meaning: "Witch of the Valley" (a named/legendary witch; a character title).
additional_notes: Usually capitalized because it works like a proper name or title (like a specific witch in a story/legend). You’ll often see it with prepositions: "da Bruxa do Vale" = "from/of the Witch of the Valley"; "pela Bruxa do Vale" can mean "by the Witch of the Valley" or be used in an oath/exclamation meaning "By the Witch of the Valley!". It can also be used to compare someone to her ("igual à Bruxa do Vale" = "like the Witch of the Valley").
target_language_example: Dizem que a Bruxa do Vale mora perto do rio.
native_language_example: They say the Witch of the Valley lives near the river.

additional_notes: Name of the holiday celebrated mainly in the U.S. (and also in Canada, on a different date). Often used with em/no: “no Dia de Ação de Graças” = “on Thanksgiving.” You may also hear “Feliz Dia de Ação de Graças!” as a holiday greeting.
target_language_example: Vamos visitar meus avós no Dia de Ação de Graças.
native_language_example: We’re going to visit my grandparents on Thanksgiving.

additional_notes: Usually written with capitals as a proper name for a specific group (e.g., a tribe, religion/cult, or fictional faction). Literally “povo” = people and “céu” = sky/heaven; in context it often implies a distinct community with authority or power.
target_language_example: O Povo do Céu não aceita estrangeiros na aldeia.
native_language_example: The People of the Sky don’t allow outsiders in the village.

additional_notes: Used after verbs of movement (like ir, levar, voltar) when the exact destination is unknown, not specified, or not important. It can be used in questions (“Ela foi a algum lugar?”) or statements (“Quero levar você a algum lugar romântico.”). In expressions like “Você vai a algum lugar com isso?”, it can mean “Are you getting anywhere with that?” (making progress), not literally going somewhere.
target_language_example: Vamos a algum lugar tranquilo para conversar.
native_language_example: Let’s go somewhere quiet to talk.

meaning: to ride a bicycle; to learn how to ride a bike.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "aprender" (to learn) and "ensinar" (to teach) to mean the activity/skill of riding a bike. Here, "a" introduces the action (similar to "to" in English), and "andar de bicicleta" literally means "to go/ride by bicycle".
target_language_example: Você sabe andar de bicicleta?
native_language_example: Do you know how to ride a bike?

additional_notes: Often used as “a” + infinitive after certain verbs (like ajudar, convencer, ensinar) to mean “to + verb” in English: “ajudou a aprender” = “helped (someone) learn.” Also common after “ter” to express “have (a lot) to learn”: “Tenho muito a aprender.”
target_language_example: Ainda tenho muito a aprender antes da prova.
native_language_example: I still have a lot to learn before the test.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "a" + infinitive ("aprender") to express purpose/goal, often after verbs like "ajudar" (help), "inspirar" (inspire), "convencer" (convince), or phrases like "me ajudou a...". You can replace "francês" with another language: "a aprender português / espanhol".
target_language_example: Ela está a aprender francês para viajar para Paris.
native_language_example: She is learning French to travel to Paris.

meaning: to learn Russian, if you want.
additional_notes: Common pattern: "ajudar (alguém) a + infinitive" = "to help (someone) to + verb". "Se quiser" means "if you want" (often short for "se você quiser"). In these examples, "ajudá-lo / ajudá-la" means "help you" (formal), while "te ajudar" means "help you" (informal, used with "você" in Brazilian Portuguese).
target_language_example: Posso te ajudar a aprender português, se você quiser.
native_language_example: I can help you learn Portuguese, if you want.

additional_notes: Used after a verb like ajudar/deixar/ensinar to describe the action someone is helping/allowing/teaching another person to do. In Portuguese, after these verbs you often use “a” + infinitive (a atravessar). You can also say “atravessar a rua” without the “a” when it’s the main verb: “Vou atravessar a rua.”
target_language_example: Você pode me ajudar a atravessar a rua?
native_language_example: Can you help me cross the street?

additional_notes: Used with time periods and quantities to express frequency/regular intervals: a cada semana (every week), a cada três horas (every three hours), a cada ano (every year), a cada três meses (every three months). It can also mean "to each" when referring to visiting/doing something for each item in a set (e.g., ir a cada monumento = go to each monument).
target_language_example: Tomo água a cada duas horas.
native_language_example: I drink water every two hours.

meaning: every day; day by day (as time goes by).
additional_notes: Often used to show gradual change or progress over time (“more and more … a cada dia”, “ficar + comparative + a cada dia”). It can mean a routine frequency (“every day”) or emphasize that something is increasing/decreasing little by little (“day by day”).
target_language_example: A cada dia, eu entendo um pouco mais de português.
native_language_example: Day by day, I understand a little more Portuguese.

meaning: on the way home; heading home.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is traveling/going back to their home at that moment. Often appears at the start of a sentence as a time phrase: "A caminho de casa, ...". You can also say "estar a caminho de casa" (to be on the way home).
target_language_example: Estou a caminho de casa, chego em dez minutos.
native_language_example: I'm on my way home; I'll be there in ten minutes.

meaning: “to sing” (as an infinitive after a verb); also “singing” (ongoing action, esp. in European Portuguese).
additional_notes: Used with many verbs to express the action that follows: e.g., "começar a cantar" (to start singing), "ensinar a cantar" (to teach to sing), "persuadir a cantar" (to persuade to sing). In European Portuguese, "estar a + infinitive" expresses an action in progress: "estais a cantar" = "you are singing". In Brazilian Portuguese, the ongoing form is more often "estar cantando".
target_language_example: Eles estão a cantar no coro hoje.
native_language_example: They are singing in the choir today.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "estar" (to be) or "ficar" to express an action in progress in European Portuguese: "estar a chorar" = "to be crying". It can also follow another verb to show the manner/state while doing something: "telefonou ... a chorar" = "called ... while crying". With "começar", it means "to start crying": "começar a chorar".
target_language_example: Ela está a chorar porque perdeu o telemóvel.
native_language_example: She is crying because she lost her phone.

additional_notes: Used with estar/ficar/continuar (and similar verbs) to talk about rain happening now or in progress: “está a chover” = “it’s raining”, “vai continuar a chover” = “it will keep raining”. With começar, it means the rain is starting: “começa a chover” = “it starts to rain”. Very common in European Portuguese; in Brazilian Portuguese you often hear “está chovendo”.
target_language_example: Está a chover muito, vamos ficar em casa.
native_language_example: It’s raining a lot, let’s stay at home.

meaning: to dance; dancing (used with another verb).
additional_notes: Common in European Portuguese after another verb, especially with verbs like aprender/ensinar/tentar/ver: “aprender a dançar” = “to learn to dance”, “ensinou o Tom a dançar” = “taught Tom to dance”, “viste-o a dançar?” = “did you see him dancing?”. It’s also used in the progressive with estar: “estou a dançar” = “I’m dancing.”
target_language_example: Eles ficaram a olhar para nós a dançar.
native_language_example: They stood there watching us dance.

additional_notes: “A + infinitive” is very common in Portuguese after verbs like ensinar (to teach), aprender (to learn), ajudar (to help), começar (to start), and others. Here, “a dirigir” refers to the action of driving. Note: “dirigir” can also mean “to manage/run/lead” (e.g., dirigir uma empresa = to run a company), but with aprender/ensinar it usually means driving a vehicle.
target_language_example: Ela está a aprender a dirigir.
native_language_example: She is learning to drive.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "a" + infinitive after words like "algo/nada/mais" or "coisa" to mean "something/nothing/more to say" (or "to tell you"). Common patterns: "tenho algo a dizer" (I have something to say), "há mais alguma coisa que me tenha a dizer?" (is there anything else you have to tell me?).
target_language_example: Não tenho mais nada a dizer.
native_language_example: I have nothing else to say.

meaning: to her (indirect object: the person who receives/benefits).
additional_notes: Used with verbs that take the preposition "a" (common with giving/telling/explaining), to indicate the female person you’re doing something to/for: "dar algo a ela" (give something to her), "dizer a ela" (tell her), "explicar a ela" (explain to her). In everyday speech, many speakers also use "para ela" in similar situations, but "a ela" is especially common with these verbs and is more standard in writing.
target_language_example: Vou enviar uma mensagem a ela hoje.
native_language_example: I’m going to send her a message today.

meaning: “to her that …” (introduces what you told/asked her).
additional_notes: Used when the verb takes an indirect object with "a" (e.g., dizer a ela, contar a ela, pedir a ela) followed by a clause with "que". In speech, Portuguese often uses "para ela" instead of "a ela" (e.g., "Diz para ela que...") but "a ela" is also correct, especially in more formal writing.
target_language_example: Vou dizer a ela que chego mais tarde.
native_language_example: I’ll tell her that I’ll arrive later.

additional_notes: Used when the verb takes the preposition “a” (often marking an indirect object), meaning “to/for him.” Common with verbs like dizer (to say/tell), explicar (to explain), dar (to give), pedir (to ask), apresentar (to introduce), and prestar atenção (to pay attention).
target_language_example: Vou mandar uma mensagem a ele mais tarde.
native_language_example: I’m going to send him a message later.

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take an indirect object (often verbs of saying, giving, showing, telling): dizer a eles (tell them), dar a eles (give them), mostrar a eles (show them). For an all-female group, use "a elas". In everyday speech, "para eles" is also common and often interchangeable depending on the verb/region.
target_language_example: Vou enviar a eles a mensagem hoje.
native_language_example: I'm going to send them the message today.

meaning: writing; to write (often in an ongoing/continuous sense).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like “continuar” or “passar” to mean “to keep/start doing” something (continuar a escrever = keep writing; passar a escrever = start writing). In European Portuguese, “estar a escrever” is the common way to say “to be writing” (right now). In Brazilian Portuguese, you’ll more often hear “estar escrevendo”. Also appears in pairs like “a ler e a escrever” = “to read and write.”
target_language_example: Estou a escrever um e-mail, já te respondo.
native_language_example: I’m writing an email; I’ll reply to you in a moment.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a topic already mentioned: “regarding that matter/issue.” Common after verbs like falar (to talk), saber (to know), ter informação (to have information), sentir-se culpado (to feel guilty). Also appears as “a este respeito” (about this) or “a respeito disso/daquilo.”
target_language_example: Não tenho nada a declarar a esse respeito.
native_language_example: I have nothing to say about that.

meaning: at this time; at this hour (of the day/night).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the current time, often with surprise or judgment about what someone is doing ("still awake at this hour?"). Very common with "da noite" (at this time of night) and "do dia" (at this time of day).
target_language_example: Você ainda está trabalhando a esta hora?
native_language_example: Are you still working at this hour?

additional_notes: Used with **a + infinitive**. Common in European Portuguese for the ongoing present: **estar a estudar** = “to be studying.” Also appears after other verbs that take **a** before an infinitive, e.g. **ajudar a estudar** (“help [someone] study”), **começar a estudar** (“start studying”), **andar a estudar** (“be going around / spend time studying,” often implying a period of time).
target_language_example: Estou a estudar para o exame agora.
native_language_example: I’m studying for the exam now.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like começar (to start), persuadir/convencer/encorajar (to persuade/convince/encourage) to describe the activity someone does. Here, the preposition “a” introduces an infinitive (“to study”) and the phrase means the person is engaged in that action (or is being encouraged to do it).
target_language_example: Ela começou a estudar francês no ano passado.
native_language_example: She started studying French last year.

meaning: 'speaking' / 'talking' (often in the sense of 'to be speaking').
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the Portuguese (especially European Portuguese) progressive form: "estar a + infinitive" → "estou a falar" = "I’m talking". It can also follow other verbs that take "a" before an infinitive, e.g. "continuar a falar" (to keep talking), "divertir-se a falar" (to have fun talking), "aprender a falar" (to learn to speak).
target_language_example: Desculpe, estou a falar ao telefone.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m talking on the phone.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like aprender (to learn), ensinar (to teach), começar (to start), or recusar-se a (to refuse to) to talk about the action of speaking French. Here, "a falar" is the infinitive phrase "to speak" (literally "to be speaking"), and "francês" is the language.
target_language_example: Ela está a falar francês com a professora.
native_language_example: She is speaking French with the teacher.

meaning: "for or against"; in favor of or opposed to.
additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion/position on an idea, plan, policy, project, etc. Often follows verbs like "ser" or "estar": "Você é/está a favor ou contra ...?" You can also answer with just "Sou a favor" / "Sou contra" (or "Estou a favor" / "Estou contra" in a specific situation).
target_language_example: Você está a favor ou contra essa mudança?
native_language_example: Are you for or against that change?

meaning: 'to do / to make' (after another verb), or 'doing' in the Portuguese progressive.
additional_notes: Common in European Portuguese. After many verbs you use "a" + infinitive to mean "to" + verb in English: "ajudar a fazer" = "help to do/make". With "estar" it forms the progressive (action happening now): "Estou a fazer" = "I’m doing/making". In Brazilian Portuguese, this idea is often expressed with "estar fazendo" instead.
target_language_example: Estou a fazer o jantar agora.
native_language_example: I’m making dinner now.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like convencer (to convince), forçar (to force), ajudar (to help), prometer (to promise) to talk about someone doing a specific action. Here, "a" introduces the infinitive ("fazer"), and "aquilo" means "that" (a specific thing/action, often something already mentioned).
target_language_example: Eu não vou te obrigar a fazer aquilo.
native_language_example: I’m not going to force you to do that.

meaning: to do that/it; (with “estar”) to be doing it.
additional_notes: Common in European Portuguese with “a + infinitive”. You’ll often see it after verbs like “estar” (continuous action: “estar a fazer isso” = “to be doing it”), and also after other verbs like “ajudar” or “acostumar-se” (“ajudar a fazer isso” = “help (to) do it”). In Brazilian Portuguese, the continuous is usually “estar fazendo isso”.
target_language_example: Estou a fazer isso agora.
native_language_example: I’m doing it now.

additional_notes: Used after verbs that take **a + infinitive** (e.g., *forçar a*, *persuadir a*, *continuar a*, *voltar a*). **-lo** means “it” and attaches to the infinitive with a hyphen: *fazer + o → fazê-lo* (accent marks the stressed syllable). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, it’s also common to say **a fazer isso** (“to do that”) instead of using **-lo**.
target_language_example: Prometi a mim mesmo que ia parar, mas acabei voltando a fazê-lo.
native_language_example: I promised myself I would stop, but I ended up doing it again.

meaning: blocking my way; stopping me from passing.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone they are physically in your way. Common in European Portuguese: "estar a" + infinitive means "to be (in the middle of) doing". "impedir" = to prevent/stop; "impedir-me" = stop me; "a passagem" = the passage/way through. You can change the person: "a impedir-nos a passagem" (blocking our way), "a impedir-te a passagem" (blocking your way).
target_language_example: Desculpe, está a impedir-me a passagem.
native_language_example: Excuse me, you're blocking my way.

meaning: 'to read'; also used in European Portuguese for the ongoing action 'reading' (estar a ler).
additional_notes: Used after some verbs + infinitive: ensinar/aprender a ler = 'to teach/learn to read'. In European Portuguese, "estar a + infinitive" expresses an action in progress: "Estou a ler" = "I am reading" (Brazilian Portuguese more often uses "estar + gerund": "Estou lendo").
target_language_example: Desculpa, não posso falar agora — estou a ler.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't talk right now — I'm reading.

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs of movement (ir, sair, levar, mandar) to mean that someone isn’t going/heading anywhere. It commonly appears with "não" (double negative in Portuguese is normal): "Não vou a lugar nenhum" = “I’m not going anywhere.”
target_language_example: Hoje eu não vou a lugar nenhum; vou ficar em casa.
native_language_example: Today I’m not going anywhere; I’m staying home.

meaning: to me (after a preposition; emphatic form).
additional_notes: Used when "me" is the object of a preposition (like a, para, de, com). You say "para mim", "comigo", "de mim", etc.—not *para eu*. Often adds emphasis/contrast: "...e não a mim?". Can appear with "mesmo" for emphasis in reflexive contexts: "a mim mesmo/a" = "to myself".
target_language_example: Ele não disse nada a mim, só a você.
native_language_example: He didn’t say anything to me, only to you.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is going/coming/visiting somewhere for work reasons, not tourism. Common with verbs like ir, vir, viajar, visitar: "viajar a negócios". Often implies a business trip.
target_language_example: Estou em Lisboa a negócios esta semana.
native_language_example: I’m in Lisbon on business this week.

meaning: "not to do that/this" (to refrain from doing it).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive after verbs like convencer (to convince), pedir/solicitar (to ask/request), tentar (to try), or persuadir (to persuade): convencer alguém a não fazer isso = “to convince someone not to do that.” In everyday Portuguese, you may also hear “pra não fazer isso” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Ela me pediu para eu não fazer isso de novo.
native_language_example: She asked me not to do that again.

additional_notes: Often used to exclude someone/something: "A não ser X" = "except for X" (similar to "exceto"). It can also introduce an exception condition: "a não ser que..." = "unless...". Usually comes right before the thing/person being excluded, or before a clause with "que".
target_language_example: Eu vou com vocês, a não ser que chova.
native_language_example: I’ll go with you, unless it rains.

meaning: with the naked eye (without a microscope/telescope).
additional_notes: Used to say something can (or cannot) be seen without any equipment. Often appears with verbs like “ver” and “ser visível/invisível”: “pode ser visto a olho nu”, “não é visível a olho nu”.
target_language_example: Essa mancha dá para ver a olho nu.
native_language_example: You can see that spot with the naked eye.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like convencer (to convince) and aconselhar (to advise) to express the action someone should do: convencer/alguém a + infinitive. Here, parar de + infinitive means “to stop doing something,” and fumar is “to smoke.”
target_language_example: O médico me pediu para parar de fumar.
native_language_example: The doctor asked me to stop smoking.

meaning: from; starting from (a point in time, place, or source).
additional_notes: Used to mark the starting point of something in time ("a partir de amanhã" = starting tomorrow), in distance/location ("a partir daqui" = from here), or in origin/source ("a partir do latim" = from Latin; "a partir destas observações" = from these observations). Very often appears as "a partir de" + noun/pronoun.
target_language_example: A partir de amanhã, vou estudar português todos os dias.
native_language_example: Starting tomorrow, I'm going to study Portuguese every day.

additional_notes: Portuguese (especially in Portugal) often uses the structure "estar a + infinitive" to talk about something happening right now. So "estar a pensar em mim" means "to be thinking about/of me" at that moment. You can change the subject and verb form (estou/estás/está/estamos/estão) depending on who is thinking.
target_language_example: Estás a pensar em mim agora?
native_language_example: Are you thinking about me now?

additional_notes:
Used with verbs like:
- "ter ... a perder" = "to have ... to lose" (often in questions: "O que você tem a perder?" = "What do you have to lose?")
- "(não) ter tempo/minuto a perder" = "(not) have time/a minute to waste" (means you must hurry)
- "deixar ... a perder" = "to let ... go to waste/ruin" (to fail to use something valuable, like love or an opportunity).
target_language_example: Vamos embora — não temos um segundo a perder.
native_language_example: Let's go—we don't have a second to waste.

meaning: “By the way, do you…?” (to introduce a new or side topic).
additional_notes: Used to casually change the subject or add an extra question/comment. Often appears at the start of a sentence: “A propósito, você…”. You can also just say “A propósito,” without “você.”
target_language_example: A propósito, você tem um minuto para conversar?
native_language_example: By the way, do you have a minute to talk?

meaning: to school on foot; walking to school.
additional_notes: Use "a pé" to mean "on foot" (walking). "Para a escola" means "to school". With the verb "ir" (to go), it often appears as "ir a pé" (to go on foot): "Eu vou a pé para a escola". You can swap "para" with "à" in many contexts: "vou a pé à escola".
target_language_example: Hoje eu vou a pé para a escola porque o ônibus está atrasado.
native_language_example: Today I'm walking to school because the bus is late.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to mean “any” in expressions like: a qualquer minuto (“any minute / at any moment”), a qualquer custo/preço (“at any cost/price”), and (often with negation) não ... a qualquer pessoa (“not to just anyone”). It can also appear in comparisons: mais do que a qualquer outra pessoa (“more than anyone else”).
target_language_example: Posso ligar a qualquer hora.
native_language_example: I can call at any time.

additional_notes: Used to say there is no specific time restriction (now, later, day or night). Often used to give permission or indicate something can happen unexpectedly: "a qualquer hora" = "whenever"/"at any moment". Common with verbs like "vir" (come), "ligar/chamar" (call), "acontecer" (happen).
target_language_example: Você pode ligar a qualquer hora, se precisar de ajuda.
native_language_example: You can call anytime if you need help.

additional_notes: Used to say something can happen (or someone can arrive) at an unspecified time, possibly very soon. Common with future or near-future situations: “vai chegar a qualquer momento” = “could arrive any minute now / any time.” It can also mean “whenever you want” with permission: “Você pode vir a qualquer momento.”
target_language_example: A entrega pode chegar a qualquer momento.
native_language_example: The delivery could arrive any moment now.

meaning: "to which" / "at what" (used when the verb or expression takes the preposition "a").
additional_notes: Common in questions and relative clauses where Portuguese requires "a" before "que" because of the verb/expression: e.g., pertencer a (a que clube?), referir-se a (a que funções?), chegar a (a que ponto?). Also used in fixed phrases like "a que horas" = "at what time" and "a que ponto" = "to what extent/point".
target_language_example: A que endereço eu devo enviar o formulário?
native_language_example: To which address should I send the form?

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask the distance from one place to another. Often followed by “de” + a reference point: “A que distância de aqui/daqui…?” You can answer with a distance: “A 2 km daqui.”
target_language_example: A que distância do hotel fica o aeroporto?
native_language_example: How far is the airport from the hotel?

additional_notes: Used to ask the distance from where you are (or from a place you mention) to a destination. Often followed by the place and/or a reference point: “A que distância fica a biblioteca daqui?” (“How far is the library from here?”). You can also omit the reference point if it’s clear: “A que distância fica a estação?”
target_language_example: Com licença, a que distância fica o centro da cidade daqui?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how far is the city center from here?

additional_notes: Used to ask the time when something happens. Common in questions like “A que horas (você) + verb…?” You may also hear the shorter “Que horas…?” in everyday speech.
target_language_example: A que horas começa a reunião?
native_language_example: What time does the meeting start?

meaning: 'What time does the…?' (asking the time something happens, with a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask at what time an event starts/ends, often with verbs like "começar" (to start) and "fechar" (to close). The "a" at the end is the feminine singular article "the" (e.g., a aula, a biblioteca, a peça). With a masculine noun, you’d use "a que horas o" (e.g., "A que horas o filme começa?").
target_language_example: A que horas a reunião termina?
native_language_example: What time does the meeting end?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time a meeting starts/ends, or inside an indirect question after verbs like "saber" (to know) and "descobrir" (to find out): "Você sabe a que horas a reunião começa?". Often followed by a verb such as "começa" (starts) or "termina/terminou" (ends/ended).
target_language_example: Você sabe a que horas a reunião vai começar?
native_language_example: Do you know what time the meeting is going to start?

additional_notes: Used to ask the time someone arrived after traveling from a place. It uses the verb **chegar** (“to arrive”) with **de** to mean “from” (coming from somewhere): *chegar de Lisboa*, *chegar do Brasil* (de + o = do). **Chegaste** is past tense for **tu** (“you”) and is especially common in European Portuguese; in Brazil you’ll often hear **A que horas você chegou de…?**
target_language_example: A que horas chegaste de Lisboa?
native_language_example: What time did you arrive from Lisbon?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a start time. “A que horas” = “at what time,” “começa” = “starts,” and “a” is used before a feminine singular noun (a escola, a reunião, a palestra, a prova, a cirurgia). For masculine nouns, use “a que horas começa o …?” (o filme, o jogo).
target_language_example: A que horas começa a aula de amanhã?
native_language_example: What time does tomorrow’s class start?

meaning: “At what time does the …” (asking when something opens/starts, with a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask the time of an event or schedule. Here it’s followed by a masculine singular noun (o museu, o parque, o restaurante) and often a verb like abrir (“to open”): “A que horas o museu abre?” For feminine nouns use “a que horas a …” (e.g., “A que horas a loja abre?”). You can also drop the article when asking generally: “A que horas abre?”
target_language_example: A que horas o supermercado abre amanhã?
native_language_example: At what time does the supermarket open tomorrow?

meaning: "At what time do you…?" (asking when someone does something).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the time when someone does an action. It’s often followed by a verb in the past, present, or future: “A que horas você acordou?” (past), “A que horas você vai…?” (future/near future), “A que horas você toma banho?” (habit). In casual speech, people may shorten it to “Que horas você…?” or “Que horas cê…?”.
target_language_example: A que horas você vai sair hoje?
native_language_example: What time are you going to leave today?

meaning: "What time do you…?" (with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used to ask at what time someone does an action, especially with reflexive verbs like "se deitar" (to go to bed) and "se levantar" (to get up). It’s typically followed by a reflexive verb: "A que horas você se deita?" / "A que horas você se levanta?". In Brazil, "você" is common; in Portugal you may hear "A que horas te…?".
target_language_example: A que horas você se levanta amanhã?
native_language_example: What time do you get up tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time of a future action or event. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb (vai dormir / vai sair / vai se encontrar) or by “estar” + phrase (vai estar de volta). In Brazilian Portuguese, “a que horas” is a common way to ask “at what time” (similar to “que horas” but a bit more complete).
target_language_example: A que horas você vai chegar amanhã?
native_language_example: What time are you going to arrive tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to ask about a specific time. "Vocês" is the common way to say "you" (plural) in Brazil (it uses 3rd-person plural verbs: vocês chegaram). Often followed by a verb: a que horas vocês chegaram/saíram/vão/fecham?
target_language_example: A que horas vocês vão sair hoje?
native_language_example: What time are you (all) going to leave today?

additional_notes: Used to introduce the subject you’re talking about, often with de: "a respeito de" + noun/pronoun ("a respeito disso" = "about that"). Common after verbs like falar (to talk), dizer (to say), saber (to know), perguntar (to ask), and in phrases like "confusão a respeito de...". In some contexts it can also mean "in that respect" (about a particular aspect), but most often it’s simply "about/regarding".
target_language_example: Não sei nada a respeito desse assunto.
native_language_example: I don't know anything about that subject.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic you’re talking about. It’s a common, neutral way to mean “about/regarding” someone or something. The pronoun changes with the person/thing: a respeito dele (about him), a respeito disso (about that), a respeito do assunto (about the topic). In sentences like “Você estava certo a respeito dela”, it means “you were right about her.”
target_language_example: Eu ouvi algumas coisas a respeito dela, mas não sei se é verdade.
native_language_example: I heard a few things about her, but I don’t know if it’s true.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific topic or situation already mentioned (“that”). Very common after verbs like falar (to talk), saber (to know), pensar (to think), and in questions like “O que vamos fazer a respeito disso?” (= “What are we going to do about that?”). Similar to “sobre isso” and “quanto a isso” (slightly more formal).
target_language_example: Ainda não decidimos nada a respeito disso.
native_language_example: We still haven't decided anything about that.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic you’re talking or thinking about. It’s a bit more formal than "sobre". It contracts with articles: a respeito do (de + o), a respeito da (de + a), a respeito dos, a respeito das; before a name you often see "a respeito de" (e.g., "a respeito do Tom" is also common in speech).
target_language_example: Ainda não decidimos nada a respeito do projeto.
native_language_example: We still haven't decided anything about the project.

additional_notes: “A” + infinitive is commonly used after verbs like “preferir” to mean “rather than (do something)”: “prefiro ficar em casa a sair” = “I prefer staying home to going out.” With “obrigar (alguém) a …”, it means “to force (someone) to …”: “obrigou-nos a sair” = “forced us to leave.”
target_language_example: Preferimos ficar aqui a sair agora.
native_language_example: We prefer to stay here rather than go out now.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to the subject (the same person), often for emphasis or contrast (e.g., “more than himself”). It commonly appears after verbs like ajudar, culpar, perdoar, amar, and can vary by gender/number: a si mesmo (masc. sing.), a si mesma (fem. sing.), a si mesmos/a si mesmas (plural). In informal speech, many people use “a você mesmo/a ti mesmo” instead.
target_language_example: Você precisa confiar mais em si mesmo.
native_language_example: You need to trust yourself more.

meaning: going up the stairs; to go up the stairs.
additional_notes: "a" + infinitive ("a subir") is commonly used in European Portuguese to mean an action in progress (like English "(was) going up"). Often appears after verbs like "ajudar" (to help someone do something) and with "ver" (to see someone doing something): "Viram-no a subir as escadas" = "They saw him going up the stairs."
target_language_example: Ele estava a subir as escadas quando o telefone tocou.
native_language_example: He was going up the stairs when the phone rang.

meaning: alone; in private (with no one else present).
additional_notes: Used after a verb to say someone is alone or that you want to speak/meet privately, without other people around. Often appears in requests like “Posso falar com você a sós?” (Can I speak to you in private?).
target_language_example: Podemos conversar a sós depois da reunião?
native_language_example: Can we talk in private after the meeting?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the action is directed back at the same person (“you yourself”). It often appears with reflexive verbs/commands: e.g., “Conhece-te a ti mesmo” (“Know yourself”). Variations: a mim mesmo (myself), a si mesmo (yourself/himself/herself—formal or 3rd person), a nós mesmos (ourselves), a vocês mesmos (yourselves).
target_language_example: Não sejas tão duro a ti mesmo.
native_language_example: Don’t be so hard on yourself.

meaning: (1) to touch; (2) to play (an instrument / music).
additional_notes: Most often, "tocar" means "to touch" someone or something: "tocar nela" = "touch her." It’s also used for playing instruments or music: "tocar violino" = "play the violin," and "tocar uma música" = "play a song." In sentences like "está aprendendo a tocar" or after verbs like "ensinar" (to teach), "a" introduces the verb in Portuguese (roughly like English "to" + verb).
target_language_example: Ela está começando a tocar piano este ano.
native_language_example: She’s starting to play the piano this year.

meaning: to play the guitar (as a skill you learn).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "aprender" (to learn) and "querer" (to want) to mean "to play the (acoustic/classical) guitar". Here, "a tocar" is like "to play" in English, and "violão" usually refers to an acoustic/classical guitar (not "guitarra"/electric guitar).
target_language_example: Ela está começando a tocar violão este mês.
native_language_example: She is starting to learn to play the guitar this month.

additional_notes: Used with verbs/expressions that require the preposition "a" (to), such as: "preferir X a Y" (to prefer X to Y), "obedecer a" (to obey/follow), and "passar a" (to pass (a subject/class)). It must agree with a feminine plural noun (e.g., "as regras", "as disciplinas"). For masculine plural, use "a todos os".
target_language_example: Ela obedeceu a todas as regras.
native_language_example: She obeyed all the rules.

additional_notes: Used to address or refer to an entire group ("everyone"). Common in greetings like "Olá a todos" / "Boa noite a todos". It can also appear with verbs like "dizer" ("Ela disse a todos...") meaning "to everyone". Note: "a" here is the preposition "to" + "todos" ("everyone/all").
target_language_example: Quero agradecer a todos pela ajuda.
native_language_example: I want to thank everyone for the help.

meaning: working; to be working (in the middle of working).
additional_notes: "A" + infinitive is a common way (especially in Portugal) to express an action in progress: "estar a trabalhar" = "to be working." It’s also often used after verbs like "voltar" (to return) to mean "to go back to doing something": "voltar a trabalhar" = "to go back to work."
target_language_example: Estou a trabalhar agora; posso falar mais tarde.
native_language_example: I’m working right now; can I talk later?

meaning: to a movie / a movie (as the object of the verb, especially with assistir a).
additional_notes: Used mainly after the verb "assistir" meaning "to watch" (assistir a + something). The "a" is a preposition required by "assistir" in this meaning, and "um filme" means "a movie." In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often drop the preposition and say "assistir um filme," but "assistir a um filme" is the more standard form.
target_language_example: A gente assistiu a um filme ontem à noite.
native_language_example: We watched a movie last night.

meaning: “(he/she/I) loved her” / “(he/she/I) used to love her.”
additional_notes: “a” is an unstressed object pronoun meaning “her” (or “it” for a feminine noun) and it usually comes before the verb: eu a amava = I loved her. “amava” is the imperfect past of amar, often used for ongoing feelings in the past or a habitual/unfinished past situation (so it can sound like “loved” or “used to love,” depending on context).
target_language_example: Naquela época, eu a amava muito, mas ela não sabia.
native_language_example: Back then, I loved her a lot, but she didn’t know.

additional_notes: “a” is an unstressed direct-object pronoun meaning “her” (or “it” for a feminine noun; also “you” in formal address to a woman). It comes before the verb in standard Portuguese: “eu a amo” = “I love her.” With names like “Mary,” you can also say “Eu amo a Mary” (without the pronoun). In writing you may see “Diga à Mary…”: “à” = “a” (to) + “a” (the), meaning “to Mary.”
target_language_example: Eu a amo muito, mas ainda não contei a ela.
native_language_example: I love her a lot, but I still haven’t told her.

additional_notes: From the verb "ver" (to see): "vi" = "I saw" (simple past). "a" is the direct-object pronoun meaning "her" (or "you" feminine in some contexts). In Portuguese, object pronouns often come before the verb ("eu a vi"), but they can also come after it ("vi-a"), especially in more formal writing. You’ll also see "o vi" (I saw him/it) and "os/as vi" (I saw them).
target_language_example: Eu a vi ontem no supermercado.
native_language_example: I saw her yesterday at the supermarket.

additional_notes: "Arma" is a feminine noun, so it uses "a" (the). It can refer to any weapon (gun, knife, etc.), but in commands like "Abaixe a arma" it often implies a firearm. Common patterns: "arma dele/dela" (his/her weapon), "arma do crime" (the weapon used in the crime).
target_language_example: A polícia encontrou a arma no carro.
native_language_example: The police found the weapon in the car.

additional_notes: Usually refers to facial hair on the chin/cheeks. Common related expression: "fazer a barba" = "to shave" (literally, "to do the beard"). You can also use it with verbs like "deixar crescer" (to grow) or "cortar" (to cut/trim).
target_language_example: Ele deixou crescer a barba durante as férias.
native_language_example: He grew his beard out during the vacation.

meaning: to grow (out) a beard; to let your beard grow.
additional_notes: Commonly used with the verb "deixar": "deixar a barba crescer" = "to let your beard grow / to grow out your beard". In the present continuous, it’s often "estar deixando a barba crescer" (I’m/he’s letting it grow).
target_language_example: No inverno, vou deixar a barba crescer.
native_language_example: In the winter, I’m going to grow out my beard.

additional_notes: Used with the feminine article a (“the”). Very common in everyday commands: Abra a boca (Open your mouth), Feche a boca (Close your mouth), Mantenha a boca fechada (Keep your mouth shut). It also appears in set expressions like até a boca (“to the brim/full to the top”) and molhar a boca (“to wet your whistle / have a drink or taste something”).
target_language_example: Abra a boca, por favor.
native_language_example: Open your mouth, please.

additional_notes: Used for a physical ball (soccer ball, toy ball, etc.). In Portuguese, nouns have gender; **bola** is feminine, so it takes **a** (“the”). In speech, **me dê a bola** and **dá-me a bola** both mean “give me the ball.”
target_language_example: Onde está a bola?
native_language_example: Where is the ball?

additional_notes: A specific weapon: an atomic/nuclear bomb. Often discussed in historical contexts (e.g., Hiroshima) or in general statements about threats to humanity. In Portuguese it’s typically used with the definite article: “a bomba atômica”.
target_language_example: Muitas pessoas ainda têm medo da bomba atômica.
native_language_example: Many people are still afraid of the atomic bomb.

additional_notes: Refers to the physical head (body part). Common in everyday expressions like “balançar a cabeça” (to shake/nod your head) and in contexts like medicine/pain: “algo para a cabeça dele” can mean something for his head (e.g., for a headache or head injury).
target_language_example: Estou com dor de cabeça.
native_language_example: I have a headache.

meaning: the box; the cash register/checkout (depending on context).
additional_notes: Most commonly means a physical box/container: "Bote a caixa na mesa" (Put the box on the table). In stores it can also mean the cash register/checkout area: "Vou pagar no caixa" (I’m going to pay at the checkout). Note: "a caixa" can also refer to a female cashier (less common than "a caixa registradora" for the machine).
target_language_example: Guardei as fotos na caixa para não estragarem.
native_language_example: I kept the photos in the box so they wouldn’t get damaged.

additional_notes: “Cama” means “bed.” With “a” (the feminine singular definite article), it means “the bed.” Common in phrases like “ir para a cama” (“to go to bed”).
target_language_example: Estou com sono; vou para a cama.
native_language_example: I’m sleepy; I’m going to bed.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb phrase “ir para” (or “ir pra” in speech): “ir para a cama cedo” = “to go to bed early.” “A cama” literally means “the bed,” but the whole expression is about the time you go to sleep, not physically going to the bed.
target_language_example: Hoje eu vou para a cama cedo porque tenho que acordar cedo amanhã.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to bed early because I have to wake up early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Commonly used with clothing verbs like tirar (to take off), colocar/vestir (to put on/wear), abotoar/desabotoar (to button/unbutton). It can also refer to a blouse or jersey depending on context, but it often means a (usually men’s) shirt.
target_language_example: Ele esqueceu a camisa no carro.
native_language_example: He forgot the shirt in the car.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a doorbell at a house/apartment. You’ll often see it with verbs like "tocar" (to ring) or "tocar a campainha" (to ring the doorbell). It can also refer to other bells (e.g., a school bell), depending on context.
target_language_example: A campainha está quebrada, então me liga quando você chegar.
native_language_example: The doorbell is broken, so call me when you arrive.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine article because it refers to the noun “cidade” (city): a capital = “the capital city” of a country/state/region. Very often followed by “de/do/da/dos/das” to say what it is the capital of: “a capital de Portugal”, “a capital do Brasil”. It can also be used more generally for the main/most important city in a context (e.g., “a capital europeia”).
target_language_example: Brasília é a capital do Brasil.
native_language_example: Brasília is the capital of Brazil.

additional_notes: Used to name the capital city of a state/country/region: “A capital da Bahia é Salvador.” Often comes before a place name (a capital da França) or as an apposition between commas (“Madrid, a capital da Espanha, ...”). Note the contraction: de + a = da (feminine), because capital is feminine (a capital).
target_language_example: Qual é a capital da Itália?
native_language_example: What is the capital of Italy?

additional_notes: Used to name the capital city of a state/country/region: “A capital da Bahia é Salvador.” Often comes before a place name (a capital da França) or as an apposition between commas (“Madrid, a capital da Espanha, ...”). Note the contraction: de + a = da (feminine), because capital is feminine (a capital).
target_language_example: Qual é a capital da Itália?
native_language_example: What is the capital of Italy?

additional_notes: Used to name the main/official city of a place. The pattern is: **A capital do + [masculine noun]** (e.g., *do Brasil*) and **A capital da + [feminine noun]** (e.g., *da França*). You can also say **capital de** with names (often cities/places) without an article: *A capital de Portugal é Lisboa.*
target_language_example: A capital do Canadá é Ottawa.
native_language_example: The capital of Canada is Ottawa.

additional_notes: Used when talking about food (beef, pork, chicken, etc.) in general. Common in shopping and cooking contexts: estar em promoção (be on sale), estragar-se/estar estragada (to go bad/be spoiled), consumir crua (eat raw), mal passada (rare/undercooked). It can also mean “flesh” in other contexts, but these examples are about food.
target_language_example: Você quer carne ou peixe no almoço?
native_language_example: Do you want meat or fish for lunch?

meaning: the letter (a written message); the card (e.g., playing card, menu item).
additional_notes: "A" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”). "Carta" most commonly means a written letter/message (like in the examples). Depending on context, it can also mean a card (e.g., "carta de baralho" = playing card) or a menu/wine list ("a carta" in restaurants).
target_language_example: Vou escrever a carta hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I’m going to write the letter tonight.

additional_notes: "A" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”), and "casa" means “house/home.” It can refer to a physical house/building or to “home” as a place of living (context decides). Very common in possession patterns like "A casa é dele" (“The house is his”) and with verbs like "consertar" (to fix/repair) or "sentir" (to feel): "Senti a casa tremer" (“I felt the house shake”).
target_language_example: A casa fica perto do trabalho.
native_language_example: The house is near work.

additional_notes: "A" = "the" (feminine singular). "Casa" = "house/home". "Dela" means "of hers" (refers to a woman), so "a casa dela" is literally "the house of hers". Often used when giving directions or asking where someone’s home is: "Onde fica a casa dela?".
target_language_example: Vou até a casa dela depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I’m going to her house after work.

additional_notes: Means “the house/home of him.” You use it to talk about where a man lives or a house that belongs to him. “Dele” = “of him / his” (for a male owner). With a female owner, you usually say “a casa dela” (“her house”).
target_language_example: Eu fui à casa dele ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I went to his house last night.

additional_notes: Used with the definite article: “a chave” = “the key” (feminine singular). Very common with prepositions: “a chave da casa” (the house key), “na fechadura” (into/in the lock), “em cima da mesa” (on top of the table). Can also mean “the solution/secret” in some contexts (e.g., “a chave do problema”), but in these examples it’s a physical key.
target_language_example: Você viu a chave do carro?
native_language_example: Have you seen the car key?

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to show possession (“the key of the car” = the car key) or a figurative meaning (“the key to knowledge”). With feminine nouns, use “a chave da” (e.g., a chave da casa). In speech, “do” = “de” + “o”.
target_language_example: Você sabe onde está a chave do escritório?
native_language_example: Do you know where the office key is?

additional_notes: Means the key (or key fob) that belongs to the car. Very common with verbs like procurar (to look for), colocar/pôr (to put/place), and in questions with onde (where): “Onde (eu) coloquei/pus a chave do carro?” You can also hear “as chaves do carro” (the car keys).
target_language_example: Não acho a chave do carro; você viu onde eu deixei?
native_language_example: I can’t find the car key; did you see where I left it?

additional_notes: Used with the definite article “a” (feminine singular) to talk about rain in a specific situation/time (“A chuva parou.” = “The rain stopped.”). Without the article, “chuva” can be more general (e.g., “Gosto de chuva.” = “I like rain.”). Common verbs: cair (to fall), parar (to stop), ouvir/escutar (to hear/listen to).
target_language_example: A chuva começou de repente, mas parou rápido.
native_language_example: The rain started suddenly, but it stopped quickly.

additional_notes: Common way to refer to a specific city that’s known from context. With verbs like conhecer (“to know”), ver (“to see”), mostrar (“to show”), it often means “the city (as a place)”—sights, streets, etc. In expressions like “a cidade toda” it means “the whole city/everyone in town.”
target_language_example: A cidade é pequena, mas tem muitas coisas para fazer.
native_language_example: The city is small, but there are lots of things to do.

meaning: the whole city; the entire city.
additional_notes: Means all of the city/all the people in the city. Used to emphasize that something affects or is known/visible throughout the entire city. Often used with verbs like "cobrir" (cover), "saber" (know), "ver" (see), and with expressions like "a cidade inteira vai saber" (“the whole city will know”).
target_language_example: O desfile parou a cidade inteira por duas horas.
native_language_example: The parade brought the whole city to a stop for two hours.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the morally correct or appropriate action in a situation. Very common with verbs like fazer (“to do”) and with certainty/opinion phrases: fazer a coisa certa, achar que fez a coisa certa, ter certeza de que está fazendo a coisa certa. You can also use it as advice: Faça a coisa certa.
target_language_example: Mesmo sendo difícil, ele decidiu fazer a coisa certa.
native_language_example: Even though it was hard, he decided to do the right thing.

a coisa certa a se fazer

target_language_multi_word_term: a coisa certa a se fazer
additional_notes: Used to talk about the morally correct or best action in a situation. Often appears in questions with "ser" (e.g., "É/Esta é a coisa certa a se fazer?"). Here, "certa" means "right/correct," not "certain" (so it can be confusing for English speakers).
target_language_example: Eu não sei qual é a coisa certa a se fazer agora.
native_language_example: I don't know what the right thing to do is now.

additional_notes: Used to form a superlative with a noun: a coisa (thing) + mais (most) + adjective. Very common in speech to emphasize opinion or experience: "a coisa mais incrível/estúpida/bonita...". Often followed by "que" + clause ("the most ... thing that...") or by a place/time phrase ("na minha vida", "do mundo"). Adjective agrees with "coisa" (feminine), so it’s usually "a coisa mais bonita/estranha", etc.
target_language_example: Isso foi a coisa mais difícil que eu já fiz.
native_language_example: That was the hardest thing I’ve ever done.

additional_notes: Used to single out what matters most in a situation or in life. Often followed by “é …” (A coisa mais importante é…) or by a clause with “que” (A coisa mais importante que você pode fazer…).
target_language_example: A coisa mais importante para mim é a saúde.
native_language_example: The most important thing for me is health.

additional_notes: "A" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”). "Comida" can mean food in general or a specific meal, depending on context. Common with verbs like comer (to eat), preparar (to prepare), and colocar na mesa (to put on the table).
target_language_example: A comida está pronta; vamos comer.
native_language_example: The food is ready; let's eat.

meaning: "the food is" (describing the food’s current state, quality, or location).
additional_notes: Used with "estar" to talk about how the food is right now: taste/quality (boa, deliciosa, ótima), readiness (pronta), or where it is (sobre a mesa). It’s about a current condition or situation (often contrasted with "ser" for more permanent characteristics).
target_language_example: A comida está quente, mas a sopa ainda não está pronta.
native_language_example: The food is hot, but the soup still isn’t ready.

meaning: the bill/check; also “the account” (e.g., online account, bank account).
additional_notes: In restaurants and cafés, “pedir a conta” means “to ask for the bill/check.” In tech or banking contexts, “conta” commonly means an account (e.g., “deletar a conta” = delete an account).
target_language_example: Pode trazer a conta, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you bring the bill/check, please?

meaning: the race; the run (as an event).
additional_notes: Used for a race/competition (running, car race, etc.) and for the act/event of running (not just one quick run to the store). In sports contexts you’ll often see verbs like terminar (finish), recomeçar (restart), vencer/ganhar (win), perder (lose), and abandonar (drop out).
target_language_example: Ele está treinando para a corrida de 10 km.
native_language_example: He is training for the 10 km race.

additional_notes: "A" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”). "Criança" means “child” and can refer to a boy or a girl (it’s grammatically feminine). Plural: "as crianças" = “the children.”
target_language_example: A criança está brincando no parque.
native_language_example: The child is playing in the park.

additional_notes: Most often means “the difference” between two things: Qual é a diferença? = “What’s the difference?” It also appears in common expressions like fazer a diferença (“to make a difference,” i.e., have a positive impact) and fazer toda a diferença (“to make all the difference,” i.e., be crucial).
target_language_example: Esse detalhe fez toda a diferença.
native_language_example: That detail made all the difference.

additional_notes: Used to compare two (or more) things/people/ideas. Common in questions: "Qual é a diferença entre A e B?" It can be followed by nouns, pronouns, or clauses (e.g., "a diferença entre fazer e não fazer").
target_language_example: Não sei qual é a diferença entre esses dois modelos.
native_language_example: I don't know what the difference is between these two models.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: definite article + noun. Often used with verbs like "sentir" (to feel), "estar" (to be), and with "para a dor" meaning "for the pain" (e.g., medicine). You may also hear "dor de" + body part ("dor de cabeça" = headache).
target_language_example: Estou com dor nas costas.
native_language_example: I have back pain.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: definite article "a" (the, feminine singular) + "escola" (school). Used for a specific school or the idea of school as an institution (e.g., "A escola não era essencial..."). In plural, "as escolas" = "the schools".
target_language_example: A escola fica perto da minha casa.
native_language_example: The school is near my house.

meaning: the right choice; the correct decision.
additional_notes: Used to say someone chose correctly in a situation. Common after verbs like "fazer" (fazer a escolha certa = to make the right choice). It agrees with feminine "escolha" (so "certa," not "certo").
target_language_example: Acho que você fez a escolha certa.
native_language_example: I think you made the right choice.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a man’s wife. "dele" means "his" (referring to him). For a woman’s wife you’d say "a esposa dela" (her wife). You’ll also hear the shorter form with a possessive: "a sua esposa" (his/her wife), which can be ambiguous without context.
target_language_example: A esposa dele está no trabalho agora.
native_language_example: His wife is at work now.

additional_notes: "A estação" most often means a transit station (train/bus/subway): "A estação fica a dois quilômetros" (The station is two kilometers away). It can also mean a season of the year, usually with a clarifying phrase or context: "Verão é a estação mais quente do ano" (Summer is the hottest season of the year).
target_language_example: Podemos nos encontrar na estação às oito?
native_language_example: Can we meet at the station at eight?

additional_notes: Used for a road that connects places, often outside cities (more like a main road than a small street). Common with verbs like cruzar (to cross), pegar (to take), and with descriptions of condition: cheia (busy), coberta de gelo (icy), danificada (damaged), estreita (narrow).
target_language_example: A estrada para a praia está fechada hoje.
native_language_example: The road to the beach is closed today.

additional_notes: Definite article + noun: "a" = "the" (feminine singular), so "a faca" means "the knife". Used for everyday knives (kitchen knife, table knife, etc.). Common with prepositions/locations: "na gaveta" (in the drawer), "em cima da mesa" (on top of the table).
target_language_example: Cadê a faca?
native_language_example: Where’s the knife?

additional_notes: Refers to someone’s family as a group. Often used after prepositions like com (with): “com a família” = “with the family.” It can mean your immediate family or your relatives in general, depending on context.
target_language_example: Vou passar o fim de semana com a família.
native_language_example: I’m going to spend the weekend with the family.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a male person's family. It’s a noun phrase made of: "a" (the) + "família" (family) + "dele" (his/of him). Often used to avoid ambiguity compared to "sua família" (which can mean his/her/your family depending on context).
target_language_example: Ele vai viajar com a família dele no fim de semana.
native_language_example: He’s going to travel with his family this weekend.

additional_notes: Commonly refers to a social gathering (a party), but can also mean a celebration or event (e.g., birthday, wedding, holiday). It’s feminine: “a festa” (the party), “uma festa” (a party). You’ll often see it with verbs like “ser” (A festa foi...), “será” (A festa será...), “dar” (Quem vai dar a festa? = Who’s hosting/throwing the party?), and “organizar” (organizar a festa = organize the party).
target_language_example: A festa começa às oito e vai até meia-noite.
native_language_example: The party starts at eight and goes until midnight.

additional_notes: A common noun for a large area covered with trees. Uses the feminine definite article “a” (“the”): “a floresta”. Often used with prepositions like “na floresta” (in the forest) and “pela floresta” (through the forest).
target_language_example: Há muitos animais na floresta.
native_language_example: There are many animals in the forest.

additional_notes: Uses the definite article a (“the”) with garota (“girl”). Often refers to a specific girl already known in the conversation or context. In some regions (especially Brazil), garota can also mean “young woman” or “girlfriend” depending on context, but it’s usually “girl.”
target_language_example: A garota está esperando o ônibus.
native_language_example: The girl is waiting for the bus.

additional_notes: Common, informal way to say goodbye or to confirm you’ll meet again. "A gente" often means "we" in everyday Brazilian Portuguese (even though it’s grammatically singular), and "se vê" means "see each other". You can add a time/place: "a gente se vê amanhã" (tomorrow), "a gente se vê em casa" (at home).
target_language_example: Tá bom, a gente se vê amanhã!
native_language_example: Alright, see you tomorrow!

additional_notes: Very common in Brazilian Portuguese as an informal way to say “nós” (we). It usually takes 3rd-person singular verb agreement: “a gente vai”, “a gente veio”. As an object, it means “us”: “com a gente” (with us), “caçando a gente” (hunting/chasing us). In more formal contexts, prefer “nós / conosco”.
target_language_example: A gente pode conversar depois?
native_language_example: Can we talk later?

additional_notes: Used as a polite way to describe someone doing you a favor. Usually followed by an infinitive: "fazer/ter a gentileza de + infinitive" (e.g., "fez a gentileza de ajudar").
target_language_example: Você teria a gentileza de repetir, por favor?
native_language_example: Would you be kind enough to repeat, please?

additional_notes: Refers to war in general or to a specific war already known from context. It’s feminine: "a guerra" (the war). You’ll often see it after prepositions: "sobre a guerra" (about the war), "entre ... e a guerra" (between ... and war).
target_language_example: Não quero falar sobre a guerra agora.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about the war right now.

meaning: “the story”; also “the history” (the account of what happened).
additional_notes: “História” can mean either a story (a tale, a narrative—sometimes invented) or history (real past events). In expressions like “contar a história”, it usually means “tell the story/account” of what happened. It’s used for a recurring situation too (“essa tem sido a história…” = “that’s been the story”).
target_language_example: Você pode me contar a história desde o começo?
native_language_example: Can you tell me the story from the beginning?

additional_notes: Refers to people as a whole (the entire human species), often in general or philosophical statements. It can also mean “humanity” in the sense of human nature/qualities (e.g., compassion), but in many contexts it simply means “all humans.” Feminine noun: a humanidade.
target_language_example: Precisamos proteger a humanidade e o planeta.
native_language_example: We need to protect humanity and the planet.

additional_notes: Most often used with a possessive to ask or talk about someone’s age: “a idade dele/dela/vocês”. It can also mean age as a concept, especially in phrases like “com a idade” (“with age/as you get older”). Often appears with “ter”: “Quantos anos você tem?” is more common than “Qual é a sua idade?” in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Com a idade, ele ficou mais paciente.
native_language_example: With age, he became more patient.

additional_notes: A common tech term meaning computer systems that can learn, recognize patterns, or make decisions. Usually used with the definite article: “a inteligência artificial”. Often shortened to “IA” (e.g., “a IA”).
target_language_example: Muitas empresas já usam a inteligência artificial para melhorar o atendimento ao cliente.
native_language_example: Many companies already use artificial intelligence to improve customer service.

meaning: 'the intention to' / 'the intention of' (planning or meaning to do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to express a plan, purpose, or what someone meant to do: "ter a intenção de + infinitive". Often appears in negatives to clarify you didn’t mean to do something (e.g., offend, trick).
target_language_example: Não tenho a intenção de sair cedo hoje.
native_language_example: I don’t intend to leave early today.

meaning: her sister (the sister of a woman/girl).
additional_notes: “dela” means “of hers/of her” and refers to a female person (ela). It’s a common way to express possession after the noun: “a irmã dela” = “her sister.” You can also say “a sua irmã,” but “a irmã dela” is often clearer (since “sua” can mean “your” or “his/her” depending on context).
target_language_example: Eu vou falar com a irmã dela amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to talk to her sister tomorrow.

additional_notes: Means “his sister” (a female sibling of a man/boy). Used when the sister has been mentioned or is clear from context. "dele" refers to “of him/his” and agrees with the owner (a male person), not with "irmã". You can also use it after the noun: "a irmã do Tom" = “Tom’s sister.”
target_language_example: Você conhece a irmã dele?
native_language_example: Do you know his sister?

additional_notes: Feminine singular noun. Often used with verbs like abrir (to open) and fechar (to close): “A janela está aberta/fechada.”
target_language_example: Por favor, abra a janela.
native_language_example: Please open the window.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific window that is in an open state. Often used with the verb “deixar” (to leave): “deixar a janela aberta” = “to leave the window open.” Word order is noun + adjective: “janela” (window) + “aberta” (open).
target_language_example: Por favor, não deixe a janela aberta quando sair.
native_language_example: Please don’t leave the window open when you leave.

additional_notes: Usually refers to an official law/rule: "A lei foi alterada" (the law was changed), "violar a lei" (break the law), "obedecer a lei" (obey the law). It can also be used more generally for a principle or 'law of nature' ("a lei da natureza"). The dramatic phrase "Eu sou a lei!" means 'I am the law!' (said by someone claiming authority).
target_language_example: Ninguém está acima da lei.
native_language_example: No one is above the law.

additional_notes: Common in school contexts to mean homework assigned by a teacher. Usually used with the verb fazer: fazer a lição de casa = “to do homework.” It’s typically treated as a singular task/set of work (even if it includes many exercises).
target_language_example: Ainda não fiz a lição de casa.
native_language_example: I still haven’t done my homework.

additional_notes: "Loja" is a feminine noun, so it commonly appears with the definite article "a" (“the”). It refers to a physical place where you buy things (a shop/store). You’ll often see it with verbs like "ir à loja" (to go to the store), "abrir/fechar a loja" (to open/close the store), and "a loja fica aberta" (the store stays open).
target_language_example: Vou à loja comprar pão.
native_language_example: I'm going to the store to buy bread.

meaning: the dishes; the dishwashing (as a chore).
additional_notes: "Louça" refers to tableware like plates, cups, glasses, and other items used for eating/drinking. In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, "lavar a louça" means to wash the dishes (do the dishwashing), and it can refer to the whole chore (washing and sometimes drying/putting away).
target_language_example: Hoje é sua vez de lavar a louça.
native_language_example: Today it’s your turn to do the dishes.

additional_notes: A feminine singular noun phrase (a + lua). Used for the Moon in general (usually lowercase in Portuguese). With names of celestial bodies, Portuguese commonly uses the definite article (o sol, a lua).
target_language_example: Hoje a lua está muito bonita.
native_language_example: The moon looks very beautiful tonight.

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to physical light (from a lamp, sun, etc.) and is used with verbs like "acender" (turn on/light) and "apagar" (turn off). It can also be figurative, meaning understanding, awareness, or someone/something that brings joy or guidance (e.g., "a luz da consciência", "a luz da minha vida"). Feminine noun: "a luz" (plural: "as luzes").
target_language_example: Pode apagar a luz, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you turn off the light, please?

additional_notes: Most commonly means “language” (a língua portuguesa = the Portuguese language). It can also mean the physical “tongue” (e.g., in the mouth). In phrases like “falar a língua” it means “to speak the language.” Depending on context, “Dobrar a língua!” can be a sharp command meaning “Hold your tongue!/Be quiet!”
target_language_example: Você fala a língua espanhola?
native_language_example: Do you speak Spanish?

additional_notes: Used to name the language officially recognized by a country, region, or organization. Often followed by “de/da/do/dos/das” to say whose official language it is (e.g., “a língua oficial da Angola”). You can also specify a context: “a língua oficial dos negócios” = “the official language for business (in that company/setting)”.
target_language_example: No Canadá, as línguas oficiais são o inglês e o francês.
native_language_example: In Canada, the official languages are English and French.

additional_notes: Feminine form of the comparative/superlative of "grande" (big/great). It’s used with feminine nouns: "a maior riqueza" (the greatest wealth), "a maior indústria" (the biggest industry). Often appears in patterns like "a maior de todas" (the greatest of all) or "a maior das ..." (the greatest of the ...). For masculine nouns, use "o maior". Note: "maior" can look like English "major," but it usually means bigger/greater, not "major" (as in a college major).
target_language_example: Esta é a maior cidade do país.
native_language_example: This is the biggest city in the country.

additional_notes: Used with "de" to mean "most of" something: "a maior parte dos..." / "a maior parte de...". It agrees with "parte" (feminine singular), even if what comes after is plural. Can also be used for time periods: "a maior parte da minha vida" = "most of my life".
target_language_example: A maior parte dos alunos chegou cedo.
native_language_example: Most of the students arrived early.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a large portion of something (often time, money, work, etc.). It usually comes before a masculine singular noun (e.g., do dia, do tempo). With feminine nouns, it becomes "a maior parte da" (e.g., da semana).
target_language_example: Eu estudo a maior parte do tempo em casa.
native_language_example: I study most of the time at home.

meaning: most of the time; the majority of the time.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens during most moments in a period (often meaning “usually”). It can go at the end of the sentence or after the verb: “Ele fica em casa a maior parte do tempo.” / “Ele passa a maior parte do tempo em casa.”
target_language_example: Eu trabalho em casa a maior parte do tempo.
native_language_example: I work from home most of the time.

meaning: most of the work; the majority of the work.
additional_notes: Used to say that more than half of the work is done (or will be done) by someone/something. Very common with verbs like fazer (to do) and estar/ser feito(a) (to be done): “A maior parte do trabalho já está feito” and “A maior parte do trabalho já foi feita” both mean “Most of the work is already done,” but the first focuses on the current state/result and the second on the completed action. Agreement: the noun “parte” is feminine, so it’s “a maior parte (…)
target_language_example: Eu já fiz a maior parte do trabalho, falta só revisar.
native_language_example: I’ve already done most of the work; I just need to review it.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the larger part of a group. Very common pattern: “a maioria de + noun/pronoun” (a maioria de nós = most of us; a maioria deles = most of them). With a following noun, you’ll often see “a maioria + plural noun”: “a maioria deles/as pessoas”.
target_language_example: A maioria dos estudantes chega cedo.
native_language_example: Most of the students arrive early.

additional_notes: Used to talk about more than half of a group of feminine plural nouns (e.g., as placas, as coisas). It’s often followed by a plural noun: “a maioria das placas”. You can also use it without repeating the noun if it’s clear from context.
target_language_example: A maioria das pessoas aqui fala português.
native_language_example: Most of the people here speak Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what is true for most members of a group. It can be followed by a relative clause ("a maioria das pessoas que...") or an aside like "se não todas" (“if not all”). Verb agreement is often plural in everyday speech ("a maioria das pessoas gostam"), though singular is also possible ("a maioria... gosta") because the subject is "a maioria".
target_language_example: A maioria das pessoas aqui trabalha de segunda a sexta.
native_language_example: Most people here work Monday to Friday.

a maioria das pessoas gosta de

target_language_multi_word_term: a maioria das pessoas gosta de
meaning: most people like to / most people like.
additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about what most people enjoy. After "gosta de", use an infinitive verb (often like "fazer", "assistir") or a noun (like "frango"). "Gosta" is singular because the subject is "a maioria" (the majority).
target_language_example: A maioria das pessoas gosta de viajar nas férias.
native_language_example: Most people like to travel on vacation.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean “more than half” or, more generally, “most.” It agrees in gender/number with the noun: most common is "a maioria dos" (before masculine plural or mixed groups), and "a maioria das" (before feminine plural). Often followed by a singular verb in Portuguese ("A maioria dos alunos é..."), though plural is also sometimes used.
target_language_example: A maioria dos clientes prefere pagar com cartão.
native_language_example: Most of the customers prefer to pay by card.

additional_notes: Used to say something lasted for the entire morning. Often follows a verb (e.g., esperar/ficar/passar) and can come after it: “esperei a manhã inteira”.
target_language_example: Fiquei estudando a manhã inteira.
native_language_example: I studied all morning.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happened during the entire morning (from morning start until around lunchtime). Often comes after the verb ("esperei a manhã toda") or after what you were doing ("passei a manhã toda ajudando..."). You can make similar phrases with other times: "a tarde toda" (all afternoon), "a noite toda" (all night), "o dia todo" (all day).
target_language_example: Fiquei a manhã toda estudando para a prova.
native_language_example: I spent all morning studying for the test.

additional_notes: A definite noun phrase: "a" = "the" (feminine singular) + "maçã" = "apple". Used when referring to a specific apple or to apples in general in a generic statement (e.g., "A maçã é vermelha" = "The apple is red"). Often appears with food-prep verbs like cortar (to cut) and descascar (to peel).
target_language_example: Vou comer a maçã depois do almoço.
native_language_example: I'm going to eat the apple after lunch.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (stated or implied): "a melhor aluna" = "the best student". It can also stand alone when the noun is understood: "Você é a melhor" = "You’re the best." Masculine is "o melhor"; plural is "as melhores".
target_language_example: Para mim, ela é a melhor professora da escola.
native_language_example: To me, she’s the best teacher at the school.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the most effective method to do an action. It’s usually followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., "a melhor forma de chegar" = "the best way to get/arrive"). You can also use it in questions ("Qual é a melhor forma de...?") and statements ("Esta é a melhor forma de...").
target_language_example: A melhor forma de economizar dinheiro é cozinhar em casa.
native_language_example: The best way to save money is to cook at home.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the most recommended method for an action. It’s usually followed by an infinitive verb: “a melhor maneira de + verb” (e.g., “a melhor maneira de fazer isso…”). You can change “melhor” to other adjectives: “a pior maneira de…” (the worst way to), “uma boa maneira de…” (a good way to).
target_language_example: A melhor maneira de aprender português é praticar um pouco todos os dias.
native_language_example: The best way to learn Portuguese is to practice a little every day.

additional_notes: Definite article + noun: a = “the” (feminine singular) + menina = “girl”. Used to talk about a specific girl already known/identified in the context, or to point her out (“the girl who…”, “the girl is Irish”).
target_language_example: A menina está brincando no parque.
native_language_example: The girl is playing in the park.

meaning: “the slightest idea (of) …”; “any idea what …” (usually in negatives).
additional_notes: Used mainly with negation to emphasize that you don’t know something at all: “não tenho a menor ideia do que…” = “I have no idea what…”. It can be followed by a clause (“do que ele está fazendo”) or by an infinitive (“do que fazer” = “what to do”).
target_language_example: Eu não tenho a menor ideia do que dizer agora.
native_language_example: I have no idea what to say now.

additional_notes: "A" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”). "Mesa" is a common noun meaning a table (often a dining or work table). It’s used both for describing what the table is like (material, covered with something) and for actions involving the surface (cleaning, setting, clearing).
target_language_example: Por favor, coloque os pratos na mesa.
native_language_example: Please put the plates on the table.

additional_notes: Used to say something is identical/equal to another. It agrees with a feminine singular noun: a mesma língua (the same language), a mesma ideia (the same idea). It can also stand alone when the noun is understood: Ela disse a mesma. = She said the same (thing). Masculine form: o mesmo; plural: as mesmas / os mesmos.
target_language_example: Não quero outra; quero a mesma.
native_language_example: I don’t want another one; I want the same one.

additional_notes: Used to say two things are identical or equivalent (“X and Y are the same thing”), or that two people have something identical (often clothes: “They wear the same thing”). Often appears after the verb ser: “são a mesma coisa.”
target_language_example: Não é a mesma coisa, mas é parecido.
native_language_example: It’s not the same thing, but it’s similar.

additional_notes: Used to compare two actions, choices, or things and say they are identical. It’s often followed by a person or clause: “a mesma coisa que o Tom…”, “a mesma coisa que eu pedi”. Common pattern: fazer/comer/pedir a mesma coisa que + someone + verb.
target_language_example: Vou pedir a mesma coisa que você pediu.
native_language_example: I’m going to order the same thing you ordered.

additional_notes: Used to say two or more people/things are equally old.
