Often followed by "de" + a person/article: "a mesma idade da Maria" (the same age as Maria), "a mesma idade do Tom" (the same age as Tom). You can also say "ter a mesma idade" (to be the same age) or soften it with "mais ou menos" (more or less).
target_language_example: Eu tenho a mesma idade que você.
native_language_example: I’m the same age as you.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun: "a minha casa" = "my house." Portuguese often includes the definite article ("a") with possessives, especially in European Portuguese; in Brazilian Portuguese it may be omitted ("minha casa"). It can also stand alone when the noun is understood: "A minha é azul" = "Mine is blue."
target_language_example: Onde está a minha carteira?
native_language_example: Where is my wallet?

additional_notes: Literally “the my grandmother” (a + minha + avó). In Portuguese it’s common to use the definite article (a/o) before possessives, especially in European Portuguese, though it can also appear in Brazilian Portuguese. You can also say “minha avó” without the article in many contexts.
target_language_example: A minha avó faz um bolo ótimo aos domingos.
native_language_example: My grandmother makes a great cake on Sundays.

additional_notes: A possessive noun phrase: "a" (the, feminine singular) + "minha" (my, feminine singular) + "bicicleta" (bicycle). Use it when the bicycle is a specific one the listener can identify (often your own). Portuguese also allows "minha bicicleta" without the article, but "a minha bicicleta" is very common in European Portuguese and also used in Brazil for emphasis or clarity.
target_language_example: Onde está a minha bicicleta?
native_language_example: Where is my bike?

additional_notes: Means “the/my pen” (feminine singular). It’s formed by the definite article + possessive: a (the, feminine) + minha (my, feminine) + caneta (pen). In Portuguese, it’s very common to use the article with possessives (a minha caneta), though you may also hear just “minha caneta” in some contexts.
target_language_example: Desculpa, esta é a minha caneta.
native_language_example: Sorry, this is my pen.

additional_notes: Commonly used when talking about losing, finding, returning, or asking who has your wallet. In Portuguese, the possessive usually comes after the article: a minha (feminine singular) + carteira. "Carteira" can also mean "handbag" or "briefcase" depending on context, but in these examples it means the wallet/purse with your money and cards.
target_language_example: Você viu a minha carteira?
native_language_example: Have you seen my wallet?

additional_notes: Uses the feminine singular definite article “a” because “casa” is feminine. Often means “home” (the place you live), not only a physical house. You can also hear “minha casa” without the article, especially after prepositions: “em minha casa” / more commonly “na minha casa” (“in my house/home”).
target_language_example: Você quer vir à minha casa hoje?
native_language_example: Do you want to come to my house/home today?

additional_notes: Used to talk about your personal preference in colors. You’ll often see it with the verb "ser": "A minha cor favorita é..." You can also point something out: "Esta é a minha cor favorita." Note: In European Portuguese, it’s very common to say "A minha cor preferida" as well.
target_language_example: A minha cor favorita é o vermelho.
native_language_example: My favorite color is red.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your own family. "A" is the definite article (“the”), and it stays when you add a possessive like "minha". You may also see "minha família" without the article, especially in more general statements (e.g., "Minha família é pequena").
target_language_example: Hoje vou jantar com a minha família.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to have dinner with my family.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the speaker’s daughter. "a" is the definite article (“the”), often used before possessives in Portuguese: "a minha filha" = literally “the my daughter” (natural in Portuguese). You can also hear "minha filha" without "a" in some contexts. "filha" is feminine; for a son, use "o meu filho".
target_language_example: A minha filha tem sete anos.
native_language_example: My daughter is seven years old.

additional_notes: Means “my sister,” with the definite article “a” (“the”) commonly used before possessives in Portuguese. Use it when talking about your sister as a specific person. In European Portuguese, “a minha irmã” is very common; in Brazilian Portuguese you may also hear “minha irmã” without the article.
target_language_example: A minha irmã mora em Lisboa.
native_language_example: My sister lives in Lisbon.

additional_notes: "Língua" can mean both "language" and "tongue" in Portuguese. In contexts with speaking/understanding (e.g., "Você fala a minha língua"), it means "my language." In physical contexts (e.g., "mordi a minha língua"), it means "my tongue."
target_language_example: Ela está a aprender a minha língua muito rápido.
native_language_example: She’s learning my language very quickly.

additional_notes: Used when the best friend is a woman/girl (amiga). For a male best friend, say “o meu melhor amigo”. You can also drop “a/o” in casual speech: “minha melhor amiga”.
target_language_example: Vou viajar com a minha melhor amiga no fim de semana.
native_language_example: I’m going to travel with my best friend this weekend.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: "a" (the, feminine) + "minha" (my, feminine) + "mãe" (mother). It’s used when the noun is feminine; for a masculine noun you’d use "o meu..." (e.g., "o meu pai"). In casual speech, "minha mãe" is often used without the article "a". You can also say "a mamãe" for “mom” (more affectionate/childlike).
target_language_example: A minha mãe mora perto daqui.
native_language_example: My mother lives near here.

additional_notes: Used when your mother is the subject and "me" is the object of the verb that follows: "A minha mãe me levou" = "My mother took me"; "A minha mãe me pede" = "My mother asks me". In Portuguese, this unstressed pronoun (me) often comes right before the verb (as in the examples).
target_language_example: A minha mãe me ligou ontem à noite.
native_language_example: My mother called me last night.

meaning: 'my mom is' (used to describe your mother).
additional_notes: Used before a noun or adjective to say what your mother is like or what she does (job/role). In European Portuguese you’ll often hear "mãe"; in Brazilian Portuguese "mamãe" is also common in more affectionate contexts. You can add emphasis with words like "mesmo" (really).
target_language_example: A minha mãe é professora.
native_language_example: My mom is a teacher.

additional_notes: Used with the feminine singular definite article (a) + possessive (minha) + noun (mão). In Portuguese, body parts are often said with an article and/or possessive depending on emphasis; here it clearly means the speaker’s hand (often in requests like "Hold my hand" or "Squeeze my hand").
target_language_example: Você pode lavar a minha mão?
native_language_example: Can you wash my hand?

additional_notes: Used to refer to your girlfriend. "a" and "minha" are feminine to match "namorada". For a male partner, say "o meu namorado" (my boyfriend). In European Portuguese you may also hear "a minha namorada" shortened to "a minha" when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Vou sair com a minha namorada hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I’m going out with my girlfriend tonight.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your personal point of view. Often appears with verbs like dar (to give), pedir (to ask for), dizer (to say), and ouvir/escutar (to hear/listen to): "Pediram a minha opinião" = "They asked for my opinion." You can also swap the possessive for other people: a tua opinião (your), a opinião dele/dela (his/her).
target_language_example: Na minha opinião, isto não vai funcionar.
native_language_example: In my opinion, this isn't going to work.

additional_notes: Used when you give someone your promise or guarantee that something is true or that you will do something. Very common with the verb “dar” (dar a minha palavra = to give my word) and also with “ter” (tens/têm a minha palavra = you have my word). You can add “de que …” to introduce what you’re promising (e.g., “Dou a minha palavra de que…”).
target_language_example: Dou a minha palavra de que vou chegar a horas.
native_language_example: I give you my word that I’ll arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun to say you experienced/owned something for the first time. It agrees with feminine nouns (a minha primeira vez, a minha primeira cerveja, a minha primeira esposa). For masculine nouns, use "o meu primeiro" (o meu primeiro carro). In Portuguese, possessives often take an article: "a minha".
target_language_example: Esta é a minha primeira vez aqui.
native_language_example: This is my first time here.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used to talk about your life in general (experiences, time, or existence). Often appears in set phrases like “a minha vida inteira” (“my whole life”) and with verbs like “mudar” (to change) or “custar” (to cost, e.g., “cost me my life”). Usually “minha vida” also works without the article, but with the article (“a”) it can sound more specific/emphatic in context.
target_language_example: A minha vida mudou muito desde que me mudei para cá.
native_language_example: My life has changed a lot since I moved here.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun: "a minha casa" = "my house." Portuguese often includes the definite article ("a") with possessives, especially in European Portuguese; in Brazilian Portuguese it may be omitted ("minha casa"). It can also stand alone when the noun is understood: "A minha é azul" = "Mine is blue."
target_language_example: Onde está a minha carteira?
native_language_example: Where is my wallet?

meaning: death; (in some contexts) the act/state of dying.
additional_notes: Usually means death as a concept ("life and death") or a specific death ("the death of someone"). With "de" it often introduces who/what died: "a morte de + person/thing" = "the death of…". In set phrases it can suggest fatal danger/certainty: "ir para a morte certa" = "to go to certain death".
target_language_example: A polícia ainda está a investigar a morte do jornalista.
native_language_example: The police are still investigating the journalist's death.

additional_notes: Definite article + noun: “a” = “the” (feminine singular) + “mulher” = “woman.” Used to refer to a specific woman already known or identified in context. In Brazilian Portuguese, “cadê a mulher?” means “where is the woman?” In some contexts, “a mulher” can also mean “the wife” (e.g., “A mulher dele chegou” = “His wife arrived”).
target_language_example: A mulher do João está no trabalho agora.
native_language_example: João’s wife is at work now.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with **que** describing which woman you mean. **Que** can refer to the subject ("the woman who called") or the object depending on the sentence, but in English it usually translates as **who/that**.
target_language_example: A mulher que mora aqui trabalha no hospital.
native_language_example: The woman who lives here works at the hospital.

meaning: the crowd; a large group of people (in one place).
additional_notes: Used for a big group of people gathered together (at a concert, in the street, etc.). It’s singular in Portuguese (“a multidão”), but it refers to many people. Common with verbs showing the group’s reaction: “A multidão adorou...”, “caiu na gargalhada”, “entrou em pânico”.
target_language_example: Havia uma multidão na porta do estádio.
native_language_example: There was a crowd at the stadium entrance.

additional_notes: Used for the household appliance that washes clothes. Often followed by the thing being washed: “máquina de lavar roupa” (washing machine) or “máquina de lavar louça” (dishwasher). Common with verbs like “usar” (to use), “consertar” (to fix), “ligar/desligar” (to turn on/off), and “fazer barulho” (to make noise).
target_language_example: A máquina de lavar quebrou, então vou lavar a roupa à mão.
native_language_example: The washing machine broke, so I'm going to wash the clothes by hand.

additional_notes: Definite article + noun: "a" = "the" (feminine singular) + "mãe" = "mother." Used to refer to a specific mother already known in the conversation, or identified by a phrase like "a mãe do Howl" (Howl’s mother). For "my mom" you usually say "minha mãe".
target_language_example: A mãe dela mora aqui perto.
native_language_example: Her mother lives nearby.

additional_notes: Means “the mother of her” (dela = de + ela). Used to refer to a female person’s mother when talking about her. It’s definite (“the”), but in English it’s usually just “her mother.”
target_language_example: A mãe dela mora aqui perto.
native_language_example: Her mother lives nearby.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a male person’s mother. Literally “the mother of him” (a + mãe + dele). In Portuguese you commonly use this structure (noun + dele/dela) instead of saying “his/her” before the noun. With a female owner, you’d say “a mãe dela” (“her mother”).
target_language_example: Eu falei com a mãe dele ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I spoke with his mother last night.

additional_notes: Portuguese often uses the definite article with body parts (a mão = “the hand”). Common phrases: **apertar a mão (de alguém)** = “to shake (someone’s) hand.” **Passar a mão (em alguém)** can mean “to run your hand over / touch someone,” and depending on context can imply groping or unwanted touching.
target_language_example: Prazer em conhecê-lo — posso apertar a mão?
native_language_example: Nice to meet you—may I shake your hand?

meaning: “the music” (a song or music in general).
additional_notes: Means music as an art form (“Music awakens feelings”) or a specific song (“He sang the song I asked for”). It’s feminine; the article changes with context (a música = the music, uma música = a song).
target_language_example: Você gosta da música brasileira?
native_language_example: Do you like Brazilian music?

meaning: 'music is…' (used to define or describe music).
additional_notes: Common sentence starter: "A música" = "music" (feminine singular), and "é" = "is" (from "ser"). Used to give a definition/opinion or say what music means to someone. Often followed by adjectives (boa, maravilhosa) or a noun phrase (a língua universal, a sua paixão).
target_language_example: A música é importante para mim.
native_language_example: Music is important to me.

additional_notes: Feminine singular noun with the definite article “a” (= “the”). Used when talking about snow in general or specific snow already known in context. Common related phrases: “Está nevando” (It’s snowing), “Tem neve na rua” (There’s snow on the street).
target_language_example: A neve cobriu a cidade durante a noite.
native_language_example: The snow covered the city overnight.

meaning: the night; the evening (the nighttime period).
additional_notes: Usually refers to nighttime in general or to a particular evening/night event (e.g., a party or the night out). With adjectives it often describes the weather or atmosphere at night: "A noite será fria" = "The night will be cold." In expressions like "encerrar a noite", it means finishing the evening's activities.
target_language_example: Vamos sair à noite.
native_language_example: Let's go out at night / in the evening.

additional_notes: Used to say something lasted for the entire night. Often follows the verb: “chorar a noite inteira” (cry all night), “ficar acordado a noite inteira” (stay awake all night). You can also say “a noite toda” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Eu trabalhei a noite inteira e agora estou exausto.
native_language_example: I worked all night and now I’m exhausted.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the previous night (yesterday night). Very common with the past tense to say what happened. You may also see the equivalent word order “na noite passada” (= “on/during last night”).
target_language_example: A noite passada eu fiquei em casa e vi um filme.
native_language_example: Last night I stayed home and watched a movie.

additional_notes: Used to say something lasted throughout the entire night. Often placed after the verb: "trabalhamos a noite toda". You can also use it with "ficar" to describe a state for the whole night (e.g., "ficou quieto a noite toda").
target_language_example: Eu fiquei acordado a noite toda estudando para a prova.
native_language_example: I stayed awake all night studying for the test.

meaning: 'our' (feminine singular), referring to something that belongs to us.
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun: a nossa família, a nossa situação, a nossa saúde, a nossa vida, a nossa empresa. It agrees in gender and number: o nosso (masc. sing.), a nossa (fem. sing.), os nossos (masc. plural/mixed), as nossas (fem. plural). Often interchangeable with just "nossa" before the noun, but "a nossa" is common when the noun is present or implied.
target_language_example: A nossa casa fica perto do centro.
native_language_example: Our house is near downtown.

meaning: the news; a piece of news; (also) the information/message someone receives.
additional_notes: Feminine noun: a notícia (sing.), as notícias (pl.). Often used with verbs like receber (to receive), ouvir (to hear), and espalhar-se (to spread): “receber/ouvir a notícia”. It can mean public news (e.g., on the radio) or simply important information someone learns.
target_language_example: Recebi a notícia ontem à noite e fiquei em choque.
native_language_example: I got the news last night and was in shock.

meaning: sense of time (awareness of time passing).
additional_notes: Most often used in the expression “perder a noção do tempo” = “to lose track of time,” especially when you’re busy, distracted, or enjoying yourself and don’t notice how much time has passed. You can also say “ter noção do tempo” (“to have a sense of time / be aware of the time”).
target_language_example: A gente estava conversando e perdeu a noção do tempo.
native_language_example: We were talking and lost track of time.

additional_notes: Most often refers to a specific word being discussed (“the word”), especially in contexts like spelling, translating, or looking it up in a dictionary. In some set expressions it can mean “promise/word” (e.g., manter a palavra = to keep your word).
target_language_example: Qual é a palavra em português para “library”?
native_language_example: What is the word in Portuguese for “library”?

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a sports game: "a partida de futebol" = "the soccer match." In other contexts, "a partida" can mean someone’s departure: "concordou com a partida" = "agreed with the departure/leaving." Note the common expression "dar a partida" (or "dê a partida!") meaning "to start" an engine/vehicle (car, ship, etc.).
target_language_example: A partida começa às oito.
native_language_example: The match starts at eight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about one specific match of tennis. "Partida" often means a match/game in sports; here it’s "of tennis" ("de tênis"). You can use verbs like "adiar" (postpone), "continuar" (continue), and "ganhar" (win) with it. In everyday speech, people may also just say "o jogo de tênis".
target_language_example: Vamos assistir à partida de tênis amanhã.
native_language_example: We’re going to watch the tennis match tomorrow.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a travel ticket: *comprar a passagem* = “to buy the ticket” (often you can specify *passagem do metrô*, *passagem de ônibus*, etc.). It can also mean a passage/corridor or crossing/way through, especially in contexts like evacuations or moving through a narrow place.
target_language_example: Preciso comprar a passagem do ônibus para amanhã.
native_language_example: I need to buy the bus ticket for tomorrow.

meaning: 1) a punishment/sentence; 2) a feather; 3) (in “valer a pena”) worth it.
additional_notes: “Pena” has two common meanings: (1) a legal punishment/sentence (cumprir a pena = to serve a sentence) and (2) a feather (pena de uma águia = an eagle feather). In the fixed expression “valer a pena”, it means “to be worth it / worthwhile” (often with “pode” or “vai”: pode valer a pena, vai valer a pena).
target_language_example: Não se preocupe: vai valer a pena.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’ll be worth it.

additional_notes: Means the leg (body part), usually from the hip down to the foot. Often used with injury verbs like "machucar a perna" (hurt your leg) and "quebrar a perna" (break your leg). "Perna" is feminine, so it takes "a" (singular) and "as" (plural: "as pernas").
target_language_example: Eu machuquei a perna ontem.
native_language_example: I hurt my leg yesterday.

meaning: “the most … person” (used to form a superlative).
additional_notes: Use this pattern to say someone is the most [adjective] person: **a pessoa mais + adjective**. You’ll often see it with **do mundo** (“in the world”) or **que eu conheço** (“that I know”): *a pessoa mais simpática do mundo* = “the nicest person in the world.”
target_language_example: Ela é a pessoa mais gentil que eu conheço.
native_language_example: She’s the kindest person I know.

additional_notes: Definite noun phrase: "a" = "the" (feminine singular) + "polícia". Used to refer to the police as an institution/force. You can also use it to mean the local police in a specific place (e.g., a city or area).
target_language_example: Chame a polícia, por favor.
native_language_example: Call the police, please.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of prender, used for a completed action: the police arrested/detained someone. The person arrested is usually introduced with a direct object: “A polícia prendeu o homem.” In everyday English, “arrest” is the most common translation when it’s official police action.
target_language_example: A polícia prendeu o suspeito ontem à noite.
native_language_example: The police arrested the suspect last night.

additional_notes: Used to report an arrest in the past. It’s a complete subject + verb phrase: a polícia (the police) + prendeu (arrested; past tense of prender) + o (the, masculine singular). Change o to a for a female person (A polícia prendeu a Maria) and to os/as for plural (A polícia prendeu os suspeitos / as suspeitas). Often followed by a name or a noun like suspeito (suspect).
target_language_example: A polícia prendeu o motorista depois do acidente.
native_language_example: The police arrested the driver after the accident.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific bridge already known from context. "Ponte" is feminine, so it goes with "a" (the) and adjectives often agree: "a ponte alta" (the tall/high bridge). Common with directions and travel: "ir para a ponte" (go to the bridge), "levar até a ponte" (take/drive me to the bridge).
target_language_example: A ponte fica perto da estação.
native_language_example: The bridge is near the station.

meaning: “the fucking …” (a very vulgar, angry intensifier before a noun).
additional_notes: Used to show strong annoyance, impatience, or emphasis before a noun: “a porra do X”. It’s profanity and can sound aggressive/hostile—avoid in polite situations. It changes with gender/number of the noun: “a porra do carro” (masc.), “a porra da chave” (fem.), “a porra dos carros” (pl. masc.), “a porra das chaves” (pl. fem.).
target_language_example: Eu não acho a porra da minha carteira!
native_language_example: I can’t find my fucking wallet!

additional_notes: "A" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”), used with feminine nouns like "porta" (door). Common with verbs like abrir/fechar (open/close), trancar/destrancar (lock/unlock), and with "chave" (key).
target_language_example: Por favor, feche a porta.
native_language_example: Please close the door.

additional_notes: Used to describe a door that is currently open or that someone left open. Common with the verb deixar (“to leave”): Deixa/Deixe a porta aberta (“Leave the door open”). Note agreement: porta (feminine) + aberta (feminine).
target_language_example: Não deixa a porta aberta, está frio.
native_language_example: Don’t leave the door open; it’s cold.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the main entrance door of a house or building. Often appears with verbs like estar (A porta da frente estava aberta.) and usar (Usa/Use a porta da frente.). In instructions, “Usa” is informal (tu) and “Use” is more formal/polite (você).
target_language_example: Por favor, bate na porta da frente.
native_language_example: Please knock on the front door.

meaning: "the door of the" (of a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to specify which door you mean: "a porta" + "do" (= de + o, "of the") + a masculine place/object (e.g., escritório, quarto, refrigerador). With feminine nouns, use "a porta da" (da = de + a).
target_language_example: A porta do banheiro está trancada.
native_language_example: The bathroom door is locked.

meaning: "the door to" / "the door for" (a place or a person).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to show destination or access: "a porta para a cozinha" (the door to the kitchen), "a porta para Kingsbury" (the door to Kingsbury). With people it often means doing someone a favor by holding/opening a door: "segurar/abrir a porta para alguém" (hold/open the door for someone). It can also be used more figuratively as "a porta para" = "the gateway to" (an opportunity/possibility).
target_language_example: Você pode segurar a porta para mim, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you hold the door for me, please?

meaning: “the door for me” (in requests: “open the door for me”).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like abrir (“to open”) or segurar (“to hold”) to ask someone to open/hold the door so you can pass. Often appears in polite questions: “Abre a porta para mim?” (informal) / “O senhor/A senhora abre a porta para mim?” (formal).
target_language_example: Você pode segurar a porta para mim, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you hold the door for me, please?

additional_notes: Feminine noun: praia. It usually appears with the definite article: a praia (“the beach”). Common with the verb ficar to talk about location/distance: “A praia fica perto/longe daqui?” You can also use it with ir para to mean “to go to the beach”: “ir para a praia”.
target_language_example: Vamos para a praia no fim de semana.
native_language_example: We're going to the beach on the weekend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what meteorologists/apps say the weather will be like (today, tomorrow, this weekend, etc.). Common patterns: “Qual é a previsão do tempo para amanhã?” (What’s the forecast for tomorrow?) and “A previsão do tempo é que…” (The forecast is that…). You may also hear “previsão meteorológica” as a more formal synonym.
target_language_example: Segundo a previsão do tempo, vai fazer frio no fim de semana.
native_language_example: According to the weather forecast, it’s going to be cold this weekend.

additional_notes: Used with the feminine definite article “a” (“the”). Common with verbs like “chegar”/“vir” to talk about the season approaching: “A primavera vai chegar logo.”
target_language_example: Na primavera, o tempo fica mais agradável.
native_language_example: In spring, the weather becomes more pleasant.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (explicit or implied). It’s the feminine form of the ordinal number: a primeira página (“the first page”). You can also use it on its own to mean “the first one” when the noun is understood from context. Masculine: o primeiro; plural: as primeiras / os primeiros.
target_language_example: A primeira vez é sempre difícil.
native_language_example: The first time is always difficult.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the first action, thought, or item in a sequence: "A primeira coisa que eu fiz/vi/disse foi..." It’s often followed by a verb phrase, and you can change it for gender/number (e.g., "O primeiro" / "A primeira"; "As primeiras coisas").
target_language_example: A primeira coisa que eu vou fazer é ligar para você.
native_language_example: The first thing I’m going to do is call you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the first occasion when something happened. It’s often followed by a verb (e.g., “a primeira vez que eu vi…”), and it can appear at the beginning or in the middle of a sentence. In questions, it commonly appears as “Quando foi a primeira vez que…?” (“When was the first time that…?”).
target_language_example: A primeira vez que visitei Lisboa, fiquei impressionado.
native_language_example: The first time I visited Lisbon, I was impressed.

additional_notes: Uses the feminine definite article “a” (= “the”) with “princesa” (princess). Often refers to a specific princess known from the story/context (e.g., in fairy tales or games: “save the princess”). Capitalize as part of a name/title: “a princesa Buttercup”.
target_language_example: Onde está a princesa?
native_language_example: Where is the princess?

additional_notes: Feminine form of the noun (professor/a). Used with the definite article a (“the”). You’ll see it for school teachers and also for female university instructors in Portuguese. If you know the teacher’s name, you can say: a professora Rosa. Plural: as professoras.
target_language_example: A professora vai explicar a lição agora.
native_language_example: The teacher is going to explain the lesson now.

additional_notes: “Prova” is a feminine noun. In many contexts it means “proof/evidence” (as in showing something is true). It can also mean “test/exam” depending on context (e.g., “Tenho uma prova amanhã.” = “I have a test tomorrow.”).
target_language_example: Você tem alguma prova disso?
native_language_example: Do you have any proof of that?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the next item in a sequence when the noun is understood from context (e.g., a próxima música = the next song). It’s feminine because it agrees with an implied feminine noun (música, história, etc.). For a masculine implied noun, use "o próximo" (e.g., o próximo trem = the next train).
target_language_example: Vamos para a próxima pergunta.
native_language_example: Let’s go to the next question.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the main point or the real problem, often followed by "que" ("a questão é que..."). Common in explanations and arguments, similar to English "The thing is, ...".
target_language_example: A questão é que eu não tenho tempo hoje.
native_language_example: The thing is, I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used for a female monarch or, more generally, for a woman seen as the most important/best in a group (“queen of…”). Often paired with "o rei" (the king).
target_language_example: A rainha vai visitar a cidade amanhã.
native_language_example: The queen is going to visit the city tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation or cause, often followed by a clause: “A razão pela qual + (subject) + verb…”. It’s fairly formal; in everyday speech you may also hear “o motivo pelo qual” or simply “por que”.
target_language_example: Não entendi a razão pela qual você saiu sem avisar.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand why you left without telling me.

additional_notes: Used for an answer to a question, problem, or situation. Often followed by a clause with the content: "A resposta foi sim/não" (“The answer was yes/no”). You can also use it more generally for a solution/result: "Só o tempo dará a resposta" (“Only time will tell / give the answer”).
target_language_example: Você já sabe a resposta?
native_language_example: Do you already know the answer?

additional_notes: Common noun used for scheduled meetings (work, school, organizations). Often appears with verbs like "ser" (to be held), "acontecer" (to happen), and "terminar" (to end). You can ask about time/place with "Quando/onde será a reunião?"
target_language_example: A reunião começa às nove, na sala 3.
native_language_example: The meeting starts at nine, in room 3.

additional_notes: "Roupa" most commonly means "clothes" in general. In contexts with washing/ironing/detergent (lavar/passar/detergente), it often means "laundry" (the clothes being washed). "Tire a roupa" means "Take off your clothes" (often implies undressing).
target_language_example: Hoje eu vou lavar a roupa.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to do the laundry.

meaning: the washed laundry; clean (already washed) clothes.
additional_notes: Used to refer to clothes that have already been washed (laundry) and are ready to be hung up to dry, put in the dryer, or folded. Common with verbs like estender/pendurar (to hang up) and with places like no varal (on the clothesline).
target_language_example: Vou dobrar a roupa lavada agora.
native_language_example: I’m going to fold the clean laundry now.

additional_notes: Used for a street in a city or town. Often followed by a clause or name to specify which one: "a rua onde ela mora" (the street where she lives), "a rua Augusta". Common with verbs like "atravessar" (to cross) and "seguir" (to follow/continue).
target_language_example: Desculpe, onde fica a rua principal?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the main street?

meaning: the room; the living room/lounge; (in some contexts) a hall/meeting room.
additional_notes: Most often refers to a room in a building. In a home, "a sala" commonly means the living room ("sala de estar"). In workplaces or events it can mean a specific room/hall, like a meeting room ("sala da reunião" / "sala de reuniões"). It’s feminine singular; plural: "as salas".
target_language_example: A sala de estar fica logo à direita.
native_language_example: The living room is right to the right.

additional_notes: Refers to the room where classes/lessons happen at a school. Often used with verbs like estar (A sala de aula está limpa) and limpar (clean). Literally “the room of class,” but in English you usually say “classroom.”
target_language_example: Os alunos já estão na sala de aula.
native_language_example: The students are already in the classroom.

additional_notes: A common name for the main room in a home where people sit, relax, and receive visitors. Often used with the definite article: "a sala de estar" (the living room). You may also hear "sala" on its own when the context is clear.
target_language_example: As crianças estão brincando na sala de estar.
native_language_example: The kids are playing in the living room.

meaning: the exit; the way out; (on roads) the exit/off-ramp.
additional_notes: Used for the place where you leave a building ("A saída é pela esquerda"), for leading someone to the door/exit ("até a saída"), and for a highway exit you might miss ("Perdemos a saída"). It comes from the verb "sair" (to leave/go out).
target_language_example: Desculpe, onde fica a saída?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the exit?

additional_notes: Means “health” as a general concept or someone’s physical condition. It’s used with the definite article “a” (literally “the”), which is common in Portuguese when speaking about abstract ideas (e.g., a saúde, a felicidade). You can also use it in phrases like “fazer bem à saúde” (to be good for your health) and “recuperar a saúde” (to recover your health).
target_language_example: Exercício regular faz bem à saúde.
native_language_example: Regular exercise is good for your health.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that health matters more than something else. It’s commonly followed by a comparison with "do que" or "que" (both mean “than”): "A saúde é mais importante do que/que o dinheiro" (“Health is more important than money”). You can also add "Nem é preciso dizer que..." (“Needless to say that...”) to strengthen the point.
target_language_example: Para mim, a saúde é mais importante do que o trabalho.
native_language_example: For me, health is more important than work.

meaning: “ma’am”; a polite/formal way to refer to an older woman (or to address a woman respectfully).
additional_notes: Used as a respectful form of address, often with the verb in the 3rd person singular: “A senhora está…”, “A senhora fala…”. It can mean “you” (formal) when speaking directly to the woman, or “the lady” when talking about her. Common pair: “o senhor” (sir).
target_language_example: A senhora precisa de ajuda?
native_language_example: Do you need help, ma’am?

additional_notes: Used to address a woman politely (often older, a customer, or someone you don’t know well). It’s “a senhora” (the lady/ma’am) + “está” (is/are), typically followed by a temporary state, location, or an action in progress: “com fome” (hungry), “de volta” (back), “ligando” (calling), “visitando” (visiting). In Brazil, “a senhora” is more formal than “você.”
target_language_example: A senhora está esperando alguém?
native_language_example: Are you waiting for someone, ma’am?

additional_notes: Very polite/formal way to address an adult woman (“a senhora” = ma’am/you, formal). Used to ask permission, make a request, or state what she is allowed to do. In questions, intonation makes it a request: “A senhora pode…?” = “Could you…?” In statements, it means “You may/can…”.
target_language_example: A senhora pode me ajudar, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you help me, please, ma’am?

additional_notes: Used to politely address an adult woman (“a senhora” = ma’am/you, formal). Often heard in customer service, with older people, or when you want to be extra respectful. The verb “quer” is from “querer” (to want), and in questions it can mean “want” or “would like.” Object pronouns may appear in formal phrasing: “A senhora quer que eu a ajude…?” = “Would you like me to help you…?”
target_language_example: A senhora quer pagar em dinheiro ou no cartão?
native_language_example: Would you like to pay in cash or by card?

meaning: the situation; the state of things.
additional_notes: Used to talk about how things are at a particular time (economy, a problem, conditions in a place, etc.). Often followed by an adjective (A situação está difícil/horrível) or a prepositional phrase (a situação em Boston).
target_language_example: A situação no trânsito hoje está complicada.
native_language_example: The traffic situation today is complicated.

additional_notes: "A" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”), and "sua" is a possessive that agrees with the possessed noun (feminine singular): a sua entrevista (“your/his/her interview”), a sua barra (“your/his/her bar”), a sua fala (“your/his/her speech”). In Brazilian Portuguese, "a sua" often means “your” (for "você"), but it can also mean “his/her/its”, so context matters; to avoid ambiguity, people may use "dele/dela" (“his/her”).
target_language_example: Posso ver a sua identidade, por favor?
native_language_example: Can I see your ID, please?

additional_notes: Means help provided by the person you’re talking to. Uses the possessive “sua” with the definite article “a.” Common in polite contexts (thanks, requests). In Brazil, “sua” can sometimes sound more formal than “sua” used in very casual speech; you may also hear “a tua ajuda” (more informal/European Portuguese and some regions) or “sua ajuda” without the article in some contexts.
target_language_example: Obrigado pela sua ajuda.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a letter belonging to the person you’re addressing, using the possessive "sua". Often sounds more formal/polite than "a tua carta" (common in Portugal and informal contexts). In Brazil, "sua" is widely used because people often address someone as "você".
target_language_example: Obrigado por enviar a sua carta; vou responder amanhã.
native_language_example: Thank you for sending your letter; I’ll reply tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive "sua" to mean "your" (formal "you" = você) or "his/her/its" depending on context; adding "a" makes it "the your house" → "your house." Often said as "sua casa" without the article, and in Brazilian Portuguese you may also hear "a casa de você" to avoid ambiguity.
target_language_example: Posso visitar a sua casa amanhã?
native_language_example: Can I visit your house tomorrow?

additional_notes: Literally “the your wife.” Portuguese often uses the definite article (a = “the”) before possessives: a sua esposa, o meu carro, etc. “Sua” agrees with the noun (esposa is feminine → sua). Depending on context, “sua” can mean “your” (formal you) or “his/her/their”; the examples here clearly mean “your wife.”
target_language_example: Você vai trazer a sua esposa para o jantar?
native_language_example: Are you going to bring your wife to dinner?

additional_notes: Literally “the your wife.” Portuguese often uses the definite article (a = “the”) before possessives: a sua esposa, o meu carro, etc. “Sua” agrees with the noun (esposa is feminine → sua). Depending on context, “sua” can mean “your” (formal you) or “his/her/their”; the examples here clearly mean “your wife.”
target_language_example: Você vai trazer a sua esposa para o jantar?
native_language_example: Are you going to bring your wife to dinner?

meaning: your absence (in “sentir a sua falta” = “to miss you”).
additional_notes: Used as the object in the very common expression “sentir falta de (alguém)” (“to miss (someone)”). “Sua” can mean “your” (often more formal, or in Brazil also for “his/her/their/your” depending on context). Don’t confuse “falta” with English “fault”: here it means “absence/lack”.
target_language_example: Vou sentir muito a sua falta quando você viajar.
native_language_example: I’m going to miss you a lot when you travel.

meaning: “your family” (formal), or “his/her family” depending on context.
additional_notes: “Sua” can mean “your” (formal singular, like to a customer/stranger) or “his/her/its/their,” so the meaning depends on who is being talked to/about. In Brazil, many people say “a família dele/dela” to be clearer. Often used when asking how someone’s relatives are or when talking about supporting/providing for one’s family.
target_language_example: Você conhece a sua família aqui na cidade?
native_language_example: Do you know your family here in the city?

additional_notes: “Sua” is a possessive that can mean “your” (formal), but also “his/her/their” in some contexts—Portuguese often relies on context to know whose daughter it is. To be clearer, people may say “a filha dele” (his daughter) or “a filha dela” (her daughter).
target_language_example: A sua filha já chegou em casa?
native_language_example: Has your daughter arrived home yet?

additional_notes: Literally “your age.” Common in comparisons and time expressions like “quando eu tinha a sua idade” (“when I was your age”). Also used in advice about maturity/behavior: “de acordo com a sua idade” (“according to/appropriate for your age”). Uses the formal/neutral possessive “sua” (also used with “você”); with “tu,” you’ll often see “a tua idade.”
target_language_example: Quando eu tinha a sua idade, eu estudava e trabalhava ao mesmo tempo.
native_language_example: When I was your age, I studied and worked at the same time.

additional_notes: Literally “the your sister.” In Portuguese, possessives often come with an article (a/o): a sua irmã, o seu irmão. In many contexts, “sua” can also mean “his/her/their,” so speakers may use “a irmã dele/dela” to be more specific.
target_language_example: A sua irmã fala inglês?
native_language_example: Does your sister speak English?

additional_notes: Used to tell or ask someone about the homework they need to do. It’s feminine singular: "a" + "lição". "sua" means "your" (formal 'you') or "his/her/their" depending on context; here it’s clearly "your". Often appears with the verb "fazer" (to do): "fazer a sua lição de casa".
target_language_example: Depois do jantar, vou fazer a minha lição de casa.
native_language_example: After dinner, I’m going to do my homework.

meaning: your mother (formal/polite) or his/her mother (depending on context).
additional_notes: "Sua" can mean "your" (especially in polite/formal speech) or "his/her". In Brazilian Portuguese, "a sua mãe" often refers to "your mother" when talking to someone using "você"; "a mãe dele/dela" is clearer for "his/her mother." With family words, Portuguese usually uses the definite article: "a mãe", "o pai".
target_language_example: Como está a sua mãe hoje?
native_language_example: How is your mother today?

additional_notes: "a" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”), and "sua" means “your” (feminine singular noun). "namorada" is “girlfriend.” Used when speaking to someone about their girlfriend. In Brazil, "sua" is often interchangeable with "a sua" (e.g., "Conheci sua namorada"); in Portugal, "a sua" is common and can sound more formal/clear. It can also be used in the sense of “your date/partner” depending on context.
target_language_example: A sua namorada vem à festa hoje?
native_language_example: Is your girlfriend coming to the party today?

additional_notes: Uses the possessive "sua" to refer to the person you’re addressing as "você" (you). Common in polite/formal contexts, but it can also sound sharp or sarcastic depending on tone (e.g., "Quem pediu a sua opinião?" = "Who asked for your opinion?"). Often appears with verbs like "dar" (to give), "pedir" (to ask for), "ter" (to have), "respeitar" (to respect).
target_language_example: Gostaria de saber a sua opinião sobre este assunto.
native_language_example: I’d like to know your opinion about this matter.

additional_notes: "Sua" is a possessive meaning “your,” and "viagem" means “trip/journey.” It’s common in polite conversation, especially with "você". In Brazil, "sua" can sometimes be ambiguous (your vs. his/her/their), but in questions like "Como foi a sua viagem?" it usually clearly means “your trip.”
target_language_example: Espero que a sua viagem tenha sido tranquila.
native_language_example: I hope your trip was smooth.

additional_notes: Used to address someone with the polite/formal possessive “sua” (especially with você/o senhor/a senhora). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often say “a sua vida” in polite contexts, and “a tua vida” in more informal contexts (common in Portugal and some regions). In formal writing, “sua” can sometimes also mean “his/her/their,” so context matters.
target_language_example: Você está arriscando a sua vida.
native_language_example: You’re risking your life.

additional_notes: Used to say an action lasted for the entire afternoon. It often comes after the verb ("Esperei a tarde toda"), and it can also appear with a gerund phrase to emphasize duration ("passaram a tarde toda conversando" = spent all afternoon talking).
target_language_example: Fiquei trabalhando a tarde toda.
native_language_example: I kept working all afternoon.

meaning: the temperature (how hot or cold something is).
additional_notes: Used with the definite article “a” (“the”). Common in weather (“a temperatura de hoje…”) and health contexts (“a temperatura dele/dela está normal” = their body temperature is normal). You can specify whose/what temperature with “de” (e.g., “a temperatura do quarto”, “a temperatura dele”).
target_language_example: Qual é a temperatura agora?
native_language_example: What is the temperature right now?

meaning: the storm; (figuratively) a crisis or difficult time.
additional_notes: Literally a strong storm (wind/rain, etc.). It can also be used figuratively for a tough period: esperar a tempestade passar = “wait for things to calm down.” Common proverb: “Quem semeia o vento colhe a tempestade” = “You reap what you sow” (bad actions bring bad consequences).
target_language_example: Vamos ficar em casa até a tempestade passar.
native_language_example: Let’s stay home until the storm passes.

meaning: the Earth; the land/ground; soil; (also) a people’s land/territory.
additional_notes: Meaning depends on context: (1) "a Terra" (often capitalized) refers to the planet Earth. (2) "a terra" can mean land/ground/soil (what you walk on or plant in). (3) With "de" + people/group ("a terra de vocês", "a terra dos nossos ancestrais"), it can mean someone’s homeland or territory.
target_language_example: Depois da chuva, a terra ficou muito molhada.
native_language_example: After the rain, the ground/soil got very wet.

meaning: “your” (feminine singular), used before a feminine noun.
additional_notes: It’s the feminine singular form of “o/a teu/tua” (“your”). Used when the thing owned/related is feminine: a tua resposta (your answer), a tua mesa (your table), a tua cara (your face). In Portugal, “a tua” is common with “tu”; in Brazil, “a sua” is often used instead in many situations.
target_language_example: Não encontrei a tua chave.
native_language_example: I didn’t find your key.

additional_notes: Often used after verbs like dizer/falar (“to tell/speak”) or querer (“to want”), especially in questions like “Querem a verdade?” = “Do you want the truth?” In Portuguese, it usually takes the definite article: a verdade.
target_language_example: Preciso saber a verdade agora.
native_language_example: I need to know the truth now.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an honest statement, often to correct a misunderstanding or admit something. It can add emphasis, like “to be honest,” and is commonly followed by a full clause (sometimes with “que,” sometimes omitted in casual speech).
target_language_example: A verdade é que eu não tenho tempo hoje.
native_language_example: The truth is I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Feminine singular noun with the definite article a. Used for a specific trip/journey: A viagem foi interessante? (“Was the trip interesting?”). Common with verbs like ser/estar (foi), ir (vai), and with cost questions: Quanto a viagem vai custar? / A viagem vai custar quanto?
target_language_example: A viagem começa amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: The trip starts tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Uses the definite article "a" (= "the") and is very common when talking about life in general or as a concept. It can also mean "someone’s life" when the context is clear (e.g., "a vida dele" = "his life").
target_language_example: A vida é curta, aproveita.
native_language_example: Life is short—enjoy it.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a description or comparison about rural/countryside life. It’s often followed by an adjective or phrase like “mais saudável” (healthier), “mais simples” (simpler), or “muito tranquila” (very peaceful).
target_language_example: Para mim, a vida no campo é mais calma.
native_language_example: For me, life in the countryside is calmer.

meaning: 'life is…' (used to describe how life is).
additional_notes: Very common sentence starter: "A vida é" + adjective/noun phrase (e.g., dura, maluca, ótima, um sonho). You can also use it in questions or contrasts: "Quem disse que a vida é justa?". Often used for general statements about life, sometimes with a reflective or philosophical tone.
target_language_example: A vida é curta, então aproveite.
native_language_example: Life is short, so enjoy it.

additional_notes: Used to say that life contains many examples of something (often good/bad experiences). The structure is: "A vida é cheia de" + plural noun, or "cheia de" + singular mass/abstract noun (e.g., "surpresas", "mistérios", "problemas"). You can also change "a vida" to another subject: "O trabalho é cheio de..."
target_language_example: A vida é cheia de mudanças, mas a gente aprende com elas.
native_language_example: Life is full of changes, but we learn from them.

meaning: "life is a..." (used to describe life with a noun/metaphor).
additional_notes: Used to define or characterize life, often in a philosophical or poetic way: “A vida é um enigma / mistério / fardo…”. The article agrees with the noun that follows: use **um** with masculine nouns (um mistério, um enigma, um espelho, um fardo) and **uma** with feminine nouns (uma viagem, uma luta, uma aventura).
target_language_example: A vida é um aprendizado constante.
native_language_example: Life is constant learning.

meaning: “life is a …” (used to introduce a description or metaphor).
additional_notes: Usually followed by a noun phrase to characterize life (e.g., “a vida é uma aventura” = “life is an adventure”). It’s a common pattern in quotes, reflections, and emphatic statements. In Portuguese you typically include the article “uma” before a singular feminine noun (“uma aventura”, “uma alegria”, “uma glória”).
target_language_example: Às vezes, a vida é uma luta, mas a gente continua.
native_language_example: Sometimes life is a struggle, but we keep going.

additional_notes: "Água" means “water” (feminine). "A" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”). Used to talk about specific water in context (e.g., the water in a pool, shower, or glass). In questions, intonation changes but the words stay the same.
target_language_example: A água do chuveiro está quente.
native_language_example: The shower water is hot.

additional_notes: Definite noun phrase: **a** = “the” (feminine singular) + **árvore** = “tree”. Used when referring to a specific tree already known from context. Plural is **as árvores** (“the trees”).
target_language_example: A árvore está no jardim.
native_language_example: The tree is in the garden.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun: a última guerra (“the last war”), a última seção (“the last section”). It can also stand alone when the noun is understood: Essa é a última (coisa) de que preciso agora (“That’s the last thing I need right now”). In “Eu fui a última a saber”, it means “the last (person)” and agrees with the speaker’s gender: a última (female), o último (male).
target_language_example: Você foi a última a chegar?
native_language_example: Were you the last to arrive?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is the least desired, least needed, or least expected option. Common with verbs like "querer" (want), "precisar" (need), and "esperar" (expect): "A última coisa que eu quero/preciso/esperava…".
target_language_example: A última coisa que eu preciso agora é de mais problemas.
native_language_example: The last thing I need right now is more problems.

meaning: “the last person to” (someone who would be last to do something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone was literally the final one in order (e.g., the last to arrive) or, very often, to emphasize that someone is least likely to do something (“He’s the last person to reveal the secret” = he would never do that). It is followed by an infinitive verb: “a última pessoa a chegar / a revelar / a falar”. You may also see “a última pessoa a quem...” when a verb needs “a” before a person (“contar a alguém”).
target_language_example: Ela é a última pessoa a desistir quando as coisas ficam difíceis.
native_language_example: She’s the last person to give up when things get difficult.

a última pessoa que eu esperava ver

target_language_multi_word_term: a última pessoa que eu esperava ver
meaning: “the last person I expected to see.”
additional_notes: Used to express surprise at seeing someone, because you really didn’t expect them to be there. You can change the location at the end (aqui, lá, no trabalho) or the tense: “a última pessoa que eu esperava ver” (I expected to see) / “a última pessoa que eu esperaria ver” (I would expect to see). Often used with “Você/Ele/Ela era…” or “Você é…”.
target_language_example: Você é a última pessoa que eu esperava ver no aeroporto.
native_language_example: You’re the last person I expected to see at the airport.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the most recent occasion when something happened. It’s often followed by a verb (e.g., “a última vez que vi…” = “the last time I saw…”). Common with time expressions like “foi há…” (it was … ago) to say how long ago it happened.
target_language_example: A última vez que fui ao Brasil foi em 2019.
native_language_example: The last time I went to Brazil was in 2019.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (“a única coisa”, “a única saída”, “a única mulher”, “a única testemunha”). It can also stand alone when the noun is understood: “Ela foi a única” = “She was the only one.” Masculine form: “o único”. Plural: “os/as únicos/únicas”.
target_language_example: Ela é a única pessoa que sabe a verdade.
native_language_example: She is the only person who knows the truth.

additional_notes: Used to point out the single option/action/thing that is possible or remains. It’s often followed by a verb phrase (a única coisa que posso fazer…) or by a clause explaining what that “only thing” is (A única coisa que se pode fazer é…).
target_language_example: A única coisa que eu quero agora é descansar.
native_language_example: The only thing I want right now is to rest.

additional_notes: Used to say there is just one person who fits a description or is present. It’s feminine because "pessoa" is grammatically feminine in Portuguese, so you say "a única pessoa" even when talking about a man. Often followed by a relative clause like "de quem" (whom/that … likes) or "em quem" (in whom/that … trusts).
target_language_example: Ela foi a única pessoa que me ajudou.
native_language_example: She was the only person who helped me.

additional_notes: Used to single out one person as the only one fitting a description; often followed by a verb ("a única pessoa que eu conheço...") or by a relative clause. It can agree for gender/number: "o único homem que" (male), "as únicas pessoas que" (plural).
target_language_example: A única pessoa que me ajudou foi a Ana.
native_language_example: The only person who helped me was Ana.

additional_notes: Used to describe (often in stories, dreams, jokes, or sci‑fi contexts) someone being kidnapped/taken away by extraterrestrials. It’s a past participle phrase: abduzido (abducted) + por (by) + alienígenas (aliens). You can change gender/number: abduzida (female), abduzidos/abduzidas (plural).
target_language_example: Ele diz que foi abduzido por alienígenas quando era criança.
native_language_example: He says he was abducted by aliens when he was a kid.

meaning: “open the …” (formal command), used before a feminine noun.
additional_notes: "Abra" is the (polite/formal) command form of the verb "abrir" (“to open”), often used with "você" implied. "A" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”), so it must be followed by a feminine noun: "abra a garrafa" (“open the bottle”), "abra a porta" (“open the door”). It can also be used figuratively: "abra a sua mente" (“open your mind”). For masculine nouns, you’ll usually see "abra o" (e.g., "abra o livro").
target_language_example: Por favor, abra a porta.
native_language_example: Please, open the door.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "abrir" (to open) using "você" (third-person) commands: "Abra". Common with kids, at the doctor/dentist, or when feeding someone. Often said with "por favor" to soften it: "Abra a boca, por favor."
target_language_example: O dentista disse: "Abra a boca, por favor."
native_language_example: The dentist said, "Open your mouth, please."

additional_notes: Polite command/request using the formal imperative of abrir (to open): (o senhor / a senhora / você) abra. Often softened with “por favor”. In questions like “Você se importa que eu abra a janela?”, it means “Do you mind if I open the window?” (subjunctive after se importar que).
target_language_example: Está muito quente aqui—abra a janela, por favor.
native_language_example: It’s very hot in here—open the window, please.

additional_notes: Uses the imperative of the verb abrir (“to open”) in the você form. It’s a common way to ask someone to open a door, often with por favor (“please”). In casual speech you may also hear abre a porta (more informal/less polite) and pra mim instead of para mim (“for me”).
target_language_example: Por favor, abra a porta que está trancada.
native_language_example: Please open the door that’s locked.

meaning: “open it” (referring to a feminine noun, e.g. a door/window).
additional_notes: Formed by the verb "abrir" (to open) + the object pronoun "a" (“it/her”), written with a hyphen as an enclitic pronoun. Use it when the thing you’re opening is grammatically feminine (e.g. "a porta", "a janela"). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many speakers also say "abrir ela" in casual speech, but "abri-la" is the standard written form.
target_language_example: Você pode abri-la, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you open it, please?

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "abrir" in the 1st person singular: "eu abri" = "I opened". Used for a completed action in the past. You can add details like how/with what ("com minha chave" = "with my key"), which door ("a porta da garagem" = "the garage door"), or for whom ("para Tom" = "for Tom"). In writing, it’s commonly spelled with an accent: "abri" (not *"abrí" in Brazilian Portuguese; "abri" has no accent).
target_language_example: Ouvi alguém bater e abri a porta devagar.
native_language_example: I heard someone knock and I opened the door slowly.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns because of the article "a" (= "the"). Common with objects you can open: "abrir a encomenda" (open the package), "abrir a cortina" (open the curtain), "abrir a gaveta" (open the drawer). If the noun is masculine, use "abrir o" (e.g., "abrir o pacote").
target_language_example: Você pode abrir a janela, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you open the window, please?

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase: "abrir" = "to open" and "a caixa" = "the box". Used for physically opening a box, often with tools (e.g., "com um pé de cabra" = "with a crowbar") or a key ("Você precisa de uma chave..."). You can use it in questions ("Posso abrir a caixa?") and with verbs like "conseguir" (manage to), "tentar" (try), and "forçar" (force someone to).
target_language_example: Não consigo abrir a caixa; você pode me ajudar?
native_language_example: I can't open the box; can you help me?

additional_notes: Used for physically opening a window. Very common in polite requests: "Você se importa se eu abrir a janela?" / "Você se incomoda se eu abrir a janela?" = "Do you mind if I open the window?". With "estar a" + infinitive it means an action in progress (European Portuguese): "Ela está a abrir a janela" = "She is opening the window."
target_language_example: Está calor aqui; você se importa se eu abrir a janela?
native_language_example: It’s hot in here; do you mind if I open the window?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to open a door, or to describe being able/trying to open it. Common in polite requests with the conditional: “Poderia, por gentileza, abrir a porta?” (Could you please open the door?).
target_language_example: Você pode abrir a porta para mim?
native_language_example: Can you open the door for me?

additional_notes: Used when asking for permission, offering, or deciding whether to open windows (often for air/ventilation). Common with polite questions like “Posso…?” (May/Can I…?) and “Podemos…?” (Can we…?).
target_language_example: Está calor aqui; posso abrir as janelas?
native_language_example: It’s hot in here; can I open the windows?

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun introduced by the definite article "a" (e.g., a bolsa, a gaveta, a geladeira, a porta, a tampa, a torneira, a carta). It’s the 3rd person singular simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "abrir": "ele/ela/você abriu" = "he/she/you opened". If the object is masculine, you’ll usually see "abriu o" (e.g., abriu o livro).
target_language_example: Ela abriu a janela para entrar ar fresco.
native_language_example: She opened the window to let fresh air in.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "abrir" (to open): "(ele/ela/você) abriu". Used for opening a physical box/container (e.g., a matchbox: "caixa de fósforo"). You can swap the article/noun depending on what was opened: "abriu a porta" (opened the door), "abriu a mala" (opened the suitcase).
target_language_example: Ela abriu a caixa e viu uma carta dentro.
native_language_example: She opened the box and saw a letter inside.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "abrir" for he/she/you (formal) + "a janela" (the window). Used to say someone opened the window, often with "para" + infinitive to explain the purpose (e.g., to let air in / get fresh air).
target_language_example: Ela abriu a janela para ventilar o quarto.
native_language_example: She opened the window to air out the room.

additional_notes: "Abriu" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "abrir" (to open). Used to describe a completed action in the past. Often followed by details about how/why the door was opened (e.g., "com um chute" = with a kick; "lentamente" = slowly; "para" + infinitive = in order to).
target_language_example: Quando cheguei, ele já abriu a porta.
native_language_example: When I arrived, he had already opened the door.

meaning: '(he/she/it) opened the door of the …' / '(someone) opened the … door'.
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "abrir" in the 3rd person singular: "abriu" = "opened". Used with "a porta" (the door) + "do" (= "de" + "o", meaning "of the") to specify what the door belongs to: "a porta do meu quarto" (my room’s door), "a porta do apartamento" (the apartment door), "a porta do forno" (the oven door).
target_language_example: Ela abriu a porta do carro devagar.
native_language_example: She opened the car door slowly.

additional_notes: Common past-tense narrative connector: "abrir" in the simple past (pretérito perfeito) + "a porta" + "e" to link to the next action. Subject is often understood from context (ele/ela). In Portuguese you can also say "abriu a porta e saiu" (“opened the door and left”).
target_language_example: Ele abriu a porta e foi embora.
native_language_example: He opened the door and went away.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "abrir" for "ele/ela/você": "abriu" = "(he/she/you) opened". "Porta-malas" means a car’s trunk/boot. Often used with "do carro" ("of the car") or with a person as subject: "Ele abriu o porta-malas."
target_language_example: Ela abriu o porta-malas para pegar as malas.
native_language_example: She opened the trunk to get the suitcases.

meaning: to put an end to; to destroy/finish off (sometimes: to kill).
additional_notes: Used with a direct object: acabar com + noun/pronoun. It can be practical/neutral (“end this problem”) or very strong (“destroy/kill”), especially in threats like “Vou acabar com você/ele” (“I’ll finish you/him off”). Often translates as “end,” “get rid of,” “ruin,” or “wipe out,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Precisamos acabar com esse barulho agora.
native_language_example: We need to put an end to this noise now.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say you did something moments ago: “acabei de + infinitive” (e.g., acabei de chegar = I just arrived). It conjugates for the person: acabei (I), acabou (he/she/you), acabamos (we), acabaram (they/you all). Often equivalent to “just” or “have just” in English, not “I finished (doing)” in the sense of completing a task (though it comes from acabar).
target_language_example: Acabei de sair de casa.
native_language_example: I just left home.

additional_notes: Used to say you discovered some information very recently. It’s built from **acabar de** (to have just done something) + **descobrir** (to discover/find out) + **que** (that). You can change the verb to match the speaker: *acabei* (I), *acabou* (you/he/she), *acabamos* (we). Often followed by a full clause: *...que ela já morou na Austrália*.
target_language_example: Acabei de descobrir que a reunião foi cancelada.
native_language_example: I just found out that the meeting was canceled.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to say you did something moments ago: "Acabo de + infinitive". It’s the present tense of "acabar" used this way; you can also change the subject: "Eu acabo de...", "Ela acaba de...", "Nós acabamos de...".
target_language_example: Acabo de chegar em casa.
native_language_example: I just got home.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say something happened very recently: “acabar de” + verb (e.g., “acabou de acordar” = “just woke up”). It conjugates to match the subject and tense (e.g., “acabei de…”, “acabaram de…”, “tinha acabado de…”).
target_language_example: Eu acabei de chegar em casa.
native_language_example: I just got home.

meaning: (He/She/It) just left; has just gone out.
additional_notes: Uses the structure **acabar de + infinitive** to say something happened very recently. Change the subject as needed: **Eu acabei de sair** (I just left), **Ela acabou de sair** (She just left).
target_language_example: Desculpa, ele acabou de sair do escritório.
native_language_example: Sorry, he just left the office.

additional_notes: Imperative form of the verb "acalmar" (to calm), with the reflexive pronoun "-se". Used to tell one person (você) to relax or stop getting upset; it can sound firm depending on tone. Often appears with intensifiers like "agora" (now) or "por um segundo" (for a second).
target_language_example: Ei, acalme-se — vai dar tudo certo.
native_language_example: Hey, calm down — everything will be fine.

meaning: to light the fire; to start a fire.
additional_notes: Used for starting a fire in a fireplace, wood stove, grill, or campfire. In questions it often appears with polite forms like “Você quer...?” (singular) or “Os senhores querem...?” (very formal/plural). The verb “acender” is also used with lights (e.g., “acender a luz” = to turn on/light the light).
target_language_example: Está frio — vou acender o fogo na lareira.
native_language_example: It’s cold—I’m going to light the fire in the fireplace.

meaning: “do you really think that…?” (expresses doubt or emphasis).
additional_notes: Used to question or challenge someone’s belief/assumption. It’s formal/polite because it uses “acha” (você/he/she thinks). Common in questions, often with a skeptical tone. More informal equivalents: “você acha mesmo que…?” or “acha que…?” (less emphatic).
target_language_example: Acha mesmo que isso vai funcionar?
native_language_example: Do you really think this is going to work?

additional_notes: From the verb "achar" (to think/to find). "Acha que…" is present tense, 3rd person singular: it can mean "he/she thinks that…" or, in Brazil, "you think that…" when speaking to someone using "você" (often with the subject omitted). Very common for stating an opinion or asking what someone thinks.
target_language_example: Acha que vai chover hoje?
native_language_example: Do you think it’s going to rain today?

meaning: "(he/she/you) thinks that the..." (introduces an opinion or belief about something feminine).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "achar" (to think/to believe) + "que" (that) + "a" (the, feminine singular). It commonly starts a clause: "Acha que a porta está trancada" = "(Do you) think the door is locked?" In questions, "Acha que...?" is often equivalent to English "Do you think...?"; in statements it means "He/She thinks that...".
target_language_example: Você acha que a reunião vai demorar?
native_language_example: Do you think the meeting will take long?

meaning: "(you/he/she) thinks that this..." / "do you think this...?"
additional_notes: From the verb **achar** (“to think / believe / guess / figure”). **Acha que isso...** is commonly used to introduce an opinion or belief about something: **(Você/Ele/Ela) acha que isso + verb...**. The subject is often omitted in questions: **Acha que isso... ?** = “Do you think this... ?” (more explicitly: **Você acha que isso...?**).
target_language_example: Você acha que isso vai dar certo?
native_language_example: Do you think this will work?

additional_notes: From the verb "achar" (to think / to find) + "que" (that) + "o" (the, masculine singular). "Acha" is the present tense for "você" (you, formal in Brazil) or "ele/ela" (he/she). It’s commonly used to introduce an opinion or expectation: "Você acha que o..." = "Do you think the...". Use "acha que a" with feminine nouns ("a" = "the" feminine).
target_language_example: Você acha que o ônibus vai demorar?
native_language_example: Do you think the bus will take long?

additional_notes: Uses the verb achar (“to think/to believe”) + que (“that”) + pode (from poder, “can/to be able to”). It can state someone’s belief about ability or possibility (Ela acha que pode cantar.), or be used in questions about who is able to do something (Quem você acha que pode consertar isto?). In a challenging tone, it can mean “you think you can get away with it?” (Você acha que pode se safar dessa?).
target_language_example: Você acha que pode me ajudar hoje?
native_language_example: Do you think you can help me today?

additional_notes: From the verb *achar* (“to think / to suppose”) + *que* (“that”) + *é* (“is”). Often used with an implied subject: **Você acha que é…?** (“Do you think it’s…?”) in questions, or **Ele/Ela acha que é…** (“He/She thinks he/she is…”) in statements. In context it can sound challenging or skeptical, like “Do you really think it’s…?” or “He thinks he’s someone important.”
target_language_example: Você acha que é fácil aprender português?
native_language_example: Do you think it’s easy to learn Portuguese?

meaning: 'they think/believe that' (also used for 'you all think that' with vocês).
additional_notes: From the verb achar (to think/feel/assume) in the 3rd-person plural (eles/elas/"you all"). It introduces an idea/opinion: acham que + clause. In questions it often shows surprise or criticism: O que acham que estão fazendo? = 'What do you think you’re doing?'
target_language_example: Eles acham que vai chover amanhã.
native_language_example: They think it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: From the verb "achar" (to think / to find). "Achava" is the imperfect past, often used for an ongoing belief in the past or a thought you had at the time (not necessarily true). Usually followed by "que" + a full clause: "Achava que ele vinha" = "I thought he was coming."
target_language_example: Eu achava que você já tinha ido embora.
native_language_example: I thought you had already left.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what someone believed in the past: "[alguém] achava que a…" = "[someone] thought that the…". "Achava" is the imperfect past of "achar" and often implies an ongoing belief or an assumption that turned out to be wrong. In this pattern, "que" = "that" and "a" is the feminine singular article "the" (so it’s usually followed by a feminine noun/name, e.g., "a Mary", "a empresa").
target_language_example: Eu achava que a reunião era hoje, mas é amanhã.
native_language_example: I thought the meeting was today, but it’s tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Achava" is the imperfect past of "achar" (to think/to find). It’s used for something you believed/assumed at the time, often later shown to be wrong or just uncertain. "que" means "that" and introduces the clause. "o" is the masculine singular article ("the") before a noun/name used like a noun (e.g., "o Tom" = "Tom"). In many sentences you’ll also see "achava que" without "o" when the next word isn’t masculine singular (e.g., "achava que era verdade" = "I thought it was true").
target_language_example: Eu achava que o ônibus chegava às oito, mas eu estava errado.
native_language_example: I thought the bus arrived at eight, but I was wrong.

additional_notes: "Achei" is the past tense of "achar" (to find). This phrase is typically followed by a relative clause with "que" (= that/which) to describe the photo, e.g., "achei a foto que você estava procurando" (I found the photo you were looking for). You can change the object: "achei o documento que…" (I found the document that…). In speech and writing, "eu" is often optional: "(Eu) achei…".
target_language_example: Achei a foto que você me mandou ontem.
native_language_example: I found the photo that you sent me yesterday.

meaning: "I thought (that)..." (often: "I assumed..." or "I was under the impression...").
additional_notes: Past of "achar" used to introduce what you believed or assumed (often later corrected). Very common before a clause in the imperfect past ("achei que ele estava...") or the imperfect subjunctive ("achei que fosse/estivesse...") especially when the thought turns out to be uncertain or wrong. Can also mean "I found that.../I realized that..." in context, but usually it’s about your belief at the time.
target_language_example: Achei que a reunião era hoje, mas é amanhã.
native_language_example: I thought the meeting was today, but it’s tomorrow.

meaning: "I thought that the..." (talking about a male person/thing).
additional_notes: Used to introduce something you believed or assumed in the past, often something that turned out to be wrong. It’s commonly followed by a name or noun (e.g., "Achei que o Tom..."). After "achei que", Portuguese often uses the imperfect subjunctive ("fosse", "tivesse", "gostasse") or "ia/iria" to express what you thought would happen.
target_language_example: Achei que o ônibus ia chegar mais cedo.
native_language_example: I thought the bus would arrive earlier.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a belief/assumption you had (often later corrected or softened). It’s the past of achar (“to think/assume”). Very commonly followed by the subjunctive in Portuguese when expressing uncertainty or a subjective assumption: achei que você estivesse / precisaria / pudesse / tivesse…
target_language_example: Achei que você já tinha chegado em casa.
native_language_example: I thought you had already gotten home.

additional_notes: Used to give an opinion or a guess, often with some uncertainty (softer than saying you're sure). It’s very common in everyday speech. You can also hear it without "que": "Acho que ele vem" / "Acho que sim".
target_language_example: Acho que vai chover amanhã.
native_language_example: I think it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an opinion or guess. It’s simply "acho que" (“I think that”) followed by the article "a" (“the”) before a feminine singular noun (e.g., a França, a Mary, a minha perna, a opinião). You can also use it before a feminine person’s name.
target_language_example: Acho que a professora vai chegar mais tarde.
native_language_example: I think the (female) teacher will arrive later.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion or suggestion about what the group ("we") should do. "Acho que" = "I think" and "devemos" (from "dever") expresses obligation/suggestion like "we should / we ought to". Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., "tentar", "usar", "tomar"). You may also hear "Eu acho que devemos..." with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Acho que devemos sair mais cedo para evitar o trânsito.
native_language_example: I think we should leave earlier to avoid traffic.

meaning: “I think we should…” / “I think we ought to…”
additional_notes: Used to suggest an action in a polite, not-too-direct way. It combines: acho que (“I think that…”) + deveríamos (conditional of dever, “we should/ought to”). Often followed by an infinitive verb (buscar, contar, conversar, ir, voltar).
target_language_example: Acho que deveríamos sair mais cedo para evitar o trânsito.
native_language_example: I think we should leave earlier to avoid traffic.
