additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion, guess, or uncertainty about what a woman/girl (ela) does, knows, is, or will do. "Acho" comes from "achar" and is very common in everyday speech; you can omit "que" in casual conversation ("Acho ela simpática"), but with a full clause you normally use "acho que...". Often translates as “I think” or the softer “I guess / I believe.”
target_language_example: Acho que ela vai chegar mais tarde.
native_language_example: I think she’s going to arrive later.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or an uncertain statement about a man/boy (ele = he). Very common in conversation. Often followed by a verb: "Acho que ele vem..." (I think he’s coming...). In questions, you can also use it to soften what you’re saying: "Acho que ele não entendeu?" (Do you think he didn’t understand?).
target_language_example: Acho que ele já saiu, mas não tenho certeza.
native_language_example: I think he’s already left, but I’m not sure.

additional_notes: Used to express a suspicion or opinion. You can add what you think he’s hiding: “algo/alguma coisa” = “something”, and who it’s hidden from with “de nós” (from us) or the more informal “da gente” (from us). Often appears as “Eu acho que…” or simply “Acho que…”.
target_language_example: Acho que ele está escondendo a verdade de nós.
native_language_example: I think he’s hiding the truth from us.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or a guess about what “they” (eles) did/are doing. It often sounds less certain than a direct statement. "Eles" is used for a group of men or a mixed group (men + women). You can also drop "que" in casual speech ("Acho eles legais"), but "acho que eles…" is the most common for full clauses.
target_language_example: Acho que eles vão chegar mais tarde.
native_language_example: I think they'll arrive later.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion, guess, or uncertainty about yourself ("eu" = "I"). Very common in everyday speech; often followed by a verb in the past, present, or conditional (e.g., "acho que eu estava...", "acho que eu posso...", "acho que eu poderia..."). In Portuguese you can often drop "eu" and just say "acho que...".
target_language_example: Acho que eu vou chegar um pouco atrasado.
native_language_example: I think I'll arrive a little late.

meaning: “I think I should…” / “I guess I should…”
additional_notes: Used to give your opinion or a tentative decision about what you think is the right thing to do. Very common in everyday speech. You can change the verb after it: “Acho que eu deveria + infinitive” (descansar, falar, partir, visitar, etc.). Often shortened in conversation to “Acho que eu devia…” or just “Acho que devia…”.
target_language_example: Acho que eu deveria pedir desculpas.
native_language_example: I think I should apologize.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or guess: acho que + a clause. “Isso” refers to “that/this” idea or situation (often something just mentioned). In full sentences you’ll often continue with a verb: “Acho que isso é…” / “Acho que isso vai…”
target_language_example: Acho que isso vai ajudar bastante.
native_language_example: I think that will help a lot.

additional_notes: Used to express a negative opinion or prediction in a softer, less certain way than a direct “não.” Common both in full sentences (followed by a clause) and as a short reply on its own. Often implies uncertainty (“I don’t think…” rather than “I’m sure not”).
target_language_example: —Você vai amanhã? —Acho que não.
native_language_example: —Are you going tomorrow? —I don't think so.

meaning: I think we should… / I think we ought to…
additional_notes: Used to politely suggest or propose an action as your opinion. Common structure: "Acho que (nós) deveríamos + infinitive" (e.g., ajudar, contar, falar, ficar). In everyday speech, "nós" is often omitted: "Acho que deveríamos…". The verb "deveríamos" is the conditional of "dever" and sounds softer/more tentative than "devemos" (we must/should).
target_language_example: Acho que nós deveríamos sair mais cedo para evitar trânsito.
native_language_example: I think we should leave earlier to avoid traffic.

additional_notes: "Acho que" is a common way to give an opinion or guess. It’s followed by a clause; "o" is the masculine singular definite article ("the") and is used when the next noun/name is treated as masculine (e.g., o Tom, o caminhão). Often you’ll see it as "Acho que o/ a/ os/ as..." depending on gender/number.
target_language_example: Acho que o ônibus já saiu.
native_language_example: I think the bus already left.

meaning: "I think I can" / "I guess I can".
additional_notes: Used to express a tentative ability or possibility: you believe you’re able to do something, but you’re not 100% sure. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., ajudar, entender, fazer). You can also say "Eu acho que posso..." (same meaning; "eu" is optional).
target_language_example: Acho que posso ir amanhã.
native_language_example: I think I can go tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to give an opinion or suggestion politely. Often the subject “eu” is omitted: “Acho que…” = “I think…”. After “precisamos”, you typically use an infinitive (“precisamos fazer/descobrir/estabelecer…”) or “de” + noun (“precisamos de ajuda” = “we need help”).
target_language_example: Acho que precisamos falar com o médico hoje.
native_language_example: I think we need to talk to the doctor today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion, assumption, or guess about the other person. Often followed by a verb (e.g., “acho que você sabe…”, “acho que você gostou…”). It can sound softer than a direct statement (“você sabe…”), but with insults or strong judgments it can still be harsh.
target_language_example: Acho que você está cansado(a).
native_language_example: I think you’re tired.

meaning: “I think you should …” / “I think you ought to …” (a suggestion/advice).
additional_notes: Used to politely give your opinion or advice. It’s built from: acho que (“I think that”) + você deveria (“you should/you ought to”, conditional of dever). Often followed by an infinitive verb: esperar, ir, perdoar, etc.
target_language_example: Acho que você deveria descansar um pouco.
native_language_example: I think you should rest a bit.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion about someone’s state or situation. It often introduces an adjective or phrase: acho que você está certa (right), enganado (mistaken), ótima (great), tendo um ataque de nervos (having a nervous breakdown). In speech, it’s commonly shortened to “acho que cê tá…/você tá…”.
target_language_example: Acho que você está com febre.
native_language_example: I think you have a fever.

additional_notes: Used to give an opinion/advice. Very often followed by an infinitive verb: “Acho que você precisa + [infinitive]” (e.g., dormir, falar, ir). You can also use it with “de” + noun: “Acho que você precisa de ajuda” (“I think you need help”).
target_language_example: Acho que você precisa falar com o médico.
native_language_example: I think you need to talk to the doctor.

additional_notes: Used to express an opinion/guess about what someone possesses, is experiencing, or is like. Very common in conversation. Verb forms: "acho" = "I think" (from achar), "você tem" = "you have" (from ter). Often followed by a noun ("um problema"), age ("vinte anos"), or an abstract idea ("condições").
target_language_example: Acho que você tem razão.
native_language_example: I think you’re right.

additional_notes: Used to express your opinion or a guess. Very common in conversation. Often followed by a noun (“acho que é um problema”), an adjective (“acho que é difícil”), or a clause (“acho que é melhor esperar”). In negative form: “não acho que é…” = “I don’t think it’s…”.
target_language_example: Acho que é melhor a gente ir agora.
native_language_example: I think it’s better for us to go now.

additional_notes: “Achou” is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of “achar”. With “que”, it introduces an opinion or belief about a situation: “Ele achou que…” = “He thought that…”. Depending on context, “achar” can also mean “to find” (e.g., “achei minhas chaves” = “I found my keys”), but in these examples it means “to think/consider”.
target_language_example: Eu achei que você já tinha saído.
native_language_example: I thought you had already left.

meaning: "(you/he/she) thought that I..." / "did you think I...?"
additional_notes: Uses the past tense of **achar** (“to think / to suppose”) + **que eu** (“that I”). Common in reported speech (**Ele achou que eu...** = “He thought I...”) and in questions (**Achou que eu... ?** = “Did you think I...?”). Often followed by another verb in the past (e.g., **ia**, **tinha**, **fosse**) depending on the situation.
target_language_example: Você achou que eu ia desistir?
native_language_example: Did you think I was going to give up?

meaning: “(a/an) … accident” (used to say what kind of accident it was).
additional_notes: Use "acidente de + noun" to specify the type of accident: "acidente de trabalho" (work accident), "acidente de avião" (plane accident/plane crash), "acidente de trem" (train accident). It often appears with "no/num" (= in a) and with verbs like "morrer" (to die) or "se machucar" (to get hurt).
target_language_example: Ela ficou ferida num acidente de carro.
native_language_example: She was injured in a car accident.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a collision involving a car. Very common in news and everyday conversation. You can add adjectives like grave (serious) or phrases like se envolver em (to be involved in) or sofrer um (to have/suffer one).
target_language_example: Ela teve um acidente de carro ontem à noite, mas está bem.
native_language_example: She had a car accident last night, but she’s okay.

meaning: traffic accident; road accident (a car crash/collision).
additional_notes: Used to talk about accidents that happen on the road/in traffic (cars, motorcycles, buses, etc.). Often appears with verbs like "houve" (there was), "aconteceu" (happened), "sofrer" (to have/suffer), and with results like "ficar ferido" (be injured) or "se machucar" (get hurt).
target_language_example: Chamei a ambulância porque houve um acidente de trânsito na esquina.
native_language_example: I called an ambulance because there was a traffic accident on the corner.

meaning: to accompany him; to walk/come with him (to escort him).
additional_notes: "Acompanhá-lo" = "acompanhar" (to accompany/escort) + "-lo" (him). It’s used when you go with someone to a place (e.g., to the elevator, to their house), often as a polite offer. In speech, Brazilians often say "acompanhar ele" instead, but "acompanhá-lo" is more standard/formal. You can also use it more generally as "to follow him" (e.g., follow someone’s work), but in these examples it means physically going with him.
target_language_example: Posso acompanhá-lo até a saída?
native_language_example: Can I walk you to the exit?

additional_notes: Used when someone gives advice against doing an action. Pattern: “(alguém) aconselhou (alguém) a não + infinitive”. In the examples, “aconselhou” is past tense (he/she advised); in other contexts you may see “aconselha” (advises) or “aconselhar” (to advise).
target_language_example: A médica me aconselhou a não beber álcool durante o tratamento.
native_language_example: The doctor advised me not to drink alcohol during the treatment.

meaning: “it happens from time to time” / “it happens occasionally.”
additional_notes: Used to say something happens sometimes, but not regularly or often. You can add a subject before it (Isso acontece de vez em quando = That happens from time to time). Very common in casual conversation; you can also use it with other verbs (Vou lá de vez em quando = I go there occasionally).
target_language_example: Eu ainda tenho dores de cabeça de vez em quando.
native_language_example: I still get headaches from time to time.

additional_notes: Used to ask if there’s a problem or something wrong with a person or thing (often implying concern). It’s the past tense of acontecer (“to happen”). Change the article to match the noun: com o (masc. sing.), com a (fem. sing.), com os / com as (plural). You can also use it as a statement: “Aconteceu alguma coisa com o meu carro.” = “Something happened to my car.”
target_language_example: Aconteceu alguma coisa com o seu telefone?
native_language_example: Did something happen to your phone?

additional_notes: Used with a person or thing to say that some event affected them: "aconteceu com você" = "happened to you." Often appears in questions like "O que aconteceu com...?" (What happened to ...?). The verb is "acontecer"; "aconteceu" is the past tense (he/she/it happened).
target_language_example: O que aconteceu com o seu telefone?
native_language_example: What happened to your phone?

additional_notes: Used to refer to an event that occurred during the previous night. "Aconteceu" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "acontecer" (to happen). "Ontem à noite" is a common time expression meaning "last night"; it’s very often used with verbs in the past to set the time of the event.
target_language_example: Não consigo parar de pensar no que aconteceu ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I can’t stop thinking about what happened last night.

additional_notes: Used to say someone wakes up early. "acorda" is the present tense (he/she/you formal) of "acordar" (to wake up), and "cedo" means "early." You can swap the subject: "Eu acordo cedo" (I wake up early), "Nós acordamos cedo" (We wake up early).
target_language_example: Eu acordo cedo para ir ao trabalho.
native_language_example: I wake up early to go to work.

additional_notes: Used to say you didn’t sleep during the night. Common with the verb "ficar" ("ficar acordado a noite toda" = "to stay awake all night"). You can change gender/number: "acordado" (male), "acordada" (female), "acordados/acordadas" (plural). Often written with the accent: "a noite toda".
target_language_example: A gente ficou acordado a noite toda estudando para a prova.
native_language_example: We stayed awake all night studying for the test.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ficar" ("ficar acordado até tarde") to mean you stayed awake/you were up late. "Acordado" agrees with the person: "acordado" (male), "acordada" (female); plural: "acordados/acordadas".
target_language_example: A gente ficou acordado até tarde conversando.
native_language_example: We stayed up late talking.

additional_notes: Used with "ter de" or "precisar" to say you have to wake up early: "tenho de/preciso acordar cedo". You can add time words like "amanhã" (tomorrow), "todo dia" (every day), or "amanhã de manhã" (tomorrow morning).
target_language_example: No fim de semana, não quero acordar cedo.
native_language_example: On the weekend, I don’t want to wake up early.

meaning: "used to" (accustomed to; in the habit of).
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb estar/ser + acostumado(a)(s) + a + infinitive: "Estou acostumado a trabalhar" = "I’m used to working." Agreement: acostumado (masc.), acostumada (fem.), acostumados/acostumadas (plural). With "não", it means you’re not used to something: "Não sou acostumado a beber" = "I’m not used to drinking."
target_language_example: Ela está acostumada a acordar cedo.
native_language_example: She’s used to waking up early.

additional_notes: Impersonal/passive-style expression used to report a generally held belief or accepted idea without saying who believes it. Common in news, formal writing, and academic contexts. Often followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., "seja", "tenha sido") because the information is presented as uncertain or reported, not a confirmed fact.
target_language_example: Acredita-se que a vacina seja segura.
native_language_example: It is believed that the vaccine is safe.

meaning: "believes in" (has faith in; accepts as true).
additional_notes: Used with the verb acreditar + em + noun/pronoun/idea. With a religion or concept (Deus, mágica), it often means “believe in” in the sense of faith. With statements or what someone says (em tudo que digo), it means “believe” as in “accept as true.”
target_language_example: Ela acredita em você, mesmo quando você duvida de si mesmo.
native_language_example: She believes in you, even when you doubt yourself.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "acreditar em" (to believe in) + "fantasmas" (ghosts). As written, "acredita" is the present tense for "você/ele/ela". It can be a question ("Acredita em fantasmas?") or a statement ("Você acredita em fantasmas.").
target_language_example: Você acredita em fantasmas ou acha que é só imaginação?
native_language_example: Do you believe in ghosts, or do you think it’s just imagination?

additional_notes: From the verb "acreditar" (to believe) + "em" (in) + "mim" (me). It can mean trusting what I’m saying ("believe me") or having confidence in me ("believe in me"), depending on context. Commonly used as "Acredita em mim!" (Believe me!) or "Você acredita em mim?" (Do you believe me / in me?).
target_language_example: Acredita em mim: eu vi tudo com meus próprios olhos.
native_language_example: Believe me: I saw everything with my own eyes.

additional_notes: Used with a noun/pronoun: acreditar em alguém/alguma coisa = believe in someone/something (have faith in them) or believe someone/something is telling the truth. For a full clause, Portuguese often uses "acreditar que" (e.g., "Acredito que é verdade" = I believe it’s true).
target_language_example: Eu acredito em você, mas preciso de provas.
native_language_example: I believe you, but I need proof.

meaning: to believe me; to trust in me.
additional_notes: Used to ask for or thank someone for trust/confidence in you. With people, Portuguese commonly uses "acreditar em" (literally “believe in”) to mean “trust” or “have faith in,” while "acreditar" without "em" can mean “believe (that something is true).” Often appears in requests like "Por favor, acredita em mim."
target_language_example: Por favor, acredita em mim — eu não faria isso.
native_language_example: Please believe me — I wouldn't do that.

meaning: to believe that / to believe in that.
additional_notes: Used to say you believe a specific statement, idea, or piece of information (often something surprising or hard to accept). 'Nisso' = 'in that'/'that' and refers back to what was just mentioned. Very common with expressions like 'É difícil acreditar nisso' (It's hard to believe that) and 'Eu mal posso acreditar nisso' (I can hardly believe it).
target_language_example: Você acredita nisso mesmo?
native_language_example: Do you really believe that?

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or belief about a statement. Very often followed by the subjunctive in Portuguese (especially in more formal speech/writing): “Acredito que ele seja…”. In everyday conversation you may also hear the indicative: “Acredito que ele é…”. With “não acredito que…”, it can mean either “I don’t believe that…” (disbelief) or “I can’t believe that…” (surprise), depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Acredito que ele esteja certo.
native_language_example: I believe (that) he’s right.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause after an admission. "admitiram" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "admitir" for "they" or "you all" (vocês). "que" means “that”, and "estavam" is the imperfect past of "estar" (“were/was being”), often followed by an adjective (errados, exaustos, etc.).
target_language_example: Eles admitiram que estavam com medo.
native_language_example: They admitted that they were afraid.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "admitir" + "que" introduces a statement someone confesses or acknowledges as true. Often followed by a full clause with a verb (e.g., "admitiu que estava...").
target_language_example: Ela admitiu que não sabia a resposta.
native_language_example: She admitted that she didn’t know the answer.

additional_notes: Used to report that someone acknowledged or confessed something about their state, feeling, or situation in the past. "admitiu" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "admitir" (to admit), and "que estava" introduces what they admitted using "estar" (to be) in the imperfect (ongoing/temporary state). Often followed by an adjective or phrase: "errada" (wrong), "assustado" (scared), "com medo" (afraid).
target_language_example: Ele admitiu que estava cansado, mas continuou trabalhando.
native_language_example: He admitted that he was tired, but he kept working.

additional_notes: Imperative form of **afastar-se** (“to move away”). Used to tell one person (você) to back away from someone or something: **Afaste-se de mim** (away from me), **Afaste-se dele/dela** (away from him/her), **Afaste-se da janela/porta** (away from the window/door). Add **por favor** to sound more polite.
target_language_example: Afaste-se um pouco, por favor.
native_language_example: Step back a little, please.

meaning: "Anyway/After all, how can I…?" (used to offer help or ask what to do).
additional_notes: "Afinal de contas" adds emphasis like "anyway" or "after all" (often when returning to the main point). It’s commonly followed by a verb phrase: "como posso ajudar…?". The rest changes with the object pronoun: "ajudá-la" (help you/her—formal feminine), "ajudá-lo" (formal masculine), "ajudá-los" (them/you all—formal), or "te ajudar" (help you—informal).
target_language_example: Afinal de contas, como posso resolver isso hoje?
native_language_example: Anyway, how can I solve this today?

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s behavior as if a situation were true (often implying it isn’t, or that the person is pretending). “Agiu” is the past tense (he/she acted) of *agir*. After *como se*, Portuguese typically uses the subjunctive: *como se não soubesse*, *como se estivesse...*
target_language_example: Ela agiu como se não me conhecesse.
native_language_example: She acted as if she didn’t know me.

meaning: to thank you (formal) / to thank him or her.
additional_notes: "Agradecer" means "to thank". The "-lhe" is an object pronoun meaning "to him/her" and is also used as the formal "to you" (to a person you address as "o senhor/a senhora"). It’s common in polite questions and statements like "Como posso agradecer-lhe?" and can be followed by "por" + noun/phrase (e.g., "agradecer-lhe por esta noite").
target_language_example: Queria agradecer-lhe pela sua ajuda.
native_language_example: I’d like to thank you for your help.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a physical post office location/branch where you can mail letters and packages and use postal services. Often appears with location verbs like "fica" (is located) and with "perto" (near): "Há uma agência dos correios aqui perto?"
target_language_example: Preciso ir à agência dos correios para enviar uma encomenda.
native_language_example: I need to go to the post office to send a package.

additional_notes: Used to express relief or gratitude about a situation or outcome. It’s typically followed by a clause in the past or present (e.g., "ainda bem que deu certo" = glad it worked out). Often implies that things could have gone badly, but didn’t. Also common as an exclamation: "Ainda bem que voltou!"
target_language_example: Ainda bem que você me avisou a tempo.
native_language_example: Good thing you warned me in time.

meaning: “Good thing it was…” / “I’m glad it was…”
additional_notes: Used to express relief or satisfaction about how something turned out in the past. It’s often followed by a time (“à noite”, “hoje”, “ontem”, “mais cedo”) or by who/what it was with (“com ele/eles”). In everyday speech you may also hear: “Ainda bem que…” without “foi”.
target_language_example: Ainda bem que foi cedo, porque depois ficou muito cheio.
native_language_example: Good thing it was early, because later it got really crowded.

meaning: “is still …” (continues to be; hasn’t changed yet).
additional_notes: Used with the verb **estar** to say a situation/state is ongoing or unchanged: **ainda está + adjective / location / gerund**. Common patterns: **ainda está aqui** (“is still here”), **ainda está aberto** (“is still open”), **ainda está chovendo** (“it’s still raining”). Related: **ainda não está…** (“is not … yet”).
target_language_example: Ele ainda está no trabalho.
native_language_example: He’s still at work.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has not gone to sleep yet. "Ainda" = "still/yet" and "estar acordado" = "to be awake". It changes for gender/number: ainda está acordada (she), ainda estão acordados/acordadas (they).
target_language_example: Você ainda está acordado?
native_language_example: Are you still awake?

additional_notes: Used to say someone has not woken up yet. "ainda" = "still/yet" and "está dormindo" is the present continuous "is sleeping" (often used for actions in progress in Portuguese). You can change the subject (ele/ela, o Tom, meu amigo, etc.) or make it a question with rising intonation or a question mark in writing.
target_language_example: Ela ainda está dormindo, então vamos falar mais baixo.
native_language_example: She’s still sleeping, so let’s speak more quietly.

meaning: “is still in” (a state or process; not finished yet).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to say something continues to be in a certain condition or ongoing process: “ainda” = “still/yet”, “estar em” = “to be in”. Common with nouns like construção (construction), andamento (progress), funcionamento (operation), movimento (motion), reforma (renovation). You can change the subject and tense (e.g., “ainda estou em…”, “ainda estava em…”).
target_language_example: O pedido ainda está em análise.
native_language_example: The request is still under review.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something continues to be alive up to now (often implying this is surprising, important, or was uncertain). You can change the person: “ainda estou vivo” (I’m still alive), “ainda está viva” (she/it is still alive — feminine), “ainda estão vivos” (they are still alive).
target_language_example: Ele foi dado como morto, mas ainda está vivo.
native_language_example: He was presumed dead, but he’s still alive.

meaning: “is still …” (continues to be; hasn’t changed yet).
additional_notes: Used with the verb **estar** to say a situation/state is ongoing or unchanged: **ainda está + adjective / location / gerund**. Common patterns: **ainda está aqui** (“is still here”), **ainda está aberto** (“is still open”), **ainda está chovendo** (“it’s still raining”). Related: **ainda não está…** (“is not … yet”).
target_language_example: Ele ainda está no trabalho.
native_language_example: He’s still at work.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something remains in the same place up to now. Often appears in statements and questions: “Ele ainda está aqui.” / “Ele ainda está aqui?” You can swap the subject and keep the phrase: “O Tom ainda está aqui.”
target_language_example: Você ainda está aqui?
native_language_example: Are you still here?

additional_notes: "Ainda" means "still" (something continues). "Estão" is the present tense of "estar" for "they/you (plural)/you (formal) are". Common patterns: (1) "ainda estão" + gerund to mean "are still doing" (e.g., "ainda estão investigando"), and (2) "ainda estão" + adjective/preposition to mean a continuing state or situation (e.g., "ainda estão juntos", "ainda estão nos procurando"). Often used in questions to check if something is still true.
target_language_example: Eles ainda estão trabalhando no projeto.
native_language_example: They are still working on the project.

meaning: "not yet" (something hasn’t happened up to now).
additional_notes: Used to say an action/state is still pending at the time you’re talking about. Often appears before the verb: "ainda não sei" (I don’t know yet), "ainda não acabou" (it hasn’t ended yet). Common in answers: "Ainda não." = "Not yet."
target_language_example: Ainda não terminei o trabalho.
native_language_example: I haven’t finished the work yet.

additional_notes: Used to say a situation or condition hasn’t happened/been reached so far. It’s often followed by an adjective or past participle (clara, seca, determinado, resolvido) or by a phrase with "com" (e.g., "não está comigo").
target_language_example: A resposta ainda não está pronta.
native_language_example: The answer isn’t ready yet.

additional_notes: Used to say someone hasn’t accepted an idea or isn’t persuaded yet. Often follows a subject (ele/ela/você/o Tom) and can be used in statements or questions: “Você ainda não está convencido?” = “Aren’t you convinced yet?” In everyday speech you may also hear “ainda não estou convencido(a)” (I’m not convinced yet) or plural “ainda não estão convencidos”.
target_language_example: Ela ainda não está convencida de que isso vai funcionar.
native_language_example: She’s still not convinced that this will work.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ter (“to have”) to say you continue to have something or that something hasn’t changed yet: Ainda tenho tempo. (“I still have time.”) You can follow it with a noun (ainda tenho dinheiro) or with “que + verb” to mean “I still have to…”: ainda tenho que fazer isso (“I still have to do that”).
target_language_example: Ainda tenho tempo para terminar o trabalho.
native_language_example: I still have time to finish the work.

additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) form of **ajudar** (“to help”) with the object pronoun **-me** (“me”) attached with a hyphen. It’s the **tu** form, common in Portugal and some regions; in more formal speech or in Brazil you’ll often hear **ajude-me** (or **me ajuda** in everyday Brazilian Portuguese). Often used as a direct request or in an urgent plea (e.g., “My God, help me!”).
target_language_example: Ajuda-me a encontrar o meu telefone, por favor.
native_language_example: Help me find my phone, please.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb to say that someone/something helps with an action: "ajudar a + verb" (e.g., ajudar a cuidar, ajudar a reduzir). Often equivalent to English “help (to) …”.
target_language_example: Você pode me ajudar a escolher um presente?
native_language_example: Can you help me choose a gift?

meaning: to help with something; to give help (with a task/problem).
additional_notes: Common polite offer of help: “Posso ajudar com alguma coisa?” = “Can I help with anything?” Often appears with pronouns (me/te/lhe): “Você pode me ajudar com…?” = “Can you help me with…?” You can add “a mais” to mean “anything else / any further help?”
target_language_example: Você pode me ajudar com isso, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you help me with this, please?

additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) form of **ajudar** (“to help”) + **-me** (“me”). Use it to ask someone directly for help; it can be polite or urgent depending on tone/context. Often followed by **com** + a noun: **Ajude-me com isso** (“Help me with that”). You can soften it with **por favor** (“please”) or **se você puder** (“if you can”).
target_language_example: Por favor, ajude-me a encontrar meu telefone.
native_language_example: Please help me find my phone.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to help you do something. It’s formed from the formal command (imperative) of "ajudar" (to help) + "-me" (me) + "a" + an infinitive verb: "Ajude-me a + [verb]". In everyday speech you may also hear "Me ajude a..." (more informal, common in Brazil).
target_language_example: Por favor, ajude-me a encontrar o meu passaporte.
native_language_example: Please help me find my passport.

meaning: “help (someone) do that / help (someone) to do that.”
additional_notes: Form of the verb "ajudar" (to help) used with "a" + infinitive: "ajudar a fazer" = "to help do/make." Often appears with object pronouns: "ajudá-lo a fazer isso" (help him do that), "ajudá-la" (her), "ajudar-me" (me). "Isso" means “that/this (thing)” and refers to an action mentioned in context.
target_language_example: Você pode me ajudar a fazer isso hoje?
native_language_example: Can you help me do that today?

additional_notes: Past tense of ajudar (“to help”) used with a following verb in the infinitive after "a": ajudou (alguém) a + infinitive. The object pronoun (me/te/o/a/nos/vos/os/as) can appear before or after the verb (e.g., "Ela o ajudou a…" = “She helped him to…”).
target_language_example: Ele me ajudou a encontrar meu celular.
native_language_example: He helped me find my phone.

additional_notes: "Ajudá-la" is "ajudar" (to help) + the object pronoun "a" (her), attached with a hyphen. The accent (ajudá-) shows the stress when the pronoun is attached. It’s often used after verbs like "deixar" (to let): "Deixe-me ajudá-la" = "Let me help her." In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many people also say "ajudar ela" (more informal), but "ajudá-la" is the standard written form.
target_language_example: Posso ajudá-la com as malas?
native_language_example: Can I help her with the bags?

additional_notes: Formed from the verb ajudar (to help) + the object pronoun -las (“them,” referring to a group of women or feminine nouns). The accent (ajudá-) appears because the pronoun is attached to the end of the verb (enclisis). You’ll often see it after infinitives like posso ajudá-las (“I can help them”) and after questions like Como posso ajudá-las?
target_language_example: Vou ajudá-las com a tarefa.
native_language_example: I’m going to help them with the assignment.

meaning: 'to help him' (help + 'him' as an object pronoun).
additional_notes: Formed from the verb "ajudar" (to help) + the object pronoun "o" (him/it), attached with a hyphen: ajudá-lo. The accent shows the stress in the infinitive when a pronoun is attached. You can use it after modal verbs too: "pode ajudá-lo" (can help him).
target_language_example: Posso ajudá-lo com isso?
native_language_example: Can I help you (him) with that?

meaning: 'to help him' (help + 'him' as an object pronoun).
additional_notes: Formed from the verb "ajudar" (to help) + the object pronoun "o" (him/it), attached with a hyphen: ajudá-lo. The accent shows the stress in the infinitive when a pronoun is attached. You can use it after modal verbs too: "pode ajudá-lo" (can help him).
target_language_example: Posso ajudá-lo com isso?
native_language_example: Can I help you (him) with that?

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say you help a male person do something: ajudR + -lo (“him”) + a + verb (infinitive). The -lo is an object pronoun attached to the verb with a hyphen. In everyday Portuguese you may also hear: ajudar ele a … (less formal).
target_language_example: Posso ajudá-lo a encontrar o hotel.
native_language_example: Can I help him find the hotel?

additional_notes: "ajudá-los" = ajudar (to help) + "-los" (them). The accent in ajudá- shows the stress when adding an object pronoun with a hyphen. It’s used after a verb in the infinitive (ajudar) and means helping a group of people (them).
target_language_example: Posso ajudá-los com o dever de casa.
native_language_example: I can help them with their homework.

meaning: 'something to' (followed by a verb), or 'something for' (someone) (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used when "algo" is followed by an infinitive introduced by "a": "algo a dizer/beber/considerar/acrescentar" = "something to say/drink/consider/ add". With an indirect object pronoun, it can mean "something for someone to...": "algo a lhe dizer" = "something to tell you". Very common in polite offers and questions: "Tem algo a... ?", "Posso oferecer algo a... ?".
target_language_example: Tenho algo a te perguntar.
native_language_example: I have something to ask you.

meaning: "something about it" / "something about that" (i.e., take action about it).
additional_notes: Used when asking or hoping that someone will do something to deal with a situation or problem. Very common with verbs like "fazer" (do/make) and in questions: "Você vai fazer algo a respeito disso?". "Disso" = "de + isso" (about this/it).
target_language_example: Precisamos fazer algo a respeito disso hoje.
native_language_example: We need to do something about it today.

meaning: something to do with it/this; some involvement in it/this.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "ter" (to have) to say someone is connected to, involved in, or related to a situation: "ter algo a ver com isso" = "to have something to do with it". Often appears in questions or accusations about responsibility ("Você teve algo a ver com isso?"). You can also say "não tenho nada a ver com isso" = "I have nothing to do with it."
target_language_example: A polícia acha que ele teve algo a ver com isso.
native_language_example: The police think he had something to do with it.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified thing or action, often implying it’s similar to what was just mentioned or shown. Common with verbs like fazer (do), acontecer (happen), comprar (buy). Depending on context, it can sound neutral, surprised, or disapproving (e.g., “Nunca pensei que algo assim aconteceria.”).
target_language_example: Você tem algo assim mais barato?
native_language_example: Do you have something like that cheaper?

additional_notes: Used to say there is a problem or that someone did something incorrectly. Very common in questions like "Fiz algo de errado?" (Did I do something wrong?) and with "haver" to express existence: "Há algo de errado" (There’s something wrong). Often followed by "com" + person/thing: "algo de errado com você" (something wrong with you).
target_language_example: Acho que há algo de errado com o meu celular.
native_language_example: I think there’s something wrong with my phone.

additional_notes: Used to say that a person or thing has a problem, isn’t working properly, or seems suspicious/odd. Very common with the verb "haver/ter" ("há/tem algo errado com..."). You can also use "alguma coisa errada com" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Acho que tem algo errado com este computador.
native_language_example: I think there’s something wrong with this computer.

additional_notes: Used when there is a purpose, recipient, or use coming next: **algo para + infinitive** (something to do/say/eat) or **algo para + noun/pronoun** (something for someone/something). Often used to offer, give, or ask for an item or task.
target_language_example: Você tem algo para beber?
native_language_example: Do you have something to drink?

additional_notes: A polite, common way to offer or ask for a drink. Often used with verbs like querer (to want), precisar (to need), and gostar (would like). You can also say: Você quer algo para beber?
target_language_example: Depois da caminhada, precisamos de algo para beber.
native_language_example: After the walk, we need something to drink.

additional_notes: Used when you don’t specify what food, just that you need food in general. Very common with verbs like pegar (grab), comprar (buy), trazer (bring), and precisar (need). You can also say “alguma coisa para comer” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Vamos parar e pegar algo para comer.
native_language_example: Let’s stop and grab something to eat.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an unspecified thing followed by a describing clause with "que" (e.g., "algo que eu vi" = "something that I saw"). Very common in everyday speech; the verb after "que" is conjugated normally.
target_language_example: Há algo que eu preciso te contar.
native_language_example: There’s something I need to tell you.

additional_notes: Used when the exact amount isn’t known or isn’t important. Often in requests or offers (e.g., asking to borrow some money). With "ter" it means "to have some money"; with "emprestar" it means lending/borrowing some money (context shows which).
target_language_example: Você tem algum dinheiro trocado?
native_language_example: Do you have some change?

additional_notes: Means an unspecified place. With affirmative sentences it often means “somewhere” (Conheço… de algum lugar = “from somewhere”). In questions and with expressions of possibility it can mean “anywhere/somewhere” depending on context (Há algum lugar…? = “Is there anywhere…?”). You can also use it with “para” + infinitive to mean “somewhere to…” (algum lugar para comer = “somewhere to eat”).
target_language_example: Vamos encontrar algum lugar para sentar e conversar.
native_language_example: Let’s find somewhere to sit and talk.

meaning: “any problem” / “any issue” (usually in questions or conditionals).
additional_notes: Common in questions to check if something is wrong: “Algum problema?” = “Any problem?” / “Is there a problem?” Also used in conditionals like “Caso você tenha algum problema…” (“If you have any problem…”). Often appears with verbs like "ter" (to have) or "haver"/"existir" (there is/are): “Tem/Há/Existe algum problema?”. In “Você tem algum problema com isso?”, it can mean “Do you have a problem with that?” (do you object).
target_language_example: Se tiver algum problema, me avise.
native_language_example: If you have any problem, let me know.

meaning: “some time” / “a while” (an unspecified amount of time).
additional_notes: Used when you don’t want to be specific about the duration. Often appears with time expressions like “após algum tempo” (after a while), “faz algum tempo” (for some time/it’s been a while), and “por algum tempo” (for a while).
target_language_example: Vou ficar aqui por algum tempo.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay here for a while.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to say the exact type/category isn’t known, isn’t specified, or doesn’t matter. Often appears in questions (to ask whether there is any kind of something) and in statements where you’re being general: “algum tipo de remédio” (some kind of medicine), “algum tipo de perigo” (some kind of danger).
target_language_example: Você tem algum tipo de alergia?
native_language_example: Do you have any kind of allergy?

meaning: “any of you?” / “does any one of you…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask a group if at least one person fits the description or can do something. It’s usually followed by a verb: “Algum de vocês sabe…?”, “Algum de vocês tem…?”. Often translates as “Does any one of you…?” or simply “Any of you…?”.
target_language_example: Algum de vocês quer ir comigo?
native_language_example: Does any one of you want to go with me?

meaning: something about it; something about that.
additional_notes: Used when talking about taking action or having information regarding a situation or topic. Very common after verbs like fazer (to do) and saber (to know): fazer alguma coisa a respeito = “do something about it”; saber alguma coisa a respeito = “know something about it.” In speech you may also hear: alguma coisa sobre isso.
target_language_example: A prefeitura precisa fazer alguma coisa a respeito.
native_language_example: City hall needs to do something about it.

meaning: "something to..." / "something for..." (something intended for a purpose).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by an infinitive with "para" to express purpose: "alguma coisa para + verb" = "something to + verb" (e.g., "para dizer", "para fazer"). It can refer to an object you use (e.g., a pen) or something meant for that action (e.g., paper), depending on context.
target_language_example: Há alguma coisa para comer?
native_language_example: Is there something to eat?

additional_notes: A very common, neutral way to say you want food without specifying what. Uses "alguma coisa" (something) + "para" (to/for) + "comer" (eat). In questions it can mean offering food ("Você quer...?" = Do you want...?) or asking if food is available ("Você tem...?" = Do you have...?).
target_language_example: Vamos parar num café para pegar alguma coisa para comer.
native_language_example: Let’s stop at a café to get something to eat.

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has an activity/task to do, or to suggest they find an activity (often meaning “stop being bored/lazy and do something”). Common in questions like “Você tem alguma coisa para fazer?” (“Do you have something to do?”). You can also hear “algo para fazer” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Se você está entediado, encontra alguma coisa para fazer.
native_language_example: If you’re bored, find something to do.

meaning: 'something that you…' / 'anything you…' (introduces what you can/need/want to do).
additional_notes: Used to ask or say that there is (or might be) something the other person can/needs to/wants to do. It’s commonly followed by a verb phrase, often in the subjunctive after expressions like "há" or "deve ter" (e.g., "alguma coisa que você possa/precise/queira..."). You’ll also hear the equivalent with "tem": "Tem alguma coisa que você...".
target_language_example: Tem alguma coisa que você possa me ajudar a resolver?
native_language_example: Is there something you can help me solve?

additional_notes: Used mainly in questions (and sometimes negatives) to ask if something has happened at least once in someone’s life or up to now. Often appears with "já" for emphasis: "Você já... alguma vez?" = "Have you ever...?" Can also mean "sometime/one day" in other contexts, but the examples here are the question-use meaning "ever".
target_language_example: Você já viajou para o exterior alguma vez?
native_language_example: Have you ever traveled abroad?

additional_notes: Common, general way to refer to an unspecified small number of tasks, items, or pieces of information. Often used with verbs like fazer (to do), comprar (to buy), cuidar (to take care of), saber (to know), and ensinar (to teach). Can imply “a few” (not many) depending on context.
target_language_example: Só preciso resolver algumas coisas antes de sair.
native_language_example: I just need to sort out a few things before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an approximate, small number of hours (not exact). Often appears with time expressions like “por algumas horas” (for a few hours) and “algumas horas atrás” (a few hours ago).
target_language_example: Vou estar ocupado por algumas horas, mas depois te ligo.
native_language_example: I’ll be busy for a few hours, but then I’ll call you.

additional_notes: "Algumas" means "some" (an unspecified quantity, plural). "Músicas" is plural of "música" (songs/music), and "francesas" agrees in gender/number with "músicas" (feminine plural) to mean "French". Often used with verbs like conhecer (to know), ouvir (to listen to), aprender (to learn), and saber cantar (to know how to sing).
target_language_example: Ela está procurando algumas músicas francesas para a viagem.
native_language_example: She’s looking for some French songs for the trip.

additional_notes: Common way to say you have a limited number of questions. "Algumas" agrees with the noun (feminine plural: perguntas). Often used with verbs like "ter" (to have) and "fazer" (to ask): "Tenho algumas perguntas" / "Vou fazer algumas perguntas". You can also say "mais algumas perguntas" = "a few more questions".
target_language_example: Antes de começarmos, tenho algumas perguntas.
native_language_example: Before we start, I have a few questions.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified group of people (not everyone). Often followed by a verb: “Algumas pessoas gostam...” / “Algumas pessoas não gostam...”.
target_language_example: Algumas pessoas preferem estudar de manhã.
native_language_example: Some people prefer to study in the morning.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an opinion or belief that is not necessarily shared by everyone (often to generalize, soften a claim, or distance yourself from the opinion). "Achar" here means “to think/believe” (not “to find”).
target_language_example: Algumas pessoas acham que trabalhar de casa é mais produtivo.
native_language_example: Some people think that working from home is more productive.

additional_notes: Used to make a general observation about certain people and to express an impression (not a proven fact). It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., reclamar, se queixar, ter esquecido) or another verb phrase.
target_language_example: Algumas pessoas parecem não entender o problema.
native_language_example: Some people seem not to understand the problem.

meaning: 'some people have' / 'some people are' (with a noun describing a condition or feeling).
additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about part of a group (“some people”). With nouns like alergia/medo/terror/dificuldade, Portuguese often uses ter (“to have”) where English might say “be” (e.g., ter alergia = to be allergic; ter medo/terror = to be afraid/terrified; ter dificuldade = to have trouble).
target_language_example: Algumas pessoas têm medo de falar em público.
native_language_example: Some people are afraid of speaking in public.

additional_notes: Used to say you need or will buy a few items of clothing that are new (not used). Common with verbs like "precisar" (to need) and "comprar" (to buy). "Algumas" is the feminine plural form of "algum" and matches "roupas" (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Vou comprar algumas roupas novas para o inverno.
native_language_example: I’m going to buy some new clothes for the winter.

additional_notes: Means an indefinite small number of weeks. Often used with time expressions like “há/atrás” (a few weeks ago) or “em” (in a few weeks). Word order can vary slightly (e.g., “mais algumas semanas” = “a few more weeks”).
target_language_example: Vou voltar em algumas semanas.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in a few weeks.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an approximate number of days (not exact). It often appears with time expressions like "alguns dias depois" (a few days later), "tem alguns dias" (a few days ago), "por mais alguns dias" (for a few more days), or with "dentro de alguns dias" (in a few days).
target_language_example: Vou ficar aqui por mais alguns dias.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay here for a few more days.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an unspecified quantity of books (plural). It agrees with the masculine plural noun “livros”: singular would be “algum livro” (“some book”/“a certain book”). Often followed by details like language (“em inglês”) or topic (“sobre Lincoln”).
target_language_example: Comprei alguns livros para a viagem.
native_language_example: I bought some books for the trip.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an approximate length of time (not an exact number). It often appears with time words like "depois" (later) or after "por" to mean "for a few months" (e.g., "por alguns meses").
target_language_example: Vou ficar aqui por alguns meses antes de voltar para casa.
native_language_example: I'm going to stay here for a few months before going back home.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a short, non-specific amount of time. Often appears with "mais" ("mais alguns minutos" = "a few more minutes"). In polite requests, you may hear "alguns minutos do seu tempo" (“a few minutes of your time”).
target_language_example: Você pode esperar alguns minutos?
native_language_example: Can you wait a few minutes?

alguém aqui tem interesse em aprender

target_language_multi_word_term: alguém aqui tem interesse em aprender
additional_notes: Used to ask a group if someone is interested in learning a subject (often a language). You typically add the topic at the end: “alguém aqui tem interesse em aprender + [língua/assunto]?” You can also change “aqui” (here) depending on context (e.g., “aí” = there), and change the verb for other activities (e.g., “em participar” = in participating).
target_language_example: Alguém aqui tem interesse em aprender português comigo?
native_language_example: Is anyone here interested in learning Portuguese with me?

additional_notes: Used when you want a person you can talk with (often for company or emotional support). Very common after verbs like "precisar" (to need) and "querer" (to want): "preciso de alguém para conversar". Literally "someone to converse (with)", but in English it’s most natural as "someone to talk to."
target_language_example: Quando eu estiver nervoso, eu só quero alguém para conversar.
native_language_example: When I’m nervous, I just want someone to talk to.

meaning: “can someone … me” / “could someone … for me” (asking for help).
additional_notes: Used to politely ask if anyone is able/willing to do something for you. It’s usually followed by a verb (dar, dizer, ajudar, levar, etc.). The “me” is an object pronoun (“to me” / “for me”) and can also come after the verb in more formal written Portuguese (e.g., “Alguém pode dizer-me...”).
target_language_example: Alguém pode me ajudar com isso, por favor?
native_language_example: Can someone help me with this, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask for an explanation (often when you’re confused). Follow it with a noun (isso/isto), or with a clause like “o que está acontecendo” (what’s happening) or “o que significa” (what it means). You can also hear “Alguém pode explicar pra mim…?” (same meaning; “pra mim” is common in speech).
target_language_example: Alguém pode me explicar como isso funciona?
native_language_example: Can someone explain to me how this works?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that describes an unspecified person. Very common after verbs like conhecer (to know), precisar de (to need), procurar (to look for), and in questions like “Há alguém que…?” / “Conhecem alguém que…?” It’s often followed by the subjunctive when the person is unknown or hypothetical: “Conhecem alguém que saiba…?” / “Preciso de alguém que eu possa confiar.”
target_language_example: Estou procurando alguém que possa me ensinar português.
native_language_example: I’m looking for someone who can teach me Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to a person with a certain language ability. It’s usually followed by the language (e.g., inglês, japonês). Here, “fale” is the present subjunctive of “falar,” commonly used after expressions like “há,” “conhece,” “procurar,” “precisar,” and “contratar,” where the person may or may not exist / is unspecified.
target_language_example: Preciso de alguém que fale português e espanhol.
native_language_example: I need someone who speaks Portuguese and Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a person capable of doing an action, often when you’re looking for help or asking if such a person is available. The verb is usually in the subjunctive: "possa" (from "poder"), because it refers to an unknown or hypothetical person (e.g., "Você conhece alguém que possa me ajudar?"). In questions, it often means “anyone who can…?”
target_language_example: Preciso de alguém que possa traduzir isto para mim.
native_language_example: I need someone who can translate this for me.

meaning: “someone who knows how to speak (… )” / “someone who can speak (… )”.
additional_notes: Used to describe a person with the ability to speak a language. After “alguém que…”, Portuguese typically uses the present subjunctive (here: “saiba”), because it refers to an unspecified person you want/need/are looking for. Very common with verbs like “precisar”, “querer”, “procurar”, “contratar”, “pretender”. You normally add the language after “falar” (e.g., “falar francês/inglês”) and can add an adverb like “fluentemente”.
target_language_example: Estamos procurando alguém que saiba falar espanhol.
native_language_example: We’re looking for someone who can speak Spanish.

additional_notes: Use this to report that something of yours was stolen. It’s usually followed by the noun for the stolen item (carro, cartão de crédito, dinheiro, passaporte, etc.). You can also change the possessive to match the item’s gender/number: o meu (masc. singular), a minha (fem. singular), os meus (masc. plural), as minhas (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Alguém roubou o meu telemóvel.
native_language_example: Someone stole my phone.

additional_notes: Used when you need a car temporarily (e.g., on a trip). The verb is "alugar" (to rent), and "um carro" means "a car." In polite requests you’ll often hear "Eu queria..." or "Gostaria de..." (I would like...).
target_language_example: Onde posso alugar um carro por dois dias?
native_language_example: Where can I rent a car for two days?

additional_notes: Used to add extra information: além de + noun/infinitive = “besides / in addition to.” In some contexts it expresses a limit or degree: estar além de = “to be beyond” (e.g., além de minha compreensão = “beyond my understanding”).
target_language_example: Além de trabalhar, eu estudo à noite.
native_language_example: Besides working, I study at night.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen or is planned for the morning of the next day. You can also hear the shorter variant “amanhã cedo” (“tomorrow early”).
target_language_example: A gente se encontra amanhã de manhã às oito.
native_language_example: We’ll meet tomorrow morning at eight.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen tomorrow during the evening or at night. In Portuguese, "à" is the contraction of "a" + "a" (meaning "at" + "the"), so "à noite" literally means "at night". You can also hear the shorter "amanhã de noite" in some regions, but "amanhã à noite" is very common and neutral.
target_language_example: A gente janta amanhã à noite?
native_language_example: Are we having dinner tomorrow night?

additional_notes: Used to specify a time on the day after today. In European Portuguese you’ll also see “amanhã de tarde.” In Brazilian Portuguese, “amanhã à tarde” is common and can also be said as “amanhã de tarde.”
target_language_example: Posso te ligar amanhã à tarde.
native_language_example: Can I call you tomorrow afternoon?

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun with a definite article (as) to mean “both (of) the…”. For masculine plural, use “ambos os”. Often agrees with what follows: ambas as peças, ambas as filhas.
target_language_example: Ambas as respostas estão corretas.
native_language_example: Both answers are correct.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean “both (of) the …”. For feminine plural nouns, use "ambas as" (e.g., "ambas as casas"). It can refer to two people/things/sides/crimes already known from context.
target_language_example: Ambos os alunos chegaram cedo.
native_language_example: Both (of) the students arrived early.

additional_notes: Used to describe friends with a strong personal bond—people you trust and share private things with. Often used when asking how many close friends someone has ("Quantos amigos íntimos você tem?"). "Íntimo" here means emotionally close, not necessarily romantic.
target_language_example: Ela só contou isso para os amigos íntimos dela.
native_language_example: She only told that to her close friends.

additional_notes: Used to say you love something/someone that belongs to you (your house, your aunt, your homeland, etc.). It must be followed by a feminine noun: **Amo a minha casa.** With a masculine noun, use **Amo o meu…** (e.g., **Amo o meu irmão.**). In Portuguese, the possessive usually comes with an article (**a** minha, **o** meu).
target_language_example: Amo a minha família, mas sinto saudades dela quando estou longe.
native_language_example: I love my family, but I miss them when I’m far away.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is (or was) the most important romantic love in your life. It often appears as "o amor da minha vida" (the love of my life) or with emphasis like "o grande amor da minha vida" (the great love of my life). You can change the possessive: "amor da sua vida" (love of your life), "amor da nossa vida" (love of our life).
target_language_example: Ele é o amor da minha vida, e eu quero me casar com ele.
native_language_example: He is the love of my life, and I want to marry him.

additional_notes: Used to define or describe what love is (often in general statements, opinions, quotes, or poetic lines). It can also be followed by a noun phrase or adjective: "Amor é coisa de adolescentes" (Love is a teenager thing) / "Amor é lindo" (Love is beautiful).
target_language_example: Amor é respeito e cuidado.
native_language_example: Love is respect and care.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the upper floor of a house/building, often contrasted with "andar de baixo" (downstairs). Common with verbs like "subir" (to go up), "ficar" (to be located), and "estar" (to be): "O banheiro fica no andar de cima" (The bathroom is upstairs) / "Ele está no andar de cima" (He’s upstairs).
target_language_example: As crianças estão no andar de cima, brincando no quarto.
native_language_example: The kids are upstairs, playing in the bedroom.

meaning: to ride a horse; to go horseback riding.
additional_notes: Used with the verb andar (“to walk/go/ride”) + a cavalo (“on a horse”) to talk about the skill of riding horses or the activity itself. Common with verbs like saber (“to know how to”), gostar de (“to like”), and aprender (“to learn”).
target_language_example: Ela aprendeu a andar a cavalo nas férias.
native_language_example: She learned to ride a horse during the vacation.

meaning: to ride a bike; to go by bicycle.
additional_notes: Uses the verb andar (“to walk/go”) + de to express the means of transport. Very common in phrases like aprender a andar de bicicleta (“to learn to ride a bike”) and prefiro andar de bicicleta a... (“I prefer riding a bike to…”).
target_language_example: No fim de semana, gosto de andar de bicicleta no parque.
native_language_example: On the weekend, I like to ride my bike in the park.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "andar" (to ride/go) + "de" + the activity/vehicle. In Brazilian Portuguese, "andar de" is very common for activities like cycling or skating (e.g., "andar de bicicleta"). You can use it with "saber" to ask/answer about ability: "Você sabe andar de skate?"
target_language_example: Eu gosto de andar de skate no parque aos sábados.
native_language_example: I like to skateboard in the park on Saturdays.

meaning: a year and a half (one and a half years).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration or time since something happened. Often appears with "há" to mean "for/since" ("Não a vejo há um ano e meio" = "I haven’t seen her for a year and a half"), or with "atrás" to mean "ago" ("um ano e meio atrás" = "a year and a half ago"). You can also say "um ano e meio" for "one year and a half."
target_language_example: Estou morando aqui há um ano e meio.
native_language_example: I’ve been living here for a year and a half.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the previous calendar year (or roughly one year ago). It often goes at the end of the sentence: “Eu fui para Boston ano passado.” You can also use it alone as a question to confirm the time: “Ano passado?”
target_language_example: A gente se conheceu ano passado.
native_language_example: We met last year.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a time in the past, often after a number: "há três anos atrás" = "three years ago". In standard Portuguese, using both "há" and "atrás" is redundant (you can say "há três anos" or "três anos atrás"), but "há ... atrás" is very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Conheci a Ana cinco anos atrás.
native_language_example: I met Ana five years ago.

additional_notes: Used to state someone’s age, often after a number: “Tenho 45 anos de idade” or more commonly just “Tenho 45 anos.” Also used with events starting at a certain age: “desde os dois anos de idade” (“since (I was) two years old”). Works with people and animals.
target_language_example: Ela tem dezoito anos de idade.
native_language_example: She is eighteen years old.

meaning: “looking forward to” (eager/excited to do or see something).
additional_notes: Used to express positive anticipation: ansioso/a (agree with the person: ansioso = male, ansiosa = female) + para + infinitive (ansioso para te ver; ansiosa para viajar). With events/clauses, you may also see “ansioso para que + subjunctive” (ansioso para que chegue o Natal). In some contexts “ansioso” can also mean “anxious/nervous,” but with “para + infinitive” it often means “looking forward to.”
target_language_example: Estou ansiosa para começar o curso amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m looking forward to starting the course tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens earlier than another event or time. Often followed by an infinitive verb: "antes de + verb" (e.g., "antes de dormir" = "before sleeping / before going to sleep"). It can also be used with nouns/pronouns: "antes de mim" = "before me". In the set phrase "antes de tudo", it means "first of all / before anything else".
target_language_example: Antes de começar a aula, vou tomar um café.
native_language_example: Before class starts, I’m going to have a coffee.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens prior to eating. It often follows an instruction or routine (e.g., wash hands/pray/take a shower) and can be used more generally as “before I/you/we eat” when the subject is understood from context.
target_language_example: Vou ligar para você antes de comer.
native_language_example: I'll call you before eating (before I eat).

additional_notes: Used to say one action happens prior to beginning another action. It’s often followed by a verb in the infinitive (comer, chover, lavar, falar). In example 2, "pouco antes de começar a" means "shortly before (it) started to".
target_language_example: Antes de começar a trabalhar, vou tomar um café.
native_language_example: Before starting to work, I’m going to have a coffee.

additional_notes: Used to say something should happen first (often a polite instruction), e.g., “Bata/Chama antes de entrar” = “Knock/Call before coming in.” You can add a place after it: “antes de entrar no banheiro/no quarto/no avião.”
target_language_example: Por favor, tire os sapatos antes de entrar.
native_language_example: Please take off your shoes before coming in.

additional_notes: Used to remind someone to think (or do something else) before saying anything. Very common in advice or rules (e.g., in class: “raise your hand before speaking”). Often appears after another verb: “Pensa/Pensem… antes de falar”.
target_language_example: Respira fundo antes de falar com ele.
native_language_example: Take a deep breath before talking to him.

additional_notes: Used to say that something should happen prior to leaving or prior to going somewhere to do an activity. It’s often followed by an infinitive to specify where/what you’re going: antes de ir trabalhar (before going to work), antes de ir estudar (before going to study), antes de ir pra cama (before going to bed). You can also use it alone (Antes de ir, …) meaning “Before I/you leave, …” (the subject is understood from context).
target_language_example: Antes de ir para o aeroporto, preciso imprimir o meu bilhete.
native_language_example: Before going to the airport, I need to print my ticket.

meaning: before going to sleep / before going to bed.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something you do earlier than the moment you go to sleep. Common in routines and reminders. Grammar: "antes de" + infinitive ("ir" + infinitive "dormir"). You can also hear "antes de dormir" (shorter, same meaning) and "antes de ir para a cama" (more literally “before going to bed”).
target_language_example: Vou tomar banho antes de ir dormir.
native_language_example: I’m going to take a shower before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened earlier than a person’s death, or something someone wants to do in their lifetime (“before I die”). Often followed by a comma when it starts the sentence: “Antes de morrer, …”. You can change the subject: “antes de eu morrer” (before I die), “antes de ele morrer” (before he dies).
target_language_example: Quero ver o mar de novo antes de morrer.
native_language_example: I want to see the sea again before I die.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that should happen prior to leaving a place or situation. Often followed by an action to check/confirm (e.g., lock the door, turn off lights). It can also appear with a complement: “antes de sair do trabalho” = “before leaving work.”
target_language_example: Antes de sair, desligue o forno.
native_language_example: Before you leave, turn off the oven.

meaning: before (a specific time/event; used with masculine singular nouns).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens earlier than a time, deadline, or event: "antes do amanhecer" (before dawn), "antes do meio-dia" (before noon), "antes do fim" (before the end), "antes do prazo" (before the deadline). It’s the contraction of "antes de" + "o". With feminine singular nouns, use "antes da"; with plural, "antes dos / antes das".
target_language_example: Preciso sair antes do jantar.
native_language_example: I need to leave before dinner.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens earlier in the morning than breakfast. Often with routines: “tomar banho” (to shower), “dar uma caminhada/passear” (to go for a walk), etc. Literally “before the morning coffee,” but it means “before breakfast” in general.
target_language_example: Eu sempre leio as notícias antes do café da manhã.
native_language_example: I always read the news before breakfast.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens earlier than dinner time. Often appears after the verb to place the time: "Cheguei antes do jantar" (I arrived before dinner). You can add words like "logo" (right/just) or "pouco" (a little) to be more specific: "logo antes do jantar", "pouco antes do jantar".
target_language_example: Vamos sair antes do jantar.
native_language_example: Let’s go out before dinner.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause meaning one action should happen earlier than another: “before (someone) does (something)” or “before (something) happens.” It’s often followed by the subjunctive in Portuguese because it refers to a future/uncertain event: "antes que ele recupere...".
target_language_example: Feche a janela antes que comece a chover.
native_language_example: Close the window before it starts to rain.

additional_notes: Contraction of "a" (to) + "o" (the) → "ao". Used after verbs of movement or arrival (e.g., ir, levar, mandar, chegar) to indicate destination: "ir ao aeroporto" = "to go to the airport". For a specific airport name, you can say "ao aeroporto Narita"; more commonly you’ll also see "ao Aeroporto de Narita".
target_language_example: Vou ao aeroporto buscar você às oito.
native_language_example: I’m going to the airport to pick you up at eight.

meaning: 'when crossing the street' / 'while crossing the street.'
additional_notes: "Ao" + infinitive ("atravessar") is a common structure meaning "when/while doing (something)." Here it introduces the situation in which something happens or advice applies. "Rua" can be translated as "street" (or sometimes "road," depending on context).
target_language_example: Ao atravessar a rua, olhe para os dois lados.
native_language_example: When crossing the street, look both ways.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (ir, chegar, levar) to indicate destination: going/heading to the central area of a city. It’s the contraction of "a" (to) + "o" (the) = "ao", plus "centro da cidade" (city center). Common in asking for directions: "Como posso chegar ao centro da cidade?"
target_language_example: Vamos ao centro da cidade de metrô.
native_language_example: Let’s go downtown by subway.

meaning: to the cinema; to the movie theater.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of going/coming (ir, ir embora, vir) to say you’re going to see a movie at a cinema. It’s the contraction of "a" + "o" (= "to" + "the"), so it’s used when "cinema" is treated as a masculine place ("o cinema"). Common in invitations and suggestions: "Vamos ao cinema?" / "Que tal irmos ao cinema?"
target_language_example: Vamos ao cinema hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Shall we go to the movies tonight?

meaning: abroad; to another country (outside one’s country).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of going/traveling (ir, viajar, estudar, morar) to mean going outside your country. It’s a fixed contraction: a + o exterior (“to the exterior/outside”), and in practice it usually means “abroad” in travel contexts.
target_language_example: Ela quer estudar ao exterior no próximo ano.
native_language_example: She wants to study abroad next year.

meaning: to the end; at the end (of).
additional_notes: Used to talk about reaching a final point or conclusion. Common in set phrases like “do início ao fim” (“from beginning to end”) and with verbs like “chegar ao fim” (“to come to an end”). It can also mean something located at the end of a text/message (“ao fim desta mensagem”).
target_language_example: Ao fim da reunião, vamos decidir o que fazer.
native_language_example: At the end of the meeting, we’ll decide what to do.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (e.g., ir, levar, chegar, vir) to indicate going/coming/arriving at a hospital. It's the contraction of "a" (to) + "o" (the) = "ao". In Portuguese you normally say "ir ao hospital" (literally "go to the hospital"), rather than English-style "go to hospital".
target_language_example: Ele precisou ir ao hospital depois do acidente.
native_language_example: He needed to go to the hospital after the accident.

additional_notes: Used after verbs of movement (like ir, ir com, levar) to say someone is going to the zoo. "Ao" is the contraction of "a" + "o" (= "to" + "the"). You’ll also see "zoológico" alone to mean "zoo" (e.g., "Vamos ao zoológico").
target_language_example: Vamos ao jardim zoológico amanhã.
native_language_example: We’re going to the zoo tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say something is immediately next to something else. It can be literal (physical location) or figurative (comparison): "Ele parece pequeno ao lado do irmão" = "He looks small next to his brother." Use "ao lado de" before masculine nouns, plurals, names, or pronouns: "ao lado do banco", "ao lado dos meus amigos", "ao lado dela".
target_language_example: O café fica ao lado da estação.
native_language_example: The café is next to the station.

additional_notes: Used for physical location: someone or something is right beside another person or place. Common with verbs like estar, sentar, morar, and with places (casa, apartamento, jardim). It can mean "in the neighboring one" with apartments/rooms (o apartamento ao lado = the apartment next door).
target_language_example: Meu carro está estacionado ao lado do seu.
native_language_example: My car is parked next to yours.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something is directly beside something else. It’s followed by a noun with a definite article: ao lado do (masc. singular), ao lado da (fem. singular), ao lado dos (masc. plural), ao lado das (fem. plural).
target_language_example: O banheiro fica ao lado da cozinha.
native_language_example: The bathroom is next to the kitchen.

meaning: along the river (following the river’s length).
additional_notes: Used to describe movement or location that follows the course/length of the river (e.g., walking, running, hiking). The core expression is "ao longo de" = "along" + a place; here it’s "do rio" ("of the river").
target_language_example: Há muitos cafés ao longo do rio.
native_language_example: There are many cafés along the river.

meaning: in half; into two equal parts.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like cortar (to cut) and dobrar (to fold) to say something is divided into two equal parts. Common patterns: cortar X ao meio (cut X in half), dobrar X ao meio (fold X in half).
target_language_example: Vamos cortar o bolo ao meio.
native_language_example: Let’s cut the cake in half.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens at exactly noon. It’s a contraction of "a" + "o" (ao) + "meio-dia" (midday). For approximate time, you can also hear "por volta do meio-dia" (around noon).
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar ao meio-dia em frente ao restaurante.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at noon in front of the restaurant.

additional_notes: Contraction of **a + o meu**. Used mainly with verbs/prepositions that take **a** (e.g., **ir a** = “to go to”, **dar a** = “to give to”). It must match a masculine singular noun (e.g., **ao meu carro** = “to my car”). For feminine: **à minha**; plural: **aos meus / às minhas**.
target_language_example: Vou ao meu apartamento agora.
native_language_example: I’m going to my apartment now.

additional_notes: Means someone is physically beside you (sitting/standing next to you) or, more figuratively, that they support you and stay with you in difficult moments. Often appears with verbs like estar/ficar/sentar-se/precisar (e.g., "Ele está ao meu lado"). You can change the possessive: ao teu lado (by your side), ao lado dela (by her side).
target_language_example: Quero você ao meu lado quando eu falar com eles.
native_language_example: I want you by my side when I talk to them.

additional_notes: "Ao" is the contraction of "a" (to) + "o" (the). It’s used with movement verbs like "ir" (to go) and also with verbs that take "a" to indicate the recipient/destination (e.g., donating something to an institution).
target_language_example: Vamos ao museu depois do almoço.
native_language_example: We’re going to the museum after lunch.

meaning: to the doctor; at the doctor’s (office).
additional_notes: "Ao" = "a" (to) + "o" (the). Used mainly with verbs like "ir" (to go), "levar" (to take someone), and "voltar" (to return): "ir ao médico" = go to the doctor / see a doctor. It can also refer to speaking with a doctor: "fiz ao médico algumas perguntas" = I asked the doctor some questions.
target_language_example: Preciso ir ao médico amanhã.
native_language_example: I need to go to the doctor tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Ao" = "a" (to) + "o" (the, masculine). Used to say you’re going to a specific park or bringing someone/something there. With a feminine noun you’d use "à" (a + a), e.g., "à praia" (to the beach).
target_language_example: Vamos ao parque depois do almoço.
native_language_example: Let’s go to the park after lunch.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something being physically around something else: around a place/object (trees around a lake), forming a circle/group around something (people around a campfire), wrapping something around (an arm around someone’s waist), or orbiting around (a satellite around the moon). It’s followed by a feminine singular noun: ao redor da lagoa. With a masculine singular noun, it’s ao redor do: ao redor do parque.
target_language_example: As crianças correram ao redor da mesa.
native_language_example: The children ran around the table.

additional_notes: Used to talk about things circling something (like planets) or people/things positioned surrounding something. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun: ao redor do Sol/do fogo. With feminine singular nouns, it becomes “ao redor da” (e.g., ao redor da mesa).
target_language_example: As crianças correram ao redor do parque.
native_language_example: The kids ran around the park.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening in many countries/places across the world. Often with verbs like viajar (to travel), ser falado (to be spoken), acontecer (to happen), and with plural nouns (e.g., pessoas/igrejas/empresas) to mean “worldwide.”
target_language_example: Essa notícia se espalhou ao redor do mundo em poucas horas.
native_language_example: That news spread around the world in just a few hours.
