additional_notes: Made of **a** (“to”) + **o** (“the”, masculine singular) + **seu** (“your/his”). It agrees with a masculine singular noun that follows: **ao seu professor** (“to your/his teacher/professor”). **Seu/sua** can mean either “your” or “his/her” depending on context; to be clearer, people may use **dele/dela** (“of him/of her”) or **de você** (“of you”).
target_language_example: Vou falar ao seu gerente amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to speak to your manager tomorrow.

meaning: next to you; by your side.
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical proximity (“right next to you”) and also, in a more emotional/supportive sense, being with someone (“by your side”). It agrees with the person: ao meu lado (next to me), ao lado dele/dela (next to him/her), ao nosso lado (next to us). Often appears with verbs like sentar (sit), ficar (stay), estar (be), ajoelhar-se (kneel).
target_language_example: Fica ao meu lado, por favor.
native_language_example: Stay next to me, please.

additional_notes: Used after verbs of going/heading (e.g., ir, voltar, passar) to show destination. It’s the contraction of "a" (to) + "o" (the) = "ao"; with feminine nouns you get "à" (a + a), e.g., "à farmácia".
target_language_example: Vou ao supermercado depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I'm going to the supermarket after work.

meaning: to the theater; to go to the theater (to see a play/show).
additional_notes: "Ao" = "a" (to) + "o" (the), used with masculine singular places. Most often used with the verb "ir": "ir ao teatro" (to go to the theater). If you mean being physically inside the building, Portuguese often uses "no teatro" (in/at the theater).
target_language_example: A gente vai ao teatro no sábado para ver uma peça.
native_language_example: We’re going to the theater on Saturday to see a play.

meaning: “on the phone” (speaking on a phone call); also “to/at the phone” in expressions like atender ao telefone.
additional_notes: Most commonly used with verbs like falar/estar ao telefone (“to be on the phone”) and atender ao telefone (“to answer the phone”). It can describe someone who is calling or being spoken to on the line.
target_language_example: Eu estava ao telefone quando você ligou.
native_language_example: I was on the phone when you called.

meaning: to work; to the workplace; (as a command) “get to work!”
additional_notes: Contraction of "a + o" before a masculine singular noun: "ao". With "ir/chegar/voltar" it means going/arriving/returning to work (the workplace or your job). On its own ("Ao trabalho!") it’s a common, punchy way to tell people to start working.
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, voltamos ao trabalho.
native_language_example: After lunch, we go back to work.

additional_notes: Contraction of "a" (to) + "o" (the) → "ao". Used with verbs of going/arriving/taking someone somewhere (ir, chegar, levar) and in questions about transport (ônibus/trem) that goes to the zoo.
target_language_example: Vamos ao zoológico no sábado.
native_language_example: We're going to the zoo on Saturday.

meaning: on Sundays; every Sunday (as a routine).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens on Sundays in general or as a habit. It’s the plural form (literally “on the Sundays”), similar to English “on Sundays.” For a single specific Sunday, Portuguese often uses “no domingo” (e.g., “No domingo passado…” = “Last Sunday…”).
target_language_example: Aos domingos, a gente almoça com a família.
native_language_example: On Sundays, we have lunch with the family.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens on weekends in general (a repeated habit), not a specific weekend. Commonly used with routine actions: "Eu trabalho aos fins de semana" (I work weekends). You can also hear the singular form "ao fim de semana" in some varieties of Portuguese.
target_language_example: Aos fins de semana, a gente costuma descansar em casa.
native_language_example: On weekends, we usually rest at home.

additional_notes: Contraction of "a + os" = "aos". It’s used before a masculine plural noun with a possessive, like "meus irmãos" (my brothers) or "meus alunos" (my students). Common with verbs like "escrever" (write [to]), "recomendar" (recommend [to]), and "adicionar" (add [to]). For feminine plural, use "às minhas"; for singular, "ao meu" (masc.) and "à minha" (fem.).
target_language_example: Vou enviar o documento aos meus colegas ainda hoje.
native_language_example: I’m going to send the document to my coworkers later today.

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take the preposition "a" (to), especially when something is directed/given/shown/said to someone. It’s the contraction of "a" + "os" (to + the, plural masculine) + "meus pais" (my parents).
target_language_example: Vou ligar aos meus pais mais tarde.
native_language_example: I’m going to call my parents later.

meaning: to the others; to other people.
additional_notes: Contraction of the preposition "a" + plural masculine article "os" ("aos") + "outros" ("others"). Used with verbs that take "a" (like ajudar a, respeitar a, juntar-se a, perguntar a) to mean doing something *to/for* other people. "Aos outros" can refer to a specific group (“the others”) or people in general (“others”).
target_language_example: Não conte isso aos outros, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t tell the others that, please.

meaning: "to his/their" (masculine plural), or "to your" (plural/formal), before a masculine plural noun.
additional_notes: Contraction of "a" + "os seus". Used with nouns like: "aos seus serviços" (to his/their services), "aos seus princípios" (to his/their principles), "aos seus advogados" (to their lawyers), "aos seus postos" (to your posts). Person depends on context: it can mean to his/its/their, and in commands it can mean to your (especially plural or formal). Feminine plural is "às suas"; singular is "ao seu" (masc.) / "à sua" (fem.).
target_language_example: Enviei os documentos aos seus assistentes.
native_language_example: I sent the documents to his/their assistants.

meaning: to your parents / to his/her/their parents.
additional_notes: Used with verbs that take the preposition “a” (e.g., apresentar algo a alguém, pedir a alguém, obedecer a alguém, mentir a alguém). “Aos” = “a + os” (“to the”). “Seus” is ambiguous in Portuguese: it can mean “your” (especially formal “you” = você), “his,” “her,” or “their,” depending on context. If you need to be clearer, you can also say “aos pais dele/dela” (to his/her parents).
target_language_example: Ela contou a verdade aos seus pais.
native_language_example: She told the truth to her parents.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a habitual/regular action that happens on Saturdays (often meaning “every Saturday” or “on Saturdays in general,” depending on context). It’s the contraction of "a + os" ("to/on" + "the" plural) + "sábados". For one specific Saturday, you’ll usually hear "no sábado" (on Saturday) or "neste sábado" (this Saturday).
target_language_example: Eu trabalho aos sábados, mas folgo aos domingos.
native_language_example: I work on Saturdays, but I’m off on Sundays.

additional_notes: Used to say the age when something happened. Pattern: "aos + [number] + anos" (for most ages). With age 1, use "ao um ano"; with “year(s) old” as description, Portuguese often uses "ter": "Ele tinha treze anos" = “He was thirteen years old.”
target_language_example: Eu me mudei para outra cidade aos treze anos.
native_language_example: I moved to another city at thirteen.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar/ser" ("estou/sou apaixonado(a) por...") or "ficar" ("fiquei apaixonado(a) por..." = "I fell in love with..."). It agrees with the speaker: apaixonado (male) / apaixonada (female). "Por" introduces the person or thing you love/are passionate about.
target_language_example: Ela é apaixonada por música brasileira.
native_language_example: She’s crazy about Brazilian music.

meaning: "in love with her" / "has a crush on her".
additional_notes: Used to express romantic feelings toward a woman: *estar apaixonado por alguém* = “to be in love with someone.” **Apaixonado** agrees with the speaker (or subject): a woman would say **apaixonada por ela**; plural **apaixonados/apaixonadas**. Often intensified with **muito** (“very”).
target_language_example: Ele está apaixonado por ela há meses, mas ainda não contou.
native_language_example: He’s been in love with her for months, but he still hasn’t told her.

meaning: in love with you / in love with you (romantically).
additional_notes: Used to express romantic feelings toward the person you’re speaking to. It agrees with the speaker: apaixonado (male speaker) / apaixonada (female speaker). You can change the person too: apaixonado por ele/ela, apaixonado por você(s). In Portuguese, "estar apaixonado(a)" often suggests being in a state of being in love (sometimes intense), while "amar" can be deeper/longer-term depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu estou apaixonado por você há meses.
native_language_example: I've been in love with you for months.

additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb phrase “apaixonar-se por (alguém)”. It’s used for starting to love someone romantically: “Ela apaixonou-se por um homem” = “She fell in love with a man.” In Portuguese you can also say “apaixonou-se por uma…” (feminine) or drop the article: “apaixonou-se por ele/ela” (fell in love with him/her).
target_language_example: Ele apaixonou-se por uma colega de trabalho.
native_language_example: He fell in love with a coworker.

additional_notes: Usually used with the reflexive pronoun: **(ele/ela) se apaixonou por + person/thing**. It’s the **past tense** (pretérito perfeito) of **se apaixonar por** (“to fall in love with”). Most often romantic, but it can also mean becoming very fond of something (e.g., a city, a hobby).
target_language_example: Ele se apaixonou por ela muito rápido.
native_language_example: He fell in love with her very quickly.

additional_notes: Used to minimize or limit something: "apenas um + noun" = "just/only a + noun" (often implying it’s nothing special or that there is a limit). With countable nouns it can also mean "only one" (e.g., "Temos apenas um hospital" = "We have only one hospital").
target_language_example: Eu sou apenas um estudante tentando aprender português.
native_language_example: I'm just a student trying to learn Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there is a single thing (quantity = one). It agrees with a feminine noun that is understood or mentioned (e.g., uma verdade, uma pessoa). With “sou apenas uma…”, it can also mean “I’m just a/an…”, downplaying importance or status. For masculine nouns, use “apenas um”.
target_language_example: Tenho apenas uma pergunta.
native_language_example: I have only one question.

additional_notes: An instruction using the polite/command form (imperative) of apertar (“to press/squeeze”) for você. Very common on devices, elevators, alarms, and computers (e.g., “aperte o botão do mouse” = “click/press the mouse button”). In Portugal you may also see “carregue no botão.”
target_language_example: Para iniciar, aperte o botão verde.
native_language_example: To start, press the green button.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "apertar o botão" (to press the button). Used for a completed action; often followed by what happened next. The subject can be "ele" (he) or "ela" (she) and is sometimes omitted in Portuguese.
target_language_example: Ela apertou o botão e a porta abriu.
native_language_example: She pressed the button and the door opened.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast between a fact (“being” + adjective/noun) and what happens anyway. It’s followed by an infinitive (ser) + description: apesar de ser jovem/rico/pobre. You can also use the plural form when the subject is plural: apesar de serem...
target_language_example: Apesar de ser difícil, eu vou tentar de novo.
native_language_example: Despite being difficult, I’m going to try again.

additional_notes: Used to express a confident guess or strong belief about what’s true or what will happen. Often followed by a full clause: "Aposto que + [subject] + [verb]". You can also say "Eu aposto que…" for extra emphasis.
target_language_example: Aposto que você vai gostar deste lugar.
native_language_example: I bet you’ll like this place.

additional_notes: Used before a verb in the infinitive to talk about acquiring a new skill or ability: aprender a + infinitive (aprender a pedir, aprender a construir, aprender a usar). It can express need/advice with verbs like precisar/ter que/dever (e.g., “preciso aprender a…”, “você deveria aprender a…”).
target_language_example: Estou aprendendo a dirigir.
native_language_example: I’m learning to drive.

additional_notes: Used for learning the ability to speak a language (often followed by the language name: “aprender a falar holandês/esperanto”). After “começar a”, the verb may appear as “começou a aprender a falar…”.
target_language_example: Estou tentando aprender a falar português.
native_language_example: I’m trying to learn to speak Portuguese.

additional_notes: "Aprender a" + infinitive means “to learn to (do something).” Here, "falar francês" is “to speak French.” You can swap in another language or skill: "aprender a falar português", "aprender a nadar".
target_language_example: Estou tentando aprender a falar francês para a minha viagem.
native_language_example: I'm trying to learn to speak French for my trip.

additional_notes: Used when talking about studying or learning the German language. The verb is "aprender" (to learn) + the language name "alemão" (German). You can use different tenses (e.g., "estou a aprender alemão" / "estou aprendendo alemão" = I’m learning German; "quero aprender alemão" = I want to learn German).
target_language_example: Estou a aprender alemão online.
native_language_example: I’m learning German online.

additional_notes: A common, neutral phrase used to talk about learning in general (skills, information, experiences). You can change the verb to match the subject/tense (e.g., "eu aprendo", "você aprende", "aprendi") and swap in similar objects like "aprender algo novo" (learn something new) or "aprender coisas diferentes" (learn different things).
target_language_example: Estou sempre tentando aprender coisas novas no trabalho.
native_language_example: I'm always trying to learn new things at work.

additional_notes: Used to talk about studying/acquiring the French language. After "aprender" you can name a language (aprender português, aprender inglês) or use a verb with "a" (aprender a nadar = to learn to swim).
target_language_example: Estou tentando aprender francês para viajar para a França.
native_language_example: I'm trying to learn French to travel to France.

additional_notes: Used to talk about studying/learning the English language. It’s a common verb + language pattern: aprender + [idioma] (e.g., aprender português). After prepositions/expressions like “estar interessado em”, Portuguese often uses “em + infinitive”: interessado em aprender inglês.
target_language_example: Eu quero aprender inglês para viajar e trabalhar.
native_language_example: I want to learn English to travel and work.

additional_notes: A common, neutral phrase. "Aprender" = "to learn"; "língua" = "language" (often used for spoken language); "estrangeira" = "foreign." You can swap in another adjective: "aprender uma língua nova" (a new language) or name the language: "aprender português / inglês". Often used with expressions like "requer" (requires), "é difícil" (is difficult), and time phrases like "em pouco tempo" (in a short time).
target_language_example: Estou tentando aprender uma língua estrangeira para viajar.
native_language_example: I'm trying to learn a foreign language to travel.

meaning: 'learned to' (did something for the first time; gained the ability).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to say someone learned how to do something: "aprendeu a + verb" (e.g., aprendeu a ler, aprendeu a tocar). It’s the past tense (Pretérito Perfeito) of "aprender" for ele/ela/você. Other common forms: "aprendi a" (I learned to), "aprendeu a" (he/she/you learned to), "aprenderam a" (they learned to).
target_language_example: Ela aprendeu a cozinhar sozinha.
native_language_example: She learned to cook by herself.

additional_notes: Past tense: “(he/she) learned to drive.” Used to talk about when or where someone got the skill of driving (usually a car). You can change the person: eu aprendi (I learned), você aprendeu (you learned), nós aprendemos (we learned). Related negative: nunca aprendeu a dirigir = “never learned to drive.”
target_language_example: Eu aprendi a dirigir no ano passado.
native_language_example: I learned to drive last year.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "aprender" (to learn) in the past ("aprendeu" = he/she/you [formal] learned) + "a" + infinitive to say someone learned how to do something. "isso" means "that/this" depending on context; you can replace it with a verb phrase (e.g., "aprendeu a cozinhar") or a noun phrase (e.g., "aprendeu a fazer pão").
target_language_example: Ela aprendeu a fazer isso assistindo a vídeos na internet.
native_language_example: She learned to do that by watching videos on the internet.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **aprender**: **ele/ela/você aprendeu** = “(he/she/you) learned.” Used to talk about the moment or period when someone acquired the skill of swimming. You can change the subject: **eu aprendi a nadar** (I learned to swim), **nós aprendemos a nadar** (we learned to swim).
target_language_example: Eu aprendi a nadar quando tinha oito anos.
native_language_example: I learned to swim when I was eight years old.

additional_notes: Past (pretérito perfeito) form of the verb aprender (“to learn”), used for a completed action. "Aprendeu" is 3rd person singular, so it can refer to ele/ela (he/she) or to você (you, informal/formal depending on region). You can add details with em + time period (em três meses = in three months) or com/a (with) to explain how someone learned.
target_language_example: Ela aprendeu francês na escola.
native_language_example: She learned French at school.

additional_notes: Used to say you gained a lot of knowledge or understanding about a topic, place, person, or culture. It’s the past tense (eu aprendi) + muito (“a lot”) + sobre (“about”). You can change the subject/person: "aprendi" (I), "aprendeu" (he/she/you formal), "aprendemos" (we), "aprenderam" (they).
target_language_example: Aprendi muito sobre a história do Brasil na escola.
native_language_example: I learned a lot about the history of Brazil at school.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than a point in time or event: após a aula, após a escola, após a meia-noite. 'Após' is a more formal/common-in-writing option; in everyday speech people often use 'depois da'. It contracts with articles: após a (feminine singular), após o (masculine singular), após as (feminine plural), após os (masculine plural).
target_language_example: Após a reunião, vamos jantar.
native_language_example: After the meeting, we'll have dinner.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens after someone dies or about life/the afterlife. You’ll often see it expanded as “após a morte de + [person]” (“after the death of [person]”). Similar in meaning to “depois da morte”.
target_language_example: Muitas pessoas acreditam em vida após a morte.
native_language_example: Many people believe in life after death.

meaning: 'that girl' (a specific girl over there / not here).
additional_notes: Uses the feminine demonstrative "aquela" (that, over there) + "garota" (girl). Common for pointing out or referring to a particular girl who is not close to the speaker. For someone nearer, you often hear "esta/essa garota" depending on region/context.
target_language_example: Quem é aquela garota ali?
native_language_example: Who is that girl over there?

meaning: 'that woman' (a woman over there / a specific woman not near the speaker).
additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative "aquela" (feminine singular) to point to or refer back to a particular woman, often someone farther away, not present, or not emotionally/physically close to the speaker. It can also refer to someone already mentioned in the conversation. Contrast: "esta mulher" (this woman, near me), "essa mulher" (that woman, near you/previously mentioned), "aquela mulher" (that woman over there).
target_language_example: Quem é aquela mulher que está falando com o João?
native_language_example: Who is that woman who is talking with João?

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative "aquele" (“that”, usually someone/something not close to the speaker) + the informal noun "cara" (“guy/dude”). Common when pointing someone out or talking about a particular man everyone knows from context; it can sound negative depending on tone (e.g., "Odeio aquele cara"). More neutral alternatives: "aquele homem" (that man).
target_language_example: Você viu aquele cara ali na porta?
native_language_example: Did you see that guy over there at the door?

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative "aquele" to point to something farther away (in space, time, or in the conversation), often contrasted with "este" (this) and "esse" (that near you/previously mentioned, depending on dialect). You can add "lá" to emphasize distance: "aquele carro lá" = "that car over there."
target_language_example: Eu não quero este; eu quero aquele carro.
native_language_example: I don’t want this one; I want that car.

meaning: 'that man' (over there; not close to the speaker).
additional_notes: Used to point out a specific man that is farther away, often with location words like ali/lá (“over there”). It contrasts with este homem (“this man,” near me) and esse homem (“that man,” near you/near what we’re talking about, depending on region).
target_language_example: Quem é aquele homem de casaco azul?
native_language_example: Who is that man in the blue coat?

meaning: "that book" (the one over there / not near the speaker).
additional_notes: "Aquele" is a demonstrative used to point to something farther away, or something already known/mentioned. It agrees with the noun: aquele (masc. sing.), aquela (fem. sing.), aqueles/aquelas (plural). Contrast: "este/esta" (this, near me) and often "esse/essa" (that, near you or previously mentioned, depending on region).
target_language_example: Você pode me emprestar aquele livro?
native_language_example: Can you lend me that book?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific person (or a general type of person) who does something. Often appears in sayings/proverbs and can sound formal or literary. It agrees with gender and number: aquele que (m.sg.), aquela que (f.sg.), aqueles que (m.pl.), aquelas que (f.pl.).
target_language_example: Aquela que chegou primeiro escolheu o melhor lugar.
native_language_example: The one who arrived first chose the best seat.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of people defined by what comes after "que". It’s the masculine plural form; it can include mixed-gender groups. Feminine plural is "aquelas que" (those who, feminine). Often used in sayings and general statements.
target_language_example: Aqueles que estudam todos os dias aprendem mais rápido.
native_language_example: Those who study every day learn faster.

additional_notes: Used to point out or identify things/people that are farther away or previously mentioned. It’s the masculine plural form, so it pairs with plural masculine nouns (or mixed-gender groups): Aqueles são os livros... Contrast with estes são os (“these are the”, near the speaker). For feminine plural nouns, use: Aquelas são as (e.g., Aquelas são as minhas chaves).
target_language_example: Aqueles são os nossos professores.
native_language_example: Those are our teachers.

additional_notes: Used to politely tell someone to do something in this spot (e.g., sign here, sit here, wait here). It often comes at the end of the instruction: "Assine aqui, por favor." In speech you may also hear "aqui por favor" (without the comma).
target_language_example: Pode deixar a mala aqui, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you leave the suitcase here, please?

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stay/wait in this place until the speaker returns. Often appears after the verb "esperar" (to wait): "Espere aqui até eu voltar". "Até" = "until"; "eu voltar" = "I return/come back" (literal: "I return"). You may also hear "aqui até eu retornar" (more formal) or "aqui até eu voltar" with singular/plural commands: "Espere" (you, singular) / "Esperem" (you all).
target_language_example: Fique aqui até eu voltar, por favor.
native_language_example: Stay here until I come back, please.

additional_notes: Used when you’re handing something over, introducing someone, or indicating that something has arrived or is located here. Often followed by a noun or name (Aqui está a minha bagagem.) or used alone with a pronoun (Aqui está ela!). In speech, you may hear it with a pause: “Aqui está, querido.”
target_language_example: Aqui está o seu recibo.
native_language_example: Here is your receipt.

additional_notes: Used when talking about repeating the same action or behavior (“do that again”). Often refers to something already known from context and is frequently used for something annoying, wrong, or not allowed: “Não faz aquilo de novo” = “Don’t do that again.”
target_language_example: Por favor, não faz aquilo de novo.
native_language_example: Please, don’t do that again.

meaning: 'That (over there) is a…' / 'Is that (over there) a…?' (masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or ask about something far from both the speaker and listener. It’s made of: aquIlo (“that over there”) + é (“is”) + um (“a/an” for masculine nouns). For feminine nouns, use "aquilo é uma" (e.g., "Aquilo é uma casa?"). In questions, Portuguese often relies on intonation (rising tone) rather than changing word order.
target_language_example: Aquilo é um restaurante?
native_language_example: Is that (over there) a restaurant?

meaning: air conditioning; an air conditioner (AC) unit.
additional_notes: Refers both to the system/feature (“air conditioning”) and the appliance/unit (“an air conditioner”). Commonly used with verbs like "ligar" (turn on), "desligar" (turn off), "funcionar" (work), and "consumir" (use/consume energy). In Brazil, people often shorten it to "ar" in casual speech (e.g., "Liga o ar").
target_language_example: Você pode desligar o ar-condicionado, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you turn off the air conditioner, please?

additional_notes: Used with the verb **arrepender-se** (to regret): **(eu) me arrependo de ter + past participle**. The **de ter** introduces a past action (something you did before): *Me arrependo de ter dito isso* = “I regret having said that.” In questions you’ll often see **Você se arrepende de ter…?**
target_language_example: Eu me arrependo de ter falado aquilo.
native_language_example: I regret having said that.

additional_notes: Feminine plural noun phrase: singular is "a abelha" (the bee). Used with the definite article "as" when talking about bees in general or about a known group of bees. Common in nature/farming contexts (honey, stings, flowers).
target_language_example: As abelhas são importantes para as plantas.
native_language_example: Bees are important for plants.

additional_notes: Feminine plural definite form: singular is “a arma” (the weapon). Used for weapons in general (guns, knives, etc.) and also for types like “armas nucleares” (nuclear weapons). Common in commands: “Abaixem as armas!” (Lower your weapons!), “Solte as armas.” (Drop the weapons.).
target_language_example: Por favor, deixe as armas no carro.
native_language_example: Please leave the weapons in the car.

additional_notes: Plural with the feminine definite article: a aula (a class/lesson) → as aulas (the classes). Used for school classes in general (e.g., when the term starts again) or for specific course sessions: as aulas de português = Portuguese classes. Common verbs: começar/recomeçar (start/restart), ir para (go to), faltar/pular (miss/skip).
target_language_example: Hoje não vou às aulas porque estou doente.
native_language_example: Today I’m not going to class because I’m sick.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the start time/date of school classes (the beginning of the school term or of a day’s classes). It’s the plural feminine subject "as aulas" (the classes) + the verb "começam" (they start). Often followed by a day/date ("amanhã", "dia oito de abril") or a time ("às oito e meia").
target_language_example: As aulas começam na próxima segunda-feira.
native_language_example: Classes start next Monday.

additional_notes: "As" is the feminine plural form of "the" in Portuguese. "Batata" (potato) is feminine, so the plural is "as batatas". Often used in cooking instructions (cut, slice, boil, etc.). If you mean sweet potatoes, you usually say "batata-doce" (plural: "as batatas-doces").
target_language_example: Vou descascar as batatas antes do jantar.
native_language_example: I’m going to peel the potatoes before dinner.

additional_notes: “As cartas” can mean (1) letters/messages (often physical mail), or (2) playing cards, depending on context. With verbs like “chegar” (arrive), “ler” (read), “enviar” (send), it usually means letters. With “embaralhar” (shuffle) or “dar as cartas” (deal the cards), it means playing cards. “Dar as cartas” can also be used figuratively as “to call the shots,” but in card-game contexts it’s literally “to deal the cards.”
target_language_example: Você já leu as cartas que eu mandei?
native_language_example: Have you read the letters I sent?

additional_notes: Used for more than one key (e.g., house keys, car keys). Often appears in requests/commands like "Dê-me as chaves" (Give me the keys) or with prepositions: "as chaves de vocês" (your keys), "as chaves ao seu irmão" (the keys to your brother), "as chaves na mesa" (the keys on the table). Singular: "a chave" = "the key".
target_language_example: Você viu onde deixei as chaves?
native_language_example: Did you see where I left the keys?

additional_notes: Means the keys of a car. Very common in requests: "Dê-me/Me dá as chaves do carro" (“Give me the car keys”). You can also say "a chave do carro" for “the car key” (singular).
target_language_example: Você viu as chaves do carro?
native_language_example: Have you seen the car keys?

additional_notes: Means the keys that belong to his car. "as chaves" = "the keys" (plural), "do carro" = "of the car" / "car's", and "dele" = "his" (referring to a male owner). You’ll often hear similar patterns like "as chaves do meu carro" (my car keys) or "as chaves do carro dela" (her car keys).
target_language_example: Você viu as chaves do carro dele?
native_language_example: Have you seen his car keys?

additional_notes: Plural of "a coisa". Often used very generally to talk about stuff, issues, or how a situation is going (e.g., "deixar as coisas como estão" = leave things as they are; "complicar as coisas" = complicate things; "acertar as coisas" = sort things out). It can also mean physical objects you can move around.
target_language_example: Vamos resolver as coisas amanhã.
native_language_example: Let's sort things out tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about reality or the true situation, often in set phrases like “as coisas como elas são” (“things as they are”) or “as coisas como elas eram” (“things as they were”). Common with verbs like aceitar (“accept”) and dizer (“say/tell”), meaning accepting reality or telling it straight. Typically followed by “são/eram” (or another form of ser).
target_language_example: Prefiro ver as coisas como elas são, mesmo quando é difícil.
native_language_example: I prefer to see things as they are, even when it’s hard.

meaning: “things are…” / “things are going…” (talking about how a situation is).
additional_notes: Used to describe the current state or direction of events in a general way (work, life, a relationship, a situation). It’s often followed by an adjective or expression like bem (well), diferentes (different), melhorando (improving), ficando fora de controle (getting out of control). In questions like “As coisas estão bem…?”, it means “Are things okay…?”.
target_language_example: Ultimamente, as coisas estão complicadas no trabalho.
native_language_example: Lately, things have been complicated at work.

additional_notes: Used to say a situation ended differently than expected. It’s typically followed by what someone expected: “as coisas não saíram como eu esperava” (things didn’t turn out the way I hoped/expected). The verb “sair” here means “to turn out” (result), not just “to leave/go out.”
target_language_example: Desculpa, mas as coisas não saíram como a gente planejou.
native_language_example: Sorry, but things didn’t turn out the way we planned.

meaning: “things are going to…” / “things will…” (talking about how a situation will develop).
additional_notes: Used to predict or expect what will happen next with “things” as a general subject (the situation, events). Usually followed by an infinitive (e.g., vão esquentar = are going to heat up) or by another verb phrase like “dar certo” (work out), “ficar bem” (be okay), “funcionar” (work). Often translates naturally as “things will…”.
target_language_example: Calma — as coisas vão melhorar.
native_language_example: Calm down — things are going to get better.

additional_notes: Definite plural feminine: singular is "a cortina". Common with verbs like "fechar" (to close) and "abrir" (to open), especially as a polite request or instruction: "Pode fechar as cortinas?" / "Feche as cortinas."
target_language_example: À noite, a gente fecha as cortinas para ter mais privacidade.
native_language_example: At night, we close the curtains to have more privacy.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the physical back (body part): "machucar as costas" (hurt your back), "quebrar as costas" (break your back), "curvar as costas" (bend/hunch your back). In the expression "dar as costas (a alguém)", it means to turn your back on someone (often implying ignoring or rejecting them).
target_language_example: Não consigo levantar peso porque machuquei as costas.
native_language_example: I can’t lift heavy things because I hurt my back.

additional_notes: Definite plural: "as" = "the" (feminine plural) + "crianças" = children/kids. Even though "criança" is grammatically feminine, "as crianças" can refer to a mixed group of boys and girls. Common with verbs in the plural (e.g., "as crianças querem...").
target_language_example: As crianças estão no parque com a professora.
native_language_example: The children are at the park with the teacher.

additional_notes: “As crianças” = “the children” (feminine plural). “Estavam” is the imperfect past of “estar,” used for ongoing/repeated past situations or descriptions (e.g., location, condition, feelings). It’s often followed by a place (“no parque”), an adjective (“famintas”), or a gerund to show an action in progress (“estavam brincando” = “were playing”).
target_language_example: As crianças estavam cansadas depois da escola.
native_language_example: The children were tired after school.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar (estão = “are”) to talk about the children’s current state/feeling or location (temporary/at the moment): As crianças estão cansadas. / As crianças estão em casa. Note: crianças is grammatically feminine plural, so adjectives usually agree (desapontadas, cansadas).
target_language_example: As crianças estão com fome agora.
native_language_example: The children are hungry now.

additional_notes: Uses the present continuous (estar + gerund) to say an action is happening right now. "As crianças" = "the children" (plural), and "brincando" is the gerund of "brincar" (to play). Often followed by a place: "na areia" (in the sand), "na piscina" (in the pool), "no jardim" (in the garden), "no parque" (in the park).
target_language_example: As crianças estão brincando lá fora.
native_language_example: The children are playing outside.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "gostar de" (= to like), which is followed by a verb in the infinitive (gostam de brincar, pular, ver) or a noun (gostam de sorvete). "As crianças" is the subject (“the children”), and "gostam" is plural (“they like”). In questions, you’ll often see "O que as crianças gostam de fazer?" = “What do children like to do?”
target_language_example: As crianças gostam de desenhar depois da escola.
native_language_example: The children like to draw after school.

meaning: "the children need" (followed by what they need).
additional_notes: "Precisar de" means "to need" and is followed by the preposition "de" before a noun, pronoun, or infinitive verb (e.g., "precisam de você", "precisam de uma casa"). "As crianças" = "the children"; "precisam" is the plural form used with "crianças".
target_language_example: As crianças precisam de ajuda agora.
native_language_example: The children need help now.

additional_notes: Used to refer to two feminine people/things (explicitly named or understood from context). It agrees with feminine nouns: as duas garotas (“the two girls”), as duas coisas (“the two things”). For masculine, use os dois; for mixed gender groups, os dois is common.
target_language_example: Eu vou levar as duas camisetas.
native_language_example: I’m going to take both T-shirts.

additional_notes: Plural feminine noun phrase: singular is "a escada" (the stair/the staircase) and plural is "as escadas" (the stairs). Very common with verbs of movement, especially "subir as escadas" (to go up the stairs) and "descer as escadas" (to go down the stairs).
target_language_example: O elevador não está funcionando, então vamos pelas escadas.
native_language_example: The elevator isn’t working, so we’ll take the stairs.

additional_notes: Plural of "a estrela" (a star). Used for stars in the sky, often in poetic or symbolic language (e.g., destiny, dreams). Common after prepositions like "sob" (under) and "para" (to/toward).
target_language_example: Hoje dá para ver as estrelas bem claras.
native_language_example: Today you can see the stars really clearly.

additional_notes: Plural feminine definite article + noun: "as" = "the" (for feminine plural nouns), "flores" = "flowers". Used to talk about specific flowers in a context (e.g., in a garden, in a vase, or in general in a sentence about nature). Singular is "a flor" (the flower).
target_language_example: Eu gosto de regar as flores de manhã.
native_language_example: I like to water the flowers in the morning.

additional_notes: Plural of "a folha" (leaf). Used for leaves on trees and plants, especially in contexts like autumn/fall when they change color and fall. In Portuguese, "folha" can also mean a sheet of paper, but in these examples it clearly means plant leaves.
target_language_example: No outono, as folhas caem das árvores.
native_language_example: In autumn, the leaves fall from the trees.

additional_notes: "Ficar" + adjective often means “to become/turn” (a change of state): "As folhas ficam vermelhas" = “The leaves turn red.” It can also mean “to stay/remain,” depending on context. "As folhas" means “the leaves” (plural), and "ficam" is present tense, often used for general facts (e.g., seasonal changes).
target_language_example: No outono, as folhas ficam marrons e caem no chão.
native_language_example: In autumn, the leaves turn brown and fall to the ground.

meaning: "the photos that" (introduces more information about which photos).
additional_notes: Used with the relative pronoun "que" to connect "as fotos" to a description/clause that identifies them: "as fotos que você tirou" = "the photos (that) you took". In Portuguese, "que" is very common and usually not omitted (even when English can drop "that").
target_language_example: Você ainda tem as fotos que tiramos na praia?
native_language_example: Do you still have the photos (that) we took at the beach?

additional_notes: A feminine plural noun almost always used in the plural: "as férias" = vacation time (school break, time off work). Common with "passar as férias" (to spend the vacation) and "entrar de férias" (to go on vacation). In Brazil it often means vacation; in Portugal "férias" is also used, while "as férias" can overlap with "as férias escolares" (school holidays).
target_language_example: Vamos passar as férias em julho.
native_language_example: We’re going to spend our vacation in July.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the school (or work) break that happens in summer. Usually plural in Portuguese: "as férias". Common with verbs like "começar" (to start) and "acabar" (to end): "As férias de verão começam..." / "acabaram".
target_language_example: Mal posso esperar pelas férias de verão.
native_language_example: I can’t wait for summer vacation.

additional_notes: Feminine plural definite noun phrase: "as" = "the" (feminine plural) + "garotas" = "girls" (often implying younger girls). Common in casual speech; a more neutral alternative is "as meninas".
target_language_example: As garotas estão prontas para sair.
native_language_example: The girls are ready to go out.

additional_notes: Feminine plural definite form: a janela (a window) → as janelas (the windows). Common with verbs like abrir (to open), fechar (to close), lavar/limpar (to wash/clean). Also appears in metaphors, e.g., "Os olhos são as janelas do coração" ("Eyes are the windows of the heart").
target_language_example: No verão, deixamos as janelas abertas para entrar ar fresco.
native_language_example: In the summer, we leave the windows open to let fresh air in.

additional_notes: "As" = "the" (feminine plural), "janelas" = "windows", "abertas" = "open" (feminine plural, agreeing with "janelas"). Often used with verbs like "deixar" (to leave) and "dormir" (to sleep): "Deixe as janelas abertas" = "Leave the windows open."
target_language_example: No verão, deixamos as janelas abertas para entrar ar fresco.
native_language_example: In the summer, we leave the windows open to let fresh air in.

additional_notes: Feminine plural noun phrase: singular is "a luz" (the light). Common with verbs like "acender" (to turn on/light), "apagar" (to turn off), and adjectives like "acesas" (on/lit) and "apagadas" (off). Often refers to the lights in a room/house.
target_language_example: Você pode apagar as luzes, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you turn off the lights, please?

meaning: the lights went out / turned off (suddenly).
additional_notes: Common way to describe lights stopping unexpectedly (e.g., a power outage). Uses the reflexive "se" to express that something happened by itself (no person mentioned as turning them off). "Apagaram" is past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "apagar".
target_language_example: As luzes se apagaram no meio do filme.
native_language_example: The lights went out in the middle of the movie.

additional_notes: "As" is the feminine plural form of “the”, and "malas" is the plural of "mala". Used most often when talking about luggage (suitcases, travel bags). Common with verbs like levar (to carry/take), ajudar com (to help with), and fazer as malas (to pack).
target_language_example: Onde estão as malas?
native_language_example: Where are the suitcases?

additional_notes: Used to refer to specific apples already known from context. "as" is the feminine plural definite article (“the”), and "maçãs" is the plural of "maçã" (“apple”). Often used when talking about apples you bought, see, or mentioned before.
target_language_example: Vou lavar as maçãs antes de comer.
native_language_example: I’m going to wash the apples before eating.

additional_notes: Definite article + plural noun. Used to refer to a specific group of girls (or “the female kids/young women”) already known from context. It’s the plural of “a menina” (the girl). In object position it appears after prepositions, e.g., “para as meninas” = “for/to the girls”.
target_language_example: As meninas estão na escola.
native_language_example: The girls are at school.

meaning: "my" (feminine plural), used before feminine plural nouns.
additional_notes: It’s the feminine plural possessive form of "meu/minha" and usually comes with the feminine plural definite article "as". Use it with feminine plural nouns: "as minhas maçãs" (my apples), "as minhas mãos" (my hands), "as minhas malas" (my suitcases). In Portuguese, the possessive agrees with the noun (feminine/masculine, singular/plural), not with the speaker.
target_language_example: Você viu as minhas chaves?
native_language_example: Have you seen my keys?

additional_notes: Feminine plural: use when talking about a group of friends who are women/girls (or a mixed group if you’re choosing the feminine form). Often used with a verb like "chamar" (to call) or "conhecer" (to meet/know). In Brazilian Portuguese, object pronouns like "me" may come before the verb ("me chamam").
target_language_example: Vou sair com as minhas amigas hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I’m going out with my (female) friends tonight.

additional_notes: Plural feminine noun phrase: "as" = "the" (plural feminine) + "minhas" = "my" + "chaves" = "keys". Common in everyday situations like losing, forgetting, or asking where you put your keys. Often used with verbs like "esquecer" (to forget), "ver" (to see), "colocar" (to put), and "estar com" (to have/be holding).
target_language_example: Não encontro as minhas chaves.
native_language_example: I can't find my keys.

additional_notes: Plural feminine noun with the definite article: "a mulher" = "the woman"; "as mulheres" = "the women". Used to talk about women as a specific group in general statements or comparisons (often paired with "os homens" = "the men").
target_language_example: As mulheres da minha família moram perto daqui.
native_language_example: The women in my family live near here.

meaning: “women like” / “women enjoy” (followed by a person, thing, or an activity).
additional_notes: "Gostar de" is the common way to say "to like" in Portuguese and it requires "de". After "de" you can use: a noun (de rosas), an infinitive verb (de falar), or a person name (de Tom). This phrase starts with "as mulheres" (“women” / “the women”), which is plural and feminine; the verb changes with the subject (e.g., "A mulher gosta de" for one woman).
target_language_example: As mulheres gostam de música brasileira.
native_language_example: Women like Brazilian music.

additional_notes: Used to make general statements about women. "As" is the plural feminine definite article (“the”), and "mulheres" means “women.” "São" is the present tense (they/you-plural are) of the verb "ser" (“to be”), used for identity and general characteristics.
target_language_example: As mulheres são importantes na sociedade.
native_language_example: Women are important in society.

additional_notes: A general statement: "As mulheres" = "women" (generic/plural), "vivem" = "(they) live", and "mais" = "more/longer". It’s commonly completed with a comparison using "(do) que": "As mulheres vivem mais (do) que os homens" = "Women live longer than men." In everyday speech, "mais que" is often used instead of the more formal "mais do que".
target_language_example: Em muitos lugares, as mulheres vivem mais do que os homens.
native_language_example: In many places, women live longer than men.

additional_notes: Plural of "a mão" (hand). Used for body parts (e.g., "lave as mãos" = wash your hands). In some expressions it can be part of idiomatic meanings, like "pôr as mãos em" (to get your hands on / lay hands on) and "tomar as mãos de alguém" (to take someone’s hands).
target_language_example: Lave as mãos antes de comer.
native_language_example: Wash your hands before eating.

additional_notes: Plural of "a noite" ("the night"). Used for nights in general or repeatedly (e.g., "during the nights" / "at night" in a general sense). Often appears with weather or seasons ("noites frias", "noites mais longas"). Not to be confused with "boa noite" (a greeting: "good evening/good night").
target_language_example: No inverno, as noites são mais frias aqui.
native_language_example: In winter, the nights are colder here.

additional_notes: Feminine plural form of the possessive 'nosso/a(s)' + the feminine plural article 'as'. Used with feminine plural nouns: 'as nossas roupas' = 'our clothes'. Contrast: 'os nossos' (masculine plural), 'a nossa' (feminine singular), 'o nosso' (masculine singular).
target_language_example: Onde estão as nossas chaves?
native_language_example: Where are our keys?

additional_notes: Literally “the our lives”: definite article + possessive + plural noun. Use it to talk about the shared lives/experiences of the speaker and others (“we/us”). Often appears with verbs like mudar (to change), arruinar (to ruin), imaginar (to imagine), and in “sem…” (without…) comparisons.
target_language_example: As nossas vidas são melhores quando passamos tempo juntos.
native_language_example: Our lives are better when we spend time together.

additional_notes: Plural feminine form of "notícia". Used for news in general or specific pieces of news/information: "escutar as notícias" (listen to the news), "surpresa com as notícias" (surprised by the news). In Portuguese it’s normally plural when talking about the news as a category.
target_language_example: Vou assistir às notícias depois do jantar.
native_language_example: I’m going to watch the news after dinner.

additional_notes: Definite plural: used for clouds in the sky. Singular is "a nuvem"; plural is "as nuvens". Very common in weather talk (e.g., clouds disappearing, darkening, being blown away). Sometimes used poetically, as in "as nuvens estão chorando" = “the clouds are crying” (it’s raining).
target_language_example: Hoje as nuvens estão bem baixas.
native_language_example: Today the clouds are very low.

additional_notes: Plural definite form of "a palavra" (word). Used to refer to words in general (spoken or written), or to specific text/phrases (e.g., words on a sign). Often appears in expressions about speech and communication, like "as palavras machucam" (words hurt) or "jogar com as palavras" (to play with words).
target_language_example: Escolha bem as palavras antes de falar.
native_language_example: Choose your words carefully before speaking.

additional_notes: Plural definite form of "parede" (wall). Used when talking about the walls of a room, apartment, building, etc. Often appears with "de" to specify which walls: "as paredes do quarto" (the bedroom walls). Singular: "a parede"; without the article: "paredes" = walls in general.
target_language_example: As paredes da sala precisam de pintura.
native_language_example: The living room walls need painting.

additional_notes: Plural definite form of "a pergunta" (a question). Used when talking about specific questions that are known from context (e.g., in an interview, a test, or a meeting). Often appears with verbs like "fazer" (to ask/pose) and "responder" (to answer).
target_language_example: No final, vou responder às perguntas.
native_language_example: In the end, I’m going to answer the questions.

additional_notes: Plural definite form of "a perna" (leg). Used for people and animals, and also in common body-related phrases (e.g., tired legs, breaking your legs). Often appears with possessives like "as minhas pernas" (my legs) or with "dele/dela" to mean "his/her legs."
target_language_example: Depois da corrida, as pernas estavam doloridas.
native_language_example: After the run, my legs were sore.

additional_notes: Plural of pessoa (“person”), with the definite article as (“the”, feminine plural). Often used to talk about people in general (e.g., “As pessoas dizem…” = “People say…”). If you mean specific people, context usually makes it clear; you can also specify with a phrase like “as pessoas daqui” (“the people from here”).
target_language_example: Às vezes, as pessoas não entendem o que eu quero dizer.
native_language_example: Sometimes people don’t understand what I mean.

meaning: 'people are' (people + the verb 'to be' in the present).
additional_notes: Used to describe what people are doing or how they are feeling right now. "As pessoas" = "the people" (often just "people" in English). "Estão" is the present tense of "estar" (temporary states/actions), commonly followed by a gerund (-ando/-endo/-indo) for ongoing actions (e.g., "estão escutando" = "are listening") or an adjective for a current condition (e.g., "estão preocupadas" = "are worried").
target_language_example: As pessoas estão esperando o ônibus.
native_language_example: People are waiting for the bus.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what people (in general) enjoy or like. After "gostam de" you typically use an infinitive verb (gostam de brigar = like to fight) or a noun/pronoun (gostam de golfe = like golf; gostam de ti = like you). In Portuguese, "gostar" normally takes "de" (you don’t say *gostam golfe*).
target_language_example: As pessoas gostam de música ao vivo.
native_language_example: People like live music.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what people in general need or must do. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., reconhecer, saber, conversar). You can use it to give advice, make a general rule, or state a necessity.
target_language_example: Às vezes, as pessoas precisam parar e respirar.
native_language_example: Sometimes, people need to stop and breathe.

meaning: "the people who" (introduces a relative clause about people).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific group of people and then describe them with a clause starting with "que" (who/that). Very common in statements and questions: "As pessoas que..." / "Quem são as pessoas que...?".
target_language_example: As pessoas que moram aqui são muito simpáticas.
native_language_example: The people who live here are very nice.

additional_notes: Used to talk about people in general. "As" is the plural feminine "the" and "pessoas" is "people"; together they mean "the people" (often just "people" in English). "São" is the present tense of "ser" (to be) for "they" (3rd person plural). Common in general statements: "As pessoas são diferentes" = "People are different."
target_language_example: Aqui, as pessoas são muito simpáticas.
native_language_example: Here, people are very friendly.

meaning: “people will / people are going to” (talking about what people will do or how they’ll react).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by an infinitive: “As pessoas vão + verb” (e.g., vão rir, vão ver). In Portuguese, “ir” (vão) is often used like “going to” in English to express a future outcome, prediction, or likely reaction.
target_language_example: Se você chegar atrasado, as pessoas vão reclamar.
native_language_example: If you arrive late, people will complain.

additional_notes: Definite article + plural noun: "as" = "the" for feminine plural nouns; singular is "a planta" (the plant). Used for plants in general or specific plants in context (e.g., houseplants, garden plants).
target_language_example: Eu rego as plantas todos os dias.
native_language_example: I water the plants every day.

additional_notes: Definite article + plural noun: "as" = "the" (feminine plural), "portas" = "doors". Used for literal doors (e.g., elevator doors), and also in phrases like "as portas de X" = "the doors of X". In Brazilian Portuguese, "porta" can also mean a "doorway/entrance" depending on context.
target_language_example: As portas do metrô se fecharam antes de eu entrar.
native_language_example: The subway doors closed before I got in.

additional_notes: Used with a plural noun: a regra (a rule) → as regras (the rules). Very common with verbs like cumprir (follow/comply with), explicar (explain), conhecer/saber (know), esquecer (forget), and observar (observe/follow). Often followed by “de + [something]”: as regras do jogo = the rules of the game.
target_language_example: Antes de começar, precisamos revisar as regras.
native_language_example: Before we start, we need to review the rules.

additional_notes: Plural feminine noun with the definite article: roupa (singular) → a roupa; roupas (plural) → as roupas. Commonly used for clothes in general, laundry, or a set of garments someone owns/wears (e.g., “as roupas da Susan” = “Susan’s clothes”).
target_language_example: Vou guardar as roupas no armário depois que secarem.
native_language_example: I’m going to put the clothes away in the closet after they dry.

additional_notes: Definite plural: a(s) + rua(s). Used to talk about streets in general in a city/area or the streets around you. Often appears with descriptions like cheias de gente (crowded), cobertas de neve (covered in snow), vazias (empty). Singular: a rua (“the street”).
target_language_example: À noite, as ruas do centro ficam mais vazias.
native_language_example: At night, the streets downtown get emptier.

additional_notes: Used to talk to or about a group of women in a polite/formal way. "as senhoras" = "the ladies" (or formal/plural "you" for women). "estão" is the present tense of "estar" (to be), used for temporary states/conditions (e.g., thirsty, tired), location (here), and ongoing actions with "a" + infinitive ("estão a ler" = "are reading").
target_language_example: As senhoras estão prontas para começar?
native_language_example: Are you ladies ready to start?

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to show possession: as suas amigas (your friends), as suas bonecas (her dolls), as suas opções (his options). It agrees with the thing possessed (feminine plural), not with who possesses it. In Portuguese, “seu/sua/seus/suas” can mean your, his, her, or its depending on context; to be clearer, people may use “as tuas” (your, informal in Portugal) or “as dela/dele” (hers/his).
target_language_example: Você trouxe as suas chaves?
native_language_example: Did you bring your keys?

additional_notes: "as" = "the" (feminine plural), "suas" = "your" (feminine plural), and "roupas" = "clothes". It’s used when speaking to someone directly (your clothes) or in a more formal way; in everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often use "as roupas de você" instead. "Suas" agrees with "roupas" (not with the person).
target_language_example: Você pode dobrar as suas roupas depois de secarem?
native_language_example: Can you fold your clothes after they dry?

meaning: "your" (feminine plural) in European Portuguese; "your" (informal, singular "you") in Brazilian Portuguese.
additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to show possession: as tuas armas (your weapons), as tuas palavras (your words). It agrees with the noun (feminine plural), not with the owner. In Brazilian Portuguese, it’s tied to the informal pronoun "tu"; in many regions, people instead use "as suas" with "você".
target_language_example: Onde estão as tuas chaves?
native_language_example: Where are your keys?

additional_notes: Plural of "a unha". Usually refers to fingernails, but it can also mean toenails (and, for animals, claws). Common with verbs like "cortar as unhas" (cut your nails), "pintar as unhas" (paint your nails), and in phrases like "passar as unhas" (run/scratch your nails lightly).
target_language_example: Preciso pintar as unhas antes da festa.
native_language_example: I need to paint my nails before the party.

additional_notes: Definite article + plural noun: "as" = "the" (feminine plural), "vacas" = "cows". Used when talking about specific cows already known or identified from context. Singular: "a vaca" (the cow).
target_language_example: As vacas estão no pasto agora.
native_language_example: The cows are in the pasture now.

additional_notes: Uses the definite article "as" (plural feminine) + the noun "árvores" (trees). It can be used as the subject or object of a sentence. Singular is "a árvore" (the tree).
target_language_example: As árvores do parque são muito antigas.
native_language_example: The trees in the park are very old.

additional_notes: Used after a condition like "Se..." or "Já que..." to show resignation or acceptance: if someone wanted it that way, you’ll accept it and move on. In natural Portuguese, many speakers would say "então pronto" or "então, pronto" (without "se").
target_language_example: Se você quer assim, então pronto.
native_language_example: If you want it that way, then so be it.

meaning: "as soon as I" (to say something happens immediately after I do something).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as a time connector: "assim que" + a clause. It’s followed by a verb, often in the past (e.g., "assim que eu acordei") or future/when possible (e.g., "assim que eu puder"). In the pattern "Foi assim que eu...", it can also mean "That’s how I..." (explaining the way something happened).
target_language_example: Vou te ligar assim que eu chegar em casa.
native_language_example: I’ll call you as soon as I get home.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "assinar" = to sign. Used to say that someone completed the action of signing a contract. Very common in formal/business contexts; you can also use it in questions: "Você assinou o contrato?" (= Did you sign the contract?) and with "já" to mean "already".
target_language_example: Ela assinou o contrato ontem à tarde.
native_language_example: She signed the contract yesterday afternoon.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **assistir a** (= to watch), which normally takes the preposition **a**: *assistir a um filme / assistir ao filme*. Often used to say what you watched and who you watched it with (*com ele*), when (*ontem de tarde*), or with details like language/subtitles (*com legendas em inglês*).
target_language_example: Hoje à noite, assisti a um filme de comédia.
native_language_example: Tonight, I watched a comedy movie.

additional_notes: "Assistindo" is the gerund of "assistir (a)", used to talk about an action in progress (like English "-ing"). It’s often used with "estar" ("estou/estava assistindo TV" = "I am/was watching TV"). In Brazil, "assistir" usually takes the preposition "a" ("assistindo à TV"), but in everyday speech it’s very common to drop it: "assistindo TV".
target_language_example: Estou assistindo TV agora.
native_language_example: I'm watching TV now.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "assistir (a)" meaning "to watch". It’s usually followed by "a" + the thing you watch; with "TV" the "a" + "a" becomes "à" (crasis): "assistindo à TV". Common in ongoing actions with "estar": "está assistindo à TV" = "is watching TV".
target_language_example: Estou assistindo à TV agora.
native_language_example: I’m watching TV now.

additional_notes: In Brazilian Portuguese, assistir a is a common verb phrase meaning “to watch” (TV, movies, games). It normally takes the preposition a: assistir a + noun (often written as “assistir a filmes”). In everyday speech, many people also say ver filmes (“to watch movies”).
target_language_example: No fim de semana, eu gosto de assistir a filmes com a minha família.
native_language_example: On the weekend, I like to watch movies with my family.

additional_notes: "Assistir a" means "to watch" in Brazilian Portuguese and normally takes the preposition "a" (assistir a + something). In everyday speech, many people drop the "a" ("assistir um filme"), but in careful/standard usage you’ll often see and hear "assistir a um filme".
target_language_example: Vamos assistir a um filme hoje à noite.
native_language_example: Let’s watch a movie tonight.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **assistir a** (to watch/attend) with the preposition **a**, so it contracts with **a** to form **à**: *assistir à TV*. Very common with other things you watch, especially events: *assistir ao jogo* (“watch the game”), *assistir ao filme* (“watch the movie”).
target_language_example: Depois do jantar, a gente gosta de assistir à TV por um tempo.
native_language_example: After dinner, we like to watch TV for a while.

additional_notes: Used when you pick up a ringing phone and respond. You can also say “atender uma ligação” (answer a call). Common in polite requests: “Pode/Poderia atender o telefone, por favor?”
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu não consegui atender o telefone a tempo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I couldn’t answer the phone in time.

meaning: crossing the street (in the act of crossing).
additional_notes: Uses the gerund "atravessando" (from "atravessar", "to cross") to describe an action in progress, often modifying a person/thing: "o homem atravessando a rua" = "the man crossing the street." It can also appear after verbs of seeing/hearing: "Eu o vi atravessando a rua" = "I saw him crossing the street."
target_language_example: Cuidado com as crianças atravessando a rua.
native_language_example: Watch out for the children crossing the street.

additional_notes: Common safety context (look left/right, be careful). Usually used with verbs like "poder" (can), "precisar" (need), or in warnings/instructions: "Antes de atravessar a rua..." / "Tome cuidado ao/para atravessar a rua."
target_language_example: Vamos atravessar a rua na faixa de pedestres.
native_language_example: Let’s cross the street at the crosswalk.

additional_notes: Used for getting from one side of a river to the other (by bridge, boat, swimming, wading, etc.). In the examples it often appears with verbs like conseguir (manage), precisar (need), or ir (be going to).
target_language_example: Vamos atravessar o rio pela ponte.
native_language_example: Let's cross the river using the bridge.

additional_notes: Literally “to cross the river by swimming.” Used with verbs like conseguir (manage), poder (be able to), or tentar (try). You can swap in another obstacle: atravessar o lago/a piscina/a baía a nado (swim across the lake/pool/bay).
target_language_example: Eles tentaram atravessar o rio a nado, mas a correnteza estava forte.
native_language_example: They tried to swim across the river, but the current was strong.

additional_notes: Used to say you cross a river by swimming. Structure: atravessar (to cross) + o rio (the river) + nadando (swimming, i.e., “by swimming”). Common with verbs of ability like conseguir/poder/ser capaz de.
target_language_example: Ela não pode atravessar o rio nadando porque a correnteza está forte.
native_language_example: She can’t swim across the river because the current is strong.

meaning: (she was) run over / hit by a car.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "ser" (often in the past: "foi") to say someone/something was struck by a car, typically involving a pedestrian being hit (sometimes with the idea of being knocked down/run over). The form changes for gender/number: "atropelado" (male), "atropelada" (female), "atropelados/atropeladas" (plural). You can add "quase" to mean "almost": "quase foi atropelada por um carro".
target_language_example: O cachorro foi atropelado por um carro, mas está bem agora.
native_language_example: The dog was hit by a car, but it’s okay now.

additional_notes: Used to say someone was struck by a car (often implying an accident). It commonly appears with the verb "ser" (to be): "foi atropelado por um carro" = "he was hit by a car." "Atropelado" changes for gender/number: "atropelada" (female), "atropelados/atropeladas" (plural).
target_language_example: Ela quase foi atropelada por um carro na rua.
native_language_example: She was almost hit by a car in the street.

additional_notes: Used to indicate position: something is behind something else. It’s the contraction of "atrás de" + "a" (the feminine singular definite article). With masculine nouns, you’ll usually see "atrás do" (de + o). Can also appear in expressions like "uma atrás da outra" = "one after another".
target_language_example: O banheiro fica atrás da cozinha.
native_language_example: The bathroom is behind the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is located on the other side of the door (not in front of it). Often used for hiding ("se esconder atrás da porta") or for placing/hanging things there ("pendurar ... atrás da porta").
target_language_example: Deixei o guarda-chuva atrás da porta.
native_language_example: I left the umbrella behind the door.

additional_notes: Literally “behind + of + me.” It can refer to physical position (something is behind you), or to someone pursuing you (“Eles estão atrás de mim” = they’re after me). Common in instructions like “Fique atrás de mim” (“Stay behind me”). In “Fechei/tranquei a porta atrás de mim,” it means you closed/locked the door after you passed through it.
target_language_example: Tem alguém atrás de mim?
native_language_example: Is there someone behind me?

meaning: behind you; also: after you / following you (pursuing).
additional_notes: Most commonly indicates physical position: something/someone is behind you (often said as a warning: “Atrás de você!”). With verbs like “estar” or “ir” (“estou/vou atrás de você”), it can also mean following you or chasing you. “Bem atrás de você” = “right behind you.”
target_language_example: Cuidado, tem alguém atrás de você.
native_language_example: Careful, there’s someone behind you.

additional_notes: Used for physical location (something is behind an object) and for chasing/going after something (running after a bus, going after what you want). It’s a contraction of "atrás de" + "o" (= "do"). With feminine nouns: "atrás da"; plural: "atrás dos/das".
target_language_example: O cachorro saiu correndo atrás do gato.
native_language_example: The dog ran after the cat.

additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns after **até**. It can mean movement/direction (**to the**): *até a estação* (“to the station”), or a time limit (**until the**): *até a hora...* (“until the time…”). With a following time expression, it often implies “up to”: *até a segunda apresentação* (“until the second performance”). In European Portuguese you may also see **até à** (até + à).
target_language_example: Vou caminhar até a praia.
native_language_example: I’m going to walk to the beach.

additional_notes: Used with a verb of movement (e.g., caminhar/andar/ir) to indicate the destination reached: going as far as the school. In everyday English this is often just “to school,” but Portuguese commonly keeps the article: “a escola.”
target_language_example: Hoje eu vou de bicicleta até a escola.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to school by bike.

meaning: to the station; until the station (as a stopping point).
additional_notes: "Até" marks an endpoint in space or time. With places, it often means movement toward a destination: "até a estação" = to the (train/bus/metro) station. In travel contexts it can also mean staying/continuing up to that stop: "ficar em pé até a estação" (stand until you reach the station).
target_language_example: Vamos de táxi até a estação porque estamos atrasados.
native_language_example: Let’s take a taxi to the station because we’re late.

additional_notes: Used to say an action continues up to the time 12:00 a.m. (midnight). Common with activities like working, talking, staying awake, etc. You’ll often see the same pattern with other times: até as duas (until 2:00), até amanhã (until tomorrow).
target_language_example: Vou ficar aqui até a meia-noite.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay here until midnight.

additional_notes: Used with a time span meaning “from X until someone dies” (até a morte dele/dela) or with a verb to mean something happened “to the point of death” (sangrar/espancar até a morte). Often appears in serious or violent contexts.
target_language_example: Ele trabalhou até a morte, sem descanso.
native_language_example: He worked himself to death, without any rest.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (e.g., andar, ir, caminhar) to show the endpoint/destination: you go/walk as far as the door. Often implies stopping there (or reaching it) before doing something else.
target_language_example: Ela correu até a porta e bateu.
native_language_example: She ran to the door and knocked.

additional_notes: Used to talk about everything that has happened (or hasn’t happened) from the past until the present moment. Very common in questions about someone’s experience: "Como você está gostando ... até agora?"
target_language_example: Até agora, está tudo bem.
native_language_example: So far, everything is fine.

additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) as a farewell meaning “see you tomorrow” (often on its own: “Até amanhã!”), and (2) to set a deadline meaning “by/until tomorrow” (e.g., “até amanhã de manhã” = “by tomorrow morning”).
target_language_example: Te ligo até amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: I’ll call you by tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to talk about reaching this place (physical) or this point (in time/progress). Very common with verbs of movement like vir (to come), chegar (to arrive), trazer (to bring), and can imply effort or distance (“all the way here”).
target_language_example: Obrigado por vir até aqui para me ajudar.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming all the way here to help me.

meaning: to a certain extent; up to a point.
additional_notes: Used to show partial agreement or partial responsibility/satisfaction—something is true, but only within limits. Often followed by a statement that adds a contrast (e.g., "..., mas...").
target_language_example: Eu entendo o que você quer dizer, até certo ponto, mas acho que precisamos tentar de outro jeito.
native_language_example: I understand what you mean, up to a point, but I think we need to try a different way.

meaning: (all the way) home; up to (someone’s) home.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement/support like acompanhar (to walk/escort), levar (to take), and dar uma carona (to give a ride). It means the person goes with you or takes you as far as your home (often for safety or convenience). Usually appears with a possessive or pronoun implied by context: até em casa (to my/your home), até a tua casa/até a sua casa.
target_language_example: Posso te acompanhar até em casa depois do jantar.
native_language_example: I can walk you home after dinner.

meaning: “until I come back / until I return.”
additional_notes: Used to set a time limit that lasts up to the moment you return. Very common after requests/commands or statements about waiting: “Espere/Fique aqui até eu voltar” (“Wait/Stay here until I come back”). You can swap “voltar” with “regressar” (more formal) with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Fica aqui até eu voltar, por favor.
native_language_example: Stay here until I come back, please.

meaning: "until then" / "until that time"; or "up to there" (to that place).
additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) time: "Até lá" = "See you/Until then" (often as a short goodbye). (2) place: "ir/caminhar até lá" = "go/walk over there" or "as far as that place". Meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Te ligo amanhã; até lá, bom trabalho.
native_language_example: I'll call you tomorrow; until then, good work.

meaning: “up to/to the” (until/to a specific masculine place, point, or time).
additional_notes: Used with masculine singular nouns (o) after até. It can indicate movement/destination (“to the…”) or a time limit (“until…”). With places, it often implies going as far as a point: até o elevador, até o Japão. With time expressions, it means “until”: até o amanhecer. Feminine version: até a; plural: até os/as.
target_language_example: Vamos esperar até o fim da reunião.
native_language_example: Let’s wait until the end of the meeting.

meaning: until the end; all the way (to the end).
additional_notes: Used for going/continuing something up to the final point in time or space: a struggle or activity ("lutar/cantar até o fim"), a time period ("até o fim do mês" = until the end of the month), or a route ("até o fim da estrada" = to the end of the road). Often implies persistence/continuing without stopping.
target_language_example: Eu vou ficar com você até o fim.
native_language_example: I’ll stay with you until the end.

meaning: by the end of the day.
additional_notes: Used to set a deadline that should be met before today finishes (often meaning before close of business). Common after words like "precisar" (to need) and "querer" (to want) when requesting a reply or delivery.
target_language_example: Você consegue me enviar o relatório até o fim do dia?
native_language_example: Can you send me the report by the end of the day?

meaning: "as far as I know" / "to the best of my knowledge."
additional_notes: Used to say you believe something is true based on the information you have, but you’re not 100% sure. Often placed at the start of a sentence, but it can also come at the end. Variations: "até onde sei" (dropping "eu"); you can change the subject: "até onde ela sabe" (as far as she knows).
target_language_example: Até onde eu sei, a reunião é amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the meeting is tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a deadline or end time that lasts up to Monday ("ficar até segunda-feira" = "stay until Monday"). As a goodbye, "Até segunda-feira!" means "See you on Monday!" Similar patterns: "até amanhã" (see you tomorrow / until tomorrow), "até mais" (see you later).
target_language_example: Então tá, até segunda-feira!
native_language_example: Alright then, see you on Monday!

additional_notes: Used with an activity to say it continues into the late hours (often implying it went on longer than usual). Common with verbs like trabalhar (work), conversar/discutir (talk/discuss), estudar (study), ficar acordado (stay up).
target_language_example: Ficamos acordados até tarde da noite vendo um filme.
native_language_example: We stayed up until late at night watching a movie.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a class/lesson where French is taught. With the verb "dar" it means to teach/give French lessons ("dar aula de francês"); with "ter"/"assistir" it means to have/attend French class.
target_language_example: Eu tenho aula de francês toda terça-feira.
native_language_example: I have French class every Tuesday.

additional_notes: Used to say what subject the class/lesson is about: "aulas de + [matéria/idioma/instrumento]". Common with languages (aulas de português), instruments (aulas de piano), and school subjects (aulas de matemática). "Ter aulas de" = to have classes in; "fazer/tomar aulas de" = to take lessons in; "dar aulas de" = to teach classes in.
target_language_example: Estou fazendo aulas de português duas vezes por semana.
native_language_example: I'm taking Portuguese classes twice a week.

additional_notes: Imperative of the verb avisar (“to let someone know, to warn, to notify”) + me (“to me”). Used to ask someone to inform you when something happens or before they do something: “Avise-me quando…” (“Let me know when…”), “Avise-me com antecedência” (“Let me know in advance”). In everyday speech, people often say “Me avise” too.
target_language_example: Avise-me se você se atrasar.
native_language_example: Let me know if you’re going to be late.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask for sugar at the table or when ordering. Often appears after what you want (e.g., "Um café com açúcar, por favor.") or by itself to request a sugar packet ("Um açúcar, por favor."). In Brazil, "um açúcar" commonly means one sugar packet/sachet.
target_language_example: Pode me trazer açúcar, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you bring me sugar, please?
