additional_notes: Used to refer to a place that is higher (upstairs, on the roof, on top of something) and relatively close to the listener. Often contrasts with aqui em cima (“up here”) and lá em cima (“up there/farther away”).
target_language_example: Espera aí em cima que eu já subo.
native_language_example: Wait up there; I’m coming up in a moment.

additional_notes: Usually appears as "deixar a barba crescer" (literally "to leave/let the beard grow"), meaning you stop shaving/trimming so it grows out. Common in everyday talk about changing your look: "Ele deixou a barba crescer" = "He grew out his beard."
target_language_example: Estou deixando a barba crescer desde outubro.
native_language_example: I’ve been growing out my beard since October.

meaning: a lot of time; quite a while.
additional_notes: Means there is plenty of time available, or that something has lasted for a long time. Common with verbs like ter (to have time), passar (to spend time), and conhecer (to have known someone) + há: "há bastante tempo" = "for quite a while."
target_language_example: Ainda temos bastante tempo antes do voo.
native_language_example: We still have plenty of time before the flight.

additional_notes: Literally “fried potatoes.” In Portugal, this usually means French fries; in the UK context it can also correspond to “chips” (as in “fish and chips”). Common when ordering food: “um hambúrguer com batatas fritas” (a burger with fries) or “um saco de batatas fritas” (a bag of chips/fries).
target_language_example: Para acompanhar, pode ser uma dose de batatas fritas?
native_language_example: As a side, can it be a portion of fries?

additional_notes: Used to say you want to drink a small amount of something, usually followed by a drink or liquid noun (água, café, suco). Very common in polite requests with “Posso…?” (“Can I…?”) or to give advice/commands (“Vá beber…”).
target_language_example: Depois do treino, vou beber um pouco de água.
native_language_example: After the workout, I’m going to drink a little water.

additional_notes: Verb + object pronoun: "beijar" (to kiss) + "-la" (her) attached with a hyphen. The accent in "beijá-" shows the stress when the pronoun is attached (common with infinitives). You can use the same pattern with other pronouns: beijá-lo (kiss him), beijá-las (kiss them, feminine), beijá-los (kiss them, masculine/mixed).
target_language_example: Eu queria beijá-la, mas fiquei com vergonha.
native_language_example: I wanted to kiss her, but I felt shy.

additional_notes: Used when greeting someone arriving/being introduced to a place, group, or situation. "Bem-vinda" is feminine; for a man, use "bem-vindo ao". "Ao" = "a" + "o" and is used before masculine singular nouns (ao clube, ao mundo); with feminine nouns you use "à" (bem-vinda à festa). Often said with an implied "Seja": (Seja) bem-vinda ao nosso restaurante!
target_language_example: Bem-vinda ao time!
native_language_example: Welcome to the team!

additional_notes: Used to welcome a female person to a place, country, event, or group. Agree it with the person: bem-vindo à (male), bem-vindos/as à (plural). It’s often followed by “à” because it commonly comes before a feminine noun (à = a + a), e.g., “à França”, “à nossa casa”. With masculine nouns, you’ll usually see “bem-vinda ao …” (ao = a + o), e.g., “Bem-vinda ao Brasil”.
target_language_example: Bem-vinda à minha cidade!
native_language_example: Welcome to my city!

meaning: “welcome to (the)” (addressed to a man) + a masculine place/thing (ao = a + o).
additional_notes: Used to greet someone arriving or joining something (“Bem-vindo ao grupo.”). For a woman, use “bem-vinda ao…”. If the noun is feminine, use “Bem-vindo à…” / “Bem-vinda à…” (à = a + a), e.g., “Bem-vindo à escola.” Often appears with “Bem-vindo(a) ao/à seu/sua…” to mean “welcome to your…”.
target_language_example: Bem-vindo ao nosso time!
native_language_example: Welcome to our team!

additional_notes: Used to say someone is welcome in this place or group. Often appears with the verb ser (“to be”): "Você é bem-vindo aqui" = “You’re welcome here.” Negative: "não é bem-vindo aqui" = “not welcome here.” You can also say it to a man or a mixed group; for a woman, use "bem-vinda aqui".
target_language_example: Fique tranquilo: você é bem-vindo aqui.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you’re welcome here.

additional_notes: Used to greet someone arriving at a place, event, or situation. 'à' = 'a' + 'a' (to the, feminine singular), so it’s used before feminine nouns (à Austrália, à China, à Wikipédia, à máquina, à primeira aula). With masculine nouns, use 'bem-vindo ao' (ao Brasil). You can also use the more formal invitation 'Seja bem-vindo(a) à…'.
target_language_example: Bem-vindo à nossa casa!
native_language_example: Welcome to our house!

additional_notes: Used to greet someone arriving at a place or joining something. Match gender/number with the person/people you’re welcoming: bem-vindo (male), bem-vinda (female), bem-vindos/bem-vindas (plural). Often followed by a place or destination with “a” (a Boston, a casa) or sometimes “à” before a feminine singular noun with the article “a” (e.g., “à cidade”).
target_language_example: Bem-vinda à nossa escola!
native_language_example: Welcome to our school!

meaning: “welcome to (the)” (addressed to a man) + a masculine place/thing (ao = a + o).
additional_notes: Used to greet someone arriving or joining something (“Bem-vindo ao grupo.”). For a woman, use “bem-vinda ao…”. If the noun is feminine, use “Bem-vindo à…” / “Bem-vinda à…” (à = a + a), e.g., “Bem-vindo à escola.” Often appears with “Bem-vindo(a) ao/à seu/sua…” to mean “welcome to your…”.
target_language_example: Bem-vindo ao nosso time!
native_language_example: Welcome to our team!

additional_notes: Used to greet someone who has returned (to a place, group, conversation, etc.). You can change gender/number: bem-vindo (male), bem-vinda (female), bem-vindos/bem-vindas (plural). It can be said alone or followed by a name/title (e.g., Bem-vindo de volta, senhor).
target_language_example: Bem-vinda de volta! Sentimos a sua falta.
native_language_example: Welcome back! We missed you.

meaning: “welcome to” (addressed to a group, or mixed gender).
additional_notes: Used to welcome people to a place or event. It agrees with who you’re welcoming: bem-vindo a (one man), bem-vinda a (one woman), bem-vindos a (men or mixed group), bem-vindas a (women only). Often followed by a city, school, house, website, etc.
target_language_example: Bem-vindos a nossa casa!
native_language_example: Welcome to our home!

meaning: “welcome to” (addressing a group; masculine or mixed group).
additional_notes: Used to greet people arriving/starting something. It’s the plural form of "bem-vindo" + "a" + "o" (ao = "to the" for masculine singular nouns). For an all-female group, use "bem-vindas à" (à = "to the" for feminine singular nouns).
target_language_example: Pessoal, bem-vindos ao nosso curso de português!
native_language_example: Guys, welcome to our Portuguese course!

additional_notes: Used to greet people arriving at a place, group, or situation. "Bem-vindos" is plural (mixed group or all men). For all women, say "Bem-vindas". For one person, use "bem-vindo" (man) / "bem-vinda" (woman). Use "à" before feminine singular nouns (a + a), e.g., "à cidade", "à família"; use "ao" before masculine singular nouns (a + o), e.g., "ao Brasil".
target_language_example: Bem-vindos à nossa empresa!
native_language_example: Welcome to our company!

meaning: 'Well, I...' (used to start a reply, often to give your opinion or explain yourself).
additional_notes: Common conversational opener. "Bem" works like English "well" to pause, soften what you’re about to say, or signal you’re thinking; then "eu" introduces what *you* think/know/do. Often followed by a statement: "Bem, eu acho..." (Well, I think...), "Bem, eu não sei..." (Well, I don’t know...).
target_language_example: Bem, eu acho melhor irmos agora.
native_language_example: Well, I think it’s better if we go now.

additional_notes: Used as a discourse marker before disagreeing, correcting someone, or backing off what was just said. "Bem" here is like English "well" to soften the response; "não" can also be repeated at the end of the sentence in Portuguese for emphasis (e.g., "..., não?").
target_language_example: Bem, não. Acho melhor a gente ir amanhã.
native_language_example: Well, no. I think it’s better if we go tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to agree with or praise a suggestion/plan. Often said alone as a quick reaction: "Boa ideia!" You can also use it inside a sentence with an article: "uma boa ideia" (a good idea) or "foi uma boa ideia" (it was a good idea).
target_language_example: Acho que é uma boa ideia sair mais cedo.
native_language_example: I think it's a good idea to leave earlier.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or ask for positive information (often after bad news). Common patterns: “Tenho uma boa notícia” (I have good news), “Você tem alguma boa notícia?” (Do you have any good news?), “A boa notícia é que...” (The good news is that...). Note: “Nenhuma notícia é uma boa notícia” is a set saying meaning “no news is good news.”
target_language_example: Tenho uma boa notícia: conseguimos resolver o problema.
native_language_example: I have good news: we managed to solve the problem.

additional_notes: Used to talk about doing well in French class/at school. "Tirar" and "obter" are common verbs with "notas" meaning “to get/earn grades” (e.g., "tirar boas notas"). "Tenho boas notas" means you generally have good grades (your overall performance), not that you physically possess them.
target_language_example: Ela sempre tira boas notas em francês, mas tem dificuldade em matemática.
native_language_example: She always gets good grades in French, but she has trouble in math.

additional_notes: Used to announce or ask about something positive. Very common with verbs like ter (tenho/temos/tens boas notícias) and with the preposition com (ficar feliz com as boas notícias = to be happy about the good news). Often appears with the definite article: as boas notícias (“the good news”).
target_language_example: Tenho boas notícias: o seu pedido foi aprovado.
native_language_example: I have good news: your request was approved.

additional_notes: Used for the cake made for a birthday celebration, often with candles on top. You can say "meu/minha" before it (e.g., "meu bolo de aniversário") to mean "my birthday cake."
target_language_example: Vamos comprar um bolo de aniversário para ela.
native_language_example: Let’s buy a birthday cake for her.

additional_notes: A common food phrase: "bolo" = cake and "de chocolate" = made with/with chocolate. Used after verbs like "adorar" (to love), "gostar" (to like), and in offers/invitations like "Quer bolo de chocolate?" or "Sirva-se de bolo de chocolate" (Help yourself to chocolate cake).
target_language_example: Você quer um pedaço de bolo de chocolate?
native_language_example: Do you want a piece of chocolate cake?

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s ability/skill in a subject. Pattern: (ser) bom/boa em + [subject]. It agrees with the person: bom (male), boa (female). You can intensify it with muito (“very”): muito bom/boa em matemática.
target_language_example: Ela é muito boa em matemática, mas eu não sou.
native_language_example: She’s very good at math, but I’m not.

additional_notes: A common greeting when you meet someone (“Bom te ver, Tom.”). In the past it becomes a goodbye-style phrase: “Foi bom te ver” = “It was nice seeing you.” You can intensify it with “muito” and add “de novo” for “again”: “Foi muito bom te ver de novo.”
target_language_example: Bom te ver de novo!
native_language_example: Nice to see you again!

additional_notes: Often used as a compliment after someone does something well: "Bom trabalho!" You can also use it literally to describe employment or work quality: "um bom trabalho" (a good job), "por seu bom trabalho" (for his/her good work).
target_language_example: Bom trabalho! Você resolveu o problema bem rápido.
native_language_example: Good job! You solved the problem really quickly.

additional_notes: Used to say people have a friendly relationship and know each other well. It agrees in gender/number: “bons amigos” (male or mixed group), “boas amigas” (female group), “bom amigo” (one man), “boa amiga” (one woman). Often appears with verbs like “ser” (to be) and “tornar-se” (to become).
target_language_example: Depois de trabalharmos juntos, viramos bons amigos.
native_language_example: After we worked together, we became good friends.

meaning: angry with me; mad at me.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" or "ficar" (to be / to get) to say someone is angry at you: "Ele está bravo comigo" (He’s mad at me) or "Ele ficou bravo comigo" (He got mad at me). "Bravo" can also mean “fierce” (e.g., an animal), but in everyday conversation it often means “angry.”
target_language_example: Desculpa — eu não queria te deixar bravo comigo.
native_language_example: Sorry — I didn’t mean to make you mad at me.

additional_notes: Used to specify the arm on the left side of the body. Often appears with body-related verbs like ferir (to injure), levantar (to raise), and with location phrases like no/meu/seu braço esquerdo (“on my/your/his/her left arm”).
target_language_example: Dói quando mexo o braço esquerdo.
native_language_example: It hurts when I move my left arm.

additional_notes: From the verb *brincar* + *com* (“with”). Used for physically playing with a toy, pet, or children (*brincando com uma boneca / o cachorro / os filhos*). With a person, it often means you’re not serious—joking or teasing (*Estou brincando com você*).
target_language_example: Calma, estou brincando com você.
native_language_example: Relax, I'm just joking with you.

additional_notes: "Brincando" is the gerund of "brincar" (to play), used to talk about an action in progress (like English "-ing"). "No" = "em" + "o" and usually means "in the" or "at the" (here, "in the park"). Often used with estar: "estou/está/estavam brincando" = "(am/is/was/were) playing."
target_language_example: As crianças estão brincando no parque agora.
native_language_example: The kids are playing in the park now.

meaning: to play with; to joke/tease about.
additional_notes: With people, it often means “to play with” (kids playing together) or “to joke/tease” someone in a friendly way, depending on context. With topics/things (assuntos/ideias), it usually means “to joke about” or “not take seriously” (sometimes with a warning tone: “don’t mess/joke with that”).
target_language_example: Não brinque com isso — é perigoso.
native_language_example: Don’t mess with that—it’s dangerous.

meaning: to pick him/it up; to go get him/it.
additional_notes: From "buscar" (to get/pick up) + the object pronoun "-lo" (him/it). The accent (buscá-) appears because in Brazilian Portuguese the final -r of the infinitive is dropped before attaching the pronoun: "buscar + o" → "buscá-lo". Very common with verbs of movement: "ir buscá-lo" (go pick him/it up), "vir buscá-lo" (come pick him/it up), often for picking someone up at places like a station or airport. "-lo" can refer to a male person (him) or to a thing (it), depending on context.
target_language_example: Posso passar às oito para buscá-lo no trabalho?
native_language_example: Can I stop by at eight to pick him up at work?

additional_notes: Plural of "cachorro-quente". Very common in menus and when ordering; you can add toppings with "com" (e.g., "com muita pimenta" = "with lots of pepper/hot sauce"). Often written with a hyphen (cachorro-quente / cachorros-quentes), though you may also see it without one in informal writing.
target_language_example: Para o lanche, vou pedir dois cachorros-quentes com mostarda e ketchup.
native_language_example: For a snack, I’m going to order two hot dogs with mustard and ketchup.

meaning: "each day" / "every day" (also: "more and more" in comparisons).
additional_notes: Literal meaning is “each day.” It can mean (1) “every day” in general statements (Cada dia conta. = Every day counts.), and (2) “more and more / increasingly” when used with comparatives like melhor/pior/maior (A situação fica cada dia pior. = The situation gets worse and worse.).
target_language_example: Estou me sentindo cada dia melhor.
native_language_example: I’m feeling better and better every day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about individual people within the group that includes the speaker (“nós” = “we/us”). Common in statements of responsibility, ability, or giving something to everyone in the group (one per person). You can change “nós” to another pronoun: “cada um de vocês” (each of you), “cada um deles” (each of them).
target_language_example: Cada um de nós tem um papel importante neste projeto.
native_language_example: Each of us has an important role in this project.

additional_notes: Common, polite phrase when ordering at a café/restaurant or asking someone to serve/make coffee. You can add details after it, like "com creme e açúcar" (with cream and sugar) or use "Um café, por favor" (a coffee, please) and "Mais café, por favor" (more coffee, please).
target_language_example: Um café, por favor, sem açúcar.
native_language_example: A coffee, please, without sugar.

additional_notes: The standard (Brazilian) Portuguese word for the morning meal. Often used with verbs like "tomar" or "comer" (to have/eat): "tomar café-da-manhã". The hyphenated form is correct; in everyday writing you may also see "café da manhã".
target_language_example: Eu tomo café-da-manhã às sete todos os dias.
native_language_example: I have breakfast at seven every day.

additional_notes: The standard word for the morning meal. It’s commonly used with the verb "tomar" (to have/consume): "tomar café da manhã" = "to have breakfast". You can also say "preparar o café da manhã" (to prepare breakfast) and "o café da manhã está pronto" (breakfast is ready).
target_language_example: Você já tomou café da manhã?
native_language_example: Have you had breakfast yet?

additional_notes: Used to say you take your coffee with no added sugar. Common in cafés when ordering: “Um café sem açúcar, por favor.” You can also specify other options, e.g., “com leite” (with milk) or “sem leite” (without milk).
target_language_example: Quero um café sem açúcar e um copo de água, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like an unsweetened coffee and a glass of water, please.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of cair + de + a (= da) + árvore. Used for something/someone that was in a tree and then fell down from it. Literal, physical meaning (not an idiom).
target_language_example: O gato caiu da árvore, mas não se machucou.
native_language_example: The cat fell from the tree, but it didn’t get hurt.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of cair: caiu = “fell.” Used for people or objects that drop/fall down. “No chão” means “on the ground/on the floor” (chão = ground/floor). You can change the subject: “Eu caí no chão” = “I fell on the ground.”
target_language_example: O copo caiu no chão e quebrou.
native_language_example: The glass fell on the floor and broke.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to say what the box contains: uma caixa de doces (a box of sweets), uma caixa de biscoitos (a box of cookies). It can also form fixed compound nouns like caixa de ferramentas (toolbox).
target_language_example: Vou comprar uma caixa de chocolate para a festa.
native_language_example: I’m going to buy a box of chocolate for the party.

additional_notes: Used for a physical route to a place (Sabe o caminho para…?), or more generally for a means/solution toward a goal (um caminho para resolver algo). In "no meu caminho para casa", it means "on my way home."
target_language_example: Qual é o melhor caminho para o aeroporto?
native_language_example: What’s the best way to the airport?

additional_notes: Used when you and at least one other person ("nós" = "we") can’t go anymore and decide to call the trip off. You can also change the possessive to match who is traveling: "cancelar a minha viagem" (my trip), "cancelar a sua viagem" (your trip), "cancelar a viagem" (the trip). Often followed by a destination with "para" (to) or "ao/à" (to + the): "viagem para Boston", "viagem ao Japão".
target_language_example: Por causa do tempo, vamos cancelar a nossa viagem amanhã.
native_language_example: Because of the weather, we’re going to cancel our trip tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has the ability/skill/opportunity to do something. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (capaz de + verb): "capaz de ler" (able to read), "capaz de fazer" (capable of doing).
target_language_example: Você é capaz de fazer isso sozinho?
native_language_example: Are you able to do that by yourself?

meaning: able to do; capable of doing.
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s ability/capacity to do an action. It’s common after forms of "ser" ("sou/é/era/será capaz de...") and it’s followed by an infinitive verb (here, "fazer", but it can be any verb: "capaz de entender", "capaz de ir"). With "não" it means "not able to". Often implies having the skill, strength, or possibility to do something.
target_language_example: Você é capaz de fazer isso sozinho?
native_language_example: Are you able to do that by yourself?

additional_notes: Used to talk about having the ability or capacity to do something. It often follows a form of the verb “ser” (to be): “sou/é/seja capaz de fazer isso” = “am/is/be able to do that.” In questions, it can mean “Can you do that?” or “Are you capable of doing that?” Depending on context, it can be neutral (skills) or more moral/judgmental (“How could someone be capable of doing that?”).
target_language_example: Não sei se sou capaz de fazer isso sozinho.
native_language_example: I don't know if I'm able to do that alone.

additional_notes: Used to name the main city/seat of government of a country, state, or region. It’s typically followed by a feminine noun (da = de + a), e.g., "a capital da Polônia". For masculine nouns, Portuguese uses "capital do" (de + o), e.g., "a capital do Brasil".
target_language_example: Lisboa é a capital de Portugal.
native_language_example: Lisbon is the capital of Portugal.

additional_notes: Used to name what place a city is the capital of: "a capital do Japão" = "the capital of Japan". "Do" is the contraction of "de" + "o" ("of" + "the") and is used with masculine singular nouns ("o Japão"); with feminine singular it becomes "da" ("de" + "a"), e.g., "a capital da Bahia".
target_language_example: Lisboa é a capital do país.
native_language_example: Lisbon is the capital of the country.

additional_notes: Used to specify the type of meat ("carne") you’re talking about. In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people more often say "carne bovina" (more formal/technical) or simply "carne" when the context already makes it clear it’s beef. You can use it in preferences and questions: "gostar de" (to like) and "preferir X a Y" (to prefer X to Y).
target_language_example: No churrasco, vamos comprar carne de boi e frango.
native_language_example: For the barbecue, we’re going to buy beef and chicken.

additional_notes: Used to talk about pork as a type of meat/food. Often appears in menu or shopping contexts. You can also say simply "porco" for "pig" (the animal), but "carne de porco" is specifically the meat.
target_language_example: Hoje vou cozinhar carne de porco com batatas.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to cook pork with potatoes.

additional_notes: "Dele" means "his" (literally "of him") and refers back to a male owner mentioned in context (e.g., Tom). It comes after the noun: "o carro dele" = "his car". Often used with possession/borrowing: "pegar o carro dele emprestado" (borrow his car), "usar o carro dele" (use his car).
target_language_example: Posso pegar o carro dele emprestado por uma hora?
native_language_example: Can I borrow his car for an hour?

meaning: (the) car in the garage; put/leave the car in the garage.
additional_notes: A common location phrase using "na" = "em" + "a" (in the + feminine singular). Often used with verbs like "colocar", "pôr" (to put), and "deixar" (to leave). You may also hear "o carro está na garagem" (the car is in the garage).
target_language_example: O carro está na garagem, pode fechar a porta.
native_language_example: The car is in the garage; you can close the door.

meaning: a new car (a car that is brand-new or recently bought).
additional_notes: "Carro" means "car" and "novo" means "new"; the adjective usually comes after the noun in Portuguese ("carro novo"). It can mean either brand-new (never used) or simply newly purchased, depending on context.
target_language_example: Eles chegaram no trabalho com um carro novo.
native_language_example: They arrived at work in a new car.

additional_notes: Means “her house/home,” referring to a female person already known from context. Often used with verbs of going/arriving (ir/chegar) and with prepositions like em/a/para: “na casa dela” = “at/to her house.”
target_language_example: Podemos nos encontrar na casa dela amanhã?
native_language_example: Can we meet at her house tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male person’s place (house/home). Often appears with prepositions: "na casa dele" (at his house), "à casa dele" (to his house), "da casa dele" (from his house / of his house). In Portuguese, possession is commonly shown with "dele/dela" (his/her) instead of an English-style possessive ("his house").
target_language_example: Vamos jantar na casa dele amanhã.
native_language_example: We’re going to have dinner at his house tomorrow.

casa no próximo fim de semana

target_language_multi_word_term: casa no próximo fim de semana
additional_notes: Means being at someone's home (or your own) during the coming weekend. Often used with verbs like "estar" (to be) or "ir" (to go): "estar em casa" = to be at home; "ir na/à sua casa" = to go to your place/house. "Sua" is more formal (often used with "você"); "tua" is more informal/familiar (often used with "tu").
target_language_example: Vou ficar em casa no próximo fim de semana.
native_language_example: I'm going to stay at home next weekend.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb: casar-se (to get married) + com (with/to). You can also hear the non-reflexive form casar com, especially in casual speech, but casar-se com is common in writing and careful speech. The pronoun agrees with the subject: eu caso-me com…, ele/ela casa-se com…, nós casamo-nos com… (often simplified in Brazilian Portuguese to eu me caso com…, ele/ela se casa com…, a gente se casa com…).
target_language_example: Você quer casar-se com ela algum dia?
native_language_example: Do you want to marry her someday?

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "com" before the person you marry: "casar com alguém". Very often appears as "casar-se com" (same meaning; "-se" emphasizes the person getting married). In everyday speech you may also hear "casar com" without "-se". Note the difference: "casar com" = marry someone; "casar" by itself can mean "to get married" (without saying who).
target_language_example: Ela vai se casar com o namorado no ano que vem.
native_language_example: She’s going to marry her boyfriend next year.

additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb “casar-se” (to get married). Used with “com” to say who someone married. In European Portuguese you often see “casou-se”; in Brazilian Portuguese it’s also common to say “casou com” (without “-se”), especially in speech.
target_language_example: Ela casou-se com um canadense em 2020.
native_language_example: She married a Canadian in 2020.

meaning: "(he/she) married a" (got married to a woman).
additional_notes: "Casou-se" is the reflexive past tense of "casar-se" (to get married). It’s used with "com" to say who someone married: "casou-se com + (a person)". "Uma" is the feminine indefinite article (“a”), so this chunk is followed by a feminine noun (e.g., "uma canadense", "uma professora"). For a man, you’d use "casou-se com um".
target_language_example: Ela casou-se com uma médica argentina.
native_language_example: She married an Argentine doctor.

additional_notes: Simple past (pretérito perfeito) of **casar com** = “to marry (someone)”. Used to say who a person married. The preposition **com** (“with”) is required: **casou com ele/ela**, **casou com o João**. In questions, it often means “Did (he/she) marry …?”
target_language_example: Ela casou com o namorado da faculdade.
native_language_example: She married her college boyfriend.

meaning: “cause of the” (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Usually appears as **a causa do + noun** to talk about the reason something happened: **a causa do acidente** (“the cause of the accident”). With a feminine noun, it changes to **a causa da** (e.g., **a causa da demora** = “the cause of the delay”).
target_language_example: A causa do problema ainda não está clara.
native_language_example: The cause of the problem is still not clear.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "cavar" (to dig) + "um buraco" (a hole). Used for physically digging a hole in the ground/sand (e.g., in a garden, on the beach, or by an animal). You can change the subject and place: "Eu cavei um buraco", "Ela cavou um buraco na areia".
target_language_example: Ontem eu cavei um buraco no quintal para plantar uma árvore.
native_language_example: Yesterday I dug a hole in the backyard to plant a tree.

additional_notes: Past tense of "cair no sono" (to fall asleep). Very common for saying you unintentionally started sleeping (often because you were tired or bored). You can add a time clue with "enquanto" (while) or "antes de" (before).
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu caí no sono no sofá.
native_language_example: Sorry, I fell asleep on the couch.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened earlier than usual on the same day. Often goes after the verb (e.g., "Cheguei cedo hoje") and can be intensified with "muito" ("muito cedo hoje" = "very early today").
target_language_example: Vou dormir cedo hoje porque estou cansado.
native_language_example: I’m going to sleep early today because I’m tired.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen at some point in the future, even if you don’t know when. Often at the beginning of a sentence for emphasis ("Cedo ou tarde, ..."), or at the end ("..., cedo ou tarde.").
target_language_example: Cedo ou tarde, vamos encontrar uma solução.
native_language_example: Sooner or later, we’ll find a solution.

meaning: “blind, deaf, and …” (used to list a third adjective).
additional_notes: This is a common structure for listing adjectives about a woman (feminine forms): cega (blind), surda (deaf), e (and) + another adjective (often muda = mute). For a man, you’d usually say: cego, surdo e … . It can be neutral/medical (e.g., “cega, surda e muda”), but it may sound insulting if the third adjective is negative (e.g., burra = stupid).
target_language_example: Ela ficou cega, surda e muda depois do acidente.
native_language_example: She became blind, deaf, and mute after the accident.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a time span (duration) or someone/something’s age. Often appears with expressions like “há cem anos” (a hundred years ago), “mais de cem anos” (more than a hundred years), and “quase cem anos” (almost a hundred years).
target_language_example: Meu bisavô viveu até os cem anos.
native_language_example: My great-grandfather lived to be 100 years old.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun (or another quantity phrase) to indicate a large approximate number. Common patterns: "centenas de pessoas" (hundreds of people), "centenas de livros" (hundreds of books), and with bigger numbers: "centenas de milhares" (hundreds of thousands), "centenas de milhões" (hundreds of millions).
target_language_example: Havia centenas de pessoas na fila.
native_language_example: There were hundreds of people in line.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the central part of a city (where shops, offices, and main sights often are). Common with verbs like morar (to live), ir (to go), and with maps/directions. Often interchangeable with "centro" or (especially in Brazil) "centro"/"downtown" depending on context.
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar no centro da cidade às seis.
native_language_example: Let’s meet downtown at six.

additional_notes: Used to give an approximate number. "cerca de" + number works with people, objects, time, money, etc. (e.g., "cerca de 10 minutos", "cerca de 50 reais"). Similar to "aproximadamente" but more common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: A reunião vai durar cerca de trinta minutos.
native_language_example: The meeting will last about thirty minutes.

additional_notes: Used to give an approximate quantity, distance, or measurement. Often followed by a noun or unit (e.g., "cerca de três litros", "cerca de três quarteirões"). You can also see it with "a" for approximate distance: "a cerca de três quarteirões daqui" = "about three blocks from here".
target_language_example: A reunião vai durar cerca de três horas.
native_language_example: The meeting will last about three hours.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like ter/haver/estar com certeza to introduce a clause with que: tenho certeza de que + [statement]. It’s a common way to confirm or check something (“Are you sure that…?”). Often appears in commands: tenha certeza de que… (“make sure that…”).
target_language_example: Tenho certeza de que ele vai chegar a tempo.
native_language_example: I'm sure that he’ll arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like "ter" or "(estar) com" certeza to introduce a clause: "ter certeza de que..." = "to be sure that...". "o" is the masculine singular article ("the") used before a masculine noun/name (e.g., "o Tom"); you can also see "certeza de que a..." (feminine), or just "certeza de que..." when no article is needed.
target_language_example: Quero ter certeza de que o ônibus sai às oito.
native_language_example: I want to make sure that the bus leaves at eight.

additional_notes: Often used after a verb like **ter**: **ter certeza que...** = “to be sure that...”. In Portugal you’ll also hear **ter a certeza de que...** (same meaning). In casual speech, **Certeza que...** by itself can mean “I’m sure (that) ...”. Related: **de certeza** = “for sure / definitely”.
target_language_example: Tenho certeza que ele vai chegar cedo.
native_language_example: I'm sure he'll arrive early.

meaning: make sure to; be sure to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to give an instruction or reminder to check that something gets done. It’s the imperative form (a command/request) of the reflexive verb “certificar-se” (to make sure). With a verb, use “certifique-se de + infinitive” (Certifique-se de salvar…). When followed by a full clause, Portuguese often uses “certifique-se de que …” (Certifique-se de que o Tom virá).
target_language_example: Certifique-se de fechar a porta antes de sair.
native_language_example: Make sure to close the door before you leave.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to check/confirm something, often as a precaution or instruction (common in rules, reminders, and checklists). It’s the imperative of the reflexive verb "certificar-se". It can be followed by the indicative (certifique-se de que ele vem) or the subjunctive (certifique-se de que ele venha), especially when expressing a desired/required action.
target_language_example: Por favor, certifique-se de que você trancou o carro antes de entrar.
native_language_example: Please make sure you locked the car before going inside.

additional_notes: Used when you want to contact law enforcement (typically by phone) to report an emergency, crime, or problem. Common patterns: "Vou chamar a polícia" (I’m going to call the police), "Temos que chamar a polícia" (We have to call the police), "Pode chamar a polícia" (You can call the police).
target_language_example: Se ele voltar, eu vou chamar a polícia.
native_language_example: If he comes back, I’m going to call the police.

additional_notes: Used as a command/request. It comes from the verb "chamar" (to call) + "um táxi" (a taxi). You can also use it in questions like "Quer que eu chame um táxi?" (Do you want me to call a taxi?). In Brazil, "chamar um táxi" can mean calling one by phone/app or asking for one to come pick you up.
target_language_example: Está tarde—chame um táxi, por favor.
native_language_example: It’s late—call a taxi, please.

meaning: to call him (something); to refer to him as (a name/title).
additional_notes: Used with the object pronoun “-lo” (= “him”) attached to the verb chamar: chamar + o → chamá-lo. It’s often followed by a name, nickname, or description: “chamá-lo de Tom” (“call him Tom”), “chamá-lo de gênio” (“call him a genius”). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese you may also hear “chamar ele de…”.
target_language_example: Podemos chamá-lo de João?
native_language_example: Can we call him João?

meaning: "a chance to" / "a chance of" (opportunity or possibility of something happening).
additional_notes: Used before a verb in the infinitive (chance de + infinitive) or before a noun to talk about the possibility/opportunity of an action or result: "chance de ganhar" (chance to win), "chance de fuga" (chance of escape). Often appears with "ter" (to have) and "existe" (there is): "tem uma chance de...", "existe alguma chance de...?". In negative form, "sem chance de..." means "no chance of...".
target_language_example: Você tem alguma chance de chegar a tempo?
native_language_example: Do you have any chance of arriving on time?

additional_notes: Used to talk about having, not having, or missing an opportunity to do something. Very common with verbs like ter (to have), nunca ter (to never have), perder (to miss/lose), and ser a única chance (to be the only chance). You can replace "isso" with another action: "chance de fazer + [verb/thing]" (e.g., "chance de ver" / "chance de falar").
target_language_example: Você ainda tem uma chance de fazer isso amanhã.
native_language_example: You still have a chance to do that tomorrow.

additional_notes: Refers to the key used to open/start a car. Often used with possessives: "a minha chave do carro" (my car key), "a chave do carro dele" (his car key). You can also say "chave do automóvel" (more formal) or simply "a chave" when context is clear.
target_language_example: Não consigo encontrar a chave do carro; você viu onde eu deixei?
native_language_example: I can’t find the car key; did you see where I left it?

meaning: to arrive on time; to make it in time.
additional_notes: Used when talking about arriving before a deadline or before something starts (e.g., class, a train/metro). Often followed by "para" + event ("chegar a tempo para a escola") or "a/ao" + place/transport ("chegar a tempo ao metro"). You can also use it in questions about whether you’ll make it: "Vamos chegar a tempo?"
target_language_example: Se sairmos agora, ainda dá para chegar a tempo para o filme.
native_language_example: If we leave now, we can still make it to the movie on time.

additional_notes: Used with "chegar" (to arrive) + "aqui" (here) to say someone arrives at the speaker’s location. Very common with time expressions ("a que horas...?"), with "acabar de" to mean "have just arrived" ("Acabei de chegar aqui"), and after conjunctions like "antes de" (before) and "até" (until).
target_language_example: Me liga quando você chegar aqui.
native_language_example: Call me when you get here.

meaning: to get home; to arrive home.
additional_notes: Used to talk about arriving at your home. In Brazil, you’ll often hear both "chegar em casa" and "chegar a casa"; "em casa" is very common in everyday speech. With "como", it can mean finding the way to your house ("how to get home").
target_language_example: Eu chego em casa às seis da tarde.
native_language_example: I get home at six in the evening.

meaning: to get there; to arrive there.
additional_notes: Used to talk about reaching a place mentioned or understood from context. Very common with time expressions (e.g., "a tempo" = "on time") and ways of travel ("de ônibus", "de trem"). In everyday speech it can also mean “to make it / achieve it” (e.g., "Ele vai chegar lá"), but in these examples it’s about arriving somewhere.
target_language_example: Se sairmos agora, a gente chega lá antes das oito.
native_language_example: If we leave now, we’ll get there before eight.

meaning: to get to / arrive at the station.
additional_notes: Used for reaching a station (train, bus, метро, etc.). In questions, it’s very common in the pattern “Como chegar à estação?” (“How do I get to the station?”). “Chegar” = to arrive; “à” = “a + a” (“to the” feminine singular), because “estação” is feminine.
target_language_example: Como posso chegar à estação de ônibus?
native_language_example: How can I get to the bus station?

additional_notes: Used to announce that the right moment has arrived to do something: "chegou a hora de + infinitive" (chegou a hora de crescer = it’s time to grow up). You can also use "chegou a hora" alone as a dramatic or decisive statement (The moment has arrived).
target_language_example: Chegou a hora de irmos embora.
native_language_example: It’s time for us to leave.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "chegar em casa" = "to get/arrive home." It’s usually used to say when someone got home (depois da meia-noite), in what condition (encharcado), or what was happening then (quando ela chegou em casa). You can change the subject: "eu cheguei em casa" (I got home), "eles chegaram em casa" (they got home).
target_language_example: Eu cheguei em casa tarde e fui direto dormir.
native_language_example: I got home late and went straight to sleep.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something arrived at the expected time (not late). Very common with transport and appointments: “O avião chegou na hora.” You can add emphasis with “na hora exata” (“exactly on time”). In sentence 7, “na hora que...” means “at the moment when...”: “Você chegou na hora que eu saí.” = “You arrived just as I left.”
target_language_example: Ainda bem que você chegou na hora para a reunião.
native_language_example: Good thing you arrived on time for the meeting.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of chegar: eu cheguei = “I arrived.” Used to say you got home, often followed by what happened next (e.g., “assim que…” = “as soon as…”). In Brazil, you’ll also hear “cheguei em casa”; in Portugal, “cheguei a casa” is common too.
target_language_example: Cheguei em casa e tomei um banho.
native_language_example: I got home and took a shower.

additional_notes: "Cheguei" is the past tense of "chegar" (to arrive) for "eu" (I). "à" = "a" (to) + "a" (the), used because "estação" is feminine, so it means “to the station.” Often used with time phrases like "a tempo" (on time) or "atrasado" (late), and can be followed by what you did next: "Assim que cheguei à estação, ..." (As soon as I arrived at the station, ...).
target_language_example: Cheguei à estação cedo, mas o trem ainda não tinha saído.
native_language_example: I arrived at the station early, but the train still hadn’t left.

additional_notes: Used to say something contains a lot of something else. It agrees with what is “full”: cheia (feminine singular), cheio (masculine singular), cheias (feminine plural), cheios (masculine plural). Common with both literal things (cheia de fotos, cheia de maçãs) and abstract ideas (cheia de energia, cheia de riscos, cheia de altos e baixos).
target_language_example: A rua estava cheia de gente.
native_language_example: The street was full of people.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to express having a lot of something, either literally (full) or figuratively (full of hope/energy, etc.). It agrees with the subject: cheio (masc.), cheia (fem.), cheios (masc. pl.), cheias (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: A sala estava cheia de gente.
native_language_example: The room was full of people.

additional_notes: Used to say what something smells like. Common patterns: "com cheiro de + noun" (having a smell of…), "estar com cheiro de…" (to smell like…), "ter cheiro de…" (to have a smell of…), and "sentir cheiro de…" (to smell/notice a smell of…). Can also be used in questions: "tem cheiro de quê?" (what does it smell like?).
target_language_example: Esse casaco está com cheiro de cigarro.
native_language_example: This coat smells like cigarettes.

additional_notes: Used to say someone felt very surprised and upset after hearing some news. "Chocados" agrees with who is shocked (chocado = masculine singular, chocada = feminine singular, chocados = masculine/mixed plural, chocadas = feminine plural). Often followed by "da/de" to specify what the news is about: "com a notícia da/de ...".
target_language_example: Eles ficaram chocados com a notícia do acidente.
native_language_example: They were shocked by the news of the accident.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "chutar a bola" (to kick the ball). Used for a completed action in the past. You can change the subject: "Eu chutei a bola" (I kicked the ball), "Ela chutou a bola" (She kicked the ball). Common with directions: "para" (to/toward) and "para fora" (out).
target_language_example: O jogador chutou a bola para o gol.
native_language_example: The player kicked the ball toward the goal.

additional_notes: Used to order or talk about tea served with lemon (usually a slice or lemon juice). In cafés/restaurants you’ll often hear it with an article: “um chá com limão” = “a lemon tea.” You can swap in other ingredients: “chá com leite” (tea with milk), “chá com mel” (tea with honey).
target_language_example: Você tem chá com limão?
native_language_example: Do you have lemon tea?

additional_notes: Common fixed choice question when offering a drink. You’ll often hear it with verbs like querer (to want), gostar (would like), tomar (to have/drink), or beber (to drink): “Você quer/gostaria de tomar/beber chá ou café?” In Portuguese, “tomar” is very common for having a drink.
target_language_example: Para acompanhar o bolo, você prefere chá ou café?
native_language_example: To go with the cake, do you prefer tea or coffee?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the city where someone was born and/or grew up. Often appears with possessives: "minha cidade natal" (my hometown), "sua cidade natal" (your/his/her hometown).
target_language_example: Sempre que posso, volto à minha cidade natal para visitar a família.
native_language_example: Whenever I can, I go back to my hometown to visit my family.

meaning: five years (a duration), or at five years old.
additional_notes: Used either to talk about a length of time (e.g., "por cinco anos" = for five years) or age ("com cinco anos" / "quando eu tinha cinco anos" = at five years old / when I was five). With time in the past, Portuguese often uses "há cinco anos" or "cinco anos atrás" (= five years ago).
target_language_example: Trabalhei nessa empresa por cinco anos.
native_language_example: I worked at that company for five years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an amount of money. With verbs like pagar/dar, it often appears with: **dar** (to give) + amount (Eu vou te dar cinco dólares.), **pagar** (to pay) + amount (Paguei cinco dólares.), and **pagar** + amount + **a mais** (to pay extra/more than expected: Paguei cinco dólares a mais.). In Brazil, you’re more likely to hear *cinco reais* in everyday life, but *dólares* is common when referring to US currency.
target_language_example: Você tem cinco dólares trocados?
native_language_example: Do you have five dollars in change?

additional_notes: Used to say something happened five minutes ago ("há cinco minutos") or to ask for a short amount of time ("só cinco minutos"). In conversation it can also mean "just a moment" even if it’s not exactly five minutes.
target_language_example: Espera cinco minutos, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait five minutes, please.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement that is obvious or made explicit. Very common after forms of estar/ficar (“Está claro que…”, “Ficou claro que…”) and in “deixar claro que…” (“to make it clear that…”). In casual speech, “Claro que sim!” also means “Of course!”.
target_language_example: Ficou claro que ela não queria continuar.
native_language_example: It became clear that she didn’t want to continue.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement that is obvious or made explicit. Very common after forms of estar/ficar (“Está claro que…”, “Ficou claro que…”) and in “deixar claro que…” (“to make it clear that…”). In casual speech, “Claro que sim!” also means “Of course!”.
target_language_example: Ficou claro que ela não queria continuar.
native_language_example: It became clear that she didn’t want to continue.

additional_notes: Used with forms of "estar" (or sometimes "ficar") to describe a surface or place that has a layer of snow on it: "está coberta de neve". Agreement matters: "coberto" (masc.) / "coberta" (fem.) and plural "cobertos/cobertas". "de" here means "with/in" (covered with snow).
target_language_example: As ruas estavam cobertas de neve depois da tempestade.
native_language_example: The streets were covered in snow after the storm.

additional_notes: A simple factual statement. "Coelhos" = rabbits, "têm" (from "ter") = have, "orelhas" = ears, "compridas" = long. Often used with the article too: "Os coelhos têm orelhas compridas" ("Rabbits/The rabbits have long ears").
target_language_example: Coelhos têm orelhas compridas, mas nem todos são do mesmo tamanho.
native_language_example: Rabbits have long ears, but not all of them are the same size.

additional_notes: Used to say an action or choice is correct or morally right. Very common in the pattern “(ser) a coisa certa a fazer” = “(to be) the right thing to do.” You can also say “fazer a coisa certa” = “do the right thing.”
target_language_example: Eu sei que é difícil, mas é a coisa certa a fazer.
native_language_example: I know it’s hard, but it’s the right thing to do.

meaning: 'something to/for' (a thing needed for a purpose, or something you’re going to do/show/say).
additional_notes: Usually appears as "uma coisa para + infinitive" (e.g., "uma coisa para escrever", "uma coisa para te mostrar"). It’s a very common, general way to refer to an object or information when you don’t want to be specific (like English "something to write with" / "something to show you").
target_language_example: Você tem alguma coisa para beber?
native_language_example: Do you have something to drink?

meaning: 'thing that/which' (used to introduce a description of a thing).
additional_notes: Used in relative clauses to add information about a noun, especially with superlatives like "a melhor coisa que..." ("the best thing that..."). Very common in questions: "Qual foi a última coisa que ela disse...?" = "What was the last thing she said...?" In everyday speech, Portuguese often uses "que" where English might use "that/which" or omit it.
target_language_example: A primeira coisa que eu fiz foi ligar para você.
native_language_example: The first thing I did was call you.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase used to talk about things that are new or different—often in the sense of new experiences or ideas (especially with verbs like "tentar" = to try). You can also use it for new items/products: "Temos coisas novas na loja" (We have new things in the store).
target_language_example: Estou tentando coisas novas este ano.
native_language_example: I’m trying new things this year.

meaning: 'things to do' (tasks/activities you need or want to do).
additional_notes: Very common everyday phrase. Often used to talk about being busy ("tenho muitas coisas para fazer", "estou cheio de coisas para fazer"). With "melhores coisas para fazer", it means you'd rather do something else ("I have better things to do").
target_language_example: Desculpa, não posso sair agora — tenho coisas para fazer.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out now—I have things to do.

meaning: “things that” / “things which” (introduces a clause describing the things).
additional_notes: Used when you want to specify or describe which “things” you mean, followed by a verb clause (often with que = “that/which”). Common in expressions like “há coisas que…” (“there are things that…”) and “as coisas que eu sei” (“the things that I know”).
target_language_example: Há muitas coisas que eu quero aprender este ano.
native_language_example: There are many things that I want to learn this year.

additional_notes: Used for people who are in the same class (at school, university, or a course). You can also say "colega de classe" (singular). Similar options: "colegas" (classmates/colleagues, depending on context) and "colegas de turma" (same group/class).
target_language_example: Eu vou estudar com meus colegas de classe depois da aula.
native_language_example: I'm going to study with my classmates after class.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the hobby of collecting postage stamps. Often appears with possessives (minha/sua/a dele) and the verb "ter" (to have) or "mostrar" (to show). "Selo" means a (postage) stamp; "selos" is plural.
target_language_example: Eu comecei uma coleção de selos quando era criança.
native_language_example: I started a stamp collection when I was a child.

additional_notes: Used when someone placed/put something somewhere in the past. It’s usually followed by the object (a bolsa, a lista) and then a location with a preposition (na/na = em + a, no = em + o, em cima de, etc.). "Colocou" agrees with the subject (ele/ela/you formal), and "a" is the feminine singular definite article for the object (use "o" for masculine: "colocou o livro...").
target_language_example: Ela colocou a chave na gaveta.
native_language_example: She put the key in the drawer.

additional_notes: "Colocou" is the simple past of "colocar" (to put/place). It’s commonly followed by "em/no/na" + place: "colocou a chave no bolso" (in the pocket), "na porta" (in/on the door), "na ignição" (in the ignition). It can also appear in indirect questions about where someone put it: "onde você colocou a chave?".
target_language_example: Eu não lembro onde eu coloquei a chave.
native_language_example: I don’t remember where I put the key.

additional_notes: “Colocou” is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of “colocar” (to put/place). It’s commonly followed by a direct object with the masculine article “o” (“the”), and then a location with a preposition: “no/na” (= em + o/a, “in/on the”), “na mesa” (on the table), “na garagem” (in the garage), “sobre a mesa” (on top of the table). Subject is often omitted in Portuguese, so “Colocou o…” can mean “He/She/Someone put the…”.
target_language_example: Ela colocou o telefone na bolsa.
native_language_example: She put the phone in her bag.

meaning: “to put/place it” or “to put him” (depending on context).
additional_notes: Colocá-lo = colocar (“to put/place”) + -lo (“it/him”). It’s the infinitive form used after expressions like “precisa”, “vamos”, “temos que”, “pode”, etc. In everyday speech, many people also say “colocar ele” instead of “colocá-lo”, but “colocá-lo” is more standard/written.
target_language_example: Você pode colocá-lo aqui na mesa.
native_language_example: You can put it here on the table.

additional_notes: Imperative of colocar (“to put/place”) + object pronoun -o (“it,” for a masculine object). Used to tell someone to put something somewhere: coloque-o ali/na mesa/na prateleira/sobre a mesa. In everyday speech, many people also say “coloca ele” or “coloca-o” depending on region and formality. With “de volta”, it means “put it back.”
target_language_example: Por favor, coloque-o aqui na bancada.
native_language_example: Please put it here on the counter.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun. It’s the contraction of "com" (with) + "a" (the). Common for being together with someone (com a Mary), sharing (dividiu... com a Mary), or helping with something (ajudando... com a tarefa).
target_language_example: Vou falar com a professora depois da aula.
native_language_example: I’m going to talk with the teacher after class.

meaning: “with (your/the) head”; also in idioms like “Onde você está com a cabeça?” = “What are you thinking?/What’s wrong with you?”
additional_notes: Used literally to describe doing something using the head (e.g., acenar com a cabeça = to nod/shake your head; bater com a cabeça = to hit/bump your head). In expressions like “Onde você está com a cabeça?” or “Não sei onde ele está com a cabeça”, it means someone is being careless, distracted, or making bad decisions.
target_language_example: Ela disse que ia dirigir depois de beber, e eu perguntei: “Onde você está com a cabeça?”
native_language_example: She said she was going to drive after drinking, and I asked, “What are you thinking?”

additional_notes: "A gente" is very common in Brazilian Portuguese and usually means "we/us" (informal/neutral in speech). So "com a gente" is a natural way to invite someone to come along: "Vem/Venha com a gente" = "Come with us." It can also mean being on someone’s side or agreeing: "Ele concordou com a gente" = "He agreed with us."
target_language_example: Se você quiser, pode almoçar com a gente hoje.
native_language_example: If you want, you can have lunch with us today.

additional_notes: "A gente" is very common in Brazilian Portuguese and usually means "we/us" (informal/neutral in speech). So "com a gente" is a natural way to invite someone to come along: "Vem/Venha com a gente" = "Come with us." It can also mean being on someone’s side or agreeing: "Ele concordou com a gente" = "He agreed with us."
target_language_example: Se você quiser, pode almoçar com a gente hoje.
native_language_example: If you want, you can have lunch with us today.

additional_notes: Used with "com" + noun to describe a condition or circumstance (here: the window is open) while doing something, often with verbs like "dormir" (to sleep), "ficar" (to stay), "deixar" (to leave), etc. It can refer to one specific moment or a habitual action depending on the verb tense.
target_language_example: Está frio; não durma com a janela aberta.
native_language_example: It’s cold; don’t sleep with the window open.

meaning: "with my" (before a feminine singular noun); often "about/concerning my" after certain verbs.
additional_notes: This is the preposition "com" + the feminine article "a" + the possessive "minha". Use it before feminine singular nouns: "com a minha saúde" (with/about my health), "com a minha proposta" (with my proposal). With some verbs, "com" is required and is best translated as "about" or "regarding" (e.g., "preocupar-se com" = to worry about; "concordar com" = to agree with; "cumprir com" = to fulfill/comply with).
target_language_example: Você concorda com a minha ideia?
native_language_example: Do you agree with my idea?

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your family or doing something alongside them. Common after verbs like ir (to go), passar (to spend), viver (to live), and mudar-se (to move). The literal structure is com (with) + a (the, feminine singular) + minha (my) + família (family).
target_language_example: Vou viajar com a minha família nas férias.
native_language_example: I’m going to travel with my family on vacation.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together with your mother (in the same place, living together, leaving someone in her care) or that you learned/did something alongside her. In Portuguese, “com” often means “with,” including living with someone (“moro com...”).
target_language_example: Vou jantar com a minha mãe hoje.
native_language_example: I’m going to have dinner with my mother today.

meaning: “with my life” (i.e., about my personal life/affairs).
additional_notes: Often used when talking about personal matters. Common in phrases like “O que isso tem a ver com a minha vida?” (“What does that have to do with my life?”) and “fazer algo com a minha vida” (“do something with my life”). Note: in this expression, it’s usually written “ter a ver” (to have to do with), not “ter haver”.
target_language_example: Isso não tem nada a ver com a minha vida.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with my life.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like "morar" (to live) or "ficar" (to stay) to say someone is with their mother. "A mãe" is "the mother" (often meaning “his/her mother” from context). In comparisons, "parecido com a mãe" means “similar to the mother.”
target_language_example: Ele mora com a mãe desde que terminou a faculdade.
native_language_example: He has been living with his mother since he finished college.

additional_notes: Means being together/accompanied by her mother, or living together with her mother (context decides). "Dela" means "of her" and refers back to a female person already mentioned (e.g., Mary). You’ll often see it after verbs like "morar/viver" (to live) and "estar" (to be): "morar com a mãe dela" = live with her mother; "estar com a mãe dela" = be with her mother (together/at the same place).
target_language_example: Hoje eu vou ao médico com a mãe dela.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to the doctor with her mother.

additional_notes: Used to say you do an action using your left hand (e.g., writing, holding something). You can also hear the variant “com a esquerda”.
target_language_example: Eu abro a porta com a mão esquerda.
native_language_example: I open the door with my left hand.

meaning: "with the news" / "upon hearing the news" (showing a reaction).
additional_notes: Often used after a feeling/reaction to show what caused it, especially with "ficar" + adjective: "ficar surpreso(a)/triste/atordoado(a) com a notícia". In English this is often more natural as "at the news" or "upon hearing the news." Note: "notícia" means "news" (not "notice").
target_language_example: Ele ficou preocupado com a notícia.
native_language_example: He got worried at the news.

meaning: "about (someone’s) mental health" / "with mental health" (in the sense of concern or dealing).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "estar preocupado(a)" to say you’re concerned about someone’s mental health: "preocupado(a) com a saúde mental de...". Also used with verbs like "cuidar/lidar/trabalhar com" to mean dealing with mental health topics. "Saúde mental" is a common, neutral term for mental health.
target_language_example: Estou preocupado com a saúde mental do meu amigo.
native_language_example: I’m worried about my friend’s mental health.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "com" (with) plus the possessive "a sua". "Sua" usually means "your" (often formal) but can also mean "his/her/its" depending on context; "a" agrees with a feminine noun (e.g., "a sua perna", "a sua faca"). It can also mean "with yours" when the noun is implied (e.g., "Posso ir com a sua?" = "Can I go with yours?").
target_language_example: Posso falar com a sua mãe um minuto?
native_language_example: Can I talk with your mother for a minute?

meaning: 'with your mother' / 'to your mother' (depending on the verb).
additional_notes: Literally means "with your mother". With verbs like "parecer" or "gritar", it’s used after the verb to show who someone is being compared to (parecida com...) or who someone is yelling at (gritar com...). It can also mean "with" in the sense of "talk to" or "have a word with" (ter uma palavra com...). "Sua" is a polite/neutral way to say "your" (often used with "você"), but in some contexts it can also mean "his/her"—context usually makes it clear.
target_language_example: Você já falou com a sua mãe sobre isso?
native_language_example: Have you already talked to your mother about that?

meaning: with someone I know; like someone I know.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a person you know, often to say something happened to them ("aconteceu com...") or that someone looks like/resembles them ("parece com...", "se parece com...", "parecido com..."). In these sentences, "com" means "with" after certain verbs/adjectives (especially in comparisons: "parecer com" = "to look like").
target_language_example: Ela se parece com alguém que eu conheço do trabalho.
native_language_example: She looks like someone I know from work.

additional_notes: This is the preposition "com" (with) + the plural feminine definite article "as" (the). It’s used before plural feminine nouns: "com as minhas mãos" (with my hands), "com as crianças" (with the children). In phrases like "para com as", it can mean "toward/regarding the" (showing attitude toward the laws, rules, etc.).
target_language_example: Vou sair com as minhas amigas hoje.
native_language_example: I’m going out with my (female) friends today.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with children or doing something alongside them. Also common after adjectives/commands to describe how you should behave toward them (e.g., "Seja paciente com as crianças" = "Be patient with the children"). "As" is the plural feminine form of "a" ("the") used with "crianças".
target_language_example: Eu trabalho com as crianças todas as tardes.
native_language_example: I work with the children every afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to say you hold, grab, carry, or do something using both hands (often for better control or safety). Common with verbs like segurar (to hold), pegar (to grab/pick up), carregar (to carry).
target_language_example: Por favor, segure o prato com as duas mãos.
native_language_example: Please hold the plate with both hands.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something using your hands (instead of a tool), or to describe what your hands are doing/where they are: “com as mãos nos bolsos” (with hands in pockets), “com as mãos pra cima” (with hands up). Often followed by a phrase describing position.
target_language_example: Ele abriu a porta com as mãos ocupadas.
native_language_example: He opened the door with his hands full.

additional_notes: Used to say the payment method. Often appears in questions and requests in shops and restaurants: “Em dinheiro ou com cartão de crédito?” (“Cash or credit card?”) and “Posso pagar com cartão de crédito?” (“Can I pay by credit card?”). You can also say “no cartão de crédito” in some contexts, but “com cartão de crédito” is the most direct for “by credit card.”
target_language_example: Desculpe, posso pagar com cartão de crédito?
native_language_example: Sorry, can I pay by credit card?

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar/ficar to talk about someone being in a jealous mood/state. It can be followed by “de” to say who/what the jealousy is about: “com ciúmes de alguém” (jealous of someone). Very common in questions like “Está com ciúmes?”
target_language_example: Ele ficou com ciúmes do meu amigo.
native_language_example: He got jealous of my friend.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing an action in a careful, cautious way (often for safety or to avoid damage). It can modify physical actions (Abra a porta com cuidado.) or more abstract actions like considering/analysing something (considerou a oferta com cuidado).
target_language_example: Pise com cuidado, o chão está molhado.
native_language_example: Step carefully; the floor is wet.

meaning: with a headache; having a headache.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (or "ficar") to describe someone’s current condition: "Estou com dor de cabeça" = "I have a headache." Also common with "acordar" to say you woke up with one: "Acordei com dor de cabeça." Often paired with other symptoms: "com dor de cabeça e garganta inflamada".
target_language_example: Estou com dor de cabeça, acho que vou deitar cedo.
native_language_example: I have a headache; I think I’m going to go to bed early.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "com" + "ela" (she/her) to mean doing something together with a female person, or comparing something/someone against her (e.g., "se comparar com ela" = "compare to/with her"). Often refers back to a woman/girl already mentioned.
target_language_example: Você pode falar com ela mais tarde.
native_language_example: Can you talk to her later?

additional_notes: Used after a verb or adjective to indicate that someone is together with him, doing something alongside him, living with him, etc. It can also appear in set expressions like "contar com ele" (to count on him) and in warnings like "cuidado com ele" (be careful with him). Contrast: "com ela" = with her; "com eles" = with them (masc./mixed); "com elas" = with them (fem.).
target_language_example: Você quer ir com ele agora?
native_language_example: Do you want to go with him now?

additional_notes: "Com" means "with" and "eles" means "they/them" (masculine plural, or a mixed group). Used for being together with people (going somewhere, doing an activity) and also after many verbs to mean "to/with them" (e.g., falar com eles = talk to them; concordar com eles = agree with them; ser rígido com eles = be strict with them).
target_language_example: Você pode ir com eles amanhã?
native_language_example: Can you go with them tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or can be done without much effort. It can describe actions (resolver, encontrar, fazer) or someone’s tendency to react quickly (se assusta/se cansa com facilidade = gets scared/tired easily).
target_language_example: Ela aprende línguas com facilidade.
native_language_example: She learns languages easily.

meaning: with a fever; having a fever.
additional_notes: Used with "estar" (or sometimes "ficar") to talk about someone’s current condition: "estar com febre" = "to have a fever" (temporary state). In Portuguese you commonly say "com" + symptom/condition (e.g., "com dor", "com gripe").
target_language_example: Acho que estou com febre desde ontem.
native_language_example: I think I’ve had a fever since yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar/ficar to talk about the temporary state of being hungry: estar com fome (to be hungry), ficar com fome (to get hungry). You can negate it with não: não estou com fome (I’m not hungry).
target_language_example: Estou com fome, vamos almoçar.
native_language_example: I'm hungry, let's have lunch.

additional_notes: Used to ask whether someone wants food or something to drink. Portuguese commonly uses "estar com" + a noun to express temporary states/feelings: "estar com fome" (to be hungry) and "estar com sede" (to be thirsty). Often used in polite questions like "O senhor/A senhora..." (formal) or "Você..." (neutral).
target_language_example: Depois da caminhada, eu estava com fome ou com sede — então parei num café.
native_language_example: After the walk, I was hungry or thirsty—so I stopped at a café.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens regularly or many times. Common with verbs to describe habits or repeated actions (e.g., "penso com frequência", "acontece com frequência").
target_language_example: Ele viaja a trabalho com frequência.
native_language_example: He travels for work often.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (or sometimes "ficar") to say you feel cold: "Estou com frio" = "I'm cold". You can add a body part with "em/no/na" (often contracted): "com frio nos pés" = "cold feet" (literally, cold in the feet).
target_language_example: Estou com frio, pode fechar a janela?
native_language_example: I'm cold—can you close the window?

meaning: "with that/with it"; also in "Para com isso" = "Stop that".
additional_notes: Literally "with that" (com + isso). Used to refer back to something already mentioned (an object, idea, situation, or behavior). Very common in questions like "O que você vai fazer com isso?" (What are you going to do with that?). In the expression "Para com isso", it’s an idiomatic, everyday way to tell someone to stop what they’re doing/saying.
target_language_example: Eu não sei o que fazer com isso.
native_language_example: I don't know what to do with that.

additional_notes: Used to politely get someone’s attention before asking the price of something. Typically followed by a verb like "custa" (costs) or "é/são" (is/are): "Com licença, quanto é isto?" / "Com licença, quanto são estes?"
target_language_example: Com licença, quanto custa esta camisa?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how much does this shirt cost?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (or other states like "ficar") to describe someone’s emotional state: "estou com medo" = "I’m afraid." You can also specify what you’re afraid of with "de": "estar com medo de" + noun/verb ("Tenho medo de altura" / "Estou com medo de cair").
target_language_example: Estou com medo de falar em público.
native_language_example: I’m afraid to speak in public.

additional_notes: Used with a noun or an infinitive to say what someone fears. Common patterns: "estar com medo de + [thing/person]" (Tenho/Estou com medo de sangue.) and "estar com medo de + infinitive" (Estou com medo de entrar.)
target_language_example: Estou com medo de falar em público.
native_language_example: I’m afraid to speak in public.

additional_notes: Often used to say you are together/doing something in your brother’s company: "Estou ... com meu irmão". With "estar" it can also mean something is in your brother’s possession/with him ("Meu computador está com meu irmão"). Note: in "confundir X com meu irmão", it means "mistake X for my brother" ("with" = "for/as").
target_language_example: Vou ao cinema com meu irmão hoje.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with my brother today.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together/doing something in the company of your friends. Often follows a verb (e.g., sair, ir, comer, encontrar-se). You may also hear variations like "com as minhas amigas" (with my [female] friends) or simply "com amigos" (with friends).
target_language_example: No sábado, vou ao cinema com meus amigos.
native_language_example: On Saturday, I'm going to the movies with my friends.

additional_notes: Used to say you are with your parents, live with them ("morar com meus pais"), or do something in interaction with them ("falar com meus pais" = talk to my parents). You can swap in other possessives: "com meus/minhas" (my, plural), "com seus/suas" (your/his/her/their, depending on context), etc.
target_language_example: No fim de semana, vou almoçar com meus pais.
native_language_example: On the weekend, I'm going to have lunch with my parents.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together/spending time with your family, or doing an activity in their company. Common with verbs like estar (to be), viver (to live), passar (to spend time), and celebrar (to celebrate). In Brazilian Portuguese, "minha" is often used where European Portuguese might use "a minha" (com a minha família).
target_language_example: Vou jantar com minha família hoje.
native_language_example: I'm going to have dinner with my family today.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your sister (company/doing something together). With some verbs, "com" can also mean comparison or confusion: "parecer com" / "ser parecido com" = "to look like"; "confundir (alguém) com" = "to mistake (someone) for".
target_language_example: Vou ao cinema com minha irmã hoje.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movie theater with my sister today.

meaning: with a lot of; very (before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to intensify by showing a large amount/degree of something. It usually comes right before a feminine noun (e.g., alegria, dor, intensidade, frequência, força, raiva, habilidade). With masculine nouns, you’ll see “com muito” (e.g., com muito cuidado). Often translates as “with a lot of …” or simply “very …” in natural English depending on context.
target_language_example: Ela falou com muita calma durante a reunião.
native_language_example: She spoke very calmly during the meeting.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" to describe how someone feels at that moment: "estar com (muita) fome" = "to be (very) hungry." "Com" here is part of the expression (literally "with hunger"), not something you translate word-for-word in English.
target_language_example: Depois do treino, eu estava com muita fome.
native_language_example: After the workout, I was very hungry.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing an action in a cautious, gentle way to avoid mistakes or accidents. It commonly follows the verb (e.g., "fale/ande/segure/abra com muito cuidado").
target_language_example: Por favor, dirija com muito cuidado na chuva.
native_language_example: Please drive very carefully in the rain.

additional_notes: This is the preposition "com" (with) + the masculine singular definite article "o" (the). Used before a masculine singular noun or name introduced with "o" (e.g., "com o filho" = with the son/child; "com o Tom" = with Tom). It can also introduce purpose or relationship phrases like "com o propósito de" (with the purpose of).
target_language_example: Vou ao mercado com o meu irmão.
native_language_example: I'm going to the market with my brother.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like ajudar (to help) to say someone helps someone else with their homework. In Portuguese, dever de casa is the common term for “homework,” and com means “with” in this context.
target_language_example: Posso te ajudar com o dever de casa depois do jantar.
native_language_example: Can I help you with the homework after dinner?

additional_notes: Formed by "com" (with) + "o" (the) + "meu" (my). It’s used before a masculine singular noun: "com o meu advogado" (with my lawyer), "com o meu cão" (with my dog). In Portuguese, you often include the article ("o") before possessives ("meu/minha") in many contexts, especially in Brazil.
target_language_example: Você pode falar com o meu irmão agora?
native_language_example: Can you talk with my brother now?

meaning: with my car; using my car (by car).
additional_notes: Often means you’re using your own car as the means of transport (like “by car”). In sentences like “um problema com o meu carro” or “alguma coisa errada com o meu carro,” it means “a problem with my car.”
target_language_example: A gente pode ir com o meu carro.
native_language_example: We can go with my car / by my car.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your father or doing something alongside him. In Portuguese, "com" often combines with articles and possessives: "com" + "o" → "com o"; "meu pai" = "my father". In Brazil you may also hear "com meu pai" (dropping "o"), but "com o meu pai" is standard and common.
target_language_example: Vou ao mercado com o meu pai.
native_language_example: I'm going to the market with my dad.

additional_notes: Used with "com" (with) + "o pai" (the father). It can mean being together with the father (doing something with him) or living with him ("morar com o pai"). In context it often means “his/her father,” even though Portuguese uses the definite article (o) instead of a possessive.
target_language_example: Ela vai viajar com o pai neste fim de semana.
native_language_example: She’s going to travel with her dad this weekend.

additional_notes: Used (1) in questions to ask what you are dealing/agreeing/living with (often after verbs that take "com", like lidar com, concordar com, viver com), and (2) as a relative phrase meaning “with what/that which” (e.g., "viver com o que ganha" = “live on what you earn”).
