target_language_example: Não sei com o que ela está preocupada.
native_language_example: I don’t know what she’s worried about.

meaning: "with the result" / "about the outcome" (showing how someone feels about what happened).
additional_notes: Used after adjectives (e.g., feliz, satisfeito, desapontado, perplexo) to say someone’s reaction to the outcome of something. You’ll also see it with possessives: com o resultado do exame/da eleição/do jogo.
target_language_example: Não estou contente com o resultado do jogo.
native_language_example: I’m not happy with the result of the game.

meaning: "with your" / "with his" / "with her" / "with its" (with + the possessive "seu").
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "com" (“with”) plus the possessive determiner "seu" (“your/his/her/its”), agreeing with the noun that follows (e.g., com o seu carro, com a sua ideia, com os seus amigos, com as suas coisas). "Seu/sua" can mean both “your” and “his/her/its” in Portuguese, so context (or using "dele/dela" for clarity) tells you whose it is.
target_language_example: Você pode me ajudar com o seu telefone?
native_language_example: Can you help me with your phone?

meaning: with your father; with his/her father.
additional_notes: Literally "com" (with) + "o" (the) + "seu" (your/his/her) + "pai" (father). "Seu/sua" can mean "your" (formal) or "his/her" depending on context. Used for being together with the father (e.g., having wine, running into him), and also appears in set phrases like "se parecer com" (to look like / resemble) and "esbarrar com" (to run into).
target_language_example: Eu vou falar com o seu pai depois do almoço.
native_language_example: I’m going to talk with your father after lunch.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun: com os cardeais (“with the cardinals”), com os próprios erros (“from/with your own mistakes”). It’s simply the preposition com (“with”) + the plural masculine article os (“the”). (Feminine plural is com as.)
target_language_example: Vou sair com os meus amigos depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I’m going out with my friends after work.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is doing an activity together with friends. Often refers to the subject’s own friends (e.g., “Tom sai com os amigos” = “Tom goes out with his friends”), though it can also mean “with the friends” in context. You’ll also hear the feminine form “com as amigas” (with the female friends) and the mixed/generic plural “com os amigos” (with friends).
target_language_example: Hoje vou jantar com os amigos.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to have dinner with my friends.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is accompanied by (or doing something together with) his friends. "dele" means "his" (referring to a male person). The feminine equivalent is "com as amigas dela" / "com os amigos dela" (“with her friends”).
target_language_example: Ele saiu para jantar com os amigos dele.
native_language_example: He went out to dinner with his friends.

meaning: "with the (his/her) children"; also "toward the children" (after an adjective).
additional_notes: Literally means “with the children.” In context it often implies “with his/her children,” since Portuguese can leave out the possessive (e.g., “com os filhos” = “with his children”). After adjectives like "severo", "duro", or "rígido", "com" can mean “toward” or “in dealing with” (e.g., "severo com os filhos" = “strict with/toward the children”).
target_language_example: Ela é muito paciente com os filhos.
native_language_example: She is very patient with her children.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun you possess or are associated with: com os meus erros (my mistakes), com os meus professores (my teachers). It’s the preposition com (“with”) + the definite article os (“the”) + the possessive meus (“my”, masculine plural). For feminine plural, you’d use com as minhas.
target_language_example: Vou jantar com os meus amigos hoje.
native_language_example: I’m going to have dinner with my friends today.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something together with your parents (e.g., talk, travel) or that you live in the same home as them. Often appears with verbs like "falar" (to speak) and "morar" (to live): "Moro com os meus pais" = "I live with my parents."
target_language_example: Vou jantar com os meus pais hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I’m going to have dinner with my parents tonight.

additional_notes: Literal phrase used to describe someone physically keeping their eyes shut (e.g., sitting, staying, thinking/resting). You can change the article/pronoun if needed: com os olhos fechados (plural, most common) or com o olho fechado (one eye).
target_language_example: Fiquei alguns minutos com os olhos fechados para relaxar.
native_language_example: I stayed with my eyes closed for a few minutes to relax.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how you interact with other people. Common after adjectives and verbs like “ser” (be), “falar” (talk), “interromper” (interrupt), “brigar” (fight), “ser gentil” (be kind). In sentence 1, the natural phrasing is: “Não interrompa os outros quando estão falando” (“Don’t interrupt others when they’re talking”).
target_language_example: Ela é muito paciente com os outros.
native_language_example: She is very patient with others.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together with their parents (e.g., going somewhere, spending time). With verbs like “morar” (to live), it means living in the same home as their parents. “os pais” is “the parents”; in context it often means “his/her parents.”
target_language_example: Hoje vou almoçar com os pais.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to have lunch with my parents.

additional_notes: Used after adjectives or verbs to say how someone feels about the outcomes (e.g., feliz/triste/satisfeito) or to indicate something is done/changes because of the results. Often translates as “with the results” or “about the results,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ela não está satisfeita com os resultados do exame.
native_language_example: She isn’t satisfied with the exam results.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **com** (“with”) + **os seus** (“your” + masculine plural noun, or “yours”). It commonly introduces things or people that belong to or are connected to someone: **com os seus gatos** (with your cats), **com os seus erros** (from/with your mistakes), **com os seus vizinhos** (with your neighbors). Note: **seus** can also mean “his/their” depending on context, but with **você** it usually means “your.”
target_language_example: Tente conversar com os seus colegas antes da reunião.
native_language_example: Try to talk with your coworkers before the meeting.

meaning: with your friends / with his (their) friends.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re doing something together with someone’s friends. "Seus" can mean "your" (formal "you"/você) or "his/their" depending on context; in Brazil it can also be used for "their" in place of "deles/delas". Often you’ll also hear "com seus amigos" (without "os").
target_language_example: Eu vou ao cinema com os seus amigos.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movies with your friends.

meaning: with your parents / with his/her/their parents.
additional_notes: Literally “with the your/their parents.” Use it to say someone is together with their parents, lives with them, travels with them, etc. "seus" can mean "your" (formal você) or "their"; in everyday Brazilian Portuguese, "seus pais" is also often used for "his/her parents" (instead of "os pais dele/dela"), so context matters.
target_language_example: Ela foi ao cinema com os seus pais.
native_language_example: She went to the movies with her parents.

meaning: with someone else; with another person.
additional_notes: Often used when talking about confusing one person for another ("confundir alguém com outra pessoa" = "to mistake someone for someone else"). It can also mean being together with someone else in a situation (e.g., "na cama com outra pessoa" = "in bed with someone else").
target_language_example: Desculpe, você me confundiu com outra pessoa.
native_language_example: Sorry, you mistook me for someone else.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (or "ficar") to mean you’re in a hurry: "Estou com pressa" = "I’m in a hurry." It can also describe how something was done: "Fiz com pressa" = "I did it in a rush." Often followed by "de" + infinitive to say what you’re rushing to do: "com pressa de ver" = "in a hurry to see."
target_language_example: Desculpa, estou com pressa de pegar o ônibus.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm in a hurry to catch the bus.

additional_notes: Used to ask about how regularly something happens (daily, weekly, etc.). Common in questions, often followed by the verb in the present: “Com que frequência você…?” In European Portuguese you may also see “Com que frequência é que…?”
target_language_example: Com que frequência vocês estudam português?
native_language_example: How often do you study Portuguese?

additional_notes: Used to ask about how frequently someone does an action. It’s typically followed by a verb (e.g., "com que frequência você vai...?"). In everyday speech, people also say "Com que frequência você..." or simply "Com que frequência...".
target_language_example: Com que frequência você vai à academia?
native_language_example: How often do you go to the gym?

additional_notes: Used to ask how regularly someone goes to a place or does an activity. Usually followed by a destination or activity: "... ao cinema" (to the movies), "... à praia" (to the beach), "... às compras" (shopping). In Brazil, "ir a" is common for cities/countries ("vai a Boston") and "ir ao/à" for specific places; in everyday speech you may also hear "vai na/no" depending on the place (regional/colloquial).
target_language_example: Com que frequência você vai à academia?
native_language_example: How often do you go to the gym?

meaning: 'with whom' (who someone is with / who they’re talking to).
additional_notes: Used to ask or specify the person someone is with, does something with, or speaks to. It often introduces a question (Com quem…?) or a relative clause after a noun (as in “as pessoas com quem…”). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many speakers also say “com quem que…?” or “com quem você…?”.
target_language_example: Com quem você vai ao cinema hoje?
native_language_example: Who are you going to the movies with today?

additional_notes: Used to ask or state the person someone is with. Common in questions like “Com quem você estava falando?” (“Who were you talking to?”). In everyday speech, it often comes at the start of a question; you can also hear “Você estava falando com quem?” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Com quem você vai ao cinema?
native_language_example: Who are you going to the movies with?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like estar/ficar to say someone is (or becomes) angry: "estar com raiva" = to be angry, "ficar com raiva" = to get angry. Often followed by "de" or "com" to say who/what you’re angry at: "com raiva do Tom" = angry at Tom, "com raiva de mim" = angry at me.
target_language_example: Ele ficou com raiva porque perdeu o ônibus.
native_language_example: He got angry because he missed the bus.

meaning: mad at me; angry with me.
additional_notes: Used after the verb "estar" (or "ficar") to say someone is angry at you: "Ele está com raiva de mim." Literally "with anger of me"; in English you normally say "angry/mad at me". You can swap "mim" for another person: "com raiva de você / dele / dela / nós".
target_language_example: Desculpa — você está com raiva de mim?
native_language_example: Sorry—are you mad at me?

additional_notes: Most commonly, **estar com sede** means “to be thirsty” (literally “to be with thirst”): *Estou com sede.* In more formal/news/business contexts, **com sede em + place** means “based in” / “headquartered in”: *uma empresa com sede em São Paulo*.
target_language_example: Depois da caminhada, estou com sede.
native_language_example: After the walk, I'm thirsty.

additional_notes: Literally **com** (“with”) + **seu** (a possessive meaning “your / his / her / their”). The exact meaning depends on context, and **seu** can be ambiguous in Portuguese (often clarified with **dele/dela** = “his/her” or **de vocês** = “your” plural). It changes for gender/number: **com sua** (with your/his/her/their [fem.]), **com seus** (plural masc.), **com suas** (plural fem.).
target_language_example: Ele saiu com seu amigo depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: He left with his friend after work.

additional_notes: "Com" means "with". "Seu" can mean "your" (informal singular) or "his/her" depending on context, so "com seu pai" can mean "with your father" or "with his/her father." If you need to be crystal clear, you can also hear/see: "com o pai dele" (with his father) / "com o pai dela" (with her father).
target_language_example: Ela mora com seu pai.
native_language_example: She lives with her father.

additional_notes: Used with masculine plural nouns (seus = “his/its/their/your (formal) + plural”). The exact meaning depends on context, because "seus" can refer to the owner (his/her/their/your) rather than the subject of the sentence. For feminine plural nouns, use "com suas"; for singular, "com seu/sua".
target_language_example: Ela chegou com seus amigos.
native_language_example: She arrived with her friends.

meaning: with your friends / with his friends (depending on context).
additional_notes: Means “with + someone’s friends.” In Brazilian Portuguese, "seu/seus" can refer to "your" (formal) or "his" (and sometimes "her"), so the exact meaning depends on who is being talked to/about. If you want to be clear, you can say "com os amigos dele" (with his friends) or "com os amigos dela" (with her friends).
target_language_example: Ela foi ao cinema com seus amigos.
native_language_example: She went to the movies with her friends.

additional_notes: Means being together/doing something in the company of one’s children. "Com" = "with". "Seus" agrees with "filhos" (masculine plural) and can mean "your" (especially in Brazil) or "his/her/their" depending on context; often clarified with "dele/dela/deles/delas" if needed.
target_language_example: Eu gosto de cozinhar com seus filhos aos domingos.
native_language_example: I like to cook with your children on Sundays.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together with their parents. In Portuguese, "seus" can mean "your" (formal) or "his/her/their" depending on context. In casual speech, Brazilians often use "com os pais" (with the parents) or "com os seus pais" for clarity; you may also see "com seus pais" after a question like "Você...".
target_language_example: Você vai viajar com seus pais neste fim de semana?
native_language_example: Are you going to travel with your parents this weekend?

meaning: sleepy; feeling like you want to sleep.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (or "ficar") to describe a temporary state: "estar com sono" = to be sleepy; "ficar com sono" = to get sleepy. Often used in everyday situations (at night, after lunch, after a long day).
target_language_example: Estou com sono, vou dormir cedo.
native_language_example: I'm sleepy, I'm going to sleep early.

meaning: “with your / with his / with her / with their” (before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: “Com” = “with” + “sua” = a possessive meaning “your / his / her / their” (it can be ambiguous; context tells you whose). It’s used with feminine singular nouns (e.g., “com sua chave”, “com sua palavra”). You may also see “com a sua…” when the article is included for emphasis or style.
target_language_example: Posso falar com sua mãe por um minuto?
native_language_example: Can I talk with your mother for a minute?

additional_notes: Means “with (the) mother.” Which person it refers to depends on context: sua mãe can mean “your mother” (common in Brazil) or “her mother.” Used for being together/living with someone (morar com sua mãe), interacting (ser gentil com sua mãe), or having conflict (brigar com sua mãe). If the mother is male-related in a sentence, you may also see com seu pai (“with your/his father”).
target_language_example: Eu vou ao médico com minha mãe hoje.
native_language_example: I’m going to the doctor with my mom today.

meaning: "with so much" / "so much" (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to intensify a feminine singular noun: com tanta fome (so hungry / with such hunger), com tanta frequência (so often), com tanta dor (in so much pain). Often followed by "que" to show a result: "com tanta fome que...". Also appears in the idiom "Não vá com tanta sede ao pote" (don’t be too eager / don’t rush into it).
target_language_example: Estou com tanta pressa que vou pegar um táxi.
native_language_example: I’m in such a hurry that I’m going to take a taxi.

meaning: in such a hurry; in such a rush.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone is very rushed. Often appears in questions like “Por que você está com tanta pressa?” (Why are you in such a hurry?). You can swap the person/verb around it: “Eu estava com tanta pressa...” / “Onde vai com tanta pressa?”.
target_language_example: Eu saí de casa com tanta pressa que nem tomei café.
native_language_example: I left home in such a rush that I didn’t even have breakfast.

meaning: so angry; with so much anger.
additional_notes: Used to intensify the emotion “raiva” (anger), often after verbs like “ficar” or “estar” (to become/be): “ficar com tanta raiva” = “to get so angry,” “estar com tanta raiva” = “to be so angry.” “Tanta” agrees with the feminine noun “raiva.” You can also add “de (alguém/algo)” to say who/what you’re angry at: “com tanta raiva de você” = “so angry at you.”
target_language_example: Ele ficou com tanta raiva que saiu sem dizer nada.
native_language_example: He got so angry that he left without saying anything.

additional_notes: Used to say something involves all people in a group or in general. Common after verbs like "se dar bem" (get along), "ser" (be), "falar" (talk), etc. Contrast: "com alguém" (with someone) vs. "com ninguém" (with nobody).
target_language_example: Ela fala com todo mundo na festa.
native_language_example: She talks to everyone at the party.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something using a tool/object or accompanied by something. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun: com um lápis (with a pencil), com um amigo (with a friend). For feminine singular, use “com uma”.
target_language_example: Posso pagar com um cartão?
native_language_example: Can I pay with a card?

additional_notes: Used to say you study, speak, or practice a language together with someone whose first language is that language. You can change the article for gender/number: com um falante nativo (a male/native speaker or unspecified), com uma falante nativa (female), com falantes nativos (plural).
target_language_example: Vou praticar português com um falante nativo amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to practice Portuguese with a native speaker tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something while smiling (often to show friendliness, politeness, or good humor). Common with verbs like cumprimentar (to greet), falar (to speak), dizer (to say), and desejar (to wish). You may also hear close variations like “com um sorriso no rosto” or “com um sorriso nos lábios” (“with a smile on his/her face/lips”).
target_language_example: Ele respondeu com um sorriso.
native_language_example: He answered with a smile.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun: com + uma + [noun]. Common uses include: accompaniment/association (casado com uma canadense), having/experiencing something (estar com uma dor de cabeça), describing what someone is wearing or a feature (vestida com uma blusa vermelha; terminou com uma nota otimista), instrument/means (andava com uma bengala; pega borboletas com uma rede), and using a body part (com uma mão). Often corresponds to English “with a,” but context can make it feel more like “having,” “using,” or “ending on.”
target_language_example: Ele escreveu a carta com uma caneta azul.
native_language_example: He wrote the letter with a blue pen.

meaning: with a knife; using a knife.
additional_notes: Uses "com" (with) to indicate the tool/instrument used to do something. Often follows a verb: "cortar ... com uma faca" (to cut ... with a knife), "gravar ... com uma faca" (to carve ... with a knife). In descriptions, it can also mean someone is carrying/holding a knife: "com uma faca nas mãos" (with a knife in (his) hands).
target_language_example: Não mexa nisso com uma faca; é perigoso.
native_language_example: Don’t mess with that using a knife; it’s dangerous.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together with the person you’re addressing, or that something is happening/being done in relation to them: ir/viajar/falar/sair com você (“go/travel/talk/go out with you”), estar bem com você (“be okay with you / be okay with you personally”). It can also mean “with you” in the sense of “in your possession” (e.g., levar com você = “take with you”).
target_language_example: Posso falar com você agora?
native_language_example: Can I talk with you now?

meaning: 'with you' (plural/formal), i.e., with you all / with you guys.
additional_notes: Used to say you are together with a group you’re speaking to. It uses the preposition "com" (with) + "vocês" (you, plural). Also appears in "estar com vocês" meaning 'to be with you (all)'. In Brazil, "vocês" is the normal plural 'you'; in Portugal, it can sound more formal in some contexts.
target_language_example: Posso ir com vocês amanhã?
native_language_example: Can I go with you all tomorrow?

meaning: feel like (doing something); be in the mood to (do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb (e.g., "com vontade de sair") to express desire or mood in the moment. Often translates as "I feel like..." / "Are you in the mood to...?". You can intensify with "muita" ("com muita vontade de" = "really feel like").
target_language_example: Hoje estou com vontade de comer pizza.
native_language_example: Today I feel like eating pizza.

meaning: feeling like going; wanting to go.
additional_notes: "Estar com vontade de" is a very common way to talk about being in the mood/feeling like doing something. It’s usually followed by an infinitive: "com vontade de ir" (to go), "com vontade de comer" (to eat). You can use it as a question ("Você está com vontade de ir?") or statement ("Eu estou com vontade de ir").
target_language_example: Hoje estou com vontade de ir ao cinema.
native_language_example: Today I feel like going to the movies.

additional_notes: Imperative of **começar a** + infinitive, used to tell someone to start doing something. It’s the more general/neutral command form often used with **você** (e.g., *Comece a falar*, *Comece a fazer as malas*).
target_language_example: Comece a estudar agora, por favor.
native_language_example: Start studying now, please.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "começar" + "a" + infinitive. Used to say you started doing something at a specific moment in the past: "comecei a falar" (I started to speak), "comecei a escrever" (I started writing). You can add time expressions like "aos trinta anos" (at 30) or "quando eu tinha cinco anos" (when I was five). Other persons: "começou a" (he/she started to), "começamos a" (we started to).
target_language_example: Quando ouvi a música, comecei a dançar.
native_language_example: When I heard the music, I started to dance.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund (comendo) to describe an action in progress, often with a form of "estar": "estou/está/estamos/estão comendo pão" = "I am / he(she) is / we are / they are eating bread." Without "estar", it can also appear as part of a longer phrase (e.g., "vi eles comendo pão" = "I saw them eating bread").
target_language_example: Eu estou comendo pão no café da manhã.
native_language_example: I am eating bread for breakfast.

additional_notes: "Comendo" is the gerund ("-ing" form) of the verb "comer" (to eat). It’s commonly used with "estar" to talk about something happening right now: "estou/está/estão comendo..." It can also describe someone while they do another action: "Ele o viu comendo um sanduíche" = "He saw him eating a sandwich."
target_language_example: Estou comendo um sanduíche agora.
native_language_example: I’m eating a sandwich now.

additional_notes: Used when you don’t want to specify exactly what will be eaten (any food will do). Very common in offers and suggestions (e.g., before going out) and can also mean “at least eat a little” when someone hasn’t eaten.
target_language_example: Estou com fome; vou comer alguma coisa antes da reunião.
native_language_example: I’m hungry; I’m going to eat something before the meeting.

additional_notes: A common everyday phrase for talking about having a healthy diet. Use it after verbs like tentar (to try), precisar (to need), dever (should), or gostar de (to like). You can also say "comer comida saudável" (eat healthy food) as a similar idea.
target_language_example: Estou tentando comer alimentos saudáveis esta semana.
native_language_example: I’m trying to eat healthy foods this week.

additional_notes: Past tense (ele/ela/você cometeu) of the verb "cometer" + "suicídio". This is a serious, formal expression; in everyday conversation you may also hear "tirou a própria vida" (“took their own life”), which can sound a bit less blunt.
target_language_example: A polícia disse que ele cometeu suicídio.
native_language_example: The police said he committed suicide.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "cometer um erro" = "to make/commit a mistake." "Cometeu" is used for he/she/you (você, formal "you") in Brazilian Portuguese; with "eu" you’d say "cometi um erro" and with "nós" "cometemos um erro." Common in situations where you’re pointing out or admitting a specific mistake.
target_language_example: Desculpe, eu cometi um erro no relatório.
native_language_example: Sorry, I made a mistake in the report.

additional_notes: Past tense of the verb “cometer” (“to commit/make,” used with mistakes and crimes). “Cometeu” is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) for ele/ela/você (“he/she/you”). You can change the subject: “Eu cometi um grande erro” (I made a big mistake), “Nós cometemos…” (We made…). Common variant: “cometer um erro” = “to make a mistake.”
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu cometi um grande erro.
native_language_example: Sorry, I made a big mistake.

additional_notes: Past tense of "cometer um erro" (to make/commit a mistake). "Cometi" is first-person singular in the simple past (pretérito perfeito), used to admit or explain a mistake. Often followed by details with "ao" + infinitive ("cometi um erro ao enviar...") or with "de" to specify the type ("erro de digitação" = typo).
target_language_example: Desculpa, cometi um erro ao preencher o formulário.
native_language_example: Sorry, I made a mistake when filling out the form.

meaning: “made a mistake” / “committed an error” (past participle, used with ter/haver).
additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb ter or haver to form the past perfect-style meaning: ter/haver cometido um erro = “to have made a mistake.” It can also appear in the passive: Foi cometido um erro = “A mistake was made.” Often followed by an adjective like grave (“serious”).
target_language_example: Acho que já tinha cometido um erro.
native_language_example: I think I had already made a mistake.

additional_notes: Used with another verb in the infinitive (começando a + verb) to say an action or change is in its early stages. Often appears with estar/estar a to describe something happening at that moment: “estava começando a…” = “was starting to…”. You can use it for actions (começando a pensar) or changes of state (começando a ficar interessante).
target_language_example: Estou começando a aprender português agora.
native_language_example: I’m starting to learn Portuguese now.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb (começar a + verb) to say someone begins an action or that something begins to happen. Often used for both deliberate actions (começar a pagar, começar a fazer) and events (começar a nevar). In speech it’s common to also hear “começar a” contracted to “começar a” (no change in writing), and you can add time words like “imediatamente”, “logo”, or “ao meio-dia”.
target_language_example: Quando eu chegar em casa, vou começar a estudar.
native_language_example: When I get home, I’m going to start studying.

meaning: "they started/began to" (followed by a verb in the infinitive).
additional_notes: This is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "começar" for "eles/elas/vocês". It’s commonly used with "a" + infinitive to say someone began doing something: "começaram a trabalhar" = "they started to work".
target_language_example: Depois do sinal, eles começaram a correr.
native_language_example: After the signal, they started to run.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "começar a" + infinitive: "começar" (to start) + "a" + "rir" (to laugh). It’s used when a group of people begins an action. Often appears with a subject like "algumas pessoas", "as raparigas", "todos". You can also add "de" to say who/what they laughed at: "começaram a rir de Tom" (= they started laughing at Tom).
target_language_example: Quando viram o vídeo, começaram a rir.
native_language_example: When they saw the video, they started to laugh.

additional_notes: It’s the past tense (ele/ela/você) of "começar a" + infinitive, used to say someone started doing something. Often followed by another verb: "começou a falar" (started to speak), "começou a entender" (started to understand). It can also describe the start of a process/event: "Começou a amanhecer" = "It started to dawn/daybreak".
target_language_example: Ontem eu comecei a estudar português.
native_language_example: Yesterday I started to study Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used to say when someone began studying French. It’s the past tense of “começar a” + infinitive (“to start to do something”): “começou a aprender” = “started to learn.” Common with time expressions like “há três anos” (three years ago), “aos treze anos” (at age 13), and “no ano passado” (last year).
target_language_example: Eu comecei a aprender francês no ano passado.
native_language_example: I started learning French last year.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of “começar a” + infinitive: “(someone) started to (do something).” Often used to describe a sudden reaction or the beginning of an action in the past. You can swap the subject: “Eu comecei a chorar”, “Ela começou a chorar”.
target_language_example: Quando ouvi a notícia, comecei a chorar.
native_language_example: When I heard the news, I started to cry.

additional_notes: Used to say that rain began at a specific moment. It’s the past tense of “começar a + infinitive” (“to start to + verb”): começou (he/she/it started) + a + chover (to rain). Often appears with time words like assim que (as soon as), quando (when), pouco depois (shortly after).
target_language_example: A gente ia fazer um piquenique, mas começou a chover.
native_language_example: We were going to have a picnic, but it started to rain.

additional_notes: Past tense: "começar a" + infinitive means "to start/begin to (do something)." Here, "começou" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "começar" and is used for a completed event in the past. "Correr" means "to run," but it can also mean "to rush" depending on context.
target_language_example: Quando ouviu o barulho, ela começou a correr.
native_language_example: When she heard the noise, she started running.

additional_notes: Past tense (ele/ela/você) of **começar a + infinitive** (“to start to do something”). You can change the subject and tense: *eu comecei a escrever*, *nós começamos a escrever*. Often used when describing the moment someone begins writing something (a report, a dictionary, a novel, etc.).
target_language_example: Depois do jantar, ela começou a escrever um e-mail importante.
native_language_example: After dinner, she started to write an important email.

additional_notes: Past tense of the pattern **começar a + infinitive** (“to start to do something”). You can add what is being studied: **começou a estudar árabe/russo/latim** (“started studying Arabic/Russian/Latin”), or **começou a estudar para a prova** (“started studying for the test”). Often used with **quando (foi que)** to ask when someone started: **Quando (foi que) você começou a estudar…?**
target_language_example: Eu comecei a estudar português no ano passado.
native_language_example: I started studying Portuguese last year.

additional_notes: Uses the past tense of **começar** (“to start”) + **a** + infinitive (**estudar**). You can swap the language: *começou a estudar português/inglês*. With **já** (“already/yet”), it often becomes a question like “Have you started studying French yet?” In questions, you may see **você** (you) or a name/subject (e.g., *Tom*).
target_language_example: Eu comecei a estudar francês no ano passado.
native_language_example: I started studying French last year.

additional_notes: Past tense: “começou” is the preterite of *começar* (“to start”), and *a falar* means “to speak/talk.” Used when someone begins speaking, often after a moment or at a specific time (e.g., *assim que...* = “as soon as...”). You can change the subject: *eu comecei a falar* (I started), *eles começaram a falar* (they started).
target_language_example: Ela começou a falar quando o professor chegou.
native_language_example: She started talking when the teacher arrived.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "começar a" + infinitive: "started to" do something. "Gritar" means "to shout/yell"; with "com" it often means shouting at someone (angrily): "começou a gritar com a mãe" / "comigo". "Novamente" means "again."
target_language_example: Ele começou a gritar com o motorista no trânsito.
native_language_example: He started shouting at the driver in traffic.

additional_notes: Used with a person’s name (“começou a namorar Maria”) or with “com” (“começou a namorar com o Paul” in some regions). In Portuguese, “namorar” often suggests dating more seriously than casual “going out,” especially with words like “sério”.
target_language_example: Ela começou a namorar o João no ano passado.
native_language_example: She started dating João last year.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "começar" + "a" + infinitive "rir". Used to say that someone began an action at a specific moment in the past. You can change the subject: "eu comecei a rir" (I started to laugh), "eles começaram a rir" (they started to laugh). Often followed by "de" to say who/what people laughed at: "começou a rir de mim" (started laughing at me).
target_language_example: Quando ouvi a piada, comecei a rir.
native_language_example: When I heard the joke, I started to laugh.

additional_notes: Used with a person or group as the subject (Tom, a orquestra) to say they began playing music or an instrument. Often followed by the instrument name: “começou a tocar bateria/trompete/violão”. The verb is in the past (pretérito perfeito): “começou” = “started/began.”
target_language_example: Quando a banda começou a tocar, todo mundo ficou em silêncio.
native_language_example: When the band started to play, everyone fell silent.

additional_notes: Past tense (3rd person singular) of the phrase “começar a trabalhar.” Used to say when someone entered the workforce or began a specific job. Often followed by details like place (em Boston), time (em junho / ontem / há três anos), job role (como carpinteiro), or employer (para o tio).
target_language_example: Ela começou a trabalhar em uma loja quando tinha 18 anos.
native_language_example: She started working in a store when she was 18.

additional_notes: Used to talk about food/cooking from China or Chinese-style dishes, often in preferences (gostar de) or when saying what someone cooks (fazer). In Portuguese, the adjective usually comes after the noun: comida (food) + chinesa (Chinese, feminine to match comida).
target_language_example: Vamos pedir comida chinesa hoje à noite.
native_language_example: Let’s order Chinese food tonight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the type of food (cuisine) from Japan. Often appears after verbs like gostar de (to like), comer (to eat), or acostumar-se com/a (to get used to). You can also say culinária japonesa for a more formal “Japanese cuisine.”
target_language_example: Hoje vamos comer comida japonesa no centro.
native_language_example: Today we’re going to eat Japanese food downtown.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens the same way it normally does (often with a hint of “no surprise”). It can go at the start of the sentence (Como de costume, …) or at the end (, como de costume).
target_language_example: Como de costume, ela chegou cedo ao trabalho.
native_language_example: As usual, she arrived early to work.

meaning: "like a" / "as a" (used to compare or describe a role).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun. It can express (1) comparison/simile: "like a ..." (e.g., "pendurado como um morcego" = "hanging like a bat"), or (2) function/role: "as a ..." (e.g., "trabalhar como um tradutor" = "work as a translator"). For feminine nouns, use "como uma".
target_language_example: Ele trabalha como um motorista.
native_language_example: He works as a driver.

additional_notes: Used with verbs to compare someone’s behavior or manner to what is considered (often stereotypically) manly: e.g., “se comportar como um homem” (“behave like a man”). It can also mean “as a (young) man” when talking about someone’s life stage (e.g., “Como um homem jovem…”).
target_language_example: Ele enfrentou o problema como um homem.
native_language_example: He faced the problem like a man.

meaning: like a fish (very well/easily; especially about swimming).
additional_notes: Used mainly in comparisons, especially with verbs like "nadar" (to swim): "nadar como um peixe" = to swim very well. It can also appear in other expressions, e.g., "beber como um peixe" = to drink a lot (alcohol). Related fixed phrase: "como um peixe fora d'água" means "like a fish out of water" (feeling out of place).
target_language_example: Ela nada como um peixe desde criança.
native_language_example: She’s been swimming like a fish since she was a child.

meaning: 'like a' / 'as a' (used to compare something to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons (similes): **como** = 'like/as' + **uma** = 'a/one' (feminine). It agrees with the noun that follows: **como um** (masculine) vs **como uma** (feminine). Often followed by a noun phrase: *como uma barata tonta* ('like a headless chicken'), *como uma luz deslumbrante* ('like a dazzling light').
target_language_example: Ele estava pálido como uma parede.
native_language_example: He was as pale as a wall.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like agir (to act), tratar (to treat), chorar (to cry), dormir (to sleep) to compare someone’s behavior to a child’s. It can be negative (immature: “Stop acting like a child”) or neutral/positive depending on context (e.g., “dormir como uma criança” = to sleep very soundly).
target_language_example: Ele respondeu como uma criança e depois pediu desculpa.
native_language_example: He replied like a child and then apologized.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or talk about the method or steps for doing something ("isso" = "that/this"). Often appears after verbs like "saber" (to know), "mostrar" (to show), "explicar" (to explain), and "dizer" (to tell): "Não sei como fazer isso" = "I don’t know how to do that."
target_language_example: Você pode me mostrar como fazer isso?
native_language_example: Can you show me how to do that?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the result/experience of an event in the past (trip, weekend, interview, flight, exam, date, etc.). Often followed by the thing you’re asking about: “Como foi a viagem?” In “Como foi que…?”, it can also mean “How did …?” asking about how something happened (e.g., “Como foi que vocês nos encontraram?” = “How did you find us?”).
target_language_example: Como foi a sua viagem?
native_language_example: How was your trip?

additional_notes: Used to ask about an event or experience that already happened. It’s often followed by a masculine noun (o show, o voo, o encontro). For feminine nouns, use “Como foi a...?” (e.g., a festa). You can also drop the article in some contexts: “Como foi?” = “How was it?/How did it go?”
target_language_example: Como foi o seu dia ontem?
native_language_example: How was your day yesterday?

meaning: “How did you…?” / “How come you…?” (asking how something happened or was done).
additional_notes: Used to ask for an explanation of how something happened, how someone did something, or how a situation came about. Adding "foi que" makes the question sound more emphatic/curious (similar to "how exactly" or "how come"). You’ll often see it followed by a past-tense verb (chegou, começou, fez, respondeu). In speech, it may be shortened to "Como você…?" with the same basic meaning but less emphasis.
target_language_example: Como foi que você descobriu isso tão rápido?
native_language_example: How did you find that out so quickly?

meaning: 'how can I...?' (asking for instructions or a way to do something).
additional_notes: Used to ask how to do something or how to make something happen, often followed by an infinitive (e.g., "entrar", "fazer", "me esquecer"). Very common in polite questions; you can also add "eu" for emphasis: "Como posso eu...".
target_language_example: Como posso chegar ao aeroporto de ônibus?
native_language_example: How can I get to the airport by bus?

meaning: How can I help you? (to a man / using formal “you”).
additional_notes: Common customer-service or polite opening question. “-lo” refers to “you” (male) as a direct object. You’ll also hear/see: “Como posso ajudá-la?” (to a woman), “Como posso ajudá-los/ajudá-las?” (to more than one person), and more informal: “Como posso te ajudar?” / “Posso te ajudar?”.
target_language_example: Boa tarde! Como posso ajudá-lo?
native_language_example: Good afternoon! How can I help you?

meaning: “how do you/does one…?” (asking how something is done/said/written).
additional_notes: Used very often with **se** to make an impersonal question (similar to English “how do you…?” or “how is it…?”). Common with verbs like **fazer** (do/make), **chamar** (call), **escrever** (write), **usar** (use), **explicar** (explain), **sentir** (feel). Note: **como se** can also mean “as if” in other contexts (e.g., *Ele fala como se soubesse tudo*), but in the examples here it’s the impersonal “how to/ how does one…?” pattern.
target_language_example: Como se diz “thank you” em português?
native_language_example: How do you say “thank you” in Portuguese?

meaning: "what is it called?" / "what’s the name of…?"
additional_notes: Used to ask for the name of something. Literally “how is it called,” but in English it’s “what is it called?” Often followed by a noun or pronoun: Como se chama este/esse…? You can also add a language: Como se chama … em inglês/japonês?
target_language_example: Como se chama isso em português?
native_language_example: What is that called in Portuguese?

meaning: "How do you say...?" (asking how to express a word/phrase in a language).
additional_notes: Used to ask for a translation or the correct way to say something. Often followed by the thing you want to say + "em" + the language: "Como se diz 'thank you' em português?" It can also be used alone ("Como se diz?") when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Como se diz "bathroom" em português?
native_language_example: How do you say "bathroom" in Portuguese?

meaning: "how do you feel?" (asking about someone’s feelings or condition).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "sentir-se" (to feel). "Como" = how, "se" is part of the reflexive verb, and "sente" is the "you" (você) form. It can ask about emotions or physical well-being: "Como se sente agora?" = right now; "Como se sente com..." = about/regarding something. More formal/polite than "Como você tá?"
target_language_example: Depois da consulta, como se sente?
native_language_example: After the appointment, how do you feel?

meaning: “How is the… going?” / “How’s the…?” (asking how someone/something is doing).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the state or progress of a specific person or thing. It’s often followed by a feminine noun because of “a” (e.g., a missão, a peça, a família). With a masculine noun, you usually say “Como vai o…?” (e.g., Como vai o trabalho?).
target_language_example: Como vai a sua saúde?
native_language_example: How is your health?

meaning: “how you…” (used to ask about the way/manner someone did something).
additional_notes: Often appears at the start of a question: **Como você + verb...?** = “How did you…?” / “How do you…?” The verb tense determines the time: **Como você chegou...?** (past) vs **Como você faz...?** (present). In European Portuguese you may also hear **Como é que você…?** for emphasis. Note: **como** can also mean “like/as” in other contexts, but in these examples it means “how.”
target_language_example: Como você aprendeu português tão rápido?
native_language_example: How did you learn Portuguese so fast?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the way or process someone learned a skill. It’s typically followed by a verb in the infinitive (often without “to” in English), like cozinhar (cook), dançar (dance), falar (speak), fazer (do/make), tocar (play an instrument). In Brazil, you’ll often hear “você”; in more formal situations you might use “Como o(a) senhor(a) aprendeu a …?”.
target_language_example: Como você aprendeu a dirigir tão cedo?
native_language_example: How did you learn to drive so early?

meaning: “How did you manage (to)?” / “How did you do it?”
additional_notes: Used to ask how someone was able to do something (often something difficult, surprising, or impressive). It’s usually followed by an infinitive verb (como você conseguiu fugir? = “how did you manage to escape?”) or by “isso” (como você conseguiu isso? = “how did you do that?”). In conversation, you can also just ask “Como você conseguiu?” when the action is clear from context. Note: in Brazil, “você” is common; in Portugal you may hear “Como conseguiste?” (informal) or “Como conseguiu?” (more formal).
target_language_example: Como você conseguiu terminar tão rápido?
native_language_example: How did you manage to finish so fast?

additional_notes: Used to express shock, anger, or disappointment about something the other person did (often rhetorical). Literally "how you could"; *pôde* is the past of *poder* ("to be able to"). Commonly followed by an infinitive: *Como você pôde fazer/falar/ser...?* You can also use *como você pode...?* for present/ongoing situations.
target_language_example: Como você pôde mentir para mim?
native_language_example: How could you lie to me?

additional_notes: Used to ask what evidence or reason someone has for a statement. It’s usually followed by a clause (subject + verb): “Como você sabe que o Tom está lá?” In everyday conversation, you’ll also hear “Como você sabe disso?” (“How do you know that?” / “How do you know?”).
target_language_example: Como você sabe que ele está dizendo a verdade?
native_language_example: How do you know that he’s telling the truth?

additional_notes: Used to ask how someone found out a piece of information. Often followed by a full clause (subject + verb): “Como você sabia que eu estava vindo?” In everyday Brazilian Portuguese you may also hear “Como é que você sabia que…?” or more informally “Como você soube que…?” (past of *saber*).
target_language_example: Como você sabia que eu não podia ir?
native_language_example: How did you know that I couldn’t go?

additional_notes: Used to ask how someone found out a fact about you. It’s followed by a verb in the past (often imperfect: “eu era/estava/gostava/queria”) or past progressive (“eu estava + gerúndio”). You can change “você” to “vocês” (plural) or “sabia” to “soube” (simple past: a specific moment of finding out).
target_language_example: Como você sabia que eu tinha chegado cedo?
native_language_example: How did you know that I had arrived early?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s emotional or physical state (question) or to say you understand/know someone’s feelings (statement). Often followed by time/place words (agora, hoje, aqui) or by “sobre + topic” (“about + topic”). In writing, questions take a question mark: “Como você se sente…?”; as a statement it appears without one: “Sei como você se sente.”
target_language_example: Depois da notícia, como você se sente?
native_language_example: After the news, how do you feel?

additional_notes: A common, friendly check-in question about someone’s situation in general. Often followed by “com + person” (Como vão as coisas com a Ana?), or “em + place” (…em casa, …em Boston). You can also use it alone as a general greeting.
target_language_example: Oi! Como vão as coisas por aí?
native_language_example: Hi! How are things going over there?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a description of something’s characteristics, condition, appearance, or how things work: Como é o clima…? (“What’s the weather like…?”). Often appears as “como é que…?” (very common in speech) for emphasis when asking how something is done. In statements, “Eu sei como é” can mean “I know what it’s like,” often implying shared experience.
target_language_example: Eu não sei como é morar sozinho.
native_language_example: I don’t know what it’s like to live alone.

additional_notes: Very common way to start a question, often adding emphasis or surprise. It’s used before a verb phrase: “Como é que você fez isso?” = “How did you do that?” It can also express disbelief: “Como é que as pessoas podem…?” = “How can people…?” Often interchangeable with plain “como” in casual speech, but “como é que” feels more emphatic.
target_language_example: Como é que você aprendeu português tão rápido?
native_language_example: How did you learn Portuguese so fast?

meaning: "how did they...?/how do they...?" (emphatic way to ask how).
additional_notes: Common in spoken Portuguese to introduce a question about method or reason, adding emphasis (similar to “how is it that they...?”). It’s followed by the verb: the tense comes from that verb (e.g., "Como é que eles fizeram...?" = past; "Como é que eles fazem...?" = present). "Eles" means “they” (masculine or mixed group; for an all-female group you can also use "elas").
target_language_example: Como é que eles chegaram tão cedo?
native_language_example: How did they get here so early?

additional_notes: Used to start questions, often with emphasis or surprise. You’ll commonly see it followed by a verb: “Como é que você faz…?”, “Como é que você se sentiu…?”, “Como é que você vai…?”. In casual speech it’s sometimes shortened to “como você…?”.
target_language_example: Como é que você aprendeu português tão rápido?
native_language_example: How did you learn Portuguese so fast?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or talk about the method or steps for doing something ("isso" = "that/this"). Often appears after verbs like "saber" (to know), "mostrar" (to show), "explicar" (to explain), and "dizer" (to tell): "Não sei como fazer isso" = "I don’t know how to do that."
target_language_example: Você pode me mostrar como fazer isso?
native_language_example: Can you show me how to do that?

meaning: how to do it; how to do so.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the method/way to do something. Common after verbs like ensinar (to teach), mostrar (to show), and saber (to know): "Ensina-me como fazê-lo" = "Teach me how to do it." The "-lo" is an object pronoun meaning "it" attached to the infinitive "fazer" (to do/make): "fazer + o" → "fazê-lo".
target_language_example: Você pode me dizer como fazê-lo com segurança?
native_language_example: Can you tell me how to do it safely?

additional_notes: Used when asking for or giving a demonstration/instructions. Literally “how one does (it)”; it often refers to a general method rather than a specific person (similar to English “how it’s done”). Common with verbs like mostrar/ensinar/explicar: “Me mostre como se faz…” = “Show me how to do it/how it’s done.”
target_language_example: Você pode me ensinar como se faz essa receita?
native_language_example: Can you teach me how to make this recipe?

additional_notes: Used to describe an unreal or hypothetical situation, or to compare something to an imagined scenario. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., estivesse, fosse, tivesse). You can change the verb to match the subject and meaning: como se eu estivesse… / como se ela estivesse….
target_language_example: Ele falava baixo, como se estivesse com medo de acordar alguém.
native_language_example: He spoke quietly, as if he were afraid of waking someone up.

meaning: “as if I were …” (introduces an unreal/imagined comparison).
additional_notes: Used after a main clause to compare something to an imagined situation: "X ... como se eu fosse Y" = "X ... as if I were Y." It typically uses the imperfect subjunctive of the verb (here, "fosse" from "ser"). You can swap "eu" for other subjects: "como se ele fosse", "como se a gente fosse", etc.
target_language_example: Ele olhou para mim como se eu fosse culpado.
native_language_example: He looked at me as if I were guilty.

meaning: as if (it) were; like if (it) were.
additional_notes: Used to compare something to an imagined or unreal situation: “as if it were…”. Very common after verbs like falar (to speak), agir (to act), parecer/soar (to seem/sound), chorar (to cry). Often implies exaggeration, make-believe, or that something isn’t really true. It uses the past subjunctive of ser: fosse (from ser = to be). You can follow it with a noun (“como se fosse meu pai” = as if he were my dad) or a clause (“como se fosse verdade” = as if it were true).
target_language_example: Ela me olhou como se fosse a primeira vez que me visse.
native_language_example: She looked at me as if it were the first time she had seen me.

additional_notes: Used to compare something to an unreal or hypothetical situation. It’s very common with the imperfect subjunctive: **como se + fosse/fossem**. Change the article to match gender/number: **como se fosse uma... / como se fossem uns/umas...**. In speech you may also hear **como se fosse** without the article when the noun is clear.
target_language_example: Ela fala comigo como se fosse uma professora.
native_language_example: She talks to me as if she were a teacher.

additional_notes: Used after a verb to say someone is acting/continuing normally, ignoring or pretending an event didn’t happen. Often follows verbs like falar (to speak), agir (to act), continuar (to continue), parecer (to seem). Subjunctive is common after "como se" (here: "tivesse acontecido").
target_language_example: Ele saiu sorrindo, como se nada tivesse acontecido.
native_language_example: He left smiling, as if nothing had happened.

meaning: to make up for lost time.
additional_notes: Used when you’re behind schedule or have wasted time and want to catch up by working faster, doing more, or taking action to recover the delay. The verb is often used with “ter que” (have to), “dever” (should), or in the inclusive “vamos/temos que” (we need to).
target_language_example: Vamos compensar o tempo perdido e terminar isso hoje.
native_language_example: Let’s make up for lost time and finish this today.

additional_notes: "Comprar" means "to buy". "Alguma coisa" means "something" (an unspecified thing). You can add what it’s for with "para": "comprar alguma coisa para o Tom" = "buy something for Tom". In questions, it often means "anything": "Você precisa comprar alguma coisa?" = "Do you need to buy anything?"
target_language_example: Vamos comprar alguma coisa para o jantar.
native_language_example: Let’s buy something for dinner.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to say you want/plan to buy one unit of something: comprar um cachorro, um suéter, um remédio. For feminine nouns, use “comprar uma” (e.g., comprar uma casa).
target_language_example: Vou comprar um presente para você.
native_language_example: I’m going to buy a present for you.

additional_notes: Common verb phrase with "comprar" (to buy) + "um carro" (a car). Often used with money/ability expressions like "não tenho condições de..." (I can’t afford to...) or "queria" (wanted/would like to). You can swap in details: "comprar um carro usado" (a used car), "comprar um carro mais barato" (a cheaper car).
target_language_example: Estou juntando dinheiro para comprar um carro.
native_language_example: I’m saving money to buy a car.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "comprar" (to buy) + the article "um" (a) + "carro" (car) + adjective "novo" (new). "Novo" agrees with "carro" (masculine singular). You can swap in other nouns/adjectives: "comprar uma casa nova" (buy a new house).
target_language_example: Estou economizando para comprar um carro novo no ano que vem.
native_language_example: I’m saving up to buy a new car next year.

additional_notes: Used when the noun is understood from context (e.g., a phone, computer, carpet). It agrees with the gender of the thing being replaced: comprar um novo (masc.), comprar uma nova (fem.). You can also say comprar um novo + noun: comprar um novo computador.
target_language_example: Meu celular quebrou, então vou comprar um novo.
native_language_example: My phone broke, so I'm going to buy a new one.

additional_notes: Used when saying you will purchase a gift and naming the recipient after "para" (for): "comprar um presente para + pessoa". The person can be a name, a pronoun (ele/ela/eles/elas), or a noun phrase (minha namorada, meu amigo). You can change the article depending on gender/number: "um presente" (a gift), "uma lembrança" (a small gift/souvenir), "os presentes" (the gifts).
target_language_example: Preciso comprar um presente para minha mãe.
native_language_example: I need to buy a gift for my mother.

meaning: “to buy a …” (with a feminine noun), or “to buy one.”
additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun (uma casa, uma motocicleta, uma moto). When the noun is understood from context, it can mean “buy one”: e.g., “Vamos comprar uma?” (“Shall we buy one?”). With masculine nouns you use “comprar um”.
target_language_example: Eu não tenho dinheiro para comprar uma moto agora.
native_language_example: I don’t have money to buy a motorcycle right now.

additional_notes: A common everyday phrase: "comprar" = to buy, "uma" = a, "casa" = house/home. Often used when talking about plans, wishes, or the real-estate market. You can swap in other things to buy: "comprar um carro" (buy a car), "comprar um apartamento" (buy an apartment).
target_language_example: Estamos pensando em comprar uma casa no próximo ano.
native_language_example: We’re thinking about buying a house next year.

additional_notes: Used to say you purchased one item (masculine singular) in the past. "Comprei" is the past tense of "comprar" (to buy) for "I". "Um" matches masculine nouns; with feminine nouns you usually use "uma" (e.g., "Comprei uma bicicleta"). Often followed by the item bought and possible descriptions: "Comprei um carro vermelho".
target_language_example: Comprei um presente para minha mãe.
native_language_example: I bought a present for my mom.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "comprar" for "eu": "comprei" = "I bought". "um carro" = "a car". Used to say you purchased a car (or in context, something described as a car, like "um carro de brinquedo" = "a toy car").
target_language_example: Comprei um carro usado na semana passada.
native_language_example: I bought a used car last week.

additional_notes: Uses the verb comprar (“to buy”) in the simple past (pretérito perfeito): comprei = “I bought.” Often appears with optional subject pronoun eu (“I”), especially for emphasis: “Eu comprei...”. Word order is typically: verb + item + adjective (chapéu novo = “new hat”).
target_language_example: Comprei um chapéu novo para o verão.
native_language_example: I bought a new hat for the summer.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of comprar: comprei = “I bought.” Used to say you purchased a book, often followed by details like what kind of book (comprei um livro de piadas) or when (comprei um livro ontem). You can swap the object: comprei um café, comprei um presente.
target_language_example: Comprei um livro novo para estudar português.
native_language_example: I bought a new book to study Portuguese.

meaning: “I bought a …” (for a feminine noun), or “I bought one.”
additional_notes: Past tense of comprar (“to buy”) with the feminine indefinite article uma (“a/one”). Use before feminine nouns: “comprei uma revista” (magazine), “comprei uma passagem” (ticket). For masculine nouns, use “comprei um …”. You can also drop the noun when it’s understood: “Comprei uma.” = “I bought one.”
target_language_example: Comprei uma camisa nova ontem.
native_language_example: I bought a new shirt yesterday.

additional_notes: "Comprou" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "comprar" = “to buy,” usually meaning a completed action. "Um" means “a/an” (masculine singular). For feminine nouns, use "comprou uma" (e.g., "comprou uma casa"). You can also swap the subject: "Eu comprei um…" (I bought a…), "Nós compramos um…" (we bought a…).
target_language_example: Ela comprou um carro usado.
native_language_example: She bought a used car.

additional_notes: Past tense of "comprar" (to buy). "Comprou" usually means "he/she/you (formal) bought"—the subject comes from context (e.g., "Ela comprou...", "Tom comprou..."). You can add details with adjectives ("um carro vermelho" = a red car) or indicate who it’s for with "para" ("comprou um carro para Maria" = bought a car for Maria).
target_language_example: Ela comprou um carro usado ontem.
native_language_example: She bought a used car yesterday.

additional_notes: "comprou" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "comprar" (to buy) for ele/ela/você. In context it usually refers to a completed purchase. You can change the subject: "Eu comprei um carro novo" (I bought a new car), "Nós compramos..." (we bought...).
target_language_example: Ela comprou um carro novo na semana passada.
native_language_example: She bought a new car last week.

additional_notes: “Comprou” is the simple past of “comprar” (to buy) for “você/ele/ela” (you/he/she). “Uma” means “a/an” for feminine singular nouns (uma banana, uma garrafa, uma tartaruga). For masculine nouns, use “comprou um” (e.g., comprou um livro).
target_language_example: Você comprou uma camisa nova?
native_language_example: Did you buy a new shirt?

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "comprar" for "he/she/you (formal) bought" + "uma casa" (a house). Used to talk about a completed purchase in the past; the subject is often a name or pronoun: "Ele comprou uma casa".
target_language_example: Ela comprou uma casa no ano passado.
native_language_example: She bought a house last year.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "comprar" (to buy): "comprou" = "bought" (3rd person singular: he/she/you formal). Often used with a subject like "O Tom" or "Papai". "câmera" can mean a photo/video camera; in Brazil people also commonly say "câmera" for a phone’s camera.
target_language_example: Ela comprou uma câmera nova ontem.
native_language_example: She bought a new camera yesterday.

additional_notes: This is a common pattern: **comprar + um/uma + item + para**. With **para + person**, it means the recipient ("for Mary"). With **para + verb (infinitive)**, it means purpose/intent ("to give to Mary"). You can also use **para si mesmo(a)** to mean "for himself/herself."
target_language_example: Eu comprei uma câmera para você usar nas férias.
native_language_example: I bought a camera for you to use on vacation.

meaning: “to buy it / to buy him” (comprar + object pronoun lo).
additional_notes: “-lo” is a clitic pronoun attached to the verb meaning “it” or “him” (masculine object). It often attaches with a hyphen: comprá-lo = comprar + o. The accent (comprá-) keeps the stress when the pronoun is attached. You may also see future forms like “comprá-lo-ei” (“I will buy it/him”).
target_language_example: Eu vou comprá-lo amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to buy it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say you agree with a person, opinion, idea, or plan. The verb is concordar com (to agree with). “Concordo” is the 1st-person singular present (“I agree”), and it’s followed by “com” + the person/thing you agree with: concordo com ele (I agree with him), concordo com o plano (I agree with the plan). You can also use it more generally: Eu geralmente concordo com o Tom (I usually agree with Tom).
target_language_example: Concordo com você, mas acho que devemos esperar um pouco.
native_language_example: I agree with you, but I think we should wait a little.

additional_notes: Used to express agreement with someone. You can soften or qualify it with phrases like “em parte” (in part) or specify the topic with “sobre isso” (about that) / “nesta questão” (on this issue). Negative form: “não concordo com você” = “I don’t agree with you.”
target_language_example: Concordo com você, mas acho que podemos tentar de outro jeito.
native_language_example: I agree with you, but I think we can try a different way.

additional_notes: Past tense (ele/ela/você) of **concordar em + infinitive** to say someone agreed to do something: *concordou em pagar / ajudar / assinar*. In the present, you’ll often see **concorda em** (“agrees to”).
target_language_example: Ele concordou em esperar mais um pouco.
native_language_example: He agreed to wait a little longer.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or encourage trust. It can be a statement (Confia em mim.) or a question (Confia em mim?). It uses the verb confiar (“to trust”) with the preposition em (“in/on”): confiar em alguém = to trust someone. Also appears as “confie em mim” (more formal/polite) and “confia em mim, [name]” when addressing someone directly.
target_language_example: Confia em mim, vai dar tudo certo.
native_language_example: Trust me, everything will be fine.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition em before the person/thing you trust: confiar em alguém / confiar em algo. In Portuguese it covers both “trust” (believe someone is honest) and “count on/rely on” (believe someone will do what they promised). Common pattern: Você pode confiar em mim. / Eu confio em você.
target_language_example: Você pode confiar em mim; eu vou te ajudar.
native_language_example: You can trust me; I’m going to help you.

meaning: to trust me; to rely on me.
additional_notes: Used when you want to reassure someone that you are reliable or honest. The verb is "confiar em" (to trust in), and you can swap the pronoun: confiar em você (trust you), confiar nele/nela (trust him/her), confiar na gente (trust us).
target_language_example: Pode confiar em mim: eu vou resolver isso hoje.
native_language_example: You can trust me: I’ll sort this out today.

meaning: to trust you; to rely on you.
additional_notes: Used to express trust (or lack of trust) in a person. The verb is usually "confiar em" + someone: "confiar em você" (you), "confiar nele/nela" (him/her), "confiar em vocês" (you all). Often appears in questions or with negatives like "não consigo confiar em você". "Fui confiar em você?" can sound like regret: "Why did I go and trust you?"
target_language_example: Eu preciso confiar em você para a gente trabalhar junto.
native_language_example: I need to trust you so we can work together.

meaning: to trust him; to rely on him.
additional_notes: Used when talking about trusting a specific man or relying on him to do something. In Portuguese, "confiar" often takes the preposition "em" (confiar em alguém), and "nele" = "em" + "ele" (“in him”). Common in questions and advice: "Posso confiar nele?" / "Você não deveria confiar nele."
target_language_example: Eu confio nele para guardar este segredo.
native_language_example: I trust him to keep this secret.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "confiar" (to trust), used to ask someone to rely on you or believe what you’re saying. You can say it alone ("Confie em mim.") or followed by a name; it can sound reassuring, but also suspicious depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Confie em mim — eu vou cuidar de tudo.
native_language_example: Trust me — I’ll take care of everything.

meaning: to meet her; to get to know her.
additional_notes: "Conhecê-la" = "conhecer" (to meet / to know someone) + "-la" (her). It’s the infinitive "conhecer" with an accent (conhecê-) because a pronoun is attached. Used when you want to meet someone for the first time or get acquainted with them (not just recognize them).
target_language_example: Estou animado para conhecê-la amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m excited to meet her tomorrow.

meaning: to meet him; to get to know him.
additional_notes: Infinitive of "conhecer" + the object pronoun "o" (= him / it / you [formal]) attached at the end. When a pronoun is attached to an infinitive, the final "-r" drops and an accent is added: conhecer + o → conhecê-lo. Often used for meeting someone for the first time ("to meet"), not just already knowing them.
target_language_example: Tenho vontade de conhecê-lo pessoalmente.
native_language_example: I’d like to meet him in person.

meaning: "to meet you too" / "nice to meet you too" (formal).
additional_notes: Used as a polite reply after someone says it was a pleasure/honor to meet you. Literally "to meet/know you also." The "-lo" is an object pronoun meaning "you" (formal, masculine) attached to the infinitive conhecer → conhecê-lo. For a woman, you may hear conhecê-la também. Very common in set phrases like: Foi um prazer conhecê-lo também / Muito prazer em conhecê-lo também.
target_language_example: Muito prazer em conhecê-lo também, senhor.
native_language_example: Nice to meet you too, sir.

additional_notes: Used to invite someone to do something together at a future time. "conosco" = "with us"; "no próximo verão" = "next summer" (literally "in the next summer"). Often appears after the activity/place: "ir para X conosco no próximo verão".
target_language_example: Quer vir conosco no próximo verão?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with us next summer?

meaning: “can do that / is able to do that.”
additional_notes: Uses the verb "conseguir" (to manage to, to be able to) + infinitive. "Consegue" is the he/she/you (formal) form in the present tense. Common in questions like "Você consegue...?" to ask if someone is capable of doing something or can manage it.
target_language_example: Você consegue fazer isso hoje?
native_language_example: Can you do that today?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "conseguir" to mean managing to obtain something. "Conseguir um emprego" focuses on successfully getting hired (not just looking). Often used with time expressions like "assim que eu puder" (as soon as I can) or "tão logo quanto eu puder" (as soon as I can).
target_language_example: Ela está tentando conseguir um emprego na área de tecnologia.
native_language_example: She is trying to get a job in the tech field.

meaning: "(he/she/you formal) managed to solve the problem."
additional_notes: Uses the verb "conseguir" (to manage to / be able to) in the past ("conseguiu") + an infinitive ("resolver") to say someone succeeded in doing something, often after effort or difficulty. "Conseguiu" can mean "you managed" when talking to someone using "você" or "he/she managed" depending on context. Negative: "não conseguiu resolver o problema" = "didn’t manage to solve the problem."
target_language_example: Finalmente, ela conseguiu resolver o problema depois de tentar várias vezes.
native_language_example: Finally, she managed to solve the problem after trying several times.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **conseguir** (“to manage to/get”) in the **pretérito perfeito** (*conseguiu* = “(he/she) got/managed to”). **Um emprego** means “a job.” Often followed by **como + profissão** (“as a…”) or **em/no/na + lugar** (“in/at…”). You can change the subject: *eu consegui*, *você conseguiu*, *eles conseguiram*.
target_language_example: Depois de muitos meses procurando, ela conseguiu um emprego em uma escola.
native_language_example: After many months of looking, she got a job at a school.

additional_notes: Used when referring to fixing a specific issue or object already known from context. “Isso” usually means “that/this” (something not in your hands right now). Can be used for repairing objects, solving problems, or correcting mistakes. Common patterns: “Você pode consertar isso?” (Can you fix this/that?) and “Vou consertar isso.” (I’ll fix it.)
target_language_example: Calma, eu vou consertar isso amanhã.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll fix it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Use this to say someone can repair anything (in general). "Consertar" is a common verb for fixing objects (a phone, a car, a computer). "Qualquer coisa" means "anything" and is used for an open, indefinite object.
target_language_example: Meu pai consegue consertar qualquer coisa na casa.
native_language_example: My dad can fix anything around the house.

meaning: to fix it; to repair it.
additional_notes: "Consertá-lo" = "consertar" (to fix/repair) + "-lo" ("it/him," masculine direct object). In everyday use, it most often means “fix it” (a computer, car, phone, etc.). In Brazil you’ll also commonly hear the pronoun before the verb: "Vou consertá-lo" or "Vou consertar isso" (more common).
target_language_example: Meu celular parou de funcionar, mas o técnico vai consertá-lo amanhã.
native_language_example: My phone stopped working, but the technician will fix it tomorrow.

meaning: "I can do that/this"; "I’m able to do it".
additional_notes: Uses the verb "conseguir" (eu consigo) to express ability or managing to do something (often after effort). It’s similar to "posso fazer isso" (“can I do this?”) but "consigo" focuses more on capability/success. "isso" usually means “that/it” (sometimes “this” depending on context). In questions, you typically just use rising intonation: "Consigo fazer isso?"
target_language_example: Não se preocupa, eu consigo fazer isso.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I can do it.

meaning: to see a doctor; to consult a doctor.
additional_notes: Used when advising or saying someone should get medical advice/attention. Very common with verbs like dever (should/ought to), precisar (need to), and poder (can) + deixar de (fail to/stop). It implies a medical consultation/appointment rather than just meeting a doctor socially.
target_language_example: Se a dor continuar, você deve consultar um médico.
native_language_example: If the pain continues, you should see a doctor.

additional_notes: Past participle form of the verb **contar** (“to tell”) + **a verdade** (“the truth”). It’s commonly used with auxiliary verbs like **ter/haver** (e.g., *ter contado a verdade* = “to have told the truth”) and especially in sentences about what someone should/shouldn’t have said (*devia/deveria ter contado a verdade*).
target_language_example: Você devia ter contado a verdade desde o começo.
native_language_example: You should have told the truth from the beginning.

additional_notes: Used when someone reveals what really happened or speaks honestly. Common with verbs like "dever" (should) and often followed by "para" + person: "contar a verdade para alguém". You can also say "contar toda a verdade" (tell the whole truth).
target_language_example: Prometo contar a verdade para você.
native_language_example: I promise to tell you the truth.

additional_notes: Used with the verb contar (“to tell”) plus the contraction ao = a + o (“to the” + masculine singular person). It introduces who you’re telling: contar ao Tom = “tell Tom.” For feminine names/nouns, use contar à (a + a): contar à Maria. You can also use contar a alguém (“tell someone”) when there’s no article: contar a mim/ela/ele.
target_language_example: Por favor, não conte ao professor o que eu disse.
native_language_example: Please don’t tell the teacher what I said.

meaning: to count to ten; (also) to take a moment to calm down.
additional_notes: Literal meaning is counting from 1 to 10 (often used when asking about language ability: “Can you count to ten in…?”). It can also be used as a way to manage anger or stress (“count to ten before you react”). In threats or games it can introduce a countdown: “I’m going to count to ten and then…”.
target_language_example: Quando eu fico com raiva, eu paro e conto até dez.
native_language_example: When I get angry, I stop and count to ten.

additional_notes: Usually used with verbs like manter (keep), ter (have), perder (lose), and entrar em contato com (get in touch with). It can mean staying in communication with a person, or being connected/in touch with something (e.g., a plane, reality, a situation).
target_language_example: Eu perdi contato com meus amigos da escola.
native_language_example: I lost contact with my school friends.

additional_notes: Imperative form of the verb **contar** (“to tell” / “to count”) + **me** (“to me”). Used to ask someone to give you information: **Conte-me a história** (“Tell me the story”), **Conte-me imediatamente se algo acontecer** (“Let me know immediately if something happens”). In Brazilian Portuguese, you’ll also commonly hear **me conte** with the pronoun before the verb, especially in everyday speech. Don’t confuse with **conte comigo** (“count on me”).
target_language_example: Conte-me quando você chegar em casa.
native_language_example: Let me know when you get home.

additional_notes: Imperative of the verb "contar" (to tell) + the object pronoun "nos" (us). It’s used to ask someone to tell a story, explain what happened, or give information. In Brazil, "Conte-nos" is quite formal; in casual speech you’ll often hear "Conta pra gente" or "Conta pra nós". It can also be followed by "o que..." (what...), "sobre..." (about...), or "de onde..." (where from...).
target_language_example: Conte-nos como foi a viagem.
native_language_example: Tell us how the trip was.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone kept doing an action: **continuar a + infinitive**. Here it’s **continuou** (he/she/it continued) + **a** + verb (e.g., *continuou a sair, a caminhar, a vencer, a gritar*). In Brazilian Portuguese you may also hear **continuou + gerund** (e.g., *continuou caminhando*), with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Mesmo cansado, ele continuou a trabalhar.
native_language_example: Even though he was tired, he kept working.

meaning: “told a story” (said a story out loud).
additional_notes: Simple past of the verb contar (“to tell”) + uma história (“a story”). Used for telling a bedtime story (história de ninar), a funny story (história engraçada), or any account/anecdote someone shares. In everyday speech it can also mean “told me a story” as in “told me something / a tale,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ontem ela contou uma história sobre a viagem dela.
