native_language_example: Yesterday she told a story about her trip.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "contar" = "to tell". The subject is usually implied by context: ele contou… (he told…), ela contou… (she told…). Often used with an indirect object pronoun: "me" (to me), "nos" (to us), "lhe" (to him/her), "lhes" (to them), or with "a/para" + a person: "contou uma história interessante à Maria" (told Maria an interesting story).
target_language_example: Ontem, meu avô contou uma história interessante para a gente.
native_language_example: Yesterday, my grandpa told us an interesting story.

additional_notes: Used to show opposition to an idea, law, person, or action (ser/estar/votar contra a…; manifestar-se contra a…). It can also mean moving in the opposite direction of something (contra a correnteza = against the current) or going against a principle/expectation (ir contra a lógica = go against logic). Changes with the noun’s gender/number: contra o, contra os, contra as.
target_language_example: Sou contra a decisão, mas vou respeitá-la.
native_language_example: I'm against the decision, but I'll respect it.

additional_notes: Used to say you did something even though you didn’t want to, often because someone pressured, forced, or made you do it (e.g., "me fez" = "made me"). You can change the possessive to match the person: contra a tua/sua vontade (against your will), contra a vontade dele/dela (against his/her will), contra a nossa vontade (against our will).
target_language_example: Assinei o contrato contra a minha vontade.
native_language_example: I signed the contract against my will.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar": "estar convencido de que" + a full clause (with a verb). It expresses a strong belief/certainty. "Convencido" changes with gender/number: "convencida", "convencidos", "convencidas".
target_language_example: Estou convencido de que ela vai aceitar a proposta.
native_language_example: I'm convinced that she will accept the proposal.

meaning: to convince him (to do something / of something).
additional_notes: "Convencê-lo" = convencer + "-lo" (him). The "-lo" is an object pronoun attached to the verb (common with infinitives), and it refers to a male person. Often used with: (1) "convencê-lo a" + infinitive (to convince him to do something), or (2) "convencê-lo de que" + clause (to convince him that...). In speech, many speakers also use "convencer ele" (more informal/colloquial), but "convencê-lo" is the more standard written form.
target_language_example: Preciso convencê-lo a vir comigo.
native_language_example: I need to convince him to come with me.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund of "conversar" + "com" to describe an ongoing conversation with someone/something. Often corresponds to English "(to be) talking to/with" depending on context.
target_language_example: Estou conversando com a minha irmã agora.
native_language_example: I’m talking with my sister right now.

meaning: to talk with; to have a conversation with.
additional_notes: Used with a person or group you’re talking to: conversar com alguém (talk to someone), conversar com meus pais (talk with my parents). It often suggests a friendly or calmer talk (a conversation) rather than just quickly saying something. Common patterns: "Preciso conversar com..." (I need to talk to...), "Quero conversar com..." (I want to talk to...).
target_language_example: Depois da reunião, posso conversar com você?
native_language_example: After the meeting, can I talk with you?

meaning: to talk with you; to have a conversation with you.
additional_notes: Used when you want to speak directly with someone, often implying a longer or more serious chat than just saying a quick thing. You can add the topic with “sobre” (about): “conversar com você sobre...”
target_language_example: Preciso conversar com você depois da reunião.
native_language_example: I need to talk with you after the meeting.

additional_notes: "Conversou" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "conversar" (to talk/chat). It’s followed by "com" to introduce the person you talked with: "conversou com a Maria" (talked to Maria). In everyday English, this is often just "talked to" rather than the more formal "conversed with".
target_language_example: Eu conversei com o médico ontem.
native_language_example: I talked to the doctor yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "convidar" (to invite). "Convidou" means “(he/she) invited”; the person invited can be shown with object pronouns (me, te, o/a, nos, vocês/os/as) or a name: "Ela me convidou..." / "Nancy o convidou...". "Para a festa" = “to the party.”
target_language_example: Eles me convidaram para a festa no sábado.
native_language_example: They invited me to the party on Saturday.

meaning: 'a cup/glass of' (often also 'a cup made of').
additional_notes: Used before a noun to say what a cup/glass contains (copo de água = a glass of water) or what it is made of (copo de isopor = a Styrofoam cup). With drinks, both beber and tomar are common: beber café / tomar café.
target_language_example: Quero um copo de água, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of water, please.

additional_notes: Used to order or talk about beer served in a glass. In restaurants/bars you can ask for another one with "outro copo de cerveja". If you want beer in a bottle or can instead, you’d usually say "uma cerveja (garrafa/lata)".
target_language_example: Para mim, um copo de cerveja, por favor.
native_language_example: For me, a glass of beer, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a serving of milk measured by a glass. Common with quantities like "meio copo" (half a glass) and with offers/questions like "Quer outro copo de leite?" (Do you want another glass of milk?). Note: in Brazilian Portuguese, "tomar" is often used with drinks ("tomar leite" = to drink milk).
target_language_example: Ele pediu um copo de leite antes de dormir.
native_language_example: He asked for a glass of milk before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Used to compare speed. Very often followed by a comparison: **do que** (or the shorter **que**) + person/thing: *Ela corre mais rápido (do) que eu.* You can also use it without saying who/what you’re comparing to when it’s clear from context. Related: *correr mais rápido* = “to run faster” (infinitive).
target_language_example: Hoje eu corro mais rápido do que antes.
native_language_example: Today I run faster than before.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "correr" (to run) in the present tense: "corre" = "he/she runs" (also "you run" in formal "você"). "todas as manhãs" means "every morning" (literally "all the mornings"). You can change the subject: "Eu corro todas as manhãs" (I run every morning), "Nós corremos..." (We run...).
target_language_example: Eu corro todas as manhãs antes de ir para o trabalho.
native_language_example: I run every morning before going to work.

additional_notes: Used to compare speed (often with **do que/que** = “than”): *correr mais rápido do que/que alguém* (“run faster than someone”). It can also be a command/encouragement: *Tem que correr mais rápido!* (“You have to run faster!”).
target_language_example: Se quisermos pegar o ônibus, precisamos correr mais rápido.
native_language_example: If we want to catch the bus, we need to run faster.

additional_notes: Used to compare speed: “as … as …”. Pattern: (subject) + pode/consegue + correr tão rápido quanto + (person/thing). Often used with pronouns (eu, você, ele/ela) or names: “tão rápido quanto eu / o Bill”.
target_language_example: Ela consegue correr tão rápido quanto o irmão dela.
native_language_example: She can run as fast as her brother.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **correr para** (“to run to/toward”), used to show quick movement in the direction of a person or place. It’s usually followed by a destination: **correu para a mãe** (to the mother), **correu para o quarto** (to the room). With a pronoun, it can be **correu para ela/ele** (“ran to her/him”).
target_language_example: Quando ouviu o barulho, ele correu para a porta.
native_language_example: When he heard the noise, he ran to the door.

meaning: to cut your hair; to get a haircut.
additional_notes: Used for both cutting hair yourself and going to a barber/salon. Very commonly said as "cortar o cabelo" (generic), or "cortar o meu/seu cabelo". In requests/commands you’ll often hear "Preciso cortar o cabelo" (I need a haircut) or "Vai cortar o cabelo" (Go get a haircut).
target_language_example: Eu vou cortar o cabelo amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to get a haircut tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the style/result (“Esse corte de cabelo ficou ótimo”) or the act of getting a haircut (“precisar de um corte de cabelo”). Very common in salons and everyday conversation. Often appears with verbs like fazer (to get/do), precisar de (to need), and ficar (to look/turn out).
target_language_example: Vou fazer um corte de cabelo amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m getting a haircut tomorrow.

meaning: “(he/she) cut the cake into …” (a number of pieces/parts).
additional_notes: Used with a number + a noun (often optional) to say how many pieces something was divided into: “em oito pedaços” (into eight pieces), “em duas partes” (into two parts). In the examples, “cortou” is the simple past of “cortar” (to cut), and the subject (who cut) is understood from context.
target_language_example: Ele cortou o bolo em quatro pedaços.
native_language_example: He cut the cake into four pieces.

additional_notes: "Costumava" is the imperfect of "costumar" and expresses a past habit or a previous, regular state. It’s commonly used to contrast the past with the present (often with "como" / "não mais").
target_language_example: Este bairro costumava ser mais tranquilo.
native_language_example: This neighborhood used to be quieter.

meaning: “I believe/think that …” (expressing an opinion or uncertainty).
additional_notes: Common, slightly formal way to introduce what you think is true. Often used with negation: “não creio que …” = “I don’t think/believe that …”. In Portuguese, what follows frequently uses the subjunctive when it’s uncertain or denied (e.g., “Não creio que seja …”, “Não creio que tenhamos …”). Similar to “acho que”, but “creio que” can sound a bit more careful or formal.
target_language_example: Creio que ele vai chegar mais tarde.
native_language_example: I think he’ll arrive later.

additional_notes: Used to say what children are doing or what state they are in. It’s the plural of “a criança está” (“the child is”). Often followed by a verb in the present continuous with “a” + infinitive (e.g., “estão a nadar” = “are swimming”), or by an adjective/past participle (e.g., “estão seguras” = “are safe”).
target_language_example: As crianças estão a brincar no parque.
native_language_example: The children are playing in the park.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "cruzar as pernas". Used to describe the action of sitting with one leg over the other. Often appears after verbs like "sentar(se)" (to sit down): "sentou-se e cruzou as pernas".
target_language_example: Ele ficou esperando e cruzou as pernas para se sentir mais confortável.
native_language_example: He waited and crossed his legs to feel more comfortable.

additional_notes: Used as a warning about a possible danger or problem. Often followed by a noun (cuidado com o cão) or with a person/pronoun (cuidado comigo/contigo). In signs and alerts it often means “Beware of…”.
target_language_example: Cuidado com o degrau na entrada.
native_language_example: Watch out for the step at the entrance.

additional_notes: Used to warn someone and introduce a risk you want them to avoid. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb (frequently with reflexive pronouns like "se": "para não se machucar"). You can also hear "cuidado pra não" in casual speech.
target_language_example: Cuidado para não esquecer as chaves.
native_language_example: Be careful not to forget the keys.

additional_notes: Used to warn someone to pay attention and avoid danger while crossing a specific place (a bridge, street, square, forest, etc.). It often appears with different verb forms like (não) ter cuidado (past: teve/tiveram), or as an instruction/command: "Tenha/Tenham/Tende cuidado ao atravessar a ...". The noun after "a" is usually feminine singular; with masculine you’ll see "ao atravessar o ...".
target_language_example: Tenha cuidado ao atravessar a rua.
native_language_example: Be careful when crossing the street.

additional_notes: Used to warn someone to be cautious while crossing a place/area (a patio, river, ocean, country, etc.). Often appears as a warning or advice: “Tenha cuidado…” (you, singular/formal) or “Tenham cuidado…” (you all). You can also use it in the past to say someone wasn’t careful: “não teve/tiveram cuidado ao atravessar o …”.
target_language_example: Tenha cuidado ao atravessar o pátio; o chão está molhado.
native_language_example: Be careful when crossing the patio; the floor is wet.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being careful with spelling/grammar in a given language. Often appears in the advice pattern "Tenha/Tenham cuidado ao + infinitive" = "Be careful when + verb" (formal/neutral), e.g., "Tenha cuidado ao escrever em português".
target_language_example: Tenha cuidado ao escrever em inglês, porque os tempos verbais mudam muito.
native_language_example: Be careful when writing in English, because the verb tenses change a lot.

additional_notes: Used as a warning about a possible danger or problem. Often followed by a noun (cuidado com o cão) or with a person/pronoun (cuidado comigo/contigo). In signs and alerts it often means “Beware of…”.
target_language_example: Cuidado com o degrau na entrada.
native_language_example: Watch out for the step at the entrance.

additional_notes: Used to warn someone and introduce a risk you want them to avoid. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb (frequently with reflexive pronouns like "se": "para não se machucar"). You can also hear "cuidado pra não" in casual speech.
target_language_example: Cuidado para não esquecer as chaves.
native_language_example: Be careful not to forget the keys.

meaning: to take care of the children / to look after the kids.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "cuidar (de)" + "de" + a noun/pronoun. Here, "das" = "de" + "as" ("of the"). Common for babysitting, supervising, or being responsible for children’s needs and safety. You can swap in other things/people: "cuidar do bebê" (the baby), "cuidar do cachorro" (the dog), "cuidar de alguém" (someone).
target_language_example: Hoje à noite eu vou cuidar das crianças enquanto você sai.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m going to take care of the kids while you go out.

additional_notes: Used when someone looks after their own needs/safety without help. It often appears with emphasis words like "próprio/própria" (e.g., "de si próprio") or with gender/number agreement: "cuidar de si mesmo" (himself), "de si mesma" (herself), "de si mesmos" (themselves, masc./mixed), "de si mesmas" (themselves, fem.).
target_language_example: Depois da cirurgia, ele teve que aprender a cuidar de si.
native_language_example: After the surgery, he had to learn to take care of himself.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "cuidar-se" used to tell someone to look after themselves, often when saying goodbye or as a warning to be careful. It can be polite ("Cuide-se, por favor") or sharp/insulting depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Está muito frio hoje—cuide-se!
native_language_example: It’s very cold today—take care!

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that describes someone by mentioning their father’s profession/identity. "Cujo/cuja/cujos/cujas" agrees with the thing possessed (here: "pai"), not with the person who owns it. It’s followed directly by a noun (no article): "cujo pai" (not *"cujo o pai"*).
target_language_example: Conheci o rapaz cujo pai é professor.
native_language_example: I met the boy whose father is a teacher.

meaning: from head to toe; completely (all over).
additional_notes: Used to mean the whole body, from the top (head) to the bottom (feet). Common with verbs like olhar (to look someone over) and with states like estar encharcado (to be soaked) to emphasize that something covers you entirely.
target_language_example: Depois da chuva, fiquei molhado da cabeça aos pés.
native_language_example: After the rain, I was wet from head to toe.

meaning: "from the bed" / "off the bed" (from the bed’s surface).
additional_notes: "da" = "de" + "a" (“from/of” + “the”, feminine). Used to show movement away from the bed (cair/rolar da cama = fall/roll off the bed) or to mean “of the bed” when talking about parts/things that belong to it (lençóis da cama = the bed sheets). Contrast: "na cama" = in/on the bed; "na beira da cama" = on the edge of the bed.
target_language_example: Ela levantou-se da cama às sete.
native_language_example: She got out of bed at seven.

meaning: “from the house” or “of the house” (de + a casa).
additional_notes: “Da” is the contraction of “de” + “a”. So “da casa” can mean movement starting from the house (“saiu correndo da casa” = ran out of the house) or something related to/belonging to the house (“o dono da casa” = the owner of the house). In the fixed expression “por conta da casa”, it means “on the house” (free, paid by the establishment/host).
target_language_example: Ele pegou as chaves da casa e saiu.
native_language_example: He grabbed the house keys and left.

additional_notes: "Da" = "de" + "a". Use it with feminine singular nouns like "chuva" to express source/cause ("molhado da chuva" = wet from the rain) or belonging ("água da chuva" = rainwater).
target_language_example: O barulho da chuva me ajuda a dormir.
native_language_example: The sound of the rain helps me sleep.

meaning: “of the city” / “in the city” (depending on context).
additional_notes: "Da" is the contraction of "de" + "a". With places, "de" can mean “of/from” (belonging to the city: "a garota … da cidade" = the girl from/of the city) or indicate location in common expressions like "no meio da cidade" (“in the middle of the city”). Often translates naturally as “in the city,” “from the city,” or “of the city,” based on the sentence.
target_language_example: Ele é o melhor médico da cidade.
native_language_example: He is the best doctor in the city.

additional_notes: "Da" = "de" + "a". Most often it links something to the kitchen: "o chão da cozinha" (the kitchen floor), "o armário da cozinha" (the kitchen cabinet), "a mesa da cozinha" (the kitchen table). With foods, "cozinha" can mean "cuisine" (style of cooking): "cozinha chinesa" = Chinese cuisine.
target_language_example: As chaves estão em cima do balcão da cozinha.
native_language_example: The keys are on top of the kitchen counter.

additional_notes: "Da" is the contraction of "de" + "a" ("of/from" + "the" feminine singular). So "da escola" can mean "of the school" (possession/association: "o jornal da escola" = "the school newspaper") or "from the school" (origin/departure). It also appears after expressions that use "de", like "gostar de" (to like) and "ter saudades de" (to miss).
target_language_example: Vou buscar você na saída da escola.
native_language_example: I’ll pick you up at the school exit.

meaning: from the station; (sometimes) of the station.
additional_notes: Contraction of "de + a". With movement verbs, it commonly means "from the station" (leaving/starting there): "sair da estação", "vim da estação". It can also mean "of the station" when describing something that belongs to or is related to a station, often clarified by context (e.g., "da estação de trem" = "of/from the train station").
target_language_example: Saí da estação e fui direto para o hotel.
native_language_example: I left the station and went straight to the hotel.

additional_notes: Contraction of **de + a** → **da**, used with the feminine noun **estrada** (“road”). It can mean **near/by the road** (*ao lado da estrada*), **on the road** (*do lado direito da estrada*), or **off the road** when used with verbs like **sair** (*sair da estrada* = to leave/go off the road). The exact meaning depends on the verb or preposition around it.
target_language_example: O carro saiu da estrada por causa da chuva forte.
native_language_example: The car went off the road because of the heavy rain.

meaning: “of the family” / “from the family” (family’s; one of the family).
additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "a" = "da". Most often marks something that belongs to the family ("o negócio da família" = the family business) or someone who is part of the family/household ("Ele é da família" = he’s one of the family). With feelings like "saudade", it can mean missing one’s family ("saudade da família").
target_language_example: Sinto saudade da família quando viajo.
native_language_example: I miss my family when I travel.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "a". Used to show possession/origin or association with the forest: "guardião da floresta" (guardian of the forest), "menino da floresta" (boy from the forest), "fronteira ... da floresta" (the forest’s border/edge).
target_language_example: Ele é o protetor da floresta.
native_language_example: He is the protector of the forest.

additional_notes: Used mainly in two common ways: (1) with nouns to mean the front one (e.g., "porta da frente" = "front door", "banco da frente" = "front seat"); (2) in expressions like "sair da frente" meaning "move out of the way". In the second use it often comes with "da minha frente" ("out of my way").
target_language_example: Pode sair da frente, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you move out of the way, please?

additional_notes: "Da" = "de" + "a". With "janela" (feminine singular), it can mean origin/source ("from the window": Ele pulou da janela.) or possession/association ("of the window": o vidro da janela = the window glass).
target_language_example: O barulho vinha da janela.
native_language_example: The noise was coming from the window.

additional_notes: Used to introduce how someone does something: *da maneira que + verb/clause*. Often follows a noun like *a maneira* (“the way/manner”) and can mean “the way that” (e.g., what someone likes about how another person speaks) or “in the way that” (how you usually do something). In everyday speech, you’ll also often hear *do jeito que* with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Faz do jeito que quiser, mas não esquece de me avisar.
native_language_example: Do it however you want, but don’t forget to let me know.

meaning: in the morning (used with a specific time).
additional_notes: Literally “of the morning” (de + a manhã). It’s very common after clock times to clarify that you mean a.m.: às oito da manhã (8 in the morning), às quatro da manhã (4 a.m.). For a general time of day, Portuguese often uses de manhã (“in the morning”) without the article: Eu trabalho de manhã (I work in the morning).
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar às nove da manhã.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at nine in the morning.

additional_notes: Formed by "de" + "a" (= "da") + "meia-noite" (“midnight”). Used to describe something connected to midnight (e.g., "o turno da meia-noite" = “the midnight shift”) or in time expressions like "por volta da meia-noite" (“around midnight”) and "já passava da meia-noite" (“it was already past midnight”).
target_language_example: Saímos do bar depois da meia-noite.
native_language_example: We left the bar after midnight.

meaning: "of/from the table" ("of the table" or "off the table").
additional_notes: "Da" = "de" + "a" (feminine singular). Use it to say something is from the table or belongs to the table: "o lado da mesa" (the side of the table), "ao redor da mesa" (around the table), "do outro lado da mesa" (on the other side of the table). With verbs like "tirar" or "pegar", it often means taking something off the table: "tirou o celular da mesa".
target_language_example: Tirei as chaves da mesa antes de sair.
native_language_example: I took the keys off the table before leaving.

meaning: "of the same" (feminine), used in comparisons or to show sameness.
additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun (explicit or implied): da mesma cidade, da mesma sala, da mesma cor, da mesma mulher. Often appears in set phrases like “da mesma forma” (“in the same way”). For masculine nouns, use “do mesmo” (e.g., do mesmo lugar).
target_language_example: Nós somos da mesma escola.
native_language_example: We are from the same school.

additional_notes: Used to say two or more people (or things) are the same age. Very common with "ser" (e.g., "Somos da mesma idade"). You can add intensifiers like "quase" (almost), "mais ou menos" (more or less), or "exatamente" (exactly). It’s often followed by "de" + a pronoun/name to compare: "da mesma idade dele/dela" or "da mesma idade do Tom".
target_language_example: Meu irmão e eu somos da mesma idade.
native_language_example: My brother and I are the same age.

meaning: in the same way; the same way.
additional_notes: Used to compare actions, feelings, or perspectives. Often appears with “que” to mean “in the same way as …” (e.g., “da mesma maneira que nós”). You can also use it on its own to mean “the same way” (e.g., “saio da mesma maneira” = “I leave the same way (I came in)”).
target_language_example: Eu penso da mesma maneira que você.
native_language_example: I think the same way as you.

additional_notes: "Da minha" is the contraction of "de" + "a" + "minha" and is used before a feminine singular noun you own or refer to (e.g., "da minha casa", "da minha cama"). The preposition "de" changes meaning by context: possession/origin ("da minha nova casa" = about/of my new house), separation ("me livrei da minha bicicleta" = got rid of my bike), need ("preciso da minha privacidade" = I need my privacy), or coming out of/away from a place ("saiam da minha cama" = get out of my bed).
target_language_example: Não mexa nas coisas da minha irmã.
native_language_example: Don’t touch my sister’s things.

additional_notes: Used to mean “of my house/home” or “from my house/home,” depending on the verb or expression. It’s the contraction of “de + a” (da) + “minha casa” (“my house/home”). Common in location phrases like “em frente da minha casa” (in front of my house) or “perto da minha casa” (near my house).
target_language_example: Tem um parque perto da minha casa.
native_language_example: There’s a park near my house.

additional_notes: "Da" is the contraction of "de" + "a". Use it to indicate possession or association (a photo *of* my family), or separation/origin (I got separated *from* my family; someone *from* my family). If the noun is masculine, it’s "do" (de + o): "do meu irmão".
target_language_example: Recebi uma mensagem da minha família ontem.
native_language_example: I got a message from my family yesterday.

additional_notes: "Da" = "de" + "a". It’s used mainly to show possession/origin ("a photo of my sister") or source ("a letter from my sister"). With verbs like "gostar", Portuguese uses "de": "gostam mais da minha irmã" = "like my sister more" (literally "like more of my sister"). "Da minha irmã" refers to something feminine singular ("a minha irmã").
target_language_example: Tenho saudades da minha irmã.
native_language_example: I miss my sister.

additional_notes: This is the contraction of "de" + "a" + "minha mãe" → "da minha mãe". Use it to show possession or origin: something that belongs to your mother ("É da minha mãe" = "It’s my mom’s") or something that comes from her ("uma carta da minha mãe" = "a letter from my mom"). In sentence 1, it appears inside a profanity/insulting outburst ("da porra da minha mãe"), which is very rude; the phrase "da minha mãe" itself is neutral.
target_language_example: Esse casaco é da minha mãe, mas eu posso pegar emprestado.
native_language_example: This coat is my mom’s, but I can borrow it.

additional_notes: Used after a superlative or strong statement to mean something is the biggest/best/worst, etc., you’ve ever experienced (e.g., “a melhor noite da minha vida” = “the best night of my life”). It can also be used more generally with “vida” in expressions about your personal life (“tomar conta da minha vida” = “take care of my own life”) and in commands like “Saiam da minha vida!” (“Get out of my life!”).
target_language_example: Foi o dia mais importante da minha vida.
native_language_example: It was the most important day of my life.

additional_notes: “da” is a contraction of “de + a” (of/from + the, feminine singular). Use it to indicate something that belongs to the mountain or is associated with it (e.g., o pico da montanha = the mountain’s peak; o ar da montanha = the mountain air).
target_language_example: Gosto do silêncio da montanha.
native_language_example: I like the quiet of the mountains.

additional_notes: “Da” is the contraction of “de + a” (“of/from + the” feminine singular). With “morte” (death), it’s used to talk about death in general (“vida depois da morte”) or a specific death (“a notícia da morte dele”, “depois da morte do autor”).
target_language_example: Tenho medo de falar da morte com as crianças.
native_language_example: I’m afraid to talk about death with the kids.

meaning: "of the night" / "evening (one)" (as in “nightly news”, “this time of night”).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify “at night” or a “nighttime/evening” version of something: a esta hora da noite (“at this time of night”), o jornal da noite (“the evening news”). Often appears in fixed expressions like antes da noite (“before nightfall”) and da noite para o dia (“overnight; suddenly”).
target_language_example: Não gosto de sair sozinho a esta hora da noite.
native_language_example: I don’t like going out alone at this time of night.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "a nossa". Used before a feminine singular noun to mean "of our" or "from our" (e.g., "da nossa missão" = "of our mission"; "da nossa classe" = "from our class"). For masculine singular, use "do nosso".
target_language_example: Você se lembra da nossa primeira viagem?
native_language_example: Do you remember our first trip?

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something belongs to your class/group. Very common with superlatives (o mais…, o melhor…, o pior…) to mean “in our class,” e.g., “o mais alto da nossa turma” = “the tallest in our class.” Here, "da" = "de + a" (“of/from the”) and "nossa turma" = “our class/group.”
target_language_example: A Maria é a melhor aluna da nossa turma.
native_language_example: Maria is the best student in our class.

additional_notes: *Da* is the contraction of *de* (“of/from”) + *a* (“the”, feminine). So *da porta* is used to talk about something belonging to the door (*a maçaneta da porta* = “the door handle”) or location/movement related to it (*de trás da porta* = “from behind the door”; *mais perto da porta* = “closer to the door”).
target_language_example: A chave caiu da porta.
native_language_example: The key fell from the door.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the next occasion something happens. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis ("Da próxima vez, ...") or after the verb ("... da próxima vez"). Common with reminders, requests, or hopes for improvement.
target_language_example: Da próxima vez, a gente conversa com mais calma.
native_language_example: Next time, we’ll talk more calmly.

meaning: vulgar insult used in phrases like “filho da puta” = “son of a bitch” / “motherf***er.”
additional_notes: Literally means “of the whore/prostitute,” but in real usage it’s almost always part of insults such as “filho da puta” (very offensive). Often appears after “seu/sua” (“you...”) when insulting someone: “Seu filho da puta!” Avoid in polite or everyday situations.
target_language_example: Sai daqui, seu filho da puta!
native_language_example: Get out of here, you son of a bitch!

meaning: “of the street” / “from the street” (used in phrases like “the other side of the street,” “end of the street”).
additional_notes: It’s the contraction of **de + a** (feminine singular) → **da**. In these examples, it commonly appears in fixed location phrases: **do outro lado da rua** (“across the street”), **dos/dois lados da rua** (“on both sides of the street”), **ao longo da rua** (“along the street”), **no fim da rua** (“at the end of the street”).
target_language_example: A farmácia fica do outro lado da rua.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is across the street.

meaning: “from the room” / “of the room” (de + a sala).
additional_notes: Contraction of **de + a**. Use **da sala** mainly in two common ways: (1) **movement out of a room**: *sair da sala* = “to leave the room”; (2) **something belonging to/located in the room**: *o canto da sala* = “the corner of the room”, *a luz da sala* = “the room light.” Often contrasts with **na sala** (“in the room”) and **para a sala** (“to the room”).
target_language_example: Pode tirar essas cadeiras da sala, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you take these chairs out of the room, please?

meaning: 'from the classroom' or 'of the classroom' (i.e., belonging to the classroom).
additional_notes: "da" = "de" + "a" ("of/from" + "the" feminine). Use it to show origin (expulso/expulsa da sala de aula = expelled from the classroom) or possession/association (o relógio da sala de aula = the classroom clock). "Sala de aula" literally means "classroom" (aula = class/lesson).
target_language_example: Preciso pegar meu caderno da sala de aula.
native_language_example: I need to get my notebook from the classroom.

additional_notes: "Da" is a contraction of "de" + "a". So "da sua" is used before a feminine singular noun: "da sua camiseta" (of your T-shirt), "da sua escola" (of your school), "da sua gripe" (from/of your flu). It often appears after verbs and expressions that take "de" (like "gostar de"). For masculine singular, you usually use "do seu" ("de" + "o" + "seu").
target_language_example: Preciso do número da sua casa.
native_language_example: I need your house number.

meaning: "of your help" / "your help" (as the object of a verb like precisar).
additional_notes: "da" = "de" + "a" and is commonly used after verbs like "precisar de" (to need). So "preciso da sua ajuda" literally means "I need of your help," but in natural English it’s just "I need your help." You can also use it with "a sua ajuda" (without "de") after other verbs (e.g., "Quero a sua ajuda" = "I want your help"). "Sua" is a polite/common way to say "your"; in some places it can also mean "his/her" depending on context.
target_language_example: Não consigo fazer isso sem a sua ajuda.
native_language_example: I can’t do this without your help.

meaning: "of your life" (your personal life; your own life).
additional_notes: Literally "from/of your life" = de + a + sua + vida. Used to refer to someone’s life in general, often in phrases like "desistir da sua vida" (give up your life) or "cuidar da sua vida" (mind your own business). In the example, it suggests giving up your own life/routine to be with someone.
target_language_example: Você não precisa abrir mão da sua vida por causa de ninguém.
native_language_example: You don’t need to give up your life for anyone.

meaning: "of (your) life"; in "O que você faz da vida?" = "What do you do for a living?"
additional_notes: Literally "de + a vida" (= "of the life"). Common after nouns like "significado da vida" ("meaning of life") or in general statements like "tempero da vida" ("spice of life"). In the very common question "O que você faz da vida?", it’s an idiomatic way to ask someone’s job/occupation (similar to "What do you do?" / "What do you do for a living?").
target_language_example: O que você faz da vida atualmente?
native_language_example: What do you do for a living these days?

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "a" + "árvore". Used to express origin or movement away from a tree (e.g., cair/descer da árvore = to fall/come down from the tree), or possession/association (e.g., galhos da árvore = the tree’s branches).
target_language_example: As folhas caíram da árvore ontem à noite.
native_language_example: The leaves fell from the tree last night.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the most recent prior occasion something happened. Common patterns: “da última vez que…” = “the last time (that)…”, and “como da última vez?” = “like last time?”
target_language_example: Da última vez que fomos lá, estava fechado.
native_language_example: The last time we went there, it was closed.

meaning: "of/from the table" ("of the table" or "off the table").
additional_notes: "Da" = "de" + "a" (feminine singular). Use it to say something is from the table or belongs to the table: "o lado da mesa" (the side of the table), "ao redor da mesa" (around the table), "do outro lado da mesa" (on the other side of the table). With verbs like "tirar" or "pegar", it often means taking something off the table: "tirou o celular da mesa".
target_language_example: Tirei as chaves da mesa antes de sair.
native_language_example: I took the keys off the table before leaving.

meaning: in an hour; an hour from now.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that will happen one hour after the present moment (or after the time being referred to). Often appears with future tense or with "vai/irá" (will). Similar patterns: "daqui a meia hora" (in half an hour), "daqui a duas horas" (in two hours).
target_language_example: Daqui a uma hora, a reunião vai terminar.
native_language_example: In an hour, the meeting will end.

meaning: "to give" / often used like "to have/do" before a noun.
additional_notes: Very common "light verb" pattern: **dar um/uma + noun**. With some nouns it’s literal (e.g., **dar um conselho** = give advice; **dar um discurso/sermão** = give a speech/lecture; **dar um autógrafo** = give an autograph). With others it’s more idiomatic and means to do something once/quickly: **dar um telefonema** = make a phone call; **dar um mergulho** = go for a swim/take a dip. Use **um** (masculine noun) or **uma** (feminine noun).
target_language_example: Vou dar um telefonema rapidinho e já volto.
native_language_example: I’m going to make a quick phone call and I’ll be right back.

meaning: to go for a walk; to take a stroll.
additional_notes: A very common, neutral way to suggest a short, leisurely walk (often for pleasure, to get some air, or to look around). Often used in invitations: “Quer/Vamos dar um passeio?” You can also say where: “dar um passeio no parque / pela cidade”.
target_language_example: Depois do jantar, vamos dar um passeio no parque.
native_language_example: After dinner, let’s go for a walk in the park.

meaning: to give a (…); to do/throw a (… ) (very often followed by a noun).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete but very common pattern in Portuguese: **dar uma + noun**. The exact meaning depends on the noun that follows. Examples: **dar uma lição** (give a lesson), **dar uma pista** (give a hint), **dar uma festa** (throw/host a party), **dar uma mão(zinha)** (give a hand/help out). You’ll often see it with an indirect object: **dar uma pista a alguém** / **me dar uma pista** (“give me a hint”).
target_language_example: Você pode me dar uma dica?
native_language_example: Can you give me a tip?

meaning: to go for a walk; to take a walk.
additional_notes: A very common, natural way to talk about going for a walk (often for leisure or light exercise). It’s often used with “sair para” (to go out to) or “ir” (to go): “sair para dar uma caminhada”, “fui dar uma caminhada”. You can add details like time/place: “de manhã cedo” (early in the morning), “no parque” (in the park).
target_language_example: Vamos dar uma caminhada depois do jantar?
native_language_example: Shall we go for a walk after dinner?

meaning: to give someone a ride (a lift).
additional_notes: Used when someone drives you somewhere in their car (or other vehicle) as a favor, usually free. Very common in requests and offers: “Pode me dar uma carona?” (Can you give me a ride?). Often followed by a destination with “para”: “dar uma carona para casa / para o trabalho”.
target_language_example: Você pode me dar uma carona até a estação?
native_language_example: Can you give me a ride to the station?

meaning: to take a look; to have a quick look.
additional_notes: Common, everyday phrase meaning to look at something briefly (often to check or examine). It’s used with many verbs: "deixar" (let), "vir" (come), "querer" (want), "ir" (go). You can add what/where you’ll look at: "dar uma olhada nisso" (take a look at that), "dar uma olhada ao redor" (look around).
target_language_example: Você pode dar uma olhada neste documento, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you take a look at this document, please?

meaning: to go for a walk/drive; to take a stroll/ride.
additional_notes: Common way to say you’re going out briefly just to walk around, get some fresh air, or drive around with no specific destination. Often used with "sair" (e.g., "saí para dar uma volta") and as an invitation ("Vamos dar uma volta?"). Depending on context, it can be on foot or by car/bike.
target_language_example: Depois do jantar, vamos dar uma volta no bairro.
native_language_example: After dinner, let’s go for a walk around the neighborhood.

additional_notes: “Das” = “de + as” (of/about/from + the, feminine plural). Use it with verbs/adjectives that take “de” to mean “about” or “of”: e.g., “cuidar das coisas” (take care of things), “esquecer das coisas” (forget things), “saber das coisas” (know about things). In “uma das coisas…”, it means “one of the things…”.
target_language_example: Não se preocupe com isso; eu cuido das coisas.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about it; I’ll take care of things.

meaning: “of the children” / “the children” (after certain verbs and prepositions).
additional_notes: Contraction of **de + as** (“of/from/about” + “the” feminine plural) → **das**. Used before **crianças** (“children”), a feminine plural noun. Common after verbs/prepositions like **cuidar de** (to take care of), **perto de** (near), and in phrases like **a educação das crianças** (“the children’s education”).
target_language_example: Não fale assim na frente das crianças.
native_language_example: Don’t talk like that in front of the children.

meaning: “of my” / “from my” (feminine plural); often “of mine” or “one of my …” depending on context.
additional_notes: Contraction of **de + as minhas**. Used with feminine plural nouns: **das minhas piadas** (“of my jokes”), **das minhas filhas** (“of my daughters”). After words like **uma** (“one”), it commonly means **“one of my …”**: **uma das minhas citações** (“one of my quotes”). With verbs that take **de** (like **precisar de** = “to need”), it can mean “(some) of my …”: **Preciso das minhas ferramentas** (“I need my tools / I need some of my tools”).
target_language_example: Esta é uma das minhas fotos favoritas.
native_language_example: This is one of my favorite photos.

meaning: “of the people” / “from the people”; also used like “(some) of the people” after a quantity or superlative.
additional_notes: Contraction of **de + as** (“of/from” + “the” feminine plural) → **das**, used with the plural noun **pessoas** (“people”). Common after expressions like **a menor** (“the smallest”), **muitas** (“many”), **algumas** (“some”), etc.: **a menor das pessoas** = “the smallest/least among people,” **muitas das pessoas** = “many of the people.” Also appears with relative clauses: **das pessoas que...** = “of the people who...”.
target_language_example: Algumas das pessoas na fila estavam com pressa.
native_language_example: Some of the people in the line were in a hurry.

meaning: "Christmas" (used to describe something related to Christmas).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean “Christmas + noun” / “for Christmas,” especially with things like cartões de Natal (Christmas cards), enfeites de Natal (Christmas decorations), presente de Natal (Christmas present). Often corresponds to English “Christmas” used as an adjective.
target_language_example: Comprei um suéter de Natal para a festa.
native_language_example: I bought a Christmas sweater for the party.

additional_notes: Used after verbs/adjectives that take the preposition "de" (especially "precisar de"): "precisar de ajuda" = "to need help". "Ajuda" is a noun (help/assistance), and "de" links it to what is needed.
target_language_example: Você precisa de ajuda com isso?
native_language_example: Do you need help with that?

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "de" + "alguma coisa" (“something”). Common after verbs/expressions that require "de", such as: "saber de" (to know about), "precisar de" (to need), "brincar de" (to play at/pretend), and "esquecer-se de" (to forget). It refers to an unspecified thing and often implies “anything” in offers ("precisar de alguma coisa?").
target_language_example: Se você souber de alguma coisa, me avise.
native_language_example: If you know about something, let me know.

meaning: 'somehow' / 'in some way' (often: 'in some way or another').
additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is possible, but you don’t know exactly how, or you’re speaking generally about a way/method. Common in questions offering help: “Posso ajudar de alguma forma?” = “Can I help in any way?” Often appears at the beginning or between commas for emphasis: “De alguma forma, …”.
target_language_example: De alguma forma, vamos resolver isso hoje.
native_language_example: Somehow, we’re going to sort this out today.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say it’s for someone’s birthday or related to a birthday: jantar de aniversário (birthday dinner), presente(s) de aniversário (birthday present(s)), cartão de aniversário (birthday card).
target_language_example: Vamos fazer um bolo de aniversário para ela.
native_language_example: Let’s make a birthday cake for her.

additional_notes: Often used after adjectives to describe how hard or easy something is: "fácil de aprender" = "easy to learn", "difícil de aprender" = "hard to learn". Here, "de" links the adjective to the infinitive verb "aprender".
target_language_example: Português é mais fácil de aprender do que alemão para mim.
native_language_example: Portuguese is easier to learn than German for me.

meaning: "to learn new things" (used after verbs like gostar).
additional_notes: Most commonly appears after verbs that take the preposition "de", especially "gostar de" (to like/enjoy). So "gostar de aprender coisas novas" = "to like learning new things." You can change the person/tense of the surrounding verb (e.g., "pensei que você gostasse...").
target_language_example: Ela gosta de aprender coisas novas todos os dias.
native_language_example: She likes learning new things every day.

meaning: “of class/lesson” (used to form phrases like “classroom,” “classmate,” “first day of class,” “hours of class,” etc.).
additional_notes: "De" means "of" and "aula" means "class/lesson." It’s used after a noun to specify that it relates to classes/lessons: sala de aula (classroom), colega de aula (classmate), dia de aula (day of class), hora(s) de aula (hour(s) of class/lesson).
target_language_example: Quantas horas de aula você tem hoje?
native_language_example: How many hours of class do you have today?

meaning: by plane; on a plane (traveling by air).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "ir", "viajar", and "andar" to say the means of transportation (how you travel). Common patterns: "ir de avião" (go by plane), "viajar de avião" (travel by plane), "andar de avião" (fly / travel by plane). Also appears in nouns like "passagem de avião" (plane ticket).
target_language_example: Vamos de avião para Lisboa amanhã.
native_language_example: We’re going to Lisbon by plane tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean that something is meant for drinking: "água de beber" (drinking water), "algo/alguma coisa de beber" (something to drink). It’s often used when offering or asking for a beverage.
target_language_example: Tem alguma coisa de beber?
native_language_example: Is there anything to drink?

meaning: “of baseball” / “baseball” (used to describe something related to baseball).
additional_notes: Uses the preposition "de" to say that something is related to baseball: "taco de beisebol" (baseball bat), "campo de beisebol" (baseball field), "jogo de beisebol" (baseball game), "equipe de beisebol" (baseball team). "Beisebol" is the Portuguese word for "baseball".
target_language_example: Ele comprou uma luva de beisebol.
native_language_example: He bought a baseball glove.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of going/traveling (ir, andar, chegar, voltar) to say the means of transportation: ir de bicicleta = to go by bike. You can contrast it with other transport using "de" (de carro, de ônibus, etc.).
target_language_example: Hoje vou de bicicleta para o trabalho.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to work by bike.

meaning: of cake; some cake (in expressions like “um pouco de bolo”).
additional_notes: "De" links something to the noun "bolo" (cake). You’ll see it after quantities, portions, or types: "um pouco de bolo" (some cake), "uma fatia de bolo" (a slice of cake), "pedaços de bolo" (pieces of cake), or to say what you like: "gosto de bolo" (I like cake).
target_language_example: Vou comer só um pouco de bolo.
native_language_example: I’m going to eat just a little cake.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (temporary state): "estar de bom humor" = to be in a good mood / cheerful. You can ask "Você está de bom humor?" or describe someone: "Ele está sempre de bom humor."
target_language_example: Hoje eu estou de bom humor.
native_language_example: Today I'm in a good mood.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s mood specifically for today. In Portuguese you say estar/ficar "de bom humor" (literally "of good humor") rather than *estar bom humor*. You can turn it into a question with rising intonation or by adding a question mark in writing.
target_language_example: Você está de bom humor hoje?
native_language_example: Are you in a good mood today?

additional_notes: Used after a number/quantity to say how many should be taken or done per turn (um de cada vez = one at a time; três de cada vez = three at a time). Common in instructions and procedures, often with verbs like entrar (to enter), pegar/tirar (to take/remove), fazer (to do).
target_language_example: Vamos resolver um problema de cada vez.
native_language_example: Let’s solve one problem at a time.

meaning: “of coffee” / “some coffee” (used to specify the thing: coffee).
additional_notes: Most commonly, **de café** marks what something is made of/contains or what you want/need: *gosto de café* (“I like coffee”), *preciso de café* (“I need coffee”), *um copo de café* (“a cup of coffee”), *mais um pouco de café* (“a little more coffee”). In English you often don’t translate **de** directly; you translate the whole phrase naturally.
target_language_example: Você quer um pouco de café?
native_language_example: Do you want a little coffee?

additional_notes: In Portuguese, *gostar* is normally followed by **de + infinitive**: *gostar de cantar* = “to like singing / to like to sing.” Here, **de** doesn’t translate word-for-word into English; it’s required by the grammar.
target_language_example: Ela gosta de cantar no carro.
native_language_example: She likes to sing in the car.

meaning: by car; in a car (using a car as transport).
additional_notes: Used to say how someone travels (mode of transportation), often after verbs like ir/vir/chegar/voltar (e.g., “vou de carro”). It contrasts with other options like “de ônibus” (by bus), “de bicicleta” (by bike), or “a pé” (on foot). In “acidente de carro,” it means “car accident.”
target_language_example: Hoje eu vou de carro porque está chovendo.
native_language_example: Today I’m going by car because it’s raining.

meaning: 'of/from home' (used to relate something to someone’s home).
additional_notes: Very common after a noun to mean it belongs to the home: chaves de casa = house keys. Also used in set phrases: trabalho/dever(es) de casa = homework; fugir de casa = run away from home; (estar) longe de casa = away from home. Often translated as “home” in English depending on context.
target_language_example: Esqueci-me das chaves de casa.
native_language_example: I forgot my house keys.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify what it is made of or what flavor/type it is. Common in foods: "barra de chocolate" (chocolate bar), "sorvete de chocolate" (chocolate ice cream). Often translates as "chocolate" before the noun in English.
target_language_example: Eu quero um bolo de chocolate.
native_language_example: I want a chocolate cake.

meaning: 'of tea' (used to describe something that contains/serves tea).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify the type/content, especially in phrases like "xícara de chá" (a cup of tea) or "colher de chá" (teaspoon). With drinks, Portuguese often uses "de" to mean "of" (content/type): "uma xícara de chá", "um copo de água". On its own, "de chá" usually sounds incomplete—you typically say the full phrase (e.g., "xícara de chá").
target_language_example: Vou fazer uma xícara de chá para você.
native_language_example: I’m going to make a cup of tea for you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about position or perspective: visto/olhado de cima = “seen from above.” With nouns it often means “upper/top”: a prateleira de cima = “the top shelf.” Common extension: de cima a baixo = “from top to bottom.”
target_language_example: Olha a cidade de cima: é linda à noite.
native_language_example: Look at the city from above: it’s beautiful at night.

additional_notes: Literally "of eating," but in everyday Portuguese it commonly follows other phrases to mean "to eat" or "something to eat." For example: "estar a fim de comer" = "feel like eating"; "algo/alguma coisa para/de comer" = "something to eat."
target_language_example: Você quer alguma coisa de comer?
native_language_example: Do you want something to eat?

meaning: “of food” / “food (type)” (used to describe cuisine or something related to food).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that something is food-related or to indicate a type of cuisine: "comida coreana" = "Korean food"; "prato de comida" = "plate of food". Very common with nationalities (comida mexicana, comida francesa) and containers/servings (prato de comida, pote de comida).
target_language_example: A gente pediu comida de restaurante italiano.
native_language_example: We ordered food from an Italian restaurant.

meaning: 'of talking/chatting with' (as in “to like/enjoy talking with”).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "gostar (de)" to express that someone enjoyed the activity of talking with a person. Structure: gostar de + conversar com + alguém. "de" is required because of "gostar de"; the core verb phrase is "conversar com" (“to talk with”).
target_language_example: Eu gostei de conversar com você ontem.
native_language_example: I enjoyed talking with you yesterday.

meaning: made of leather; leather (as a material).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say what it’s made from: "um cinto de couro" (a leather belt), "luvas de couro" (leather gloves). It describes the material (couro = leather/hide) and is very common in shopping/product descriptions.
target_language_example: Você tem uma carteira de couro?
native_language_example: Do you have a leather wallet?

meaning: of credit; credit (used in phrases like “cartão de crédito” = “credit card”).
additional_notes: “De” + “crédito” is used to describe something related to borrowing/credit, especially in fixed combinations like “cartão de crédito” (credit card) and “linha de crédito” (line of credit). It typically follows the noun it describes (cartão/linha + de crédito).
target_language_example: Você aceita cartão de crédito?
native_language_example: Do you accept credit cards?

additional_notes: Used after nouns to specify that something is money or involves money (e.g., quantia de dinheiro = an amount of money, fonte de dinheiro = a source of money, desperdício de dinheiro = a waste of money). It can also follow verbs or expressions that require "de" before a noun (e.g., precisar de dinheiro = to need money).
target_language_example: Eu preciso de dinheiro para pagar o aluguel.
native_language_example: I need money to pay the rent.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like sofrer (to suffer), reclamar (to complain), or morrer (to be dying) to say the cause is back pain: sofrer de dor nas costas, reclamar de dor nas costas, morrer de dor nas costas. Also common: ter dor nas costas (“to have back pain”).
target_language_example: Ela não foi ao trabalho porque estava sofrendo de dor nas costas.
native_language_example: She didn’t go to work because she was suffering from back pain.

additional_notes:
Most common in the pattern: 
- O que há de errado com ...? = What’s wrong with ...?
- Há algo/nada de errado com ... = There is something/nothing wrong with ...
It’s a fixed expression with 'errado' (wrong) and usually comes with verbs like 'haver' (há/havia), 'ter' (tem/tinha), or 'estar' (está).
target_language_example: Há algo de errado com este computador.
native_language_example: There’s something wrong with this computer.

meaning: 'to write' (used after de in expressions like 'have to write' or 'finish writing').
additional_notes:
Often appears after certain verbs and adjectives:
- ter de + infinitive = 'to have to' do something (Eu tenho de escrever... = I have to write...)
- terminar/acabar de + infinitive = 'to finish' doing something (terminar de escrever = finish writing)
- adjective + de + infinitive describes something as easy/fun/hard/etc. to do (divertidas de escrever = fun to write).
target_language_example: Preciso terminar de escrever o e-mail hoje.
native_language_example: I need to finish writing the email today.

meaning: 'of being' / 'to be' (with estar), often after another verb.
additional_notes: This is the preposition "de" + the infinitive "estar". It commonly follows verbs like "acusar (alguém) de..." (to accuse someone of...), "culpar (alguém) de..." (to blame someone for...), or expressions like "antes de estar..." (before being...). Note that "de estar" also appears inside the fixed phrase "sala de estar" (living room).
target_language_example: Eles me acusaram de estar atrasado de propósito.
native_language_example: They accused me of being late on purpose.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean it’s someone’s pet/kept for companionship: “animal de estimação” (pet) and also “meu cachorro de estimação” (my pet dog). By extension it can describe a favorite/cherished personal item (“meu violão de estimação”), meaning one you’re fond of.
target_language_example: Você tem algum animal de estimação?
native_language_example: Do you have any pets?

meaning: 'to study' (used after verbs/expressions like 'precisar de', 'ter de', or 'com o propósito de').
additional_notes: Portuguese often uses **de + infinitive** after certain expressions. Common ones in the examples are **ter de estudar** = “to have to study” and **precisar de estudar** = “to need to study”. With **com o propósito de estudar**, it means “with the purpose of studying / in order to study.” In English this is usually translated with **to + verb** (not “of studying”).
target_language_example: Eu preciso de estudar hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I need to study tonight.

meaning: 'to talk/speak' (used after certain words), or 'about talking/speaking'.
additional_notes: "De" + infinitive is common in Portuguese. It often comes after nouns/adjectives (e.g., "necessidade de falar" = "need to talk") and after some verbs like "terminar de" ("terminar de falar" = "to finish talking"). It can also introduce the topic with "falar de" ("falar de amor" = "talk about love").
target_language_example: Não tenho vontade de falar agora.
native_language_example: I don't feel like talking right now.

meaning: 'to talk/speak with the' (used after verbs that take **de** before an infinitive).
additional_notes: This chunk often appears after verbs/expressions that require **de + infinitive**, such as **gostar de** (to like), **ter de** (to have to), **não deixar de** (don’t fail to / make sure to), and **não se esquecer de** (don’t forget to). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun/name with **o** (e.g., **o Tom**). With a feminine noun, you’d use **de falar com a** (e.g., **a Maria**).
target_language_example: Não se esqueça de falar com o professor depois da aula.
native_language_example: Don’t forget to talk to the teacher after class.

meaning: 'to do' / 'doing' (used as 'de' + infinitive after certain verbs).
additional_notes: Portuguese often uses the preposition "de" before an infinitive: "parar de fazer" (to stop doing), "terminar de fazer" (to finish doing), "lembrar-se de fazer" (to remember to do), and "ter de fazer" (to have to do, obligation). In English, this usually becomes "to do" or "doing" depending on the verb (e.g., "stop doing", "remember to do").
target_language_example: Eu me esqueci de fazer o relatório.
native_language_example: I forgot to do the report.

meaning: 'to do that' / 'from doing that' (de + infinitive, depending on the verb).
additional_notes: Used after certain verbs that require **de + infinitive**. With **impedir/proibir** it usually means **“from doing that”** (blocking an action): *impedir alguém de fazer aquilo*. With **convencer** it usually means **“to do that”** (persuading someone to do something): *convencer alguém de fazer aquilo*. **Aquilo** means “that (thing/that action)” (something more distant or already known from context).
target_language_example: Ela me convenceu de fazer aquilo, mas depois me arrependi.
native_language_example: She convinced me to do that, but later I regretted it.

additional_notes: Used after certain verbs, adjectives, or expressions that require the preposition "de" before an infinitive ("de" + "fazer"). Very common with ideas like necessity/obligation ("ter de fazer isso" = "have to do this"), possibility/need ("precisar de fazer isso"), feelings ("ficar envergonhado de fazer isso" = "be embarrassed to do this"), and being excused ("ser dispensado de fazer isso" = "be exempt from doing this"). In Brazil it’s also common to say "precisar fazer isso" (without "de"), but "ter de" is widely used.
target_language_example: Eu não quero ter de fazer isso de novo.
native_language_example: I don't want to have to do this again.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say it belongs to the science fiction genre: "um filme de ficção científica" (a science fiction movie), "romances de ficção científica" (sci-fi novels). Often shortened in speech to "sci-fi" in English, but in Portuguese you commonly say the full phrase "ficção científica".
target_language_example: Você prefere filmes de ficção científica ou de ação?
native_language_example: Do you prefer science fiction movies or action movies?

additional_notes: Used after verbs and expressions that take "de" (like gostar de) to say what someone likes or is interested in. Here, "filmes" = movies and "ficção científica" = science fiction; you can swap in another genre (ex.: de filmes de comédia).
target_language_example: Ela não gosta de filmes de ficção científica, mas adora filmes de comédia.
native_language_example: She doesn't like science fiction movies, but she loves comedy movies.

additional_notes: Used with estar/ficar (“to be”) to say someone isn’t working that day/shift: Estou de folga hoje. It also appears in phrases like dias de folga (“days off”) and tirar X de folga (“to take X off / take time off”), often referring to work or school.
target_language_example: Estou de folga amanhã, então posso te ajudar à tarde.
native_language_example: I’m off tomorrow, so I can help you in the afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to ask or say that someone is not working during the evening/night. It uses the common expression “estar de folga” (= to be off work / have time off) plus the time phrase “hoje à noite” (= tonight). In questions, it’s often used to check someone’s availability.
target_language_example: Estou de folga hoje à noite, então posso sair mais cedo.
native_language_example: I’m off tonight, so I can go out earlier.

meaning: 'of French' / 'in French' (relating to the French language).
additional_notes: Uses "de" to link something to the French language: a subject you study (aula/curso de francês), an exam (teste de francês), a dictionary (dicionário de francês), or a person’s ability (falante de francês). With verbs like "gostar", "francês" can be the thing you like/study ("gosto de francês" = "I like French").
target_language_example: Você tem um livro de francês?
native_language_example: Do you have a French book?

meaning: “seafood” / “of seafood” (used to describe something made with seafood, or a seafood place).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify type: restaurante de frutos do mar (seafood restaurant), sopa de frutos do mar (seafood soup), prato de frutos do mar (seafood dish). The base phrase is frutos do mar (“seafood”); adding de often means “of/with”.
target_language_example: Vamos a um restaurante de frutos do mar hoje?
native_language_example: Shall we go to a seafood restaurant today?

meaning: "of smoking" / "to smoke" (used with an infinitive after certain words).
additional_notes:
It’s the preposition "de" + the infinitive "fumar". Common in structures like: 
- "deixar de fumar" = to quit smoking / to stop smoking
- "parar de fumar" = to stop smoking
- "hábito de fumar" = (the) habit of smoking
Also appears in set phrases like "salão de fumar" (smoking room/lounge).
target_language_example: Estou a tentar deixar de fumar.
native_language_example: I’m trying to quit smoking.

meaning: of soccer; soccer (as an adjective phrase).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify it’s related to soccer: partida de futebol (soccer match), clube de futebol (soccer club), time/equipe de futebol (soccer team), bola de futebol (soccer ball), torneio de futebol (soccer tournament). It’s the preposition de (“of”) + futebol (“soccer/football”), so it works like “soccer” in English (a soccer match). In Brazil, futebol usually means soccer; in Portugal it can also mean football (soccer) in general.
target_language_example: A gente vai assistir a um jogo de futebol hoje à noite.
native_language_example: We’re going to watch a soccer match tonight.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like estar/ficar to say someone is currently on vacation or has time off: "Estou de férias". Also appears with sair ("sair de férias" = to go on vacation) and with a time period: "estavam de férias em julho passado". Note: "férias" can also mean vacation days/leave ("dias de férias").
target_language_example: Estou de férias na semana que vem.
native_language_example: I’m on vacation next week.

meaning: of English; in English (as a subject).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that something is related to the English language, especially as a school subject or course: "curso de inglês" (English course), "aulas de inglês" (English classes), "professor(a) de inglês" (English teacher). Also used in questions like "Você gosta de inglês?" meaning "Do you like English?" (the language/subject).
target_language_example: Eu tenho prova de inglês amanhã.
native_language_example: I have an English test tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used after many nouns and adjectives to introduce an action in the infinitive, similar to English “to …” or “of …-ing”. Common with words like decisão (decision) and medo (fear): decisão de ir = “decision to go”, medo de ir = “fear of going / fear to go”. Often followed by a destination with para: de ir para o exterior = “to go abroad”.
target_language_example: Estou com vontade de ir ao cinema hoje.
native_language_example: I feel like going to the movies today.

meaning: 'to go to' (often 'the opportunity/order/need to go to …').
additional_notes: Used after a noun or verb that requires "de" (e.g., oportunidade/ordem/necessidade + de) and before the infinitive "ir". "Ir a" introduces the destination. Common patterns: "oportunidade de ir a...", "ordens de ir a...", "ter de ir a...".
target_language_example: Não tenho vontade de ir ao trabalho hoje.
native_language_example: I don't feel like going to work today.

additional_notes: Used with verbs/nouns that take the preposition “de” before an infinitive (often “ter de”, “planos de”, “costume de”), followed by “ir” (to go) and “ao” = “a + o” (to the + masculine singular place). For feminine singular, you’ll usually see “de ir à” (e.g., de ir à praia).
target_language_example: Eu estava com vontade de ir ao cinema hoje.
native_language_example: I felt like going to the movies today.

additional_notes: A very common structure: **de + infinitive** links an action to another verb/noun/adjective (e.g., *gostar de*, *a ideia de*, *o desejo de*). **ir para** means “to go to” with the sense of going/moving toward a destination, and **para a** is used before a feminine singular noun (*a Austrália, a praia, a escola*). In many contexts you’ll also hear **concordar em ir para...** rather than *concordar de ir para...*.
target_language_example: A ideia de ir para a praia amanhã é ótima.
native_language_example: The idea of going to the beach tomorrow is great.

meaning: “to go to …” (used after verbs/expressions with “de” + infinitive).
additional_notes: Used when a previous verb or expression requires the preposition “de” before an infinitive (e.g., “gostar de…”, “impedir alguém de…”, “ter de…”). “à” is the contraction of “a + a” and is used before feminine singular nouns/places (e.g., “à ópera”, “à aula”). With masculine singular you usually see “ao” (a + o), e.g., “ir ao cinema”.
target_language_example: Eu preciso de ir à farmácia hoje.
native_language_example: I need to go to the pharmacy today.

additional_notes: You’ll often see the infinitive jogar preceded by the preposition de after certain verbs/expressions, especially: lembrar-se de jogar (“to remember playing/to remember to play”), ter o costume de jogar (“to have the habit of playing”), gostar de jogar (“to like playing/to like to play”), and ter de jogar (“to have to play”). In English, the de usually doesn’t get translated directly; you translate the whole expression.
target_language_example: Ela gosta de jogar videogame com os amigos.
native_language_example: She likes playing video games with her friends.

meaning: 'to play soccer/football' (used after verbs like gostar de, parar de).
additional_notes: This is the preposition + infinitive structure "de + verb" used after certain verbs. Common ones: "gostar de" (to like), "parar de" (to stop), "precisar de" (to need). Here, "jogar futebol" means "to play soccer" (American English) / "to play football" (British English). You can also replace "futebol" with another activity: "de jogar tênis", "de estudar", etc.
target_language_example: Ela parou de jogar futebol no ano passado.
native_language_example: She stopped playing soccer last year.

additional_notes: Used with verbs and nouns that take the preposition “de” before an infinitive, like “gostar de lavar” (to like washing). It also appears in common noun phrases such as “máquina de lavar” (washing machine) and “sabão de lavar” (laundry soap/soap for washing).
target_language_example: Preciso de lavar a roupa antes de amanhã.
native_language_example: I need to wash the clothes before tomorrow.

meaning: 'of milk' / 'made with milk' (used to describe something milk-related).
additional_notes: Uses "de" + a noun to describe the type/material/flavor of something. Common in phrases like "chá de leite" (milk tea), "café de leite" (coffee with milk), "produtor de leite" (milk producer/dairy farmer), or to identify containers/products: "jarra de leite" (milk jug).
target_language_example: Quero um café de leite, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like a coffee with milk, please.

meaning: 'to read' (used after certain verbs/adjectives with the preposition “de”).
additional_notes: Portuguese often uses “de” + infinitive after certain verbs/adjectives. Common patterns: **parar/deixar de ler** = to stop reading; **estar cansado de ler** = to be tired of reading; **gostar de ler** = to like reading; **(é) fácil/difícil de ler** = (it’s) easy/hard to read; **terminar de ler** = to finish reading.
target_language_example: Eu gosto de ler antes de dormir.
native_language_example: I like to read before going to sleep.

meaning: to read the book (used after verbs that take “de” + infinitive).
additional_notes: In Portuguese, some verbs are followed by **de + infinitive**. So **de ler o livro** is the action “to read the book,” attached to another verb: **terminar de ler o livro** (to finish reading the book), **estar terminando de ler o livro** (to be finishing reading the book), **esquecer-se de ler o livro** (to forget to read the book). In English we usually don’t translate the “de” as “of.”
target_language_example: Eu me esqueci de ler o livro ontem.
native_language_example: I forgot to read the book yesterday.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say what material something is made of: "X é de madeira" (X is wooden / made of wood) or "um/uma X de madeira" (a wooden X).
target_language_example: Preciso de uma estante de madeira para o meu quarto.
native_language_example: I need a wooden bookshelf for my bedroom.

additional_notes: Used after the preposition "de" in expressions like "de mais" (= "of more"). Very common with verbs/expressions that take "de" (precisar de mais..., gostar de mais...) and with nouns (mais chuva, mais homens, mais voluntários). Note: don't confuse with "demais" (one word), which usually means "too much/too many" or "very".
target_language_example: Você quer de mais alguma coisa?
native_language_example: Do you want anything else?

additional_notes: Used to say something happens during the morning (time of day). Commonly placed at the end of the sentence (e.g., "Eu trabalho de manhã"), but it can also come earlier for emphasis. You’ll often see it alongside "à tarde" (in the afternoon) and "à noite" (at night).
target_language_example: Eu sempre tomo café de manhã.
native_language_example: I always have coffee in the morning.

meaning: 'of peanut butter' (used to describe something made with/containing peanut butter).
additional_notes: Uses "de" to link a noun to what it’s made of or flavored with. Common in food phrases like "sanduíche de manteiga de amendoim" (peanut-butter sandwich). In questions like "Você gosta de manteiga de amendoim?", the "de" isn’t used because it’s just the food name.
target_language_example: Quero uma torrada de manteiga de amendoim.
native_language_example: I want a piece of toast with peanut butter.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (or "ficar") to describe someone’s current mood/temporary state: "Estou/Ele está de mau humor". You can add time expressions: "hoje", "de manhã", "nessa manhã".
target_language_example: Hoje eu estou de mau humor porque dormi pouco.
native_language_example: Today I’m in a bad mood because I slept poorly.

additional_notes: Used when "eu" becomes the object of a preposition like "de". Common with expressions like "ter/fazer pena (de mim)" or "ter piedade de mim" ("have mercy on me"), "falar de mim" ("talk about me"), and with nouns like "parte de mim" ("part of me"). You generally say "de mim" (not *"de eu").
target_language_example: Não falem de mim pelas costas.
native_language_example: Don't talk about me behind my back.

additional_notes: Very common with verbs that take **de + noun**, such as **gostar de** (to like), **entender de** (to know about / be knowledgeable about), and **falar de** (to talk about). In these cases, **de música** usually means “about music,” not literally “of music.”
target_language_example: A gente estava falando de música no almoço.
native_language_example: We were talking about music at lunch.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say it’s related to classical music: "concerto de música clássica" (classical music concert), "festival de música clássica" (classical music festival). Often appears with "música clássica" by itself when talking about the genre.
target_language_example: Ela toca piano em um grupo de música clássica.
native_language_example: She plays piano in a classical music group.

meaning: “of snow”; “snow-” (used to describe something made of/covered with snow).
additional_notes: Usually follows a noun to specify snow as the material or type: bola de neve (“snowball”), queda de neve (“snowfall”), coberto de neve (“covered in snow”). It’s the preposition de + neve (“snow”).
target_language_example: As montanhas estavam cobertas de neve.
native_language_example: The mountains were covered in snow.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to repeat something or to do something one more time. Often follows what you want repeated: "Diga isso de novo, por favor" (Say that again, please) or "Posso ver o cardápio de novo, por favor?" (Can I see the menu again, please?). "De novo" literally means "again" and "por favor" means "please".
target_language_example: Pode repetir de novo, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you repeat that again, please?

additional_notes: Used to say an action happens another time (repeat) or returns after stopping. Very common in requests like “Diga de novo” (“Say it again”) and with verbs for repeated actions/events (ligar, tossir, pensar, ver, etc.).
target_language_example: Pode repetir de novo, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you say it again, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about the origin/source of someone or something. Common in questions like “De onde você é?” (Where are you from?) and “De onde você veio?” (Where did you come from?). Can also introduce an indirect question: “Não sei de onde...” (I don’t know where from...).
target_language_example: De onde é este vinho?
native_language_example: Where is this wine from?

additional_notes: Literally “from where (it) came.” Used either as a direct question (“De onde veio isso?”) or inside a longer sentence (“o lugar de onde veio” = “the place where (you) came from”). “Veio” is the past of “vir” (to come) for ele/ela/você; for “you all” it’s “de onde vieram?”.
target_language_example: De onde veio essa informação?
native_language_example: Where did this information come from?

meaning: made of paper; paper (as the material).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say what something is made from: "aviões de papel" (paper airplanes), "saco de papel" (paper bag). It’s a literal, compositional use of "de" (of/from) + "papel" (paper).
target_language_example: Você tem um saco de papel?
native_language_example: Do you have a paper bag?

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say what material it’s made of: "copo de plástico" (plastic cup), "garrafa de plástico" (plastic bottle). It contrasts with other materials like "de vidro" (glass) or "de papel" (paper).
target_language_example: Você tem uma garrafa de plástico?
native_language_example: Do you have a plastic bottle?

meaning: "to be able to" ("can") used before another verb.
