It can also describe people/things that are hard to deal with in a certain way (e.g., difícil de contentar = hard to please). Often appears as "é/foi/será difícil de..." or after a noun: "uma teoria difícil de explicar".
target_language_example: Este texto é difícil de ler sem um dicionário.
native_language_example: This text is hard to read without a dictionary.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is hard for a person or group. It agrees in gender/number with what is difficult: difícil (m./sing.), difícil (f./sing.), difíceis (plural). Often followed by a pronoun: difícil para mim/ele/ela/nós/vocês.
target_language_example: Isso é difícil para mim, mas vou tentar.
native_language_example: This is hard for me, but I’ll try.

additional_notes: Used to instruct someone (often politely/formally) to pass a message on to a third person. The pronoun “-lhe” means “to him/her” (indirect object), attached to the imperative form “diga” (from dizer, “to say/tell”). Common in requests like “Diga-lhe que espere” (“Tell him/her to wait”).
target_language_example: Por favor, diga-lhe que eu chego às oito.
native_language_example: Please tell him/her that I’ll arrive at eight.

additional_notes: Imperative of "dizer" (to say/tell) addressed to "você"/"o senhor/a senhora". The “-me” is an object pronoun meaning “to me.” Often used to ask for information: "Diga-me por quê…", "Diga-me quando…", "Diga-me com que frequência…". Less formal: "Diz-me" (to tu) or "Me diga" (common in Brazil).
target_language_example: Diga-me onde fica a estação, por favor.
native_language_example: Tell me where the station is, please.

additional_notes: Uses the formal command (imperative) of dizer (“to say/tell”) + the object pronoun me (“to me”) + o que (“what”). Common in questions or requests for information, especially polite/formal situations. In casual speech, people often say “me diga o que …” or “diz pra mim o que …”.
target_language_example: Diga-me o que você precisa para concluir o trabalho.
native_language_example: Tell me what you need to finish the job.

meaning: “tell me where …” (a polite/formal request for a location).
additional_notes: Uses the formal command form of the verb dizer (“to say/tell”): diga + the object pronoun me (“to me”), followed by onde (“where”). Common in requests for information: “Diga-me onde fica…”, “Diga-me onde está…”. In everyday spoken Brazilian Portuguese, people often say “Me diga onde…” or “Me diz onde…”.
target_language_example: Diga-me onde fica a estação, por favor.
native_language_example: Tell me where the station is, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (often politely or formally) to provide information or instructions: “Tell us what they’re saying,” “Tell us what to do,” “Tell us what you thought.” It’s made up of diga (command form of “dizer,” used with “você”), nos (“to us”), and o que (“what”). In more informal speech you’ll often hear “diz pra gente o que…” or “fala pra gente o que…”.
target_language_example: Por favor, diga-nos o que você precisa.
native_language_example: Please tell us what you need.

additional_notes: "Diga" is the formal (você / o senhor, a senhora) imperative of "dizer" (“to say/tell”). It’s commonly followed by "a" before an indirect object (the person you’re telling): "diga a ele" (tell him), "diga a ela" (tell her), "diga ao professor" (tell the teacher). Often used with "que" to introduce what you’re telling: "Diga a ele que…".
target_language_example: Diga a ela que eu chego às oito.
native_language_example: Tell her that I’ll arrive at eight.

additional_notes: Used to give an instruction/request to pass a message to a woman/girl (“ela” = her). The verb is in the imperative (formal ‘you’): diga. Informal equivalents are often “diz pra ela que…” / “fala pra ela que…”.
target_language_example: Por favor, diga a ela que eu vou ligar mais tarde.
native_language_example: Please tell her that I’ll call later.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to pass a message on to a woman (“her”). You normally follow it with a verb in the present continuous: “estou + gerúndio” (e.g., estou trabalhando = I’m working). “Diga” is the imperative of dizer for você (neutral/polite in Brazil). If speaking to someone informally (tu), you may hear “diz a ela que estou…”.
target_language_example: Diga a ela que estou chegando agora.
native_language_example: Tell her that I'm arriving now.

additional_notes: Imperative form (formal) of "dizer" + "a verdade". Used to ask/tell someone to be honest: "Diga a verdade!" You can make it more polite with "por favor" or use "me/nos/lhe" to say who should be told: "Diga-me a verdade" (tell me the truth), "Diga-nos a verdade" (tell us the truth). In informal speech, you’ll often hear "diz a verdade" (to one person) or "digam a verdade" (to multiple people).
target_language_example: Por favor, diga a verdade: você quebrou o celular?
native_language_example: Please tell the truth: did you break the phone?

additional_notes: Used to give an instruction: diga (formal imperative of "dizer") + ao (= a + o). It means "tell/say to [someone]" where the person is masculine singular and usually introduced by a name/title: "Diga ao Tom...". For feminine singular, use "diga à" (a + a). Often followed by "que..." (tell him that...) or "para..." (tell him to...).
target_language_example: Diga ao João que eu ligo mais tarde.
native_language_example: Tell João that I’ll call later.

additional_notes: Uses the formal imperative of **dizer** (“to say/tell”): **diga** = “tell/say” (to you, formal). It’s typically followed by a clause: **diga o que + (verb)** (“tell what… / tell me what to do”). In everyday speech with friends, you’ll often hear **diz o que…** instead (informal).
target_language_example: Por favor, diga o que você precisa.
native_language_example: Please tell me what you need.

additional_notes: Used with the verbs pegar/pedir (to borrow/ask to borrow): pegar dinheiro emprestado de alguém (borrow money from someone) and pedir dinheiro emprestado a alguém (ask someone to lend you money).
target_language_example: Não quero pegar dinheiro emprestado de ninguém.
native_language_example: I don’t want to borrow money from anyone.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has (or doesn’t have) enough money in order to buy something. Often followed by the thing being bought: “dinheiro para comprar um/uma …”. You can change the verb for other purposes (e.g., “dinheiro para pagar” = money to pay).
target_language_example: Não tenho dinheiro para comprar ingressos hoje.
native_language_example: I don’t have money to buy tickets today.

additional_notes: Used to say that the available or earned money is enough to do something. Common patterns: **dinheiro suficiente para + infinitive** (Eu tenho dinheiro suficiente para viajar.) and **dinheiro suficiente para que + subjunctive** (Há dinheiro suficiente para que ele compre um carro.).
target_language_example: Não tenho dinheiro suficiente para pagar o aluguel este mês.
native_language_example: I don’t have enough money to pay the rent this month.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has the necessary amount of money to purchase something. Often followed by the item (e.g., “uma casa”, “tudo que precisa”). Word-by-word it’s dinheiro (money) + suficiente (enough) + para comprar (to buy).
target_language_example: Não tenho dinheiro suficiente para comprar esse computador agora.
native_language_example: I don’t have enough money to buy that computer right now.

meaning: "the right to" (to be allowed/entitled to do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb (direito de + verb) to say someone is entitled to do something, or that it’s fair/legitimate for them to do it. Common with forms of ter (e.g., tenho/tem/temos direito de...). Also appears as ter direito a + noun (e.g., direito a férias = the right to vacation).
target_language_example: Você tem direito de pedir uma explicação.
native_language_example: You have the right to ask for an explanation.

meaning: straight to bed; directly to bed.
additional_notes: Used when someone goes to bed immediately, without doing anything else first (often because they’re tired). With verbs like "ir" or "ser" in the past: "foi/fomos/foram direto para a cama". "Direto" works like "straight/directly" here, and it can also agree as "direta" depending on the speaker/context.
target_language_example: Depois da viagem, eu fui direto para a cama.
native_language_example: After the trip, I went straight to bed.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. "Dirigir" means "to drive"; "um carro" means "a car." You’ll often hear it with ability ("Eu consigo dirigir um carro"), permission/age ("muito jovem/novo para dirigir"), and requirements ("precisa de uma licença"). In Brazil, "carteira de motorista" / "CNH" is the driver’s license; in Portugal, "carta de condução."
target_language_example: Eu não posso dirigir um carro sem carteira de motorista.
native_language_example: I can't drive a car without a driver's license.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb: "estar (ou ficar) disposto a + infinitive". It expresses willingness, readiness, or being prepared to do something (often implying a decision/attitude). It changes with gender/number: disposto (m. sing.), disposta (f. sing.), dispostos (m. pl.), dispostas (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Estou disposto a tentar de novo.
native_language_example: I’m willing to try again.

additional_notes: Past tense of dizer ('to say/tell'). Used to report what someone told you: [Someone] disse-me que + clause. In Brazilian Portuguese, this is often phrased as "me disse que"; in Portugal, "disse-me que" is common. You can replace the person: "Ele/ela disse-me que..."
target_language_example: O meu chefe disse-me que a reunião foi cancelada.
native_language_example: My boss told me that the meeting was canceled.

additional_notes: "Disse" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "dizer" (to say/to tell). "Disse a" introduces the person you spoke to: "disse a + name" (often with an article: "disse ao/à"). After that you can add what was said: "disse a Maria o que..." (told Maria what...), "disse a Maria para..." (told Maria to...), "disse a Maria que..." (told Maria that...). With male names it commonly becomes "disse ao": "Ele disse ao Tony."
target_language_example: Eu disse ao João que estava atrasado.
native_language_example: I told João that I was late.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **dizer a verdade** (“to tell the truth”). Used to report that someone was truthful about something in a completed situation. Often appears with a subject: **Eu/Ele/Ela/Tom disse a verdade**. In English, “tell the truth” is more common than the literal “say the truth.”
target_language_example: Ela disse a verdade sobre o que aconteceu.
native_language_example: She told the truth about what happened.

additional_notes: From the verb "dizer" (to say) in the past (ele/ela/você disse = he/she/you said) + "alguma coisa" (something/anything). In questions like "Ele disse alguma coisa?", it often means "Did he say anything?". You can add "para" + a person ("disse alguma coisa para a Maria") or "sobre" + a topic ("disse alguma coisa sobre isso").
target_language_example: Você disse alguma coisa para o médico?
native_language_example: Did you say anything to the doctor?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "dizer" (to say) in the simple past ("disse" = "I/you/he/she said") plus "isso" (that/it). Very common when denying, confirming, or asking about something someone said: "Eu não disse isso" (I didn’t say that), "Por que disse isso?" (Why did you say that?). Often you’ll hear it with a subject ("Eu/Você/O senhor") or without it when it’s clear from context.
target_language_example: Eu nunca disse isso para você.
native_language_example: I never said that to you.

additional_notes: "Disse" is the past tense of "dizer" (to say/tell). "Dizer para + [person]" introduces who you spoke to and is very common before: (1) "que" + a full statement: "Disse para a Mary que..." (= he told Mary that...); or (2) an instruction: "Disse para ele fazer..." (= he told him to do...). In everyday English you often translate it as "told" rather than "said".
target_language_example: Eu disse para ele que não podia ir hoje.
native_language_example: I told him I couldn't go today.

additional_notes: Used to report an instruction or advice in the past: **disse** (said/told) + **para** (for/to) + **não** (not) + infinitive verb. The subject is the person who gave the instruction. The person receiving it can appear as an indirect object: **me/lhe/nos disse para não…** (“told me/him/her/us not to…”). Often followed by an infinitive like **ir, tocar, mentir, estacionar**; it can also be followed by a verb phrase with **se** (e.g., **não se preocupar** = “not to worry”).
target_language_example: Eu disse para não abrir a porta para estranhos.
native_language_example: I told (you/them) not to open the door to strangers.

additional_notes: "Disse" is the past tense of "dizer" (to say/tell). "para o" is a contraction of "para" + "o" meaning "to the" (masculine), so it’s used before masculine nouns and names treated as masculine (e.g., "o Tom"). Very common pattern: "disse para o + [person] + [verb]" = "told [person] to [verb]" (often giving an instruction). With a clause, it can mean "told [person] that...": "disse para o Tom que...". For feminine, you’ll see "disse para a" ("para" + "a").
target_language_example: Eu disse para o Pedro esperar aqui.
native_language_example: I told Pedro to wait here.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said. It’s the past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **dizer** (“to say”) + **que** (“that”), introducing a clause: **[someone] disse que + sentence**. You can change **disse** to match the subject: **eu disse que**, **você/ele/ela disse que**, **nós dissemos que**, **eles/elas disseram que**.
target_language_example: Ela disse que vai chegar mais tarde.
native_language_example: She said that she’ll arrive later.

meaning: "said that the" (referring to a feminine singular noun/name).
additional_notes: "Disse" is the past tense of "dizer" (to say). "Que" introduces what was said (“that…”). "A" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”) and is used before many feminine nouns and sometimes before women’s names (e.g., "a Mary" in some contexts/varieties). Used to report what someone said: "[Someone] disse que a [person/thing]..."
target_language_example: Ele disse que a professora estava cansada.
native_language_example: He said that the teacher was tired.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said and what they believed at the time. It’s common in storytelling/reporting: **disse que** (“said that”) + **achava que** (“(he/she/I) thought that”). The subject of **achava** is often implied by context (e.g., “Tom said that he thought that…”).
target_language_example: Ela disse que achava que eu já tinha saído.
native_language_example: She said she thought I had already left.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said and what they believed/assumed. It often appears before a feminine noun because of “a” (= “the”, feminine singular): e.g., “a Mary”, “a professora”, “a situação”. You can change person/tense: “eu disse que achava que a…”, “eles disseram que achavam que a…”.
target_language_example: Ela disse que achava que a reunião ia começar mais tarde.
native_language_example: She said that she thought the meeting was going to start later.

additional_notes: Used to report what a woman/girl said. **disse** is the simple past of *dizer* (“to say”), **que** means “that” and introduces the reported clause, and **ela** means “she.” In Portuguese, the subject pronoun (**ela**) is sometimes optional (you may also hear/see *disse que…* without *ela*).
target_language_example: O João disse que ela vai chegar mais tarde.
native_language_example: João said that she’s going to arrive later.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech: "disse" (past of "dizer", 'said') + "que" ('that') + "ele" ('he'). Common for telling what a man/boy said. Often you can omit "ele" if it's clear from context (e.g., "Tom disse que quebrou o copo"), but keeping it is also normal.
target_language_example: Ela disse que ele não podia ir hoje.
native_language_example: She said that he couldn't go today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about a man’s identity/state/characteristic (era = “was”). It’s common in storytelling or when repeating information. Often followed by an adjective or noun: “disse que ele era solteiro” (said he was single), “disse que ele era forte” (said he was strong). In everyday speech you may also hear/see the shorter version “disse que ele…” without repeating “era” if the next part uses a different verb.
target_language_example: Ela disse que ele era professor, mas na verdade ele trabalhava em outra área.
native_language_example: She said that he was a teacher, but actually he worked in another field.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about a man/boy’s state or condition. **disse** is the past of *dizer* (“said/told”), **que** = “that,” and **ele estava** is the imperfect past of *estar* (“he was/was feeling/was located”). Very common in indirect speech: *Ela disse que ele estava cansado.*
target_language_example: Ela disse que ele estava cansado demais para sair.
native_language_example: She said that he was too tired to go out.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man said he wanted. Common in indirect/reported speech: **disse que** (“said that”) + **ele queria** (“he wanted”). In Portuguese, **que** (“that”) is usually kept (more than in English), and **queria** is the imperfect past, often used for what someone wanted at that time.
target_language_example: Ela disse que ele queria sair mais cedo.
native_language_example: She said he wanted to leave earlier.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech to introduce what a man said in the past: *X disse que ele tinha…* (“X said that he had…”). Very often you’ll see **tinha que** right after it: **disse que ele tinha que…** = “said that he had to / needed to …”. In everyday Portuguese, people may drop **que** or **ele** depending on context, but this fuller form is clear and common in learners’ materials.
target_language_example: Ela disse que ele tinha que sair mais cedo.
native_language_example: She said that he had to leave earlier.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said (indirect speech). "Disse" is the past of "dizer" (to say/tell). "Que" introduces the reported clause (“that”). "Era" is the imperfect past of "ser" (to be), often used for descriptions/identities or background information in the past (e.g., "era casada" = was married; "era importante" = was important). The subject is usually understood from context (I/he/she said).
target_language_example: Ele disse que era tarde demais para ligar.
native_language_example: He said it was too late to call.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about their state/feeling or situation in the past. "disse" is the past of "dizer" (to say), and "que" introduces the reported clause. "estava" is the imperfect past of "estar" (to be), often used for temporary states (hungry, available, irritated, etc.). The subject pronoun (ele/ela/você/eu) is often omitted because it’s understood from context.
target_language_example: Ela disse que estava cansada, então foi para casa cedo.
native_language_example: She said she was tired, so she went home early.

additional_notes: Past tense reporting of what someone said: "disse" = "(he/she) said" and "que" introduces the reported clause. "estava cansado" means "was tired" (cansado = masculine; cansada = feminine). You can swap the subject: "Eu disse que estava cansado/a" (I said I was tired), "Ela disse que estava cansada" (She said she was tired). Often followed by "de" + infinitive to mean "tired of" doing something (e.g., "cansado de esperar" = tired of waiting).
target_language_example: Ele disse que estava cansado e foi para casa mais cedo.
native_language_example: He said he was tired and went home early.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said: "X disse que estava muito + adjective" (e.g., cansado/a, frio, assustado/a). The adjective usually agrees with the person being described (cansada for Mary; cansado for Tom). Often followed by the reason/result (e.g., "para..." = too... to...).
target_language_example: Ela disse que estava muito feliz com a notícia.
native_language_example: She said she was very happy about the news.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech: "disse" (said) + "que" (that) + "estava com" (was with / had). Very common with temporary states and feelings: "estar com saudade" (to miss), "estar com frio" (to be cold), "estar com pressa" (to be in a hurry), "estar com sede" (to be thirsty), "estar com um resfriado" (to have a cold). You change it for person/tense as needed (e.g., "Eu disse que estava com...", "Ela disse que está com...").
target_language_example: Ele disse que estava com dor de cabeça.
native_language_example: He said he had a headache.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech to introduce what someone said about you. Often followed by a verb in the imperfect (e.g., "podia", "parecia") to describe a past situation or impression.
target_language_example: Ela disse que eu precisava estudar mais.
native_language_example: She said that I needed to study more.

meaning: 'said that I should' / 'told me I should.'
additional_notes: Used to report someone’s advice, recommendation, or opinion in the past. Structure: (someone) disse que eu deveria + infinitive (tomar, estudar, aprender) = “(someone) said I should…”. With a past infinitive (ter + past participle), it refers to something you should have done: “disse que eu deveria ter ido…” = “said I should have gone…”. Often you’ll also hear it with a person’s name instead of “eu” (e.g., “disse que você deveria…”).
target_language_example: Ela disse que eu deveria dormir mais.
native_language_example: She said that I should sleep more.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech to say what someone said they were going to do. The verb "ir" in the imperfect ("ia") commonly expresses a planned/expected future from a past point of view (similar to English “was going to”). The subject changes with context ("eu disse que ia...", "ele disse que ia..."). Often "que" can be omitted in casual speech ("disse que ia" → "disse que ia"/"disse que ia"), but it’s standard to include it.
target_language_example: Ela disse que ia chegar mais cedo, mas se atrasou.
native_language_example: She said she was going to arrive earlier, but she got delayed.

additional_notes: Past tense: "disse" = "(he/she) said" (from dizer). "que" introduces what was said (“that…”). "me" = “me.” "amava" is the imperfect past of amar (“loved/used to love”), often used in storytelling or to describe an ongoing feeling in the past. You can change the subject: "Ele disse que me amava" (He said…), "Ela disse que me amava" (She said…).
target_language_example: Eu nunca esqueci quando ele disse que me amava.
native_language_example: I never forgot when he said he loved me.

additional_notes: Used to report that someone/something stated a refusal or negated something. Often followed by a verb clause: "disse que não viu" = "said (he) didn’t see"; or used alone as a complete answer: "Disse que não." = "(He/She) said no." "Disse" is the past of "dizer" (to say/tell).
target_language_example: Ele me disse que não podia ir hoje.
native_language_example: He told me he couldn’t go today.

meaning: “(someone) said that the …” (reporting what someone said; 'que' = 'that', 'o' = 'the').
additional_notes: Used to introduce a reported statement: **[person] disse que + clause**. Here **o** is the masculine singular definite article (“the”) starting a noun phrase (**o Tom**, **o reino**, **o time**, etc.). In questions, it can be part of a reminder/confirmation: **Quantos anos você disse que o Tom tinha?** = “How old did you say Tom was?” In Portuguese, the main verb often stays in the past (**disse**) even if the reported info is still true.
target_language_example: Ele disse que o ônibus ia atrasar.
native_language_example: He said that the bus was going to be late.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech to describe what someone said they needed to do. You usually follow it with an infinitive verb (e.g., estudar, comprar, dormir, ficar) or with a noun phrase (precisava de + noun). The subject is often understood from context (e.g., “Tom disse…” → “Tom said…”). Note: precisava comes from precisar (“to need”) and is not related to English “precise.”
target_language_example: Ele disse que precisava sair mais cedo.
native_language_example: He said that he needed to leave earlier.

additional_notes: "disse" is the past of "dizer" (to say). "precisava de" is the imperfect past of "precisar de" (to need) and is followed by a noun or noun phrase (e.g., "precisava de dinheiro" = needed money). In real use, the subject can change: "Eu disse que precisava de..." (I said I needed...), "Ela disse que precisava de..." (She said she needed...).
target_language_example: Ela disse que precisava de ajuda com a tarefa.
native_language_example: She said she needed help with the homework.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said they want. It combines the past tense of "dizer" (disse = said) + "que" (that) + the present of "querer" (quer = wants). You can change the subject and object pronouns as needed: "Ele/ela disse...", "me/te/nos disse...".
target_language_example: Ele me disse que quer mudar de emprego.
native_language_example: He told me he wants to change jobs.

meaning: 'said (that) he/she wanted' (reported speech in the past).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said they wanted. "disse" is the past of "dizer" (to say), and "que" introduces the content of what was said. "queria" is the imperfect past of "querer" (to want), often used after "disse que" to describe the desire/intention at that time (like "wanted" / "was wanting"). You can change the subject: "Eu disse que queria...", "Ela disse que queria..."
target_language_example: Ela disse que queria falar com você amanhã.
native_language_example: She said she wanted to talk to you tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Disse" is the past tense of "dizer" (to say). "Que" introduces reported speech (“that…”). "Queria" is the imperfect of "querer" (to want) and often corresponds to “wanted” in English. "Ir" means “to go.” You can change the subject before "disse" (Tom disse…, Ela disse…) and add a destination after "ir" (ir à praia, ir ao cinema).
target_language_example: Ela disse que queria ir ao cinema hoje.
native_language_example: She said she wanted to go to the movies today.

additional_notes: Past reporting of someone’s statement + knowledge: **disse** (preterite of *dizer*, “said/told”) + **que** (“that”) + **sabia** (imperfect of *saber*, “knew/used to know”). Often introduces an indirect statement: *Ela disse que sabia as regras* (“She said she knew the rules”). With **me/te/lhe disse**, it means “told me/you/him/her.”
target_language_example: Ele me disse que sabia a resposta, mas não quis falar.
native_language_example: He told me he knew the answer, but he didn’t want to say it.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about their own feelings or physical/emotional state. In Portuguese, "se sentia" agrees with the subject (e.g., "ele disse que se sentia..." / "ela disse que se sentia...") and the adjective that follows usually agrees too ("cansado" for a man, "cansada" for a woman). It’s common in indirect/reported speech after verbs like "disse" (said).
target_language_example: Ela disse que se sentia nervosa antes da entrevista.
native_language_example: She said that she felt nervous before the interview.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said (reported speech). "disse" = "(he/she) said"; "que" = "that"; "tinha" is the imperfect of "ter" (to have), often used after "disse que" to express past information or obligations: "disse que tinha algo" = "said (she) had something"; "disse que tinha que" + verb = "said (she) had to" (meaning "said she needed to/was supposed to"). The subject is usually understood from context (e.g., "Ela disse...", "Tom disse...").
target_language_example: Ele disse que tinha que sair mais cedo.
native_language_example: He said he had to leave early.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said (indirect speech). "disse" is the past tense of "dizer" (to say/tell), and "que" introduces the reported clause. "você" is the subject of that clause (common for "you" in Brazil). You can replace "você" with another subject: "disse que ele…" (said that he…), "disse que eu…" (said that I…).
target_language_example: Ela disse que você pode entrar agora.
native_language_example: She said that you can come in now.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about “you” in the past. It’s a common pattern: [name] disse que você estava + adjective/verb phrase (e.g., ocupado/irritado/dirigindo). Note: “disse” can refer to “he said” or “she said” (Portuguese doesn’t specify gender here).
target_language_example: Ela disse que você estava cansado.
native_language_example: She said that you were tired.

meaning: 'they told me that…' / 'I was told that…'.
additional_notes: Used to report information you heard from other people. Literally 'they told me that', with the indirect object pronoun -me ('to me') attached to the verb. Often followed by a full clause in the past or present. Can also introduce advice/instructions: "Disseram-me que eu devia…" (they told me I should…) or a command in the subjunctive: "Disseram-me que voltasse…" (they told me to come back…).
target_language_example: Disseram-me que a reunião foi cancelada.
native_language_example: They told me that the meeting was canceled.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "dizer": "eles/elas disseram" + "que" to introduce what someone reported. Used to relay information or repeat what other people claimed. Often followed by another verb in the past (e.g., "disseram que precisavam...") or present (e.g., "disseram que o pai está...").
target_language_example: Eles disseram que iam chegar cedo.
native_language_example: They said they were going to arrive early.

meaning: “(they) said that they …” (reporting what someone said about them).
additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech: "disseram" = “(they) said” (past tense), "que" = “that,” and "eles" = “they” (the group being talked about). You can replace "eles" with another subject (e.g., "disseram que eu...", "disseram que ela...").
target_language_example: Eles disseram que eles vão chegar mais tarde.
native_language_example: They said that they will arrive later.

additional_notes: Used to report what people said (reported speech). "Disseram" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "dizer" for "they" (3rd person plural). "Estavam" is the imperfect past of "estar" (they were), often used to describe a situation/state in progress at that time (e.g., being afraid, being in a hurry). It’s commonly followed by an expression like "com medo" (afraid), "com pressa" (in a hurry), or another verb phrase ("voltando" = coming back/returning).
target_language_example: Eles disseram que estavam cansados, então foram embora cedo.
native_language_example: They said they were tired, so they left early.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said in the past. "disseram" = “they said” (also used for “you all said” in some regions), "que" = “that,” and "precisavam de" = “needed” + "de" before a noun/thing needed (e.g., de um favor, de mais tempo, de algo para beber).
target_language_example: Eles disseram que precisavam de ajuda.
native_language_example: They said they needed help.

additional_notes: Used to report what other people said (reported speech). "disseram" is past tense of "dizer" (they said); "que" means "that"; "vocês" is "you" (plural); "eram" is the imperfect past of "ser" (you were). Often followed by a noun/adjective phrase: "disseram que vocês eram amigos/amigas" (they said you were friends).
target_language_example: Disseram que vocês eram novos na cidade.
native_language_example: They said you were new in the city.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **dividir**: **dividiu** = “divided.” Used with **em + number/parts** to say how something was split (e.g., *em cinco pedaços* = “into five pieces”). You can replace **o bolo** with any item: *dividiu a pizza em oito fatias*.
target_language_example: Ele dividiu o bolo em quatro pedaços para todo mundo comer.
native_language_example: He divided the cake into four pieces so everyone could eat.

additional_notes: Imperative form of the reflexive verb "divertir-se" (to have fun). It’s the polite/standard command used with "você"; for "tu" you often hear "diverte-te" (more common in Portugal) or "se diverte" (common in Brazil). Often followed by "com" (with), "na/no" (at/in), or "enquanto" (while).
target_language_example: Divirta-se no passeio e me conte depois!
native_language_example: Have fun on the outing and tell me about it afterward!

additional_notes: Impersonal/passive way to report a general belief, rumor, or hearsay without saying who is speaking (similar to English “they say…”). Common in news, writing, and everyday speech. Often introduces information you’re not fully confirming.
target_language_example: Diz-se que este restaurante é o melhor da cidade.
native_language_example: They say this restaurant is the best in the city.

additional_notes: Used after a subject (person/thing) to introduce what they say: “X diz que …”. The verb is present tense of dizer (to say), but it can report information in general, or something someone said recently.
target_language_example: Ela diz que vai chegar cedo.
native_language_example: She says that she’ll arrive early.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone (or something like a letter/legend) says about a man. In everyday speech, you can omit the repeated subject and just say “diz que…” if it’s clear who “he” is (e.g., “O Tom diz que está melhor hoje.”).
target_language_example: O médico diz que ele precisa descansar mais.
native_language_example: The doctor says that he needs to rest more.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone claims or states they want. "diz" is the present tense of "dizer" (to say) for ele/ela/você. "que" means "that" and introduces the next clause. Portuguese often omits the subject in the second clause when it’s the same person (so "diz que quer" = "diz que ele/ela quer"). You can change the subject/tense: "eu digo que quero" (I say I want), "eles dizem que querem" (they say they want).
target_language_example: Ela diz que quer aprender português.
native_language_example: She says she wants to learn Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used with the verb dizer (to say) + que (that). It can be literal (“they tell me that…”) or a general/impersonal rumor or common opinion (“they say…”). Often the subject is explicit (e.g., Tom e Maria dizem que…), but it can also be omitted as an impersonal “they” (Dizem que...).
target_language_example: Dizem que vai chover amanhã.
native_language_example: They say it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report something you’ve heard (rumors, general talk, or information from unspecified people). "Dizem" is the 3rd-person plural of "dizer" (“to say”) and often works like English “they say…”. You can also use it without "ele": "Dizem que…" = “They say that…” / “It’s said that…”.
target_language_example: Dizem que ele vai voltar amanhã.
native_language_example: They say he’s coming back tomorrow.

meaning: “they say that the…” / “people say that the…”
additional_notes: Used to report what people say or what is rumored, without saying who exactly. It’s the verb "dizer" in the 3rd person plural ("dizem" = "they say") + "que" (“that”) + the masculine singular article "o" (“the”). You can change the article depending on the noun: "dizem que a…" (feminine), "dizem que os…" (masc. plural), "dizem que as…" (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Dizem que o restaurante daqui é o melhor da cidade.
native_language_example: They say the restaurant here is the best in the city.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund ("dizendo") to describe the ongoing act of telling the truth, often in questions or statements about whether someone is being honest. Common patterns: "estar dizendo a verdade" (to be telling the truth), "acabar dizendo a verdade" (to end up telling the truth), "me/te/lhe dizendo a verdade" (telling me/you/him/her the truth).
target_language_example: Você está dizendo a verdade ou está brincando comigo?
native_language_example: Are you telling the truth or are you kidding with me?

additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech or the content of what someone says. Often follows verbs like estar/fazer/receber/responder/ligar: e.g., “recebi um telegrama dizendo que…” = “I got a telegram saying that…”. It can mean either (1) someone is literally speaking (“ela estava me dizendo que…”) or (2) a message/report contains information (“estão dizendo que…”, “um telegrama dizendo que…”).
target_language_example: Ele me mandou uma mensagem dizendo que ia se atrasar.
native_language_example: He sent me a message saying that he was going to be late.

additional_notes: Formed by the verb "dizer" + the object pronoun "me" (“me”), joined with a hyphen when the pronoun comes after the verb (common in European Portuguese), especially with infinitives in polite questions: "Pode/Poderia dizer-me...". You’ll also see the same idea with other verb forms, e.g. "Diga-me..." (“Tell me...”).
target_language_example: Pode dizer-me a que horas começa a reunião?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what time the meeting starts?

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object (the person who receives the information): dizer a + person. With pronouns: dizer a ele/ela, or contracted forms like dizer-lhe (more formal). Often followed by what you’re telling them: “dizer a alguém o que/que…”.
target_language_example: Preciso dizer a você uma coisa importante.
native_language_example: I need to tell you something important.

additional_notes: Used when you want to be honest or admit something. Very common after verbs like "ter que" (to have to) and "pretender" (to intend). You can also say "a verdade" alone to mean “the truth” (e.g., "A verdade é que..." = "The truth is that...").
target_language_example: Vou dizer a verdade: eu esqueci o seu aniversário.
native_language_example: I’ll tell the truth: I forgot your birthday.

additional_notes: Used with a direct object (algo = “something”) to indicate you speak or state an unspecified thing. It often appears with prepositions like “a/para” to show who you’re speaking to: “dizer algo a/para alguém” (to say something to someone). The verb “dizer” changes with the subject (eu digo, você/ele diz, nós dizemos, vocês/eles dizem).
target_language_example: Quero dizer algo importante para você.
native_language_example: I want to say something important to you.

additional_notes: Used when someone wants/needs to speak, make a comment, or express an opinion. Often appears in questions like “Você gostaria de dizer alguma coisa?” (“Would you like to say something?”). In “Isso deve nos dizer alguma coisa”, it means “tell us something” (i.e., be a sign/indicate something).
target_language_example: Se você quiser dizer alguma coisa, pode falar agora.
native_language_example: If you want to say something, you can speak now.

additional_notes: Used when referring to a specific thing someone said or is about to say (“isso” = “that/this”). Often appears after verbs like fazer (“make”) in questions ("O que te faria dizer isso?" = "What would make you say that?") or in requests to stop repeating something ("Para de dizer isso" = "Stop saying that").
target_language_example: Não acredito que você vai dizer isso na reunião.
native_language_example: I can’t believe you’re going to say that in the meeting.

meaning: to say what (to say the thing that...).
additional_notes: Used when the object of dizer (“to say/tell”) is introduced by o que (“what/that which”). Common in questions ("Dizer o quê?" = “Say what?”) and in phrases like "dizer o que pensa" (“say what you think”) or "dizer o que tem para dizer" (“say what you have to say”). Word order can change depending on the sentence (e.g., "o que você disse" = “what you said”).
target_language_example: Pode dizer o que aconteceu?
native_language_example: Can you say what happened?

additional_notes: Used to introduce what someone says, thinks, or claims: **dizer que + clause**. Often appears with an object pronoun for who you’re telling: **dizer-lhe(s) que** (“tell him/her/them that”). Very common inside other expressions like **ouvir dizer que** (“to hear that / to have heard that”).
target_language_example: Preciso dizer que não posso ir hoje.
native_language_example: I need to say that I can’t go today.

dizer que ele é um gênio

target_language_multi_word_term: dizer que ele é um gênio
meaning: to say that he is a genius.
additional_notes: Often used after expressions that comment on how reasonable the statement is: "pode-se dizer" (one can say), "pode-se facilmente dizer" (it’s easy to say), "não é exagero dizer" / "não é demais dizer" (it’s not an exaggeration to say). "Gênio" can mean a genius (a very talented person), especially in something like music, math, etc.
target_language_example: Não é exagero dizer que ele é um gênio no piano.
native_language_example: It’s not an exaggeration to say that he’s a genius at the piano.

meaning: to say/tell something (often to introduce a point).
additional_notes: Often used to preface what you’re about to say, like “I have to say something” or “Let me tell you something.” The something can be stated next ("Dizer uma coisa: ...") or left implied ("Vou te dizer uma coisa." can mean “Let me tell you something” with suspense). Common variants: "querer dizer uma coisa" (to want to say something), "ter que dizer uma coisa" (to have to say something).
target_language_example: Tenho que dizer uma coisa: não concordo com isso.
native_language_example: I have to say something: I don’t agree with that.

additional_notes: Used after comparative words like "mais" (more), "menos" (less), "melhor" (better), "pior" (worse), "maior" (bigger/older), and "menor" (smaller/younger): "mais/menos … do que" = "more/less … than". It’s a contraction of "de" + "o que" (literally “of what/that which”), but in modern Portuguese it functions like "than" in comparisons.
target_language_example: Ela fala mais devagar do que eu.
native_language_example: She speaks more slowly than I do.

additional_notes: Used after comparative words like mais/menos/melhor/pior to compare someone or something with yourself. It’s the same idea as English “than I/me.” Often appears as “mais … do que eu” (more … than me) or “melhor … do que eu” (better … than me).
target_language_example: Ela fala inglês melhor do que eu.
native_language_example: She speaks English better than me.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "o" = "do". Used to link something to a specific accident (e.g., "a cena do acidente" = "the scene of the accident"), or after certain verbs to mean "about the accident" (e.g., "me contou do acidente" = "told me about the accident").
target_language_example: Ainda não sabemos a causa do acidente.
native_language_example: We still don't know the cause of the accident.

meaning: “of the lunch” / “before lunch” (in phrases like “antes do almoço”).
additional_notes: “Do” is the contraction of “de + o” (“of/from the”). “Almoço” means “lunch.” You’ll very often see it after time expressions like “antes do almoço” (before lunch) or “depois do almoço” (after lunch).
target_language_example: Vamos conversar depois do almoço.
native_language_example: Let’s talk after lunch.

meaning: “of the year” (also used in expressions like “this time of year”).
additional_notes: It’s the contraction of “de + o” → “do”, so it literally means “of the year.” Common in superlatives and descriptions (e.g., “a estação mais quente do ano” = “the hottest season of the year”) and in time expressions like “nesta altura do ano” = “at this time of year.”
target_language_example: Dezembro é uma das épocas mais movimentadas do ano.
native_language_example: December is one of the busiest times of the year.

meaning: “of the car,” “from/out of the car,” or “about the car,” depending on context.
additional_notes: It’s the contraction of **de + o** (“of/from/about” + “the”) → **do**. Common uses: **pneu do carro** (“the car’s tire”), **controle do carro** (“control of the car”), **sair do carro** (“to get out of the car,” literally “leave from the car”), and **reclamar do carro** (“to complain about the car”).
target_language_example: Tira as compras do carro, por favor.
native_language_example: Take the groceries out of the car, please.

meaning: 'of the day when' (used to introduce the event that happened on that day).
additional_notes: Used when you mention a specific day and then add a clause explaining what happened on that day. It often follows verbs like lembrar (to remember): "(Eu) lembro/me lembro do dia em que...". The full structure is "de + o dia" → "do dia" + "em que" (when/that).
target_language_example: Nunca vou me esquecer do dia em que a gente se mudou para esta cidade.
native_language_example: I’ll never forget the day when we moved to this city.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say something/someone is from, in, or related to high school: "estudantes do ensino médio" (high school students), "time ... do ensino médio" (high school team). It’s the contraction of "de + o" ("do") + "ensino médio". In Brazil, "ensino médio" is the stage after "ensino fundamental" (roughly grades 10–12).
target_language_example: Ela é professora do ensino médio.
native_language_example: She is a high school teacher.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de + o" → "do", used before a masculine singular noun. With verbs like "gostar" (to like) and "achar" (to think/find), "do filme" means "the movie" in the sense of "about the movie" (your opinion of it).
target_language_example: O que você achou do filme?
native_language_example: What did you think of the movie?

additional_notes: Used to say the direction of a translation (source language → target language). Often appears with verbs like "traduzir" (to translate): "traduzir X do francês para o inglês".
target_language_example: Você pode traduzir este e-mail do francês para o inglês?
native_language_example: Can you translate this email from French into English?

meaning: from the bottom of my heart; sincerely, deeply.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize strong, genuine feelings (often love or gratitude, but it can also intensify negative feelings like hate). It commonly follows verbs like "amar" (to love), "agradecer" (to thank), "sentir" (to feel), and "odiar" (to hate). The literal parts are: "do" (from the), "fundo" (bottom/depth), "do meu" (of my), "coração" (heart).
target_language_example: Obrigado por tudo, do fundo do meu coração.
native_language_example: Thank you for everything, from the bottom of my heart.

meaning: "of the dinner" / "for dinner time" (refers to dinner as an event/time).
additional_notes: "Do" = "de" + "o" and is used before a masculine singular noun like "jantar". Very common in the expression "(estar/ser) hora do jantar" = "(it’s) dinner time". "Jantar" can mean both "dinner" and "to have dinner" depending on context, but in "do jantar" it’s the noun "dinner".
target_language_example: Vamos conversar depois do jantar.
native_language_example: Let’s talk after dinner.

meaning: 'the way (that)' / 'how' (something is done or how someone is).
additional_notes: Used to describe manner or style: how someone does something or how something should be done. Often follows verbs like gostar de (to like), amar (to love), fazer (to do), and should/ought expressions: do jeito que deveria (“the way it should”). It can introduce a clause: do jeito que + subject + verb.
target_language_example: Quero que você faça isso do jeito que eu expliquei.
native_language_example: I want you to do it the way I explained.

meaning: (right) next to; on someone’s side (supporting them).
additional_notes: Common in two patterns: (1) location: “do lado de + person/place” = “next to/beside” (Tem um jardim do lado de sua casa.). (2) support/opinion: “ficar/estar do lado de alguém” = “to side with someone” (Você está do lado de quem?). Can also appear with directions: “do lado esquerdo/direito” = “on the left/right side”.
target_language_example: Ela mora do lado do supermercado.
native_language_example: She lives next to the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is outdoors or not inside a building/room. Often used with verbs like esperar (to wait), assistir (to watch), ficar/estar (to be), and trabalhar (to work).
target_language_example: Vamos esperar do lado de fora.
native_language_example: Let’s wait outside.

additional_notes: Used to indicate position/location on the right, or to say you should stay/drive/park on the right side of something (e.g., the road, a bed, a person). Often followed by “de/da/do” to specify what it’s the right side of: “do lado direito da estrada” = “on the right side of the road.”
target_language_example: O banheiro fica do lado direito da recepção.
native_language_example: The bathroom is on the right side of the reception desk.

meaning: "of the sea" / "from the sea" (contraction of "de + o mar").
additional_notes: Used to link something to the sea (origin, type, location, etc.). It’s the contraction of "de" + "o" + "mar". Common in phrases like "água do mar" (sea water), "ondas do mar" (sea waves), "perto do mar" (near the sea), and "no fundo do mar" (at the bottom of the sea).
target_language_example: O som do mar me acalma.
native_language_example: The sound of the sea calms me.

meaning: the same way; just the same.
additional_notes: Used to say something is done or happens in an identical or very similar way. Often appears with comparisons: "do mesmo jeito que..." (the same way as...). It can also mean "anyway / regardless" in phrases like "...do mesmo jeito" (I’ll do it/it’ll happen just the same).
target_language_example: A gente pode ir a pé ou de ônibus; vamos chegar lá do mesmo jeito.
native_language_example: We can go on foot or by bus; we’ll get there either way.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de + o + meu". It’s used before a masculine singular noun: "do meu chefe" (of my boss), "do meu braço" (from my arm). The exact meaning depends on context: possession/association ("o discurso do meu amigo" = my friend's speech / the speech of my friend) or origin/separation ("tirou do meu bolso" = took it from my pocket). It can also appear inside set expressions like "Larga do meu pé!" (informal: leave me alone / get off my back).
target_language_example: Você pegou isso do meu prato?
native_language_example: Did you take that from my plate?

meaning: “of my car” / “from my car” (also “in/on/under my car,” depending on context).
additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "o" (= "do"), followed by "meu" (my) + "carro" (car). Portuguese uses "de" in many place/possession expressions, so "do meu carro" can mean possession (something belonging to your car: "a bateria do meu carro"), origin (taken from your car), or location when combined with another word: "na mala do meu carro" (in the trunk of my car), "debaixo do banco do meu carro" (under the seat of my car).
target_language_example: Esqueci a carteira no porta-luvas do meu carro.
native_language_example: I forgot my wallet in my car’s glove compartment.

additional_notes: “Do” is the contraction of “de + o” and often means “of” (possession/relationship: “a casa do meu pai” = “my father’s house”) or “from” (origin/source: “ganhei isso do meu pai” = “I got this from my father”). The exact meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Peguei o carro do meu pai para ir ao trabalho.
native_language_example: I took my father’s car to go to work.

meaning: 'from my room' or 'of my room' (my room’s).
additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "o" = "do". With "quarto" it can mean: (1) origin/location: "from my room" (e.g., hearing something do meu quarto), or (2) possession/identification: "the number of my room" (número do meu quarto). Often used in commands like "Sai do meu quarto!" = "Get out of my room!"
target_language_example: Não mexa nas coisas do meu quarto.
native_language_example: Don’t touch the things in my room.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "o" + "nosso". Used to show belonging or association with "our" something masculine singular (e.g., "do nosso clube" = "of our club"). It changes with gender/number: "da nossa" (fem. sing.), "dos nossos" (masc. plural), "das nossas" (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Ele é do nosso time.
native_language_example: He is on our team.

additional_notes: "Do" = "de" + "o" (“of/from the”), and "nosso" means “our” (masculine singular to match "time"). Used to say someone belongs to your group/team (sports team, work team, project group).
target_language_example: Precisamos de mais alguém do nosso time para ajudar com isso.
native_language_example: We need someone else from our team to help with this.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something located opposite or across from something else. Very common with a reference point introduced by "de" (e.g., do outro lado do rio/da rua) or in phrases like "do outro lado da mesa" (across the table).
target_language_example: A farmácia fica do outro lado da rua.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is on the other side of the street.

meaning: across the street (on the other side of the street).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located on the opposite side of the street from where you are (often implying it’s nearby). Common with verbs like morar (to live) and ficar/estar (to be located). You can add bem for emphasis: bem do outro lado da rua = right across the street.
target_language_example: A farmácia fica bem do outro lado da rua.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is right across the street.

meaning: 'of the other' / 'the other person's' (also 'others' depending on context).
additional_notes: Contraction of **de + o** = **do**. Used to refer to another person/thing: **cuidar do outro** = “to care for others / for the other person.” Changes with gender/number: **da outra**, **dos outros**, **das outras**. Common in patterns like **um atrás do outro** (“one after the other”) and **um do lado do outro** (“next to each other”).
target_language_example: Ajudar é pensar no bem do outro.
native_language_example: Helping is thinking about the other person's well-being.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "o" + "país". Most often means "of the country" (e.g., "a capital do país" = "the capital of the country"). It can also mean "from the country" depending on the verb/context (e.g., "fora do país" = "outside the country").
target_language_example: O presidente do país falou na televisão.
native_language_example: The country's president spoke on TV.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like saber, lembrar-se, falar, ter ideia to refer back to an event. It’s the contraction de + o (“do”) + que aconteceu (“what happened”), so it often translates as “about what happened” or “of what happened,” depending on the verb: falar do que aconteceu (talk about what happened), lembrar-se do que aconteceu (remember what happened), não ter ideia do que aconteceu (have no idea what happened).
target_language_example: Ela ainda está chateada por causa do que aconteceu ontem.
native_language_example: She’s still upset because of what happened yesterday.

meaning: “what you …” / “what are you … about?” (literally “of what you …”).
additional_notes: Commonly used after verbs that take the preposition **de** (e.g., **falar de** = talk about, **gostar de** = like, **rir de** = laugh at, **ter medo de** = be afraid of). **do** is a contraction of **de + o**, so **do que** = **de + o que** (“of/about what”). It can introduce (1) a question: **Do que você estava falando?** (“What were you talking about?”) and (2) a relative clause: **Não entendi nada do que você falou.** (“I didn’t understand anything you said.”).
target_language_example: Eu já te contei do que você precisa para a viagem.
native_language_example: I already told you what you need for the trip.

additional_notes: Used after comparative words like "mais" (more), "menos" (less), "melhor" (better), "pior" (worse), "maior" (bigger/older), and "menor" (smaller/younger): "mais/menos … do que" = "more/less … than". It’s a contraction of "de" + "o que" (literally “of what/that which”), but in modern Portuguese it functions like "than" in comparisons.
target_language_example: Ela fala mais devagar do que eu.
native_language_example: She speaks more slowly than I do.

meaning: "than the" (used after a comparison with mais/menos).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons to introduce the second item being compared. "Do que" means "than"; "a" is the feminine singular definite article "the" (used before feminine nouns like "a riqueza", "a sua mãe"). It can also appear as "do que o" (masculine), "do que os/as" (plural), or just "do que" if no article is needed.
target_language_example: Este livro é mais interessante do que a revista.
native_language_example: This book is more interesting than the magazine.

additional_notes: Used to compare preferences or quantities, especially with verbs that require the preposition “de” (like gostar de). Structure: “mais/menos + de + X + do que + de + Y”. “do que” = “than/than what”. The extra “de” before the second item is there because the verb still needs “de”. It may change with gender/number: “do que do” (de + o), “do que da” (de + a), “do que dos/das” (de + os/as).
target_language_example: Eu preciso mais de ajuda do que de tempo.
native_language_example: I need help more than time.

additional_notes: Used after comparative words like mais/menos/melhor/pior to compare someone or something with yourself. It’s the same idea as English “than I/me.” Often appears as “mais … do que eu” (more … than me) or “melhor … do que eu” (better … than me).
target_language_example: Ela fala inglês melhor do que eu.
native_language_example: She speaks English better than me.

additional_notes: Used after comparatives with mais/menos/melhor/pior/etc. to compare a reality with your expectation: “more/less/better/worse … than I expected.” It’s very common in the pattern “(um pouco/muito) mais/menos … do que eu esperava.”
target_language_example: O voo foi bem mais longo do que eu esperava.
native_language_example: The flight was much longer than I expected.

additional_notes: Used after a comparison (usually with mais/menos: “more/less”) to say reality is different from your expectation: “more/less … than I thought.” Often follows adjectives (mais caro do que eu pensava) or time/quantity expressions (mais tempo do que eu pensava).
target_language_example: A viagem foi mais longa do que eu pensava.
native_language_example: The trip was longer than I thought.

additional_notes: Used after comparatives like "mais" (more) or "menos" (less) to compare something to a masculine singular noun: "mais ... do que o + noun". It’s the contraction of "de" + "o" (= "do") plus "que". For feminine singular, you’ll often see "do que a"; for plurals, "do que os/as".
target_language_example: Este café é mais forte do que o chá.
native_language_example: This coffee is stronger than tea.

meaning: “than the” (comparing with a plural masculine group/thing).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons with "mais/menos ... do que". "do que" = "than"; "os" is the plural masculine "the" (also used for mixed groups). It often stands in for an implied noun: "do que os seus" = "than yours" (your ones).
target_language_example: Este restaurante é mais caro do que os outros.
native_language_example: This restaurant is more expensive than the others.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (melhor, pior, mais/menos, etc.) to say someone/something is greater or better than every other person/thing in a group: "melhor do que qualquer outro" = "better than any other." You’ll also see it with people: "do que qualquer um/qualquer pessoa" = "than anyone/any person," and with relative clauses: "do que qualquer pessoa que eu conheça" = "than anyone I know."
target_language_example: Ela é mais organizada do que qualquer outra pessoa da equipe.
native_language_example: She is more organized than anyone else on the team.

meaning: “what you …” / “what are you … about?” (literally “of what you …”).
additional_notes: Commonly used after verbs that take the preposition **de** (e.g., **falar de** = talk about, **gostar de** = like, **rir de** = laugh at, **ter medo de** = be afraid of). **do** is a contraction of **de + o**, so **do que** = **de + o que** (“of/about what”). It can introduce (1) a question: **Do que você estava falando?** (“What were you talking about?”) and (2) a relative clause: **Não entendi nada do que você falou.** (“I didn’t understand anything you said.”).
target_language_example: Eu já te contei do que você precisa para a viagem.
native_language_example: I already told you what you need for the trip.

additional_notes: Used after a comparison (often with "mais" or "menos") to say something is more/less true than the listener expects: "mais … do que você pensa" = "more … than you think." It can also appear as "do que você imagina" (same idea).
target_language_example: Isso é mais importante do que você pensa.
native_language_example: This is more important than you think.

meaning: “of the river” / “from the river” (de + o rio).
additional_notes: “Do” is the contraction of **de + o** (“of/from the”). So **do rio** literally means “of/from the river” and is very common in location phrases like **ao longo do rio** (along the river), **na beira do rio** (on the riverbank), **na margem do rio** (on the river’s edge), and **do lado (leste/oeste) do rio** (on the east/west side of the river).
target_language_example: O hotel fica do outro lado do rio.
native_language_example: The hotel is on the other side of the river.

additional_notes: Contraction of **de + o seu**. Used before a **masculine singular** noun (e.g., *carro, tempo*): *do seu carro*, *do seu tempo*. With **seu/sua**, this usually refers to the person you’re speaking to (often with **você**), but it can also mean “his/her/their” depending on context; use **dele/dela** if you need to be very clear.
target_language_example: Posso pegar uma cópia do seu documento?
native_language_example: Can I take a copy of your document?

meaning: “of your car” (sometimes “from your car,” depending on the verb).
additional_notes: This is the contraction of **de + o** → **do**, plus **seu carro** (“your car”). It’s used to show possession or relation: **as chaves do seu carro** = “the keys of your car / your car keys.” With some verbs, **de** can mean “from,” so context matters (e.g., “take [something] from your car”).
target_language_example: Tire tudo do seu carro antes de vender.
native_language_example: Take everything out of your car before selling it.

additional_notes: Used to show possession or relationship with “pai” (father): “do” = “de” (of/from) + “o” (the), and “seu” = “your” (also can mean “his/her/their” depending on context). Common in phrases like “a jaqueta do seu pai” (your father’s jacket) and “a idade do seu pai” (your father’s age).
target_language_example: Eu me lembro do seu pai quando ouço essa música.
native_language_example: I remember your father when I hear that song.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something belonging to (or related to) someone’s work/job. It’s made of **de + o = do** (“of the”) + **seu** (“your/his/her”) + **trabalho** (“work/job”). In Portuguese, **seu/sua** can sometimes be ambiguous (your vs. his/her), so context matters; if you need to be extra clear for “your,” you can also hear **do trabalho dele/dela** (of his/her work) in other contexts.
target_language_example: O que você mais gosta do seu trabalho?
native_language_example: What do you like most about your job?

meaning: “of the sofa” or “from the sofa” (de + o).
additional_notes: Do is the contraction of de + o (“of/from the”). It commonly appears inside location phrases like embaixo do sofá (“under the sofa”) and atrás do sofá (“behind the sofa”), and with verbs like sair do sofá (“get off the sofa / leave the sofa”).
target_language_example: Tire as moedas debaixo do sofá.
native_language_example: Take the coins from under the sofa.

meaning: “of the sun” / “from the sun” (and sometimes just “the sun”).
additional_notes: “Do” = “de + o” and it commonly links something to the sun: origin (“luz do sol” = sunlight), relationship (“planetas… do sol” = planets of the sun/solar system), or proximity (“mais próximo do sol” = closest to the sun). With verbs like “gostar de”, “do sol” can mean “the sun” as the object (“Gosto do sol.”).
target_language_example: A energia do sol é muito forte hoje.
native_language_example: The sun’s energy is very strong today.

meaning: 'from the roof' / 'off the roof' (from a roof).
additional_notes: Contraction of "de + o" → "do". Used after verbs that express coming/falling/jumping from somewhere (e.g., "cair do telhado", "pular do telhado"). Not the same as "no telhado" (= on the roof) or "no telhado" with "em cima do telhado" (= up on the roof).
target_language_example: O gato caiu do telhado e eu corri para ajudar.
native_language_example: The cat fell off the roof and I ran to help.

meaning: 'of the time' / 'about the time' (sometimes: 'about the weather').
additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "o" (= "of/from/about the"). Used with the masculine singular noun "tempo". Common in fixed phrases about time (e.g., "a roda do tempo" = "the wheel of time") and in time comparisons like "um terço do tempo" ("a third of the time"). With verbs like "falar"/"reclamar", "do tempo" often means talking/complaining about the weather.
target_language_example: Não tenho muito do tempo hoje, mas posso te ajudar amanhã.
native_language_example: I don’t have much time today, but I can help you tomorrow.

meaning: “from work” / “from the job/workplace”; sometimes “of the work” depending on context.
additional_notes: Contraction of "de + o" → "do". Most often used with verbs of leaving/coming back to indicate origin: "sair do trabalho" (leave work), "voltar do trabalho" (come back from work). It can also mean "of the work" in phrases like "cansado do trabalho duro" (tired of hard work) or "gosta do trabalho dele" (likes his work).
target_language_example: Chego do trabalho às seis e meia.
native_language_example: I get home from work at six thirty.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de + o" → "do". Used with verbs like "descer" (to get off) or "ser expulso" (to be kicked out) to show movement away from the bus or leaving it.
target_language_example: Ele desceu do ônibus na próxima parada.
native_language_example: He got off the bus at the next stop.

additional_notes: Used to talk about age ("aos dois anos" = "at age two"), time spans ("por dois anos" = "for two years"), time in the future ("daqui a dois anos" = "in two years"), and comparisons in age ("dois anos mais velha" = "two years older"; also "dois anos a mais").
target_language_example: Fiquei no Brasil por dois anos.
native_language_example: I stayed in Brazil for two years.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened two years before now (or before the time being talked about). It often goes at the beginning or end of the sentence: “Dois anos atrás, ...” / “... dois anos atrás.” You can swap the number: “um ano atrás”, “três anos atrás”, etc.
target_language_example: Nós nos mudamos para cá dois anos atrás.
native_language_example: We moved here two years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say there are exactly two cars. Often appears after verbs like “ter” (to have) or with an article: “os dois carros” = “the two cars.”
target_language_example: Eu só tenho dois carros, não três.
native_language_example: I only have two cars, not three.

additional_notes: Used to say an amount of time (duration) or a time difference (e.g., late/early by two days). You can place it after a verb or after the time word you’re describing (e.g., “dois dias atrasado” = “two days late”).
target_language_example: Vamos ficar aqui por dois dias.
native_language_example: We’re going to stay here for two days.

additional_notes: Literally “two sons” (filho = son; plural filhos). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, “filhos” is also often used generically to mean “children” when the gender isn’t important or is mixed. If you want to be explicitly gender-neutral you can say “dois filhos/duas filhas” as appropriate, or “duas crianças” (“two kids/children”).
target_language_example: Nós temos dois filhos e moramos em São Paulo.
native_language_example: We have two children and we live in São Paulo.

additional_notes:
Used to express a duration or time reference of two months. Common with:
- "durante/por dois meses" = for two months (length of time)
- "há dois meses" = two months ago
- "faz/já faz dois meses" = it’s been two months (since something happened)
Also used in contexts like pregnancy to indicate how far along someone is: "grávida de dois meses" (two months pregnant).
target_language_example: Estou trabalhando aqui há dois meses.
native_language_example: I’ve been working here for two months.

additional_notes: Used in math to state equality: “X é igual a Y” = “X equals Y / is equal to Y”. Here, “dois” is the subject (the left side) and you typically say the whole expression, e.g. “Cinco vezes dois é igual a dez.” Also common in everyday comparisons: “Isso é igual a aquilo” (“That’s the same as that”).
target_language_example: Dois é igual a um mais um.
native_language_example: Two equals one plus one.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the upcoming Sunday relative to today. Often used without a preposition: "Domingo que vem...". You can also say "no domingo que vem" (on next Sunday). Similar pattern: "semana que vem" (next week), "mês que vem" (next month).
target_language_example: No domingo que vem, a gente pode almoçar juntos.
native_language_example: Next Sunday, we can have lunch together.

additional_notes: Common pattern: **estar com dor de + [body part]** (“to have pain in…”). The body part usually comes without an article: **dor de cabeça** (headache), **dor de barriga** (stomachache), **dor de garganta** (sore throat), **dor de dente(s)** (toothache), **dor de ouvido** (earache). You can also say **ter dor de + ...**.
target_language_example: Estou com dor de cabeça desde ontem.
native_language_example: I’ve had a headache since yesterday.

additional_notes: Commonly used with the verb/structure “estar com” to mean you currently have a toothache: “Estou com dor de dente.” You can add intensity with adjectives like “forte” (strong) or “uma bela” (a nasty/big, often ironic way to say it’s bad).
target_language_example: Estou com dor de dente desde ontem.
native_language_example: I’ve had a toothache since yesterday.

additional_notes: A common way to say you have pain in your stomach. Often used with "estar com" (temporary condition) or "ter" (to have): "Estou com dor de estômago" / "Tenho dor de estômago".
target_language_example: Acho que comi demais e estou com dor de estômago.
native_language_example: I think I ate too much and I have a stomachache.

meaning: back pain; pain in the back.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "estar com" or "ter" to say someone has back pain. Often appears as "com dor nas costas" (without an article) or "com uma dor nas costas" (emphasizing one particular pain/episode).
target_language_example: Depois de carregar as caixas, fiquei com dor nas costas.
native_language_example: After carrying the boxes, I ended up with back pain.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who is in a very deep sleep and hard to wake up. It’s built from the gerund/continuous form "dormindo" (sleeping) + the adverb "profundamente" (deeply), often used with "estar": "está dormindo profundamente".
target_language_example: Fala baixo: ele está dormindo profundamente.
native_language_example: Speak quietly: he’s fast asleep.

meaning: to go to sleep before midnight.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the time you fall asleep (not just being in bed). Often appears with verbs like ir (vou/fui dormir) and precisar (preciso dormir). You can negate it with nunca/não: “Nunca vou dormir antes da meia-noite.”
target_language_example: Hoje vou tentar dormir antes da meia-noite.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to try to go to sleep before midnight.

meaning: to sleep a little / to get some sleep.
additional_notes: Used to say you need (or could use) some rest, often because you’re tired. It can mean literally sleeping for a short time (a nap) or more generally “get some sleep.” In Brazil, it’s common to say “precisar dormir um pouco”; in Portugal you may also hear “precisar de dormir um pouco.”
target_language_example: Estou muito cansado(a); vou dormir um pouco.
native_language_example: I’m very tired; I’m going to get some sleep.

meaning: 'of the Dead Poets' (as in the title/name “Sociedade dos Poetas Mortos” = “Dead Poets Society”).
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the proper name “Sociedade dos Poetas Mortos” (a reference to the film/book title “Dead Poets Society”). Grammatically, it’s a contraction: “de + os” → “dos” (“of the”), followed by “poetas mortos” (“dead poets”).
target_language_example: Eles estão falando sobre a Sociedade dos Poetas Mortos na aula.
native_language_example: They’re talking about Dead Poets Society in class.

additional_notes: Used to compare or choose between two people/things: superlatives like "o mais... dos dois" (the ...-est of the two), and also with "nenhum dos dois" (neither of the two). It’s the contraction of "de + os" ("dos") + "dois".
target_language_example: Eu prefiro este dos dois.
native_language_example: I prefer this one out of the two.

additional_notes: Contraction of **de + os** (“of/from” + “the”): **dos**. Used to show possession or association (“the lives of men”), or to mean humans/mankind in general (“the world of men”). In comparisons, it can mean “one of the (men)” (e.g., *um dos homens mais inteligentes* = “one of the smartest men”).
target_language_example: A história dos homens é cheia de mudanças.
native_language_example: The history of mankind is full of changes.

additional_notes: Used after "um/uma" to mean someone/something belongs to the group of the best: "um dos melhores" = "one of the best (ones)". It’s the contraction of "de + os" ("dos") + "melhores" (comparative plural of "bom" = good). For feminine nouns, use "uma das melhores".
target_language_example: Este restaurante é um dos melhores da cidade.
native_language_example: This restaurant is one of the best in the city.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de + os meus". Used to link something to "my" masculine plural nouns (e.g., "meus móveis", "meus colegas"). It often appears after verbs/expressions that take "de" like "precisar de" (to need), "separar-se de" (to get rid of / separate from), or phrases like "em nome de" (on behalf of).
target_language_example: Estou com saudade dos meus amigos.
native_language_example: I miss my friends.

additional_notes: "Dos" is a contraction of "de + os" ("of/from + the"). Use "dos meus amigos" to say something is part of your friends ("some of my friends" = "alguns dos meus amigos"), belongs to them/comes from them ("favores dos meus amigos" = "favors from my friends"), or to talk about something related to them ("falar dos meus amigos" = "talk about my friends").
target_language_example: Vou falar dos meus amigos para você mais tarde.
native_language_example: I’ll talk about my friends to you later.

additional_notes: Contraction of **de + os** → **dos** (“of the” / “from the”) + **meus filhos** (“my children”). Used to show possession or relation: **a mãe dos meus filhos** (“the mother of my children”), **a língua materna dos meus filhos** (“my children’s mother tongue”), **longe dos meus filhos** (“far from my children”).
target_language_example: Preciso falar com a professora dos meus filhos.
native_language_example: I need to talk to my children’s teacher.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say it’s your ideal version of that thing (a dream place, dream job, dream girl/guy, etc.). Very common in romantic contexts: “a garota/o garoto dos meus sonhos” = “the girl/guy of my dreams.” Literally “from the my dreams” (de + os).
target_language_example: Este é o emprego dos meus sonhos.
native_language_example: This is the job of my dreams.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "os" + "nossos". Used to talk about something that belongs to you/your group: "alguns dos nossos colegas" = "some of our colleagues". It can also stand alone when the noun is understood: "um dos nossos" = "one of ours". It agrees with gender/number: "das nossas" (feminine plural), "do nosso" (masc. singular), "da nossa" (fem. singular).
target_language_example: Alguns dos nossos amigos não podem vir hoje.
native_language_example: Some of our friends can’t come today.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de + os" → "dos". Used to show possession or relation: "a vida dos outros" = “other people’s lives,” "os erros dos outros" = “other people’s mistakes.” It can also appear with verbs that take "de" to mean “(different) from others”: "diferente dos outros" = “different from the others.”
target_language_example: Não gosto de falar dos outros.
native_language_example: I don’t like talking about other people.

meaning: “of your” / “of his/her/its” / “of their” (plural masculine), used before a plural noun.
additional_notes: "Dos" = "de" + "os" (“of the”). "Seus" is the possessive (your/his/her/their) agreeing with a masculine plural noun (e.g., pecados, trabalhos, cachorros). So "dos seus + noun" means “of your/his/her/their + noun.” Note: "seu(s)/sua(s)" can be ambiguous (your vs his/her/their); context usually clarifies.
target_language_example: Preciso de alguns dos seus documentos para fazer o cadastro.
native_language_example: I need some of your documents to register you.

additional_notes: Contraction of de + os: dos. Use it to mean belonging to your parents (e.g., a casa dos seus pais = your parents’ house) or referring to something involving them (depender dos seus pais = depend on your parents; sentir falta dos seus pais = miss your parents). You can swap in their/your/his/her by changing seus: dos meus pais (my), dos pais dele (his), dos pais dela (her).
target_language_example: Vou jantar na casa dos seus pais amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to have dinner at your parents’ house tomorrow.

meaning: two things at the same time; multitasking.
additional_notes: Used to say someone does two activities simultaneously. Often appears with verbs like "fazer" (to do) or "conseguir" (to manage to/can): "fazer duas coisas ao mesmo tempo". You can also swap in another number or item: "três coisas ao mesmo tempo", "duas tarefas ao mesmo tempo".
target_language_example: Não consigo fazer duas coisas ao mesmo tempo.
native_language_example: I can't do two things at the same time.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has two female children. Agreement matters: "duas" is feminine plural to match "filhas" (daughter).
