Compare: "duas filhas" (two daughters) vs. "dois filhos" (two sons) and "dois filhos" can also mean "two children" in general (mixed gender). Often appears with "ter": "Ele tem duas filhas."
target_language_example: Minha irmã tem duas filhas e um filho.
native_language_example: My sister has two daughters and one son.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (por duas horas = for two hours), how long something took (demorou duas horas para... = it took two hours to...), and time relative to now or another event (duas horas depois = two hours later; duas horas atrás = two hours ago).
target_language_example: A reunião vai durar duas horas.
native_language_example: The meeting will last two hours.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has exactly two sisters. "irmãs" is the plural of "irmã" (sister), and "duas" agrees with the feminine noun (you’d say "dois irmãos" for "two brothers"). In "(as) duas irmãs", it means "the two sisters" (a specific pair).
target_language_example: Ela tem duas irmãs e um irmão.
native_language_example: She has two sisters and one brother.

duas ou três vezes por semana

target_language_multi_word_term: duas ou três vezes por semana
meaning: two or three times a week.
additional_notes: Used to express frequency per week. It’s approximate: you’re saying it happens around 2–3 times weekly, not an exact fixed schedule. Common with routine activities (work out, go somewhere, eat out, etc.).
target_language_example: Eu estudo português duas ou três vezes por semana.
native_language_example: I study Portuguese two or three times a week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a 2-week length of time or a point in time relative to now. Common patterns: "daqui a duas semanas" = "in two weeks" (from now); "faz duas semanas" = "two weeks ago" / "it’s been two weeks"; "duas semanas atrás" = "two weeks ago." Note: "duas" (feminine) agrees with "semanas" (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Vou ficar em Portugal por duas semanas.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay in Portugal for two weeks.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens two times (Eu fui duas vezes.) or to compare quantities with "duas vezes mais" = "twice as ..." (duas vezes mais velho/forte/comprido). Often placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Eu li este livro duas vezes.
native_language_example: I read this book twice.

additional_notes: Used to describe how often something happens in a daily routine. It’s common in health and schedule contexts (e.g., taking medicine, brushing teeth). You can swap the number: “uma vez ao dia” (once a day), “três vezes ao dia” (three times a day).
target_language_example: Tome este remédio duas vezes ao dia.
native_language_example: Take this medicine twice a day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency. It’s usually followed by a time period like dia (day), semana (week), mês (month), ano (year): “duas vezes por ano” = “twice a year.” You can also say “duas vezes ao ano,” which is very common with time periods.
target_language_example: Eu faço exercício duas vezes por semana.
native_language_example: I work out twice a week.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens two times each day. Common in routines, schedules, and instructions (e.g., medicine, hygiene). Often follows the verb: "Tom alimenta o cachorro duas vezes por dia."
target_language_example: Tomo este remédio duas vezes por dia.
native_language_example: I take this medicine twice a day.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens in a typical week. The order is: number + "vezes" (times) + "por" (per) + time period ("semana" = week). You can swap the number: "uma vez por semana" (once a week), "três vezes por semana" (three times a week).
target_language_example: Eu vou à academia duas vezes por semana.
native_language_example: I go to the gym twice a week.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens within a period of time or throughout an event. It’s "durante" + the feminine singular article "a"; with masculine nouns it’s "durante o" (e.g., durante o jantar). Often followed by time periods/events: durante a faculdade, durante a refeição, durante a recessão, durante a aula.
target_language_example: Eu li muito durante a viagem.
native_language_example: I read a lot during the trip.

additional_notes: Used to place an event or situation in the time period when a war was happening. Often appears after the main verb or at the end of the sentence. You can swap in another time period: "durante a noite" (during the night), "durante o dia" (during the day).
target_language_example: Muitas famílias se mudaram durante a guerra.
native_language_example: Many families moved during the war.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened at some point in the nighttime period (not necessarily all night). Common in weather updates and describing things that occurred while people were sleeping. Often equivalent to “overnight” in English.
target_language_example: A temperatura caiu durante a noite.
native_language_example: The temperature dropped overnight.

meaning: during the vacation(s) / during the holidays.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens in the time period when you’re on vacation or when a school/work break is happening. "Férias" is often plural in Portuguese even when English would say "vacation." You can also specify which break: "durante as férias de primavera" (during spring break).
target_language_example: Durante as férias, eu gosto de viajar e descansar.
native_language_example: During vacation, I like to travel and rest.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens within the time period of summer break (often school holidays). "Durante" = "during" + "as férias" = "the holidays/vacation" + "de verão" = "of summer". You can swap in other times: "durante as férias de inverno" (during winter break).
target_language_example: Vou descansar durante as férias de verão.
native_language_example: I’m going to rest during the summer vacation.

additional_notes: Used to say something lasts or happens over a long period. Common with verbs like ficar (to stay), pensar (to think), esperar (to wait), and with negatives (e.g., Não… durante muito tempo = “not for a long time”).
target_language_example: Esperei durante muito tempo, mas ele não apareceu.
native_language_example: I waited for a long time, but he didn’t show up.

meaning: “during the” (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens within a period of time. It’s “durante” + the definite article “o” (= “the” for masculine singular nouns): durante o inverno (during the winter), durante o trabalho (during work). With other nouns, the article changes: durante a noite (during the night), durante os anos (during the years), durante as férias (during the vacation).
target_language_example: Vou descansar durante o fim de semana.
native_language_example: I’m going to rest during the weekend.

meaning: during the day; in the daytime.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens at some point within the daytime period (not at night). Common with routines or time-limited actions: trabalhar/dormir/cuidar de alguém durante o dia.
target_language_example: Eu estudo durante o dia e trabalho à noite.
native_language_example: I study during the day and work at night.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens within the summer period. Often comes at the beginning of a sentence (“Durante o verão, …”) or after the verb (“… durante o verão”).
target_language_example: Durante o verão, a cidade fica muito cheia de turistas.
native_language_example: During the summer, the city gets very crowded with tourists.

additional_notes: Used to express doubt about a statement. It’s typically followed by a clause with a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., “Duvido que ele esteja…”, “Duvido que ele vá…”). You can also use it in other persons: “Duvidamos que…” (we doubt that), “Você duvida que…?” (Do you doubt that…?).
target_language_example: Duvido que ela chegue a tempo.
native_language_example: I doubt that she’ll arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to express doubt about a statement or situation. It’s the start of a clause with “duvidar que…”, which typically takes the subjunctive (e.g., esteja, vá). “o” is the masculine singular definite article (“the”) and can change depending on the noun: duvido que a… / duvido que os… / duvido que as….
target_language_example: Duvido que o ônibus chegue a tempo.
native_language_example: I doubt that the bus will arrive on time.

additional_notes: Contraction of “dá” (tu imperative of dar, “to give”) + “me” (“to me”). Used to ask/order someone you address as tu to hand you something. In European Portuguese it’s common to use this with family/close people; with strangers you’d usually say “dê-me …” (formal). Often add “por favor” to be polite.
target_language_example: Dá-me a caneta, por favor.
native_language_example: Give me the pen, please.

additional_notes: Usually used as the reflexive expression **se dar bem com**: *Eu me dou bem com...*, *Você se dá bem com...*, *Ela/Ele se dá bem com...*. It means having a good relationship with someone (no conflict, friendly). In the negative: *não se dar bem com* (“not get along with”).
target_language_example: Eu me dou bem com os meus colegas de trabalho.
native_language_example: I get along with my coworkers.

additional_notes: Informal form of "dá para". Used to say something is possible: "Dá pra fazer" = "You can do it / It’s possible to do it." In questions/requests it can sound impatient or annoyed: "Dá pra parar?" = "Can you stop?" Also, "dar pra alguém" can be slang meaning "to sleep with someone" (sexual), depending on context.
target_language_example: Não dá pra sair hoje; está chovendo muito.
native_language_example: We can’t go out today; it’s raining a lot.

additional_notes: From the verb dar (“to give”) in the imperative form dê (used with você / o senhor / a senhora) + the object pronoun me (“to me”). Common in requests and commands: Dê-me + noun. In everyday speech, many people also say Me dê…, especially in Brazil.
target_language_example: Por favor, dê-me um copo de água.
native_language_example: Please give me a glass of water.

additional_notes: Formed from the formal imperative of dar (“to give”) + me (“to me”) + a (“the” feminine singular). Used to ask someone to hand you a specific object. Often said as a request; you can soften it with “por favor”. For masculine nouns, use “dê-me o” (e.g., “Dê-me o livro.”).
target_language_example: Por favor, dê-me a garrafa de água.
native_language_example: Please give me the bottle of water.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to hand you an object close to them (“that”). It’s an imperative of dar (to give): dê + me (“to me”). Common with a noun: “Dê-me essa chave.” You can soften it with “por favor.” In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, “Me dá essa…” is more informal.
target_language_example: Dê-me essa caneta, por favor.
native_language_example: Give me that pen, please.

additional_notes: "Dê" is the formal (você) imperative of "dar" (to give). "-me" means "to me" and attaches to the verb in formal commands. Used to politely ask for an object, often with "por favor". For feminine nouns, use "dê-me a" (e.g., "Dê-me a chave").
target_language_example: Por favor, dê-me o passaporte.
native_language_example: Please, give me the passport.

additional_notes: “Dê-me” is the formal command (imperative) of dar (“to give”) + “me” (“to me”). “Sua” means “your” in a formal/polite way (also used when speaking to someone as você). It must be followed by a noun: dê-me sua carteira / sua espada / sua mão. In informal speech to a friend, you’d more often hear: “Me dá a sua …” or “Dá-me a tua …” depending on region.
target_language_example: Por favor, dê-me sua identidade.
native_language_example: Please, give me your ID.

additional_notes: Imperative of **dar** (“to give”) + object pronoun **me** (“to me”) + **um** (“a/one”, masculine). Used to ask for something in a direct but polite/formal way, especially in written instructions or more formal speech. You can change **um** to **uma** (feminine) or add a noun/complement: **Dê-me um café**, **Dê-me um exemplo**, **Dê-me um copo de água**. In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often say **Me dá um…** instead.
target_language_example: Por favor, dê-me um café sem açúcar.
native_language_example: Please give me a coffee without sugar.

additional_notes: Formal (você/o senhor/a senhora) imperative of dar (“to give”) + object pronoun me (“to me”) + uma (“a/one”, feminine). Commonly followed by a feminine noun (uma dica, uma pista). Can also mean “give me one (of them)” when the noun is understood from context. In Brazilian Portuguese, the pronoun placement here (dê-me) is more formal; in everyday speech you’ll often hear me dá/ me dê.
target_language_example: Por favor, dê-me uma água.
native_language_example: Please give me a water.

meaning: “give a …” (often used like “take/have a …” in English, e.g., “take a step/break”).
additional_notes: From the verb **dar** (“to give”). **Dê** is a polite command (“give!”) or can appear in wishes/requests with the subjunctive (e.g., “May God give us…”). Very common in fixed expressions: **dê um passo** = “take a step”, **dê um tempo** = “take a break / give it some time.”
target_language_example: Por favor, dê um minuto e eu já volto.
native_language_example: Please give me a minute and I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: Polite, common way to ask someone to look at something briefly. It’s the imperative form of “dar uma olhada” (literally “to give a look”). Often followed by em/na/no/nas/nesse/nisto + the thing/place you want someone to look at: “Dê uma olhada nessa foto.”
target_language_example: Dê uma olhada no documento e me diga o que você acha.
native_language_example: Take a look at the document and tell me what you think.

additional_notes: Used when buying or counting eggs. "Uma dúzia" = 12 (a full dozen). "Meia dúzia" = 6 (half a dozen). Often appears with prices in shops (e.g., "Quanto custa a dúzia de ovos?").
target_language_example: Preciso de uma dúzia de ovos para a receita.
native_language_example: I need a dozen eggs for the recipe.

meaning: "and the" (feminine singular), or simply "and" before a feminine noun/name.
additional_notes: Used to connect two items in a sentence: "X e a Y" = "X and (the) Y". The "a" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”), used with many feminine nouns and with some female names (common in European Portuguese and also seen in Brazilian Portuguese in certain contexts).
target_language_example: O João e a Ana vão ao cinema hoje.
native_language_example: João and Ana are going to the movies today.

additional_notes: Used to connect to what happens next or the current situation. As a question ("E agora?"), it means "What now?" or "So what do we do now?" It can also introduce a new development or consequence: "...e agora" = "...and now / and now (because of that)".
target_language_example: Perdi o ônibus, e agora não sei como vou chegar a tempo.
native_language_example: I missed the bus, and now I don't know how I'm going to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to link actions in a story: first one thing happens, and then someone starts doing another action. After "começou a" you use an infinitive verb (e.g., "ler", "conversar"). The subject is understood from context; you can also say "e eu comecei a…", "e ela começou a…".
target_language_example: Ele abriu a porta e começou a explicar o problema.
native_language_example: He opened the door and started to explain the problem.

additional_notes: Used to connect actions/events in sequence. Often followed by a verb ("e depois me telefone" = "and then call me"). It can also introduce a follow-up question or comment, similar to "and then?" / "what about after that?" ("E depois?" or "E depois, ..."). With "de" it becomes "e depois de ..." = "and after ...".
target_language_example: A gente almoça e depois vai ao cinema.
native_language_example: We’ll have lunch and then go to the movies.

additional_notes: Used either (1) to prompt someone or move a conversation along, like “So…?” (“E então, o que você acha?”), or (2) to link events in sequence, like “and then/and after that” (“…e então eu vou morrer”). Often appears at the start of a question or between two clauses.
target_language_example: E então, o que vamos fazer agora?
native_language_example: So, what are we going to do now?

additional_notes: Used to join yourself to someone else: "Tom e eu" = "Tom and I". Portuguese often uses "eu" after "e" even in places where English prefers "me" (e.g., after a preposition you’d typically say "para mim", but with simple coordination you’ll often see "e eu").
target_language_example: A Ana e eu vamos amanhã.
native_language_example: Ana and I are going tomorrow.

meaning: “and I are” (used after another subject, to make “X and I are …”).
additional_notes: Used in the subject of a sentence: “(Name) e eu estamos …” = “(Name) and I are …”. The verb is plural (estamos) because it refers to two or more people. Common with names and family terms (Tom e eu; meu irmão e eu).
target_language_example: Maria e eu estamos cansados hoje.
native_language_example: Maria and I are tired today.

meaning: “and I are” (used to say you and another person are something).
additional_notes: Used after another subject: “(Name/Person) e eu somos …” = “(Name/Person) and I are …”. With “eu” (I), Portuguese uses the verb form “somos” (we are). You can also use it with “você e eu somos …” = “you and I are …”.
target_language_example: Minha irmã e eu somos brasileiras.
native_language_example: My sister and I are Brazilian.

additional_notes: Used to add that the speaker is the same as the person just mentioned (they also like/do/are the same thing). Often comes at the end of the sentence after a comma: "..., e eu também." The subject pronoun "eu" is emphasized here; in casual speech you may also hear just "eu também". With verbs, Portuguese often drops the second verb because it’s understood from context ("Ela gosta..., e eu também" = "...and I do too").
target_language_example: Ele vai ao cinema amanhã, e eu também.
native_language_example: He’s going to the movies tomorrow, and I am too.

meaning: "and I have" (as part of a plural subject: "X and I have").
additional_notes: Used when the subject is two or more people including you: "Tom e eu" = "Tom and I". In Portuguese, the verb must agree with the plural subject, so you use "temos" (we have), not "tenho" (I have). Common patterns: "[Pessoa] e eu temos ..." (something in common / the same age / the same problem).
target_language_example: Minha irmã e eu temos a mesma opinião.
native_language_example: My sister and I have the same opinion.

meaning: 'and a half' (used with time and durations).
additional_notes: Used after an hour or time to mean “:30” or “half an hour more.” Examples: “duas e meia” = 2:30; “uma hora e meia” = 1.5 hours (one hour and a half). You can also say “meia-noite e meia” = 12:30 a.m.
target_language_example: A reunião é às três e meia.
native_language_example: The meeting is at 3:30.

additional_notes: Used to ask what happened/was found/should be done next, often after someone has given some information. Very common in conversation to keep the story going (similar to English “and then what?” / “so what should I do?”). It’s usually followed by a verb: “E o que você fez?” (“And what did you do?”).
target_language_example: E o que aconteceu depois?
native_language_example: And what happened after that?

additional_notes: Used to add an additional event/result: “and broke an arm.” The subject (he/she) is usually understood from the previous sentence. In Portuguese, “o braço” (literally “the arm”) often means “his/her arm” from context; you can also say “o braço dele/dela” to be explicit.
target_language_example: Ela escorregou no banheiro e quebrou o braço.
native_language_example: She slipped in the bathroom and broke her arm.

meaning: "and your friends" / "and his friends" / "and their friends" (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to add "and [someone’s] friends" to a subject: "você e seus amigos" = "you and your friends"; "Tom e seus amigos" = "Tom and his friends." Portuguese uses "seus" for both "your" (formal) and "his/their" in many contexts, so the meaning comes from who is being talked to/about. For female friends/possessor you may see "e suas amigas" / "e suas amigas".
target_language_example: Você e seus amigos querem jogar hoje?
native_language_example: Do you and your friends want to play today?

additional_notes: Used to add another occasional/variable action or item after something already mentioned. Common in patterns like “Às vezes…, e às vezes…” or “... e às vezes ...” to show that things change from one time to another.
target_language_example: Eu trabalho em casa e às vezes vou ao escritório.
native_language_example: I work from home and sometimes I go to the office.

additional_notes: Used to call out to someone directly before a question or comment. Often sounds informal and can come across as a bit blunt depending on tone and context; you can soften it with the person’s name or “com licença”. Written with a comma after “ei” to mark direct address.
target_language_example: Ei, você pode me ajudar um minuto?
native_language_example: Hey, can you help me for a minute?

additional_notes: Used to say that a woman/girl began doing something. Pattern: (subject) + começou a + infinitive verb (andar, cantar, ficar, orar, suar). In speech you can change the subject: eu comecei a (I started to), ele começou a (he started to), a gente começou a (we started to).
target_language_example: Ela começou a estudar português ontem.
native_language_example: She started studying Portuguese yesterday.

meaning: she started to cry / she began crying.
additional_notes: Used to describe the moment someone begins crying. Structure: "ela" (she) + "começou a" (started to) + infinitive (here, "chorar" = to cry). Often appears with time/contrast words like "de repente" (suddenly), "assim que" (as soon as), and can take intensifiers like "alto" (loudly) or "de novo" (again).
target_language_example: Quando ouviu o resultado, ela começou a chorar.
native_language_example: When she heard the result, she started to cry.

meaning: “she bought a …” (feminine subject + past of “to buy” + “a/an” for a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say that “she” (ela) bought something. In Portuguese, the article changes with the gender of the thing bought: um (masculine) vs. uma (feminine). Examples: Ela comprou um frango. / Ela comprou uma cadeira. The verb is in the simple past (pretérito perfeito): comprou = “bought”.
target_language_example: Ela comprou um livro para o filho.
native_language_example: She bought a book for her son.

meaning: "she must have been" (a guess/deduction about the past).
additional_notes: Used to infer something about a past situation based on evidence or what seems likely. It’s often followed by an adjective or description (e.g., bonita, feliz, professora). You can change the subject: "ele deve ter sido" (he must have been), "eles devem ter sido" (they must have been).
target_language_example: Ela deve ter sido muito inteligente na escola.
native_language_example: She must have been very smart in school.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of dizer. Use it to report what a woman/girl said or to introduce reported speech: “Ela disse que…” (“She said that…”). With an indirect object it often translates as “told”: “Ela disse ao filho…” (“She told her son…”). You can also use it in questions about someone’s words: “do que ela disse” (“what she said”).
target_language_example: Ela disse que não podia vir hoje.
native_language_example: She said she couldn’t come today.

additional_notes: Used to report what a woman said. Very common before a full clause: "Ela disse que" + verb. In Portuguese, "que" often corresponds to English "that" and is usually required here. Tense can shift depending on timing (e.g., "ela disse que vai" = she said she is going; "ela disse que iria/voltaria" = she said she would go/come back).
target_language_example: Ela disse que não podia vir hoje.
native_language_example: She said that she couldn't come today.

additional_notes: Used to report what a woman/girl claims, states, or tells you, introducing a clause with **que** (“that”). In Portuguese you often don’t repeat the subject in the second clause (e.g., **Ela diz que seguiu as regras** is more natural than **Ela diz que ela seguiu...**).
target_language_example: Ela diz que vai chegar mais tarde.
native_language_example: She says she’s going to arrive later.

additional_notes: "Ela" means "she". "Era" is the imperfect past of "ser" (to be), used for descriptions in the past (traits, states, professions, background) and for ongoing/habitual situations in the past. Often followed by an adjective or noun (e.g., "ela era corajosa", "ela era estudante").
target_language_example: Quando eu a conheci, ela era professora.
native_language_example: When I met her, she was a teacher.

meaning: "she was a" (describing what she used to be / was at that time).
additional_notes: Used with a noun phrase after it to describe someone in the past: a profession, type of person, or description ("Ela era uma professora", "Ela era uma mentirosa"). "Era" is the imperfect past of "ser" and often implies a continuing state or a background description (not a one-time event). "Uma" is feminine singular; for masculine, use "ele era um".
target_language_example: Quando eu a conheci, ela era uma estudante de medicina.
native_language_example: When I met her, she was a medical student.

additional_notes:
Used to describe an ongoing situation in the past or background information. Often followed by: 
- an adjective/state: "ela estava triste" (she was sad)
- "a" + infinitive (common in European Portuguese): "ela estava a chorar" (she was crying)
- or a place: "ela estava em casa" (she was at home). Note: "estar" is for temporary states/locations (vs. "ser" for more permanent identity/characteristics).
target_language_example: Quando eu cheguei, ela estava em casa.
native_language_example: When I arrived, she was at home.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" to talk about where she is or how she is (feelings, temporary situations, readiness, being late, etc.). For more permanent identity/characteristics, Portuguese often uses "ela é" (ser) instead.
target_language_example: Ela está no trabalho agora, mas está cansada.
native_language_example: She is at work now, but she is tired.

additional_notes: Used to say something is typical or happens very often with her. It’s usually followed by an action or a description: (1) European Portuguese often uses "estar sempre a + infinitive" ("Ela está sempre a fazer..."); (2) Brazilian Portuguese often uses "estar sempre + gerund" ("Ela está sempre fazendo..."). It can also be followed by an adjective ("ela está sempre ocupada/diferente").
target_language_example: Ela está sempre a reclamar do trabalho.
native_language_example: She's always complaining about work.

additional_notes: "Ela" = "she" and "fala" is the present tense of "falar" (to speak/talk). Use it to say what languages a woman speaks (often with "idiomas" or "línguas") or what she talks about (often with "sobre" = "about").
target_language_example: Ela fala inglês muito bem, mas fala devagar.
native_language_example: She speaks English very well, but she speaks slowly.

additional_notes: A simple subject + verb + language pattern: "ela" (she) + "falar" (to speak) + the language name. Often followed by an adverb like "bem" (well), "muito bem" (very well), or "fluentemente" (fluently). For a question, you can use rising intonation or add a question mark in writing: "Ela fala inglês?"
target_language_example: Ela fala inglês, mas prefere falar português em casa.
native_language_example: She speaks English, but she prefers to speak Portuguese at home.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "fazer" for "ela" (she). Use it for a completed action in the past: doing something ("Ela fez tudo que pôde"), making/creating something ("Ela fez um vestido"), taking/doing an exam ("o exame que ela fez"), making friends/relationships ("Ela fez amizade"), or causing something with "fazer com que" ("Ela fez com que ele..." = "She made him..." / "She caused him to...").
target_language_example: Ela fez o jantar ontem.
native_language_example: She made dinner yesterday.

additional_notes: “Ela ficou” is “she + ficou” (past tense of ficar). It can mean (1) she stayed/remained in a place or position: “Ela ficou num hotel barato.” / “Ela ficou parada…”, or (2) she became/ended up in a new state, often with an adjective: “Ela ficou cega.”, “Ela ficou surpresa.” The exact translation depends on what comes after it (a place/position vs. an adjective).
target_language_example: Ela ficou nervosa antes da entrevista.
native_language_example: She got nervous before the interview.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a completed action in the past (pretérito perfeito) with the subject ela (“she”). Often followed by para/a + place to say where she went: “Ela foi para o ponto de ônibus.” In some contexts it can also mean “she was” (from ser), but with destinations like para fora it clearly means “went.”
target_language_example: Ela foi ao mercado comprar pão.
native_language_example: She went to the market to buy bread.

additional_notes: Used to say where she went. "Foi" is the past tense of "ir" (to go). "Para" introduces the destination or direction: a city/country ("para Paris"), a specific place ("para o seu quarto"), or a direction/side ("para aquele lado"). In Portuguese you can often shorten this to "Ela foi pra..." in casual speech/writing.
target_language_example: Ela foi para casa depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: She went home after work.

ela foi aconselhada por ele a

target_language_multi_word_term: ela foi aconselhada por ele a
additional_notes: Passive voice of aconselhar (“to advise”). Structure: [someone] foi aconselhado(a) por [someone] a + infinitive. Use aconselhada (feminine) for “she” and aconselhado (masculine) for “he”. You can also change the agent: por ele (by him), por ela (by her), por um médico (by a doctor), etc.
target_language_example: Ela foi aconselhada por ele a descansar mais.
native_language_example: She was advised by him to rest more.

additional_notes: Used to say what a woman or girl likes (a person, thing, or activity). After "gosta de" you often use a noun ("animais", "jazz", "você") or an infinitive verb to talk about an activity ("cozinhar", "dormir", "nadar"). In Portuguese it normally requires "de" (you don’t say "ela gosta" + direct object).
target_language_example: Ela gosta de café, mas não gosta de chá.
native_language_example: She likes coffee, but she doesn’t like tea.

additional_notes: Used when a woman (ela) does something *to/for someone* and that person is the indirect object (lhe). Common with verbs like dar (to give), entregar (to hand/deliver), pedir (to ask/request), perguntar (to ask), prometer (to promise). In Brazilian Portuguese, many speakers use "para ele/ela/você" instead of "lhe" in everyday speech, but "lhe" is still correct and common in writing and more formal contexts.
target_language_example: Ela lhe contou a verdade.
native_language_example: She told him/her/them/you (formal) the truth.

additional_notes: Uses the verb dar (to give) in the simple past: deu = “gave”. The pronoun lhe means “to him / to her / to you” (formal), i.e., “to someone” as an indirect object. In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often use "ela deu para ele/ela/você" or "ela te deu" instead of "ela lhe deu".
target_language_example: Ela lhe deu um copo de água.
native_language_example: She gave him/her/you a glass of water.

additional_notes: Used to report what a woman (ela) said to someone. “lhe” is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him/to her/to you (formal)”, and “disse” is the past tense of “dizer” (to say/tell). Usually followed by a clause with “que” (“that …”). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often use “ela disse pra ele/ela que …” instead of “ela lhe disse que …”.
target_language_example: Ela lhe disse que não podia ir hoje.
native_language_example: She told him/her that she couldn’t go today.

meaning: “she (to) me” — used when she does something to me / for me (she + object pronoun “me”).
additional_notes: Common subject + object pronoun order in Portuguese: “ela” (she) + “me” (to me). It usually comes right before the verb: “Ela me disse...” = “She told me...”. In everyday speech, people may also say “Ela disse pra mim...”, but “ela me + verb” is very common and natural.
target_language_example: Ela me ajudou a encontrar meu celular.
native_language_example: She helped me find my phone.

additional_notes: "Ela" = she, "me" = to me, and "deu" is the past (preterite) of "dar" (to give): “she gave.” It’s used both for giving physical things ("Ela me deu vários livros") and in common expressions like "ela me deu um abraço" (“she gave me a hug”), "ela me deu motivos" (“she gave me reasons”), and "ela me deu as costas" (“she turned her back on me,” idiomatic).
target_language_example: Ela me deu um presente ontem.
native_language_example: She gave me a present yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to report what a woman said. After **que** (“that”), you add the content of what she said; the verb tense can shift depending on when the original statement happened (e.g., past, present, future-in-the-past). In Brazil, **ela me disse** is common, but **ela disse para mim** / **ela me falou** can also be heard.
target_language_example: Ela me disse que não podia ir hoje.
native_language_example: She told me that she couldn’t go today.

additional_notes: "Ela" = "she" and "mora" is the present tense of "morar" (to live/reside). Often followed by a place (Ela mora aqui / no Brasil), by "com" + someone (Ela mora com ele = She lives with him), or by an adverb describing distance (Ela mora perto = She lives nearby). Common in questions: "Onde ela mora?" = "Where does she live?"
target_language_example: Ela mora perto do trabalho.
native_language_example: She lives close to work.

meaning: "she doesn't / she didn't / she can't" (negating what she does/can do).
additional_notes: Used to negate a verb phrase about a woman/girl: "ela não" + verb (e.g., "ela não pode" = "she can't"). In questions it can be used like a confirmation question depending on intonation/context (e.g., "Ela não matou...?" ≈ "Didn't she kill...?" / "She didn't kill..., did she?").
target_language_example: Ela não quer ir hoje.
native_language_example: She doesn't want to go today.

additional_notes: Used to say that a woman/girl does not possess something or does not have something (money, a phone, children, motivation, etc.). It’s the negative form of the verb “ter” (to have): “ela tem” (she has) → “ela não tem” (she doesn’t have). In speech, you may hear a tag question like “..., tem?” to check/confirm information (similar to “..., does she?” / “..., right?”).
target_language_example: Ela não tem tempo hoje.
native_language_example: She doesn’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to say that a woman/girl is not something (identity, nationality, relationship, etc.). Often followed by a noun/adjective (e.g., "Ela não é americana") or by "...mas..." to correct/contrast ("Ela não é X, mas sim Y"). In casual speech, "não" is often pronounced like "num".
target_language_example: Ela não é professora; ela é médica.
native_language_example: She is not a teacher; she is a doctor.

additional_notes: Used to start a comparison or degree statement about a woman/girl: **Ela não é tão + adjective + quanto...** = “She isn’t as + adjective + as…”. It can also appear with **a ponto de** to mean “not so… that…” (e.g., *Ela não é tão tola a ponto de...* = “She’s not so foolish that…”). You can swap **ela** for another subject (e.g., *ele não é tão...*, *você não é tão...*).
target_language_example: Ela não é tão rápida quanto o irmão.
native_language_example: She isn’t as fast as her brother.

additional_notes: "Ela" is the subject pronoun "she". "O" is a direct object pronoun meaning "him" (or sometimes "it"). In Portuguese, object pronouns like "o/a/os/as" often come right before the verb: "Ela o lembra..." = "She reminds him..." (more natural English: "She reminds him of his mother.").
target_language_example: Ela o vê todos os dias.
native_language_example: She sees him every day.

additional_notes: Used to report advice/warnings. Structure: **Ela** (she) + **o** (“him,” object pronoun) + **aconselhou** (advised) + **a** + **não** + infinitive. Very common pattern: **aconselhar alguém a (não) fazer algo** (“to advise someone to (not) do something”). You can swap **o** for **a** (her) or **me/te/nos/vos** (me/you/us/you all) depending on who receives the advice.
target_language_example: Ela o aconselhou a não falar com estranhos na internet.
native_language_example: She advised him not to talk to strangers on the internet.

additional_notes: “Ela” = “she” and “quer” is the 3rd-person singular present of “querer” (“to want”). It’s followed by an infinitive (quer pintar/quer saber/quer ver) or by a noun (quer um café). In questions you may hear “O que é que ela quer?” = “What does she want?”
target_language_example: Ela quer um copo d’água, por favor.
native_language_example: She wants a glass of water, please.

additional_notes: Used before a verb when the subject is “ela” (she) and the verb takes the pronoun “se”. Often it’s the equivalent of English “she” with certain verbs (e.g., ela se levanta = she gets up), but sometimes it adds a reflexive sense (“herself”) depending on the verb. The pronoun changes with the subject: eu me, você/tu te, ele se, nós nos, vocês se, eles se.
target_language_example: Ela se veste rapidamente antes de sair.
native_language_example: She gets dressed quickly before leaving.

additional_notes: Based on the verb phrase **se apaixonar por (alguém)** = “to fall in love with (someone).” It’s a common, neutral way to talk about starting to love someone romantically. The **se** is part of the reflexive verb (**apaixonar-se**). In the examples, **por um** is followed by a noun (e.g., *um príncipe, um jovem artista*). You can change the subject: *Eu me apaixonei por…* (I fell in love with…), *Ele se apaixonou por…* (He fell in love with…).
target_language_example: Ela se apaixonou por um colega de trabalho.
native_language_example: She fell in love with a coworker.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **se casar com** (“to marry / to get married to”). **Ela** is “she”, so this whole chunk is used to say who she married: **Ela se casou com ele** = “She married him.” The **com** introduces the spouse/partner. You can add a reason with **por**: **por dinheiro** (“for money”), **porque...** (“because...”).
target_language_example: Ela se casou com ele no ano passado.
native_language_example: She married him last year.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of the reflexive verb "sentar-se" (to sit down). "Ela" = she, "se" marks the reflexive action, and "sentou" is the past form of "sentar". Often followed by a place ("ali", "aqui", "na cadeira") or combined with another action using "e" ("Ela se sentou e..." = She sat down and...).
target_language_example: Ela se sentou no sofá e ficou em silêncio.
native_language_example: She sat down on the couch and stayed silent.

meaning: 'she sat down near him' / 'she sat next to him'.
additional_notes: "Sentar-se" means "to sit down" (often used with the reflexive "se": "ela se sentou"). "Perto de" means "near/close to"; with "dele" it becomes "perto dele" ("near him"). Often used to describe choosing a place close to someone (e.g., on a bus).
target_language_example: Ela se sentou perto dele para conversar.
native_language_example: She sat down near him to talk.

meaning: 'she has' / 'she has to' (present tense of ter).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what a woman/girl possesses, has as a characteristic, or experiences: Ela tem cabelo curto. With "tem que + infinitive", it means obligation: Ela tem que parar de fumar = "She has to stop smoking." In questions, you can ask what she has/what’s wrong: O que ela tem?
target_language_example: Ela tem que estudar hoje.
native_language_example: She has to study today.

additional_notes: Used to say that a woman/girl possesses something or has a characteristic/feature. It’s typically followed by a singular masculine noun (um + noun): “Ela tem um diploma…”, “Ela tem um sotaque…”. For singular feminine nouns, you’d use “ela tem uma …” (e.g., “Ela tem uma casa”).
target_language_example: Ela tem um irmão mais velho.
native_language_example: She has an older brother.

additional_notes: Used to say that a woman/girl possesses something or has a characteristic. Very common with nouns: "Ela tem uma bolsa" (She has a bag). It can also describe appearance or traits: "Ela tem uma cara engraçada" literally 'She has a funny face' → meaning 'She looks funny' / 'She has a funny-looking face'.
target_language_example: Ela tem uma irmã mais velha.
native_language_example: She has an older sister.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **tentar** for **ela** (she). Very commonly followed by an infinitive: **ela tentou + verbo** (e.g., *ela tentou esconder...* = she tried to hide...). It can also take a direct object: *ela tentou pará-lo* = she tried to stop him/it. Often contrasts with success/failure: *ela tentou, mas não conseguiu* = she tried, but she couldn’t.
target_language_example: Ela tentou ligar para você ontem, mas não conseguiu.
native_language_example: She tried to call you yesterday, but she couldn’t.

additional_notes: Used to say a woman tried to convince a man to do (or not do) something. Grammar: ela (she) + tentou (tried) + persuadi-lo (to persuade him; persuadir + o = him) + a + infinitive verb (e.g., comprar, ir, organizar). With negation: “a não” + infinitive (a não baixar = not to lower).
target_language_example: Ela tentou persuadi-lo a ficar mais um pouco.
native_language_example: She tried to persuade him to stay a little longer.

meaning: 'she is' (used to describe who/what she is, or what she’s like).
additional_notes: "Ela" = "she" and "é" is the present of "ser" (to be) for "he/she/it". Use it with nationality (Ela é inglesa.), identity (Ela é médica.), and general characteristics (Ela é legal.). In questions, intonation often changes or you can add a question mark in writing: Ela é italiana? Often followed by an adjective or noun.
target_language_example: Ela é minha amiga.
native_language_example: She is my friend.

additional_notes: Use it to describe a woman/girl with an adjective: "Ela é muito" + adjective (atraente, linda, esperta, etc.). In Portuguese you typically need an adjective after "muito"; by itself it sounds incomplete unless the adjective is understood from context.
target_language_example: Ela é muito simpática com todo mundo.
native_language_example: She is very friendly with everyone.

meaning: "she is a" (introduces what she is, her role, or a description).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun (uma). Common with jobs/roles and descriptions: “Ela é uma cozinheira / artista / estudante.” For masculine, use “ele é um…”. If the next word starts with a vowel, Portuguese may use “uma” as usual (no special change), e.g., “Ela é uma artista.”
target_language_example: Ela é uma médica excelente.
native_language_example: She is an excellent doctor.

additional_notes: Basic description sentence with "ela" (she) + "é" (is) + "uma" (a) + "garota" (girl). Often followed by an adjective: "Ela é uma garota bonita/educada/gentil." In some contexts, "garota" can mean "young woman" rather than a child; for a more child-specific word, you can also hear "menina".
target_language_example: Ela é uma garota inteligente e divertida.
native_language_example: She is a smart and fun girl.

additional_notes: Basic identifying/describing sentence: ela (she) + é (is) + uma mulher (a woman). Often followed by an adjective ("adorável", "egoísta") or a descriptive phrase with de ("uma mulher de grande beleza" = "a woman of great beauty"). If you mean "the woman" (a specific one), you’d usually say "Ela é a mulher..." instead of "uma".
target_language_example: Ela é uma mulher muito inteligente.
native_language_example: She is a very intelligent woman.

additional_notes: “Elas” means “they” referring to a group of women/girls (or feminine nouns). “Estavam” is the imperfect past of “estar,” used for states or ongoing situations in the past. It commonly appears with: (1) a gerund to mean “were + -ing” (Elas estavam dormindo. = They were sleeping.), or (2) an adjective/past participle to describe a past state (Elas estavam zangadas. = They were angry.). In questions, it often sets a past-time scene: O que elas estavam tomando? = What were they drinking?
target_language_example: Quando eu cheguei, elas estavam estudando.
native_language_example: When I arrived, they were studying.

meaning: “they are” (for a group of women/girls, or a mixed group when referring specifically to females).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" for temporary states, locations, and actions happening now (present continuous). Common patterns: "elas estão aqui" (location), "elas estão prontas" (state/ready), "elas estão + gerund" like "comendo/jantando/jogando" (they are eating/having dinner/playing). Contrast: "elas são" is for more permanent identity/characteristics.
target_language_example: Elas estão no parque agora.
native_language_example: They are in the park right now.

additional_notes: "Elas" is the subject pronoun for an all-female group (for a mixed group, Portuguese usually uses "eles"). "Querem" is the present tense (they want) of the verb "querer". It’s commonly followed by an infinitive (e.g., "elas querem viajar" = they want to travel) or by a noun/clause ("o que elas querem" = what they want). In many sentences, the pronoun can be omitted because the verb ending already shows "they" (e.g., "Querem conversar.").
target_language_example: Elas querem um café agora.
native_language_example: They want a coffee now.

meaning: 'they are' (talking about a group of females).
additional_notes: Used with the subject pronoun "elas" = "they" (for women/girls or feminine things) + "são" = "are" (3rd person plural of "ser", “to be”). It can describe identity or characteristics ("Elas são professoras"), origin ("Elas são do Brasil"), age/qualities ("Elas são da mesma idade"), or be used as a short answer meaning “Yes, they are.”
target_language_example: Elas são brasileiras.
native_language_example: They are Brazilian.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine plural subject (“elas” = “they,” referring to a group of women/things treated as feminine). “têm” is the present tense of **ter** (“to have”) for **eles/elas**; it has a tilde to distinguish it from **tem** (“he/she has”). Often followed by a noun (“elas têm dinheiro”) or an expression like **em comum** (“in common”).
target_language_example: Elas têm dois filhos.
native_language_example: They have two children.

additional_notes: Used when “a” (“her”) comes before the verb: Ele a viu = “He saw her.” This is common in more formal/written Portuguese. In everyday speech (especially in Brazil), many people instead say “ele + verb + ela” (e.g., “Ele abraçou ela”). Note: “a” refers to a female person/thing and changes with gender/number (o/os/as).
target_language_example: Ele a viu na rua, mas não falou com ela.
native_language_example: He saw her on the street, but he didn’t talk to her.

additional_notes: "Ele" = "he". "Chegou" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "chegar" (to arrive/to get to a place). Often used with time expressions like "a tempo" (on time), "cedo" (early), and clauses like "depois que..." (after...).
target_language_example: Ele chegou em casa às oito.
native_language_example: He got home at eight.

additional_notes: A common way to say someone arrived at their home. Uses the verb "chegar" (to arrive) in the past ("chegou" = "arrived") plus "em casa" (“at home/home”). You can change the subject and time: "eu cheguei em casa" (I got home), "ela chegou em casa" (she got home), "cheguei em casa tarde" (I got home late), "chegou em casa às dez" (got home at ten). In some places you may also hear "chegar a casa".
target_language_example: Ele chegou em casa cansado depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: He got home tired after work.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man/boy began an action or started to become a certain way. Pattern: "ele começou a" + infinitive verb (comer, cantar, ficar, etc.). For other subjects: "eu comecei a", "ela começou a", "a gente começou a", "nós começamos a", "eles/elas começaram a".
target_language_example: Ele começou a estudar português ontem.
native_language_example: He started studying Portuguese yesterday.

additional_notes:
"Deixar" is a very common verb with a few everyday meanings:
- "deixar + place/person/thing" = to leave (e.g., leave a country; leave family behind).
- "deixar + verb (infinitive)" = to let/allow (e.g., "deixou a barba crescer" = let his beard grow).
- In some contexts it can mean to drop/let fall (e.g., "deixou a salsicha cair" = he dropped/let the sausage fall).
- "deixar a função/cargo" = to resign/step down from a role/job.
Here it’s "ele" (he) + "deixou" (left/let) + "a" (the, feminine), so the next word is typically a feminine noun (a barba, a família, a África, a função...).
target_language_example: Ele deixou a porta aberta por engano.
native_language_example: He left the door open by mistake.

additional_notes: Past tense of the verb "dizer" (to say/tell). Often followed by "que" + a clause ("Ele disse que..."). It can also take an indirect object: "Ele disse-me" = "He told me". Used when reporting what a man said.
target_language_example: Ele disse que vai chegar mais tarde.
native_language_example: He said he’ll arrive later.

meaning: “he said that…” (to report what a man said).
additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech (what a male person said), followed by a clause with que (“that”). Very common in storytelling and conversation. You can change ele to ela (“she”) or eles/elas (“they”).
target_language_example: Ele disse que não podia vir hoje.
native_language_example: He said that he couldn’t come today.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man/boy said in the past. After "disse que" (“said that”), Portuguese typically uses the imperfect tense "estava" to describe an ongoing state at that time (e.g., happy, alone, returning). Often followed by an adjective ("feliz", "solitário") or by a verb in -ndo for an action in progress ("estava voltando" = "was coming back").
target_language_example: Ele disse que estava cansado demais para sair.
native_language_example: He said he was too tired to go out.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man says, followed by a statement (a clause introduced by "que" = "that"). In everyday speech, Portuguese often repeats the subject ("ele diz que ele...") even though it can be omitted ("ele diz que gosta...").
target_language_example: Ele diz que vai chegar mais tarde.
native_language_example: He says he’s going to arrive later.

additional_notes: Used with the imperfect past tense (era) to describe what someone was like, used to be, or something that was happening/habitual in the past. Often followed by an adjective, noun, or a passive construction like "era chamado" (was called).
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, ele era muito tímido.
native_language_example: When I was a kid, he was very shy.

meaning: “he was very …” (used before an adjective or description).
additional_notes: "Ele era" is the imperfect past of "ser" (to be), used to describe a continuing state or characteristic in the past (appearance, personality, social/economic situation, etc.). "Muito" works like “very/a lot” to intensify what comes next: "ele era muito alto" (very tall), "ele era muito pobre" (very poor).
target_language_example: Quando criança, ele era muito tímido.
native_language_example: When he was a child, he was very shy.

additional_notes: Used to describe who/what someone was in the past. It uses the imperfect past of **ser** (era = “was/used to be”) for descriptions and background information. **um** is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”); with feminine nouns you’d say **ela era uma**.
target_language_example: Ele era um professor muito paciente.
native_language_example: He was a very patient teacher.

additional_notes: Used to say what the topic/subject of a book is. After sobre you add the topic (a person, place, animal, event, etc.). You can change ele (he) to ela (she) or a person’s name, and escreveu (wrote) can change with tense (e.g., vai escrever, escreveu, tinha escrito).
target_language_example: Ele escreveu um livro sobre a história do Brasil.
native_language_example: He wrote a book about the history of Brazil.

additional_notes: Used to describe a past state or ongoing situation in the past (appearance, feelings, condition, location, or what someone was doing): ele estava ocupado (he was busy), ele estava no segundo ano (he was in second year), ele estava nadando (he was swimming). Often sets background context rather than a one-time completed event.
target_language_example: Ontem, ele estava cansado, então foi dormir cedo.
native_language_example: Yesterday, he was tired, so he went to bed early.

meaning: 'he is' (temporary state, condition, or action in progress).
additional_notes: Uses estar (not ser) to talk about how someone is feeling, their condition, location, or what they’re doing right now. Often followed by: atrás de (looking for), com (with), dando... (doing/going for), em (in), sem (without).
target_language_example: Ele está cansado hoje.
native_language_example: He is tired today.

meaning: “he is always …” (he does something all the time / very often).
additional_notes: Used before a verb (often in the gerund: "está sempre + verb-ndo") to complain or comment on a repeated habit: "Ele está sempre estudando" = “He’s always studying.” It can also be used with "com" to mean he is consistently with someone: "Ele está sempre comigo" = “He’s always with me.”
target_language_example: Ele está sempre falando alto.
native_language_example: He’s always talking loudly.

additional_notes: "Ele" means "he" and "fala" is the present tense of "falar" (to speak/to talk). Use it to say what language(s) he speaks ("Ele fala russo.", "Ele fala quatro línguas."), or how he speaks ("Ele fala com o coração.", "Ele fala como se fosse um especialista."). The next words give the detail: a language, a number of languages, or an expression like "com..." (with) or "como se..." (as if).
target_language_example: Ele fala muito rápido quando está nervoso.
native_language_example: He talks very fast when he's nervous.

additional_notes: Basic subject + verb phrase: ele (he) + fala (speaks) + inglês (English). Used to state a skill/ability. For questions, raise intonation (Ele fala inglês?) or add a question word: Ele fala inglês, francês ou alemão? You can intensify with adverbs like bem (well), fluente (fluently), perfeitamente (perfectly), or compare: melhor do que eu (better than me).
target_language_example: Ele fala inglês muito bem, mas eu ainda estou aprendendo.
native_language_example: He speaks English very well, but I'm still learning.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something a man did in the past. Common patterns: (1) "Ele fez + noun" = he made/did (e.g., fez uma viagem = took a trip; fez progresso = made progress; fez dinheiro = made money). (2) Causative: "Ele fez + person + infinitive" = he made/caused someone to do something (e.g., Ele fez o Tom perder a esperança = He made Tom lose hope).
target_language_example: Ele fez um bolo para o aniversário dela.
native_language_example: He made a cake for her birthday.

additional_notes: Uses the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of **fazer**: **ele fez** = “he did/made.” **isso** means “this/that/it” (referring to an action already mentioned or understood). Very common in explanations and questions like **Por que ele fez isso?** (“Why did he do that?”).
target_language_example: Ele fez isso para ajudar a mãe dele.
native_language_example: He did that to help his mother.

meaning: "he became" / "he got" (often used before an adjective).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective or state to show a change/result: "ele ficou + adjective" = he ended up/turned/became (e.g., ficou louco = went crazy; ficou triste = got sad). "Ficou" is the past tense of "ficar" and doesn’t usually mean "stayed" in these change-of-state sentences.
target_language_example: Ele ficou cansado depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: He got tired after work.

meaning: 'he went' / 'he left' (past of *ir*); sometimes 'he was' in passive-style expressions (*foi* = 'was').
additional_notes: **Ele** = 'he' and **foi** is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of **ir** ('to go'): *Ele foi para a cama cedo* = 'He went to bed early.' Very common with destinations using **para** or **a/à/ao**: *foi para...*, *foi à...*. In questions, you’ll often see **aonde ele foi?** = 'Where did he go?' Also note **foi** can be the past of **ser** ('to be') in passive or fixed expressions (e.g., *Ele foi demitido* = 'He was fired'), but in the provided examples it mainly means 'went.' In *ele foi de mal a pior*, it’s an idiom meaning 'he went from bad to worse.'
target_language_example: Ele foi ao mercado depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: He went to the market after work.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man left a place or departed. Common with details like destination ("para Paris" = to Paris), manner ("sem dizer adeus" = without saying goodbye), or time ("Quando ele foi embora?" = When did he leave?). "Ir embora" is the verb phrase meaning “to go away/leave”; "foi" is the past (he went).
target_language_example: Ele foi embora cedo porque estava cansado.
native_language_example: He left early because he was tired.

meaning: 'he went to' / 'he went for' (to a place or toward a destination).
additional_notes: Used to say that a male person traveled/moved to a destination: "Ele foi para + place" (He went to...). It can also express going somewhere for a purpose when followed by an infinitive: "Ele foi para Portugal para trabalhar" (He went to Portugal to work). In everyday speech you may also hear "ele foi pra" (shorter form of "para").
target_language_example: Ele foi para o trabalho cedo hoje.
native_language_example: He went to work early today.

additional_notes: "Ele" = he. "Foi" is the past (pretérito perfeito) of "ir" (to go): "he went". "Para" means "to" (destination). "A" is the feminine singular definite article "the" (used before many place nouns like "a biblioteca", and some regions/continents like "a África"). With masculine nouns it changes: "ele foi para o ..." (e.g., "para o Brasil"). With many city and country names you may not use an article at all (e.g., "para Itália" is also common depending on variety), but the pattern "para a" is very common when the noun takes "a".
target_language_example: Ontem, ele foi para a escola bem cedo.
native_language_example: Yesterday, he went to school very early.

meaning: 'he went' / 'he left' (past of *ir*); sometimes 'he was' in passive-style expressions (*foi* = 'was').
additional_notes: **Ele** = 'he' and **foi** is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of **ir** ('to go'): *Ele foi para a cama cedo* = 'He went to bed early.' Very common with destinations using **para** or **a/à/ao**: *foi para...*, *foi à...*. In questions, you’ll often see **aonde ele foi?** = 'Where did he go?' Also note **foi** can be the past of **ser** ('to be') in passive or fixed expressions (e.g., *Ele foi demitido* = 'He was fired'), but in the provided examples it mainly means 'went.' In *ele foi de mal a pior*, it’s an idiom meaning 'he went from bad to worse.'
target_language_example: Ele foi ao mercado depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: He went to the market after work.

meaning: “he likes” / “he enjoys” (followed by a noun or a verb in the infinitive).
additional_notes: Use this to talk about what a man/boy likes or enjoys. Structure: **ele gosta de + noun** (Ele gosta de futebol.) or **ele gosta de + infinitive verb** (Ele gosta de cantar.). Often translated as “he likes to…”. You can swap the subject: **eu gosto de** (I like), **ela gosta de** (she likes), **você gosta de** (you like).
target_language_example: Ele gosta de cozinhar em casa.
native_language_example: He likes to cook at home.

additional_notes: Common pattern where **ele** is the subject (“he”) and **me** is the object pronoun (“me”). In Brazilian Portuguese, **me** often comes **before** the verb: *ele me viu* (“he saw me”), *ele me convidou* (“he invited me”). In European Portuguese you may also see the pronoun after the verb: *ele viu-me*, *ele convidou-me*.
target_language_example: Ele me ajudou a encontrar o endereço.
native_language_example: He helped me find the address.

additional_notes: Past tense of "dar" (to give): "deu" = "gave" (simple past). "me" is the object pronoun "to me". Often followed by the thing given: "ele me deu dinheiro" (he gave me money). It can also be used for non-physical things like advice, a ride, or an answer.
target_language_example: Ele me deu um conselho muito útil.
native_language_example: He gave me very useful advice.

additional_notes: Used to report something a man (ele) said to you. Very common before "que" + a clause ("Ele me disse que...") or before an infinitive phrase (often informal "pra" = "para"): "Ele me disse pra...". In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, "me" often comes before the verb ("ele me disse"), while in more formal writing you may also see "ele disse-me".
target_language_example: Ele me disse que vai chegar mais tarde.
native_language_example: He told me he’s going to arrive later.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man said. It’s the start of an indirect statement: **ele** (he) + **me** (to me) + **disse** (told/said) + **que** (that). After **que**, you add the information being reported. In speech, people may also say **ele disse que…** (without *me*) if “to me” is understood.
target_language_example: Ele me disse que não podia vir hoje.
native_language_example: He told me that he couldn’t come today.

additional_notes: Common past tense structure: subject (ele) + indirect object pronoun (me) + verb in the simple past (mostrou, from mostrar). Used when someone showed you something. You’ll often follow it with the thing shown (a foto, o álbum, a coleção) and sometimes a preposition like “em” + manner (e.g., em segredo = secretly).
target_language_example: Ele me mostrou onde fica a estação.
native_language_example: He showed me where the station is.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives. Very common pattern: "Ele mora em" + place (e.g., em Lisboa, em algum lugar perto do parque). You can also add details like "sozinho" (alone) or "numa casa" (in a house).
target_language_example: Ele mora aqui há dois anos.
native_language_example: He has lived here for two years.

additional_notes: Used to say where a man/boy lives. "morar" = to live/reside, and "em" is the preposition for location (in/at/on). Often followed by a city, country, neighborhood, or a type of place (e.g., "uma casa", "um apartamento").
target_language_example: Ele mora em São Paulo desde 2020.
native_language_example: He has lived in São Paulo since 2020.

additional_notes: Used to state that a male person has died. You can add details with time (e.g., "dez anos atrás" = ten years ago), manner/cause ("de repente" = suddenly; "de" + illness/cause), place ("onde"/"em"), or "na hora" meaning immediately/on the spot after an accident. In more formal or sensitive contexts, Portuguese also uses softer expressions like "ele faleceu" (he passed away).
target_language_example: Ele morreu há três anos.
native_language_example: He died three years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man/boy did not do something at any time. It’s simply the pronoun ele (“he”) + the adverb nunca (“never”), followed by a verb: ele nunca falou (“he never spoke”). In Portuguese, nunca usually comes right before the main verb.
target_language_example: Ele nunca chega na hora.
native_language_example: He never arrives on time.

additional_notes: Used to negate a verb or statement about a male person (“ele”). In Portuguese, “não” usually comes right before the verb: “Ele não está…”, “Ele não tem…”. You’ll also see it before forms like “conseguia” (could/manage to) and with lists: “Ele não fala nem inglês nem francês” (“He speaks neither English nor French”).
target_language_example: Ele não quer ir hoje.
native_language_example: He doesn’t want to go today.

meaning: 'he isn't' / 'he is not' (not in/at a place, or not in a certain state).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" to say a man/boy is not somewhere or is not in a temporary condition/state. Often followed by a place or condition: "ele não está em casa" (he's not at home), "ele não está na cidade" (he's not in the city), "ele não está louco" (he isn't crazy). In Portuguese, "estar" is commonly used for location and temporary states (vs. "ser" for more permanent characteristics).
target_language_example: Ele não está no trabalho hoje.
native_language_example: He isn't at work today.

additional_notes: Used to say a man/boy lacks something (money, time, interest, respect, shame, etc.). Often followed by a noun ("Ele não tem dinheiro") or by "para" + verb to express lack needed to do something ("Ele não tem dinheiro para comprar...").
target_language_example: Ele não tem tempo para ir hoje.
native_language_example: He doesn't have time to go today.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man ("ele" = he) will not do something, often in the near future. Very commonly followed by an infinitive verb: "Ele não vai + verb" (e.g., "Ele não vai conseguir" = He won’t manage). In questions, it can suggest surprise or concern: "Ele não vai... ?"
target_language_example: Ele não vai chegar a tempo.
native_language_example: He isn't going to arrive on time.

meaning: "he is not" (used to negate who/what he is).
additional_notes: Used to say that a male person (ele) does not have a certain identity, relationship, or quality. It’s the negative of "ele é". Often followed by an adjective (Ele não é bobo.), a noun with an article (Ele não é um amigo.), or a possessive phrase (Ele não é seu filho.). You can add contrast with "e sim" ("but rather").
target_language_example: Ele não é brasileiro; ele é português.
native_language_example: He isn’t Brazilian; he’s Portuguese.

meaning: 'he seems' / 'he looks (like)' (based on appearance or impression).
additional_notes: Used to say the speaker’s impression about a man. Follow it with an infinitive for actions/situations ("Ele parece nos conhecer" = he seems to know us), or with an adjective/noun for description ("Ele parece saudável" = he looks healthy; "Ele parece um modelo" = he looks like a model). For a woman, use "ela parece".
target_language_example: Ele parece estar cansado hoje.
native_language_example: He seems to be tired today.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb (parar de + infinitive) to say someone stopped an activity or habit: Ele parou de beber (he stopped drinking). You can use it for something happening in the moment (stopped crying/talking) or for quitting a longer-term habit (stopped drinking/smoking). For other subjects, change ele: eu parei de, ela parou de, nós paramos de, etc.
target_language_example: Ele parou de trabalhar cedo hoje.
native_language_example: He stopped working early today.

additional_notes: This is the start of a sentence with the verb **perder** (“to lose/miss”) in the past: **ele perdeu** = “he lost/he missed”. It’s followed by a masculine noun with **o** (“the”). With people (e.g., **o filho**), **perder** can mean “to lose” in the sense of someone dying. With travel or events (e.g., **o voo**), it often means “to miss” (arrive too late).
target_language_example: Ele perdeu o ônibus e chegou atrasado ao trabalho.
native_language_example: He missed the bus and arrived late to work.

additional_notes: Used to say that a male person needs something: ele (he) + precisar de (to need + de). After "precisa de" you typically use a noun or noun phrase (e.g., mais tempo, novos sapatos, uma xícara de açúcar). With verbs, Portuguese usually uses "precisar de" + infinitive (e.g., "Ele precisa de dormir" = He needs to sleep), though in Brazil many people also say "Ele precisa dormir" without "de".
target_language_example: Ele precisa de ajuda agora.
native_language_example: He needs help now.

additional_notes: "Ele" = “he” and "quer" is the present-tense (3rd person singular) of "querer" (“to want”). It’s commonly followed by an infinitive ("Ele quer jogar" = “He wants to play”) or by a noun ("Ele quer um" = “He wants one”). With "quer que" + subjunctive, it means “he wants (someone) to…” ("Ele quer que eu vá" = “He wants me to go”).
target_language_example: Ele quer comer agora.
native_language_example: He wants to eat now.

meaning: "he wanted" / "he would like" (past tense of querer).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a man’s desire, intention, or preference in the past. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., "ele queria dançar" = "he wanted to dance") or by a noun ("ele queria comida" = "he wanted food"). It also appears in reported speech after "disse que..." ("he said that he wanted...").
target_language_example: Ele queria comprar um carro novo, mas não tinha dinheiro.
native_language_example: He wanted to buy a new car, but he didn’t have money.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to mean “he knows how to” do something: “Ele sabe nadar” = “He can swim.” It can also refer to knowing facts (“Ele sabe a resposta” = “He knows the answer”). In questions, you’ll often hear: “Ele sabe fazer isso?” = “Does he know how to do that?”
target_language_example: Ele sabe falar português muito bem.
native_language_example: He can speak Portuguese very well.

meaning: 'he can speak' / 'he knows how to speak' (a language).
additional_notes: Used to say that a man has the ability to speak a language. Often followed by the language ("Ele sabe falar japonês") or by how many languages ("cinco idiomas / cinco línguas"). You can add another skill with "e": "Ele sabe falar e escrever...". For "only a little", use "só um pouco (de)": "Ele sabe falar só um pouco de inglês".
target_language_example: Ele sabe falar português muito bem.
native_language_example: He can speak Portuguese very well.

meaning: "He can speak French." / "He knows how to speak French."
additional_notes: "saber" + infinitive ("sabe falar") is a common way to say someone knows how to do something or can do it. You can swap the language or the subject: "Eu sei falar inglês" (I can speak English), "Ela sabe falar português" (She can speak Portuguese). In questions, just raise intonation or add a question mark: "Ele sabe falar francês?"
target_language_example: Ele sabe falar francês e espanhol.
native_language_example: He can speak French and Spanish.

meaning: 'he left' / 'he went out' (past tense of sair).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say a man left a place (saiu de casa/da sala/da estação) or went out to do something (saiu para comer/dar uma caminhada). You can add time (saiu duas semanas atrás) or manner (saiu rapidamente).
target_language_example: Ele saiu cedo para trabalhar.
native_language_example: He left early to go to work.

additional_notes: "Ele" means “he.” "Se" is a very common clitic pronoun placed before the verb, often making the action reflexive (he does it to himself) or showing that the verb is used in a “reflexive-style” way. Examples: "ele se manteve" = “he kept himself/remained,” "ele se ofende" = “he gets offended,” "ele se deu conta" = “he realized.” In English you often won’t translate "se" as a separate word, or it may become “himself.”
target_language_example: Ele se levantou cedo hoje.
native_language_example: He got up early today.

additional_notes: Past tense of **casar-se com** (“to marry / to get married to”). **Ele** = “he”; **se casou** = “got married” (completed action); **com** introduces the person he married (“to/with”). Often followed by a name or pronoun: **Ele se casou com ela** (“He married her”).
target_language_example: Ele se casou com a Maria em 2020.
native_language_example: He married Maria in 2020.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man/boy physically resembles someone. It’s the verb phrase **se parecer com** (“to look like / resemble”) + **o** (“the”, masculine singular). Change **o** depending on the noun: **com a** (feminine: *Ele se parece com a mãe.*), **com os/as** (plural). You can also change the subject: **Ela se parece com o pai.** / **Eu me pareço com o meu pai.**
target_language_example: Ele se parece com o professor.
native_language_example: He looks like the teacher.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man (ele) did not agree to do an action. The verb is reflexive: recusar-se a + infinitive (recusou-se a contar, a desistir, a receber, a vir). You can change the subject: eu me recusei a…, ela se recusou a…, nós nos recusamos a…. In writing, you may see the hyphen: recusou-se.
target_language_example: Ele se recusou a assinar o contrato.
native_language_example: He refused to sign the contract.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase “tornar-se” (to become). It’s commonly used to talk about someone becoming a profession or a new role: “Ele se tornou pianista/policial.” You may see it with or without an article before professions (“Ele se tornou policial” and “Ele se tornou um policial” are both possible; using “um/uma” can sound a bit more specific, like “a (certain) police officer”).
target_language_example: Depois de muitos anos de estudo, ele se tornou médico.
native_language_example: After many years of studying, he became a doctor.

meaning: 'he always' (talking about something he habitually does, or something that will always be true).
additional_notes: "Ele" = "he" and "sempre" = "always". "Sempre" usually goes before the main verb: "Ele sempre chega cedo" (He always arrives early). It can also be used with the future to mean "will always": "Ele sempre estará..." (He will always be...).
target_language_example: Ele sempre esquece o meu aniversário.
native_language_example: He always forgets my birthday.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **sentar-se** (“to sit down”), with the reflexive pronoun **-se**. In European and more formal Brazilian Portuguese, **-se** is often attached to the verb (**sentou-se**). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese you may also hear **ele sentou** (without **-se**) with the same meaning. Often followed by a place/position: **ao lado (de)** (next to), **na minha frente** (in front of me), or a purpose with **para**: **sentou-se para ler** (sat down to read).
target_language_example: Ele sentou-se no sofá para descansar.
native_language_example: He sat down on the sofa to rest.

meaning: "he has" / "he's got" (he possesses; he has a trait; he is a certain age).
additional_notes: "Ele" = "he" + "tem" = "has" (from the verb "ter", to have). Used for possession (ele tem dicionários), relationships (a família que ele tem), physical traits (ele tem cabelo rebelde), age (ele tem uns trinta anos = he’s about 30), and in common expressions like "ele tem algo a ver com isso" = "he has something to do with this".
target_language_example: Ele tem dois irmãos e tem 25 anos.
native_language_example: He has two brothers and he is 25 years old.

additional_notes:
Used to say that a man/boy possesses something or has a characteristic. 
- "ele" = he 
- "tem" (from "ter") = has 
- "um" = a/an (masculine singular), used before masculine singular nouns (e.g., "um blog", "um coração"). 
For feminine nouns, use "ele tem uma" (e.g., "ele tem uma ideia"). "Tem" is also used for age: "Ele tem 30 anos."
target_language_example: Ele tem um carro novo.
native_language_example: He has a new car.

meaning: “he has a …” (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb ter (“to have”) to say someone possesses something (Ele tem uma empregada.), has family (Ele tem uma esposa…), or has a quality/trait (Ele tem uma personalidade irritante.). It must be followed by a feminine singular noun; for masculine nouns you use “ele tem um …”.
target_language_example: Ele tem uma casa pequena, mas confortável.
native_language_example: He has a small but comfortable house.

additional_notes: Used to say that a male person made an effort to do something. It’s usually followed by an infinitive verb: "ele tentou + verb" (e.g., ele tentou escapar = he tried to escape). You can also use it with "tentar" + noun in some cases (e.g., tentar uma coisa = try something).
target_language_example: Ele tentou abrir a porta, mas estava trancada.
native_language_example: He tried to open the door, but it was locked.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man possessed something, experienced something, got a result, or was obliged to do something in the past. Very common patterns: **ele teve + noun** (“he had/experienced…”, e.g., *ele teve um mau dia* = “he had a bad day”); **ele teve + number + noun** (“he had…”, e.g., children); **ele teve + result** (“he made/earned…”, e.g., profit); and **ele teve que + verb** (“he had to…”, obligation).
target_language_example: Ele teve que sair mais cedo hoje.
native_language_example: He had to leave earlier today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone had good luck in finding something (a job, hotel, doctor, parking spot, etc.). The pattern is: "ter sorte de" + infinitive verb (here, "encontrar"). You can change the subject and tense: "Eu tive sorte de encontrar..." / "Ela teve sorte de encontrar..."
target_language_example: Eu tive sorte de encontrar um apartamento perto do trabalho.
native_language_example: I was lucky to find an apartment close to work.

additional_notes: “Ele” = “he”. “Tinha” is the imperfect past of “ter” (to have). It’s used for past possession (things he had), past situations/background, and habitual actions or states in the past (often like “used to” in English): “Ele tinha o hábito…” = “He used to have the habit… / He had the habit…”.
target_language_example: Ele tinha um carro, mas vendeu.
native_language_example: He had a car, but he sold it.

meaning: “he took a photo / he took a picture.”
additional_notes: In Portuguese, you usually say tirar uma foto (literally “to take/throw out a photo”) to mean “to take a photo.” In real use you’ll change the subject: eu tirei uma foto (I took a photo), ela tirou uma foto (she took a photo), etc. You can add details with de: tirou uma foto da família (a photo of the family), tirou uma foto dele mesmo (a photo of himself).
target_language_example: Ele tirou uma foto do documento e mandou para mim.
native_language_example: He took a photo of the document and sent it to me.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "trabalhar" (to work) conjugated for "ele" (he). Portuguese often drops the subject pronoun when it’s clear from context, so you may also hear just "Trabalha muito" (He works a lot). Can describe a general habit, a current situation, or someone’s job.
target_language_example: Ele trabalha em um hospital.
native_language_example: He works in a hospital.
