meaning: 'he goes' or 'he is going to' (he will).
additional_notes: Commonly used with another verb in the infinitive to talk about the near future: "Ele vai + infinitive" = "He is going to ..." (Ele vai jogar = He’s going to play). Depending on context, it can also mean literal movement: "Ele vai ao mercado" = "He goes/is going to the market."
target_language_example: Ele vai comprar pão mais tarde.
native_language_example: He’s going to buy bread later.

additional_notes: "Ele" = "he". "Veio" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "vir" (to come). It’s used for a completed action in the past and is often followed by where/from/how someone came: "veio até aqui" (came up to here), "veio de ônibus" (came by bus), "veio para casa" (came home).
target_language_example: Ele veio cedo, mas eu ainda não estava pronto.
native_language_example: He came early, but I still wasn’t ready.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of voltar: it indicates that he returned and the action is finished. Often used with destinations: voltou para casa/para o Japão (“returned home/to Japan”) and with origin: voltou da Holanda (“came back from Holland”). As an exclamation (“Ele voltou!”) it can mean “He’s back!”
target_language_example: Ele voltou para casa ontem à noite.
native_language_example: He came back home last night.

additional_notes: Refers to a man (ele) who returned to his home. Use it to say someone went back home after being away; it often appears with time expressions (e.g., muito tarde, há alguns instantes) or details about the trip (e.g., via Hong Kong). In everyday speech you may also hear: “ele voltou pra casa” (pra = para a).
target_language_example: Quando acabou o trabalho, ele voltou para casa de ônibus.
native_language_example: When work ended, he went back home by bus.

meaning: 'he is' (used to describe or identify a man/boy).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective or noun to say what he is like or what he is: Ele é atraente (He's attractive), Ele é louco por... (He's crazy about...), Ele é membro... (He's a member...), Ele é viciado em... (He's addicted to...). In Portuguese you often drop the subject pronoun; you can also just say "É atraente" if it's clear who you're talking about.
target_language_example: Ele é muito simpático, mas hoje ele está cansado.
native_language_example: He is very nice, but today he is tired.

meaning: "he is the last person" (the least likely / least wanted person).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone is the least appropriate, least expected, or least desired person for something: **Ele é a última pessoa (para / com quem / que...)**. It’s often figurative (not literally “last in a line”). Note: **última** usually means **“last”**, not “ultimate.”
target_language_example: Ele é a última pessoa em quem eu confiaria com esse segredo.
native_language_example: He’s the last person I’d trust with that secret.

additional_notes: Use it to describe a male person with an adjective: "Ele é muito" + adjective (cuidadoso, honesto, jovem). With expressions like "sensível ao frio" it means he is very sensitive to the cold. The same pattern works with other subjects: "ela é muito" (she is very), "você é muito" (you are very).
target_language_example: Ele é muito simpático com todo mundo.
native_language_example: He is very nice to everyone.

meaning: 'he is the' (used to identify or define who someone is).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun or title to say who someone is: a name (Ele é o Tim.), a role/job (Ele é o capitão da equipe.), or a description (Ele é o verdadeiro idiota.). You can also use it with superlatives like “o mais…” (“the most…”). For feminine nouns, use “ela é a”.
target_language_example: Ele é o responsável pelo projeto.
native_language_example: He is the person in charge of the project.

meaning: "he is a" / "he is an" (used to describe what a man/boy is).
additional_notes: Used with a noun phrase to identify or describe a male person (profession, role, or type of person): "Ele é um escoteiro" (He is a scout). The article "um" is masculine; for a female person you usually use "Ela é uma...". You can also put adjectives before the noun: "Ele é um ótimo professor" (He’s a great teacher).
target_language_example: Ele é um bom amigo.
native_language_example: He is a good friend.

meaning: 'he is a good …' (talking about a man).
additional_notes: Used to describe a man positively before a masculine singular noun (bom + noun): "Ele é um bom advogado." The adjective "bom" agrees with the noun; for feminine it changes to "Ela é uma boa …" and for plural "Eles/Elas são bons/boas …".
target_language_example: Ele é um bom professor.
native_language_example: He is a good teacher.

additional_notes: Used to say a man/boy is extremely intelligent or talented. It can be literal (real genius) or sometimes enthusiastic praise (like 'he’s brilliant'). For a woman, say "ela é um gênio". In Brazilian Portuguese, "gênio" can also mean someone’s temper/mood ("mau gênio" = bad temper), but in this phrase it means 'genius'.
target_language_example: Na escola, todo mundo diz que ele é um gênio.
native_language_example: At school, everyone says he is a genius.

additional_notes: Used to describe a male person, often followed by an adjective or phrase that characterizes him (e.g., "de poucas palavras" = "of few words", "enérgico" = "energetic"). You can swap "ele" for a name ("João é um homem...") or change the gender: "ela é uma mulher" (she is a woman).
target_language_example: Ele é um homem honesto e trabalhador.
native_language_example: He is an honest and hard-working man.

meaning: 'he is a person' / 'he’s a … person' (to describe what he’s like).
additional_notes: Often followed by an adjective to describe someone’s personality or character: "Ele é uma pessoa cruel/estranha/quieta." In an exclamation ("Ele é uma pessoa!"), it can mean something like "He’s quite a character!" depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Ele é uma pessoa muito gentil com todo mundo.
native_language_example: He’s a very kind person with everyone.

additional_notes: "Eles" = "they" (masculine or mixed group). "Eram" is the imperfect past of "ser" (to be), used for descriptions/background in the past (age, personality, states) and in "I didn’t know (that) they were..." statements.
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, eles eram meus vizinhos.
native_language_example: When I was a child, they were my neighbors.

additional_notes: Used with **estar** to describe a past state or condition (“they were tired/weak”) or an ongoing action in the past when followed by a **gerund** (-ndo): “eles estavam rindo” = “they were laughing.” It’s the **imperfect** tense, often implying something was happening/true for a while in the past.
target_language_example: Quando cheguei, eles estavam esperando na porta.
native_language_example: When I arrived, they were waiting at the door.

additional_notes: Used with a location (where they are: "Eles estão no caminho") or a temporary state/condition ("Eles estão cansados" = They are tired). It's the verb "estar" (to be) for temporary states and locations, not "ser" (more permanent identity/traits).
target_language_example: Eles estão em casa agora.
native_language_example: They are at home now.

additional_notes: "Eles" = "they". "Foram" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "ir" (to go) and also of "ser" (to be). In passive sentences it often appears with a past participle to mean "were" (e.g., "foram escolhidos" = "were chosen"). With adjectives, it can mean "were" in the past ("foram felizes" = "they were happy"). Context tells you whether it’s "went" or "were".
target_language_example: Eles foram ao cinema ontem.
native_language_example: They went to the movies yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to report information someone gave you. "Eles" = "they" (plural), "me" = "to me", "disseram" is the past tense of "dizer" (to say/tell), and "que" introduces what they said ("that"). In everyday speech, "me disseram" can also appear as "disseram-me" (more formal/European style).
target_language_example: Eles me disseram que o restaurante já estava fechado.
native_language_example: They told me that the restaurant was already closed.

meaning: “they don’t / they aren’t / they didn’t” (they + not).
additional_notes: Used to negate a statement about “they” (a group of males or a mixed group). In Portuguese, **não** typically comes right before the verb: **Eles não são...** (“They aren’t...”), **Eles não tinham...** (“They didn’t have...”). It can also appear in questions: **Eles não são uma boa diversão?** often means “Aren’t they fun?” or “Don’t they make good company?” depending on context.
target_language_example: Eles não querem ir agora.
native_language_example: They don’t want to go now.

meaning: “they don’t have” (they do not possess / there isn’t, for them).
additional_notes: Used to say that a group of people/animals/things (eles) lacks something or does not possess it. Very common with nouns: “eles não têm dinheiro/emprego/filhos”. In Portuguese, “não têm” is the negative of “têm” (they have).
target_language_example: Eles não têm tempo hoje.
native_language_example: They don’t have time today.

additional_notes: "O" is an unstressed direct-object pronoun meaning “him” (for a man/boy) or “it” (for a masculine noun). In Portuguese it often comes before the verb: "Eles o prenderam" = “They arrested him.” (In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many speakers might instead say "Eles prenderam ele", but "eles o" is more formal/standard.)
target_language_example: Eles o viram na estação.
native_language_example: They saw him at the station.

additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive to say what “they want to do” (e.g., eles querem saber = they want to know; eles querem adotar = they want to adopt). Often appears in questions like “O que é que eles querem…?” = “What do they want…?”
target_language_example: Eles querem ir embora agora.
native_language_example: They want to leave now.

additional_notes: Used when the subject is plural (eles = they) and the action is reflexive (they did it to themselves) or reciprocal (they did it to each other). Very common with verbs like: eles se amam (they love each other), eles se aceitaram (they accepted each other), eles se transformaram (they turned into…). In writing, the pronoun typically comes right before the verb: eles se + verbo.
target_language_example: Depois da discussão, eles se desculparam.
native_language_example: After the argument, they apologized to each other.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "casar-se". "Se" is a reflexive pronoun here, meaning the action happens between them (they married each other). Very often followed by time or place: "em" + place/date/month (e.g., "em Las Vegas", "em maio"). In questions you’ll often see: "Quando eles se casaram?" (When did they get married?).
target_language_example: Eles se casaram no ano passado.
native_language_example: They got married last year.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (to be) to identify or describe what people/things are. Often appears in questions like “O que eles são?” (“What are they?”). For an all-female group, use “elas são”.
target_language_example: Eles são brasileiros.
native_language_example: They are Brazilian.

meaning: “they go” / “they are going to” (future with ir + infinitive).
additional_notes: "Eles" = "they". "Vão" is the present tense of "ir" (to go) for "they". It’s often used as the near-future pattern "eles vão" + infinitive (e.g., "eles vão ajudar" = "they’re going to help"). It can also mean simple movement/going somewhere when followed by a place or context.
target_language_example: Eles vão chegar mais cedo hoje.
native_language_example: They’re going to arrive earlier today.

additional_notes: Used to report what “they” (a group of people) said. After **que** you usually put a full clause, often in the past (e.g., *foi*, *nunca viram*) or in the future/conditional (*fariam*, *vamos ter*, *virão*). In everyday speech you can also say **disseram que** when it’s clear who “they” are.
target_language_example: Eles disseram que não tinham tempo hoje.
native_language_example: They said that they didn’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to report hearsay or a general rumor, without saying who exactly. Often introduces information you didn’t verify yourself. In speech you may also hear the shorter “dizem que…” (“they say…”).
target_language_example: Eles dizem que vai chover amanhã.
native_language_example: They say it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **fazer** for **eles/elas/vocês**. Used for completed actions in the past. **Fazer** can mean “to do” (tasks/activities: *fizeram o dever de casa*) or “to make” (something created or done: *fizeram uma promessa*). It’s also common in set phrases like *fizeram as pazes* (“they made up”).
target_language_example: Eles fizeram tudo o que podiam.
native_language_example: They did everything they could.

additional_notes: "Eles" = "they". "Foram" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "ir" (to go) and also of "ser" (to be). In passive sentences it often appears with a past participle to mean "were" (e.g., "foram escolhidos" = "were chosen"). With adjectives, it can mean "were" in the past ("foram felizes" = "they were happy"). Context tells you whether it’s "went" or "were".
target_language_example: Eles foram ao cinema ontem.
native_language_example: They went to the movies yesterday.

meaning: “they like” / “they enjoy” (followed by a noun or a verb in the infinitive).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "de" after "gostar": "Eles gostam de + [noun]" (They like + noun) or "Eles gostam de + [infinitive verb]" (They like/enjoy + -ing). To say what they don’t like, use "Eles não gostam de...".
target_language_example: Eles gostam de música brasileira.
native_language_example: They like Brazilian music.

additional_notes: Used to say that a group of people (eles = “they”) needs something. With precisar, Portuguese normally uses de before a noun or pronoun: precisar de ajuda (to need help), precisar de voluntários (to need volunteers).
target_language_example: Eles precisam de mais tempo para terminar o trabalho.
native_language_example: They need more time to finish the work.

additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive to say what “they want to do” (e.g., eles querem saber = they want to know; eles querem adotar = they want to adopt). Often appears in questions like “O que é que eles querem…?” = “What do they want…?”
target_language_example: Eles querem ir embora agora.
native_language_example: They want to leave now.

meaning: “they have” / “they’ve got” (and in “eles têm que…”, “they have to…”).
additional_notes: "Eles" = "they" and "têm" is the present tense of "ter" (to have) for "they". It’s used for possession (Eles têm dois gatos.), for having an amount of something (Eles têm bastante tempo.), and in the common structure "ter que + infinitive" to express obligation/necessity: "Eles têm que se comportar" = "They have to behave."
target_language_example: Eles têm que sair agora.
native_language_example: They have to leave now.

meaning: “they have a” (for a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "ter" (to have). "têm" is the present tense for "eles/elas/vocês" (they/you all). "um" means "a/an" for a masculine singular noun; for feminine you’d use "uma".
target_language_example: Eles têm um carro novo.
native_language_example: They have a new car.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is written, spoken, or done using French. Common after verbs like falar (to speak), escrever (to write), dizer (to say), colocar (to put), and aprender (to learn). Portuguese also uses similar patterns with other languages: em inglês, em espanhol, em português.
target_language_example: Você pode repetir isso em Francês, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you repeat that in French, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a place that isn’t known, isn’t important to specify, or hasn’t been decided yet. Very common with verbs like estar (to be), ir (to go), encontrar-se (to meet), and with questions like "Você viu...?".
target_language_example: Acho que deixei meu celular em algum lugar aqui em casa.
native_language_example: I think I left my phone somewhere here at home.

meaning: somewhere around here (nearby, but not exactly sure where).
additional_notes: Used when you know something/someone is in the general area, but you don’t know the exact location. Very common with verbs like "ficar" (to be located), "morar" (to live), "estar" (to be), and "perder" (to lose). Word-by-word: "em" (in) + "algum lugar" (some place) + "por aqui" (around here).
target_language_example: O banheiro deve ser em algum lugar por aqui.
native_language_example: The bathroom should be somewhere around here.

meaning: in trouble; in a difficult situation.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (e.g., "estar em apuros") to say someone is in trouble or has a serious problem (often needing help). It can refer to legal trouble, financial trouble, or just being in a bad situation.
target_language_example: Se você não pagar a tempo, vai ficar em apuros.
native_language_example: If you don’t pay on time, you’ll be in trouble.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen in the near future. Common with future or near-future expressions (e.g., "vou", "devo", "provavelmente"). It can also mean "in short" in some contexts, but the most common beginner meaning is time-related: "soon".
target_language_example: Eu volto em breve.
native_language_example: I'll be back soon.

additional_notes: Used with nouns to express that someone is trying to find something or going somewhere with the goal of finding it (often a solution, adventure, evidence, a place to live, etc.). Common after verbs like ir/andar/viajar/procurar (e.g., "foi em busca de...").
target_language_example: Ela veio à cidade em busca de trabalho.
native_language_example: She came to the city in search of work.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is at home (not out/at work/school) specifically today. Common with the verb "estar" (temporary state): "estou/está/estão em casa hoje". You can also use "ficar" to mean 'stay'/'remain': "vou ficar em casa hoje".
target_language_example: Não posso sair; vou ficar em casa hoje.
native_language_example: I can’t go out; I’m going to stay home today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" to describe something burning (often strongly): "está em chamas". It can describe objects, vehicles, buildings, or places. With verbs like "entrar" it means "to catch fire" (e.g., "entrou em chamas").
target_language_example: O prédio está em chamas; chame os bombeiros!
native_language_example: The building is on fire; call the firefighters!

additional_notes: Used to indicate position or placement on a surface or at a higher point: em cima da cadeira (on the chair), em cima da colina (on top of the hill). Often contrasts with embaixo de/da (under/below). Contraction: em + a = na, so you’ll often see em cima da (feminine singular), em cima do (masculine singular), em cima das/dos (plural).
target_language_example: Deixe o livro em cima da mesa, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the book on the table, please.

meaning: on top of the wallet (or purse).
additional_notes: "Em cima de" means "on (top of)" in the sense of something resting above and touching another object. "Carteira" can mean a wallet/purse; in other contexts it can also mean a school desk or a portfolio, but in these examples it’s a wallet/purse. You can swap in other nouns: "em cima da mesa" (on the table), "em cima do livro" (on top of the book).
target_language_example: Deixei meu celular em cima da carteira.
native_language_example: I left my phone on top of the wallet.

meaning: on top of the table; on the table (resting on its surface).
additional_notes: Literally “on top of the table.” Use it to say that something is located resting on the table’s surface (a book, plates, a tablecloth, etc.). In everyday speech it often corresponds to English “on the table.”
target_language_example: Deixa as chaves em cima da mesa, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the keys on the table, please.

meaning: on top of the table; on the table (resting on its surface).
additional_notes: Literally “on top of the table.” Use it to say that something is located resting on the table’s surface (a book, plates, a tablecloth, etc.). In everyday speech it often corresponds to English “on the table.”
target_language_example: Deixa as chaves em cima da mesa, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the keys on the table, please.

meaning: “to meet you” (addressing a woman, formal/polite) / “to meet her”.
additional_notes: Used mainly in the structure “(É) um prazer em conhecê-la” or “Prazer em conhecê-la,” meaning “(It’s a) pleasure to meet you.” Here, “em” + infinitive (“conhecer”) is a common way to say “to …” after words like “prazer” (pleasure). “-la” is the object pronoun “her/you (female, formal).”
target_language_example: É um prazer em conhecê-la pessoalmente.
native_language_example: It’s a pleasure to meet you in person.

meaning: in contact with; to get in touch with.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "estar/ficar/manter-se" (to be/stay/keep in contact) and "entrar" (to contact/get in touch). Often refers to communication by phone, email, message, etc.: "entrar em contato com alguém".
target_language_example: Vou entrar em contato com você amanhã.
native_language_example: I’ll get in touch with you tomorrow.

meaning: in ten minutes; within ten minutes (after 10 minutes).
additional_notes: Used to talk about how long something takes (duration) or when something will happen (in 10 minutes from now). In schedules, you’ll also see the pattern “de X em X” meaning “every X” (e.g., “de dez em dez minutos” = “every ten minutes”).
target_language_example: A reunião começa em dez minutos.
native_language_example: The meeting starts in ten minutes.

meaning: toward; in the direction of (to the).
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or orientation toward a specific masculine singular place/person/thing introduced by "o" (ao = a + o). With feminine nouns, use "em direção à" (à = a + a): "em direção à praia". Common with verbs of motion like "ir", "correr", "caminhar".
target_language_example: O ônibus vai em direção ao centro.
native_language_example: The bus goes toward downtown.

meaning: toward the door / in the direction of the door.
additional_notes: Used to describe movement or orientation toward a place. Common with verbs of movement (ir, correr, seguir, mover-se) and also with gestures (acenou com a cabeça em direção à porta = nodded toward the door). Here, "à" is the contraction of "a" + "a" (feminine singular), because "porta" is feminine: em direção a + a porta → em direção à porta.
target_language_example: Ela caminhou em direção à porta e saiu sem dizer nada.
native_language_example: She walked toward the door and left without saying anything.

additional_notes: Used after many verbs/adjectives that take the preposition **em** before an infinitive, like **concordar em** (agree to), **sonhar em** (dream of/about), **hesitante em** (hesitant to/about), **melhor em** (better at). In English it often becomes “to do that” or “doing that,” depending on the context.
target_language_example: Ela insistiu em fazer isso sozinha.
native_language_example: She insisted on doing that alone.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like falar/conversar/escrever/ler to say what language something is spoken or written in, or with a noun to describe something that is in that language (e.g., "um livro em francês"). Also common when talking about studying a language ("me especializar em francês").
target_language_example: Você pode explicar isso em francês?
native_language_example: Can you explain that in French?

additional_notes: Common with verbs like "seguir" or "ir" to mean "to move on / continue" ("seguir em frente"). It can also mean "in front (of)" in locations: "em frente de/do/da". As an encouragement, "vá/vão em frente!" means "go ahead!" (permission or urging someone to proceed).
target_language_example: Pode ir em frente; eu vou te alcançar depois.
native_language_example: You can go ahead; I’ll catch up with you later.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a position directly before a place/thing, often outside it (e.g., in front of a building) or facing it (e.g., in front of a mirror). It contracts with masculine singular nouns: em + frente + a + o = em frente ao. With feminine singular: em frente à; plural: em frente aos / em frente às.
target_language_example: O café fica em frente ao banco.
native_language_example: The café is in front of the bank.

additional_notes: Used to locate something directly in front of another place/object (often a building): *em frente à casa/loja*. It can also mean “opposite” in the sense of facing across a street or space. In Brazilian Portuguese it’s commonly followed by the article: *em frente à* (= *em frente a + a*), *em frente ao* (= *a + o*), *em frente aos/às*.
target_language_example: O ponto de ônibus fica em frente ao supermercado.
native_language_example: The bus stop is in front of the supermarket.

additional_notes: Location phrase. "em frente a" means "in front of" (facing something). With a feminine singular noun like "a escola", it contracts to "à" (= a + a). You can swap in other places: "em frente ao banco" (in front of the bank), "em frente à minha casa" (in front of my house).
target_language_example: Vou esperar por você em frente à escola.
native_language_example: I’ll wait for you in front of the school.

additional_notes: Used to give a location: something is directly opposite/at the front side of the station. "em frente a" + "a" often contracts to "à" before a feminine noun like "a estação".
target_language_example: O café fica em frente à estação de metrô.
native_language_example: The café is in front of the subway station.

additional_notes: Used to make a broad, general statement (a generalization) about men. Em geral = “in general / generally”. Often followed by a comparative: mais … do que/que (“more … than”). The comma after em geral is common but optional in short sentences.
target_language_example: Em geral, os homens são mais pesados do que as mulheres.
native_language_example: In general, men are heavier than women.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is spoken, written, read, or done using the English language. It often comes after the verb (falar/escrever/ler em inglês), and it can also describe a noun (frases em inglês = phrases in English).
target_language_example: Você consegue explicar isso em inglês?
native_language_example: Can you explain that in English?

em ir fazer compras com a

target_language_multi_word_term: em ir fazer compras com a
additional_notes: This chunk often appears after verbs that require the preposition “em”, especially **insistir em** (“to insist on”). **Ir fazer compras** means “to go shopping” (literally “to go do shopping”), and **com a** means “with the” before a feminine noun (e.g., *com a mãe* = “with (the) mom”). In full sentences, it’s typically followed by a feminine person/thing: *com a mãe / com a sua mãe / com a professora*.
target_language_example: Ele insistiu em ir fazer compras com a irmã.
native_language_example: He insisted on going shopping with his sister.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened during the month of June. "em" is the common preposition for months in Portuguese (em janeiro, em fevereiro, etc.).
target_language_example: Vamos viajar em junho.
native_language_example: We’re going to travel in June.

meaning: in less than (a period of time).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens within a shorter time than the amount mentioned. It’s followed by a time expression (e.g., um minuto, uma semana, dois anos, três meses). Often answers “How long did it take?” or “When will it happen?”
target_language_example: Eu termino o trabalho em menos de uma hora.
native_language_example: I’ll finish the work in less than an hour.

meaning: in my heart (in my feelings; deeply cared about).
additional_notes: Used to express strong affection, love, or emotional importance. Common in romantic, family, or heartfelt contexts (e.g., remembering someone, saying they matter to you). You can change the possessive: em seu coração (in your heart), em nosso coração (in our hearts).
target_language_example: Mesmo longe, você está em meu coração todos os dias.
native_language_example: Even far away, you’re in my heart every day.

meaning: in me; on me; about me.
additional_notes: Preposition + stressed pronoun: em + mim (never *em eu*). Use it after verbs that take **em** (e.g., *confiar em* = to trust, *pensar em* = to think about) and to say how clothes/items fit **on** your body (*fica bem/ruim/apertada/folgada em mim*). Also used for thoughts/feelings directed at you (*pensar em mim*).
target_language_example: Você pode confiar em mim.
native_language_example: You can trust me.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your personal view (similar to “I think” or “as far as I’m concerned”). It can come at the start of the sentence or be inserted in the middle, often set off by commas. Also commonly said as “na minha opinião” and, more formally, “em minha opinião”.
target_language_example: Em minha opinião, este filme é bom, mas é muito longo.
native_language_example: In my opinion, this movie is good, but it’s too long.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true in a lot of countries (not necessarily all). Often appears at the start of a sentence to give general context ("Em muitos países, ..."), or after a verb to describe where something happens ("é falado em muitos países").
target_language_example: Em muitos países, as pessoas falam mais de uma língua.
native_language_example: In many countries, people speak more than one language.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like colocar, ordenar, or organizar to say a list, words, names, or files should be arranged A–Z (or by the alphabet). Common in instructions: “Coloque X em ordem alfabética.”
target_language_example: Você pode colocar os nomes em ordem alfabética?
native_language_example: Can you put the names in alphabetical order?

additional_notes: Used to say a person/thing is in a different location, or to suggest moving the conversation/activity to a different place. Often used with verbs like estar/ficar (to be/stay), ir (to go), or conversar (to talk).
target_language_example: Vamos comer em outro lugar.
native_language_example: Let’s eat somewhere else.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something existing or happening somewhere other than Earth. Common with verbs like existir/haver (“to exist/there is/are”) and with the topic “vida” (life): “Há/Existe vida em outros planetas?” “Em” + place = “in/on/at” depending on context; here it’s best translated as “on”.
target_language_example: Os cientistas procuram sinais de vida em outros planetas.
native_language_example: Scientists look for signs of life on other planets.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened (or will happen) during the month of October. Common with past and future events: "aconteceu em outubro" (happened in October), "vai acontecer em outubro" (will happen in October).
target_language_example: As aulas começam em outubro.
native_language_example: Classes start in October.

additional_notes: Used when you want to speak away from other people, often to discuss something personal, sensitive, or confidential. It commonly follows verbs like falar (to speak) and conversar (to talk): “falar com alguém em particular”.
target_language_example: Depois da reunião, posso falar com você em particular?
native_language_example: After the meeting, can I speak with you in private?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is not fighting and wants peace (often in phrases like “vir em paz” = “come in peace”), or to describe a situation/relationship without conflict (“viver em paz com…” = “live in peace with…”).
target_language_example: Quero viver em paz com meus vizinhos.
native_language_example: I want to live in peace with my neighbors.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar (e.g., "estar em perigo") to say someone is in a dangerous situation or at risk of harm. Common in warnings and emergencies ("Você está em perigo!").
target_language_example: Não te aproximes do fogo — estás em perigo.
native_language_example: Don’t go near the fire—you’re in danger.

additional_notes: Used to describe photos, movies, or images without color, or (more broadly) a way of seeing things as having only two options (no nuance). With verbs like "ver"/"enxergar" it means someone sees without color.
target_language_example: Prefiro o filme em preto e branco.
native_language_example: I prefer the movie in black and white.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "estar" (to be) or "entrar" (to go into) to describe a sudden state of fear/anxiety and loss of calm. Common in warnings/advice: "Não entre em pânico" = "Don’t panic."
target_language_example: Quando ouvi o alarme, fiquei em pânico.
native_language_example: When I heard the alarm, I panicked.

meaning: "in which" (asking which place/option something is in).
additional_notes: Used in questions with the preposition "em" + "qual" to ask which specific location/container/option (city, office, hotel, shelf, etc.) something is in. It agrees with the noun: "em qual" (singular) / "em quais" (plural). Often interchangeable with "em que" in everyday speech (e.g., "Em que cidade mora?").
target_language_example: Em qual rua fica o restaurante?
native_language_example: On which street is the restaurant?

additional_notes: Used to say there is no specific location (it doesn’t matter where). Often appears with relative phrases like “em qualquer lugar onde...” (“anywhere where...”) or “em qualquer lugar que...” (“wherever...”). In questions it can sound like “wherever you are?”.
target_language_example: Você pode me ligar em qualquer lugar, eu atendo.
native_language_example: You can call me anywhere, I’ll answer.

meaning: “in which / where” (asking or specifying the place, time, or situation something is in).
additional_notes: Used in questions like “Em que rua?” = “On which street?” and “Em que ano...?” = “In which year...?” It can also introduce a relative clause meaning “in which/where” (e.g., “o ano em que nasceram” = “the year in which they were born”). Often translates as “where” when talking about places.
target_language_example: Em que bairro você mora?
native_language_example: Which neighborhood do you live in?

em que ano da faculdade de medicina

target_language_multi_word_term: em que ano da faculdade de medicina
meaning: “what year of medical school (are you in)?”
additional_notes: Used to ask which year/stage someone is currently in within a medical degree program. It’s a question fragment that usually needs a verb like “você está” / “tu estás” / “vocês estão” (“are you”). You can swap the program: “em que ano da faculdade” (what year of college/university) or “em que ano de medicina” (what year of med school).
target_language_example: Em que ano da faculdade de medicina você está?
native_language_example: What year of medical school are you in?

additional_notes: Used after adjectives like rico/pobre/abundante (or phrases like sem igual) to specify what the country is rich/poor/abundant in. Common pattern: “ser + adjective + em + [noun]” (e.g., “rico em…”, “pobre em…”).
target_language_example: O Brasil é muito rico em recursos naturais.
native_language_example: Brazil is very rich in natural resources.

additional_notes: "Em" + "seu" expresses location or context associated with a masculine singular noun: "em seu quintal" (in his yard), "em seu tempo livre" (in his free time). It can mean "his" or "its" depending on what "seu" refers to, and it can also be formal "your" (referring to "você"), though in everyday Brazilian Portuguese people often use "dele/dela" to avoid ambiguity.
target_language_example: Ela guardou o celular em seu bolso.
native_language_example: She put her phone in her pocket.

additional_notes: Literally “in your room,” but in Portuguese the possessive "seu" can mean "his," "her," "your" (formal), or "their". Context usually makes it clear; if needed, speakers may use "no quarto dele/dela" to be specific.
target_language_example: Ela ficou em seu quarto o dia todo.
native_language_example: She stayed in her room all day.

additional_notes: Used to describe something visible on someone’s face (a smile, an expression) or something applied to the face (e.g., water). It agrees with the person: em meu rosto (on my face), em seu rosto (on your face / on his/her face), em nosso rosto (on our face), em seus rostos (on your/their faces).
target_language_example: Havia preocupação em seu rosto.
native_language_example: There was worry on his/her face.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like pegar, tomar, carregar, segurar to mean holding or carrying someone in one’s arms (often romantic or protective). "Seus" agrees with the person who is doing the holding; it can mean "his," "her," "your" (formal), or "their" depending on context. You may also see "em meus braços" (in my arms) or "em seus próprios braços" (in their own arms).
target_language_example: Ela adormeceu em seus braços.
native_language_example: She fell asleep in his arms.

additional_notes: Used after verbs and expressions like "acreditar" (to believe), "pensar" (to think), and "ter confiança" (to have confidence) to refer back to the subject. It can change with gender/number: "em si mesma" (herself), "em si próprios/mesmos" (themselves). Common in fixed phrases like "acreditar em si mesmo" = "believe in yourself."
target_language_example: Você precisa confiar mais em si mesmo.
native_language_example: You need to trust yourself more.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like ficar, estar, permanecer, ouvir, and trabalhar to say someone is quiet or something happens with no talking/noise. Often describes a temporary state: "ficar em silêncio" = "to fall/go quiet."
target_language_example: Por favor, fiquem em silêncio durante o filme.
native_language_example: Please stay quiet during the movie.

meaning: in/on/at his, her, or your (formal) (feminine noun).
additional_notes: "Em" is a preposition meaning "in/on/at" depending on context. "Sua" means "his/her/your (formal)" and agrees with a feminine noun (e.g., "sua mesa", "sua casa"). It can refer to "his" or "her"; if you need to be clearer, Portuguese often uses "dele" (his) / "dela" (hers).
target_language_example: Ela deixou o celular em sua bolsa.
native_language_example: She left her phone in her bag.

additional_notes: Literally means something is physically being held (e.g., a book, a drink). It’s also used figuratively to say someone controls or is responsible for something ("My future is in your hands") or to blame someone for harm ("You have their blood on your hands"). The possessive (suas) can mean your, his, her, or their depending on context; in Brazil people often use "nas suas mãos" or "em suas mãos" with the same idea.
target_language_example: Agora a decisão está em suas mãos.
native_language_example: Now the decision is in your hands.

meaning: 'in you' / 'in you (singular, informal)' after certain verbs (e.g., believe, trust, be interested).
additional_notes: "Em ti" is used with verbs that take the preposition "em" + a person, especially "confiar em" (to trust), "acreditar em" (to believe in), and "estar interessado/a em" (to be interested in). "Ti" is the object form used with "tu" (you, informal singular).
target_language_example: Eu confio em ti.
native_language_example: I trust you.

additional_notes: Used to say something is in many places or throughout an area. Very common with verbs like estar (to be), encontrar (to find), procurar (to look for), aparecer (to appear). You can also say "por toda parte" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Deixei meus óculos em casa e procurei em toda a parte.
native_language_example: I left my glasses at home and looked everywhere.

meaning: in all the / in every (plural feminine).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens or exists in every case/place/item within a group. It’s the preposition “em” (in/on/at) + “todas as” (all the, feminine plural). It must be followed by a feminine plural noun (e.g., línguas, redes sociais, estações, direções). For masculine plural, use “em todos os”.
target_language_example: Ele para em todas as cidades pequenas no caminho.
native_language_example: It stops in every small town along the way.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is true globally/in many countries. Often with verbs like "ser conhecido" (to be known), "ser falado" (to be spoken), "ser estudado" (to be studied), etc.
target_language_example: Esse filme fez sucesso em todo o mundo.
native_language_example: That movie was a hit all over the world.

additional_notes: Used to say something applies to each item in a plural set: em todos os dedos (on all the fingers), em todos os aspectos (in all aspects), em todos os tipos (in all kinds of). It’s followed by a plural masculine noun; for feminine, use "em todas as" (e.g., em todas as cidades).
target_language_example: Há câmeras em todos os quartos do hotel.
native_language_example: There are cameras in all the hotel rooms.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or can be found in many places, with no specific location. Common with verbs like estar/ir/andar/olhar/encontrar (to be/go/walk or ride/look/find). It can emphasize thoroughness ("They looked everywhere") or general presence ("People like us are everywhere").
target_language_example: Eu vejo essas placas em todos os lugares.
native_language_example: I see those signs everywhere.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something surrounding something else (physical) or moving in a circular path around it (orbiting). It’s a contraction: em torno de + o = em torno do. With other articles: em torno da (de + a), em torno dos (de + os), em torno das (de + as).
target_language_example: As crianças correram em torno do parque.
native_language_example: The kids ran around the park.

meaning: in everything that; in all that.
additional_notes: Used to refer to all the things within a category or situation, followed by a verb clause: “em tudo o que + (subject) + verb”. Often used with verbs like acreditar (to believe), fazer (to do), dizer (to say), esforçar-se (to make an effort). It’s a literal combination of em (in) + tudo (everything) + o que (that/what).
target_language_example: Eu confio em tudo o que você faz.
native_language_example: I trust everything you do.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: em um foguete (in a rocket), em um prato (on a plate), em um hotel (in a hotel). In everyday Portuguese it’s often contracted to "num" (e.g., "Trabalho num hotel"). Which English preposition fits best depends on the noun (in a hotel vs. on a plate).
target_language_example: Moro em um apartamento pequeno.
native_language_example: I live in a small apartment.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened as a result of a car crash/traffic accident. Common after verbs like morrer/falecer (“to die”) and ser morto (“to be killed”). Also appears as em + um/uma + acidente de + [vehicle]: em um acidente de moto, em um acidente de ônibus. In Portugal, you’ll often hear num acidente de carro (em + um = num).
target_language_example: Ela ficou ferida em um acidente de carro ontem à noite.
native_language_example: She was injured in a car accident last night.

additional_notes: Used with events that happened because of a road/vehicle accident (car, motorcycle, etc.). Common with verbs like "morrer" (to die), "ser morto" (to be killed), "se ferir" (to get injured), and "quebrar" (to break). Also appears as "num acidente de trânsito" (in a traffic accident) in speech/writing.
target_language_example: Ela se feriu em um acidente de trânsito, mas já está melhor.
native_language_example: She was injured in a traffic accident, but she's already better.

additional_notes: Used for location: someone is seated on a bench. In Portugal you’ll often see the contraction “num banco” (= em um banco). Don’t confuse with “um banco” meaning “a bank” (financial institution); context like “sentado” usually makes it clear it’s a bench.
target_language_example: Ela estava sentada em um banco no parque.
native_language_example: She was sitting on a bench in the park.

meaning: in one day; (sometimes) one day / someday.
additional_notes: Most often used for a time limit or duration: doing something within 24 hours ("finish it in one day"). In some contexts (especially with verbs like "sonhar", "esperar"), it can mean "one day" in the sense of "someday" ("Sonho em um dia..." = "I dream that one day..."). Also appears as "em um só dia" for extra emphasis.
target_language_example: Acho que consigo resolver isso em um dia.
native_language_example: I think I can solve this in one day.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens. "em" = in/at, "um" = a (masculine singular), "restaurante" = restaurant. In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, you’ll also often hear "num restaurante" (contraction of "em um").
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar em um restaurante perto do hotel.
native_language_example: Let’s meet in a restaurant near the hotel.

additional_notes: Used to place something/someone inside or at a location, situation, or event: em uma fazenda (on a farm), em uma queda (in a fall), em uma agência (at a travel agency). It’s the preposition "em" + the indefinite article "uma" (for feminine nouns). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, it’s often contracted to "numa" (same meaning).
target_language_example: Eu moro em uma cidade pequena.
native_language_example: I live in a small city.

meaning: in a house; at a house (inside a house).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like morar/viver/entrar to indicate being or going inside a particular (not necessarily specified) house. "Em" + "uma" (feminine singular of "um/uma" = "a/an"). In Portuguese you often say "em casa" to mean "at home" in general, but "em uma casa" means "in a (specific/unspecified) house" (e.g., not necessarily your own).
target_language_example: Eles passaram a noite em uma casa perto da praia.
native_language_example: They spent the night in a house near the beach.

meaning: in a small town (in a small city).
additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives/grew up/was born. Very common with verbs like "morar" (to live), "crescer" (to grow up), and "nascer" (to be born). "Uma" is the feminine form of "a" meaning "a/one"; you can also hear "numa cidade pequena" (= "em uma").
target_language_example: Ela mora em uma cidade pequena no interior.
native_language_example: She lives in a small town in the countryside.

meaning: in one hour; in an hour (from now).
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen one hour from the present moment (a future time). Very common with the future tense or near-future expressions. Also appears as "em 1 hora" or "em uma hora"; in casual speech you may hear "numa hora" (= em + uma).
target_language_example: A reunião começa em uma hora.
native_language_example: The meeting starts in an hour.

additional_notes: Often used in hypothetical questions like “If you were stuck/stranded on a deserted island…”. You may also hear “numa ilha deserta” (same meaning; contraction of “em uma”). “Ilha deserta” usually means an uninhabited island, not a sandy desert.
target_language_example: Se eu ficasse em uma ilha deserta, eu levaria água e um rádio.
native_language_example: If I ended up on a deserted island, I would take water and a radio.

additional_notes: This is "em" + infinitive "ver" with the object pronoun "-lo" (= "ele"; also "você" in formal address). It often appears after expressions like "feliz em..." (happy to...), "prazer em..." (nice to...), or with emphasis like "só em vê-lo..." (just seeing him...). In English, it’s usually translated as "to see him" or "seeing him" rather than literally "in seeing him".
target_language_example: Fiquei muito feliz em vê-lo hoje.
native_language_example: I was very happy to see you/him today.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located below something else. It’s the contraction of "em" + "baixo" + "de" + "a" (da = de + a), so it’s followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., "a cama", "a árvore"). With a masculine singular noun, you’ll see "embaixo do" (do = de + o). Often used with verbs like "estar" (to be) and "olhar" (to look): "Está embaixo da cama" / "Olhe embaixo da cama".
target_language_example: O gato está embaixo da mesa.
native_language_example: The cat is under the table.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a location directly beneath a table. Very common with verbs like estar/ficar (to be), colocar/pôr (to put), esconder-se (to hide), and olhar/procurar (to look/search). Often interchangeable with “debaixo da mesa” in everyday speech.
target_language_example: O cachorro está embaixo da mesa.
native_language_example: The dog is under the table.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to lend you something: “Empreste-me X” = “Lend me X.” It’s the command form of *emprestar* (“to lend”) + the object pronoun *me* (“to me”). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese you’ll also hear/see **Me empresta...** (more casual). Note: English “borrow” can cause confusion—*emprestar* means “to lend,” while “to borrow” is *pegar emprestado*.
target_language_example: Empreste-me sua caneta por um minuto, por favor.
native_language_example: Lend me your pen for a minute, please.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of the verb phrase "encher o balde" (to fill the bucket). Very common with "de" + material/liquid ("encheu o balde de água/areia") or "com" ("encheu o balde com água fria"). You can also add how full it got: "até a boca" = "all the way to the top / to the brim".
target_language_example: Ela encheu o balde de água e levou para o jardim.
native_language_example: She filled the bucket with water and took it to the garden.

additional_notes: Used when you have an arranged meeting with a person (often like “meet up”). It takes a person after com: encontrar com o Tom / com ela. In many places you’ll also hear the more formal/standard variant “encontrar-se com”.
target_language_example: Vou encontrar com a Ana amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to meet up with Ana tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used when you’re going to find something specific but not yet identified ("a/an ..."). Often followed by a noun: "encontrar um jornal" (find a newspaper), "encontrar um jeito" (find a way). Note: "encontrar" can look like English "encounter", but it commonly means "find" in Portuguese.
target_language_example: Preciso encontrar um lugar para estacionar.
native_language_example: I need to find a place to park.

meaning: to find a job (to get a job).
additional_notes: Used when talking about getting employment (job-hunting). Often appears with verbs like precisar de / ter de (need to) and with adjectives like novo (new) or permanente (permanent). You can also say “arrumar um emprego” (common in Brazil) with a very similar meaning.
target_language_example: Ela está tentando encontrar um emprego desde o mês passado.
native_language_example: She has been trying to find a job since last month.

additional_notes: Used when someone succeeds in finding an item, person, or information they were searching for. "Encontrou" is the simple past of "encontrar" (to find). "O que" means "what/that which," and "estava procurando" means "was looking for" (ongoing past action). Often appears as a question: "Você encontrou o que estava procurando?"
target_language_example: Finalmente encontrei o que estava procurando na internet.
native_language_example: I finally found what I was looking for on the internet.

meaning: to find her / to find it (feminine).
additional_notes: This is the infinitive verb "encontrar" (to find) + the direct object pronoun "-la" (= her/it, for a feminine person or thing). The pronoun is attached with a hyphen; the accent (encontrá-) shows the stress when the pronoun is attached. It can refer to a woman/girl ("her") or to a feminine noun ("it"), e.g., "a chave" (the key).
target_language_example: Preciso encontrá-la antes que seja tarde.
native_language_example: I need to find her/it before it's too late.

additional_notes: "Encontrá-las" is "encontrar" (to find) + "-las" (them, feminine plural). The accent in "encontrá-" appears when the pronoun is attached to the end of the verb (enclisis). Used for objects that are feminine plural (e.g., "as chaves" = the keys, "as meninas" = the girls). In everyday speech, many people also say "encontrar elas", but in careful/standard writing you’ll see "encontrá-las".
target_language_example: Temos que encontrá-las antes que escureça.
native_language_example: We have to find them before it gets dark.

additional_notes: This is the infinitive verb encontrar (“to find/meet”) + the object pronoun -lo (“him/it”), attached with a hyphen (enclisis). The accent (encontrá-) marks the stressed syllable when the pronoun is added. Common after infinitives: "Vou encontrá-lo" = “I’m going to find/meet him.” In context it can mean either “find” (locate) or “meet” (run into/meet up), depending on the situation.
target_language_example: Preciso encontrá-lo antes da reunião.
native_language_example: I need to find him before the meeting.

meaning: to find them; to meet them.
additional_notes: "Encontrá-los" = "encontrar" (to find/meet) + "-los" (them, masculine or mixed group). It’s an infinitive with the object pronoun attached, common in Brazilian Portuguese (often after another verb like "tentar" or "poder"). In everyday speech you may also hear "encontrar eles", but "encontrá-los" is more standard/written.
target_language_example: Se você vir meus amigos, me avise: eu preciso encontrá-los.
native_language_example: If you see my friends, let me know: I need to find them.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s email contact (like name@example.com). You’ll often hear/see it with possessives: "meu/teu/seu endereço de e-mail". Also commonly shortened to "e-mail" in casual conversation when context is clear.
target_language_example: Você pode me mandar o seu endereço de e-mail, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you send me your email address, please?

additional_notes: Used to describe an action or situation in progress in the past that forms the background for another event. Often followed by a verb in the gerund (e.g., "lendo") or another ongoing past action; "estava" is the imperfect past of "estar".
target_language_example: Eu vi um acidente enquanto eu estava dirigindo para casa.
native_language_example: I saw an accident while I was driving home.

additional_notes: Used with a subject (who teaches) + "ensina francês" + optional details like where ("em Boston"), to whom ("para crianças"), to you ("me"), and how often ("duas vezes por semana"). "Ensinar" is the verb "to teach"; "francês" is the language "French".
target_language_example: Ela ensina francês online.
native_language_example: She teaches French online.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ensinar" (to teach) + the subject/language being taught (here, "francês"). You can add who you teach with "ensinar francês a alguém" (to teach French to someone). In everyday speech, many people also say "dar aulas de francês" (to give/teach French classes).
target_language_example: Ela ensina francês numa escola perto daqui.
native_language_example: She teaches French at a school near here.

additional_notes: Used with the verb “ensinar” (to teach) plus the subject “inglês” (English). You can use it to talk about your job/profession (“Ensinar inglês é minha profissão.”) or to ask someone for lessons (“Você pode/poderia me ensinar inglês?”). “Pode” is more direct; “poderia” is more polite.
target_language_example: Ela começou a ensinar inglês online este ano.
native_language_example: She started teaching English online this year.

additional_notes: Past tense (ele/ela/você) of "ensinar" + "a" + infinitive: "ensinou a + verb" = "taught to + verb" (who taught someone to do something). The person being taught is often introduced with "a" (indirect object): "ensinou a seus estudantes a..." or with a pronoun: "me/te/lhe ensinou a...".
target_language_example: Meu pai me ensinou a dirigir.
native_language_example: My dad taught me to drive.

meaning: to contact; to get in touch with.
additional_notes: Used to talk about reaching someone by phone, email, message, etc. Very common in polite questions and requests: “Como posso/posso entrar em contato com…?” Also often used with verbs like tentar (“try”) and ir (“will”): “tentei entrar em contato…”, “vou/irá entrar em contato…”.
target_language_example: Vou entrar em contato com você amanhã.
native_language_example: I’ll get in touch with you tomorrow.

meaning: to enter/go into (a place) or to start/join (an institution/event).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun after the contraction **na = em + a** (“in/into the”). For masculine nouns, you usually use **entrar no** (**em + o**). Common with places (**entrar na casa**, **entrar na sala**) and with institutions/events in the sense of being admitted or starting (**entrar na escola**).
target_language_example: Não posso entrar na sala agora.
native_language_example: I can't go into the room right now.

meaning: to enter the room; to go into the room.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "entrar" (to enter) + "na" (= em + a, “in/into the”) + "sala" (room/classroom). Very common for physically going into a room, and also often refers to entering a classroom. You can also say "entrar em uma sala" (enter a room) when it’s indefinite.
target_language_example: Por favor, bata na porta antes de entrar na sala.
native_language_example: Please knock on the door before entering the room.

meaning: to enter / go into (a place, group, or institution).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun: entrar + em + o = entrar no (“into the”). For feminine singular, you’ll usually see “entrar na” (em + a). Common with rooms, vehicles, and organizations (e.g., entrar no quarto, entrar no ônibus, entrar no exército).
target_language_example: Você pode entrar no prédio pela porta da frente.
native_language_example: You can enter the building through the front door.

additional_notes: Used as a polite instruction/request. It’s the formal imperative of the verb phrase “entrar em contato com” (“to contact”). Common in emails, notices, and customer service. You can also say “Entre em contato comigo” (“Contact me”).
target_language_example: Se você precisar de ajuda, entre em contato comigo.
native_language_example: If you need help, contact me.

additional_notes: Used with feminine plural nouns (as + plural) after entre to indicate location, separation, or a time range: entre as ruínas (among/between the ruins), entre as linhas (between the lines), entre as três e as cinco (between three and five). Also appears in relative clauses: entre as quais… (“among/between which…”).
target_language_example: O gato se escondeu entre as árvores.
native_language_example: The cat hid among the trees.

meaning: “between me and …” (used to indicate the two people/things involved).
additional_notes: Used to show that something involves only the speaker (“mim” = “me”) and another person or thing: “entre mim e você” = “between you and me” / “just between us” (often implying it’s private). In Brazilian Portuguese, it’s normal to say “entre mim e você” (not *entre eu e você*). It can also be literal/physical (“O gato está entre mim e você.”).
target_language_example: Isso fica entre mim e você, ok?
native_language_example: This stays between you and me, okay?

additional_notes: Most commonly means "among us" (within our group): "Há um médico entre nós?" It can also mean "between us" in the sense of sharing or dividing something: "Há um pouco de dinheiro entre nós" (= we have some money among us / between us). Context usually makes the meaning clear.
target_language_example: Entre nós, ninguém quer sair hoje.
native_language_example: Between us, nobody wants to go out today.

additional_notes: Used with plural masculine nouns (os) to mean (1) “among the” in the sense of being in a group or within a set of people/things: "popular entre os garotos" (popular among the boys); and (2) “between the” when talking about a relationship or comparison involving two sides/groups: "entre os Estados Unidos e a Grã-Bretanha" (between the U.S. and Great Britain). For feminine plural, use "entre as".
target_language_example: Há muita competição entre os candidatos.
native_language_example: There’s a lot of competition among the candidates.

meaning: among themselves; with each other (within a group).
additional_notes: Used when the action happens mutually inside a group (two or more people/animals/things) and doesn’t involve outsiders. Often follows the verb: falar entre si, sorrir entre si, trocar algo entre si, comunicar-se entre si.
target_language_example: Depois da reunião, os colegas combinaram tudo entre si.
native_language_example: After the meeting, the coworkers agreed on everything among themselves.

meaning: to deliver it; to hand it over (to someone).
additional_notes: "Entregá-lo" = "entregar" (to deliver/hand over/surrender) + "-lo" ("it/him"). It’s used for physically delivering something, handing something to someone, or turning someone in/surrendering them to authorities. Often followed by "a/à" (to) or informal "pra/pro" (to/for): "entregá-lo à polícia".
target_language_example: Vou entregá-lo ao gerente amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: I'll deliver it to the manager tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: "Entrou" is the past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "entrar" for ele/ela/você: "(he/she/you) entered". "Na" = "em" + "a" and is used before feminine singular places/nouns (e.g., "na casa", "na mesquita", "na escola"). With masculine nouns you use "no" ("entrou no carro"). Often used to talk about entering a building/place.
target_language_example: Ela entrou na loja sem dizer nada.
native_language_example: She went into the store without saying anything.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **entrar**: **ele/ela entrou** = “he/she entered.” **na** is a contraction of **em + a** (“in/into + the”), so **entrou na sala** is literally “entered in the room,” but in English you normally say “entered the room” or “came into the room.” You can swap the subject: **Eu entrei na sala** (I entered), **eles entraram na sala** (they entered).
target_language_example: Quando ela entrou na sala, todo mundo ficou em silêncio.
native_language_example: When she entered the room, everyone went quiet.

meaning: "(he/she/it) entered" or "got into" (a masculine singular place/vehicle).
additional_notes: "Entrou" is the past tense (pret. perfeito) of "entrar" for ele/ela/você. "No" = "em" + "o" and is used before masculine singular nouns (no trem, no carro, no prédio, no ônibus). Often used for entering buildings/places ("enter") and for getting into vehicles ("get into").
target_language_example: Ela entrou no cinema e comprou pipoca.
native_language_example: She went into the movie theater and bought popcorn.

additional_notes: Past tense of entrar (“to enter”). The "no" is a contraction of "em + o" and is commonly used with entrar (entrar em algum lugar). In English you usually say “enter the room” (without “in”). Change the subject to match who entered: "Eu entrei no quarto" (I entered the room), "Eles entraram no quarto" (They entered the room).
target_language_example: Ela entrou no quarto devagar.
native_language_example: She entered the room slowly.

meaning: "So, what…?" / "Well then, what…?" (used to start a question).
additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a question to move a conversation forward, ask for an opinion, or ask what happens next. It can sound slightly impatient or challenging depending on tone (like English “So, what now?”). Often followed by a verb: “Então, o que fazemos agora?”
target_language_example: Então, o que você quer fazer hoje?
native_language_example: So, what do you want to do today?

additional_notes: Used after a condition (often introduced by “Se…”) to mean “in that case, prepare yourself” or “be ready for what comes next.” In standard Portuguese you’d more commonly hear “então se prepara” or “então se apronte.” This exact wording (“se pronto”) sounds nonstandard/colloquial and may appear as a shortened or mistaken form.
target_language_example: Se você vai mesmo falar com ela hoje, então se pronto: ela pode ficar chateada.
native_language_example: If you’re really going to talk to her today, then get ready: she might get upset.

additional_notes: Imperative of "enviar" (to send) + the object pronoun "-me" (me). Common in polite requests, often with "por favor": "Envie-me um e-mail" / "Envie-me uma mensagem". In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many people also say "Me envie" (more informal/colloquial) with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Por favor, envie-me os documentos por e-mail.
native_language_example: Please send me the documents by email.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "enviar uma mensagem". Used for sending a text/DM/email/message in general. Often followed by the recipient with "para" or "a" ("enviou uma mensagem para ela" / "enviou uma mensagem a uma amiga"). With an indirect object pronoun: "enviou-lhe uma mensagem" = "sent him/her a message".
target_language_example: Ele enviou uma mensagem para mim ontem à noite.
native_language_example: He sent me a message last night.

additional_notes: Used to say that one female person/thing was the only one in a group or situation. It’s the imperfect past of "ser" (era = was). Change for gender/number: "era o único" (masc.), "eram os/as únicos(as)" (plural). Often followed by "a" + infinitive ("a usar") or "que" + verb ("que conseguia ver").
target_language_example: Ela era a única que sabia a resposta.
native_language_example: She was the only one who knew the answer.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of **ser** (*era*) + an adjective/nationality (*canadense*). Common for describing someone’s identity/background in the past (e.g., nationality): **Eu era canadense** = “I was Canadian,” **Ele era canadense** = “He was Canadian.”
target_language_example: Quando eu morava no Brasil, muita gente achava que eu era canadense.
native_language_example: When I lived in Brazil, many people thought I was Canadian.

meaning: (someone) was a child / when (someone) was a child.
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of "ser" (era) to describe an ongoing past state: being a child. Often appears after "quando" (when): "quando eu/ele/ela era criança". With plural subjects it becomes "eram crianças" (they were children). You can also say "quando eu era pequeno/a" as a similar idea.
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, eu brincava na rua todos os dias.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I played in the street every day.

meaning: "was young" (imperfect past: used for background/past description).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of ser (era) + adjective (jovem) to describe someone’s age/state in the past. Very common in sentences like "Quando eu era jovem, ..." meaning "When I was young, ..." to talk about habits, routines, or general situations in the past (not a one-time event).
target_language_example: Quando eu era jovem, eu morava perto da praia.
native_language_example: When I was young, I lived near the beach.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of **ser** (**era**) to describe a past state/characteristic, often as background description (not a one-time event). **muito** intensifies an adjective: *era muito diferente/pequena/maduro*.
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, a escola era muito longe.
native_language_example: When I was a child, the school was very far away.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of "ser" (era) to describe an ongoing state in the past (age/background), often with "quando" (“when”). It can refer to “I was very young” or “he/she was very young,” depending on context; Portuguese often drops the subject pronoun.
target_language_example: Eu era muito jovem quando comecei a trabalhar.
native_language_example: I was very young when I started working.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of the verb "ser" (to be): "ele era" = "he was" / "it was". "Era o" is used before a masculine singular noun: "era o lugar" (it was the place), "era o Sami" (it was Sami). For feminine, use "era a"; for plural, "eram os/as". Note: Portuguese "era" here means "was" and is not the English noun "era" (a time period).
target_language_example: Eu achava que era o Paulo, mas era o Pedro.
native_language_example: I thought it was Paulo, but it was Pedro.

additional_notes: Used to say that one person (male) was the only person in a place or doing an action. It’s the imperfect past of ser (era = “was”), often describing an ongoing situation or background in the past. For a female, say “era a única”. You can add a noun after it: “era o único amigo” (“was the only friend”).
target_language_example: Eu era o único que sabia a resposta.
native_language_example: I was the only one who knew the answer.

additional_notes: Used to say that one person (he/she/it) was the only one with a certain ability, knowledge, or situation. It’s the past tense of “é o único que” (“is the only one who”). The verb after “que” is usually in the imperfect past (e.g., sabia, estava, podia) to describe an ongoing state in the past.
target_language_example: Ela era a única que entendia a pergunta.
native_language_example: She was the only one who understood the question.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of "ser" ("era" = "was") + "tão" ("so/that") to intensify an adjective or adverb: "Ele era tão amável" (He was so kind). It often appears in the structure "tão ... que" ("so ... that"). With comparisons, Portuguese uses "tão ... quanto" ("as ... as").
target_language_example: Ela era tão cansada que foi dormir cedo.
native_language_example: She was so tired that she went to bed early.

additional_notes: “Era” is the imperfect past of “ser” (to be). Use “era um” to describe someone’s identity/profession or what something was in the past, often as background description or a past state that lasted for some time. It agrees with gender/number: “era uma” (feminine), “eram um/uns/umas” (plural).
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, meu pai era um professor.
native_language_example: When I was a child, my father was a teacher.

meaning: “was a man” (used to describe a man in the past).
additional_notes: "Era" is the imperfect past of "ser" (to be), often used for descriptions/background information (age, personality, reputation, appearance). It’s commonly followed by adjectives or descriptions: "era um homem forte", "era um homem de má reputação". Often corresponds to English “used to be” or “was” for ongoing past descriptions.
target_language_example: Ele era um homem muito gentil quando era jovem.
native_language_example: He was a very kind man when he was young.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ser** in the imperfect (**era**) + **uma** (“a/an” feminine) to describe what someone/something was, or to set the scene in the past (background details like time, weather, a typical morning). For masculine nouns, use **era um**.
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, era uma escola pequena.
native_language_example: When I was a child, it was a small school.

additional_notes: Used to say you (or someone else) thought something was a good idea in the past. Often appears after verbs like achar/pensar (“to think”), and it can be followed by an infinitive phrase explaining the action: “era uma boa ideia fazer isso” (“it was a good idea to do that”). Note: “era” is the imperfect past of ser (“to be”), commonly used for background opinions or ongoing states in the past.
target_language_example: No começo, eu achava que era uma boa ideia sair cedo.
native_language_example: At first, I thought it was a good idea to leave early.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of "ser" (era) to describe someone as a child in the past, often giving background or describing what someone was like back then. You can add adjectives after "criança" (e.g., normal, delicada, extraordinária).
target_language_example: Quando eu era uma criança, eu gostava muito de desenhar.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I really liked drawing.

meaning: “was a person” (used to describe what someone was like).
additional_notes: From the verb ser in the imperfect (era = “was/used to be”) + uma pessoa (“a person”). Commonly followed by an adjective or description: era uma pessoa legal/aberta/diferente (“she was a nice/open-minded/different person”). It can describe a lasting trait in the past, or highlight that someone acted like a different person in a certain situation (e.g., at night).
target_language_example: Antes, ele era uma pessoa muito tímida.
native_language_example: Before, he was a very shy person.

meaning: "Once upon a time there was a..." (story opening).
additional_notes: Traditional opening used to begin fairy tales and stories. It sets the scene in the past and introduces a character. It can change to match gender/number: "era uma vez uma" (a woman/a queen), "era uma vez" (no noun said), "era uma vez uns/umas" (some).
target_language_example: Era uma vez um gato que queria viajar pelo mundo.
native_language_example: Once upon a time there was a cat who wanted to travel the world.

additional_notes: Used for plants that grow where you don’t want them, especially in gardens. Often appears with verbs like "puxar" (pull up) and expressions like "estar tomado de" (to be overrun with). Singular: "erva daninha".
target_language_example: Precisamos tirar as ervas daninhas antes de plantar.
native_language_example: We need to remove the weeds before planting.

meaning: to school on foot; (go) to school walking.
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of a full phrase like “ir para a escola a pé” (to go to school on foot) or “ir à escola a pé” (to go to school on foot). “a pé” means “on foot” and is used to say you go somewhere by walking.
target_language_example: Hoje eu vou para a escola a pé.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to school on foot.

additional_notes: Used almost always in the pattern (não) ter escolha a não ser + infinitive, meaning you’re forced to do something: “I (don’t) have any choice but to…”. It expresses lack of alternatives. You can change tense and person: não tenho / não tive / não temos escolha a não ser…
target_language_example: Não temos escolha a não ser esperar.
native_language_example: We have no choice but to wait.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund "escondendo" (from "esconder", to hide) to describe an ongoing action or suspicion that someone is keeping a secret. Often used with verbs like "estar" (to be) or in questions: "Você está escondendo alguma coisa?".
target_language_example: Acho que ele está escondendo alguma coisa de nós.
native_language_example: I think he’s hiding something from us.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of the reflexive verb “esconder-se” (to hide). Used for a person, animal, or even things like the sun: “O sol escondeu-se...” (The sun hid / disappeared behind...). Often followed by location words like “atrás de” (behind), “debaixo de” (under), “na” (in).
target_language_example: Ele escondeu-se atrás da porta.
native_language_example: He hid behind the door.

additional_notes: "Escondeu" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "esconder" (to hide). It’s often used with a pronoun object (o/a/os/as = him/it, her/it, them), as in "O Tom o escondeu..." = "Tom hid it/him...". "Atrás da porta" means "behind the door" (a common place to hide something or someone).
target_language_example: Ela escondeu o presente atrás da porta.
native_language_example: She hid the present behind the door.

additional_notes: From the verb "escovar" (to brush) + "os dentes" (the teeth). In Portuguese you often don’t say “your” here; it’s understood from context (e.g., "Eu escovo os dentes" = “I brush my teeth”). Common with time/frequency words like "toda manhã" (every morning), "depois de" (after), and "com que frequência?" (how often?).
target_language_example: Eu escovo os dentes antes de dormir.
native_language_example: I brush my teeth before going to sleep.

additional_notes: A very common daily-routine phrase. In Portuguese you typically say it with the definite article: “os dentes” (“the teeth”), even when talking about your own teeth. Often used with time expressions like “pelo menos duas vezes por dia” (at least twice a day) or with obligation: “preciso/tenho que/devo escovar os dentes” (I need to / have to / should brush my teeth).
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, vou escovar os dentes.
native_language_example: After lunch, I’m going to brush my teeth.

additional_notes: An instruction using the command form (imperative) of "escovar" (to brush) + "os dentes" (the teeth). Common in reminders and routines, often followed by time expressions like "antes de" (before) or "depois/após" (after).
target_language_example: Escove os dentes duas vezes por dia.
native_language_example: Brush your teeth twice a day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your daily routine or habits. It’s the 1st-person singular present tense of “escovar” (to brush) + “os dentes” (the teeth). You can add time/frequency expressions like “toda manhã” (every morning) or “duas vezes ao dia” (twice a day).
target_language_example: Depois do café da manhã, escovo os dentes.
native_language_example: After breakfast, I brush my teeth.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "escovar os dentes" (to brush your teeth). It often implies the person finished brushing. In questions, Portuguese can drop the subject ("Escovou os dentes?") or include it for clarity ("Você escovou os dentes?"). "Já" adds the idea of "already/yet" ("Você já escovou os dentes?").
target_language_example: Eu já escovei os dentes.
native_language_example: I already brushed my teeth.

additional_notes: A polite/formal instruction using the imperative of "escrever" (to write) directed at "você". Common on forms, signs, and in requests. You may also hear "Escreva seu nome" (less formal) or "Escreve o teu nome" in Portugal when addressing someone with "tu".
target_language_example: Por favor, escreva o seu nome e a sua assinatura no final do formulário.
native_language_example: Please write your name and your signature at the bottom of the form.

additional_notes: An instruction (imperative) often seen on forms, lists, or signs. “Escreva” is the formal/neutral command form of “escrever” (to write), used with “você” (even if “você” isn’t said). “Seu” here means “your” (your name). You may also see: “Escreva o seu nome” (with the article) or “Escreva seu nome completo” (full name).
target_language_example: Por favor, escreva seu nome e assine aqui.
native_language_example: Please write your name and sign here.
