It also appears in indirect questions and reported speech: "perguntou-me quem eu era" (asked me who I was), "disse que eu era..." (said that I was...).
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, eu era muito tímido.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I was very shy.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past (era) to describe a continuing state in the past (“when I was young…”), often to set background or explain motivations. Commonly followed by time words like antes (“before”) or quando (“when”), or combined with another verb to describe what you used to want/need.
target_language_example: Eu era jovem quando me mudei para esta cidade.
native_language_example: I was young when I moved to this city.

additional_notes: “Eu” = “I”. “Escrevi” is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of “escrever” (to write), used for a completed action. “Uma carta” = “a letter” (a written message). You can add details with “para” (to/for someone): “Eu escrevi uma carta para a minha professora.”
target_language_example: Eu escrevi uma carta para a minha mãe.
native_language_example: I wrote a letter to my mother.

additional_notes: From the verb *esperar* (“to wait”, “to expect”, “to hope”). In these examples it’s in the imperfect past (*esperava*), often used for an expectation/hope you had over a period of time or in the background (“I was expecting…”). Common patterns: **Eu esperava que +** (subjunctive) to mean “I was expecting/hoping that…”, e.g. *Eu esperava que o teste fosse mais fácil*. Also used to compare reality vs expectation: *como eu esperava* (“as I expected”).
target_language_example: Eu esperava que você chegasse mais cedo, mas tudo bem.
native_language_example: I was expecting you to arrive earlier, but it’s okay.

meaning: "I hope that..." (introduces a hope/wish, usually followed by the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Use it to express hope about something that may happen or be true. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the present subjunctive: "Eu espero que alguém faça isso". In casual speech, you may also hear the indicative in some contexts, but learners should treat "esperar que" as a subjunctive trigger.
target_language_example: Eu espero que você consiga um bom emprego.
native_language_example: I hope you get a good job.

meaning: “I hope that the …” (introduces what you hope will happen).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause with something you hope is true or will happen. After "(eu) espero que", Portuguese normally uses the subjunctive mood (e.g., "esteja", "venha", "seja", "possa", "vá"). "o" is the masculine singular definite article (“the”) and is usually followed by a noun or name ("o Tom"). Note: "esperar" can also mean “to wait (for)”, but in this pattern it means “to hope (that)”.
target_language_example: Eu espero que o ônibus chegue logo.
native_language_example: I hope the bus arrives soon.

additional_notes: Used to express a wish or hope about what the other person will do or how they are. Very common in polite messages (e.g., “Eu espero que você esteja bem.”). The verb after “que” is often in the subjunctive, especially for hopes/wishes (e.g., “aprenda”, “aproveite”, “esteja”).
target_language_example: Eu espero que você goste do seu novo trabalho.
native_language_example: I hope you like your new job.

meaning: “I hope you can…” / “I hope you’ll be able to…”
additional_notes: Used to express a hope or polite request about what someone is able to do. It’s followed by a verb (often in the infinitive), e.g., “eu espero que você possa ajudar / vir / fazer isso”. Note: “espero” can look like English “expect,” but here it usually means “(I) hope.”
target_language_example: Eu espero que você possa vir amanhã.
native_language_example: I hope you can come tomorrow.

meaning: "I hope you have..." / "I hope you did..."
additional_notes: Used to express hope about something the other person has done or has experienced. It’s followed by the subjunctive form of "ter" ("tenha") plus a past participle to talk about a past action: "eu espero que você tenha + (feito/gostado/dado/lavado...)". In English this often becomes "I hope you (did)..." or "I hope you’ve (done)...".
target_language_example: Eu espero que você tenha encontrado o lugar sem problemas.
native_language_example: I hope you found the place without any problems.

additional_notes: Used to say you didn’t remember something. Often followed by a direct object (“Eu esqueci algo.” = “I forgot something.”) or by “que” + a clause (“Eu esqueci que hoje é feriado.” = “I forgot that today is a holiday.”). In Brazil, “Esqueci!” is also common by itself.
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu esqueci o seu nome.
native_language_example: Sorry, I forgot your name.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb (de + verb) to say you forgot an action: “Eu esqueci de trazer…” = “I forgot to bring…”. You can change the subject: “Você esqueceu de…?” (Did you forget to…?). In Brazilian Portuguese, you may also hear “esqueci de + infinitive” without the “eu” when the subject is clear: “Esqueci de perguntar.”
target_language_example: Eu esqueci de mandar a mensagem ontem.
native_language_example: I forgot to send the message yesterday.

additional_notes: "Eu" = I. "Estava" is the imperfect past of "estar" and is used for ongoing states, descriptions, or situations in the past (e.g., hungry, interested, curious, in a place), and for actions in progress in the past (often + gerund: "eu estava vendo..." = I was watching...).
target_language_example: Eu estava cansado, então fui dormir cedo.
native_language_example: I was tired, so I went to bed early.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of estar (eu estava) to describe a past state/condition (how you felt). “Cansado” agrees with the speaker: a man says “cansado”; a woman says “cansada” (“eu estava cansada”). You can add time expressions (hoje, ontem à noite) or intensifiers like “demais” (too).
target_language_example: Quando cheguei em casa, eu estava cansado e fui dormir cedo.
native_language_example: When I got home, I was tired and went to sleep early.

meaning: “I was afraid to…” / “I was scared of…”
additional_notes: Used to talk about a past fear. It’s typically followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., dizer, fazer, ficar, conseguir, passar) to say what you were afraid to do or what might happen. Often translates naturally as “I was afraid to…” in English, even though Portuguese uses “with fear of” (estar com medo de).
target_language_example: Eu estava com medo de perguntar, mas acabei perguntando.
native_language_example: I was afraid to ask, but I ended up asking.

additional_notes: Used to admit a past mistake or incorrect opinion. Literally "I was mistaken" (masculine speaker); a feminine speaker usually says "eu estava errada". Often followed by "sobre" + topic ("eu estava errado sobre isso" = "I was wrong about that").
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu estava errado sobre o horário da reunião.
native_language_example: Sorry, I was wrong about the time of the meeting.

additional_notes:
Uses the imperfect past (estava) to describe an ongoing state in the past. Often followed by:
- "que" + verb: "Eu estava esperando que você viesse" = “I was expecting you to come.”
- an infinitive: "Eu estava esperando surpreender o Tom" = “I was hoping/expecting to surprise Tom.”
Context determines whether it sounds more like “waiting” (for someone/something) or “expecting/hoping” (for an outcome).
target_language_example: Eu estava esperando o ônibus quando você me ligou.
native_language_example: I was waiting for the bus when you called me.

additional_notes: Used to describe how you felt in the past. It’s the imperfect past of sentir-se (“to feel”), often followed by an adjective (feliz, triste, doente) or a phrase like do mesmo jeito (“the same way”). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, you may also hear: “eu estava me sentindo” (more formal/explicit) or “eu estava me sentindo” with “me” sometimes dropped in casual speech (“eu estava sentindo”).
target_language_example: Eu estava me sentindo cansado(a) ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I was feeling tired last night.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of *estar* (*eu estava*) to describe how you were feeling (a state/condition) in the past. *Muito* intensifies it (“very”). *Cansado* agrees with the speaker: a man typically says *cansado*; a woman says *cansada*. Common with connectors like *porque* (because) and *então* (so/then), or with *para* + infinitive to mean “too tired to…” (e.g., *muito cansado para continuar*).
target_language_example: Eu estava muito cansado ontem à noite, então fui dormir cedo.
native_language_example: I was very tired last night, so I went to bed early.

meaning: “I was about to …” (I was just going to do something).
additional_notes: Used to say you were very close to doing something (often a moment before it happened or before you changed your mind). Commonly followed by an infinitive verb: “Eu estava prestes a sair” = “I was about to leave.” You can swap the subject and tense as needed: “Eu estou prestes a …” (I’m about to …), “Ele/ela estava prestes a …” (He/She was about to …).
target_language_example: Eu estava prestes a te ligar quando você mandou mensagem.
native_language_example: I was about to call you when you texted.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past (estava + gerund) to describe an action in progress in the past. It’s commonly followed by an infinitive (tentar + infinitive): “Eu estava tentando ajudar… / lembrar… / pensar…”. You can swap the subject and verb for other people: “ele/ela estava tentando…”, “nós estávamos tentando…”.
target_language_example: Eu estava tentando ligar para você quando você me mandou mensagem.
native_language_example: I was trying to call you when you texted me.

additional_notes: "Eu" = I. "Estava" is the imperfect past of "estar" and is used for ongoing states, descriptions, or situations in the past (e.g., hungry, interested, curious, in a place), and for actions in progress in the past (often + gerund: "eu estava vendo..." = I was watching...).
target_language_example: Eu estava cansado, então fui dormir cedo.
native_language_example: I was tired, so I went to bed early.

additional_notes: Used with "estar" in the past (imperfect): "eu estava" = "I was". With "com" + noun, it commonly means: (1) being with someone: "Eu estava com Tom" (I was with Tom); (2) having/experiencing a state or symptom: "com fome" (hungry), "com dores" (in pain), "com as mãos ocupadas" (hands were full/occupied), "com a palavra na ponta da língua" (had the word on the tip of my tongue). In English you often translate it without "with" (e.g., "I was hungry").
target_language_example: Eu estava com muita sede, então bebi água.
native_language_example: I was very thirsty, so I drank water.

additional_notes: Form of the verb "estar" with "eu" (I). Use "estou" to talk about temporary states/conditions (feelings, health, location, situations): "Eu estou cansado" (I’m tired), "Eu estou em casa" (I’m at home). (Contrast: "eu sou" from "ser" is more for permanent traits/identity.) In questions, Portuguese often drops the subject: "Estou certa?" is also common.
target_language_example: Eu estou com fome agora.
native_language_example: I’m hungry now.

meaning: "I have" / "I'm feeling" (a temporary condition, emotion, symptom, or situation).
additional_notes: Used with nouns to say you’re experiencing something right now: pain/illness (dor, torcicolo), emotions (medo, pena, vergonha), or a temporary situation/amount (pouco dinheiro). Often corresponds to English “I have…” or “I’m …” depending on the noun. You can replace “eu” with other subjects: “ele está com…”, “nós estamos com…”.
target_language_example: Eu estou com fome e estou com pressa.
native_language_example: I'm hungry and I'm in a hurry.

meaning: “I feel like / I’m in the mood to (do something).”
additional_notes: Used to express a desire or urge to do something right now or these days. It’s followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., beber, comer, caminhar, ligar). You can also use it without “eu” when the subject is clear: “Estou com vontade de…”. Very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Estou com vontade de sair hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I feel like going out tonight.

additional_notes: Present continuous: "eu" (I) + "estou" (am) + "comendo" (eating). Used to say what you’re doing right now (often with food: "Eu estou comendo cereal/uma banana"). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people also commonly say "Estou comendo..." without "eu" (the subject is understood).
target_language_example: Desculpa, não posso falar agora — eu estou comendo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t talk right now — I’m eating.

additional_notes: Used to say what you study (a subject) or where you study (a school/university). In Portuguese, the subject pronoun "eu" (I) is often optional, so you may also hear just "Estudo Direito". "Eu estudo" can describe a general habit (I study every day) or what you’re doing these days (I’m studying Spanish).
target_language_example: Eu estudo português à noite.
native_language_example: I study Portuguese at night.

additional_notes: Used to say you are learning/studying the French language. "Eu" = I, "estudo" (from estudar) = I study, "francês" = French. You can add time/frequency phrases after it, like "no colégio" (at school), "todo dia" (every day), "pelo menos uma hora" (at least an hour), and "sempre que (eu) posso" (whenever I can)—the "eu" is often omitted in the second part.
target_language_example: Eu estudo francês desde o ano passado.
native_language_example: I’ve been studying French since last year.

additional_notes:
Past tense of falar (“to speak/to talk/to say”) with eu (“I”). Often used with:
- com + person: “Eu falei com ele/ela/eles” = “I talked to him/her/them.”
- que + clause: “Eu falei que…” = “I said that…”
It can also be used to insist or repeat an order/statement: “Pra trás, eu falei!” = “Back up, I said!” (informal tone). In “eu falei, mas ninguém me ouviu / não fui ouvido”, it means “I spoke, but no one listened to me / I wasn’t heard.”
target_language_example: Eu falei com a médica ontem, mas ela não respondeu.
native_language_example: I talked to the doctor yesterday, but she didn’t reply.

additional_notes: Used to say you talked to someone (a completed action). The person comes after com: eu falei com Maria / com ele / com elas / com uns amigos. In everyday English, “I talked to …” is often the most natural translation. In European Portuguese you may also hear “falei com” meaning “I talked to” (same idea).
target_language_example: Eu falei com o meu chefe sobre o horário.
native_language_example: I talked to my boss about the schedule.

meaning: “I told [him/them] / I said to the …” (male person or “the …” masculine singular).
additional_notes: Used to report what you said to someone: eu falei para o Tom… = “I told Tom…” / “I said to Tom…”. In Portuguese, falar para + someone is very common for “tell” or “say to”. The “o” is the masculine singular article (often with a name: o Tom) or “the” before a masculine noun (o médico). With a female person or feminine noun, use “eu falei para a …”.
target_language_example: Eu falei para o meu irmão esperar em casa.
native_language_example: I told my brother to wait at home.

additional_notes: First-person singular of the verb "falar" (to speak/to talk). Commonly used with languages: "Eu falo inglês/árabe" = "I speak English/Arabic." It can also describe how you speak: "Eu falo rápido" = "I speak fast."
target_language_example: Eu falo português um pouco.
native_language_example: I speak Portuguese a little.

additional_notes: Used to say you can speak the French language. You can add adverbs like “um pouco” (a little), “muito bem” (very well), or time expressions like “todos os dias” (every day). In conversation you may also hear it without the subject: “Falo francês.”
target_language_example: Desculpe, eu não falo espanhol; eu falo francês.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t speak Spanish; I speak French.

additional_notes: Use this to say you have basic ability in a language. It’s followed by the language name (often without an article): “Eu falo um pouco de francês.” You can also hear “Eu falo um pouco de português/inglês…”. For a slightly stronger statement, people may say “Eu falo um pouco de francês, mas não muito bem” (“…but not very well”).
target_language_example: Eu falo um pouco de português, mas ainda estou aprendendo.
native_language_example: I speak a little Portuguese, but I’m still learning.

additional_notes: Used to talk about actions, habits, or things you create/prepare. Common in questions like “O que é que eu faço agora?” (“What do I do now?”). In Portuguese, fazer is also used where English might use another verb: “fazer caminhadas” = “to go on walks,” “fazer café” = “to make coffee,” “fazer tudo por alguém” = “to do everything for someone.” Word order is flexible, but “Eu faço…” often adds emphasis (you can also just say “Faço…” in context).
target_language_example: Se você precisar de ajuda, eu faço isso para você.
native_language_example: If you need help, I’ll do that for you.

additional_notes: Used to say that you perform an action or habit. Often appears when explaining how you do something (e.g., “como eu faço isso” = “how I do this”), giving the reason (“porque quero” = “because I want to”), or talking about frequency (“uma vez por semana/ao ano” = “once a week/a year”). The verb is fazer (to do/to make) in the present tense: eu faço.
target_language_example: Eu faço isso todo dia antes do trabalho.
native_language_example: I do this every day before work.

meaning: “I get / I become” (a feeling or state).
additional_notes: Used with **ficar + adjective** to talk about how you end up feeling or a change of state: *Eu fico nervoso/a* (“I get nervous”). The adjective agrees with the speaker: **nervoso** (male), **nervosa** (female). **Ficar** can also mean “to stay/remain” in other contexts, but with emotions it often means “to get/become.” You may also see *ficar + adjective + em + infinitive*: *Eu fico feliz em gastar…* (“I’m happy to spend…”).
target_language_example: Eu fico cansado depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I get tired after work.

meaning: 'I got / I became' (and sometimes 'I stayed / I ended up').
additional_notes: "Eu fiquei" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "ficar" for "I". It’s very common with emotions/conditions ("eu fiquei chocada" = I got shocked), with life-status changes ("eu fiquei noivo" = I got engaged), and to say you stayed somewhere for a period of time ("eu fiquei em casa" = I stayed at home). Depending on context, it can also mean "I ended up" (unexpected result).
target_language_example: Eu fiquei muito feliz com a notícia.
native_language_example: I got very happy when I heard the news.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **ficar** (“to stay/remain”) in the past (**fiquei**) to say you stayed in a place. Very common for giving a reason with **porque** (“because”), like staying home due to rain or illness. You can also replace **em casa** with another place: *Eu fiquei no hotel* (“I stayed at the hotel”).
target_language_example: Ontem eu fiquei em casa para descansar.
native_language_example: Yesterday I stayed at home to rest.

additional_notes:
Literally “I became surprised.” Used to say you felt surprise after something happened. Often followed by:
- **ao + infinitive**: *Eu fiquei surpreso ao ouvir...* (“I was surprised to hear...”)
- **com + noun**: *Eu fiquei surpreso com a resposta.* (“I was surprised by/at the answer.”)
You can change **surpreso** to match the speaker: **surpresa** (female), **surpresos/surpresas** (plural).
target_language_example: Eu fiquei surpreso ao ver que já estava tudo pronto.
native_language_example: I was surprised to see that everything was already ready.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something you did in the past. "Fazer" can mean both “to do” (tasks/actions) and “to make” (create/prepare), so the best translation depends on context. Common in questions like "O que eu fiz...?" (“What did I do...?”) and in phrases like "Eu fiz de tudo..." (“I did everything I could...”).
target_language_example: Eu fiz o jantar ontem.
native_language_example: I made dinner yesterday.

meaning: I did that / I did it.
additional_notes: "Eu" = "I" and "fiz" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "fazer" (to do/make). "Isso" means "that" or "it" (a thing/idea), often something already known from context. Use it to say you were the one who did/made something; you can add details with phrases like "com as minhas próprias mãos" (with my own hands), "corretamente" (correctly), or "por ela" (for her).
target_language_example: Eu fiz isso ontem à noite, mas ninguém percebeu.
native_language_example: I did it last night, but nobody noticed.

meaning: “I did what …” (I did the thing that …).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause explaining what you did: "Eu fiz o que [someone wanted/asked/ordered]". Very common with verbs like "querer" (to want), "pedir" (to ask/request), and "mandar" (to order). In speech, you’ll often hear it as part of a longer sentence (not usually a standalone phrase).
target_language_example: Eu fiz o que pude para ajudar.
native_language_example: I did what I could to help.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (uma). It’s the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of fazer: eu fiz = “I did/I made.” Common with things you create (uma lista, uma mesa) or actions/events (uma aposta, uma tentativa). With masculine nouns, you’ll usually see “eu fiz um …”.
target_language_example: Eu fiz uma pergunta para o professor.
native_language_example: I asked the teacher a question.

additional_notes: Simple past (pretérito perfeito) of the verb ir. Used for a completed action in the past. Often followed by a destination with a/ao/à (eu fui a um show; eu fui à festa). It can also be used with an infinitive to show you went somewhere to do something (eu fui surfar).
target_language_example: Eu fui ao mercado ontem.
native_language_example: I went to the market yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say you went somewhere in the past. "Fui" is the past tense of "ir" (to go). "Ao" = "a" + "o" and is used before masculine singular places/nouns (e.g., ao banco, ao centro, ao correio). For feminine singular, use "eu fui à" (à praia). For plural, "eu fui aos" / "eu fui às".
target_language_example: Eu fui ao mercado ontem.
native_language_example: I went to the market yesterday.

additional_notes: Uses the past tense of *ir* (eu fui = I went/I have gone) plus *lá* (“there,” usually meaning a place not near the speaker). Often followed by details like how you went (*de trem*), when (*ontem*), why (*para...*), or with whom (*sozinho*). In many contexts English might say “I went” when “there” is implied, but Portuguese commonly keeps *lá* to emphasize the place.
target_language_example: Eu fui lá na semana passada para visitar meus avós.
native_language_example: I went there last week to visit my grandparents.

additional_notes: Used to say you went to a place. It’s the past tense of “ir” (to go): eu fui = I went. “para” = to/for. “a” is the feminine singular definite article (“the”), so it’s used before feminine nouns (e.g., a cozinha, a praça). With masculine nouns, you use “eu fui para o …” (o = the). With many countries, you may see “eu fui para a Austrália”, but some countries take no article or use “ao/à” depending on the name.
target_language_example: Ontem eu fui para a escola bem cedo.
native_language_example: Yesterday I went to the school very early.

additional_notes: Used to say you went somewhere in the past: eu (I) + fui (I went, past of ir) + à (= a + a). Use à before feminine singular nouns (à academia, à livraria) and some place expressions like à casa (dela). For masculine places, use eu fui ao (ao mercado).
target_language_example: Ontem eu fui à praia com meus amigos.
native_language_example: Yesterday I went to the beach with my friends.

additional_notes: Simple past (pretérito perfeito) of the verb ir. Used for a completed action in the past. Often followed by a destination with a/ao/à (eu fui a um show; eu fui à festa). It can also be used with an infinitive to show you went somewhere to do something (eu fui surfar).
target_language_example: Eu fui ao mercado ontem.
native_language_example: I went to the market yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say you were the last person to do something or to find out something. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (often after "a"): "Eu fui o último a saber" (I was the last to know). For a woman, say "Eu fui a última a..."; for a mixed/unknown group, "os últimos a...". In Brazil, you also commonly hear "Eu fui o último a + infinitive" without "a" in casual speech, but "a" is standard.
target_language_example: Eu fui o último a chegar na reunião.
native_language_example: I was the last to arrive at the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to express a polite desire or preference. Very common with **que + verb (subjunctive)** to mean “I’d like/wish that…”, especially when talking about what you want someone else to do or how you wish something were: *Eu gostaria que ela parasse…* (“I’d like her to stop…”). In everyday speech you’ll also hear *Eu queria…* with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Eu gostaria que você chegasse mais cedo amanhã.
native_language_example: I’d like you to arrive earlier tomorrow.

meaning: "I would like to" (polite way to say you want to do something).
additional_notes: Used to make polite requests or express a desire, often in service situations (ordering, booking, asking for information). It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., fazer, saber, trocar). In everyday speech, people may also say “Queria...” with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Eu gostaria de pedir a conta, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like to ask for the bill/check, please.

meaning: “I would like to be able to …”
additional_notes:
Used to express a wish/desire to have the ability or opportunity to do something. It’s polite and common: 
- eu gostaria de = “I would like / I’d like” (more polite than “eu quero”).
- poder + infinitive = “to be able to” + verb (poder comprar, poder explicar, etc.).
With the perfect infinitive (poder ter feito), it means wishing you had been able to do something in the past (“I would like to have been able to have done that” → usually “I wish I could have done that”).
target_language_example: Eu gostaria de poder falar português com mais confiança.
native_language_example: I’d like to be able to speak Portuguese with more confidence.

meaning: "I’d like to know" / "I would like to know."
additional_notes: Polite way to ask for information. Often followed by a question word (o que = what, onde = where, qual = which/what) or an indirect question: "Eu gostaria de saber o que aconteceu" (“I’d like to know what happened”). It can also mean “I’d like to be able to / know how to” with an infinitive: "Eu gostaria de saber tocar piano" (“I’d like to know how to play the piano / I’d like to be able to play the piano”).
target_language_example: Eu gostaria de saber quanto custa este bilhete.
native_language_example: I’d like to know how much this ticket costs.

meaning: “I’d like (that) …” / “I wish (that) …” (polite desire about a situation).
additional_notes: Used to introduce something you want to happen or to be true, often with a different subject after que (e.g., “eu gostaria que ela…”). It commonly requires the subjunctive in the following clause (e.g., desse, estivéssemos, fosse, houvesse). It can express a polite request (“I’d like you to…”) or a wish about an unreal/imagined situation (“I wish today were Friday”).
target_language_example: Eu gostaria que você falasse mais devagar.
native_language_example: I’d like you to speak more slowly.

meaning: “I would like you to…” (polite; often followed by a verb in the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to make polite requests or express wishes about what someone should/could do. In Portuguese it commonly triggers the subjunctive in the following verb (e.g., você venha, você entenda, você fosse).
target_language_example: Eu gostaria que você me ajudasse com isso.
native_language_example: I would like you to help me with that.

meaning: 'I used to like/love (to)…' or 'I would like (to)…' (depending on context).
additional_notes: "Gostava" is the imperfect past of "gostar". Most often it means a past habit/state: "I used to like/love" or "I liked" (especially with activities: "gostava de + infinitive"). In some contexts (especially in polite requests), "eu gostava de" can mean "I would like to…" (similar to "eu gostaria de"). With a person, "gostar de você" means "to like you" (not necessarily romantic).
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, eu gostava de ler antes de dormir.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I used to like reading before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Past tense of "gostar" (to like). It’s usually followed by "de" (often contracted: de + o = do; de + a = da; de + este = deste), e.g., "Eu gostei do peixe" (= I liked the fish). You can also use it alone as a response: "Eu gostei." (= I liked it / I enjoyed it). Often appears with "muito" to mean "really liked."
target_language_example: Eu gostei muito do filme, mas achei o final meio triste.
native_language_example: I really liked the movie, but I found the ending kind of sad.

additional_notes: "Eu gostei de" is the past tense of gostar de. It’s followed by "de" + a noun/pronoun (Eu gostei de Tom. / Eu gostei de ambos.) or by "de" + an infinitive verb to say you enjoyed doing something (Eu gostei de falar... / Eu gostei de ficar...). For "I like" in the present, use "Eu gosto de".
target_language_example: Eu gostei de conhecer sua família.
native_language_example: I enjoyed meeting your family.

additional_notes: Usually used as **eu gosto de + noun/infinitive** (“I like (something) / I like doing (something)”). With pronouns/people you also use **de**: **Eu gosto dele/dela** (“I like him/her”). For emphasis or contrast, **eu gosto** can appear later in the sentence: **Esse aí eu gosto** (“That one, I like”).
target_language_example: Eu gosto de cozinhar em casa.
native_language_example: I like cooking at home.

additional_notes: Used to say you like something. "Gosto" comes from "gostar de" (to like), which requires "de". "Da" is the contraction of "de" + "a" and is used before a feminine singular noun (e.g., "a ideia", "a foto", "a China", "a primavera"). For masculine singular you usually say "eu gosto do" (de + o).
target_language_example: Eu gosto da comida portuguesa.
native_language_example: I like Portuguese food.

additional_notes: Used to say you like a specific color (often followed by a color adjective: amarela, azul, verde) or the color of something (eu gosto da cor de + noun). Often you’ll also hear: “Eu gosto da cor azul” or simply “Eu gosto do azul.”
target_language_example: Eu gosto da cor do seu casaco.
native_language_example: I like the color of your coat.

additional_notes: Used to say you like/enjoy something. Follow it with a noun (eu gosto de rosas) or a verb in the infinitive (eu gosto de dormir / de fazer compras). Often shortened in speech to “gosto de …” when “eu” is understood.
target_language_example: Eu gosto de aprender português.
native_language_example: I like learning Portuguese.

additional_notes: Uses the verb structure **gostar de + infinitive** to talk about things you enjoy doing. Add the food or activity after **comer** (e.g., *comer bolo*, *comer fora* = eat out). You can also add a person with **com** (*comer com você* = eat with you).
target_language_example: Eu gosto de comer pizza no fim de semana.
native_language_example: I like to eat pizza on the weekend.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "gostar" + "de" + infinitive to say you like doing something: "Eu gosto de + [verb]". You can add what you study ("história", "línguas", "russo") or how you study ("sozinho"). Often you can drop "eu" in conversation: "Gosto de estudar."
target_language_example: Eu gosto de estudar à noite.
native_language_example: I like to study at night.

additional_notes: Used to say you enjoy going somewhere to do an activity. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb: "Eu gosto de ir + verb" (ir assistir, ir caminhar, ir comprar, ir nadar, ir ver). You can also shorten it to "Eu gosto de" when the idea of “going” is obvious from context.
target_language_example: Eu gosto de ir jantar fora nos fins de semana.
native_language_example: I like to go out for dinner on the weekends.

additional_notes: Used to say you enjoy music in general. The verb phrase is "gostar de" (to like), so it normally takes "de" before what you like: "Eu gosto de música", "Eu gosto de rock". You can add details with adjectives or adverbs: "música alta" (loud music), "especialmente" (especially).
target_language_example: Eu gosto de música, mas não gosto de música muito alta.
native_language_example: I like music, but I don't like very loud music.

additional_notes: Used to say you enjoy being a certain way or having a certain characteristic/role. It’s often followed by an adjective (direto, pontual, ruivo) or a noun describing a role/identity (professor). You can change the verb for the person: "você gosta de ser" (you like being), "ele/ela gosta de ser" (he/she likes being).
target_language_example: Eu gosto de ser honesto com as pessoas.
native_language_example: I like being honest with people.

additional_notes: Used to say you like something/someone. It’s “eu gosto de” + “do” (= de + o) before a masculine singular noun or name treated as masculine. For feminine singular, use “eu gosto da” (de + a). With plural, “dos/das”. In Portuguese, “gostar” uses “de” (gostar de algo).
target_language_example: Eu gosto do café.
native_language_example: I like coffee.

meaning: "I like my ..." (talking about something you own or someone close to you).
additional_notes: "Gostar" is used with "de": "eu gosto de...". "Do" is a contraction of "de + o" and is used before a masculine singular noun with "meu" (e.g., "do meu café"). Variations: "da minha" (feminine singular), "dos meus" (masculine plural), "das minhas" (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Eu gosto do meu trabalho.
native_language_example: I like my job.

additional_notes: Used to say you like something that belongs to the person you’re speaking to. It’s made of: eu gosto de + o seu (“your”, masculine). After this, you usually add a masculine noun: Eu gosto do seu chapéu. With feminine nouns, use “da sua”: Eu gosto da sua roupa. If you’re talking to multiple people, use “dos seus / das suas”.
target_language_example: Eu gosto do seu trabalho.
native_language_example: I like your work.

additional_notes: Used to compare preferences. It’s usually followed by de/do/da/dos/das + a noun (e.g., do verão, das frases) or by “de” + verb in the infinitive (e.g., eu gosto mais de viajar). You can add “do que …” to say what you’re comparing against: “Eu gosto mais do verão do que do inverno.”
target_language_example: Eu gosto mais de café do que de chá.
native_language_example: I like coffee more than tea.

additional_notes: Used to express preference. Often appears in comparisons with **do que** (“than”): *Eu gosto mais de X do que de Y* (“I like X more than Y / I prefer X to Y”). You can also use it without a comparison to mean you generally prefer that thing.
target_language_example: Eu gosto mais de chá do que de café.
native_language_example: I like tea more than coffee.

meaning: I like (it) a lot / I really like (it).
additional_notes: Used to express strong liking. It’s often followed by **de** + noun/verb: *Eu gosto muito de frutos do mar* (“I really like seafood”) or *Eu gosto muito de viajar* (“I really like traveling”). With **de + demonstrative**, it can be *deste/desta* (“this”): *Eu gosto muito desta cidade* (“I like this city a lot”).
target_language_example: Eu gosto muito de música brasileira.
native_language_example: I really like Brazilian music.

additional_notes: Used to say you like something/someone a lot. It’s: eu (I) + gosto (I like) + muito (a lot) + da (= de + a), which is used before feminine singular nouns (a Austrália, a culinária, a língua, a minha avó). For masculine singular, you usually use “eu gosto muito do …” (do = de + o).
target_language_example: Eu gosto muito da sua cidade.
native_language_example: I really like your city.

additional_notes: Used to express a strong liking for a person, thing, or activity. After "de" you can use: (1) a noun: "Eu gosto muito de morangos" (I really like strawberries); (2) an infinitive verb: "Eu gosto muito de ajudar" (I really like helping). With people you also use "de": "Eu gosto muito de você" (I like you a lot / I’m very fond of you).
target_language_example: Eu gosto muito de aprender português.
native_language_example: I really like learning Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used to strongly express liking/enjoying something or someone. It’s the first-person singular of gostar (“to like”), with muito (“a lot”). The do is a contraction of de + o (“of the”), used before masculine singular nouns or names treated as masculine (e.g., do Tom, do meu trabalho). Before feminine nouns you’d use da (de + a): Eu gosto muito da música. Before verbs or many place names, it’s often just de: Eu gosto muito de viajar / de São Paulo. With clauses, you often get do que: Eu gosto muito do que ele escreveu (“I really like what he wrote”).
target_language_example: Eu gosto muito do café daqui.
native_language_example: I really like the coffee here.

meaning: “I was going to…” / “I would…” (past intention or planned future-from-the-past).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of ir ("to go") to talk about an intention/plan in the past: “I was going to call…”. It’s often followed by an infinitive (eu ia fazer, eu ia chamar). It can also mean something that was about to happen (“I was going to be late”) or what someone expected you would do (“Você achou que eu ia…?”).
target_language_example: Eu ia te ligar, mas meu celular ficou sem bateria.
native_language_example: I was going to call you, but my phone ran out of battery.

meaning: "I already…" / "I’ve already…"; sometimes "I’m about to…" (with verbs like ir).
additional_notes: Used with the adverb "já" to say something has happened before now (often like English "already" or "ever" in superlatives: "a mais… que eu já…" = "the most… I’ve ever…"). With "já vou" it often means you’re leaving/going right away ("I’m off / I’m going now"). Tense changes the nuance: "eu já li" (I already read / I’ve read), "eu já havia saído" (I had already left).
target_language_example: Eu já terminei o meu trabalho.
native_language_example: I’ve already finished my work.

eu já sei o que o

target_language_multi_word_term: eu já sei o que o
meaning: “I already know what (the/that) …” (used before a masculine noun/name).
additional_notes: This is the start of the structure **Eu já sei o que + o/a + [person/thing] + [verb]** to say you already know what someone did/is doing/is going to do. **o** is the masculine article (“the”) used before a man’s name or a masculine noun (e.g., *o Tom*). With a woman’s name, it becomes **eu já sei o que a…** (e.g., *a Maria*). In English you usually don’t translate the article: *o Tom* → “Tom.”
target_language_example: Eu já sei o que o João vai dizer.
native_language_example: I already know what João is going to say.

additional_notes: Used to say you read in general or habitually, or that you are reading something (depending on context). Often followed by what you read: *eu leio um livro / eu leio o poema*. In comparisons like *quanto mais eu leio...*, it means “the more I read...”.
target_language_example: Eu leio notícias todos os dias.
native_language_example: I read the news every day.

meaning: “I … to you/him/her” (with lhe = indirect object: “to you” formal, or “to him/her”).
additional_notes: Used when the speaker (eu) does something for/to someone, and that person is expressed with lhe (an indirect object pronoun). It commonly means “to you” in formal address (você/o senhor/a senhora), or “to him/her.” It typically comes before the verb: eu lhe deixei (I left you/him/her), eu lhe mandei (I sent you/him/her), eu lhe emprestei (I lent you/him/her).
target_language_example: Eu lhe enviei o endereço por e-mail.
native_language_example: I sent you the address by email.

additional_notes: "Lhe" is an object pronoun meaning "to you" (formal) or "to him/her". This uses the verb "dar" (to give) in the simple past (pretérito perfeito): "dei" = "I gave". In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often say "eu te dei" (to you, informal) or "eu dei para você" instead of "eu lhe dei".
target_language_example: Eu lhe dei minha palavra.
native_language_example: I gave you my word.

meaning: “I read” (past: I read / I have read).
additional_notes: “Eu” = “I”. “Li” is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) form of the verb “ler” (“to read”), used for a completed reading in the past. It can mean “I read (it)” or “I have read (it)” depending on context. Often followed by what you read: “eu li o livro/a nota”, or by “que” to mean “I read that…”.
target_language_example: Eu li esse artigo hoje de manhã.
native_language_example: I read that article this morning.

meaning: “I read this book” (completed action in the past).
additional_notes: Uses the simple past (pretérito perfeito): eu li = “I read” (past, finished). From the verb ler (to read); li is irregular. You can add time expressions like “dois anos atrás” / “há dois anos” (two years ago) or “quando…” (when…) to say when you read it.
target_language_example: Eu li este livro no ano passado.
native_language_example: I read this book last year.

additional_notes: Used when the verb is reflexive and the subject is “eu” (I). It often corresponds to English “I … myself” or just “I …” (since English doesn’t always mark reflexives). Common with daily-routine verbs and actions done to yourself: eu me levanto (I get up), eu me casei (I got married), eu me machuquei (I hurt myself). In Brazilian Portuguese, “eu me” is standard; you may also hear “me” before the verb in some contexts (e.g., “Eu me levanto” / “Eu levanto-me” (more formal in Portugal)).
target_language_example: Eu me sinto bem hoje.
native_language_example: I feel good today.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "se apaixonar por" = "to fall in love with" (often meaning to start having romantic feelings). Commonly followed by a time expression like "desde o instante em que..." (since the moment that...) or "no dia/momento que..." (on the day/moment that...). You can change the person/object: "ele se apaixonou por ela" (he fell in love with her), "eu me apaixonei por você" (I fell in love with you).
target_language_example: Eu me apaixonei por ela desde o primeiro dia.
native_language_example: I fell in love with her from the first day.

additional_notes: Used to express regret about a past action. It’s formed with "arrepender-se de" + "ter" + past participle (e.g., "ter feito", "ter dito", "ter ido"). Often followed by a verb in the past participle to say what you regret doing.
target_language_example: Eu me arrependo de ter dito isso.
native_language_example: I regret having said that.

additional_notes: Very common and neutral in Brazilian Portuguese. It literally means “I call myself” (chamar = to call), and it’s followed by your name: “Eu me chamo Ana.” Often shortened in speech to “Me chamo Ana.” Alternatives you may also hear: “Meu nome é…” (more direct: “My name is…”).
target_language_example: Oi, eu me chamo Laura. Prazer!
native_language_example: Hi, my name is Laura. Nice to meet you!

meaning: I had a lot of fun.
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of the reflexive verb "divertir-se" = "to have fun". "Me" matches "eu" (I). Often followed by "em/na/no" + place/event (Eu me diverti muito na festa.) or with a gerund to say how you had fun (Eu me diverti muito fazendo isso.).
target_language_example: Eu me diverti muito com vocês ontem.
native_language_example: I had a lot of fun with you guys yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say you met someone, either on purpose (meeting up) or by chance (running into). Very common in Brazilian Portuguese with people: “Eu me encontrei com a Ana.” You can also hear the non-reflexive version with the same meaning: “Eu encontrei a Ana.”
target_language_example: Eu me encontrei com o João depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I met up with João after work.

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive pronoun “me” with the verb “esconder-se” (to hide oneself). It’s the pretérito perfeito (completed past action): “eu me escondi” = I hid (at a specific time). Common with place phrases like “atrás de…” (behind) or “em/no/na…” (in/on + the).
target_language_example: Quando ouvi um barulho, eu me escondi atrás da porta.
native_language_example: When I heard a noise, I hid behind the door.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say you forgot to do something (eu me esqueci de dizer…). It can also introduce a noun/idea you forgot about (eu me esqueci do seu nome). In Brazil, people also commonly say “eu esqueci de …” (without “me”).
target_language_example: Eu me esqueci de comprar pão.
native_language_example: I forgot to buy bread.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **(se) lembrar (de)** = “to remember.” It often comes with **de**: *Eu me lembro de você* (“I remember you”). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many people also say **Eu lembro** (without *me*), with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Eu me lembro de quando a gente se conheceu.
native_language_example: I remember when we met.

additional_notes: Used to say you remember a person/thing (“Eu me lembro de vocês dois.”) or to remember doing something in the past (“Eu me lembro de ter ouvido…”, “Eu me lembro de tê-lo encontrado…”). The pattern is usually: eu me lembro de + noun/pronoun, or eu me lembro de + verb in the infinitive (often ter + past participle to mean “having done”). In everyday speech, many people also say “eu lembro de” (without “me”).
target_language_example: Eu me lembro de ter visto esse filme quando era criança.
native_language_example: I remember seeing that movie when I was a kid.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **levantar-se** (“to get up / to stand up”). It can mean standing up from a seat (**da cadeira**) or getting out of bed / starting your day, often with a time (**muito cedo**, **trinta minutos atrás**, **às seis**). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people also say **eu levantei** (without **me**) with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Eu me levantei do sofá quando a campainha tocou.
native_language_example: I got up from the sofa when the doorbell rang.

additional_notes: Used to say you changed where you live and relocated to a destination. "mudar-se" is the verb “to move (house),” and it’s commonly used with "para" + city/house/apartment. Often followed by a time expression like "ontem", "recentemente", or "logo após...".
target_language_example: Eu me mudei para São Paulo no ano passado.
native_language_example: I moved to São Paulo last year.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a question you’re thinking about (often with words like por que/porque, o que, qual, quanto, etc.). It can also be followed by “sobre” to mean “I wonder about…”. In Brazil you’ll also hear “eu me pergunto se…” (“I wonder if…”).
target_language_example: Eu me pergunto se ele vai chegar a tempo.
native_language_example: I wonder if he’ll arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a question you’re thinking about (often with curiosity or uncertainty). It’s followed by a clause, like a question embedded in a sentence: “Eu me pergunto como ele fez isso” (“I wonder how he did that”). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people also often say “Eu me pergunto como…” or simply “Me pergunto como…”.
target_language_example: Eu me pergunto como isso vai terminar.
native_language_example: I wonder how this will end.

additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or uncertainty about something (often followed by a full clause: eu me pergunto o que + subject + verb). Very common in conversation and writing. You may also hear the shorter form “me pergunto o que …” when the subject “eu” is implied.
target_language_example: Eu me pergunto o que vai acontecer amanhã.
native_language_example: I wonder what will happen tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or uncertainty about a place/location. It’s typically followed by a full clause ("...onde ele foi", "...onde ela mora") or by an infinitive to talk about what to do ("...onde colocar/pendurar...").
target_language_example: Eu me pergunto onde fica a estação de metrô.
native_language_example: I wonder where the subway station is.

additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or uncertainty about the reason for something. Often followed by a full clause (subject + verb). In Portuguese you’ll see both “por que” and “por quê”; “por que” is typically used before the explanation, and “por quê” is often used at the end of a question or before punctuation.
target_language_example: Eu me pergunto por que ele não respondeu à minha mensagem.
native_language_example: I wonder why he didn’t reply to my message.

eu me pergunto por que o

target_language_multi_word_term: eu me pergunto por que o
additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or puzzlement about a reason. It’s typically followed by a masculine noun (o) or a male name/title (o Tom, o professor). For feminine nouns, you’ll usually see: "eu me pergunto por que a...". "por que" here means "why" in an indirect question.
target_language_example: Eu me pergunto por que o ônibus está atrasado.
native_language_example: I wonder why the bus is late.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or curiosity about something. It’s often followed by a yes/no idea introduced by "se" (if/whether). You can use it when you’re thinking out loud: "Eu me pergunto se ele vem." = "I wonder if he’s coming."
target_language_example: Eu me pergunto se vai chover hoje.
native_language_example: I wonder if it’s going to rain today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a question you’re thinking about (you don’t know the answer). It often continues with a person or thing: “Eu me pergunto se o Tom...” = “I wonder if Tom...”. Note: Portuguese also uses “se” for “if/whether” (not just “if” in conditions). “o” is the masculine singular article (“the”); in other sentences you may see “a” (fem.), “os” (masc. plural), or “as” (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Eu me pergunto se o professor vai chegar cedo.
native_language_example: I wonder if the teacher is going to arrive early.

meaning: “I refuse to …” (I won’t / I’m not willing to).
additional_notes: Used to strongly say you will not do something. It’s followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., aceitar, desistir, sair). In everyday speech you may also hear “eu recuso” or “recuso-me a”, but “eu me recuso a” is very common in Brazil.
target_language_example: Eu me recuso a mentir para você.
native_language_example: I refuse to lie to you.

additional_notes: Used to describe your emotional or physical state in the past. It’s the past tense of "eu me sinto" (“I feel”), with the reflexive pronoun "me". You typically follow it with an adjective: "Eu me senti cansado(a), culpado(a), envergonhado(a), impotente." Adjectives often change for gender (cansado/cansada, culpado/culpada, envergonhado/envergonhada).
target_language_example: Eu me senti melhor depois de descansar.
native_language_example: I felt better after resting.

additional_notes: Used to describe your physical or emotional state. In Portuguese it often appears with an adjective ("Eu me sinto bem/mal/normal") or with "cansado/cansada" (agreeing with the speaker’s gender). In everyday speech, many people also say "Eu sinto" or "Me sinto" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Hoje eu me sinto bem, mas ontem eu me senti mal.
native_language_example: Today I feel good, but yesterday I felt bad.

additional_notes: Often refers to feeling physically sick (“I don’t feel well”) or emotionally bad/guilty (“I feel bad about…”). Common patterns: “Eu me sinto mal.” (I feel bad/unwell.) / “Eu me sinto mal em + infinitive” (I feel bad about doing something: “...em mentir” = about lying) / “Eu me sinto mal por/pelo/pela + person/thing” (I feel sorry for someone: “...pelo Tom”).
target_language_example: Hoje eu me sinto mal, então vou ficar em casa.
native_language_example: Today I feel unwell, so I’m going to stay home.

additional_notes: Use this to talk about how you’re feeling, usually followed by an adjective: eu me sinto muito bem/mal (I feel very good/bad), muito animado(a) (very excited), muito sozinho(a) (very lonely), muito melhor (much better). The adjective often changes for gender (animado/animada, sozinho/sozinha, gordo/gorda).
target_language_example: Eu me sinto muito cansado hoje.
native_language_example: I feel very tired today.

additional_notes: Use this to express a strong feeling or emotional state, followed by an adjective (or an adjective phrase): eu me sinto tão + adjective. Often used with feelings like desanimado (discouraged), humilhado (humiliated), sem esperança (hopeless), sozinho/sozinha (alone), vivo (alive). Adjectives usually agree with the speaker’s gender (sozinho/sozinha).
target_language_example: Eu me sinto tão cansado hoje.
native_language_example: I feel so tired today.

additional_notes: Used to say where you live or who you live with. Often followed by a place (eu moro aqui / em Lisboa / na casa...) or an adverb like “agora” (now). The verb is morar (“to live/reside”); eu moro is the present tense for “I.”
target_language_example: Eu moro perto do trabalho.
native_language_example: I live near work.

additional_notes: Use this to say where you live (city, state, country, etc.). The verb is **morar** (“to live/reside”), and **em** means “in.” The place name usually comes right after: *Eu moro em Boston.*
target_language_example: Eu moro em São Paulo, mas trabalho no Rio.
native_language_example: I live in São Paulo, but I work in Rio.

meaning: “I live in (the)…”, used before certain place names.
additional_notes: Use "eu moro" + a preposition + place. "no" = "em" + "o" (in the), so it’s used with masculine singular places that take the article "o" (e.g., no Japão, no Rio de Janeiro). Many cities don’t use an article, so you’d say "Eu moro em São Paulo" (not *no*). Some places are feminine and use "na" (em + a), e.g., "na França".
target_language_example: Eu moro no Brasil.
native_language_example: I live in Brazil.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of the verb "nascer" (to be born). Often followed by where or when you were born: "eu nasci em..." (in), "eu nasci no/na..." (in the + masc./fem. place), or "eu nasci em [year/decade]". In relative clauses you’ll often see "onde eu nasci" (where I was born) or "em que eu nasci" (in which I was born).
target_language_example: Eu nasci no Brasil, mas cresci nos Estados Unidos.
native_language_example: I was born in Brazil, but I grew up in the United States.

additional_notes: Used to say your birthplace. It’s the past tense of “nascer” (to be born): “eu nasci” = “I was born,” followed by “em” + a city/country (often without an article with city names). You can add more info with “mas cresci em …” (“but I grew up in …”).
target_language_example: Eu nasci em Lisboa, mas moro em Londres agora.
native_language_example: I was born in Lisbon, but I live in London now.

meaning: “I never” (used to say something has never happened, or would never happen).
additional_notes: Used with a verb to say you have never done/experienced something: “Eu nunca fiz isso.” It can refer to the past/present (“I’ve never… / I never…”) or to a hypothetical/conditional situation with the conditional or “teria” (“I would never… / I would never have…”), e.g. “Eu nunca poderia…” / “Eu nunca teria conseguido…”.
target_language_example: Eu nunca vi esse filme.
native_language_example: I’ve never seen that movie.

additional_notes: Used to express surprise about something you didn’t expect or imagine. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., “pudesse”, “fosse”) or by a future form (e.g., “iria acontecer”, “aconteceria”). Often implies “I never expected…” in English.
target_language_example: Eu nunca pensei que isso fosse tão difícil.
native_language_example: I never thought it would be so difficult.

additional_notes: Used to say that up to a point in the past, you had not had the experience of seeing something. It uses the past perfect in Portuguese: eu + nunca + tinha + visto (ver = to see). Often followed by a thing/person ("Eu nunca tinha visto algo assim") or by a clause ("Eu nunca tinha visto o Tom chorando").
target_language_example: Eu nunca tinha visto tanta gente aqui antes do show começar.
native_language_example: I’d never seen so many people here before the show started.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence or clause to negate what follows. Typically followed by a verb: "Eu não sei" (I don’t know), "Eu não quero" (I don’t want). In Portuguese, "não" can also come before the verb without "eu" when the subject is understood.
target_language_example: Eu não entendo.
native_language_example: I don’t understand.

meaning: “I’m not …” (using estar: not in a certain state/condition).
additional_notes: Used to say you are *not* in a temporary state or condition (feelings, health, mood, being sleepy, being used to something, being sure/ready, etc.). Often contrasts with **eu não sou** (ser) for more permanent identity/traits. Common pattern: **Eu não estou + adjective** (e.g., *Eu não estou cansado* = I’m not tired).
target_language_example: Eu não estou pronto agora.
native_language_example: I’m not ready right now.

eu não fazia ideia de que

target_language_multi_word_term: eu não fazia ideia de que
additional_notes: Used to say you didn’t know something before (often something surprising). The verb is in the imperfect past (fazia), so it’s like “I didn’t use to have any idea / I had no idea” at that time. You’ll also hear: “Eu não tenho ideia de que …” (present, “I have no idea that …”) and “Eu não fazia ideia!” (by itself: “I had no idea!”).
target_language_example: Eu não fazia ideia de que o filme era tão longo.
native_language_example: I had no idea the movie was so long.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t like something or someone. It’s the verb gostar (to like) in the present tense: eu gosto = I like, eu não gosto = I don’t like. It normally takes de before what you like/dislike: eu não gosto de café. With pronouns it stays the same: eu não gosto de você = I don’t like you. You can also use it before a verb in the infinitive: eu não gosto de estudar = I don’t like studying.
target_language_example: Eu não gosto de acordar cedo.
native_language_example: I don’t like waking up early.

meaning: "I can’t" / "I’m not able to" (also used for "I’m not allowed to").
additional_notes: Used to say you cannot do something because it’s impossible, you don’t have the ability, you don’t have permission, or you refuse ("I can’t" meaning "I won’t"). It’s followed by a verb in the infinitive: "eu não posso aceitar / ir / pagar". In Portuguese, "não" comes before the verb: "eu não posso".
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu não posso falar agora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t talk right now.

meaning: "I don't want" (I do not want to).
additional_notes: Used to refuse something, say you don’t desire something, or say you don’t intend to do something. Often followed by a verb in the infinitive (eu não quero incomodar = I don’t want to bother) or by a noun/pronoun (eu não quero nenhuma banana = I don’t want any banana; eu não quero ninguém = I don’t want anyone). In casual speech, you may also hear just "não quero" when the subject is obvious.
target_language_example: Eu não quero sair hoje.
native_language_example: I don't want to go out today.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have the information or aren’t sure. It can stand alone as a full answer ("Eu não sei.") or introduce a clause: "Eu não sei que..." (“I don’t know what/that...”), "Para onde..., eu não sei" (“Where to..., I don’t know”).
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu não sei a resposta.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know the answer.

additional_notes: First-person singular negative of **ser** (“to be”). Use it to say what you are not (identity, profession, characteristics), often followed by a noun or adjective: *Eu não sou um herói* (“I’m not a hero”), *Eu não sou ambicioso* (“I’m not ambitious”). For temporary states, Portuguese often uses **não estou** (from **estar**) instead.
target_language_example: Eu não sou médico, mas posso ajudar.
native_language_example: I’m not a doctor, but I can help.

additional_notes: Used to say you lack something (an object, time, plans, etc.). Often followed by a noun: eu não tenho tempo (I don’t have time), eu não tenho dinheiro (I don’t have money). In Portuguese you typically keep the subject “eu” when emphasizing or contrasting, but it can be omitted in context: Não tenho tempo.
target_language_example: Desculpe, eu não tenho dinheiro agora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have money right now.

meaning: “I don’t have anything / I have nothing.”
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t possess anything, don’t have anything to do, or don’t have any objection/complaint. Very common in longer patterns like: “Eu não tenho nada contra…” (I have nothing against…), “Eu não tenho nada de que me queixar.” (I have nothing to complain about), and “Eu não tenho nada para fazer.” (I have nothing to do). Often pronounced in speech like “eu num tenho nada” (very informal pronunciation).
target_language_example: Hoje eu não tenho nada para fazer, então vou ficar em casa.
native_language_example: Today I don’t have anything to do, so I’m going to stay at home.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of ter (tinha) to say you didn’t have something in the past, often describing a situation/state over a period of time. It can be followed by a noun (eu não tinha amigos) or by a phrase like certeza de/que (eu não tinha certeza se/que...).
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, eu não tinha tempo para brincar.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I didn’t have time to play.

eu não tinha ideia de que

target_language_multi_word_term: eu não tinha ideia de que
additional_notes: Used to say you didn’t know or didn’t realize something in the past, and it introduces a clause with que (“that”). Often followed by a verb in the past or conditional (e.g., estaria, poderia, era). In the present you can say: Eu não tenho ideia de que… (“I have no idea that…”), though more common is Eu não fazia ideia de que… for “I had no idea that…”.
target_language_example: Eu não tinha ideia de que a reunião começava tão cedo.
native_language_example: I had no idea that the meeting started so early.

eu não tinha ideia de que você

target_language_multi_word_term: eu não tinha ideia de que você
additional_notes: Used to express surprise about something you didn’t know before. Literally “I didn’t have an idea that you…”. It’s commonly followed by a verb clause (e.g., "era", "podia", "trabalhava"). You can also change the subject: "Eu não tinha ideia de que ele/ela/vocês…"
target_language_example: Eu não tinha ideia de que você morava tão longe.
native_language_example: I had no idea that you lived so far away.

additional_notes: Used to refuse or state you will not do something. It’s very common before another verb in the infinitive: “Eu não vou + infinitive” (Eu não vou dizer / fazer / falar). In speech, “não vou” can sound like “num vou” (informal pronunciation). Also used for plans: “Eu não vou ao trabalho amanhã” = “I’m not going to work tomorrow.”
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu não vou responder a essa pergunta.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m not going to answer that question.

additional_notes: Used when the speaker (eu) is doing an action to a male person or a masculine thing already known in context. The "o" is a direct object clitic meaning "him" or "it" (masculine). It often appears before the verb in formal/standard Portuguese: "Eu o vejo" = "I see him." In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people very often avoid "o" and say "Eu vejo ele" (him) or just drop the pronoun if it’s clear.
target_language_example: Eu o encontrei ontem no trabalho.
native_language_example: I found him yesterday at work.

additional_notes: "O" is the direct-object pronoun (“him/it”) placed before the verb. "Vi" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "ver" (“to see”). Used for a completed action in the past; for a woman/thing referred to as feminine, use "eu a vi" (“I saw her/it”). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many speakers more often say "eu vi ele" / "eu vi isso" instead of "eu o vi".
target_language_example: Eu o vi na rua mais cedo.
native_language_example: I saw him on the street earlier.

additional_notes: Used to express a strong negative feeling about something (a thing, an activity, or a situation). Common patterns: "Eu odeio + noun" (Eu odeio química.) and "Eu odeio + infinitive" (Eu odeio esperar.), and "Eu odeio quando..." to complain about a situation (Eu odeio quando tem muita gente.).
target_language_example: Eu odeio quando alguém chega atrasado.
native_language_example: I hate when someone arrives late.

additional_notes: "Os" is the direct-object pronoun “them” (usually masculine or mixed group) and "vi" is the past tense of "ver" (to see): “I saw.” In Portuguese, object pronouns like "o/os/a/as" can come before the verb ("eu os vi") in more formal/written style. In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many speakers prefer "Eu vi eles/elas" instead. You can also follow it with another verb to mean “I saw them [do something]”: "Eu os vi entrar" (I saw them enter).
target_language_example: Eu os vi chegando tarde na reunião.
native_language_example: I saw them arriving late to the meeting.

additional_notes: Past tense of **ouvir** (“to hear”). Often just means you perceived a sound or someone speaking: **Eu ouvi um trovão** (“I heard thunder”), **Eu ouvi alguém entrar** (“I heard someone come in”). With a direct object that’s a person, it can mean “I listened to” (paid attention): **Eu ouvi o Tom cuidadosamente**. In **Eu ouvi falar**, it means “I’ve heard (about it)” / “I heard people say.”
target_language_example: Eu ouvi dizer que a loja fecha cedo hoje.
native_language_example: I heard that the store closes early today.

meaning: “I heard that…” / “I’ve heard that…” (reporting information you heard from someone else).
additional_notes: Used to introduce second-hand information or a rumor. It often implies you’re not fully sure it’s true (similar to “I hear that…”). The verb is the past of ouvir (“to hear”): eu ouvi = “I heard.” You can also use it without “eu”: “Ouvi dizer que…”
target_language_example: Eu ouvi dizer que vai chover amanhã.
native_language_example: I heard it’s going to rain tomorrow.

meaning: I stopped smoking / I quit smoking.
additional_notes: "Parar de" + infinitive means "to stop doing" something. "Eu parei de fumar" is in the past (pretérito perfeito) and refers to a completed action: you stopped smoking. In conversation, people may also say "Parei de fumar" (dropping "eu").
target_language_example: Eu parei de fumar no ano passado.
native_language_example: I quit smoking last year.

additional_notes:
Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **passar** for “I”. Meaning depends on what comes next:
- **passar por (aqui/lá)** = to pass by, stop by briefly: *Eu passei por aqui.*
- **passar + time period** (a manhã, o dia, a semana) = to spend time: *Eu passei a semana inteira em Boston.*
- **passar em/na (prova)** = to pass an exam/test: *Eu passei na prova.*
- **passar por cima de** (figurative) = to disregard/step over others to get what you want.
target_language_example: Eu passei a tarde toda estudando para a prova.
native_language_example: I spent the whole afternoon studying for the test.

additional_notes: Used to say how you spent your day (who you were with, where you were, or what you did). It’s the past tense of passar o dia (“to spend the day”). Very commonly followed by: com + person (Eu passei o dia com a Ana.), em/na/no + place (Eu passei o dia na praia.), or a gerund (-ando/-endo/-indo) to describe an activity (Eu passei o dia estudando.).
target_language_example: Eu passei o dia estudando para a prova.
native_language_example: I spent the day studying for the test.

meaning: "I spent the whole day" (doing something / somewhere / with someone).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "passar" in the past ("passei" = "I spent"). It’s commonly followed by: (1) a gerund to say what you did: "passei o dia inteiro lendo" (reading), "assistindo" (watching); (2) a place: "em casa" (at home); or (3) a person: "com o Tom" (with Tom). Often implies it took basically all day.
target_language_example: Eu passei o dia inteiro trabalhando e nem vi o tempo passar.
native_language_example: I spent the whole day working and didn’t even notice the time go by.

eu passei o fim de semana com

target_language_multi_word_term: eu passei o fim de semana com
additional_notes: Used to say who you were with during the weekend. The verb is in the past (passei = I spent). You can replace the person/group after com (with): com ele/ela (with him/her), com eles/elas (with them), com meus/minhas… (with my…).
target_language_example: Eu passei o fim de semana com a minha família.
native_language_example: I spent the weekend with my family.

additional_notes: Past tense of pedir (pretérito perfeito): used for a completed action. Common uses: pedir algo = ask/request something (Eu pedi ajuda.); pedir comida/bebida = order (Eu pedi o almoço.; Eu pedi só um café.); pedir com/sem… = request a feature/option (Eu pedi com vista pro mar.); pedir para + person + infinitive = ask someone to do something (Eu pedi para o Tom assinar…); pedir para que + subjunctive = more formal “ask that …” (Eu pedi para que ele nos enviasse…); pedir permissão a alguém = ask permission from someone (Eu pedi permissão ao Tom.).
target_language_example: Eu pedi a conta, por favor.
native_language_example: I asked for the bill/check, please.

meaning: 'I took' / 'I got' / 'I caught' (past tense of pegar).
additional_notes: "Eu peguei" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "pegar" and its meaning depends on what comes next. Common beginner uses: **pegar + transport** = “to take” (Eu peguei o elevador / um ônibus / um táxi); **pegar + something** = “to catch/get” (Eu peguei um peixe!); **pegar no sono** = “to fall asleep” (Eu peguei no sono enquanto lia).
target_language_example: Eu peguei um táxi para casa.
native_language_example: I took a taxi home.

meaning: "I thought that" / "I used to think that."
additional_notes: Used to introduce a belief or expectation you had (often in the past), sometimes implying it turned out to be wrong or different than expected. The verb is in the imperfect tense (pensava), which often suggests an ongoing or habitual thought in the past. Often followed by another verb in the past (e.g., conhecia) or conditional (e.g., seria).
target_language_example: Eu pensava que ele já tinha chegado.
native_language_example: I thought he had already arrived.

meaning: “I thought that the …” (about a man/masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to introduce something you believed in the past (often something that turns out not to be true). It’s the imperfect tense of pensar (“to think”), common for past beliefs/assumptions. Use “que a” with feminine nouns (Eu pensava que a Maria era canadense) and just “que” before names/pronouns (Eu pensava que ele era canadense).
target_language_example: Eu pensava que o seu irmão morava aqui.
native_language_example: I thought that your brother lived here.

meaning: "I thought you..." / "I used to think you..."
additional_notes: Used to introduce a belief or assumption you had (often that turned out to be wrong). "Pensava" is the imperfect tense of "pensar" (to think), so it often implies an ongoing or repeated thought in the past. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the past (e.g., "conhecia", "gostava", "tinha"). In everyday speech, "que" is sometimes omitted: "Eu pensava você..." (less formal).
target_language_example: Eu pensava que você já sabia disso.
native_language_example: I thought you already knew that.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you believed or assumed in the past (often something that turns out to be wrong or surprising). In Portuguese it’s very common for the verb in the next clause to be in the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., “fosse”, “tivesse”, “pudesse”) or in the past (e.g., “tinha ido”).
target_language_example: Eu pensei que você já tinha saído.
native_language_example: I thought you had already left.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed in the past (often something that turned out to be different). Common before an adjective or noun phrase: “Eu pensei que era óbvio” (I thought it was obvious), “Eu pensei que era pouco demais” (I thought it was too little). Often implies a mistaken assumption depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu pensei que era hoje, mas é amanhã.
native_language_example: I thought it was today, but it’s tomorrow.

meaning: “I thought it was…” / “I thought it would be…”
additional_notes: Used to talk about a past belief or assumption that may have been wrong or later corrected. After verbs like pensar (to think) in the past, Portuguese commonly uses the imperfect subjunctive (fosse, from ser) after que: “pensei que fosse…”. Often followed by a noun (“…o Tom”), an adjective (“…muito legal”), or a clause.
target_language_example: Eu pensei que fosse hoje, mas é amanhã.
native_language_example: I thought it was today, but it’s tomorrow.

meaning: “I thought that the …” (I believed the … was/ would be …).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed in the past. After "pensei que", Portuguese often uses the subjunctive in the following clause (e.g., "estivesse", "fosse", "falasse"), especially when expressing uncertainty, a mistaken assumption, or reported expectation. In everyday speech, many people also use the indicative (e.g., "estava"). "o" is the masculine singular article (“the”); it can change to "a/os/as" depending on the noun (e.g., "eu pensei que a Maria...").
target_language_example: Eu pensei que o ônibus chegaria mais cedo.
native_language_example: I thought the bus would arrive earlier.

meaning: “I thought you…” (introducing what you believed, often in the past).
additional_notes: Used when you assumed something about the other person. "Pensei" is the simple past of "pensar" (to think), and "que" introduces the clause that follows. In speech you can change "você" to another subject (e.g., "eu pensei que ele/ela…", "eu pensei que vocês…").
target_language_example: Eu pensei que você estava em casa.
native_language_example: I thought you were at home.

meaning: "I thought you were..." (I assumed you were...).
additional_notes: Used to say you had an (often mistaken) assumption about someone. After "pensei que", Portuguese typically uses the imperfect subjunctive ("fosse") when referring to an imagined/uncertain situation in the past. "Fosse" is the past subjunctive of "ser" (to be), and it can be followed by a noun/adjective ("médico", "canadense"), a place phrase ("de Boston"), or a person ("Tom").
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu pensei que você fosse a gerente.
native_language_example: Sorry, I thought you were the manager.

additional_notes: “Eu penso” is the first-person singular of the verb “pensar” (to think). It’s often followed by a preposition: “penso em” + person/thing (think about; also used for “miss/think of” someone: “Eu penso em você”) and “penso sobre” + topic/issue (think about/reflect on a subject). In Portuguese you can also drop “eu” because the verb ending already shows the subject: “Penso em você.”
target_language_example: Eu penso no trabalho durante a noite.
native_language_example: I think about work at night.

additional_notes: From the verb "perder" in the simple past (pretérito perfeito): "eu perdi" = "I lost". It’s used with a direct object: "eu perdi o livro" (I lost the book). With transport/events/appointments, "perder" often means "to miss": "eu perdi o trem" (I missed the train).
target_language_example: Acho que eu perdi minhas chaves.
native_language_example: I think I lost my keys.

additional_notes: From the verb **perder** (to lose / to miss). Use it when you didn’t catch part of something in time (**perdi o começo / o final do filme** = “I missed the beginning/end of the movie”) or when you stopped having something like control or interest (**perdi o controle** = “I lost control”, **perdi o interesse** = “I lost interest”). **o** is the masculine singular article (“the”); with a feminine noun you use **a** (**eu perdi a…**).
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu perdi o que você disse.
native_language_example: Sorry, I missed what you said.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun you possess (o meu + noun). With objects (cartão, caderno), perder usually means "to lose." With scheduled transport (voo, ônibus), perder often means "to miss" (arrive too late). You can also change it for feminine nouns: "eu perdi a minha…" (e.g., "a minha mala").
target_language_example: Eu perdi o meu passaporte no aeroporto.
native_language_example: I lost my passport at the airport.

additional_notes: Used when you want to say you asked a question in the past. Common patterns: **eu perguntei a/à [person]** (I asked [someone]), **eu perguntei para [person]** (also: I asked [someone]), and **eu perguntei [question word]...** (I asked what/where/if...).
target_language_example: Eu perguntei ao professor se a prova era hoje.
native_language_example: I asked the teacher if the exam was today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **perguntar** (“to ask”). **Eu perguntei a + person** means “I asked + person” (the **a** introduces the person you asked). You can then add what you asked using **se** (“if/whether”), a question word (**o que**, **onde**, etc.), or the topic with **sobre** (“about”). Common pattern: **Eu perguntei ao/à + person …** (a + o = **ao**; a + a = **à**).
target_language_example: Eu perguntei ao professor se a prova era hoje.
native_language_example: I asked the teacher if the test was today.

meaning: 'I could' / 'I would be able to' (often polite: 'could I...?').
additional_notes: Literally 'I' (eu) + 'could/was able to' (poderia). Used to talk about ability/possibility in a hypothetical situation ('I could/would be able to...') and to make polite requests or questions ('Could I see...?'). Often followed by an infinitive: 'eu poderia + verbo' (eu poderia ver, eu poderia dizer). It can also appear in conditional sentences: 'Se..., eu poderia...' ('If..., I could/would be able to...').
target_language_example: Eu poderia pagar com cartão?
native_language_example: Could I pay by card?

meaning: “I could have” (a past possibility/ability that didn’t happen).
additional_notes: Used with a past participle (e.g., comprado, evitado, visitado) to talk about something you were able/likely to do in the past, but didn’t. Often appears with a condition (Se eu soubesse..., Se eu tivesse...) to mean “I could have (done it) if…”.
