native_language_example: Can you tell me exactly what happened yesterday?

meaning: "exactly what I (… )" (used to emphasize that something matches perfectly).
additional_notes: Used when you’re about to say what you needed, wanted, meant, said, asked for, etc. It’s typically followed by a verb phrase, e.g. "Exatamente o que eu precisava" (needed), "Exatamente o que eu quis dizer" (meant), "Exatamente o que eu pedi" (asked for). Often appears after "é/era" (is/was): "Isso é/era exatamente o que eu…"
target_language_example: Isso é exatamente o que eu estava procurando.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what I was looking for.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause describing the thing you want to explain (often followed by a verb like "significa" / "aconteceu"). Common in questions ("Você pode explicar o que…?") and when introducing an explanation ("Deixe-me explicar o que…").
target_language_example: Você pode explicar o que você quis dizer com isso?
native_language_example: Can you explain what you meant by that?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ser" (often in the past: "foi") to say someone was expelled from a school. "Expulso" is the masculine form; for a woman you say "expulsa da escola". You can also specify the school: "expulso da escola X".
target_language_example: Ele foi expulso da escola por brigar com outro aluno.
native_language_example: He was expelled from school for fighting with another student.

meaning: 'people speak' / 'it is spoken'; also 'it is said/rumored'.
additional_notes: Impersonal/passive use of "falar" with "se" (no specific subject). Common for talking about what language is spoken in a place ("Aqui fala-se português" = "Portuguese is spoken here") and for general talk/rumors ("Fala-se que..." = "People say/It’s said that...").
target_language_example: Nesta cidade fala-se muito de política.
native_language_example: In this city, people talk a lot about politics.

additional_notes: Uses the impersonal construction "fala-se" (verb + "se") to talk about what people in general speak, without naming who. Very common for languages: "Fala-se inglês aqui" = "English is spoken here." Word order can vary (often after a place: "No Canadá, fala-se inglês").
target_language_example: Aqui fala-se inglês e espanhol.
native_language_example: English and Spanish are spoken here.

additional_notes: Used to compare the way someone speaks to a different type of person/thing (often to criticize or tease). After **como se**, Portuguese typically uses the **imperfect subjunctive**: **fosse** (from *ser*). The article changes with gender/number: **um/uma/uns/umas** (e.g., *fala como se fosse uma professora*).
target_language_example: Ele fala como se fosse um especialista, mas nunca estudou o assunto.
native_language_example: He talks as if he were an expert, but he never studied the topic.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **falar** (to speak) + the language name. It usually appears with a subject: **Ele fala francês.** You can change the person: **Eu falo francês** (I speak French), **Você fala francês?** (Do you speak French?). For emphasis you can add adverbs like **fluentemente** (fluently) or **só** (only).
target_language_example: Você fala francês?
native_language_example: Do you speak French?

additional_notes: Used to compare speaking ability. Structure: (subject) + fala + (language) + melhor do que + (person/thing being compared). You can turn it into a yes/no question with intonation or by adding a question mark in writing: "Ele fala francês melhor do que você?" It also works with other verbs and skills, e.g., "canta melhor do que" (sings better than), and with other languages: "fala inglês melhor do que".
target_language_example: Ela fala francês melhor do que eu.
native_language_example: She speaks French better than I do.

additional_notes: Used to compare someone’s ability (here, speaking French) to another person’s ability. Pattern: [subject] fala [língua] tão bem quanto [pessoa/pronome]. You can swap in other languages or verbs (e.g., fala inglês…, canta tão bem quanto…).
target_language_example: Ela fala inglês tão bem quanto o professor.
native_language_example: She speaks English as well as the teacher.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone can speak the Japanese language. It’s the verb "falar" (to speak) conjugated for "he/she/you (formal)/it" in the present tense: "(ele/ela/você) fala". In questions you’ll often see it as "Você fala japonês?" (Do you speak Japanese?) or "Alguém aqui fala japonês?" (Does anyone here speak Japanese?).
target_language_example: Ela fala japonês e inglês.
native_language_example: She speaks Japanese and English.

meaning: “speaks a little (bit) of …” (has basic ability in a language).
additional_notes: Used mainly with languages: "falar" (to speak) + "um pouco" (a little) + "de" + the language. It often implies limited/basic proficiency. Can be modified with words like "também" (also) or "só" (only): "Ele só fala um pouco de francês" = he only speaks a little French.
target_language_example: Eu falo um pouco de português, mas ainda estou aprendendo.
native_language_example: I speak a little Portuguese, but I’m still learning.

additional_notes: Present tense of the verb "falar" (to speak) with "eles/elas/vocês": "(they/you all) speak". Used to say that a group knows/speaks the French language. For a singular person: "fala francês" (he/she/you speak French).
target_language_example: Eles falam francês muito bem.
native_language_example: They speak French very well.

additional_notes: “Falando com” is the gerund (present participle) of “falar” + “com” (“to talk/speak with”). It describes an ongoing action: someone is in the middle of talking with someone else. In many situations it translates as “talking to” in English, even though Portuguese uses “com” (“with”). It often appears after verbs like “estar/ficar/passar (tempo)” to emphasize duration or that the action is happening right now.
target_language_example: Estou falando com a minha mãe agora; posso te ligar depois?
native_language_example: I'm talking to my mom now; can I call you later?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "falar" (to speak) with "no telefone" (= "on the phone"). Often appears with "estar" to describe an action in progress: "está falando no telefone" (he/she is talking on the phone). You can also use it to describe how long someone has been on the phone: "há horas" (for hours).
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu não posso atender agora; estou falando no telefone.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t answer right now; I’m talking on the phone.

additional_notes: Used with the verb falar + sobre + noun/pronoun to introduce the topic of the conversation. It can refer to something you’re discussing now (Estamos falando sobre...) or something you were discussing earlier (Eu estava falando sobre...). Often takes pronouns like ele/ela/você/isso: falando sobre ele (about him), falando sobre isso (about that).
target_language_example: A gente estava falando sobre o seu trabalho ontem.
native_language_example: We were talking about your job yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to show you mean what you're saying or to check if someone is joking. Often appears with verbs like “estar” (estou falando sério) or on its own in conversation: “Tá falando sério?” / “Tô falando sério.”.
target_language_example: Falando sério, eu preciso ir embora agora.
native_language_example: Seriously, I need to leave now.

additional_notes: Used to talk about people who speak a language as their first language (from childhood). Common in language-learning contexts: "praticar [uma língua] com falantes nativos" = to practice [a language] with native speakers. Singular: "falante nativo"; feminine forms: "falante nativa", "falantes nativas".
target_language_example: Estou procurando falantes nativos de português para praticar.
native_language_example: I’m looking for native Portuguese speakers to practice with.

additional_notes: Used to express the goal/ability of speaking English in a confident way. Common with verbs like "gostaria de" (I’d like to) and "poder" (to be able to): "Gostaria de poder falar Inglês com confiança" = “I’d like to be able to speak English confidently.”
target_language_example: Quero falar Inglês com confiança nas reuniões.
native_language_example: I want to speak English confidently in meetings.

meaning: to speak/talk with; to talk to.
additional_notes: Used to indicate who you are speaking to (person, group). Common after verbs like querer/precisar/tentar/decidir + falar com. In European Portuguese you may also see the extra preposition: “preciso de falar com…”.
target_language_example: Posso falar com você um minuto?
native_language_example: Can I talk to you for a minute?

additional_notes: Used to say you need or want to talk to/with a woman or a feminine noun. In Portuguese, some female names are used with the article “a” (especially in Brazil): “falar com a Susan” = “talk to Susan.” It’s also used in comparisons like “falar com a parede” (“talking to a wall,” i.e., the other person doesn’t listen).
target_language_example: Preciso falar com a gerente agora.
native_language_example: I need to speak with the (female) manager now.

meaning: to talk to her; to speak with her.
additional_notes: Used when you want (or managed) to have a conversation with a woman/girl. "Falar" = to speak/talk, "com" = with/to (in this context), "ela" = she/her. In questions, it often means "Did you manage to reach her and talk?"
target_language_example: Preciso falar com ela hoje à tarde.
native_language_example: I need to talk to her this afternoon.

meaning: to talk to him; to speak with him.
additional_notes: "Falar com" is the common way to say "to talk to / speak with" someone. "Ele" = "him" (a male person). You’ll often hear it in requests or commands: "Deixe-me falar com ele" (Let me talk to him), "Vá falar com ele" (Go talk to him).
target_language_example: Eu preciso falar com ele agora.
native_language_example: I need to talk to him now.

meaning: to talk to them; to speak with them.
additional_notes: "Falar com" is the common way to say “talk to / speak with.” "Eles" means “they/them” (masculine or mixed group). Often used with verbs like "querer" (to want), "dever" (should), "ter que" / "precisar" (have to/need), and "tentar" (to try): e.g., "Eu tenho que falar com eles" = “I have to talk to them.”
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, vou falar com eles sobre o trabalho.
native_language_example: After lunch, I’m going to talk to them about work.

meaning: to talk/speak with (a man); “to talk to him”.
additional_notes: Used when the person you’re talking to/about is masculine. It’s made of “falar” (to speak) + “com” (with) + “o” (the, masculine). Very often you’ll see the contraction “com o” → “com o” (kept separate in standard Portuguese), followed by a man’s name: “falar com o Tom” = “talk to/with Tom”. With a woman, it’s “falar com a …” (e.g., “falar com a Maria”).
target_language_example: Preciso falar com o gerente agora.
native_language_example: I need to talk to the manager now.

meaning: 'to talk to you' / 'to speak with you'.
additional_notes: Used when you want or need to have a conversation with someone. "Falar" = to talk/speak, "com" = with, "você" = you (common in Brazil). Often appears after verbs like "querer" (to want) or "precisar" (to need): "Quero/Preciso falar com você."
target_language_example: Posso falar com você um minuto?
native_language_example: Can I talk to you for a minute?

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic of a conversation: “I need/want/was hoping to talk to you about…” It’s common before a noun (“sobre as suas notas”), “algo” (something), “uma coisa” (a thing), or “outra coisa” (another thing). In more formal situations, you may hear “falar com o senhor / com a senhora sobre…”.
target_language_example: Posso falar com você sobre o trabalho amanhã?
native_language_example: Can I talk to you about work tomorrow?

meaning: to talk to you (plural) / to speak with you (plural).
additional_notes: Used when addressing two or more people. In Brazil, "vocês" is the common plural "you" in both formal and informal situations; in Portugal you may also hear "falar convosco". Often used for requests or urgency: "Preciso falar com vocês" = "I need to talk to you all."
target_language_example: Depois da reunião, eu quero falar com vocês por cinco minutos.
native_language_example: After the meeting, I want to talk to you all for five minutes.

meaning: to talk to me; to speak with me.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone talks (or wants/needs to talk) with you. It’s the verb "falar" (to talk/speak) + "comigo" (with me). Common in questions and invitations: "Quer falar comigo?" (Do you want to talk to me?) and "Se quiser falar comigo..." (If you want to talk to me...).
target_language_example: Pode falar comigo agora?
native_language_example: Can you talk to me now?

additional_notes: Used to address one person with the informal pronoun “tu” (“contigo” = “with you”). Common in Portugal and in some regions of Brazil; in many Brazilian contexts you’ll also hear “falar com você”. Often used when you want to speak to someone about something or in private: “falar contigo sobre/a respeito de…”; “falar contigo em particular”.
target_language_example: Quando tiver um minuto, queria falar contigo.
native_language_example: When you have a minute, I’d like to talk to you.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition “em” to say what language you’re speaking: “falar em + idioma” (also common: “falar francês” without “em”). It can describe ability (“Ele sabe falar em francês”) or what you’ll use in a situation (“Você vai falar em francês com o Tom?”).
target_language_example: No trabalho, eu preciso falar em francês com alguns clientes.
native_language_example: At work, I need to speak in French with some clients.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone can speak the French language, wants to learn it, or likes speaking it. After the verb "falar" (to speak), you can name a language directly (e.g., "falar inglês", "falar português").
target_language_example: Ela sabe falar francês muito bem.
native_language_example: She can speak French very well.

additional_notes: Used to compliment or express surprise about someone’s ability in French. "tão bem" means "so well" and often pairs with "como" in comparisons (e.g., "tão bem como" = "as well as"). You can swap in other languages: "falar espanhol tão bem", "falar inglês tão bem", etc.
target_language_example: Eu queria falar francês tão bem quanto você.
native_language_example: I wish I could speak French as well as you.

additional_notes: "Falar" means "to speak" (a language). Use it with the language name: falar português, falar espanhol, etc. Common in questions about ability with "poder": "Você pode falar inglês?" You can also use "saber" to mean "to know how to" in general: "Não sei falar inglês" = "I don't know how to speak English."
target_language_example: Eu falo um pouco de inglês, mas entendo melhor do que falo.
native_language_example: I speak a little English, but I understand better than I speak.

meaning: to speak badly about others; to gossip/badmouth people.
additional_notes: Literally “to speak badly of others.” Often used to talk about criticizing people behind their backs or gossiping. Common patterns: “nunca falar mal dos outros” (never badmouth others), “ouvir/ver alguém falar mal dos outros” (hear/see someone gossip), “estar pronto para falar mal dos outros” (be quick to criticize others).
target_language_example: Não gosto de gente que fica falando mal dos outros no trabalho.
native_language_example: I don't like people who keep badmouthing others at work.

meaning: to talk about; to speak about.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic of a conversation. Very common with a noun or pronoun (falar sobre o assunto, falar sobre ela) or with "isso" (falar sobre isso). In "ouvir falar sobre", it means "to have heard about" something/someone.
target_language_example: Podemos falar sobre isso depois do jantar?
native_language_example: Can we talk about it after dinner?

meaning: to talk about it; to discuss it.
additional_notes: Common way to bring up (or avoid) a topic. "Isso" = "it/that" (something known from context). Often used with "com" + person: "falar sobre isso com você" (talk about it with you). You can soften or strengthen it with phrases like "em privado" (in private) or "já não quero" (I don't want to anymore).
target_language_example: Podemos falar sobre isso depois do jantar?
native_language_example: Can we talk about it after dinner?

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: falar sobre o Tom / o incidente / o exército. For feminine nouns, use “falar sobre a” (a Maria). For plural, “falar sobre os/as”. Often interchangeable with “falar do/da” in everyday speech, but “falar sobre” can sound a bit more neutral/formal (“talk about/on the subject of”).
target_language_example: Podemos falar sobre o plano depois do almoço?
native_language_example: Can we talk about the plan after lunch?

additional_notes: Used to bring up or discuss a past event or situation. Very common when referring to something sensitive or difficult to discuss. Verb changes with the subject/tense: quero falar… (I want to talk…), ninguém quer/queria… (no one wants/wanted…).
target_language_example: Podemos falar sobre o que aconteceu ontem?
native_language_example: Can we talk about what happened yesterday?

additional_notes: A polite request when you can’t hear someone well. Often used with polite phrases like "poderia...?", "por favor", or "você se importaria de...?". You can also say "Fale um pouco mais alto, por favor" (imperative) — still polite with "por favor".
target_language_example: Desculpe, não estou ouvindo bem — você pode falar um pouco mais alto, por favor?
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't hear well—can you speak a little louder, please?

meaning: to speak a little more slowly.
additional_notes: A polite, common request when you don’t understand someone or they’re speaking too fast. Often used with “Por favor” and “Você poderia...?” for extra politeness. You can also say “Pode falar um pouco mais devagar?” (more direct) or “mais devagar, por favor” (short).
target_language_example: Desculpe, eu ainda estou aprendendo português—você pode falar um pouco mais devagar?
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m still learning Portuguese—can you speak a little more slowly?

meaning: Talk to me / speak to me.
additional_notes: Imperative form of **falar** (“to speak/talk”), used to ask or demand that someone talk to you. Often sounds firm or direct, especially in arguments. You can soften it with **por favor** (“Fale comigo, por favor.”). In the negative: **não fale comigo** (“don’t talk to me”).
target_language_example: Por favor, fale comigo quando tiver um minuto.
native_language_example: Please talk to me when you have a minute.

additional_notes: Past of "falar" used to say you talked to someone. Very common in conversation; often followed by a person ("falei com o Tom", "falei com ela") or with "sobre" to say what you talked about ("falei com ele sobre..." or "falei sobre... com ele").
target_language_example: Já falei com o médico, e está tudo certo.
native_language_example: I already spoke with the doctor, and everything is fine.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "falar" for a completed action. "Com ele" means "with/to him" (you can also translate it as "I talked to him"). Often used to report that you already contacted someone: "Eu já falei com ele" = "I already spoke to him." In the negative: "Não falei com ele" = "I didn’t speak to him."
target_language_example: Falei com ele ontem, mas ele não respondeu.
native_language_example: I spoke to him yesterday, but he didn’t reply.

additional_notes: Past tense of falar (to speak/talk): falei = “I spoke/I talked.” Used with com (“to/with”) and the masculine definite article o (“the”) before a man’s name or a masculine noun: “Falei com o Tom” = “I spoke to/with Tom.” For a woman’s name, you typically use “falei com a …” (e.g., “Falei com a Ana”). Also common with a role/title: “Falei com o médico” = “I spoke to the doctor.”
target_language_example: Já falei com o gerente sobre o problema.
native_language_example: I already spoke to the manager about the problem.

additional_notes: Used to say you (the speaker) speak French. It’s the present tense of *falar* (“to speak”): *eu falo* = “I speak / I am speaking.” You can add frequency or context: *todos os dias* (every day), *em casa* (at home), *no trabalho* (at work), *com os meus pais* (with my parents).
target_language_example: Desculpe, não falo francês muito bem.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t speak French very well.

additional_notes: Used to say you have basic ability in a language. It’s the 1st-person singular present of "falar" (falo = I speak) + "um pouco" (a little) + "de" before the language name. You can also say "Eu falo um pouco de..." (with "eu" for emphasis).
target_language_example: Desculpe, eu falo um pouco de português.
native_language_example: Sorry, I speak a little Portuguese.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of the verb phrase “falar com” = “to talk to/with.” It’s used to say you had a conversation or addressed someone: “falou com ele” (spoke to him), “falou com a gente” (spoke with us). In Portuguese, “com” is required after “falar” when you mention the person you spoke to.
target_language_example: Eu já falei com o médico hoje.
native_language_example: I already spoke with the doctor today.

meaning: “(he/she/you) spoke/talked with the …” (to a male person/thing).
additional_notes: “Falou” is the simple past of falar (“to speak/talk”) and is also commonly used in conversation as “you spoke” (você) in Brazilian Portuguese. “Com” means “with/to”. “O” is “the” (masculine singular), so it’s followed by a masculine noun or a man’s name/title: “falou com o Tom”, “falou com o pai”, “falou com o garçom”. For feminine, use “falou com a …”.
target_language_example: Você já falou com o gerente?
native_language_example: Have you talked to the manager?

meaning: lack of; (in "sentir falta de") to miss.
additional_notes: Often used with a noun to say something is missing or unavailable: "falta de tempo" (lack of time). Very common in the phrase "sentir falta de [someone/something]" = to miss [someone/something]. You may also see "por falta de" = because of a lack of.
target_language_example: Sinto falta de você.
native_language_example: I miss you.

additional_notes: "Farei" is the future tense of "fazer" (to do/make): "I will do." "Qualquer coisa" means "anything." Often followed by "por" + person to mean you’d do anything for someone ("Farei qualquer coisa por você"). With "menos" it means “anything except” ("Farei qualquer coisa, menos isso"). You can also add a clause with "que" to specify: "Farei qualquer coisa que você pedir" = “I’ll do anything you ask.”
target_language_example: Eu farei qualquer coisa para te ajudar.
native_language_example: I’ll do anything to help you.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional form of the verb (here, fazer → faria) to talk about what someone would do in a hypothetical situation, or to ask if someone would do something. Often appears with a subject pronoun: eu faria isso (I would do that), você faria isso? (Would you do that?), ele/ela faria isso (He/She would do that).
target_language_example: Eu não faria isso no seu lugar.
native_language_example: I wouldn’t do that in your place.

meaning: "would do something like that" (often showing shock/disapproval).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of fazer (faria = would do) to talk about a hypothetical action. Common in questions like “Quem faria uma coisa dessas?” to express disbelief, suspicion, or moral judgment about an act. “dessas” means “like that/like those,” referring back to something just mentioned or understood.
target_language_example: Eu jamais faria uma coisa dessas com você.
native_language_example: I would never do something like that to you.

additional_notes: From the verb **fazer** (to do/make) + **isso** (“that/this”). It commonly appears in questions with **como** (“how”) or **por que/porque** (“why”) to ask how/why someone does something: *Como ele faz isso?* / *Por que faz isso?* In these examples it’s often used with an implied subject (he/she/you), but **faz** specifically is the present tense for **ele/ela/você** (and also for **a gente** in informal Brazilian Portuguese).
target_language_example: Por que você faz isso toda vez?
native_language_example: Why do you do that every time?

additional_notes: Used to say that an activity or habit has a negative effect on health. The subject is often an infinitive phrase (e.g., Fumar/Beber/Comer demais faz mal à saúde). You can also use "fazer mal a" with other things: "Faz mal ao estômago" (it’s bad for the stomach).
target_language_example: Dormir pouco faz mal à saúde.
native_language_example: Sleeping too little is bad for your health.

meaning: “How long has it been since you…?” / “How long have you…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask about the amount of time from a starting point until now. Commonly followed by a verb in the present tense (conhece, está, joga, fuma) to mean “have been … for how long?” Often equivalent to “Há quanto tempo você…?” In answers, Portuguese often uses: “Faz dois anos que…” or “Estou aqui há dois anos.”
target_language_example: Faz quanto tempo que você trabalha aqui?
native_language_example: How long have you been working here?

additional_notes: Used to say something is logical/understandable. Often appears as a question (Faz sentido?) meaning “Does it make sense?” or as an answer (Faz sentido.) meaning “That makes sense.” You can also use it with a subject: Isso faz sentido. / Esta frase faz sentido?
target_language_example: Isso faz sentido para você?
native_language_example: Does that make sense to you?

meaning: "three years ago" / "it’s been three years" (talking about time elapsed).
additional_notes: Uses the impersonal verb "fazer" to say how much time has passed. Very common in patterns like "Faz três anos que..." (It’s been three years since...) or at the end of a sentence: "Eu moro aqui faz três anos." In this use, "faz" stays in the 3rd-person singular (not *faço*).
target_language_example: A gente se mudou para cá faz três anos.
native_language_example: We moved here three years ago.

meaning: "(they/you all) do that" / "(they/you all) do it".
additional_notes: "Fazem" is the present tense (they / you all) form of "fazer" (to do, to make). "Isso" means "that" or "it" (referring to an action or thing already understood). Often appears in questions like "Como é que vocês fazem isso?" (How do you do that?).
target_language_example: Por que tantas pessoas fazem isso?
native_language_example: Why do so many people do that?

meaning: 'doing here' (used in questions like “What are you doing here?”).
additional_notes: Common in the pattern “O que + [person] + estar + fazendo aqui?” to ask why someone is here or what they’re doing in this place. The verb is usually in the present progressive (estou/está/estamos/estão fazendo). Depending on tone, it can sound surprised, suspicious, or just curious.
target_language_example: O que você está fazendo aqui tão cedo?
native_language_example: What are you doing here so early?

additional_notes: “Fazendo” is the gerund of **fazer** (“to do/make”), used to talk about an action in progress or repeated. **Isso** usually means “that/this/it” (often “that/it” in English). Common in questions and descriptions: *estava fazendo isso* (“was doing that”), *continuei fazendo isso* (“I kept doing it”).
target_language_example: Eu estava fazendo isso sem perceber.
native_language_example: I was doing it without realizing it.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is currently in the middle of doing something at this moment. Often appears with the verb estar to form the present continuous: “está/estava/esteja fazendo isso agora” = “is/was/might be doing that now.” “Isso” can mean “that” or “it,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu estou fazendo isso agora, mas posso te ligar depois.
native_language_example: I’m doing that now, but I can call you later.

meaning: to do something; to make something.
additional_notes: Very common, general phrase for taking an action or creating something. In everyday speech it usually means “do something” (an action): Tenho de fazer algo. It can also mean “make something” (create/produce), depending on context. Often followed by an adjective or noun: fazer algo grande (“do something big/great”).
target_language_example: Vamos fazer algo hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Shall we do something tonight?

additional_notes: Used when there’s a problem or situation and you want someone to take action to change it. Often appears with "temos que/temos de" (we have to) or "você tem que/tem de" (you have to). "A respeito (disso/disto)" can be added to specify what you mean: "fazer algo a respeito disso" = "do something about that".
target_language_example: Se isso continuar, vamos ter que fazer algo a respeito.
native_language_example: If this keeps going, we’ll have to do something about it.

additional_notes: Common way to say you need to take action (often when there’s a problem): "Temos de fazer alguma coisa" = "We have to do something." You can add what it’s about with "a respeito" (about it) or "sobre" (about), or specify the action after "fazer". Also used with modal/need verbs like "precisar", "ter de", "dever", and "tentar".
target_language_example: Vamos fazer alguma coisa para ajudar.
native_language_example: Let’s do something to help.

meaning: to do something to / in order to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to say you will take an action with a purpose or goal: “do something to help/solve/avoid…”. Very common pattern: fazer alguma coisa para + infinitive (para ajudar, para resolver, para evitar). You can also ask someone: Você pode fazer alguma coisa para…? = “Can you do something to…?”
target_language_example: Vou fazer alguma coisa para melhorar a situação.
native_language_example: I’m going to do something to improve the situation.

additional_notes: A polite, common way to say you want to ask several (not many) questions. You can add who you’re asking with "a/ao/à/aos/às" (e.g., "a você", "ao senhor", "às senhoras"). Often used with verbs like "querer", "pretender", or "poder" to soften the request: "Eu queria/poderia fazer algumas perguntas..."
target_language_example: Posso fazer algumas perguntas sobre o contrato?
native_language_example: Can I ask a few questions about the contract?

additional_notes: Used to politely request or state that you want to question someone. Very common with modal verbs like "posso" (can I) and "querer" (to want): "Posso fazer algumas perguntas para o Tom?" In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, "fazer algumas perguntas ao" or "fazer algumas perguntas para" are also used; "perguntar a" / "perguntar para" is another common alternative ("Posso te perguntar algumas coisas?").
target_language_example: Posso fazer algumas perguntas para o senhor antes de começarmos?
native_language_example: Can I ask you (sir) some questions before we start?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "fazer" (to do/make) + "aquilo" (that, over there/that specific thing) to refer to a specific action already known from the context. Often implies “that (thing we’re talking about)” and can sound a bit more emphatic or distant than "fazer isso" (“do this/that”).
target_language_example: Eu não vou fazer aquilo de novo.
native_language_example: I’m not going to do that again.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific action already known from context (aquilo = “that”), often with “nunca mais” to mean “never again” or with “temos que” to mean “we have to.” The object (aquilo) is usually something previously mentioned or understood by both speakers.
target_language_example: Por favor, não faça aquilo de novo.
native_language_example: Please, don’t do that again.

meaning: to do things; to handle things (in a certain way).
additional_notes: A very common, general phrase used to talk about someone’s way/method of doing something (often followed by phrases like “de uma certa maneira”, “do jeito dela”, “assim/desta maneira”). It can refer to routines, decisions, or how you approach tasks, not necessarily physical “making” of objects.
target_language_example: Podemos fazer as coisas com calma.
native_language_example: We can do things calmly.

meaning: to pack (your bags) / to pack up.
additional_notes: Used when you’re preparing to leave (for a trip, moving out, being sent somewhere, etc.). Very common with "ter que" or "precisar" (Ter que fazer as malas = I have to pack). You can also say "começar a fazer as malas" (to start packing).
target_language_example: A gente sai amanhã cedo, então vou fazer as malas hoje à noite.
native_language_example: We leave early tomorrow, so I’m going to pack tonight.

meaning: to go shopping; to do the shopping (buy things).
additional_notes: Literally “to make purchases.” Very common with places: “fazer compras no supermercado/no shopping.” It can mean shopping in general (“Eu gosto de fazer compras”) or doing necessary errands/groceries (“Tenho que fazer compras”).
target_language_example: Vamos fazer compras amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: Let’s go shopping tomorrow morning.

meaning: to do next; to do afterwards.
additional_notes: Used when talking about the next step in a sequence of actions. Very common after questions like “O que (você) vai fazer em seguida?” (“What are you going to do next?”). Similar to “o que fazer a seguir”.
target_language_example: Terminamos aqui. O que você vai fazer em seguida?
native_language_example: We’re done here. What are you going to do next?

meaning: to do that / to do it.
additional_notes: Used to refer to doing an action that’s already known from context. "Isso" means “that/it” (a thing or action). You’ll also see "fazer isto" (“do this”) and "fazer aquilo" (“do that over there/that other thing”). "Fazer" is irregular (e.g., eu faço, você/ele faz).
target_language_example: Eu não vou fazer isso.
native_language_example: I’m not going to do that.

meaning: to do that now / to do it now.
additional_notes: Used to talk about doing a specific thing immediately. Often appears with obligation/necessity verbs like “dever” (should), “ter que” (have to), “precisar” (need to), or permission like “poder” (can). Word order is flexible in speech (e.g., “fazer isso agora” / “agora fazer isso”), but “fazer isso agora” is the most common.
target_language_example: Eu não posso fazer isso agora; faço mais tarde.
native_language_example: I can’t do that now; I’ll do it later.

meaning: "to do this before" (doing something earlier than another event/time).
additional_notes: Used to say an action must be completed prior to a specific moment or another action. It’s followed by either: (1) a noun/time expression (e.g., "antes de amanhã" = before tomorrow), or (2) a verb in the infinitive (e.g., "antes de irmos" = before we go). With a person + verb, Portuguese often uses "antes de você" + infinitive (common in Brazil): "antes de você chegar".
target_language_example: Vou fazer isso antes de sair.
native_language_example: I’ll do this before leaving.

meaning: to do that again; to do it again.
additional_notes: Used to talk about repeating an action. "Fazer" = "to do/make", "isso" = "that/it" (refers to something just mentioned or understood), and "de novo" = "again". Very common in questions and plans: "Você quer fazer isso de novo?" (Do you want to do it again?).
target_language_example: Não vou fazer isso de novo.
native_language_example: I’m not going to do that again.

additional_notes: Common, flexible phrase built from: fazer (to do/make) + isso (that/it) + hoje (today). Use it to talk about completing a task today. You can swap the time word: fazer isso amanhã (tomorrow), fazer isso agora (now). In questions, it often becomes: Você/Vocês quer(em) fazer isso hoje? (“Do you want to do that today?”).
target_language_example: Eu posso fazer isso hoje, mas não amanhã.
native_language_example: I can do that today, but not tomorrow.

meaning: to do that again; to do it again.
additional_notes: Use this to say someone will repeat an action. It’s built from: fazer (to do/make) + isso (that/it) + novamente (again). In everyday speech, you’ll often also hear "fazer isso de novo" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Não vou fazer isso novamente.
native_language_example: I’m not going to do that again.

meaning: to do that again (to repeat it).
additional_notes: Used to ask or say that an action should be repeated. Very common with polite add-ons like “por favor” (“please”). You can swap “isso” for “isto” (“this”) depending on variety/context, and “outra vez” can also be said as “de novo”. Often appears with “ter que / ter de” (“have to”): “Você tem que fazer isso outra vez.”
target_language_example: Desculpa, não ouvi bem — podes fazer isso outra vez?
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t hear well — can you do that again?

additional_notes: Used when asking or offering to do something on someone else’s behalf, or as a favor. The person helped usually comes after "por" (por mim, por você, por nós, por ela/ele). In everyday speech you’ll often hear it as "fazer isso por mim/você". Similar idea: "fazer algo por alguém".
target_language_example: Você pode fazer isso por mim, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you do this for me, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone for a favor or to thank them for it. Common with polite questions: “Você pode…?” (Can you…?) and “Você poderia…?” (Could you…?) where “poderia” sounds more polite/less direct. The verb changes with the subject: “Eu faço…”, “Você faz…”, “Ele/Ela faz…”.
target_language_example: Você pode, por favor, fazer isso por mim?
native_language_example: Can you please do this for me?

additional_notes: Used when someone offers, agrees, or is willing to do something on another person’s behalf. You can change the pronoun: fazer isso por mim (for me), por ele/ela (for him/her), por nós (for us), por vocês (for you all). In questions: Você pode fazer isso por mim?
target_language_example: Posso fazer isso por você hoje.
native_language_example: I can do that for you today.

meaning: “doing that would be” (introducing a hypothetical result/judgment).
additional_notes:
Used to talk about what the consequence or evaluation would be if someone did something. It combines:
- fazer = to do/make
- isso = that/this
- seria = would be (conditional of ser)
Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase: divertido (fun), romântico (romantic), uma perda de tempo (a waste of time), impossível (impossible). You can also say “Fazer isso seria + [adjective/noun]” as a full sentence.
target_language_example: Acho que fazer isso seria uma boa ideia.
native_language_example: I think doing that would be a good idea.

meaning: to do it by yourself (female speaker).
additional_notes: Used when a woman/girl is the one doing the action alone, without help. It’s built from: fazer (to do/make) + isso (that/it) + sozinha (alone, feminine). If the person is male, use “fazer isso sozinho.” With “você,” speakers choose sozinho/sozinha based on the person being addressed.
target_language_example: Não se preocupe — eu consigo fazer isso sozinha.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — I can do it by myself.

meaning: to do this alone / by yourself.
additional_notes: Used when someone will do a task without help. It often implies independence or that help is needed (especially in negatives like “não posso fazer isso sozinho”). You can swap in another object: “fazer isso” (do it) + “sozinho/sozinha” (alone), matching the person’s gender. In Portuguese, “sozinho” can mean both “alone” and “on your own” (without help).
target_language_example: Você consegue fazer isso sozinho ou quer ajuda?
native_language_example: Can you do this on your own, or do you want help?

meaning: to do this; to make this.
additional_notes: "Fazer" is a very common verb meaning "to do" (an action/task) or "to make" (create something). "Isto" means "this" (usually something close to the speaker or something being shown/pointed to). In conversation, it often refers to the current task or action: "Você pode fazer isto" = "You can do this."
target_language_example: Não quero fazer isto agora.
native_language_example: I don't want to do this now.

additional_notes: Used before a verb (often 'querer') to mean doing whatever someone wants or doing what is necessary/appropriate in context. Very common in patterns like: 'fazer o que eu quero' (do what I want), 'fazer o que você quiser' (do whatever you want), 'deixar alguém fazer o que…' (let someone do what…).
target_language_example: Você pode fazer o que quiser, mas tem que avisar antes.
native_language_example: You can do whatever you want, but you have to let me know first.

additional_notes: Used to give permission or emphasize freedom of choice. Often appears after verbs like "poder" (can/may): "Você pode fazer o que quiser." The verb "quiser" is the (future) subjunctive of "querer" (to want), used in phrases meaning "whatever ...".
target_language_example: Aqui você pode fazer o que quiser, desde que respeite as regras.
native_language_example: Here you can do whatever you want, as long as you follow the rules.

additional_notes: Used with an object or implied action: "fazer" = to do/make, and "para ajudar" = in order to help. Often appears with "nada"/"algo" and the structure "não havia nada que eu/ele pudesse fazer para ajudar" (“there was nothing I/he could do to help”).
target_language_example: Sinto muito, mas não há nada que eu possa fazer para ajudar agora.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but there’s nothing I can do to help right now.

meaning: to do anything; to do whatever (someone wants).
additional_notes: Common with the idea of having no limits or being free/able to choose: Você pode fazer qualquer coisa! (“You can do anything!”). In questions it often means “anything at all”: Se você pudesse fazer qualquer coisa… (“If you could do anything…”). With fear/hesitation it means being afraid to take any action: medo de fazer qualquer coisa (“afraid to do anything”). You’ll also see it followed by a clause: qualquer coisa que (eu/ele) quisesse = “whatever (I/he) wanted.”
target_language_example: Hoje eu posso fazer qualquer coisa que eu quiser.
native_language_example: Today I can do whatever I want.

additional_notes: Used before a clause to mean you did all the actions needed/possible: “fazer tudo o que + verb (past/infinitive)”. Often followed by phrases like “tinha que” (had to) or “pude” (could).
target_language_example: Vou fazer tudo o que for possível para ajudar.
native_language_example: I’ll do everything that’s possible to help.

meaning: “to make/do a …” (used before a singular noun).
additional_notes: Very common pattern in Portuguese: use "fazer" + "uma" + noun to express doing an action, especially when the action is named by a noun (e.g., "fazer uma chamada" = make a call, "fazer uma reserva" = make a reservation, "fazer uma pergunta" = ask a question, "fazer uma observação" = make a comment, "fazer uma dieta" = go on a diet). It changes with gender/number: "fazer um" (masc.), "fazer umas/uns" (plural).
target_language_example: Você pode fazer uma reserva para hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Can you make a reservation for tonight?

additional_notes: Used when you need to call someone, usually by phone. You can specify the type: "fazer uma ligação telefônica" (make a phone call), or the destination: "fazer uma ligação para o Japão" (make a call to Japan). Very common with "precisar" and "ter que/ter de" to say you need to call.
target_language_example: Vou fazer uma ligação rapidinho e já volto.
native_language_example: I’m going to make a quick call and I’ll be right back.

meaning: to take a break; to pause.
additional_notes: Used when you stop an activity for a short rest. Common at work or while studying: "Preciso fazer uma pausa" (I need a break). Often used with "precisar", "querer", "poder", or "dever" + infinitive. It can also mean pausing a conversation or task briefly, depending on context.
target_language_example: Vamos fazer uma pausa de cinco minutos.
native_language_example: Let’s take a five-minute break.

additional_notes: A very common, polite way to introduce a question. Often used with permission or a softener: “Posso te/lhe fazer uma pergunta?” (Can I ask you a question?), “Deixa eu/Deixe-me te/lhe fazer uma pergunta” (Let me ask you a question). “Te” is informal (you), “lhe” is more formal.
target_language_example: Posso te fazer uma pergunta rápida?
native_language_example: Can I ask you a quick question?

meaning: “to do it” / “to do him” (fazer + the object pronoun -lo).
additional_notes: This is the verb fazer (“to do/make”) with an attached object pronoun -lo (= o, “him/it”), often used after an infinitive form. It can mean “do it” (referring to something previously mentioned) or “make him do it / make him…” depending on context (e.g., fazê-lo mudar = “make him change”). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, you’ll often hear/see fazer isso or fazer ele instead.
target_language_example: Não consigo fazê-lo hoje.
native_language_example: I can’t do it today.

additional_notes: Imperative (command) form of **fazer** + the object pronoun **o** (“it” or “him”), written with a hyphen. Often used as a direct command: **Faça-o agora mesmo.** It can also be followed by an infinitive to mean “make him/it (do something)”: **Faça-o entrar** (“Make him/it come in”), **Faça-o parar** (“Make him/it stop”).
target_language_example: Se você acha melhor, faça-o hoje.
native_language_example: If you think it’s best, do it today.

additional_notes: Imperative form of the verb “fazer” (“to do/make”) for “você”. It’s used to tell someone to do something. In negative commands you often see: “Não faça isso” (“Don’t do that”).
target_language_example: Por favor, faça isso com cuidado.
native_language_example: Please do it carefully.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to do whatever is mentioned next (often implying “whatever is necessary/appropriate”). It’s built with the imperative of fazer (“faça” = “do/make” in the você form) + “o que” (“what”). Common patterns: “Faça o que achar melhor.” (“Do what you think is best.”), “Faça o que tem de fazer.” (“Do what you have to do.”), “Faça o que quiser.” (“Do what you want.”).
target_language_example: Faça o que for melhor para você.
native_language_example: Do what’s best for you.

additional_notes: Uses the formal command form (imperative) of fazer: faça (“do/make”). Often said to give someone permission, show indifference, or end an argument: “Go ahead—do whatever you want.” You can also say “faça o que você quiser” (same meaning, with você).
target_language_example: Se você não quer ouvir meu conselho, faça o que quiser.
native_language_example: If you don’t want to listen to my advice, do whatever you want.

additional_notes: From the verb "fazer" (to do/make): "faço" = "I do/make" (present tense). "Isso" means "that/it" (often something just mentioned or understood from context). Used to talk about doing an action or habit: "Eu faço isso" = "I do that", but Portuguese can drop "eu" and just say "Faço isso".
target_language_example: Não faço isso com frequência.
native_language_example: I don’t do that often.

additional_notes: Used to say that the speaker’s group ("we") permanently shut the restaurant, or that it stopped operating. Commonly followed by a time expression like “há/tem + time” to mean “(we) closed it + time ago” (e.g., “há três anos / tem três anos” = “three years ago”). Can also mean “we closed up the restaurant (for the day)” depending on context, but with “há/tem três anos” it clearly means closed down three years ago.
target_language_example: Fechamos o restaurante no ano passado.
native_language_example: We closed the restaurant last year.

additional_notes: Used when asking for permission or offering to close a window (e.g., because of cold, noise, or rain). In Portuguese, you can use "Devo..." (Should I...?) or "Posso..." (May/Can I...?) before it. The verb is "fechar" (to close) + "a janela" (the window).
target_language_example: Está frio aqui — vou fechar a janela.
native_language_example: It’s cold in here — I’m going to close the window.

additional_notes: Used when asking or reminding someone to shut the door. Common in polite requests with "pode/poderia" (can/could), "por favor" (please), or "você se importaria em..." (would you mind...). Often followed by "ao sair" = "when you leave/on your way out."
target_language_example: Por favor, feche a porta porque está frio.
native_language_example: Please close the door because it’s cold.

additional_notes: Imperative form of the verb “fechar” (to close) used to give an instruction. Commonly said to one person; to be more polite you can add “por favor” (“Feche a porta, por favor.”). “Feche a porta atrás de você” means “Close the door behind you.”
target_language_example: Feche a porta, por favor, está fazendo frio.
native_language_example: Close the door, please—it's cold.

additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) form of "fechar" (to close) + "os olhos" (the eyes). It’s typically used when giving instructions (e.g., during a test, exercise, meditation, or to help someone remember something). You can soften it with "por favor" ("Feche os olhos, por favor.").
target_language_example: Feche os olhos por um momento e respire fundo.
native_language_example: Close your eyes for a moment and take a deep breath.

additional_notes: "Fechou" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "fechar" (to close). It’s used for a completed action in the past. Often appears with "a porta" (the door) or with a specific door: "fechou a porta do escritório" (closed the office door). You can also use it as a question: "Quem fechou a porta?" (Who closed the door?).
target_language_example: Antes de sair, ele fechou a porta.
native_language_example: Before leaving, he closed the door.

additional_notes: Usually appears with a helper verb like ter/haver to form the past (“ter feito isso” = “to have done that/it”). It refers back to something already mentioned (isso = “that/it”). You’ll often see it in different tenses/moods: “já tinha feito isso” (had already done it), “nunca tenha feito isso” (have never done it), “pode ter feito isso” (may have done it).
target_language_example: Eu nunca tinha feito isso antes.
native_language_example: I had never done that before.

additional_notes: Used to express pleasure or willingness about doing something: **feliz em + infinitive** (feliz em ajudar, feliz em ver, feliz em ouvir, feliz em saber). In conversation you’ll also often hear **fico feliz em...** (“I’m happy to...”) or **ficaria feliz em...** (“I’d be happy to...”, more polite/conditional). In some contexts **feliz em + noun/pronoun** can mean “happy to see/meet” (e.g., *Feliz em te ver*).
target_language_example: Fico feliz em ajudar, se você precisar.
native_language_example: I’m happy to help if you need it.

additional_notes: Used as a polite way to say you’re pleased to see someone. It’s built from feliz em (“happy to”) + ver (“to see”). The -lo means “him/you” in formal address (você/o senhor). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese people often say “feliz em te ver” (informal) or simply “feliz em ver você”. Tense changes with the verb (estou/fiquei/ficarei feliz em vê-lo).
target_language_example: Ficamos muito felizes em vê-lo novamente.
native_language_example: We were very happy to see you again.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a party celebrating someone’s birthday. Often appears with possessives (minha/teu/sua) or with “de + someone” (festa de aniversário dela). You can use “ir à” (go to) and “convidar (alguém) para” (invite someone to) with it.
target_language_example: Você vai à minha festa de aniversário no sábado?
native_language_example: Are you going to my birthday party on Saturday?

additional_notes: "Fez" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "fazer" (to do/to make) for ele/ela/você. "Aquilo" means "that" (often something more distant, previously mentioned, or a specific thing/situation). The phrase is often used to point to or take responsibility for an action: "Quem fez aquilo?" = "Who did that?"
target_language_example: Ele fez aquilo de propósito.
native_language_example: He did that on purpose.

additional_notes: "Fez" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "fazer" (to do/make) for "ele/ela/você". "Isso" means "that/this" (something previously mentioned or understood). The phrase is often used to refer back to an action: "Ele fez isso" = "He did that/this."
target_language_example: Quem fez isso com o meu carro?
native_language_example: Who did this to my car?

additional_notes: Uses the verb fazer in the past (fez = “did/made”) plus isso (“that/it”) and de propósito (“on purpose”). It often implies the action was deliberate (sometimes with a negative tone, like blaming someone). You can change the subject: “Eu fiz isso de propósito” (I did it on purpose), “Ela fez isso de propósito” (She did it on purpose).
target_language_example: Ele fez isso de propósito para me irritar.
native_language_example: He did that on purpose to annoy me.

additional_notes: Past tense of fazer (“to do/make”) + o que (“what/that which”). Used to say someone did what another person said/asked, or did what was necessary (often followed by a clause: “fez o que + [someone said/was needed]”).
target_language_example: Ela fez o que eu pedi.
native_language_example: She did what I asked.

meaning: “did what he …” (he did the thing that he …).
additional_notes: Common sentence pattern: **fez** (past of *fazer*, “to do/make”) + **o que** (“what/that which”) + **ele** (“he”) introduces a clause explaining what he did: *fez o que ele queria / pretendia / achava correto / pediu*. Often followed by a verb in the imperfect (*queria*, *pretendia*, *achava*) or past perfect (*tinha pedido*).
target_language_example: Ela fez o que ela achava melhor.
native_language_example: She did what she thought was best.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "fazer o seu melhor" = “to do your best.” It agrees with the subject: eu fiz o meu melhor, você/ele/ela fez o seu melhor, nós fizemos o nosso melhor, vocês/eles/elas fizeram o seu melhor. Common for encouragement or reassurance when someone tried hard.
target_language_example: Você fez o seu melhor, e isso é o que importa.
native_language_example: You did your best, and that's what matters.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "fazer" + "tudo o que". Used to introduce a clause describing all the actions someone did: "fez tudo o que + verb/phrase". The subject can change (Eu fiz / você fez / ela fez / nós fizemos, etc.), and it can also be future/other tenses (faz / vai fazer / tinha feito).
target_language_example: Ela fez tudo o que podia para ajudar.
native_language_example: She did everything she could to help.

additional_notes: Past tense of "fazer" + "um" (“a/an”). Used with many nouns to mean “make/do something”: fez um sinal (made a sign/gesture), fez um café (made coffee), fez um esforço (made an effort). The subject is usually ele/ela/você (he/she/you formal).
target_language_example: Ela fez um bolo para o aniversário.
native_language_example: She made a cake for the birthday.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "fazer" used to praise someone for a completed action. You can change the subject (e.g., eu fiz, você fez, ela fez, nós fizemos) and add emphasis like "realmente" (really). Often used with "Você" (informal) or "O senhor/A senhora" (formal).
target_language_example: Parabéns, você fez um bom trabalho no relatório.
native_language_example: Congratulations, you did a good job on the report.

meaning: 'made a' / 'did a' (past tense of fazer + a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun to say someone created, prepared, built, or carried out something: fez uma salada (made a salad), fez uma doação (made a donation), fez uma lista (made a list). It’s the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of fazer for ele/ela/você: ele fez uma…. For a masculine noun, you usually see fez um….
target_language_example: Ela fez uma reserva para amanhã.
native_language_example: She made a reservation for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is located. "fica" (from "ficar") here means "is located". "ao lado de" = "next to/beside". It changes with gender/number: "ao lado do" (masc. sing.), "ao lado da" (fem. sing.), "ao lado dos" (masc. plural), "ao lado das" (fem. plural).
target_language_example: O restaurante fica ao lado do banco.
native_language_example: The restaurant is next to the bank.

additional_notes: Used to give the location of something. Common pattern: "[lugar] fica do outro lado de/da/do ..." = "[place] is on the other side of ..." (street, river, building, etc.). You can also say just "Fica do outro lado" when the reference point is understood (e.g., the other side of the street).
target_language_example: O banheiro fica do outro lado do corredor.
native_language_example: The bathroom is on the other side of the hallway.

additional_notes: Used to say that a place is located far away from where you are now. It’s built with: ficar (to be/ to be located) + longe (far) + daqui (from here). Very common in questions and negatives: "Fica longe daqui?" (Is it far from here?), "Não fica longe daqui." (It’s not far from here.).
target_language_example: O supermercado fica longe daqui?
native_language_example: Is the supermarket far from here?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ficar" (to be located) + "no" (= em + o, “in/on/at the”). It introduces where something is: buildings, floors, parts of a city, regions, etc. Often corresponds to English “is on the third floor / is in the southwest…”. (Also varies with gender/number: fica na, fica nos, fica nas.)
target_language_example: A estação fica no centro da cidade.
native_language_example: The station is in the city center.

meaning: “is located in the city center / downtown.”
additional_notes: Uses ficar to talk about where a place is located. You can swap the subject: O banco fica no centro da cidade. In many places, centro da cidade is equivalent to “downtown.”
target_language_example: O hotel fica no centro da cidade, perto do metrô.
native_language_example: The hotel is located downtown, near the subway.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is located. "Fica" (from "ficar") is common for locations, and "perto de" means "near". Use "da" (= de + a) before a feminine singular noun with the article (e.g., "da Itália", "da parede"). With masculine singular, you’d say "fica perto do"; without an article, use "fica perto de".
target_language_example: O supermercado fica perto da estação.
native_language_example: The supermarket is near the station.

additional_notes: Used with a following adjective or comparative phrase to show gradual change over time. Very common patterns: (1) "ficar cada vez + adjective/comparative": "ficando cada vez pior" (getting worse and worse). (2) "ficar cada vez mais/menos + adjective": "ficando cada vez mais bonita" (getting more and more beautiful), "ficando cada vez menos eficaz" (getting less and less effective). Often appears with time phrases like "com o passar do tempo/dos meses/dos anos" (as time goes by).
target_language_example: O trânsito está ficando cada vez mais complicado.
native_language_example: Traffic is getting more and more complicated.

meaning: to stay here; to remain here.
additional_notes: Uses "ficar" (to stay/remain) + "aqui" (here). Common for talking about staying in a place (temporarily or for a while), or about something needing to remain in a specific location (e.g., an object: "Isso deve ficar aqui."). Often appears with modal verbs or obligations like "poder" (can/may), "ter que" (have to), "dever" (should), and in questions ("Posso ficar aqui?").
target_language_example: Podemos ficar aqui até o ônibus chegar?
native_language_example: Can we stay here until the bus arrives?

additional_notes: Used to give permission or say it’s okay for someone to remain in a place for whatever length of time they want. Very often followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., quiser/quiserem = “(you) want”). You can swap the place: ficar aí o tempo que… (“stay there as long as…”).
target_language_example: Você pode ficar aqui o tempo que precisar.
native_language_example: You can stay here as long as you need.

meaning: 'to stay here as long as' (you want).
additional_notes: Used with a verb in the subjunctive, most commonly "quanto quiser" (you—singular) or "quanto quiserem" (you all / they). It gives permission and emphasizes there’s no time limit: "Pode(m) ficar aqui quanto quiser(em)."
target_language_example: Você pode ficar aqui quanto quiser.
native_language_example: You can stay here as long as you want.

meaning: to be okay; to be fine (especially after a problem).
additional_notes: Often used to reassure someone or express confidence that a situation will turn out fine: "vai/ vão ficar bem" (you/they will be okay), "vamos ficar bem" (we’ll be okay). With people, it can mean recovering/being safe; with "as coisas" or a situation, it means things will work out. Also note a different common meaning: "ficar bem com" can mean "to look good with" (clothes/colors), depending on context.
target_language_example: Não se preocupe, vai ficar tudo bem.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything will be okay.

meaning: to keep; to stay with; (often) to hook up/make out with.
additional_notes:
"Ficar com" is very common and has a few meanings depending on context:
- Possession/choice: "Pode ficar com..." = “You can keep ... / You can have ...” (e.g., keeping the apples).
- Staying/remaining with someone: "ficar com eles" = “stay with them.”
- Romance (Brazilian Portuguese, very common): "ficar com alguém" usually means “to hook up/make out with someone” (often casual, not necessarily a serious relationship like "namorar").
Because of these different uses, the surrounding words usually clarify the meaning.
target_language_example: Pode ficar com o meu casaco; está frio lá fora.
native_language_example: You can keep my coat; it's cold outside.

meaning: to stay in; to remain in (a place/state).
additional_notes: Used with a location ("ficar em Boston" = stay in Boston) or with some situations/states when the complement works like a noun phrase ("ficar em segurança" = stay safe / remain in safety). Often implies staying for a period of time. Common future/plan forms: "vou ficar em...", "quero ficar em...", "planejo ficar em...".
target_language_example: Vou ficar em Lisboa por três dias.
native_language_example: I'm going to stay in Lisbon for three days.

additional_notes: Used to say you remain at home instead of going out. With "prefiro" it expresses preference ("Prefiro ficar em casa" = "I’d rather stay home"). With "ter que" / "deveria" it expresses obligation/advice ("tem que/deveria ficar em casa" = "has to/should stay home"), often because of illness, weather, etc.
target_language_example: Hoje vai chover, então vamos ficar em casa.
native_language_example: It’s going to rain today, so we’re going to stay at home.

meaning: to stand up; to remain standing (on your feet).
additional_notes: Used when someone moves into a standing position or stays standing instead of sitting/lying down. Common in rules/instructions (e.g., “Não é pra ficar em pé” = “You’re not supposed to stand up/be standing”). With places like buses, it often means “to stand (not sit)” during the ride.
target_language_example: Se você estiver cansado, pode sentar; não precisa ficar em pé.
native_language_example: If you’re tired, you can sit down; you don’t need to stand.

meaning: to be alone; to stay alone (by yourself).
additional_notes: "Ficar" often means "to stay" or "to end up" in a situation. "Ficar sozinho" is commonly used to say you want some time by yourself (often to rest, think, or have privacy). You can add a reason with "para": "ficar sozinho para pensar".
target_language_example: Vou ficar sozinho um pouco para descansar.
native_language_example: I’m going to be alone for a bit to rest.

meaning: "I will be happy to" (to do something).
additional_notes: Polite, friendly way to offer or agree to do something. It’s the future tense of "ficar" ("ficarei" = "I will be"), used with "feliz" + "em" + infinitive: "ficarei feliz em ajudar". In everyday speech you may also hear "vou ficar feliz em..." or simply "fico feliz em..." (present).
target_language_example: Ficarei feliz em responder às suas perguntas.
native_language_example: I’ll be happy to answer your questions.

additional_notes: Used to express a polite/positive reaction that depends on a future condition. It’s built with the future tense of **ficar** (“ficarei” = “I will be”) + **muito feliz** (“very happy”) + **se** (“if”). After **se**, Portuguese often uses the **future subjunctive** for future events (e.g., **se eu/tu/ele vir**, “if I/you/he see”). You can add object pronouns to mean “see you/him/her/them”: **se vos vir** (you all), **se as/os/o/a vir** (them/him/her).
target_language_example: Ficarei muito feliz se você puder vir amanhã.
native_language_example: I’ll be very happy if you can come tomorrow.

meaning: 'will be fine/OK' or 'will look good (on someone)'.
additional_notes: Future tense of "ficar" + "bem". Most commonly used to reassure someone: "Tudo ficará bem" = "Everything will be fine." With people, it often means someone’s health/situation will turn out OK: "Ele ficará bem." With clothes or appearance, it means something will suit/look good on someone: "Este chapéu ficará bem nela."
target_language_example: Não se preocupe, tudo ficará bem amanhã.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything will be fine tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Ficou" is the past (pretérito perfeito) of "ficar" and often means "to become" in these contexts. "Ficou doente" is used for a change of state (someone wasn’t sick before, then got sick). You can add time expressions like "neste final de semana" (this weekend) or "há alguns dias" (a few days ago).
target_language_example: Depois da viagem, eu fiquei doente.
native_language_example: After the trip, I got sick.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ficar** in the past (**ficou**) to say someone remained at home instead of going out/work/school. Common with time expressions (e.g., **ontem**, **o dia todo**, **a semana inteira**) or reasons (**porque estava doente**). The subject is understood from context or stated earlier (e.g., *Maria ficou em casa*).
target_language_example: Eu fiquei em casa porque estava cansado.
native_language_example: I stayed at home because I was tired.

additional_notes: "Ficou" is the past tense of "ficar" and often means "to become" or "to remain." "Em silêncio" means "in silence." Used to describe a person or a place that suddenly becomes quiet, or someone who stops talking for a moment.
target_language_example: Quando ouviu a notícia, ela ficou em silêncio.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she fell silent.

additional_notes: Used with ficar (past: ficou) to describe a change of state or how someone ended up feeling/being. It’s commonly followed by an adjective: ficou muito impressionada (became very impressed), ficou muito preocupado (got very worried), ficou muito cético (became very skeptical), ficou muito rico (became very rich). Person and number change: eu fiquei, você/ele ficou, nós ficamos, eles ficaram.
target_language_example: Depois da notícia, eu fiquei muito feliz.
native_language_example: After the news, I became very happy.

additional_notes: From ficar (to become/to end up) + surpreso (surprised). It describes a change of state: someone ends up surprised after something happens or after learning something. Common patterns: “ficou surpreso com…” (surprised at/by…), and “ficou surpreso que…” (surprised that…). Gender/number agreement: “ficou surpresa” (female), “ficaram surpresos/surpresas” (plural).
target_language_example: Eu fiquei surpreso com a notícia.
native_language_example: I was surprised by the news.

additional_notes: A common genre label. Use it after verbs like gostar de, preferir, assistir a, or with articles (os filmes de ação = “action movies”). In European Portuguese, you may also see “filmes de acção” (older spelling).
target_language_example: Hoje à noite vamos ver filmes de ação.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re going to watch action movies.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for the horror genre. Often used with verbs like gostar de (to like), assistir a (to watch), and ter medo de (to be afraid of). Singular: filme de terror.
target_language_example: Eu não assisto a filmes de terror porque fico com medo.
native_language_example: I don’t watch horror movies because I get scared.

meaning: “end of the” (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns: fim da semana (“end of the week”), fim da mensagem (“end of the message”), fim da linha (“end of the line”). With masculine nouns, use fim do (e.g., fim do dia). Can also appear as a heading/announcement: “Fim da competição.”
target_language_example: Preciso entregar o relatório antes do fim da tarde.
native_language_example: I need to submit the report before the end of the afternoon.

additional_notes: Plural of "final de semana". Very common with "no(s)/aos" to mean "on/during the weekends": "nos finais de semana". You can also say "no fim de semana" for "on the weekend" (singular). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, "fim de semana" is more common than "final de semana".
target_language_example: Nos finais de semana, a gente costuma descansar e ver amigos.
native_language_example: On weekends, we usually rest and see friends.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun introduced by "do" (= de + o): "o final do show/do filme/do mês". Common with "até o final do..." = "until the end of...". For feminine nouns, use "final da" (e.g., "final da semana").
target_language_example: Vamos ficar até o final do jogo.
native_language_example: Let’s stay until the end of the game.

additional_notes: Plural of "fim de semana" (weekend). Common after frequency expressions like "todos os" (every) and "quase todos os" (almost every). You may also hear "no fim de semana" (on the weekend) and "aos fins de semana" (on weekends, regularly).
target_language_example: Aos fins de semana, a gente descansa e vê filmes.
native_language_example: On weekends, we rest and watch movies.

additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) using the você form of the verb ficar (“to stay”). Used to tell someone to remain in the same place, often temporarily (e.g., while you do something).
target_language_example: Fique aqui, por favor, e espere um minuto.
native_language_example: Stay here, please, and wait a minute.

additional_notes: Imperative form of ficar + de olho (“to keep an eye”), used to tell someone to pay attention or monitor someone/something. Often followed by em/no/na/nos/nas: “Fique de olho no Tom” = “Keep an eye on Tom.” You may also hear “ficar de olho” (infinitive) or “fica de olho” (informal command).
target_language_example: Fique de olho na sua mochila no metrô.
native_language_example: Keep an eye on your backpack on the subway.

additional_notes: Common imperative (usually to você) meaning “monitor” or “look after” something for a moment so nothing bad happens (e.g., your bag, the road, a child). It’s often followed by a noun with an article: fique de olho na estrada / no celular / nas crianças. You can also hear: "ficar de olho em" (same idea).
target_language_example: Fique de olho na minha mochila, por favor, enquanto eu vou ao caixa.
native_language_example: Keep an eye on my backpack, please, while I go to the register.

meaning: “keep an eye on the (plural feminine)” / “watch the”.
additional_notes: Imperative/formal command using ficar de olho em (“to keep an eye on; to watch over; to monitor”). It’s used to ask someone to pay attention, supervise, or make sure something/someone is safe. Here, nas = em + as, used with feminine plural nouns (e.g., nas crianças, nas malas). For masculine plural, you’ll often hear: fique de olho nos.
target_language_example: Fique de olho nas bolsas enquanto eu pago.
native_language_example: Keep an eye on the bags while I pay.

additional_notes: Imperative form (você) of "ficar" + "longe": a command/request telling someone not to come near something/someone, often for safety or to set a boundary. Common patterns: "Fique longe de + [thing/person]" (Stay away from...), "Fique longe daqui" (Stay away from here). Can also be used alone: "Fique longe!".
target_language_example: Fique longe da janela, por favor.
native_language_example: Stay away from the window, please.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "ficar" (to stay) + "longe" (far) + "de" (from). Used to tell someone not to come near a person/thing, often as a warning or for safety. You can also say "Fique longe!" (Stay away!) without naming what to avoid.
target_language_example: Fique longe do fogo, por favor.
native_language_example: Please stay away from the fire.

additional_notes: Imperative in the você form (formal or neutral), from ficar (“to stay”) + quieto (“quiet/still”). Used to tell someone to stop talking or stop moving, often as a warning (e.g., so someone won’t hear you). You can also hear: “Fique quieta” (to a woman) and “Fiquem quietos/quietas” (plural).
target_language_example: Fique quieto por um minuto, por favor.
native_language_example: Be quiet for a minute, please.

additional_notes: Polite phrase used to give someone permission or to make them feel welcome. It can mean (1) “feel free to do X” (Fique à vontade para...) or (2) “make yourself at home/comfortable,” often when inviting someone to sit, take off a coat, etc. It’s the imperative of “ficar” (to stay/become): “fique” (you, formal) + “à vontade” (at ease).
target_language_example: Pode entrar e fique à vontade.
native_language_example: Come in and make yourself comfortable.

meaning: 'feel free to' (polite invitation/permission to do something).
additional_notes: Uses the imperative of "ficar" ("fique") + "à vontade" ("at ease/comfortable") to politely encourage someone to do an action: "Fique à vontade para + infinitive" (e.g., perguntar, ligar, sentar, usar). Common in hosts/customer service and friendly professional messages. You can also say "Fique à vontade" alone meaning "Make yourself comfortable."
target_language_example: Fique à vontade para mandar uma mensagem se tiver dúvidas.
native_language_example: Feel free to send a message if you have questions.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "ficar" + "em casa". Use it to say you remained at home (often because of weather, being sick, or choosing not to go out). You can also say "não fui a/ao/à + place; fiquei em casa" (“I didn’t go to…; I stayed home”).
target_language_example: Hoje eu não saí: fiquei em casa e descansei.
native_language_example: Today I didn’t go out: I stayed at home and rested.

additional_notes: From the verb "ficar" (to become) + "surpreso" (surprised). It’s used to say you ended up feeling surprised after something happened. Common patterns: "Fiquei surpreso ao/ao ver..." (I was surprised to/when I saw...), "Fiquei surpreso com..." (I was surprised by...), and "Fiquei surpreso que..." / more naturally "Fiquei surpreso por ele ter..." (I was surprised that...). Gender/number change: "fiquei surpresA" (female speaker), "ficamos surpresos/surpresas" (we were surprised).
target_language_example: Fiquei surpreso quando ele me ligou tão tarde.
native_language_example: I was surprised when he called me so late.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a past moment that caused surprise. "Fiquei" is the simple past of "ficar" (to become / to end up), and it’s common to say "ficar surpreso/a" = “to be (get) surprised.” Change "surpreso" to "surpresa" if the speaker is female. You can also make it plural: "ficamos surpresos/surpresas" = “we were surprised.”
target_language_example: Fiquei surpreso quando ela chegou tão cedo.
native_language_example: I was surprised when she arrived so early.

additional_notes: "Fiz" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "fazer" (to do/make) for "eu" (I). "Isso" means "that/it" (something not close to the speaker, or just a general "it"), and can refer back to an action already mentioned: "Nunca fiz isso" = "I’ve never done that." Often used to explain a reason with "porque" or "pelo/pela" (because of/for): "Fiz isso pelo Sami" = "I did it for Sami."
target_language_example: Desculpa — fiz isso sem pensar.
native_language_example: Sorry — I did it without thinking.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you did (often in response to instructions, expectations, or necessity). It’s the past tense of "fazer" (to do/make): "fiz" = "I did". The phrase is usually followed by a clause like "(eu) tinha que fazer" (I had to do), "você me disse" (you told me), or "ele queria" (he wanted). In speech and writing, the subject "eu" is often omitted: "(Eu) fiz o que…".
target_language_example: Desculpa, fiz o que você pediu.
native_language_example: Sorry, I did what you asked.

meaning: “I did what I could” / “I did my best.”
additional_notes: Used to say you made the maximum effort possible, often when you couldn’t fully achieve the desired result. It can sound defensive or apologetic depending on tone/context. Grammar note: past tense of fazer (fiz = “I did/made”) + o que pude (“what I was able to”). Common variations: “fiz o que pude para…” (“I did what I could to…”), “fiz o possível” (“I did what was possible”).
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu fiz o que pude, mas não deu tempo de terminar.
native_language_example: Sorry, I did what I could, but there wasn’t time to finish.

meaning: "(I/you/he/she) do that" (future subjunctive: "if/when" someone does that).
additional_notes: "Fizer" is the future subjunctive of "fazer" (to do/make), used after triggers like "quando" (when), "se" (if), "caso" (in case), "assim que" (as soon as). "Isso" means "that/this" (something previously mentioned). Often implies a condition or a future event: "quando eu fizer isso" = "when I do that"; "se ela fizer isso" = "if she does that".
target_language_example: Se eu fizer isso hoje, amanhã teremos mais tempo.
native_language_example: If I do that today, tomorrow we'll have more time.

additional_notes: "Fizeram" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "fazer" for "eles/elas" (they) or "vocês" (you all). "isso" means "that/it" (a specific action or thing already known from context). Often used in questions ("Como fizeram isso?" = "How did you do that?") or statements ("Eles fizeram isso" = "They did it").
target_language_example: Por que vocês fizeram isso?
native_language_example: Why did you (all) do that?

meaning: "(if someone) did that" / "were to do that" (imperfect subjunctive of fazer + isso).
additional_notes: Used with the imperfect subjunctive (fizesse) to talk about a hypothetical or uncertain action in the past or future. Common after "se" (if) and after verbs/expressions that trigger the subjunctive, like "querer que" (to want someone to…), "pedir que" (to ask that…), and "permitir que" (to allow that…).
