It’s very common for descriptions and background information ("There used to be...", "There was..."), and it’s **impersonal** (you don’t say who did it). In everyday speech, many people also use **tinha um** with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Havia um café aqui perto, mas fechou no ano passado.
native_language_example: There was a café near here, but it closed last year.

meaning: "there was a" / "there used to be a" (in the past).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "haver" to indicate existence in the past (an impersonal form like English "there was"). "Uma" is the feminine form of "a/an", so it’s followed by a feminine noun (e.g., "uma razão"). In everyday spoken Portuguese, people often use "tinha uma" with a similar meaning, but "havia uma" is more neutral/formal.
target_language_example: Naquela rua, havia uma padaria muito boa.
native_language_example: On that street, there was a really good bakery.

meaning: “There used to be a bridge here.”
additional_notes: Uses **havia** (imperfect of *haver*) to say that something **existed in the past**. Very common for background description: *Havia um supermercado aqui* (“There used to be a supermarket here”). Often appears with time expressions like **há muito tempo** (“a long time ago”) or **havia um tempo em que...** (“there was a time when…”).
target_language_example: Antes da estrada, havia uma ponte aqui.
native_language_example: Before the road, there used to be a bridge here.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened earlier today during the morning. Often answers “when?” and can go at the beginning or end of the sentence: Hoje de manhã, eu fui ao mercado. / Eu fui ao mercado hoje de manhã.
target_language_example: Hoje de manhã eu tomei café e saí cedo.
native_language_example: This morning I had coffee and left early.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen later today, during the evening or nighttime. Often used with future plans or expectations (e.g., "vou", "posso", "espero"). In Portuguese, "à noite" means "at night"; adding "hoje" specifies "tonight."
target_language_example: A gente se encontra hoje à noite.
native_language_example: We’ll meet tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later today during the afternoon. "à tarde" = "in the afternoon"; adding "hoje" specifies that it’s today. Common in questions and plans (e.g., what you’ll do, when you arrive, weather).
target_language_example: Vamos nos ver hoje à tarde.
native_language_example: We’re going to see each other this afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that describes which man you mean: “o homem que…” = “the man who/that…”. Often followed by a verb (e.g., "o homem que eu vi" = "the man (that) I saw"). In English you can sometimes drop “that,” but in Portuguese you normally keep “que.”
target_language_example: O homem que está ali é o meu professor.
native_language_example: The man who is over there is my teacher.

additional_notes: Used to say it’s the right moment to start (or stop) an action, often in the patterns: “(Já) está na hora de + infinitive” (It’s time to…), “É hora de + infinitive” (It’s time to…), and “Não é hora de + infinitive” (It’s not the time to…). Typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., ir, discutir, encerrar).
target_language_example: Já está na hora de dormir.
native_language_example: It’s time to sleep.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how many hours something happens each day, often after a number: "dez horas por dia" (ten hours a day). Very common in questions with "quantas": "Quantas horas por dia...?".
target_language_example: Eu durmo oito horas por dia.
native_language_example: I sleep eight hours a day.

meaning: “hours you …” — used in questions about how many hours you spend/do something.
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed expression by itself; it’s most commonly seen in the pattern **Quantas horas você + verb…?** meaning **“How many hours do you …?”** (asking about duration). Example: **Quantas horas você dorme?** = “How many hours do you sleep?”
target_language_example: Quantas horas você trabalha por dia?
native_language_example: How many hours do you work per day?

additional_notes: Used to report an event in the past. "Houve" is the past form of the impersonal verb "haver" meaning “there is/are/there was/were”; it doesn’t change for singular/plural (e.g., "Houve dois acidentes" = “There were two accidents”). Often used in news-style or formal descriptions; in everyday speech many people also use "teve" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Houve um problema com o voo ontem à noite.
native_language_example: There was a problem with the flight last night.

additional_notes: Uses haver (há) to say that something exists/is happening, often when you don’t know exactly what it is. Very common in questions: “Há algo...?” = “Is there something...?” Also used with adjectives or phrases: “Há algo estranho/misterioso...” (There’s something strange/mysterious...), “Há algo acontecendo” (Something is happening), “Há algo entre vocês?” (Is something going on between you two?).
target_language_example: Há algo que eu deveria saber?
native_language_example: Is there something I should know?

meaning: 'there is something that…' / 'is there something that…?'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce important information or a question about something specific. Usually followed by a clause with a verb: “há algo que + (subject) + precise saber/fazer/proteger…”. In questions, Portuguese often relies on intonation rather than changing the word order: “Há algo que você quer me dizer?” = “Is there something you want to tell me?”.
target_language_example: Há algo que eu quero te dizer antes de você ir embora.
native_language_example: There’s something I want to tell you before you leave.

additional_notes: A polite way to ask if someone has something they want to say/ask/request. Literally “there is something that you want,” but it functions like “Is there anything you’d like…?” Often followed by an infinitive (dizer, pedir, perguntar) or by “que + subjunctive” to express what you want someone else to do: “...que eu leve?” = “...that I bring?”
target_language_example: Há algo que você queira fazer antes de irmos embora?
native_language_example: Is there anything you want to do before we leave?

meaning: "Is there any…?" / "there is (some)…"; with time, "for some (time)".
additional_notes: Uses the verb "haver" in the impersonal sense meaning "there is/are" (it stays in the singular: "Há algum cinema…?", "Há alguns cinemas…?"). With "algum/alguma/alguns/algumas" it often corresponds to English "any" in questions (asking if something exists nearby/available). With time expressions ("há algum tempo"), it means "for some time" (not "ago"—"há" can also mean "ago" in other patterns, e.g., "há dois anos").
target_language_example: Há alguma farmácia aberta por aqui?
native_language_example: Is there any pharmacy open around here?

meaning: a few weeks ago; for a few weeks (depending on context).
additional_notes: Uses "há" (from "haver") to indicate time passed between then and now. With past events it usually means "a few weeks ago" (e.g., "morreu há algumas semanas" = "died a few weeks ago"). With states/relationships it often means "for a few weeks" (duration up to now): "conhece... há algumas semanas" = "has known... for a few weeks". Common alternative: "faz algumas semanas".
target_language_example: Mudei para esta cidade há algumas semanas.
native_language_example: I moved to this city a few weeks ago.

meaning: a few days ago; for a few days (depending on context).
additional_notes: Uses "há" (from "haver") to talk about time relative to now. With past actions/events, it means "a few days ago" (e.g., "Ele ficou doente há alguns dias"). With a continuing situation plus a duration, it means "for a few days" (e.g., "Ele está lá há alguns dias" = he has been there for a few days).
target_language_example: Comecei a trabalhar aqui há alguns dias.
native_language_example: I started working here a few days ago.

meaning: about three years ago (three years ago, approximately).
additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. "há" means "ago" (literally "there is" in time expressions), and "cerca de" means "about/around". You can swap the time: "há cerca de duas semanas" (about two weeks ago), "há cerca de um mês" (about a month ago). Common structure: "Foi há cerca de X" or "Aconteceu há cerca de X".
target_language_example: Cheguei aqui há cerca de três anos.
native_language_example: I arrived here about three years ago.

meaning: "five years ago" / "for five years" (depending on context).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "haver" (há) to express time distance from the present. With a completed past event, it means "five years ago" (Ela morreu há cinco anos.). With an action/state that started in the past and continues now, it means "for five years" (Está fechado há cinco anos.; Está fazendo caminhadas há cinco anos.). In English you often choose between "ago" vs "for"; in Portuguese "há" can cover both.
target_language_example: Moro aqui há cinco anos.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here for five years.

meaning: “ten years ago” / “for ten years” (with a time ago expression).
additional_notes: Uses the verb haver (há) to express time distance from now. With a past event, it means “ten years ago” (Aconteceu há dez anos.). With an action/state that started in the past and continues to now (often with present tense), it means “for ten years” (Moro aqui há dez anos.).
target_language_example: Trabalho aqui há dez anos.
native_language_example: I’ve worked here for ten years.

meaning: "two" with há: either "there are two" or "two ago" (two units of time ago).
additional_notes: Há is from the verb haver. With a noun, it often means “there is/there are”: Há dois botes no lago. With a time expression (anos, dias, minutos, etc.), it means “ago”: há dois anos = two years ago. In the “ago” meaning, you usually use há + number + time unit (and you typically don’t need atrás, though many people say há dois anos atrás in casual speech).
target_language_example: Eu cheguei aqui há dois minutos.
native_language_example: I arrived here two minutes ago.

meaning: two years ago; for two years (ago).
additional_notes: Uses "há" (from "haver") to talk about time elapsed up to now. With past events: "...há dois anos" = "two years ago" (e.g., he quit two years ago). With actions/states that started in the past and continue: "(só) ... há dois anos" = "for (only) two years" (e.g., he has been studying for two years). Often appears at the end of the sentence. You can also see it with "desde" ("desde há dois anos"), meaning "for the past two years"/"since two years ago".
target_language_example: Moro nesta cidade há dois anos.
native_language_example: I’ve lived in this city for two years.

meaning: two days ago; for two days (up to now).
additional_notes: Uses "há" (from the verb "haver") to talk about time elapsed. With a completed past event, it means "two days ago" (e.g., "Ele chegou há dois dias"). With something continuing until now, it means "for two days" / "for the past two days" (often with a negative or ongoing situation: "Não tem... há dois dias", "Procuro vocês há dois dias"). Common alternatives: "faz dois dias" (same idea) and "dois dias atrás" (usually "two days ago" only).
target_language_example: Estou esperando uma resposta há dois dias.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for an answer for two days.

additional_notes: Used to ask if there is anything additional to do, say, or provide. Very common in polite contexts (customer service, finishing a conversation). It’s often followed by a verb phrase, e.g. “eu precise fazer”, “me tenha a dizer”, “podemos fazer por você”.
target_language_example: Há mais alguma coisa que eu possa ajudar?
native_language_example: Is there anything else I can help with?

additional_notes: Used to say that many of something exist or are present. "há" (from "haver") is an impersonal verb meaning "there is/are" and doesn’t change with the noun; "muitas" agrees with a feminine plural noun (e.g., casas, estantes, lojas, ilhas). For masculine plural, use "há muitos".
target_language_example: Aqui há muitas pessoas todos os dias.
native_language_example: There are many people here every day.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a general statement or list of things. "há" means "there is/there are" (from the verb haver). It’s followed by a relative clause with "que" ("that") describing those things. Very common with verbs like "precisar", "ter que", "querer", "saber".
target_language_example: Há muitas coisas que eu ainda não entendo.
native_language_example: There are many things that I still don’t understand.

additional_notes: Uses **há** (from **haver**) to say that people exist/are present somewhere (“there is/there are”). Very common to describe how crowded a place is: **Há muitas pessoas no parque.** You can make it a question with intonation or a question mark: **Há muitas pessoas na sala de espera?**
target_language_example: Hoje há muitas pessoas na praia.
native_language_example: Today there are many people at the beach.

meaning: a long time ago; for a long time (depending on context).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "haver" (há) to express elapsed time, like "ago" in English: "Vi esse filme há muito tempo" = "I saw that movie a long time ago." You can also use it to emphasize that something has been true for a long time: "Morta há muito tempo" = "dead for a long time." Often appears at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Não te vejo há muito tempo.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen you in a long time.

meaning: "there are many" / "there is a lot of".
additional_notes: Uses the verb "há" (from "haver") to mean "there is/there are" in an impersonal way, followed by a plural noun: "Há muitos + noun" = "There are many + noun". Common in neutral/formal speech and writing. Note: "há" is also used for time expressions ("há dois anos" = "two years ago"), but in this pattern it means existence/quantity.
target_language_example: Há muitos turistas aqui no verão.
native_language_example: There are many tourists here in the summer.

additional_notes: Uses "há" (from haver) to mean "there is/there are" in the sense of existence/availability. Very common in statements about what exists in a place: "Há muitos livros na biblioteca" = "There are many books in the library." (In everyday speech, people also often say "Tem muitos livros..." with the same meaning.)
target_language_example: Aqui há muitos livros interessantes para ler.
native_language_example: There are many interesting books here to read.

additional_notes: Used to ask about duration from a starting point up to now (e.g., how long someone has lived/studied/worked). With events, it can mean “How long ago…?”. The verb usually comes right after: “Há quanto tempo o Tom mora…?”. You can change “o” to “a/os/as” depending on the noun (e.g., “Há quanto tempo a Maria…”).
target_language_example: Há quanto tempo o seu irmão trabalha aqui?
native_language_example: How long has your brother worked here?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the duration of an action or state that started in the past and continues to now. Very common with the present tense in Portuguese (e.g., "Há quanto tempo você mora aqui?"), which corresponds to English present perfect ("have you lived") or "have you been ...". You can answer with "Há..." (Há dois anos.) or "Faz..." (Faz dois anos.)
target_language_example: Há quanto tempo você trabalha aqui?
native_language_example: How long have you worked here?

additional_notes:
Used to ask about the length of time since you first met someone. 
- Structure: "Há quanto tempo" + (subject) + verb in the present ("você conhece") + person.
- In English it often maps to the present perfect (“have you known”), even though Portuguese commonly uses the present ("conhece") with "há" to express duration.
- You can replace "você" with "ele/ela" or a name: "Há quanto tempo você conhece a Ana?"
target_language_example: Há quanto tempo você conhece a Maria?
native_language_example: How long have you known Maria?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the duration of an ongoing situation or action that started in the past and continues now. You usually add a place or an action after "está": "aqui/aí" (here/there), "ocupada" (busy), "sentada" (sitting), "olhando" (watching/looking). Common variants: "Há quanto tempo você está..." (you, formal in Brazil), "Há quanto tempo você está..." / "Há quanto tempo você tá..." (more casual speech), and "Há quanto tempo você está..." can also be asked as "Faz quanto tempo que você está...?"
target_language_example: Há quanto tempo você está esperando aqui?
native_language_example: How long have you been waiting here?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the duration of an ongoing situation or action that started in the past and continues now. You usually add a place or an action after "está": "aqui/aí" (here/there), "ocupada" (busy), "sentada" (sitting), "olhando" (watching/looking). Common variants: "Há quanto tempo você está..." (you, formal in Brazil), "Há quanto tempo você está..." / "Há quanto tempo você tá..." (more casual speech), and "Há quanto tempo você está..." can also be asked as "Faz quanto tempo que você está...?"
target_language_example: Há quanto tempo você está esperando aqui?
native_language_example: How long have you been waiting here?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the length of time someone has been working somewhere, with someone, for someone, or on something. Often followed by: com (with), em (in/at), para (for), nisso/nisso aqui (on this). Uses the expression “há quanto tempo” (“for how long/since when”), which refers to a time period up to now, similar to English present perfect (“have you been working”).
target_language_example: Há quanto tempo você trabalha aqui?
native_language_example: How long have you been working here?

meaning: "How long have you been …?" (asking since when someone has been something).
additional_notes: Used to ask about duration up to now with the verb ser (to be). It commonly appears with a noun/adjective after é: "Há quanto tempo você é professor(a)?" / "… é vegetariano(a)?" It can also be used with “dono(a) de …” to mean ownership: "Há quanto tempo você é dono(a) deste carro?" Literally it’s like “there is how much time you are…”, but in English you usually say “How long have you been…?”
target_language_example: Há quanto tempo você é casado?
native_language_example: How long have you been married?

additional_notes:
Uses the impersonal verb "haver" ("há"):
- With a noun: "Há três crianças" = "There are three children".
- With a time expression (usually "há três + [time unit]"): "há três anos" = "three years ago" / "three years ago from now". Many speakers add "atrás" (e.g., "há três anos atrás"), but "há três anos" already has the "ago" meaning.
target_language_example: Há três pessoas esperando lá fora.
native_language_example: There are three people waiting outside.

meaning: three years ago; for three years (in the past).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "haver" (há) to talk about time. With a completed past action, it usually means "three years ago" (e.g., "Fui lá há três anos" = I went there three years ago). With the imperfect to describe an ongoing situation in the past, it can mean "for three years" / "had been ... for three years" (e.g., "Eu morava lá há três anos" = I had been living there for three years).
target_language_example: Comecei a trabalhar aqui há três anos.
native_language_example: I started working here three years ago.

meaning: "three days ago" / "for three days" (depending on context).
additional_notes: Uses "há" (from "haver") to express time relative to now. With a completed past event (e.g., "chegou"), it means "three days ago." With an action/state that started in the past and continues to now (often with "estar"), it means "for three days" (="has been ... for three days").
target_language_example: Estou esperando há três dias.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for three days.

meaning: three months ago; for three months (with duration up to now).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "haver" (há) to talk about time. With a completed past action, it means "... ago" (Fui promovido há três meses = I was promoted three months ago). With an action/state that started in the past and continues now, it means "for ..." (Tom está na Austrália há três meses = Tom has been in Australia for three months). You can also hear the structure "Há três meses que..." meaning "It’s been three months since..." / "For three months, ...". Note: "há" is invariable here (always "há", not changing with person).
target_language_example: Moro aqui há três meses.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here for three months.

meaning: three weeks ago; for three weeks (up to now).
additional_notes: Uses "há" (from the verb "haver") to express elapsed time. With past events, it means "three weeks ago" (Eu o vi há três semanas.). With actions/states that started in the past and continue now, it means "for three weeks" (Estamos aqui há três semanas.). It’s common to place the time phrase at the beginning or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Moro aqui há três semanas.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here for three weeks.

additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is present somewhere. It’s the verb haver in the present: há. Common in statements and questions (Há um...? = Is there a...?). Very often followed by a noun (há um lago, há um problema).
target_language_example: Há um problema com o meu pedido.
native_language_example: There’s a problem with my order.

meaning: a year ago; for a year (up to now).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "haver" (há) to express elapsed time. With past events, it means "a year ago" (Aconteceu há um ano.). With actions/states that continue into the present, it means "for a year" (Eles estão no Brasil há um ano. = they’ve been in Brazil for a year). Many speakers also say "há um ano atrás", but "há um ano" already contains the idea of "ago".
target_language_example: Moro aqui há um ano.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here for a year.

meaning: "there is/there’s a" (referring to a singular feminine noun).
additional_notes: Uses the verb haver (impersonal) to state that something exists or is present. Very common in more formal or neutral writing/speech. It’s followed by a feminine singular noun (uma + noun), e.g., “há uma dúvida”, “há uma chance”. Often interchangeable with “existe uma” or “tem uma” (more informal in some regions).
target_language_example: Há uma possibilidade de chuva amanhã.
native_language_example: There’s a chance of rain tomorrow.

meaning: an hour ago; for an hour (depending on context).
additional_notes: Uses the verb haver (há) to express elapsed time. With a completed past action, it usually means “an hour ago” (e.g., Ele partiu há uma hora.). With an action/state that continues up to now, it means “for an hour” (e.g., Estou procurando há uma hora.). Many speakers add “atrás” (há uma hora atrás), but “há uma hora” already includes the idea of “ago,” so “atrás” is redundant.
target_language_example: Estou esperando há uma hora.
native_language_example: I've been waiting for an hour.

meaning: one week ago; for a week (up to now).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "haver" (há) to express time distance from now. With past events, it means "a week ago" (Ele ganhou o prêmio há uma semana). With actions/states that started in the past and continue to the present, it means "for a week" (Eu estou aqui há uma semana). In Brazil you may hear "há uma semana atrás"; it’s common but redundant because "há" already means "ago."
target_language_example: Estou estudando português há uma semana.
native_language_example: I've been studying Portuguese for a week.

meaning: "idea of" / "any idea about" (knowledge or guess about something).
additional_notes: Common with verbs like "ter" (to have): "Tem alguma ideia de...?" = "Do you have any idea...?". Often followed by an indirect question: "ideia de onde/como/quando/por que...". With "a ideia de que..." it means "the idea that..." (a belief/assumption). In the negative, it emphasizes not knowing: "não ter ideia de..." / "não ter a mínima ideia de..." = "to have no idea" / "not have the slightest idea".
target_language_example: Você tem alguma ideia de quanto isso vai custar?
native_language_example: Do you have any idea how much this is going to cost?

additional_notes: Used after verbs like "ter" (to have) or "fazer" (to have, in the sense of grasp/realize): "Você tem alguma ideia de como…?" = “Do you have any idea how…?” and "Você não faz ideia de como…" = “You have no idea how…”. Often expresses surprise, emphasis, or that something is hard to imagine.
target_language_example: Você tem ideia de como chegar lá de ônibus?
native_language_example: Do you have any idea how to get there by bus?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question about location. Very common in negatives: “não tenho (nem) ideia de onde…” = “I have no idea where…”. You can also use it in questions: “Você tem ideia de onde…?” = “Do you have any idea where…?”. Often follows verbs like ter (“to have”) or saber (“to know”).
target_language_example: Você tem ideia de onde fica a estação de metrô?
native_language_example: Do you have any idea where the subway station is?

meaning: (to have) an idea of who it was / who someone was.
additional_notes: Used when you don’t know (or are asking if someone knows) a person’s identity. Very common with negatives: "não tenho ideia de quem era…" / "não faço a mínima ideia de quem era…" (= "I have no idea at all who it was"). You can change the tense: "quem é" (who it is) vs. "quem era" (who it was).
target_language_example: Eu não tenho ideia de quem era a pessoa que ligou ontem.
native_language_example: I have no idea who the person who called yesterday was.

meaning: an idea of what… / any idea what…
additional_notes: Used with (ter/fazer) ideia to talk about knowing or having an understanding of something: “Tens/Você tem ideia do que…?” = “Do you have any idea what…?” and “Não tenho/Não faço ideia do que…” = “I have no idea what…” It’s followed by a clause with the verb (often in the infinitive: “do que vestir”, “do que comprar”).
target_language_example: Você tem ideia do que ele quis dizer?
native_language_example: Do you have any idea what he meant?

meaning: an idea of what to do; know what to do.
additional_notes: Used with (não) ter/fazer ideia to say someone (doesn't) know what to do in a situation. Very common in the negative: “não tenho ideia do que fazer” = “I have no idea what to do.” You can change the verb after “do que…”: “ideia do que dizer” (what to say), “do que comprar” (what to buy).
target_language_example: Eu não tenho ideia do que fazer agora.
native_language_example: I have no idea what to do now.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ir (often in the past perfect: tinha ido embora) to say someone had already left by the time something else happened. In exclamations/conditionals like "Se tivesse ido embora!", it expresses regret: "If only (I/he) had left!"
target_language_example: Quando liguei, ela já tinha ido embora.
native_language_example: When I called, she had already left.

meaning: blocking my way; preventing me from passing.
additional_notes: Used to complain that someone is physically obstructing you. "impedindo" is the gerund of "impedir" (to prevent/stop), and "-me" means "me" (object pronoun). "a passagem" is "the passage/way through". Often said to ask someone to move aside; can also be phrased as "O senhor está me impedindo de passar".
target_language_example: Com licença, você está impedindo-me a passagem.
native_language_example: Excuse me, you’re blocking my way.

additional_notes: Used to say that something matters to someone (or is significant for something). The thing that is important comes before, and the person/thing it matters to comes after: “É importante para mim/ele/nós” (It’s important to me/him/us). It can also describe importance for a purpose or result: “importante para a felicidade” (important for happiness).
target_language_example: Isso é muito importante para mim.
native_language_example: This is very important to me.

additional_notes: Used to say someone can’t do something (often physically or emotionally). It’s usually followed by an infinitive (incapaz de + verb). The adjective agrees with the person: incapaz (m./f. singular), incapazes (plural).
target_language_example: Ela ficou incapaz de falar.
native_language_example: She was unable to speak.

additional_notes: Often used with the verb ir (to go), especially in the structure “vai indo bem” to mean something is progressing well/turning out fine. It can suggest things are generally okay, sometimes with a modest or gradual tone (not necessarily “perfect”).
target_language_example: O projeto está indo bem até agora.
native_language_example: The project is going well so far.

additional_notes: Used with a destination after the preposition "para". It’s the gerund of "ir" (to go) and commonly appears in the past continuous: "estava indo para..." = "was going to..." (was on the way / was heading to).
target_language_example: Estou indo para casa agora.
native_language_example: I'm going home now.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ir in the gerund (indo) to describe movement in progress or a planned trip: "(estar) indo" = "to be going". "para a" means "to the" before a feminine noun (e.g., a academia, a estação). For masculine nouns, you usually use "indo para o".
target_language_example: Estou indo para a estação agora.
native_language_example: I'm going to the station now.

additional_notes: "Indo" is the gerund of "ir" (to go), so this phrase describes an action in progress: someone is currently headed home. It’s often used with "estar" to form the present/past continuous: "estou/estava indo para casa" (I’m/I was going home). You can also use it after verbs like "imaginar" (to imagine): "me imaginei indo para casa".
target_language_example: Já estou indo para casa; te ligo quando chegar.
native_language_example: I’m already on my way home; I’ll call you when I arrive.

additional_notes: Used to say someone studies/does English daily. Most often appears after a verb like estudar (to study): “(Eu) estudo inglês todos os dias.” You can also use the pattern with other subjects (ela/ele/você/nós) and other activities: “Eu treino todos os dias” (I train every day).
target_language_example: Eu pratico inglês todos os dias, nem que seja por 10 minutos.
native_language_example: I practice English every day, even if it’s only for 10 minutes.

additional_notes: Used to say what someone intends or does not intend to do: "ter intenção de" = "to intend to". It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., "intenção de ir", "intenção de ficar"). You’ll often see it in the negative: "não tenho intenção de..." = "I don’t intend to...". Also common with "com a intenção de" = "with the intention of".
target_language_example: Eu não tenho intenção de voltar hoje.
native_language_example: I don’t intend to come back today.

additional_notes: Used with a noun or an infinitive verb: "interessado em música" (interested in music), "interessado em aprender" (interested in learning). It can describe curiosity/enthusiasm or romantic interest depending on context (e.g., "interessado em você" can mean interested in you romantically). Agreement: interessado (masc.), interessada (fem.), interessados/interessadas (plural).
target_language_example: Ela está interessada em trabalhar aqui.
native_language_example: She is interested in working here.

meaning: to go to (a place/event) / to go and (do something).
additional_notes: "Ir" is "to go" and it’s commonly followed by "a" to say where you’re going: "ir a Paris", "ir a uma reunião", "ir a um médico" (= go to the doctor). You can also use it with another verb to mean "go and do": "ir a ajudar". In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often say "ir para" instead of "ir a" for destinations ("ir para Boston"), but "ir a" is still correct and common, especially in more formal or written contexts and with events/appointments.
target_language_example: Eu vou a uma reunião amanhã cedo.
native_language_example: I'm going to a meeting early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about going to an unspecified destination. After verbs like querer/quererem (“to want”) or ter que (“to have to”), it often means “go anywhere/go someplace” depending on context. Uses the preposition “a” with “ir” (ir a + place).
target_language_example: Depois do trabalho, eu vou a algum lugar para jantar.
native_language_example: After work, I'm going somewhere for dinner.

additional_notes: Means being free/allowed/able to go to any place, with no restriction. Often used with forms of “poder” (can/may): “Você pode ir a qualquer lugar.”
target_language_example: Com esse passe, você pode ir a qualquer lugar na cidade.
native_language_example: With this pass, you can go anywhere in the city.

additional_notes: Used before masculine singular nouns: ir + a + o = ao. Common with places and events: ir ao bar, ir ao shopping, ir ao show. With feminine nouns you usually use ir à (ir a + a), and with plural you use ir aos (ir a + os).
target_language_example: Vamos ir ao cinema hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Do you want to go to the movies tonight?

additional_notes: Used for physically going to a bank (the financial institution), often to do things like withdraw money (sacar dinheiro), deposit money, or talk to a bank employee. In Portuguese, “banco” can also mean “bench,” but with “ir ao banco” it usually means the bank, especially in money-related contexts.
target_language_example: Vou ao banco amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to the bank tomorrow morning.

meaning: to go to the bathroom (to use the toilet).
additional_notes: Common, polite way to say you need to use the restroom. Often used with precisar/ter de: "Eu preciso/tenho de ir ao banheiro." In Brazil you may also hear "ir ao toalete" or "ir ao banheiro"; in more formal settings you can say "ir ao banheiro, por favor?" or "Posso ir ao banheiro?" (May I go to the bathroom?).
target_language_example: Com licença, posso ir ao banheiro?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I go to the bathroom?

additional_notes: Used for the activity of going to a movie theater to watch a film. The verb is "ir" (to go) + "ao" (= a + o, “to the”) + "cinema" (cinema/movie theater). Often used after verbs like "querer" (to want) and "planejar" (to plan).
target_language_example: Vamos ir ao cinema hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Do you want to go to the movies tonight?

meaning: to go to the movies with me.
additional_notes: Used to invite someone to the cinema. Often appears after an invitation verb like "querer" (to want), "gostar de" (to like/would like), or "aceitar" (to accept): e.g., "Você gostaria de ir ao cinema comigo?". "ao" = "a" + "o" (to the). You can change "comigo" to "com você" (with you), "com ele" (with him), etc.
target_language_example: Você quer ir ao cinema comigo hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Do you want to go to the movies with me tonight?

additional_notes: Used when someone needs medical care or needs to be checked by a doctor. Often appears with advice/urgency words like "deveria" (should) or "imediatamente" (immediately). In negative sentences, "não" makes it "not go / can't go".
target_language_example: Se a dor piorar, vou ao hospital.
native_language_example: If the pain gets worse, I’m going to the hospital.

meaning: to go to the doctor (for an appointment/checkup).
additional_notes: Used when you need medical care or a checkup. Common with obligation/advice: "tenho de" (I have to), "preciso" (I need to), "deveria" (should). It can refer to visiting a general doctor; for a specific specialist you can say "ir ao dentista" (dentist), "ir ao cardiologista" (cardiologist), etc.
target_language_example: Estou com febre, então vou ao médico amanhã.
native_language_example: I have a fever, so I’m going to the doctor tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about visiting a zoo. It’s built from ir (to go) + ao = a + o (“to the”, masculine singular) + zoológico (zoo). With other masculine places you’ll often see the same pattern: ir ao cinema (to go to the movies).
target_language_example: No domingo, vamos ir ao zoológico com as crianças.
native_language_example: On Sunday, we’re going to the zoo with the kids.

additional_notes: Used to say you will accompany someone. It often appears with verbs like "gostar de" (eu gostaria de ir com você = I’d like to go with you), "poder" (eu posso/poderia ir com você = I can/could go with you), and in negatives (não posso ir com você = I can’t go with you). In Brazil, "você" is common; in Portugal, you’ll often hear "ir contigo" instead.
target_language_example: Eu vou com você.
native_language_example: I'll go with you.

meaning: to go to sleep; to go to bed.
additional_notes: Used when you’re about to stop what you’re doing and head off to sleep. Very common with verbs like "dever" (should) and "ter que" (have to): "deveríamos ir dormir" (we should go to bed), "tenho que ir dormir" (I have to go to sleep).
target_language_example: Estou cansado; vou dormir agora.
native_language_example: I'm tired; I'm going to sleep now.

additional_notes: Used to say you will go to a specific place that’s understood from context. Very common with verbs like "deixar" (to let) and "mandar/falar para" (to tell). In everyday speech, "lá" can sometimes just mean “over there” or “to that place,” not necessarily far away.
target_language_example: Posso ir lá depois do trabalho?
native_language_example: Can I go there after work?

meaning: to go there alone / by yourself.
additional_notes: "Ir" = to go, "lá" = there (usually somewhere not right here), and "sozinho" = alone (masc.; use "sozinha" for a woman). Often used with advice or warnings like "não ir lá sozinho" (don’t go there alone).
target_language_example: Não quero ir lá sozinho à noite.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go there alone at night.

additional_notes: Used to talk about going somewhere to swim (a pool, the beach, a lake, etc.). It often follows verbs like querer (to want) and poder (can/may): “Quero ir nadar”, “Posso ir nadar?”. You can add a time expression (hoje à tarde) or company (com vocês).
target_language_example: Vamos ir nadar na piscina amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: Let's go swimming in the pool tomorrow morning.

meaning: to go to (a destination); to head for.
additional_notes: Used with a place/destination (a cidade, a praia, casa, etc.). Often followed by a definite article when the place takes one: ir para a praia, ir para o Brasil; but you’ll also hear the contraction forms: ir pra/pra + article (informal spoken) and ir pro/ir pra (para + o/a).
target_language_example: Amanhã eu vou para casa cedo.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going home early.

meaning: 'to go to' (toward a place; often feminine singular).
additional_notes: Used to express going/traveling to a destination. It’s the verb ir (to go) + para (to/toward/for) + a (the, feminine singular), so it’s used with places that take the article a: ir para a biblioteca, ir para a cadeia. With masculine places use ir para o; with plural use ir para os/as. Many countries don’t use an article in Portuguese, so you often say ir para Portugal/Irlanda (no a/o).
target_language_example: Vamos ir para a praia amanhã.
native_language_example: We’re going to the beach tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about going to sleep earlier than usual. Often used with advice or recommendations (e.g., "Você deveria...", "É melhor...") and with time expressions like "hoje" (today), "esta noite" (tonight).
target_language_example: Tenho prova amanhã, então vou para a cama cedo.
native_language_example: I have a test tomorrow, so I’m going to bed early.

additional_notes: Used with a destination ("para" = "to/toward"). Often implies going there as part of your routine (classes), not just visiting the building. You can change the subject and tense: "eu vou", "ele vai", "preciso ir", "quero ir".
target_language_example: Hoje eu vou para a escola de manhã.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to school in the morning.

additional_notes: Used for attending/going to a party or event. Often followed by who you go with (com ele/ela) or reason/obligation (tem que ir, me fez ir). You’ll also see it negated: não ir para a festa (“not go to the party”).
target_language_example: A gente vai para a festa hoje à noite.
native_language_example: We’re going to the party tonight.

meaning: to go home (to go to one’s house).
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase: *ir* (to go) + *para* (to/for) + *casa* (home/house). Often used without an article (*para casa*, not *para a casa*) when it means “home” in general. You can change the subject and tense: *Vou para casa* (I’m going home), *Vamos para casa* (Let’s go home), *Ele foi para casa* (He went home).
target_language_example: Estou cansado; vou para casa agora.
native_language_example: I’m tired; I’m going home now.

additional_notes: A common, everyday phrase used to say you are leaving (or someone should/can leave) and go home at this moment. You can change the subject and tense as needed (e.g., "eu vou", "você vai", "ele deve ir"), and "agora" can be moved for emphasis ("agora" = now).
target_language_example: Estou cansado; vou para casa agora.
native_language_example: I’m tired; I’m going home now.

meaning: to go to the (a destination with a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to talk about going to a place/destination. It’s literally "ir" (to go) + "para" (to/toward) + "o" (the, masculine). For feminine destinations, use "ir para a". In everyday speech in Brazil, "para o" is often contracted to "pro" (e.g., "Vou pro shopping"). With cities/countries, usage of the article (o/a) varies by place name and by region, so sometimes you’ll also hear "ir para" without the article.
target_language_example: Vamos ir para o restaurante depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: Let’s go to the restaurant after work.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ir" (to go) + an activity verb in the infinitive. You can talk about plans or invitations: "Quero ir pescar" (I want to go fishing), "Vamos ir pescar" (Let’s go fishing), "Quer ir pescar comigo?" (Do you want to go fishing with me?).
target_language_example: No fim de semana, vamos ir pescar no lago.
native_language_example: On the weekend, let’s go fishing at the lake.

additional_notes: Used with destinations introduced by the preposition “a” + the definite article. “à” = “a” + “a” (feminine singular), so it’s used before feminine singular places like “à loja”, “à França”, “à casa dele”. Common variants: “ir ao” (masculine singular: ao supermercado), “ir aos/às” (plural), and “ir a” (no article, e.g., “ir a Portugal” in some varieties).
target_language_example: Vamos ir à praia amanhã.
native_language_example: Let’s go to the beach tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about attending school (physically going there), often in everyday routines or obligations. In Portuguese, "à" = "a" + "a" (to + the) before a feminine singular noun like "escola". You can change the verb for tense/person: "vou à escola" (I go/I’m going), "fui à escola" (I went), "preciso ir à escola" (I need to go).
target_language_example: Hoje eu não vou à escola porque estou doente.
native_language_example: Today I’m not going to school because I’m sick.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "ir" (to go) + "a" (to) + "a festa" (the party). Because "a" + "a" contracts to "à", you say "ir à festa" (not *ir a a festa*). You can change the party to other places the same way: "ir à escola" (go to school), "ir ao cinema" (go to the cinema; "a" + "o" = "ao").
target_language_example: A gente vai à festa depois do jantar.
native_language_example: We’re going to the party after dinner.

additional_notes: Used to talk about going to the beach as an activity or plan. It’s literally “to go to the beach” (ir = to go; à = to + a, feminine singular; praia = beach). You can change the subject (eu/você/vocês/ela) and add time words like hoje (today), amanhã (tomorrow), etc.
target_language_example: No verão, a gente gosta de ir à praia no fim de semana.
native_language_example: In the summer, we like to go to the beach on the weekend.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of ir (iria = "would go") + infinitive (acontecer = "to happen") to talk about something that was expected/predicted to happen, often from a past point of view (e.g., "I knew it would happen"). Common with verbs like saber (to know), achar (to think), sentir (to feel), ouvir dizer (to hear say).
target_language_example: Eu não imaginava que isso iria acontecer tão cedo.
native_language_example: I didn’t imagine that was going to happen so soon.

meaning: “would want to” (would be likely to want).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of ir (iria) + infinitive (querer) to talk about a hypothetical/conditional desire: what someone would want in a given situation. Very common in questions like “Por que eu iria querer…?” (“Why would I want to…?”), often implying doubt or “what reason would I have?”
target_language_example: Eu não sei por que ela iria querer trocar de emprego agora.
native_language_example: I don’t know why she would want to change jobs now.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional form of ir (iria) to talk about what someone would want in a hypothetical situation or from a past point of view. Often appears after verbs like saber/pensar/achar: “Eu sabia/pensei que ele iria querer fazer isso.”
target_language_example: Achei que você iria querer fazer isso comigo.
native_language_example: I thought you would want to do that with me.

meaning: younger sister (the youngest sister, or a sister younger than you).
additional_notes: Used to describe a sister who is younger than someone else (often the speaker). It can mean “my younger sister” (minha irmã mais nova) or “his/her younger sister” (sua irmã mais nova). More generally, it can also mean “the younger/youngest sister” among sisters. The phrase is straightforward: irmã = sister, mais nova = younger (literally “more new/younger”).
target_language_example: Vou buscar minha irmã mais nova na escola.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick up my younger sister at school.

meaning: older sister (a female sibling who is older).
additional_notes: Used to specify that your sister is older than you or older than another sister. Often appears with possessives: "a minha irmã mais velha" (my older sister), "a irmã mais velha dela" (her older sister).
target_language_example: A minha irmã mais velha mora em Lisboa.
native_language_example: My older sister lives in Lisbon.

meaning: younger brother (younger sibling who is male).
additional_notes: Used to specify that your brother is younger than you (or younger than another sibling). It contrasts with "irmão mais velho" (older brother). "Caçula" can also be used as a noun/adjective meaning "the youngest" in the family/group, and it can be used with other family words (e.g., "filho caçula" = youngest son).
target_language_example: Meu irmão caçula começou a escola este ano.
native_language_example: My younger brother started school this year.

additional_notes: Used to say that a male person is the brother of a previously mentioned male. In Portuguese you often express possession with "dele" (= of him / his), especially when you want to be clear who the brother belongs to. (For a female: "irmã dele".)
target_language_example: Ele veio com o irmão dele para a festa.
native_language_example: He came with his brother to the party.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s male twin sibling. In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often just say “meu gêmeo” (my twin) or “irmão gêmeo” when they want to be clear it’s a brother (not a twin sister). For fraternal/non-identical twins, you may hear “irmão gêmeo fraterno”, but many speakers still say “irmão gêmeo” in general.
target_language_example: Ele confundiu o João com o irmão gêmeo dele.
native_language_example: He confused João with his twin brother.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male sibling who is younger than someone else (often the speaker or another person mentioned). You can also say "meu/minha/seu/sua irmão mais novo" (“my/your younger brother”). Literally “brother more new/younger.”
target_language_example: Meu irmão mais novo tem dez anos.
native_language_example: My younger brother is ten years old.

meaning: older brother (the brother who is older).
additional_notes: Used to specify an older male sibling, often with a possessive (meu/seu/nosso): "meu irmão mais velho" = "my older brother". In Portuguese you can also say "irmão mais novo" (younger brother) and for sisters "irmã mais velha/mais nova".
target_language_example: Meu irmão mais velho mora em outra cidade.
native_language_example: My older brother lives in another city.

additional_notes: Used literally to talk about someone’s male and female siblings. It’s also commonly used as a form of address to a group (“brothers and sisters”), sometimes in religious or motivational contexts. You can also just say “irmãos” to mean “siblings” in general.
target_language_example: Eu tenho dois irmãos e uma irmã, mas às vezes digo só: “Tenho irmãos e irmãs.”
native_language_example: I have two brothers and one sister, but sometimes I just say: “I have brothers and sisters.”

meaning: 'that/it, please' (polite way to refer to something and ask).
additional_notes: Used when you’re politely asking someone to do something with a specific thing or topic you’re indicating (a document, an object, an idea, etc.). Very common in requests with verbs like corrigir (correct), revisar (review), explicar (explain), ajudar a levar (help carry). In speech it often sounds like one unit: "isso, por favor".
target_language_example: Pode olhar isso, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you look at this/that, please?

additional_notes: Used to say that an event really occurred, often referring back to something just mentioned ("isso" = “that”). In questions, it’s a way to confirm or show surprise: “Did that really happen?”
target_language_example: Não acredito que isso aconteceu ontem.
native_language_example: I can’t believe that happened yesterday.

additional_notes: Often used to add urgency or immediacy: *isso* = “that/it” (referring to something already known from context) and *agora* = “now.” Common in requests and commands: *Faça isso agora.* / *Para com isso agora!* Word order can vary depending on what’s emphasized (e.g., *agora* can also come earlier: *Agora, faça isso!*).
target_language_example: Não consigo fazer isso agora; posso fazer mais tarde.
native_language_example: I can’t do that right now; I can do it later.

additional_notes: Used when you want to repeat an action, experience, or look at something one more time. Common with verbs like ver (to see), fazer (to do), sentir (to feel), and olhar (to look). Word order is fixed: isso (that/it) + de novo (again).
target_language_example: Vamos fazer isso de novo amanhã?
native_language_example: Shall we do that again tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to say (often accusingly or to confirm) that someone did something intentionally rather than by accident. Very common with verbs like "fazer" (to do/make): "fez isso de propósito" = "did that on purpose." You can also use just "de propósito" after the verb: "Ele fez de propósito."
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu não fiz isso de propósito.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t do that on purpose.

meaning: 'that was' (referring to something that happened in the past).
additional_notes: Used to comment on or evaluate a past action, event, or situation. Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase: "isso foi nojento" (that was disgusting), "isso foi um desperdício" (that was a waste). It can also introduce an explanation: "isso foi o que..." (that was what...).
target_language_example: Isso foi muito bom, obrigado.
native_language_example: That was very good, thank you.

meaning: 'That was very…' / 'That was so…' (used to emphasize a description).
additional_notes: Used to comment on something that just happened or something you’re talking about. It’s usually followed by an adjective: "isso foi muito engraçado" (that was very funny), "isso foi muito difícil" (that was very hard). You can also add comparisons after it, e.g. "isso foi muito mais difícil do que…" (that was much harder than…).
target_language_example: Nossa, isso foi muito cansativo.
native_language_example: Wow, that was very tiring.

meaning: “that more than once” / “it more than once.”
additional_notes: Used to say someone did the same thing repeatedly (two or more times). "isso" (“that/it”) refers to an action or thing already mentioned or understood from context. It often comes after the verb phrase: "fiz isso mais de uma vez" (“I did that more than once”).
target_language_example: Eu já fiz isso mais de uma vez.
native_language_example: I’ve done that more than once.

additional_notes: Used to say that something causes an emotional state. It’s often followed by an adjective describing how you feel (e.g., furioso/a, triste, nervoso/a, feliz). You can swap the object pronoun: isso te deixa (makes you), isso o/a deixa (makes him/her), isso nos deixa (makes us).
target_language_example: Isso me deixa muito feliz.
native_language_example: That makes me very happy.

isso não tem nada a ver

target_language_multi_word_term: isso não tem nada a ver
meaning: "That has nothing to do with (it/me/you/etc.)" / "That’s not related."
additional_notes: Used to say something is unrelated or irrelevant to a person or topic. Very common with "com" + someone/something: "Isso não tem nada a ver com ele" (…with him), "…com você" (…with you), "…com o que nós falamos" (…with what we talked about). It can also be used alone to dismiss a connection: "Isso não tem nada a ver."
target_language_example: Desculpa, mas isso não tem nada a ver com a pergunta.
native_language_example: Sorry, but that has nothing to do with the question.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is not true, not the case, or not a certain thing. Very common with adjectives ("isso não é importante/seguro") and with "o que" to correct someone or clarify meaning ("isso não é o que eu quis dizer" = “that’s not what I meant”). "Isso" often refers to something just mentioned or happening now.
target_language_example: Desculpa, mas isso não é verdade.
native_language_example: Sorry, but that isn’t true.

meaning: “that all the time” / “that all the time.”
additional_notes: Used to say someone does/says/uses that very frequently or repeatedly. Often appears after the verb: “Eu faço isso o tempo todo.” You can swap “isso” for another object: “Eu faço isso o tempo todo” (I do that all the time) vs. “Eu faço isso” (I do that).
target_language_example: Ele reclama disso o tempo todo.
native_language_example: He complains about that all the time.

meaning: 'it or not' / 'whether or not' (used to force a yes-or-no answer).
additional_notes: Used after a verb or request to emphasize the choice between doing/having something and not doing/having it. Common in questions like "Vai fazer isso ou não?" (Are you going to do it or not?) and in statements with "se" meaning "whether": "Não sei se ele vai fazer isso ou não" (I don’t know whether he’ll do it or not). "Isso" can refer to an action (“do it”) or a thing (“want it”).
target_language_example: Você vem comigo, isso ou não?
native_language_example: Are you coming with me or not?

meaning: 'that/it for me' (i.e., for my benefit; on my behalf; to/for me).
additional_notes: Commonly used when asking someone to do/get/take something for you: "Faça/pegue/levar isso para mim" = "Do/get/take that for me." It can also introduce a personal opinion: "Isso, para mim, ..." = "To me, ... / In my opinion, ..." In writing, commas are often used in the opinion sense ("Isso, para mim, parece estranho").
target_language_example: Você pode guardar isso para mim por um instante?
native_language_example: Can you hold onto that for me for a moment?

additional_notes: Used to give an impression or opinion based on what you see/know. Very common before an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., bom, improvável, muito caro, uma má ideia). You can also change the subject: “Isso” = that, “Ele/Ela” = he/she, “Isso aqui” = this.
target_language_example: Isso parece ser perigoso.
native_language_example: That seems to be dangerous.

additional_notes: Used to say something is possible, or to guess/speculate about what something is like (often followed by an adjective or noun: "isso pode ser difícil" = "that could be hard", "isso pode ser verdade" = "that might be true"). In questions ("Isso pode ser...?"), it expresses surprise or doubt: "Can that be...?".
target_language_example: Isso pode ser uma boa ideia.
native_language_example: That could be a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to say something is possible or feasible. Common in explanations/instructions: "como isso pode ser feito" = "how this can be done." You can also use it as a question: "Isso pode ser feito?" = "Can this be done?"
target_language_example: Não se preocupe — isso pode ser feito em poucos minutos.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — it can be done in a few minutes.

meaning: “that for me” / “it for me” (as in “do it for me”).
additional_notes: Used after a verb (often fazer/refazer) to ask or say someone is doing an action on your behalf: “Façam isso por mim” = “Do that for me.” In “Não estou dizendo isso por mim”, it means “I’m not saying this for myself” (i.e., not for my own benefit).
target_language_example: Você pode fazer isso por mim, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you do that for me, please?

additional_notes: Used to check whether your explanation was enough. Common in customer service, interviews, meetings, and polite conversation. It’s often followed by a person or group: "Isso responde à pergunta do senhor/da senhora/de vocês?" (sir/ma’am/you all). You can also say "Isso não responde à pergunta" (“That doesn’t answer the question”).
target_language_example: Desculpe se fui confuso — isso responde à sua pergunta?
native_language_example: Sorry if I was unclear—does that answer your question?

additional_notes: Used to talk about an imaginary or possible situation/result (often like English “that would be…”). It’s the conditional of the verb “ser” (to be): “seria” = “would be.” Common for giving opinions politely or imagining outcomes: “Isso seria bom/legal/rude.”
target_language_example: Isso seria ótimo, mas não tenho tempo hoje.
native_language_example: That would be great, but I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to explain the meaning or consequence of something just mentioned. Very common in clarifications: “Isso significa que…” = “That means that…”. You can also use it as a question: “O que isso significa?” = “What does that mean?”
target_language_example: Isso significa que temos que sair agora.
native_language_example: That means we have to leave now.

additional_notes: Used when the speaker emphasizes doing something without help or without anyone else involved. In practice, Portuguese often uses just "sozinho" (alone/by myself) after the verb; "isso sozinho" specifically highlights "that/it" (the task or situation) as being handled alone. For a woman, use "isso sozinha."
target_language_example: Não se preocupe — eu consigo resolver isso sozinho.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — I can handle that by myself.

meaning: 'that is' / 'this is' (referring to something just mentioned).
additional_notes: Used to identify or describe something: “Isso é + adjective/noun” (Isso é intolerável; Isso é algo…). “Isso” usually points to an idea/situation already in the conversation (often like English “that”), and it can also mean “this” depending on context. Common in reactions and evaluations.
target_language_example: Isso é uma boa ideia.
native_language_example: That’s a good idea.

meaning: 'That/this is very…' (used to intensify an adjective).
additional_notes: Used to comment on something and emphasize a quality: "isso" = "that/this", "é" = "is", "muito" = "very/a lot". Usually followed by an adjective (complicado, estranho, fácil, injusto), but you can also add a noun phrase like "Isso é muito trabalho" (That’s a lot of work).
target_language_example: Isso é muito caro para o meu orçamento.
native_language_example: That’s very expensive for my budget.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or emphasize the specific thing being referred to or identified. Often followed by a clause (e.g., "isso é o que eu acho") or used as a pointed question: "E isso é o quê, exatamente?". In speech and writing, you may also see variants like "isso é o que eu quero" and the more formal-sounding "isto é o que…".
target_language_example: Isso é o que eu quero dizer.
native_language_example: That’s what I mean.

additional_notes: Used to say there is nothing more beyond what follows. It’s commonly followed by a verb clause: “Isso é tudo o que eu sei” (That’s all I know), “Isso é tudo o que importa” (That’s all that matters). In English you often omit “that”: “That’s all I know.”
target_language_example: Isso é tudo o que precisamos por hoje.
native_language_example: That’s all we need for today.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe something. "Isso" means “that/this” (a neutral demonstrative often used for things/ideas), "é" = “is”, and "um" = “a/an” for masculine singular nouns. For feminine nouns, use "isso é uma" (e.g., "Isso é uma ideia").
target_language_example: Isso é um problema sério.
native_language_example: That’s a serious problem.

meaning: 'that is a...' / 'this is a...' (introducing a noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or describe something with a feminine noun: "Isso é uma + [noun]". With masculine nouns, use "isso é um". "Isso" often means "that" (something already mentioned), but it can also point to something near you like "this" depending on context.
target_language_example: Isso é uma boa ideia.
native_language_example: That’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to say what language a text/sign/document is in. Common pattern: “Isto está escrito em + [língua]” (e.g., português, inglês, espanhol). You can also use “Está escrito em...” when “isto” (this) is clear from context.
target_language_example: Desculpe, isto está escrito em português.
native_language_example: Sorry, this is written in Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used to say that something (isto = “this”) is not a certain thing or does not have a certain quality. Very common in simple statements and in corrections/contradictions: “Isto não é verdade!” You can also add intensifiers like “assim tão” to mean “not (all) that”: “Isto não é assim tão fácil.”
target_language_example: Desculpe, mas isto não é o que eu pedi.
native_language_example: Sorry, but this isn’t what I ordered.

additional_notes: Used to deny or correct what something is (or how it should be understood). Because it ends in “uma”, it must be followed by a feminine singular noun (uma brincadeira, uma derrota, uma mesa, uma opinião). For masculine nouns, use “isto não é um …”.
target_language_example: Isto não é uma piada, é sério.
native_language_example: This is not a joke, it’s serious.

isto é tudo o que posso fazer

target_language_multi_word_term: isto é tudo o que posso fazer
meaning: “This is all I can do.” / “That’s all I can do.”
additional_notes: Used to say you can’t do more than what you’re already doing. Often followed by who it’s for: “por ti” (for you, informal singular), “por você / pelo senhor / pela senhora” (for you, formal), “por vocês” (for you all). “Isto” can also be “isso” depending on what you’re referring to (this vs. that).
target_language_example: Desculpe, isto é tudo o que posso fazer agora.
native_language_example: Sorry, this is all I can do right now.

meaning: "this is a" (introducing a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify/describe something: "Isto" = "this" and "é" = "is". The article must match the noun’s gender/number: "isto é um" (masc. sing.), "isto é uma" (fem. sing.), "isto são uns/umas" (plural, less common in beginners’ speech). You’ll also see "isso é um" (“that is a”, often for something already mentioned).
target_language_example: Isto é um problema sério.
native_language_example: This is a serious problem.

additional_notes: Used to identify or point something out. "Isto" = "this" (neutral), "é" = "is", and "uma" is the feminine form of "a/an" (use before feminine nouns like "catedral", "gaivota", "lei", "nota"). With masculine nouns, use "isto é um".
target_language_example: Isto é uma escola.
native_language_example: This is a school.

additional_notes: From the verb "jogar" (to play, for games/sports) + "futebol" (soccer/football). In Brazil, "futebol" usually means soccer. You can use it with subjects like "eu jogo futebol", "você joga futebol?", "ele/ela joga futebol". Often followed by "com" to say who you play with ("joga futebol com amigos") and time expressions like "há quanto tempo" / "faz quanto tempo" (how long have you been playing).
target_language_example: Eu jogo futebol aos sábados com meus amigos.
native_language_example: I play soccer on Saturdays with my friends.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **jogar** (“to play”) + the sport **golfe** (“golf”). The form **joga** is present tense for **ele/ela/você** (“he/she/you”). Other common forms: **eu jogo golfe** (I play golf), **você joga golfe?** (Do you play golf?), **eles jogam golfe** (They play golf).
target_language_example: Meu chefe joga golfe depois do trabalho às sextas-feiras.
native_language_example: My boss plays golf after work on Fridays.

additional_notes: From the verb "jogar" (to play, for sports/games) + "tênis" (tennis). Often used in questions about ability, place, or time: "joga tênis bem?" (plays tennis well?), "onde joga tênis?" (where do you play tennis?), "quando é que joga tênis?" (when do you play tennis?). For other subjects: "eu jogo tênis", "você joga tênis", "nós jogamos tênis".
target_language_example: Eu jogo tênis aos sábados.
native_language_example: I play tennis on Saturdays.

additional_notes: From the verb "jogar" (to play) + "xadrez" (chess). Used to talk about someone playing chess. You can change the subject and verb form: "Eu jogo xadrez" (I play chess), "Você joga xadrez?" (Do you play chess?), "Nós jogamos xadrez" (We play chess).
target_language_example: Você joga xadrez nos fins de semana?
native_language_example: Do you play chess on weekends?

additional_notes: Used before the sport/game: jogador de basquete (basketball player), jogador de golfe (golfer). In Brazilian Portuguese you’ll also hear jogador de bola, a looser way to say “ball player” (often meaning a good soccer player).
target_language_example: Ela é jogadora de tênis.
native_language_example: She is a tennis player.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone who plays baseball (professionally or as an amateur). You can change the sport after "jogador de" (e.g., "jogador de futebol"). Feminine form: "jogadora de beisebol".
target_language_example: Meu irmão quer ser jogador de beisebol quando crescer.
native_language_example: My brother wants to be a baseball player when he grows up.

additional_notes: Common way to specify a person who plays the sport futebol (soccer). In Brazil, futebol usually means soccer, so this typically refers to a soccer player; when talking about American football, people usually say jogador de futebol americano.
target_language_example: Ele quer ser jogador de futebol quando crescer.
native_language_example: He wants to be a soccer player when he grows up.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone who plays tennis, especially as their sport or hobby. You’ll often see it with adjectives like bom/boa (good), melhor (best), or ávido (avid), and with the verb ser (to be): “Ele é um jogador de tênis.”
target_language_example: Ela é jogadora de tênis há cinco anos.
native_language_example: She has been a tennis player for five years.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who plays chess. Often appears with verbs like “ser” (to be) and “derrotar” (to defeat), and with comparisons like “melhor do que” (better than). You can also add adjectives: “um bom jogador de xadrez” (a good chess player).
target_language_example: Ela é uma jogadora de xadrez excelente.
native_language_example: She is an excellent chess player.

additional_notes: "Jogando" is the gerund of "jogar" (to play), used like English “playing.” "Jogando futebol" often describes what someone is doing right now (with "estar": "estão jogando futebol") or how/when something happened: "Feri meu joelho jogando futebol" (“I hurt my knee playing soccer”).
target_language_example: Eu me machuquei jogando futebol ontem.
native_language_example: I got hurt playing soccer yesterday.

additional_notes: "Jogando" is the gerund of "jogar" (to play), used to talk about an action in progress or as an explanation of how/when something happened. Common patterns: "estar jogando tênis" = "to be playing tennis (right now)"; "machucou... jogando tênis" = "got hurt while playing tennis"; "passou a tarde... jogando tênis" = "spent the whole afternoon playing tennis".
target_language_example: Estou jogando tênis agora.
native_language_example: I’m playing tennis right now.

additional_notes: "Jogar" is the verb used for playing games/sports; "jogando" is the gerund (-ing form) often used with "estar" to talk about what someone is doing right now ("estou/está/estamos... jogando xadrez"). It can also be used after another verb to mean "by playing" or "playing" as an activity (e.g., "nos divertimos jogando xadrez").
target_language_example: Estou jogando xadrez com um amigo agora.
native_language_example: I'm playing chess with a friend right now.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "jogar" (to play) + the sport name. You can conjugate "jogar" depending on the subject (eu jogo, ele joga, nós jogamos) and keep "beisebol" the same. Often used after verbs like "gostar de" (to like) and "ir" (to go) to say you like to play or you’re going to play.
target_language_example: A gente vai jogar beisebol no parque hoje.
native_language_example: We’re going to play baseball in the park today.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "jogar" (to play) + the sport "futebol". You can talk about plans with "vou/vai jogar futebol" (I’m going to / he’s going to play soccer) and likes with "gosto de jogar futebol" (I like playing soccer).
target_language_example: Aos sábados, a gente joga futebol no parque.
native_language_example: On Saturdays, we play soccer in the park.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "jogar" (to play) + the sport "golfe" (golf). You can conjugate "jogar" to talk about different times: "eu jogo golfe" (I play), "vou jogar golfe" (I’m going to play), "queria/gostaria de jogar golfe" (I’d like to play).
target_language_example: A gente pode jogar golfe depois do almoço?
native_language_example: Can we play golf after lunch?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "jogar" (to play) + the sport "tênis" (tennis). You can say "jogar tênis" for the activity in general, and add time expressions like "hoje", "esta tarde", or "nos fins de semana". Common patterns: "gostar de jogar tênis" (to like playing tennis), "aprender a jogar tênis" (to learn to play tennis), "saber jogar tênis" (to know how to play tennis).
target_language_example: A gente pode jogar tênis amanhã de manhã?
native_language_example: Can we play tennis tomorrow morning?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "jogar" (to play) + the game name "xadrez" (chess). Common in questions and with "saber" (to know how to): "Você sabe jogar xadrez?" = "Do you know how to play chess?" Also appears with "ensinar a" (to teach to): "ensinar a jogar xadrez" = "teach (someone) to play chess."
target_language_example: Eu aprendi a jogar xadrez na escola.
native_language_example: I learned to play chess at school.

meaning: "game of" / "(a) game" (followed by the type of game or sport).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to specify what kind of game you mean: jogo de tabuleiro (board game), jogo de damas (checkers), jogo de futebol (soccer match). In sports contexts, jogo de + [sport] often means a match (e.g., um jogo de ontem = yesterday’s match/game).
target_language_example: Vamos assistir a um jogo de futebol amanhã.
native_language_example: Let’s watch a soccer match tomorrow.

meaning: "I played tennis for the first time."
additional_notes: Uses the simple past (pretérito perfeito): "joguei" = "I played" (from "jogar"). "Pela primeira vez" means "for the first time" and can be used with many verbs: "fiz isso pela primeira vez" (I did this for the first time), "viajei pela primeira vez" (I traveled for the first time). Word order is flexible, especially with time words like "ontem" (yesterday).
target_language_example: Eu joguei tênis pela primeira vez nas férias.
native_language_example: I played tennis for the first time on vacation.

additional_notes: Used to say someone doesn’t have the age or maturity for an activity. Pattern: (ser/estar) jovem demais para + infinitive. You can change for gender/number: jovem demais / jovens demais.
target_language_example: Eles são jovens demais para assistir a esse filme.
native_language_example: They’re too young to watch that movie.

additional_notes: Polite/formal imperative of the reflexive verb juntar-se ("to join"), used as an invitation or request. It takes the preposition a before the person/group you’re joining: junte-se a mim (join me), junte-se a nós (join us). You’ll also see other polite imperative forms like junte-se ao grupo (join the group) and junte-se à reunião (join the meeting).
target_language_example: Junte-se a nós para o jantar.
native_language_example: Join us for dinner.

additional_notes: Used with **já** (“already”) + **comeu** (past of *comer*, “to eat”) to say someone has eaten before/earlier, or to ask if they’ve eaten yet. In questions like **Você já comeu?**, it often means “Have you eaten yet?” (whether the action has happened up to now).
target_language_example: Você já comeu hoje?
native_language_example: Have you eaten today yet?

meaning: "has already been" / "has been" (somewhere), referring to a past visit or presence.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "estar" in the simple past ("esteve") with "já" (already). Common for talking about having visited a place before or having already been somewhere at an earlier time: "Ela já esteve no Havaí" = she has been to Hawaii (before/already). In questions, it often means "Have you been there before?"
target_language_example: Você já esteve em Portugal?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Portugal?

meaning: 'have/has already been to/in' (often: 'have/has ever been to').
additional_notes: Uses the past of **estar** (**esteve**) with **já** to ask or state whether someone has had the experience of being in a place or situation. Very common in questions like **Você/O senhor já esteve em... ?** = 'Have you ever been to...?' Can be used with places (em Roma) and also experiences/situations (em algum relacionamento...). In English you often translate it with the present perfect ('have been') rather than a literal 'already was'.
target_language_example: Você já esteve em São Paulo?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to São Paulo?

additional_notes: Used to report that someone (often an unspecified group: “they”) has already told a man/boy to do (or not do) something. Structure: **Já falaram para o + [male name/noun] + infinitive**. For a woman/girl, use **já falaram para a**. In this context, **falar para** often means **to tell/instruct**, not just “to talk.”
target_language_example: Já falaram para o Pedro esperar aqui.
native_language_example: They've already told Pedro to wait here.

meaning: "has already done that/this" (referring to something someone has done before now).
additional_notes: Used to say that an action is already completed. "já" = already; "fez" is the past of "fazer" (to do/make); "isso" = that/this (a general “it/that thing”). Often appears in questions like "Será que ele já fez isso?" (“Has he done that yet/already?”).
target_language_example: Você já fez isso alguma vez?
native_language_example: Have you ever done that?

additional_notes: Uses "já" (already) + the past of "ir" (to go): "foi" (went). It often means someone already left or already went somewhere ("Ele já foi dormir"). With places, it can mean "has been to" ("Você já foi a Boston?"). In conversation, "Ok, já foi" can mean “Done,” “All set,” or “That’s taken care of.”
target_language_example: Calma, já foi — agora é só esperar o resultado.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s done — now we just have to wait for the result.

additional_notes: Uses "já" (already) + the past of "ir" (to go): "foi" (went). It often means someone already left or already went somewhere ("Ele já foi dormir"). With places, it can mean "has been to" ("Você já foi a Boston?"). In conversation, "Ok, já foi" can mean “Done,” “All set,” or “That’s taken care of.”
target_language_example: Calma, já foi — agora é só esperar o resultado.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s done — now we just have to wait for the result.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ler (“to read”) in the past: já indicates the action is already completed. In questions like “Já leu...?”, it often means “Have you read... yet?”. You may also see it with a subject (e.g., “você já leu”, “Tom já leu”).
target_language_example: Você já leu este livro?
native_language_example: Have you read this book yet?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has heard something before. It’s the verb ouvir (to hear) in the 3rd person singular of the present perfect in Portuguese (já + [verb]): “já ouviu…?” = “have you already heard…?”. Very common in questions like “Já ouviu esta música?” and in the fixed expression “Já ouviu falar de/sobre…?” = “Have you heard of/about…?”. Often implies the speaker thinks it’s possible (or likely) the person knows it.
target_language_example: Você já ouviu falar desse restaurante?
native_language_example: Have you heard of that restaurant?

meaning: "Have you ever thought about…?" / "Have you considered…?"
additional_notes: Used to introduce an idea or suggestion, often as a question. It can be about a general reflection ("Have you ever thought about how…") or about considering doing/becoming something ("Have you considered being a teacher?"). Commonly followed by a noun or by a verb in the infinitive ("em fazer", "em ser", "em virar").
target_language_example: Já pensou em morar fora do país?
native_language_example: Have you ever thought about living abroad?

additional_notes: Used to ask or state that someone has finished something earlier than expected or by now. Often appears as a question: "Já terminou?" = "Are you done already?/Have you finished yet?" You can add what was finished with "de" + infinitive ("já terminou de lavar") or with a direct object ("já terminou os deveres").
target_language_example: Você já terminou de estudar?
native_language_example: Have you finished studying yet?

additional_notes: Used to say something was already completed before another past event.
