- **Asking to be dropped off/left somewhere:** **Me deixa em/no + place** = “Drop me off at / leave me at …” (e.g., *Me deixa no hotel.*)
- **Cause/result:** **[Thing/person] me deixa + adjective / com + noun** = “(Something) makes me … / leaves me …” (e.g., *Ler me deixa com sono.*)
Often said as **Deixa eu…** in casual speech, but **Me deixa…** is also natural.
target_language_example: Me deixa falar com ele um minuto, por favor.
native_language_example: Let me talk to him for a minute, please.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **deixar** + **me** (“me”). It often means **to allow** someone to do something: *me deixar ajudar/falar/experimentar* (“let me help/speak/try”). With certain phrases it means **to leave (someone) in a state/situation**, e.g. *me deixar irritado* (“make/leave me annoyed”) and *me deixar em paz* (“leave me alone”). Word order can be **me deixar** or **deixar-me** (more formal/European Portuguese).
target_language_example: Você pode me deixar entrar?
native_language_example: Can you let me come in?

additional_notes: A direct request to stop bothering you or to go away. Uses the imperative of "deixar" (to leave): "deixe" (you, formal) + "me" (me). Often used with "por favor" to soften it; without it, it can sound firm or irritated.
target_language_example: Estou ocupado agora — me deixe em paz, por favor.
native_language_example: I'm busy right now—please leave me alone.

additional_notes: "Me" = "me" (object pronoun). "Deixou" is the past of "deixar" and commonly means: (1) "made me" + adjective/feeling: "Isso me deixou brava" = "That made me angry"; (2) "let/allowed me" + infinitive: "me deixou fazer" = "let me do"; (3) "didn't let me" is very common: "não me deixou" = "didn't allow me". The subject is who caused it or who allowed/forbade it.
target_language_example: A notícia me deixou muito triste.
native_language_example: The news made me very sad.

additional_notes: From the verb "dar" (to give) in the simple past (pretérito perfeito): "deu" = "gave" for he/she/it/you (formal). "me" is the indirect object pronoun (to me). Very common with gifts, help, opportunities, information, etc. Word order is usually "[subject] me deu [something]"; you can also say "deu-me" (more formal/written).
target_language_example: Ela me deu um conselho muito bom.
native_language_example: She gave me some very good advice.

meaning: 'gave me a' / 'gave me one' (simple past of 'dar').
additional_notes: Used with the verb "dar" (to give) in the simple past: "(ele/ela) me deu" = "(he/she) gave me". "um" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”) or can mean “one,” and it’s followed by what was given: "me deu um álbum". With some nouns, "dar" can also mean “to deal/land” (e.g., "me deu um soco" = "punched me"). Word order can vary: "A minha tia me deu um álbum" and "Minha tia me deu um álbum".
target_language_example: Ele me deu um presente de aniversário.
native_language_example: He gave me a birthday present.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **dar** (“to give”) in the **simple past** (**deu** = “gave”). **Me** is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to me,” and **uma** is the feminine form of “a/an” (use **um** for masculine nouns: *me deu um livro*). You can add the giver before the verb: *Minha mãe me deu uma…*
target_language_example: Ele me deu uma garrafa de água.
native_language_example: He gave me a bottle of water.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **dever** to say someone owes you **money** (*Ela me deve dinheiro*), **a favor** (*Tom me deve um favor*), or more generally “owes you one” (*Ele me deve uma* — informal, meaning they should do you a favor later). In questions, it often appears as **Quanto o senhor me deve?** (“How much do you owe me?”).
target_language_example: Você me deve um favor.
native_language_example: You owe me a favor.

additional_notes: Uses the indirect object pronoun “me” (“to me”) + the imperative/subjunctive form “diga” of “dizer” (“to say/tell”). Very common in requests for information, often with details like “me diga onde…” (“tell me where…”). It can sound firm depending on context; “me fala” is more informal.
target_language_example: Por favor, me diga seu nome completo.
native_language_example: Please tell me your full name.

additional_notes: "Me" is an object pronoun meaning “to me.” "Disse" is the past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "dizer" (“to say/tell”). It’s used when someone told you something at a specific time. The subject is often understood from context (ele/ela/você), and you can also hear "disse-me" (more formal/literary).
target_language_example: Ela me disse que vai chegar mais tarde.
native_language_example: She told me she’s going to arrive later.

additional_notes: Used when reporting what someone instructed you to do. Pattern: "[Someone] me disse para + infinitive" (e.g., "me disse para vir" = "told me to come"). In everyday speech you may also hear "me falou para" with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Ela me disse para esperar aqui.
native_language_example: She told me to wait here.

meaning: “told me not to …” (told me to not do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to say someone advised/ordered you not to do an action: “me disse para não + verb”. You can swap the subject: “Ele/Ela me disse para não…” (“He/She told me not to…”).
target_language_example: Ela me disse para não contar a ninguém.
native_language_example: She told me not to tell anyone.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said to you. Structure: (person) me disse que + clause. You can change the pronoun: te disse que (told you), lhe disse que (told him/her/you formal), nos disse que (told us). Often followed by a verb in the past, present, or conditional, depending on what was said.
target_language_example: Ele me disse que não podia vir hoje.
native_language_example: He told me that he couldn't come today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said and their opinion/belief at the time. "me disse" = "told me" (to me). "achava" is the imperfect of "achar" and often means "thought/believed" (a past opinion, not necessarily true). Usually followed by a full clause with "que".
target_language_example: Ela me disse que achava que o filme ia ser chato.
native_language_example: She told me that she thought the movie was going to be boring.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said: **me disse** = “told me” and **que ela** introduces what “she” said/did/wanted/felt. Often followed by a verb in the past (*queria, tinha, gostou, sentiu, foi*) or present (*quer*). You can swap **ela** for another subject: *me disse que ele…* (“told me that he…”), *me disse que vocês…* (“told me that you all…”).
target_language_example: Ela me disse que ela não podia ir hoje.
native_language_example: She told me that she couldn’t go today.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man said (indirect speech). The pattern is: (someone) + me disse que + ele + verb/statement. In Portuguese, “que” = “that” introducing the reported clause, and “ele” = “he” referring to the man being talked about.
target_language_example: Ela me disse que ele vai chegar tarde.
native_language_example: She told me that he’s going to arrive late.

additional_notes: Used for reported speech: someone (ele = he) told you something about his past state or condition. Structure: [Name] me disse (that person told me) + que (that) + ele estava (he was) + adjective or expression (desapontado, satisfeito, solitário; or com fome, com pressa, etc.). In Portuguese, after verbs like dizer (to say/tell), you typically use que to introduce what was said.
target_language_example: A Ana me disse que ele estava doente ontem.
native_language_example: Ana told me that he was sick yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone told you about their identity, condition, or a description in the past. Portuguese often drops the subject pronoun here: "era" implies "ele/ela era" (= he/she was). "Me" means "to me" (indirect object), and "disse" is the past of "dizer" (to say/tell).
target_language_example: O João me disse que era professor.
native_language_example: João told me that he was a teacher.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone told you (indirect speech). In this pattern, **disse** is the simple past of *dizer* (“said/told”), and **estava** is the imperfect of *estar*, often used for an ongoing state/feeling at that time. The subject after *que* is often omitted when it’s clear (e.g., “Tom me disse que estava…” = “Tom told me he was…”).
target_language_example: Ela me disse que estava cansada.
native_language_example: She told me she was tired.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech: "me disse" = "told me" and "que queria" introduces what the person said they wanted to do. "Queria" is the imperfect of "querer" (to want), often used to report someone’s intention in the past or in a more indirect/softer way. It’s commonly followed by an infinitive: "que queria estudar / conhecer / mudar / parar / vencer".
target_language_example: Ela me disse que queria ir embora mais cedo.
native_language_example: She told me that she wanted to leave earlier.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said to you (indirect/reported speech). It’s built from: me (to me) + disse (said/told; past of dizer) + que (that) + você (you). Often appears after a subject (e.g., “O Tom me disse que você…”) and is followed by whatever was said (e.g., “estava doente”, “gosta de…”, “ia viajar…”). In everyday Portuguese, “disse” commonly translates as “told” when there’s an indirect object (“me/te/lhe”).
target_language_example: A Ana me disse que você já chegou.
native_language_example: Ana told me that you already arrived.

additional_notes: Past tense of "me dizer" (to tell me). You use it to report information someone told you. It’s often followed by a verb in the past (e.g., "eram", "tinham"). You can change the subject: "ele/ela me disse que" (he/she told me that) or "me disseram que" (they told me that).
target_language_example: Me disseram que a reunião foi cancelada.
native_language_example: They told me that the meeting was canceled.

additional_notes: Used to report what other people told you in the past. It’s common in indirect speech: “me disseram que …” (“they told me that …”) + “estavam” (imperfect past of “estar”, meaning “were/used to be” in a temporary state or ongoing situation). The verb after “estavam” often comes as an adjective (felizes, seguros) or as a gerund for an ongoing action (estavam ensinando, estavam se divertindo).
target_language_example: Me disseram que estavam prontos para sair.
native_language_example: They told me that they were ready to leave.

meaning: to tell me; to say to me.
additional_notes: "Me" is an object pronoun meaning “to me/me,” placed before the verb in these examples. It’s common in Brazilian Portuguese to use "me dizer" for “tell me,” especially in questions and requests. In more formal or European Portuguese, you may also see the pronoun after the verb ("dizer-me"). Often followed by "o que" (“what”) or an indirect question: "me dizer o que..." (“tell me what...”).
target_language_example: Você pode me dizer onde fica o banheiro?
native_language_example: Can you tell me where the bathroom is?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to give you information about a place or where something/someone is, often followed by an infinitive (e.g., "onde encontrar..." = where to find...) or by a full clause ("onde ele mora" = where he lives). With "poder" it becomes more polite: "Você poderia me dizer onde...?" In everyday speech you may also hear "me dizer aonde" when it implies movement/destination (where to go/put something).
target_language_example: Você pode me dizer onde fica a estação de metrô?
native_language_example: Can you tell me where the subway station is?

additional_notes: Used after verbs like **poder**, **saber**, **vir** to ask for an explanation: *Você pode/sabe me dizer por que…?* In everyday speech, **me dizer** is often said as **me dizer** or **dizer-me** (more formal). **Por que** (two words) is used in questions and indirect questions meaning “why”.
target_language_example: Você pode me dizer por que está tão nervoso?
native_language_example: Can you tell me why you’re so nervous?

meaning: to tell me who (…); to let me know who (…).
additional_notes: Used to ask for the identity of a person or people. It’s usually part of a longer question like “Você pode me dizer quem…?” (“Can you tell me who…?”). Word order is flexible: “me dizer quem” and “dizer-me quem” both mean the same. Common polite starters: “Você pode…?”, “Você se importaria de…?”, “Por gentileza…?”.
target_language_example: Você pode me dizer quem está responsável por isso?
native_language_example: Can you tell me who is responsible for this?

additional_notes: Literally “(you) give me,” from **dar** (to give) + **me** (to me). Very common in requests and commands: **Me dá isso.** (“Give me that.”) You can soften it by adding **por favor** or using **você pode me dar…?** (“can you give me…?”). It’s also used in fixed expressions like **Me dá licença?** (“Excuse me?” / “May I…?”) and with feelings/physical reactions: **Me dá água na boca** (“It makes my mouth water,” literally “it gives me water in my mouth”).
target_language_example: Me dá um copo de água, por favor.
native_language_example: Can you give me a glass of water, please?

meaning: "it gives me chills" / "it gives me the creeps."
additional_notes: Used to say something makes you feel a shiver—often from fear, disgust, or being creeped out (sometimes from strong emotion). It literally means “(it) gives me shivers,” from "dar" (to give) + "arrepios" (shivers/goosebumps). You can swap the object pronoun: "te dá arrepios" (gives you chills), "me deu arrepios" (gave me chills).
target_language_example: Esse filme de terror me dá arrepios.
native_language_example: That horror movie gives me chills.

additional_notes: Used to ask or tell someone to give something to you. It’s the imperative of "dar" (to give) for "você" (not "tu"). Very common in requests: "Me dê + noun" (Me dê um copo de água.). In more informal speech you may also hear "me dá".
target_language_example: Por favor, me dê seu nome e seu telefone.
native_language_example: Please, give me your name and your phone number.

additional_notes: Used when the subject lends something to you (“me” = to me). It’s the verb *emprestar* (to lend) with the object pronoun *me*. Common in polite requests: “Você pode/poderia me emprestar…?”
target_language_example: Você pode me emprestar uma caneta, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you lend me a pen, please?

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive verb "encontrar-se" + "com" + a person/group. It often means arranging to meet (an appointment) or going to meet someone (e.g., at the airport). The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject: eu vou me encontrar com…, você vai se encontrar com…, ele/ela vai se encontrar com…, nós vamos nos encontrar com…, vocês vão se encontrar com…, eles/elas vão se encontrar com…. In casual speech, people also say "encontrar com" without the reflexive ("Vou encontrar com ele"), but "me encontrar com" is common and correct.
target_language_example: Vou me encontrar com a Ana depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I’m going to meet up with Ana after work.

additional_notes: From the verb **encontrar-se com** (“to meet with/to run into”), used with **com** + a person. **Me** indicates the subject is “I” (reflexive form). In Brazil you’ll often hear **Eu me encontrei com...**; in Portugal, **Encontrei-me com...** is also common. It can mean a planned meeting (“meet up with”) or an unexpected one (“run into”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Hoje me encontrei com a Ana para tomar um café.
native_language_example: Today I met up with Ana to have a coffee.

meaning: "teach me" (show me how to do something).
additional_notes: "Me" means "to me" (object pronoun), and "ensinar" means "to teach". Common patterns: "Pode me ensinar?" (Can you teach me?), "me ensinar a + verb" (teach me to + verb), and "me ensinar como + verb" (teach me how to + verb). In Brazil you may also hear "ensinar-me" (more formal) or "me ensina?" (informal).
target_language_example: Você pode me ensinar a cozinhar arroz?
native_language_example: Can you teach me to cook rice?

additional_notes: “Me” is the object pronoun “me,” and “ensinou” is the past (preterite) form of “ensinar” (“to teach/show”). It’s used for a completed action in the past: someone taught you something, showed you how to do something, or instructed you. Common patterns: “me ensinou a + infinitive” (taught me to + verb) and “me ensinou + noun” (taught me + a subject/thing).
target_language_example: Meu avô me ensinou a cozinhar.
native_language_example: My grandfather taught me to cook.

meaning: 'taught me to' (said about someone teaching you how to do something).
additional_notes: Used when the subject is the person who taught you a skill or behavior. Structure: (Alguém) me ensinou a + infinitive verb. In the examples, the action comes after "a" (xingar, esquiar, surfar, tocar). You can change "me" to other object pronouns: te ensinou a (taught you), nos ensinou a (taught us).
target_language_example: Minha mãe me ensinou a cozinhar.
native_language_example: My mom taught me to cook.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to help you or do something for you. Commonly appears in questions like “Você pode/poderia me fazer um favor?” and can be followed by “de” + infinitive to specify the action: “me fazer um favor de preencher…” (do me the favor of filling out…). In Brazilian Portuguese, “me” is an object pronoun meaning “to/for me.”
target_language_example: Você pode me fazer um favor e fechar a janela, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you do me a favor and close the window, please?

additional_notes: "Me" is the object pronoun “me,” placed before the verb. "Fez" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "fazer" (to make/do). Common uses: (1) make/appoint someone: "Ele me fez seu sucessor" = “He made me his successor.” (2) do/make something for someone: "Minha mãe me fez um bolo" = “My mom made me a cake.” (3) ask/pose something to someone: "Ninguém nunca me fez essa pergunta" = “No one has ever asked me that question.” (4) cause a reaction: "Seu gesto me fez chorar" = “His/Her gesture made me cry.”
target_language_example: Isso me fez pensar.
native_language_example: That made me think.

additional_notes: From the verb "lembrar-se" (to remember), used with a reflexive pronoun: "(eu) me lembro". In speech and writing, the subject "eu" is often omitted. It’s commonly followed by "de" + a thing/person: "me lembro de você", "me lembro disso", "me lembro desse rapaz". You may also hear the non-reflexive variant "lembro" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Não me lembro do nome dele.
native_language_example: I don’t remember his name.

additional_notes: From the verb "lembrar-se (de)", which usually takes "de" before a noun, name, or a verb in the infinitive: "me lembro de + coisa" (I remember + something) or "me lembro de + verbo" (I remember doing/to do). In the negative, it’s very common as "não me lembro de..." (I don’t remember...). You can swap the pronoun for other people: "eu me lembro", "você se lembra", "ele/ela se lembra", "nós nos lembramos", etc.
target_language_example: Não me lembro de onde deixei as chaves.
native_language_example: I don’t remember where I left the keys.

additional_notes: Past (pretérito perfeito) of “(eu) me levanto” from the verb “levantar-se” (to get up / stand up). In these examples it often means getting out of bed (“I got up”). It can also mean standing up from a chair. The “me” is a reflexive pronoun and can come before or after the verb: “me levantei” or “levantei-me” (more formal).
target_language_example: Me levantei cedo para pegar o ônibus.
native_language_example: I got up early to catch the bus.

additional_notes: Imperative form of the verb "ligar" (to call/phone) with the object pronoun "me" (me). Used to ask someone to call you, often with a time or condition: "me liga quando/assim que...". You can also add where to call: "me liga no escritório" (call me at the office). In everyday speech, people also say "me liga" instead of the more formal "liga pra mim".
target_language_example: Quando você chegar em casa, me liga.
native_language_example: When you get home, call me.

additional_notes: From the verb "ligar" meaning "to call" (by phone). "Me" is the object pronoun "me," so it refers to the person who received the call. Often used with time expressions like "ontem à noite" (last night), "no dia seguinte" (the next day), or "no meio da noite" (in the middle of the night).
target_language_example: Ele me ligou mais tarde para confirmar o horário.
native_language_example: He called me later to confirm the time.

meaning: to kill me; (also) to be furious with me (“they’re going to kill me”).
additional_notes: Literally "matar" (to kill) + "me" (me). It can be used in a real, literal sense (someone tried to kill me) or as an exaggeration meaning someone will be very angry or punish you (e.g., "Minha mãe vai me matar" = "My mom is going to kill me" → meaning she’ll be really mad). Word order can vary: "vai me matar" / "vai matar-me" (more formal/written).
target_language_example: Se eu chegar tarde em casa, meu pai vai me matar.
native_language_example: If I get home late, my dad is going to kill me.

additional_notes: "Me" is the object pronoun “to me,” and "mostrar" means “to show.” You’ll often see it after another verb (e.g., "podia" / "queria") or after a preposition, meaning someone shows something to you, or shows you how to do something: "me mostrar alguns trabalhos" (show me some work), "me mostrar como fazer" (show me how to do).
target_language_example: Você pode me mostrar onde fica o banheiro?
native_language_example: Can you show me where the bathroom is?

meaning: "to show me the way" / "to give me directions".
additional_notes: Used when asking for or thanking someone for directions. The verb is usually conjugated (e.g., “pode me mostrar…” or more formal “pode-me mostrar…”). “Obrigado/a” changes with the speaker’s gender (male: obrigado; female: obrigada).
target_language_example: Você pode me mostrar o caminho até a estação, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you show me the way to the station, please?

me mostrar o caminho para o

target_language_multi_word_term: me mostrar o caminho para o
additional_notes: Polite phrase for asking for directions. "me" = "to me"; "mostrar" = "to show"; "o caminho" = "the way/path"; "para" = "to". It’s usually followed by a destination noun (often with an article: "o"/"a", e.g., "para o museu", "para a estação"). Common polite variants include: "Você pode..." (can you), "Você poderia..." (could you, more polite), and "Vocês poderiam..." (plural: you all could you).
target_language_example: Com licença, você poderia me mostrar o caminho para a estação?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you show me the way to the station?

meaning: “showed me” / “has shown me” (he/she/it showed something to me).
additional_notes: "Me" is the object pronoun “me,” placed before the verb. "Mostrou" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "mostrar" for ele/ela/você: "(he/she/you) showed." It’s used when someone showed you something specific (a photo, a letter, a place). In conversation, "me mostrou" can also translate as “has shown me,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ele me mostrou onde fica a estação de metrô.
native_language_example: He showed me where the subway station is.

additional_notes: "Me" is the object pronoun "me" (the person receiving the action), and "odeia" is "(he/she/you formal) hates" from the verb "odiar". Used with a subject: "Ela me odeia" (She hates me). In Brazil, you may also hear "me odeia" after the verb (more formal): "Ela odeia-me" (less common in everyday speech).
target_language_example: Acho que ele me odeia, mas nunca me disse nada.
native_language_example: I think he hates me, but he never told me anything.

additional_notes: Used at the table to ask someone to hand you the salt. Very common with politeness words like “por favor” and “você pode/poderia…?”. The structure is: passar + object (o sal) + indirect object pronoun (me = to me). You can also hear “passa o sal pra mim” in more casual speech.
target_language_example: Você pode me passar o sal, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the salt, please?

additional_notes: "Me" is an object pronoun meaning “me,” and "pediu" is the past (simple past) of "pedir" (“to ask for / to request”). It’s used when someone asked you to do something ("me pediu para..." = “asked me to...”) or asked you for something ("me pediu permissão" = “asked me for permission”).
target_language_example: Ele me pediu para fechar a janela.
native_language_example: He asked me to close the window.

additional_notes: Used when someone asks you to do something: **[alguém] me pediu para + infinitive** (me pediu para fazer, me pediu para ir). Pronouns change with the person: *me pediu para* (asked **me**), *te pediu para* (asked **you**), *lhe pediu para* (asked **him/her/you** formal), *nos pediu para* (asked **us**).
target_language_example: Ela me pediu para esperar aqui um minuto.
native_language_example: She asked me to wait here for a minute.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "pedir" (to ask/request) + an indirect object pronoun ("me" = to me) + "que" + a verb in the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., "trouxesse", "ajudasse", "tirasse", "deixasse"). It introduces what someone asked you to do. Often equivalent to English "asked me to + verb."
target_language_example: Ele me pediu que eu esperasse um minuto.
native_language_example: He asked me to wait a minute.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a question you’re thinking about (often followed by words like qual/quem/o que/quando/como or by se = “whether/if”). It’s the present tense of perguntar with the reflexive pronoun me, literally “I ask myself.”
target_language_example: Me pergunto se ele vai ligar hoje.
native_language_example: I wonder if he’s going to call today.

meaning: "I wonder how" (I’m curious about how something happened/works/is done).
additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or uncertainty about the way something happens or is done. It’s formed from "me pergunto" (I ask myself) + "como" (how). Often followed by a clause: "Me pergunto como isso funciona." You can also use other persons: "Eu me pergunto como..." / "Ela se pergunta como...".
target_language_example: Me pergunto como você aprendeu português tão rápido.
native_language_example: I wonder how you learned Portuguese so fast.

additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or uncertainty about something, often before an indirect question. It’s the reflexive verb "perguntar-se" (to wonder/ask oneself) + "o que" (what). You can change the subject: "Me pergunto..." (I wonder), "Ele/Ela se pergunta..." (he/she wonders), "Nos perguntamos..." (we wonder).
target_language_example: Me pergunto o que vai acontecer amanhã.
native_language_example: I wonder what will happen tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or uncertainty about a reason in an indirect question. Here, “por que” (two words) is used before a clause (e.g., “por que ele fez isso”) and means “why.” Often followed by a full sentence explaining what you’re wondering about.
target_language_example: Me pergunto por que ela não respondeu à minha mensagem.
native_language_example: I wonder why she didn’t reply to my message.

additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or uncertainty about the reason for something. It’s the reflexive verb "perguntar-se" (to wonder/ask oneself) + "por que" (why). In real speech, you’ll usually see it followed by a person’s name ("por que o Tom...") or a noun ("por que o carro..."). If the next word is a feminine noun/name, use "a" instead: "Me pergunto por que a Maria...".
target_language_example: Me pergunto por que o ônibus está atrasado hoje.
native_language_example: I wonder why the bus is late today.

additional_notes: Used to express doubt/curiosity about whether something is true or will happen. It’s often followed by a full clause in the present or past (e.g., “Me pergunto se ele sabe…”). The verb is “perguntar-se” (to wonder), so you may also hear other persons: “Eu me pergunto se…”, “A gente se pergunta se…”.
target_language_example: Me pergunto se vai chover amanhã.
native_language_example: I wonder if it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or uncertainty: me pergunto (I wonder) + se (if/whether) + o (the, masculine singular). It’s commonly followed by a noun (o Tom, o professor, o carro) or another masculine singular subject. For feminine singular, you’ll often see “me pergunto se a …”.
target_language_example: Me pergunto se o ônibus já passou.
native_language_example: I wonder if the bus has already gone by.

additional_notes: "Me" is an object pronoun meaning "to me"/"me." "Perguntou" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "perguntar" (to ask). Often followed by a question word (onde, qual, o que) or a noun phrase with "sobre" (perguntar sobre algo = ask about something).
target_language_example: Ela me perguntou se eu tinha tempo amanhã.
native_language_example: She asked me if I had time tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report a yes/no question someone asked you. It’s the combination of: "me" (to me) + "perguntou" (asked, past) + "se" (if/whether) + "eu" (I). Very common in storytelling and reported speech; the verb is usually in the past (perguntou), but can change with tense (e.g., "me pergunta se eu…").
target_language_example: Ela me perguntou se eu queria ir ao cinema.
native_language_example: She asked me if I wanted to go to the movies.

additional_notes: Used to report a yes/no question someone asked you. Structure: [person] me perguntou se eu estava + adjective (bem, com fome, ocupada) or + verb in the gerund (estudando, gostando) to describe what you were doing/feeling at that moment. Often translated as “asked me if I was…” or “asked me whether I was…”.
target_language_example: Ela me perguntou se eu estava pronto para sair.
native_language_example: She asked me if I was ready to leave.

additional_notes: Used to report a question someone asked you. It’s in the past: "perguntar" (to ask) → "perguntou" (asked), and "querer" (to want) → "queria" (wanted/was willing to). It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., "dirigir", "ir", "tomar").
target_language_example: Ela me perguntou se eu queria ajudar.
native_language_example: She asked me if I wanted to help.

meaning: 'asked me if I had' / 'asked me whether I had'.
additional_notes: Used in reported speech to say that someone asked a yes/no question. "me perguntou" = "asked me"; "se" = "if/whether"; "eu tinha" is the imperfect of "ter" (to have), commonly used after "perguntar" to report what was asked (often about having/possessing something or having something with you).
target_language_example: Ela me perguntou se eu tinha tempo para conversar.
native_language_example: She asked me if I had time to talk.

meaning: “I felt …” (past tense of “to feel,” about your physical or emotional state).
additional_notes: From the verb **sentir-se** (“to feel,” reflexive). It’s the **preterite** (completed past) form: **(eu) me senti**. Very commonly followed by an adjective: **me senti mal/cansado/relaxado/sozinho/amado**. You can add time words like **ontem** (yesterday) or **depois** (after).
target_language_example: Depois da reunião, me senti confiante.
native_language_example: After the meeting, I felt confident.

additional_notes: Used with the verb sentir-se (“to feel”) in continuous tenses to talk about your physical or emotional state. It usually appears with estar (e.g., estou/estava me sentindo…) and is followed by an adjective or phrase: me sentindo bem (well), mal (sick/bad), confuso (confused), solitário (lonely). In European Portuguese you often see a more direct form: sinto-me / estou a sentir-me.
target_language_example: Hoje estou me sentindo cansado, então vou dormir cedo.
native_language_example: Today I’m feeling tired, so I’m going to sleep early.

meaning: “I feel” / “I’m feeling” (about your physical or emotional state).
additional_notes: From the verb sentir-se (“to feel”), used with reflexive pronouns. You’ll often see it with an adjective: me sinto cansado(a) (I feel tired), me sinto melhor (I feel better), me sinto pra baixo (I feel down), me sinto seguro(a) (I feel safe). In Portuguese, the adjective usually agrees with the speaker’s gender: cansado (male), cansada (female).
target_language_example: Hoje me sinto bem melhor.
native_language_example: Today I feel much better.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your physical or emotional state. It’s the reflexive verb "sentir-se" (to feel), conjugated for "eu" (I): "(eu) me sinto". Word order can vary in everyday speech: "Eu me sinto bem" / "Me sinto bem" / "Hoje me sinto bem".
target_language_example: Depois de descansar um pouco, me sinto bem.
native_language_example: After resting a bit, I feel good.

meaning: 'I feel more…' (increasingly, to a greater degree).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verb "sentir-se" to describe your emotional/physical state increasing in degree. It’s typically followed by an adjective or phrase: "me sinto mais à vontade" (more at ease), "me sinto mais seguro" (safer), "me sinto mais fresco" (cooler), or comparisons like "me sinto mais X do que Y" (I feel more X than Y). You can also say "eu me sinto mais…" (with "eu" for emphasis).
target_language_example: Depois de conversar com você, me sinto mais confiante.
native_language_example: After talking with you, I feel more confident.

additional_notes: Used with sentir-se + mal. Depending on context, it can mean feeling physically sick (“Me sinto mal hoje”) or feeling emotionally bad/guilty/sorry about something (“Me sinto mal por ter mentido”; “Me sinto mal a respeito disso”). With por/pelo(a), it often means “I feel bad about…” or “I feel sorry for…” someone.
target_language_example: Desculpa, me sinto mal por ter esquecido o seu aniversário.
native_language_example: Sorry, I feel bad for forgetting your birthday.

meaning: “I feel bad / guilty about” (something) or “I feel sorry for” (someone).
additional_notes: Used with **por + person** to express pity/compassion ("I feel sorry for them"), and with **por + infinitive** to express regret or guilt about an action ("I feel bad for forgetting..."). Often appears without the subject **eu** in conversation: **(Eu) me sinto mal por...**. You can swap **me** for other pronouns: **ele se sente mal por...**, **a gente se sente mal por...**.
target_language_example: Eu me sinto mal por ter dito aquilo.
native_language_example: I feel bad for having said that.

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive verb **sentir-se** (“to feel”), so **me** = “myself” (I feel). **muito melhor** intensifies **melhor** (“better”) to mean “much better.” Often used with time words like **hoje** (today), **já** (already), **agora** (now), or after a change like quitting smoking.
target_language_example: Depois de descansar um pouco, me sinto muito melhor.
native_language_example: After resting a bit, I feel much better.

additional_notes: Used when the subject changes into a new state/role: *I become X*. It’s the verb **tornar-se** (“to become”) with the reflexive pronoun **me** (= myself). In Brazil you’ll also see **tornar-me** (more formal) and, in speech, often just **virar** with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Um dia quero me tornar médico.
native_language_example: One day I want to become a doctor.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive after verbs like querer/esperar/planejar/sonhar to talk about a future change in identity or profession: “(eu) me tornar um/uma + noun”. Agree the article with the noun’s gender: um dentista, uma professora. In casual speech, people also say “virar” or “me transformar em”.
target_language_example: Um dia, quero me tornar um engenheiro.
native_language_example: One day, I want to become an engineer.

additional_notes: Used to say how someone behaves toward you. Structure: (someone) me trata como + noun (criança, escravo, irmão, princesa). You can change the object pronoun: te trata como (treats you), o/a trata como (treats him/her), nos trata como (treats us).
target_language_example: Ela me trata como um amigo, não como um cliente.
native_language_example: She treats me like a friend, not like a customer.

meaning: to see me; to come see me / visit me.
additional_notes: "Me" is the object pronoun ("me"), and "ver" means "to see". In invitations it often appears with "vir" ("vir me ver") meaning "come see me / come visit me". It can also be used for requesting a meeting: "Você quer me ver?" = "Do you want to see me?"
target_language_example: Você pode vir me ver no fim de semana?
native_language_example: Can you come see me this weekend?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ter" (to have): "ter medo da morte" = "to be afraid of death". You can also use "não ter medo da morte" to say you’re not afraid of death, or "não ter mais medo" for “not afraid anymore.”
target_language_example: Ela sempre teve medo da morte, mas agora está mais calma.
native_language_example: She always feared death, but now she’s calmer.

additional_notes: Used after ter/estar/com (and sometimes other verbs) to say what someone is afraid of: medo de + noun (medo de avião) or medo de + infinitive (medo de andar, medo de me perder). You can intensify it with "morrendo de medo" = "terrified".
target_language_example: Tenho medo de falar em público.
native_language_example: I'm afraid of speaking in public.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is afraid of snakes. You can swap in another thing after "medo de" (e.g., "medo de altura" = fear of heights). Common with "ter" (to have): "ter medo de cobras".
target_language_example: Ela tem medo de cobras, então não vai ao zoológico.
native_language_example: She’s afraid of snakes, so she doesn’t go to the zoo.

additional_notes: Used with expressions like **ter medo de...** (to be afraid of...), **estar com medo de...** (to be afraid/scared of...), and **sentir medo de...** (to feel afraid of...). **De mim** means “of me”; you can also say **medo de mim mesmo(a)** for “fear of myself” (mesmo = male speaker, mesma = female speaker).
target_language_example: Você não precisa ter medo de mim.
native_language_example: You don’t need to be afraid of me.

meaning: fear of dying; afraid to die.
additional_notes: Used after "ter medo de" or "estar com medo de" + infinitive to say you’re afraid of something happening (here, dying). "Estar com medo" often emphasizes a current/temporary feeling; "ter medo" can be more general.
target_language_example: Ela tem medo de morrer sozinha.
native_language_example: She is afraid of dying alone.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being scared when it’s dark. Often appears with verbs like "ter" (to have): "Tenho medo do escuro"; "estar com" (to be afraid right now): "Estou com medo do escuro"; and intensifiers like "muito" (very) or "morrer de" (to be extremely afraid).
target_language_example: Quando falta luz, eu fico com medo do escuro.
native_language_example: When the power goes out, I get scared of the dark.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the middle of the day. Very common in time expressions like "antes do meio-dia" (before noon) and "ao meio-dia" (at noon). With "do" it usually means "before noon" or "by noon" depending on context.
target_language_example: Vamos almoçar ao meio-dia.
native_language_example: Let’s have lunch at noon.

meaning: “the middle of the” / “through, by means of” (with por).
additional_notes: With location expressions, (no) meio da = “in the middle of the”: No meio da Europa (“in the middle of Europe”), pelo meio da multidão (“through the middle of the crowd”). With por meio da, it means “through/by means of” and is common in more formal writing or speech: por meio da experiência (“through experience”), por meio da força (“by means of force”). The noun after da is usually feminine singular (da = de + a).
target_language_example: Cheguei lá por meio da ajuda de um amigo.
native_language_example: I got there with the help of a friend.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things/people (superiority). Often followed by a noun/pronoun (“melhor do que a minha”, “melhor do que Maria”) or a clause (“melhor do que nada”). In many contexts, especially in Brazil, you may also hear “melhor que” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Este café é melhor do que aquele.
native_language_example: This coffee is better than that one.

additional_notes: Used to compare abilities, performance, or how well someone knows something, with eu as the reference point. Often follows a verb (fazer, conhecer, falar, etc.): "Ela dança melhor do que eu." In everyday speech you may also hear "melhor do que eu" even when the full idea is "melhor do que eu faço/conheço/falo" (the verb is understood from context).
target_language_example: Ele dirige muito melhor do que eu.
native_language_example: He drives much better than I do.

additional_notes: Used to compare how you feel (or how something is) today versus yesterday. Very common with verbs like "(se) sentir" (to feel): "Estou/me sinto melhor hoje do que ontem." You can intensify it with "muito" (much): "muito melhor hoje do que ontem."
target_language_example: Depois de descansar, estou melhor hoje do que ontem.
native_language_example: After resting, I’m better today than yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s closest friend. It can be literal (a person) or figurative, as in saying something like a book is your “best friend.” Often appears with possessives: meu/minha (my), seu/sua (your), nosso/nossa (our).
target_language_example: A Ana é minha melhor amiga desde a escola.
native_language_example: Ana has been my best friend since school.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things/people (superiority). Often followed by a noun/pronoun (“melhor do que a minha”, “melhor do que Maria”) or a clause (“melhor do que nada”). In many contexts, especially in Brazil, you may also hear “melhor que” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Este café é melhor do que aquele.
native_language_example: This coffee is better than that one.

additional_notes: Used to compare abilities, performance, or how well someone knows something, with eu as the reference point. Often follows a verb (fazer, conhecer, falar, etc.): "Ela dança melhor do que eu." In everyday speech you may also hear "melhor do que eu" even when the full idea is "melhor do que eu faço/conheço/falo" (the verb is understood from context).
target_language_example: Ele dirige muito melhor do que eu.
native_language_example: He drives much better than I do.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things/people. Very common in both formal and informal speech. Often appears with intensifiers like "muito" (much) or "bem" (really): "muito melhor que" / "bem melhor que". In more formal Portuguese you may also see "melhor do que" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Este restaurante é melhor que aquele.
native_language_example: This restaurant is better than that one.

meaning: “lies to me all the time” (usually: *mente para mim o tempo todo/inteiro*).
additional_notes: In practice, this expression is almost always completed as **mente para mim o tempo todo** or **mente para mim o tempo inteiro** (“lies to me all the time”). **mente** is the present tense of *mentir* (“to lie”). **para mim** = “to me.” Both **o tempo todo** and **o tempo inteiro** mean “all the time,” with no important difference in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Você mente para mim o tempo todo.
native_language_example: You lie to me all the time.

additional_notes: "Mentiu" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "mentir" (to lie). It’s commonly followed by "para" + a person/pronoun to say who was lied to: "mentiu para a Maria" (lied to Maria), "mentiu para mim" (lied to me), "mentiu para ti" (lied to you, informal in many regions), "mentiu para você" (lied to you). You can also add an infinitive to explain why: "mentiu para proteger..." (lied to protect...).
target_language_example: Ela mentiu para mim porque estava com medo.
native_language_example: She lied to me because she was afraid.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "mentir" + "para mim". The subject is implied by context (ele mentiu / ela mentiu / você mentiu). In speech, Brazilians often say "mentiu pra mim".
target_language_example: Por que você mentiu para mim?
native_language_example: Why did you lie to me?

additional_notes: Used to say two things/situations are identical or basically equivalent. Often appears with the article: “a mesma coisa” (the same thing), or with “uma” when talking more generally: “uma mesma coisa” (one and the same thing). You can also use it to say something repeats or doesn’t change: “Aqui é sempre a mesma coisa” (“It’s always the same here”).
target_language_example: Pra mim, isso tudo é a mesma coisa.
native_language_example: To me, it’s all the same thing.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male friend (“amigo”). It can also be used as a friendly form of address when speaking to a man (like “my friend”/“buddy”), sometimes to soften advice or make a point (e.g., “O truque, meu amigo, ...”). For a female friend, use “minha amiga.” In plural: “meus amigos” / “minhas amigas.”
target_language_example: Meu amigo mora aqui perto.
native_language_example: My friend lives nearby.

meaning: “my love” (a term of affection; also “my beloved”).
additional_notes: Used as a romantic endearment when addressing someone (often like “honey/sweetheart”), or to refer to your love/feelings for someone (“declarar o meu amor”). Can also be used alone as a form of address (e.g., “Meu amor.”).
target_language_example: Meu amor, eu sinto muito a sua falta.
native_language_example: My love, I miss you so much.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the date you were born and the yearly celebration of it. You’ll often see it with or without the article: “meu aniversário” and “o meu aniversário” both mean “my birthday.” Common with time expressions like “é amanhã” (it’s tomorrow), “foi na semana passada” (it was last week), and “é em outubro” (it’s in October).
target_language_example: No meu aniversário, quero jantar com a minha família.
native_language_example: On my birthday, I want to have dinner with my family.

additional_notes: Means an apartment that belongs to or is used by the speaker. Both “meu apartamento” and “o meu apartamento” are common; adding “o” (“the”) often makes it sound more specific/emphatic. “Meu/minha” agree with the noun: apartamento (masculine) → meu; casa (feminine) → minha.
target_language_example: Você quer vir ao meu apartamento hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Do you want to come to my apartment tonight?

additional_notes: Used to talk about your paternal or maternal grandfather. In Portuguese, family words often use a possessive (meu/minha, seu/sua, nosso/nossa) instead of “of me.” The stress is on the last syllable: avô (grandfather) vs avó (grandmother).
target_language_example: Meu avô mora perto daqui.
native_language_example: My grandfather lives near here.

additional_notes: "Meu" = "my", "avô" = "grandfather", "morreu" = "died" (past tense of "morrer"). Often used with time expressions like "faz" or "há" to say how long ago it happened: "Meu avô morreu há três anos" = "My grandfather died three years ago."
target_language_example: Meu avô morreu quando eu tinha dez anos.
native_language_example: My grandfather died when I was ten years old.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific piece of clothing that belongs to you. "Meu" agrees with a masculine noun like "blusão" (compare: "minha blusa listrada" for a feminine noun). "Listrado" means "striped" and also agrees in gender/number ("listrado/listrada/listrados/listradas"). Common in questions when you’re looking for something: "Você viu...?" / "Sabe(s) onde está...?"
target_language_example: Não consigo achar o meu blusão listrado.
native_language_example: I can’t find my striped jacket/sweatshirt.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: meu (my) + cabelo (hair). It can refer to the hair on your head in general. Common with verbs like estar (Meu cabelo está sujo.), soltar (Solte meu cabelo! = let go of my hair / loosen my hair), and deixar/fazer + infinitive to describe effects (Isso faz meu cabelo ficar arrepiado. = That makes my hair stand on end).
target_language_example: Preciso lavar meu cabelo hoje.
native_language_example: I need to wash my hair today.

additional_notes: "Meu" means "my" (used with masculine singular nouns). "Cachorro" usually means "dog" (often a male dog), and in everyday speech it can refer to a dog of any gender. You can also say "a minha cadela" for "my (female) dog."
target_language_example: Meu cachorro se chama Toby.
native_language_example: My dog is named Toby.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the speaker’s own car. Often appears in everyday situations like locating your car, talking about your keys, or asking someone to carry something to your car. Note: in sentence 3, “a porra do” is a swear-word intensifier (very informal/impolite), but “meu carro” itself is neutral.
target_language_example: Vou pegar algo no meu carro.
native_language_example: I'm going to get something from my car.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your own credit card. In Portuguese, possessives like "meu" (my) agree with the noun: "cartão" is masculine, so it’s "meu cartão" (not *minha*). You’ll also often hear/see it with the article: "o meu cartão de crédito" (also means "my credit card").
target_language_example: Não consigo pagar: perdi meu cartão de crédito.
native_language_example: I can’t pay: I lost my credit card.

additional_notes: "Meu" means "my" and changes to match the noun (here, masculine singular: "celular"). In Portuguese you’ll often also hear/see the article with possessives: "o meu celular" = "my cell phone". Common related verbs: "carregar" (charge), "devolver" (give back/return), "achar/encontrar" (find).
target_language_example: Não consigo achar meu celular; você viu?
native_language_example: I can’t find my cell phone; have you seen it?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the person you share a room (or sometimes an apartment/house) with. You can change the possessive: "meu/minha" (my), "seu/sua" (your/his/her), "nosso/nossa" (our). You may also hear "colega de quarto" or, in Brazil, "meu/minha roommate".
target_language_example: Meu companheiro de quarto chega tarde quase todos os dias.
native_language_example: My roommate gets home late almost every day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your own computer (desktop or laptop). "Meu" agrees with masculine singular nouns like "computador". You can swap in another possessive: "seu computador" (your computer), "nosso computador" (our computer).
target_language_example: Não consigo trabalhar hoje porque meu computador travou.
native_language_example: I can’t work today because my computer froze.

additional_notes: Use this to describe your computer’s state or condition (e.g., está lento = is slow) or where it is (está com meu irmão = my brother has it / it’s with my brother). Portuguese often uses the article with possessives: meu computador / o meu computador are both common.
target_language_example: Meu computador está com problema hoje.
native_language_example: My computer is having a problem today.

additional_notes: Used to give or refer to advice you are offering. Often appears with verbs like ouvir (to listen to), ignorar (to ignore), and seguir (to follow): ouvir/ignorar/seguir meu conselho. You can also change the possessive: meu/minha (my), seu/sua (your), nosso/nossa (our), etc. Note: conselho is masculine, so it’s meu conselho.
target_language_example: Se eu fosse você, eu seguiria meu conselho e começaria hoje.
native_language_example: If I were you, I’d follow my advice and start today.

additional_notes: Used both literally (the organ: “my heart beats”) and figuratively to express strong emotion, affection, or devotion (“with all my heart”). In romantic/poetic language, it can mean someone’s love or the place where someone is cherished (“I lost my heart to…” = “I fell in love with…”). Often appears in set phrases like “com todo o meu coração” (“with all my heart”).
target_language_example: Eu confio em você de todo o meu coração.
native_language_example: I trust you with all my heart.

additional_notes: Dever de casa means “homework” (school work you do at home). You can change the possessive to match the person: meu/minha (my), seu/sua (your), nosso/nossa (our). Often used with fazer (to do) and ajudar com (to help with): fazer o dever de casa; ajudar com o dever de casa.
target_language_example: Vou terminar meu dever de casa antes de sair.
native_language_example: I’m going to finish my homework before going out.

additional_notes: Used to talk about money that belongs to the speaker. Often appears with verbs like gastar (to spend), querer (to want), pagar (to pay), roubar (to steal), pegar (to take), and receber ... de volta (to get back/refund). You may also hear the more formal/standard form with the article: "o meu dinheiro" (same meaning).
target_language_example: Quero meu dinheiro de volta.
native_language_example: I want my money back.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your email in general (your account/inbox), especially with verbs like olhar (to check/look at) and checar (to check). You may also hear/access it as "meus e-mails" when talking about individual messages. "E-mail" is masculine in Portuguese, so it takes "meu".
target_language_example: Vou abrir meu e-mail rapidinho e já volto.
native_language_example: I’m going to check my email quickly and I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your office as a place (a room in a building) or, more generally, your workplace. In Portuguese you can say both "meu escritório" and "em meu escritório" (without "o")—both mean "in my office"; the second is a bit more formal. "Escritório" can also mean an office as a business (e.g., a law firm), depending on context.
target_language_example: Pode me encontrar no meu escritório depois do almoço?
native_language_example: Can you meet me in my office after lunch?

meaning: "my son"; also used to address a boy/young man like “my son” (sometimes like “son”).
additional_notes: Literally “my” (meu) + “son” (filho). Used both to talk about your son (Meu filho está brincando...) and as a form of address (Tudo bem, meu filho?), which can sound affectionate, protective, or gently admonishing depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Venha cá, meu filho, preciso falar com você.
native_language_example: Come here, my son, I need to talk to you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your (male) cat. In everyday speech, Portuguese often drops the article, so you’ll commonly hear "meu gato" instead of "o meu gato". For a female cat, say "minha gata".
target_language_example: Meu gato está dormindo no sofá.
native_language_example: My cat is sleeping on the couch.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an umbrella that belongs to you. In Brazilian Portuguese, possessives like "meu" often appear without the article ("meu guarda-chuva"), while you may also hear "o meu guarda-chuva" for emphasis or clarity. "Guarda-chuva" is masculine, so it takes "meu/o meu".
target_language_example: Você viu meu guarda-chuva?
native_language_example: Have you seen my umbrella?

additional_notes: "Irmão" means "brother" and "meu" means "my". "Caçula" refers to the youngest child/sibling in the family; with "irmão," it means the youngest brother (often just understood as the younger brother). You can also say "minha irmã caçula" (my youngest sister) or use it after names: "O João é o caçula" (João is the youngest).
target_language_example: Meu irmão caçula mora comigo.
native_language_example: My younger brother lives with me.

meaning: "my brother is" (talking about his current state, location, or what he’s doing).
additional_notes: "Meu irmão" means "my brother" (you can also say "o meu irmão"). "Está" is from "estar" and is used for temporary states/conditions (ferido), location (fora), status (online), and actions in progress when followed by a gerund ("está vivendo", "está jogando").
target_language_example: Meu irmão está cansado hoje.
native_language_example: My brother is tired today.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male sibling who is younger than you. Often appears with the verb ser/estar for introductions and descriptions ("Este é..." / "Meu irmão mais novo está...") and with "viver" (to live) or "ir" (to go). In Portuguese, "mais novo" means "younger" (literally "more new"), and you can also say "meu irmão mais velho" for "my older brother."
target_language_example: Meu irmão mais novo mora comigo, mas trabalha perto do centro.
native_language_example: My younger brother lives with me, but works near downtown.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male sibling who is older than you. "Mais velho" means "older" (literally "more old"). You can also drop the article "o" and just say "meu irmão mais velho" in many sentences; both are common.
target_language_example: Meu irmão mais velho mora em outra cidade.
native_language_example: My older brother lives in another city.

meaning: 'my brother is…' (used to describe your brother).
additional_notes: Use this to state or describe something about your brother, followed by an adjective, age/number, or a noun with an article (e.g., a job): "Meu irmão é alto." / "Meu irmão é oito anos mais velho." / "Meu irmão é professor." You can also say "O meu irmão é…" (often a bit more specific/emphatic, like “my brother”).
target_language_example: Meu irmão é muito engraçado, mas é tímido com pessoas novas.
native_language_example: My brother is very funny, but he’s shy with new people.

meaning: "my side"; (in context) "by my side" / "on my side".
additional_notes: Often used with "do" ("do meu lado") to mean physically next to you ("beside me") or to mean someone supports you ("on my side"). With verbs like "ficar/estar" it often implies support ("to be on my side"), and with movement/position verbs like "sentar/vir" it usually means location ("next to me").
target_language_example: Fica do meu lado durante a reunião.
native_language_example: Stay by my side during the meeting.

additional_notes: Used by a woman to refer to her spouse. With "marido" you use the masculine possessive "meu" (often written as "o meu marido"), even though the speaker is female. In Brazil, "meu marido" is often used without the article; in Portugal, "o meu marido" is more common.
target_language_example: Meu marido vai chegar mais tarde.
native_language_example: My husband will arrive later.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your closest friend who is male. For a female best friend, say “minha melhor amiga.” In Portuguese you can also say “o meu melhor amigo,” especially in European Portuguese, but “meu melhor amigo” is common too.
target_language_example: Vou sair com meu melhor amigo hoje.
native_language_example: I'm going out with my best friend today.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your male partner. Often appears as either "meu namorado" or "o meu namorado" (both mean “my boyfriend”). In Brazilian Portuguese, dropping the article is very common ("meu namorado"); in European Portuguese, the article ("o meu") is also very common. If speaking to/about a female partner, use "minha namorada".
target_language_example: Vou jantar com meu namorado hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I’m going to have dinner with my boyfriend tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say what your name is (Meu nome é...) or to refer to your name in general. It can also mean your reputation/good name in expressions like limpar meu nome (“clear my name”).
target_language_example: Meu nome é Ana, prazer em conhecer você.
native_language_example: My name is Ana, nice to meet you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce yourself or correct your name. Often followed by your first name: “Meu nome é Ana.” In everyday conversation, Brazilians also commonly say “Eu sou…” (“I’m…”) instead. You may hear “O meu nome é…” with the article for extra emphasis, but the meaning is the same.
target_language_example: Oi! Meu nome é Lucas.
native_language_example: Hi! My name is Lucas.

additional_notes: Used to give or talk about your phone number. Often appears with verbs like pedir (to ask for), dar (to give), esquecer (to forget), and mudar (to change). You can also say: "Qual é o seu número de telefone?" (What’s your phone number?) or more commonly in Brazil: "Qual é o seu número?"
target_language_example: Anota aí: meu número de telefone é 555-1234.
native_language_example: Write it down: my phone number is 555-1234.

additional_notes: "Meu" means "my" and changes with the gender/number of the thing you own: meu pai (my father), minha mãe (my mother), meus pais (my parents). In Portuguese, you can also use it more generally for “Dad” when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Meu pai trabalha perto daqui.
native_language_example: My dad works near here.

meaning: “my father was …” (talking about what your father used to be, or was in the past).
additional_notes: Used with the imperfect tense of "ser" (era) to describe a past state or identity, often a job, role, or characteristic. You can also say "o meu pai era" (“my father was”), which is a bit more explicit/emphatic. Common pattern: "Meu pai era" + profissão/adjetivo (e.g., "Meu pai era professor.").
target_language_example: Meu pai era muito paciente quando eu era criança.
native_language_example: My father was very patient when I was a child.

additional_notes: Used before an adjective, place, or verb in the -ndo form to say your father’s current state, location, or an action in progress. With *estar*, it often suggests something temporary or changing (e.g., *está cansado*, *está na garagem*, *está consertando*).
target_language_example: Meu pai está trabalhando agora.
native_language_example: My dad is working right now.

meaning: “my father” + “me” (object pronoun), as in “My father (verb) me …”
additional_notes: Common sentence pattern: the object pronoun (me = “me/to me”) comes before the verb in Portuguese: “Meu pai me ajudará” = “My father will help me.” Depending on the verb, “me” can mean a direct object (“see me”) or an indirect object (“give me,” “buy me”).
target_language_example: Meu pai me ligou ontem à noite.
native_language_example: My father called me last night.

additional_notes: A complete sentence using the past tense of **morrer** (“to die”). Common patterns: **morreu de + illness/cause** (“died of/from…”): *Meu pai morreu de câncer.*; **morreu há + time** (“died … ago”): *Meu pai morreu há dois anos.*; **desde que meu pai morreu** (“since my father died”): *Passaram-se cinco anos desde que meu pai morreu.*
target_language_example: Sinto muito, meu pai morreu quando eu era criança.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, my father died when I was a child.

meaning: 'my dad/father doesn’t / isn’t / didn’t' (negative statement about my father).
additional_notes: "Meu pai" means "my father" (or "my dad" in a casual tone). "Não" is the basic word for "not" and is placed before the verb: "meu pai não gosta" = "my father doesn’t like". In English you usually need an auxiliary verb (doesn’t/isn’t/didn’t), so it’s not translated word-for-word as "my father not".
target_language_example: Meu pai não quer sair hoje.
native_language_example: My dad doesn’t want to go out today.

meaning: "My dad/father is…" (used to say what your father is/does or where he’s from).
additional_notes: Use it to introduce information about your father: a job/profession (Meu pai é médico.), a nationality/origin (Meu pai é de Donegal.), or another description. It’s often followed by a profession without an article: "Meu pai é médico/arqueólogo." (not *um médico* in the most common phrasing).
target_language_example: Meu pai é professor.
native_language_example: My dad is a teacher.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your own passport. It’s a common travel/airport phrase. You may also hear/see "o meu passaporte" (with the definite article) and sometimes people drop the article: "meu passaporte". Feminine is "minha" (e.g., "minha mala"), but "passaporte" is masculine, so it uses "meu".
target_language_example: Eu não consigo achar meu passaporte.
native_language_example: I can't find my passport.

additional_notes: Use it to introduce an activity you do for fun. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., ler, pescar) or a noun phrase (e.g., colecionar moedas). You may also hear/see "O meu passatempo é…" (same meaning; "o" is just the article).
target_language_example: Meu passatempo é cozinhar para os amigos.
native_language_example: My hobby is cooking for friends.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the speaker’s own country. Often appears with the verb ser/estar (e.g., “A capital do meu país é…”) and after prepositions like em/ao/do (e.g., “ao meu país” = “to my country”, “do meu país” = “of/from my country”). Gender/number agreement: meu/minha/meus/minhas depending on the noun (país is masculine singular, so it’s meu).
target_language_example: Sinto saudades do meu país.
native_language_example: I miss my country.

additional_notes: "Primo" is a male cousin; for a female cousin, use "minha prima". You can say "meu primo" with or without the person’s name (e.g., "meu primo João").
target_language_example: Meu primo mora em São Paulo.
native_language_example: My cousin lives in São Paulo.

meaning: “my own” (emphasizes that it belongs to me personally).
additional_notes: Used to stress ownership, independence, or that something is personal and not shared: meu próprio dinheiro = money I earned/paid myself; meu próprio quarto/carro = my own room/car. It agrees with the noun: minha própria casa (feminine), meus próprios livros (plural), minhas próprias coisas (feminine plural). Often corresponds to English “my very own.”
target_language_example: Quero ter meu próprio negócio um dia.
native_language_example: I want to have my own business one day.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your own room; commonly a bedroom in a home. You can swap the possessive for other people: “seu quarto” (your room), “nosso quarto” (our room).
target_language_example: Vou arrumar meu quarto hoje.
native_language_example: I’m going to tidy my room today.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a wristwatch: Relógio está quebrado = “My watch is broken.” With household clocks you can also say relógio (e.g., relógio de parede = wall clock). “Meu” agrees with a masculine noun like relógio.
target_language_example: Você viu meu relógio? Acho que deixei na mesa.
native_language_example: Have you seen my watch? I think I left it on the table.

meaning: “my dream is …” (what you want to be/do).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a personal ambition or life goal. It’s followed by an infinitive (ser, ter, viajar, etc.). You’ll also hear/see it with the article: “O meu sonho é …” (same meaning, a bit more emphatic).
target_language_example: Meu sonho é viajar pelo mundo.
native_language_example: My dream is to travel around the world.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your own phone. In Brazilian Portuguese, "telefone" often means a mobile phone; you can also say "meu celular". It can appear with or without the article: "meu telefone" / "o meu telefone". Common in everyday situations like talking about settings, problems, or lending your phone.
target_language_example: Posso pegar meu telefone um minuto?
native_language_example: Can I grab my phone for a minute?

additional_notes: Used to refer to your uncle (your parent’s brother, or your aunt’s husband). Portuguese possessives agree with the noun: "meu" (masc. singular), "minha" (fem. singular), "meus" (masc. plural), "minhas" (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Meu tio mora em São Paulo.
native_language_example: My uncle lives in São Paulo.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "dar" (to give) in the past: "deu" = "gave". "Me" is an object pronoun meaning "to me / me" and usually comes before the verb: "(ele) me deu" = "(he) gave me". You can replace the noun: "minha tia me deu..." (my aunt gave me...), "meu amigo me deu..." (my friend gave me...).
target_language_example: Meu tio me deu um livro no meu aniversário.
native_language_example: My uncle gave me a book on my birthday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your job (occupation) or the work/task you’re responsible for. Context decides the meaning: with verbs like "terminar" it often means a task/project ("My work is finished"), while with "amar" or "é no departamento" it often means your job/position. You can also use it to emphasize responsibility: "É o meu trabalho" = "It’s my job."
target_language_example: Desculpa, não posso sair agora — preciso terminar meu trabalho.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out now—I need to finish my work.

additional_notes: "Vizinho" is masculine; for a female neighbor, use "minha vizinha". You may also see "o meu vizinho" / "a minha vizinha" (with the article), which is also common and still means “my neighbor.” Used both for someone who lives next door and more generally in the neighborhood.
target_language_example: Meu vizinho mora no apartamento ao lado.
native_language_example: My neighbor lives in the apartment next door.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: "meus" (my, masculine plural) + "amigos" (friends, or male friends / mixed-gender group). Often used with "de" as "(alguns/muitos/um) de meus amigos" = "(some/many/one) of my friends." For an all-female group, you’d say "minhas amigas."
target_language_example: Vou sair com meus amigos hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I’m going out with my friends tonight.

additional_notes: "Meus amigos" = "my friends" (plural, masculine or mixed group). "Estão" is the 3rd person plural of "estar" (to be), used for temporary states, location, or condition (e.g., "aqui" = here, "em perigo" = in danger, "fora da cidade" = out of town). Often followed by a place or an adjective.
target_language_example: Meus amigos estão cansados, então vão embora cedo.
native_language_example: My friends are tired, so they’re leaving early.

additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression; it’s a very common sentence pattern: subject + object pronoun + verb. Here, "meus amigos" (my friends) is the subject, and "me" means "me" (the person receiving the action). In Portuguese, object pronouns like "me" usually come before the verb: "Meus amigos me convidaram" = "My friends invited me". The verb changes depending on what your friends did: convidaram (invited), visitaram (visited), viraram as costas (turned their backs on).
target_language_example: Meus amigos me ajudaram com a mudança.
native_language_example: My friends helped me with the move.

additional_notes: Plural form referring to your grandparents as a pair/group. Uses the masculine plural (avós) even if you mean one grandfather + one grandmother. For one grandparent: “meu avô” (my grandfather) / “minha avó” (my grandmother).
target_language_example: Meus avós moram perto da praia.
native_language_example: My grandparents live near the beach.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the other students who are in the same class as you. You can change the possessive: meus/minhas (my), seus/suas (your), nossos/nossas (our). Singular: "meu colega de classe" / "minha colega de classe". Often shortened to "meus colegas" when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Meus colegas de classe vão fazer um trabalho em grupo hoje.
native_language_example: My classmates are going to do a group project today.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase used to talk about your teeth. Often appears with hygiene verbs like escovar (to brush) and in dreams/stories about teeth falling out (meus dentes caíram). You may also see it as “os meus dentes” (more explicit/emphatic) vs. “meus dentes” (more common/neutral).
target_language_example: Preciso ir ao dentista porque meus dentes estão doendo.
native_language_example: I need to go to the dentist because my teeth hurt.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your kids. "Meus" is the plural masculine form of "my" and is also the default for mixed-gender groups; use "minhas filhas" for “my daughters” (all female). Often appears with a preposition + article: "dos meus filhos" (of my children), "nos meus filhos" (about/in my children). You may also hear the shorter form "meus filhos" without "os" (the).
target_language_example: Vou buscar meus filhos na escola às cinco.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick up my kids at school at five.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: “meus” (my, plural masculine) + “olhos” (eyes). Very common with body parts, often after a preposition like “nos”/“em” (“in/into”): “olhe nos meus olhos” = “look into my eyes.”
target_language_example: Meus olhos estão irritados hoje.
native_language_example: My eyes are irritated today.

additional_notes: “Meus” is the masculine plural form of “my,” used because “pais” (parents) is masculine plural in Portuguese. It can also literally mean “my fathers,” but in everyday use “meus pais” means “my parents.” You’ll often see it with verbs like “ver” (to see/visit), “morar” (to live), “morrer” (to die), “ficar” + adjective (to become/feel), and “ter medo” (to be afraid).
target_language_example: Meus pais vão chegar mais tarde.
native_language_example: My parents are going to arrive later.

meaning: “my parents are …” (talking about what your parents are doing, where they are, or what state they’re in right now).
additional_notes: "Meus pais" = "my parents". "Estão" is the verb "estar" (to be), used for temporary situations, location, actions in progress (often with a gerund: "estão discutindo" = "are arguing"), and current states (including "estão mortos" = "are dead"). Often used without "os"; adding "os" ("os meus pais") can sound more specific/emphatic.
target_language_example: Meus pais estão trabalhando agora, então não podem atender o telefone.
native_language_example: My parents are working right now, so they can’t answer the phone.

meaning: 'my parents (to) me' + a verb (e.g., 'my parents gave/told/made/forbade me…').
additional_notes: Used when your parents are the subject and you are the object of the verb. Typically followed by a verb in the past or present: "Meus pais me deram..." (gave me), "me disseram..." (told me), "me fizeram..." (made me), "me proibiram..." (forbade me). In Portuguese, the object pronoun "me" often comes right before the verb.
target_language_example: Meus pais me ajudaram muito quando eu era criança.
native_language_example: My parents helped me a lot when I was a child.

additional_notes: Used to describe or identify your parents (plural) with an adjective or a noun. The verb "são" is the plural form of "ser" (to be) for "eles/elas". Often followed by adjectives ("meus pais são legais") or professions/roles ("meus pais são professores").
target_language_example: Meus pais são muito ocupados durante a semana.
native_language_example: My parents are very busy during the week.

meaning: "my own eyes" (i.e., personally; with direct evidence).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like ver (“to see”) to emphasize that you witnessed something yourself, not just heard about it. It often appears in the pattern "(Eu) vi com os/meus próprios olhos" (“I saw it with my own eyes”). You can change the possessive/person: "seus próprios olhos" (your own eyes), "nossos próprios olhos" (our own eyes), etc.
target_language_example: Eu não acreditei até ver com meus próprios olhos.
native_language_example: I didn’t believe it until I saw it with my own eyes.

additional_notes: Plural body-part noun with the possessive adjective "meus" (used with masculine plural nouns). Often appears with health/pain verbs like "doer" (Meus pés doem.) or with actions like washing (Lavei meus pés.). You may also hear "os meus pés" for emphasis/contrast ("my feet" as opposed to someone else’s).
target_language_example: Depois da caminhada, meus pés estavam cansados.
native_language_example: After the walk, my feet were tired.

meaning: "my feet are" (used to describe how your feet feel).
additional_notes: Use it with an adjective or expression to talk about a condition: meus pés estão frios (cold), dormentes (numb), doendo (hurting). You can add emphasis with sempre (always) or with strong/idiomatic phrases like meus pés estão me matando (“my feet are killing me”). Often shortened in speech to "meus pés tão...".
target_language_example: Meus pés estão muito cansados depois da caminhada.
native_language_example: My feet are very tired after the walk.

additional_notes: Used to talk about shoes that belong to the speaker. "Meus" (my) agrees with the plural masculine noun "sapatos" (shoes). For a single shoe, you’d say "meu sapato."
target_language_example: Não encontro meus sapatos em lugar nenhum.
native_language_example: I can’t find my shoes anywhere.

additional_notes: Used when talking about your emotional state, often in a personal or serious conversation: "falar sobre meus sentimentos" (to talk about my feelings). With verbs like "ferir" it can mean hurting someone emotionally: "feriu os meus sentimentos" (hurt my feelings). You can also say "os meus sentimentos"; the article "os" is common after a verb.
target_language_example: Preciso falar com você sobre meus sentimentos.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you about my feelings.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your own glasses. In Portuguese, óculos is usually plural even when referring to one pair. You may also hear “meus óculos de sol” (“my sunglasses”).
target_language_example: Onde estão meus óculos? Não consigo ler sem eles.
native_language_example: Where are my glasses? I can’t read without them.

additional_notes: Plural imperative of the reflexive verb "mexer-se" (to move). Used to tell a group ("you all"/vocês) to hurry up or start moving; often said with urgency: "Mexam-se, vamos!" = "Come on, get moving!"
target_language_example: Pessoal, mexam-se! O ônibus já chegou.
native_language_example: Guys, get moving! The bus has already arrived.

additional_notes: Used to talk about amounts of money in dollars. In Portuguese, the number comes before the currency name (mil dólares, dez mil dólares, etc.).
target_language_example: Esse celular custa mil dólares.
native_language_example: This phone costs a thousand dollars.

additional_notes: Used when talking about amounts of Japanese money. You can change the number: três mil ienes (3,000 yen), dez mil ienes (10,000 yen), vinte mil ienes (20,000 yen). Often used with prices, payments, and budgeting.
target_language_example: Só tenho mil ienes comigo.
native_language_example: I only have one thousand yen with me.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to indicate a very large (but not exact) quantity: milhares de pessoas/ruas/empregos. As with most quantity expressions in Portuguese, it’s followed by "de" (literally “of”).
target_language_example: Havia milhares de pessoas na rua.
native_language_example: There were thousands of people in the street.
