additional_notes: Used to indicate a large number of people in a general, approximate way. Often appears in news or statistics, and can combine with other quantities (e.g., "centenas de milhares de pessoas" = "hundreds of thousands of people").
target_language_example: Milhares de pessoas participaram da manifestação.
native_language_example: Thousands of people took part in the protest.

additional_notes: Used to name a specific amount of money (1,000,000 dollars), often for prices or hypothetical questions. In casual speech it can also mean “about a million dollars” when paired with algo como (“something like”).
target_language_example: Eu não pagaria um milhão de dólares por isso.
native_language_example: I wouldn’t pay a million dollars for that.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to express a very large (often approximate) number. Common in facts, news, and statistics. You can also expand it (e.g., "centenas de milhões de" = "hundreds of millions of").
target_language_example: Milhões de pessoas assistiram ao jogo ontem.
native_language_example: Millions of people watched the game yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about very large amounts of money in dollars (the currency). It’s a noun phrase that usually follows a number: "três milhões de dólares" (three million dollars), "cem milhões de dólares" (one hundred million dollars).
target_language_example: O projeto custou milhões de dólares.
native_language_example: The project cost millions of dollars.

additional_notes: Used when politely asking someone to do something involving you, usually after a preposition like por (for/by) or de (from), or in phrases like para mim (“to/for me”). Mim is the object form of “I” (used after prepositions), while eu is used as the subject (e.g., Eu espero.).
target_language_example: Pode repetir para mim, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you repeat that for me, please?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a friend who is a woman/girl. It agrees with the speaker: a man or a woman can say “minha amiga.” With a noun like “amiga,” the possessive is typically “minha” (feminine singular). You may also see “a minha amiga” (“my friend” with the definite article), which is very common in European Portuguese and also possible in Brazilian Portuguese for emphasis/clarity. For a male friend: “meu amigo.” Plural: “minhas amigas.”
target_language_example: Vou sair com a minha amiga hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I’m going out with my (female) friend tonight.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your grandmother (your mother’s or father’s mother). Often appears as either “minha avó” (more common before the noun) or “a minha avó” (with the definite article for emphasis/clarity). In Brazilian Portuguese, “vó” is a very common, informal short form for “avó” (e.g., “minha vó”).
target_language_example: Vou visitar minha avó no fim de semana.
native_language_example: I’m going to visit my grandmother this weekend.

additional_notes: Used when talking about your own luggage (suitcase(s), backpack(s), etc.), especially while traveling (airports, hotels, stations). In these contexts, bagagem is usually uncountable in Portuguese, even if you have multiple items.
target_language_example: Desculpe, você pode guardar a minha bagagem por algumas horas?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you store my luggage for a few hours?

additional_notes: "Minha" means "my" (used with feminine nouns), and "bicicleta" is feminine, so you say "minha bicicleta". You may also hear "a minha bicicleta" (“my bicycle”), especially for emphasis or clarity. In Brazil, "bike" is also common in casual speech.
target_language_example: Você pode pegar minha bicicleta emprestada hoje.
native_language_example: You can borrow my bike today.

additional_notes: "Bolsa" commonly means a handbag/purse in everyday contexts, especially with theft/travel situations ("roubaram minha bolsa"). It can also mean a backpack or bag depending on context. "Minha" agrees with the feminine noun "bolsa".
target_language_example: Vou colocar minha bolsa aqui na cadeira.
native_language_example: I’m going to put my bag here on the chair.

meaning: “my bag/purse must be…” / “my bag/purse is probably…”
additional_notes: Used to make a guess about where your bag/purse is. "deve estar" expresses probability ("must be" / "should be" / "is probably"). It’s usually followed by a location ("em casa", "no carro") or by "com" + a person to mean someone has it/it’s with them ("com ela", "com ele", "com eles").
target_language_example: Minha bolsa deve estar no escritório.
native_language_example: My bag/purse is probably at the office.

meaning: “my head”; also “in my mind” (inside my head).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: the physical head (part of your body). It’s also commonly used for thoughts/inner voice: "na/dentro da minha cabeça" = “in my head/in my mind.” In the expression "(nunca) passou pela minha cabeça", it means “(never) crossed my mind/occurred to me.”
target_language_example: Isso nunca passou pela minha cabeça.
native_language_example: That never crossed my mind.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a pen that belongs to the speaker. It’s feminine: caneta (a caneta), so it takes minha (“my,” feminine singular). Often used when looking for something or describing where it is (e.g., Você viu minha caneta? / Minha caneta está...).
target_language_example: Eu não encontro minha caneta.
native_language_example: I can’t find my pen.

additional_notes: "Carteira" most commonly means a wallet (especially in Brazil), but depending on context it can also mean a purse/handbag. Used with "minha" to show possession (feminine noun: a minha carteira).
target_language_example: Não encontro a minha carteira.
native_language_example: I can't find my wallet.

additional_notes: Used to talk about where you live. You can say just "minha casa" (more casual) or "a minha casa" (with the article, often used for emphasis or clarity). It can mean the physical house or your home in general depending on context.
target_language_example: Você quer vir à minha casa depois do trabalho?
native_language_example: Do you want to come to my place after work?

additional_notes: Used to say where you live in relation to another place. Very common pattern: “A minha casa fica perto de + place” (near), or “... fica longe de + place” (far). “Fica” here means “is located,” not “stays.” You can use “minha” without “a” (Minha casa...), or with it (A minha casa...).
target_language_example: Minha casa fica perto do centro.
native_language_example: My house is close to downtown.

additional_notes: Used to describe where your home is or what it’s like. After “é”, you can add an adjective (longe, perto) or a place description (perto da escola, perto de um ponto de ônibus). Note: “casa” can mean both “house” and “home” in Portuguese, depending on context.
target_language_example: Minha casa é pequena, mas muito confortável.
native_language_example: My house is small, but very comfortable.

additional_notes: Used by a male or female speaker to refer to their wife. Often appears after a preposition like de/para/com (e.g., "para a minha esposa"). In informal speech, the article "a" may be dropped ("pra minha esposa"). The possessive can change with the person: minha esposa (my), sua esposa (your/his/her), nossa esposa (our).
target_language_example: Vou falar com minha esposa antes de decidir.
native_language_example: I’m going to talk to my wife before deciding.

additional_notes: Used by a male or female speaker to refer to their wife. Often appears after a preposition like de/para/com (e.g., "para a minha esposa"). In informal speech, the article "a" may be dropped ("pra minha esposa"). The possessive can change with the person: minha esposa (my), sua esposa (your/his/her), nossa esposa (our).
target_language_example: Vou falar com minha esposa antes de decidir.
native_language_example: I’m going to talk to my wife before deciding.

meaning: “my wife is …” (used to describe your wife’s job, nationality, religion, personality, etc.).
additional_notes: Used before a noun or adjective to give information about your wife. You can say “Minha esposa é …” or “A minha esposa é …”; both mean “My wife is …”. After it, you can add a profession (often without an article: “Minha esposa é advogada”) or an adjective/nationality (“Minha esposa é polonesa”).
target_language_example: Minha esposa é professora e muito paciente.
native_language_example: My wife is a teacher and very patient.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase used to talk about your relatives (immediate or extended). It often appears with a preposition like “em” (in) or “com” (with): “em minha família” = “in my family”, “com minha família” = “with my family”. In everyday speech, “minha” is often shortened to “minha” but you may also hear “a minha família” (“my family” with the article).
target_language_example: No fim de semana, vou visitar minha família.
native_language_example: On the weekend, I'm going to visit my family.

additional_notes: Used to identify or refer to your daughter (often in introductions: “Esta é minha filha…”). It can also be used as a direct address to your daughter (“Minha filha, vem cá.”). In some contexts, especially with older speakers or in religious language, it can be used to address a younger woman in a caring way (similar to “my child”).
target_language_example: Esta é minha filha, Ana.
native_language_example: This is my daughter, Ana.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your sister. "Minha" agrees with the feminine noun "irmã" (sister). Before a vowel sound, it may be shortened to "minh'" in speech (e.g., "minh' irmã").
target_language_example: Vou ligar para minha irmã mais tarde.
native_language_example: I’m going to call my sister later.

meaning: “my sister is …” (my sister is + a temporary state or an action happening now).
additional_notes: Use **minha irmã** (“my sister”) + **está** (from **estar**, “to be”) to talk about how your sister is feeling/doing right now, or what she is doing (often with a gerund: **está + verb-ndo**). It’s typically for temporary states (e.g., sick, in love) or ongoing actions (traveling, knitting). For more permanent characteristics, Portuguese often uses **ser** instead (**minha irmã é…**).
target_language_example: Minha irmã está cansada hoje.
native_language_example: My sister is tired today.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your sister who is older than you. It’s a normal, neutral family phrase. Word-by-word: minha = my, irmã = sister, mais velha = older/eldest (literally “more old”). If you have more than one older sister, you can still use it when the context makes clear which one you mean; otherwise you might add her name.
target_language_example: Vou sair com a minha irmã mais velha hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I’m going out with my older sister tonight.

meaning: "my sister has" (she has/possesses; she has something scheduled).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "ter" (to have). It can mean possession (qualities, body parts, objects) or having something planned/regularly scheduled (e.g., classes). With "o mesmo ... que", it refers to something your sister owns: "o mesmo relógio que a minha irmã tem" = "the same watch that my sister has."
target_language_example: A minha irmã tem um carro novo.
native_language_example: My sister has a new car.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information about your sister (job, age, personality, etc.). Portuguese usually omits the subject pronoun “ela” here; you can just say “Minha irmã é …”. After “é”, use a noun/adjective (“secretária”, “minha melhor amiga”) or an age comparison (“… anos mais velha/mais nova que eu”).
target_language_example: Minha irmã é muito simpática.
native_language_example: My sister is very nice.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the homework you have to do for school. It’s often said with the verb “fazer” (to do): “fazer a lição de casa” = “to do homework.” You can also say “me ajudar com a (minha) lição de casa” = “help me with (my) homework.” In Brazil, “lição de casa” is very common; you may also hear “dever de casa” in some regions.
target_language_example: Vou fazer minha lição de casa depois do jantar.
native_language_example: I'm going to do my homework after dinner.

additional_notes: Usually means the language you speak/understand (“Falam minha língua.” = “They speak my language.”). In more physical contexts, it can mean your tongue (“queimei minha língua” = “I burned my tongue”). Often used with verbs like falar (to speak) and ouvir (to hear), and can appear with or without the article: “a minha língua” / “minha língua.”
target_language_example: Você pode falar na minha língua, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you speak my language, please?

meaning: my native language / my mother tongue.
additional_notes: Used to say what language you learned first as a child. You can change the possessive to match the person: minha/sua/a nossa língua materna (my/your/our native language). Often used with the verb "ser": "Minha língua materna é...".
target_language_example: Minha língua materna é o inglês, mas estou aprendendo português.
native_language_example: My native language is English, but I’m learning Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used to say what language you grew up speaking. It’s a common phrase in introductions and language-learning contexts. You can also change the possessive: "minha" (my, for a female speaker or as the set form with "língua"), "sua" (your), "a nossa" (our), etc.
target_language_example: Qual é a sua língua nativa?
native_language_example: What is your native language?

additional_notes: Used to say which school class/subject you like the most. Often appears with the verb "ser": "A matemática é a minha matéria favorita" / "Minha matéria favorita é biologia". You may see the article "a" before "minha" ("a minha") or omitted ("minha"); both are common.
target_language_example: História é minha matéria favorita.
native_language_example: History is my favorite subject.

additional_notes: Used by a female speaker to refer to her closest friend who is a woman/girl. Grammar: "minha" agrees with the feminine noun "amiga" (so it’s "minha melhor amiga" but "meu melhor amigo" for a male best friend). You can also use it for male speakers; the gender here describes the friend, not the speaker.
target_language_example: Vou viajar com a minha melhor amiga no fim de semana.
native_language_example: I’m going to travel with my best (female) friend this weekend.

meaning: "my wife" (also sometimes "my woman/partner," depending on context).
additional_notes: Most commonly means "my wife". In some contexts, especially in Brazil, "minha mulher" can also be used more loosely to refer to a long-term female partner (similar to "my woman"), but it’s still strongly associated with being a spouse. It agrees with the speaker: a woman would usually say "meu marido" (“my husband”). Often appears as "a minha mulher" with the article for emphasis or style.
target_language_example: Vou jantar com a minha mulher hoje.
native_language_example: I'm going to have dinner with my wife today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your own mother. It agrees with the feminine noun “mãe” (mother): “minha” = “my” (feminine singular). In casual speech, people often say “minha mãe” even when just meaning “mom.”
target_language_example: Vou ligar para minha mãe mais tarde.
native_language_example: I’m going to call my mom later.

meaning: "my mom is" (my mother is + an action/state).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what your mother is doing right now or what condition/location she is in. Often followed by a verb in the -ndo form for actions in progress (e.g., "minha mãe está preparando...") or by an adjective/place to describe a temporary state or location (e.g., "minha mãe está fora"). In Portuguese you can say either "A minha mãe" or "Minha mãe" for "my mother/my mom."
target_language_example: Minha mãe está trabalhando agora.
native_language_example: My mom is working right now.

meaning: “my mother (to) me …” (my mom + “me” before a verb).
additional_notes: Used to say your mother does something to/for you, with the object pronoun “me” (= me) placed before the verb: “Minha mãe me ajuda” (My mother helps me), “Minha mãe me ensinou…” (My mother taught me…). In Portuguese, pronouns like “me/te/o/a/nos” often come before the verb, unlike English where “me” usually comes after the verb.
target_language_example: Minha mãe me ligou ontem à noite.
native_language_example: My mother called me last night.

additional_notes: Used to describe or identify your mother. It’s the possessive “minha” (my) + “mãe” (mother) + the verb “é” (is, from ser). Follow it with an adjective (minha mãe é bonita), a noun/profession (minha mãe é enfermeira), or a phrase (minha mãe é a primeira a levantar). In Portuguese, “mãe” takes a feminine adjective: bonita, bela, etc.
target_language_example: Minha mãe é muito trabalhadora.
native_language_example: My mother is very hardworking.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your own hand, often with actions like raising it (levantar), pushing it (empurrar), or holding it (segurar a mão de alguém). In Portuguese you can also say "a minha mão" for emphasis/clarity, similar to “my hand” vs “my own hand.”
target_language_example: Por favor, pegue na minha mão.
native_language_example: Please hold my hand.

additional_notes: "Namorada" is a girlfriend (someone you’re dating). Use "minha" because "namorada" is feminine. The masculine version is "meu namorado" (my boyfriend). It’s common in both Brazil and Portugal.
target_language_example: Vou ao cinema com minha namorada hoje.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movies with my girlfriend today.

additional_notes: Use this to state your girlfriend’s identity, nationality, origin, or a trait. Follow it with a noun (“atriz”), an adjective (“linda”, “chinesa”), or a phrase like “de + place” (“de Boston”). Remember agreement: adjectives describing a woman usually end in -a (linda, chinesa).
target_language_example: Minha namorada é muito inteligente.
native_language_example: My girlfriend is very smart.

additional_notes: Used to state your personal view, often with the verb "ser" ("Minha opinião é...") or after asking for someone’s view ("Se querem minha opinião..." = "If you want my opinion..."). "Opinião" is feminine, so it goes with "minha"; in more formal writing you may also see "a minha opinião".
target_language_example: Na minha opinião, isso não faz sentido.
native_language_example: In my opinion, that doesn’t make sense.

additional_notes: Used when you give your promise (Dou-lhe minha palavra), when you keep/break your promise (manter/quebrar minha palavra), or to emphasize sincerity/strong belief (Por minha palavra, ... = “I swear / honestly ...”). It can also mean “my version/testimony” in a disagreement (É a minha palavra contra a sua = “It’s my word against yours.”).
target_language_example: Eu dou a minha palavra de que vou pagar amanhã.
native_language_example: I give you my word that I’ll pay tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your own leg (or sometimes the lower part of your body). In Portuguese, the possessive can appear with or without the definite article: “a minha perna” and “minha perna” both mean “my leg.” Common in injury/health contexts with verbs like machucar (to hurt/injure), quebrar (to break), and morder (to bite).
target_language_example: Minha perna está doendo muito.
native_language_example: My leg hurts a lot.

meaning: 'my own' (emphasizing that it belongs to me or is chosen/done by me).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun (because própria is feminine): minha própria casa/verdade/escolha. It adds emphasis, like “my very own” or “of my own,” and often highlights independence or personal responsibility/choice. For masculine nouns, you’d say meu próprio (e.g., meu próprio carro).
target_language_example: Preciso de um tempo só para mim, para seguir a minha própria vida.
native_language_example: I need some time just for myself, to live my own life.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your aunt (your mother’s or father’s sister, or an aunt by marriage). In Portuguese, family words often take a possessive before the noun: minha (my). You may also hear/see it with an article, especially in Portugal: a minha tia (“my aunt”).
target_language_example: Vou visitar a minha tia no fim de semana.
native_language_example: I’m going to visit my aunt this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your aunt (your mother’s or father’s sister, or an aunt by marriage). In Portuguese, family words often take a possessive before the noun: minha (my). You may also hear/see it with an article, especially in Portugal: a minha tia (“my aunt”).
target_language_example: Vou visitar a minha tia no fim de semana.
native_language_example: I’m going to visit my aunt this weekend.

additional_notes: Literally “my life.” Used both for talking about your life in general (past or present) and, in context, to mean “the most important thing in my life” (A guitarra é minha vida). It can also appear in a welcoming/ironic phrase: “Seja bem-vinda à minha vida” = “Welcome to my life.”
target_language_example: Este trabalho está a consumir a minha vida.
native_language_example: This job is taking over my life.

additional_notes: Plural feminine: use when the group is all women/girls (or you’re referring to a feminine group). It can be a warm form of address in thanks (e.g., “Obrigado, minhas amigas!”). As a possessive, it can appear with or without an article depending on the sentence: “Eu gosto das minhas amigas” (I like my friends) vs. “Minhas amigas foram...” (My friends went...).
target_language_example: Vou sair com minhas amigas hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I'm going out with my (female) friends tonight.

additional_notes: "Minhas" is the feminine plural form of "my" and agrees with "chaves" (keys). Often used when talking about house/apartment or car keys. You may also hear "as minhas chaves" (“my keys,” with the definite article).
target_language_example: Você viu minhas chaves em algum lugar?
native_language_example: Have you seen my keys anywhere?

meaning: “my things / my stuff” (my belongings or personal matters).
additional_notes: Usually refers to your personal belongings (clothes, items, documents, etc.). In some contexts it can also mean your personal business/affairs (e.g., problems to deal with or tasks to sort out: “resolver minhas coisas” = “take care of my things”). Often said as “minhas coisas” or “as minhas coisas” for emphasis.
target_language_example: Preciso passar em casa para pegar minhas coisas.
native_language_example: I need to stop by home to get my things.

meaning: “my back” (my back area; often used when talking about back pain).
additional_notes: Literally “my backs,” but Portuguese uses the plural (as in English “my back” is singular). Common with verbs like doer/estar doendo (“to hurt”) and expressions like “estão me matando” (“are killing me,” meaning they hurt a lot). Can also be used for actions involving your back, like “coçar” (“to scratch”).
target_language_example: Depois de carregar a mala, minhas costas começaram a doer.
native_language_example: After carrying the suitcase, my back started to hurt.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your own hands, literally (washing, sweating, full) or figuratively to emphasize personal responsibility or direct involvement (e.g., "with my own hands"). In European Portuguese you often hear/see "as minhas mãos"; in Brazilian Portuguese both "minhas mãos" and "as minhas mãos" are common.
target_language_example: Eu fiz isso com as minhas mãos.
native_language_example: I did this with my own hands.

additional_notes: Used with **estar** to describe a temporary state or condition of your hands. Common patterns: **minhas mãos estão + adjective** (sujas, cheias, frias) or **minhas mãos estão + gerund** to describe what they’re doing (doendo = hurting, tremendo = shaking). You may also hear **as minhas mãos estão...** (same meaning, a bit more explicit).
target_language_example: Minhas mãos estão frias.
native_language_example: My hands are cold.

additional_notes: Used to talk about clothing that belongs to the speaker. You may also see the more common form with the article: “as minhas roupas” (“my clothes”). Often appears with verbs like gostar de (to like), roubar (to steal), estar (to be), or lavar/torcer (to wash/wring).
target_language_example: Preciso lavar minhas roupas hoje.
native_language_example: I need to wash my clothes today.

additional_notes: Refers to coins from a long time ago, often used in contexts like collecting (colecionar) or archaeology/history (found in tombs, etc.). In everyday Portuguese, it can mean simply “old coins,” but it often suggests coins with historical or collectible value.
target_language_example: Ele coleciona moedas antigas desde criança.
native_language_example: He has collected old/antique coins since he was a child.

meaning: a lot of; lots of; a bunch of (often: “um monte de”).
additional_notes: Literally means “a pile/mound of,” but it’s usually used to mean “a lot of” before a noun: “um monte de + noun” (um monte de pessoas, um monte de coisas). It’s common and fairly informal. With “Que monte de…”, it expresses criticism/surprise, like “What a load of… / What a bunch of…”.
target_language_example: Tenho um monte de coisas para fazer hoje.
native_language_example: I have a lot of things to do today.

meaning: a lot of things to do; tons of stuff to do.
additional_notes: "Um monte de" is a very common, informal way to say "a lot of". It often means “many/much” (quantity) and is used in everyday speech. You can swap "coisas" for something more specific: "um monte de trabalho" (a lot of work), "um monte de tarefas" (lots of tasks).
target_language_example: Hoje eu tenho um monte de coisas para fazer, então não posso sair.
native_language_example: Today I have a lot of things to do, so I can't go out.

additional_notes: From the verb *morar* (“to live/reside”) + *aqui* (“here”). Common in questions like *Há quanto tempo você mora aqui?* (“How long have you lived here?”). In Brazilian Portuguese, *você mora aqui?* means “Do you live here?” (about someone’s residence).
target_language_example: Você mora aqui ou está só de passagem?
native_language_example: Do you live here, or are you just passing through?

additional_notes: Used to say someone still lives in the same home as their parents. You can change the subject and tense: "Eu moro com os meus pais" (I live with my parents), "Ela morava com os pais" (She used to live with her parents). Often used with "ainda" to mean "still."
target_language_example: Ela ainda mora com os pais.
native_language_example: She still lives with her parents.

additional_notes: From the verb “morar” (to live/reside) + “em” (in/at). Used to say where someone lives (city, country, neighborhood) or sometimes the type of place (e.g., “em um apartamento”). Often followed by a place name or by “um/uma” + noun.
target_language_example: Ele mora em Lisboa, mas trabalha no Porto.
native_language_example: He lives in Lisbon, but works in Porto.

meaning: "lives in" (when the place is feminine or takes "na").
additional_notes: Used with the verb "morar" (to live) + "na" (= "em" + "a"), meaning “in the” or “in” before a feminine noun/place name. Many countries and places take "na" (e.g., na Alemanha), while others take "no" (no Brasil) or just "em" (em Portugal). You can also use it for neighborhoods/parts of a city ("na pior parte da cidade") and for specific places like houses ("na casa grande").
target_language_example: Eu moro na mesma rua que você.
native_language_example: I live on the same street as you.

additional_notes: Used with the verb morar (to live/reside). "no" is a contraction of "em" + "o" and is used before masculine singular places: "no centro", "no Brasil", "no terceiro andar". For feminine singular, use "na" (em + a); plural: "nos" (em + os) and "nas" (em + as).
target_language_example: Ela mora no centro da cidade.
native_language_example: She lives in the city center.

additional_notes:
Used to say where someone lives relative to a place. 
- mora = “(he/she) lives” (from morar)
- perto de = “near”
- da = de + a (“of/from” + “the” feminine singular), used before feminine nouns (a escola, a biblioteca). With a masculine noun, you usually use “perto do” (do = de + o), e.g., “mora perto do parque”.
target_language_example: Ela mora perto da estação de metrô.
native_language_example: She lives near the subway station.

additional_notes: Used with a place to say where people live. "Moram" is the present tense (they/you all live) of "morar" + "em" (in). Often followed by a city/country: "moram em Berlim", "moram no Brasil" (em + o = no), "moram na Alemanha" (em + a = na).
target_language_example: Meus pais moram em São Paulo.
native_language_example: My parents live in São Paulo.

additional_notes: "Morando" is the gerund of "morar" (to live/reside). With "estar" (e.g., "estou/está/estamos"), it often means someone is currently living somewhere, sometimes suggesting a temporary situation. Use "em" before the place: "morando em Roma", "morando em Boston", "morando em casa".
target_language_example: Ela está morando em Lisboa por alguns meses.
native_language_example: She is living in Lisbon for a few months.

additional_notes: Used with cities, countries, neighborhoods, etc. to say where someone lives (permanently or long-term). The verb is "morar" and it normally takes the preposition "em" before the place: "moro em São Paulo" (I live in São Paulo). For temporary stays, Portuguese often uses "ficar" (to stay), but "morar" is for living/residing.
target_language_example: Eu moro em Lisboa, mas quero morar em Porto.
native_language_example: I live in Lisbon, but I want to live in Porto.

meaning: "used to live in" / "was living in" (past, ongoing/habitual).
additional_notes: "Morava" is the imperfect past of "morar" (to live/reside). Use it for past situations that were ongoing, repeated, or background information (often with "quando" = "when"). It commonly contrasts with "morei em" (simple past: lived in, completed period). It’s followed by a place: "morava em Boston", "morava em Singapura".
target_language_example: Naquela época, eu morava em Lisboa e trabalhava no centro.
native_language_example: Back then, I used to live in Lisbon and I worked downtown.

meaning: “I live in” (used to say where you live).
additional_notes: “Moro” is the present tense of the verb “morar” (to live/reside) for “eu” (I). It’s followed by “em” + a place (city, country, neighborhood), often with a contraction: em + o = no (moro no Brasil), em + a = na (moro na Itália), em + um/uma = num/numa (moro numa cidade pequena).
target_language_example: Moro em Lisboa, mas trabalho em Cascais.
native_language_example: I live in Lisbon, but I work in Cascais.

additional_notes: Literal meaning is “dying of hunger,” but it’s commonly used as an exaggeration to mean you’re extremely hungry. Often used with estar: “Estou morrendo de fome.”
target_language_example: Depois da caminhada, eu estava morrendo de fome.
native_language_example: After the hike, I was starving.

meaning: “died from lack of …” / “died due to not having enough …”.
additional_notes: Used to explain the cause of death/withering as a shortage of something. It’s the past tense (they died): *morreram* = “(they) died”. You can change the subject and verb form: *morreu por falta de* (he/she/it died), *morri por falta de* (I died), *morrer por falta de* (to die from lack of). Common with plants/flowers and essentials like *água* (water), *chuva* (rain), *comida* (food), *oxigênio* (oxygen).
target_language_example: Os peixes morreram por falta de oxigênio na água.
native_language_example: The fish died from lack of oxygen in the water.

additional_notes: Used to say the cause of death. In Portuguese, morrer de + [disease/cause] = “to die of/from [disease/cause]”. You can also specify the type/location: “câncer no pulmão” = “lung cancer.”
target_language_example: Minha avó morreu de câncer há cinco anos.
native_language_example: My grandmother died of cancer five years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone died because of an accident. It’s usually followed by the type of accident/vehicle: de carro (car), de bicicleta (bike), de avião (plane), de trem (train). You can also say: morreu num acidente de… (more common in speech).
target_language_example: Ele morreu em um acidente de moto.
native_language_example: He died in a motorcycle accident.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone died in the previous calendar year. It’s the past tense of morrer (“to die”) + no ano passado (“last year”). You can swap the subject: Ele/Ela/Meu avô/Minha mãe morreu no ano passado.
target_language_example: Minha avó morreu no ano passado.
native_language_example: My grandmother died last year.

meaning: to show (someone) how to do that/this.
additional_notes: Used when offering or promising to demonstrate a process/steps. Often appears with an implied or stated object (the person): “me mostrar como fazer isso” = “show me how to do it,” “lhe mostrar como fazer isso” = “show you (formal)/him/her how to do it,” “nos mostrar…” = “show us…”. “Isso” usually means “that/it” (something already mentioned), but in some contexts it can be “this.”
target_language_example: Eu posso te mostrar como fazer isso depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I can show you how to do it after work.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "mostrar" (to show) + the object pronoun "me" (me). Used to ask someone to show you something: "Mostre-me o seu passaporte". In Brazil, it’s also very common to place the pronoun after the verb: "Mostre-me" = "Mostra-me" (informal) and "Me mostre" (especially in casual speech).
target_language_example: Mostre-me onde fica o banheiro, por favor.
native_language_example: Show me where the bathroom is, please.

additional_notes: "Mostrou" is the past tense (ele/ela/você) of "mostrar" (to show). It’s used with an indirect object (who you show it to): "me" (to me), "lhe" (to him/her), "nos" (to us), etc. You can add what the photo is of with "uma foto de…" (a photo of…).
target_language_example: Eu mostrei uma foto do meu irmão para ela.
native_language_example: I showed her a photo of my brother.

additional_notes: Used when you want to stop talking about the current topic and start talking about something else. Common in conversations (sometimes to avoid an uncomfortable topic). Often used with "vamos" (let’s) or "podemos" (can we) + "por favor" (please).
target_language_example: Podemos mudar de assunto? Isso me deixa desconfortável.
native_language_example: Can we change the subject? This makes me uncomfortable.

additional_notes: From the verb "mudar" (to change / to move) + "para" (to/for). With places, it often means "moved to" (especially as "(se) mudou para" = moved to). With situations/results, it means "changed to" or "changed for": "mudou para sempre" = changed forever; "mudou para melhor" = changed for the better.
target_language_example: Ela mudou para Lisboa no ano passado.
native_language_example: She moved to Lisbon last year.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an unspecified large amount or many events/things. Common in everyday speech: "Muita coisa mudou" = "A lot has changed"; "Não é muita coisa" = "It’s not much"; "Tem muita coisa rolando" uses "rolando" (informal) to mean "going on/happening," so the whole phrase means "There’s a lot going on."
target_language_example: Desculpa a demora — aconteceu muita coisa esta semana.
native_language_example: Sorry for the delay — a lot happened this week.

meaning: very hungry; a lot of hunger.
additional_notes: Most commonly used with "estar com" (or "ficar com") to describe how hungry someone is: "Estou com muita fome" = "I’m very hungry." "Fome" (hunger) is feminine, so it takes "muita" (not "muito").
target_language_example: Depois da caminhada, estou com muita fome.
native_language_example: After the hike, I’m very hungry.

meaning: a lot of people; many people.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a large number of people in general (often like English “lots of people”). It’s very common in everyday speech and can be the subject of a sentence: “Muita gente + verb (singular)”.
target_language_example: Hoje tem muita gente no shopping.
native_language_example: There are a lot of people at the mall today.

additional_notes: Used to talk generally about a large number or variety of items, facts, events, or topics. It can refer to things you like (Gosto de muitas coisas), things that were said (Disseram-se muitas coisas), or events that happened (Muitas coisas aconteceram). Often appears as the subject or object of the sentence.
target_language_example: Eu tenho muitas coisas para fazer hoje.
native_language_example: I have many things to do today.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re busy or have many tasks/responsibilities. Common pattern: ter + muitas coisas para fazer (to have a lot of things to do). You can change the amount: poucas coisas para fazer (few things to do), algumas coisas para fazer (a few things to do).
target_language_example: Não posso sair agora; tenho muitas coisas para fazer.
native_language_example: I can’t go out now; I have a lot of things to do.

additional_notes: Used when you’re about to add more information about “many things” using a relative clause with **que** (“that/which”). Very common before verbs like **precisar** (to need) and **fazer** (to do): *muitas coisas que preciso fazer* = “many things that I need to do.”
target_language_example: Ainda tenho muitas coisas que preciso terminar hoje.
native_language_example: I still have many things that I need to finish today.

additional_notes: Commonly used with the verb "tirar" ("tirar fotos" = "to take photos"). "Muitas" agrees with the feminine plural noun "fotos". In negatives, "não... muitas" means "not many".
target_language_example: A gente tirou muitas fotos na praia.
native_language_example: We took a lot of pictures at the beach.

additional_notes: Used to say that there are a lot of different languages, or that someone learns/speaks several languages. Feminine plural: muita (f.) → muitas; língua → línguas. Often used with verbs like aprender (to learn), falar (to speak), and ensinar (to teach).
target_language_example: Ela fala muitas línguas, mas quer aprender mais uma.
native_language_example: She speaks many languages, but she wants to learn one more.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about a large number of people. Often used as the subject of a sentence ("Muitas pessoas...") or after a verb like "havia" (there were) to describe how many people were in a place.
target_language_example: Hoje há muitas pessoas no parque.
native_language_example: Today there are many people in the park.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens frequently or repeatedly. It can go at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis ("Muitas vezes, ...") or right before the verb ("ele muitas vezes chega...").
target_language_example: Muitas vezes eu esqueço minhas chaves.
native_language_example: I often forget my keys.

additional_notes: Used to intensify how well someone does something: *falar/dançar/cozinhar muito bem* (“to speak/dance/cook very well”). It can also mean “(to know/understand/hear) very well”: *conhecer muito bem*, *ouvir muito bem*. With *sentir-se*, it means “to feel very well / (not) feel very well”: *Não estou me sentindo muito bem*. In expressions like *sei muito bem (quem/que...)*, it emphasizes certainty: “I know very well (who/that...).”
target_language_example: Eu entendi muito bem o que você disse.
native_language_example: I understood very well what you said.

meaning: “very well (made good use of) the year that …”
additional_notes: Used as part of the pattern **aproveitar muito bem o ano que + verb**, meaning you used/spent that year really well. The verb after **o ano que** usually agrees with the subject or with **o ano**: **o ano que passou** (the year that passed) is common; you may also see **o ano que passaram** (the year that they/you all spent/passed).
target_language_example: Eu aproveitei muito bem o ano que passei em Portugal.
native_language_example: I made very good use of the year I spent in Portugal.

additional_notes: Used to describe a feminine noun (or a person referred to with a feminine word): e.g., memória, ideia, comida. With masculine nouns, use “muito bom”. Often comes after the noun: “uma memória muito boa”.
target_language_example: A comida daqui é muito boa.
native_language_example: The food here is very good.

additional_notes: Used to praise someone/something (“Ele é muito bom”) or to say a place/thing is of good quality (“O caminho não é muito bom”). In speech it can also be an enthusiastic reaction meaning “Great!” or “Sounds good!”.
target_language_example: A comida daqui é muito boa!
native_language_example: The food here is really good!

additional_notes: Used to compliment a woman/girl or to describe a feminine noun (e.g., cidade, lua, letra). “Muito” intensifies the adjective. Change “bonita” to “bonito” with masculine nouns/people (e.g., “um lugar muito bonito”, “ele está muito bonito”).
target_language_example: Essa foto ficou muito bonita.
native_language_example: That photo turned out very beautiful.

additional_notes: Used to strongly compliment the appearance, sound, or quality of something (a name, accent, dog, scenery, etc.). It agrees with the noun: muito bonito (masc. sing.), muito bonita (fem. sing.), muito bonitos (masc. pl.), muito bonitas (fem. pl.). You can also use it on its own to react: "Eu acho muito bonito" / "Isso é muito bonito".
target_language_example: Seu desenho ficou muito bonito!
native_language_example: Your drawing turned out very beautiful!

additional_notes: Used to say you’re extremely tired. Agree it with the person: muito cansado (male) / muito cansada (female). Common with estar: Estou muito cansado/cansada. You can also use it in guesses or advice: Você deve estar muito cansado/cansada (“You must be very tired”).
target_language_example: Depois do voo, estou muito cansada.
native_language_example: After the flight, I’m very tired.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize the price/cost of something. Often said as an exclamation ("Isso é muito caro!") and can also be used with "não" to soften/negate it ("não é muito caro" = "it’s not very expensive").
target_language_example: Esse celular é muito caro para mim.
native_language_example: This phone is too expensive for me.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something is hard (an activity, exam, book, situation, etc.). It can come after the verb ("é muito difícil") or before an infinitive ("é muito difícil de ler" = "it’s very hard to read").
target_language_example: Aprender a dirigir numa cidade grande pode ser muito difícil.
native_language_example: Learning to drive in a big city can be very difficult.

additional_notes: Used to describe an activity or experience as being a lot of fun. Common with verbs like "ser" and "foi" (was), or after verbs of opinion like "achar" (to think/find): "Achei muito divertido" = "I found it very fun." You can also use it with an infinitive to talk about an activity in general: "É muito divertido + verb".
target_language_example: Foi muito divertido assistir ao jogo com você.
native_language_example: It was very fun to watch the game with you.

additional_notes: Used to intensify the feeling of being happy/glad. Often with forms of "ser/estar" (e.g., "Estou muito feliz") or to express polite enthusiasm about something ("Ficaria muito feliz de..." = "I’d be very happy to...").
target_language_example: Estou muito feliz com a notícia.
native_language_example: I’m very happy about the news.

additional_notes: Used to describe a group of people (or “we”) being very happy. It’s plural, so it matches plural subjects like “todos”, “eles/elas”, or “nós”. Singular is “muito feliz”.
target_language_example: Estamos muito felizes com a notícia.
native_language_example: We’re very happy about the news.

meaning: "very kind" / "very nice" (about a person or something they did).
additional_notes: Used to praise someone's kindness or politeness. Common pattern: "É muito gentil de sua parte + infinitive" = "It’s very kind of you to..." (also: "da sua parte"). In Brazil you’ll also hear "muito legal" in more casual situations.
target_language_example: Foi muito gentil da sua parte me ajudar com as malas.
native_language_example: It was very kind of you to help me with the bags.

additional_notes: Used to describe size or extent. Often appears with “não é muito grande” (“it’s not very big”). With people (e.g., “Você é muito grande”), it can mean physically big/tall/large; depending on context, it may sound a bit direct, so speakers might soften it (e.g., “bem alto/a” = “quite tall”).
target_language_example: O apartamento é muito grande para mim.
native_language_example: The apartment is very big for me.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize the importance of something. "Muito" means "very" and typically comes right before the adjective: "muito importante", "muito bom", "muito difícil".
target_language_example: Isso é muito importante para mim.
native_language_example: This is very important to me.

additional_notes: Used to express strong interest or that you found something engaging. Common with verbs like achar (“to think/find”): “Achei muito interessante…”. Word order is flexible: “Isso é muito interessante” / “Isso foi muito interessante” / “Muito interessante foi…”. You can add emphasis with “mesmo” (“really/indeed”): “Foi muito interessante mesmo.”
target_language_example: Achei a conversa muito interessante.
native_language_example: I found the conversation very interesting.

additional_notes: Common, informal-friendly way to say you like something or someone. Used for people, objects, events, and experiences (e.g., "Foi muito legal" = "It was really cool"). In speech it can stand alone as a reaction: "Muito legal!".
target_language_example: O show foi muito legal!
native_language_example: The show was really cool!

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities or degrees (knowledge, effort, intensity, etc.). Often followed by "do que" to mean "much more than" (e.g., "muito mais do que eu" = "much more than me"). Can also be used without a comparison to mean "a lot more" in general ("Preciso aprender muito mais").
target_language_example: Ela ganha muito mais do que eu.
native_language_example: She earns much more than I do.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities, degree, value, etc. Pattern: **(subject) + verb + muito mais do que + (comparison)**. Often pairs with **antes** (“before”) for time comparisons (e.g., “more than before”), or with a person/thing (e.g., “more than him/that”).
target_language_example: Esta casa custa muito mais do que eu esperava.
native_language_example: This house costs much more than I expected.

additional_notes: Used to compare amounts of money. The pattern is **muito mais + noun + do que** (“much more + noun + than”). You can change the noun: **muito mais tempo do que** (“much more time than”). Often followed by a person/pronoun (**do que eu**) or a time/comparison point (**do que agora**).
target_language_example: Ela tem muito mais dinheiro do que antes.
native_language_example: She has much more money than before.

additional_notes: Used to compare improvement or a higher quality/skill. Common with verbs like sentir-se (to feel): “sinto-me muito melhor” = “I feel much better.” Also used in comparisons with do que/que (“than”): “muito melhor do que/que…” = “much better than…”.
target_language_example: Depois de descansar, estou muito melhor.
native_language_example: After resting, I’m much better.

meaning: “thank you very much for the…” (addressing one person; speaker is usually male).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for something specific. "pela" = "por" + "a" and is used before feminine singular nouns (pela ajuda, pela visita). For masculine singular, use "pelo" (ex.: "muito obrigado pelo tempo"); for plural, "pelos/pelas". If the speaker is female, it's common to say "muito obrigada" instead of "muito obrigado".
target_language_example: Muito obrigado pela sua paciência.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your patience.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific thing or action. It’s followed by **por** + a noun (“por sua ajuda”) or **por** + an infinitive (“por organizar…”). You can also use **por ter + past participle** to mean “for having …” (“por ter vindo”). **Obrigado** agrees with the speaker: **muito obrigado** (male / mixed), **muito obrigada** (female).
target_language_example: Muito obrigado por me ajudar com isso.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for helping me with this.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" to talk about a temporary state (being busy right now/these days). "Ocupado" agrees with the person: "ocupado" (male or mixed group), "ocupada" (female). Can also be used to make a polite assumption: "Você deve estar muito ocupado" (You must be very busy).
target_language_example: Desculpa, hoje estou muito ocupado, mas posso falar amanhã.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm very busy today, but I can talk tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to describe something with a high temperature (an object, a room, the weather, etc.). Often appears with estar/ficar (e.g., "está muito quente", "ficou muito quente"). "Quente" can also mean "sexy" in some contexts, but here it’s about heat/temperature.
target_language_example: Cuidado: a panela está muito quente.
native_language_example: Careful: the pot is very hot.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is bad (a thing, situation, day, dream, news, etc.). It can stand alone as a short reaction ("Muito ruim.") and can be intensified further with repetition or words like "mesmo" ("Muito ruim mesmo" = "Really bad").
target_language_example: O serviço aqui é muito ruim.
native_language_example: The service here is very bad.

additional_notes: Used to intensify speed. With verbs, it usually means “very quickly” (Ele está aprendendo muito rápido). With actions like driving/swimming, it can also mean “very fast” (Dirijo muito rápido / Nado muito rápido). Word order is typically muito + rápido right after the verb.
target_language_example: Não fale muito rápido, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t speak too fast, please.

additional_notes: Used to intensify the adjective "triste" (sad). It can describe a person’s emotional state ("Eu fiquei muito triste") or something that makes you sad ("Isso me deixa muito triste"). With "ficar", it often means "to become/get" sad; with "estar/ser", it describes someone as sad ("O Tom é/está muito triste").
target_language_example: Fiquei muito triste quando ouvi a notícia.
native_language_example: I was very sad when I heard the news.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is really helpful or serves a practical purpose. It can describe people (Você foi muito útil.) or things/animals (O cavalo é um animal muito útil.). Often used in polite feedback/thanks. Word order is fixed: muito + adjective (útil).
target_language_example: Este aplicativo é muito útil para aprender português.
native_language_example: This app is very useful for learning Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used as a warning or emphasis to act carefully. Common with verbs like ter (have), tomar (take), and especially in the imperative: Tenha muito cuidado. You can also say Com muito cuidado (“with great care”) when describing how to do something.
target_language_example: Tenha muito cuidado ao atravessar a rua.
native_language_example: Be very careful when crossing the street.

additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about having, not having, earning, or making a large amount of money. With verbs like ter (to have): "não tem muito dinheiro" = "doesn’t have much money." With fazer (to make/earn): "fez muito dinheiro" = "made a lot of money."
target_language_example: Eu não preciso de muito dinheiro para ser feliz.
native_language_example: I don’t need a lot of money to be happy.

meaning: a long time; a lot of time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about duration. Often follows verbs like gastar/passar/ficar (“to spend/stay”) to mean “spend a lot of time,” and with “já faz” to mean “(it’s been) a long time” (e.g., “já faz muito tempo”).
target_language_example: Faz muito tempo que eu não vejo meus amigos.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen my friends in a long time.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened far in the past. Often comes at the end of the sentence (e.g., "aconteceu ... atrás"). You can also say "há muito tempo" with the same meaning (more common in some contexts).
target_language_example: Eu vi esse filme muito tempo atrás.
native_language_example: I saw that movie a long time ago.

meaning: 'a long time to' / 'plenty of time to'.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about how much time something takes or how much time someone has to do something. Often appears with verbs like "levar" (to take): "levou muito tempo para + infinitive" = "it took a long time to...". It can also mean "plenty of time to" depending on context (having enough time).
target_language_example: Demorei muito tempo para entender essa parte.
native_language_example: It took me a long time to understand that part.

meaning: “a lot of work” / “a lot of trouble (for someone)”
additional_notes: Most commonly means “a lot of work” (often with verbs like fazer/ter/precisar de: "Muito trabalho precisa ser feito"). With "dar muito trabalho a alguém", it means “to cause someone a lot of trouble/effort” (e.g., a task, situation, or person is hard to deal with).
target_language_example: Esse projeto deu muito trabalho, mas valeu a pena.
native_language_example: That project was a lot of work, but it was worth it.

additional_notes: Used to say there are many tasks still pending. The pattern is common and flexible: (ter) muito trabalho a fazer = “(to) have a lot of work to do.” You can change the verb tense (tenho/tinha/tive/teremos) or add time words (hoje, amanhã, antes de...).
target_language_example: Ainda temos muito trabalho a fazer antes da reunião.
native_language_example: We still have a lot of work to do before the meeting.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *ter* (“to have”): *ter muito em comum (com alguém)* = to share many interests, traits, or experiences with someone. You can also say *não ter muito em comum* (“not have much in common”).
target_language_example: Acho que nós dois temos muito em comum.
native_language_example: I think we have a lot in common.

additional_notes: Common in the pattern (ainda) ter/restar + muito que aprender, meaning someone still has a lot to learn. Often followed by com + someone (Tenho muito que aprender com você.) to say you can learn a lot from them. Note: in everyday speech you may also hear simply muito para aprender with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Nós ainda temos muito que aprender antes da prova.
native_language_example: We still have a lot to learn before the exam.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has a large number of friends. "Muitos" agrees with the masculine plural noun "amigos" (for a mixed group or a group of men; for all women, you’d say "muitas amigas"). Often followed by details like where the friends are from ("de Recife") or where they are ("em Boston"), or by an infinitive phrase describing what they do ("para ajudar").
target_language_example: Ele fez muitos amigos na escola.
native_language_example: He made many friends at school.

additional_notes:
Used to talk about a long period of time. Common with time expressions like:
- "há muitos anos" = many years ago / for many years (depending on context)
- "durante/por muitos anos" = for many years
- "muitos e muitos anos" = many, many years (emphasis)
- "Passaram-se muitos anos" = Many years have passed.
target_language_example: Não nos vemos há muitos anos.
native_language_example: We haven't seen each other in many years.

additional_notes: Used to say someone made lots of mistakes. Often appears with the verb "cometer" (to make/commit): "cometer muitos erros". You can add what kind of mistakes with "erros de ..." (e.g., "erros de ortografia" = spelling mistakes).
target_language_example: No começo, eu cometi muitos erros, mas aprendi com eles.
native_language_example: At the beginning, I made many mistakes, but I learned from them.

additional_notes: "Muitos" agrees in gender and number with the noun. With "livros" (masculine plural), it becomes "muitos". Used to talk about a large quantity of books, often after verbs like comprar (to buy) and ler (to read).
target_language_example: Ela tem muitos livros em casa.
native_language_example: She has many books at home.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a large number of countries in general. It’s the plural of "muito país" ("many/a lot of country"), with "muitos" agreeing in gender and number with "países". Often followed by more information about those countries (region, a shared situation, laws, etc.).
target_language_example: Muitos países da Europa usam o euro.
native_language_example: Many countries in Europe use the euro.

additional_notes: A fixed phrase used to refer to the non-combatant/civilian group in a community, especially in urgent or dangerous situations (e.g., evacuation orders, “women and children first”). Often appears as a subject or object: “as mulheres e crianças” (the women and children).
target_language_example: Em caso de emergência, levem as mulheres e crianças para um lugar seguro.
native_language_example: In an emergency, take the women and children to a safe place.

additional_notes: Used to mean all countries/places on Earth (“the whole world”). Often appears with prepositions like “no mundo inteiro” (in the whole world) and “do mundo inteiro” (from all over the world).
target_language_example: Esse filme ficou famoso no mundo inteiro.
native_language_example: That movie became famous worldwide.

additional_notes: Used to say something is a poor choice or not a good plan. Often appears with the verb "ser": "É/era uma má ideia" (It is/was a bad idea). In Brazilian Portuguese you’ll also hear "má" pronounced like "máh"; it agrees with feminine nouns like "ideia".
target_language_example: Acho que foi uma má ideia sair sem guarda-chuva.
native_language_example: I think it was a bad idea to go out without an umbrella.

additional_notes: Literally “mother of her.” Portuguese often puts the possessive after the noun using **de + pronoun**: **dela** = **de + ela** (“of her”), **dele** = **de + ele** (“of him”). So **a mãe dela** = “her mother.” You’ll also see it in expressions like **língua-mãe dela** (“her mother tongue / native language”).
target_language_example: Vou falar com a mãe dela amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to talk to her mother tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a man/boy’s mother. Dele means “of him / his” and is common after nouns (mãe dele, pai dele, amigo dele). For “her mother,” use mãe dela; for “your mother” (informal), mãe de você; or “your mother” (more common in Brazil), sua mãe.
target_language_example: A mãe dele mora perto daqui.
native_language_example: His mother lives near here.

additional_notes: Used to specify which hand (right vs. left), especially in instructions (e.g., “Erga a mão direita.”). Often appears with possessives: “a minha mão direita” (my right hand), “a sua mão direita” (your right hand), “na mão direita” (in/on the right hand).
target_language_example: Escrevo com a mão direita, mas seguro o telefone com a esquerda.
native_language_example: I write with my right hand, but I hold the phone with my left.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the left hand as a body part, often with a possessive: “minha/sua/a mão esquerda” (my/your/the left hand). Common in instructions and descriptions (e.g., levantar a mão esquerda = raise the left hand).
target_language_example: Escrevo com a mão esquerda, mas como com a direita.
native_language_example: I write with my left hand, but I eat with my right.

meaning: (to raise your) hand to ask a question.
additional_notes: Usually appears in the full expression **levantar/erguer a mão para fazer uma pergunta** (“to raise (your) hand to ask a question”), commonly used in classrooms or meetings when you want to speak. You can add a possessive: **a minha mão** (my hand), **a mão** (the hand/your hand, from context).
target_language_example: Eu levantei a mão para fazer uma pergunta.
native_language_example: I raised my hand to ask a question.

additional_notes: Used in hygiene instructions, usually with the verb "lavar" (to wash): "lavar as mãos antes das refeições" = "wash your hands before meals." In Portuguese you’ll often see "as minhas mãos" (my hands) or simply "minhas mãos"; and in general instructions it’s common to use the definite article: "lavar as mãos" (wash the hands = wash your hands).
target_language_example: As crianças devem lavar as mãos antes das refeições.
native_language_example: Children should wash their hands before meals.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened in the previous month. It’s common with or without the article: "mês passado" or "o mês passado". With "desde" (since), it marks the starting point: "desde o mês passado" = "since last month."
target_language_example: A gente se mudou para cá mês passado.
native_language_example: We moved here last month.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that will happen in the month after the current one. Often used with the future tense (e.g., “vai”, “irá”, “vai ter”) or with a future time reference.
target_language_example: A reunião é mês que vem.
native_language_example: The meeting is next month.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like ver/assistir (to watch/see) and estar/aparecer (to be/appear) to talk about something being shown or broadcast on television. It’s the contraction of em + a (“in/on the”) + TV.
target_language_example: Hoje vai passar um jogo na TV.
native_language_example: A game is going to be on TV today.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens. "na" = "em" + "a" (in/at + the), so it’s used with feminine singular places/nouns like "a biblioteca".
target_language_example: Vou estudar na biblioteca depois da aula.
native_language_example: I'm going to study at the library after class.

additional_notes: Used literally for something physically resting or falling on your head (e.g., a hat, a raindrop). It’s also used figuratively to mean “in your mind/inside your head,” referring to thoughts, feelings, or panic happening internally. Often appears in expressions like “Mãos na cabeça!” (“Hands on your head!”).
target_language_example: Fiquei com essa ideia na cabeça o dia todo.
native_language_example: I had that idea in my head all day.

additional_notes: Used mainly in Brazilian Portuguese with verbs like estar/ficar (to be), ir (to go), and mandar/prender (to send/arrest): “Ele está na cadeia.” Although cadeia literally means “chain,” in everyday speech it commonly means “jail/prison.” You can also say “na prisão” (more neutral/formal).
target_language_example: Se continuar assim, vai acabar na cadeia.
native_language_example: If you keep going like that, you’ll end up in jail.

additional_notes: "Na" = "em" + "a" (in + the, feminine). Used to say something is inside a box/container. For a masculine container you'd use "no" (e.g., "no saco" = in the bag).
target_language_example: Deixei as chaves na caixa.
native_language_example: I left the keys in the box.

meaning: in bed; to bed (in the bed).
additional_notes: "Na" = "em" + "a" (in + the), so it literally means "in the bed". Used for being in bed (resting, sleeping, sick) and, with some verbs, for putting someone into bed (e.g., "pôr na cama").
target_language_example: Estou na cama porque não me sinto bem.
native_language_example: I'm in bed because I don't feel well.

meaning: in the house; at home (inside the house).
additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "a" → "na" (feminine singular), used to say someone/something is inside a specific house: "na casa". Often appears in questions like "Tem alguém na casa?" (= Is anyone in the house?). For possession/whose house, you can add "de" + name/article: "na casa da Mickey" (at Mickey’s house), "na casa dos pais" (at the parents’ house).
target_language_example: Tem crianças na casa agora?
native_language_example: Are there children in the house right now?

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located or happens in an urban area. "Na" is the contraction of "em" + "a" (feminine), because "cidade" is feminine: "em a cidade" → "na cidade". Often contrasted with "no campo" (in the countryside).
target_language_example: Eu moro na cidade, mas trabalho no campo.
native_language_example: I live in the city, but I work in the countryside.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is happening or where someone/something is located. It’s the contraction of "em" + "a" + "cozinha" (feminine), so you say "na" with feminine places/rooms like "na cozinha", "na sala".
target_language_example: Estou na cozinha preparando o jantar.
native_language_example: I’m in the kitchen preparing dinner.

additional_notes: "Na" is the contraction of "em" (in/at) + "a" (the, feminine). Use "na escola" to talk about being at school (the place/institution) or something happening there. With verbs of being/doing, it often means "at school" (e.g., studying/working there).
target_language_example: Vou te encontrar na escola depois da aula.
native_language_example: I’ll meet you at school after class.

additional_notes: Contraction of "em + a" → "na". Most commonly refers to a train/metro/bus station. Used for location ("We’re at the station") or drop-off/pick-up ("Leave me at the station").
target_language_example: Vou te encontrar na estação às seis.
native_language_example: I’ll meet you at the station at six.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens or where someone is. "na" = "em" (in/at) + "a" (the, feminine singular), because "estação" is feminine: "a estação" → "na estação". You may also see "estação ferroviária" for a more formal "train station".
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar na estação de trem às oito.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the train station at eight.

additional_notes: "Na" = "em + a" (in/at + the). Used to talk about being a university student or being physically at the university, often in past-time stories: "quando eu estava na faculdade" = "when I was in college." In Brazil, "faculdade" commonly refers to higher education (college/university).
target_language_example: Eu estudava muito na faculdade, mas também saía com os amigos.
native_language_example: I studied a lot in college, but I also went out with friends.

additional_notes: "Na" is the contraction of "em" + "a" and means "in/on/at the" for feminine singular places/events. Use it to say you were at a party or that something happened there: "na festa" (at the party).
target_language_example: A gente se viu na festa ontem à noite.
native_language_example: We saw each other at the party last night.

meaning: in the line/queue; waiting in line.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "ficar/estar/esperar" (to stay/be/wait) to say someone is standing in a queue, often for service or their turn: "na fila aguardando a vez". You can also hear commands like "Entre na fila" (“Get in line”).
target_language_example: A gente ficou na fila para comprar ingressos.
native_language_example: We waited in line to buy tickets.

additional_notes: "na" = "em" (in) + "a" (the, feminine). Used to say someone/something is located in the forest or something happens there. "Floresta" is feminine, so you say "na floresta" (not *no*).
target_language_example: Vamos caminhar na floresta amanhã.
native_language_example: We’re going to hike in the forest tomorrow.

meaning: in front (of); ahead; out in front.
additional_notes: Used for position or location: "na frente do Tom" = "in front of Tom". It can also mean going ahead/leading: "Eu vou na frente" = "I’ll go ahead". Common with "do/da/dos/das" to mean "in front of the" or "in front of (someone/something)". Also used for doing something in someone’s presence: "na frente das meninas" = "in front of the girls".
target_language_example: Pode esperar na frente da loja?
native_language_example: Can you wait in front of the store?

meaning: 'in front of' (in front of a place/thing).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a location directly in front of something (a building, station, house, TV, etc.). It’s a contraction of "em a" → "na" + "frente" + "de" + article ("da" = de + a). With masculine nouns you’ll usually see "na frente do" (de + o).
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar na frente do restaurante às sete.
native_language_example: Let’s meet in front of the restaurant at seven.

additional_notes: Used to talk about position in space (physically in front of someone/something) or position/order in a race, line, ranking, etc. It can also mean doing/saying something with someone present (“in front of Tom”).
target_language_example: A farmácia fica na frente do supermercado.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is in front of the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located inside the garage. Common with verbs like pôr/colocar (to put), ter (to have), estar (to be), and precisar de (to need). "Na" is the contraction of "em" + "a" (in + the), because "garagem" is usually feminine: "a garagem".
target_language_example: Deixe as bicicletas na garagem, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the bikes in the garage, please.

additional_notes: “na” = “em + a” (in + the, feminine singular). “Geladeira” means “refrigerator/fridge.” Used to talk about where food/drinks are stored (location).
target_language_example: Tem suco na geladeira?
native_language_example: Is there juice in the fridge?

meaning: at the time; on time; right away/instantly (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally “in the hour,” but it most often means “at that time” (na hora de + infinitive/noun: “at the time of / when,” e.g., na hora de dormir). With arrivals it commonly means “on time” (chegar na hora). In phrases like “morreu na hora,” it means “instantly/on the spot.”
target_language_example: Eu cheguei na hora e o filme começou na hora.
native_language_example: I arrived on time, and the movie started right away.

meaning: at the right time; on time (when it matters).
additional_notes: Used to say something happened at the ideal/matching moment (often with “lugar certo” = “right place”). It can mean arriving exactly when expected (“Chegou na hora certa!”) or finding/doing something early enough for a good result (“descoberto na hora certa”).
target_language_example: Se você me ligar na hora certa, eu posso te buscar na estação.
native_language_example: If you call me at the right time, I can pick you up at the station.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is included in a list (guest list, waiting list, to-do list, etc.). Often used with the verb "estar": "estar na lista" = "to be on the list". You can specify which list: "na lista de espera" (on the waiting list), "na lista de convidados" (on the guest list).
target_language_example: Desculpe, mas seu nome não está na lista.
native_language_example: Sorry, but your name isn’t on the list.

meaning: on the table; at the table.
additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "a" (feminine singular): "na" = "in/on/at the". Most commonly it means "on the table" (location of an object): "O livro está na mesa." It can also mean "at the table" (where someone is sitting/eating): "Ele comeu na mesa." In set phrases like "na mesa de operação", it means "on the operating table".
target_language_example: Deixa as chaves na mesa, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the keys on the table, please.

meaning: "in the same" (feminine singular), used before a feminine noun like foto, aula, rua.
additional_notes: It’s the contraction of "em" + "a" + "mesma". Use it when something/someone is in the same place/group/thing as someone else: "na mesma foto" (in the same photo), "na mesma aula" (in the same class), "na mesma rua" (on the same street). For masculine singular, you’ll usually see "no mesmo" (ex.: "no mesmo lugar").
target_language_example: A gente trabalha na mesma empresa.
native_language_example: We work at the same company.

additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "a" + "minha". Used before a feminine noun to mean “in my / on my / at my,” depending on the place or surface: "na minha cidade" (in my city), "na minha mesa" (on my table). Common with nouns like "casa" (home), "mesa" (table), "mudança" (move), etc.
target_language_example: Vou deixar o casaco na minha cadeira.
native_language_example: I’m going to leave the coat on my chair.

meaning: "in my face" (right in front of me, or directly/insultingly to me).
additional_notes: Literally “on/in my face.” Used both for something happening physically right in front of you and for rude/direct actions toward you (e.g., laughing at you, hanging up on you: “desligar na minha cara”). You can change the possessive: na sua cara (in your face), na cara dele/dela (in his/her face).
target_language_example: Ele riu na minha cara quando eu contei a novidade.
native_language_example: He laughed in my face when I told the news.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located or staying at your home. Often appears with verbs like ficar (to stay), dormir (to sleep), estar (to be), and with “há” to say there is/are something at your house. It’s the contraction of “em” + “a” (“na”) + “minha casa” (“my house”).
target_language_example: Hoje vamos jantar na minha casa.
native_language_example: Today we're going to have dinner at my house.

meaning: in my life (ever / in my lifetime).
additional_notes: Often used to emphasize that something has never happened before (or is happening for the first time) in your whole life: "nunca... na minha vida" = "never in my life." You may also see stronger versions like "na minha vida toda" (in my whole life). It can also mean "in my personal life" in a broader sense (things that matter or happen to me).
target_language_example: Eu nunca pensei nisso na minha vida.
native_language_example: I never thought about that in my life.

meaning: in the hand; (also) to let someone down.
additional_notes: Most commonly means something is physically being held: "com X na mão" = "with X in (your) hand". In expressions like "deixar (alguém) na mão", it means "to let (someone) down / abandon them" (not literal).
target_language_example: Estou com o passaporte na mão, pronto para sair.
native_language_example: I have my passport in hand, ready to leave.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened during the previous night. Often follows the verb: "Cheguei em casa na noite passada". Also commonly appears as "ontem à noite" (same meaning).
target_language_example: Eu fiquei em casa na noite passada porque estava cansado.
native_language_example: I stayed home last night because I was tired.

additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "a" + "nossa". Used with feminine singular nouns: "na nossa missão" (in our mission), "na nossa cidade" (in our city), "na nossa empresa" (at our company). With movement words like "direção", it can mean "toward us/our direction" ("na nossa direção").
target_language_example: Eles chegaram na nossa casa cedo.
native_language_example: They arrived at our house early.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located/placed on a wall (e.g., a map, picture, painting). It’s the contraction of "em" + "a" (= "na") + "parede". Often appears after verbs like "estar" (to be) or "olhar/veja" (to look/see): "está na parede", "olhe na parede".
target_language_example: A foto está na parede da sala.
native_language_example: The photo is on the living room wall.

meaning: in the back; at the back (rear).
additional_notes: Used to say where someone/something is located, especially in a room, vehicle, line, or group. Often implies a specific area (“the back part”), e.g., the back seats or the back of the room. Variants: “atrás” is a more general “behind/in back of,” while “na parte de trás” points to the back section.
target_language_example: As mochilas estão na parte de trás do carro.
native_language_example: The backpacks are in the back of the car.

meaning: in the back of; at the back of.
additional_notes: Used to locate something in the rear area of a place/object. It’s common with rooms and buildings (na parte de trás da sala, da igreja, da loja). After "da" you typically have a feminine singular noun (da = de + a). For masculine singular nouns, it changes to "do" (na parte de trás do carro).
target_language_example: O banheiro fica na parte de trás da casa.
native_language_example: The bathroom is in the back of the house.

meaning: in the pool; at the swimming pool.
additional_notes: "Na" is the contraction of "em" + "a" and means "in/on/at the" (feminine singular). Use "na piscina" for being inside the pool (swimming) or located at the pool area, depending on context. Common with verbs like "nadar" (to swim), "estar" (to be), "cair" (to fall), "entrar" (to enter), and "ficar" (to stay).
target_language_example: As crianças estão brincando na piscina.
native_language_example: The kids are playing in the pool.

additional_notes: Used when you almost remember a word or name but can’t quite say it yet: "Está na ponta da língua" / "Estou com ___ na ponta da língua". It can also mean something is very well-known or everyone is talking about it (e.g., "Estava na ponta da língua de todo mundo").
target_language_example: O endereço está na ponta da língua, mas eu não consigo lembrar agora.
native_language_example: The address is on the tip of my tongue, but I can’t remember it right now.

meaning: at/on the door; at the doorway/entrance.
additional_notes: Literally "em + a porta" → "na porta". Used for location (someone is standing/waiting at the door) and with common verbs like bater na porta (to knock on the door) and deixar/colocar algo na porta (to leave/put something at the door or in the door/lock area, depending on context). Often implies the entrance area rather than a specific point.
target_language_example: Tem alguém na porta; vou atender.
native_language_example: There’s someone at the door; I’ll answer it.

additional_notes: "Na" is the contraction of "em" (in/at/on) + "a" (the, feminine), so it literally means "in/at/on the beach." It’s used to say where someone is or where something happens: "estar/ficar na praia" (to be/stay at the beach), "passar o dia na praia" (to spend the day at the beach). In English you usually say "at the beach" or "on the beach" depending on context.
target_language_example: Vamos ficar na praia até o pôr do sol.
native_language_example: We’re going to stay at the beach until sunset.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or should be placed on a shelf. It’s the contraction of "em" + "a" (feminine singular) → "na", followed by "prateleira" (shelf).
target_language_example: Deixe os copos na prateleira de cima, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the cups on the top shelf, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened on the first occasion you did something (often followed by “que” + a verb: “na primeira vez que…”).
