It can also mean “on the first try” when correcting/referencing a previous attempt: “Você tinha razão na primeira vez” (= you were right the first time).
target_language_example: Eu acertei na primeira vez que tentei.
native_language_example: I got it right the first time I tried.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is incarcerated or serving time. It’s the contraction of "em" + "a" (feminine singular) → "na", so you’ll also see "na cadeia" (more colloquial) and "no presídio" (in a prison facility).
target_language_example: Ele ficou na prisão por roubo.
native_language_example: He was in prison for theft.

additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "a" = "na". Often appears with verbs like "passar": "passar na prova" = "to pass the exam/test" (get a passing grade). "Prova" usually means an exam/test (not "proof" in the mathematical/legal sense).
target_language_example: Eu estou nervoso(a) para a prova, mas acho que vou passar na prova.
native_language_example: I’m nervous about the test, but I think I’ll pass the exam.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the next occurrence of something in time or sequence. It’s feminine because it usually modifies an implied feminine noun like semana (week), vez (time/occasion), parada (stop), or eleição (election): e.g., na próxima segunda(-feira), na próxima parada, na próxima eleição. You can also say "no próximo" with masculine nouns (e.g., no próximo ano).
target_language_example: Eu te ligo na próxima semana.
native_language_example: I’ll call you next week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an event happening on the Monday of next week. It’s a common way to schedule plans or appointments. Often appears with the future tense (será, voltará) or with modal verbs (pode, poderei, precisa/tem que).
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar na próxima segunda-feira às 9h.
native_language_example: We’re going to meet next Monday at 9 a.m.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen during the week after the current one. It’s a common time expression: “na” = “em + a” (“in the”), “próxima” agrees with “semana” (feminine). You can also hear “semana que vem” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Podemos conversar na próxima semana?
native_language_example: Can we talk next week?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a future occasion when something will happen again. Often follows a verb (e.g., "vou fazer melhor na próxima vez") or can introduce a more specific time with "na próxima vez que..." (“the next time that...”).
target_language_example: Na próxima vez, vou chegar mais cedo.
native_language_example: Next time, I’ll arrive earlier.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on a Wednesday. Often appears with time words like que vem (“next”) and passada (“last/past”), e.g., na quarta-feira que vem = “next Wednesday”, na quarta-feira passada = “last Wednesday”. You can also use it to ask about availability: Você está livre na quarta-feira? (“Are you free on Wednesday?”).
target_language_example: Tenho uma reunião na quarta-feira de manhã.
native_language_example: I have a meeting on Wednesday morning.

additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "a" = "na". Used to say something happened or someone was present during a specific meeting. Often followed by details: "na reunião do nosso povo" (in our people’s meeting) or "na reunião na casa da Mickey" (at the meeting at Mickey’s house).
target_language_example: Vou falar disso na reunião de amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to talk about that at tomorrow’s meeting.

meaning: in/on the street; out on the street (homeless).
additional_notes: Literally “in the street.” Used for being physically in the street/public space (walking, meeting, playing), and also in the expression “acabar/ficar na rua” meaning to end up homeless or without a place to live. It can also be used with street names (e.g., “na Rua Park” = “on Park Street”).
target_language_example: Não brinque na rua, porque passam muitos carros.
native_language_example: Don’t play in the street, because a lot of cars go by.

meaning: in the room; in the living room.
additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "a" → "na". "Sala" often means a room in general, but very commonly refers to the living room ("sala de estar"). Used to say where someone/something is (location) or where something happened.
target_language_example: O celular está na sala.
native_language_example: The phone is in the living room.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is inside a specific type of room. It’s the contraction of "em + a" → "na" plus "sala" (room) and "de" introducing the room’s purpose: "na sala de reuniões" (in the meeting room), "na sala de cirurgia" (in the operating room). Often followed by a singular noun, or a plural like "reuniões" depending on the fixed name of the room.
target_language_example: Vou esperar por você na sala de espera.
native_language_example: I’ll wait for you in the waiting room.

additional_notes: "Na" is the contraction of "em" (in) + "a" (the, feminine singular). "Sala de aula" literally means “classroom” (a room for lessons). Used to say someone/something is physically inside the classroom; often appears in rules or instructions (e.g., "Não se pode fumar na sala de aula" = “You can’t smoke in the classroom”).
target_language_example: Por favor, falem baixo na sala de aula.
native_language_example: Please speak quietly in the classroom.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located in a waiting room (often at a doctor’s office, clinic, or hospital). "na" is the contraction of "em" (in) + "a" (the), so it literally means "in the" + "waiting room" ("sala" = room, "de espera" = of waiting).
target_language_example: Vou ficar na sala de espera até chamarem meu nome.
native_language_example: I’ll stay in the waiting room until they call my name.

additional_notes: "na" = "em" + "a" (in + the), used with feminine singular places like "a sala". "Sala de estar" is the common word for a home’s living room/sitting room. Often used with verbs like colocar (put), ficar/estar (be/stay), conversar (talk), dormir (sleep), escrever (write).
target_language_example: Deixa as chaves na sala de estar, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the keys in the living room, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening on Monday. It’s very common to say the day name without "feira" in Brazil: "segunda" = "segunda-feira" (Monday). "na" = "em" + "a" (in/on the). You can also use this pattern with other weekdays: "na terça", "na quarta", etc.
target_language_example: A reunião é na segunda, às nove.
native_language_example: The meeting is on Monday, at nine.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on a specific Monday. It’s the contraction of “em” + “a” → “na” + “segunda-feira” (“Monday”). You’ll often hear similar forms: “na terça(-feira)” (on Tuesday), “na quarta(-feira)” (on Wednesday), etc.
target_language_example: A reunião é na segunda-feira de manhã.
native_language_example: The meeting is on Monday morning.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the Monday of the previous week relative to today (a specific day in the past). You can swap the weekday: na terça-feira passada (last Tuesday), etc. Often contrasts with "na próxima segunda-feira" (next Monday).
target_language_example: Na segunda-feira passada, eu tive uma reunião muito cedo.
native_language_example: Last Monday, I had a meeting very early.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens within a week or with weekly frequency. Common patterns: (1) frequency: "X vezes na semana" = "X times a week"; (2) time reference: "na semana anterior/seguinte" = "the previous/next week"; (3) within a specific week as a period: "na semana inteira" = "in the whole week". Also appears as "durante a semana" (during the week, weekdays) depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu vou ao mercado duas vezes na semana.
native_language_example: I go to the market twice a week.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened during the previous week (the week before this one). Often answers “when?” questions and can go at the end or beginning of the sentence.
target_language_example: A gente se viu na semana passada.
native_language_example: We saw each other last week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something planned or expected for the week after the current one. Often comes after the verb (e.g., "podemos nos encontrar na semana que vem") but can also be placed at the beginning for emphasis: "Na semana que vem, ...".
target_language_example: Vou começar o curso na semana que vem.
native_language_example: I’m going to start the course next week.

additional_notes: "na" = "em" + "a" (in/on the + feminine singular), and "sexta" is short for "sexta-feira" (Friday). "à noite" means "at night" and is used for the evening/night time (not the afternoon). Common in invitations and scheduling questions: "Você está ocupado(a) na sexta à noite?"
target_language_example: A gente pode se encontrar na sexta à noite.
native_language_example: We can meet on Friday night.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on a specific Friday. It’s the contraction of "em" + "a" → "na" + "sexta-feira" (Friday). You can also add time words like "na sexta-feira passada" (last Friday) or "na sexta-feira que vem" (next Friday).
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar na sexta-feira.
native_language_example: We’re going to meet on Friday.

additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "a" + "sua". Used before a feminine noun: "na sua perna" (on your leg), "na sua meia" (in your sock), "na sua casa" (to/at your house), "na sua sala" (in your classroom). With places, "ir na sua casa" is common in Brazil meaning "go to your house" (also "ir à sua casa").
target_language_example: Tem uma mancha na sua camisa.
native_language_example: There’s a stain on your shirt.

meaning: at the university; in university (at college).
additional_notes: "Na" is a contraction of "em" + "a" and usually means "in/at the" (feminine singular). Use "na universidade" for being at the campus/institution, studying there, or working there (a job at a university). In English you might say "at the university" or just "in college/university" depending on context.
target_language_example: Ela trabalha na universidade e estuda à noite.
native_language_example: She works at the university and studies at night.

meaning: on the porch / on the balcony (outside area attached to a building).
additional_notes: "Na" = "em" + "a" (in/on the), used before a feminine singular noun like "varanda". "Varanda" can mean a porch/veranda (often at the front/side of a house) or a balcony (outside platform of an apartment). Which one it is depends on the building and context.
target_language_example: Vamos tomar café na varanda.
native_language_example: Let’s have coffee on the porch/balcony.

meaning: “actually” / “in fact” (to correct, clarify, or emphasize what’s true).
additional_notes: Used to add a correction or clarification (often contrasting with what someone might think), or to emphasize a true detail. It can appear at the start of the sentence (“Na verdade, …”) or inserted later (“…, na verdade.”).
target_language_example: Na verdade, eu prefiro ficar em casa hoje.
native_language_example: Actually, I’d rather stay home today.

additional_notes: Literally 'in the life' (em + a vida). Often used to talk about life in general: 'momentos na vida' = 'moments in life'. With a possessive or name it means 'in someone’s life': 'na vida dele' = 'in his life'. With negatives it can mean 'ever': 'nunca na vida' = 'never ever'. It also appears in expressions like 'se meter na vida dos outros' = 'to meddle in other people’s business'.
target_language_example: Eu nunca vi isso na vida.
native_language_example: I’ve never seen that in my life.

meaning: on the table; at the table.
additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "a" (feminine singular): "na" = "in/on/at the". Most commonly it means "on the table" (location of an object): "O livro está na mesa." It can also mean "at the table" (where someone is sitting/eating): "Ele comeu na mesa." In set phrases like "na mesa de operação", it means "on the operating table".
target_language_example: Deixa as chaves na mesa, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the keys on the table, please.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a personal opinion, often at the beginning of the sentence and followed by a comma. You can change the possessive to match the speaker: na tua/sua opinião (in your opinion), na nossa opinião (in our opinion).
target_language_example: Na minha opinião, este lugar é perfeito para morar.
native_language_example: In my opinion, this place is perfect to live in.

meaning: in the room; in the living room.
additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "a" → "na". "Sala" often means a room in general, but very commonly refers to the living room ("sala de estar"). Used to say where someone/something is (location) or where something happened.
target_language_example: O celular está na sala.
native_language_example: The phone is in the living room.

additional_notes: Used to correct, clarify, or add a more accurate point—often contrasting with what was just said or assumed. Very common as a sentence opener: “Na verdade, eu…” + verb (e.g., “não sei”, “queria”, “esperava”). You can also drop “eu” if the subject is clear: “Na verdade, não sou.”
target_language_example: Na verdade, eu pensei que você já soubesse.
native_language_example: Actually, I thought you already knew.

additional_notes: Used when a verb takes an indirect object introduced by "a" (to). In negative sentences, Portuguese uses "nada" where English often uses "anything": "Não direi nada a eles" = "I won’t say anything to them." Common with verbs like "dizer" (to say), "contar" (to tell), "provar" (to prove), "mostrar" (to show).
target_language_example: Não tenho nada a te dizer.
native_language_example: I don’t have anything to tell you.

additional_notes: Used when someone has no comment, explanation, or contribution left. Often appears with verbs like "ter" or "haver": "não tinha nada a dizer" (he had nothing to say), "não havia mais nada a dizer" (there was nothing left to say). As a question ("Nada a dizer?"), it can sound challenging or ironic: “Nothing to say?”
target_language_example: Depois da reunião, não havia mais nada a dizer.
native_language_example: After the meeting, there was nothing more to say.

additional_notes: Used to say there’s no risk or downside, so you might as well try (often after “ter”: “não tenho nada a perder” = “I have nothing to lose”). You can also see the longer pattern “não há nada a perder” (“there’s nothing to lose”).
target_language_example: Vamos tentar—não temos nada a perder.
native_language_example: Let’s try— we have nothing to lose.

meaning: “nothing to do with it” / “not involved in this.”
additional_notes: Used to say someone has no connection, responsibility, or involvement in a situation (“isso” = “that/it”). Very common with the verb TER: “não tenho/tinha/tive nada a ver com isso.” You can also hear it in the sense of “that has nothing to do with that” (“isso não tem nada a ver com…”).
target_language_example: Pode ficar tranquilo(a): eu não tenho nada a ver com isso.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I have nothing to do with this.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the only thing involved (often with a negative tone or complaint). It commonly follows a negative verb: “não … nada além de …” = “doesn’t … anything except …”. Can also be used as a standalone phrase: “Nada além de …” = “Nothing but …”.
target_language_example: Este relatório não é nada além de uma cópia do anterior.
native_language_example: This report is nothing but a copy of the previous one.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the only thing involved (often with a negative tone or complaint). It commonly follows a negative verb: “não … nada além de …” = “doesn’t … anything except …”. Can also be used as a standalone phrase: “Nada além de …” = “Nothing but …”.
target_language_example: Este relatório não é nada além de uma cópia do anterior.
native_language_example: This report is nothing but a copy of the previous one.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like fazer (“do”) or dizer (“say”) to deny having done/said anything wrong. Very common in defensive explanations: “não fiz nada de errado” = “I didn’t do anything wrong.” You can also use it about a situation: “Não tem nada de errado” = “There’s nothing wrong.”
target_language_example: Não tem nada de errado em pedir ajuda.
native_language_example: There’s nothing wrong with asking for help.

meaning: “none of that” / “nothing of that” (i.e., not any of it).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something already mentioned or understood from context. Common with negatives to emphasize absence or rejection (e.g., “não tem nada disso” = “doesn’t have any of that”). Can also express disapproval: “Não estou gostando nada disso” = “I’m not liking this at all / any of this.”
target_language_example: Eu não quero nada disso agora.
native_language_example: I don’t want any of that right now.

additional_notes: Used to say there are no shared interests, characteristics, or similarities between people/things. Often appears with forms of the verb *ter* (to have): *não ter nada em comum com* (“to have nothing in common with”).
target_language_example: A gente não tem nada em comum com aquele grupo.
native_language_example: We have nothing in common with that group.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like saber, conhecer, dizer, falar to say you don’t know/tell anything about a topic. Often appears in negatives: “não … nada sobre …”. In Portuguese, double negatives are normal: “não sei nada sobre isso” = “I don’t know anything about that.”
target_language_example: Eu não sei nada sobre esse filme.
native_language_example: I don't know anything about that movie.

additional_notes: Used to say there is no information, knowledge, or comment about a topic. Very common with verbs like saber (to know), dizer (to say), falar/comentar (to talk/comment): "não sei nada sobre isso" = "I don’t know anything about that." You can intensify it with words like "absolutamente": "absolutamente nada sobre isso" = "absolutely nothing about that."
target_language_example: Eu não sei nada sobre isso ainda.
native_language_example: I don’t know anything about that yet.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that one thing has top priority. Very often followed by “do que” (or the shorter “que”) + the thing being compared: “Nada é mais importante (para mim) do que você.” You can add “para mim/para você/para nós” to say “to me/to you/to us.”
target_language_example: Nada é mais importante para nós do que a saúde.
native_language_example: Nothing is more important to us than health.

additional_notes: Used to say that you (or someone else) will join the speaker’s group to swim. "a gente" literally means "the people," but in everyday Portuguese it commonly means "we/us" (often with singular verb forms: "a gente vai").
target_language_example: Você quer nadar com a gente depois do almoço?
native_language_example: Do you want to swim with us after lunch?

additional_notes: Used to say you swim in the ocean (as opposed to a pool). It’s common after verbs like “gostar de” (to like) and “ir” (to go): “gosto de nadar no mar”, “vou nadar no mar”.
target_language_example: No verão, a gente vai nadar no mar todo dia.
native_language_example: In the summer, we’re going to swim in the sea every day.

additional_notes: Used to compare swimming ability. Structure: **nadar** (to swim) + **tão bem quanto** (“as well as / just as well as”). The person you’re comparing to comes after **quanto** (e.g., **você**, **o senhor**, **os senhores**, **vós**).
target_language_example: Ela não nada tão bem quanto o irmão, mas está melhorando.
native_language_example: She doesn’t swim as well as her brother, but she’s improving.

meaning: “that night” (a specific night, usually already mentioned).
additional_notes: Uses the contraction em + aquela → naquela (“in/on that”). Common when referring back to a particular night in a story or conversation: Naquela noite... You can also ask about it: Onde você estava naquela noite?
target_language_example: Naquela noite, a cidade estava muito silenciosa.
native_language_example: That night, the city was very quiet.

meaning: back then; at that time (in the past).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific period in the past that both speakers can identify from context. Often contrasts with the present ("naquela época... hoje"). Similar to "naquele tempo".
target_language_example: Naquela época, eu morava com meus pais.
native_language_example: Back then, I lived with my parents.

meaning: "on that day" / "that day" (referring to a specific day in the past or previously mentioned).
additional_notes: Used to point to a particular day that the speaker and listener can identify from context (often a past event). It’s the contraction of "em aquele" → "naquele" ("on/in that" + masculine singular), plus "dia". Common with past-tense narration: "aconteceu naquele dia", "choveu naquele dia".
target_language_example: Eu nunca vou esquecer o que aconteceu naquele dia.
native_language_example: I’ll never forget what happened that day.

meaning: “at that moment” / “at that time” (a specific moment in the past).
additional_notes: Refers to a particular point in time already known from context, usually in a story or past situation. It often contrasts with another time (before/after). Also appears at the start of a sentence for emphasis: “Naquele momento, ...”.
target_language_example: Naquele momento, eu não entendi o que estava acontecendo.
native_language_example: At that moment, I didn’t understand what was happening.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has a runny nose (often from a cold or allergies). In conversation you’ll usually include a possessive: "Meu nariz está escorrendo" (my), "Seu nariz está escorrendo" (your), "O nariz dele/dela está escorrendo" (his/her).
target_language_example: Acho que estou resfriado; meu nariz está escorrendo desde ontem.
native_language_example: I think I have a cold; my nose has been running since yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to locate something on your body, especially pain or a sensation in the back area. With verbs like passar (“to apply/rub”), it means applying something to the skin on your back. Often used with pain: dor nas minhas costas = “back pain.”
target_language_example: Estou com uma dor forte nas minhas costas.
native_language_example: I have a strong pain in my back.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition “ao” (“at”) or “antes do/até o” (“before/until”) to talk about the time when the sun comes up. Literally “the birth of the sun,” and contrasts with “pôr do sol” (sunset).
target_language_example: Vamos sair ao nascer do sol.
native_language_example: Let’s leave at sunrise.

additional_notes: Past tense (ele/ela/você) of **nascer** (“to be born”) + **em** (“in/on”). Use **nasceu em** with places (cities, countries) and also with dates (e.g., **nasceu em 10 de agosto**). It can also be used more literally for something that “sprang up/grew” somewhere (e.g., a flower was born/appeared).
target_language_example: Ela nasceu em 1998, no Brasil.
native_language_example: She was born in 1998, in Brazil.

meaning: “not even” (emphasizes that something is true in the most extreme/unlikely case).
additional_notes: Used to strengthen a negative statement: it says that something doesn’t apply even in a case you would expect it to. Often comes before the thing being emphasized (a person/thing/situation): “Nem mesmo um deus…” = “Not even a god…”. It can also appear after a negative clause: “..., nem mesmo quando…” = “..., not even when…”.
target_language_example: Eu não tenho tempo, nem mesmo hoje.
native_language_example: I don’t have time, not even today.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not true in every case or doesn’t happen every time. It often softens a statement and can be followed by a verb (e.g., "Nem sempre é fácil...").
target_language_example: Nem sempre eu concordo com ele, mas tento entender o ponto de vista dele.
native_language_example: I don’t always agree with him, but I try to understand his point of view.

meaning: “not even” (emphasizes that something didn’t happen at all).
additional_notes: Used before a word or phrase to stress how surprising/strong the negation is: it didn’t happen even in the smallest/most basic case. Often comes with another negative word like “não”, but can also appear without it depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Eu nem sequer tenho tempo para almoçar hoje.
native_language_example: I don’t even have time for lunch today.

additional_notes: Used to say that a statement is true for some, but not for every member of a feminine plural group. It’s followed by a feminine plural noun (e.g., pessoas, crianças, leis). For masculine, you’d say “nem todos os”. Often used to soften generalizations.
target_language_example: Nem todas as pessoas gostam de café.
native_language_example: Not everyone likes coffee.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true for some people, but not for all. Often followed by a verb: "Nem todo mundo gosta..." (= Not everyone likes...). Similar meaning: "não é todo mundo que...".
target_language_example: Nem todo mundo quer sair hoje.
native_language_example: Not everyone wants to go out today.

additional_notes: Used to say a generalization is not true for every member of a group. It’s typically followed by a masculine plural noun (e.g., nem todos os alunos). For feminine plural nouns, use "nem todas as" (nem todas as pessoas...). Often translates as “Not all…” or “Not everyone…”.
target_language_example: Nem todos os brasileiros falam inglês.
native_language_example: Not all Brazilians speak English.

additional_notes: Used with a negative (usually “não”) to emphasize that something is zero or not in the slightest: “não … nem um pouco” = “not at all.” It can modify adjectives (“não é nem um pouco normal”) or verbs (“não gosto … nem um pouco”). Often placed at the end of the clause for emphasis.
target_language_example: Eu não estou nem um pouco cansado hoje.
native_language_example: I’m not tired at all today.

meaning: none of us; not one of us.
additional_notes: Used to say that zero people in the group (“we/us”) do, want, or know something. It’s often followed by a verb in the 3rd person singular: “Nenhum de nós quer…”. Feminine form: “nenhuma de nós” (none of us women).
target_language_example: Nenhum de nós tem tempo hoje.
native_language_example: None of us have time today.

meaning: "none of my" (referring to your friends/kids/siblings, etc.).
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to say that zero people/things in your group have/do something: "Nenhum dos meus amigos..." (none of my friends...). Grammatically, "nenhum" is singular, so the verb is often singular too ("Nenhum dos meus amigos fala..."); in everyday Brazilian Portuguese you may also hear plural agreement ("Nenhum dos meus amigos falam/podem..."). Feminine: "nenhuma das minhas" (e.g., "Nenhuma das minhas amigas...").
target_language_example: Nenhum dos meus colegas mora perto daqui.
native_language_example: None of my coworkers live near here.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something located or happening in the city where you are (or the city being discussed). It’s the contraction of "em" + "esta" + "cidade"; with a masculine noun you’d use "neste" (e.g., "neste bairro" = "in this neighborhood").
target_language_example: Tem um bom restaurante nesta cidade.
native_language_example: There’s a good restaurant in this city.

meaning: in this area; around here (in this field).
additional_notes: Literally "in this area" ("nesta" = "em" + "esta"). It can refer to a physical location/neighborhood (restaurants, hospitals, post office) or to an area of work/study/experience ("nesta área" = "in this field").
target_language_example: Não conheço muitos bons cafés nesta área.
native_language_example: I don’t know many good cafés around here.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weekend closest to now (the coming weekend, or the one that just happened depending on context). It’s a contraction of "em" + "este" ("in" + "this"), so it often answers “when?” (Quando?).
target_language_example: Vamos viajar neste fim de semana.
native_language_example: We’re going to travel this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what is happening at the present time. Common with the present tense to describe an action in progress or a situation that is currently true. It can also be used alone as a short answer meaning “Right now.”
target_language_example: Não posso falar neste momento.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now.

meaning: 'nobody likes' (followed by a noun or a verb in the infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to say that no one likes something in general, or that no one likes a particular person. After "de", you can use a noun ("más notícias") or an infinitive verb ("perder", "ser enganado"). It can sound like a general statement or complaint depending on context.
target_language_example: Ninguém gosta de esperar na fila.
native_language_example: Nobody likes waiting in line.

meaning: "nobody" / "no one" + "me" (as the object): "no one (does something) to me".
additional_notes: Used when the subject is nobody (ninguém) and "me" is an unstressed object pronoun meaning "to me" or "me". Very common before verbs: "Ninguém me ouviu" (Nobody heard me), "Ninguém me respeita" (Nobody respects me). In Brazil it can also be phrased with the pronoun after the verb in more formal writing: "Ninguém ouviu-me" (less common in everyday speech).
target_language_example: Ninguém me ajudou quando eu precisei.
native_language_example: No one helped me when I needed it.

additional_notes: Used to say that it’s impossible for anyone to do something. Often followed by an infinitive verb: "ninguém pode + verbo" (e.g., ajudar, viajar). In European Portuguese you may also see "ninguém pode" with "o/a" in between in some contexts, but the core meaning stays the same.
target_language_example: Ninguém pode entrar aqui sem autorização.
native_language_example: No one can enter here without authorization.

additional_notes: Used to say that no person wants to do something. Common patterns: (1) "ninguém quer" + infinitive (e.g., "ninguém quer falar", "ninguém quer ser..."); (2) "ninguém quer que" + subjunctive to express wanting someone else to do/be something (e.g., "ninguém quer que você seja..."). It can also take object pronouns: "ninguém quer te ouvir" (nobody wants to hear you).
target_language_example: Hoje ninguém quer sair de casa.
native_language_example: Today nobody wants to leave the house.

additional_notes: Used to say that there is no person who has the information. Often followed by a noun or clause: "ninguém sabe a verdade" (no one knows the truth), "ninguém sabe que..." (no one knows that...), or set phrases like "ninguém sabe ao certo" (no one knows for sure).
target_language_example: Ninguém sabe quando a reunião vai começar.
native_language_example: No one knows when the meeting is going to start.

additional_notes: Used to say that nobody knows the explanation, details, or outcome of something. It’s often followed by a verb or clause (e.g., “ninguém sabe o que aconteceu” = no one knows what happened).
target_language_example: Ninguém sabe o que vai acontecer amanhã.
native_language_example: No one knows what will happen tomorrow.

meaning: “no one is going to / will …” (negative about the future).
additional_notes: Used to say that nobody will do something in the future. Often followed by an infinitive verb: “Ninguém vai + infinitive” (e.g., acreditar, falar, notar, saber). “Vai” is from “ir” and works like English “going to” for future plans/predictions. You can also use it to reassure (“Ninguém vai mexer com você” = “No one will mess with you”) or to warn (“Ninguém vai acreditar em você” = “No one will believe you”).
target_language_example: Não se preocupe: ninguém vai descobrir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: no one is going to find out.

meaning: at the airport; in the airport.
additional_notes: "No" is the contraction of "em" (in/at) + "o" (the), so "no aeroporto" = "in/at the airport" (a specific airport). Common with verbs like esperar (to wait), deixar (to drop off/leave), chegar (to arrive), buscar (to pick up), trabalhar (to work). With "chegar" you’ll often see both "chegar ao aeroporto" and "chegar no aeroporto" in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.
target_language_example: Vou te encontrar no aeroporto amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: I’ll meet you at the airport tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Refers to the lower level of a building (the floor below where you are, or the lower floor in general). Often used with verbs like morar (to live), deixar (to leave), estar (to be), and ir/descer (to go down).
target_language_example: O banheiro fica no andar de baixo.
native_language_example: The bathroom is downstairs (on the downstairs floor).

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened within a particular year. "No" is a contraction of "em" + "o" (= "in" + "the"), so "no ano" literally means "in the year". Very common in phrases like "no ano seguinte" (the following year) and "no ano em que..." / "no ano que..." (in the year when...).
target_language_example: Eu me mudei para Lisboa no ano passado.
native_language_example: I moved to Lisbon last year.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened during the previous calendar year. Commonly placed at the end of the sentence, but it can also come at the beginning for emphasis (often followed by a comma). Literally: “in the past year” (no = em + o).
target_language_example: No ano passado, nós viajamos para o Chile.
native_language_example: Last year, we traveled to Chile.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about something planned or expected for the following year. Often used with future plans: "vou... no ano que vem" (I’m going to... next year). Literal structure: "no" (in the) + "ano" (year) + "que vem" (that comes).
target_language_example: A gente vai viajar no ano que vem.
native_language_example: We’re going to travel next year.

additional_notes: "No" is the contraction of "em + o" and often means "in/on" depending on the context. Use "no avião" to talk about being aboard the aircraft or doing something while traveling by plane (e.g., reading, seeing someone, already being there).
target_language_example: Vou dormir no avião para chegar descansado.
native_language_example: I’m going to sleep on the plane so I arrive rested.

meaning: in/at the bank; in/on the seat/bench.
additional_notes: "No" = "em + o" (in/at the). "Banco" can mean (1) a financial bank (money, loans, account), or (2) a seat/bench (like a car seat: "no banco de trás" = in the back seat; "no banco do passageiro" = in the passenger seat). The context usually makes it clear which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Vou deixar o dinheiro no banco antes de viajar.
native_language_example: I’m going to leave the money in the bank before traveling.

additional_notes: “No” is a contraction of “em + o” and means “in the” (masculine singular). Use “no banheiro” to say someone/something is located inside the bathroom. With verbs of movement (e.g., “entrar”), it can refer to going into the bathroom.
target_language_example: Deixa a toalha no banheiro, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the towel in the bathroom, please.

additional_notes: "No" is the contraction of "em" + "o" ("in/at" + "the"). Used for being at a bar, meeting someone there, waiting there, etc. Similar contractions: "na" = em + a (in/at the [fem.]), "nos" = em + os, "nas" = em + as.
target_language_example: A gente se encontra no bar às oito.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the bar at eight.

additional_notes: Used to say something is inside a pocket (usually of clothing or a bag). Very common after verbs like colocar/pôr (to put), guardar (to keep), and ter (to have). It’s a contraction of em + o → no.
target_language_example: Estou com o celular no bolso.
native_language_example: I have my phone in my pocket.

additional_notes: Common way to say what you eat or do at breakfast. It’s the contraction of "em + o" → "no" + "café da manhã". Often used with verbs like "comer", "beber", "tomar" (have/drink), and "fazer" (have breakfast).
target_language_example: Eu tomo café no café da manhã.
native_language_example: I drink coffee at breakfast.

meaning: on the way; on the path/road; sometimes: in the way.
additional_notes: Used for being along a route or during a trip (often with "de" or "para": "no caminho de casa" = on the way home; "no caminho para" = on the way to). It can also mean being on/within a path or area ("Eles estão no caminho"), and with adjectives it forms common phrases like "no caminho errado" (on the wrong way/path). Depending on context, it may imply blocking someone’s way (similar to "in the way").
target_language_example: Estou no caminho para o trabalho.
native_language_example: I’m on the way to work.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened while traveling from where you were to the school (walking, driving, bus, etc.). Often used at the start of the sentence: “No caminho para a escola, …”. You can swap the destination: “no caminho para casa” (on the way home), “no caminho para o trabalho” (on the way to work).
target_language_example: No caminho para a escola, eu parei para comprar um lanche.
native_language_example: On the way to school, I stopped to buy a snack.

meaning: in the countryside; in a field.
additional_notes: Used with places to mean being located in or going to a rural area (“the countryside”) or an open field. Often contrasts with “na cidade” (in the city).
target_language_example: No fim de semana, vamos caminhar no campo.
native_language_example: On the weekend, we’re going for a walk in the countryside.

additional_notes: "No" = "em" + "o" (in + the). Used to say someone/something is inside the car (often waiting, sitting, or something located there). With movement into the car, Portuguese often uses "no carro" too (e.g., "Entrem no carro" = "Get in the car").
target_language_example: Deixa a mochila no carro, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the backpack in the car, please.

additional_notes: Used to locate something in the central area of a city or town. Often appears with places and activities: "morar no centro" (live downtown), "fazer compras no centro" (shop downtown). It can also be followed by "de" + a place name: "no centro de Boston" (in the center of Boston).
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar no centro às seis.
native_language_example: Let’s meet downtown at six.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located in the central area of a city. It’s the contraction of "em + o" → "no" (literally, "in the center of the city"). Often used with places like shops, offices, monuments, restaurants, etc.
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar no centro da cidade às seis.
native_language_example: Let’s meet downtown at six.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something is located or happens on the surface of the floor (inside) or the ground (outside). Often follows verbs like cair (to fall), derramar (to spill), colocar/deixar (to put/leave), or deitar (to lie down).
target_language_example: Deixei minhas chaves no chão perto da porta.
native_language_example: I left my keys on the floor near the door.

additional_notes: Literally "in the sky/heaven" ("no" = "em" + "o"). Most commonly it means "in the sky" (things you see above you: clouds, stars, planes). In some contexts—especially religious or poetic—it can mean "in heaven".
target_language_example: Hoje tem muitas estrelas no céu.
native_language_example: There are lots of stars in the sky today.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens on a particular day/date. It’s a contraction of "em + o" → "no" (so "no dia" = "em o dia"). Often followed by a number/month: "no dia 11 de junho".
target_language_example: A reunião é no dia 15 de março.
native_language_example: The meeting is on March 15th.

meaning: "on the day when" (the day that something happened).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that specifies what happened on that particular day. Often followed by a verb in the past: "no dia em que eu fui", "no dia em que ele se aposentou". You can also use it to set the scene for a story: "Tudo começou no dia em que...".
target_language_example: Conheci a Ana no dia em que cheguei a Lisboa.
native_language_example: I met Ana on the day I arrived in Lisbon.

meaning: the next day; the following day.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the day after a referenced day/event in the past or future. Often appears at the start of a sentence as a time marker: “No dia seguinte, …”.
target_language_example: No dia seguinte, a gente conversou com mais calma.
native_language_example: The next day, we talked more calmly.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on a Sunday. "no" = "em" + "o" (on + the), so it literally means "on the Sunday". You’ll often hear it with time expressions like "no domingo passado" (last Sunday) or "no domingo à tarde" (on Sunday afternoon).
target_language_example: Vamos almoçar no domingo.
native_language_example: Let’s have lunch on Sunday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being in or during the period of Brazilian high school (ensino médio), usually grades 10–12. Literally it’s "in the middle education" (no = em + o), but it corresponds to English "in/during high school." Also used with "estar" to say someone is currently in high school.
target_language_example: A gente se conheceu no ensino médio.
native_language_example: We met in high school.

additional_notes: "No" is the contraction of "em + o" and commonly translates as "in" or "at". "No escritório" is used for location (being in the office) and can also mean calling someone at their office/workplace number.
target_language_example: Hoje eu vou trabalhar no escritório.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to work at the office.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is in a place without light (literal darkness). It can also be used figuratively to mean "not knowing" or "being uninformed" (e.g., "Estou no escuro" = "I’m in the dark").
target_language_example: Fiquei no escuro porque ninguém me contou o que aconteceu.
native_language_example: I was kept in the dark because nobody told me what happened.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like olhar (to look), ver (to see), and se olhar (to look at oneself) to say someone is looking/seeing themselves reflected in a mirror. It’s a contraction of em + o → no.
target_language_example: Olhe no espelho antes de sair.
native_language_example: Look in the mirror before you leave.

meaning: 'in the exam' / 'on the exam' (during the test).
additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "o" = "no". Often used to talk about what happens during a test (e.g., cheating) or performance/results related to the test (e.g., passing).
target_language_example: Ela tirou uma boa nota no exame.
native_language_example: She got a good grade on the exam.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is outside their home country. Very common with verbs like viver (to live), morar (to live), trabalhar (to work), estudar (to study), viajar (to travel), estar (to be). It can refer generally to “foreign countries” rather than one specific place.
target_language_example: Ela mora no exterior desde 2020.
native_language_example: She has been living abroad since 2020.

additional_notes: Used for the end of a time period or sequence: "no fim do ano" (at the end of the year), "no fim de outubro" (at the end of October). It can also mean the final result/outcome: "no fim, tudo deu certo" (in the end, everything worked out). Common fixed expressions include "no fim das contas" (when all is said and done) and "no fim da linha" (at the end of the line; with no more options).
target_language_example: No fim, a gente encontrou a solução.
native_language_example: In the end, we found the solution.

meaning: on the weekend; during the weekend.
additional_notes: Means something happens on/over the weekend (Saturday and Sunday). Often used with the verb in the future: "No fim de semana vou...". In Brazil you also commonly hear "no final de semana" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: No fim de semana, a gente vai à praia.
native_language_example: On the weekend, we’re going to the beach.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weekend immediately before the current week. Common with past-tense verbs (e.g., fui, voltei, comi). You can also say “no último fim de semana” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: O que você fez no fim de semana passado?
native_language_example: What did you do last weekend?

additional_notes: Used to point to the final part of a time period (no fim do mês = at the end of the month), a text or event (no fim do livro = at the end of the book), or a physical location (no fim do corredor = at the end of the hallway). It’s the contraction of em + o (no) + fim + de + o (do).
target_language_example: A farmácia fica no fim do quarteirão.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is at the end of the block.

additional_notes: Used for either (1) a conclusion/outcome: "No final, ..." = "In the end, ...", or (2) a physical position at the far end of something: "no final deste corredor" (at the end of this hallway), "no final da fila" (at the end of the line). Often followed by de + noun (no final de…).
target_language_example: No final do filme, ela decide ir embora.
native_language_example: At the end of the movie, she decides to leave.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens when an event, period, or object finishes. Very common with time periods (no final do mês, no final do dia) and events (no final do jogo, no final do encontro). The following noun is usually masculine singular because of "do" (= de + o). With a feminine noun, it changes to "no final da" (de + a).
target_language_example: No final do filme, todo mundo aplaudiu.
native_language_example: At the end of the movie, everyone applauded.

meaning: at the end of the hallway/corridor.
additional_notes: Used to indicate location: something/someone is located at the far end of a corridor (often with extra directions like “à direita” = “on the right”). Common in giving directions in buildings (hotels, apartments, offices). You may also hear “no fim do corredor” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: A sala de reuniões fica no final do corredor, perto do elevador.
native_language_example: The meeting room is at the end of the hallway, near the elevator.

additional_notes: Used to say something is inside the oven (usually cooking/baking or being kept warm). Often used with verbs like estar (to be), pôr/colocar (to put), and assar (to bake/roast).
target_language_example: O bolo já está no forno.
native_language_example: The cake is already in the oven.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what will happen at a later time. It can mean the distant future or simply “from now on” depending on context.
target_language_example: No futuro, quero morar perto do mar.
native_language_example: In the future, I want to live near the sea.

additional_notes: "No" is the contraction of "em + o" and usually means being in/at a specific place. With "hospital", Portuguese commonly uses "no hospital" both for being inside the hospital (as a patient) and for being there for something (e.g., visiting someone).
target_language_example: Meu avô está no hospital desde ontem.
native_language_example: My grandfather has been in the hospital since yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens during winter in general. It's the contraction of "em" + "o" → "no" + "inverno". Often contrasts with other seasons: "no verão" (in summer), "na primavera" (in spring), "no outono" (in autumn/fall).
target_language_example: No inverno, escurece mais cedo.
native_language_example: In winter, it gets dark earlier.

additional_notes: "No" = "em" + "o" (in + the), so it means "in the" with a masculine singular noun. "Jardim" usually means a garden (plants/flowers), and in some contexts can refer to the yard/outdoor area around a house. Very common with actions or things located there: trabalhar/cavar/deixar/ver/encontrar no jardim. In "no jardim do teto", it means "in/on the rooftop garden" (a garden area on the roof).
target_language_example: As crianças estão brincando no jardim.
native_language_example: The kids are playing in the garden.

meaning: in the lake; on the lake.
additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "o" → "no". Used to say something is located in/inside the lake (e.g., fish, birds, boats) or happening there. Often translates as "in the lake"; with boats it can also be "on the lake" in English.
target_language_example: Tem muitos peixes no lago.
native_language_example: There are many fish in the lake.

meaning: in his place; instead of him.
additional_notes: Used to say you (or someone else) does something as a substitute for a man/boy (“dele” = “of him”). Very common in hypothetical questions with “O que você teria feito...?” = “What would you have done...?” You can change the pronoun: “no lugar dela” (in her place), “no lugar deles/delas” (in their place).
target_language_example: Se eu estivesse no lugar dele, eu falaria a verdade.
native_language_example: If I were in his place, I would tell the truth.

meaning: “on the map, where (the) … is/it is located.”
additional_notes:
Used when you’re about to point out a place on a map. It typically appears in sentences like “Deixa/Deixe-me mostrar-te no mapa onde fica a Austrália” (“Let me show you on the map where Australia is.”). 

Grammar notes for beginners: 
- **no mapa** = “on the map” (em + o → no). 
- **onde fica** = “where it is located / where it is.” 
- **a** is the feminine article “the” used with many place names (e.g., **a Austrália**). Some places take **o** (e.g., **o Brasil**) or no article depending on usage/region.
- Often followed by a country/city/region name: **no mapa onde fica a França / o Brasil / Lisboa**.
target_language_example: Posso mostrar-te no mapa onde fica a França?
native_language_example: Can I show you on the map where France is?

additional_notes: Contraction of "em + o" → "no" + "mar". Use it for location (being in the sea) or destination/movement (throwing/falling into the sea), depending on the verb and context.
target_language_example: Eles nadaram no mar a manhã toda.
native_language_example: They swam in the sea all morning.

meaning: 'in the middle' / 'in the middle of' (in the center, or involved in something).
additional_notes: Often followed by "de" + noun: "no meio de" = "in the middle of" (place, time, situation). It can be literal (in the center) or figurative (caught up in an event): "no meio de um tiroteio". "Fique no meio" means "stay in the middle/center".
target_language_example: Eu estava no meio de uma reunião quando você ligou.
native_language_example: I was in the middle of a meeting when you called.

meaning: in the middle of; halfway through; in the midst of.
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun after da (= de + a): no meio da avenida (in the middle of the avenue), no meio da discussão (in the middle of the discussion), no meio da tarde (mid-afternoon). With a masculine noun, it becomes no meio do (de + o). It can refer to a physical place (in the middle of a street), a situation/event (in the middle of a battle/discussion), or a time period (mid-afternoon).
target_language_example: Ele me ligou no meio da reunião.
native_language_example: He called me in the middle of the meeting.

meaning: in the middle of the road.
additional_notes: Used to say something is located halfway across the road (often in the center). Common with things like holes, lines/markings, objects, or people. Literally: “in the middle of the road.”
target_language_example: Não pare no meio da estrada.
native_language_example: Don’t stop in the middle of the road.

meaning: in the middle of the night.
additional_notes: Used for something that happens very late at night, often unexpectedly, while people are asleep. Common with verbs like acordar (to wake up), ouvir (to hear), ligar (to call), and vir (to come). It can also be used to complain about being disturbed: “no meio da noite?!”
target_language_example: Eu acordei no meio da noite com um barulho estranho.
native_language_example: I woke up in the middle of the night because of a strange noise.

meaning: in the middle of the street/road.
additional_notes: Used to say something (a car, bus, person, etc.) is stopped or located right in the center of the roadway, often blocking traffic. Common with verbs like estacionar (to park) and parar (to stop).
target_language_example: Não pare no meio da rua.
native_language_example: Don’t stop in the middle of the street.

meaning: in the middle of (during; in the center of).
additional_notes: Used to say something happened halfway through an activity/event (“no meio do concerto”) or right in the center of a place (“no meio do cruzamento / do deserto / do mato”). It’s the contraction of “em” + “o” → “no” + “meio” + “de” + “o” → “do”. With a feminine noun, use “no meio da” (e.g., “no meio da rua”).
target_language_example: O celular descarregou no meio do filme.
native_language_example: The phone died in the middle of the movie.

meaning: in the middle of nowhere; far from everything.
additional_notes: Used to say a place is very remote/isolated (often countryside), with few people, services, or things nearby. Common with verbs like morar/viver/estar (to live/be). It’s a fixed phrase: literally “in the middle of nothing.”
target_language_example: O sinal de celular não pega aqui porque estamos no meio do nada.
native_language_example: There’s no cell signal here because we’re in the middle of nowhere.

meaning: “at the market” or “on the market / available for sale.”
additional_notes: "No" = "em" + "o" (“in/at the”). Most often it means a physical place (a market, marketplace, or grocery market): "comprar no mercado" = to buy at the market. In business/product contexts, it can mean something is available for purchase: "estar no mercado" / "chegar ao mercado" = to be on the market / to come onto the market.
target_language_example: Esse produto já está no mercado?
native_language_example: Is this product already on the market?

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun (because of 'no' = em + o): no mesmo time, no mesmo ônibus, no mesmo apartamento, no mesmo lugar. For feminine nouns, use 'na mesma' (na mesma sala). Often expresses being in the same group/vehicle/location, or doing something in the same year/day, etc.
target_language_example: A gente trabalha no mesmo prédio.
native_language_example: We work in the same building.

additional_notes: Used to say two people/things are in (or were in) the same neighborhood. Often appears with verbs like morar (to live) and crescer (to grow up). Structure: no = em + o (“in the”), mesmo = “same”, bairro = “neighborhood.” You can change it for gender/number: na mesma rua (on the same street), no mesmo lugar (in the same place), nos mesmos bairros (in the same neighborhoods).
target_language_example: A gente mora no mesmo bairro, mas quase nunca se encontra.
native_language_example: We live in the same neighborhood, but we almost never run into each other.

additional_notes: Used to say two events happened on the exact same calendar day. Often links two clauses: “Aconteceu X no mesmo dia em que aconteceu Y.” In Portuguese, “em que” can often be understood as “when/that” here.
target_language_example: Cheguei no mesmo dia em que você saiu da cidade.
native_language_example: I arrived on the same day (that) you left the city.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to say something is in/on/at something that belongs to you. It’s a contraction: em + o = no, so you’ll see it with places or surfaces (no meu quarto, no meu ombro). For feminine nouns use "na minha"; for plural, "nos meus" / "nas minhas".
target_language_example: Deixei minhas chaves no meu bolso.
native_language_example: I left my keys in my pocket.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located in your office, or to tell someone to come/wait/meet there. It's made from "em" (in) + "o" (the) → "no", plus "meu" (my) and "escritório" (office). You can change the owner: "no seu escritório" (in your office), "no nosso escritório" (in our office).
target_language_example: Vou estar no meu escritório às três; pode passar lá.
native_language_example: I’ll be in my office at three; you can stop by.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what is (or was) typical in the country you come from. It’s the contraction of "em" + "o" (no) + "meu" + "país". You can swap "meu" for other possessives: "no seu país" (in your country), "no nosso país" (in our country).
target_language_example: No meu país, as pessoas jantam mais cedo.
native_language_example: In my country, people eat dinner earlier.

meaning: in my room / in my bedroom.
additional_notes: “No” = “em + o” (“in the”). With “meu quarto” it usually means “in my room” (often your bedroom at home). It’s used to say where someone is, goes, stays, sleeps, or where something is located. If you mean “to my room,” you’ll often hear “para o meu quarto” (or “pro meu quarto” in informal speech).
target_language_example: Vou ficar no meu quarto hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay in my room tonight.

meaning: in my free time; in my spare time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what you do when you’re not working or studying. It can go at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis ("No meu tempo livre, ...") or later in the sentence ("... no meu tempo livre"). You can change the possessive to match the person: no teu/seu tempo livre (your), no nosso tempo livre (our).
target_language_example: No meu tempo livre, eu gosto de cozinhar.
native_language_example: In my free time, I like to cook.

additional_notes: Means “in/on the world” in a general sense (often with superlatives like “the most … in the world”). It’s the contraction of "em" + "o" → "no" (so "no mundo" = "em o mundo"). Can also appear in phrases like "no mundo da ciência" (“in the world/field of science”).
target_language_example: Ela diz que esta é a melhor praia no mundo.
native_language_example: She says this is the best beach in the world.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is true everywhere in the world. Often goes with verbs like "ser visto" (to be seen), "ser conhecido" (to be known), and "ser popular" (to be popular). In a more personal/hyperbolic sense, it can mean “in the whole world” (e.g., "meu melhor amigo no mundo todo").
target_language_example: Essa marca é famosa no mundo todo.
native_language_example: That brand is famous all over the world.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened during the previous calendar month. Often comes at the end of the sentence, but it can also be moved to the beginning for emphasis (e.g., "No mês passado, ...").
target_language_example: No mês passado, eu viajei para São Paulo.
native_language_example: Last month, I traveled to São Paulo.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening in the month after the current one. Common with future tenses and plans: “vou…”, “vai…”, “irá…”, “estará…”, “terá…”. Similar to “na semana que vem” (next week) and “no ano que vem” (next year).
target_language_example: Vamos viajar no mês que vem.
native_language_example: We’re going to travel next month.

additional_notes: Used to talk about things that happen or are true during the autumn season. It’s a contraction of "em" + "o" → "no" ("in the" + "autumn"). You can also place it at the start of the sentence: "No outono, ...".
target_language_example: No outono, eu gosto de caminhar no parque.
native_language_example: In the fall, I like to walk in the park.

additional_notes: "No" is the contraction of "em" (in/at) + "o" (the). Use it to say someone/something is located or doing an activity in/at the park. For "parks" in general (no specific one), you can also say "em parque" (less common) or rephrase (e.g., "em um parque" = in a park).
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar no parque depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: Let’s meet in the park after work.

additional_notes: Means someone/something is located or waiting at the bus stop. It’s the contraction of em + o = no, so you’ll also see: "no ponto de ônibus" (at the bus stop) vs. "no ponto" (at the stop).
target_language_example: A gente se encontra no ponto de ônibus às 8.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the bus stop at 8.

additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "o" → "no" (= "in the"). Used to say something/someone is located in or happening in the basement of a house/building. Without a specific "the," you may also see "num porão" (= "in a basement").
target_language_example: As bicicletas estão guardadas no porão.
native_language_example: The bikes are stored in the basement.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the next upcoming stop, time period, or event. It’s the contraction of "em" + "o" (= "no") plus "próximo". Common with nouns like "ponto" (stop), "inverno" (winter), "final de semana" (weekend), "mês" (month), etc. Word order stays the same: "no próximo + noun".
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar no próximo fim de semana.
native_language_example: Let’s meet next weekend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something planned, expected, or scheduled to happen in the year after the current one. Often used with future or intention expressions like "pretender" (to intend), "ter de" (to have to), or "vão" (they are going to).
target_language_example: Vamos viajar no próximo ano.
native_language_example: We’re going to travel next year.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an event happening on the Sunday that’s coming up (the next one). It’s the contraction of "em + o" → "no" ("on the"). You can also hear "domingo que vem" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: A gente se vê no próximo domingo.
native_language_example: See you next Sunday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weekend immediately coming after now. It’s literally “in/on the next weekend”: "no" = "em + o" (in/on + the), "próximo" agrees with "fim de semana". Often used with future plans: "Vou... no próximo fim de semana" / "Você pode... no próximo fim de semana?".
target_language_example: A gente pode se encontrar no próximo fim de semana?
native_language_example: Can we meet next weekend?

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen during the month after the current one. Often appears with future expressions like "vou" (I’m going), "irei" (I will go), or "estarei" (I will be).
target_language_example: Vou começar um curso de português no próximo mês.
native_language_example: I’m going to start a Portuguese course next month.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the summer of the next year/coming summer relative to now. Very common for future plans: ir/viajar/fazer algo no próximo verão. In Portuguese you normally include the preposition + article: "no" (= em + o) before seasons in this kind of time expression.
target_language_example: Vamos viajar no próximo verão.
native_language_example: We're going to travel next summer.

additional_notes: "No" = "em" (in/on) + "o" (the). Used for writing or putting something on a board. With teaching contexts, "o quadro" usually means the classroom board (blackboard/whiteboard). In other contexts, it can mean another kind of board, e.g., "quadro de avisos" = notice board/bulletin board.
target_language_example: Escreve a data no quadro, por favor.
native_language_example: Write the date on the board, please.

meaning: in the room; in the bedroom.
additional_notes: "No" is the contraction of "em + o" (“in/on/at the” + masculine singular “the”). "Quarto" can mean a general room, but very commonly means “bedroom” (e.g., "no quarto de hóspedes" = “in the guest room”). Used to say where someone/something is or where an action happens.
target_language_example: Deixa as malas no quarto, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the suitcases in the bedroom, please.

meaning: in his room / in his bedroom.
additional_notes: "no" = "em + o" (in the). "quarto" is a room; in many everyday contexts it means "bedroom". "dele" means "his" (of him) and is often used to make possession clear (e.g., to avoid confusion with "seu"). You can swap the owner: "no quarto dela" (in her room), "no meu quarto" (in my room), "no quarto do Tom" (in Tom’s room).
target_language_example: Ele está no quarto dele estudando.
native_language_example: He’s in his room studying.

meaning: in the backyard / in the yard.
additional_notes: "No" is the contraction of "em + o" (= "in the"). "Quintal" is the yard area of a house (often the backyard in Brazil). Used to say something is located or happening in that outdoor space: trees, animals, activities, etc.
target_language_example: As crianças estão brincando no quintal.
native_language_example: The kids are playing in the backyard.

meaning: in the river / into the river (also: on the river).
additional_notes: Contraction of "em + o" → "no" + "rio". Use it for being or doing something in the river (Eu nadei no rio.) and also for movement into the river with verbs like "mergulhar" (to dive) or "jogar" (to throw) (Ele mergulhou no rio.; Joguei-a no rio.). For clear direction, Portuguese may also use "para o rio" (to the river).
target_language_example: No verão, a gente nada no rio quase todo dia.
native_language_example: In the summer, we swim in the river almost every day.

additional_notes: Used to say that an expression, emotion, or a physical feature is visible on someone’s face. Very common with nouns like expressão, sorriso, medo, lágrimas. It contracts de+o → do (e.g., no rosto dele = on his face; no rosto dela = on her face).
target_language_example: Ela tinha um olhar de surpresa no rosto.
native_language_example: She had a look of surprise on her face.

additional_notes: "No seu" is the contraction of "em" + "o" + "seu" and is used before a masculine singular noun: "no seu universo" (in your universe), "no seu lugar" (in your place). It often corresponds to English "in your" or "in your shoes" (when followed by "lugar"). With verbs like "confiar" (to trust), Portuguese uses "em" + a person: "confiar no seu irmão" = "trust your brother".
target_language_example: Não mexa no seu celular durante a aula.
native_language_example: Don’t use your phone during class.

meaning: in your room / in his (or her) room.
additional_notes: "no" is the contraction of "em" + "o" (= “in the”). "seu/sua" can mean “your” (formal) or “his/her/its” depending on context, so "no seu quarto" may refer to the listener’s room or someone else’s room.
target_language_example: Pode deixar suas coisas no seu quarto.
native_language_example: You can leave your things in your room.

additional_notes: "no" is the contraction of "em" + "o" and usually means "in/on the" for masculine singular places/objects. With furniture like "sofá", it’s typically translated as "on the sofa" (sitting/lying/sleeping there). In casual speech you may also hear "sentei no sofá" meaning "I sat on the sofa."
target_language_example: Depois do trabalho, gosto de ficar no sofá e assistir TV.
native_language_example: After work, I like to stay on the sofa and watch TV.

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like "cair no sono" (to fall asleep) and "pegar no sono" (to manage to fall asleep). "Cair" suggests dozing off (often quickly), while "pegar" emphasizes finally getting to sleep, sometimes after having trouble.
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, eu caí no sono no sofá.
native_language_example: After lunch, I fell asleep on the couch.

additional_notes: "No" is the contraction of "em + o" and is used for masculine singular places: "no supermercado" = "in/at the supermarket". Common with verbs like "fazer compras" (to shop/buy groceries), "procurar" (to look for someone), "esbarrar com" (to bump into/run into), and "trabalhar" (to work).
target_language_example: Vou passar no supermercado depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I’m going to stop by the supermarket after work.

meaning: in the attic / up in the attic.
additional_notes: "No" = "em + o" (in the). "Sótão" is the attic: the space under the roof, above the main rooms. Often used for storage, hiding, noises, or a small workspace ("uma oficina no sótão").
target_language_example: Guardamos as malas no sótão.
native_language_example: We keep the suitcases in the attic.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is located in a building. Common with verbs like estar/ficar/morar (location) and with movement like sair do elevador (getting off the elevator). Literally: em + o = no (“in/on the”) + terceiro andar (“third floor”).
target_language_example: A sala de reuniões fica no terceiro andar.
native_language_example: The meeting room is on the third floor.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened during an exam or regarding your performance/results on it (e.g., “fui bem no teste” = “I did well on the test”; “passei/não passei no teste” = “I passed/didn’t pass the test”). It’s the contraction of “em + o” → “no” (“in/on the”).
target_language_example: Tirei uma nota boa no teste de matemática.
native_language_example: I got a good grade on the math test.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the highest point or upper part of something (no topo da colina, no topo da árvore). Also used figuratively for being first/best in a ranking or group (no topo da lista, no topo da aula). Structure: no topo de + feminine singular noun (da = de + a). With a masculine noun, it’s "no topo do".
target_language_example: Seu nome está no topo da lista.
native_language_example: Your name is at the top of the list.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is at their job/place of work. Very common with verbs like estar/ficar (to be/stay), ligar (to call), passar tempo (to spend time), and conhecer alguém (to meet someone) to describe what happens while working or in the workplace.
target_language_example: Não posso falar agora; estou no trabalho.
native_language_example: I can't talk right now; I'm at work.

meaning: on the train; in the train (car).
additional_notes: "No" = "em" + "o" (in/on the + masculine singular). Used to say you are traveling by train or located inside the train. Often contrasts with "na estação" (at the station) and pairs with verbs like "embarcar" (to board) and "conversar" (to talk).
target_language_example: Eu vou ler um livro no trem.
native_language_example: I'm going to read a book on the train.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens during the summer season. It’s the contraction of "em" + "o" (in + the): "no". Often placed at the start of the sentence to set the time frame: "No verão, ...".
target_language_example: No verão, a gente vai à praia quase todo fim de semana.
native_language_example: In the summer, we go to the beach almost every weekend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened during the previous summer. Literally “in the past summer” (no = em + o). You can also hear: “no último verão”.
target_language_example: No verão passado, eu trabalhei em um café perto da praia.
native_language_example: Last summer, I worked at a café near the beach.

meaning: on the bus; in the bus.
additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "o" → "no" (meaning "in/on the"). Used to say where someone/something is or where something happened while riding the bus. You can also use it in time/sequence contexts (e.g., "no ônibus, eu li" = "on the bus, I read").
target_language_example: Eu esqueci minha mochila no ônibus.
native_language_example: I forgot my backpack on the bus.

additional_notes: Used to talk about things that happened during the most recent Saturday/Sunday. Often follows the verb or goes at the end of the sentence. You can also hear/see: "no fim de semana passado" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: A gente ficou em casa no último fim de semana.
native_language_example: We stayed home last weekend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the most recent weekend that has already passed. Common in Brazil; you may also hear "no fim de semana passado" with the same meaning. Structure: "no" = "em + o" ("on/in the") + "último" ("last") + "final de semana" ("weekend").
target_language_example: A gente ficou em casa no último final de semana.
native_language_example: We stayed home last weekend.

meaning: at the last minute; at the very last moment.
additional_notes: Used when something happens very late, just before a deadline or before it’s too late (often implying little time left and sometimes stress or urgency). It can describe doing something (finished the project), changing plans (canceled), arriving right before something ends (before the store closes), or even losing your ability to speak right at the end (“Faltaram-me palavras no último minuto.” = “I was lost for words at the last minute”).
target_language_example: Consegui enviar o formulário no último minuto.
native_language_example: I managed to submit the form at the last minute.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened during the previous night (the night before today). Commonly placed at the end of the sentence as a time expression. Often interchangeable with "ontem à noite" in everyday use.
target_language_example: Eu cheguei tarde em casa noite passada.
native_language_example: I got home late last night.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a female person’s name. Often appears after question words like "Qual"/"Como" (e.g., "Qual era o nome dela?") or with verbs like "saber" (to know) and "esquecer" (to forget): "Eu sei o nome dela" / "Eu esqueci o nome dela". For a male person, use "nome dele"; for “your name,” use "seu nome" or "o teu nome" (Portugal).
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu não lembro o nome dela.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t remember her name.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male person’s name. Common after verbs and expressions like “precisar de” (to need), “lembrar-se de” (to remember), and in questions like “Qual era...?” (What was...?). In Portuguese you often say “o nome dele” / “do nome dele” instead of a single word like “his.” For a female person, use “nome dela” (“her name”).
target_language_example: Desculpa, esqueci o nome dele.
native_language_example: Sorry, I forgot his name.

additional_notes: Used to contrast someone’s real name with a nickname, stage name, online username, or a false name. Often appears with possessives: "meu nome verdadeiro" (my real name), "o nome verdadeiro dela" (her real name).
target_language_example: Qual é o seu nome verdadeiro?
native_language_example: What is your real name?

additional_notes: Used to identify a person/thing: "O meu nome é..." (My name is...), "O seu nome é...?" (Is your name...?). You can also use it in a more dramatic/metaphorical way to label something: "X, o teu nome é Y" (“X, your name is Y!” meaning “X is the very definition of Y”).
target_language_example: Prazer, o meu nome é Ana.
native_language_example: Nice to meet you, my name is Ana.

additional_notes: Used as an adjective or noun: um autor norte-americano (a North American author), uma empresa norte-americana (a North American/U.S. company). In many contexts it specifically means “from the United States,” though it can literally mean “from North America” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ela trabalha para uma empresa norte-americana.
native_language_example: She works for a North American/U.S. company.

additional_notes: Means that something happens during weekends in general (habitually/typically). Literally “in the ends of the week,” and often used when talking about how busy a place gets or whether someone works on weekends.
target_language_example: O shopping fica lotado nos finais de semana.
native_language_example: The mall gets crowded on weekends.

additional_notes: Literally “in the ends of the week.” Used to talk about what you usually do on Saturdays and Sundays. Very common with habitual expressions like sempre (always), geralmente (usually), and with verbs like gostar de (to like to), ir (to go), jogar (to play).
target_language_example: Nos fins de semana, eu costumo dormir até mais tarde.
native_language_example: On weekends, I usually sleep in.

meaning: in the back; at the back (in the rear area).
additional_notes: Used for location: the back of a room, classroom, bus, theater, etc. Can also mean in a back area of a place/building (e.g., the backyard or back part of a store). Often answers “where?” (onde?).
target_language_example: O banheiro fica nos fundos do restaurante.
native_language_example: The bathroom is in the back of the restaurant.

additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "os" (= "nos") + "meus" (= "my", masculine plural). Used before a masculine plural noun to mean “in my / on my / during my,” depending on the noun: "nos meus planos" (in my plans), "nos meus dias de folga" (on my days off), "nos meus tempos de escola" (in my school days). Feminine plural is "nas minhas".
target_language_example: Nos meus fins de semana, eu gosto de descansar em casa.
native_language_example: On my weekends, I like to relax at home.

additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "os" + "olhos" → "nos olhos". Often used with verbs like "olhar" to mean looking someone directly in the eyes ("olhar nos olhos"). It can also describe something seen in someone’s eyes (e.g., truth, tears) or physical sensations in the eyes (e.g., pain).
target_language_example: Ele olhou nos meus olhos e disse a verdade.
native_language_example: He looked me in the eyes and told the truth.

meaning: in the last / over the past (…); in the final (…).
additional_notes: Used with a time period or part of something to refer to the most recent part: nos últimos anos/dias/meses (“in the last / over the past years/days/months”), nos últimos cem metros (“in the last 100 meters”). Often implies a change or something happening during that recent period.
target_language_example: Nos últimos meses, tenho trabalhado muito.
native_language_example: In the last few months, I’ve been working a lot.

additional_notes: "Nos" is an object pronoun meaning "us" (the people receiving the action). "Ajudar" means "to help." In Brazilian Portuguese, object pronouns like "nos" often come before the verb in many sentences (e.g., "vai nos ajudar" = "is going to help us"). You may also see it after the verb in formal European Portuguese or in set structures (e.g., "ajudar-nos").
target_language_example: Você pode nos ajudar com essa tarefa?
native_language_example: Can you help us with this task?

additional_notes: From the verb casar-se (“to get married”), in the nós form of the past (pretérito perfeito): nós nos casamos. The pronoun nos shows it’s reflexive/reciprocal (“we married each other”). Often used with time expressions: há/tem um ano (“a year ago”), há três anos (“three years ago”). In speech it’s common to just say “A gente se casou” or even “A gente casou” (more informal).
target_language_example: Nós nos casamos no ano passado.
native_language_example: We got married last year.
