additional_notes: Used to introduce who/what something is called. It’s a set phrase made from "o nome" (the name) + "do" (= de + o, “of the”). It agrees with masculine singular nouns; with feminine singular use "o nome da" (de + a), and with plural use "o nome dos / o nome das".
target_language_example: Você sabe o nome do professor?
native_language_example: Do you know the teacher’s name?

additional_notes: Used with masculine singular nouns: "o nosso + [masc. singular noun]" (e.g., "o nosso relatório" = "our report"). It can also stand alone as a possessive pronoun meaning "ours" when the noun is understood from context (e.g., "O nosso é melhor" = "Ours is better"). The form changes with gender/number: "a nossa" (fem. sing.), "os nossos" (masc. plural), "as nossas" (fem. plural).
target_language_example: O nosso carro está na garagem.
native_language_example: Our car is in the garage.

additional_notes: Uses the definite article + possessive: "o" (the) + "nosso" (our) + "professor". In Portuguese you often say "o nosso..." where English usually just says "our...". Refers to a specific teacher known to the speaker and listener. Feminine form: "a nossa professora".
target_language_example: O nosso professor vai chegar atrasado hoje.
native_language_example: Our teacher is going to arrive late today.

meaning: "the number" (often a phone number or a specific number).
additional_notes: Means “the number” in general, but in everyday speech it commonly refers to a phone number when the context is contact information (e.g., “Dê-me o número” = “Give me the number”). You’ll also see it with qualifiers: “o número de telefone” (the phone number), “o número errado” (the wrong number).
target_language_example: Você pode me passar o número dela?
native_language_example: Can you give me her number?

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to talk about how many there are, often in statistics or formal writing. It can also appear in the structure “O número de X é de Y” = “The number of X is Y.” The verb often agrees with “número” (singular): “O número de estudantes está caindo…”.
target_language_example: O número de pessoas na fila é de vinte.
native_language_example: The number of people in the line is twenty.

additional_notes: Used to ask for, give, remember/forget, or write down someone’s phone number. Often followed by "de" + person/pronoun: "o número de telefone dele/dela" (his/her phone number), "o número de telefone do João" (João’s phone number). You may also hear the shorter "o telefone" meaning "the phone number" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Você pode me passar o seu número de telefone?
native_language_example: Can you give me your phone number?

meaning: the other side; the other party/side (in a dispute).
additional_notes: Literally "the other side" (o = "the", outro = "other", lado = "side"). Used for a physical opposite side ("do outro lado da rua" = "across the street"), a faraway place ("do outro lado do mundo" = "on the other side of the world"), or the opposing side in a conflict/argument ("o outro lado" = "the other team/party"). It can also be used in everyday contexts like turning a pillow to the cooler side.
target_language_example: Antes de decidir, tente ouvir o outro lado da história.
native_language_example: Before deciding, try to hear the other side of the story.

additional_notes: Used to contrast with "um/uma" (“one”) or to refer to the other person/thing in a pair or group: "Um é vermelho e o outro é branco." It can refer to people or things. In sequences you may also see "um após o outro" (“one after the other”). Feminine form: "a outra".
target_language_example: Pegue uma cadeira e traga a outra para cá.
native_language_example: Take one chair and bring the other one here.

additional_notes: Used with a specific father already known in context (e.g., in a family: o pai, a mãe). It can also mean the “father” of something (founder/creator), as in o pai de uma língua. As an exclamation ("O pai!"), it calls out to or refers to “Dad!”
target_language_example: O pai do Pedro trabalha aqui.
native_language_example: Pedro’s father works here.

additional_notes: Uses the definite article (o = “the”) and the possessive pronoun dela (“of her” / “hers”). It refers to the father of a female person already clear from context. Often used instead of “seu pai” to avoid ambiguity (since seu can mean “his/her/your”).
target_language_example: O pai dela trabalha aqui.
native_language_example: Her father works here.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male person’s father. "dele" means "of him / his" and agrees with the person who owns the father (not with "pai"). For a woman, use "o pai dela" (her father). You may also see "o pai do João" (João’s father).
target_language_example: Eu não conheço o pai dele, mas conheço a mãe dele.
native_language_example: I don't know his father, but I know his mother.

meaning: 'the paper' (material/sheet) or 'the role/part' (in a play, job, or situation).
additional_notes: Most commonly means paper as a material or a sheet/document: "Corte o papel" (cut the paper), "Você leu o papel?" (did you read the document/paper?). It can also mean a role or part someone plays: "Faz o papel de Hamlet" (plays Hamlet) and "conseguiu o papel" (got the role). Context usually makes it clear.
target_language_example: Ele conseguiu o papel principal no filme.
native_language_example: He got the lead role in the movie.

additional_notes: Common in European Portuguese for the first meal of the day. Often used with the verb “tomar” (tomar o pequeno-almoço = to have/eat breakfast). In Brazilian Portuguese, “café da manhã” is more common.
target_language_example: Normalmente tomo o pequeno-almoço às sete.
native_language_example: I usually have breakfast at seven.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular article “o” with the superlative “pior” to refer to the worst situation, outcome, or part of something. Common in fixed expressions like “o pior está por vir” (the worst is yet to come) and “o pior já passou” (the worst is over), and in contrasts like “o melhor / o pior”.
target_language_example: Achei que ia ser difícil, mas o pior já passou.
native_language_example: I thought it was going to be hard, but the worst is over.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an idea/strategy for what you’re going to do: "Qual é o plano?" = "What’s the plan?". "Plano" can also mean a "plan" in the sense of a subscription/tariff (e.g., phone or health plan: "o plano de saúde"), and in film it can mean a "shot" ("um plano"). Gender: masculine (o).
target_language_example: Qual é o plano para amanhã?
native_language_example: What’s the plan for tomorrow?

additional_notes: Masculine singular form used with the definite article o (“the”). Refers to one specific police officer (known from context) or can be used generically (“the officer”). Feminine: a policial. Plural: os policiais / as policiais.
target_language_example: O policial pediu meus documentos.
native_language_example: The police officer asked for my ID.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the place where you wait for the bus. Common in directions with verbs like "ficar" (to be located) and "estar" (to be). In many places, people also say "ponto de autocarro" (more common in Portugal).
target_language_example: Desculpe, onde fica o ponto de ônibus mais próximo?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the nearest bus stop?

additional_notes: Used as a noun meaning “the reason” or “the explanation,” often after verbs like saber/entender/explicar/descobrir. It’s commonly followed by "de" ("o porquê de..." = “the reason for.../why...”), or it can stand alone: "Você quer saber o porquê?". Note the accent: "porquê" (with ê) when it’s a noun with an article (o/um) or when it stands alone as “the why.”
target_language_example: Ninguém sabe o porquê de tanta pressa.
native_language_example: Nobody knows the reason for such a rush.

additional_notes: Used for the storage compartment of a car, usually at the back. Common with the verbs abrir (to open) and fechar (to close): abrir/fechar o porta-malas. Not to be confused with o capô, which is the hood (bonnet) over the engine.
target_language_example: Você pode colocar as malas no porta-malas?
native_language_example: Can you put the suitcases in the trunk?

meaning: the gate (a large door/entrance, often for a yard or building).
additional_notes: Refers to a gate you pass through (e.g., at a house, garden, school, or entrance). In commands like "Para o portão!", it can mean "Go/Head to the gate!" or "Stop at the gate!" depending on context. Feminine: "a porta" = (regular) door; "o portão" is typically bigger.
target_language_example: Encontra-me no portão principal às oito.
native_language_example: Meet me at the main gate at eight.

meaning: the people; the population (as a group).
additional_notes: Refers to people as a collective (a community, the general public, or a nation’s citizens). Often used in political or historical contexts (e.g., voting, fighting, protesting). Singular in form but can mean many people; plural is “os povos” (peoples/nations).
target_language_example: O povo quer mudanças.
native_language_example: The people want change.

meaning: “the president” (a leader of a country, organization, or committee).
additional_notes: Used with the masculine singular definite article o (“the”). It can refer to the head of a country (“o presidente do Brasil”) or the chair/leader of a group (“o presidente do comitê”). Feminine form: a presidenta / a presidente (varies by preference and context).
target_language_example: O presidente do comitê vai falar primeiro.
native_language_example: The committee president will speak first.

additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about how much something costs. Often followed by de + noun to specify what: o preço da entrada (the ticket price). Common in questions like “Qual é o preço…?” or “Você pode me dizer o preço…?”
target_language_example: O preço deste café é muito alto.
native_language_example: The price of this coffee is very high.

meaning: 'the first' (the one in position 1; the earliest).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun (often implied) to mean “the first.” It can refer to a rank/order (o primeiro prêmio = “the first prize”) or to the first person/thing to do something (ser o primeiro = “to be the first”). Feminine form: a primeira.
target_language_example: Ele foi o primeiro a chegar.
native_language_example: He was the first to arrive.

additional_notes: Used for the leader of the government in many parliamentary systems. It’s a masculine noun phrase; for a woman you can also hear/see “a primeira-ministra”. Often appears in news contexts with verbs like renunciar (to resign), se reunir (to meet), and fazer uma declaração (to make a statement).
target_language_example: O primeiro-ministro vai falar na TV hoje à noite.
native_language_example: The prime minister is going to speak on TV tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say who is first to perform an action. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., "o primeiro a entrar"). It agrees with the person: "o primeiro a" (masc. singular), "a primeira a" (fem. singular), "os primeiros a" (masc. plural), "as primeiras a" (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Ela foi a primeira a chegar.
native_language_example: She was the first to arrive.

meaning: the first train (of the day / earliest train).
additional_notes: Used when talking about catching the earliest scheduled train on a route, often in travel or commuting contexts. It’s literal: "o primeiro" = "the first" + "trem" = "train".
target_language_example: Se quisermos chegar cedo, precisamos pegar o primeiro trem.
native_language_example: If we want to arrive early, we need to take the first train.

additional_notes: "Problema" is a masculine noun, so it uses the masculine article "o" (singular). Often used with verbs like "resolver/solucionar" (to solve) or "ter" (to have): "resolver o problema". Plural: "os problemas" (the problems).
target_language_example: Precisamos resolver o problema hoje.
native_language_example: We need to solve the problem today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the main difficulty or bad news before explaining it. Very common in spoken and written Portuguese. Often followed by a full clause: “O problema é que + [subject] + [verb] …”. You can also omit “que” in some cases, but “o problema é que” is the most natural for beginners.
target_language_example: Eu queria ir, mas o problema é que estou sem tempo hoje.
native_language_example: I wanted to go, but the problem is that I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male teacher/instructor, often at school or university. In Portuguese, the article “o” means “the” (masculine singular). You can also use “professor” as a title before a name (e.g., “o professor Quirrell”). Female: “a professora”.
target_language_example: O professor vai explicar a lição de novo.
native_language_example: The teacher is going to explain the lesson again.

meaning: sunset; the setting of the sun.
additional_notes: A common, neutral noun phrase for the time/event when the sun goes down. Often used with verbs like assistir/ver (“watch/see”) and with adjectives like lindo (“beautiful”). The literal sense is “the putting/setting of the sun,” but in English you normally just say “sunset.”
target_language_example: Vamos ver o pôr do sol na praia.
native_language_example: Let's watch the sunset at the beach.

meaning: “as much as you want” / “as long as you want.”
additional_notes: Used to emphasize freedom or permission to do something without a limit. It typically follows a verb (often in the imperative or after “poder”): “Estude o quanto quiser” = “Study as much as you want.” Here, “o quanto” means “how much/how long,” and “quiser” is the subjunctive of “querer” used after expressions of permission/indefinite amount. Often interchangeable with “quanto quiser” in casual speech.
target_language_example: Pode ficar aqui o quanto quiser.
native_language_example: You can stay here as long as you want.

additional_notes: Used for a room in a house or building; very commonly refers to a bedroom. For specific types, it’s often followed by “de …”: “quarto de hóspedes” (guest room). Also used with possession: “o quarto dela” (her room).
target_language_example: Vou arrumar o quarto antes de dormir.
native_language_example: I’m going to tidy the room before going to sleep.

additional_notes: "Quarto" means "room" and often specifically "bedroom" in everyday Portuguese. "Dele" means "his" (literally "of him") and is used after the noun: "o quarto dele" = "his room". You can change the person: "o quarto dela" (her room), "o meu quarto" (my room), "o quarto deles" (their room, masc./mixed), "o quarto delas" (their room, fem.).
target_language_example: Vou deixar suas coisas no quarto dele.
native_language_example: I'll leave your things in his room.

meaning: “what does the…?” / “what is the…?” (used before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to start a question with a feminine singular subject (a + noun): “O que a + [person/thing] + [verb]?” For masculine singular, use “o que o…”, and for plural “o que as…” / “o que os…”. Often translates as “What does…?” or “What is…?” rather than word-for-word.
target_language_example: O que a professora explicou hoje?
native_language_example: What did the teacher explain today?

meaning: "What do you think?" / "What do you think of ...?"
additional_notes: Common way to ask for someone’s opinion. Often used alone ("O que acha?") or with "de" + noun/verb to mean “What do you think about...?” ("O que acha de quatro ou cinco?", "O que acha de irmos agora?"). You can also add who you’re talking to: "O que acha, filha?". In "fazer o que acha certo", it means “do what you think is right.”
target_language_example: O que acha de jantar aqui hoje?
native_language_example: What do you think about having dinner here today?

additional_notes: Used with the verb achar (“to think/to find”) to ask for someone’s opinion or guess about something: o que acha que vai acontecer? (“what do you think will happen?”). In questions like O que acha que está fazendo? it often sounds like a reprimand/challenge (“What do you think you’re doing?”). You’ll also see variations for politeness or formality: O que você acha que…? / O que o senhor(a) acha que…?
target_language_example: O que acha que vai acontecer se a gente atrasar?
native_language_example: What do you think will happen if we’re late?

additional_notes: Used to talk about events or outcomes. Often appears in the pattern "É o que acontece..." = "That’s what happens..." (a general result), or as a question "O que acontece?" = "What’s happening?".
target_language_example: É o que acontece quando você não estuda.
native_language_example: That’s what happens when you don’t study.

additional_notes: Used to ask or state the future outcome of a situation. Literally “the/that which will happen” (o que + future tense of acontecer). Often appears in questions like “O que acontecerá (se...)?” or with “a/ao” to mean “what will happen to...?”
target_language_example: Ninguém sabe o que acontecerá amanhã.
native_language_example: Nobody knows what will happen tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to ask about an event or to refer back to an event that already happened. Often appears after verbs like ver (to see), saber (to know), contar (to tell), and explicar (to explain): “Você viu o que aconteceu?” / “Eu contei o que aconteceu.”
target_language_example: Ninguém sabe o que aconteceu depois da festa.
native_language_example: Nobody knows what happened after the party.

additional_notes: Used to ask about an event or change involving someone or something (often a problem, accident, or unexpected situation). It’s typically followed by a person or thing: "O que aconteceu com o Tom?" / "O que aconteceu com a minha mala?" You’ll also see it inside a longer sentence: "Temos que descobrir o que aconteceu com..."
target_language_example: O que aconteceu com você ontem à noite?
native_language_example: What happened to you last night?

meaning: “what happened to the…?” (referring to a feminine noun/person).
additional_notes: Used to ask about an event or change involving someone/something. It’s the combination of: o que (“what”) + aconteceu (“happened”) + com (“to/with”) + a (“the”, feminine). Replace “a” with “o” for masculine (o que aconteceu com o Tom?) and with a name without the article in some varieties (o que aconteceu com a Maria?).
target_language_example: O que aconteceu com a sua mala?
native_language_example: What happened to your suitcase?

additional_notes: Used to ask about or report an event involving a man/boy (“ele” = him). Very common in questions: “Você sabe o que aconteceu com ele?” You can swap the pronoun: “o que aconteceu com ela?” (to her), “com você?” (to you), “com eles/elas?” (to them). Often used after verbs like “saber” (to know), “perguntar” (to ask), and “se perguntar” (to wonder).
target_language_example: Ninguém sabe ao certo o que aconteceu com ele depois da festa.
native_language_example: No one knows for sure what happened to him after the party.

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone/something’s situation or fate (often when you haven’t seen them/it in a while or something seems wrong). It’s followed by a masculine noun or name with the article “o” (e.g., o Marcus). For feminine nouns/names, use “o que aconteceu com a…?” (e.g., a Maria). In speech and informal writing, you’ll also see “O que aconteceu com…” without the article when it’s clear from context.
target_language_example: O que aconteceu com o seu celular?
native_language_example: What happened to your phone?

o que aconteceu com o seu

target_language_multi_word_term: o que aconteceu com o seu
additional_notes: Used to ask what happened to something that belongs to the person you’re speaking to (often a body part or an object). It’s followed by a masculine noun (o seu braço, o seu carro). With a feminine noun, you’d say: “o que aconteceu com a sua …?” (ex.: a sua perna).
target_language_example: O que aconteceu com o seu celular?
native_language_example: What happened to your phone?

additional_notes: Used to ask about events from a specific past night. "O que aconteceu" is a common way to say "what happened" (past tense). "Naquela" means "that" (referring to a particular night you both know about). Often appears after verbs like "dizer" (to tell) or "contar" (to tell/recount).
target_language_example: Você pode me contar o que aconteceu naquela noite?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what happened that night?

additional_notes: Commonly used in the fixed expression **Aconteça o que aconteça, ...** or placed at the end of a sentence (**..., aconteça o que aconteça.**) to mean “regardless of the situation.” It uses the subjunctive of **acontecer** (“to happen”) and often introduces advice, determination, or reassurance.
target_language_example: Aconteça o que aconteça, eu vou te ajudar.
native_language_example: Whatever happens, I’m going to help you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the necessary or correct action in a situation. Often appears after verbs like dizer (to tell), saber (to know), or fazer (to do): dizer/saber/fazer o que deve ser feito. Literally "what should be done," and it can sound a bit serious or duty-focused (doing what’s necessary).
target_language_example: Vamos fazer o que deve ser feito, mesmo que seja difícil.
native_language_example: Let's do what must be done, even if it's difficult.

meaning: “what should we do” / “what are we supposed to do”.
additional_notes:
Used to ask for advice or the next step to take. It can be followed by:
- “a respeito disso” = about that/that situation
- “com …” = with … / about … (what to do with something/someone)
- “se …” = if … (what to do in a condition)
Verb: “devemos” is the “we” form of “dever” (should/ought to).
target_language_example: Não sei o que devemos fazer agora.
native_language_example: I don’t know what we should do now.

additional_notes: Used to ask what you should say to a specific person or group. The person comes after "a": "a ela" (to her), "a ele" (to him), "a eles" (to them). Often appears as a direct question: "O que devo dizer a ela?"
target_language_example: O que devo dizer a eles sobre o atraso?
native_language_example: What should I tell them about the delay?

additional_notes: Used to ask for advice or instructions about the right next action. "devo" is from "dever" (should/ought to) + "fazer" (to do). You can add context after it, e.g., "O que devo fazer em seguida?" (next), "...com isso?" (with this), "...se eu encontrar um?" (if I find one).
target_language_example: Estou perdido. O que devo fazer agora?
native_language_example: I’m lost. What should I do now?

additional_notes: Used to refer back to something someone said. It’s often used after verbs like retirar (“to take back”) or lamentar (“to regret”). The subject is usually understood from context (e.g., "o que disse" can mean “what I said” or “what he/she said”). "disse" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of dizer (“to say”).
target_language_example: Desculpe, eu não quis dizer o que disse.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t mean what I said.

meaning: “what she …” (used in questions or in the middle of a sentence).
additional_notes: Built from **o que** (“what/that which”) + **ela** (“she”). It can start a question (**O que ela faz aqui?** = “What is she doing here?”) or introduce a clause meaning “what she …” (**…o que ela queria saber** = “…what she wanted to know”). Word order is fixed: **o que** comes before the subject **ela**.
target_language_example: Eu não entendi o que ela disse.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what she said.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of something a woman/girl said. Very common after verbs like entender (to understand), ouvir (to hear), saber (to know), and ficar claro (to be clear): e.g., "Você entendeu o que ela disse?". It’s literally "the what she said" (o que = what/that which; ela disse = she said).
target_language_example: Eu não ouvi o que ela disse.
native_language_example: I didn’t hear what she said.

meaning: 'what she was doing' / 'what was she doing?'.
additional_notes: Used to ask about her actions in the past, often with a sense of surprise or suspicion. "Estava fazendo" is the past progressive (imperfect of estar + gerund), meaning an ongoing action: 'was doing'. It can be a direct question ("O que ela estava fazendo aqui?") or part of a larger sentence after verbs like "saber" ("Só Deus sabe o que ela estava fazendo lá.").
target_language_example: Ninguém entendeu o que ela estava fazendo naquela hora.
native_language_example: Nobody understood what she was doing at that moment.

meaning: 'what they' (refers to a group of females, or a mixed group when referring to women).
additional_notes: Used to start a question or a clause about information/actions involving “elas” (= “they”, feminine plural). Often followed by a verb: “O que elas disseram?” (“What did they say?”). In statements, it can mean “what they ...” as the object of another verb: “Eu sei o que elas fizeram” (“I know what they did”).
target_language_example: Não entendi o que elas quiseram dizer.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what they meant.

meaning: what they mean (what they want to say).
additional_notes: Used to ask about or state the meaning/intention of what “they” (elas) said or did. Often appears as a question: “O que elas querem dizer?” (“What do they mean?”). You can also add “com isso” to mean “by that/with that”: “O que elas querem dizer com isso?”
target_language_example: Não entendi — o que elas querem dizer com isso?
native_language_example: I didn’t understand—what do they mean by that?

additional_notes: Used to introduce what a man said, thinks, did, wants, etc. It often appears before a verb: “o que ele disse” (what he said), “o que ele acha” (what he thinks), “o que ele pediu” (what he asked for). In questions, “O que ele…?” means “What does he…?”.
target_language_example: Não entendi o que ele quis dizer.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what he meant.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of something a man (ele = he) said. Often appears after verbs like entender (to understand), ouvir (to hear), repetir (to repeat), and achar (to think). You can swap ele for other subjects: o que ela disse (what she said), o que você disse (what you said).
target_language_example: Eu não acredito no que ele disse.
native_language_example: I can't believe what he said.

meaning: “what he was doing” / “what was he doing?”
additional_notes: Literally “what he was doing.” It can be used as (1) an embedded clause after another verb: "...terminar o que ele estava fazendo" (“...finish what he was doing”), or (2) as a direct question: "O que ele estava fazendo aqui/lá?" (“What was he doing here/there?”). Uses the imperfect past "estava fazendo" to talk about an ongoing action in the past.
target_language_example: Eu não entendi o que ele estava fazendo.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what he was doing.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an action done by a specific man (“he”). Often introduces a clause as the subject of the sentence (“O que ele fez foi…” = “What he did was…”). In questions, it asks about his action (“O que ele fez?” = “What did he do?”).
target_language_example: Eu não consigo esquecer o que ele fez.
native_language_example: I can’t forget what he did.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the thing a man/boy wants. It can be a statement (Ele está fazendo o que ele quer. = “He’s doing what he wants.”) or a direct question (O que ele quer? = “What does he want?”). In conversation, people often drop the subject for a more natural sound: “o que quer?” / “o que você quer?”.
target_language_example: Eu não sei o que ele quer de verdade.
native_language_example: I don’t know what he really wants.

additional_notes: Used to say you are giving a male person freedom to choose an action or thing. It often follows verbs like deixar (“to let”) or poder (“to be allowed/can”): “deixar + [person] + o que ele quiser” = “let [him] do whatever he wants.” The structure is literally “what he wants,” but it functions like English “whatever he wants.” (For a woman: “o que ela quiser.”)
target_language_example: Deixa ele escolher o que ele quiser.
native_language_example: Let him choose whatever he wants.

additional_notes: Used to refer to something done, said, known, or thought by a group of people (eles = “they”). Common in questions (e.g., “O que eles sabem?” = “What do they know?”) and in sentences where it means “what(ever) they…” (e.g., “comer o que eles me dão” = “eat what they give me”).
target_language_example: Eu vou perguntar o que eles decidiram.
native_language_example: I’m going to ask what they decided.

additional_notes: Used to ask about or refer to the content of what a group of people (“eles” = they) said. Very common after verbs like ouvir (to hear), descobrir (to find out), and saber (to know): “Você ouviu o que eles disseram?” You can swap “eles” for other pronouns: “o que ela disse” (what she said), “o que você disse” (what you said).
target_language_example: Eu não entendi o que eles disseram.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what they said.

meaning: "what were they …" (used to ask what they were doing/using/wearing, etc.).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question. It’s typically followed by a verb in the gerund (estavam + verb ending in -ando/-endo/-indo) to mean “were doing” (past continuous): e.g., “O que eles estavam fazendo?” = “What were they doing?” The pronoun “eles” means “they” (masculine or mixed group). For “they” (all women), you can also see “elas”: “O que elas estavam…”.
target_language_example: O que eles estavam fazendo ontem à noite?
native_language_example: What were they doing last night?

meaning: “what are they …” (used to start a question).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a verb in the -ndo form to ask about an action happening now: “O que eles estão fazendo?” = “What are they doing?” In statements, the word order can change (“… é o que eles estão …”).
target_language_example: O que eles estão procurando?
native_language_example: What are they looking for?

meaning: "what are they doing?" / "what they are doing."
additional_notes: Literally "what they are doing." Use it as a direct question (often with a question mark): "O que eles estão fazendo?" = "What are they doing?" It can also appear inside a longer sentence without being a question: "Eu sei o que eles estão fazendo." = "I know what they are doing." Here, "eles" = "they" (masculine/mixed group), and "estão fazendo" is the present continuous (estar + gerund) for actions happening now/around now.
target_language_example: Você viu o que eles estão fazendo na rua?
native_language_example: Did you see what they're doing in the street?

additional_notes: Often used to ask about an action ("What did they do?") or to introduce a statement about their action ("What they did was wrong"). Tense depends on context: in questions it can be simple past (“did”) or present perfect (“have done”). If you add a complement, it specifies the target or purpose: "com você" (to you/with you), "para você" (for you).
target_language_example: Eu não acredito no que eles fizeram.
native_language_example: I can’t believe what they did.

additional_notes: Used to ask about or state their desire/goal. Often appears in questions ("O que eles querem?") and in statements like "Sei..." (I know...) or "Você tem..." (You have...). In phrases like "O que eles querem com o Tom?", it can mean "What do they want with Tom?" (= what is their purpose involving Tom).
target_language_example: Não entendo o que eles querem de nós.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what they want from us.

meaning: "what they mean" / "what they’re trying to say."
additional_notes: Used to ask about or state the meaning/intent behind someone’s words or actions. Often followed by "com isso?" (= "by that?" / "with that?") when you’re asking what someone means by a specific thing. "querer dizer" is the common verb phrase for "to mean" (literally "to want to say").
target_language_example: Não entendi o que eles querem dizer com essa mensagem.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what they mean by that message.

meaning: "what it/that used to be"; or "what it was" (in indirect questions).
additional_notes: Common in two patterns: (1) "não é mais o que era" = “it’s not what it used to be anymore” (often about quality, power, status, etc.). (2) In indirect questions after verbs like perguntar/perguntar-se/saber/dizer: "perguntei-lhe o que era" = “I asked him what it was.” It can also refer back to a whole idea: "..., o que era uma mentira" = “..., which was a lie.”
target_language_example: Este restaurante não é mais o que era.
native_language_example: This restaurant isn’t what it used to be anymore.

additional_notes: Used to ask what you and other people ("we") are doing, often to question the plan, what you’re doing in a place ("aqui" = here), what you’re doing wrong ("de errado" = wrong), or why you’re standing still ("parados" = stopped/standing around). Can also be used inside a longer sentence to refer to the action you’re doing now (e.g., "...o que estamos fazendo agora" = what we’re doing now).
target_language_example: O que estamos fazendo aqui tão cedo?
native_language_example: What are we doing here so early?

meaning: "what was" / "that which was" (followed by a verb phrase).
additional_notes: Used to refer to something that was happening/being/owing at a past moment: (1) as a relative clause after a verb like esconder/ler/pagar (“hide/read/pay what was…”), or (2) in a question meaning “what was …?” Often followed by a present participle or past participle: "o que estava acontecendo" (what was happening), "o que estava escrito" (what was written).
target_language_example: Não entendi o que estava acontecendo na reunião.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what was happening in the meeting.

meaning: what was happening / what was going on.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a situation or event that was in progress in the past. Very common after verbs like ver (to see), perceber (to notice/realize), contar (to tell), and perguntar (to ask): "Ele viu/percebeu o que estava acontecendo". In questions, you’ll often hear the shorter form "O que está acontecendo?" (What’s happening?) for the present.
target_language_example: Eu não entendi o que estava acontecendo na reunião.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what was happening in the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to an activity already in progress in the past. Often appears after verbs like parar (to stop), terminar (to finish), continuar (to continue), or saber (to know), and can refer to the subject (ele/ela) or another person from context.
target_language_example: Ela continuou o que estava fazendo quando eu cheguei.
native_language_example: She continued what she was doing when I arrived.

meaning: 'what is' / 'what’s' (used to ask what is happening or going on).
additional_notes: Used at the start of questions. Often followed by a verb to form expressions like: "O que está acontecendo?" (What’s happening?), "O que está havendo?" (What’s going on?), or more informal options like "O que está rolando?" / "O que está pegando?". In European Portuguese you may also see "o que está a + infinitive" (e.g., "o que está a pedir" = what you’re asking for).
target_language_example: O que está acontecendo aqui?
native_language_example: What’s happening here?

additional_notes: Used to ask what is happening right now (often because something seems strange or unexpected). Very common in conversation. You can add a place/person for emphasis: “O que está acontecendo aqui?” (“What’s going on here?”). Also used inside a longer sentence: “Você sabe o que está acontecendo?” (“Do you know what’s happening?”).
target_language_example: Ei, o que está acontecendo aqui?
native_language_example: Hey, what’s going on here?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the text you can read on something (a sign, wall, shirt, book, etc.). Often used in questions like “O que está escrito aqui/ali?” = “What does it say here/there?”
target_language_example: O que está escrito na placa?
native_language_example: What does the sign say?

additional_notes: A very common question using the verb "fazer" (to do/make) in the present continuous: "estar" + gerund ("está fazendo" = "is doing"). Often said as a direct question to someone, sometimes with extra words like "agora" (now) or "aí" (there/over there). You’ll also hear the more informal short form: "O que você tá fazendo?"
target_language_example: Ei, o que está fazendo aqui?
native_language_example: Hey, what are you doing here?

meaning: “what are you (plural) doing?” / “what they are doing.”
additional_notes: Built from: o que (“what”) + estão (present of estar for “you all/they”) + fazendo (gerund of fazer, “doing”). It can be a direct question (often with a question mark): “O que estão fazendo aqui?” = “What are you (all) doing here?” It can also be used inside a longer sentence as an embedded question/statement: “Eu sei o que estão fazendo.” = “I know what they’re doing.” The subject is usually “you all” (vocês) or “they” (eles/elas), depending on context.
target_language_example: Não entendo o que estão fazendo com esse computador.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what they’re doing with that computer.

meaning: 'what I' / 'what that I…' (introduces a clause about something you do/think/say).
additional_notes: Used to start a question (“O que eu faço?” = “What do I do?”) or to introduce a relative clause after a verb (“Eu comprei o que eu precisava” = “I bought what I needed”). Often followed by a verb: o que eu preciso, o que eu disse, o que eu acho. With a direct object verb like “entender”, it can mean “what I meant/said”: “Você entendeu o que eu quis dizer?”
target_language_example: Eu não sei o que eu devo dizer agora.
native_language_example: I don’t know what I should say now.

meaning: “What should I do?” / “What was I supposed to do?”
additional_notes: Used to ask for advice or guidance. In the present/future sense, it’s often like “What should I do (now)?” even though it uses the conditional form deveria. It can also refer to an expectation in the past: “What was I supposed to do?” You can swap the subject: “O que você deveria fazer?” (What should you do?).
target_language_example: Não sei o que eu deveria fazer; você pode me ajudar?
native_language_example: I don’t know what I should do; can you help me?

meaning: "What should I do?" / "What am I supposed to do?"
additional_notes: Used to ask for advice or instructions. You can add details with "com" (what to do with something), "por" (what to do for someone), or "se" (what to do if something happens). In conversation, people often shorten it to "O que devo fazer?"
target_language_example: Não sei o que eu devo fazer agora.
native_language_example: I don’t know what I should do now.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of what the speaker says. Very common after verbs like escutar/ouvir (“listen”), entender (“understand”), acreditar (“believe”), and fazer (“do”): e.g., “Escute o que eu digo” = “Listen to what I’m saying.” In commands it can sound firm (like “Do what I say”). Often appears with tudo (“everything”): tudo o que eu digo = “everything I say.”
target_language_example: Por favor, preste atenção no que eu digo.
native_language_example: Please pay attention to what I’m saying.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to your own words (something you said earlier). Often appears after verbs like entender (to understand), esquecer (to forget), lembrar (to remember), repetir (to repeat). Can also be used as a question: "O que eu disse?" = "What did I say?"
target_language_example: Repete o que eu disse, por favor.
native_language_example: Repeat what I said, please.

meaning: "What do I do?" / "What should I do?"
additional_notes: Often used as a question asking for advice or what action to take next ("So what do I do?", "What do I do until then?"). It can also be used more literally to ask what to do with something/someone: "O que eu faço com você?" = "What am I going to do with you?". In statements, it can mean "what I do" as the subject: "O que eu faço é problema meu." = "What I do is my problem."
target_language_example: Eu estou perdido—o que eu faço agora?
native_language_example: I’m lost—what do I do now?

additional_notes: Used to talk about an action you performed, often introducing an explanation or asking someone to notice it. It can be a direct question/statement ("Você viu o que eu fiz?"), or part of a longer sentence ("O que eu fiz foi errado" / "Espero que o que eu fiz tenha ajudado").
target_language_example: Vou te contar o que eu fiz depois da aula.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you what I did after class.

meaning: “What can I do?” / “What can I do to…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask what actions are possible or advisable, often offering help or asking for guidance (e.g., “...para ajudar” = “to help”, “...para me proteger” = “to protect myself”, “...por vocês” = “for you”). It can be a full question by itself (“O que eu posso fazer?”) or followed by a purpose with para + infinitive.
target_language_example: Não sei como resolver isso — o que eu posso fazer?
native_language_example: I don’t know how to solve this—what can I do?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the thing(s) you desire. Often appears after a main clause (e.g., “Dá-me…”) or at the start of a sentence to introduce your desire. In requests, Portuguese commonly uses the verb querer (“to want”) in the present tense; for politeness you can add words like “por favor” or use “eu gostaria” (“I would like”).
target_language_example: Eu sei exatamente o que eu quero.
native_language_example: I know exactly what I want.

o que eu quero agora é

target_language_multi_word_term: o que eu quero agora é
additional_notes: Used to introduce (and often emphasize) the specific thing you want at the moment. Very common in spoken Portuguese. You can also hear/see it with intensifiers like “Tudo o que eu quero agora é...” (“All I want right now is...”).
target_language_example: O que eu quero agora é descansar um pouco.
native_language_example: What I want right now is to rest a little.

meaning: 'what I mean' / 'what I'm trying to say'.
additional_notes: Used to clarify your meaning or check if someone understands you. Often appears in questions like “Você entende o que eu quero dizer?” (= “Do you know what I mean?”). Literally it’s “what I want to say,” but in everyday Portuguese it commonly means “what I mean.”
target_language_example: Não sei se você entendeu o que eu quero dizer.
native_language_example: I don't know if you understood what I mean.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize your real desire/intention, often introducing a noun or an infinitive phrase (e.g., "amor", "sair daqui"). Very common in spoken Portuguese to clarify or contrast with other possibilities (similar to “What I really want is…”).
target_language_example: O que eu quero é descansar um pouco.
native_language_example: What I want is to rest a little.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to something you previously said to the other person. Often appears in reminders or checks, like “Remember what I told you,” “Tell him what I told you,” or “What did I tell you about that?” You may also see variations like “o que eu disse” (what I said) or “o que eu te disse sobre…” (what I told you about…).
target_language_example: Não esquece o que eu te disse ontem, tá?
native_language_example: Don’t forget what I told you yesterday, okay?

additional_notes: Literally "the thing that I have." Often appears as a question: "O que eu tenho?" (“What’s wrong with me?” / “What do I have?”). Very common in the pattern "o que eu tenho a + infinitive" to mean “what I have to + verb,” especially in set phrases like "o que eu tenho a ganhar?" (“what do I have to gain?”) and "o que eu tenho a perder?" (“what do I have to lose?”).
target_language_example: No fim das contas, o que eu tenho a perder?
native_language_example: At the end of the day, what do I have to lose?

meaning: “what am I going to do?” / “what I’m going to do.”
additional_notes: Common with **vou** (near-future with *ir* + infinitive): *eu vou fazer* = “I’m going to do (something).” It can be a **question** (*O que eu vou fazer?* “What am I going to do?”) or a **statement introducing a plan** (*O que eu vou fazer é…* “What I’m going to do is…”). Often followed by **com isso** (“with this”), **sobre isso** (“about this”), etc.
target_language_example: Não sei o que eu vou fazer agora.
native_language_example: I don’t know what I’m going to do now.

additional_notes:
Literally "what (you/he/she/it) does" (o que + fazer). Very common as a question:
- To ask what someone is doing, often when you see them somewhere unexpected: "O que faz aí/aqui?" = "What are you doing there/here?"
- In more general/abstract questions, it means "What makes...": "O que faz de nós humanos?" = "What makes us human?"
By itself ("O que faz?"), it usually means "What are you doing?" and can sound a bit abrupt depending on tone; you can soften with "Desculpe" or "O que você está fazendo?" (Brazil) / "O que estás a fazer?" (Portugal).
target_language_example: Ei, o que faz aqui tão cedo?
native_language_example: Hey, what are you doing here so early?

o que faz você pensar que

target_language_multi_word_term: o que faz você pensar que
additional_notes: Used to challenge or ask for the reason/evidence behind someone’s belief or assumption. Very common in conversation. You can also say "O que te faz pensar que..." (more informal) or "O que o(a) faz pensar que..." (more formal). Often followed by a full clause: "... ele gosta de você", "... você pode fazer isso".
target_language_example: O que faz você pensar que isso vai dar certo?
native_language_example: What makes you think that this will work?

additional_notes: Used when you’re talking about the best action or next step. Often appears after verbs like saber (to know) and discutir (to discuss): "não sei o que fazer" (I don’t know what to do). It can also imply being told what actions to take: "me dizem o que fazer" (they tell me what to do).
target_language_example: Não sei o que fazer agora.
native_language_example: I don’t know what to do now.

additional_notes: Used to ask for instructions or advice about how to handle something. Often appears after verbs like saber (to know): "Você sabe o que fazer com isto?". "Isto" means "this" (usually something close to the speaker); you can also hear "o que fazer com isso" with "isso" (that/this near the listener or already mentioned).
target_language_example: Não sei o que fazer com isto.
native_language_example: I don’t know what to do with this.

additional_notes: Used in two very common ways: (1) as “what (someone) did” in statements like "Vi o que fez" (“I saw what you did”); (2) in questions with fazer meaning “to make/cause,” often followed by a person + infinitive: "O que fez o Tom parar?" (“What made Tom stop?”). It can also appear with "fazer com" meaning “do with”: "O que fez com ele?" (“What did you do with him?”).
target_language_example: Não entendi o que fez você mudar de ideia.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what made you change your mind.

additional_notes: Used mostly in questions to add emphasis or insistence, similar to “what on earth…?” but not necessarily rude. It combines: o que (“what”) + foi (past of ser, “was”) + que (linking “that”). It can also appear in a relative structure like “seja o que foi que…” = “whatever it was that…”. In everyday speech, people often shorten it to “o que que…?” or just “o que…?”.
target_language_example: O que foi que você disse agora?
native_language_example: What was it that you just said?

additional_notes: Used to refer to an event in the past that happened before another past moment (past perfect: "havia" + past participle). Often appears after verbs like saber (to know), contar (to tell), and pedir (to ask). You may also hear/see: "o que tinha acontecido" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Eu expliquei ao policial o que havia acontecido.
native_language_example: I explained to the police officer what had happened.

additional_notes: Used to ask about an event or problem, often with "com" + a person/thing: "O que houve com a Dani?" = "What happened to Dani?" You can also use it with a time word like "ontem" (yesterday) or as a statement: "Já sabemos o que houve" = "We already know what happened."
target_language_example: Ei, o que houve com você?
native_language_example: Hey, what happened to you?

additional_notes: Used to ask about an event or change affecting a person/thing (often when something seems wrong, surprising, or you’re looking for an update). It’s the past of haver (“houve” = “there was/there happened”), so it typically refers to something that already happened.
target_language_example: O que houve com o seu celular? Ele não está ligando.
native_language_example: What happened to your phone? It won’t turn on.

additional_notes: Used to ask what exists or is present in a place or container, often followed by a location phrase like "na caixa" (in the box), "na geladeira" (in the fridge), or "embaixo" (underneath). Literally "the/what + there is" (from "haver" = to exist/be present), but in everyday questions it corresponds to "what's there?" or "what's inside?".
target_language_example: O que há dentro dessa bolsa?
native_language_example: What’s inside that bag?

additional_notes: Used to ask what the problem is. Often followed by "com" + a person/thing: "O que há de errado com ele?" (“What’s wrong with him?”). It can also be used with a place/situation: "O que há de errado nesta fazenda?" (“What’s wrong on this farm/with this farm?”).
target_language_example: O que há de errado com o computador?
native_language_example: What’s wrong with the computer?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the meaning or interpretation of something (“isso” = “that/this” in context). Often appears as a direct question: “O que isso significa?” or inside a longer sentence: “Você pode me dizer o que isso significa?” It can also mean “what does this mean for…?” as in “O que isso significa para o Tom?”
target_language_example: Desculpe, não entendi—o que isso significa?
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t understand—what does that mean?

o que isso tem a ver com

target_language_multi_word_term: o que isso tem a ver com
meaning: “what does that have to do with …?” / “what does that have to do with it …?”
additional_notes: Used to question the connection or relevance between two things, often when something seems unrelated (sometimes with an annoyed or skeptical tone). Usually followed by a noun or person: “O que isso tem a ver com o Tom?” You’ll also hear variations like “O que isso tem a ver?” (What does that have to do with it?)
target_language_example: O que isso tem a ver com o trabalho que precisamos fazer hoje?
native_language_example: What does that have to do with the work we need to do today?

additional_notes: Used when **lhe** refers to the person affected/concerned (an indirect object), common in questions and statements: *O que lhe aconteceu?* (“What happened to you/him/her?”). **Lhe** can mean **to him / to her / to you (formal)** depending on context. You’ll often see it before the verb: *O que lhe falta é...* (“What you lack is...”), or in rhetorical questions: *O que lhe interessa...?* (“What business is it of yours...?/Why do you care...?”).
target_language_example: O que lhe disseram sobre a reunião?
native_language_example: What did they tell you/him/her about the meeting?

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask for additional information or another option (“What else can you tell me?”). It can also appear in statements like “o que mais você precisa fazer” = “what else you need to do” (i.e., additional things).
target_language_example: O que mais você quer saber?
native_language_example: What else do you want to know?

meaning: “What else did you…?” / “What more did you…?” (asking for additional things or information).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to ask for extra items, actions, details, or information beyond what was already mentioned. The verb comes after it: “O que mais você fez/viu/quer/precisa…?”. Often translates naturally as “What else…?” rather than literally “What more you…”.
target_language_example: O que mais você quer saber?
native_language_example: What else do you want to know?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause referring to something done, said, wanted, asked for, etc., by 'we' (nós). Often appears in phrases like "o que nós fizemos" (what we did) or "o que nós queremos" (what we want). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people also commonly say "o que a gente" instead of "o que nós".
target_language_example: Vou explicar o que nós decidimos na reunião.
native_language_example: I’m going to explain what we decided in the meeting.

additional_notes:
A common question used to ask about plans, next steps, or how to deal with a problem. Often followed by:
- "com" + noun/pronoun: "O que nós vamos fazer com isso?" (What are we going to do with this?)
- "hoje/amanhã" etc.: "O que nós vamos fazer hoje?" (What are we going to do today?)
- "sobre" + person/thing: "O que nós vamos fazer sobre o Tom?" (What are we going to do about Tom?)
"nós" can be replaced by "a gente" in informal speech: "O que a gente vai fazer?"
target_language_example: O que nós vamos fazer depois do almoço?
native_language_example: What are we going to do after lunch?

meaning: "what" / "that which" (followed by a masculine singular subject, often a name).
additional_notes: This is really the common structure **o que** (“what/that which”) + **o** (“the”, masculine singular) that appears right before a masculine noun/name that is the subject of the clause: **o que o Tom fez** = “what Tom did.” It can introduce a statement (**Eu vi o que o Tom fez.**) or a question (**O que o Tom fez agora?**). With a feminine subject, you’d see **o que a...** (e.g., **o que a Maria disse**).
target_language_example: Eu não entendi o que o professor explicou.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what the teacher explained.

meaning: "what the" (introduces a question or statement about a plural masculine group/thing).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun with the article "os" (e.g., "O que os médicos disseram?" = "What did the doctors say?"). It often starts a question meaning "What do the ...? / What did the ...?" and the verb comes later. It can also appear in statements like "X é o que os Y merecem" ("X is what the Y deserve"). For feminine plural, use "o que as"; for singular, "o que o" / "o que a".
target_language_example: O que os alunos querem aprender hoje?
native_language_example: What do the students want to learn today?

additional_notes: Used to ask about possible actions or solutions. Often followed by “para + infinitive” (purpose): “O que podemos fazer para ajudar?” (= What can we do to help?). It can also be used with “por você” meaning “for you” (what we can do to help you).
target_language_example: O que podemos fazer agora para resolver isso?
native_language_example: What can we do now to solve this?

meaning: 'what can I do' / 'what can I do (to help)?'
additional_notes: Used to ask what actions are possible or appropriate in a situation, often when offering help or looking for a solution. Very common pattern: “O que posso fazer para + verb” (e.g., para ajudar, para te convencer). Pronouns can change: “para lhe ajudar” (more formal), “para te ajudar” (informal). You may also see different prepositions depending on meaning: “pela vida dele” (“for his life / on his behalf”) or “sem os meus amigos” (“without my friends”).
target_language_example: O que posso fazer para melhorar o meu português?
native_language_example: What can I do to improve my Portuguese?

additional_notes: Common polite question to offer help or service. Usually followed by a person/pronoun (por você/ti/ela/ele/eles/elas) or a name. In customer-service contexts, you’ll also hear: “O que posso fazer por você?”
target_language_example: Olá! O que posso fazer por você hoje?
native_language_example: Hi! What can I do for you today?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the necessary actions in a situation. It’s a common, neutral phrase in instructions and explanations. Literally: o que (what) + precisa (needs) + ser feito (to be done). You can change the tense/person of "precisar": e.g., "o que precisava ser feito" (what needed to be done).
target_language_example: Vamos decidir o que precisa ser feito primeiro.
native_language_example: Let’s decide what needs to be done first.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified item or set of items that a person needed. It often appears after verbs like pegar (to pick up), comprar (to buy), encontrar (to find), or conseguir (to manage to). The subject is understood from context (e.g., “você” in “o que precisava” = “what you needed”).
target_language_example: Eu já tenho o que precisava para a viagem.
native_language_example: I already have what I needed for the trip.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a task or set of actions that are necessary. Often appears after verbs like saber (“to know”), dizer (“to say”), or haver (“there is/are”) and is common in more formal or written Portuguese. Grammar note: “precisava” = “needed/was necessary,” and “ser feito” = “to be done” (passive/impersonal).
target_language_example: Eu já sei o que precisava ser feito, então vou começar agora.
native_language_example: I already know what needed to be done, so I’m going to start now.

meaning: 'what do you want…?' / 'what would you like…?'.
additional_notes: Uses "quer" (from *querer*, 'to want') with an implied subject, usually **você**: "O que quer comer?" = "O que (você) quer comer?" Common in questions before an infinitive (comer, fazer, beber). You may also hear "O que você quer…?" (more explicit).
target_language_example: O que quer fazer hoje?
native_language_example: What do you want to do today?

additional_notes: Used to ask for clarification about the meaning or intention of something. Often appears as a question ("O que quer dizer?"), and you can add "com ..." to specify what exactly you’re asking about: "O que quer dizer com 'muito tempo'?". In statements, it can also mean 'to mean' in the sense of intention: "Entendo o que quer dizer" = 'I understand what you mean.'
target_language_example: Desculpa, o que quer dizer com isso?
native_language_example: Sorry, what do you mean by that?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a concession: the speaker says something will be true in all cases. Often appears at the beginning of a sentence, followed by a comma. The verb is in the present subjunctive (aconteça from acontecer). You can also use it after another clause: “Eu vou te ajudar, o que quer que aconteça.”
target_language_example: O que quer que aconteça, vamos ficar juntos.
native_language_example: Whatever happens, we’ll stay together.

o que quer que eu faça

target_language_multi_word_term: o que quer que eu faça
meaning: “What do you want me to do?” / “Whatever you want me to do.”
additional_notes: Used to ask what action someone expects from you, often with a frustrated, resigned, or challenging tone (“What do you expect me to do?”). Literally uses the subjunctive (faça) after “quer que…”. You can add a name/title (Tom, senhor) or an interjection like “hein?” to emphasize the tone.
target_language_example: O que quer que eu faça agora?
native_language_example: What do you want me to do now?

additional_notes: Literally “the thing that we want.” Used to introduce or refer back to a specific desired thing/goal (“O que queremos é…”) or to mean “whatever we want” after verbs like fazer/ter (“Fazemos/temos o que queremos”). Often contrasts desire vs. reality: “Não é o que queremos, mas…”.
target_language_example: O que queremos agora é descansar.
native_language_example: What we want now is to rest.

additional_notes: Often used after verbs like conseguir (to get/achieve), encontrar (to find), comer (to eat), dizer (to tell) to refer to the desired thing. Queria is the imperfect of querer (to want), so it commonly describes an ongoing desire in the past or what someone wanted at that time. The subject is often understood from context (e.g., ele/ela queria; você queria).
target_language_example: Finalmente encontrei o que queria.
native_language_example: I finally found what I wanted.

additional_notes: Often used as part of a longer structure like "(Eu faço) o que quero" (“I do what I want”) or "O que quero é..." (“What I want is...”), where "o que" means “what/that which” + "quero" (“I want”).
target_language_example: O que quero é um café sem açúcar.
native_language_example: What I want is a coffee without sugar.

additional_notes: Used to give someone complete freedom of choice. It’s built from "o que" (what) + "quiser" (subjunctive of querer, 'to want'), and often follows verbs like comer, beber, escolher, fazer: "Beba o que quiser" = "Drink whatever you want." (In practice, many people also say "o que quiserem" with "eles/elas".)
target_language_example: Pode pedir o que quiser no cardápio.
native_language_example: You can order whatever you want from the menu.

meaning: "whatever you want" (to do/eat/read/etc.), addressed to more than one person.
additional_notes: Uses the plural (vocês) form: quiserem = "(you all) want". It often expresses permission or indifference: "do/read/eat whatever you want". With an imperative or permission phrase (podem/tem permissão), it can sound friendly or dismissive depending on tone.
target_language_example: Podem escolher o que quiserem para o jantar.
native_language_example: You can choose whatever you want for dinner.

additional_notes: Common in questions when you’re guessing or wondering about something, often without expecting a definite answer. It can sound softer/more thoughtful than simply "O que...?". The "será" here is from "ser" and helps express uncertainty (similar to "could it be that...").
target_language_example: O que será que ela quis dizer com isso?
native_language_example: I wonder what she meant by that.

additional_notes: Used to ask for the meaning of a word, phrase, sentence, paragraph, or situation. Often followed by what you’re asking about: “O que significa esta palavra/frase/isso?” You can also embed it in a longer question: “Você pode me dizer o que significa …?”
target_language_example: Desculpe, o que significa “saudade”?
native_language_example: Sorry, what does “saudade” mean?

meaning: “what … you” (used to start a question about what causes/affects you).
additional_notes: Used at the beginning of questions. "o que" = “what”; "te" is the unstressed object pronoun “you” (to you). It often appears with verbs like "faz" (makes), "impediu" (prevented), "mantém" (keeps), etc., to mean “what makes you…?”, “what stopped you…?”, “what keeps you…?” The verb that follows determines the exact meaning.
target_language_example: O que te deixou tão feliz hoje?
native_language_example: What made you so happy today?

o que te faz pensar que

target_language_multi_word_term: o que te faz pensar que
additional_notes: Used to challenge or ask for the reason/evidence behind someone’s belief or assumption. It’s a question that often sounds skeptical or confrontational (depending on tone). Typically followed by a full clause with que: “O que te faz pensar que ele está mentindo?”
target_language_example: O que te faz pensar que ela vai aceitar o convite?
native_language_example: What makes you think she’s going to accept the invitation?

o que te fez pensar que eu era

target_language_multi_word_term: o que te fez pensar que eu era
meaning: “What made you think that I was…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason/evidence behind someone’s belief about you. Very common with an adjective or description after “era”: “O que te fez pensar que eu era mais jovem?” You can swap “te” for “lhe” for a more formal tone (“O que lhe fez pensar…”). Often followed by “que” + a clause describing what they believed.
target_language_example: O que te fez pensar que eu era brasileiro?
native_language_example: What made you think I was Brazilian?

meaning: "what’s the matter? / what’s wrong?"; also "what does it have?" (in questions like "what has…?")
additional_notes:
Used in questions with different meanings depending on context:
- Alone ("O que tem?") often means “What’s wrong?” / “What is it?”
- With a person/pronoun ("O que tem ele?" / "O que você tem?") means “What’s wrong with him/you?”
- In riddle-style questions ("O que tem cabeça…?") it literally means “What has…?”
- With "de + adjective/noun" ("O que tem de novo/engraçado?") means “What’s new/funny (about it)?”
target_language_example: Você está quieto hoje. O que tem?
native_language_example: You’re quiet today. What’s wrong?

additional_notes: Used to ask what is wrong with someone/something, often showing concern, surprise, or criticism. Very commonly followed by "com" + person/thing: "O que tem de errado com você/eles?" It can also refer to an idea or situation with "nisso" (= "in that"): "O que tem de errado nisso?" You can also say it alone when asking generally: "O que tem de errado?"
target_language_example: O que tem de errado com o computador?
native_language_example: What's wrong with the computer?

additional_notes: Used to report/explain an earlier event (past perfect: tinha acontecido) from the point of view of another moment in the past (e.g., he told her what had happened). Very common after verbs like contar (to tell), explicar (to explain), and saber (to know).
target_language_example: Eu expliquei para ela o que tinha acontecido antes da reunião.
native_language_example: I explained to her what had happened before the meeting.

additional_notes: Uses "tinha" (imperfect of "ter") in the common meaning “there was / there were.” It often appears in questions or clauses asking what was inside something or what existed in a situation: "O que tinha dentro...?" (What was inside...?), "ver o que tinha de errado" (see what was wrong).
target_language_example: Ela abriu a gaveta para ver o que tinha lá dentro.
native_language_example: She opened the drawer to see what was inside.

additional_notes: Used to start a question or an embedded question addressed to someone you use **tu** with. It’s typically followed by a verb: **O que tu disseste?** (“What did you say?”). In many varieties you’ll also hear **O que é que tu…** with the same meaning. Common in informal speech and in regions/contexts where **tu** is used.
target_language_example: O que tu queres comer hoje?
native_language_example: What do you want to eat today?

meaning: “what is going to happen” / “what will happen.”
additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about a future event or outcome. Very common with "Eu não sei..." (“I don’t know...”) and with "com" + a person/thing to mean “what will happen to (someone/something)?” You can also add a time (e.g., "às onze horas") to ask what will happen at that time.
target_language_example: Ninguém sabe o que vai acontecer depois da reunião.
native_language_example: Nobody knows what will happen after the meeting.

additional_notes: A common question using **ir + infinitive** (**vai fazer**) to ask about someone’s plans or what action they will take. You can add details after it: **agora** (now), **amanhã** (tomorrow), **no verão** (in the summer), **a respeito de...** (about/regarding...), **com...** (with...), **então** (then/so). Often the subject **você** is implied: **(Você) o que vai fazer?**
target_language_example: E se chover, o que vai fazer?
native_language_example: And if it rains, what are you going to do?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the next plan/decision for a group (“we”). Often followed by a time word (agora, depois) or by phrases like a respeito disso (“about that”), com… (“with…”), para… (“in order to…” / “for…”). In writing it may appear as “O que vamos fazer?”; in speech it can sound like “Que vamos fazer?” or “O que a gente vai fazer?” (more informal).
target_language_example: O que vamos fazer se chover?
native_language_example: What are we going to do if it rains?

meaning: “what you…?” / “what do you…?” (used to ask a question).
additional_notes: Used at the start of questions directed to someone. Often followed by a verb: "O que você quer?" (What do you want?), "O que você está fazendo?" (What are you doing?). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, it can alternate with "o que cê" or "o que você" vs. the more formal "o que o senhor/a senhora".
target_language_example: O que você quer fazer hoje?
native_language_example: What do you want to do today?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion about something. It’s often followed by a preposition + what you’re asking about: “O que você acha de...?” (common in Brazil; “você” is neutral/informal in most Brazilian contexts, while in more formal situations you might hear “O que o senhor/a senhora acha...?”).
target_language_example: O que você acha do restaurante?
native_language_example: What do you think of the restaurant?

meaning: “what do you think of …?” / “how do you feel about …?”
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion about a thing, person, situation, or idea. Very often followed by a noun (O que você acha de minha casa?) or by a verb in the infinitive to suggest an activity (O que você acha de ir…? “How about going…?”). In more formal situations, you may hear “O que o senhor/a senhora acha de…?”.
target_language_example: O que você acha de a gente almoçar juntos amanhã?
native_language_example: What do you think about us having lunch together tomorrow?

meaning: "What do you think of…?" / "What’s your opinion about…?"
additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion about a thing/topic. It’s the start of a question and is followed by a noun (often with the contraction "do" = "de" + "o"). With feminine nouns you’ll usually see "da" (de + a): "O que você acha da comida?" You can also ask about a plural noun with "dos/das": "O que você acha dos filmes?"
target_language_example: O que você acha do meu plano?
native_language_example: What do you think of my plan?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion/guess about a situation or what should be done. Often followed by a full clause: “o que você acha que aconteceu / devemos fazer / está aqui”. In questions it commonly starts the sentence, and you can make it more formal by using “o que o senhor/a senhora acha que…”.
target_language_example: O que você acha que vai acontecer amanhã?
native_language_example: What do you think is going to happen tomorrow?

meaning: “What did you think?” / “What did you think of …?”
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion after an experience (a city, movie, speech, etc.). It can also mean “What did you think (that…)?” when followed by a clause, e.g., “O que você achou que o Tom faria?” = “What did you think Tom would do?” In Brazil, “você” is common in everyday speech; in more formal contexts you may also hear “O que o senhor/a senhora achou?”.
target_language_example: O que você achou do restaurante?
native_language_example: What did you think of the restaurant?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion after experiencing something (an event, speech, show, food/drink, a person, etc.). It’s the past tense of achar (“to think/find”), so it often refers to something that already happened or that the person has already tried/seen. With feminine nouns, use “da” instead of “do” (e.g., “O que você achou da festa?”). In informal speech, “você” is often shortened to “cê”: “O que cê achou do filme?”
target_language_example: O que você achou do restaurante novo?
native_language_example: What did you think of the new restaurant?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone ate in the past. Often followed by a time expression (hoje de manhã, ontem à noite) or by a meal (no café da manhã, no jantar). In speech, Brazilians often shorten it to "O que você comeu?" or "O que cê comeu?".
target_language_example: O que você comeu no almoço?
native_language_example: What did you eat for lunch?

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s previous words. Common in questions ("O que você disse?" = "What did you say?") and in statements ("Acredito que o que você disse é verdade" = "I believe what you said is true"). Adding "mesmo" can mean "again" or "exactly" ("O que você disse mesmo?" = "What did you say again/What exactly did you say?").
target_language_example: Eu não entendi o que você disse.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what you said.

meaning: “What do you say?” (asking for someone’s opinion/response).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone thinks or how they respond to a suggestion or situation. Depending on tone, it can also sound like “What did you say?” / “Come again?” in a conversational way.
target_language_example: Vamos jantar fora hoje. O que você diz?
native_language_example: Let’s have dinner out today. What do you say?

meaning: "what were you..." (introduces a question in the past, often with an ongoing action).
additional_notes: Used at the start of questions to ask what someone was doing at a particular moment in the past. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the gerund (estava + verb ending in -ndo): "O que você estava fazendo?" = "What were you doing?" You can also use it with other complements when the context makes the action clear.
target_language_example: O que você estava fazendo quando eu liguei?
native_language_example: What were you doing when I called?

additional_notes: Used to ask about an action in progress at a specific time in the past (past continuous). Often followed by a time reference (agora, na semana passada) or by a clause with quando (“when…”). In speech, you’ll also hear the shorter forms “O que você tava fazendo…?” and (more informal) “O que cê tava fazendo…?”.
target_language_example: O que você estava fazendo ontem à noite?
native_language_example: What were you doing last night?

meaning: "what are you" / "what are you (currently) ..." (used to ask what someone is doing, saying, thinking, etc.).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question, followed by a verb phrase to ask what someone is doing right now: "O que você está + [verb in the -ndo form]" (e.g., fazendo, pensando, cozinhando) or (especially in Portugal) "O que você está a + infinitive" (e.g., a dizer). Often translates as "What are you ...?" or "What are you ...ing?".
target_language_example: O que você está fazendo agora?
native_language_example: What are you doing right now?

meaning: what you’re saying / what you’re telling me.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of what someone is saying (often to evaluate it: if it makes sense, is true, is important, etc.). Literally “that which you are saying.” In speech, it’s common to shorten to “o que você tá dizendo”.
target_language_example: Eu entendi o que você está dizendo, mas eu não concordo.
native_language_example: I understand what you’re saying, but I don’t agree.

additional_notes: A very common question using the present continuous (estar + gerund). It can be neutral (“What are you doing right now?”) or sound surprised/angry depending on tone (like “What do you think you’re doing?”). Often followed by extra info: “...aqui?” (here), “...comigo?” (to/with me), “...em casa tão cedo?” (at home so early). In Portuguese, you may also hear the informal version “o que você tá fazendo?” or “o que cê tá fazendo?”.
target_language_example: Ei, o que você está fazendo aí na minha cadeira?
native_language_example: Hey, what are you doing there in my chair?

o que você está fazendo aqui

target_language_multi_word_term: o que você está fazendo aqui
additional_notes: A common question to ask why someone is in a place, often showing surprise, suspicion, or curiosity. You can add details after "aqui" (e.g., "de volta" = back/again, "aqui dentro" = in here/inside, "tão cedo" = so early, "tão tarde" = so late). It can sound a bit confrontational depending on tone; for a more neutral/polite option, you can say "Posso ajudar?" (Can I help?) or "O que você veio fazer aqui?" (What did you come here to do?).
target_language_example: Oi, Ana—o que você está fazendo aqui sozinha?
native_language_example: Hi, Ana—what are you doing here by yourself?

o que você está fazendo aí

target_language_multi_word_term: o que você está fazendo aí
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone is doing in a specific place, often showing surprise or concern. Aí refers to where the other person is (near them or just “there” from the speaker’s point of view), and you can add a location after it: aí em cima (up there), aí fora (out there), aí no telhado (on the roof). In Brazil, você is common; in Portugal you might hear o que estás a fazer aí?
target_language_example: Ei, o que você está fazendo aí na rua tão tarde?
native_language_example: Hey, what are you doing out there on the street so late?

meaning: “what would you do” (asking about a hypothetical situation).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone would do in an imagined scenario. Often followed by “se...” (“if...”) to introduce the condition: “O que você faria se...?” In Brazil, “você” is common; in Portugal you may also hear “O que farias...?” (more informal) or “O que você faria...?” (less common).
target_language_example: O que você faria se perdesse o passaporte?
native_language_example: What would you do if you lost your passport?

meaning: “what would you do if …” (asking a hypothetical question).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone would do in an imagined situation. Follow it with a clause in the subjunctive (e.g., “se ganhasse”, “se fosse”, “se visse”). You can change “você” to “vocês” (plural) or use a more formal/less direct “o que o senhor / a senhora faria se …”.
target_language_example: O que você faria se perdesse o seu passaporte no exterior?
native_language_example: What would you do if you lost your passport abroad?

meaning: "what do you do?" / "what are you doing?" (what you do).
additional_notes: Literally “what you do.” Used in questions to ask about someone’s job/routine/plans (“O que você faz da vida?” = “What do you do for a living?”) or about what someone does with something (“O que você faz com isso...?” = “What you do with this/that...?”). Meaning depends on context and time: it can be general (“What do you do?”) or right now (“What are you doing?”).
target_language_example: O que você faz nos fins de semana?
native_language_example: What do you do on weekends?

additional_notes: Literally “the/that which you did.” It can be a statement referring to an action (“I forgive what you did”) or a direct question, often shocked or accusing (“What did you do to my baby?” / “What have you done to me?”). In speech, “você” is often reduced to “cê” (“o que cê fez?”).
target_language_example: Eu não acredito no que você fez.
native_language_example: I can’t believe what you did.

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone did with an object/person (often implying it’s missing or you disapprove).
