native_language_example: The students arrived early for the test.

additional_notes: Plural of "o fato". Used to refer to true information or the real details of a situation. Often appears after verbs like "conhecer" (to know) or "precisar de" (to need).
target_language_example: Antes de decidir, quero ouvir os fatos.
native_language_example: Before deciding, I want to hear the facts.

additional_notes: Plural definite form of "o filho" (son/child). Often used to mean "the kids/children" in general (especially when gender isn’t important), or specifically "the sons" depending on context. Possession is commonly shown with "de": "os filhos deles" (their children), "os filhos do Sully" (Sully’s children).
target_language_example: Os filhos da Ana estudam aqui.
native_language_example: Ana’s children study here.

additional_notes: Definite article + plural noun. Used to talk about cats in general (“Cats …”) or about specific cats known from context. Singular: “o gato” (the cat). Feminine plural: “as gatas” (the female cats).
target_language_example: Os gatos dormem muito durante o dia.
native_language_example: Cats sleep a lot during the day.

additional_notes: Plural of “o homem” (“the man”). Used either to refer to a specific group of men (“the men”) or to men as a category in general statements (often contrasted with “as mulheres” = “women”).
target_language_example: Os homens desta turma são muito simpáticos.
native_language_example: The men in this class are very nice.

additional_notes: Uses the verb ser (to be) in the present tense: são = “are” (3rd person plural). It can refer to men in general (“Men are…”) or a specific group (“The men are…”) depending on context. It’s commonly followed by an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., os homens são gentis = “men are kind”).
target_language_example: Os homens são diferentes, mas todos merecem respeito.
native_language_example: Men are different, but everyone deserves respect.

additional_notes: Plural form with the masculine plural article “os”, used for mixed-gender groups or people in general. Often used when contrasting humans with animals, gods, aliens, or robots. Singular: “o humano” (the human) or more commonly “o ser humano” (the human being).
target_language_example: Os humanos precisam de água e comida para sobreviver.
native_language_example: Humans need water and food to survive.

additional_notes: Definite plural: os + japonês. Used to talk about Japanese people in general, or a specific group already known in context. For an all-female group you can also see “as japonesas.”
target_language_example: Os japoneses gostam muito de comida japonesa.
native_language_example: Japanese people really like Japanese food.

meaning: 'the Japanese are' (talking about Japanese people in general).
additional_notes: Used to make general statements about Japanese people as a group. "Os" is the plural masculine definite article ('the'), "japoneses" is plural ('Japanese people'), and "são" is the verb "ser" in the present tense for "they are". Often appears with adverbs like "em geral" or "geralmente" ('in general/usually') when making broad generalizations.
target_language_example: Os japoneses são muito pontuais.
native_language_example: The Japanese are very punctual.

additional_notes: Plural of "o jovem" (a young person). Used with "os" to talk about young people as a group in general (e.g., "popular among young people"). In speech, "Cadê os jovens?" is a casual way to ask where they are.
target_language_example: Esse evento é voltado para os jovens.
native_language_example: This event is aimed at young people.

additional_notes: Masculine plural definite article + noun. Used to talk about specific books that are already known from context (e.g., a set of textbooks, library books, or books on a shelf). Singular: "o livro"; indefinite plural: "uns livros" (some books).
target_language_example: Eu coloquei os livros na mochila.
native_language_example: I put the books in the backpack.

meaning: “the best” (plural masculine; can also be mixed-gender).
additional_notes: Used for more than one person/thing. It’s the plural of “o melhor” (“the best”). Often appears with “de/do mundo” (“in/of the world”), or in comparisons like “entre os melhores” (“among the best”). With a noun: “os melhores sanduíches” = “the best sandwiches.”
target_language_example: Quais são os melhores restaurantes aqui perto?
native_language_example: Which are the best restaurants near here?

additional_notes: Definite plural of menino (“boy”). Used to refer to a specific group of boys (already known from context). In Brazilian Portuguese it can also be a casual way to refer to a group of male kids/guys (“the guys”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Os meninos estão brincando no parque.
native_language_example: The boys are playing in the park.

additional_notes: Used with masculine plural nouns: “os meus irmãos” = “my brothers.” It can also stand alone as a possessive pronoun meaning “mine” (referring to a masculine plural group): “Os meus são do Brasil” = “Mine are from Brazil.” The article “os” is required in these cases.
target_language_example: Os meus amigos moram perto daqui.
native_language_example: My friends live near here.

additional_notes: Means a group of male friends or a mixed group (men and women). It’s the plural of "o meu amigo". Often used after prepositions like "com" (with), "sem" (without), and "para" (for/to). In Brazilian Portuguese you may also hear "meus amigos" without "os" depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Hoje vou sair com os meus amigos depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: Today I’m going out with my friends after work.

additional_notes: Refers to more than one child of the speaker; filhos is masculine plural and can mean “sons” specifically or “children” in general (mixed group). Often shortened in speech to “meus filhos” without os. Singular: “o meu filho” (my son/child) or “a minha filha” (my daughter).
target_language_example: Vou buscar os meus filhos na escola às três.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick up my kids at school at three.

additional_notes: Used to say where your children live. You typically follow it with a city, country, or neighborhood. Common variants: “meus filhos moram em …” (more common; you can drop “os”) and singular “meu filho / minha filha mora em …”.
target_language_example: Os meus filhos moram em São Paulo.
native_language_example: My children live in São Paulo.

additional_notes: Used to talk about books that belong to the speaker. It includes the definite article “os” (“the”) plus the possessive “meus” (“my”) and the plural noun “livros” (“books”). In Portuguese, it’s very common to use the article before a possessive (os meus / as minhas), especially in European Portuguese.
target_language_example: Preciso encontrar os meus livros antes da aula.
native_language_example: I need to find my books before class.

additional_notes: Literally “the my parents.” In Portuguese, possessives are often used with the definite article (o/a/os/as), especially in European Portuguese, but it’s also common in Brazilian Portuguese. Use it to talk about your mother and father together. The verb may agree in plural: “Os meus pais moram...” (“My parents live...” ).
target_language_example: Hoje vou jantar com os meus pais.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to have dinner with my parents.

additional_notes: Used to talk about shoes that belong to the speaker. Includes the masculine plural definite article + possessive: os (the, plural) + meus (my, masculine plural) + sapatos (shoes). For feminine plural items, you’d use “as minhas …” (e.g., as minhas botas).
target_language_example: Não encontro os meus sapatos.
native_language_example: I can’t find my shoes.

meaning: "my glasses" (the ones I wear to see).
additional_notes: Used to talk about your eyeglasses. "Óculos" is normally plural in Portuguese, even if you’d say "a pair" in English. The article changes with context: "os meus óculos" (my glasses), "meus óculos" (my glasses, slightly more direct), "os óculos" (the glasses). Often used with verbs like "esquecer" (forget), "perder" (lose), "deixar" (leave), "colocar" (put/place).
target_language_example: Preciso encontrar os meus óculos antes de sair.
native_language_example: I need to find my glasses before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to refer to multiple people’s or things’ names. Common after verbs like dizer (to tell), saber (to know), or pesquisar (to look up/research): “dizer os nomes”, “saber os nomes”, “pesquisar os nomes”. Often followed by “deles/delas” (“their”).
target_language_example: Você lembra os nomes de todos os alunos?
native_language_example: Do you remember all the students’ names?

additional_notes: Plural masculine form of "o nosso". Used to mean "our" before a masculine plural noun (e.g., "os nossos vizinhos") or on its own as a pronoun meaning "ours" (e.g., "os nossos" = "our people/our things" from context). Feminine plural is "as nossas".
target_language_example: Os nossos amigos chegam amanhã.
native_language_example: Our friends arrive tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to refer to children belonging to “us” (the speaker plus another person or group). You can also say “nossos filhos” without “os” in many sentences (especially after a preposition like “para nossos filhos”). “Filhos” can mean children in general (not only sons), depending on context.
target_language_example: Vamos pensar no futuro dos nossos filhos.
native_language_example: Let’s think about our children’s future.

additional_notes: Plural noun with the definite article: *o olho* (the eye) → *os olhos* (the eyes). Common in everyday commands and expressions like **Abre os olhos!** (“Open your eyes!/Pay attention!”) and in the idiom **Custa os olhos da cara** (“It costs an arm and a leg,” literally “it costs the eyes of the face”).
target_language_example: Ele fechou os olhos por um segundo.
native_language_example: He closed his eyes for a second.

additional_notes: A common way to express possession with body parts in Portuguese: definite article + noun + possessive phrase. Here, "dela" = "de" + "ela" (“of her”), and it usually refers to a specific person (not “hers” in general). You can change the owner: "os olhos dele" (his eyes), "os olhos da Maria" (Maria’s eyes). The article agrees with the noun: "os olhos" (plural), but "o olho" (one eye).
target_language_example: Eu não conseguia parar de olhar para os olhos dela.
native_language_example: I couldn’t stop looking at her eyes.

additional_notes: Plural masculine form used to refer to the remaining people/things in a group. Often appears after a number ("os outros três" = "the other three") or after "todos" ("todos os outros" = "all the other"). It can also mean "other people" in general depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu vou primeiro, e os outros vêm depois.
native_language_example: I'll go first, and the others will come later.

additional_notes: Plural masculine form used to refer to the remaining people/things in a group. Often appears after a number ("os outros três" = "the other three") or after "todos" ("todos os outros" = "all the other"). It can also mean "other people" in general depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu vou primeiro, e os outros vêm depois.
native_language_example: I'll go first, and the others will come later.

additional_notes: Plural definite form of "o ovo" (egg). Used when talking about eggs as specific items (e.g., in a store, on a tray) or as a general category in context. Often appears in shopping/food situations and in fixed expressions like "quebrar os ovos" (to break the eggs).
target_language_example: Preciso de comprar os ovos para o bolo.
native_language_example: I need to buy the eggs for the cake.

additional_notes: Plural of “o pai” (the father). Often used to mean both parents together (mother and father). Don’t confuse with “o país” (the country) — note the accent: país.
target_language_example: Os pais da Ana trabalham muito.
native_language_example: Ana’s parents work a lot.

additional_notes: Definite article + plural noun: **os** = “the” (masculine plural) and **peixes** = “fish” (plural of *peixe*). Used when talking about specific fish in general or a known group (e.g., the fish in a tank/river).
target_language_example: Os peixes estão no aquário.
native_language_example: The fish are in the aquarium.

additional_notes: Plural of "o prato". It can mean physical plates (tableware) or, in some contexts, the dishes/food being served (e.g., "os pratos típicos" = typical dishes). Often used with kitchen verbs like "pôr" (to put/place), "trazer" (to bring), "lavar" (to wash), "quebrar" (to break).
target_language_example: Depois do jantar, eu lavo os pratos.
native_language_example: After dinner, I wash the dishes.

additional_notes: Plural of "o preço". Used when talking about prices in general (e.g., in shops, rent, the economy). Often appears with verbs like "subir" (to go up) and "cair" (to go down).
target_language_example: Os preços no supermercado estão muito altos.
native_language_example: Prices at the supermarket are very high.

meaning: "the first ones" / "the first" (plural, masculine or mixed group).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the people or things that come before all others in order or time. Common in expressions like "durante os primeiros dias" (“during the first days”) or "ser os primeiros" (“to be the first”). For an all-female group, use "as primeiras"; singular is "o primeiro" / "a primeira".
target_language_example: Chegámos cedo e fomos os primeiros a entrar.
native_language_example: We arrived early and were the first to go in.

additional_notes: Definite plural: "os" = "the" (masculine plural) + "pássaros" = birds. Used for literal birds ("Os pássaros voam") and in the phrase "os pássaros e as abelhas" (“the birds and the bees,” i.e., talking about sex/reproduction, often with children).
target_language_example: De manhã, eu gosto de ouvir os pássaros cantando.
native_language_example: In the morning, I like to hear the birds singing.

meaning: "the feet"; in expressions like "pôr/meter os pés", "set foot" (go/enter a place).
additional_notes: Literal meaning is body parts: "Levante os pés dela" = "Lift her feet." In the common idioms "pôr os pés" and "meter os pés", it means going somewhere/entering a place, often used with "nunca" to mean you’ll never go back: "nunca mais meter os pés" = "never set foot (there) again."
target_language_example: Eu nunca mais vou meter os pés naquele bar.
native_language_example: I’m never going to set foot in that bar again.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase with the definite article (os = “the” for masculine plural). Common for exam/test results, medical results, research results, election results, or the outcome of a process. Often used after verbs like saber/receber/ver/enviar (to know/receive/see/send the results).
target_language_example: Já saíram os resultados do exame?
native_language_example: Are the exam results out already?

additional_notes: Definite plural: used when talking about a specific pair of shoes or shoes in general. Often appears with verbs like tirar (to take off): tirar os sapatos = to take off your shoes.
target_language_example: Por favor, tire os sapatos antes de entrar.
native_language_example: Please take off your shoes before coming in.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like tirar/retirar (“to take off/remove”) or bater (“to knock/tap,” e.g., to clean dirt off) to talk about what you do with your shoes before going into a house or room. Very common in house rules: “Tire os sapatos antes de entrar.”
target_language_example: Por favor, tire os sapatos antes de entrar no apartamento.
native_language_example: Please take off your shoes before entering the apartment.

additional_notes: Used to address two or more men (or a mixed group, in some contexts) in a polite/formal way, like “you gentlemen / you sirs.” It’s the present tense of “estar” with the subject “os senhores.” Common in formal speech, customer service, or when speaking respectfully. In Brazil, people often use “vocês estão” instead; “os senhores estão” sounds more formal. In Portugal, you may also see “Os senhores estão a + infinitive” for “you are (doing) …”.
target_language_example: Os senhores estão prontos para começar?
native_language_example: Are you gentlemen ready to start?

meaning: human beings; humans (people as a species).
additional_notes: Used in a general, scientific, or formal way to talk about people as a whole (not specific individuals). Often appears in statements comparing humans to animals or nature. Singular: "o ser humano".
target_language_example: Os seres humanos precisam de água para sobreviver.
native_language_example: Human beings need water to survive.

additional_notes: Used to state general facts about humans. "Os seres humanos" = “human beings / humans” (plural), and "têm" is the 3rd person plural of "ter" (“to have”). Often followed by something people possess (body parts, abilities, etc.).
target_language_example: Os seres humanos têm cinco sentidos.
native_language_example: Human beings have five senses.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun: os seus irmãos (“his/her/your/their brothers”), os seus filmes (“…films”). In Portuguese, seu/sua/seus/suas can mean “your” (often formal) or “his/her/their” depending on context, so speakers may use dele/dela/deles/delas to avoid ambiguity (e.g., os talentos dele = “his talents”).
target_language_example: Ela vai trazer os seus documentos amanhã.
native_language_example: She will bring her documents tomorrow.

meaning: your friends (plural, masculine or mixed group).
additional_notes: Means “your friends.” It uses the possessive "seus" (your), which can also mean “his/her/their” depending on context, so speakers may use "os amigos dele/dela" to be extra clear. "Os" and "amigos" agree in gender/number: for an all-female group, say "as suas amigas".
target_language_example: Você vai sair com os seus amigos hoje?
native_language_example: Are you going out with your friends today?

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s children in a polite or more formal way. Literally “the your children” (os = “the” for plural masculine/mixed groups; seus = “your”; filhos = “children/sons”). Often used when addressing someone with “você”. For only daughters, you can say “as suas filhas”.
target_language_example: Os seus filhos vão à escola hoje?
native_language_example: Are your children going to school today?

meaning: “your eyes” (formal or plural) / “his/her/their eyes” (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally “the your eyes.” In Portuguese, the possessive (seus/suas) can refer to “your” (especially formal ‘you’) or to “his/her/their,” so context usually makes it clear. Common with verbs like fechar (to close): “Feche os seus olhos.”
target_language_example: Por favor, feche os seus olhos por um momento.
native_language_example: Please close your eyes for a moment.

additional_notes: Uses "seus" (plural) to agree with "pais". In Brazilian Portuguese, "seus" often refers to the person you’re talking to, especially in more formal speech or when using "você(s)"; in everyday conversation many people also say "os teus pais" (more informal/closer) depending on region. Can also mean "his/her/their parents" if the context is talking about someone else.
target_language_example: Os seus pais moram aqui perto?
native_language_example: Do your parents live nearby?

additional_notes: Uses the possessive “seus/suas” (“your”), which is common in Brazil especially with “você” and can sound more formal or less direct than “teus/tuas.” It agrees with the noun: “os seus problemas” (masculine plural). Often used when talking about someone’s personal issues, difficulties, or troubles (financial, personal, etc.).
target_language_example: Eu não posso resolver os seus problemas por você.
native_language_example: I can't solve your problems for you.

additional_notes: Definite plural form: "os" = "the" (masculine plural) + "soldados" = "soldiers". Use it when referring to a specific group of soldiers. Singular: "o soldado" (the soldier).
target_language_example: Os soldados chegaram cedo ao quartel.
native_language_example: The soldiers arrived early at the barracks.

meaning: "yours" (masculine plural), or "your" + a masculine plural noun.
additional_notes: "Os" is the masculine plural definite article (“the”), and "teus" is the masculine plural form of the possessive "teu" (“your”). It’s used with masculine plural nouns: "os teus olhos" = “your eyes”, "os teus pais" = “your parents”. It can also stand alone to mean “yours” when the noun is understood: "Os teus são maiores" = “Yours are bigger.” (In Brazil, "os seus" is often used instead; in Portugal, "os teus" is common in informal contexts.)
target_language_example: Os teus amigos vêm hoje?
native_language_example: Are your friends coming today?

additional_notes: Used with the plural article "os" because in Portuguese "óculos" is normally plural even when referring to one pair. You can specify the type: "óculos de leitura" (reading glasses), "óculos de sol" (sunglasses). Possession is often shown with "de": "os óculos dele/dela" (his/her glasses).
target_language_example: Onde estão os meus óculos?
native_language_example: Where are my glasses?

additional_notes: Used at the end of a phrase to be intentionally vague, meaning “or something similar.” Common in casual speech when you’re not sure of the exact detail or you don’t want to be too specific. Also used in questions to suggest a possible category (e.g., “an artist or something like that?”).
target_language_example: A gente pode tomar um café, ou algo do tipo.
native_language_example: We can have a coffee, or something like that.

meaning: “or less” (used in “mais ou menos” = “more or less / about”).
additional_notes: You’ll most often see it in the fixed expression "mais ou menos". With numbers/quantities it means “about/approximately” ("São mais ou menos oito quilômetros." = “It’s about eight kilometers.”). With comparisons or descriptions it means “more or less / roughly / kind of” (approximate, not exact). By itself, "ou menos" can mean “or less,” but in everyday Portuguese it’s usually part of "mais ou menos."
target_language_example: Chego em casa em uma hora, mais ou menos.
native_language_example: I’ll get home in about an hour.

meaning: "or not" (used to show alternatives or insist on a yes/no answer).
additional_notes: Common after a clause introduced by "se" (if/whether): "se ... ou não" = "whether ... or not". It can also appear in direct questions to pressure for a clear yes/no: "Vai responder ou não?" In patterns like "goste ou não" it means "whether you like it or not" and signals that something will happen anyway.
target_language_example: Diga logo se você vem ou não.
native_language_example: Just tell me whether you're coming or not.

additional_notes: Used when switching to a different option, topic, activity, or idea. Often appears after verbs like pensar em (think about), fazer (do), tentar (try), precisar (need). It can also appear in comparisons like "mais do que qualquer outra coisa" = "more than anything else."
target_language_example: Vamos fazer outra coisa hoje?
native_language_example: Shall we do something else today?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a different person from the one already mentioned or expected. Often appears with "por" after verbs like "esperar" ("esperar por outra pessoa" = to wait for someone else). You may also see "uma outra pessoa" to emphasize "a different person".
target_language_example: Desculpe, eu achei que você fosse outra pessoa.
native_language_example: Sorry, I thought you were someone else.

additional_notes: Used when offering, requesting, or suggesting a refill. Word order is flexible: you can say “outra xícara de café” or place it later in the sentence (“pegar para você outra xícara de café”). “Outra” agrees with the feminine noun “xícara” (so it’s “outra,” not “outro”).
target_language_example: Você quer outra xícara de café?
native_language_example: Do you want another cup of coffee?

additional_notes: Used to refer to additional items, tasks, or topics besides the ones already mentioned. Very common in expressions like “entre outras coisas” (“among other things”) and “ter outras coisas para fazer” (“to have other things to do”). In Portuguese it often implies “more things” or “different things” that remain.
target_language_example: Desculpa, não posso sair agora — tenho outras coisas para resolver.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out now—I have other things to take care of.

additional_notes: Used to talk about people different from the ones already mentioned, or people in general besides yourself/your group. Often appears with the definite article: "as outras pessoas" = "the other people" (a specific group), while without the article it can be more general.
target_language_example: Não compare sua vida com a das outras pessoas.
native_language_example: Don’t compare your life with other people’s.

meaning: “the other day” (recently; on a different day, not today).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a recent past day that isn’t specified (“the other day”). With "no outro dia" it can mean “that other day / the day before” depending on context (often a past occasion you both remember). Also used at the start of a sentence as a time marker: "Outro dia, ..." = “The other day, ...”.
target_language_example: Outro dia, eu te vi no mercado, mas você estava com pressa.
native_language_example: The other day, I saw you at the market, but you were in a hurry.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the opposite side of something (a place, street, door, river, etc.). Very common with prepositions like "do outro lado" (on/from the other side), "pelo outro lado" (by/through the other side), and "até o outro lado" (to the other side).
target_language_example: A entrada fica do outro lado da rua.
native_language_example: The entrance is on the other side of the street.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a different location than the current/mentioned one. Often appears with prepositions: em outro lugar (“in another place”), para outro lugar (“to another place”), de outro lugar (“from another place”), or with nenhum: em nenhum outro lugar (“nowhere else”).
target_language_example: A gente pode comer em outro lugar.
native_language_example: We can eat somewhere else.

additional_notes: "Ouvi-lo" = "ouvir" (to hear / to listen to) + "-lo" (him, as a direct-object pronoun). It’s used when "him" comes after the verb (common in European Portuguese and more formal in Brazilian Portuguese). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many people would say "ouvir ele" instead. In context it can mean simply hearing a sound ("I can hardly hear him") or listening to what someone says ("Why should I listen to him?").
target_language_example: Não consigo ouvi-lo bem por causa do barulho.
native_language_example: I can’t hear him well because of the noise.

meaning: "I heard (that)..." / "I’ve heard (that)..." (a rumor or second-hand information).
additional_notes: Used to introduce information you heard from someone else (not something you know for sure). Often implies hearsay/gossip. You can change the tense/person: "ouço dizer que" (I hear people say that), "ouvi dizer que" (I heard), "tenho ouvido dizer que" (I’ve been hearing).
target_language_example: Ouvi dizer que vai chover amanhã.
native_language_example: I heard that it’s going to rain tomorrow.

meaning: "I heard that the..." (introducing something you heard/learned).
additional_notes: Used to report hearsay or information you learned from other people, without saying it’s confirmed. You can change the article to match the noun: "ouvi dizer que a..." (feminine), "ouvi dizer que os..." (plural masculine/mixed), "ouvi dizer que as..." (plural feminine). Often followed by a name or noun phrase: "Ouvi dizer que o Tom..."
target_language_example: Ouvi dizer que o novo restaurante é muito bom.
native_language_example: I heard that the new restaurant is very good.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information you heard from someone else (a rumor, news, or secondhand info). It’s a neutral, common way to start a conversation about what you’ve heard. You can swap the subject: “ouvi dizer que ele/ela…”, “ouvi dizer que vocês…”.
target_language_example: Ouvi dizer que você vai se mudar no mês que vem.
native_language_example: I heard that you’re going to move next month.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund ("ouvindo") to describe an action in progress, often with "estar": "estou/estava ouvindo música" = "I am/was listening to music." You can add a genre after "música" (e.g., "música country").
target_language_example: Estou ouvindo música agora.
native_language_example: I’m listening to music right now.

additional_notes: "Ouvir" means "to listen/hear." With "gostar de" (to like) or verbs like "adorar" (to love), you typically use "de" + infinitive: "gosto de ouvir...". You can also add time expressions like "quando tenho um tempinho livre" (when I have a little free time).
target_language_example: Eu costumo ouvir música clássica enquanto estudo.
native_language_example: I usually listen to classical music while I study.

additional_notes: Literally “(you) heard what I said.” It’s often used as a pointed question to check if someone was listening, and can sound impatient or confrontational depending on tone. With insults or swear words (like in some examples), it becomes very aggressive and rude. You can also say “Você ouviu o que eu disse?” (more explicit) or “Você ouviu?” (“Did you hear?”).
target_language_example: Você ouviu o que eu disse? Preciso de uma resposta.
native_language_example: Did you hear what I said? I need an answer.

additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) of the verb ouvir (“to listen/hear”) + object pronoun me (“me”). Used to get someone’s attention before giving instructions or asking them to take you seriously. You can soften it with por favor (“please”).
target_language_example: Ouça-me um minuto, eu posso explicar.
native_language_example: Listen to me for a minute, I can explain.

meaning: to pay the bill (in a restaurant/bar) or pay the check.
additional_notes: Used when paying what you owe after eating/drinking somewhere (the "conta" is the bill/check). Common with verbs like "pedir" (to ask for) and "dividir" (to split): "Podemos pedir a conta?" / "Vamos dividir a conta?"
target_language_example: Desculpe, você pode trazer a conta? Eu vou pagar a conta.
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you bring the bill? I’m going to pay the bill.

additional_notes: Used for paying rent on a home/apartment. You can add time expressions like "este mês" (this month) or "hoje" (today). In Brazil, "aluguel" is common; in some places you may also hear "renda" (especially in Portugal).
target_language_example: Tenho que pagar o aluguel hoje.
native_language_example: I have to pay the rent today.

meaning: “to pay for it/that” (pay the cost) or “to pay for it” (suffer consequences).
additional_notes: Often used literally about money: “pagar por isso” = “pay for it/that.” It can also be used figuratively as a warning or threat meaning someone will face consequences: “Você vai pagar por isso!” (“You’ll pay for this!”). Context and tone make the meaning clear.
target_language_example: Se você mentir, vai pagar por isso.
native_language_example: If you lie, you’ll pay for it.

additional_notes: Past tense of "pagar" (to pay) + "a conta" (the bill). Used for restaurant bills and also for household bills (e.g., electricity). You can specify whose bill with "a conta dele/dela" (his/her bill) or what kind with "a conta de eletricidade / de energia elétrica" (the electricity bill).
target_language_example: Eu já paguei a conta, podemos ir embora.
native_language_example: I already paid the bill; we can leave.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a man’s father. "dele" means "of him / his" and refers back to a male person already mentioned (e.g., ele, Tom). You can also hear "o pai dele" = "his dad/father". Similar patterns: "pai dela" (her father), "mãe dele" (his mother).
target_language_example: Eu conheci o pai dele ontem.
native_language_example: I met his father yesterday.

meaning: "a pair of"; also "a couple of" (a small number, e.g., days).
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean a matched set of two things (par de tênis/luvas/chinelos/óculos). With time or amounts (e.g., par de dias), it means “a couple of / a few,” not necessarily exactly two.
target_language_example: Preciso comprar um par de meias.
native_language_example: I need to buy a pair of socks.

additional_notes: Used to talk about two shoes as one set. Very common with purchases and shopping: "comprar um par de sapatos" (to buy a pair of shoes).
target_language_example: Preciso de um par de sapatos confortáveis para o trabalho.
native_language_example: I need a comfortable pair of shoes for work.

additional_notes: Made of the preposition “para” (to/for) + the feminine singular article “a”. It’s used to show destination, recipient, or purpose before a feminine noun: e.g., “para a economia” (for the economy). With some female names, Portuguese may also use the article (“para a Kate”). In casual speech/writing, “para a” is often shortened to “pra” (e.g., “pra Kate”).
target_language_example: Comprei um presente para a minha mãe.
native_language_example: I bought a gift for my mom.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like "ir" (to go) to say someone is going to bed/going to sleep: "ir para a cama". It refers to the act of going to bed (often meaning going to sleep), not just physically going toward a bed.
target_language_example: Estou cansado, vou para a cama cedo hoje.
native_language_example: I’m tired; I’m going to bed early today.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "para" to indicate destination/goal (going/taking someone to school). Often follows verbs like "ir" (to go), "voltar" (to return), "caminhar" (to walk), and "levar" (to take/bring).
target_language_example: Vou para a escola agora.
native_language_example: I'm going to school now.

additional_notes: Used to say how someone goes to school: "para a escola" (to school) + "de" + transport (by). You can swap the transport: "de carro" (by car), "de trem" (by train), "a pé" (on foot). Word order is flexible in conversation: "Vou para a escola de ônibus" / "Vou de ônibus para a escola."
target_language_example: Hoje eu vou para a escola de ônibus porque está chovendo.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to school by bus because it’s raining.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction/destination (often a train, subway/metro, or bus station). It commonly follows movement verbs like ir (to go), correr (to run), voltar (to return), levar (to take/bring someone), and pegar (to catch a bus/train). You may also hear a more general version: para a estação ferroviária (to the train station) or para a estação do metrô (to the метро/subway station).
target_language_example: Preciso ir para a estação agora.
native_language_example: I need to go to the station now.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (like ir, mandar, levar) to say someone is going to university/college (often meaning to attend or start studying there). In Brazil, "faculdade" often refers to a college/university program or institution; in Portugal you may also hear "universidade". "Para" expresses direction/destination (“to”).
target_language_example: Ela vai para a faculdade de manhã.
native_language_example: She goes to college in the morning.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is going to a party, something is intended for a party, or relates to a party (e.g., clothes, invitations). It’s formed by "para" (to/for) + "a" (the, feminine) + "festa" (party).
target_language_example: Você vai para a festa hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Are you going to the party tonight?

meaning: 'to us' / 'for us' (using the informal pronoun a gente = 'we/us').
additional_notes: Used with verbs that take para to indicate the recipient or beneficiary: escrever para a gente (write to us), fazer/pegar algo para a gente (do/get something for us), pagar para a gente (pay for us), trabalhar para a gente (work for us). A gente is very common in everyday speech and usually takes singular verb forms (a gente vai, a gente está). More formal: para nós.
target_language_example: Você pode explicar isso para a gente?
native_language_example: Can you explain that to us?

meaning: "to my" / "for my" (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used when something is directed toward you or done for your benefit: para = “to/for”, a = “the” (feminine singular), minha = “my” (feminine singular). It must be followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., para a minha casa, para a minha festa, para a minha esquerda). In everyday speech, it’s often pronounced like “pra minha” when the noun doesn’t need the article (e.g., “pra minha casa”).
target_language_example: Você pode vir para a minha casa depois do trabalho?
native_language_example: Can you come to my house after work?

meaning: to the police (e.g., call/report/turn someone in to the police).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like “ligar/telefonar para a polícia” (to call the police) and “denunciar/relatar algo para a polícia” (to report something to the police). It can also appear with “ir para a polícia” (to go to the police) or “levar alguém para a polícia” (to take someone to the police station).
target_language_example: Se você vir algo suspeito, ligue para a polícia.
native_language_example: If you see something suspicious, call the police.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "para" to show direction/purpose (going/taking someone somewhere): "ir para a praia" (to go to the beach), "levar alguém para a praia" (to take someone to the beach). In the expression "de frente para a praia", "para" means "facing/toward": a house with an ocean/beach view.
target_language_example: Vamos para a praia amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: Let's go to the beach tomorrow morning.

meaning: “for/to your” (before a feminine singular noun); can also mean “for/to his/her” depending on context.
additional_notes: Formed by: para (“to/for”) + a (“the”, feminine singular) + sua (“your / his / her”). In Portuguese, possessives like seu/sua can be ambiguous (your vs. his/her), so context often clarifies. Used when the noun is feminine singular (ex.: para a sua amiga, para a sua casa, para a sua dor de cabeça).
target_language_example: Tenho um presente para a sua mãe.
native_language_example: I have a present for your mother.

additional_notes: Used to say something is intended for someone’s party ("for") or someone is going to the party ("to"). "Sua" can mean "your" (informal you) or "your" (formal you); if you’re talking to a friend using "tu", you might also hear "para a tua festa".
target_language_example: Comprei um presente para a sua festa.
native_language_example: I bought a gift for your party.

additional_notes: Uses "para" + infinitive to show purpose (why someone does something): "Nós viemos para ajudar" = "We came to help." Often used when offering assistance: "Posso fazer algo para ajudar?" You can add who you’re helping: "para ajudar o Tom" (to help Tom).
target_language_example: Estou aqui para ajudar você.
native_language_example: I’m here to help you.

meaning: "to help him" / "in order to help him."
additional_notes: Used to express purpose (para + infinitive) followed by the object pronoun -lo (= "him"). In Brazilian Portuguese, many speakers often say "para ajudar ele" in everyday speech, but "para ajudá-lo" is more formal/standard and common in writing. The verb is accented: ajudar + -lo → ajudá-lo.
target_language_example: Vou ligar para ajudá-lo com o trabalho.
native_language_example: I’m going to call to help him with the work.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to mean something is intended or suitable “for drinking” (e.g., água para beber). Used after an adjective + demais/muito to mean “too (adj.) to drink” (quente demais para beber). With people, it can also mean being old enough to drink alcohol (muito novo para beber cerveja). In phrases like sair para beber, it means “to go out drinking.”
target_language_example: Você tem água para beber?
native_language_example: Do you have drinking water?

additional_notes: Used with a verb of movement (usually "ir" or "voltar") to say someone is going home immediately. "Para casa" means "(to) home," and "agora" means "now." In commands, it can be: "Vai para casa agora" = "Go home now."
target_language_example: Vamos para casa agora porque já está tarde.
native_language_example: Let's go home now because it's already late.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement like ir/voltar (to go/come back) to say you’re going home earlier than expected or earlier than normal. Often appears as part of a longer phrase: “ir para casa mais cedo” (to go home earlier), “voltar para casa mais cedo” (to come back home earlier).
target_language_example: Hoje vou para casa mais cedo porque tenho uma consulta.
native_language_example: Today I'm going home earlier because I have an appointment.

meaning: “to get there” / “in order to arrive there.”
additional_notes: Used after a verb to express the goal of arriving at a place (lá = “there”). Very common with time expressions and travel verbs like levar/demorar (“to take”), pegar (“to take” a bus), and with transport phrases like de ônibus (“by bus”).
target_language_example: Qual é o melhor caminho para chegar lá?
native_language_example: What’s the best way to get there?

additional_notes: Most often it means purpose: **para + verb** = “in order to …” (e.g., *sair para comer* = “go out to eat”). It can also mean suitability: “good/ready/OK **to eat**” (e.g., *bom para comer*). In service contexts it can contrast **para comer aqui** (“to eat here”) vs **para levar** (“to take away/to go”).
target_language_example: Vamos parar aqui para comer antes do filme.
native_language_example: Let’s stop here to eat before the movie.

meaning: to buy; in order to buy.
additional_notes: Uses para + infinitive (comprar) to express purpose: why someone does something ("in order to buy"). It can also come after verbs like pedir/precisar: "me pediu para comprar" = "asked me to buy"; "precisam de dinheiro para comprar" = "need money to buy".
target_language_example: Preciso ir ao mercado para comprar pão.
native_language_example: I need to go to the market to buy bread.

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or direction toward where the speaker is (or toward the current place). Common in commands: "Vem para cá!" (Come here!) and "Para cá!" (Over here!/This way!). It can also mean "to here" in the sense of moving to this location: "mudei de Boston para cá" = "I moved from Boston to here."
target_language_example: Vem para cá, por favor.
native_language_example: Come here, please.

additional_notes: Used to express movement or direction from outside to the interior of a place (often with verbs like entrar, vir, ir, trazer, colocar, carregar). It can appear by itself (“Vá para dentro.” = “Go inside.”) or with a location (“para dentro da casa” = “into the house”).
target_language_example: Está frio lá fora; vem para dentro.
native_language_example: It’s cold outside; come inside.

additional_notes: Used with movement verbs (e.g., pular, empurrar, correr) to show motion from outside to inside. It’s the combination of para dentro de (“into”) + a (“the”, feminine singular), so it’s followed by a feminine singular noun: para dentro da piscina/caverna. With masculine singular you’ll usually see para dentro do (e.g., para dentro do carro).
target_language_example: Ela entrou para dentro da casa rapidamente.
native_language_example: She went into the house quickly.

meaning: 'to/for her' (addressing a woman or referring to a female person).
additional_notes: Used with verbs that take "para" to show the recipient/target or beneficiary of an action (e.g., speaking to her, barking at her, buying something for her). "Ela" means "she/her" (female), and after the preposition "para" it stays "ela" (not "a ela"). In fast speech/writing, you may also see the contraction "pra ela" (informal).
target_language_example: Vou explicar isso para ela depois.
native_language_example: I’ll explain that to her later.

additional_notes: Uses para + ele to show who benefits from something ('for him') or who something is directed to ('to him'), especially with giving, bringing, buying, cooking, telling. With some verbs (like ligar), Portuguese often uses a preposition: "Liguei para ele" = "I called him." Also note the contraction: para + o = pro, but para + ele does not contract (you say "para ele").
target_language_example: Comprei um presente para ele.
native_language_example: I bought a present for him.

additional_notes: Uses para + infinitive to express purpose (“in order to…”): Fui lá para estudar. It can also follow verbs like dizer (“to tell”) to mean “to tell someone to study”: Eu disse a ele/ela para estudar. Often followed by what you’re studying: para estudar música/arte/vocabulário.
target_language_example: Comprei um caderno novo para estudar para a prova.
native_language_example: I bought a new notebook to study for the test.

meaning: "to do" / "to make"; often "(in order) to do" or "to do" (as in "things to do").
additional_notes: Uses the infinitive after "para" to express purpose: "para fazer X" = "(in order) to do/make X". It’s also common after a noun to mean "to do": "coisas para fazer" = "things to do". "Fazer" can mean both "to do" and "to make", depending on the context.
target_language_example: Tenho muita coisa para fazer hoje.
native_language_example: I have a lot to do today.

meaning: “to do that” / “in order to do that.”
additional_notes: Used after a verb, adjective, or noun to express purpose or what someone needs/gets/has trouble with: e.g., “help to do that,” “take weeks to do that,” “difficulty doing that,” “a chance to do that.” In everyday speech it can often be replaced by “para isso” when the verb is understood.
target_language_example: Eu preciso de mais tempo para fazer isso.
native_language_example: I need more time to do that.

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs of movement or taking/bringing to indicate going from inside to outside (e.g., ir para fora = to go outside; levar para fora = to take outside). It can refer to leaving a building/room or moving something out.
target_language_example: Vamos para fora tomar um ar.
native_language_example: Let’s go outside to get some fresh air.

additional_notes: Used to talk about plans, reservations, or arrangements happening later today in the evening/night. Common with verbs like planejar (to plan) and with requests like booking a room: “um quarto para hoje à noite”.
target_language_example: Você tem uma mesa para hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Do you have a table for tonight?

meaning: 'to go (in order to go)'; used to say the destination or purpose of going.
additional_notes: Often follows a verb (e.g., pedir, dizer) to introduce an action someone should do: "pedir ... para ir" = "ask ... to go". It’s also very common before a destination or direction: "para ir à estação" (to get to the station), "para ir de X a Y" (to go from X to Y). In questions, it can mean "to get to" when asking for directions or transport.
target_language_example: Qual é a melhor rota para ir ao aeroporto?
native_language_example: What’s the best route to get to the airport?

additional_notes: Often used after verbs like "convidar" (to invite), "sair" (to go out), or "ir" (to go) to say the purpose is dinner: "convidou-me para jantar" = invited me to have dinner. It can also appear after "estar" in the sense of being about to do something: "estava para jantar" = I was about to have dinner.
target_language_example: Vamos sair para jantar hoje à noite.
native_language_example: Let's go out for dinner tonight.

additional_notes: Uses "para" + infinitive to express purpose: something is intended/used so that you can read it. Often after a noun: "um livro para ler" (a book to read), "óculos para ler" (reading glasses). It can also appear alone as a short answer/title meaning “to read.”
target_language_example: Peguei um artigo para ler mais tarde.
native_language_example: I grabbed an article to read later.

meaning: to help me / in order to help me.
additional_notes: Used with "para" + infinitive to express purpose ("in order to..."). "Me" is an object pronoun meaning "me"; it can come before the infinitive: "para me ajudar". After adjectives like "muito bêbado", it often means "too ... to": "muito bêbado para me ajudar" = "too drunk to help me".
target_language_example: Você pode ficar um pouco mais para me ajudar?
native_language_example: Can you stay a little longer to help me?

meaning: to/for me; for my part (as far as I’m concerned).
additional_notes: Used after the preposition "para" to show who something is directed to or done for: "Ligue para mim" (call me), "um presente para mim" (a gift for me). It can also mean "for me/as far as I’m concerned" when talking about your perspective or what is easy/important to you: "Para mim, é fácil". After prepositions in Portuguese, you say "mim" (not "eu").
target_language_example: Isso é muito importante para mim.
native_language_example: This is very important to me.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to do something for you or direct an action toward you. Often comes after the verb: "Abra a porta para mim, por favor." With verbs like "olhar" or "sorrir", "para mim" means "at me" (direction), not "for me". In speech you may also hear "pra mim, por favor" (more casual pronunciation of "para").
target_language_example: Você pode guardar isso para mim, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you keep this for me, please?

meaning: 'for us' / 'to us' (directed toward us or for our benefit).
additional_notes: Used with verbs to show the recipient or beneficiary is a group that includes the speaker (“us”). Common with giving/making/preparing ("fazer/preparar algo para nós" = do/make something for us), reactions directed at you ("sorrir/acenou para nós" = smiled/waved at us), or evaluation/importance ("uma honra/uma vitória para nós" = an honor/a victory for us). In "trabalhar para nós", it means “work for us” (for our company/household).
target_language_example: Você pode explicar isso para nós?
native_language_example: Can you explain that to us?

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun with the definite article “o”. It commonly indicates destination (going to a place), recipient (for someone/something), or purpose (intended for something). In informal speech/writing, it’s often contracted to “pro” (e.g., “Vou pro México”).
target_language_example: Comprei um presente para o meu irmão.
native_language_example: I bought a present for my brother.

meaning: for breakfast (to have/eat at breakfast time).
additional_notes: Used to say something is intended as breakfast or that someone is going somewhere in order to have breakfast. Common with verbs like fazer (to make), querer (to want), descer (to go down), convidar (to invite), encontrar-se (to meet). You may also hear: "no café da manhã" = at breakfast / during breakfast.
target_language_example: Vou tomar fruta e iogurte para o café da manhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to have fruit and yogurt for breakfast.

meaning: toward the sky; up at the sky.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like olhar (to look), levantar (to raise), and apontar (to point) to indicate direction—upward, toward the sky. Often translates as “up at the sky” in natural English.
target_language_example: À noite, gosto de olhar para o céu e ver as estrelas.
native_language_example: At night, I like to look up at the sky and see the stars.

meaning: abroad; to another country (outside your country).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of going/traveling (ir, viajar, mudar-se) to say someone goes outside their home country. Often used without naming a destination: “viajar para o exterior” = “travel abroad.” It contrasts with “no exterior” (“abroad” as a place/state: “Ele mora no exterior.”).
target_language_example: No ano que vem, vou para o exterior a trabalho.
native_language_example: Next year, I’m going abroad for work.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "traduzir" (to translate) to say the target language of a translation. Literally "to/for the French (language)"; in English you usually say "into French".
target_language_example: Você pode traduzir isso para o francês?
native_language_example: Can you translate this into French?

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (ir, levar, ser levado, transportar) to show destination. Often appears in urgent/medical contexts (e.g., "às pressas para o hospital" = "to the hospital in a hurry"). In European Portuguese you may also hear "para o hospital" and "ao hospital" with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Precisamos ir para o hospital agora.
native_language_example: We need to go to the hospital now.

additional_notes: Used to say something is intended for dinner time or for a dinner meal/event. Common with verbs like "ficar" (to stay) and "convidados" (guests): "ficar para o jantar" = stay for dinner; "convidados para o jantar" = guests for dinner. You can also use it with plans and timing: "voltar para o jantar" (come back for dinner).
target_language_example: Você vai voltar para o jantar?
native_language_example: Are you going to come back for dinner?

meaning: to the sea; facing/toward the sea.
additional_notes: Often expresses movement/direction (e.g., "fugiu para o mar" = ran off into the sea). With "de frente" or "vista", it means orientation/view toward the sea: "de frente para o mar" (facing the sea), "com vista para o mar" (with a sea view).
target_language_example: Quero um quarto de hotel com vista para o mar.
native_language_example: I want a hotel room with a sea view.

additional_notes: Used to say something is good/bad for nature and the planet. Common after comparatives ("melhor/pior para o meio ambiente") and with verbs like "fazer mal" (to harm) or "ser bom" (to be good). "Meio ambiente" literally means "environment."
target_language_example: Essa embalagem é ruim para o meio ambiente.
native_language_example: This packaging is bad for the environment.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction, recipient, or purpose involving something that belongs to you: *para* + *o* = **para o** (“to the/for the”), and **meu** means “my” (masculine singular). It must match the noun: **para a minha** (feminine), **para os meus** (masc. plural), **para as minhas** (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Comprei um presente para o meu pai.
native_language_example: I bought a gift for my dad.

additional_notes:
Common in patterns like:
- **de X para o outro** = "from one X to the next" (sudden change): *De um momento para o outro...*
- **um/uma ... para o outro/a** = "for each other": *feitos um para o outro*
- **de um ... para o outro** = "from one ... to the other": *do fone de um ouvido para o outro*
target_language_example: Passei a mala de uma mão para a outra e continuei andando.
native_language_example: I moved the suitcase from one hand to the other and kept walking.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like “se preparar” (to prepare) or “estar preparado” (to be prepared) to talk about being ready for a negative possibility. Common in the fixed contrast “esperar o melhor e se preparar para o pior” (“hope for the best and prepare for the worst”).
target_language_example: Vamos torcer para dar certo, mas precisamos nos preparar para o pior.
native_language_example: Let’s hope it works out, but we need to prepare for the worst.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction/destination. "para" = "to/toward" + "o" ("the") + "ponto de ônibus" ("bus stop"). Very common in questions asking for directions ("o caminho para...") and with verbs of movement like "ir" (to go) and "correr" (to run).
target_language_example: Vou para o ponto de ônibus agora.
native_language_example: I’m going to the bus stop now.

additional_notes: Used to indicate the recipient/beneficiary is "you" and the noun that follows is masculine singular: "para o seu + noun". Example: "para o seu casamento" = "for your wedding". (Feminine: "para a sua"; plural: "para os seus / para as suas".)
target_language_example: Comprei um presente para o seu irmão.
native_language_example: I bought a gift for your brother.

additional_notes: Used to say something is necessary, important, or contributes to achieving success. Very common after phrases like “a chave para o sucesso” (the key to success), “fundamental para o sucesso” (fundamental for success), and “vital para o sucesso” (vital for success). It can also appear as “para o sucesso de + [noun]” to specify what is meant (e.g., “para o sucesso do nosso plano” = for the success of our plan).
target_language_example: A prática diária é essencial para o sucesso.
native_language_example: Daily practice is essential for success.

additional_notes: Uses "para" to show destination or purpose. Common with verbs of movement ("ir para o trabalho" = to go to work) and with "aparecer para o trabalho" (to show up for work). It can also mean being chosen/selected for a job or task ("escolher alguém para o trabalho" = choose someone for the job).
target_language_example: Hoje vou cedo para o trabalho.
native_language_example: Today I’m going early to work.

additional_notes: Used to ask about or refer to a destination or direction someone/something is going. Often appears with verbs of movement like ir (to go), viajar (to travel), or with going constructions like estar indo. Contrast: "onde" = where (location), "para onde" = where to (destination).
target_language_example: Você sabe para onde ele foi?
native_language_example: Do you know where he went (to)?

additional_notes: Contraction of “para” + “os”. Used before a masculine plural noun meaning destination (“to the…”) or intended recipient/purpose (“for the…”): e.g., “para os fundos” (to the back), “para os meus pais” (for/to my parents), “para os botes” (to the lifeboats).
target_language_example: Vou mandar uma mensagem para os meus amigos.
native_language_example: I’m going to send a message to my friends.

meaning: to go for a walk; for a walk (often with a dog).
additional_notes: Used after verbs of movement/action like levar (to take), sair (to go out), ir (to go) to say the purpose: going out in order to walk around. Very common with pets: levar o cachorro para passear = take the dog for a walk.
target_language_example: Vou levar o cachorro para passear depois do almoço.
native_language_example: I’m going to take the dog for a walk after lunch.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to express purpose: para + infinitive = “in order to…”. PegAR can mean physically “grab/pick up” (para pegar o livro, o chapéu) or “catch/take” a means of transport (para pegar o trem). The “o” is the masculine singular definite article (“the”); change it with the noun: para pegar a (fem.), para pegar os/as (plural).
target_language_example: Saí cedo para pegar o ônibus.
native_language_example: I left early to catch the bus.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive after "para" to express purpose/goal: you do something in order to catch the train (often because of time pressure). "Pegar" here means "to catch" (a train/bus), not "to pick up". You can swap in other transport: "para pegar o ônibus / o metrô / o voo".
target_language_example: Vou sair mais cedo para pegar o trem das 7.
native_language_example: I’m going to leave earlier to catch the 7 o’clock train.

additional_notes: Used after a verb to show purpose: "(do something) para pegar o ônibus" = "(do something) in order to catch the bus". With "pegar", it often means "catch" (especially when you might miss it), but it can also mean simply "take" the bus as a means of transport. "Ônibus" is commonly shortened to "ônibus" (same word) or, informally in Brazil, "busão".
target_language_example: Saí mais cedo para pegar o ônibus.
native_language_example: I left earlier to catch the bus.

additional_notes: Used to explain the purpose of an action (para + infinitive = “in order to…”). Common in health/first-aid contexts: gelo (ice) helps reduzir (reduce) o inchaço (swelling). You may also hear “pra reduzir o inchaço” in casual speech.
target_language_example: Tome este remédio para reduzir o inchaço.
native_language_example: Take this medicine to reduce the swelling.

additional_notes: Usually means being ready or about to leave a place. Common with verbs like "preparar-se" (to get ready) and "estar" (to be): "preparou-se para sair" = got ready to go out/leave; "já está para sair" = he’s already about to leave.
target_language_example: Estou pronto(a) para sair, só falta pegar as chaves.
native_language_example: I’m ready to go out/leave; I just need to grab the keys.

meaning: "to be" / "in order to be" (for becoming or serving as something).
additional_notes: Used mainly to express purpose or suitability: (1) destiny/intention: "nascer para ser..." = "be born to be..."; (2) requirements/qualities needed: "para ser professor..." = "to be a teacher..."; (3) being chosen/called/asked to take a role: "escolher/chamar alguém para ser..." = "choose/call someone to be...". Often followed by a noun or profession/role.
target_language_example: Ela estudou muito para ser médica.
native_language_example: She studied a lot to become a doctor.

additional_notes: Used with the reflexive pronoun “si” to mean that an action is done for the benefit of the same person as the subject. It agrees in gender/number: “para si mesma” (for herself), “para si mesmos/as” (for themselves). Often used to emphasize doing something for your own benefit or deceiving yourself (e.g., “mentir para si mesmo” = “to lie to yourself”).
target_language_example: Ele guardou o último pedaço de bolo para si mesmo.
native_language_example: He saved the last piece of cake for himself.

meaning: 'for you' (to you), addressing one person informally.
additional_notes: Used with "tu" (informal 'you') and common in European Portuguese; in Brazilian Portuguese, people more often use "para você". It can indicate the recipient of something (a message, a song) or who something is meant for, and with verbs like "mentir" it can mean 'to you'.
target_language_example: Isto é para ti.
native_language_example: This is for you.

additional_notes: Used to show the recipient or who something applies to: telling something to everyone (Conte para todo mundo), sending something to everyone (mandar e-mail para todo mundo), obvious to everyone (óbvio para todo mundo), lying to everyone (mentir para todo mundo), or enough space for everyone (espaço suficiente ... para todo mundo). Often interchangeable with the more formal "para todos" / "para todo o mundo" depending on region.
target_language_example: Vou explicar isso para todo mundo na reunião.
native_language_example: I’m going to explain this to everyone in the meeting.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement to mean “back/backwards” (e.g., dar um passo para trás, cair para trás, nadar para trás). With “deixar” it often means “leave behind” (deixar algo/alguém para trás). It can also be used figuratively for going back in time or reversing something (fazer girar para trás a roda do tempo).
target_language_example: Esqueci minha mochila para trás.
native_language_example: I left my backpack behind.

additional_notes: Used to express purpose: someone does something "para ver" (to see/watch/check/find out). It’s often followed by a noun (para ver um filme, para ver a filha) or by an indirect question with "se" (para ver se... = to see if...).
target_language_example: Vou ligar para ver se ele está em casa.
native_language_example: I’m going to call to see if he’s home.

para ver o que estava acontecendo

target_language_multi_word_term: para ver o que estava acontecendo
meaning: "to see what was happening / going on."
additional_notes: Uses **para + infinitive** to express purpose (“in order to…”). **o que estava acontecendo** means “what was happening/going on” at that moment (past continuous: **estava + -ndo**). Common when someone reacts to a noise or commotion and goes to check.
target_language_example: Ouvi um barulho na rua e fui lá fora para ver o que estava acontecendo.
native_language_example: I heard a noise in the street and went outside to see what was going on.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person you address as “você.” With verbs of giving/bringing/leaving, it often means “for you” (intended for you). With verbs of saying/telling, it often means “to you.” You’ll also hear it in fixed expressions like “Parabéns para você!” (“Congratulations to you!”).
target_language_example: Comprei um presente para você.
native_language_example: I bought a gift for you.

meaning: 'to see him' / 'in order to see him'.
additional_notes: Used to express purpose with para + infinitive ("in order to..."). "Vê-lo" = "ver" (to see) + the object pronoun "-lo" (him/it). Very common in Brazilian Portuguese in formal or neutral speech; in everyday conversation people also say "para ver ele". In "Dá para vê-lo daqui", it means "You can see him/it from here" (i.e., it’s possible to see him/it).
target_language_example: Vou passar na sua casa para vê-lo antes da reunião.
native_language_example: I’ll stop by your house to see you (him) before the meeting.

meaning: “to do that” / “in order to do that.”
additional_notes: Used after a verb, adjective, or noun to express purpose or what someone needs/gets/has trouble with: e.g., “help to do that,” “take weeks to do that,” “difficulty doing that,” “a chance to do that.” In everyday speech it can often be replaced by “para isso” when the verb is understood.
target_language_example: Eu preciso de mais tempo para fazer isso.
native_language_example: I need more time to do that.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop an action: **Para de** + infinitive verb (e.g., *para de correr* = “stop running”). It’s the informal **tu** command of *parar*; in Brazil you’ll also often hear **Pare de** as a more formal/polite option, especially with *você* or in customer-service situations.
target_language_example: Para de mexer no celular durante a aula.
native_language_example: Stop using your phone during class.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb to mean stopping an activity: "parar de" + infinitive (parar de tocar, parar de reclamar). Often used in requests/complaints ("Por favor, pare de..."). In the present/future it can also mean 'won’t stop' ("não vai parar de...").
target_language_example: Eu preciso parar de procrastinar.
native_language_example: I need to stop procrastinating.

additional_notes: Used to ask or tell someone to stop speaking. Very common in requests and commands: "Pare de falar" (Stop talking), "Você poderia parar de falar?" (Could you stop talking?). Often appears after verbs like "pedir" (to ask): "Ele pediu para ela parar de falar".
target_language_example: Por favor, pare de falar um minuto.
native_language_example: Please stop talking for a minute.

additional_notes: Uses the verb pattern "parar de + infinitive" to mean "to stop doing (something)". "Aquilo" means "that" (something over there / something already known in context). Often used after verbs like "pedir" (to ask), "mandar" (to order), or "convencer" (to convince): "Pede/Manda/Convence alguém a parar de fazer aquilo."
target_language_example: Por favor, pare de fazer aquilo agora.
native_language_example: Please, stop doing that now.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone (or yourself) to stop an action. Common patterns: "precisar parar de..." (need to stop...), "ter de parar de..." (have to stop...), "dever parar de..." / "deveria parar de..." (should / should stop...). You can replace "isso" with a verb or noun phrase: "parar de fumar" (stop smoking), "parar de falar" (stop talking).
target_language_example: Por favor, pare de fazer isso agora.
native_language_example: Please stop doing that now.

meaning: to stop smoking; to quit smoking.
additional_notes: Uses the verb pattern **parar de + infinitive** (“to stop doing something”). Here, **fumar** = “to smoke.” Common with advice/obligation verbs like **ter que** (have to), **precisar** (need to), **dever** (should/must), and with **tentar** (try): *tentar parar de fumar*.
target_language_example: Eu parei de fumar no ano passado.
native_language_example: I quit smoking last year.

additional_notes: "Parasse" is the imperfect subjunctive of "parar" (to stop). It’s commonly used after expressions like "querer que" (to want that), "gostar que" (to wish/like that), "pedir para que" (to ask that), "sugerir que" (to suggest that), and "advertir que" (to warn that), when talking about what you want/ask/suggest someone should do: "Eu queria que ela parasse de fumar" = "I wanted her to stop smoking."
target_language_example: Ele pediu que eu parasse de fumar.
native_language_example: He asked me to stop smoking.

additional_notes: "Pare" is the formal/neutral imperative (command) of "parar" (to stop). It’s followed by "de" + infinitive: "Pare de falar" (Stop talking). With someone you address as "tu," you may also hear "pára de". It can sound firm or annoyed depending on tone.
target_language_example: Pare de mexer no seu celular, por favor.
native_language_example: Stop messing with your phone, please.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop doing something to you. Grammatically: **pare** (imperative of *parar*) + **de** + verb in the infinitive + **me** (object pronoun “me”). In the examples, **me** comes before the infinitive: *Pare de me copiar.* You can also drop **me** if there’s no “me” object (e.g., *Pare de falar!* = “Stop talking!”).
target_language_example: Pare de me interromper, por favor.
native_language_example: Stop interrupting me, please.

additional_notes: An imperative used to tell someone to stop having a certain behavior or trait. It’s followed by an adjective (e.g., curioso/curiosa, emotivo, teimoso). The verb form "pare" is a formal/neutral command (often used with "você"); in informal speech with "tu," you may hear "para de ser tão".
target_language_example: Pare de ser tão impaciente!
native_language_example: Stop being so impatient!

meaning: "It seems to me that..." / "I think that..."
additional_notes: Used to give your opinion or impression in a softer, less direct way than stating something as a fact. Often followed by a clause with "que" (e.g., "parece-me que ele está atrasado"). You can also hear the simpler "parece que..." ("it seems that...") without "me".
target_language_example: Parece-me que hoje vai chover.
native_language_example: It seems to me that it’s going to rain today.

additional_notes: Used to say something looks or sounds true, without being certain. It’s the verb phrase "parecer" (to seem) + "estar" (to be, temporary state), so it’s often followed by an adjective (cansado, feliz) or by "-ndo" (gerund) to describe an ongoing action (dormindo, tendo...). You can change the subject/tense: "Eu pareço estar..." (I seem to be...), "Parecia estar..." (He/She seemed to be...).
target_language_example: Você parece estar com pressa.
native_language_example: You seem to be in a hurry.

meaning: "seems to be very" (or "seems to be a lot").
additional_notes: Used to describe your impression of someone’s state/feeling: parece (it seems) + estar (to be, temporary state) + muito (very/a lot). Commonly followed by an adjective (assustado, confuso, feliz, nervoso) or by "mais" for comparisons ("muito mais feliz" = "much happier"). You can swap the subject: "Ela parece estar muito cansada."
target_language_example: Você parece estar muito cansado hoje.
native_language_example: You seem to be very tired today.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective or adverb phrase to say something appears to a strong degree: “parece muito + adjective/adverb” (e.g., parece muito confiante = seems very confident). It can also appear in comparisons: “parece muito mais …” = “seems/looks much more …”.
target_language_example: Ela parece muito cansada hoje.
native_language_example: She looks very tired today.

additional_notes: Used to express an impression or inference rather than certainty, often based on what you see, hear, or know. Common in everyday speech: "Parece que vai chover" (It looks like it’s going to rain). You can also use it to soften a statement or opinion.
target_language_example: Parece que eles se esqueceram da reunião.
native_language_example: It seems like they forgot about the meeting.

meaning: "it seems that the..." / "it looks like the..."
additional_notes: Used to introduce something you think is true based on what you know or see (often with some uncertainty). It’s the verb "parecer" (to seem) + "que" + the article "o" (“the” for masculine singular nouns). You can also say "Parece que a..." (feminine), "Parece que os..." (masculine plural), "Parece que as..." (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Parece que o ônibus está atrasado.
native_language_example: It looks like the bus is late.

meaning: “it seems like you…” / “it looks like you…”
additional_notes: Used to introduce an impression, inference, or something you’ve heard, often with some uncertainty. It’s followed by a verb clause (usually in the past or present): "Parece que você + verbo...". Common in both formal and informal speech.
target_language_example: Parece que você não entendeu a pergunta.
native_language_example: It seems like you didn’t understand the question.

additional_notes: Used to say something is likely true based on what you see/know, but you’re not 100% sure. Conjugate "parecer" for the subject (eu pareço, ele/ela parece, nós parecemos, etc.) + infinitive "ser". Often followed by an adjective or noun: "parece ser rico" (seems to be rich), "parece ser um oficial" (seems to be an officer). It can also be used without a subject as a general statement: "Parece ser difícil" (It seems to be difficult).
target_language_example: Isso parece ser uma ideia melhor do que a última.
native_language_example: That seems to be a better idea than the last one.

meaning: “seems to be a person (who is)…”, used to describe someone’s apparent character.
additional_notes: Used when you’re giving an impression rather than stating a fact. It’s commonly followed by an adjective (amigável, confiável, honesta) or a longer description: “Parece ser uma pessoa muito inteligente.” You can change the subject (Eu/Tu/Você/Ele/Ela/Nome) and keep the structure. Note: “parece” = “it seems/you seem”; “ser” = “to be”; “uma pessoa” = “a person.”
target_language_example: Ela parece ser uma pessoa muito gentil.
native_language_example: She seems to be a very kind person.

additional_notes: Used to soften an opinion or observation. It comes from the verb "parecer" (to seem/to look). You can change it to match the subject: "pareço um pouco" (I seem a bit), "pareces um pouco" (you seem a bit), "parecem um pouco" (they seem a bit). Note: "se parece" (as in "Você se parece...") is different and means "to look like / resemble" someone.
target_language_example: O seu plano parece um pouco arriscado.
native_language_example: Your plan seems a little risky.

meaning: 'they seem to be' / 'they appear to be'.
additional_notes: Used with a plural subject (eles/elas/vocês) to express an impression, not a certainty. It’s the verb *parecer* (to seem) + *estar* (to be, temporary state). Often followed by an adjective (*parecem estar cansados*) or by a gerund (*parecem estar se divertindo* = “seem to be having fun”).
target_language_example: Eles parecem estar com pressa.
native_language_example: They seem to be in a hurry.

meaning: “seemed to be; appeared to be” (in the past).
additional_notes:
Used to describe how someone/something appeared, based on what you observed, without certainty. It combines the imperfect of 
parcer
 (parecia = “seemed”) + the infinitive 
estar
 (“to be”), often followed by an adjective (impressionado, satisfeito, doente) or a state (com fome). The imperfect 
parecia
 suggests an ongoing impression in the past.
target_language_example: Ela parecia estar cansada depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: She seemed to be tired after work.

additional_notes: Used to describe your impression about someone’s state or feelings: **[subject] parecia estar muito + adjective**. **Parecia** is past (imperfect) of *parecer* (“to seem”), and **estar** is used for temporary states (e.g., *animado, assustado, irritado*). In casual speech, Portuguese may drop **estar**: *O Tom parecia muito animado.*
target_language_example: Ela parecia estar muito cansada depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: She seemed to be very tired after work.

additional_notes: Used before a noun that describes a feeling, mood, or state: com saudades (missing someone/home), com raiva (angry), com pressa (in a hurry), com sono (sleepy). It’s a descriptive way to say how someone appeared based on what you observed. Often followed by an article/intensifier: com muita pressa (very rushed).
target_language_example: Ela parecia estar com medo de falar em público.
native_language_example: She seemed to be afraid of speaking in public.

additional_notes: "Parei" is the past of "parar" (to stop), so this is typically said to announce you quit (often recently) or that you stopped at some point in the past. You can add time expressions: "parei de fumar faz três anos" = "I quit smoking three years ago". It can also be paired with other actions: "parei de fumar e de beber" = "I quit smoking and drinking."
target_language_example: Parei de fumar no ano passado e me sinto muito melhor.
native_language_example: I quit smoking last year and I feel much better.

additional_notes: Used to say how long it has been since you stopped smoking: "Parei de fumar há + time period" (há seis meses, há um ano). The word "há" here means "ago" / "for" in the sense of elapsed time. In everyday speech you may hear "há ... atrás" (e.g., "há três meses atrás"), but it’s redundant because both "há" and "atrás" already express "ago".
target_language_example: Parei de fumar há dois anos.
native_language_example: I quit smoking two years ago.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "parar" used to tell more than one person (or "you" plural) to stop doing something. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb: "Parem de + infinitive" (Parem de correr = Stop running). For one person, use "para de"; for a more formal plural, you may also hear "parem de" addressing "vocês".
target_language_example: Parem de falar e prestem atenção!
native_language_example: Stop talking and pay attention!

meaning: “Stop fighting!” / “Stop arguing!” (addressing more than one person).
additional_notes: Imperative command to a group (you plural). Uses "parar de" + infinitive ("brigar" = to fight/argue), meaning “to stop doing something.” The verb form "parem" is used when speaking to multiple people (vocês).
target_language_example: Parem de brigar agora, por favor.
native_language_example: Stop arguing now, please.

additional_notes: Used to count shoes as a set of two (left + right). Often used with numbers and quantity words (e.g., “dois/três/muitos pares de sapatos”).
target_language_example: Preciso comprar dois pares de sapatos para o trabalho.
native_language_example: I need to buy two pairs of shoes for work.
