additional_notes: Past tense of **parar de + infinitive** (“to stop doing”). It’s followed by a verb in the infinitive: **parou de falar** (stopped talking), **parou de chover** (stopped raining). Often used with time words like **depois que** (“after”) to say something happened once an action stopped.
target_language_example: Ele parou de fumar no ano passado.
native_language_example: He stopped smoking last year.

additional_notes: Past tense: "parar de" + infinitive means "to stop (doing something)". "Parou" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) for ele/ela/você. Common time expressions: "há dois anos" = "two years ago" (literally "there is two years"). You can change the subject: "Eu parei de fumar" (I stopped), "Nós paramos de fumar" (we stopped).
target_language_example: Eu parei de fumar no ano passado.
native_language_example: I stopped smoking last year.

additional_notes: Used when something used to work but suddenly doesn’t anymore (often because of an accident, damage, or a problem/update). It’s the past tense (ele/ela/você) of “parar de funcionar” (“to stop working”). You can replace the thing that broke: “O X parou de funcionar.”
target_language_example: A internet parou de funcionar do nada.
native_language_example: The internet stopped working out of nowhere.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a portion/section of something ("uma parte da história") or an area within a place ("em que parte da cidade"). Very often appears with the verb phrase "fazer parte de" (= "to be part of / belong to"), and in general statements like "faz parte da vida" (= "it’s part of life"). Note: with a plural noun, it becomes "parte dos/das" (e.g., "parte dos alunos").
target_language_example: Quero fazer parte da equipe.
native_language_example: I want to be part of the team.

additional_notes: Used to say that something belongs to a larger whole (“parte do nosso jogo”), or to talk about someone’s share/portion (“sua parte do aluguel”). In the expression “por parte de/alguém”, it means “on the part of / from (someone)”, often used to assign responsibility (“um erro por parte do motorista”). It changes to match gender/number of the next noun: parte do (masc. sing.), parte da (fem. sing.), parte dos (masc. pl.), parte das (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Essa é a melhor parte do filme.
native_language_example: This is the best part of the movie.

meaning: a tennis match (a game of tennis).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a match you watch or play. In Portuguese, "partida" often means a match/game (especially in sports), and "de tênis" specifies the sport. Common with verbs like "assistir (a)" (to watch), "ver" (to see/watch), "jogar" (to play), and "desafiar" (to challenge someone to a match).
target_language_example: Vamos marcar uma partida de tênis para sábado de manhã.
native_language_example: Let’s schedule a tennis match for Saturday morning.

passa a maior parte do tempo

target_language_multi_word_term: passa a maior parte do tempo
additional_notes: Used with a subject (ele/ela/você + passa) to say how someone usually spends their time. It’s often followed by a place (em/na/no + lugar) or an activity in the gerund (fazendo, lendo, trabalhando). You can change the verb form: eu passo, ele/ela passa, nós passamos, eles/elas passam.
target_language_example: Eu passo a maior parte do tempo trabalhando em casa.
native_language_example: I spend most of my time working at home.

additional_notes: Used with a subject + passar + muito tempo + em/no/na + place/activity. In the examples, "passa" is the present tense (he/she/it spends). You can also change the subject: "Eu passo muito tempo..." (I spend a lot of time...).
target_language_example: Eu passo muito tempo estudando português.
native_language_example: I spend a lot of time studying Portuguese.

meaning: to spend the night (somewhere); to stay overnight.
additional_notes: Used with a place to say where you’ll be for the night: “passar a noite aqui/num hotel/na casa de alguém”. It can be a statement (“Vou passar a noite aqui.”) or a request (“Posso passar a noite?” = “Can I stay over/overnight?”).
target_language_example: A gente pode passar a noite na sua casa?
native_language_example: Can we stay the night at your place?

additional_notes: Used with com/with someone (passar mais tempo com você) or doing something (passar mais tempo estudando = spend more time studying). Often appears with deveria/probably should (suggestion/advice) or queria/queria que (wish).
target_language_example: A gente precisa passar mais tempo com a família.
native_language_example: We need to spend more time with the family.

additional_notes: Used to talk about dedicating/allocating more time to be with someone (family, friends, kids, etc.). The verb is usually conjugated (eu passo, você passa, ele/ela passa) and you can change the amount: "passar menos tempo com", "passar muito tempo com". Often followed by a person or group: "com a família", "com os meus filhos".
target_language_example: Neste mês, vou passar mais tempo com meus amigos.
native_language_example: This month, I’m going to spend more time with my friends.

passar mais tempo com minha família

target_language_multi_word_term: passar mais tempo com minha família
meaning: to spend more time with my family.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "passar" to mean "to spend" (time). "Mais tempo" = "more time" and "com minha família" = "with my family." You’ll often hear it with phrases like "eu gostaria de poder..." (I wish I could...), "tenho que..." (I have to...), and "preciso..." (I need to...).
target_language_example: Neste ano, quero passar mais tempo com minha família.
native_language_example: This year, I want to spend more time with my family.

additional_notes: Used when you succeed in an exam/test (i.e., you get a passing grade). Common structure: "passar em/na" + exam/test: "passar na prova", "passar no exame", "passar na prova de matemática". It’s different from "fazer a prova" (to take/sit the test).
target_language_example: Se eu estudar hoje, acho que vou passar na prova amanhã.
native_language_example: If I study today, I think I’ll pass the test tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used for getting a passing grade/result on a test. In Portuguese, “passar” can mean “to pass (succeed)” and it often takes “em/no/na” + the test: “passar no exame”, “passar na prova”. The opposite is “não passar/reprovar no exame” (to fail the exam).
target_language_example: Preciso passar no exame para conseguir o certificado.
native_language_example: I need to pass the exam to get the certificate.

additional_notes: Use "passar" + "em/no/na" (passar em um teste / passar no teste) to say you passed an exam/test. It focuses on meeting the required score/criteria. Contrast: "fazer um teste" = to take a test; "reprovar no teste" = to fail the test.
target_language_example: Se eu estudar hoje, vou passar no teste amanhã.
native_language_example: If I study today, I’ll pass the test tomorrow.

meaning: to spend the rest of (your) life.
additional_notes: Used with an activity or situation to talk about what someone will do for the remainder of their lifetime. Often followed by a gerund (-ando/-endo/-indo), e.g., “passar o resto da vida trabalhando” = “spend the rest of your life working.” You can add “com alguém” (with someone) or “em + lugar” (in a place): “passar o resto da vida com a Mary / na Austrália.”
target_language_example: Não quero passar o resto da vida fazendo a mesma coisa.
native_language_example: I don’t want to spend the rest of my life doing the same thing.

additional_notes: Used at the table to ask someone to hand you the salt (usually because it’s out of your reach). Common polite patterns: “Pode me passar o sal, por favor?” (more direct) and “Poderia/Você se importaria em passar o sal?” (more polite). You can swap in other items: “passar a pimenta”, “passar o pão”, etc.
target_language_example: Você pode passar o sal e a pimenta, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you pass the salt and pepper, please?

additional_notes:
From the verb **passar** (“to spend” time). It’s commonly followed by:
- **a + infinitive** (more common in Portugal): *Passei a tarde toda a arrumar o quarto.*
- **gerund (-ndo)** (more common in Brazil): *Passei a tarde toda arrumando o quarto.*
You can also use it with a place: *Passei a tarde toda no parque.*
target_language_example: Passei a tarde toda a estudar para o exame.
native_language_example: I spent the whole afternoon studying for the exam.

meaning: 'I spent the day (doing something)' / 'I spent all day'.
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "passar o dia". Often followed by "com + person" (passei o dia com a Maria) or by a gerund to say what you did all day (passei o dia estudando, trabalhando, limpando). You can change the time word: passei a tarde (afternoon), passei a noite (night).
target_language_example: Hoje passei o dia estudando para a prova.
native_language_example: Today I spent the day studying for the test.

additional_notes: Used to say you were with someone for the entire day. It’s the past tense (pretérito perfeito) of passar: eu passei = “I spent.” You typically add a person after com (com meu amigo, com a minha mãe, com o Tom). You can drop the subject pronoun “Eu” in Portuguese: “(Eu) passei…”.
target_language_example: Passei o dia inteiro com minha família no parque.
native_language_example: I spent the whole day with my family at the park.

meaning: bus tour; a ride/tour by bus.
additional_notes: Used when asking whether there’s an organized sightseeing tour that goes by bus (often sold to tourists), or referring to that activity ending/being unavailable. It’s typically a noun phrase: fazer um passeio de ônibus (to take a bus tour).
target_language_example: A gente vai fazer um passeio de ônibus pela cidade amanhã.
native_language_example: We’re going to take a bus tour around the city tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **passar** (“to spend” time) + **a noite** (“the night”). Very common with a place: **passou a noite em/no/na...** (in/at). In the past tense (**passou**), it usually means someone stayed there overnight.
target_language_example: Ela passou a noite no hospital.
native_language_example: She spent the night at the hospital.

meaning: “spent the afternoon” (used to say how someone used their afternoon).
additional_notes: Used with the verb passar (“to spend” time) in the past: passou + a tarde. It’s commonly followed by an activity in the gerund (e.g., estudando, lendo, cozinhando) or by “com + person” to say who you spent the afternoon with. You can intensify with toda/a tarde toda (“the whole afternoon”) or inteira/a tarde inteira (“the entire afternoon”).
target_language_example: Eu passei a tarde trabalhando em casa.
native_language_example: I spent the afternoon working at home.

additional_notes: From the verb "passar" + "em/na". In Brazilian Portuguese, "passar na prova" means to get a passing grade (to succeed) on a test/exam. You can change the subject and tense: "Eu passei na prova" (I passed), "Você vai passar na prova" (You will pass).
target_language_example: Passei na prova, mas foi difícil.
native_language_example: I passed the exam, but it was hard.

meaning: passed the exam (achieved a passing grade).
additional_notes: "Passar em" + exam/test means to pass it (i.e., succeed). In the past tense it’s often said as "(ele/ela) passou no exame"; "no" = "em" + "o" (in/on the). The opposite is usually "não passou no exame" or "reprovou no exame".
target_language_example: Finalmente passei no exame de direção!
native_language_example: I finally passed the driving test!

additional_notes: From the verb passar (to pass) + em + o = no. Used with tests/exams: passar no teste = to pass the test (get a passing grade). You can change the subject and tense: Eu passei no teste (I passed), Você passou no teste? (Did you pass?). "Mal passou" means "barely passed."
target_language_example: Eu passei no teste, mas por pouco.
native_language_example: I passed the test, but barely.

additional_notes: From the verb "passar" (to spend/time to pass). Used to say how someone spent the whole day or most of it, often followed by a place ("no parque"), with someone ("com Maria"), or doing an activity, frequently in the gerund ("lendo", "escrevendo", "pensando"). "Passou o dia todo" adds emphasis: "the whole day." You can change the subject/tense: "Eu passei o dia...", "Ela passou o dia..."
target_language_example: Eu passei o dia todo estudando para a prova.
native_language_example: I spent the whole day studying for the test.

meaning: "(he/she) spent the whole day" (doing something / somewhere).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "passar" (to spend, to pass) in the past tense ("passou") + "o dia inteiro" (the whole day). Often followed by a gerund to say what someone was doing all day: "passou o dia inteiro estudando". You can change the subject and tense: "passei o dia inteiro..." (I spent), "passamos..." (we spent), "vai passar o dia inteiro..." (will spend).
target_language_example: Eu passei o dia inteiro trabalhando.
native_language_example: I spent the whole day working.

meaning: "spent the whole day at/in the" (feminine place).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "passar" (to spend time). "Passou" is the past tense (he/she/you-form). "o dia todo" means "all day / the whole day." "na" = "em" + "a" and is used before feminine singular nouns (na biblioteca, na livraria, na floresta). For masculine places, use "no" (no parque); for plural, "nos/nas".
target_language_example: Ela passou o dia todo na praia.
native_language_example: She spent the whole day at the beach.

additional_notes: Past tense of "passar" meaning "to spend" (time). It’s used to say how someone spent their weekend, often followed by a place ("em Boston"), a person ("com o pai"), or an adverb like "sozinho/a" (alone). You can change "passou" to match the subject: "passei" (I spent), "passamos" (we spent).
target_language_example: Nós passamos o fim de semana na praia.
native_language_example: We spent the weekend at the beach.

meaning: "it crossed my mind" / "it occurred to me."
additional_notes: Used to say an idea/thought came to you (often suddenly). Very common with "nunca" to mean you never even thought of something: "Nunca passou pela minha cabeça". Tense can change (e.g., "passa", "passou"); the pronoun can change too: "passou pela sua cabeça" (your mind), "pela cabeça dele/dela" (his/her mind).
target_language_example: Sinceramente, nem passou pela minha cabeça que ele pudesse estar mentindo.
native_language_example: Honestly, it didn’t even cross my mind that he could be lying.

additional_notes: Used to say a country has a lot of a certain kind of resource. It’s often followed by an adjective specifying the type: recursos naturais (natural resources), recursos minerais (mineral resources), recursos hídricos (water resources). You can swap in a specific country name (O Brasil é rico em recursos naturais) or add “muito” for emphasis (é muito rico em…).
target_language_example: O Canadá é rico em recursos naturais, mas muitas áreas são pouco povoadas.
native_language_example: Canada is rich in natural resources, but many areas are sparsely populated.

meaning: "a piece of" / "a slice of" (some food or material).
additional_notes: Used to indicate an amount that’s a piece or portion of something. Very common with food (pedaço de carne, pedaço de melancia) and can also be used for things like paper, wood, etc. Often interchangeable with "um pedaço de" (a piece of) or "um bocado de" (a bit of), depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu só quero um pedaço de bolo, por favor.
native_language_example: I just want a piece of cake, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about one portion of a cake. In everyday speech you may also hear "fatia de bolo" (slice of cake), especially when it’s a clean slice.
target_language_example: Quero só um pedaço de bolo, por favor.
native_language_example: I just want a piece of cake, please.

additional_notes: Used when you mean a small sheet or scrap of paper, often for writing something down (a name, phone number, note). Very common with verbs like escrever (to write) and anotar (to jot down), and with em/num (on/in a piece of paper).
target_language_example: Você tem um pedaço de papel para eu anotar o endereço?
native_language_example: Do you have a piece of paper so I can write down the address?

additional_notes: "Pedi" is the past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "pedir" = "to ask/request". The pattern is usually: "pedi a + [person] + que + [verb in the subjunctive]" to say you asked someone to do something. In speech, Portuguese often uses "para" instead of "que": "Pedi ao Tom para fechar a porta." ("a" + "o" = "ao"). With feminine names it stays "a": "pedi à Maria" (written with crase: à).
target_language_example: Pedi ao meu chefe que me desse mais um dia para terminar o relatório.
native_language_example: I asked my boss to give me one more day to finish the report.

additional_notes: Used when you request assistance from someone. Common patterns: "pedir ajuda a alguém" (ask someone for help) and "pedir ajuda com/em alguma coisa" (ask for help with something).
target_language_example: Se você não entender, pode pedir ajuda ao professor.
native_language_example: If you don’t understand, you can ask the teacher for help.

meaning: to apologize; to say you’re sorry.
additional_notes:
Common way to apologize in Portuguese. Use it with:
- a/alguém (who you’re apologizing to): "Quero pedir desculpas ao João." (or "à Maria")
- por/pelo/pela + noun/thing you did: "Pedir desculpas pelo que eu disse." / "pela demora"
You can also say "Desculpa" (informal) or "Desculpe" (more formal), but "pedir desculpas" is neutral and works in many situations.
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu preciso pedir desculpas pelo atraso.
native_language_example: Sorry, I need to apologize for being late.

meaning: to ask a favor (to ask someone for help).
additional_notes: Polite way to ask someone to do something for you. Very common in requests, often with polite verbs like "posso" (can I) or "poderia" (could I), and with indirect object pronouns: "Posso lhe pedir um favor?" (Can I ask you a favor?). You can add who you’re asking with "a" + the person: "pedir um favor ao senhor / à senhora / a vocês / a um amigo".
target_language_example: Posso te pedir um favor? Você pode me ajudar com isso?
native_language_example: Can I ask you a favor? Can you help me with this?

additional_notes: Past tense of the verb "pedir" (to ask/request) used with an indirect object: "pediu a ele/ela" = "asked him/her". Very commonly followed by "para" + infinitive ("pediu a ela para esperar") or by "que" + subjunctive ("pediu a ela que esperasse"). With "desculpas", it means "to apologize to" ("pediu a ela desculpas").
target_language_example: Ele pediu a ela que falasse mais devagar.
native_language_example: He asked her to speak more slowly.

additional_notes: Past tense of pedir desculpas (“to apologize”). Common patterns: pedir desculpas a alguém (to apologize to someone): “pediu desculpas ao funcionário / à professora”; pedir desculpas por algo (to apologize for something): “pediu desculpas por estar atrasado / por isso”. “Ao” = a + o, “à” = a + a (used before feminine nouns).
target_language_example: Ele pediu desculpas por não ter respondido.
native_language_example: He apologized for not having replied.

additional_notes: Past tense of “pedir” (“to ask/request”) + “para”, used to introduce what someone asked another person to do. Very often followed by an infinitive: “pediu para ele se sentar” (“asked him to sit down”). You may also see “pediu para que …” followed by the subjunctive: “pediu para que ficássemos quietos” (“asked that we stay quiet”). Pronouns can attach to the verb: “perdoá-lo” = “forgive him.”
target_language_example: Ele pediu para eu esperar mais um pouco.
native_language_example: He asked me to wait a little longer.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *pedir* in the pattern **pedir para + [person] + infinitive** to say you asked someone to do something: *Ele pediu para a Maria fazer isso.* In many varieties of Portuguese (especially in Brazil), some names can appear with an article (*a Maria*), so **para a** = “to the (female person)”. You may also hear/see **pediu à** (formal) or **pediu para** without an article depending on the name/dialect.
target_language_example: Ele pediu para a Ana esperar um pouco.
native_language_example: He asked Ana to wait a little.

additional_notes: "Pediu" is the past tense of "pedir" (to ask/request). "à" = "a" (to) + "a" (the, feminine), used before a feminine person or noun: "pediu à Mary" / "pediu à sua mãe". Often followed by "para" + infinitive (pediu à Mary para ajudar) or by "que" + past subjunctive (pediu à Mary que ajudasse / que falasse mais devagar).
target_language_example: Eu pedi à professora para repetir, por favor.
native_language_example: I asked the teacher to repeat, please.

additional_notes: Used with forms of **estar** to describe something that is burning or has started burning: **A casa estava pegando fogo** (“The house was on fire”). It can also be used figuratively (more informal) to mean someone/something is “on a roll” or “really heating up” (doing very well or getting intense): **Eles estão pegando fogo!**
target_language_example: Quando cheguei, a cozinha já estava pegando fogo.
native_language_example: When I arrived, the kitchen was already on fire.

additional_notes: “Pegar” is a very common verb with several meanings depending on context: grabbing/taking something (“pegar o frango”), catching an animal (“pegar o coelho”), picking up/collecting something, etc. The “o” is the masculine singular definite article (“the”) and must match the noun’s gender; with a feminine noun you use “pegar a …”. In “pegar o que quiser”, “o que” means “whatever/what(ever)”.
target_language_example: Pode pegar o livro na mesa?
native_language_example: Can you grab the book on the table?

meaning: to catch the first train (the earliest train).
additional_notes: Uses pegar = “to catch/take (a means of transport)”. O primeiro trem refers to the earliest train available that day/schedule. Often used with verbs like acordar cedo, sair cedo, levantar-se cedo, and apressar-se to explain why you’re leaving early.
target_language_example: Se a gente quiser chegar a tempo, precisamos pegar o primeiro trem.
native_language_example: If we want to arrive on time, we need to catch the first train.

meaning: to catch/take the train (usually in time to board).
additional_notes: Uses pegar in the sense of “catch” (like catching a bus/flight). Very common when talking about rushing or being on time: pegar o trem das 8, correr para pegar o trem, conseguir/não conseguir pegar o trem.
target_language_example: Se a gente sair agora, ainda dá tempo de pegar o trem das 8.
native_language_example: If we leave now, we can still catch the 8 o’clock train.

additional_notes: Very common in Brazil for using public transport. "Pegar" here means "catch" (like catching a bus), not "pick up". You can use it with a time ("pegar o ônibus das seis" = the 6 o’clock bus) or a destination ("pegar o ônibus para a estação" = take the bus to the station).
target_language_example: Se a gente sair agora, dá tempo de pegar o ônibus.
native_language_example: If we leave now, we can still catch the bus.

additional_notes: Used when you manage (or hope) to board the final train service of the day. In Portuguese, "pegar" often means "to catch/take" for transport (pegar o trem/ônibus/metro).
target_language_example: Se a gente correr, dá tempo de pegar o último trem.
native_language_example: If we run, we can still catch the last train.

pegar um pouco de ar fresco

target_language_multi_word_term: pegar um pouco de ar fresco
additional_notes: Used when someone goes outside, takes a short walk, or opens a window to breathe cleaner/cooler air. Very common and natural in everyday speech. You’ll also hear: "tomar um pouco de ar fresco" with the same meaning. Often used as a suggestion or encouragement ("Você precisa pegar um pouco de ar fresco").
target_language_example: Vou sair cinco minutos para pegar um pouco de ar fresco.
native_language_example: I’m going out for five minutes to get some fresh air.

meaning: "(he/she) took/got one" (picked up, grabbed, or caught/used a means of transport).
additional_notes: From the verb pegar (“to take/get/catch”). It’s commonly used with an object: pegou um espelho (picked up a mirror), pegou um biscoito (took a cookie), pegou um voo/avião (took/caught a flight/plane). The exact English verb depends on context (take, grab, get, catch).
target_language_example: Ela pegou um táxi para o hotel.
native_language_example: She took a taxi to the hotel.

additional_notes: Uses the verb “pegar” (to catch/get) + “um resfriado” (a cold). You can change the tense/person: “peguei” (I caught), “pegou” (he/she caught), “pegamos” (we caught). Often followed by “porque” to give a reason (real or believed), e.g., “porque saí com o cabelo molhado.”
target_language_example: Acho que peguei um resfriado ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I think I caught a cold last night.

meaning: “I took a taxi” / “I got a taxi.”
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "pegar" meaning “to take/catch” in the sense of transportation. Used when you chose that mode of transport (often with a reason like being late, rain, missing the bus). In conversation it’s common to omit the subject "eu": "Peguei um táxi" = “I took a taxi.”
target_language_example: Ontem, peguei um táxi para voltar para casa.
native_language_example: Yesterday, I took a taxi to get back home.

additional_notes: This is the infinitive verb pegar (“to take/get/grab/catch”) with the object pronoun -lo (“him/it”) attached. It’s common after another verb (e.g., tentar pegá-lo, precisa pegá-lo) and often means “pick it up,” “go get it,” or “catch him” depending on context. With emprestado, it means “borrow it” (pegá-lo emprestado).
target_language_example: Vou pegá-lo na estação amanhã.
native_language_example: I’ll pick him/it up at the station tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of looking, entering, throwing, etc. to indicate that something happens through the window as a passage or opening. It’s the contraction of por + a (“pela”) + janela (“window”). Often means “out the window” with verbs like jogar (to throw), and “through the window” with verbs like entrar (to enter).
target_language_example: O gato saiu pela janela.
native_language_example: The cat went out through the window.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens during the morning period (often as a time-of-day). Common with routines ("Trabalho pela manhã") or with a specific day: "amanhã pela manhã" (tomorrow morning), "hoje pela manhã" (this morning), "ontem pela manhã" (yesterday morning). Similar to "de manhã"; "pela manhã" can sound a bit more specific/formal and emphasizes the time period.
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar amanhã pela manhã, antes do trabalho.
native_language_example: Let’s meet tomorrow morning, before work.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the first occurrence of an event or the first time you met/saw/did something. Often comes after the verb (e.g., "vi ... pela primeira vez"), and it can also be placed earlier for emphasis.
target_language_example: Estou viajando para o Brasil pela primeira vez.
native_language_example: I’m traveling to Brazil for the first time.

meaning: for the first time in; for the first time in (a place).
additional_notes: Used to say something is happening after a long period of not happening ("for the first time in months/years") or that something happened in a particular place for the first time ("for the first time in Boston"). Often followed by a time expression (um mês, meses, anos) or a location (Boston, o Japão).
target_language_example: Estou aqui pela primeira vez em cinco anos.
native_language_example: I’m here for the first time in five years.

additional_notes: “Pela” is the contraction of “por” + “a” (“for/by the” feminine singular). It’s used to express cause/responsibility (“responsável pela sua morte” = responsible for his/her death), a characteristic (“famoso pela sua cozinha” = famous for its cuisine), or purpose (“lutar pela sua liberdade” = fight for his/her freedom). “Sua” can mean “your” (often formal) or “his/her/its,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Obrigado pela sua ajuda.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help.

meaning: for the last time; the last time (that).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the most recent/previous occasion when something happened or someone was seen (often with verbs like ver, encontrar, estar, visitar). Common in phrases like “Quando o vi pela última vez…” (“When I saw him last…”). It can also mean “for the last time” in the sense of “never again after this,” but in everyday past-storytelling it usually means “the last time (I did X).”
target_language_example: Quando nos falamos pela última vez, você estava morando em Lisboa.
native_language_example: The last time we talked, you were living in Lisbon.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the first occurrence of an event or the first time you met/saw/did something. Often comes after the verb (e.g., "vi ... pela primeira vez"), and it can also be placed earlier for emphasis.
target_language_example: Estou viajando para o Brasil pela primeira vez.
native_language_example: I’m traveling to Brazil for the first time.

meaning: behind (someone’s) back; from behind (in the back).
additional_notes: Often means doing or saying something without the person knowing (“behind their back”), especially criticizing or speaking badly about them: falar mal/criticar alguém pelas costas. It can also be literal in physical descriptions: levar/receber um tiro pelas costas (“be shot in the back/from behind”).
target_language_example: Não faça isso pelas costas dela; fale diretamente com ela.
native_language_example: Don’t do that behind her back; talk to her directly.

additional_notes: Used to set a minimum end point in time: you want something to continue up to that time (and possibly longer). It’s typically followed by a masculine singular time reference with an article, e.g. "o Natal". Variations: "pelo menos até a" (feminine), "pelo menos até" (no article).
target_language_example: Fique aqui pelo menos até o fim da reunião.
native_language_example: Stay here at least until the end of the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to give a minimum number of occurrences (three is the minimum, it could be more). Common with past events ("já aconteceu") and routines ("por dia", "por semana"). Often placed right before the quantity: "pelo menos" + number + "vez/vezes".
target_language_example: Eu já vi esse filme pelo menos três vezes.
native_language_example: I’ve already seen that movie at least three times.

additional_notes: Used to say a minimum number of times something happens. Often followed by a time period: “pelo menos uma vez por dia/na semana/ao ano”.
target_language_example: Você precisa visitar Lisboa pelo menos uma vez na vida.
native_language_example: You need to visit Lisbon at least once in your life.

pelo menos uma vez por semana

target_language_multi_word_term: pelo menos uma vez por semana
additional_notes: Used to express a minimum frequency. Often comes after the verb phrase it modifies (e.g., “Eu vou… pelo menos uma vez por semana”). You can swap in other time periods: “pelo menos uma vez por dia” (a day), “por mês” (a month), “por ano” (a year).
target_language_example: Eu vou à academia pelo menos uma vez por semana.
native_language_example: I go to the gym at least once a week.

meaning: “for what” / “based on what” (e.g., “as far as I know/remember,” “from what it seems”).
additional_notes: Often introduces the basis for what you’re saying: information you have (pelo que sei = as far as I know), memory (pelo que me lembro = as far as I remember), evidence/appearance (pelo que parece / pelo que se pode perceber = it seems / from what one can tell), or reason/blame/thanks (grato pelo que você fez = grateful for what you did; culpar alguém pelo que aconteceu = blame someone for what happened). It’s the contraction of por + o + que.
target_language_example: Pelo que ouvi, a reunião foi cancelada.
native_language_example: From what I heard, the meeting was canceled.

meaning: 'as far as I know' / 'to the best of my knowledge'.
additional_notes: Used to qualify a statement as being based on your current information, and to signal that you might not be 100% sure. Often placed at the start of the sentence, but it can also come after the main clause. More formal variant: "que eu saiba".
target_language_example: Pelo que eu sei, a reunião começa às três.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the meeting starts at three.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information that you believe is true, but you’re not 100% certain. Often followed by a clause (e.g., *ela ainda não é casada*). You can also use it without *ela*: *Pelo que eu sei, ele…*, *Pelo que eu sei, isso…*, or simply *Pelo que eu sei,*.
target_language_example: Pelo que eu sei, ela mora aqui há pouco tempo.
native_language_example: As far as I know, she’s only lived here for a short time.

meaning: As far as I know, he…
additional_notes: Used to introduce information you believe is true based on what you know or have heard, but with some uncertainty (“to the best of my knowledge”). Very common in conversation to soften a statement. You can change the subject pronoun: “pelo que eu sei, ela… / eles…”, or drop it if context is clear: “Pelo que eu sei, ainda não chegou.”
target_language_example: Pelo que eu sei, ele trabalha aqui desde 2022.
native_language_example: As far as I know, he has worked here since 2022.

pelo que eu sei, ele é

target_language_multi_word_term: pelo que eu sei, ele é
meaning: "As far as I know, he is…"
additional_notes: Used to qualify what you’re saying: it’s true to the best of your knowledge, but you’re not 100% sure. You can swap the person: "pelo que eu sei, ela é…" (she), "pelo que eu sei, eles são…" (they). Often appears with adjectives or descriptions (e.g., honesto, confiável, americano).
target_language_example: Pelo que eu sei, ele é casado.
native_language_example: As far as I know, he is married.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to mean “for your …”, often when thanking, congratulating, or giving credit/blame: Obrigado pelo seu apoio. It’s the contraction of por + o (“pelo”) + seu (“your”). Variations: pela sua (feminine singular), pelos seus (masculine plural), pelas suas (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Obrigado pelo seu apoio durante o projeto.
native_language_example: Thank you for your support during the project.

meaning: "(you/he/she) think(s) that…" (often in a challenging/rhetorical question).
additional_notes: Form of the verb pensar (“to think”) + que (“that”). Very common in questions like “O que você pensa que…?” (“What do you think…?”) and in confrontational phrases like “Quem você pensa que é?” (“Who do you think you are?”). Often appears as “você pensa que…”, “ele pensa que…”, etc.
target_language_example: Quem você pensa que é para falar assim comigo?
native_language_example: Who do you think you are to talk to me like that?

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "ter" (e.g., "tenho/tens/tem/têm pensado em mim") to mean "have/has been thinking about me". The verb is "pensar em" (= to think about/of), and "em mim" means "about me". Common in questions like "Você tem pensado em mim?".
target_language_example: Tenho pensado em mim e no que eu quero para o futuro.
native_language_example: I’ve been thinking about myself and what I want for the future.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar + pensando em + noun/pronoun/infinitive to say what someone is thinking about or considering (e.g., 'pensando em você' = thinking about you; 'pensando em viajar' = thinking about traveling). With pronouns: 'em mim' (about me), 'em você' (about you).
target_language_example: Estou pensando em comprar um carro novo.
native_language_example: I’m thinking about buying a new car.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause with an idea/opinion/assumption: “pensar que + sentence.” Often implies a belief that may or may not be true (sometimes like “to assume”). In questions like “O que te fez pensar que…?”, it means “What made you think that…?”
target_language_example: Eu pensei que você já tinha saído.
native_language_example: I thought you had already left.

additional_notes: Used when you want to reflect or consider something (an idea, proposal, decision). Very common after phrases like "Tenho que..." (I have to...), "Vou..." (I’m going to...), "Preciso..." (I need to...), or "Concordou em..." (agreed to...). In conversation, you can also say "Vou pensar nisso" (same meaning, more natural in many cases).
target_language_example: Deixa eu pensar sobre isso e te respondo amanhã.
native_language_example: Let me think about it and I’ll answer you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone believed or assumed in the past. It often suggests an ongoing belief at the time, a background thought, or something later corrected (like “I thought (but I was wrong)”). In Portuguese it can be followed by the indicative for a past belief about a fact (Pensava que ele estava...) or by the subjunctive when the context calls for it (e.g., after certain verbs/tenses: Pensava que estivéssemos...).
target_language_example: Eu pensava que você já tinha chegado.
native_language_example: I thought you had already arrived.

meaning: "I thought that the…" / "I used to think that the…" (introduces what you believed).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an assumption or belief that may be wrong or is being corrected. "Pensava" is the imperfect of "pensar" and often means a past, ongoing belief ("I thought / I used to think"). "Que" means "that". "O" is the masculine singular "the" and is also used before many male names (e.g., "o Tom" = "Tom"). For a female name or feminine noun, use "pensava que a…".
target_language_example: Pensava que o restaurante abria às oito.
native_language_example: I thought the restaurant opened at eight.

meaning: “I thought you…” / “I was under the impression you…”
additional_notes: Used to introduce a past belief/assumption about the person you’re talking to (“você”). The subject “eu” is often omitted: “(Eu) pensava que você…”. After “pensava que…”, you may see different verb forms depending on certainty/time, e.g. indicative for facts (“precisava”) or subjunctive/conditional for uncertainty or hypotheticals (“precisasse”, “faria”).
target_language_example: Pensava que você ia chegar mais cedo.
native_language_example: I thought you were going to arrive earlier.

meaning: "I thought you (plural)" / "I was under the impression you (plural)".
additional_notes: Used to introduce something you believed or assumed in the past (often something you later found out was wrong). "Pensava" is the imperfect past of "pensar" and can sound like an ongoing belief/assumption rather than a single moment. "Vocês" is "you" (plural, and also used as singular "you" in much of Brazil). The subject "eu" is often omitted: "(Eu) pensava que vocês...".
target_language_example: Pensava que vocês já tinham terminado o trabalho.
native_language_example: I thought you had already finished the work.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed in the past—often a mistaken assumption or expectation. It’s the past tense of *pensar* (“to think”). It commonly comes before another verb (often in the imperfect tense or conditional/subjunctive, depending on meaning): *Pensei que estava…* (“I thought I was/you were…”), *Pensei que poderia…* (“I thought I could/might…”).
target_language_example: Pensei que você já tinha chegado.
native_language_example: I thought you had already arrived.

meaning: 'I thought it was' / 'I thought (that) I was/you were/etc.'
additional_notes: Used to express a past belief or assumption that may be corrected later. You can follow it with a noun/adjective ("pensei que era meu", "pensei que era fascinante") or with a subject + description ("pensei que era a sua vez"). Often implies “but I was wrong / but it wasn’t.”
target_language_example: Desculpa, pensei que era hoje, não amanhã.
native_language_example: Sorry, I thought it was today, not tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say what you believed at the time, often realizing later it wasn’t true. It commonly introduces a description/state after it (brincando, chorando, dormindo, namorando…). Grammatically, it’s the past of “pensar” (“pensei”) + “que” + the imperfect subjunctive of “estar” (“estivesse”), which is typical in Portuguese after verbs of thinking in the past when reporting an assumption.
target_language_example: Pensei que estivesse doente, mas era só cansaço.
native_language_example: I thought you were sick, but it was just tiredness.

additional_notes: Used to express a mistaken belief or assumption in the past. It’s built from the past tense of pensar (pensei = “I thought”) + que + the imperfect subjunctive of ser (fosse = roughly “was/were”) after a past “thought/believed” statement. Very common for identifying someone/something or having an expectation: “Pensei que fosse o Tom, mas era o John.”
target_language_example: Desculpa, pensei que fosse você.
native_language_example: Sorry, I thought it was you.

meaning: "I thought that the..." (about a masculine noun/name).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed in the past. "Pensei" is the past of "pensar" (to think). "Que" means "that," and "o" is "the" for masculine singular nouns (e.g., "o Tom", "o carro"). Often followed by the subjunctive in Portuguese when describing an assumption or uncertain belief (e.g., "pensei que o Tom estivesse...").
target_language_example: Pensei que o ônibus já tivesse saído.
native_language_example: I thought the bus had already left.

meaning: "I thought it would be" (I expected it to be).
additional_notes: Used to talk about an expectation in the past that turned out to be true or (often) wrong. It’s the past of "pensar" (pensei = I thought) + "que" (that) + conditional of "ser" (seria = would be). Common in comparisons like "mais ... do que pensei que seria" (more ... than I thought it would be) and with adjectives/nouns: "pensei que seria fácil" / "pensei que seria uma boa ideia".
target_language_example: Pensei que seria mais barato, mas estava enganado.
native_language_example: I thought it would be cheaper, but I was mistaken.

additional_notes: Used to say what you believed before, often when you’re surprised it wasn’t true or you’re correcting a misunderstanding. "Pensei" is past tense of "pensar" (to think). After "pensei que", Portuguese commonly uses the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., "pensei que você fosse") or pluperfect subjunctive (e.g., "pensei que você tivesse ido"), though in everyday speech you may also hear the indicative (e.g., "pensei que você tinha...").
target_language_example: Pensei que você ia chegar mais cedo.
native_language_example: I thought you were going to arrive earlier.

meaning: "I thought you were going to..." / "I thought you would..."
additional_notes: Used to say an expectation or assumption you had in the past that may be wrong or surprising. Very common in conversation. Structure: (Eu) pensei que + subject + fosse + infinitive. Here, "fosse" is the past subjunctive of "ser" used after verbs of thinking in the past (pensei/achei) when talking about what you thought would happen.
target_language_example: Pensei que você fosse chegar mais cedo.
native_language_example: I thought you were going to arrive earlier.

meaning: "I thought you were going to..." / "I thought you would..."
additional_notes: Used to say an expectation or assumption you had in the past that may be wrong or surprising. Very common in conversation. Structure: (Eu) pensei que + subject + fosse + infinitive. Here, "fosse" is the past subjunctive of "ser" used after verbs of thinking in the past (pensei/achei) when talking about what you thought would happen.
target_language_example: Pensei que você fosse chegar mais cedo.
native_language_example: I thought you were going to arrive earlier.

meaning: “I think the same as …” / “I agree with … (about that).”
additional_notes: Used to say your opinion is the same as someone else’s. It’s built from: penso (“I think”) + o mesmo (“the same”) + que (“as/that”). You normally follow it with a person/pronoun (ele/ela, eles/elas, você, vocês, tu) or sometimes with a clause (e.g., “penso o mesmo que você: isso não vai dar certo”).
target_language_example: Penso o mesmo que você sobre esse assunto.
native_language_example: I think the same as you about this topic.

additional_notes: Past tense of "pensar" + "que" to introduce what someone believed or assumed. The verb in the next clause can be in the indicative (e.g., "pensou que ele era...") or, often in more formal Portuguese, in the subjunctive after verbs of opinion/thought when reporting an assumption (e.g., "pensou que ele fosse...").
target_language_example: Eu pensei que você já tinha ido embora.
native_language_example: I thought you had already left.

meaning: “little chef” (often used as a nickname or teasing form of address).
additional_notes: Used to address someone directly (like “buddy” or “kiddo”), often playfully or sarcastically—especially if the person is cooking, acting like they’re in charge, or being told what to do. Capitalizing “Chef” can make it feel more like a title or nickname. You can also say “o pequeno chef” (“the little chef”).
target_language_example: Ei, pequeno Chef, o jantar não vai se fazer sozinho!
native_language_example: Hey, little chef, dinner isn’t going to make itself!

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "perceber" + "que" to introduce a clause: "X percebeu que + [sentence]". Use it when someone becomes aware of a fact or notices something (sometimes suddenly). Often translates as "realized that" or "noticed that" depending on context.
target_language_example: Ela percebeu que tinha esquecido a carteira em casa.
native_language_example: She realized she had forgotten her wallet at home.

additional_notes: Used to talk about losing body weight. The verb "perder" means "to lose," and "alguns quilos" means "a few kilograms" (often said even in countries where people also say "emagrecer" = "to slim down"). Common with "precisar" (to need), "dever" (should), "ter de" (have to), and "querer" (to want).
target_language_example: Depois das festas, quero perder alguns quilos.
native_language_example: After the holidays, I want to lose a few kilos.

additional_notes: Used for body weight (health/fitness). You’ll often see it with “como” (how) or “para” (in order to): “Como posso perder peso?” / “Para perder peso, eu…”.
target_language_example: Estou tentando perder peso, então estou comendo menos açúcar.
native_language_example: I’m trying to lose weight, so I’m eating less sugar.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about wanting/needing to slim down a bit. The verb is "perder" (to lose) + "peso" (weight). You’ll often see it with "precisar" (to need to), "querer" (to want to), or "dever" (should).
target_language_example: Depois das festas, quero perder um pouco de peso.
native_language_example: After the holidays, I want to lose a little weight.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun after it (because of “a” = “the” feminine singular). With perder, it can mean literally losing something (Perdeu a sua bolsa? = “Did you lose your bag?”) and also missing something related to time (Perdeu a hora = “He missed the time / overslept / was late”). With some nouns it can mean “lose” in a figurative sense (perdeu a esperança = “lost hope”) or “lose track” (perdeu a conta = “lost count”). For masculine nouns you’ll often see “perdeu o”.
target_language_example: Ele perdeu a chave de casa ontem.
native_language_example: He lost the house key yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun after perder (“to lose”): perdeu o celular (lost the phone), perdeu o passaporte (lost the passport), perdeu o emprego (lost the job), perdeu o trem (missed the train). With abstract nouns it can mean “lost” in a figurative sense, e.g., perdeu o interesse (lost interest). In fixed expressions it can be idiomatic: Você perdeu o juízo? = “Have you lost your mind?”
target_language_example: Ele perdeu o bilhete e não conseguiu entrar.
native_language_example: He lost the ticket and couldn’t get in.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "perder o emprego" = “to lose one’s job,” often meaning to be fired or laid off. It changes with the person: "eu perdi o emprego" (I lost my job), "você/ele/ela perdeu o emprego" (you/he/she lost their job), "nós perdemos o emprego" (we lost our job), "eles/elas perderam o emprego" (they lost their job).
target_language_example: Ele perdeu o emprego no mês passado.
native_language_example: He lost his job last month.

additional_notes: Formal/polite way to ask someone’s forgiveness or to apologize. Common before/after saying what you did wrong (often with “por” + infinitive: “Perdoe-me por me atrasar.”). Also used to get someone’s attention or soften a question (“Perdoe-me, você está bem?”).
target_language_example: Perdoe-me por ter falado assim com você.
native_language_example: Forgive me for speaking to you like that.

additional_notes: "Perdoá-lo" = "perdoar" (to forgive) + "-lo" (him). The pronoun attaches to the end of the infinitive (common after verbs like "pedir para", "precisar", "convencer alguém a"). Often used when talking about forgiving someone for something: "perdoá-lo por...".
target_language_example: Ela disse que não consegue perdoá-lo pelo que aconteceu.
native_language_example: She said she can't forgive him for what happened.

meaning: to ask something; to ask a question.
additional_notes: Very common when introducing a question, often as “Posso perguntar uma coisa?” (“Can I ask you something?”). You can also swap “uma coisa” for a specific topic: “Posso te perguntar uma coisa sobre o trabalho?”
target_language_example: Posso perguntar uma coisa?
native_language_example: Can I ask you something?

additional_notes: "Pergunte" is the formal imperative (você) of "perguntar" (to ask). Use "pergunte a + person" to say who you’re asking: "Pergunte a Mary..." / "Pergunte a ele..." / "Pergunte a um especialista...". It’s often followed by an indirect question with "se" (if/whether) or a question word like "como" (how). With topics, you’ll usually see "pergunte a + person + sobre + [topic]".
target_language_example: Pergunte ao professor se há tarefa para amanhã.
native_language_example: Ask the teacher if there’s homework for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to ask a question. It’s the formal singular imperative of **perguntar** (“to ask”). **ao** = **a + o** (“to the”), used before masculine singular nouns/names: *Pergunte ao Tom…* (“Ask Tom…”). With feminine singular: *pergunte à Maria…*; with plurals: *pergunte aos/às…*. You may also see **pergunte para** in some varieties, but **pergunte a/ao/à** is very common.
target_language_example: Pergunte ao professor se a prova vai ser amanhã.
native_language_example: Ask the teacher if the test will be tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report a question you asked in the past. "perguntei" = “I asked” (past tense of perguntar). "-lhe" is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him/to her” (common in more formal European Portuguese; in Brazil many people would say "perguntei a ele/ela" or "perguntei pra ele/ela"). "se" introduces an indirect yes/no question (“if/whether”).
target_language_example: Perguntei-lhe se podia ajudar com as malas.
native_language_example: I asked him/her if I could help with the bags.

additional_notes: "Perguntei" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "perguntar" (to ask). It’s commonly followed by "a" before the person you asked: "Perguntei a Maria...". What you asked can come after, often introduced by "por que" (why) or with a question word like "quais" (which/what).
target_language_example: Perguntei ao professor onde fica a biblioteca.
native_language_example: I asked the teacher where the library is.

additional_notes: Used to say you asked a question to a specific person in the past. It’s the verb *perguntar* (“to ask”) in the first-person past (*perguntei* = “I asked”) + *ao* (“to the”), which is *a* + *o* and is used before a masculine singular noun/name (e.g., *ao Tom*). With feminine names you usually use *à* (e.g., *perguntei à Maria*). Often followed by *se* (“if/whether”) for yes/no questions or a question word like *quando* (“when”), *quantos* (“how many”).
target_language_example: Perguntei ao meu professor se a prova vai ser difícil.
native_language_example: I asked my teacher if the test is going to be difficult.

additional_notes: Formed from the verb perguntar (to ask) + the object pronoun me (myself). It’s used to express curiosity or uncertainty, often followed by a question word (onde, por que, como, quando) or by se (“whether/if”). Common in writing and more formal speech; in casual conversation you might also hear "eu me pergunto" or just "será que...".
target_language_example: Pergunto-me se ele vai chegar a tempo.
native_language_example: I wonder if he’ll arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or uncertainty about whether something is true or will happen. It literally means “I ask myself if…”. The verb is reflexive (perguntar-se). You can also hear/see other persons: "perguntas-te se" (you wonder if), "pergunta-se se" (one wonders if / it is wondered if).
target_language_example: Pergunto-me se ela já chegou em casa.
native_language_example: I wonder if she has already gotten home.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect yes/no question, expressing curiosity or uncertainty. Often appears as "(Eu) me pergunto se..." (I wonder if...). You can use it about present or past situations, and it’s common in both speech and writing.
target_language_example: Me pergunto se vai chover amanhã.
native_language_example: I wonder if it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Perguntou" is the past tense (he/she/it asked) of "perguntar". The "a" introduces the person being asked: "perguntou a Mary" = "asked Mary". It’s often followed by a question word (aonde, de onde, por que, que tipo...) or by "se" meaning "if/whether" when reporting a yes/no question: "perguntou ... se ...".
target_language_example: Ela perguntou ao professor se a prova era difícil.
native_language_example: She asked the teacher if the test was difficult.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect (reported) yes/no question after the verb perguntar in the past (perguntou). Often followed by a verb in the past or imperfect: “perguntou se estava…”, “perguntou se ia…”. If you see “se perguntou se…”, it means “asked himself/herself whether… / wondered if…”.
target_language_example: Ela perguntou se eu precisava de ajuda.
native_language_example: She asked if I needed help.

additional_notes: Used to report a yes/no question someone asked you. "perguntou" is the past of "perguntar" (to ask) and "se" means "if/whether" in indirect questions. Often followed by a verb phrase: "perguntou se eu precisava..." (asked if I needed...), "perguntou se eu queria..." (asked if I wanted...).
target_language_example: Ele perguntou se eu tinha tempo para conversar.
native_language_example: He asked if I had time to talk.

additional_notes: Used to report a yes/no question in the past. "perguntou" = "(he/she) asked"; "se" = "if/whether"; "eu" = "I"; "gostava de" = "liked" (imperfect past), commonly used when talking about general preferences in the past. After "gostar de", you normally use a noun ("de chocolate") or a verb in the infinitive ("de viajar").
target_language_example: Ela perguntou se eu gostava de música brasileira.
native_language_example: She asked if I liked Brazilian music.

additional_notes: Past tense of "perguntar a" (“to ask someone”). It’s used before a person (or a feminine noun) because "a" + "a" = "à" (crase). With a masculine noun you’ll usually see "perguntou ao" (a + o). Common patterns: "perguntou à [pessoa] por que..." (asked ... why...), "perguntou à [pessoa] se..." (asked ... if/whether...), "perguntou à [pessoa] como..." (asked ... how...).
target_language_example: Ela perguntou à professora se podia sair mais cedo.
native_language_example: She asked the teacher if she could leave earlier.

meaning: “permission to” (to be allowed to do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb: "permissão para + [verb]" (e.g., "permissão para entrar"). Common with verbs like "ter" (to have) and "dar" (to give): "ter permissão para..." = to be allowed to..., "dar permissão para..." = to give permission to... . You can also use it to ask politely: "Permissão para ...?"
target_language_example: Você tem permissão para usar o banheiro?
native_language_example: Do you have permission to use the bathroom?

additional_notes: Formal, polite way to ask permission or to introduce what you’re about to do (offer help, make a suggestion, etc.). It uses the imperative of "permitir" + the object pronoun "me". You may also hear "permite-me" (less formal) and in very formal speech "permita que eu...".
target_language_example: Permita-me explicar melhor.
native_language_example: Allow me to explain better.

additional_notes: Used to specify the left leg (body part). Often appears with possessives (minha/sua) and with pain or injury verbs like doer (to hurt) and ser baleado (to be shot).
target_language_example: Machucei a perna esquerda jogando futebol.
native_language_example: I hurt my left leg playing soccer.

additional_notes: From the verb **persuadir** (“to persuade”), commonly used as **persuadir alguém a + infinitive**: *persuadiu-me a ir* (“persuaded me to go”). In your examples, the person persuaded can be shown with pronouns like **o** (“him”) or **te** (“you”). **Isso** means “that/this (thing)” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ele me persuadiu a fazer isso, mas eu não queria.
native_language_example: He persuaded me to do that, but I didn’t want to.

additional_notes: Used with the verb pertencer + a + person/thing to show ownership or that something is associated with someone/something. The pronoun after a often combines: a ele = to him, a ela = to her, a você = to you, a mim = to me. It can be literal (property/object) or figurative (e.g., Meu coração pertence a você).
target_language_example: Este livro pertence à Maria, não a mim.
native_language_example: This book belongs to Maria, not to me.

meaning: 'belongs to' (is owned by; is part of).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is someone’s property or is associated with/part of something. "ao" is the contraction of "a" + "o" (to the + masculine singular): pertence ao Tom = belongs to Tom. With feminine singular, use "pertence à"; with plural, "pertence aos/às". It can also be used in a more abstract sense: "pertence ao passado" = belongs to the past.
target_language_example: Este casaco pertence ao meu irmão.
native_language_example: This coat belongs to my brother.

additional_notes: Used to say something is at a short distance from a place/thing. It combines perto (near) + da (= de + a, “of/from the” feminine singular). With masculine singular it’s perto do; with plural: perto dos/perto das. Also appears in expressions like chegar perto de (“to get close to / approach”).
target_language_example: O hotel fica perto da estação.
native_language_example: The hotel is near the station.

additional_notes: Used to say something is close to a (train/metro/bus) station. Often answers “Where?” (Onde?) and can be swapped with other places: perto do hotel, perto da escola. Contrast with longe da estação (“far from the station”).
target_language_example: Tem um café perto da estação.
native_language_example: Is there a café near the station?

meaning: near my house / close to my home.
additional_notes: Used to indicate something is located nearby where you live. Common with verbs like "há/tem" (there is/are) to mention places around your home. You can swap the possessive to match the person: "perto da sua casa" (near your house), "perto da casa dele/dela" (near his/her house). Often also said as "perto de casa" (near home).
target_language_example: Tem um supermercado perto da minha casa.
native_language_example: There’s a supermarket near my house.

additional_notes: Used to say a place (where someone lives, stays, etc.) is close to the beach. Often follows verbs like "morar" (to live) or "ficar" (to stay).
target_language_example: O hotel fica perto da praia.
native_language_example: The hotel is near the beach.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located a short distance from where you are now. Very common in questions with "Fica...?" ("Is it located...?") and with places (praia, correio, hospital, banco). You can also use "mais perto daqui" to mean "closer to here" (e.g., the closest bank).
target_language_example: Tem algum restaurante bom perto daqui?
native_language_example: Is there any good restaurant near here?

additional_notes: Used to talk about physical proximity to you. Very common with verbs like chegar (come), ficar (stay), morar (live), and with tirar… de perto de mim (“take it/him away from me”). Often interchangeable with “perto de mim” vs. “próximo de mim” (more formal).
target_language_example: Não fique tão perto de mim, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t stand so close to me, please.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is nearby. It’s the contraction of "perto de" + "o" (masculine singular: de + o = do). Use "perto da" for feminine singular (de + a), "perto dos" for masculine plural, and "perto das" for feminine plural. Often used for locations ("near the subway"), and sometimes for being in someone’s company ("when she’s with her boyfriend").
target_language_example: Moro perto do centro.
native_language_example: I live near downtown.

additional_notes: Uses perto de (“near”) + the definite article + noun. With masculine singular nouns like rio, de + o becomes do: perto do rio. You can swap in other places: perto do parque (“near the park”), perto da escola (“near the school”).
target_language_example: Há um restaurante perto do rio.
native_language_example: There is a restaurant near the river.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe someone by what they did/are, followed by a verb clause. In Portuguese you can also say “quem …” with a similar meaning (“Quem escreveu este livro…” = “The person who wrote this book…”). Often appears as “a pessoa que …” (the person who) or “uma pessoa que …” (a person who).
target_language_example: Ela é a pessoa que me ajudou quando eu cheguei aqui.
native_language_example: She’s the person who helped me when I arrived here.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar (present tense, 3rd person plural) to describe what people are doing right now (often + gerund: estão morrendo = 'are dying'), their current condition (estão feridas = 'are injured'), or where they are (estão aqui = 'are here'). Estar is generally for temporary states/locations (vs. ser for more permanent characteristics).
target_language_example: Muitas pessoas estão cansadas hoje.
native_language_example: Many people are tired today.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "pintar" (to paint) + "a minha casa" (my house). In everyday use it usually means painting the house walls (inside and/or outside), not making an artistic painting. Often used with time or help questions: "Quanto tempo vai levar...?" / "Preciso de ajuda para...".
target_language_example: No fim de semana vou pintar a minha casa e depois vou limpar tudo.
native_language_example: This weekend I’m going to paint my house and then I’m going to clean everything up.

additional_notes: Used when someone steps on your foot, often by accident (e.g., in a crowd), but it can also be intentional. The verb is "pisar" (to step on); "pisou" is the past tense (he/she/you stepped). You can change the person: "pisou no seu pé" (stepped on your foot), "pisei no seu pé" (I stepped on your foot).
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu pisei no seu pé sem querer.
native_language_example: Sorry, I stepped on your foot by accident.

additional_notes: Used to ask or say that someone intends to do something in the future. It uses the present continuous style in Portuguese: "estar" + "planejando" (planning) + "fazer" (to do). You can swap "isso" (this/that) for another object: "planejando fazer aquilo" (planning to do that over there) or "planejando fazer isso sozinho(a)" (planning to do this alone).
target_language_example: Eu não estava planejando fazer isso hoje, mas mudei de ideia.
native_language_example: I wasn’t planning to do that today, but I changed my mind.

additional_notes: Used to talk about intentions or arrangements for a future time/event or goal. Usually followed by a day/time ("planos para amanhã", "planos para segunda") or an action/goal ("planos para viajar", "planos para destruir..."), and it often comes with the verb "ter" (to have) or "fazer" (to make).
target_language_example: Você tem planos para o feriado?
native_language_example: Do you have plans for the holiday?

meaning: “one can… / you can… / it’s possible to …” (impersonal).
additional_notes: Formed by **pode** (can/is able to) + **-se** (impersonal “one/people”). It’s used when you don’t want to say who exactly can do something (a general statement). Very common in written Portuguese and formal speech. Often followed by an infinitive: **pode-se + infinitive** (e.g., *pode-se entrar*, *pode-se dizer*).
target_language_example: Aqui pode-se pagar com cartão.
native_language_example: Here you can pay by card.

additional_notes: Common way to say that something is possible (not certain). Often used with subjects like "isso" (that/this), "algo" (something), or "qualquer coisa" (anything). In the past tense, you’ll often see "pode" change to "podia" (“could happen”) or "pôde" (“was able to happen / could happen” in a specific situation).
target_language_example: Calma—isso pode acontecer com todo mundo.
native_language_example: Relax—that can happen to anyone.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is able to help a woman/girl. It’s made of pode (“can”) + ajudar (“to help”) + -la (“her,” direct object). In Brazil it’s common to also hear/see "pode ajudar ela" in informal speech, but "ajudá-la" is the more standard written form. For other people, the pronoun changes: "pode ajudá-lo" (him), "pode ajudá-los" (them, masc./mixed), "pode ajudá-las" (them, fem.).
target_language_example: A recepcionista pode ajudá-la com o formulário.
native_language_example: The receptionist can help her with the form.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is able to help. It’s made of pode (“can” / “is able to”) + ajudá-lo (“help you”), where -lo means “you” in a more formal style (often written/very polite, and more common in Brazil than in everyday speech). In casual Brazilian Portuguese, people often say pode te ajudar or pode ajudar você.
target_language_example: A recepcionista pode ajudá-lo com o check-in.
native_language_example: The receptionist can help you with check-in.

additional_notes: Formed by **poder** (can/may) + **estar** (to be, temporary state). Used to say something is **possibly true** or to make a **guess**: *Ele pode estar cansado* (“He might be tired”). It often comes before an adjective or state (*perdida, sozinho, vivo, bêbado*). It can also be followed by **gerund** to mean “may be happening/doing”: *Não pode estar acontecendo!* (“That can’t be happening!”).
target_language_example: O ônibus pode estar atrasado.
native_language_example: The bus might be late.

meaning: "can speak" / "may speak"; also "go ahead, you can speak."
additional_notes: Form of the verb phrase "poder + falar". It can express ability (speaking a language), permission/possibility, or a polite request. In conversation, "Pode falar." often means “Go ahead, you can talk/speak now” (e.g., inviting someone to start). With a question or request it’s common: "Pode falar mais rápido?" = “Can you speak faster?” (polite).
target_language_example: Pode falar agora, estou ouvindo.
native_language_example: Go ahead, you can speak now—I'm listening.

meaning: “can do” / “is able to do” (he/she/you-formal/it can do).
additional_notes: From **poder** (can/to be able to) + **fazer** (to do/make). **Pode** is the present tense for **ele/ela/você** (he/she/you formal). Often used in general statements with **se** (“one can / it’s possible to”), e.g., **não se pode fazer...** = “you can’t/one can’t do...”. Also used in questions: **Quem pode fazer...?** = “Who can do...?”
target_language_example: Você pode fazer isso hoje?
native_language_example: Can you do that today?

meaning: “can do it/that” (is able to do it).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone has the ability/possibility to do something. The subject changes: eu posso fazer isso (I can do it), você pode fazer isso? (Can you do it?). In questions it can mean either ability (“Are you able to?”) or permission depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu não sei se posso fazer isso hoje.
native_language_example: I don’t know if I can do it today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is able to do a task without help. "Pode" can also sound like “may” (permission), but here it’s about ability. You can change the subject: "eu posso...", "ele pode...", "você pode..."; and change gender/number: "sozinho" (male), "sozinha" (female), "sozinhos/sozinhas" (plural).
target_language_example: Eu não posso fazer isso sozinho; preciso de ajuda.
native_language_example: I can’t do this alone; I need help.

meaning: “can do whatever you want” / “is free to do whatever (they) want.”
additional_notes: Used to say someone has the freedom/permission to choose any option. It can be about ability (“can”) or permission (“may”), depending on context. The verb changes with the subject (eu posso, você/ele pode, nós podemos, eles podem). Often appears with “com…” to specify what it’s about (e.g., com o dinheiro dele = with his money).
target_language_example: Aqui você pode fazer o que quiser, desde que respeite as regras.
native_language_example: Here you can do whatever you want, as long as you follow the rules.

meaning: “can do it” / “can make him do it.”
additional_notes: "pode" = "(he/she/you) can". "fazê-lo" is "fazer" (to do/make) + the object pronoun "-lo" (him/it), attached to the infinitive. Often means "can do it" (Ele pode fazê-lo. = He can do it). With another verb after it, "fazer" can be causative: "fazer alguém + verb" = "make someone do something" (Pode fazê-lo lavar as mãos? = Can you make him wash his hands?). In everyday speech you may also hear "pode fazer isso" instead of "pode fazê-lo."
target_language_example: Você acha que pode fazê-lo hoje?
native_language_example: Do you think you can do it today?

additional_notes:
Literally 'can stay/remain' (poder + ficar). Very common with an extra phrase that clarifies the meaning:
- ficar + em/na/no... = 'stay' in a place: "Pode ficar na nossa casa." (You can stay at our house.)
- ficar + para... = 'stay' for something / 'stay until': "Pode ficar para o jantar?" (Can he stay for dinner?)
- ficar + com... = 'keep' or 'end up with': "Pode ficar com o cachecol." (You can keep the scarf.)
- ficar + adjective/noun = 'become/turn': "Pode ficar ótimo." (It can turn out great.) / "pode ficar rico" (can become rich) / "ficar com raiva" (get angry).
target_language_example: Se quiser, você pode ficar com este livro.
native_language_example: If you want, you can keep this book.

additional_notes: Used to give permission or state possibility that someone is allowed to stay in this place. Often followed by a time expression (e.g., “só uma noite”, “duas ou três noites”, “o tempo que quiser”). In questions, it can sound like asking for permission (“Pode ficar aqui?” = “Can I stay here?”). The negative form is “não pode ficar aqui” (“you can’t stay here / you may not stay here”).
target_language_example: Você pode ficar aqui esta noite, mas amanhã precisa ir embora.
native_language_example: You can stay here tonight, but tomorrow you need to leave.

meaning: 'there may be' / 'there can be' (it’s possible that something exists or happens).
additional_notes: Uses the impersonal verb "haver" to mean "there is/are" in the sense of existence. It stays in the singular: "Pode haver problemas" (not *podem haver*). Often interchangeable with "pode existir" (may exist) or "pode ter" in casual speech, but "pode haver" is more standard/formal.
target_language_example: Pode haver um atraso por causa do trânsito.
native_language_example: There may be a delay because of traffic.

additional_notes: It’s the verb "poder" (to be able to / may) + "ir" (to go): "(ele/ela/você) pode ir". Use it for permission ("You may go") or possibility/ability ("can go"). With destinations, add "para" ("pode ir para casa" = can go home). In the negative, "não pode ir" means "can’t go" or "mustn’t go" depending on context.
target_language_example: Você pode ir comigo amanhã?
native_language_example: Can you go with me tomorrow?

meaning: “can you … for me?” / “could you … for me?” (polite request).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone politely to do something for you. It’s the verb "poder" (can/could) in the present tense ("pode" = "you can" / "can you") + the unstressed object pronoun "me" (to me / for me). It’s typically followed by an infinitive or another verb phrase: "Pode me ajudar?" (Can you help me?), "Pode me enviar…?" (Can you send me…?). In Brazilian Portuguese you’ll also often hear the variant "pode me" in speech even though in more formal writing you may see different pronoun placement.
target_language_example: Pode me ajudar a encontrar a estação, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you help me find the station, please?

meaning: “Can you help me?” / “Could you help me?”
additional_notes: Literally “(you) can help me.” It’s a common way to ask for help; you can add “por favor” to be more polite (“Pode me ajudar, por favor?”). Often used with context words like “aqui” (here) or “com isso” (with this). With “alguém” it means “Can someone help me?”
target_language_example: Com licença, pode me ajudar a encontrar a estação?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you help me find the station?

additional_notes: Polite way to ask someone for help doing a specific action. You’ll normally follow it with a verb in the infinitive (e.g., dobrar, escolher, lavar, levar, preencher, tirar). Often used with “por favor” to sound extra polite. Common variations: “Pode me ajudar?” (Can you help me?) and “Você pode me ajudar a…?” (Can you help me to…?).
target_language_example: Pode me ajudar a encontrar a saída, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you help me find the exit, please?

meaning: "you can call me …" (a name or nickname).
additional_notes: Used to give permission/preference for how someone should address you, usually after stating your full name. After "de" you put the name, nickname, or title you want to be called. It’s polite and common in introductions.
target_language_example: Meu nome é Gabriela, mas pode me chamar de Gabi.
native_language_example: My name is Gabriela, but you can call me Gabi.

meaning: “can you give me…?” / “could you give me…?”
additional_notes: Literally “(you) can give me.” Used to politely ask someone to give you something (an object, time, help, etc.). Often appears in questions: “Pode me dar + [noun]?” In Brazil, you’ll also hear “Pode me dar…” and the slightly more formal “Pode me dar…” with “por favor” added.
target_language_example: Pode me dar a conta, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you give me the bill/check, please?

additional_notes: Polite way to ask for information. Usually followed by a question word like "onde" (where), "por que" (why), "como" (how), etc. You can also make it more formal by adding a title/name: "A senhora/Senhor pode me dizer…?" In Brazil, you may also hear "pode me dizer" without the "você"; it still means "can you tell me".
target_language_example: Pode me dizer onde fica a estação de metrô?
native_language_example: Can you tell me where the subway station is?

meaning: "Can you lend me…?" / "Could you lend me…?"
additional_notes: Polite request using "pode" (can/could) + "me" (to me) + "emprestar" (to lend). It’s usually followed by what you want to borrow: "Pode me emprestar o seu?" = “Can you lend me yours?” You’ll also hear "Você pode me emprestar…?" (more explicit) or the more formal "O senhor/A senhora pode me emprestar…?".
target_language_example: Pode me emprestar sua caneta por um minuto?
native_language_example: Can you lend me your pen for a minute?

meaning: “can you explain it to me?” / “could you explain it to me?”
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to explain something to you. It’s a polite request with the verb "poder" (can/could) + "me" (to me) + "explicar" (to explain). You can add what you want explained after it: "Pode me explicar o que significa...?" or "Pode me explicar como...?". In Brazil, "pode me" is common; in Portugal you may also hear "pode explicar-me".
target_language_example: Pode me explicar como chegar na estação?
native_language_example: Can you explain to me how to get to the station?

meaning: “Can you show me…?” / “Could you show me…?”
additional_notes: Polite request using the verb “poder” (can/could) + “me” (to me) + “mostrar” (to show). Often followed by what you want to see: “Pode me mostrar o cardápio?” You can also use it on its own (“Pode me mostrar?”) when the object is understood from context. In Brazil, you’ll also commonly hear “Pode mostrar?” (more direct) or “Pode me mostrar, por favor?” (more polite).
target_language_example: Pode me mostrar onde fica o banheiro?
native_language_example: Could you show me where the bathroom is?

meaning: “can help us” / “may be able to help us.”
additional_notes: Used to say that someone is able (or possibly able) to help your group. It’s built from pode (“can/may be able to”), nos (“us”), and ajudar (“to help”). In questions it’s often about who could help: “Quem pode nos ajudar?”
target_language_example: Você pode nos ajudar com isso, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you help us with this, please?

meaning: "it can be" / "it may be" (possibility); also "it could be".
additional_notes: From "poder" (to be able to / can) + "ser" (to be). Used to say something is possible, might happen, or could be true (often like English "may/might"). It can also be used for deduction: "Só pode ser..." = "It can only be..." / "It must be..." depending on context.
target_language_example: Pode ser verdade, mas não tenho certeza.
native_language_example: It may be true, but I'm not sure.

additional_notes: Common passive construction: *pode* (can/may) + *ser* (to be) + *feito* (done/made). Used to talk about what is possible or feasible, often in instructions, plans, or problem-solving contexts (e.g., *Veja o que pode ser feito a respeito* = “See what can be done about it”). Often implies possibility rather than certainty.
target_language_example: Isso pode ser feito amanhã, sem pressa.
native_language_example: That can be done tomorrow—no rush.
