additional_notes: Used to say that something is possibly a certain thing, or that someone sometimes has a certain characteristic. It’s the verb phrase **poder** (to be able to / can) + **ser** (to be) + **um** (a, masculine). Often the subject is implied by context (e.g., “it/he”). For feminine nouns, use **pode ser uma**.
target_language_example: Isso pode ser um problema se chover.
native_language_example: That could be a problem if it rains.

meaning: "it could be a..." / "it might be a..." (a possibility).
additional_notes: Used to speculate or suggest a possible explanation/option: "Pode ser uma opção" = "It could be an option." It’s the verb phrase "pode ser" (can be / may be) + the feminine article "uma" (a/an), so it’s followed by a feminine noun (e.g., "uma farsa", "uma missão"). With masculine nouns, you’ll usually see "pode ser um" (e.g., "pode ser um problema").
target_language_example: Pode ser uma boa ideia, mas vamos pensar melhor.
native_language_example: It could be a good idea, but let’s think it through better.

meaning: "it can be" / "it may be" (possibility); also "it could be".
additional_notes: From "poder" (to be able to / can) + "ser" (to be). Used to say something is possible, might happen, or could be true (often like English "may/might"). It can also be used for deduction: "Só pode ser..." = "It can only be..." / "It must be..." depending on context.
target_language_example: Pode ser verdade, mas não tenho certeza.
native_language_example: It may be true, but I'm not sure.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. It’s typically followed by a verb in the subjunctive: "Pode ser que ele venha" (may/might come), "Pode ser que não tenham" (may not have). Often translates as “may/might” or “it could be that.”
target_language_example: Pode ser que eu chegue tarde hoje.
native_language_example: I might arrive late today.

additional_notes: Uses the common structure "pode ser que + (subjunctive)" to express possibility/uncertainty. Here, "chova" is the present subjunctive of "chover" (to rain). You can swap in other verbs: "Pode ser que eu chegue tarde" (I might arrive late).
target_language_example: Leva um guarda-chuva; pode ser que chova.
native_language_example: Bring an umbrella; it might rain.

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to talk about something that is possible in the past: "pode ter acontecido" = "may have happened". With negation, "não pode ter" often means logical impossibility: "can't have" (e.g., "Ele não pode ter passado" = "He can't have passed").
target_language_example: Ela pode ter esquecido as chaves em casa.
native_language_example: She may have forgotten the keys at home.

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to talk about something that is possible in the past: "pode ter acontecido" = "may have happened". With negation, "não pode ter" often means logical impossibility: "can't have" (e.g., "Ele não pode ter passado" = "He can't have passed").
target_language_example: Ela pode ter esquecido as chaves em casa.
native_language_example: She may have forgotten the keys at home.

meaning: “you can use” / “(someone) can use” (permission or possibility).
additional_notes: From the verb phrase “poder” (can/may) + “usar” (to use). It often gives permission (“You may use…”) or says something is possible/available (“You can use…”). The subject can be implied (pode usar = you can use) or stated (Tom pode usar… = Tom can use…).
target_language_example: Você pode usar meu computador por alguns minutos.
native_language_example: You can use my computer for a few minutes.

additional_notes: From the verb "poder" (to be able to/can) + "ver" (to see). It can be literal (someone is able to see something) or used as a polite phrase meaning "as you can see" to point to evidence or what’s obvious in the situation. Often appears with implied subjects: "você pode ver" (you can see), "ele/ela pode ver" (he/she can see).
target_language_example: Você pode ver a placa daqui?
native_language_example: Can you see the sign from here?

additional_notes: Used to ask or say that someone is able/allowed to come somewhere. Very common in polite requests and invitations (often with the subject implied): “Pode vir?” / “Pode vir mais cedo?” It can also be used alone as permission/encouragement: “Pode vir.” = “You can come / Go ahead and come.”
target_language_example: Se quiser, pode vir comigo.
native_language_example: If you want, you can come with me.

additional_notes: "Podem" is the present tense of "poder" (to be able to / to be allowed to) for "eles/elas/vocês". It’s followed by an infinitive like "fazer" (to do/to make). Use it for ability ("Computadores podem fazer..." = computers can do...) or permission ("Eles podem fazer o que quiser" = they may/can do whatever they want).
target_language_example: Vocês podem fazer este exercício agora.
native_language_example: You (plural) can do this exercise now.

meaning: "can do that" / "are able to do that."
additional_notes: "Podem" is the present tense of "poder" (to be able to / can) for "they/you (plural)". It’s used to say someone has the ability or permission to do something: "Eles/Elas podem fazer isso" = "They can do that"; "Vocês podem fazer isso" = "You (all) can do that." Often appears in questions: "Como podem fazer isso?" = "How can they do that?"
target_language_example: Vocês podem fazer isso amanhã?
native_language_example: Can you (all) do that tomorrow?

meaning: “can be” / “may be” (they can be/are able to be; it’s possible they are).
additional_notes: Podem = “can/may” (3rd person plural of poder), ser = “to be.” Used with plural subjects (eles/elas/essas coisas/as pessoas) to talk about possibility, ability, or what is generally true. Often followed by an adjective (podem ser tolas), a noun (podem ser animais), or alternatives (podem ser reais ou imaginários).
target_language_example: Os resultados podem ser diferentes amanhã.
native_language_example: The results may be different tomorrow.

additional_notes: Passive voice: the subject is what is visible, not who is seeing it. Used for general statements or possibility/availability. Plural masculine form (vistos) is used with mixed or masculine plural nouns (e.g., anúncios, coelhos); for feminine plural use “podem ser vistas”. Also common with “só” = “can only be seen”.
target_language_example: Esses animais podem ser vistos aqui durante o inverno.
native_language_example: These animals can be seen here during the winter.

additional_notes: Used to ask for permission or suggest having a conversation. Often followed by details like where or when: em particular (“in private”), a sós (“alone”), em outro lugar (“somewhere else”), sobre isso (“about that”), pela manhã (“in the morning”). In questions it commonly means “Can we talk?”
target_language_example: Podemos conversar depois do trabalho?
native_language_example: Can we talk after work?

additional_notes: "Podemos" means "we can" (also used as "can we...?" to ask permission), and "falar" means "to talk/speak." Use it to ask to have a conversation (often about something important): "Podemos falar?" You can add details: "podemos falar a sós?" (can we talk in private?), "podemos falar sobre..." (can we talk about...), or "podemos falar em [língua]" (can we speak in [language]).
target_language_example: Podemos falar depois da aula?
native_language_example: Can we talk after class?

meaning: “Can we speak with…?” / “May we talk to…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask permission or propose speaking to someone. "Podemos" = "we can" (also used politely like "could we"), "falar" = "to speak," and "com" = "with/to". The person you want to speak to comes after "com" (e.g., "com Tom", "com a senhora", "com os senhores").
target_language_example: Podemos falar com você por um minuto?
native_language_example: Can we talk to you for a minute?

additional_notes: A polite, common way to suggest discussing a topic now or later. You can add a time word to be specific: amanhã (tomorrow), depois (later), mais tarde (later), depois do almoço (after lunch). Often used to postpone a sensitive or longer conversation.
target_language_example: Podemos falar sobre isso quando você tiver um tempo?
native_language_example: Can we talk about that when you have some time?

meaning: “we can do” / “can we do” (depending on context).
additional_notes: From the verb "poder" (to be able to/can) in the 1st person plural present tense: "podemos" = "we can". Used to talk about what’s possible or allowed. In questions like "O que mais podemos fazer?" it means "What else can we do?"; in statements like "Podemos fazer tudo isso" it means "We can do all of that."
target_language_example: Podemos fazer isso amanhã?
native_language_example: Can we do that tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to say something is possible or doable, to propose a plan, or to encourage someone (like “We’ve got this”). Often followed by details such as time (antes de segunda), place (aqui), or conditions (sem nenhuma ajuda). "Isso" usually means “this/that” depending on context.
target_language_example: Se trabalharmos juntos, podemos fazer isso hoje.
native_language_example: If we work together, we can do this today.

meaning: “we can do it” / “we can do it (it = something already mentioned).”
additional_notes: Used to say the group ("we") is able to do something. "fazê-lo" = "fazer" (to do/make) + "-lo" ("it"), and this "it" refers to something understood from context (a task, plan, etc.). In questions it often means "Can we do it...?" or "Are we able to do it...?"
target_language_example: Acho que podemos fazê-lo hoje, se todo mundo ajudar.
native_language_example: I think we can do it today if everyone helps.

meaning: “we can go” / “can we go?” (asking permission or saying it’s possible).
additional_notes: From "poder" (can/to be able to) + "ir" (to go). Often used to ask for permission or if it’s time to leave: "Já podemos ir?" = “Can we go now?” You can add where you’re going with "para" (destination): "podemos ir para casa" = “we can go home.” You can add company with "com": "podemos ir com você?" = “can we go with you?”
target_language_example: Se você estiver pronto, podemos ir agora.
native_language_example: If you’re ready, we can go now.

additional_notes: Used to suggest or ask about meeting up. Literally “we can meet (each other)”: podemos (“we can”) + nos (“each other/ourselves”) + encontrar (“to meet/find”). Very common when discussing a time and place (amanhã, na semana que vem, às X horas, em algum lugar). In Brazilian Portuguese, you may also hear “podemos nos ver” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Podemos nos encontrar às 18h na estação?
native_language_example: Can we meet at 6 p.m. at the station?

meaning: to be able to spend more time with.
additional_notes: Used to talk about having the opportunity/ability to spend more time together with someone (often as a wish or desire: "Eu gostaria de poder...", "Quem dera...", "Você já desejou..."). After "com" you typically use a person or group ("com minha família", "com os amigos"). You can change the time amount: "passar mais/menos tempo com", "passar muito tempo com".
target_language_example: Eu queria poder passar mais tempo com você esta semana.
native_language_example: I wanted to be able to spend more time with you this week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a possible event or outcome (often something uncertain or worrying). It’s the conditional form of "poder" + infinitive: "poderia" = "could/might" and "acontecer" = "to happen."
target_language_example: Se chover, isso poderia acontecer de novo.
native_language_example: If it rains, that could happen again.

meaning: “could do that / could do it” (would be able to do it).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of poder (poderia) + fazer isso (“do that/it”). Often expresses possibility/ability in a hypothetical or uncertain way, and can sound polite/less direct than “pode fazer isso”. With a subject, it becomes “eu/ele/ela poderia fazer isso” (“I/he/she could do it”). In questions like “Como … poderia fazer isso?”, it can also express disbelief (“How could … do that?”).
target_language_example: Você acha que eu poderia fazer isso sozinho?
native_language_example: Do you think I could do it by myself?

additional_notes: "Poderia" is the conditional of "poder" and is commonly used to make polite requests (often meaning “Could you…?”) or to talk about possibility (“I could…”). "Me" is the object pronoun “me/to me/for me.” In requests, Portuguese often drops the subject "você": "Poderia me dar…?" = “Could you give me…?” Also used with reflexive verbs: "poderia me machucar" = “I could hurt myself.”
target_language_example: Poderia me ajudar com isso, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you help me with this, please?

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of poder (“poderia” = “could”) to sound more polite/less direct than “pode me ajudar?”. Often followed by “por favor” and can be made more formal with “O senhor / A senhora poderia me ajudar?”. Common with complements like “com isso” (with this) or “em + [something]” (in/with + a topic/task).
target_language_example: Você poderia me ajudar a encontrar a estação de metrô, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you help me find the subway station, please?

additional_notes: A polite way to ask for help, commonly followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., carregar, dobrar, preencher). Often used as a request (especially with “por favor”). You may also see “Você poderia me ajudar a…?” (directly addressing someone) or “Alguém poderia me ajudar a…?” (asking if anyone can help).
target_language_example: Você poderia me ajudar a encontrar a estação de metrô, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you help me find the subway station, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask politely for something. "Poderia" is the conditional of "poder" (can/could) and makes the request softer than "pode". Often followed by the item you want: "Poderia me dar um copo de água, por favor?" In everyday speech you may also hear "podia me dar" or with the pronoun after the verb in more formal Portuguese: "poderia dar-me".
target_language_example: Poderia me dar um copo de água, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you give me a glass of water, please?

meaning: "Could you tell me...?" (polite request for information).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of "poder" (poderia = could/would be able to) + "me dizer" (tell me). Very common in polite questions, often with "Com licença". Typically followed by a question word (onde, qual, como) or by a noun phrase (o caminho, a senha). You may also hear/see "poderia dizer-me" (more formal) or in Brazil "poderia me falar" (same idea).
target_language_example: Você poderia me dizer onde fica a estação mais próxima?
native_language_example: Could you tell me where the nearest station is?

additional_notes: Formed by the conditional of "poder" (poderia = could/would be able to) + "ser" (to be). Used to suggest a possibility or make a softer, more polite statement than "pode ser". Often followed by a noun or adjective: "poderia ser um médico" (could be a doctor), "poderia ser verdade" (could be true).
target_language_example: Isso poderia ser uma boa ideia.
native_language_example: That could be a good idea.

meaning: "could have" (past possibility/ability; often implies something didn’t happen).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a possible past action or situation: either (1) a missed/alternative action (“You could have added more salt”), (2) something that was possible but didn’t happen (“I could have helped”), or (3) what was/wasn’t possible to know/do in the past (“I couldn’t have known”). It’s formed with poder in the conditional (poderia) + ter + past participle (feito, ajudado, posto, sabido, machucado, etc.).
target_language_example: Você poderia ter me avisado antes.
native_language_example: You could have told me earlier.

meaning: “could have done” (past possibility/ability; often about something that didn’t happen).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of poder (poderia) + ter + past participle (feito) to talk about what was possible in the past. It often implies regret, criticism, or a missed chance: “I/you/he could have done better.” Common in questions (O que você poderia ter feito?) and with conditions using se + past subjunctive (se tivesse tentado = “if (he) had tried”).
target_language_example: Eu poderia ter feito isso ontem, mas esqueci.
native_language_example: I could have done that yesterday, but I forgot.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a past possibility (often implying uncertainty, speculation, or a missed opportunity). It’s the conditional of poder (poderia = could/would be able to) + ter feito (have done) + isso (that/it). Common in questions (“Ele poderia ter feito isso?” = “Could he have done that?”) and in statements about who was able/likely to do something.
target_language_example: Ela poderia ter feito isso, mas não teve tempo.
native_language_example: She could have done that, but she didn’t have time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that was possible in the past, often to speculate about what might have happened or what something/someone might have been. It’s the conditional of "poder" + "ter sido" (to have been) and is commonly followed by a noun/adjective ("um de nós", "muito pior") or a past participle in passive meaning ("detido", "morto").
target_language_example: Ele poderia ter sido mais cuidadoso.
native_language_example: He could have been more careful.

additional_notes: Used mostly with verbs like aprender/saber/recitar: "aprender um poema de cor" = to memorize/learn a poem by heart; "saber um poema de cor" = to know a poem by heart. Although it contains "cor" ("color"), here "de cor" is an idiom meaning “from memory,” not “of color.”
target_language_example: Ela recitou o poema de cor na aula.
native_language_example: She recited the poem by heart in class.

additional_notes: Used to name the exact place where people agree to meet (often for an appointment, group, or event). Common with verbs like "marcar" (to set/arrange) and "chegar" (to arrive): "Qual é o ponto de encontro?" / "Vamos chegar ao ponto de encontro às 8." It can also be used more figuratively for a place where people gather (e.g., a library as a gathering place).
target_language_example: Vamos marcar a estação de metrô como ponto de encontro.
native_language_example: Let’s set the subway station as the meeting point.

meaning: 'by chance' / 'accidentally'; also used to soften a question: 'by any chance...?'.
additional_notes: Often means something happened unexpectedly (like “by chance”). In questions, it commonly means “by any chance…?”, making the question more polite or tentative: “Você por acaso sabe...?” = “Do you happen to know…?” It can also be used to express surprise/uncertainty: “Por acaso eu estava certo.” = “I was right, as it turns out.”
target_language_example: Você por acaso tem um carregador de celular?
native_language_example: Do you happen to have a phone charger?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a temporary period of time lasting several days (not exact). Common with verbs like ficar (to stay), sair/ir (to leave/go), and emprestar (to lend): “ficar por alguns dias” = “stay for a few days.”
target_language_example: Vou pegar o carro emprestado por alguns dias.
native_language_example: I’ll borrow the car for a few days.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a nearby place (“around here”), to say someone passed by (“passed through here”), or to indicate the route/way something goes (“breathe through here”). Also common in “novo(a) por aqui” = “new around here.”
target_language_example: Você conhece algum mercado bom por aqui?
native_language_example: Do you know any good grocery store around here?

additional_notes: Used to give the reason/cause of something. It’s usually followed by a noun or pronoun: por causa de + (thing/person) (e.g., "por causa do acidente", "por causa dela"). You can also use it with "disso/daquilo" (“because of that”).
target_language_example: Não vou sair por causa da chuva.
native_language_example: I’m not going out because of the rain.

meaning: because of (due to) + a feminine singular noun (“the”).
additional_notes: Used to give a reason/cause before a noun or noun phrase: por causa da fumaça (because of the smoke). It’s the contraction of por causa de + a = por causa da. (Also: por causa do = de + o; por causa de + no article.) For reasons with a full clause, Portuguese often uses porque: Não fui porque estava doente (I didn’t go because I was sick).
target_language_example: Cheguei atrasado por causa da chuva.
native_language_example: I arrived late because of the rain.

meaning: because of the rain / due to the rain.
additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something, specifically that rain caused it. The pattern is often "por causa de" + noun (e.g., por causa do trânsito = because of traffic). In everyday speech you can also hear "por causa da" or "por causa do" depending on the noun’s gender (chuva is feminine → da).
target_language_example: O voo atrasou por causa da chuva.
native_language_example: The flight was delayed because of the rain.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something. "por causa de" + noun = "because of" (cause/reason). Here, "da" = "de" + "a" (feminine singular) because "tempestade" is feminine; with a masculine noun you’d use "do" (e.g., "por causa do trânsito").
target_language_example: O voo foi cancelado por causa da tempestade.
native_language_example: The flight was canceled because of the storm.

meaning: because of (due to) + masculine singular noun.
additional_notes: Used to give the reason or cause for something. It’s the contraction of “por causa de” + “o” (the): por causa do incêndio = because of the fire. With feminine singular use “por causa da”, with plural “por causa dos/das”, and with a verb you often use “por causa de” + infinitive (e.g., por causa de chover). It can go before or after the main clause: “O jogo foi adiado por causa do mau tempo.” / “Por causa do mau tempo, o jogo foi adiado.”
target_language_example: Cancelamos a reunião por causa do trânsito.
native_language_example: We canceled the meeting because of the traffic.

additional_notes: Used to express duration of time. With actions/states that last over a period (like living somewhere), Portuguese often uses "por + [time period]" (e.g., por dois dias, por três meses, por muitos anos).
target_language_example: Trabalhei nessa empresa por dez anos.
native_language_example: I worked at that company for ten years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency or an amount averaged for each day (how many times/how much in one day). Common after numbers and expressions like “uma vez” (once), “três copos” (three cups), “quantas vezes” (how many times).
target_language_example: Eu caminho 30 minutos por dia.
native_language_example: I walk 30 minutes a day.

additional_notes: Used to say the method/channel of communication or sending something (e.g., send a file, share an address). Common with verbs like enviar (to send), mandar (to send), and conversar (to talk).
target_language_example: Vou te mandar os detalhes por e-mail ainda hoje.
native_language_example: I’ll send you the details by email later today.

additional_notes: Used when politely asking someone to accept something (e.g., apologies, condolences, help, an offer, a gift). "Aceite" is the formal/polite imperative of "aceitar" (to accept) used with "você" (and also with "o senhor / a senhora"). It can take an object: "aceite isso" (accept this) or a pronoun attached with a hyphen in more formal writing: "aceite-a" (accept it/her) and "aceite-o" (accept it/him).
target_language_example: Por favor, aceite este presente.
native_language_example: Please accept this gift.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to add something (a name, an item, a sentence, punctuation, etc.). **Adicione** is the imperative form of **adicionar** for **você** (e.g., *Adicione o meu nome...* = “Add my name...”). In writing you’ll often see a comma after **por favor**, but it’s also common to say it without the comma in speech.
target_language_example: Por favor, adicione meu e-mail ao formulário.
native_language_example: Please add my email to the form.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask for help. "Por favor" = "please" and "ajude-me" is the formal/standard command "help me" (from "ajudar"). Often followed by "a" + infinitive to say what you need help with: "ajude-me a limpar" (help me clean). You can also say "Por favor, me ajude"—same meaning, more common in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.
target_language_example: Por favor, ajude-me a encontrar meu passaporte.
native_language_example: Please, help me find my passport.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to call or summon help/services. In Portuguese, "chamar" can mean "to call" (phone) or "to summon/get" (e.g., call the police/doctor/taxi). With an object it’s often "chame a polícia / um médico / um táxi". With a person as the object pronoun it can also mean “call me (by a name)”: "Chame-me de Joe" = “Call me Joe.”
target_language_example: Por favor, chame um táxi para mim.
native_language_example: Please call a taxi for me.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to put/place something somewhere. It’s common in instructions and service situations. "Coloque" is the formal command form (imperative) of "colocar" for "você"; in everyday Brazilian Portuguese you may also hear "por favor, coloca" (more informal). The preposition after it is often "em" or "na/no" (e.g., "coloque na mesa", "coloque no lixo").
target_language_example: Por favor, coloque seu casaco na cadeira.
native_language_example: Please put your coat on the chair.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to allow something or to keep something in a certain state. With an infinitive (deixe + verb), it often means “let (someone) do (something)” (e.g., deixe Tom dormir). With a noun/adjective, it can mean “leave/keep” (deixe as janelas abertas; deixe as minhas coisas como estão). It can also mean “leave (a message)” (deixe uma mensagem) and “let it go/let it pass (this time)” (deixe passar dessa vez).
target_language_example: Por favor, deixe a porta fechada.
native_language_example: Please, leave the door closed.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask for permission or to request that someone allow you to do something. It’s usually followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., dormir, entrar, falar, ir, ajudar). Note: “deixe-me” = “let me” (formal-ish). In everyday speech you may also hear “deixa eu …” (more informal).
target_language_example: Por favor, deixe-me explicar.
native_language_example: Please, let me explain.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to say something or to tell someone a message. "Diga" is the formal command form (imperative) of "dizer" for "você". Common patterns: "Por favor, diga a verdade" (tell the truth), "Por favor, diga a [pessoa] que..." (tell [someone] that...), and "Por favor, diga olá" (say hi).
target_language_example: Por favor, diga ao professor que eu vou chegar atrasado.
native_language_example: Please tell the teacher that I'm going to be late.

additional_notes: Very polite/formal. "diga-me" is the formal command (imperative) of "dizer" (“to say/tell”) + "-me" (“to me”). Often used to ask questions: "Por favor, diga-me como..." (how...), "...qual..." (which/what...), "...o seu..." (your...). In casual speech you might also hear "Por favor, me diga" or "Por favor, diz-me" (more informal in Portugal).
target_language_example: Por favor, diga-me a que horas começa a reunião.
native_language_example: Please tell me what time the meeting starts.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to pass a message to a man or to someone referred to with a masculine noun/title (e.g., Tom, o chefe, o cozinheiro). The structure is: “Por favor, diga ao + [person] + para + infinitive” (to ask them to do something) or “Por favor, diga ao + [person] + que + clause” (to say something). For a woman/ feminine noun, use “diga à” (e.g., “diga à Maria”).
target_language_example: Por favor, diga ao Pedro que eu chego em dez minutos.
native_language_example: Please tell Pedro that I’ll be there in ten minutes.

meaning: "please, give" / "please, do" (polite command using "dê", the formal "you" command form of "dar").
additional_notes: Used to politely tell someone to give something or to perform an action. "Dê" is the imperative for "você" (formal/polite). Common patterns: "dê isso a ele" = "give this to him"; "dê uma olhada" = "take a look"; "dê um passo" = "take a step"; "dê banho" = "give (someone) a bath"; "dê o melhor de si" = "do your best".
target_language_example: Por favor, dê esta carta à professora.
native_language_example: Please give this letter to the teacher.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to hand you something or provide something (an item, help, information, etc.). “Dê-me” is the formal imperative of “dar” (to give) + “me” (to me). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many people also say “por favor, me dê …”.
target_language_example: Por favor, dê-me um copo de água.
native_language_example: Please, give me a glass of water.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to lend you something (or some money) temporarily. "Empreste-me" is the formal written form of "emprestar" (to lend) + the object pronoun "me" (to me). In everyday speech, many people say "Me empresta..." or "Me empreste..." (especially in Brazil). Typically followed by the thing you want to borrow: "por favor, empreste-me este livro".
target_language_example: Por favor, empreste-me sua caneta por um minuto.
native_language_example: Please lend me your pen for a minute.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to write something, often as an instruction (e.g., on a form). “Escreva” is the formal/you form (você) imperative/subjunctive of “escrever”. You can add what to write next: “Por favor, escreva seu nome aqui.”
target_language_example: Por favor, escreva seu nome e sua assinatura aqui.
native_language_example: Please write your name and your signature here.

additional_notes: Polite way to ask someone to wait. Often followed by where/for how long: espere ali (wait there), espere só mais um instante/momento (wait just one more moment), espere um pouco mais (wait a little longer). Common in service situations (shops, phone calls, appointments).
target_language_example: Por favor, espere na sala de espera.
native_language_example: Please, wait in the waiting room.

additional_notes: Polite way to ask someone to wait until a specific time/day ("até amanhã", "até segunda") or until an action is finished. In everyday speech you’ll often hear both "espere até eu terminar" and "espere até que eu termine" (both mean “wait until I finish”).
target_language_example: Por favor, espere até eu voltar.
native_language_example: Please wait until I get back.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to speak or to say/tell something. With a language: "Por favor, fale comigo em francês" = "Please speak to me in French." With "fale para + pessoa + verbo" it means "please tell (someone) to do something" (e.g., "fale para o Tom ficar mais quieto"). With "fale para + pessoa + que ..." it means "please tell (someone) that ...". You can add adverbs like "lentamente" and comparisons like "tão ... quanto possível" to ask how they should speak.
target_language_example: Por favor, fale mais devagar.
native_language_example: Please speak more slowly.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to do something. "Faça" is the formal imperative of "fazer" (used with "você"), so it often appears in requests to a professional or someone you’re being polite/formal with: "Por favor, faça isso" (Please do this). It can also introduce structures like "faça com que..." (please make it so that...).
target_language_example: Por favor, faça isso agora.
native_language_example: Please do that now.

additional_notes: Polite request. “Feche” is the formal command form (imperative) of fechar (to close), commonly used with você (e.g., “Feche a porta, por favor.”). You may also hear the more informal version “Por favor, fecha a porta” (with tu, in some regions). Often followed by details like “ao sair” (when leaving), “atrás de você” (behind you), or “com cuidado” (carefully).
target_language_example: Por favor, feche a porta porque está frio aqui.
native_language_example: Please close the door because it’s cold in here.

additional_notes: A polite request using the imperative form of the verb "ficar" (to stay/remain). Common when inviting someone to stay longer ("Por favor, fique com a gente.") or in set phrases like "Fique à vontade" (“Make yourself comfortable / Feel free”). In speech, it can also be said without the comma: "Por favor fique".
target_language_example: Está tarde, mas por favor, fique mais um pouco.
native_language_example: It’s late, but please stay a little longer.

additional_notes: "Ligue" is the polite command form (você imperative) of "ligar". It can mean (1) turn something on: "ligue a TV / ligue a luz"; (2) call someone, usually with "ligue para + person": "ligue para mim"; or (3) call/contact if something happens: "ligue se...". The meaning depends on what comes next (an object like "a televisão" vs. "para + person").
target_language_example: Por favor, ligue para o seu médico se a febre voltar.
native_language_example: Please call your doctor if the fever comes back.

meaning: "please, keep" / "please, maintain" (a polite request to continue doing something or to keep something in a certain state).
additional_notes: Used in polite instructions or requests. "Mantenha" is the formal command form (imperative) of "manter" (to keep/maintain). Often followed by a noun or phrase describing what should be kept: "mantenha a voz baixa" (keep your voice down), "mantenha contato" (keep in touch), "mantenha segredo" (keep it secret), "mantenha alguém informado" (keep someone informed).
target_language_example: Por favor, mantenha a porta trancada.
native_language_example: Please keep the door locked.

meaning: "Please, (to) me…" used to make a polite request (e.g., “please send me…”, “please forgive me”).
additional_notes: "Por favor" means “please.” The pronoun "me" means “me/to me” and is commonly placed before the verb in Brazilian Portuguese: "Por favor, me envie…". In European Portuguese you’ll often see it after the verb with a hyphen: "Por favor, envie-me…". Usually followed by a verb (envie, explique, perdoe, diga, ajude, etc.).
target_language_example: Por favor, me ajude com isso.
native_language_example: Please help me with this.

meaning: “please, tell me …” (a polite way to ask for information).
additional_notes: Used to politely request an answer or explanation, often followed by a question word like como (how), qual (which), quando (when), or quanto (how much). Common in customer service and when asking for directions. In Brazil, you’ll also hear “por favor, diga-me …” (more formal) or “por favor, me fala …” (more casual).
target_language_example: Por favor, me diga onde fica o banheiro.
native_language_example: Please, tell me where the bathroom is.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to hand you something or provide something (e.g., information, advice, a document). The verb form “dê” is the formal/polite command (imperative) of “dar” (“to give”) used with “você”; “me” means “to me.” Often followed by a noun phrase: “por favor, me dê + [item].”
target_language_example: Por favor, me dê um minuto para explicar.
native_language_example: Please, give me a minute to explain.

additional_notes: Common polite request on the phone or in messages. In Brazil, "me ligue" uses "ligar" (to call by phone). You can add time/place info: "antes de vir" (before coming), "mais tarde" (later), "quando você chegar" (when you arrive), "no meu hotel" (at my hotel). Also common: "Me liga" (more informal) and "me ligue" (a bit more formal/polite).
target_language_example: Se você tiver alguma dúvida, por favor, me ligue.
native_language_example: If you have any questions, please call me.

additional_notes: Polite way to ask someone to show you something or demonstrate how to do something. “Mostre-me” is the formal command (imperative) of “mostrar” + “me” (“to me”), so it’s common in instructions and customer-service situations. In casual speech, people often say “Por favor, me mostra …” or simply “Mostra …, por favor.”
target_language_example: Por favor, mostre-me onde fica o banheiro.
native_language_example: Please, show me where the bathroom is.

meaning: “Please, … us” / “Please, … to us” (asking someone to do something for us).
additional_notes: Used when making a polite request and the verb takes the object pronoun “nos” (“us”). Common patterns: “Por favor, nos diga…” (Please tell us…), “Por favor, nos dê…” (Please give us…), “Por favor, nos leve…” (Please take us…). In Portuguese, the object pronoun often comes before the verb in these requests.
target_language_example: Por favor, nos ajude com isso.
native_language_example: Please help us with this.

meaning: 'please don't' (a polite request not to do something).
additional_notes: Used before a verb to politely ask someone not to do an action. In Brazilian Portuguese you’ll often see it with você forms (Por favor, não abra...), and in European Portuguese it can appear with tu forms (Por favor, não te esqueças...). You can also add 'por favor' at the end: 'Não abra a janela, por favor.'
target_language_example: Por favor, não faça barulho.
native_language_example: Please don't make noise.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to stop an action. "Pare" is the formal command form of "parar" (stop) for você/a pessoa; it’s followed by "de" + infinitive (e.g., "pare de falar", "pare de fazer isso"). You can also say "Por favor, pare." without adding an action.
target_language_example: Por favor, pare de mexer no meu celular.
native_language_example: Please stop messing with my phone.

additional_notes: Used in polite instructions, especially in formal contexts (forms, applications, registration). In Brazilian Portuguese, "preencher" commonly means “to fill in” a form; it can take an object like "este formulário" or "o formulário abaixo". You may also see it without the comma: "Por favor preencha...".
target_language_example: Por favor, preencha seus dados aqui e assine no final.
native_language_example: Please fill in your details here and sign at the end.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to respond. "Responda" is the formal command form (você / o senhor / a senhora). You can add what you want them to respond to: "responda à pergunta" (answer the question), "responda-me" (reply to me), or "responda em inglês" (reply in English).
target_language_example: Por favor, responda quando puder.
native_language_example: Please reply when you can.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to adopt a quality or behave in a certain way. Followed by an adjective or noun phrase: “Por favor, seja + adjective” (seja educado/gentil/honesto) or “seja + noun” (seja paciente). “Seja” is the present subjunctive (used for requests) of “ser” (to be) for você/ele/ela.
target_language_example: Por favor, seja paciente comigo.
native_language_example: Please be patient with me.

additional_notes: Polite way to ask someone to take a seat. "Sente-se" is the formal/polite command form (from "sentar-se" = to sit down) and the "-se" means "yourself" (reflexive). Often followed by where to sit: "aqui" (here), "lá atrás/na parte de trás" (back there/in the back), "no sofá" (on the sofa). You can also add a name: "Por favor, sente-se, Tom."
target_language_example: Por favor, sente-se e fique à vontade.
native_language_example: Please, sit down and make yourself comfortable.

meaning: "Please remove/take" (or "please make" in the sense of making a copy/photo).
additional_notes: "Tire" is the polite imperative of "tirar" (to take out/remove; to take off clothes; to take someone out of a place; to make copies or take a photo). Often followed by an object: "tire a camisa" (take off the shirt), "tire da mesa" (remove from the table), "tire meu nome da lista" (take my name off the list), "tire três cópias" (make three copies), "tire-me daqui" (get me out of here).
target_language_example: Por favor, tire uma foto de nós.
native_language_example: Please take a photo of us.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to bring something to you. "Traga" is the formal (você) imperative of "trazer" (to bring), and "-me" means "to me". Common in service situations (restaurants, hotels) or polite requests; you can replace the object: "Por favor, traga-me a conta" (the bill).
target_language_example: Por favor, traga-me a conta.
native_language_example: Please bring me the bill.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to come to a place or event, or to come at a specific time/date. "Venha" is the imperative/subjunctive form of "vir" (to come) used for "você"; with "tu" you’ll often hear "vem" (e.g., "Por favor, vem aqui"). It can be followed by location words ("aqui", "para casa"), invitations ("à minha casa", "à inauguração"), and time phrases ("hoje", "na próxima sexta-feira").
target_language_example: Por favor, venha comigo ao médico amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: Please, come with me to the doctor tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to return, either to a place (volte ao seu lugar / volte para casa / volte para dentro) or at a future time (volte amanhã / daqui a meia hora / na semana que vem). In Brazil you’ll also hear "por favor, volte" in customer service contexts meaning “please come back (again)”. It’s a polite request (imperative form of "voltar").
target_language_example: Por favor, volte mais tarde — ainda não estamos abertos.
native_language_example: Please come back later — we’re not open yet.

additional_notes: Uses the imperative of ir (“vá” = “go”). Commonly followed by a destination with a preposition: ao/à (a + o/a) for specific places (ex: ao banco), para for a destination/city (ex: para São Francisco), and em frente (fixed phrase) meaning “ahead/forward” (vá em frente = “go ahead”). This is polite but direct, like giving instructions.
target_language_example: Por favor, vá para casa agora.
native_language_example: Please, go home now.

meaning: 'please' + 'me' (used before a verb to make a polite request).
additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to do something for you. It’s usually followed by a verb (often in the imperative): "Por favor me diga...", "Por favor me mostre...", "Por favor me passe...". "Me" is an object pronoun meaning "to me" or "for me" depending on the verb. In everyday speech, people also say simply "Por favor" or place it at the end: "Me diga, por favor."
target_language_example: Por favor me ajude com isso.
native_language_example: Please help me with this.

additional_notes: Used to explain a reason or justify what was said or happened. Often comes after (or with) emphasis like "é (exatamente) por isso que…" = "that’s (exactly) why…". In speech, it can also be used on its own: "Por isso." = "That’s why / for that reason."
target_language_example: Eu não tinha dinheiro, por isso que não fui ao cinema.
native_language_example: I didn’t have money, so that’s why I didn’t go to the movies.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an extension in time: staying/waiting/continuing for an additional three days beyond what was planned or expected. Common with verbs like ficar (to stay), esperar (to wait), continuar (to continue). Word order in English is usually “for three more days.”
target_language_example: Posso ficar aqui por mais três dias?
native_language_example: Can I stay here for three more days?

meaning: 'for me' / 'on my behalf' / 'as far as I’m concerned'.
additional_notes: Used in several common ways: (1) someone is asking/waiting for you: "perguntou/esperando por mim" = "asked for me / waiting for me"; (2) a favor or doing something for your benefit: "faz isso por mim" = "do it for me"; (3) opinion/permission: "Por mim, tudo bem" = "As far as I’m concerned, it’s fine"; (4) representation: "falar por mim" = "to speak for me"; and also "feliz por mim" = "happy for me".
target_language_example: Você pode ligar para eles por mim?
native_language_example: Can you call them for me?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a long duration. It can refer to the past ("I lived... for a long time"), the future ("you won’t see... for a long time"), or a general/lasting effect ("will be remembered for a long time").
target_language_example: Não falo com ele por muito tempo.
native_language_example: I haven’t spoken to him for a long time.

additional_notes: Used to express a duration of time that something lasted in the past, present, or future. Often comes after the verb it describes: "morei lá por muitos anos" (I lived there for many years).
target_language_example: Eu trabalhei aqui por muitos anos.
native_language_example: I worked here for many years.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens or how much you get/pay in one month (rate or frequency). Often after a number or quantity: "três vezes por mês" (three times per month), "mil peças por mês" (a thousand pieces per month), "R$ 2.000 por mês" (R$2,000 a month).
target_language_example: Eu pago 50 reais por mês pela internet.
native_language_example: I pay 50 reais a month for internet.

additional_notes: Used to ask about duration (how long something will last) or to refer to an unknown/unspecified length of time. Often appears in questions: “Por quanto tempo…?” = “For how long…?” In statements it can mean “for how long (still/anymore)”: “Não sei por quanto tempo (ainda)” = “I don’t know for how much longer.”
target_language_example: Por quanto tempo você vai ficar aqui?
native_language_example: How long are you going to stay here?

meaning: "for how long" (asking about the duration of time you).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the length/duration of an action or stay. It’s a question phrase; the verb comes after it (e.g., "por quanto tempo você ficou...?"). You can change "você" to "ele/ela" or "vocês" depending on who you’re asking about.
target_language_example: Por quanto tempo você vai ficar aqui?
native_language_example: How long are you going to stay here?

por quanto tempo você pretende ficar

target_language_multi_word_term: por quanto tempo você pretende ficar
meaning: "How long do you intend to stay?"
additional_notes: A polite question asking about someone’s planned duration of stay in a place (country, city, hotel, etc.). You can swap in the place after "ficar" (e.g., "aqui", "em São Paulo", "no Brasil"). Common variants: "Por quanto tempo você vai ficar...?" (more casual/neutral) and "Por quanto tempo o(a) senhor(a) pretende ficar...?" (more formal).
target_language_example: Por quanto tempo você pretende ficar em São Paulo?
native_language_example: How long do you intend to stay in São Paulo?

meaning: "for how long have you (plural)" / "how long will you (plural)".
additional_notes: Used to ask about the duration of something involving "vocês" (you all). "Por quanto tempo" = "for how long". It’s usually followed by a verb in the past (e.g., "vocês ficaram..." = you stayed) or future/intentions (e.g., "vocês pretendem ficar..." = you plan to stay). In Brazil, "vocês" is the normal plural "you" (it takes 3rd-person plural verb forms: "vocês ficaram", "vocês pretendem").
target_language_example: Por quanto tempo vocês vão ficar aqui?
native_language_example: How long are you (all) going to stay here?

meaning: “why the…?” / “why is the…?” (used before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason. It’s the question form: por que = “why”, followed by a = “the” (feminine singular). Common with nouns like a bruxa (the witch), a fumaça (the smoke), a casa (the house). Note: por que (two words) = “why”; porque (one word) = “because,” which learners often mix up.
target_language_example: Por que a porta está aberta?
native_language_example: Why is the door open?

additional_notes: Used to ask a woman “why…?” in a polite or formal way. “A senhora” is a respectful form of address (like “ma’am”), common with strangers, older women, customers, etc. In everyday conversation it often takes third-person verb forms: “Por que a senhora está…?”, “Por que a senhora quer…?”
target_language_example: Por que a senhora não me disse antes?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you tell me earlier, ma’am?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s possible motive or reason for doing something, often with surprise, disbelief, or confusion. "Por que" = "why"; "alguém" = "someone/anyone"; "iria" is the conditional of "ir" and works like "would" here. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb: "Por que alguém iria fazer.../querer...".
target_language_example: Por que alguém iria mentir sobre isso?
native_language_example: Why would anyone lie about that?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason behind people’s actions or behavior. Often followed by a verb in the present tense (e.g., "mentem", "dizem", "são"). In questions, it’s typically written as "por que" (two words).
target_language_example: Por que as pessoas falam tão alto aqui?
native_language_example: Why do people talk so loudly here?

meaning: “why do people have …?” / “why do people feel …?”
additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for something people have or experience. **por que** = “why” (question), **as pessoas** = “people”, **têm** (ter) = “have” (present tense). With feelings, Portuguese often uses **ter** (“to have”) where English uses “to be/feel”: **ter medo de** = “to be afraid of.”
target_language_example: Por que as pessoas têm tanta pressa hoje em dia?
native_language_example: Why are people in such a hurry nowadays?

meaning: "why she" / "why is she" (asking for the reason).
additional_notes: Used in questions and indirect questions. In direct questions, it often comes at the beginning: "Por que ela..." (= "Why is she...?"). In indirect questions, it follows a verb like perguntar/saber: "Perguntei ... por que ela..." (= "I asked ... why she...").
target_language_example: Não sei por que ela saiu tão cedo.
native_language_example: I don't know why she left so early.

por que elas estão fazendo isso

target_language_multi_word_term: por que elas estão fazendo isso
meaning: "Why are they doing that?" (about a group of women / "they" feminine).
additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason behind an action. "Por que" = "why" in questions. "Elas" means "they" referring to a group of women (or a group treated as feminine); for mixed/masculine groups you usually use "eles". You can add "com + pronoun" to mean "to/against (someone)": "com a gente" (to us), "com ela" (to her), "com ele" (to him).
target_language_example: Por que elas estão fazendo isso agora?
native_language_example: Why are they doing that now?

meaning: "why he..." (used to ask why a man/boy did something).
additional_notes: Used in both direct questions (Por que ele está...?) and indirect questions (Eu não sei por que ele fez isso.). Note the spelling: **por que** = “why” (question/indirect question), while **porque** = “because” (answer/reason).
target_language_example: Você sabe por que ele foi embora tão cedo?
native_language_example: Do you know why he left so early?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or talk about the reason for a specific action done by a male person (ele = he). Very common after verbs like contar (to tell), saber (to know), perguntar (to ask), and in indirect questions: "me contou por que ele fez aquilo" = "told me why he did that." Note: "por que" (two words) is used in questions (direct or indirect); "aquilo" means "that" (over there / that thing).
target_language_example: Ninguém entende por que ele fez aquilo.
native_language_example: Nobody understands why he did that.

meaning: "why they" / "why did they" (asking for a reason, with "they").
additional_notes: Used at the start of a direct question (Por que eles...?) or inside an indirect question after verbs like perguntar-se (Eu me pergunto por que eles...). In direct questions it often translates as "Why did they...?" in English; in indirect questions it’s "why they..." (no inversion in Portuguese).
target_language_example: Eu não entendo por que eles fizeram isso.
native_language_example: I don’t understand why they did that.

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason behind what a group of people (eles) is doing or how they are. It’s made of: por que (why) + eles (they) + estão (are, from estar). After estão you’ll often see: an adjective (com medo, com raiva), a gerund (-ando: chorando, protestando), or a place/position (abaixados).
target_language_example: Por que eles estão rindo?
native_language_example: Why are they laughing?

por que eles estão fazendo isso

target_language_multi_word_term: por que eles estão fazendo isso
additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason behind an action that “they” (eles) are doing right now (estão fazendo). You can add “com + pronoun/name” to mean “to/with someone,” often implying the person is being affected: com ela (to her), com ele (to him), com você (to you), comigo (to me). Note: “Por que” (two words) is used in questions meaning “why.”
target_language_example: Por que eles estão fazendo isso com a gente?
native_language_example: Why are they doing this to us?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason or explanation about something happening now. "Por que" = "why" and "estamos" = "we are" (present tense of "estar"), so it’s typically followed by a verb in the -ndo form (gerund) like "fazendo", "indo", "rindo": "Por que estamos fazendo isso?"
target_language_example: Por que estamos esperando aqui?
native_language_example: Why are we waiting here?

meaning: "why is" / "why are you" (asking the reason for a current state or action).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to ask the reason for how something is right now or what someone is doing. Often followed by an adjective or a verb: "Por que está vazio?" (why is it empty?), "Por que está sorrindo?" (why are you smiling?). In speech and informal writing, you’ll also see "por que tá" (short for "está").
target_language_example: Por que está tão difícil hoje?
native_language_example: Why is it so difficult today?

meaning: “Why is it so…?” / “Why are you so…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for a situation or someone’s state. Follow it with an adjective (e.g., preocupado, triste) or a description of the environment (e.g., escuro aqui, quieto). In everyday writing you’ll also see the question written as “Por que está tão…?” or “Por que tá tão…?” (more informal).
target_language_example: Por que está tão barulhento lá fora?
native_language_example: Why is it so noisy outside?

meaning: “why are you … ?” (asking the reason for what someone is doing/feeling).
additional_notes: Used to ask why someone is doing something or in a certain state: “Por que estás + (verb in -ndo)” (Por que estás rindo? = Why are you laughing?) or “Por que estás + adjective” (Por que estás triste? = Why are you sad?). Common with “estás” in European Portuguese; in Brazil you’ll often hear “Por que você está …?”.
target_language_example: Por que estás tão cansado hoje?
native_language_example: Why are you so tired today?

additional_notes: Common in European Portuguese: "estar a" + infinitive expresses an action happening right now (similar to English present continuous). Use it to ask the reason for what someone is doing: "Por que estás a beber...?" = "Why are you drinking...?" In Brazilian Portuguese, you’ll more often hear "Por que você está ..." or "Por que você está + gerund" (e.g., "Por que você está bebendo...?").
target_language_example: Por que estás a falar tão alto?
native_language_example: Why are you talking so loudly?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason something is happening. **Por que** = “why” in direct questions, and **estão** is the present tense of *estar* for **eles/elas/vocês** (“they/you all are”). In speech, **vocês** is often the implied subject even if it isn’t written.
target_language_example: Por que estão tão quietos hoje?
native_language_example: Why are you all so quiet today?

meaning: “why I…?” / “the reason why I…”; sometimes “(the path/way) that I go through.”
additional_notes: Most commonly starts a question: “Por que eu + verb…?” = “Why am I…?” or “Why did I…?”. In more formal/older usage, especially after a noun like caminho/estrada/motivo (“path/road/reason”), “por que” can mean “by/through which” or “for which” (e.g., “o caminho por que eu passo…” = “the path that I go through…”).
target_language_example: Por que eu não posso entrar?
native_language_example: Why can't I come in?

additional_notes: Used to question the reason or motivation for doing something. It’s often followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., ajudar, confiar, ficar, dar). You can change the subject pronoun: "por que você deveria..." (why should you...), "por que a gente deveria..." (why should we...).
target_language_example: Por que eu deveria aceitar essa proposta?
native_language_example: Why should I accept this offer?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason you are required/forced to do something. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb (fazer, ir, ajudar, decidir). In speech it’s common to shorten it to "Por que tenho que…?" or "Por que eu tenho que fazer isso?"
target_language_example: Por que eu tenho que esperar aqui?
native_language_example: Why do I have to wait here?

additional_notes: Used to question someone’s motive or the logic of an action. It’s a rhetorical-sounding way to say there’s no reason to do something. Grammar: "por que" = "why" (in questions); "iríamos" is the conditional of "ir" and helps form "would"; "querer" = "to want". Usually followed by an infinitive verb: "por que iríamos querer + [verb]".
target_language_example: Por que iríamos querer fazer isso agora?
native_language_example: Why would we want to do that now?

additional_notes: Used at the start or in the middle of a question to ask the reason for a situation or fact previously mentioned ("this/that"). Often followed by a verb: "por que isso acontece?" = "why does this happen?". Note: "por que" (two words) is used in questions; "porque" (one word) means "because" in answers.
target_language_example: Você sabe por que isso não funciona?
native_language_example: Do you know why this doesn't work?

meaning: 'why did/does the …' (asking for the reason; used before a masculine singular noun/name).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question. "por que" = "why". "o" is the masculine singular definite article (“the”), often used before a man’s name in some varieties of Portuguese (e.g., "o Tom" = “Tom”). If the noun is feminine, use "por que a"; plural: "por que os/as".
target_language_example: Por que o João chegou tão tarde?
native_language_example: Why did João arrive so late?

additional_notes: Used to ask a “why” question politely/formally to a man. It’s made of **por que** (“why”) + **o senhor** (“you”, formal). Verbs usually go in the **3rd person singular**: *Por que o senhor está…?* / *Por que o senhor achou…?*
target_language_example: Por que o senhor não me avisou antes?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you tell me earlier, sir?

meaning: 'why do the' / 'why are the' (introduces a question about a plural noun).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question: "por que" = "why", and "os" is the masculine plural definite article ("the") before a plural noun (os motores, os adultos, os exercícios). For feminine plural, use "por que as". After "por que os", Portuguese may use a verb in the plural (e.g., "Por que os motores pararam?") or a singular verb like "é/são" depending on the noun ("Por que os exercícios são importantes?").
target_language_example: Por que os alunos estão cansados hoje?
native_language_example: Why are the students tired today?

meaning: 'I wonder why…' / 'why could it be that…?'
additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or speculation about a reason (often with some surprise). It’s more tentative than a plain question with "por que"—you’re wondering, not necessarily expecting a clear answer. Common in spoken Portuguese before a clause: "Por que será que ele não veio?"
target_language_example: Por que será que ela ainda não respondeu?
native_language_example: I wonder why she still hasn’t replied.

meaning: 'I wonder why…' / 'why could it be that…?'
additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or speculation about a reason (often with some surprise). It’s more tentative than a plain question with "por que"—you’re wondering, not necessarily expecting a clear answer. Common in spoken Portuguese before a clause: "Por que será que ele não veio?"
target_language_example: Por que será que ela ainda não respondeu?
native_language_example: I wonder why she still hasn’t replied.

meaning: "why you...?" (used to ask why someone did/does something).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question with the pronoun "tu" (you, informal/singular). It’s followed by a verb: "Por que tu foste...?" / "Por que tu gostas...?" In Brazil, many speakers more often say "Por que você..."; with "tu", the verb is typically in the "tu" form (e.g., "tu foste", "tu gostas").
target_language_example: Por que tu não me ligaste ontem?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you call me yesterday?

additional_notes: Used at the start (or in the middle) of a question to ask for someone’s reason or explanation. "Por que" = "why" and is followed by "você" + a verb (e.g., "Por que você foi...?", "Por que você quer...?"; in indirect questions it can appear after another verb: "Vão lhe perguntar por que você quer...").
target_language_example: Por que você não me contou antes?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you tell me earlier?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s reasoning or opinion before a clause. In questions, it’s written as two words: “por que”. Often followed by a full sentence (e.g., “Por que você acha que ele fez isso?”).
target_language_example: Por que você acha que ela está chateada?
native_language_example: Why do you think she’s upset?

por que você acha que o

target_language_multi_word_term: por que você acha que o
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s reasoning or opinion. It’s a common question pattern: “Por que” = “why”, “você acha que” = “you think (that)”, and “o” is the masculine singular definite article (“the”), so it’s typically followed by a masculine noun or a male person’s name/title (e.g., “o Tom”, “o professor”). For a female name/title, you’d use “a” instead: “por que você acha que a…”. In speech, “que” is often optional in similar sentences, but it’s very common to include it here.
target_language_example: Por que você acha que o João não veio hoje?
native_language_example: Why do you think João didn’t come today?

additional_notes: Used to ask why someone continues to be in a state or situation. Follow it with an adjective (acordada, chateado), a place (aqui), or a verb in the -ndo form for an ongoing action (reclamando). Note agreement: você is used with está; adjectives can change for gender (acordada/acordado, chateada/chateado).
target_language_example: Por que você ainda está esperando?
native_language_example: Why are you still waiting?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason someone bought something. "Por que" (usually written separately in questions) means “why,” and "você comprou" means “you bought” (past). You normally add the thing after it: "Por que você comprou isso/esse carro/tantas coisas?"
target_language_example: Por que você comprou esse livro?
native_language_example: Why did you buy that book?

por que você comprou um carro

target_language_multi_word_term: por que você comprou um carro
additional_notes:
A question asking for the reason someone bought a car. 
- **por que** = “why” (question form)
- **você** = “you”
- **comprou** = “bought” (past; from *comprar*)
- **um carro** = “a car”
You can add an adjective after **carro** to specify the type (e.g., **um carro alemão** = “a German car”).
target_language_example: Por que você comprou um carro usado?
native_language_example: Why did you buy a used car?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s reason behind a decision. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., aprender, estudar, vender, não ir). In questions, "por que" is usually written as two words; "porque" (one word) is used in answers meaning "because."
target_language_example: Por que você decidiu mudar de emprego?
native_language_example: Why did you decide to change jobs?

meaning: "Why were you..." (asking for the reason someone was doing/feeling something in the past).
additional_notes:
Used to ask about a past situation, action, or emotion. It’s formed by:
- por que = why
- você = you
- estava = were (imperfect past of "estar")
Often followed by a gerund (fazendo, gritando) or an adjective (zangado, desapontado). In questions, it’s usually written "Por que" (two words).
target_language_example: Por que você estava tão nervoso ontem?
native_language_example: Why were you so nervous yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason someone is in a certain state or is doing something right now. It’s followed by an adjective (por que você está nervoso?) or by a verb in the -ando/-endo/-indo form to describe an action in progress (por que você está segurando...?). In questions, Portuguese often uses “por que” as two words.
target_language_example: Por que você está falando tão baixo?
native_language_example: Why are you speaking so quietly?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason someone is present in a place. It can sound neutral or suspicious depending on tone/context. Often followed by details like “hoje” (today), “tão cedo” (so early), or “novamente” (again). You may also hear “Por que você está aqui?” as a standalone question.
target_language_example: Por que você está aqui neste horário?
native_language_example: Why are you here at this time?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason someone is crying. In questions, **por que** usually means “why.” **você** = “you” (common in Brazil), and **está chorando** is the present continuous (“are crying”). You can add a term of affection like **meu amor** (“my love”) or **de novo** (“again”).
target_language_example: Por que você está chorando? Posso ajudar?
native_language_example: Why are you crying? Can I help?

por que você está fazendo isso com

target_language_multi_word_term: por que você está fazendo isso com
additional_notes: Used to question someone's action involving a person. With "com" it can sound like "with" (involving them) or, in many contexts, like English "to" (treating them in a certain way): "Por que você está fazendo isso com ela?" = "Why are you doing this to her?" The person comes right after: "com ele/ela/eles/elas" or a name ("com o Fadil").
target_language_example: Por que você está fazendo isso com a sua irmã?
native_language_example: Why are you doing this to your sister?

meaning: "Why are you ...ing me?" (asking why someone is doing something to you).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question. It’s a common pattern: "Por que você está me" + verb (gerund), e.g., "contando" (telling), "olhando" (looking at), "seguindo" (following), "tratando" (treating). "Você está" is like "you are" (often used for actions happening now), and "me" means "me" as the object.
target_language_example: Por que você está me ignorando?
native_language_example: Why are you ignoring me?

por que você está sendo tão

target_language_multi_word_term: por que você está sendo tão
additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s current behavior (often criticizing it). Add an adjective after tão (e.g., duro/dura = harsh, mau/má = mean/bad, malvado/malvada = evil/cruel). Often sounds accusatory; for a softer tone you can add "assim": "Por que você está sendo tão assim?"
target_language_example: Por que você está sendo tão impaciente comigo?
native_language_example: Why are you being so impatient with me?

por que você está sendo tão

target_language_multi_word_term: por que você está sendo tão
additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s current behavior (often criticizing it). Add an adjective after tão (e.g., duro/dura = harsh, mau/má = mean/bad, malvado/malvada = evil/cruel). Often sounds accusatory; for a softer tone you can add "assim": "Por que você está sendo tão assim?"
target_language_example: Por que você está sendo tão impaciente comigo?
native_language_example: Why are you being so impatient with me?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s current state or behavior. It’s normally followed by an adjective (e.g., chateado, nervoso, quieto). In speech, você is often shortened to "cê": "Por que cê tá tão...?".
target_language_example: Por que você está tão preocupado com isso?
native_language_example: Why are you so worried about that?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason someone is using something (an object, clothes, a device, etc.). You normally follow it with the thing: “Por que você está usando isso?” (“Why are you using that?”). In Brazilian Portuguese, you may also hear “Por que você tá usando…?” (more casual).
target_language_example: Por que você está usando o meu carregador?
native_language_example: Why are you using my charger?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason behind someone’s past action. Often followed by the thing done: "Por que você fez isto?" (Why did you do this?) or "Por que você fez aquela pergunta...?" (Why did you ask that question...?). In Portuguese, "por que" is usually written as two words in questions meaning "why".
target_language_example: Por que você fez isso ontem?
native_language_example: Why did you do that yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason behind someone’s action. Often appears as a question ("Por que você fez isso?") but can also be part of a statement ("Sabemos por que você fez isso" = “We know why you did that”). In Brazil, “você” is common; in Portugal you may hear “Por que fizeste isso?” / “Por que fez isso?”.
target_language_example: Por que você fez isso ontem?
native_language_example: Why did you do that yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s liking something/someone. It’s often followed by “de” + noun/verb: “Por que você gosta de café forte?” (“Why do you like strong coffee?”). If you’re asking about a specific person/object, you can add a pronoun after: “por que você gosta dela/dele/disso” (“why do you like her/him/that”). As an indirect question after another phrase, it stays the same: “Você pode me dizer por que você gosta dela?” (“Can you tell me why you like her?”).
target_language_example: Por que você gosta de morar aqui?
native_language_example: Why do you like living here?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason someone likes something or doing something. "Por que" introduces the question (why), "você" is "you" (informal singular in Brazil), and "gosta de" is "like" but it requires "de" before a noun or a verb in the infinitive (e.g., "gosta de Boston", "gosta de cavalos", "gosta de trabalhar"). In more formal speech you can replace "você" with "o senhor / a senhora".
target_language_example: Por que você gosta de morar aqui?
native_language_example: Why do you like living here?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason someone likes something a lot. Often followed by "de" + a noun/place/person ("Por que você gosta tanto de Boston?") or by "disso/daquilo" ("Por que você gosta tanto disso?"). You can drop "você" in informal conversation: "Por que gosta tanto...?"
target_language_example: Por que você gosta tanto desse filme?
native_language_example: Why do you like this movie so much?

meaning: "why did you/why do you ... me" (asking the reason someone did/does something to you).
additional_notes: Used to start a direct question: por que = why; você = you; me = me (object pronoun). You normally add a verb right after: "Por que você me acordou?" (Why did you wake me up?). In questions, "por que" is commonly written as two words. Word order is usually: Por que + você + me + verb.
target_language_example: Por que você me ajudou ontem?
native_language_example: Why did you help me yesterday?

meaning: "why don’t you…?" / "why didn’t you…?" (a suggestion or asking for a reason).
additional_notes: Used to (1) suggest an action: “Por que você não vem comigo?” = “Why don’t you come with me?”, or (2) ask why something didn’t happen in the past: “Por que você não me contou?” = “Why didn’t you tell me?”. The verb form after it shows whether it’s present (não vem) or past (não veio). Can sound neutral or accusatory depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Por que você não me ajuda com isso?
native_language_example: Why don’t you help me with this?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason someone needs something or needs to do something. Often followed by a noun ("Por que você precisa desta informação?") or an infinitive verb ("Por que você precisa fazer isso?"). In indirect questions, it can appear as "por que" after another verb: "Preciso saber por que você precisa disso."
target_language_example: Por que você precisa de ajuda agora?
native_language_example: Why do you need help now?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason someone needs an object, person, or service. After "precisar", Portuguese normally uses "de" before a noun or pronoun: "preciso de troco", "precisa de um médico", "precisa de minha permissão". Often followed by a noun phrase (e.g., "de tantas roupas").
target_language_example: Por que você precisa de ajuda agora?
native_language_example: Why do you need help now?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s desire/decision. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb: “Por que você quer + verb” (e.g., estudar, morar, ir). In questions, it’s usually written “por que” (two words). “Você” is common in Brazilian Portuguese; with “tu,” you’d often say “Por que tu quer…” (or in some regions “Por que tu queres…”).
target_language_example: Por que você quer trocar de emprego?
native_language_example: Why do you want to change jobs?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s reason for wanting to become something (a job/role) or to have something happen to them (passive voice with “ser”, e.g., “ser apresentado” = “to be introduced”). Often followed by a profession (“médico”, “enfermeira/o”) or a past participle (“apresentado/a”).
target_language_example: Por que você quer ser professor(a)?
native_language_example: Why do you want to be a teacher?

meaning: “Why did you…?” (used before a reflexive verb with se).
additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason. It’s typically followed by a reflexive verb, where se matches você (e.g., se divorciou = “got divorced”, se escondeu = “hid”). In writing, it’s usually followed by the verb right away: “Por que você se mudou?”
target_language_example: Por que você se atrasou hoje?
native_language_example: Why were you late today?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for a repeated or habitual action by the person you’re talking to. Structure: por que (why) + você (you) + sempre (always) + verb. In writing, question form is usually "Por que" (two words) at the start of a question. Often sounds annoyed or complaining depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Por que você sempre chega atrasado?
native_language_example: Why do you always arrive late?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone possessing something or having a certain feeling/state. "Por que" = “why” in questions, "você" = “you,” and "tem" (from "ter") = “have.” Often followed by a noun ("por que você tem dois carros?") or by an expression like "medo de..." (“fear of...”).
target_language_example: Por que você tem tanta pressa?
native_language_example: Why are you in such a hurry?

meaning: “why did you come?” / “why have you come?”
additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s arrival. Often followed by a place (“ao Japão”, “à Coreia”, “para a Malásia”) or by a time-related detail (“tão cedo” = “so early”). In casual speech, people may also say “Por que você veio aqui?” (“Why did you come here?”).
target_language_example: Por que você veio tão cedo hoje?
native_language_example: Why did you come so early today?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone having a strong quality or behaving in a certain way. You usually follow it with an adjective (feio = ugly, malvado = mean/evil, pessimista = pessimistic). In writing, the question form here is typically “por que” (two words).
target_language_example: Por que você é tão nervoso hoje?
native_language_example: Why are you so nervous today?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason, addressing more than one person. In questions, it’s usually written as two words: **por que** (“why”). **Vocês** means “you” plural in Brazilian Portuguese (often used in both formal and informal situations). The verb form that follows is typically 3rd-person plural (e.g., **vocês disseram**, **vocês fugiram**).
target_language_example: Por que vocês chegaram tão tarde?
native_language_example: Why did you all arrive so late?

additional_notes: Used to begin a question asking the reason for what a group of people is doing or how they are. "Vocês" is "you" plural (common in Brazil). After "estão" you typically add a verb in the -ndo form (gerund) for an action happening now (e.g., "fazendo", "esperando") or an adjective/state (e.g., "tristes", "nervosos"). Often written without an accent as "por que" in questions; "por quê" can appear at the end of a question.
target_language_example: Por que vocês estão esperando aqui?
native_language_example: Why are you all waiting here?

meaning: "Why are you (plural) …ing me" / "Why are you (plural) …ing to me".
additional_notes: Used to start a question asking the reason for what a group of people (vocês = you all) is currently doing to you. The structure is: "Por que" + "vocês estão" (you all are, right now) + "me" (me) + a verb (often in the -ando/-endo/-indo form, like ajudando, encarando, perseguindo). In questions, "por que" is written as two words.
target_language_example: Por que vocês estão me ignorando?
native_language_example: Why are you all ignoring me?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for a state/feeling of a group of people. Pattern: "Por que vocês estão tão + adjective?" (bravos = angry, felizes = happy, tristes = sad). With quiet, the adjective agrees with the group: quietos (masc./mixed) vs quietas (fem.).
target_language_example: Por que vocês estão tão cansados hoje?
native_language_example: Why are you all so tired today?

additional_notes: Very common in speech to emphasize a 'why' question; often interchangeable with just "por que". It’s typically followed by the verb (e.g., "Por que é que você está...?"). Also appears as "por que é que" or "porque é que" depending on spelling preference/region.
target_language_example: Por que é que você não me contou antes?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you tell me earlier?

additional_notes: Used to express frequency or an amount within one week. Common with numbers and time/quantity words: "X dias/horas/vezes por semana" (X days/hours/times per week).
target_language_example: Eu treino duas vezes por semana.
native_language_example: I work out twice a week.

meaning: by yourself; on your own; by itself.
