additional_notes: Used to say someone does something independently ("Decida/Pense por si mesmo" = don’t rely on others), or that something happens without outside help ("resolveu-se por si mesmo" = it solved itself). It agrees with the subject: por si mesmo (he/you masc.), por si mesma (she/you fem.), por si mesmos/mesmas (they). Often interchangeable with "sozinho(a)" in the “by yourself” sense.
target_language_example: Ele preferiu fazer o trabalho por si mesmo.
native_language_example: He preferred to do the work by himself.

additional_notes: Used after verbs/adjectives of thanks or gratitude (e.g., “agradecer”, “ser grato”) to say what you’re thankful for. It also appears in expressions like “Se não fosse por sua ajuda…” / “Se não tivesse sido por sua ajuda…” (“If it weren’t for your help…”). “Sua” is the formal ‘your’ (often addressing você); with friends people often say “por tua ajuda” (tu) or simply “pela ajuda” (“for the help”).
target_language_example: Muito obrigado por sua ajuda com o relatório.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help with the report.

meaning: because of you; due to you (your fault/credit).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone is the reason something happened. Depending on context and tone, it can be negative (blame: “It’s your fault”) or positive (credit: “Thanks to you”). You can also change it for formality/person: por sua causa (you – formal/singular), por tua causa (you – informal/singular, common in Portugal), por causa dele/dela (because of him/her), por nossa causa (because of us), etc.
target_language_example: Eu consegui este emprego por sua causa.
native_language_example: I got this job because of you.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason for an apology, thanks, forgiveness, etc. It’s commonly followed by a past participle (por ter feito, por ter perdido, por ter avisado) to mean “for having done / because you did.” In everyday speech you may also hear the simpler form with an infinitive: por fazer, por perder, por avisar.
target_language_example: Desculpe por ter chegado atrasado.
native_language_example: Sorry for arriving late.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun (por toda a + noun) to talk about something being spread everywhere in a place ("all over the house") or happening/lasting during an entire period ("throughout my life"). With masculine singular: "por todo o"; feminine plural: "por todas as"; masculine plural: "por todos os".
target_language_example: Temos lojas por toda a cidade.
native_language_example: We have stores all over the city.

additional_notes: Used when thanking someone for everything they did to help you. Often follows words like "obrigado/a" (thank you) or "agradecido/a" (grateful). You can change "sua" to match formality/number: "por toda a tua ajuda" (informal singular), "por toda a ajuda" (more general).
target_language_example: Obrigado por toda a sua ajuda com o relatório.
native_language_example: Thank you for all your help with the report.

additional_notes: Used to say something is in many places, spread around, or easy to find in any location. Very common with verbs like estar/haver/ter (Está/Há/Tem ... por toda parte) and with procurar (procurar ... por toda parte = to search everywhere).
target_language_example: Depois da festa, tinha lixo por toda parte.
native_language_example: After the party, there was trash everywhere.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun (o + noun) to mean something is spread everywhere on/over something (por todo o chão, por todo o corpo) or happens across an entire place/area (por todo o país). In travel contexts it can also mean “all the way (along the whole route)” (por todo o caminho). For feminine nouns, use “por toda a”; for plural, “por todos os / por todas as”.
target_language_example: Fiquei procurando minhas chaves por todo o apartamento.
native_language_example: I kept looking for my keys all over the apartment.

meaning: for three hundred dollars (as the price).
additional_notes: Use por + amount to say the selling/buying price (how much something cost or was sold for). In many situations, por = “for” in the sense of “in exchange for.” (Contrast: para is “to/for (recipient)”, as in 'vendeu para a Mary'.)
target_language_example: Comprei esse celular por trezentos dólares.
native_language_example: I bought this phone for three hundred dollars.

meaning: for three (units); for three (as a price); by three (people).
additional_notes:
“Por” + number is very common and the exact English preposition depends on context: 
- Duration: “por três minutos/dias…” = “for three minutes/days…”
- Price/exchange: “por três milhões (de dólares)” = “for three million (dollars)”
- Passive agent: “foi assaltado por três homens” = “was robbed by three men.”
target_language_example: Espere aqui por três minutos.
native_language_example: Wait here for three minutes.

additional_notes: Used to express the duration of an action or state. Common with the past ("morei..."), with "estar" + state ("estive..."), and with ongoing actions in the present perfect continuous ("venho estudando...", "tem estudado..."). You can swap the number: "por dois anos", "por cinco anos", etc.
target_language_example: Trabalhei nessa empresa por três anos.
native_language_example: I worked at that company for three years.

additional_notes: "Por" + a time period expresses duration (how long something lasts): ficar, esperar, viajar, viver de algo, etc. It answers "Por quanto tempo?" (For how long?).
target_language_example: Vamos viajar por três dias e depois voltar.
native_language_example: We’re going to travel for three days and then come back.

additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasts or how long someone waits/does something. Common pattern: "por + [amount of time]" (por duas horas, por cinco minutos, por um ano).
target_language_example: Fiquei no aeroporto por três horas.
native_language_example: I stayed at the airport for three hours.

additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasts. With verbs like ficar/estar/ter (in some situations), it indicates duration in time. You can swap in other time periods: por dois dias, por uma semana, por seis meses.
target_language_example: Vou ficar aqui por três meses.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay here for three months.

meaning: for having (done something) to him; for having + him.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like desculpar/perdoar to say the reason: por + ter (infinitive) + object pronoun. Here, tê-lo = ter + o (“him/it”) with hyphen and accent when the pronoun attaches to the infinitive. Common variants: por tê-la (her/it), por tê-los (them masc.), por tê-las (them fem.). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese you may also hear: por ter incomodado ele (more colloquial).
target_language_example: Obrigado por tê-lo avisado a tempo.
native_language_example: Thanks for having warned him in time.

additional_notes: This is the preposition **por** + the masculine singular article **um** (“a/an”). Common uses: **passive voice** to show the agent (*Foi destruída por um robô* = “was destroyed by a robot”); **exchange** with *trocar X por um Y* (“trade X for a Y”); **duration** (*por um breve período* = “for a short period”); and after some verbs like *procurar por um...* (“look for a ...”).
target_language_example: O livro foi escrito por um autor brasileiro.
native_language_example: The book was written by a Brazilian author.

meaning: for a moment; for a brief instant.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is needed for a very short time. Common with verbs like hesitar (to hesitate), esperar (to wait), falar (to talk), and usar (to use). In requests, it can sound polite and minimizing: “...por um instante?” = “...for a moment?”.
target_language_example: Espere aqui por um instante, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait here for a moment, please.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a long duration. It can refer to the past ("for a long time"), or—depending on context—to the future ("for a long time"). Often interchangeable with "por muito tempo" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Não te vejo por um longo tempo.
native_language_example: I haven't seen you for a long time.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to do something briefly (wait, come here, listen, talk). In everyday speech it often just means “a moment/briefly,” not exactly 60 seconds.
target_language_example: Espere aqui por um minuto, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait here for a minute, please.

meaning: for a moment; for a short time.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens briefly or temporarily. Common with actions/states like waiting, being quiet, staying, holding/caring for something, etc. It can also be used as a quick apology/interrupting phrase meaning “sorry, just a moment.”
target_language_example: Espere por um momento, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait for a moment, please.

meaning: by lightning; by a lightning bolt.
additional_notes: Used with passive verbs like "ser atingido" (to be struck/hit) or "ser morto" (to be killed) to say the cause was lightning. "Raio" can mean a lightning bolt (not just a 'ray' of light).
target_language_example: O telhado foi atingido por um raio durante a tempestade.
native_language_example: The roof was struck by lightning during the storm.

meaning: for a while; for some time.
additional_notes: Used to say something lasts for a limited period (often temporary), like staying somewhere, resting, or continuing an activity. Very common after verbs (ficar, continuar, descansar).
target_language_example: Vou esperar aqui por um tempo.
native_language_example: I’ll wait here for a while.

additional_notes: Used to give a reason/explanation. "porque" = "because" and "estava chovendo" is the past continuous (imperfect) form meaning "it was raining" (ongoing background situation). Often follows a main clause: "Fiquei em casa porque estava chovendo."
target_language_example: Não fomos ao parque porque estava chovendo.
native_language_example: We didn’t go to the park because it was raining.

meaning: "the door, please" (used when politely asking about the door—e.g., to open it or move away from it).
additional_notes: "Porta" means "door" and "por favor" means "please." You’ll usually hear this as part of a longer request, like "Abra a porta, por favor" (Open the door, please) or "Afastem-se da porta, por favor" (Move away from the door, please). In Portuguese, "por favor" can go at the end of the sentence for a polite tone.
target_language_example: Pode fechar a porta, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you close the door, please?

additional_notes: Used to say that a door is locked (you can’t open it). Often appears as "A porta está trancada" or "Esta/essa porta está trancada". You can add details like "por dentro" (locked from the inside) or "por fora" (locked from the outside). "Trancar" means “to lock; to bolt.”
target_language_example: Não consigo entrar porque a porta está trancada.
native_language_example: I can’t get in because the door is locked.

meaning: “can do / be able to do” (subjunctive: “may be able to do”).
additional_notes: “Possa” is the present subjunctive of “poder” (to be able to / can). It’s commonly used after expressions like “que” (that), “talvez” (maybe), “duvido que” (I doubt that), and in sentences about possibility, doubt, or uncertainty: “algo que eu possa fazer” = “something I can do.”
target_language_example: Não sei se eu possa fazer isso hoje.
native_language_example: I don’t know if I can do that today.

meaning: "can help us" (with "possa" in the subjunctive, often after hopes, doubts, or possibilities).
additional_notes: Used when you’re not stating a fact, but a wish, uncertainty, or possibility. Very common after expressions like "espero que" (I hope that), "talvez" (maybe), and in questions like "você sabe de alguém que..." (do you know someone who...). Literally: "(that he/she/you) may be able to help us."
target_language_example: Espero que você possa nos ajudar com isso.
native_language_example: I hope you can help us with this.

additional_notes: Used to offer help politely. “Posso” = “can I / may I” and “ajudá-la” = “help her / help you (formal, feminine)”. The “-la” refers to a female person and is common in more formal or written Portuguese; in everyday Brazilian Portuguese many people instead say “Posso te ajudar?” or “Posso ajudar você?”. You can add what you’re helping with: “a + infinitive” (posso ajudá-la a encontrar…) or “em algo” (with something).
target_language_example: Boa tarde, posso ajudá-la com alguma coisa?
native_language_example: Good afternoon, can I help you with anything?

meaning: “Can I help you (all)?” (speaking to women / a group including women).
additional_notes: Used to politely offer help. "Posso" = “can I”, "ajudar" = “to help”, and "-las" is an object pronoun meaning “you/them” (feminine plural). It’s common in customer-service situations (e.g., in a store) when addressing two or more women. If you’re addressing men or a mixed group, you’ll often hear "posso ajudá-los"; for one woman: "posso ajudá-la"; for one man: "posso ajudá-lo". Often followed by "a" + infinitive: "posso ajudá-las a encontrar..." (“can I help you find...”).
target_language_example: Boa tarde — posso ajudá-las a escolher um presente?
native_language_example: Good afternoon — can I help you choose a gift?

meaning: “I can help you” / “Can I help you?” (formal “you,” masculine).
additional_notes: Used to offer help or ask how you can help someone. “Posso” = “I can,” “ajudar” = “to help,” and “-lo” means “him/you (formal)” as an object pronoun; in practice it often means “you” when addressing someone with você/o senhor. For a woman, you may hear “posso ajudá-la.”
target_language_example: Posso ajudá-lo com as malas?
native_language_example: Can I help you with the bags?

additional_notes: Used when offering help to more than one person, or as a polite/formal way to address someone (depending on region and context). Literally “I can help you (them)” where posso = “I can” and ajudá-los = “help you (plural)” (help + -los “you/them” masc. plural). Common in customer service: “Em que posso ajudá-los?” = “How can I help you?” You can add what you’re helping with: “a encontrar algo” (to find something), “com seus casacos” (with your coats), “em algo” (with something).
target_language_example: Olá! Posso ajudá-los a escolher um tamanho?
native_language_example: Hi! Can I help you choose a size?

meaning: "I can say" / "Can I say?" (asking or stating permission/ability to speak).
additional_notes: Literally "(I) can say" (poder + dizer). Used either as a question to ask permission to say/tell something (often followed by a clause or "a eles" = "to them"), or as a statement meaning you’re only able/willing to say what you know (e.g., "Só posso dizer..." = "I can only say...").
target_language_example: Posso dizer a verdade agora?
native_language_example: Can I tell the truth now?

meaning: "Can I speak to ...?" / "May I talk to ...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask permission to talk to someone, especially on the phone or when requesting to see someone. It’s polite and common in customer service contexts; you can add "por favor" to be extra polite. Verb pattern: "falar com" (to speak with/to). You then add the person’s name or a pronoun: "com ele/ela" (with him/her).
target_language_example: Olá, posso falar com a gerente, por favor?
native_language_example: Hi, may I speak to the manager, please?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask to speak to someone, especially on the phone or in a formal setting. "Posso" = “may/can I,” "falar" = “to speak,” "com" = “with,” and "o" is the masculine singular “the” (used before male names/titles). For a woman, you usually say: "Posso falar com a …?"
target_language_example: Olá, bom dia. Posso falar com o senhor Carlos, por favor?
native_language_example: Hello, good morning. May I speak with Mr. Carlos, please?

meaning: “Can I talk to you?” / “May I speak with you?”
additional_notes: A polite, very common way to ask to speak with someone. You can add details like time (por um minuto/por um segundo = “for a minute/for a second”), privacy (a sós/em particular = “in private”), place (lá fora = “outside”), language (em inglês = “in English”), or topic (sobre X = “about X”). Often used to start a request that feels a bit serious or personal.
target_language_example: Oi, posso falar com você em particular por um minuto?
native_language_example: Hi, can I talk to you in private for a minute?

meaning: “Can I talk to you (plural)?” / “May I speak with you (plural)?”
additional_notes: Used to ask permission to talk to two or more people (vocês = “you” plural, common in Brazil). Often followed by details like em particular (“in private”), por um minuto/um segundo (“for a minute/second”), or rapidamente (“quickly”). In “Sinto que posso falar com vocês”, it means “I feel like I can talk to you (plural)” in the sense of feeling comfortable opening up.
target_language_example: Oi, posso falar com vocês depois da reunião?
native_language_example: Hi, can I talk to you after the meeting?

additional_notes: From "poder" (to be able to / can) + "fazer" (to do/make). Used to ask for permission or make an offer: "Posso fazer uma pausa?" (permission) / "Posso fazer algo para ajudar?" (offering help). It can also state ability/possibility in context: "Não posso fazer mais." (I can't do any more).
target_language_example: Posso fazer uma pergunta?
native_language_example: Can I ask a question?

meaning: "Can I do that?" / "I can do that."
additional_notes: From the verb phrase "poder" (to be able to / can) + "fazer" (to do/make) + "isso" (that/this). It can be a statement about ability/permission ("I can do that") or a question asking permission/possibility ("Can I do that?"). In speech, you’ll often hear the question with rising intonation: "Posso fazer isso?" You can add "também" (too) or "com você(s)" (with you [pl.]) depending on the situation.
target_language_example: Posso fazer isso agora ou é melhor esperar?
native_language_example: Can I do that now, or is it better to wait?

meaning: “can I do for you?” / “I can do for you.”
additional_notes: Used to offer help or ask how you can assist someone. It often appears in full questions like “O que (mais) posso fazer por você?” (“What else can I do for you?”). In statements, it means “what I can do for you,” as in “Isso é o que eu posso fazer por você.” Uses the verb “poder” (posso = I can) + “fazer” (to do) + “por você” (for you).
target_language_example: Posso fazer por você um café?
native_language_example: Can I make you a coffee?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask permission to do something, especially before a noun like observação (comment), pergunta (question), reserva (reservation/booking), sugestão (suggestion). Often followed by the specific thing: “Posso fazer uma pergunta?” = “Can I ask a question?” You can also use “Posso…” with other verbs (e.g., “Posso falar…?”).
target_language_example: Com licença, posso fazer uma pergunta rápida?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I ask a quick question?

additional_notes: A polite, common way to ask permission before asking something. You can add an adjective after "pergunta" (e.g., "uma pergunta rápida" = a quick question, "uma pergunta idiota" = a stupid/silly question) and you can add who you’re asking with "para você" or "a ela". Often used by itself: "Posso fazer uma pergunta?"
target_language_example: Com licença, posso fazer uma pergunta rápida?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I ask a quick question?

meaning: “I can do it.” / “I’m able to do it.”
additional_notes: Used to say you’re capable of doing something. "posso" = “I can”, "fazer" = “to do/make”, and "-lo" means “it” (referring to something masculine or a general “it”). Often used for reassurance (e.g., “Don’t worry, I can do it myself”) or to offer to handle a task. In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often say "posso fazer" or "eu consigo fazer" instead of the more formal-sounding "fazê-lo".
target_language_example: Se você quiser, posso fazê-lo hoje mesmo.
native_language_example: If you want, I can do it today.

meaning: “can I stay?” / “can I remain?” (also: “can I keep…?” with *ficar com*).
additional_notes: *Posso* = “I can / may I”, *ficar* = “to stay/remain.” Often used to ask permission: *Posso ficar aqui até…?* (“Can I stay here until…?”). With **ficar com + noun/pronoun**, it commonly means “to keep” or “to hold on to”: *Posso ficar com isto?* (“Can I keep this?”). With **ficar com + person**, it can mean “to stay with (someone)”: *Posso ficar com você por um tempo?* (“Can I stay with you for a while?”).
target_language_example: Posso ficar aqui mais um pouco?
native_language_example: Can I stay here a little longer?

additional_notes: Used to ask for permission or possibility to go somewhere or go with someone. It’s the 1st-person singular present of the verb phrase “poder” (to be able to / can) + “ir” (to go). Often followed by “a” + place (posso ir ao cinema?) or “com” + person (posso ir com você/vocês?). In Brazil you may also hear “posso ir em/na…” with places (posso ir na sua casa?).
target_language_example: Posso ir com vocês depois do trabalho?
native_language_example: Can I go with you (all) after work?

additional_notes: "Posso" is the 1st-person singular of "poder" (can/may). "Lhe" is an object pronoun meaning "to you" (formal) or "to him/her" depending on context; in these examples it’s a polite "to you". Common in customer-service/polite requests: "Em que posso lhe ajudar?" (How can I help you?), "Posso lhe pedir...?" (Can I ask you...?).
target_language_example: Posso lhe mostrar o caminho.
native_language_example: Can I show you the way?

additional_notes: Used to ask permission. With an object, it often means “Can I take/grab…?” In requests to borrow, it commonly appears as “posso pegar … emprestado/a?” (“Can I borrow …?”). In “posso pegar isso de volta?”, it means “Can I get/take that back?”.
target_language_example: Posso pegar este livro por um minuto?
native_language_example: Can I take this book for a minute?

additional_notes: Used to ask permission to take/get one item (often understood from context). With "pegar" it can mean take/grab (a napkin, a piece of cake), get/catch (a bus), or borrow (money) depending on what comes next.
target_language_example: Posso pegar um copo d’água?
native_language_example: Can I get a glass of water?

meaning: “Can I … (for you)?” / “I can … you …” (usually followed by a verb).
additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese before another verb + a pronoun: “Posso te ajudar?” = “Can I help you?” Here, “posso” = “I can / may I”, and “te” = “you” (object pronoun). In more formal or European Portuguese you may see “posso ajudá-lo(a)?” or “posso-te ajudar?” (with a hyphen).
target_language_example: Posso te ajudar com isso?
native_language_example: Can I help you with that?

meaning: “Can I help you?” / “I can help you.”
additional_notes: Common offer of help. Literally “(I) can help you.” In questions it often means “Can I help you?” or “May I help you?”, especially in customer service: “Posso te ajudar com…?” The pronoun “te” is informal (used with você/tu in Brazil); more formal alternatives include “Posso ajudá-lo/ajudá-la?” or “Posso ajudar você?”
target_language_example: Oi! Posso te ajudar a encontrar o seu pedido?
native_language_example: Hi! Can I help you find your order?

meaning: "Can I give you…?" / "I can give you…"
additional_notes: Literally “(I) can give you.” Used to offer or ask permission to give something (an object, time, help, information) or something more abstract like a hug or a kiss. In speech you may also hear it as “posso lhe dar” (more formal) or “posso dar pra você” (more explicit). The object usually comes right after: “Posso te dar um abraço?”
target_language_example: Posso te dar uma ajuda com isso?
native_language_example: Can I help you with that?

additional_notes: Used to offer to teach someone how to do an action. It’s built from posso (“I can”), te (“you” informal object pronoun), ensinar (“to teach”), and a + infinitive verb (e.g., a cantar, a cozinhar). You can also say: posso ensinar você a … (a bit more explicit), or (polite): posso lhe ensinar a … / posso te ensinar a …? as a question.
target_language_example: Posso te ensinar a falar português bem rápido.
native_language_example: I can teach you to speak Portuguese really fast.

meaning: “Can I call you?” / “May I give you a call?”
additional_notes: Used to ask permission to phone someone. Very common in everyday conversation; you can add a time like “mais tarde” (later), “amanhã” (tomorrow), or “uma hora dessas” (one of these days/sometime). “Te” = “you” (informal, singular), so with more formal “you” you’d say “Posso ligar para você?” or “Posso te ligar?” depending on region.
target_language_example: Posso te ligar mais tarde, depois do trabalho?
native_language_example: Can I call you later, after work?

additional_notes: Used to ask permission to take a photo. You can add context like “aqui” (here) or specify the person: “Posso tirar uma foto sua?” / “...tua?” = “Can I take a photo of you?” (“sua” is common in Brazil; “tua” is used in some regions and often with “tu”.) You can also say “uma foto de você” (of you).
target_language_example: Com licença, posso tirar uma foto aqui?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I take a photo here?

additional_notes: Used to ask permission to use something. "posso" is the 1st-person singular of "poder" (to be able to / can) and "usar" means "to use." You can follow it with an object ("Posso usar isto?"), or add time words like "por um instante" (for a moment). For a more polite version, you can say "Posso usar o seu…?" or "Eu posso usar…?"
target_language_example: Posso usar a cadeira, por favor?
native_language_example: Can I use the chair, please?

meaning: “Can I use yours?” / “May I use your …?”
additional_notes: Used to ask permission to use something that belongs to the person you’re speaking to. Usually followed by a noun: “Posso usar o seu computador?” (your computer), “Posso usar o seu banheiro?” (your bathroom). “o seu / a sua” agrees with the noun’s gender (o = masculine, a = feminine). In Brazil, “banheiro” commonly means “bathroom/restroom.”
target_language_example: Posso usar o seu carregador por um minuto?
native_language_example: Can I use your charger for a minute?

additional_notes: From "poder" (to be able to/can) + "ver" (to see). Used to ask permission to look at something (common in service situations: documents, tickets), or to say you’re able to see something. You’ll often add an object ("posso ver seu passaporte?") or an activity ("posso ver televisão?").
target_language_example: Posso ver o seu bilhete, por favor?
native_language_example: Can I see your ticket, please?

meaning: "Can I see him/it?" or "May I see you?" (formal).
additional_notes: Used to ask for permission or possibility of seeing someone/something. "vê-lo" = "ver" (to see) + the object pronoun "-lo" attached with a hyphen. "-lo" usually means "him" or "it", and can also mean "you" in formal address (replacing "o senhor/a senhora"). Common in questions like "Posso vê-lo?" and "Quando posso vê-lo?"
target_language_example: Posso vê-lo agora ou só amanhã?
native_language_example: Can I see him now, or only tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to say that only a small number of people do something or exist in a place. It’s the feminine plural form of “pouco” because “pessoas” is feminine. Often contrasted with “muitas pessoas” (many people).
target_language_example: Poucas pessoas entendem essa regra no começo.
native_language_example: Few people understand that rule at first.

meaning: a short time; not much time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a brief duration. Often appears with "por" (for) to mean "for a short time" ("por pouco tempo"), or with "em" (in) to mean "in a short time" / "quickly" ("em pouco tempo"). Can be intensified as "muito pouco tempo" (very little time).
target_language_example: Vou precisar de pouco tempo para terminar isso.
native_language_example: I’ll need only a short time to finish this.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to say you have/want/need a small quantity of something. It commonly appears as "um pouco de" (a little of) or "pouco de" after words like "há" (there is/are).
target_language_example: Você pode me dar um pouco de água, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little water, please?

additional_notes: Very common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese. Used after verbs to show the receiver/benefit or direction: explicar pra mim (explain to me), fazer pra mim (do for me), olhar pra mim (look at me), é pra mim (it’s for me). Note: with a subject pronoun before a verb, people often say 'pra eu' (Pra eu fazer isso...), not 'pra mim' + verb.
target_language_example: Você pode mandar a foto pra mim?
native_language_example: Can you send the photo to me?

additional_notes: Common informal form of “para você”. Used to indicate the person who receives something, is affected by something, or who something is done for. In some contexts it can sound like “as far as you’re concerned” (e.g., “Acabou pra você.” = “It’s over for you.”).
target_language_example: Comprei um presente pra você.
native_language_example: I bought a present for you.

meaning: “Nice to meet you.” (formal, said to a man)
additional_notes: Used when meeting someone for the first time or in introductions. It’s more formal/polite than just “prazer”. The “-lo” means “you (him)”, referring to a male person you’re addressing; for a woman, say “prazer conhecê-la”. You’ll also hear it with “foi/é um prazer conhecê-lo” (“It was/is a pleasure to meet you”) and with intensifiers like “grande” (“a great pleasure”).
target_language_example: Olá, senhor Almeida. Prazer conhecê-lo.
native_language_example: Hello, Mr. Almeida. Nice to meet you.

meaning: “Nice to meet you.” (to a man, formal/polite)
additional_notes: Used when being introduced or meeting someone for the first time. Literally “a pleasure to meet you.” The ending “-lo” refers to “you” (him) as a direct object in formal Brazilian Portuguese; to a woman you can say “prazer em conhecê-la.” A common shorter option is just “Prazer!”
target_language_example: Prazer em conhecê-lo, senhor Silva.
native_language_example: Nice to meet you, Mr. Silva.

additional_notes: Used with a person/thing + precisar de + noun/pronoun to say someone needs something: “Eu preciso de ajuda.” In the negative, “não precisa de” = “doesn’t need (it).” In everyday speech, “precisar de” can also be used like “to have to,” but then it’s followed by an infinitive (without “de”): “Preciso estudar.”
target_language_example: Você precisa de alguma coisa?
native_language_example: Do you need anything?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "precisar de" + noun to say someone needs something. It’s often followed by a time word like "agora" (now). You can change the subject: "Eu preciso de ajuda" (I need help), "Você precisa de ajuda?" (Do you need help?).
target_language_example: Você precisa de ajuda com isso?
native_language_example: Do you need help with that?

additional_notes: Used with the verb precisar de (“to need”) plus mais (“more”). It’s usually followed by a noun: precisa de mais água/sal (“needs more water/salt”). Sometimes the noun is implied from context: Ninguém precisa de mais. Note: precisa looks like English “precise,” but here it means “(he/she/it) needs.”
target_language_example: Este projeto precisa de mais tempo.
native_language_example: This project needs more time.

additional_notes: From the verb "precisar de" (to need). It’s used to say someone needs your help, presence, or something you can provide. Often appears in questions like "Você precisa de mim?" (Do you need me?). In Portuguese, "precisar" typically takes "de" before the thing/person needed: "precisa de + noun/pronoun".
target_language_example: Se você precisar de mim, é só ligar.
native_language_example: If you need me, just call.

additional_notes: Used with the verb precisar de (“to need”) + the preposition de + the masculine singular indefinite article um. The thing needed comes right after: precisa de um casaco (“needs a coat”). With você/ele/ela it’s precisa; with eu it’s preciso; with nós it’s precisamos. For feminine nouns, use precisa de uma (e.g., precisa de uma ajuda).
target_language_example: Ele precisa de um médico agora.
native_language_example: He needs a doctor now.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun: precisa de um novo + noun (e.g., gerente, teclado). For feminine nouns, use “precisa de uma nova …” (e.g., uma nova ideia). “Precisar de” = “to need” (and it takes “de”).
target_language_example: Meu computador precisa de um novo teclado.
native_language_example: My computer needs a new keyboard.

additional_notes: Used when someone requires a medical transplant. The verb is usually in the form “(ele/ela) precisa de…” + “um transplante de” + the organ (rim/kidney, coração/heart, fígado/liver). You can change the subject and tense: “Eu preciso…”, “Ele vai precisar…”.
target_language_example: Ela precisa de um transplante de medula óssea.
native_language_example: She needs a bone marrow transplant.

additional_notes: From the verb "precisar" (“to need”). It’s followed by "de" + a noun: "precisa de uma" + feminine singular noun (e.g., "uma mão", "uma pintura"). With a masculine noun you use "precisa de um" ("Ele precisa de um carro"). In speech/writing you may also see "precisa de" without an article in some cases (e.g., "precisa de ajuda").
target_language_example: Ela precisa de uma ajuda com a tarefa.
native_language_example: She needs some help with the homework.

additional_notes: Used with a subject (often ele/ela/você/a gente) to say something is necessary: "(alguém) precisa fazer (algo)". In questions it often means “Does someone really have to…?” (e.g., "Será que alguém precisa fazer tanto barulho?"). You can also use it with "o que" to mean “what (someone) needs to do”: "o que ele precisa fazer".
target_language_example: Eu não sei o que eu preciso fazer agora.
native_language_example: I don’t know what I need to do now.

meaning: (he/she/you) needs to do that/this; has to do that/this.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has a necessity or obligation to do something. "precisa" is the present tense of "precisar" (to need), and "fazer isso" means "to do that/this" (isso usually refers to something already mentioned). You can change the subject: "Eu preciso fazer isso" (I need to do this), "Ela precisa fazer isso" (She needs to do this). In questions, it often expresses doubt or checking: "Você acha que... precisa...?" = "Do you think ... needs to...?"
target_language_example: Eu preciso fazer isso hoje.
native_language_example: I need to do this today.

additional_notes: Used to say something is necessary or required. It’s from "precisar" (to need) + "ser" (to be). Often followed by a past participle to express passive meaning ("precisa ser consertado" = "needs to be fixed") or by an adjective/noun ("precisa ser prudente" = "needs to be careful"). It can also be used without an explicit subject, meaning "it needs to be...".
target_language_example: Precisa ser hoje, senão vai ficar tarde demais.
native_language_example: It has to be today, otherwise it’ll be too late.

additional_notes: Impersonal phrase used to say that something must be done, without saying who will do it. Very common in to-do lists and instructions: “o que precisa ser feito” = “what needs to be done.” Often used with time words like “imediatamente” (immediately) or “hoje” (today).
target_language_example: Ainda há muito que precisa ser feito antes da reunião.
native_language_example: There’s still a lot that needs to be done before the meeting.

additional_notes: "Precisam" is the 3rd person plural of "precisar" (eles/elas/vocês precisam). It is usually followed by "de" + a noun or pronoun: "precisam de amor", "precisam de você". In questions, it can be used alone as "Precisam de...?" (= Do you/they need ...?).
target_language_example: Vocês precisam de ajuda?
native_language_example: Do you need help?

additional_notes: Used to say that a conversation is necessary, often about something important or possibly serious. You can add a topic with "sobre" (e.g., "precisamos conversar sobre isso"). In direct situations, it can also imply “we need to talk (about a problem).”
target_language_example: Precisamos conversar sobre o que aconteceu ontem.
native_language_example: We need to talk about what happened yesterday.

additional_notes: "Precisamos" is the "we" form of the verb "precisar" (to need). It is typically followed by "de" + a noun/pronoun: "precisamos de ajuda" (we need help), "precisamos de você" (we need you).
target_language_example: Precisamos de mais tempo para terminar o trabalho.
native_language_example: We need more time to finish the work.

additional_notes: Used to say your group ("we") needs a greater quantity/number of something: "precisamos" = "we need" and "de" is used before the thing needed. Put the item after it (e.g., "mais tempo", "mais café", "mais voluntários"). In Portuguese you normally say "precisar de" + noun/infinitive.
target_language_example: Precisamos de mais tempo para terminar isso hoje.
native_language_example: We need more time to finish this today.

additional_notes: Used to say the group would benefit from having more people with the same qualities as the person named next (often as a compliment). It’s built from: precisamos de (“we need”) + mais pessoas (“more people”) + como (“like/as”). Often followed by você/ele/ela or a name: “Precisamos de mais pessoas como você.”
target_language_example: Precisamos de mais pessoas como você aqui.
native_language_example: We need more people like you here.

additional_notes: Used to say you (we) need something: precisar de + noun. Use “um” with masculine singular nouns (um contrato, um tradutor). For feminine singular, use “precisamos de uma …” (uma sala). In many situations you can also say “precisamos de + [noun]” without the article, especially with general/abstract things (e.g., “precisamos de tempo”).
target_language_example: Precisamos de um médico agora.
native_language_example: We need a doctor now.

additional_notes: Common way to say you (as a group) need to figure out what to do. Uses the verb pattern "precisar de" + noun ("to need" + something): "precisamos de" = "we need". Often intensified with "e rápido!" ("and fast!") or modified with adjectives: "um plano melhor" ("a better plan").
target_language_example: Antes de começar, precisamos de um plano.
native_language_example: Before we start, we need a plan.

additional_notes: Used to say that you/your group needs something. "Precisamos" = "we need"; "de" is required after "precisar"; "uma" is the feminine form of "a" (use "um" for masculine nouns: "precisamos de um carro"). Often followed by a noun or noun phrase: "precisamos de uma escada/mesa/senha".
target_language_example: Precisamos de uma resposta até amanhã.
native_language_example: We need an answer by tomorrow.

additional_notes: From the verb "precisar" (to need). Used with "de" before a noun or an infinitive: "precisando de ajuda" (needing help), "precisando de dormir" (needing to sleep). Very common in questions to offer help or check if someone needs something: "Você está precisando de...?"
target_language_example: Estou precisando de um pouco de tempo para terminar isso.
native_language_example: I need a little time to finish this.

additional_notes: Used before a noun, pronoun, or infinitive phrase: precisar de ajuda (need help), precisar de uma chave (need a key), precisar de alguém para conversar (need someone to talk to). Often appears in the conditional/future: Se você precisar de..., me avise (If you need..., let me know). Don’t drop the preposition: it’s usually "precisar de" (not *precisar algo*).
target_language_example: Se você precisar de mais tempo, podemos terminar amanhã.
native_language_example: If you need more time, we can finish tomorrow.

meaning: "needed" / "was in need of" (imperfect past of "precisar de").
additional_notes: Used to say someone needed something in the past or as an ongoing situation in the past. It’s often followed by a noun or quantity (e.g., mais tempo, uma, um pouco mais de dinheiro). You can also use it in a polite/soft way to explain why something happened: "Eu precisava de..." = "I needed...".
target_language_example: Eu precisava de ajuda ontem, mas ninguém atendeu o telefone.
native_language_example: I needed help yesterday, but no one answered the phone.

additional_notes: "Precisava" is the imperfect past of "precisar" (to need), often used for an ongoing situation in the past. "Precisar de" is followed by a noun (here, "dinheiro"). It can mean needing money in general, not necessarily right at that moment.
target_language_example: Naquela época, eu precisava de dinheiro para pagar o aluguel.
native_language_example: At that time, I needed money to pay the rent.

additional_notes: "Precisava" is the imperfect past of "precisar" (to need), used for an ongoing situation in the past or as background context (not a one-time completed action). "De" is required with "precisar" when it means "to need" + a noun ("precisar de algo" = to need something). You can change the subject: "Eu precisava...", "Ele/Ela precisava...", or omit it when it’s clear from context: "Precisava de mais tempo."
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu precisava de mais tempo para terminar.
native_language_example: Sorry, I needed more time to finish.

meaning: "needed to do that" / "had to do that".
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of precisar (precisava) to talk about a past necessity or obligation. Often appears in indirect questions or reported speech with "se" (whether/if): "Ele perguntou se precisava fazer isso" = "He asked whether he needed to do that." Similar in meaning to "tinha que fazer isso" (had to do that).
target_language_example: Eu precisava fazer isso ontem, mas esqueci.
native_language_example: I needed to do that yesterday, but I forgot.

meaning: “I need to buy” / “I have to buy.”
additional_notes: Used to say you need to purchase something. It’s the verb precisar (to need) + infinitive comprar (to buy). Often followed by the item (preciso comprar uma agenda) or by “mais” (more): preciso comprar mais canetas. You can add “de” for emphasis in Brazilian Portuguese: “Preciso (mesmo) de comprar…”.
target_language_example: Preciso comprar pão e leite hoje.
native_language_example: I need to buy bread and milk today.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone formally/politely for help. "Preciso" = “I need”; "da" = “of the” (de + a); "sua ajuda" = “your help” (formal your). With friends you’ll often hear "preciso da tua/da sua ajuda" or in Brazil "preciso da sua ajuda" / "preciso da sua ajuda, cara" (“dude”).
target_language_example: Desculpe, preciso da sua ajuda com este formulário.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need your help with this form.

additional_notes: Used with a noun or noun phrase: "Preciso de tempo" = "I need time." In European Portuguese it can also be followed by an infinitive with "de": "Preciso de falar" = "I need to talk." (In Brazilian Portuguese, "preciso falar" is more common.) Note: "preciso" looks like English "precise" but here it means "(I) need."
target_language_example: Preciso de ajuda com isto.
native_language_example: I need help with this.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or state that you need assistance. It comes from "precisar de" (to need) + "ajuda" (help). You can add details with "com" to say what you need help with (e.g., "Preciso de ajuda com..."), or add a place like "aqui" (here). You can also change the subject: "Você precisa de ajuda?" (Do you need help?), "Ele/Ela precisa de ajuda" (He/She needs help).
target_language_example: Desculpe, preciso de ajuda para encontrar este endereço.
native_language_example: Sorry, I need help finding this address.

additional_notes: Used to say you need a greater quantity of something. It’s often followed by a noun: "Preciso de mais água." You can also add a number or amount: "Preciso de mais dois minutos." (Literally "I need of more" in Portuguese, but the natural English translation is "I need more").
target_language_example: Desculpe, não consigo terminar hoje; preciso de mais tempo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t finish today; I need more time.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "precisar de" + an indefinite article. "Um" is for masculine singular nouns; for feminine use "preciso de uma" (e.g., "Preciso de uma ajuda"). In natural Portuguese, with uncountable nouns you often drop the article: "Preciso de dinheiro" (more natural than "Preciso de um dinheiro"). You can also use it before an infinitive with "um" + noun phrase: "Preciso de um tempo para relaxar."
target_language_example: Estou com dor de cabeça; preciso de um remédio.
native_language_example: I have a headache; I need a medicine.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun to say you need something: preciso de uma + noun (e.g., uma bolsa, uma mudança). For masculine nouns, use “preciso de um”. You can drop “eu” because it’s often implied: “Preciso de uma…”.
target_language_example: Preciso de uma ajuda com isso.
native_language_example: I need some help with this.

additional_notes: Used to say you need to speak with someone. Add the person after “com”: preciso falar com ele/ela/você; preciso falar com o/a (name). You can also add when/conditions: “Preciso falar com ele quando…”
target_language_example: Preciso falar com você agora.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you now.

additional_notes: Used to say you need to speak with a specific male person. Structure: "Preciso falar com o + [man’s name/title]". You can add time/urgency words like "agora mesmo" (right now) or "a sós/em particular" (alone/in private). For a woman, use "preciso falar com a ...".
target_language_example: Preciso falar com o gerente agora mesmo.
native_language_example: I need to talk to the manager right now.

additional_notes: Used to say you have something important or necessary to discuss with someone. You can add details like a sós / em particular (“in private”), agora (“now”), mais tarde (“later”), or sobre X (“about X”). In Brazilian Portuguese, você is common; in European Portuguese you may hear preciso falar contigo.
target_language_example: Preciso falar com você sobre o trabalho depois da reunião.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you about work after the meeting.

meaning: “I need to do” / “I have to do”.
additional_notes: Used to say you must do something. It’s formed by preciso (“I need”) + fazer (“to do/make”). Often followed by a noun (preciso fazer uma ligação/uma cópia) or by an infinitive phrase (preciso fazer algo antes de...).
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu preciso fazer isso hoje.
native_language_example: Sorry, I need to do this today.

meaning: "I need to do this" / "I have to do this."
additional_notes: "Preciso" is the 1st-person singular of the verb "precisar" (to need). It’s commonly followed by an infinitive: "preciso + fazer" (I need to do). "Isso" means "this/that" (the thing you’re talking about). Often used inside longer sentences after verbs like "achar" (to think) or "dizer" (to say): "Ele acha que preciso fazer isso" (He thinks I need to do this).
target_language_example: Não gosto, mas preciso fazer isso hoje.
native_language_example: I don’t like it, but I need to do this today.

additional_notes:
Used to say you have to repeat an action. 
- preciso = “I need” (from precisar)
- fazer = “to do/make”
- isso = “this/that” (near the speaker)
- outra vez = “again / one more time”
Often appears in questions with achar (“to think”): “Você acha que preciso fazer isso outra vez?” = “Do you think I need to do this again?” You can swap “isso” for a specific task: “preciso fazer o exercício outra vez.”
target_language_example: Acho que preciso fazer isso outra vez para entender melhor.
native_language_example: I think I need to do this again to understand better.

meaning: I need to go / I have to go.
additional_notes: Used to say you must leave or go somewhere, often because of an obligation or necessity. It can be followed by a destination with "a" (often with "ao/à": "preciso ir ao dentista") or "para" (often shortened in speech to "pra": "preciso ir pra casa"). It can also be followed directly by an activity: "preciso ir trabalhar". By itself ("Preciso ir."), it commonly means "I need to leave."
target_language_example: Desculpa, preciso ir agora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go now.

additional_notes: Used to ask or insist that someone does something. After "preciso que você", Portuguese normally uses the present subjunctive: "preciso que você continue/ajude/me dê/pare/quebre". It can sound direct; to soften it, add "por favor" or use "eu queria que você...".
target_language_example: Preciso que você chegue cedo amanhã, por favor.
native_language_example: I need you to arrive early tomorrow, please.

additional_notes: Used to say you require information, often before you can decide or act. Typically followed by a question word or clause: "preciso saber se..." (I need to know if...), "preciso saber que..." (I need to know that...), or a direct object like "preciso saber seu nome" (I need to know your name). "Preciso" is from the verb "precisar" (to need), and the subject "eu" (I) is usually implied.
target_language_example: Preciso saber a que horas você chega.
native_language_example: I need to know what time you arrive.

additional_notes: Used to say you must find out a place/location. It’s typically followed by a clause with a verb: “Preciso saber onde fica…”, “Preciso saber onde você mora”, “Preciso saber onde colocar isto.” You can change the person/tense: “Você precisa saber onde…”, “Eu precisava saber onde…”.
target_language_example: Preciso saber onde fica a estação de metrô.
native_language_example: I need to know where the subway station is.

additional_notes: Used when asking someone to complete a form by writing the required information. Common in offices, schools, websites, and applications. Word order can vary slightly (e.g., “preencher esse/este formulário, por favor”). “Preencher” = “to fill in/out”; “formulário” = “form”.
target_language_example: Por favor, preencha este formulário com seus dados pessoais.
native_language_example: Please fill out this form with your personal information.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **preencher** (“to fill out”). Used to say someone has completed a form; often with **já** (“already”) or **ainda não** (“not yet”). In questions, it asks whether the form has been filled out.
target_language_example: Você já preencheu o formulário online?
native_language_example: Have you already filled out the online form?

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar/ficar to describe someone’s current state of worry or concern about a person, thing, or situation: estar preocupado com + noun/pronoun/infinitive. Often followed by alguma coisa (“something”) or alguém (“someone”).
target_language_example: Estou preocupado com a prova de amanhã.
native_language_example: I'm worried about tomorrow's test.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar (or estava) to describe an action in progress: “está/estava preparando o jantar” = “is/was preparing dinner.” You can add time words like “agora” (now) or “neste momento” (right now), and place words like “na cozinha” (in the kitchen).
target_language_example: Estou preparando o jantar agora, então não posso atender o telefone.
native_language_example: I'm preparing dinner now, so I can't answer the phone.

additional_notes: Imperative form of the reflexive verb preparar-se (to prepare oneself). Often used to warn or set expectations about what’s coming next (e.g., prepare-se para o pior, para uma surpresa), or to tell someone to get ready to do something (prepare-se para partir). In writing, the hyphen connects the verb to the object pronoun: prepare-se.
target_language_example: Prepare-se para a reunião de amanhã.
native_language_example: Get ready for tomorrow’s meeting.

additional_notes: Used for a gift given for someone’s birthday. Very common with verbs like dar (to give), ganhar/receber (to get/receive), comprar (to buy), and pedir (to ask). You can also shorten it to presente for “gift/present” when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Qual presente de aniversário você quer este ano?
native_language_example: What birthday present do you want this year?

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "estar" to describe what someone is doing right now: "estou/ele está prestando atenção". It’s also common with "prestar atenção em" or "prestar atenção a" (to pay attention to someone/something). Negative form: "não estava prestando atenção" (wasn’t paying attention).
target_language_example: Você está prestando atenção no que eu estou dizendo?
native_language_example: Are you paying attention to what I’m saying?

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they should focus more on something. It’s often followed by “a/ao/à/às” + the thing you should focus on: “prestar mais atenção à aula” (to class), “prestar mais atenção ao que eu digo” (to what I say). You can also use it on its own as advice or a warning: “Você precisa prestar mais atenção.”
target_language_example: Preste mais atenção ao trânsito ao atravessar a rua.
native_language_example: Pay more attention to traffic when crossing the street.

meaning: “pay attention” / “pay attention to …” (formal or polite command).
additional_notes: This is the imperative form (você) of **prestar atenção** (“to pay attention”). It’s common with **por favor** to sound more polite. Use **preste atenção a + person/thing** (often **preste atenção nele/nela** = “pay attention to him/her”).
target_language_example: Preste atenção ao que o professor está dizendo.
native_language_example: Pay attention to what the teacher is saying.

additional_notes: Imperative form used to address a group (you all). Often used alone as a warning or to get people to focus. It’s commonly followed by a preposition: **prestar atenção a** alguém/algo (“pay attention to someone/something”); in Brazil you may also hear **prestar atenção em/no/na** with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Pessoal, prestem atenção ao que o professor está dizendo.
native_language_example: Guys, pay attention to what the teacher is saying.

meaning: about to leave / about to depart.
additional_notes: Used with the verb estar: (estar) prestes a + infinitive = “to be about to” do something. Here, partir means “to leave” or “to depart” (people: leave; trains/buses: depart). Common in time-sensitive situations (e.g., a train/bus is about to depart).
target_language_example: Desculpe, estou prestes a partir — falamos mais tarde.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m about to leave — we’ll talk later.

meaning: about to leave; just about to go out.
additional_notes: Used with the verb estar (or similar) to say something is going to happen very soon: estar prestes a + infinitive. Here, sair means “to leave / to go out,” and it’s often followed by extra detail (e.g., sair correndo = “run out”). Very common with interruptions: “Eu estava prestes a sair quando…” (“I was just about to leave when…”).
target_language_example: Eu estava prestes a sair, mas você me ligou.
native_language_example: I was about to leave, but you called me.

additional_notes: Past tense of the set phrase “prestar atenção” (“to pay attention / to notice”). It often takes a preposition: prestar atenção em/no/na (“pay attention to” something) or prestar atenção em/a alguém (“pay attention to” someone).
target_language_example: Você prestou atenção no que eu disse?
native_language_example: Did you pay attention to what I said?

additional_notes: Used before a school subject, language, or area to say what someone teaches (or who teaches that subject). In Brazil, "professor" is commonly used for school teachers as well as professors. With subjects/languages, it’s usually "professor de + [subject]" (e.g., professor de francês, professor de artes).
target_language_example: Ela é professora de matemática.
native_language_example: She is a math teacher.

additional_notes: Used for someone who teaches the French language (at school, a course, etc.). In Brazilian Portuguese, "professor" is used for teachers in general; "de francês" specifies the subject. For a woman, you’ll often hear "professora de francês". You can also say "meu/minha professor(a) de francês" (my French teacher).
target_language_example: Minha professora de francês é muito paciente.
native_language_example: My French teacher is very patient.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a teacher who teaches the English language. In Portuguese, "professor" can mean a school teacher (not necessarily a university professor). You can change the subject (meu/minha, seu/sua, o/a) to match who you're talking about and the teacher’s gender: "meu professor de inglês" / "minha professora de inglês".
target_language_example: Minha professora de inglês é muito paciente.
native_language_example: My English teacher is very patient.

additional_notes: Used to say someone made a promise to meet another person. Structure: (alguém) prometeu + se encontrar com + (alguém) + (place/time). In everyday speech you may also hear “prometeu encontrar com” (without “se”), but “se encontrar com” is very common and means “to meet up with.”
target_language_example: Ele prometeu se encontrar com a gente depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: He promised to meet up with us after work.

additional_notes: Used with estar (estou/está/estamos...) to say someone is ready. Often followed by a noun (pronto para a tempestade = ready for the storm) or by an infinitive verb (pronto para aceitar = ready to accept). The adjective agrees with the person: pronto (male), pronta (female), prontos/prontas (plural).
target_language_example: Você está pronto para começar?
native_language_example: Are you ready to start?

additional_notes: Used with the plural adjective "prontos" (feminine: "prontas") plus "para". Use it before an infinitive verb: "prontos para fazer" (ready to do), or before a noun: "prontos para a festa" (ready for the party). Often appears with "estar": "estamos/eles estão prontos para...".
target_language_example: Estamos prontos para sair agora.
native_language_example: We’re ready to leave now.

additional_notes: Infinitive + object pronoun. “proteger” = to protect, and “-la” = “her” (direct object). In Portuguese, object pronouns are often attached to the end of the verb with a hyphen. The accent in “protegê-” marks a stressed vowel when the pronoun is attached (compare: “proteger” vs. “protegê-la”).
target_language_example: Vou protegê-la a qualquer custo.
native_language_example: I’ll protect her at any cost.

additional_notes: Infinitive verb + object pronoun: proteger (“to protect”) + -lo (“him/it”). The pronoun attaches with a hyphen, and the verb gets an accent shift: proteger → protegê- before -lo/-la/-los/-las. Common after infinitives (and some other forms).
target_language_example: Vou protegê-lo a qualquer custo.
native_language_example: I’m going to protect him at any cost.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is likely continuing in the same state or place up to now. It’s made of: provavelmente (probably) + ainda (still/yet) + está (is, temporary/state/location). Often followed by an adjective or a location: "provavelmente ainda está confuso" (still confused), "provavelmente ainda está na escola" (still at school).
target_language_example: Ela provavelmente ainda está no trabalho.
native_language_example: She is probably still at work.

additional_notes: Used to say something is likely to happen in the future. It’s “provavelmente” (probably) + “vai” (goes/is going to), often followed by an infinitive verb: “provavelmente vai chegar” (will probably arrive). In everyday speech, it may also appear as “provavelmente vai” or with the subject omitted when it’s clear from context.
target_language_example: A gente provavelmente vai sair mais cedo hoje.
native_language_example: We’ll probably leave earlier today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the Monday of the next week (the upcoming Monday). Common after prepositions like "até" (until/by) and "para" (for/by a deadline): "até a próxima segunda-feira" = by/until next Monday; "para a próxima segunda-feira" = due for next Monday. Often appears as "na próxima segunda-feira" = on next Monday.
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar na próxima segunda-feira às 9h.
native_language_example: We’re going to meet next Monday at 9 a.m.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening in the month after the current one. Often used without an article in casual speech ("próximo mês"), but you can also say "no próximo mês" or "o próximo mês" depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: A gente se vê no próximo mês.
native_language_example: We’ll see each other next month.

additional_notes: A noun for the time when the sun goes down and the sky changes color. Often used with verbs like ver (to see), admirar (to admire), and with adjectives like belo (beautiful).
target_language_example: Vamos ver o pôr-do-sol na praia.
native_language_example: Let’s watch the sunset at the beach.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the time of day when the sun goes down. Often appears with verbs like ver/assistir (to watch/see) and can also refer to the sunset itself (the colors in the sky).
target_language_example: Vamos ver o pôr do sol na praia.
native_language_example: Let’s watch the sunset at the beach.

meaning: 'which are' / 'what are' (used to ask for a list or options).
additional_notes: Usually starts a question asking someone to name specific items (e.g., “Quais são…?” = “What are…?/Which are…?”). It agrees with plural nouns: quais (plural of qual) + são (they are). For singular, you use “qual é?”. Often followed by a noun phrase: “Quais são as opções?”, “Quais são os melhores?”.
target_language_example: Quais são os horários disponíveis?
native_language_example: What times are available?

additional_notes: Used to ask about multiple feminine plural items: "Quais são as alternativas?" = "Which are the alternatives?" Often followed by a feminine plural noun (as alternativas, as chances, as fontes). For masculine plural, use "quais são os"; for singular, "qual é a" (fem.) / "qual é o" (masc.).
target_language_example: Quais são as opções mais baratas?
native_language_example: Which are the cheapest options?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the rules (e.g., of a group, game, place, or situation). Often followed by “do/da/deste/dessa…” to specify whose rules: “Quais são as regras do grupo?” = “What are the group’s rules?” In statements, it can also introduce a clause meaning “which are the rules” (e.g., “Eu sei quais são as regras.” = “I know what the rules are.”).
target_language_example: Antes de começar, quais são as regras?
native_language_example: Before we start, what are the rules?

meaning: “what are your” (asking about someone’s plural noun: impressions, concerns, priorities, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to list or describe their views, concerns, priorities, expectations, etc. It must be followed by a plural noun (often feminine plural because it refers to “as” + a feminine plural noun like impressões/preocupações/prioridades/expectativas). For a masculine plural noun, you’d say “quais são os seus …?”. Often used in polite/professional contexts.
target_language_example: Quais são as suas dúvidas sobre o contrato?
native_language_example: What are your questions/doubts about the contract?

meaning: 'which are the' (asking about plural masculine items).
additional_notes: Used to ask for a list/selection of items: “Which are the …?” It agrees with plural masculine nouns (os limites, os pilares). For plural feminine, use “quais são as”. In speech it often introduces a noun: “Quais são os seus planos?”
target_language_example: Quais são os seus objetivos para este ano?
native_language_example: What are your goals for this year?

additional_notes: Used to ask which ones belong to the person you’re speaking to: “Quais” = “which/what (plural)”, “são” = “are”, “os seus” = “your (plural masculine)”. It’s typically followed by a plural noun (planos, desejos, esportes, hobbies, sonhos). For feminine nouns, you’ll usually hear: “Quais são as suas …?” (e.g., “as suas ideias”). For singular, it changes to “Qual é o seu/a sua …?”
target_language_example: Quais são os seus objetivos para este ano?
native_language_example: What are your goals for this year?

additional_notes: Used when there are exactly two options and you’re asking someone to choose between them. Often followed by a noun (“qual dos dois livros...”), or used alone as a short question (“Qual dos dois?”). It can refer to people or things.
target_language_example: Eu tenho duas camisas: qual das duas você prefere?
native_language_example: I have two shirts: which of the two do you prefer?

meaning: "what was the..." (in the past, with a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask about something in the past. It’s made of: qual (which/what) + era (was) + o (the, masculine). With feminine nouns, use "qual era a" (e.g., "Qual era a sua favorita?"). Common with nouns like "nome", "segredo", "ponto", "sonho".
target_language_example: Qual era o problema?
native_language_example: What was the problem?

meaning: 'what was the name' (asking for a name in the past).
additional_notes: Used to ask (or to remember) someone/something's name when you’re talking about a past situation. Common pattern: "Qual era o nome de..." (someone’s name) or "Qual era o nome do/da..." (the name of a thing/person with a noun). In conversation it can imply you’ve forgotten: "Qual era o nome mesmo?" = "What was the name again?".
target_language_example: Qual era o nome do restaurante onde a gente jantou ontem?
native_language_example: What was the name of the restaurant where we had dinner yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to ask (or report) what the issue was in a past situation. Common in indirect questions after verbs like perguntar (“ask”) and dizer/falar (“tell”), or as a direct question: “Qual era o problema?” Literally: “what was the problem?”.
target_language_example: Eu não entendi qual era o problema com o pedido.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what the problem was with the order.

meaning: “what was the…?” / “which was the…?” (asking about a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask about something in the past, especially for facts, reasons, results, or impressions. It agrees with a feminine noun that follows (e.g., causa, resposta, impressão). For a masculine noun, use “qual foi o…?”; for plural, “quais foram os/as…?”.
target_language_example: Qual foi a sua resposta?
native_language_example: What was your answer?

meaning: 'what was the…?' (asking about something in the past).
additional_notes: Used to ask about a past situation, outcome, or item, usually followed by a noun: "Qual foi o problema?" / "Qual foi o resultado?". It’s the past of "ser" (foi = was). Change to match gender/number: "qual foi a" (feminine), "quais foram os/as" (plural).
target_language_example: Qual foi o motivo da sua viagem?
native_language_example: What was the reason for your trip?

meaning: “what is the…?” (asking which one / what definition, conclusion, relation, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to ask for identification or a specific piece of information about a feminine noun (because of “a”): e.g., a coisa, a conclusão, a definição, a espécie, a graça, a relação, a idade. For masculine nouns, use “qual é o…?”. Often followed by a noun or noun phrase, and commonly used in questions like “Qual é a sua…?” (“What is your…?”).
target_language_example: Qual é a resposta certa?
native_language_example: What is the correct answer?

meaning: “what color is the …?” (asking the color of something masculine).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the color of a masculine singular noun: Qual é a cor do carro? = “What color is the car?” For feminine nouns, use “Qual é a cor da …?” (da casa). With plural nouns: “Qual é a cor dos …?” / “das …?”. In Brazil you may also hear “Que cor é …?” as a shorter alternative.
target_language_example: Qual é a cor do seu casaco?
native_language_example: What color is your coat?

meaning: 'what's the difference between' (used to compare two things).
additional_notes: Used to ask how two people/things/ideas differ. It’s usually followed by two items connected with "e" (and): "Qual é a diferença entre X e Y?" You can also use it in more formal contexts without changing the meaning.
target_language_example: Qual é a diferença entre este plano e aquele?
native_language_example: What’s the difference between this plan and that one?

meaning: “what is the distance” / “how far is it”.
additional_notes: Used to ask how far one place is from another, or how far it is to reach a destination. Common patterns: **Qual é a distância até...** (to/until...), **Qual é a distância de X a Y / de X para Y** (from X to Y), and **Qual é a distância entre X e Y** (between X and Y). It can also ask about a distance someone usually covers (e.g., running).
target_language_example: Qual é a distância daqui até a estação de metrô?
native_language_example: How far is it from here to the subway station?

additional_notes: Used to ask the distance starting from your current location (daqui = “from here”). You can add a destination with “até” or “para”: “Qual é a distância daqui até ali?” (to there), “Qual é a distância daqui para Boston?” (to Boston). Often followed by “ao/à + place” as well: “daqui ao hotel” (from here to the hotel).
target_language_example: Com licença, qual é a distância daqui até a estação?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how far is it from here to the station?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s age. It’s often followed by "de" + person/pronoun (Qual é a idade dela? = How old is she?) or "da/do" + noun/name (Qual é a idade do Tom? = How old is Tom?). More natural in everyday speech is "Quantos anos tem ...?" or "Que idade tem ...?"
target_language_example: Qual é a idade do seu irmão?
native_language_example: How old is your brother?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the number of people living in a place. It’s usually followed by “de/da/do” + place: “Qual é a população da Índia?” (of India), “... de Boston?” (of Boston), “... do país?” (of the country). Often used in questions like “Você sabe qual é a população de...?”
target_language_example: Você sabe qual é a população do Brasil?
native_language_example: Do you know what the population of Brazil is?

meaning: “which one is yours?” / “what is your …?” (addressing someone formally).
additional_notes: Used to ask about something that belongs to the person you’re speaking to, or to ask which item is theirs. It’s the feminine form because it refers to a feminine noun (e.g., banda, caneta, carteira). For masculine nouns, use “Qual é o seu…?”; in informal speech with friends you’ll often hear “Qual é a tua…?”. Often followed by a noun: “Qual é a sua banda favorita?”
target_language_example: Qual é a sua senha do Wi‑Fi?
native_language_example: What’s your Wi‑Fi password?

meaning: "what is your" (asking a question about something belonging to you / your opinion).
additional_notes: Used to ask which one is yours or what your choice/opinion is. It must be followed by a feminine noun (e.g., "desculpa", "fruta", "guitarra", "força", "fraqueza", "resposta", "sugestão"). For masculine nouns, use "qual é o teu" (e.g., "Qual é o teu nome?"). Often implies "which" when there are multiple options (e.g., "Qual é a tua guitarra?" = Which one is your guitar?).
target_language_example: Qual é a tua opinião sobre isto?
native_language_example: What is your opinion about this?

meaning: “what is the…?” (asking which one/what thing it is).
additional_notes: Used to ask for the identity, choice, or value of something: Qual é o truque? (“What’s the trick?”), Qual é o aluguel médio…? (“What’s the average rent…?”). It agrees with the noun that follows: qual é o… (masc. singular), qual é a… (fem. singular), quais são os/as… (plural). Often followed by a noun: qual é o segredo / significado / som.
target_language_example: Qual é o endereço do hotel?
native_language_example: What is the hotel’s address?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the name of a person, place, street, thing, etc. It’s often followed by "de" + noun/pronoun (e.g., "Qual é o nome da rua?", "Qual é o nome dela?"). In speech you may also hear the shorter "Qual o nome...?".
target_language_example: Desculpe, qual é o nome do restaurante?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what’s the name of the restaurant?

meaning: "what is his name?" / "do you know his name?"
additional_notes: Used to ask (or talk about) a male person’s name. Literally “what is the name of him.” Often used as a direct question (Qual é o nome dele?) or inside another sentence after verbs like saber (“to know”): Você sabe qual é o nome dele? For a woman, use qual é o nome dela; for a person you address as “you,” use qual é o seu nome?
target_language_example: Desculpe, qual é o nome dele mesmo?
native_language_example: Sorry, what’s his name again?

additional_notes: Used to ask the name of something you’re pointing to or referring to. Often followed by a masculine noun: “Qual é o nome desse filme/jogo/rios?”. For feminine nouns, use “dessa”: “Qual é o nome dessa música?”. In casual speech, it’s common to shorten to “Qual o nome desse…?”.
target_language_example: Qual é o nome desse restaurante?
native_language_example: What’s the name of this restaurant?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a specific number tied to someone or something (phone number, room number, ID/reference number, etc.). Often followed by “de” + noun (“Qual é o número do quarto?”) or “dela/dele” (“Qual é o número dela?”). In Brazilian Portuguese you’ll also hear “Qual é o número?” on its own when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Com licença, qual é o número do pedido?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is the order number?

additional_notes: A common question to ask what is wrong or why something is an issue. It can be neutral (“What’s the issue?”) or sound confrontational depending on tone (like “So what’s the problem?”). Often used on its own as a complete question. Literally: “which is the problem?”.
target_language_example: Qual é o problema com este computador?
native_language_example: What’s wrong with this computer?

meaning: “what is your…?” (asking for someone’s specific thing, like problem, salary, destination).
additional_notes: Used to ask which specific one applies to the person you’re talking to. It must match the gender/number of the noun that follows: **Qual é o seu** + masculine singular (seu salário), **Qual é a sua** + feminine singular (sua profissão), **Quais são os seus** + masculine plural, **Quais são as suas** + feminine plural. In some contexts it can sound accusatory (e.g., *Qual é o seu problema?* = “What’s your problem?”).
target_language_example: Qual é o seu endereço?
native_language_example: What’s your address?

additional_notes: Common, polite way to ask someone’s name (formal/polite “seu”). You can add words after it for more detail: “nome todo” = full name; “nome real” = real name. In informal speech with friends, you’ll often hear “Qual é o teu nome?” (Portugal) or “Qual é o seu nome?” / “Como você se chama?” (Brazil).
target_language_example: Desculpe, qual é o seu nome?
native_language_example: Sorry, what is your name?

meaning: “what size is it?” / “how big is it?”
additional_notes: Used to ask for the size or dimensions of something. Often followed by "de" or "do/da" + the thing: "Qual é o tamanho deste vestido?" (clothing size) or "Qual é o tamanho da memória...?" (amount/capacity). In some contexts it refers to length/area/overall size rather than a specific measurement unit.
target_language_example: Qual é o tamanho do seu sapato?
native_language_example: What size is your shoe?

additional_notes: Used to ask for information about something that belongs to or is associated with the person you’re talking to. It needs a noun after it (e.g., nome, apelido, tamanho, destino). "Teu" is an informal/regionally common form of "your" (same meaning as "seu" / "teu" vs. "o seu" depending on dialect). With feminine nouns, it becomes "qual é a tua ...?"; with plural, "quais são os teus/as tuas ...?".
target_language_example: Qual é o teu nome completo?
native_language_example: What is your full name?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause describing an unspecified thing (followed by a verb): qualquer coisa que + verb. Often refers to actions or tasks ("anything you do", "whatever you want"). You’ll often see it with the subjunctive when the action is uncertain or general (e.g., "qualquer coisa que eu faça").
target_language_example: Eu topo qualquer coisa que você sugerir.
native_language_example: I’m up for anything you suggest.

additional_notes: Used to mean an unspecified location (it doesn’t matter which). Often appears with "em" ("em qualquer lugar" = "anywhere") or as a standalone option ("Qualquer lugar está bom" = "Anywhere is fine"). You can also use it to exclude a place: "Qualquer lugar, menos aqui" = "Anywhere but here."
target_language_example: Podemos nos encontrar em qualquer lugar perto da estação.
native_language_example: We can meet anywhere near the station.

additional_notes: Used to say that it’s possible for any person (no special skill/permission required), or that anyone is capable of doing something. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., fazer, ler, cometer). You can also hear it with feminine agreement: “qualquer uma pode” (“any woman can” / “anyone can,” referring to a woman).
target_language_example: Com um pouco de prática, qualquer um pode aprender português.
native_language_example: With a little practice, anyone can learn Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time or date of a past event. Very common in the pattern “Quando foi que…?” to add emphasis; it’s still just asking “When was it that…?” Often followed by “a primeira vez que…”, or by a subject + past-tense verb.
target_language_example: Quando foi que você chegou em casa?
native_language_example: When did you get home?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the most recent occasion something happened. It’s typically followed by “que” + a verb: “Quando foi a última vez que você…?” You may also see “em que” in more formal writing, but “que” is most common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Quando foi a última vez que você veio aqui?
native_language_example: When was the last time you came here?

quando foi a última vez que

target_language_multi_word_term: quando foi a última vez que
additional_notes: Used to ask about the most recent occurrence of an action. It’s typically followed by a verb (often in the past), and it can be formal (tomou, assistiu, cortou, falou) or informal (falaste). In speech, people may shorten it to “Quando foi a última vez que…?” without extra context, and the answer often uses “Foi…” or a time expression (e.g., “na semana passada”, “faz dois dias”).
target_language_example: Quando foi a última vez que você viajou de avião?
native_language_example: When was the last time you traveled by plane?

quando foi a última vez que
