target_language_example: Quero que você fique mais um pouco.
native_language_example: I want you to stay a little longer.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone what you want them to do: “I want (that) you stay here.” In Portuguese it commonly takes the present subjunctive after “quero que” (here: “você fique”). You can add time/place details with “até…” (until) and locations like “aqui” (here) or “em Boston”.
target_language_example: Quero que você fique aqui comigo esta noite.
native_language_example: I want you to stay here with me tonight.

meaning: “I want you to … (for me / to me)” (used before another verb).
additional_notes: This is the start of a request or desire: **quero** (I want) + **que** + **você** (you) + **me** (me). It’s followed by another verb, usually in the **subjunctive** because it expresses what you want someone else to do: *Quero que você me diga…* (“I want you to tell me…”). The **me** is an object pronoun and typically comes before the verb: *me ajude* (“help me”), *me ligue* (“call me”).
target_language_example: Quero que você me ajude com isso.
native_language_example: I want you to help me with this.

meaning: “I want you to write to me.”
additional_notes: Used to say you want someone to contact you in writing (a message, email, letter). After "quero que" (I want that), Portuguese typically uses the present subjunctive: "você me escreva". Often followed by details like how often (frequentemente), what to write (uma carta), or when (assim que você chegar lá = as soon as you get there).
target_language_example: Quero que você me escreva quando tiver tempo.
native_language_example: I want you to write to me when you have time.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information you want to make sure the other person knows, often to express feelings (apologies, gratitude, reassurance) or to emphasize a point. It’s followed by what you want the person to know (e.g., “quero que você saiba que…” = “I want you to know that…”). Note: “você” is common in Brazil; in more formal contexts you may also hear “quero que o senhor/a senhora saiba”.
target_language_example: Quero que você saiba que pode contar comigo.
native_language_example: I want you to know that you can count on me.

additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone else to do. After "quero que" (“I want that...”), Portuguese uses the present subjunctive: "você vá" (from "ir" = to go). You can add where/with whom: "ao correio" (to the post office), "com o Tom" (with Tom), "conosco" (with us), "lá" (there).
target_language_example: Quero que você vá comigo amanhã.
native_language_example: I want you to go with me tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express what the speaker wants a group of people ("vocês" = you all) to do. It is followed by a verb in the subjunctive (usem, parem, fiquem, saibam, se sentem, sejam, vão), often giving an instruction, request, or strong desire.
target_language_example: Quero que vocês me ajudem com isso.
native_language_example: I want you all to help me with this.

meaning: "I want to know" / "I’d like to know."
additional_notes: Used to ask for information or express curiosity/interest. Often followed by a clause or question (e.g., "Quero saber a que horas..." = "I want to know what time...") or by "mais" + "sobre" to mean "I want to know more about...". It’s neutral and common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Quero saber se você vai amanhã.
native_language_example: I want to know if you’re going tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to ask for a person’s identity or to find out who did something. It’s followed by a clause, e.g., “quero saber quem fez isso” (“I want to know who did this”). In European Portuguese, you may also see “quero saber quem és” with “tu”; in Brazilian Portuguese, “quero saber quem você é” is more common.
target_language_example: Quero saber quem ligou para mim ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I want to know who called me last night.

meaning: "I want to be" / "I want to become".
additional_notes: Used to talk about what you want to be in the future (a job, role, identity): "Quero ser médico." It can also be used more broadly to express wanting to be in a certain state or situation: "Quero ser dispensado" = "I want to be excused/exempt". The verb changes with the subject (e.g., "eu quero ser", "você quer ser", "ele quer ser").
target_language_example: Quando eu crescer, quero ser engenheiro.
native_language_example: When I grow up, I want to be an engineer.

meaning: "I want to be a" (for a masculine noun/profession).
additional_notes: Used to say what you want to become (a job, role, or identity). It’s made of: quero (I want) + ser (to be) + um (a/an, masculine). Use "quero ser uma" before feminine nouns (e.g., "quero ser uma médica"). With plural: "quero ser um dos..." = "I want to be one of the...".
target_language_example: Quando crescer, quero ser um engenheiro.
native_language_example: When I grow up, I want to be an engineer.

meaning: "I want to" + "you" (object), as in "I want to (do something) to/for you".
additional_notes: "Quero" = "I want" and "te" is an unstressed object pronoun meaning "you" (singular, informal) used with verbs like "fazer" (to do/make), "agradecer" (to thank), etc.: "Quero te agradecer" (I want to thank you). In Brazil, many speakers also say "quero agradecer a você" instead of using "te".
target_language_example: Quero te ajudar com isso.
native_language_example: I want to help you with that.

meaning: “I want to see you.” (often: “I want you to come see me / I need to see you.”)
additional_notes: Used to say you want to meet someone in person or see them (sometimes urgently, like an order/request: “Come see me now”). “Te” is an informal object pronoun (= “you”); in more formal speech you might hear “quero ver você.” Tone depends on context: it can be affectionate (“I miss you”) or confrontational (“I don’t want to see you again”).
target_language_example: Quero te ver hoje à noite para conversarmos.
native_language_example: I want to see you tonight so we can talk.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to see someone or something masculine (singular) right now or at a specific time. It’s made of: quero (I want) + ver (to see) + o (the, masculine). For a female noun, use "quero ver a"; for plural, "quero ver os/as". Often followed by a person’s name with an implied "o": "Quero ver o Tom" = “I want to see Tom.”
target_language_example: Quero ver o médico hoje.
native_language_example: I want to see the doctor today.

meaning: “we wanted him to do (it)” / “we wanted that he do (it)” (past).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of querer (queríamos = “we wanted/used to want”) + que + imperfect subjunctive (ele fizesse = “that he did/should do”). This structure is common after verbs of wanting/requesting (querer, pedir, exigir) when you talk about what you wanted someone else to do. Often followed by o que (“what”): o que queríamos que ele fizesse = “what we wanted him to do.”
target_language_example: Eu expliquei de novo porque eles queriam que ele fizesse tudo sozinho.
native_language_example: I explained again why they wanted him to do everything by himself.

meaning: "fifteen years" (an age or a period of 15 years).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s age (Tenho quinze anos. = I’m fifteen) or about time that has passed (Faz/Se passaram quinze anos… = It’s been fifteen years…). In Brazil, "festa de quinze anos" refers to a girl’s 15th birthday celebration (similar to a quinceañera).
target_language_example: Quando eu tinha quinze anos, eu morava no Rio.
native_language_example: When I was fifteen, I lived in Rio.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (how long something takes or lasts) or a time interval. Common patterns: "esperar quinze minutos" (to wait 15 minutes), "levar quinze minutos" (to take 15 minutes), "passaram quinze minutos?" (have 15 minutes passed?), "de quinze em quinze minutos" (every 15 minutes), and "quinze minutos de caminhada" (a 15-minute walk).
target_language_example: A reunião vai durar quinze minutos.
native_language_example: The meeting will last fifteen minutes.

additional_notes: Used to clarify or ask about someone’s intended meaning, often after confusion or misunderstanding. Typically followed by "que" (quis dizer que...) or by "com" to specify what something meant (quis dizer com isso...). Can also be used negatively: "não quis dizer" = “didn’t mean (it/that)”.
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu quis dizer que chego às oito, não às sete.
native_language_example: Sorry, I meant (to say) that I arrive at eight, not at seven.

meaning: ram-don (a Korean noodle dish made by mixing instant ramen and udon).
additional_notes: A borrowed term (popularized internationally by the film *Parasite*) used to name a specific dish. In Portuguese it’s treated like a food name: you can say “fazer ram-don” (to make it), “comer ram-don” (to eat it), or “gostar de ram-don” (to like it).
target_language_example: Hoje eu vou fazer ram-don para o jantar.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to make ram-don for dinner.

additional_notes: Means the racket used to play tennis. It’s a straightforward noun phrase: raquete (racket) + de (of/for) + tênis (tennis). You can add a possessive (minha/sua) or specify the type, e.g., raquete de tênis de mesa (table tennis/ping-pong paddle).
target_language_example: Esqueci minha raquete de tênis em casa.
native_language_example: I forgot my tennis racket at home.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation or cause. Often follows words like “a única” (the only), “a mesma” (the same), or “qual foi a” (what was the). In speech you may also hear “razão por que” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Essa é a razão pela qual eu não fui à festa.
native_language_example: That’s the reason why I didn’t go to the party.

additional_notes: "Recebeu" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "receber" (to receive) for ele/ela/você. "Uma carta" means "a letter" (a piece of mail). Often followed by "de" to say who it’s from: "recebeu uma carta de + pessoa". You can swap the subject: "Eu recebi uma carta", "Nós recebemos uma carta".
target_language_example: Ontem eu recebi uma carta do banco.
native_language_example: Yesterday I received a letter from the bank.

additional_notes: Past tense: "recebi" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "receber" (to receive). "Uma carta" means "a letter" (usually a physical letter; for email you’d more often say "recebi um e-mail"). Common with "de" (from someone) and "do/da" (from + the): "Recebi uma carta dela" / "Recebi uma carta do meu amigo."
target_language_example: Recebi uma carta do banco ontem.
native_language_example: I received a letter from the bank yesterday.

additional_notes: Used when telling someone you got a (paper) letter from a person. "Recebi" is the past tense of "receber" (to receive) for "eu" (I), so it refers to a completed action. In conversation, people may also use "recebi uma mensagem/e-mail de" for a message/email instead of a physical letter.
target_language_example: Ontem, recebi uma carta de minha avó.
native_language_example: Yesterday, I received a letter from my grandmother.

meaning: to recommend a good (one) (e.g., doctor, restaurant, etc.).
additional_notes: Used when asking someone to suggest a good option from a category. It’s usually followed by a noun: "recomendar um bom médico/restaurante/dicionário". You’ll also hear the more explicit form "me recomendar" (“recommend me…”). In polite requests, "pode" is common; "poderia" is more polite/formal (“could you”).
target_language_example: Você pode me recomendar um bom café por aqui?
native_language_example: Can you recommend a good coffee shop around here?

meaning: to make up for lost time.
additional_notes: Used when you want to catch up after a delay or period of inactivity (work, study, projects, relationships, etc.). It often implies working faster or doing extra to compensate. You can also say “recuperar o tempo” with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Depois das férias, vou recuperar o tempo perdido no trabalho.
native_language_example: After the vacation, I’m going to make up for lost time at work.

additional_notes: Refers to materials and sources found in nature that people use, like water, forests, minerals, oil, and gas. Often used in discussions about a country’s wealth, development, or environmental issues (e.g., protecting or wasting natural resources).
target_language_example: Precisamos proteger nossos recursos naturais para o futuro.
native_language_example: We need to protect our natural resources for the future.

additional_notes: Past tense (ele/ela/você) of the verb phrase “(se) recusar a + infinitive” (“to refuse to do something”). Very common with the reflexive pronoun: “se recusou a aceitar / a falar / a fazer…”. You can also hear “recusou aceitar…”, but “recusou a + infinitive” is a standard, clear pattern for beginners.
target_language_example: Ele se recusou a pedir desculpas.
native_language_example: He refused to apologize.

meaning: reluctant to do that/this; unwilling to do it.
additional_notes: Used to say someone doesn’t want to do something, often because they’re hesitant, unsure, or don’t feel comfortable. Common with the structure “relutante em + verb (infinitive)”: “relutante em falar”, “relutante em aceitar”. You can also say “estar relutante” (to be reluctant) or “ficar relutante” (to become reluctant).
target_language_example: Eu estava relutante em fazer isso sozinho.
native_language_example: I was reluctant to do that alone.

additional_notes: Used when talking about finding a solution to a specific issue or difficulty. In everyday speech, you’ll also hear it with different demonstratives ("resolver esse problema" / "resolver aquele problema") or without them ("resolver o problema"). "Resolver" is a very common verb for solving problems, issues, questions, or situations.
target_language_example: Vamos trabalhar juntos para resolver este problema hoje.
native_language_example: Let’s work together to solve this problem today.

additional_notes: Common with verbs like "tentar" (try) or phrases like "com facilidade" (easily). In everyday speech it can mean either finding the solution (solve) or taking action so the issue goes away (fix).
target_language_example: Vamos resolver o problema juntos.
native_language_example: Let’s solve the problem together.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "resolver" + "o problema". Used to say someone found a solution and fixed/dealt with an issue. Subject comes from context (ele/ela/você). Often followed by adverbs like "facilmente" (easily), "com facilidade" (with ease), "rapidinho" (very quickly; informal), or phrases like "sozinho/por conta própria" (alone/by oneself).
target_language_example: Ela resolveu o problema em poucos minutos.
native_language_example: She solved the problem in a few minutes.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition “a” before the person/thing you answer or respond to: “responder a uma pergunta” (answer a question), “responder a alguém” (answer someone). In some contexts, “responder a (um adulto/uma autoridade)” can mean “talk back” (respond in a rude/defiant way).
target_language_example: Você já respondeu ao e-mail do professor?
native_language_example: Have you already replied to the teacher’s email?

additional_notes: Used when you reply to a specific question. In Portuguese you say “responder a” (to answer) + “a pergunta” (the question). The “a + a” becomes “à” (with the accent) before a feminine singular noun like “pergunta”. You can also say “responder a uma pergunta” = “answer a question.”
target_language_example: Desculpe, não sei responder à pergunta agora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t answer the question right now.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the specific answer for a particular question. It often appears with verbs like “ser” (A resposta… é…), “saber” (saber a resposta…), and “encontrar” (encontrar resposta…). Note the preposition “a” after “resposta” when it’s followed by what the answer is to: “resposta a + (pergunta)”.
target_language_example: Ainda não tenho a resposta a esta pergunta.
native_language_example: I still don’t have the answer to this question.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "atravessar" (to cross): "atravessar um rio a nado" = to swim across a river. "A nado" means "by swimming" (similar to "a pé" = on foot, "de carro" = by car).
target_language_example: Eles atravessaram o rio a nado porque não havia ponte.
native_language_example: They swam across the river because there was no bridge.

additional_notes: Usually appears with a verb like atravessar (“to cross”): atravessar um rio nadando = “to cross a river by swimming.” Here, nadando is the gerund (“swimming”) and it describes how the action is done (like “by -ing” in English).
target_language_example: Ele atravessou o rio nadando porque a ponte estava quebrada.
native_language_example: He crossed the river by swimming because the bridge was broken.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **rir de** (“to laugh at”) + **mim** (“me”). It often implies being laughed at/mocked. **Riram** can mean “they laughed” or “you all (vocês) laughed,” depending on context. You can swap the pronoun: **riram de você** (laughed at you), **riram dele/dela** (laughed at him/her), **riram da gente** (laughed at us).
target_language_example: Eu fiquei triste porque riram de mim.
native_language_example: I was sad because they laughed at me.

additional_notes: "Grana" is slang for "money" (like "cash"), so this phrase is informal and often suggests stealing cash or taking the money from someone. In many contexts, you can also hear "roubar grana" without "a". Verb: roubar (to steal).
target_language_example: Ele tentou roubar a grana do caixa.
native_language_example: He tried to steal the money from the register.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **roubar** (“to steal”) in the simple past (**roubou** = “(he/she/you) stole”). **A minha** means “my” for a **feminine singular** thing: *a minha bicicleta, a minha bolsa, a minha mala*. For masculine nouns, you’d say **roubou o meu...** (*o meu celular*). Can also be used figuratively: *Você roubou a minha ideia* (“You stole my idea”).
target_language_example: Alguém roubou a minha carteira no metrô.
native_language_example: Someone stole my wallet on the subway.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone took your wallet without permission. It’s the past tense of "roubar" (to steal): "(ele/ela/você) roubou" = "(he/she/you) stole." "Carteira" is usually "wallet" (it can also mean "ID card/driver’s license" depending on context, but with "roubou" it typically means wallet). You can swap "minha" for another possessive: "roubou sua carteira" (stole your wallet), "roubou a carteira dele" (stole his wallet).
target_language_example: Desculpe, mas alguém roubou minha carteira no ônibus.
native_language_example: Sorry, but someone stole my wallet on the bus.

additional_notes: Used when accusing or reporting that someone stole something that belongs to you. "Roubou" is the past tense of "roubar" (to steal), and "o meu" means "my" for a masculine noun (e.g., o relógio, o chapéu). For feminine nouns, you’d say "roubou a minha" (e.g., a bolsa).
target_language_example: Alguém roubou o meu telefone no ônibus.
native_language_example: Someone stole my phone on the bus.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **saber** + an infinitive to talk about having a skill: **saber dirigir** = to know how to drive. It can take an object for what kind of vehicle: **dirigir um carro / caminhão**. Often used in questions: **Você sabe dirigir?** = “Can you drive?”
target_language_example: Eu não sei dirigir, mas minha irmã sabe.
native_language_example: I can’t drive, but my sister can.

meaning: (he/she/you) can speak; knows how to speak (a language).
additional_notes: Used with languages to say someone has the ability to speak them: "sabe falar inglês" = "can speak English." Literally "knows (how) to speak." It often appears with adverbs like "bem" (well) or "um pouco" (a little): "só sabe falar um pouco de francês" = "only can speak a little French."
target_language_example: Você sabe falar português?
native_language_example: Can you speak Portuguese?

meaning: “(he/she/you) can speak French” / “knows how to speak French.”
additional_notes: Uses the verb "saber" + infinitive ("falar") to talk about knowing how to do a skill. Conjugation changes with the subject: "eu sei falar francês" (I can speak French), "você/ele/ela sabe falar francês" (you/he/she can), "nós sabemos falar francês" (we can). In questions, it often means “Can you speak French?” ("Você sabe falar francês?") or “Does anyone speak French?” ("Alguém sabe falar francês?").
target_language_example: Eu não sei falar francês, mas sei falar um pouco de espanhol.
native_language_example: I can’t speak French, but I can speak a little Spanish.

meaning: 'can speak French almost…' / 'almost speaks French… (as well as …)'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone can speak French nearly as well as someone else, or nearly at a native level. In Portuguese, you’ll often see it as “sabe falar francês quase tão bem quanto/como …” (= almost as well as …) or “quase como um nativo” (= almost like a native). Note: the most natural word order is usually “sabe falar francês quase …”, with “quase” introducing the comparison that follows.
target_language_example: Ela sabe falar francês quase tão bem quanto o professor.
native_language_example: She can speak French almost as well as the teacher.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "saber" + infinitive to talk about an acquired skill/ability. It can mean ordinary reading ("sabe ler e escrever") or reading/understanding something like lips or body language ("sabe ler os movimentos dos lábios" = can interpret/understand). You can change the subject: "eu sei ler", "você sabe ler", "eles sabem ler".
target_language_example: Você sabe ler em português?
native_language_example: Can you read in Portuguese?

meaning: "(he/she) can swim" / "(he/she) knows how to swim."
additional_notes: "Saber" + infinitive expresses an ability/learned skill: "saber nadar" = to know how to swim. It changes with the subject: "eu sei nadar", "você sabe nadar", "ele/ela sabe nadar", "nós sabemos nadar". For questions, you can use "Você sabe nadar?" (= Can you swim?).
target_language_example: Você sabe nadar?
native_language_example: Can you swim?

meaning: "(he/she) knows how to play" (a musical instrument).
additional_notes: Used with a person as the subject + "saber" (to know how to) + "tocar" (to play) + an instrument. You can change the verb to match the subject: "eu sei tocar", "você sabe tocar", "eles sabem tocar". Often followed by the instrument without an article: "sabe tocar flauta/violão/piano".
target_language_example: Você sabe tocar violão?
native_language_example: Do you know how to play the guitar?

meaning: “(he/she) knows how to play the piano.”
additional_notes: Used to say that someone has the skill/ability to play the piano. It’s the 3rd-person singular of "saber" (to know how to) + "tocar" (to play an instrument) + "piano". For other subjects: "Eu sei tocar piano" (I know how to play the piano), "Você sabe tocar piano?" (Do you know how to play the piano?), "Eles sabem tocar piano" (They know how to play the piano).
target_language_example: Você sabe tocar piano ou outro instrumento?
native_language_example: Do you know how to play the piano or another instrument?

meaning: "do you know who it belongs to?"
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone knows the owner of something. It usually appears as a polite question ("Você sabe a quem pertence este/esse...?"). "a quem" means "to whom" and is common in more formal speech; in everyday conversation many people also say "de quem é" ("whose is it?"). "pertencer" means "to belong (to)."
target_language_example: Você sabe a quem pertence esta bolsa?
native_language_example: Do you know who this bag belongs to?

additional_notes: From the verb "saber" (to know, as a fact) + "a resposta" (the answer). Used to say someone knows the answer to a question: "sabe a resposta para essa pergunta". With "você", it means "you know"; with "ele/ela", it means "he/she knows". You can also negate it: "não sabe a resposta" (doesn’t know the answer).
target_language_example: Você sabe a resposta?
native_language_example: Do you know the answer?

additional_notes: Used with a following verb or clause to talk about knowing how to do something (“Ele sabe como se fecha…” = “He knows how to close…”), or to ask if someone knows how (“Sabe como…?” = “Do you know how…?”). In conversation, it can also introduce an explanation or shared understanding (often as “Sabe como é…” = “You know how it is…”), which is more informal in tone.
target_language_example: Você sabe como chegar lá de ônibus?
native_language_example: Do you know how to get there by bus?

additional_notes: Used with a following verb or clause to talk about knowing how to do something (“Ele sabe como se fecha…” = “He knows how to close…”), or to ask if someone knows how (“Sabe como…?” = “Do you know how…?”). In conversation, it can also introduce an explanation or shared understanding (often as “Sabe como é…” = “You know how it is…”), which is more informal in tone.
target_language_example: Você sabe como chegar lá de ônibus?
native_language_example: Do you know how to get there by bus?

additional_notes: "Sabe" is the (present tense) 'you/he/she knows' form of "saber". "Disso" means 'of that/about that' (de + isso). Used to say someone is aware of a fact or piece of information, or to ask if someone knows it. Polite question uses "O senhor/A senhora sabe disso?"
target_language_example: Você sabe disso, né?
native_language_example: You know that, right?

additional_notes: Used to say someone has a lot of knowledge about a topic or person. It’s the verb saber (to know facts/information) in the 3rd-person singular present (ele/ela/você sabe) + muito (a lot) + sobre (about). You can change the subject: eu sei muito sobre…, nós sabemos muito sobre…, eles sabem muito sobre….
target_language_example: Eu sei muito sobre essa cidade, porque morei aqui por anos.
native_language_example: I know a lot about this city because I lived here for years.

additional_notes: From the verb *saber* (“to know”) + *o* (“the”, masculine singular). In conversation, Portuguese often drops the subject pronoun, so **Sabe o…?** usually means **“Do you know…?”** (addressing *você*), but it can also mean **“He/she knows the…”** depending on context. Very common before nouns (**Sabe o caminho…?** = “Do you know the way…?”) and before **o que** (**Sabe o que…?** = “Do you know what…?”).
target_language_example: Você sabe o endereço da loja?
native_language_example: Do you know the store’s address?

meaning: "(he/she/you) knows the name" / "do you know the name?".
additional_notes: From the verb "saber" (to know) + "o nome" (the name). It’s used both as a statement ("Ele sabe o nome") and as a yes/no question, often just by intonation in speech ("Sabe o nome deles?"). In Portuguese you can omit the subject pronoun ("você/ele/ela") because the verb form often makes it clear from context. Common with "de": "sabe o nome de todos os clientes" (knows the names of all the customers).
target_language_example: Você sabe o nome da rua?
native_language_example: Do you know the name of the street?

meaning: "do you know what…?" / "you know what…?" (often to introduce something important or surprising).
additional_notes: Used to start a question or a (sometimes rhetorical) comment that sets up what comes next: "Sabe o que eu ouvi?" It can be genuinely asking if someone knows, or used for emphasis like English "You know what?" It agrees with the person: "Você sabe o que…" (you know what…), "O senhor sabe o que…" (formal), "Vocês sabem o que…" (plural).
target_language_example: Sabe o que? Eu mudei de ideia.
native_language_example: You know what? I changed my mind.

meaning: "(you/he/she) knows what happened"; often used as "Do you know what happened?"
additional_notes: Built from "sabe" (knows; also the formal "you know") + "o que" (what) + "aconteceu" (happened). Common in questions: "Você sabe o que aconteceu?" (formal you) or "Tu sabes o que aconteceu?" (Portugal/informal). Can also appear with a person: "Sabe o que aconteceu ao Sammy?" = "Do you know what happened to Sammy?"
target_language_example: Você sabe o que aconteceu ontem à noite?
native_language_example: Do you know what happened last night?

meaning: “do you know what … is?” / “you know what … is.”
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone knows what something is (often followed by a noun or “isto/isso”: “Sabe o que é isto?”). It can also be used on its own (“Sabe o que é?”) when the thing is understood from context. With a name or pronoun instead of “você” (e.g., “Tom sabe o que é”), it means “Tom knows what it is.”
target_language_example: Você sabe o que é saudade?
native_language_example: Do you know what saudade is?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question about location. It’s the verb saber (“to know”) in the 3rd-person singular (ele/ela/você) + onde (“where”). Often appears in questions like “Você (por acaso) sabe onde…?” = “Do you (happen to) know where…?”
target_language_example: Você sabe onde fica a estação de metrô?
native_language_example: Do you know where the subway station is?

additional_notes: Literally “(you/he/she) know(s) where I live.” Often used as a question (with rising intonation or a question mark). "sabe" is from "saber" (to know). Use "Você sabe onde eu moro?" (neutral), "O senhor sabe..." (formal to a man), "A senhora sabe..." (formal to a woman), or with a name: "Tom sabe...".
target_language_example: Você sabe onde eu moro? Posso te mandar a localização.
native_language_example: Do you know where I live? I can send you my location.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone knows the reason for something, or to ask if someone knows the reason. "sabe" is the present tense of "saber" (to know), and "por que" means "why" (the reason). You can change the subject/pronoun: "eu sei por que...", "ela sabe por que...", "você sabe por que...?".
target_language_example: Você sabe por que ele não veio?
native_language_example: Do you know why he didn’t come?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause with a fact someone knows. It’s the verb saber (to know a fact) + que (“that”). In questions, it can be “(Do you) know that…?” or “Does (he/she) know that…?”; with no subject stated (“Sabe que…?”) it often implies “you” (você) in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Você sabe que hoje é feriado?
native_language_example: Do you know that today is a holiday?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question about a person’s identity (who did something). Very common in phrases like “não se sabe quem…” = “it’s not known who…”. With just “Sabe quem…?” it can be a direct question (“Do you know who…?”) or a rhetorical lead-in (“You know who…?”).
target_language_example: Você sabe quem vai apresentar a reunião amanhã?
native_language_example: Do you know who is going to lead the meeting tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to say that someone recognizes your identity, or (often in arguments) to challenge someone who doesn’t know you well. It’s usually part of a longer phrase like “Você sabe quem eu sou?” (Do you know who I am?) or “Você não sabe quem eu sou!” (You don’t even know who I am!).
target_language_example: Você sabe quem eu sou, mas não sabe o que eu passei.
native_language_example: You know who I am, but you don't know what I've been through.

meaning: "(they) can speak French" / "(they) know how to speak French."
additional_notes: "Sabem" is the 3rd-person plural of "saber" (to know), used to talk about knowing how to do something. The pattern is "saber" + infinitive verb: "saber falar" = "to be able to speak". Here it’s in the plural (“they”): "Eles/Elas sabem falar francês." In questions, you can keep the same order: "Eles sabem falar francês?"
target_language_example: Vocês sabem falar francês?
native_language_example: Can you (all) speak French?

additional_notes: "Sabem" is the present tense (3rd person plural) of "saber" (to know). It’s used before an embedded question with "o que" (“what”), like in "Eles sabem o que fazer" (“They know what to do”). Often followed by a verb in the infinitive ("o que fazer") or by a full clause ("o que está acontecendo").
target_language_example: Vocês sabem o que precisam fazer agora?
native_language_example: Do you (plural) know what you need to do now?

additional_notes: Present tense of **saber** (to know) in the **3rd person plural** (**eles/elas sabem** = they know; **vocês sabem** = you all know) + **que** (“that”) to introduce a clause. Often the subject is omitted because it’s understood from context.
target_language_example: Vocês sabem que a reunião começa às nove?
native_language_example: Do you all know that the meeting starts at nine?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question about a person’s identity. "Sabem" is the 3rd person plural of "saber" (to know), and "quem" means “who”. Often followed by a clause (e.g., "quem é", "quem você é", "quem sois").
target_language_example: Eles sabem quem você é.
native_language_example: They know who you are.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what “we” know about a fact, action, or meaning. It’s often followed by a full clause ("Sabemos o que você fez" = “We know what you did”) or by an infinitive in more general statements ("Todos sabemos o que fazer" = “We all know what to do”). In negative form, it becomes "não sabemos o que" (“we don’t know what …”).
target_language_example: Sabemos o que precisamos fazer agora.
native_language_example: We know what we need to do now.

meaning: to know the truth; to find out the truth.
additional_notes: Used when someone wants or needs the true facts about a situation. Often appears with verbs like querer (to want), precisar (to need), merecer (to deserve), ter direito de (to have the right to), and ter que (to have to). You can also use descobrir a verdade for “to discover/find out the truth.”
target_language_example: Eu preciso saber a verdade antes de tomar uma decisão.
native_language_example: I need to know the truth before making a decision.

meaning: to know how; to find out how.
additional_notes:
Used when talking about having (or wanting) the knowledge/skill to do something, or asking for an explanation of the way something is done. Very often followed by a verb (often in the subjunctive after "como"):
- "Quero saber como fazer isso." = I want to know how to do this.
It can also stand alone when the action is understood from context: "Eu quero saber como."
target_language_example: Quero saber como você aprendeu português tão rápido.
native_language_example: I want to know how you learned Portuguese so fast.

meaning: to know what (to do / what something is).
additional_notes: Used when you know the correct information, choice, or action. Very common with an infinitive to express knowing what to do: "saber o que fazer" (to know what to do). You can also use it without "fazer" when the verb is understood from context (e.g., "saber o que fizemos" = know what we did).
target_language_example: Eu não sei o que dizer.
native_language_example: I don't know what to say.

additional_notes: Used when someone wants information or an explanation about a past event. With "quero" it often expresses insistence or concern: "Quero saber o que aconteceu" (“I want to know what happened”). In questions you’ll often hear: "Você sabe o que aconteceu?" (“Do you know what happened?”).
target_language_example: Eu preciso saber o que aconteceu ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I need to know what happened last night.

meaning: “to know what you …” / “let me know what you …” (introducing what someone will decide/do/say).
additional_notes: Used most often inside a longer request like “Deixe-me saber o que você decide (fazer)” (“Let me know what you decide (to do)”). Literally it’s “to know what you,” and it normally needs a verb afterward (decide, want, did, etc.). You can also use “me avise o que você…” for “let me know…”.
target_language_example: Me avise o que você decidiu, por favor.
native_language_example: Let me know what you decided, please.

additional_notes: Used when you need information about a location or place. Often followed by a clause with a verb: “saber onde + (someone) está/foi/mora/escondeu…”. Common in polite requests: “Quero/Gostaria/Preciso saber onde…”.
target_language_example: Você sabe onde fica a estação de metrô?
native_language_example: Do you know where the subway station is?

additional_notes: Used when you want to know the reason for something. It’s often followed by a clause (por que + subject + verb): “saber por que você fez isso” (“to know why you did that”). In questions, “por que” is usually written as two words (why).
target_language_example: Eu preciso saber por que você saiu tão cedo.
native_language_example: I need to know why you left so early.

meaning: to know why; to find out why.
additional_notes: Used when you want an explanation or reason for something. Here, **por quê** (two words, with an accent) is used at the **end of a question** or clause: *Eu quero saber por quê.* In other positions you often see **por que** (no accent): *Eu quero saber por que você foi embora.* (Beginners often confuse **por quê / por que / porque / porquê**.)
target_language_example: Preciso saber por quê você fez isso.
native_language_example: I need to know why you did that.

meaning: to know who (someone is) / to find out who.
additional_notes: Used with an indirect question (quem + verb) to say you know or want to learn a person’s identity. Often appears as "querer/gostaria de saber quem..." (want/would like to know who...) or "acreditar saber quem..." (believe you know who...). You can also use it to emphasize mutual knowledge: "sabemos quem você é" (we know who you are).
target_language_example: Eu quero saber quem pegou o meu celular.
native_language_example: I want to know who took my phone.

meaning: to know/find out who did that.
additional_notes: Used when you want information about the person responsible for something. "Saber" can mean either already knowing (“I know who did it”) or wanting to find out (“I want to know who did it”), depending on context. "Fez" is the past tense of "fazer" (to do/make), and "isso" means “that/it.”
target_language_example: Preciso saber quem fez isso antes de decidir o que fazer.
native_language_example: I need to know who did that before deciding what to do.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect yes/no question (uncertainty about whether something is true or will happen). Often appears after verbs like "querer", "gostaria", "precisar", "resta" (e.g., "Quero saber se...", "Resta saber se..."). In requests, "deixe-nos saber se..." means "let us know if...".
target_language_example: Não sei se ele já chegou.
native_language_example: I don't know if he has arrived yet.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has (or wants) complete knowledge about a topic/person/thing. Very common with verbs like querer/precisar/parecer + saber tudo sobre. The preposition “sobre” means “about” here, and it’s followed by a noun or pronoun: sobre você/isto/este banheiro.
target_language_example: Eu quero saber tudo sobre o seu trabalho.
native_language_example: I want to know everything about your job.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a question or statement about some specific information (often followed by a verb, e.g., “é”, “fazer”, “disse”). In speech it can be a real question (“Do you know what Tom said?”) or a reminder/assumption (“You already know what to do.”). Usually followed by a clause starting with a verb: “sabes o que é…?”, “sabes o que fazer?”, “sabes o que aconteceu?”
target_language_example: Sabes o que aconteceu aqui ontem à noite?
native_language_example: Do you know what happened here last night?

meaning: "(He/She/I) knew how to speak French" / "could speak French" (in the past).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of "saber" (sabia) + infinitive to talk about an ability/skill someone had (often as background information or something you discovered/assumed). In the present you’d say "sei falar francês". You can swap "francês" for another language: "sabia falar inglês/espanhol".
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, eu sabia falar francês, mas esqueci quase tudo.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I could speak French, but I forgot almost everything.

additional_notes: Used with the imperfect of "saber" (sabia) + "disso" (“of that/that”) to say someone already had that knowledge. Often contrasts with new information or surprise, and can be turned into a question: "Você sabia disso?" = “Did you know that?” (implies “before now”).
target_language_example: Eu não sabia disso até agora.
native_language_example: I didn’t know that until now.

additional_notes: Used when someone knows the specific thing/action/information that follows. "Sabia" is the imperfect past of "saber" (to know), often used for ongoing/background knowledge in the past. It’s commonly followed by a clause with another verb: "sabia o que dizer" (knew what to say), "sabia o que fazer" (knew what to do).
target_language_example: Eu sabia o que fazer, mas fiquei nervoso na hora.
native_language_example: I knew what to do, but I got nervous at the moment.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of **saber** (*sabia*) to talk about what someone knew in a situation in the past. It’s often used after a negative word: **não sabia o que fazer** = “didn’t know what to do.” You can change the subject: **eu sabia**, **você sabia**, **nós sabíamos**, **eles sabiam**. Common extensions: **sabia o que fazer a seguir** (“knew what to do next”).
target_language_example: Eu sabia o que fazer, mas estava com medo.
native_language_example: I knew what to do, but I was scared.

additional_notes: Past (imperfect) form of the verb "saber" + "que" (“that”). Used to say someone had knowledge of a fact in the past or already knew something. The subject is often understood from context: "(Eu) sabia que..." = “I knew that…”, "Ele/Ela sabia que..." = “He/She knew that…”.
target_language_example: Eu sabia que você ia chegar cedo.
native_language_example: I knew that you were going to arrive early.

meaning: “knew that the …” (said about a woman/thing, since it’s followed by “a”).
additional_notes: Used in the imperfect past of saber (“to know”): “(ele/ela) sabia” = “he/she knew.” “Que” introduces a clause (“that …”), and “a” is the feminine singular definite article (“the”) that usually comes right before a feminine noun/name with a title (e.g., a Maria). Often followed by verbs like estava (was), tinha (had), ia (was going to), etc.
target_language_example: Eu sabia que a professora estava doente.
native_language_example: I knew that the teacher was sick.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of saber (sabia = “knew/used to know”) + que (“that”) + era (imperfect past of ser, “was”). Often introduces something you were sure about in the past: Eu sabia que era mentira. You can change the subject: eu sabia (I knew), ele/ela sabia (he/she knew), você sabia (you knew), a gente sabia (we knew).
target_language_example: Eu sabia que era ele pelo jeito de falar.
native_language_example: I knew it was him by the way he spoke.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of saber (sabia) to describe knowledge/thoughts you had at that time in the past. It’s followed by que + estava (imperfect of estar) to set the situation/state that was happening then. What comes after estava can be an adjective (errado/a), a place (em casa), or a gerund to describe an ongoing action (cometendo um erro). In questions, it can mean “Did you know that … was …?”
target_language_example: Eu sabia que estava atrasado, mas não consegui sair mais cedo.
native_language_example: I knew I was late, but I couldn’t leave earlier.

additional_notes: From the verb **saber** (“to know”). **Sabia** is the **imperfect past**, often used for background/ongoing knowledge in the past (“knew”). Very commonly followed by a clause with **que** (“that”) + **eu** (“I”) + a verb: *Sabia que eu estava aqui* (“(He) knew that I was here”). In questions, it can mean “How did you know that I…?”
target_language_example: Eu não sabia que eu tinha esquecido o celular em casa.
native_language_example: I didn’t know that I had forgotten my phone at home.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of **saber** (**sabia**) to describe past knowledge/background information. **que** = “that,” and **eu estava** (“I was”) is often followed by an adjective or a condition: *cansado(a)* (tired), *com sede* (thirsty), *deprimido(a)* (depressed), *pronto(a)* (ready). The ending changes with the subject: *eu sabia* (I knew), *ele/ela sabia* (he/she knew).
target_language_example: Ela sabia que eu estava nervoso antes da entrevista.
native_language_example: She knew that I was nervous before the interview.

meaning: “(he/she) knew I was going to …” / “(you) knew I was going to …”
additional_notes: Used to say someone already knew a future/intended action (“eu ia” = “I was going to”). “sabia” is the imperfect of *saber* (“to know”), often implying an ongoing/past knowledge: *Ele sabia que eu ia…* = “He knew I was going to…”. You may also see it with *você sabia que eu ia…* (“You knew I was going to…”) or *sabia que eu ia…?* as a question (“Did you know I was going to…?”).
target_language_example: Você sabia que eu ia chegar cedo?
native_language_example: Did you know I was going to arrive early?

additional_notes: Used to report knowledge about a specific masculine noun that follows (o = “the” for a masculine singular noun). “Sabia” is the imperfect past of saber (“to know”), and it often appears in statements like “Ele/Ela sabia que o …” or can be said without the subject when it’s understood from context.
target_language_example: Eu sabia que o voo ia atrasar.
native_language_example: I knew that the flight was going to be delayed.

meaning: “(I/he/she) knew there was/that there were…” or “knew (someone) had…”
additional_notes: Often used with and without “não” (“não sabia que tinha…” = “I didn’t know there was/that you had…”). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, “tinha” is commonly used where more formal writing might use “havia/existia” (there was) or “tinha” in the sense of “possessed/owned” depending on context. It can also introduce a necessity: “sabia que tinha que + verb” = “knew (someone) had to + verb.”
target_language_example: Eu não sabia que tinha um mercado aqui perto.
native_language_example: I didn’t know there was a market nearby.

additional_notes: "Sabia" is the imperfect past of "saber" (to know). The subject is often implied by context: "(Eu) sabia que você…" = "I knew that you…"; "(Ele/Ela) sabia que você…" = "He/She knew that you…". In questions, intonation or a question mark makes it "Did (someone) know that you…?".
target_language_example: Eu sabia que você ia gostar do filme.
native_language_example: I knew that you were going to like the movie.

meaning: "Get out of my…" / "Get away from my…" (telling someone to leave a place or move away).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to say what you want someone to leave: "saia da minha casa" (get out of my house), "saia da minha frente" (get out of my way/in front of me), "saia da minha varanda" (get off my porch). The full form is "saia" (formal/neutral command) or "sai" (informal). By itself ("Sai/saia da minha!") it can mean "Leave me alone!/Get off my back!" and is more informal/annoyed.
target_language_example: Saia da minha frente, por favor.
native_language_example: Get out of my way, please.

additional_notes: An imperative telling someone to leave the place you are in. It comes from the verb **sair** (“to leave/go out”) + **daqui** (“from here”). It can sound very strong or rude, especially with exclamation marks or words like **imediatamente** (“immediately”); you can soften it with **por favor** (e.g., *Saia daqui, por favor.*).
target_language_example: Saia daqui agora, por favor — é perigoso.
native_language_example: Get out of here now, please — it’s dangerous.

meaning: "get out of my..." / "get off my..." (a forceful order).
additional_notes: Used as an imperative command to tell someone to leave your space or stop blocking you. It’s usually followed by a noun like caminho (way), escritório (office), quarto (room). Verb: sair (to leave). This form can sound rude/angry; for a softer version you can say "Por favor, saia do meu..." or "Pode sair do meu...?".
target_language_example: Por favor, saia do meu quarto agora.
native_language_example: Please get out of my room now.

meaning: 'to leave' / 'to get out of' / 'to get out of (a situation)'.
additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (da = de + a). It can mean physically leaving a place (sair da casa, sair da sala de aula) or escaping a condition/situation (sair da pobreza = get out of poverty). With time limits, it often means “be out by…” or “leave within…” (Tem meia hora pra sair da casa = You have half an hour to leave the house).
target_language_example: Preciso sair da reunião mais cedo hoje.
native_language_example: I need to leave the meeting early today.

meaning: to leave here; to get out of here.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to leave the current place (often with urgency: “Let’s get out of here!”). Conjugates as the verb *sair* (“to leave”): *vamos sair daqui* (let’s leave), *sai daqui!* (get out of here! – informal singular), *saia daqui!* (more formal).
target_language_example: Está tarde — vamos sair daqui agora.
native_language_example: It’s late—let’s get out of here now.

meaning: to leave home; to go out (from home).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "sair" (to leave/go out) + "de" + "casa" (home/house). It often means leaving your home to go somewhere else, and can be used literally (step out of the house) or more generally (go out for the day). Common in advice or routines: "antes de sair de casa" = "before leaving home."
target_language_example: Vou sair de casa cedo para evitar o trânsito.
native_language_example: I'm going to leave home early to avoid traffic.

meaning: 'to leave' or 'to get out of' (a place or situation).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine noun after de + o → do (e.g., do escritório, do Japão, do banheiro). It can mean physically leaving a place ("sair do escritório") or getting out/away from something ("sair do caminho" = move out of the way). With some expressions it can mean removing yourself from a state or condition (e.g., "sair do chão" = get up off the floor/ground).
target_language_example: Vou sair do trabalho às seis.
native_language_example: I'm going to leave work at six.

meaning: to leave earlier; to leave early.
additional_notes: Used when someone departs before the usual/expected time (e.g., leaving work or school early). It can refer to leaving earlier than planned (mais cedo do que o normal/do que previsto). Common patterns: “sair mais cedo do trabalho/da escola”, “ter que sair mais cedo” (have to leave early).
target_language_example: Hoje vou sair mais cedo para ir ao médico.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to leave early to go to the doctor.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re leaving earlier than normal today (often from work/school). It can appear with verbs like "precisar" (need to), "querer" (want to), or "ter que" (have to): "Tenho que sair mais cedo hoje." You can add a comparison: "... do que de costume" = "... than usual."
target_language_example: Posso sair mais cedo hoje? Tenho uma consulta médica.
native_language_example: Can I leave early today? I have a doctor’s appointment.

additional_notes: Uses the verb sair (“to leave/go out”) + correndo (“running”). Very common for sudden actions, often after hearing/seeing something: "Assim que... saiu correndo" (“As soon as... he/she ran out”). Can be followed by a place/direction with de/para ("saiu correndo da casa" = ran out of the house; "saiu correndo para o jardim" = ran to the garden) or by atrás de (“after/chasing”). Changes with the subject: eu saí correndo, você saiu correndo, eles saíram correndo.
target_language_example: Quando viu o ônibus chegando, ela saiu correndo para o ponto.
native_language_example: When she saw the bus arriving, she took off running to the bus stop.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **sair de** (“to leave / to go out of”), used with **da = de + a** (“from the” feminine singular). It’s followed by a place or situation: **saiu da loja/sala/casa/piscina/cidade** (“left the store/room/house/pool/city”). It can also mean something is no longer in a certain state or situation: **sair da cadeia** (“get out of jail”). In phrases like **saiu da moda**, it means “went out of fashion.” (For masculine singular you’ll often see **saiu do** = de + o.)
target_language_example: Ele saiu da reunião cedo porque estava cansado.
native_language_example: He left the meeting early because he was tired.

meaning: (he/she) left home; went out (from the house).
additional_notes: Past tense of "sair de casa" (to leave home / to go out). It can mean simply leaving the house at a certain time ("Saiu de casa às seis") or leaving home to live elsewhere/going away and not coming back ("saiu de casa e não retornou"). Often followed by details like time (às seis), manner (às pressas = in a hurry), or context (sem se despedir = without saying goodbye).
target_language_example: Ele saiu de casa cedo para pegar o ônibus.
native_language_example: He left home early to catch the bus.

meaning: 'left' / 'came out of' (went out from a place).
additional_notes: Past tense of "sair de" (to leave / to go out of). Used to say someone or something exited a place: "saiu do quarto" (left the room), "saiu do estacionamento" (left the parking lot), "saiu do buraco" (came out of the hole). With feminine nouns, it changes to "saiu da" (e.g., "saiu da casa").
target_language_example: Ela saiu do trabalho mais cedo hoje.
native_language_example: She left work earlier today.

additional_notes: Used to form compound nouns that name a room by its purpose or function: "sala de reuniões" (meeting room), "sala de leitura" (reading room), "sala de estudos" (study room), "sala de cirurgia" (operating room). It’s typically followed by a noun (often plural) describing what happens there.
target_language_example: A entrevista vai ser na sala de espera.
native_language_example: The interview will be in the waiting room.

additional_notes: A common room in a home where people relax, talk, watch TV, etc. Often used with verbs like estar (to be) and ficar (to stay): "Estou na sala de estar." Literal idea is “room for being/staying,” but the natural English translation is “living room.”
target_language_example: Vamos assistir a um filme na sala de estar.
native_language_example: Let’s watch a movie in the living room.

meaning: “to save / to rescue (someone/something)” (with a feminine direct object).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun or feminine pronoun object: salvar a criança (save the child), salvar a Terra (save the Earth), salvar a espécie humana (save the human species). It can mean rescuing from immediate danger (drowning), or preventing something bad from happening (extinction, disaster). Common set phrase: salvar a pele = “to save your skin” (save yourself).
target_language_example: Precisamos agir agora para salvar a cidade.
native_language_example: We need to act now to save the city.

additional_notes: Uses the past tense of salvar (“to save”): salvou = “saved” (3rd person singular). It can mean literally rescuing someone from danger, or figuratively meaning “you really helped me a lot / you were a lifesaver.” Often said to thank someone: “Você salvou a minha vida!”
target_language_example: Obrigado por me ajudar com o carro — você salvou a minha vida!
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me with the car—you saved my life!

meaning: to save her; to rescue her.
additional_notes: This is the verb "salvar" (to save/rescue) + the object pronoun "a" (= her/it, feminine), written with a hyphen after an infinitive: salvar + a → salvá-la. The accent (salvá-) keeps the original stress of "salvar" when the pronoun is attached. Used for saving someone from danger or saving someone medically (e.g., with an antidote).
target_language_example: Temos de salvá-la antes que seja tarde demais.
native_language_example: We have to save her before it's too late.

additional_notes: Used to say you are pleased/content with something: **estar/ficar satisfeito(a) com** + noun. It agrees with the subject: **satisfeito** (male), **satisfeita** (female), **satisfeitos/satisfeitas** (plural). The article changes with the noun: **com a** (feminine singular), **com o** (masc. singular), **com as** (fem. plural), **com os** (masc. plural).
target_language_example: Ela ficou satisfeita com a resposta do professor.
native_language_example: She was satisfied with the teacher’s answer.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is happy/pleased with an outcome. Common with verbs like "estar" (to be) and "ficar" (to become/end up): "estar satisfeito" = be satisfied; "ficar satisfeito" = become satisfied after something happens. "Satisfeito" agrees with the person: "satisfeito" (male), "satisfeita" (female).
target_language_example: Estou satisfeito com o resultado do exame.
native_language_example: I'm satisfied with the exam result.

additional_notes:
"Saudade" is the feeling of missing someone or something, often with nostalgia or affection. It commonly appears as:
- "ter saudade de" = to miss (Eu tenho saudade de você.)
- "estar com saudade de" = to miss / to be missing (Estou com saudade de casa.)
- "sentir saudade de" = to miss / to feel longing for (Sinto saudade dos meus amigos.)
You can also use it alone as an exclamation: "Saudade de você!" = "Miss you!" (very common in messages).
target_language_example: Estou com saudade de você desde que você viajou.
native_language_example: I’ve missed you since you traveled.

additional_notes: Used with a verb like sentir/ter + saudades de + person/thing/activity. "Saudade(s)" is a very common Portuguese idea of missing someone or something with affection and nostalgia. With an infinitive after "de", it means you miss doing that activity (e.g., "saudades de sair"). Often appears as "sinto saudades de..." (I miss...), "tenho saudades de..." (I miss...), or "vai ter/sentir saudades de..." (you will miss...).
target_language_example: Estou com saudades de você e das nossas conversas.
native_language_example: I miss you and our conversations.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb phrase “estar com” (e.g., “estar com saudades de casa”) to say you miss your home/your place. “Saudade(s)” is a very common word for a deep feeling of missing someone or something; adding “de casa” specifies that it’s home you miss.
target_language_example: Depois de duas semanas viajando, eu já estava com saudades de casa.
native_language_example: After two weeks traveling, I was already homesick.

meaning: "I miss you" / "missing you" (a feeling of longing for you).
additional_notes: Used with the noun "saudade" (almost always in the plural: "saudades") to express that you miss someone. Common patterns: "sentir saudades de você" (to miss you), "ficar com saudades de você" (to end up missing you / to start missing you). You can swap "você" for another person: "saudades de você" / "saudades de ti" / "saudades do João".
target_language_example: Estou com saudades de você.
native_language_example: I miss you.

meaning: “... yourself, please” (a polite request with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used after an imperative/reflexive verb to politely ask someone to do something to themselves: apresse-se (hurry up), levante-se (stand up), apresente-se (introduce yourself), sirva-se (help yourself), vista-se (get dressed). The “se” is the reflexive pronoun (“yourself/yourselves”), and “por favor” means “please.” Often you’ll see it as: Verb-se, por favor.
target_language_example: Sente-se, por favor.
native_language_example: Sit down, please.

additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb **se apaixonar (por)**. It’s used with **por** + a person/thing: **se apaixonou por mim** (“fell in love with me”). It can also be used more broadly for becoming passionate about something (a hobby, a place, an idea), depending on context.
target_language_example: Ele se apaixonou por ela na primeira semana.
native_language_example: He fell in love with her in the first week.

additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb pattern "apaixonar-se por" = "to fall in love with." It’s used with a person or sometimes a place/thing. "pela" is "por" + "a" (feminine singular); with masculine you’ll often see "pelo" ("por" + "o").
target_language_example: Ela se apaixonou pela cidade na primeira semana.
native_language_example: She fell in love with the city in the first week.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of the reflexive verb phrase “se apaixonar por” (to fall in love with / to develop strong romantic feelings for someone). It normally takes “por” before the person/thing you fall for: “se apaixonar por alguém”. You can change it for other subjects and tenses (e.g., “eu me apaixonei por…”, “ela se apaixonou por…”).
target_language_example: Eu me apaixonei por ele muito rápido.
native_language_example: I fell in love with him very quickly.

additional_notes: Gerund of the reflexive verb **aproximar-se** (“to approach / to come closer”). Very common with **estar** to describe an action in progress: **está se aproximando** = “is approaching.” Often followed by **de** + person/thing: **se aproximando de mim** (“approaching me”). Can be literal (walking closer) or figurative (getting closer in a race, in distance, etc.).
target_language_example: Tem alguém se aproximando da porta.
native_language_example: Someone is approaching the door.

meaning: to be late; to end up running late.
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nos/vocês/se) to say someone arrives later than expected or planned. Very common with "para" + event/time ("se atrasar para o jantar" = be late for dinner). You can also add how much: "se atrasar um pouco" (be a little late).
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu me atrasei para a reunião.
native_language_example: Sorry, I was late for the meeting.

meaning: to get married; to marry (each other).
additional_notes: Very common verb phrase meaning “to marry” in the sense of entering marriage. It’s reflexive (casar-se), so you’ll often see it with pronouns: eu me caso, você se casa, eles se casam. It’s frequently used with “com” (to marry someone): Ela vai se casar com o João. Also used with “vai/vão se casar” for future plans.
target_language_example: Eles vão se casar no ano que vem.
native_language_example: They’re going to get married next year.

meaning: to marry (someone); to get married to (someone).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase: casar = “to marry,” and se casar = “to get married.” Use com before the person you marry (se casar com alguém). In the past: se casou com; in the future: vai se casar com / irá se casar com. Not the same as casar alguém (“to marry two people,” e.g., a priest marrying a couple).
target_language_example: Ela vai se casar com o namorado no ano que vem.
native_language_example: She’s going to marry her boyfriend next year.

meaning: “(they/you all) got married” / “(they/you all) married (each other)” (past tense).
additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of **casar-se** (“to get married”). The **se** shows it’s reflexive/reciprocal: **eles se casaram** = “they married each other / they got married.” With **vocês**, **se casaram** means “you (plural) got married.” Often used with **onde** (“where”) or **quando** (“when”) to ask about the wedding.
target_language_example: Eles se casaram no civil no ano passado.
native_language_example: They got married at city hall last year.

additional_notes: Past form of the reflexive verb "se casar". It often appears with time expressions (e.g., "o mês passado" = last month) and with places using "em" (e.g., "se casou em Boston" = got married in Boston). You can say "se casou" without mentioning who the person married.
target_language_example: Ela se casou no ano passado.
native_language_example: She got married last year.

additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb "casar-se". Used with "com" to say who someone married: "Ele se casou com ela." In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often also say "casou com" (dropping "se").
target_language_example: Ela se casou com o namorado do colégio.
native_language_example: She married her high school boyfriend.

meaning: “(he/she) married (a woman) / got married to (a woman)”
additional_notes: From the verb casar-se (“to get married”), used reflexively: casar-se com alguém = “to marry/get married to someone.” The "a" is the feminine definite article (“the”) and appears before a woman’s name or a noun like "a mamãe" (“mom”). With a man, you’d say "se casou com o" (o = “the” masculine). Often used in the past ("se casou") to talk about when someone got married.
target_language_example: Ela se casou com a Ana no ano passado.
native_language_example: She married Ana last year.

additional_notes: From the verb "casar-se com" (to get married to). "Se casou" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito): "he/she got married". "Com" = "to/with" in Portuguese, but in English you normally translate it as "married" + direct object (“married a nurse”). "Uma" is used before feminine nouns (uma moça, uma canadense, uma enfermeira, uma viúva). With a masculine noun, use "um": "se casou com um médico".
target_language_example: Ela se casou com uma advogada.
native_language_example: She married a lawyer.

meaning: "is called" / "is named" (referring to the name of a person or thing).
additional_notes: Used with the verb chamar-se (“to be called”), especially for names/labels: Ela se chama Ana. = “Her name is Ana.” In questions: Como isso se chama? = “What is this called?” In Portuguese you can also say O nome dele é…; calling someone a nickname often uses chamar without se: Nós o chamamos Ken.
target_language_example: Este lugar se chama Praia Azul.
native_language_example: This place is called Blue Beach.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of the reflexive verb phrase “se conhecer” = “to meet each other / to first get to know each other.” Often used in questions about when/where/how two people first met: “Onde se conheceram?”, “Como vocês se conheceram?”. With names: “Tom e Maria se conheceram…”. With “vocês”, it can mean “you two/you all met.”
target_language_example: Nós nos conhecemos no trabalho, mas só viramos amigos depois.
native_language_example: We met at work, but we only became friends later.

additional_notes: A reflexive verb: the person apologizing is also the subject (Eu me desculpo; Você se desculpa; Ele/Ela se desculpa; Nós nos desculpamos; Vocês se desculpam; Eles/Elas se desculpam). Common in advice/requests like “Pare de se desculpar” (“Stop apologizing”). Often followed by “por” to say what you’re sorry for: “Me desculpe por chegar tarde.”
target_language_example: Desculpe, eu preciso me desculpar por ontem.
native_language_example: Sorry, I need to apologize for yesterday.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **dar-se conta (de)** = “to realize / notice / become aware (of)”. **Se deu conta de que** is past tense (he/she/it realized that…). Often followed by a clause starting with **que**. Common alternatives: **percebeu que**, **notou que**.
target_language_example: Eu me dei conta de que tinha esquecido a carteira em casa.
native_language_example: I realized that I had forgotten my wallet at home.

additional_notes: Gerund form of the reflexive verb “se divertir” (“to have fun”). Often used with “estar” to describe something happening at the moment: “estar se divertindo” = “to be having fun.” The subject is the one having fun (they are enjoying themselves).
target_language_example: As crianças estão se divertindo no parque.
native_language_example: The kids are having fun at the park.

meaning: to have fun; to enjoy oneself.
additional_notes: A common reflexive verb (divertir-se). It’s used for enjoying yourself at an event or activity: “se divertir muito” = “have a lot of fun.” Often follows “ir” (going to) to talk about future plans: “vai se divertir” = “you’re going to have fun.”
target_language_example: A gente se divertiu muito na festa ontem.
native_language_example: We had a lot of fun at the party yesterday.

additional_notes: Past (pretérito perfeito) of the reflexive verb "se divertir" (to have fun). It agrees with the subject: eu me diverti, você/ele/ela se divertiu, nós nos divertimos, vocês/eles/elas se divertiram. Often used with places/events: "se divertiu em Boston?", "se divertiu na festa?"
target_language_example: A gente se divertiu muito na praia ontem.
native_language_example: We had a lot of fun at the beach yesterday.

meaning: to get along with; to have a good relationship with.
additional_notes: Used with the reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nos/vos/se) + "dar-se bem" + "com" someone (or an animal). It means you have no problems with them and interact well. Common in the present: "Eu me dou bem com...", "Ele/ela se dá bem com...". In Brazil you may also hear both "com Mary" and "com a Mary" (article before a person’s name is regional/style).
target_language_example: Eu me dou bem com os meus colegas de trabalho.
native_language_example: I get along with my coworkers.

meaning: to meet up with; to meet (someone).
additional_notes: Used when you arrange or intend to meet another person. The verb is reflexive (encontrar-se): you’ll often see it conjugated like “eu me encontro com…”, “ele/ela se encontra com…”, “vamos nos encontrar com…”. You can also say “se encontrar” without “com” when the other person is implied (e.g., “Vamos nos encontrar às 5”).
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar com a Ana amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: Let’s meet up with Ana tomorrow morning.

meaning: hiding (oneself); in the act/process of hiding.
additional_notes: This is the gerund (-ndo form) of the reflexive verb "se esconder" (to hide oneself). It’s commonly used with "estar" to describe an action in progress: "está/estava se escondendo" = "is/was hiding." It can be followed by "de" to say who/what someone is hiding from ("se escondendo de mim"), or by a place with "em/atrás de" etc. to say where they’re hiding.
target_language_example: As crianças estavam se escondendo no quarto para assustar os pais.
native_language_example: The kids were hiding in the bedroom to scare their parents.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of the reflexive verb "se esconder" (“to hide oneself”), used with "atrás (de)" to say someone hid behind something. It agrees with the subject: "eu me escondi", "ele/ela se escondeu", "nós nos escondemos", "eles/elas se esconderam".
target_language_example: Ela se escondeu atrás da porta quando ouviu um barulho.
native_language_example: She hid behind the door when she heard a noise.

additional_notes: Past tense of "se esquecer de". It’s used with a subject (ele/ela/você/nós, etc.) + "se esqueceu de" + noun or verb in the infinitive. Example patterns: "se esqueceu de você" = forgot you; "se esqueceu de apagar a luz" = forgot to turn off the light.
target_language_example: Eu me esqueci de levar o guarda-chuva.
native_language_example: I forgot to take the umbrella.

meaning: Vulgar: “to fuck oneself” / “to get screwed”; often used as “go fuck yourself!”
additional_notes: Very offensive/vulgar in Brazilian Portuguese. Commonly used in the imperative as an insult: “Vai se foder!” (to one person), “Vão se foder!” (to multiple people). In other contexts it can mean “to get screwed / to be in trouble / to go badly” (e.g., “Se eu perder esse emprego, eu me fodo.”).
target_language_example: Vai se foder, eu não vou te ajudar.
native_language_example: Go fuck yourself, I’m not going to help you.

additional_notes: From the verb “importar-se” (“to care, to mind, to be bothered”). Very common in questions like “Quem se importa…?” = “Who cares…?”. Often followed by “com” + noun/pronoun: “se importa com isso” (“cares about that”). Note: despite looking like English “import”, “importar-se” usually means “to care/mind,” not “to import goods.”
target_language_example: Ele não se importa com o que os outros pensam.
native_language_example: He doesn't care what other people think.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **se importar com** (“to care about / to mind”). It’s usually followed by **o que** (“what”) plus a clause: *se importa com o que eu penso* = “cares what I think.” Very common in negatives and questions: *Ninguém se importa...* (“Nobody cares...”), *Quem se importa...?* (“Who cares...?”).
target_language_example: Eu não me importo com o que os outros dizem.
native_language_example: I don't care what other people say.

meaning: to join us; to come with us (as part of the group).
additional_notes: Uses the reflexive verb "se juntar (a)" = "to join (someone/a group)". "a nós" means "to us". Very common for invitations: "Quer se juntar a nós?" (Do you want to join us?). You can swap in other people: "se juntar a mim" (join me), "se juntar a eles" (join them).
target_language_example: Quer se juntar a nós para jantar hoje?
native_language_example: Do you want to join us for dinner today?

additional_notes: "Se juntar a" means "to join" (a group/organization). Here it’s used with the plural feminine noun phrase "as forças especiais" (the special forces), so it becomes "às" = "a" + "as". Very common in questions like "Você quer... ?" or "Tem certeza de que quer... ?".
target_language_example: Ele decidiu se juntar às forças especiais no ano passado.
native_language_example: He decided to join the special forces last year.

additional_notes: From the verb **lembrar-se (de)** = “to remember (something/someone).” It uses a reflexive pronoun (**me/te/se/nos/vocês se**) and usually takes **de** before the thing remembered: **Você se lembra de mim?** = “Do you remember me?” Common in questions with **ainda** (“still”): **Ainda se lembra...?**
target_language_example: Eu não me lembro do nome dele.
native_language_example: I don’t remember his name.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "lembrar-se" (to remember) in the reflexive form + "de" + a noun/pronoun/thing remembered: "Ela se lembra de você." In questions, it often means "Do you remember…?" Note: In Brazil, you may also hear "lembra de" without "se" in informal speech.
target_language_example: Você se lembra do nome dele?
native_language_example: Do you remember his name?

additional_notes: From the verb "lembrar-se de" (to remember). It’s reflexive ("se") and needs the preposition "de". With masculine singular nouns or names it usually becomes "do" (= de + o): "se lembra do Tom?". For feminine singular, use "da" (= de + a): "Você se lembra da Maria?". You can also say "Eu me lembro de...", "Você se lembra de...", "Ele/Ela se lembra de...". Often used in questions and negatives: "Você se lembra do...?")
target_language_example: Você se lembra do nosso professor de português?
native_language_example: Do you remember our Portuguese teacher?

meaning: to get up; to stand up.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb (levantar + se). Commonly used for getting up from bed or standing up after sitting/lying down. In Brazilian Portuguese, you’ll often hear it without the pronoun in casual speech (e.g., “Levanta!”), but “se levantar” is the standard form.
target_language_example: Eu preciso me levantar cedo amanhã.
native_language_example: I need to get up early tomorrow.

meaning: "got up" / "stood up" (past tense of se levantar).
additional_notes: Used in the past to talk about rising from bed (wake up and get out of bed) or standing up from a chair/seat. Context tells which meaning fits. Common with time questions (A que horas…?) and with events (Quando… entrou, todo mundo…).
target_language_example: Eu me levantei cedo hoje, mas ele se levantou tarde.
native_language_example: I got up early today, but he got up late.

meaning: “(he/she) stood up and went” (got up and left/went).
additional_notes: Common in storytelling to show two actions in sequence: first someone gets up (from sitting/lying), then goes somewhere. Often followed by a destination with “até” (to/as far as) or “em direção a” (toward), or by “embora” meaning “away/left.” Changes with the subject and tense: “me levantei e fui” (I stood up and went), “se levantaram e foram” (they stood up and went).
target_language_example: Ela se levantou e foi até o balcão para pagar.
native_language_example: She stood up and went to the counter to pay.

additional_notes: Past tense of "se machucar" (a reflexive verb). It’s used when someone is injured or hurts themselves, often with details like when or how: "se machucou em uma queda" (in a fall), "no acidente" (in the accident). You can use it as a question: "Você se machucou?" (Did you get hurt?).
target_language_example: Ele se machucou jogando futebol.
native_language_example: He got hurt playing soccer.

additional_notes: Used for changing where you live (relocating) to a destination. It’s a reflexive verb phrase: *mudar-se* + *para* + place. In everyday speech, it’s common to say *vou me mudar para...* or *vai se mudar para...* (the reflexive pronoun changes with the subject: *me/te/se/nos/vocês se*).
target_language_example: A gente vai se mudar para um apartamento perto do trabalho.
native_language_example: We’re going to move to an apartment near work.

additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb "mudar-se" (often written as "se mudar") + "para" to talk about changing where you live. "Para a" is used before feminine singular places/nouns ("a França", "a Alemanha", "a Austrália"); with masculine it’s "para o" ("para o Brasil"), and with plural it’s "para as/para os".
target_language_example: No ano que vem, a gente vai se mudar para a Espanha.
native_language_example: Next year, we’re going to move to Spain.

meaning: "(they) moved to" (changed residence to a place).
additional_notes: From the verb "mudar-se" = to move (house). "Se" is a reflexive pronoun, and "mudaram" is the 3rd-person plural past (preterite): "they moved". Use "para" before the destination: "se mudaram para Boston". You can change the subject/person: "eu me mudei para...", "você se mudou para...", "nós nos mudamos para...".
target_language_example: Depois que se mudaram para o Rio, começaram um novo trabalho.
native_language_example: After they moved to Rio, they started a new job.

additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb "mudar-se" (to move/relocate). The pattern is: "[person] se mudou para + place". In the past, you’ll often see "se mudou" (moved). It refers to moving house/city/country, not moving an object.
target_language_example: Ela se mudou para São Paulo no ano passado.
native_language_example: She moved to São Paulo last year.

additional_notes: Used when someone volunteers to do an action, often to help: “(Ele/Ela) se ofereceu para + infinitive”. The verb is "oferecer" in the reflexive form (se oferecer) = to offer oneself / to volunteer.
target_language_example: Eu me ofereci para buscar você no aeroporto.
native_language_example: I offered to pick you up at the airport.
