additional_notes: Used with "com" to say someone/something resembles someone/something else: "se parece com você" = "looks like you". In questions, "Como ele se parece?" asks what someone looks like (their appearance). You can also ask for a comparison: "Com que se parece isto?" = "What does this look like?"
target_language_example: Ela se parece com a irmã, mas tem o cabelo mais curto.
native_language_example: She looks like her sister, but she has shorter hair.

additional_notes: Used to compare appearance or similarity. It’s the verb "parecer" in the reflexive form ("se parecer") + "com" (with): "X se parece com Y" = "X resembles Y".
target_language_example: Ela se parece muito com a irmã.
native_language_example: She looks a lot like her sister.

meaning: looks like her mother; resembles her mother.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has a similar appearance to their mother. It comes from the verb phrase "se parecer com" = "to look like / to resemble". You can swap in other people: "se parece com o pai" (looks like his/her father), "se parece com você" (looks like you).
target_language_example: Ele se parece com a mãe, mas tem os olhos do pai.
native_language_example: He looks like his mother, but he has his father's eyes.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "parecer" in the reflexive form "se parecer com" to say someone or something resembles another. "com" = "like"/"with" in this sense. "o" is the masculine singular definite article (“the”); use "a" for feminine ("se parece com a mãe"), "os/as" for plural, or drop the article with names ("se parece com o João" / "se parece com João").
target_language_example: Esse desenho se parece com o original.
native_language_example: This drawing looks like the original.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has a similar appearance (or sometimes personality) to their father. It comes from the verb phrase "se parecer com" = "to look like / to resemble". You can swap in other people: "se parece com a mãe" (his/her mother), "me parece com você" (I look like you). In questions, it often appears as "Você acha que... ?" = "Do you think... ?"
target_language_example: Ela se parece com o pai, mas tem o sorriso da mãe.
native_language_example: She looks like her father, but she has her mother's smile.

additional_notes: Used to say someone (or something) has a strong resemblance to another person/thing. The base verb is "parecer (com)" = "to look like / to seem like"; with "se" it commonly means physical resemblance: "ele se parece com o pai". "muito" intensifies it (a lot). You can also say "parece muito com" without "se" in many contexts.
target_language_example: Ela se parece muito com a irmã mais velha.
native_language_example: She looks a lot like her older sister.

meaning: “have passed since” (a period of time up to now, since an event happened).
additional_notes: Used with a time expression (e.g., "dois meses", "dez anos") + "se passaram" (from "passar") to say that this amount of time has gone by since a past event introduced by "desde que". Very common with "já" to emphasize that time has already passed: "Dez anos já se passaram desde que..." Also appears with other tenses or numbers: "Um mês se passou..." / "Muitos anos se passaram...".
target_language_example: Três semanas já se passaram desde que comecei o curso.
native_language_example: Three weeks have already passed since I started the course.

additional_notes: From the verb **se preocupar (com)** = “to worry (about)” or “to care (about).” It often comes with **com** + a thing/person: *se preocupa com as florestas* (“cares about the forests”). As a suggestion/reassurance, **Não se preocupa.** means “Don’t worry.” (In Brazil, you’ll more commonly hear **Não se preocupe** / **Não se preocupe não**.)
target_language_example: Ela se preocupa com a mãe todos os dias.
native_language_example: She worries about her mom every day.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb: preocupar-se (often written as “se preocupar”). Common patterns: “se preocupar com + noun/pronoun” (to worry about) and “(não) se preocupar” (don’t worry). In speech you’ll often hear “Não se preocupe” (formal/you) or “Não se preocupa” (informal/you), meaning “Don’t worry.”
target_language_example: Não precisa se preocupar com isso agora.
native_language_example: You don’t need to worry about that now.

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive form "se" with the verb "preparar" to describe someone getting themselves ready. Very common with an infinitive after "para" ("se preparando para sair" = getting ready to leave) or with a noun ("se preparando para a viagem" / "se preparando para seu encontro" = preparing for the trip/meeting). Often appears in the progressive: "estar + se preparando" = "to be getting ready".
target_language_example: Estou me preparando para a entrevista amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m getting ready for the interview tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with a subject + (se) recusar a + infinitive to say someone refuses to do something. It’s fairly strong (suggests resistance or unwillingness), similar to “refuse to” in English. The verb is pronominal here: eu me recuso a, você/ele/ela se recusa a, nós nos recusamos a, eles/elas se recusam a.
target_language_example: Ela se recusa a assinar o contrato.
native_language_example: She refuses to sign the contract.

additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb “recusar-se a” (“to refuse to”). It’s followed by a verb in the infinitive: “se recusou a fazer” (refused to do). In the present tense: “(ele) se recusa a …”. In everyday speech you may also hear “recusou” without “se,” but “recusar-se a” is the standard form.
target_language_example: Ela se recusou a responder às perguntas.
native_language_example: She refused to answer the questions.

additional_notes: Past tense (3rd person singular) of "se recusar a" + infinitive. Used when someone decides not to do something (often strongly or firmly): "Ele se recusou a pagar" = "He refused to pay." The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject: eu me recusei, você/ele/ela se recusou, nós nos recusamos, eles/elas se recusaram.
target_language_example: Ela se recusou a pagar porque a conta estava errada.
native_language_example: She refused to pay because the bill was wrong.

meaning: to sit down; to take a seat.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb (sentar-se): the object pronoun (se) is often placed before the verb in Brazilian Portuguese (e.g., “pode se sentar”, “vá se sentar”). Common in polite invitations and instructions. You can also hear “sentar” without “se” in casual speech, but “sentar-se / se sentar” is the standard form.
target_language_example: Pode se sentar, por favor.
native_language_example: Please have a seat.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb "sentir-se" (to feel). Used with adjectives/adverbs to describe someone’s physical or emotional state: "Ele se sente melhor" (He feels better). Common in questions like "Como você se sente?" (How do you feel?). Often also said without the reflexive in casual speech (e.g., "Eu sinto muito" = I’m very sorry), but for describing your state, "sentir-se" is standard.
target_language_example: Eu me sinto cansado hoje.
native_language_example: I feel tired today.

additional_notes: Form of the reflexive verb "sentir-se" (to feel, emotionally/physically). "Se" refers back to the subject (he/she). "Se sentia" is the imperfect past, used for an ongoing feeling in the past, a habitual past feeling, or background description (often after "disse que...": "he/she said (that) he/she felt..."). Common patterns: "se sentia + adjective" (se sentia cansado/a, culpado/a, confiante), "se sentia melhor" (felt better), "não se sentia tão..." (didn’t feel so...).
target_language_example: Eu me sentia nervoso antes da prova.
native_language_example: I felt nervous before the test.

additional_notes: Used with estar (+ se sentindo) to talk about a temporary emotional or physical state. It’s the gerund of the reflexive verb "sentir-se" (to feel), often used after verbs like "estar", "ficar", "parecer".
target_language_example: Estou me sentindo melhor hoje.
native_language_example: I’m feeling better today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "(se) sentir" (to feel) + "bem" (well) to talk about someone’s physical or emotional state. Very common in questions like "Você está se sentindo bem?" and in reported speech like "Ele disse que estava se sentindo bem."
target_language_example: Depois de descansar um pouco, estou me sentindo bem.
native_language_example: After resting a bit, I'm feeling well.

meaning: 'feeling better' (about one’s health, mood, or situation).
additional_notes: From the verb "se sentir" (to feel) + "melhor" (better). Often used to ask or say if someone’s condition has improved: "Você está se sentindo melhor?" You can change tense/person: "estou/me sinto", "estava me sentindo", "vai se sentir". Very common when talking about illness or recovery.
target_language_example: Depois de descansar um pouco, estou me sentindo melhor.
native_language_example: After resting a bit, I’m feeling better.

meaning: to feel (oneself); to feel (in a certain way).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb used with a subject to describe how someone feels physically or emotionally. Often followed by an adjective or expression: se sentir sozinho/a (to feel lonely), se sentir à vontade (to feel comfortable/at ease), se sentir em casa (to feel at home), se sentir confiante (to feel confident). Conjugates like sentir: eu me sinto, você/ele se sente, nós nos sentimos, eles se sentem.
target_language_example: Depois da conversa, eu me senti muito melhor.
native_language_example: After the conversation, I felt much better.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective or past participle to describe how someone felt emotionally or physically. It agrees with the subject: *ele se sentiu cansado* (he felt tired), *ela se sentiu cansada* (she felt tired). Often followed by an adjective like *incrível*, *mal*, *bem*, *usado*, *triste*.
target_language_example: Depois da reunião, ela se sentiu aliviada.
native_language_example: After the meeting, she felt relieved.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **sentar-se** (“to sit down”). Used with **ele/ela/você** (and also with a named subject like “Tom”). Often followed by a place: **se sentou no/na/em...** (“sat (down) on/in/at…”).
target_language_example: Ela se sentou ao meu lado.
native_language_example: She sat down next to me.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about a change of state or identity (profession, size, role, etc.). It often comes with a noun/adjective: "se tornar veterinária" (become a vet), "se tornar maior" (become bigger). In everyday speech, "virar" can be a more informal alternative in some contexts.
target_language_example: Com o tempo, ele se tornou um ótimo líder.
native_language_example: Over time, he became a great leader.

additional_notes: Used to talk about changing into a new state, role, or profession. It’s followed by a noun (often a job/title): se tornar um professor, se tornar um monge. Commonly used with goals or plans (objetivo, querer, decidir, gostar).
target_language_example: Ela quer se tornar uma médica.
native_language_example: She wants to become a doctor.

additional_notes: Past tense (3rd person plural) of the verb phrase “se tornar” = “to become.” Used with plural subjects (“they”) to say a change happened or a new state/identity was reached. Often followed by an adjective or a noun (sometimes with an article): “se tornaram vermelhas” (became red), “se tornaram músicos/advogados” (became musicians/lawyers), “se tornaram uma potência” (became a power).
target_language_example: Com o tempo, as cidades pequenas se tornaram grandes centros.
native_language_example: Over time, small towns became big hubs.

additional_notes: Used to say that two or more people started being friends (often after meeting or spending time together). It’s the past tense of "se tornar" (“to become”). You can specify the people: "O Tom e a Mary se tornaram amigos." You can also add time words like "logo" (soon) or "recentemente" (recently).
target_language_example: Depois de trabalharem juntos por alguns meses, eles se tornaram amigos.
native_language_example: After working together for a few months, they became friends.

additional_notes: Form of the verb "tornar-se" (= to become). Used to say someone/something changed state or became something over time. Often followed by a noun or adjective: "se tornou juiz" (became a judge), "se tornou fluente" (became fluent). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, "virou" is a common alternative.
target_language_example: Com o tempo, isso se tornou mais fácil.
native_language_example: Over time, this became easier.

additional_notes: From the verb "tornar-se" (to become), used with an indefinite masculine noun: "tornou-se um + noun". It often describes a change over time or a new status/role (e.g., "se tornou um símbolo", "se tornou um cidadão"). For feminine nouns, use "se tornou uma".
target_language_example: Com o tempo, ele se tornou um especialista no assunto.
native_language_example: Over time, he became an expert on the subject.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "se tornar" = "to become" in the past ("tornou-se"). You use "uma" because the next word is feminine (e.g., "uma enfermeira", "uma policial"). Often used for someone changing into a new state or role (profession, social status, etc.). Word order can also appear as "tornou-se uma" (more formal).
target_language_example: Depois de anos estudando, ela se tornou uma médica.
native_language_example: After years of studying, she became a doctor.

additional_notes: Used with "se" + subject pronoun "ela" (she). In a conditional sentence, it means "if she" (e.g., "Se ela descobrir..." = "If she finds out..."). In indirect questions after verbs like "perguntar" (to ask) or "saber" (to know), it often means "whether she" ("Ele perguntou se ela..." = "He asked whether she..."). "E se ela...?" commonly means "What if she...?".
target_language_example: Não sei se ela vem hoje.
native_language_example: I don't know whether she's coming today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition ("if he...") or an indirect yes/no question ("whether he..."). Often followed by a verb phrase: "se ele vier" (if he comes), "não sei se ele vai" (I don’t know if he’s going).
target_language_example: Não sei se ele vai conseguir chegar a tempo.
native_language_example: I don’t know whether he’ll manage to arrive on time.

meaning: 'if I' (introduces a condition) or 'whether I' (in indirect questions).
additional_notes: Used to start a clause about a possible condition: "Se eu..." = "If I...". With past subjunctive it often expresses hypothetical situations ("Se eu estivesse..." = "If I were..."). It can also appear after verbs like "imaginar"/"perguntar" meaning "whether" ("Imaginei se eu conseguiria..." = "I wondered if/whether I could...").
target_language_example: Se eu tiver tempo, eu te ligo mais tarde.
native_language_example: If I have time, I’ll call you later.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an unreal or imagined situation, usually followed by what you would do in that case. It uses the imperfect subjunctive of "ser" (fosse) and often pairs with the conditional in the next clause (e.g., "eu faria", "eu ajudaria").
target_language_example: Se eu fosse você, eu falaria com o professor.
native_language_example: If I were you, I would talk to the teacher.

meaning: “if I knew / if I had known.”
additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical condition. With a past result (often with “teria” + past participle), it usually means “if I had known” (a regret about the past). It uses the imperfect subjunctive of “saber” (to know): “soubesse”.
target_language_example: Se eu soubesse antes, eu teria chegado mais cedo.
native_language_example: If I had known earlier, I would have arrived sooner.

meaning: "if I had" / "if I were to have" (hypothetical).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical or unreal condition. "Tivesse" is the imperfect subjunctive of "ter" (to have). It’s commonly followed by a result in the conditional tense: "Se eu tivesse..., eu ajudaria/faria/falaria...". With "tivesse de" it often means "if I had to".
target_language_example: Se eu tivesse mais dinheiro, eu viajaria mais.
native_language_example: If I had more money, I would travel more.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical or unreal situation (often paired with a conditional result): Se eu tivesse dinheiro, eu compraria… / eu poderia… / eu viajaria…. The verb form “tivesse” is the imperfect subjunctive of ter (to have), commonly used after “se” (if) for ‘if I had…’ ideas.
target_language_example: Se eu tivesse dinheiro, alugaria um apartamento maior.
native_language_example: If I had money, I would rent a bigger apartment.

additional_notes: Uses the future subjunctive of the verb **ser** (*for*). It’s very common after **se** to talk about a condition that may happen in the future: **se for encontrado** = “if he is found”, **se for descoberto a tempo** = “if it is discovered in time”. You can also use it for identity/description: **Se for homem...** = “If you’re a man...”.
target_language_example: Eu vou com você se for possível.
native_language_example: I’ll go with you if it’s possible.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical or contrary-to-fact situation. It’s made of **se** (“if”) + **fosse** (imperfect subjunctive of **ser**, “to be”). Often pairs with the conditional in the other clause: **Se fosse..., seria...** (“If it were..., it would be...”). The subject can be implied or stated: **se fosse eu** (“if it were me”), **se fosse verdade** (“if it were true”).
target_language_example: Se fosse você, eu não aceitaria esse trabalho.
native_language_example: If I were you, I wouldn’t take that job.

additional_notes: Used in conditions: "Se não chover..." = "If it doesn’t rain...". It can also mean "otherwise" as a warning or consequence (often followed by a comma): "Se não, ..." = "Otherwise, ...". In set phrases it can add emphasis, like "a maioria..., se não todas" ("most people, if not all") and "não é nada, se não ..." ("is nothing if not ...").
target_language_example: Se não tiveres tempo hoje, podemos ir amanhã; se não, tudo bem.
native_language_example: If you don’t have time today, we can go tomorrow; otherwise, that’s fine.

additional_notes: Uses the future subjunctive of ser (for) after se (if). Common in warnings and conditions: Se não for tratado, vai morrer. It can also mean “if not” in time/choice questions: Se não for agora, quando será? and “unless” in some contexts: Não serei X se não for Y.
target_language_example: Se não for possível hoje, podemos fazer amanhã.
native_language_example: If it isn’t possible today, we can do it tomorrow.

meaning: “if it weren’t for …” / “if it hadn’t been for …” (a condition that didn’t happen).
additional_notes: Used to say that something would have been different without a certain person/thing/circumstance. Very common with the conditional perfect: “eu teria…” (“I would have…”). Often appears as “se não fosse por/pela/pelo …” (especially before nouns), but you can also say “se não fosse + noun” in many cases.
target_language_example: Se não fosse por você, eu não teria terminado a tempo.
native_language_example: If it weren’t for you, I wouldn’t have finished on time.

additional_notes: Used when introducing an indirect yes/no question or a condition, followed by a masculine noun (o fotógrafo, o Tom, o urso) or something treated as masculine. It often translates as “if/whether the …” or simply “if/whether …” in English. Contrast: “se a” for feminine singular, “se os/as” for plural.
target_language_example: Não sei se o ônibus já passou.
native_language_example: I don't know if the bus has already passed.

additional_notes: Used to offer assistance or leave the option open for the other person to ask for help. It’s a conditional clause with "se" (if) + "precisar" (to need) + "de" + a noun (here, "ajuda"). Often paired with an invitation like "me avise" (let me know), "me chama" (call me), or "é só pedir" (just ask). You can change the noun: "se precisar de informações" (if you need information).
target_language_example: Se precisar de ajuda com o formulário, posso explicar.
native_language_example: If you need help with the form, I can explain.

additional_notes: Common in offers of help and polite instructions. Uses the future subjunctive after "se" (if): "se precisar" (“if you need”). Often followed by what to do: "me avise" (let me know), "me chame" (call me), "peça" (ask), "nos ligue" (call us).
target_language_example: Se precisar de algo, estou aqui.
native_language_example: If you need anything, I’m here.

additional_notes: Common polite offer of help. Uses the future subjunctive after "se" (if): "se precisar..." You can add who to contact: "me ligue" (call me), "me diga" (tell me), or "é só pedir" (just ask). Often said as reassurance before someone leaves or starts something.
target_language_example: Se precisar de alguma coisa, estou aqui.
native_language_example: If you need anything, I’m here.

additional_notes: Common polite way to make something optional or to soften a suggestion/offer. It can come at the end (“Pode sair, se quiser.”) or at the beginning (“Se quiser, podemos…”). Often the subject “you” (você) is implied. Uses the future subjunctive of "querer" (quiser).
target_language_example: Se quiser, eu posso te ajudar com isso.
native_language_example: If you’d like, I can help you with that.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition (often at the start of a sentence): if a situation happens, then something else follows. It can be followed by different verb tenses depending on the situation: present (Se você é...), future subjunctive (Se você precisar...), etc.
target_language_example: Se você tiver tempo, podemos conversar depois.
native_language_example: If you have time, we can talk later.

se você fizer alguma coisa contra

target_language_multi_word_term: se você fizer alguma coisa contra
additional_notes: Used to warn or threaten consequences if someone harms, attacks, betrays, or acts against a person or group. Very common in spoken Portuguese in protective/angry contexts. It’s followed by a person (mim, ele, ela) or by a noun phrase (a minha família, o meu pai). Often comes with a consequence in the next clause (ex: "... chamo a polícia", "... vou te prender").
target_language_example: Se você fizer alguma coisa contra a gente, eu vou chamar a polícia.
native_language_example: If you do anything against us, I’m going to call the police.

additional_notes: Used to set up an "if" condition before a result. Common pattern: "Se você fizer isso, (then) ...". In Portuguese, "fizer" is the future subjunctive used after "se" when talking about a possible future action (similar to English "if you do" / "if you ever do"). "Isso" usually refers to something already mentioned; you can also hear "se você fizer isso" = "if you do it".
target_language_example: Se você fizer isso de novo, vou chamar o gerente.
native_language_example: If you do that again, I’m going to call the manager.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition (usually followed by an action or advice). It’s often followed by an infinitive ("se você quer realizar..." = "if you want to achieve...") or by a full clause with "que" ("se você quer que ele..." = "if you want him to..."). You can also drop the subject in conversation: "Se quer...".
target_language_example: Se você quer aprender português mais rápido, pratique um pouco todos os dias.
native_language_example: If you want to learn Portuguese faster, practice a little every day.

additional_notes: Used to offer an option politely or to make something conditional on the other person’s preference. It often comes at the end of the sentence (“…se você quiser”) or at the beginning (“Se você quiser, …”). The verb is in the future subjunctive: quiser (from querer, “to want”).
target_language_example: Podemos sair mais cedo, se você quiser.
native_language_example: We can leave earlier, if you’d like.

additional_notes: Used when talking about obeying rules or instructions (at school, work, games, etc.). Often appears with verbs like poder (can), precisar (need to), dever (should/must), and ter de (have to). You can also specify whose rules: seguir as regras da escola (follow the school rules).
target_language_example: Se você quiser jogar, tem de seguir as regras.
native_language_example: If you want to play, you have to follow the rules.

additional_notes: Plural of "segunda-feira" (Monday). Used with days of the week to talk about something that happens regularly: "todas as segundas-feiras" = "every Monday". Also used for recurring time off: "tirar segundas-feiras" = to take Mondays off.
target_language_example: A academia fecha às segundas-feiras.
native_language_example: The gym is closed on Mondays.

meaning: 'I can speak' / 'I know how to speak'.
additional_notes: Used to say you have the ability to speak a language. It’s the verb saber (sei = “I know/can”) + infinitive falar (“to speak”). Often followed by a language name (sei falar francês) and can be modified with adverbs like só (“only”), um pouco (“a little”), or muito bem (“very well”). In negatives: não sei falar… (“I can’t/don’t know how to speak…”).
target_language_example: Eu sei falar português, mas não muito bem.
native_language_example: I can speak Portuguese, but not very well.

additional_notes: Used to say you know what someone is doing or what needs to be done. It’s the present tense of the verb "saber" (to know facts/information): "(eu) sei" = "I know", followed by "o que" = "what". Often followed by a verb phrase: "Sei o que você quer" (I know what you want).
target_language_example: Eu sei o que você quer dizer.
native_language_example: I know what you mean.

meaning: “I know what the …” / “I know what …” (starting a clause).
additional_notes: This is usually the beginning of a longer sentence: **Sei o que o Tom está fazendo** (“I know what Tom is doing”). **o que** = “what”. The extra **o** is the masculine article (“the”) used before a masculine noun/name (e.g., **o Tom**, **o amanhã** in many dialects). You’ll also see **sei o que a…** with feminine nouns (**a Maria**) or just **sei o que…** without an article.
target_language_example: Sei o que o professor quer dizer.
native_language_example: I know what the teacher means.

additional_notes: Used to say you know the location of someone/something, often before an indirect question or clause: “Sei onde ele mora” (“I know where he lives”). It’s formed by “sei” (I know, from *saber*) + “onde” (where). You can also negate it: “Não sei onde…” (“I don’t know where…”).
target_language_example: Sei onde fica a estação de metrô.
native_language_example: I know where the subway station is.

additional_notes: Used to say you understand the reason for something. "sei" is the 1st-person singular present of "saber" (to know). Here, "por que" (two words) means "why" in indirect questions/statements (e.g., "Eu sei por que ele fez isso"). Don’t confuse it with "porque" (one word), which usually means "because."
target_language_example: Sei por que você está preocupado.
native_language_example: I know why you’re worried.

meaning: “I know why the …” (introducing a reason for what someone did/feels).
additional_notes: Used before a clause to say you know the reason for something: “Sei por que o Tom…” = “I know why Tom…”. Here, **por que** (two words) means **“why”** in indirect questions/statements (I know why…, I don’t know why…). The **o** is the masculine singular definite article (“the”), often used before a name/title in Portuguese (e.g., *o Tom*), but it can also introduce a masculine noun (*o motivo*, *o problema*).
target_language_example: Sei por que o João saiu mais cedo.
native_language_example: I know why João left early.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you know as a fact. "Sei" is the 1st-person singular present of "saber" (to know), and it’s typically followed by a clause with "que" (that). Often used to reassure someone or state certainty (e.g., "Sei que você consegue" = "I know you can do it").
target_language_example: Sei que você está ocupado, mas preciso falar com você.
native_language_example: I know you’re busy, but I need to talk to you.

additional_notes: Used when you (the speaker) are certain about some information and then continue with a statement about someone/something: “Sei que o Tom...” = “I know that Tom...”. It’s made of sei (I know) + que (that) + o (the/masculine singular), so you typically follow it with a masculine noun/name (o Tom, o professor). For feminine you’d say “sei que a...”. Often used with future: “sei que o Tom estará...” = “I know Tom will be...”.
target_language_example: Sei que o ônibus chega às oito.
native_language_example: I know the bus arrives at eight.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something the speaker claims to know about the listener ("you"). Very common for stating facts, assumptions, or showing understanding: "Sei que você entende" (I know you understand). Word-by-word: sei (I know) + que (that) + você (you). In conversation, "você" is common in Brazil; in more formal contexts you may also see "sei que o senhor / a senhora...".
target_language_example: Sei que você está ocupado, mas preciso falar com você por um minuto.
native_language_example: I know you're busy, but I need to talk to you for a minute.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a period of time ("for six years" / "six years ago") or someone’s age. With age, Portuguese often says "ter X anos" (to be X years old): "tinha seis anos" = "I was six." With time periods, it commonly appears with "há" (for/ago) and "desde" (since): "há seis anos" = "for six years" or "six years ago" depending on context.
target_language_example: Moro aqui há seis anos.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here for six years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (por seis meses = for six months), someone’s age (tem seis meses de idade = is six months old), or time after/before something (seis meses depois = six months later). Also common in phrases like seis meses de vida (six months of life).
target_language_example: Fiquei no Brasil por seis meses.
native_language_example: I stayed in Brazil for six months.

additional_notes: Used to greet and welcome a female guest or newcomer. It’s the formal/standard imperative of ser (“to be”): “be welcome.” It often appears with “de volta” (welcome back) or with “a/à” + place/group (e.g., à família, à minha casa). For a man, say “seja bem-vindo”; for more than one person or a mixed group, “sejam bem-vindos/bem-vindas.”
target_language_example: Seja bem-vinda ao time!
native_language_example: Welcome to the team!

additional_notes: Used to greet and welcome more than one person (or a mixed group) in a formal/neutral way. Literally “be well-welcomed,” using the verb ser in the present subjunctive (“sejam”). For one person, you’ll often hear “seja bem-vindo(a).” You can add “a/ao/à + place/event” (e.g., “à nossa aula”).
target_language_example: Sejam bem-vindos ao nosso curso!
native_language_example: Welcome to our course!

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone left, reacted, or did something in complete silence. You can add who they didn’t speak to: “sem dizer uma palavra a ninguém” = “without saying a word to anyone.”
target_language_example: Ele foi embora sem dizer uma palavra.
native_language_example: He left without saying a word.

additional_notes: Used to agree to help or say something is doable. Often followed by an infinitive (podemos ajudar / podemos fazer / podemos ir). “Sem problema” is a common, casual way to say “no problem” (similar to “sem problemas” or “sem stress”).
target_language_example: Sem problema; podemos resolver isso amanhã.
native_language_example: No problem; we can solve that tomorrow.

meaning: at a loss for words; not knowing what to say.
additional_notes: Used to describe being speechless or unsure what to say next, often because of surprise, embarrassment, or a difficult moment. You can use it as a standalone phrase at the beginning of a sentence ("Sem saber o que dizer, ...") or after a verb like "estar" ("Eu estava sem saber o que dizer").
target_language_example: Fiquei sem saber o que dizer quando ouvi a notícia.
native_language_example: I was at a loss for words when I heard the news.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened in the previous week. It often appears without a preposition (e.g., "Vi ela semana passada"), but you can also say "na semana passada" (more explicit: "in the last week").
target_language_example: Eu comecei meu novo trabalho semana passada.
native_language_example: I started my new job last week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the week after the current one. Often appears with or without the article: "na semana que vem" / "a semana que vem" / just "semana que vem" (especially in casual speech). Common with future time expressions like "até" (see you).
target_language_example: A reunião ficou marcada para a semana que vem.
native_language_example: The meeting was scheduled for next week.

meaning: “has always been” / “was always” (something was consistently true in the past).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a lasting characteristic, situation, or opinion from the past up to a reference point (often up to now). It’s the verb "ser" (foi = past of "to be") with "sempre" (“always”). Common with descriptions: "sempre foi + adjective/noun" (e.g., "sempre foi reservado", "sempre foi meu favorito").
target_language_example: Ela sempre foi muito gentil com todo mundo.
native_language_example: She has always been very kind to everyone.

meaning: “always” + “me” (i.e., something always happens to me / affects me).
additional_notes: Used before a verb: **sempre** (always) + **me** (object pronoun “me”). It often translates as “always + verb + me,” “always tells me,” “always reminds me,” “always makes me,” etc. The **me** means *to me* (indirect object) or *me* (direct object), depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Eles sempre me ajudam quando preciso.
native_language_example: They always help me when I need it.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has had a desire for something for a long time. It’s the imperfect tense of "querer" (quis = "wanted"), often with an infinitive ("sempre quis estudar") or with "que" + subjunctive to express what someone wanted another person to do ("sempre quis que fôssemos...").
target_language_example: Eu sempre quis aprender a tocar violão.
native_language_example: I always wanted to learn to play the guitar.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a habitual action: someone consistently uses or wears something. Often followed by a noun (e.g., "sempre usa preto" = always wears black). Note: "usa" is the 3rd-person singular form of "usar" (he/she/it uses; you (formal) use).
target_language_example: Ela sempre usa óculos quando lê.
native_language_example: She always wears glasses when she reads.

additional_notes: A strong romantic or affectionate phrase. "sempre" = always; "vou" is from "ir" (to go) used to form the near-future: "vou amar" = "I’m going to love" / "I will love". "te" means "you" (informal singular, used with someone you call "você"), and it can also appear after the verb: "vou amar-te" (more formal/literary).
target_language_example: Não importa a distância: sempre vou te amar.
native_language_example: No matter the distance, I will always love you.

meaning: to sit down; to seat oneself.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb (sentar + se). Often used in invitations or instructions: "Pode/Podem sentar-se" (You can sit down), "Vem sentar-se" (Come sit down). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, it’s also common to say "sentar" without "-se" (e.g., "Pode sentar").
target_language_example: Pode sentar-se aqui, por favor.
native_language_example: You can sit here, please.

meaning: to sit back there (in the back).
additional_notes: Used to ask or say that someone will sit in the back area (often the back seat of a car, or the back of a room/bus). You can use it as a polite request with “posso…?” (can I…?) or “permita-me…” (allow me…).
target_language_example: Eu prefiro sentar lá atrás para ter mais espaço.
native_language_example: I prefer to sit back there (in the back) to have more room.

meaning: to sit in the back (rear seat/at the back).
additional_notes: Used to say someone will sit in the back part of a vehicle (like the back seat of a car) or at the back of a place (like the back of a classroom). Often appears with verbs like "deixar" (to let), "mandar" (to tell/order), or in a question asking permission ("Podemos...?").
target_language_example: As crianças vão sentar na parte de trás do carro.
native_language_example: The kids are going to sit in the back of the car.

meaning: to sit in the back (back seats / back row).
additional_notes: Used to say someone sits at the back of a place like a car, bus, classroom, or room. Often implies “in the back seats” or “in the back row.” You’ll also see: “no fundo” (in the back, singular) and “lá no fundo” (way in the back).
target_language_example: Se não houver lugar na frente, podemos sentar nos fundos.
native_language_example: If there’s no room in the front, we can sit in the back.

additional_notes: Imperative form of **sentar-se** (“to sit down”), used when speaking to **você**. Often comes with polite words like **por favor**. More informal alternatives are **senta** (to tu) or **senta aí** (“sit there/over there”).
target_language_example: Pode entrar e sente-se, por favor.
native_language_example: You can come in and sit down, please.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "sentir" with the object pronoun "me" (= me). Very common for describing how you felt at a specific moment (emotionally or physically): "Senti-me triste" (I felt sad), "Senti-me tonto" (I felt dizzy). In everyday English, you usually translate it simply as "I felt..." rather than the more literal "I felt myself...".
target_language_example: Senti-me melhor depois de descansar.
native_language_example: I felt better after resting.

meaning: we miss you / we miss you (formal).
additional_notes: From the expression "sentir falta de" = "to miss" (literally, "to feel (someone’s) absence"). "Sentimos" is "we miss" (present tense). "a sua" is a more formal way to say "your" (often used with "você"), but depending on context it can also mean "his/her" (formal) in some varieties. You can also say "Sentimos a sua falta" by itself as a message to someone who’s away.
target_language_example: Sentimos a sua falta aqui em casa.
native_language_example: We miss you here at home.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of “sentir-se” (to feel). Very common with adjectives to describe how someone felt at a specific moment: “sentiu-se tímida/só/tonto/humilhado”. The adjective agrees with the person (e.g., tímida for a woman; tonto for a man).
target_language_example: Depois da notícia, ele sentiu-se aliviado.
native_language_example: After the news, he felt relieved.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of the reflexive verb sentar-se (“to sit down”). It commonly appears with a place introduced by em/num/na (“on/in”) or with à (“at/to,” as in à mesa = “at the table”).
target_language_example: Ela sentou-se ao meu lado.
native_language_example: She sat down next to me.

additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb "sentar-se" (to sit down). "Ao lado de" means "next to/beside" and is followed by a person or object: "ao lado dele" (next to him), "ao lado da cama" (next to the bed). You can change the subject: "sentei-me ao lado" (I sat down), "sentaram-se ao lado" (they sat down).
target_language_example: Eu me sentei ao lado da minha amiga no ônibus.
native_language_example: I sat down next to my friend on the bus.

additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb **sentar-se** (“to sit down”). **na** is the contraction of **em + a** (“in/on/at + the”) and is used before a **feminine singular** noun: *na cadeira, na cama, na terra*. With a masculine noun, you usually use **no** (*sentou-se no sofá*). The **-se** doesn’t translate directly into English; it’s part of how Portuguese forms “sit down.”
target_language_example: Ela sentou-se na cadeira ao lado da janela.
native_language_example: She sat down in the chair next to the window.

meaning: 'sat next to me' / 'sat by my side.'
additional_notes: Past tense of "sentar-se" (to sit down). "Ao meu lado" means "next to me" or "by my side" and is used for physical position (e.g., in a church, on a bus). You’ll also often see it with "se": "(Ele/Ela) se sentou ao meu lado."
target_language_example: Um senhor sentou ao meu lado no ônibus.
native_language_example: A man sat next to me on the bus.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "ser" + past participle "amado" to form a passive idea: someone loves you. It often appears with "por" to say who loves you (e.g., "ser amado por alguém" = "to be loved by someone"). You can also use it in a negative form: "não ser amado" = "not to be loved".
target_language_example: Todo mundo quer ser amado.
native_language_example: Everyone wants to be loved.

meaning: 'to be able to' (to be capable of).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: ser capaz de + verb (e.g., ser capaz de fazer). Often expresses ability, capacity, or what someone is expected to manage: 'Você deve/deveria ser capaz de...'. In the negative, it means not being able to: 'não ser capaz de...'.
target_language_example: Eu não sou capaz de terminar hoje, mas posso entregar amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m not able to finish today, but I can deliver it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive after verbs/expressions like "dever" (should), "precisar" (need), or in phrases like "o que tem que ser feito" = "what has to be done." It’s the passive form of "fazer" (to do/make): "fazer" (active) → "ser feito" (to be done). Often used when the focus is on the task/result, not who does it.
target_language_example: Ainda há muito trabalho a ser feito antes do prazo.
native_language_example: There is still a lot of work to be done before the deadline.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "ser" (to be) + the adjective "feliz" (happy) to talk about being happy in general, as a state/goal (often translated as "to be happy"). Common in sentences about what someone wants or what matters in life (e.g., "quer ser feliz", "para ser feliz...").
target_language_example: Tudo o que eu quero é ser feliz.
native_language_example: All I want is to be happy.

meaning: to be honest; to be truthful.
additional_notes: Used both literally (someone is an honest person) and as a conversational filler meaning “to be honest / honestly,” often to introduce a frank opinion (e.g., “Para ser honesto, ...”). In everyday speech, you’ll also hear “pra ser honesto” (short for “para”).
target_language_example: Para ser honesto, eu não entendi a pergunta.
native_language_example: To be honest, I didn’t understand the question.

additional_notes: Used to advise or warn someone to pay more attention and avoid mistakes or accidents. Common with verbs like "dever" (should) and "precisar" (need to): "Você deveria/precisa ser mais cuidadoso." You can add a time frame like "de agora em diante" (from now on). The adjective agrees with the person: "cuidadoso" (male), "cuidadosa" (female), "cuidadosos/cuidadosas" (plural).
target_language_example: Ao atravessar a rua, você precisa ser mais cuidadoso.
native_language_example: When crossing the street, you need to be more careful.

meaning: to be so (adjective); to be that + adjective.
additional_notes: Used with an adjective to emphasize a quality: "ser tão + adjetivo" (e.g., "ser tão cruel"). Often appears in complaints or praise ("Como você pôde ser tão..." / "Obrigado por ser tão..."). You can also use it in comparisons with "tão ... quanto" = "as ... as" (e.g., "não ser tão valioso quanto..."). The adjective agrees with the person described (estúpida/estúpido, cooperativo/cooperativa, etc.).
target_language_example: Desculpa por ser tão impaciente.
native_language_example: Sorry for being so impatient.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ser** + the masculine indefinite article **um** to identify what someone/something is (profession, category, identity, or what it’s meant to be). For feminine nouns, use **ser uma**. Often contrasts with **estar** (temporary states): **ser um médico** = to be a doctor (identity/profession).
target_language_example: O meu irmão quer ser um engenheiro.
native_language_example: My brother wants to be an engineer.

meaning: to be a good (one) / to make a good (something).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to describe someone’s character or suitability for a role (e.g., ser um bom marido, ser um bom terapeuta). Often appears with parecer (seem) or in the future tense (vai ser) to talk about how someone is or will be.
target_language_example: Ela quer ser um bom exemplo para os filhos.
native_language_example: She wants to be a good example for her children.

meaning: to be a bit more (…); to be a little more (…).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective (discreto, exato, modesto, preciso, etc.) to make a polite suggestion or request for a change in behavior or quality. Often appears in questions/requests: “Você poderia ser um pouco mais…?”
target_language_example: Você pode ser um pouco mais paciente comigo?
native_language_example: Can you be a bit more patient with me?

meaning: “to be a/an” (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "ser" (“to be”) + the feminine indefinite article "uma" (“a/an”) to describe what someone/something is (identity, role, category). It must agree with gender: use "ser um" before masculine nouns ("ser um professor"), and "ser uma" before feminine nouns ("ser uma professora"). In the past or with modals it often appears as "para ser uma..." (“to be a... / to become a...”).
target_language_example: Ela quer ser uma médica.
native_language_example: She wants to be a doctor.

meaning: to be a person (often: to be a certain kind of person).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective or description to say what someone’s character/identity is like: “ser uma pessoa honesta” (to be an honest person), “ser uma pessoa melhor” (to be a better person). It often expresses a lasting quality (ser) rather than a temporary state. You can also add “de + noun” to describe character: “uma pessoa de mau caráter” (a person of bad character).
target_language_example: Eu tento ser uma pessoa responsável no trabalho.
native_language_example: I try to be a responsible person at work.

additional_notes: Plural of "ser humano". Used in a general, collective sense (often in scientific, philosophical, or formal contexts) to talk about people as a species. Can appear as an apposition for emphasis: "nós, seres humanos" = "we humans".
target_language_example: Como seres humanos, precisamos uns dos outros.
native_language_example: As human beings, we need each other.

additional_notes: Used to politely say that something would be helpful/appreciated. It agrees with the noun: bem-vinda (feminine singular), bem-vindo (masculine singular), bem-vindas/bem-vindos (plural). Often used with offers or requests for help, a drink, etc.
target_language_example: Um pouco de água agora seria bem-vinda.
native_language_example: Some water now would be welcome.

meaning: "would be able to" / "could" (would be capable of).
additional_notes: Conditional form of **ser capaz de**. It’s used to talk about a hypothetical ability or possibility in the past/future, or to make a request/polite question: **Você seria capaz de…?** = “Could you…?”. In some contexts it can also mean “I wouldn’t have the heart / I couldn’t bring myself to…”, especially in negatives (e.g., **Não seria capaz de fazer isso**).
target_language_example: Você seria capaz de me ajudar com isso?
native_language_example: Could you help me with this?

meaning: "it would be better if" (suggesting an alternative).
additional_notes: Used to give advice or make a polite suggestion about what someone should do. It’s the conditional of "ser" ("seria" = "would be"), followed by "melhor" (better) and "se" (if). Often followed by the imperfect subjunctive: "seria melhor se você fizesse..." (it would be better if you did...).
target_language_example: Seria melhor se você chegasse mais cedo amanhã.
native_language_example: It would be better if you arrived earlier tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is welcome to come/enter/join, often after phrases like “quem quiser…” (whoever wants to…) or “qualquer um que…” (anyone who…). It can also imply “feel free to come.” Agree the ending with the person: você/ele será bem-vindo; ela será bem-vinda; vocês/eles serão bem-vindos; elas serão bem-vindas.
target_language_example: Se você quiser vir amanhã, será bem-vindo.
native_language_example: If you want to come tomorrow, you’ll be welcome.

meaning: “will be able to”; “will be capable of”.
additional_notes: Future tense of “ser capaz de” (to be able to / be capable of) + an infinitive verb. Used for ability/possibility in the future, often with “não/nunca” for impossibility (“não/nunca será capaz de…”). In sentence 4, it means being willing/ready to do anything (“ser capaz de tudo”).
target_language_example: Você será capaz de terminar hoje?
native_language_example: Will you be able to finish today?

meaning: Used to express wonder/uncertainty: “I wonder… / could it be that…?”
additional_notes: Often inserted into a question to show you’re guessing, curious, or not sure about the answer. It can follow question words like quem (who), onde (where), o que (what), etc.: “Quem será que…?” = “I wonder who…”. It doesn’t change the basic question, but makes it sound more speculative.
target_language_example: Será que ele já chegou?
native_language_example: I wonder if he’s arrived already.

additional_notes: Used to say someone will be good at a role/job (often followed by a noun like médico, professor, colega de quarto). From ser (to be) in the future tense: ele será = “he will be”. You can also use it for things: Será um bom dia. = “It will be a good day.”
target_language_example: A Ana será uma boa líder.
native_language_example: Ana will be a good leader.

meaning: "I wonder if he..." / "Could it be that he...?"
additional_notes: Used to introduce a doubt or question when you’re not sure about the answer. It’s very common in spoken Portuguese and often sounds softer/more tentative than a direct question. You can use it with many verbs: "Será que ele vem?" (I wonder if he’s coming). The subject can change: "será que eu/ela/vocês...".
target_language_example: Será que ele já chegou em casa?
native_language_example: I wonder if he’s already gotten home.

meaning: "I wonder if they..." / "could it be that they..." (a way to ask a question with doubt).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a question when you’re unsure or speculating. It often corresponds to English “I wonder if…” rather than a simple yes/no question. In Brazil it’s very common in everyday speech. Note: the verb after it can be in the present or future (e.g., “Será que eles vêm?” / “Será que eles vão vir?”).
target_language_example: Será que eles já chegaram?
native_language_example: I wonder if they’ve arrived already.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a question when you’re unsure and are speculating (often like “Do you think…?” / “I wonder whether…”). "Será que" can be used with other subjects too (será que a…, será que ele/ela…, será que eu…). In English you usually don’t translate it word-for-word.
target_language_example: Será que o ônibus já passou?
native_language_example: I wonder if the bus has already passed.

additional_notes: A very polite, formal way to make a request—often to a man you don’t know well (e.g., staff, an older man). Literally it’s like “would it be that you could…”, but it functions as “Could you…?” / “Would you be able to…?” In Brazil, you’ll often hear the less formal version with "você": "Será que você poderia...?"
target_language_example: Será que o senhor poderia me ajudar com estas malas?
native_language_example: Could you help me with these suitcases?

additional_notes: A time expression used to say a duration ("for seven years") or a point in time later ("seven years later"). Common patterns: "por sete anos" = for seven years; "há sete anos" = (since) seven years ago / for seven years (with ongoing situations); "sete anos depois" = seven years later. "Sete anos." alone can be a short answer meaning "Seven years."
target_language_example: Trabalhei nessa empresa por sete anos.
native_language_example: I worked at that company for seven years.

meaning: “seven is a number …” (used to say what kind of number seven is, often “a lucky number”).
additional_notes: This is a simple statement pattern: “[number] é um número + (de/da…)”. You’ll very often hear it completed as “sete é um número da sorte” or “sete é um número que dá sorte” (“seven is a lucky number”). In Portuguese you can say either “O sete é um número…” or just “Sete é um número…” (both are common).
target_language_example: Para muita gente, sete é um número da sorte.
native_language_example: For many people, seven is a lucky number.

additional_notes: “Seu” agrees with the thing owned (amigo = masculine), not with the owner. So “seu amigo” can mean “your friend” (to you) or “his/her friend” (3rd person), depending on context. In Brazil, to avoid ambiguity people often say “o amigo dele/dela” (= his/her friend).
target_language_example: Você já falou com seu amigo sobre isso?
native_language_example: Have you already talked to your friend about that?

additional_notes: Seu = “your” (formal, or used when speaking to/with someone you address as “você”; also can mean “his/her/their” in some contexts). Aniversário usually means “birthday,” but it can also mean another kind of anniversary, so you may see clarifications like “aniversário de casamento” (wedding anniversary).
target_language_example: Não vou esquecer do seu aniversário este ano.
native_language_example: I won’t forget your birthday this year.

additional_notes: “Seu” means “your” (also “his/her/its” depending on context). With family words it’s often used as a polite way to address someone: “seu avô” = “your grandfather.” You may also hear “o seu avô” (with the article) without changing the meaning. If you want to be extra clear, you can say “o avô dele/dela” = “his/her grandfather.”
target_language_example: Seu avô mora aqui perto?
native_language_example: Does your grandfather live nearby?

additional_notes: “Seu/sua” is a possessive that can mean “your” (especially with você), but it can also mean “his/her/their.” In Brazilian Portuguese, to avoid ambiguity, people often use “o cabelo dele/dela” (= his/her hair). With “seu cabelo,” context usually makes clear whose hair it is.
target_language_example: Seu cabelo está lindo hoje.
native_language_example: Your hair looks beautiful today.

additional_notes: “Seu” can mean “your” (formal singular) or “his/her/its,” so you use context to know whose dog it is. With “você,” Portuguese often uses “seu” (e.g., “Seu cachorro tem pulgas?” = “Does your dog have fleas?”). If you want to be clearer, you can say “o cachorro dele/dela” (his/her dog) or “o seu cachorro” (your dog).
target_language_example: Seu cachorro é muito amigável.
native_language_example: Your dog is very friendly.

meaning: your car / his car / her car / their car.
additional_notes: "Seu" can mean "your" (formal or plural) or "his/her/their" depending on context. In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often use "o seu carro" for "your car" and "o carro dele/dela" to be clearer about "his/her car."
target_language_example: Onde você estacionou o seu carro?
native_language_example: Where did you park your car?

additional_notes: “Seu/sua” is a possessive that can mean “your” (formal singular, or in some regions also informal) and can also mean “his/her/their” (especially in Brazil). Context usually makes it clear. “Casaco” is “coat” (often also used for a jacket). You may also see “o casaco dele/dela” to be unambiguous (“his/her coat”).
target_language_example: Pegue seu casaco antes de sair.
native_language_example: Grab your coat before you leave.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the listener’s phone. “Seu” agrees with the noun (here, “celular”), and can mean “your” (to one person) or “your” (to you all) depending on context. In many places you’ll also hear “o seu celular” (“your cell phone”).
target_language_example: Você trouxe seu celular para a reunião?
native_language_example: Did you bring your cell phone to the meeting?

additional_notes: "Seu" means "your" (informal singular) or "his" / "her" / "its" / "their" (because "seu/sua" can be ambiguous). In these examples, context makes it clear it means "your". "Conselho" is a countable noun: you can ask for "um conselho" (a piece of advice) or "seu conselho" (your advice). Common with verbs like "precisar de" (Preciso do seu conselho), "seguir" (Vou seguir o seu conselho), and "agradecer" (Sou grato pelo/pelo seu conselho).
target_language_example: Obrigado pelo seu conselho — vou tentar de novo.
native_language_example: Thanks for your advice — I’m going to try again.

meaning: “your heart”; also “your feelings/affection (love)” in romantic contexts.
additional_notes: Literal meaning is a physical heart (“your heart”). Very common in phrases about emotions: ganhar o seu coração = “to win your heart”; ouvir/escutar o seu coração = “listen to your heart” (follow your feelings/intuition); perder o (seu) coração = “to lose your heart,” i.e., fall in love.
target_language_example: Eu não quero partir, mas preciso seguir o meu coração.
native_language_example: I don’t want to leave, but I need to follow my heart.

additional_notes: Common way to refer to a student’s homework. Often used with verbs like fazer (to do), terminar/acabar (to finish), esquecer (to forget), and ajudar com (to help with). In Brazilian Portuguese, dever de casa is very common; lição de casa is also used.
target_language_example: Você já fez o seu dever de casa?
native_language_example: Have you done your homework yet?

additional_notes: “Seu/sua” is a possessive that can mean “your” (especially with você / formal you) or “his/her/its,” depending on context. If you want to avoid ambiguity, people often say “o dinheiro dele” (his money) or “o dinheiro dela” (her money). You can also say “teu dinheiro” for “your money” in places where “tu” is used.
target_language_example: Eu não quero o seu dinheiro; eu só quero ajuda.
native_language_example: I don’t want your money; I just want help.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to someone’s address. "Seu" is a possessive that usually means "your" (often formal, or when speaking to someone as "você"), but it can also mean "his/her/their" depending on context. In forms you may see "endereço residencial" for "home/residential address."
target_language_example: Você pode confirmar seu endereço, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you confirm your address, please?

meaning: your office; his/her/their office (depending on context).
additional_notes: “Seu” is a possessive that can mean “your” (often formal) or “his/her/their,” so context tells you whose office it is. “Escritório” is an office (workplace room). For clarity, Brazilians often say “o seu escritório” (your office) or use “dele/dela” (his/her): “no escritório dele/dela.”
target_language_example: Posso falar com você no seu escritório depois do almoço?
native_language_example: Can I talk to you in your office after lunch?

meaning: your son (or: his/her son, depending on context).
additional_notes: "Seu" can mean "your" (formal singular or in many places also plural) or "his/her". In speech, Brazilians often prefer "o seu filho" for clarity, or use "dele/dela" ("o filho dele/dela") to avoid ambiguity.
target_language_example: Como está o seu filho hoje?
native_language_example: How is your son today?

additional_notes: “Seu” can mean “your” (formal singular / you) or “his/her/its” (third person). In Brazil, to avoid confusion people often say “o guarda-chuva dele/dela” (“his/her umbrella”) or “o seu guarda-chuva” for “your umbrella.” You may see it with or without the article: “seu guarda-chuva” / “o seu guarda-chuva.”
target_language_example: Você esqueceu seu guarda-chuva aqui.
native_language_example: You forgot your umbrella here.

additional_notes: “Seu” can mean “your” (formal or in some regions) or “his/her,” depending on context. It agrees with the thing owned (irmão = masculine singular). If you want to be unambiguous for “his brother,” you can say “o irmão dele”; for “her brother,” “o irmão dela.”
target_language_example: Ela foi ao cinema com seu irmão.
native_language_example: She went to the movies with her brother.

additional_notes: "Seu" can mean "your" (formal singular) or "his/her" depending on context. "Irmão mais velho" means the older brother (older than the other sibling being compared). Often used in comparisons: "diferente de...", "igualzinho a...".
target_language_example: Meu irmão mais novo é alto, mas seu irmão mais velho é mais alto ainda.
native_language_example: My younger brother is tall, but your/his older brother is even taller.

additional_notes: "Seu/sua" is a possessive that can mean "your" (when talking to someone as você) and can also mean "his" or "her" depending on context. Because it can be ambiguous, Brazilians often say "o livro dele/dela" for "his/her book". In classroom instructions, "Abra seu livro..." usually means "Open your book...".
target_language_example: Você pode colocar seu livro na mochila?
native_language_example: Can you put your book in your backpack?

additional_notes: "Seu" is a possessive that can mean "your" (formal), "his", "her", or "their" depending on context. "Seu marido" means "someone’s husband" (often "her husband" in sentences like the examples). If you want to be extra clear, you can also say "o marido dela" (her husband) or "o marido dele" (his husband).
target_language_example: Você já conheceu o seu marido?
native_language_example: Have you met your husband yet?

meaning: your boyfriend (or her/his boyfriend, depending on context).
additional_notes: "Seu" can mean "your" (informal in many parts of Brazil) or "his/her"; context tells you whose boyfriend it is. "Namorado" is a male partner/boyfriend; for a female partner you’d say "sua namorada". Often you’ll also hear "o namorado dele/dela" to make it clearly "his/her boyfriend."
target_language_example: Você já conheceu seu namorado?
native_language_example: Have you met your boyfriend (or her/his boyfriend)?

meaning: your name (or his/her/your formal name, depending on context).
additional_notes: "Seu" can mean "your" (informal singular in Brazil; also formal "your" with você/o senhor/a senhora) and can also mean "his" or "her" depending on context. In "limpar seu nome", it refers to clearing someone’s reputation/record (literally "to clean your/his/her name").
target_language_example: Qual é o seu nome completo?
native_language_example: What is your full name?

additional_notes: Used when requesting or filling in someone’s identifying information, especially on forms, envelopes, registrations, or deliveries. Can appear as a full sentence/request: "Seu nome e endereço, por favor." Variations include "o seu nome e endereço" (more explicit) and the polite "por favor."
target_language_example: Preciso do seu nome e endereço para enviar a encomenda.
native_language_example: I need your name and address to send the package.

meaning: 'your name is' (formal) / 'his or her name is'.
additional_notes: Uses "seu" (your/his/her) + "nome" (name) + "é" (is). In Brazilian Portuguese, "seu" is commonly used as formal 'your' (especially with "você") and can also mean 'his/her' depending on context, so it can be ambiguous. Often used to ask or confirm someone’s name, typically with a question intonation or a question mark (e.g., "Seu nome é Ken?").
target_language_example: Desculpe, seu nome é Ana?
native_language_example: Sorry, is your name Ana?

additional_notes: "Seu" is a possessive that can mean "your" (especially formal or in Brazil) but it can also mean "his/her/their" depending on context, so sometimes it’s ambiguous. "Novo" agrees with the noun: seu novo carro (masc. sing.), sua nova casa (fem. sing.), seus novos amigos (masc. pl.), suas novas ideias (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Você já conheceu seu novo professor?
native_language_example: Have you met your new teacher yet?

meaning: your phone number (or his/her phone number, depending on context).
additional_notes: "Seu/sua" can mean "your" (informal singular in Brazil) or "his/her/their". In these sentences it usually means "your" when speaking directly to someone, and "his/her" when talking about another person. You’ll also hear "o seu número de telefone" (with the article) and just "seu número de telefone"—both are common.
target_language_example: Pode me dizer seu número de telefone, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you tell me your phone number, please?

meaning: your goal; his/her goal (depending on context).
additional_notes: "Seu" can mean "your" (informal singular) or "his/her/its". In Brazil, "seu objetivo" is often understood as "your goal" if you’re speaking directly to someone; for clarity, people also use "o seu objetivo" (your) or "o objetivo dele/dela" (his/her). Common with verbs like "alcançar" (to achieve/reach) and "atingir" (to hit/reach).
target_language_example: Qual é seu objetivo para este ano?
native_language_example: What is your goal for this year?

meaning: your father / his father / her father.
additional_notes: "Seu" (and "sua") can mean "your" (formal or when using "você"), or "his/her/their" depending on context. So "seu pai" can mean "your dad" or "his/her dad". If you need to be extra clear, Portuguese often uses "o pai dele" (his father) or "o pai dela" (her father).
target_language_example: Você pode chamar seu pai para vir aqui?
native_language_example: Can you call your father to come here?

meaning: 'your father is' (introduces what someone’s father is like or what his job/identity is).
additional_notes: Used to describe or ask about someone’s father (appearance/personality) or profession: "Seu pai é alto" (tall), "Seu pai é médico?" (a doctor?). "Seu" here means “your” in the formal sense (also used for “his/her” depending on context). In casual speech with friends, many people use "teu pai é" (common in some regions) or "o seu pai é" for clarity/emphasis.
target_language_example: Seu pai é professor de matemática?
native_language_example: Is your father a math teacher?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person informally (você) or as a polite form in Brazil. In Portugal, “seu” can also mean “his/your (formal)” depending on context; to be extra clear, you may hear “o teu passaporte” (informal) or “o seu passaporte” (formal). Often used at airports, hotels, border control, etc., especially in requests like “Seu passaporte, por favor.”
target_language_example: Preciso do seu passaporte para fazer o check-in.
native_language_example: I need your passport to check in.

additional_notes: Used to talk to someone about the country they are from/live in. "Seu" agrees with the noun (país, masculine), not the person; it can mean “your” (you) or “his/her/its” depending on context, though with "você" it’s usually “your.” Often appears with the article: "o seu país".
target_language_example: Como é o clima no seu país?
native_language_example: What’s the weather like in your country?

additional_notes: "Seu" is a possessive that can mean "your" (informal singular), or "his/her/their". Because it can be ambiguous, people often use "o plano dele/dela" to be clearer. "Seu plano" is used just like English "your/his/her plan" (subject or object in a sentence).
target_language_example: Eu entendi o seu plano, mas acho que podemos melhorar.
native_language_example: I understood your plan, but I think we can improve it.

meaning: your point of view; your opinion/perspective.
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s opinion or perspective on a topic. It often appears with verbs like apreciar (to appreciate), explicar (to explain), compartilhar (to share), and defender (to defend). You may also see variations like o seu ponto de vista (more explicit) and meu/teu/nosso ponto de vista (my/your(Portugal)/our point of view).
target_language_example: Entendo seu ponto de vista, mas não concordo.
native_language_example: I understand your point of view, but I don’t agree.

meaning: "your first" / "his first" / "her first" (before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: "Seu" can mean "your" (formal or in some regions) or "his/her" depending on context. Use it with a masculine singular noun (e.g., "seu primeiro encontro"). With a feminine noun, it becomes "sua primeira" (e.g., "sua primeira viagem").
target_language_example: Você se lembra do seu primeiro dia de trabalho?
native_language_example: Do you remember your first day of work?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something belongs specifically to that person (not someone else). It agrees with what comes after it: seu próprio + masculine singular noun (seu próprio nome), sua própria + feminine singular noun (sua própria casa), seus próprios / suas próprias for plurals. In Brazil, "seu" often means "your" (for "você"), while "dele/dela" can be used for clarity as "his/her".
target_language_example: Ela quer abrir seu próprio negócio.
native_language_example: She wants to open her own business.

additional_notes: Means “your room” (often “your bedroom”), using the possessive adjective “seu” (“your”). It can also mean “his/her room” depending on context, but in direct questions to someone (e.g., “Este é o seu quarto?”) it usually means “your.” In everyday speech, many Brazilians often say “o teu quarto” (informal/region-dependent) or “o quarto de você” to avoid ambiguity.
target_language_example: Vou deixar sua mala no seu quarto.
native_language_example: I’ll leave your suitcase in your room.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the listener’s face. "Seu" agrees with the thing owned ("rosto" is masculine), not with the person; it can also mean “his/her/their face” depending on context. Very common with prepositions: "no seu rosto" (on your face), "do seu rosto" (from your face).
target_language_example: Tem alguma coisa no seu rosto.
native_language_example: There’s something on your face.

additional_notes: "Seu/Sua" is a possessive that can mean "your" (formal, often used with você), but it can also mean "his/her/their". Context usually makes it clear. You’ll often see it with an article: "o seu telefone" (your/his/her/their phone).
target_language_example: Você pode me passar o seu telefone?
native_language_example: Can you give me your phone number?

meaning: your free time; your spare time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about time when someone is not working/studying and has no obligations. It often appears with "no/durante o seu tempo livre" (in/during your free time) or with "passar" (to spend): "passar o seu tempo livre fazendo...". The possessive "seu" can mean "your" (you) or "his/her/their" depending on context; here it’s typically "your" because it’s a question.
target_language_example: No seu tempo livre, eu gosto de ler e caminhar.
native_language_example: In my free time, I like to read and go for walks.

additional_notes: Means “your work/job” in a general sense. It can refer to someone’s employment (Ele odeia seu trabalho.) or to the work they produce (Gosto do seu trabalho.). Often used with “o seu trabalho” for emphasis/clarity. Note: “seu” can also mean “his/her/their/your (formal)” depending on context; “o seu trabalho” helps make it clear.
target_language_example: Você terminou o seu trabalho hoje?
native_language_example: Did you finish your work today?

additional_notes: "Seus" is a possessive meaning "his/her/your/their" (it agrees with the thing owned: alunos = masculine plural). In many situations, "seus" can be ambiguous (his vs her vs your vs their), so context matters; you may also see "dele" (his) / "dela" (her) to be more specific: "os alunos dele/dela." Often used when talking about a teacher and the students they teach.
target_language_example: A professora conversou com seus alunos depois da aula.
native_language_example: The teacher talked with her students after class.

meaning: your friends (plural; can also mean “his/her/their friends” depending on context).
additional_notes: “Seus” is a possessive meaning “your” in the formal sense (for “você”) and often agrees with the noun: “seus amigos” (masculine plural). It can also refer to someone else’s friends (“his/her/their”) when “seu/sua/seus/suas” refers back to a third person; in Brazil, speakers often use “dele/dela/deles/delas” to avoid ambiguity.
target_language_example: Você pode trazer seus amigos para a festa?
native_language_example: Can you bring your friends to the party?

additional_notes: Used to say what your friends are like/doing/where they are right now. It uses **estar (estão)**, which is common for temporary states, location, and actions in progress (e.g., *estão preocupados*, *estão vindo*, *estão lá embaixo*). You may also see **os seus amigos estão** with the article **os**; it usually means the same thing here.
target_language_example: Seus amigos estão esperando lá fora.
native_language_example: Your friends are waiting outside.

additional_notes: "Seus" is a possessive that can mean "your" (to you-all or to one person in formal Brazilian Portuguese) or "his/her/their" depending on context. "Colegas" means colleagues/classmates/buddies in a neutral way. Often clarified with "dele/dela/deles/delas" if needed (e.g., "os colegas dele").
target_language_example: Ele saiu para almoçar com seus colegas.
native_language_example: He went out to have lunch with his colleagues.

additional_notes: Means “(someone’s) classmates.” Here, "seus" can mean "your" (formal/plural) or "his/her/their" depending on context; Portuguese often uses "dele/dela" to be extra clear (e.g., "os colegas de classe dele"). "Colegas" is plural; singular is "colega de classe".
target_language_example: Ela sempre estuda com seus colegas de classe depois da aula.
native_language_example: She always studies with her classmates after class.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive "seus/suas" (“your” or sometimes “his/her/their”) + a plural noun. With "filhos" it commonly refers to children in general (sons and/or daughters). In sentences with "vocês" (you all), it clearly means "your"; with "ele/ela" it could mean "his/her" depending on context.
target_language_example: Vocês cuidam bem dos seus filhos.
native_language_example: Do you take good care of your children?

additional_notes: "Seus" is the plural possessive and can mean either "your" (to you all / formal you) or "their," depending on context. "Guarda-chuvas" is plural of "guarda-chuva" (umbrella). In many situations, Brazilians prefer "os guarda-chuvas de vocês" (your umbrellas) or "os guarda-chuvas deles/delas" (their umbrellas) to avoid ambiguity.
target_language_example: Vocês pegaram seus guarda-chuvas antes de sair?
native_language_example: Did you all grab your umbrellas before leaving?

additional_notes: “Seus” is a possessive meaning “your” (especially formal or plural) or “his/her/their,” depending on context. It agrees with the noun: livros (masculine plural). Often you’ll also see “os seus livros” (“your/his/her/their books”). In Brazilian Portuguese, “os livros dele/dela” is commonly used to avoid ambiguity.
target_language_example: Você trouxe seus livros para a aula?
native_language_example: Did you bring your books to class?

additional_notes: “Seus” is a possessive that can mean “your” (especially in Brazil, often used with você) or “his/her/their,” depending on context. It agrees with the plural noun “objetivos.” Often used with verbs like escrever (write), pensar (think about), and atingir/alcançar (reach/achieve).
target_language_example: Você já definiu seus objetivos para este ano?
native_language_example: Have you already defined your goals for this year?

additional_notes: "Seus" is a possessive that can refer to "your" (formal/with você), "his," "her," or "their." In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, to avoid ambiguity people often say "os olhos dele/dela" (his/her eyes) or "os olhos de vocês" (your plural).
target_language_example: Eu gosto da cor dos seus olhos.
native_language_example: I like the color of your eyes.

additional_notes: In Portuguese, "seu(s)" can mean "your" (informal singular), "his", "her", or "their". So "seus pais" is often ambiguous and the meaning depends on the situation (or can be clarified with "os pais dele/dela" = his/her parents). Note that "pais" can also mean "countries" in other contexts, but with family topics it usually means "parents".
target_language_example: Você mora perto dos seus pais?
native_language_example: Do you live near your parents?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something belongs to the subject itself (not someone else). It agrees with what follows: "seus" (masc. plural) + "próprios" (masc. plural), e.g., "seus próprios mitos" = "their own myths." In fixed expressions like "com seus próprios olhos" it means "with your own eyes" (the possessive matches the person being addressed).
target_language_example: Eles querem tomar suas próprias decisões.
native_language_example: They want to make their own decisions.

additional_notes: "Seus" is a possessive that can be ambiguous in Portuguese: it may refer to "his", "her", "your" (formal), or "their". In many contexts, people use "dele/dela/deles/delas" to clarify (e.g., "os sapatos dele" = "his shoes"). With the definite article, you often see "os seus sapatos" (same meaning).
target_language_example: Você pode tirar os seus sapatos aqui, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you take off your shoes here, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s personal dreams, plans, or life goals. It agrees with the person being addressed: seus sonhos = your dreams (to você / vocês) or his/their dreams depending on context; for a single person you may also hear teus sonhos (more common in Portugal and parts of Brazil). Often appears with verbs like realizar (achieve), tornar realidade (make come true), and correr atrás de (go after/chase).
target_language_example: Não desista dos seus sonhos.
native_language_example: Don’t give up on your dreams.

additional_notes: Plural of "sexta-feira" (Friday). Often used with the preposition "às" to mean "on Fridays" (habitual action): "às sextas-feiras". You can also say "nas sextas-feiras" (more like "on the Fridays"), but "às sextas-feiras" is the most common for routines.
target_language_example: Às sextas-feiras, eu termino o trabalho mais cedo.
native_language_example: On Fridays, I finish work earlier.

meaning: 'herself' (reflexive; referring back to the same woman/person).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive structures like "para si mesma" (to herself) and "de si mesma" (at herself). It refers back to the subject (usually "ela"), especially after prepositions (para, de, por, em). Related forms: "si mesmo" (himself/itself), "si" (oneself), "a si" (to oneself).
target_language_example: Ela prometeu a si mesma que ia descansar mais.
native_language_example: She promised herself that she would rest more.
