additional_notes: Used after a preposition (often "a", "de", "para", "por") to refer back to the same person as the subject: "a si mesmo" = "to yourself/himself"; "sobre si mesmo" = "about himself". The form changes with the person: "a mim mesmo" (myself), "a ti mesmo" (yourself, informal), "a si mesmo" (yourself formal / himself / herself), "a nós mesmos" (ourselves), "a vocês mesmos" (yourselves), "a si mesmos" (themselves).
target_language_example: Antes de decidir, pergunte a si mesmo o que você realmente quer.
native_language_example: Before deciding, ask yourself what you really want.

additional_notes: Used to express that something (a gesture, support, friendship, someone being there) is very important or emotionally significant to you. The subject can be a thing ("Seu apoio..."), an action/idea ("Você estar aqui..."), or even a person ("Você significa muito para mim" = "You mean a lot to me"). Formality-neutral and common in spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: Obrigado por ter vindo — isso significa muito para mim.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming — it means a lot to me.

meaning: 'yes, I…' (confirming and emphasizing that you are the one doing/saying it).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a reply to confirm something and then continue with a sentence in the first person. The comma shows a short pause and adds emphasis (similar to “Yes, I do.”). Often followed by a verb: “Sim, eu pago.”
target_language_example: Sim, eu entendo, mas não posso ir hoje.
native_language_example: Yes, I understand, but I can’t go today.

meaning: “Yes, but …” (agreeing, then adding a contrast or correction).
additional_notes: Used to acknowledge what someone said (“sim”) and immediately introduce a counterpoint, limitation, objection, or clarification (“mas”). The comma often marks a pause in speech: “Sim, mas…” You can follow it with a full sentence or a short phrase.
target_language_example: Sim, mas eu não posso hoje.
native_language_example: Yes, but I can’t today.

additional_notes: Used to confirm something and then continue with a comment (often adding an adjective or clarification): “Sim, é claro.” / “Sim, é lindo.” In Portuguese you’ll often hear just “Sim.” or “É.” as a short confirmation; “Sim, é …” sounds a bit more explicit and is commonly followed by more information. Change “é” if needed: “Sim, sou.” (Yes, I am), “Sim, está.” (Yes, it is/they are [temporary state]), “Sim, são.” (Yes, they are).
target_language_example: —A comida é boa? —Sim, é muito boa.
native_language_example: —Is the food good? —Yes, it’s very good.

meaning: “feel” (polite command), used in invitations like “feel free / make yourself at home.”
additional_notes: Imperative form of the reflexive verb sentir-se (“to feel”). It’s a polite way to invite someone to be comfortable or to do something: sinta-se em casa (“make yourself at home”), sinta-se à vontade (“feel comfortable”), sinta-se livre (para…) (“feel free to…”). Often used with por favor.
target_language_example: Sinta-se à vontade para fazer perguntas.
native_language_example: Feel free to ask questions.

additional_notes: First-person singular of the reflexive verb "sentir-se". Used to describe your physical or emotional state: "Sinto-me bem/mal" (I feel good/bad), "Sinto-me melhor" (I feel better), "Sinto-me triste/feliz" (I feel sad/happy). Often followed by an adjective or an expression like "à vontade" (comfortable).
target_language_example: Sinto-me cansado, mas feliz.
native_language_example: I feel tired, but happy.

additional_notes: Used to express a subjective feeling or impression, often followed by a verb in the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., estivesse, fosse): "Sinto como se algo estivesse errado." It’s common in both spoken and written Portuguese. You can also say "sinto-me como se" (more formal).
target_language_example: Sinto como se eu não tivesse dormido nada.
native_language_example: I feel like I didn’t sleep at all.

additional_notes: Used before a person, thing, or action to show you feel bad about it. With a person ("por você/por ele") it often means sympathy ("I feel sorry for you/him"). With an event/thing ("por isso/por aquilo/por tudo") or an action in the past ("por ter..."), it often works like an apology ("I'm sorry for having..."). You can omit "eu" in conversation: "Sinto muito por...".
target_language_example: Sinto muito por ter chegado tão tarde.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for arriving so late.

meaning: “Help yourself (to) …” / “Please take (some) …” (polite invitation to serve yourself).
additional_notes: Imperative form of the reflexive verb "servir-se (de)", used when offering food/drinks or inviting someone to take something for themselves. It’s a polite command, often used with "por favor". Common patterns: "Sirva-se de + noun" (Sirva-se de um pouco de café) and "Sirva-se de mais + noun" (Sirva-se de mais biscoitos).
target_language_example: Sirva-se de água à vontade, por favor.
native_language_example: Help yourself to as much water as you like, please.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic of what you’re talking or writing about. It’s the preposition "sobre" + the feminine singular definite article "a". It usually comes before a feminine noun (e.g., "sobre a sua família", "sobre a Argélia"). The masculine version is "sobre o".
target_language_example: Vamos conversar sobre a viagem amanhã.
native_language_example: Let’s talk about the trip tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is placed on top of a table (resting on its surface). Often follows verbs like colocar (to put), pôr (to put), deixar (to leave), estender (to spread out), and largar (to set down). It can also be used more generally as “on the table” with other surfaces (e.g., sobre a cama = on the bed).
target_language_example: Deixe os documentos sobre a mesa, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the documents on the table, please.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what someone is talking, writing, or asking about. Common after verbs like falar (to talk), saber (to know), dizer (to say), escrever (to write). You’ll also see it with other demonstratives: sobre este assunto (this subject, more formal/European Portuguese) or sobre aquele assunto (about that subject).
target_language_example: Eu tenho uma pergunta sobre esse assunto.
native_language_example: I have a question about this topic.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific topic or thing already mentioned or understood in context. Common after verbs like falar (to talk), dizer (to say), mencionar (to mention), saber (to know), and perguntar (to ask): “falar sobre isso” = “talk about it/that.”
target_language_example: Podemos conversar sobre isso amanhã?
native_language_example: Can we talk about it tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic of a question, statement, request, complaint, etc. It’s the contraction of "sobre" (about/on) + "o" (the, masculine singular). Often appears in phrases like "perguntar/falar/pensar/reclamar sobre o ..." and in questions like "Sobre o que...?" (“About what...?”).
target_language_example: Queria falar sobre o seu plano.
native_language_example: I wanted to talk about your plan.

meaning: about the subject/topic; on the matter.
additional_notes: Used to say something is related to a specific topic under discussion. Very common with verbs like falar/conversar (to talk), saber (to know), ler (to read), and with nouns like livro (book), especialista (expert). Often interchangeable with “a respeito do assunto” or “sobre isso” (about it).
target_language_example: Não tenho nada a acrescentar sobre o assunto.
native_language_example: I have nothing to add on the matter.

meaning: 'about what'; 'what ... about' (used to introduce the topic).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition **sobre** (“about”) + **o que** (“what”) to ask or refer to the subject of something: **Sobre o que vamos falar?** (“What are we going to talk about?”). It often appears after a verb that normally takes **sobre** (e.g., **falar sobre** = “talk about”, **mentir sobre** = “lie about”, **contar sobre** = “tell about”). In more formal writing you may also see **a respeito do que** with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Não entendi sobre o que eles estavam discutindo.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what they were arguing about.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic of a conversation or discussion: *talk about / discuss / find out about what happened*. Often follows verbs like **falar** (to talk), **conversar** (to chat/talk), **discutir** (to discuss/argue), **descobrir** (to find out/discover). You can add a time expression after **aconteceu**: **ontem**, **hoje à noite**, etc.
target_language_example: Podemos conversar sobre o que aconteceu mais tarde?
native_language_example: Can we talk about what happened later?

additional_notes: Used after verbs like falar/conversar (to talk) or tentar falar (to try to talk) to say the topic is your emotions. In everyday speech you can also hear: “sobre meus sentimentos” (dropping “os”), or “sobre os meus sentimentos por você” (“about my feelings for you”).
target_language_example: Preciso falar com você sobre os meus sentimentos.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you about my feelings.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like falar/conversar/discutir (to talk/chat/discuss) to say the topic is your shared plans. "Sobre" = "about/on" + "os nossos" = "our" + "planos" = "plans". In the examples, "falamos" is simple past (we talked) and "falávamos" is imperfect past (we used to talk / we were talking).
target_language_example: Podemos conversar sobre os nossos planos para o fim de semana?
native_language_example: Can we talk about our plans for the weekend?

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "sofrer um acidente". Used to say someone was involved in an accident (car, work, etc.), often implying injury or harm. You can add details with "de" (type) or "em/no/na" (place): "acidente de carro", "acidente no trabalho".
target_language_example: Ela sofreu um acidente de moto ontem.
native_language_example: She had a motorcycle accident yesterday.

additional_notes: A common, neutral phrase used to talk about fixing or resolving an issue. It’s built from solução (“solution”) + para (“to/for”) + o problema (“the problem”). You’ll often see it with verbs like procurar (“to look for”), ter (“to have”), and encontrar (“to find”).
target_language_example: Precisamos encontrar uma solução para o problema antes de amanhã.
native_language_example: We need to find a solution to the problem before tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to state a friendship relationship. Often you’ll also hear it with the subject: “(Nós) somos amigos.” In casual speech Portuguese may drop “nós” because “somos” already means “we are.” It can refer to close friends or more loosely (e.g., being friends on Facebook).
target_language_example: Não se preocupe — somos amigos.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—we’re friends.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "sorrir" + "para" + "mim". Used to describe a completed action in the past: someone smiled at you. Often appears in storytelling or describing a moment (e.g., "enquanto" = "while"). If you change the person: "sorri para você" (I smile at you), "sorrimos para ele" (we smiled at him).
target_language_example: Quando eu cheguei, ele sorriu para mim e abriu a porta.
native_language_example: When I arrived, he smiled at me and opened the door.

additional_notes: Used to name the flavor of ice cream. In Brazil, "sorvete" is ice cream, and "de" often means "of" to indicate flavor (sorvete de chocolate, sorvete de morango, etc.).
target_language_example: Você quer sorvete de baunilha ou de chocolate?
native_language_example: Do you want vanilla ice cream or chocolate?

meaning: "I am a" (used before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: From the verb "ser" (to be): "eu sou" = "I am" + "um" = "a/an" (masculine). Use it to say what you are (identity, profession, category): "Sou um estudante." For feminine nouns, use "sou uma". In negatives you often hear "não sou um..." = "I'm not a...".
target_language_example: Sou um estudante, mas não sou um atleta.
native_language_example: I'm a student, but I'm not an athlete.

additional_notes: Used to describe yourself (male speaker) and often followed by an adjective or description: "Sou um homem solitário" (a lonely man), "Sou um homem de palavra" (a man of my word). Also appears in comparisons like "como qualquer outro" (like any other) or "tão... quanto" (as... as).
target_language_example: Sou um homem simples, mas honesto.
native_language_example: I’m a simple man, but honest.

additional_notes: "Soube" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of *saber* (“to know / to find out”). With **que** it introduces information: **(Eu/Ele/Ela) soube que...** = “(I/he/she) found out that…” or sometimes “(I/he/she) heard that…”. In Portuguese the subject is often omitted, so **Soube que...** can mean “I found out that…” (or “He/She found out that…”) depending on context.
target_language_example: Soube que você vai se mudar.
native_language_example: I found out that you’re going to move.

additional_notes: "Soube" is the simple past of "saber" and often means you learned some new information (heard it, found out) rather than that you already knew it. It’s commonly followed by "que" + a clause: "Soube que você..." (= I heard that you...). You can also use it as a question: "Como foi que X soube que você...?" (= How did X find out that you...?).
target_language_example: Soube que você vai se mudar para outra cidade.
native_language_example: I heard you’re going to move to another city.

additional_notes: Common in polite requests and thanks. "Sua" is the possessive used with "você" (and also as a formal "your" with "o senhor / a senhora"). Often appears with "precisar de" (to need) and "obrigado(a) por" (thank you for).
target_language_example: Você pode me dar sua ajuda com isso?
native_language_example: Can you give me your help with this?

additional_notes: Literally refers to someone’s head (“a sua cabeça dói” = “your head hurts”). Very commonly used in a figurative sense to mean thoughts/ideas: “Está tudo aqui, na sua cabeça.” = “It’s all in your head.” It appears in set expressions like “passar pela sua cabeça” (to cross your mind) and “fizeram sua cabeça” (they got into your head / influenced or brainwashed you). Note: “sua” can also mean “his/her/their” depending on context, but in questions like “Como está a sua cabeça?” it’s typically “your.”
target_language_example: Já passou pela sua cabeça mudar de emprego?
native_language_example: Has it ever crossed your mind to change jobs?

additional_notes: “Sua” is a possessive that can mean “your” (formal singular) or “his/her/its/their,” so you often rely on context. In Brazil, “sua casa” is also common when addressing someone informally, even though “seu/sua” is traditionally more formal; “te” in a sentence often signals the speaker is addressing “you,” so “sua casa” = “your home.” Use “em sua casa” for “at your (someone’s) place/home,” and “para sua casa” for “to your home.”
target_language_example: Posso passar na sua casa mais tarde?
native_language_example: Can I stop by your place later?

additional_notes: Means the city where someone was born or grew up. "Sua" can mean "your" (formal singular) or "his/her/its" depending on context; to be clearer, speakers may also say "a cidade natal dele/dela" (his/her hometown). Often used with verbs like "voltar" (to return) and "partir" (to leave).
target_language_example: Depois de muitos anos, ela voltou à sua cidade natal para visitar a família.
native_language_example: After many years, she returned to her hometown to visit her family.

additional_notes: "Sua" is a possessive that can mean "your" (formal/with você) or "his/her" (and sometimes "their"). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often use "a esposa dele/dela" to avoid ambiguity. Usually used with the article: "a sua esposa".
target_language_example: Você vai trazer a sua esposa para o jantar?
native_language_example: Are you going to bring your wife to dinner?

additional_notes: "Sua" is a possessive that can mean "your" (formal/with você) or "his/her" (and sometimes "their"). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often use "a esposa dele/dela" to avoid ambiguity. Usually used with the article: "a sua esposa".
target_language_example: Você vai trazer a sua esposa para o jantar?
native_language_example: Are you going to bring your wife to dinner?

meaning: “your absence”; used in the expression “sentir sua falta” = “to miss you.”
additional_notes: Most commonly appears with the verb “sentir”: “(Eu) sinto sua falta” (I miss you), “senti sua falta” (I missed you), “vou sentir sua falta” (I’m going to miss you). “Sua” agrees with the person being missed (your), and “falta” literally means “lack/absence.” You can also say “sinto falta de você” (same meaning).
target_language_example: Vou sentir sua falta quando você viajar.
native_language_example: I’m going to miss you when you travel.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the listener’s family. "Sua" agrees with the noun (família is feminine), not with the person; it can mean "your" (singular or plural) and sometimes "his/her/their" depending on context. In Brazil, many people also say "a sua família" (with the article) and often use "a família de você" to avoid ambiguity.
target_language_example: Como está a sua família?
native_language_example: How is your family?

additional_notes: Means the birthday celebration/party of the person you’re talking to. "Sua" can mean "your" (formal or plural) and can also mean "his/her" depending on context; in these examples it’s "your." Often appears with the preposition "para" (invite someone to your birthday party) and with "ir à" (go to your birthday party). You may also hear "a sua festa de aniversário" (with the article) or just "sua festa de aniversário."
target_language_example: Você vai fazer sua festa de aniversário este sábado?
native_language_example: Are you going to have your birthday party this Saturday?

additional_notes: "Sua" is a possessive that can mean "your" (especially formal "you" = você/o senhor/a senhora) or "his/her/their," depending on context. "Filha" is "daughter." To avoid ambiguity, Portuguese often uses "a filha dele/dela" (his/her daughter) or "a sua filha" (your daughter).
target_language_example: Eu conheci a sua filha ontem.
native_language_example: I met your daughter yesterday.

additional_notes: Used when talking about the photo that represents someone on a social network, messaging app, or online account. "Sua" agrees with the noun (foto) and can mean "your" (informal) or "your" (formal) depending on context. You may also see "a sua foto de perfil" (= "your profile picture") with the article for emphasis/clarity.
target_language_example: Sua foto de perfil ficou muito bonita.
native_language_example: Your profile picture looks really nice.

additional_notes: Often used when talking about what someone says happened (their version of events), not necessarily a fictional story. "Sua" can mean "your" (formal singular) or "his/her/your/their" depending on context; if you need to be extra clear, you can say "a sua história" (your story) or "a história dele/dela" (his/her story).
target_language_example: Ninguém acreditou na sua história.
native_language_example: Nobody believed your story.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s age (Qual é a sua idade?) or to compare someone to what’s typical at that age (para a sua idade = “for your age”). In “quando era da sua idade,” it means “when I was your age” (literally “when I was of your age”).
target_language_example: Quando eu era da sua idade, eu já morava sozinho.
native_language_example: When I was your age, I already lived on my own.

additional_notes: "Sua" is a possessive that can mean "your" (formal or in Brazil often with "você"), or "his/her/its" depending on who is being talked about. In speech, Brazilians often say "a sua irmã" / "sua irmã" for emphasis; "a irmã dele/dela" can be used to avoid ambiguity.
target_language_example: Você conhece a sua irmã?
native_language_example: Do you know your sister?

additional_notes: Used to talk about schoolwork you have to do at home. The possessive can change with the person and number: minha lição de casa (my), sua lição de casa (your—also his/her/its in some contexts), a lição de casa dele/dela (his/her), nossa lição de casa (our), a lição de casa deles/delas (their).
target_language_example: Você já fez sua lição de casa?
native_language_example: Have you done your homework yet?

additional_notes: Língua can mean both “language” and “tongue” in Portuguese. In questions like “Como se diz … na sua língua?”, it means “in your language.” In physical contexts (examining, biting, cutting), it means the body part “tongue.” Sua is a possessive meaning “your” (formal) or “his/her/its,” so context tells you whose it is. To be extra clear, Portuguese may also say “língua materna” (mother tongue/native language).
target_language_example: Como se diz “thank you” na sua língua?
native_language_example: How do you say “thank you” in your language?

meaning: your native language; your mother tongue.
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s first language (the language they grew up speaking). It can be adapted to match the person/number: "minha língua materna" (my), "sua" (your/his/her), "nossa" (our), "a língua materna dele/dela" (his/her). In questions, it’s very common: "Qual é a sua língua materna?"
target_language_example: Minha língua materna é o português, mas também falo inglês.
native_language_example: My native language is Portuguese, but I also speak English.

meaning: your native language; your mother tongue.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the language someone learned first and speaks naturally from childhood. It commonly appears in questions like “Qual é a sua língua nativa?” and can address one person (você: sua) or, in more formal contexts, “o senhor / a senhora” (also uses “sua”). For “you all” (vocês), people still often say “sua língua nativa” in casual speech, but “a língua nativa de vocês” is also very common and clearer.
target_language_example: Eu queria praticar sua língua nativa para entender melhor a sua cultura.
native_language_example: I wanted to practice your native language to better understand your culture.

additional_notes: Used when talking to someone using the formal address (você). It can refer to a suitcase or a travel bag, depending on context. With a question word you often hear it as: “Qual é a sua mala?” = “Which one is your suitcase?”
target_language_example: Posso pegar sua mala para você?
native_language_example: Can I take your suitcase for you?

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: sua = “your” (also can mean “his/her/their” depending on context), mente = “mind.” Often used in expressions like “Abra (a) sua mente” (“Open your mind”) and “Alimente a sua mente” (“Feed your mind”) to talk about being open to ideas or learning. The article “a” is optional in some contexts: “Abra a sua mente” and “Abra sua mente” are both common.
target_language_example: Tente manter sua mente aberta a novas ideias.
native_language_example: Try to keep your mind open to new ideas.

additional_notes: Mulher means “woman” and also “wife.” With sua (“your/his/her”), sua mulher is often “your wife” when you’re speaking directly to someone (Você), but it can also mean “his wife” or “her wife” when talking about a third person (because seu/sua can refer to “your,” “his,” or “her”). To avoid ambiguity, Portuguese often uses dele/dela: a mulher dele (his wife), a mulher dela (her wife).
target_language_example: Você já falou com sua mulher hoje?
native_language_example: Have you already talked to your wife today?

additional_notes: "Sua" is a possessive that can mean "your," "his," "her," or "their" (formal/standard Portuguese). Often the context (who is being talked to/about) makes it clear. If you want to be more explicit in Brazilian Portuguese, people sometimes say "a mãe dele/dela" (his/her mother).
target_language_example: Sua mãe trabalha perto daqui?
native_language_example: Does your mother work near here?

meaning: "your hand" (formal or "your" = his/her/its/your, depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally "your hand," but "sua" can also mean "his/her/its" (especially in Brazil, where "seu/sua" is often used instead of "dele/dela"). Used for giving/holding something ("em sua mão" = "in your/his/her hand"), for physical contact ("Tire sua mão..." = "Take your hand..."), and in the expression "como a palma de sua mão" = "like the back of your hand" (know something very well).
target_language_example: Coloque sua mão aqui, por favor.
native_language_example: Put your hand here, please.

additional_notes: "Sua" can mean "your" (formal) or "his/her" depending on context, since "você" uses 3rd-person possessives in Portuguese. "Namorada" is a girlfriend (female partner); "seu namorado" is a boyfriend. You can also say "a namorada dele/dela" to be clearer (his/her girlfriend).
target_language_example: Você vai trazer sua namorada para a festa?
native_language_example: Are you going to bring your girlfriend to the party?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the other person’s point of view. Often appears with verbs like respeitar (to respect), compartilhar (to share), concordar com (to agree with), and in questions like “Na sua opinião…?” (“In your opinion…?”). “Sua” is the possessive for “you” (você) and also for “his/her/their” in some contexts, so it can sometimes mean “his/her/their opinion” depending on who is being addressed.
target_language_example: Na sua opinião, esse filme vale a pena?
native_language_example: In your opinion, is this movie worth it?

additional_notes: “Sua” is a possessive that can mean “your” (formal you / você) or “his/her/its/their,” so the exact meaning depends on who is being talked about. Often used with verbs like manter (to keep), cumprir (to fulfill/keep), and quebrar (to break) a promessa.
target_language_example: Você vai cumprir sua promessa?
native_language_example: Are you going to keep your promise?

meaning: 'your/his/her/their own' (emphasizing that it belongs to that person).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to stress that something is that person’s own (not someone else’s): "sua própria língua" = their own language, "sua própria vida" = his own life. It agrees with the noun: use "próprio" (masc. sing.), "própria" (fem. sing.), "próprios" (masc. pl.), "próprias" (fem. pl.). "Sua" can mean your (formal)/his/her/their depending on context; to avoid ambiguity, people may use "dele/dela" (e.g., "a própria opinião dele").
target_language_example: Ela quer ter a sua própria casa.
native_language_example: She wants to have her own house.

additional_notes: Used to address someone directly or refer to what they answered (in conversation, a form, an exam, or an official statement). 'Sua' is a possessive meaning 'your' (also used as 'his/her/its' in some contexts), and 'resposta' means 'answer/response'. Often appears with verbs like 'ser' (foi) or 'dar' (dará).
target_language_example: Obrigado pela sua resposta.
native_language_example: Thank you for your answer.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s wellbeing. "Sua" means "your" (formal) and also "his/her/its" depending on context; if you want to be very clear about "your" (informal), people often say "a tua saúde" (Portugal) or "a sua saúde" / "a saúde de você" (Brazil). Often appears with prepositions like "para a sua saúde" (for your health) and verbs like "afetar" (to affect).
target_language_example: Você precisa cuidar da sua saúde.
native_language_example: You need to take care of your health.

additional_notes: "Sua" means "your" (also can mean "his/her/its" depending on context). "Viagem" is a trip or journey. Very common when asking about or talking about someone’s travel plans or a recent trip; you’ll also hear the more explicit "a sua viagem" ("your trip").
target_language_example: Como foi sua viagem?
native_language_example: How was your trip?

additional_notes: “Sua” can mean “your” (formal/with você) or “his/her/its,” depending on context. Often used in expressions like “estar em perigo” (to be in danger), “perder a vida” (to lose one’s life), “salvar a vida” (to save someone’s life), and “lutar pela vida” (to fight for one’s life).
target_language_example: Eu não quero mudar sua vida, só quero ajudar.
native_language_example: I don’t want to change your life, I just want to help.

additional_notes: Refers to possessions that belong to the person you’re talking to. Often used in everyday situations like packing/leaving ("Pegue(m) suas coisas") or to mean someone’s personal affairs/responsibilities ("cuide das suas coisas" = mind your own business/take care of your own matters). "Suas" agrees with a plural noun (coisas) and can be used with "você" or "vocês".
target_language_example: Pegue suas coisas e vamos embora.
native_language_example: Get your things and let’s go.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s vacation time during the summer. "Suas" is a polite/standard way to say "your" (often used with "você"); with "tu" you’d usually say "tuas férias de verão". In Portuguese, "férias" is usually plural.
target_language_example: O que você fez nas suas férias de verão?
native_language_example: What did you do on your summer vacation?

additional_notes: Means "your hands" when speaking to one person (você). Often used in commands/instructions: Deixe-me ver suas mãos! (Let me see your hands!), Levante suas mãos! (Raise your hands!), Lave bem suas mãos. (Wash your hands well.). Can also be figurative: "Meu destino está em suas mãos" = "My fate is in your hands" (you are responsible / in control). Note: "suas" can also mean "his/her/their" in other contexts, but with você it commonly means "your."
target_language_example: Coloque suas mãos na mesa, por favor.
native_language_example: Put your hands on the table, please.

meaning: “your words” (formal/plural ‘you’) or “his/her/their words,” depending on context.
additional_notes: “Suas” can mean ‘your’ (addressing someone as você/vocês) or ‘his/her/their’. Context (who is being talked to/about) tells you which. Often used when referring to what someone said (sometimes with an emotional tone), e.g., “Retire as suas palavras!” = “Take back your words!”
target_language_example: Eu nunca vou esquecer suas palavras.
native_language_example: I’ll never forget your words.

meaning: “your own” / “his/her/their own” (feminine plural), emphasizing that something belongs to that person.
additional_notes: Used with a feminine plural noun (e.g., coisas, músicas, mãos, razões, piadas). It adds emphasis, like “your own (things)” or “their very own”. The possessive "suas" can mean “your” (formal), “his”, “her”, or “their” depending on context; "próprias" agrees with the noun (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Ele prefere usar suas próprias palavras.
native_language_example: He prefers to use his own words.

meaning: your clothes (formal/plural ‘you’), or his/her/their clothes (depending on context).
additional_notes: “Suas” is a possessive that agrees with the noun (here, plural feminine “roupas”). It can mean ‘your’ when addressing someone with você/vocês (common in Brazil), and it can also mean ‘his/her/their’ in some contexts (especially if referring to ele/ela/eles/elas). If you need to be clearer, you may hear: “as roupas dele/dela/deles/delas” (his/her/their clothes).
target_language_example: Você já lavou suas roupas?
native_language_example: Have you washed your clothes?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "subir" (to go up/climb) + "em" + a plural noun. It can describe a playful activity (kids climbing trees) or an animal’s ability. You can also say "subir na árvore" (climb the tree) for a specific tree.
target_language_example: Ele não consegue subir em árvores muito altas.
native_language_example: He can't climb very tall trees.

meaning: “(he/she) went up the stairs” / “climbed the stairs.”
additional_notes: “Subiu” is the past tense (preterite) of *subir* (“to go up”), used for a completed action. It usually implies going upward; for going down you’d use *desceu as escadas*. You can add details like *com dificuldade* (“with difficulty”) or *correndo* (“running”), and specify which stairs with *de/ do/ da* (e.g., *as escadas do sótão* = “the attic stairs”).
target_language_example: Ela subiu as escadas bem devagar porque estava cansada.
native_language_example: She went up the stairs very slowly because she was tired.

meaning: 'juice of' / 'juice made from' (used before an ingredient).
additional_notes: Use "suco de + [fruit/vegetable]" to say the type/flavor of juice: "suco de laranja" (orange juice), "suco de uva" (grape juice), "suco de cenoura" (carrot juice). In everyday speech, people often shorten it to just "suco" when the flavor is clear from context.
target_language_example: Quero um suco de laranja, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like an orange juice, please.

additional_notes: Common drink order in cafés/restaurants. You can add details like "fresco" (fresh) or "um pouco de" (a little).
target_language_example: Para o café da manhã, eu vou tomar um suco de laranja.
native_language_example: For breakfast, I’m going to have an orange juice.

additional_notes: A common drink. You can use it when ordering or offering a beverage. Also appears as “sumo de maçã” in some varieties of Portuguese (especially Portugal).
target_language_example: Pode me dar um suco de maçã, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me an apple juice, please?

additional_notes: Used to say that an amount/degree is enough for a purpose or result. Often followed by an infinitive (suficiente para + verb), e.g., "idade suficiente para beber" = "old enough to drink."
target_language_example: Não tenho dinheiro suficiente para comprar isso.
native_language_example: I don't have enough money to buy that.

meaning: 'suggested that' (introduces a suggestion, often followed by the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used after the past tense of "sugerir" ("he/she suggested"). Very commonly followed by a verb in the imperfect subjunctive in Portuguese (e.g., "sugeriu que eu fosse", "sugeriu que fizéssemos"), especially when the subject changes (she suggested that I...).
target_language_example: O médico sugeriu que eu descansasse mais.
native_language_example: The doctor suggested that I rest more.

additional_notes: Used when the speaker is giving advice or a recommendation. After "sugiro que", Portuguese typically uses the present subjunctive: "coma" (that you eat), "comece" (that you start), "cozinhe" (that you cook), "faça" (that you do), "fique" (that you stay), "guarde" (that you keep). Depending on tone and context, it can sound polite or like a firm warning/command (e.g., "Sugiro que você fique fora do meu caminho").
target_language_example: Sugiro que você fale com o seu chefe primeiro.
native_language_example: I suggest that you talk to your boss first.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a guess or suspicion, often with limited evidence. After "suspeito que", Portuguese can use either the indicative (more neutral: "suspeito que ele está") or the subjunctive (more doubtful/formal: "suspeito que ele esteja").
target_language_example: Suspeito que ele não venha hoje.
native_language_example: I suspect he won’t come today.

meaning: "I suspect that the..." (about a male person/thing).
additional_notes: Used to express a suspicion/guess. In Portuguese, "suspeito que" often introduces a clause with the subjunctive when you’re unsure (e.g., "Suspeito que o Tom esteja..." = “I suspect Tom is...” ). "o" is the masculine singular “the” (used with male names like Tom, or masculine nouns).
target_language_example: Suspeito que o vizinho esteja em casa.
native_language_example: I suspect the neighbor is at home.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ser** (“to be”) to classify or define what something is. **São** is the **they/you(pl.) are** form (also used with plural nouns like *as abelhas*, *os golfinhos*). **Animais** is plural; for singular you’d say **é um animal** (“is an animal”).
target_language_example: Os gatos são animais domésticos.
native_language_example: Cats are domestic animals.

additional_notes: Form of the verb **ser** (to be): **são** = “are” (3rd person plural) + **as** = “the” (feminine plural). Used to identify or describe something: *As maçãs são as melhores frutas.* It’s also common in questions and short answers, sometimes with the subject after the verb (inversion): *São as famosas panquecas...?* / *São as piores.*
target_language_example: Estas são as minhas chaves.
native_language_example: These are my keys.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (“to be”) to describe more than one thing/person as good. It agrees in gender/number: são boas (plural feminine). Often followed by a noun: são bons professores (“are good teachers”).
target_language_example: Esses livros são bons, mas caros.
native_language_example: These books are good, but expensive.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ser" (são = "are") + nationality adjective (canadenses = "Canadian" in the plural for mixed or all-female groups). For an all-male group you can also say "são canadenses" (same form). Question form can be just intonation or a question mark in writing: "Eles são canadenses?" Adding "mesmo" can mean "really/actually": "Vocês são canadenses mesmo?"
target_language_example: Meus vizinhos são canadenses, mas moram aqui há anos.
native_language_example: My neighbors are Canadian, but they've lived here for years.

meaning: “are from the same …” / “are of the same …”.
additional_notes: Used to say two or more people/things share the same group, origin, category, measurement, etc. It’s normally followed by a noun: são da mesma equipe (same team), são da mesma altura (same height), são da mesma parte do país (same part of the country). The adjective agrees with the noun: mesma (feminine singular), mesmo (masculine singular), mesmas/mesmos (plural).
target_language_example: Nós somos da mesma turma.
native_language_example: We’re in the same class (group).

additional_notes: Used to describe more than one thing/ person as big/large. It’s the plural form: “são” (they are) + “grandes” (big/large, plural). With “demais,” it means “too big” (e.g., “são grandes demais”). It can also be figurative: “são grandes amigos” = “they are good/close friends.”
target_language_example: Esses sapatos são grandes para mim.
native_language_example: These shoes are big for me.

additional_notes: Used to say that two or more people are brothers (male siblings). In mixed or unspecified gender, Portuguese often uses the masculine plural "irmãos" to mean "siblings" in general. For a specific pair with one sister, you can also say "são irmão e irmã" or "são irmãos" (generic). For two sisters: "são irmãs". The verb "são" is from "ser" (to be) and is used for identity/relationships.
target_language_example: Eles são irmãos, mas não se parecem nada.
native_language_example: They are brothers/siblings, but they don’t look alike at all.

additional_notes: "São" is the present tense of "ser" (to be) for "they/you all": "they are". "Mais" means "more". Together, "são mais" is commonly followed by an adjective/adverb and then a comparison: "do que" (than) or sometimes just "que". Example patterns: "Eles são mais + adjective + (do) que..." = "They are more ... than ...".
target_language_example: Essas ruas são mais seguras do que as do centro.
native_language_example: These streets are safer than the ones downtown.

additional_notes: Used to say that multiple things belong to you: "são" = "are" and "meus" = "mine" (for masculine plural nouns, or mixed groups). Often appears after a noun ("Os erros são meus") or by itself when the noun is understood ("Esses são meus"). For feminine plural, use "são minhas".
target_language_example: Esses livros são meus, mas aquela caneta não é minha.
native_language_example: These books are mine, but that pen isn’t mine.

additional_notes: Used with plural subjects in the present tense of ser (são = “are”) + muito to intensify an adjective: são muito antigas (“are very old”), são muito populares (“are very popular”). With nouns/quantities, muito can mean “a lot/too much” depending on context. Negative: não são muito... (“are not very...”).
target_language_example: Essas ruas são muito estreitas.
native_language_example: These streets are very narrow.

additional_notes: Used with plural feminine subjects (e.g., praias, rosas, tardes, irmãs, filhas) to describe that they are very beautiful. It’s the present tense of “ser” (são = are) + intensifier “muito” (very) + adjective “bonitas” (pretty/beautiful, feminine plural). With masculine or mixed groups, use “são muito bonitos.”
target_language_example: Essas fotos são muito bonitas.
native_language_example: These photos are very beautiful.

meaning: "are the" / "(they) are the" (plural of "ser" + masculine plural "the").
additional_notes: Used to identify or point out who/what something is in the plural: "X são os Y" = "X are the Y". It can also be used for emphasis in a cleft-like structure, similar to "It’s the..." in English: "São os dados" = "It’s the data/facts." (For feminine plural, use "são as".)
target_language_example: Eles são os responsáveis pelo projeto.
native_language_example: They are the ones responsible for the project.

meaning: "are so" / "are as" (used to intensify an adjective, or in comparisons).
additional_notes: Used with adjectives to mean “so” (intensity): “Eles são tão simpáticos.” It’s also commonly used in the structure “tão + adjective + quanto” to mean “as + adjective + as”: “As mulheres são tão inteligentes quanto os homens.” “São” is the present tense of “ser” for “they/you (plural)/you (formal plural)”, so it agrees with plural subjects (e.g., “As pessoas são…”).
target_language_example: Essas casas são tão bonitas!
native_language_example: These houses are so beautiful!

additional_notes: Used to soften or defend an action: the speaker says the intention was harmless or helpful. Commonly followed by an infinitive (e.g., ajudar, evitar, ser, fazer, proteger). In speech, subject is often understood from context: “Só estava tentando ajudar.” = “I was just trying to help.”
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu só estava tentando ajudar.
native_language_example: Sorry, I was just trying to help.

additional_notes: Used to say you need just one thing (and nothing more). Use it with a noun or an infinitive phrase turned into a noun idea (e.g., tempo para pensar). The verb is precisar de (“to need”), which requires de before what you need: preciso de água. You can change the person: só precisamos de (“we only need”), só precisa de (“you/he/she only needs”).
target_language_example: Só preciso de um pouco de ajuda.
native_language_example: I only need a little help.

additional_notes: Used to soften what you’re about to say (often an explanation, apology, or clarification). It’s the imperfect past of "querer" ("queria" = "I wanted"), and it’s commonly followed by an infinitive: "só queria dizer/perguntar/avisar…". Can also appear with other subjects (e.g., "ele só queria" = "he just wanted").
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu só queria perguntar uma coisa.
native_language_example: Sorry, I just wanted to ask something.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that your intention is simple or limited (often to reassure, soften a request, or insist on a single goal). It’s commonly followed by an infinitive (Só quero ajudar.) or by "que" + subjunctive (Só quero que ela vá embora.).
target_language_example: Eu só quero descansar um pouco.
native_language_example: I just want to rest a little.

só quero ir para casa e

target_language_multi_word_term: só quero ir para casa e
meaning: “I just want to go home and …”
additional_notes: Used to express a simple desire after something (often after being tired, stressed, or finished with an activity). It’s usually followed by another verb in the infinitive (e.g., dormir, ver, descansar, tomar banho). Often appears with or without the subject “eu” (“Eu só quero…” / “Só quero…”).
target_language_example: Só quero ir para casa e descansar.
native_language_example: I just want to go home and rest.

additional_notes: Used to express a simple or main wish/request: só = “just/only”, quero = “I want”, que introduces what you want to happen. Very often followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., recupere, melhore, relaxe, saiba, vá). The subject after que can be left unstated when it’s understood (often “you”).
target_language_example: Só quero que você fique bem.
native_language_example: I just want you to be okay.

additional_notes: Used to limit quantity ("só um café" = only one coffee) or to downplay/minimize something ("ele é só um tonto" = he’s just a fool). Very common in polite requests for time: "Só um segundo/segundinho" (just a second).
target_language_example: Me dá só um minuto, por favor.
native_language_example: Just give me a minute, please.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an action, statement, or idea in a general way, often with judgment, surprise, or disbelief (e.g., "Nunca vi tal coisa" = "I’ve never seen such a thing"). It can point back to something already mentioned or to something hypothetical. Common with verbs like fazer/dizer/acreditar/concordar em.
target_language_example: Eu nunca disse tal coisa.
native_language_example: I never said such a thing.

additional_notes: Used to propose an idea in a softer, less direct way. Literally “maybe” + “we should” (from the verb *dever*, “to have to/should,” here in the conditional/subjunctive form *devêssemos*). Often followed by an infinitive: *talvez devêssemos esperar / ligar / ir*.
target_language_example: Talvez devêssemos sair mais cedo para evitar o trânsito.
native_language_example: Maybe we should leave earlier to avoid traffic.

additional_notes: Used to make a cautious suggestion about your own actions (less direct than saying "I should"). After "talvez" (“maybe/perhaps”), Portuguese often uses the subjunctive; here, "devesse" is the imperfect subjunctive of "dever" (“to should/ought to”). Commonly followed by an infinitive: "talvez eu devesse ir" (maybe I should go). To talk about something you think you should have done in the past, you can use: "talvez eu devesse ter + past participle" (e.g., "talvez eu devesse ter estudado" = maybe I should have studied).
target_language_example: Talvez eu devesse ligar para ela amanhã.
native_language_example: Maybe I should call her tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to suggest a possibility politely or tentatively. "Talvez" (“maybe/perhaps”) often triggers the subjunctive; "possa" is the present subjunctive of "poder" (“can/to be able to”). Common with an infinitive after it: "talvez eu possa ajudar / consertar / fazer".
target_language_example: Talvez eu possa ligar para você mais tarde.
native_language_example: Maybe I can call you later.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty about a situation. "Talvez" means "maybe/perhaps" and is commonly followed by the subjunctive: "seja" (from "ser", to be). It often introduces a possible explanation ("Talvez seja porque...") or a cautious opinion ("Talvez seja melhor...").
target_language_example: Talvez seja tarde demais para ligar agora.
native_language_example: Maybe it’s too late to call now.

additional_notes: Used to give a suggestion or advice, often implying what the speaker thinks is a better idea. It’s polite but can sound a bit critical depending on tone. Grammar: "talvez" (“maybe”) commonly triggers the subjunctive, so you’ll often see "talvez você devesse" (from "dever", “should/ought to”). You can also use it with other people: "talvez eu devesse" (maybe I should), "talvez a gente devesse" (maybe we should).
target_language_example: Talvez você devesse descansar um pouco antes de continuar.
native_language_example: Maybe you should rest a little before continuing.

meaning: “maybe you want to…” / “perhaps you’d like to…”
additional_notes: Used to make a suggestion or recommendation more polite/less direct. It’s usually followed by an infinitive (e.g., ler, ir, contar) or a noun (e.g., quinze queijos). You can also use it to offer an option: “Talvez você queira…” = “Maybe you’d like…”
target_language_example: Talvez você queira experimentar este prato.
native_language_example: Maybe you’d like to try this dish.

meaning: "as much as" / "as ... as" (equal amount or degree).
additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things/actions and say they are equal in degree or quantity. It often follows a verb (e.g., trabalhar, querer, gostar): "Eu trabalho tanto quanto você" = “I work as much as you.” It can also be used with a general comparison: "Tanto quanto qualquer..." = “as much as any...”.
target_language_example: Eu gosto de café tanto quanto você.
native_language_example: I like coffee as much as you.

meaning: "as much as I do / as ... as I am".
additional_notes: Used to compare yourself with someone or something else. With verbs, it means “as much as I do” (e.g., gosta/faz/bebe/come tanto quanto eu). With adjectives/adverbs, it means “not as … as I am” (e.g., não tão alto quanto eu = not as tall as me). Often shortened to “tanto quanto eu” or “tão ... quanto eu,” depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Ela não estuda tanto quanto eu.
native_language_example: She doesn’t study as much as I do.

meaning: so long; such a long time.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize a long duration (“for so long”) or a large amount of time (“spend so much time”). Very common with verbs like esperar (to wait), conhecer (to know), ficar (to stay), passar (to spend time), and with “há” to mean “for” a past duration: “há tanto tempo” = “for so long / for such a long time.”
target_language_example: Eu não te via há tanto tempo!
native_language_example: I hadn’t seen you in so long!

additional_notes: Used to say something happened very late in the evening/night, often when it’s already quite dark and people are usually at home or asleep. It often follows the verb it describes (e.g., "voltava... tarde da noite").
target_language_example: Cheguei tarde da noite e fui direto dormir.
native_language_example: I arrived late at night and went straight to sleep.

additional_notes: Used when something happens after the right time has passed (often implying it’s no longer possible to change the outcome). Very common as a full sentence: "É tarde demais" / "Já é tarde demais" (“It’s already too late”). Can also be used after a verb: "Cheguei tarde demais" (“I arrived too late”). "Antes que fosse tarde demais" means “before it was too late.”
target_language_example: Vamos embora agora — se esperarmos mais, vai ser tarde demais.
native_language_example: Let’s leave now—if we wait longer, it’ll be too late.

additional_notes: Used to say there isn’t enough time left to do something or to change what happened. It’s followed by an infinitive (verb) (e.g., “tarde demais para fazer...”) or by a noun/pronoun (e.g., “tarde demais para isso”). Often appears as “É tarde demais para...” (“It’s too late to/for...”).
target_language_example: É tarde demais para mudar de ideia agora.
native_language_example: It’s too late to change your mind now.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened late during the previous night (yesterday night). Often appears after the verb: “chegou tarde ontem à noite” (arrived late last night). You can intensify it with “muito”: “muito tarde ontem à noite” (very late last night).
target_language_example: Eu fui dormir tarde ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I went to sleep late last night.

meaning: a glass of wine (a wine glass, with wine).
additional_notes: Used when talking about a serving of wine in a glass (often a stemmed wine glass). In Brazilian Portuguese, you may also hear “copo de vinho,” but “taça” is the more typical word for wine in a stemmed glass. Plural: “taças de vinho.”
target_language_example: Você quer uma taça de vinho branco ou tinto?
native_language_example: Do you want a glass of white wine or red?

additional_notes: "Te" is an object pronoun meaning "you" used with "ajudar" (to help), mainly in Brazil in informal speech. You’ll often hear it in: "posso te ajudar?" (can I help you?), "vou te ajudar" (I’ll help you), "pode te ajudar" (can help you). In more formal situations, you may see/hear "ajudá-lo/ajudá-la" or "ajudar você" instead.
target_language_example: Posso te ajudar com isso?
native_language_example: Can I help you with that?

additional_notes: Used with the object pronoun "te" (= you, informal singular) plus the verb "ajudar" and then an infinitive verb: "te ajudar a + verb". Very common in offers and questions ("Posso te ajudar a...?" / "Quem pode te ajudar a...?"). In Brazil you may also hear "ajudar você a" or "te ajudar" (dropping "a") in casual speech.
target_language_example: Posso te ajudar a preencher este formulário?
native_language_example: Can I help you fill out this form?

meaning: to meet you / to get to know you.
additional_notes: "Te" is an object pronoun meaning "you" (informal singular, common in Brazil). "Conhecer" means "to know" in the sense of being familiar with a person/place or meeting someone for the first time. You’ll often hear it in greetings like "Prazer te conhecer" (= "Nice to meet you"). For knowing facts/information, Portuguese usually uses "saber" instead of "conhecer".
target_language_example: Foi muito bom te conhecer pessoalmente.
native_language_example: It was really nice to meet you in person.

additional_notes: "Te" is the object pronoun meaning "to you" (informal singular), and "contar" means "to tell" (also "to count" in other contexts). Very common before a noun: "te contar um segredo/uma história". You can also see variations like "vou te contar" (I’m going to tell you) and "pode te contar" (can tell you).
target_language_example: Preciso te contar uma coisa importante.
native_language_example: I need to tell you something important.

additional_notes: Used when introducing a piece of information you’re about to share, often something personal, important, or a bit surprising. Literally "to tell you a thing" (te = "to you" in informal speech; contar = "to tell"; uma coisa = "something"). You can swap te for other pronouns: "me contar uma coisa" (tell me something), "lhe contar uma coisa" (tell you—more formal).
target_language_example: Preciso te contar uma coisa importante.
native_language_example: I need to tell you something important.

meaning: to give you (something); to offer you.
additional_notes: Te is an object pronoun meaning “to you” (informal singular). It commonly comes before the verb: “Eu vou te dar isso” = “I’m going to give you that.” With “dar” it can also mean giving something non-physical, like “um abraço” (“a hug”) or “um trabalho” (“a job”). In more formal Portuguese, you may also hear “lhe dar” for “to give you,” depending on region and whether the person is “você/senhor(a)”.
target_language_example: Posso te dar uma carona?
native_language_example: Can I give you a ride?

additional_notes: Used with the indirect object pronoun **te** (“to you”) plus **dar** (“to give”) and **um** (“a/an” masculine singular): **te dar um + [noun]**. Very common before a thing or abstract item: **te dar um caderno** (give you a notebook), **te dar um conselho** (give you advice). In informal speech, **te** can also come after the verb: **vou dar-te um…** (more formal/European). Note: some fixed expressions use this pattern, e.g. **dar um pé** can mean “to kick someone out / dump someone” depending on context.
target_language_example: Posso te dar um copo d’água?
native_language_example: Can I give you a glass of water?

meaning: “I owe you …” / “How much do I owe you?”
additional_notes: Used when you owe someone money, a favor, or want to pay them back for something. Common in questions: “Quanto te devo?” or “Quanto é que te devo?” = “How much do I owe you?” The fixed expression “Te devo uma!” means “I owe you one!” and is informal.
target_language_example: Obrigado por me ajudar hoje — te devo uma!
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me today — I owe you one!

additional_notes: Past tense of "dizer" (to say/tell) with the object pronoun "te" = "to you" (informal singular, like "you" meaning one person). Often appears as "já te disse" = "I already told you" and can be used to remind someone of something you said before. More formal: "lhe disse" (to you/ him/ her).
target_language_example: Eu te disse para chegar cedo.
native_language_example: I told you to arrive early.

additional_notes: Common way to introduce information (often important, serious, or personal). The full phrase is usually "preciso/tenho que/quero/gostaria de te dizer uma coisa" (= "I need/have to/want/would like to tell you something"). "Te" is an informal/object-pronoun form meaning "to you" (common in Brazil); in more formal contexts you may hear "lhe dizer uma coisa" or "dizer uma coisa para você".
target_language_example: Antes de você ir, preciso te dizer uma coisa importante.
native_language_example: Before you go, I need to tell you something important.

meaning: to ask you a few questions.
additional_notes: Used to politely introduce that you want to ask someone some questions. "Te" means "to you" (informal singular object pronoun). You may also hear "lhe fazer algumas perguntas" (more formal) or "fazer algumas perguntas para você".
target_language_example: Antes de começar, eu queria te fazer algumas perguntas.
native_language_example: Before we start, I wanted to ask you a few questions.

additional_notes:
A polite, common way to introduce a question. 
- "te" = "to you" (informal singular object pronoun). In more formal situations you may hear "lhe fazer uma pergunta" or "fazer uma pergunta para você".
- Very often used with modal/polite verbs: "posso" (can I), "queria/gostaria" (I’d like), "preciso" (I need).
- Word order can vary: "Posso te fazer uma pergunta?"
target_language_example: Desculpa, posso te fazer uma pergunta rapidinho?
native_language_example: Sorry, can I ask you a quick question?

meaning: to kill you (literally), or (informally) “to get you in big trouble” / “to be furious with you.”
additional_notes: Literally, it’s the verb phrase “matar” (to kill) with the object pronoun “te” (you). It can be used in real, physical contexts (“That could kill you”) and also as an exaggeration meaning someone will be extremely angry or you’ll be in serious trouble (e.g., “Your mom will kill you!”). When used as a threat (“Eu vou te matar”), it’s very aggressive and can be offensive; the added swear word in the examples makes it even stronger.
target_language_example: Se você chegar atrasado de novo, o chefe vai te matar.
native_language_example: If you’re late again, the boss will kill you (i.e., will be furious with you).

additional_notes: Common structure: mostrar (to show) + te (to you, informal singular). Used when offering to show something or explain how to do something: “Deixa/Deixe-me te mostrar…” = “Let me show you…”. In more formal or common Brazilian Portuguese, you may also hear “mostrar para você” or “te mostrar” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Posso te mostrar onde fica a estação?
native_language_example: Can I show you where the station is?

additional_notes: Used to politely introduce a request. "Te" means "you" (informal singular object pronoun), so it’s common with friends, family, or people you’re on first-name terms with. Often appears with polite/softening verbs like "posso", "poderia", "queria", or "gostaria" (e.g., "Posso te pedir um favor?"). You can add emphasis with "um favor enorme" (a huge favor).
target_language_example: Posso te pedir um favor? Você pode me ajudar com isso?
native_language_example: Can I ask you a favor? Can you help me with this?

additional_notes: Literally “I see you” (te = you, vejo = I see). Commonly used to talk about seeing someone at a specific time/place (“Te vejo amanhã/no domingo/no avião”) and also as a casual farewell meaning “See you!” or “See you later” (“Te vejo amanhã!”, “Te vejo depois.”). You can also hear the plural form “Vejo vocês” = “I’ll see you (all).”
target_language_example: Te vejo mais tarde no café.
native_language_example: See you later at the café.

additional_notes: "Te" is an unstressed object pronoun meaning "you" (informal/singular), very common in Brazil in speech and in casual writing. The verb stays in the infinitive (ver = "to see"), often after another verb like querer (to want) or estar ansioso para (to look forward to). You may also see "ver você" (more explicit) or, in more formal contexts, "vê-lo/vê-la" (to see you/him/her).
target_language_example: Preciso te ver hoje à tarde.
native_language_example: I need to see you this afternoon.

additional_notes: Used when you want to meet someone again or are happy to see them again. Literally “see you again,” with the object pronoun **te** = “you” (informal singular, common in Portugal and in some parts of Brazil). In Brazil, you may also hear **ver você de novo**. Often follows verbs like **esperar** (to hope), **precisar** (to need), **ter que** (to have to), or expressions like **estar contente por** (to be happy to).
target_language_example: Mal posso esperar para te ver de novo amanhã!
native_language_example: I can’t wait to see you again tomorrow!

meaning: "has been" / "has been doing" (recently, over a period of time).
additional_notes: Present perfect of "estar" used to describe a state or repeated situation that has been happening lately or over a recent period (often with words like "ultimamente"). It’s common before adjectives ("tem estado triste") or expressions like "com fome". It can also be used with frequency to mean "has been (there)" repeatedly ("tem estado mais vezes...").
target_language_example: Ele tem estado muito ocupado esta semana.
native_language_example: He has been very busy this week.

additional_notes: "Tem feito" is the present tense of "ter" + past participle (fazer → feito). It talks about something that has happened up to now, often with the idea of repeated/ongoing actions or recent past. Very common in Brazilian Portuguese; in European Portuguese you may hear "tem feito" especially for actions repeated over time.
target_language_example: Ela tem feito muito progresso este mês.
native_language_example: She has made/been making a lot of progress this month.

meaning: “has been doing that” / “has done that (repeatedly, up to now)”.
additional_notes: Uses the Portuguese present perfect: **ter** (in the present) + past participle (**feito**). It often describes something that has been happening repeatedly or continuously from the past until now. Common time expressions with it: **há meses** (“for months”), **todas as noites** (“every night”).
target_language_example: Ela tem feito isso com muita frequência ultimamente.
native_language_example: She has been doing that very often lately.

additional_notes: Form of the verb "ser" using "ter" + past participle ("sido"). It’s used to describe a state, situation, or behavior that started in the past and continues into the present, or has been true repeatedly over a period of time. Often followed by an adjective or noun: "tem sido difícil" (has been difficult), "tem sido nossa casa" (has been our home).
target_language_example: Ultimamente, ele tem sido muito paciente comigo.
native_language_example: Lately, he has been very patient with me.

meaning: 'has been very' / 'has been really' (recently, up to now).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "ter" in the present perfect ("tem sido") to describe an ongoing situation or repeated behavior from the recent past until now. It’s commonly followed by an adjective (simpático, egoísta, paciente) to comment on someone’s behavior. Often implies “lately / these days.”
target_language_example: Você tem sido muito gentil comigo ultimamente.
native_language_example: You’ve been very kind to me lately.

additional_notes: Used to ask or say that something is connected to something else. Very common in questions like “O que X tem a ver com Y?” (“What does X have to do with Y?”). The verb changes with the subject: “tenho a ver com” (I), “tem a ver com” (he/she/you), “têm a ver com” (they/you all).
target_language_example: Isso não tem nada a ver com você.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with you.

additional_notes: Used to say two people (or things) have equal ages. Structure: [person] tem a mesma idade que + [other person/pronoun]. You can change “tem” to match the subject (e.g., “eu tenho…”, “eles têm…”).
target_language_example: Eu tenho a mesma idade que a minha irmã.
native_language_example: I’m the same age as my sister.

meaning: 'there is/are something' or 'has something' (often: 'is there anything…?' / 'do you have anything…?').
additional_notes: Uses the verb **ter** (“to have”). With a stated subject, it literally means **“(someone) has something”**: *Ela tem algo na mão* (“She has something in her hand”). Without a subject, Portuguese often uses **tem** to mean **“there is/are”** (like *há*): *Tem algo aqui para fazer?* (“Is there anything to do here?”). Very common in questions: *Tem algo mais…?* (“Is there anything else…?”) and in expressions like *Você tem algo contra ele?* (“Do you have something against him?”).
target_language_example: Tem algo que eu possa fazer para ajudar?
native_language_example: Is there anything I can do to help?

additional_notes: Used with nouns to mean an unspecified amount or existence. In questions, it often means “any”: “Tem algum restaurante por aqui?” = “Is there any restaurant around here?” It can also mean “has some/any” when talking about someone/something possessing something: “Eles têm algum plano B?” = “Do they have a plan B?” Note: in Brazilian Portuguese, “tem” is commonly used impersonally to mean “there is/are,” even though it’s literally “has.”
target_language_example: Tem algum problema se eu chegar um pouco mais tarde?
native_language_example: Is there any problem if I arrive a little later?

meaning: 'Is there any...?' / 'Do you have any...?' (asking if any exists).
additional_notes: Used to ask if there is any of something (usually a feminine noun) available or present. Common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese as a shorter form of "Tem alguma..." instead of "Há alguma..." or "Você tem alguma...". Often followed by a noun: "Tem alguma sugestão?" (any suggestion), "Tem alguma dúvida?" (any question).
target_language_example: Tem alguma farmácia aberta agora?
native_language_example: Is there any pharmacy open right now?

additional_notes: Uses "ter" in an impersonal way to mean "there is/are" (like "há"). Very common in speech. Often implies suspicion or concern: "Tem alguma coisa com ele" = "Something's wrong with him" / "There's something going on with him." In questions it can mean "Is there anything...?": "Tem alguma coisa aí?" = "Is there something/anything there?"
target_language_example: Acho que tem alguma coisa errada com o computador.
native_language_example: I think there's something wrong with the computer.

additional_notes: Used to say you suspect a problem or that something isn’t right. Very common in speech; often followed by “com” + person/thing: “Tem alguma coisa errada com o meu carro” (“There’s something wrong with my car”). In questions, it can mean “Is something wrong?”
target_language_example: Tem alguma coisa errada com o ar-condicionado; não está esfriando.
native_language_example: There’s something wrong with the air conditioner; it isn’t cooling.

meaning: 'are you sure?' / 'is he/she sure?'; literally 'have certainty'.
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is confident about something. Often appears as a full question by itself (“Tem certeza?”). Common patterns: “Tem certeza de que...?” / informal in speech: “Tem certeza que...?”. Can also be used with a subject: “Ele/ela tem certeza?”.
target_language_example: Tem certeza de que você quer sair agora?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to leave now?

additional_notes: Used to express certainty or to ask someone to confirm something. Often appears as a question without the subject: "Tem certeza de que...?" (= "Are you sure that...?"). With a named subject, it means "[someone] is sure that...": "O Tom tem certeza de que...". The "de que" introduces the clause that follows.
target_language_example: Você tem certeza de que quer sair agora?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to leave now?

additional_notes:
Used to ask for confirmation about a past event or identity. 
- tem certeza = “are you sure” (informal “cê tem certeza”) 
- de que = “that” 
- foi = past of “ser/ir” here meaning “was” (it was). 
Often followed by the person/thing (“foi o Tom…”) or by an emphasized structure like “foi X que/quem…” (“was it X who/that…”).
target_language_example: Tem certeza de que foi a Ana que ligou ontem?
native_language_example: Are you sure it was Ana who called yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to ask for confirmation that no one did something (or is doing something). It’s typically followed by a verb: “Tem certeza de que ninguém te viu?” (“Are you sure no one saw you?”). You can change the object pronoun depending on who: te (you, informal), você (you), o/a (him/her), nos (us).
target_language_example: Tem certeza de que ninguém ouviu a conversa?
native_language_example: Are you sure nobody heard the conversation?

additional_notes: Used to confirm someone’s decision, often before buying/choosing something or doing an action. It’s a shortened form of “Você tem certeza de que quer…?” and can be followed by a noun (“…este/esta?”) or an infinitive verb (“…ir”, “trabalhar”, etc.).
target_language_example: Tem certeza de que quer cancelar a reserva?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to cancel the reservation?

additional_notes: Used to ask for confirmation or express doubt. It’s the verb *ter* (“to have”) + *certeza* (“certainty”), so literally “(you) have certainty that…”. The subject is often omitted and understood as “you” (e.g., *Tem certeza que…?*). You can add a subject for clarity: *Você tem certeza que…?* / *Ele(a) tem certeza que…?*. Very common in conversation; in more formal writing you may also see *Tem certeza de que…*.
target_language_example: Você tem certeza que quer ir agora?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to go now?

additional_notes: Used to confirm someone’s decision or double-check before they do something. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., conhecer, fazer, ficar) or by "isso" (“that/this”). You may also hear the fuller form "Você tem certeza que quer…?"; both mean the same.
target_language_example: Tem certeza que quer sair agora?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to leave now?

meaning: “has to do” / “must do” (is required to do).
additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity. It’s the verb ter (to have) + de + infinitive: eu tenho de fazer, você tem de fazer, ele/ela tem de fazer, nós temos de fazer, eles/elas têm de fazer. Common in instructions: “Tudo o que (você) tem de fazer é…” = “All you have to do is…”. Similar in meaning to “ter que fazer”.
target_language_example: Você tem de fazer isso hoje.
native_language_example: You have to do this today.

additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase **ter de + infinitive** to express obligation/necessity (“have to / must”). **Tem** is the 3rd-person singular present (“he/she/it has to”). You can change the subject: **eu tenho de…**, **você/ele/ela tem de…**, **nós temos de…**, **eles têm de…**. In Brazilian Portuguese, **ter que** is also very common with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Ele tem de fazer isso hoje.
native_language_example: He has to do that today.

additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity to leave or go somewhere. It’s the 3rd person singular present of "ter de" + infinitive (here, "ir"). Common variants: "tenho de ir" (I have to go), "tem que ir" (very common in speech, same meaning), and the fixed phrase "Tenho de ir" = "I have to go (now)".
target_language_example: Desculpa, já é tarde e eu tenho de ir.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s already late and I have to go.

meaning: “has to be / must be” (it’s necessary or logically certain).
additional_notes: Used to express necessity/obligation or a strong conclusion based on what you know. It’s the verb phrase **ter de + infinitive** (“to have to”), here with **ser** (“to be”): **(ele/ela/você) tem de ser** = “he/she/you has to be”; **(isso) tem de ser** = “this has to be.” In everyday speech, **ter que** is also common: **tem que ser**.
target_language_example: Desculpa, mas tem de ser hoje.
native_language_example: Sorry, but it has to be today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has enough money for a purchase. The subject changes with the person (e.g., eu tenho, você tem, ele/ela tem, nós temos). Often followed by the thing being bought: "...para comprar uma casa" / "...para comprar isso". In questions, it can be used to check if someone can afford something.
target_language_example: Acho que não tenho dinheiro suficiente para comprar esse computador agora.
native_language_example: I think I don’t have enough money to buy that computer right now.

meaning: "has two" (there are two; someone/thing possesses two).
additional_notes: "Tem" is the 3rd-person singular of "ter" (to have). It’s used to say someone/it has a quantity of 2: "Ele tem dois amigos" (He has two friends), or that something contains/has two parts/features: "Este carro tem dois lugares" (This car has two seats). With "você" you use "tem" too, but often add the pronoun: "Você tem dois...".
target_language_example: A casa tem dois banheiros.
native_language_example: The house has two bathrooms.

meaning: "has two" (there are two / he-she-it has two of something).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "ter" (to have) in the 3rd person singular: "ele/ela/você" or a thing ("a cidade", "o gato"). It expresses possession or that something contains/has two of something. The number and noun can change: "tem duas praias", "tem duas casas".
target_language_example: A escola tem duas entradas.
native_language_example: The school has two entrances.

additional_notes: Used (often in the negative: “não tem ideia do que…”) to say someone doesn’t know or understand something, or to emphasize surprise (“You have no idea what…!”). It’s followed by a clause starting with “o que” (“what”). In questions, Brazilian Portuguese often adds a tag like “tem?” or “não é?” to confirm (“…, right?”).
target_language_example: Você tem ideia do que aconteceu ontem?
native_language_example: Do you have any idea what happened yesterday?

meaning: "Is there anything else?" / "Do you have anything else?"
additional_notes: Used to ask if there is something additional (another item, more food, another task). Very common in shops, restaurants, and service situations. Often followed by a specific area or purpose: "...lá em cima?" (up there), "...para comer?" (to eat), or "...que eu possa fazer por você?" (that I can do for you). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, "tem" is often used instead of "há" to mean "there is/are."
target_language_example: Tem mais alguma coisa que você precisa hoje?
native_language_example: Is there anything else you need today?

meaning: “has more than” (i.e., is over; has over).
additional_notes: Used with quantities (numbers, ages, amounts) to say something is greater than a stated value. With age or time, it often translates as “is over” (Ela tem mais de 30 anos = She’s over 30). With objects/amounts, it’s literally “has more than” (Ele tem mais de 30 pares de sapatos = He has more than 30 pairs of shoes).
target_language_example: O filme tem mais de duas horas.
native_language_example: The movie is over two hours long.

tem mais ou menos a mesma idade que

target_language_multi_word_term: tem mais ou menos a mesma idade que
additional_notes: Used to compare ages. "mais ou menos" means "more or less / approximately" and softens the statement (you’re not giving an exact age). Usually followed by a person/pronoun (e.g., "que eu", "que nós", "que a gente"). You can swap the subject: "Eu tenho mais ou menos a mesma idade que ele."
target_language_example: Ela tem mais ou menos a mesma idade que o meu irmão.
native_language_example: She’s about the same age as my brother.

additional_notes: From the verb "ter" (to have): "ter medo (de)" = "to be afraid (of/to)". It’s commonly followed by "de" + a thing/person ("tem medo do cavalo" = afraid of the horse) or "de" + an infinitive ("tem medo de ir" = afraid to go). You can also negate it: "não tem medo" = not afraid.
target_language_example: Ela tem medo de falar em público.
native_language_example: She is afraid to speak in public.

additional_notes: Used with a person (ele/ela/você/Tom) + "tem medo de" + a noun or an infinitive verb: "tem medo de cobra" (afraid of snakes), "tem medo de voar" (afraid to fly). For other people, conjugate "ter": "tenho medo de" (I’m afraid of), "temos medo de" (we’re afraid of).
target_language_example: Eu tenho medo de falar em público.
native_language_example: I’m afraid of speaking in public.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ter (to have): eu tenho medo do escuro; você tem medo do escuro? It describes a fear/phobia. You can swap escuro for other fears: tenho medo de aranhas (spiders), tenho medo de altura(s) (heights).
target_language_example: Eu não tenho medo do escuro, mas tenho medo de aranhas.
native_language_example: I'm not afraid of the dark, but I'm afraid of spiders.

meaning: “has a lot of” / “there is (a) lot of” (with a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb ter (“to have”) plus muita (“a lot of”). It can describe possession/characteristics (e.g., alguém tem muita coragem) or existence in a place (common in Brazilian Portuguese: Tem muita neve aqui. = “There’s a lot of snow here.”). Agreement matters: muito (masc. sing.), muita (fem. sing.), muitos (masc. pl.), muitas (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Esse trabalho tem muita importância.
native_language_example: This job has a lot of importance.

additional_notes: Used with feminine plural nouns (muitas + noun): "tem muitas virtudes". In Portuguese, the subject is often omitted, so "Tem muitas vantagens" can mean "It has many advantages" or "There are many advantages," depending on context. A common alternative for the “there are” meaning is "há muitas...".
target_language_example: Aqui tem muitas opções vegetarianas.
native_language_example: There are many vegetarian options here.

additional_notes: From the verb "ter" (to have) in the 3rd person singular present: "ele/ela/você tem". It can refer to having money in general, money available to spend, or money saved (e.g., "no banco"). Often used with "parece que" (it seems that) or "fingir que" (to pretend that).
target_language_example: Ela tem muito dinheiro, mas prefere viver de forma simples.
native_language_example: She has a lot of money, but she prefers to live simply.

additional_notes: From **ter** (to have).
