Common add-ons: "todo dia" (every day), "de ouvido" (by ear), and comparisons like "melhor do que" (better than).
target_language_example: Ela toca piano muito bem.
native_language_example: She plays the piano very well.

additional_notes: From the verb **tocar** (“to play” an instrument) + **violão** (acoustic guitar). **Toca** is the present tense for **ele/ela/você** (“he/she/you”). For **I play**, say **eu toco violão**; for **we play**, **nós tocamos violão**. Common in questions like **Você toca violão?** (“Do you play guitar?”).
target_language_example: Você toca violão todos os dias?
native_language_example: Do you play the (acoustic) guitar every day?

additional_notes: “Tocando” is the gerund of “tocar” (to play an instrument). It’s commonly used with “estar” to talk about something happening right now: “Alguém está tocando piano” = “Someone is playing the piano.”
target_language_example: Ela está tocando piano na sala.
native_language_example: She is playing the piano in the living room.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "tocar" to mean "to play" a musical instrument (also: tocar violão, tocar guitarra). You can say "Eu sei tocar piano" (I can play the piano) or use it after another verb: "começar a tocar piano" (to start playing the piano), "ensinar a tocar piano" (to teach how to play the piano).
target_language_example: Eu gosto de tocar piano à noite.
native_language_example: I like to play the piano at night.

additional_notes: "Tocar" is used for playing musical instruments. "Violão" usually means an acoustic (classical) guitar (as opposed to "guitarra", often electric). Common patterns: "saber tocar violão" (to know how to play), "aprender a tocar violão" (to learn to play), "ensinar a tocar violão" (to teach someone to play). You may also hear "tocar no violão" with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Ele toca violão muito bem.
native_language_example: He plays the guitar very well.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of “tocar a campainha” = to ring the doorbell. Used when someone presses/rings the doorbell at a house, apartment building, gate, etc. You can ask who did it with “Quem tocou a campainha?” or confirm with “Você tocou a campainha?”
target_language_example: Quando cheguei, toquei a campainha e esperei na porta.
native_language_example: When I arrived, I rang the doorbell and waited at the door.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to mean the totality of something: toda a verdade (“the whole truth”), toda a esperança (“all hope”), toda a noite (“all night/the whole night”). It agrees with the noun’s gender/number (compare: todo o, todos os, todas as).
target_language_example: Passei toda a tarde estudando.
native_language_example: I spent the whole afternoon studying.

additional_notes: Means “all people” in general. Very common in everyday speech (often more casual than “todos”). With negation it can mean “not everyone”: “Nem toda a gente…” = “Not everyone…”.
target_language_example: Toda a gente sabe disso.
native_language_example: Everybody knows that.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happened (or never happened) at any point in your entire life. Often appears with superlatives (e.g., “the best … of my life”), with “nunca” (“never”) to stress something has never happened, or with “durante” (“during/for”) to mean “for my whole life.”
target_language_example: Eu queria visitar Lisboa em toda a minha vida, e finalmente consegui este ano.
native_language_example: I had wanted to visit Lisbon all my life, and I finally managed to this year.

meaning: everywhere; all around (usually in “por toda a parte”).
additional_notes: Most often used with the preposition “por”: “por toda a parte” = “everywhere / all over the place.” It can describe people looking in many places (“procurar por toda a parte”) or something being present in many places (“há lixo por toda a parte”).
target_language_example: Procurei meu celular por toda a parte e não encontrei.
native_language_example: I looked for my phone everywhere and didn’t find it.

meaning: "all your" / "all his" / "all her" (referring to a feminine singular thing).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun: toda a sua + noun (e.g., toda a sua carne). It can also be used without the noun when the noun is understood from context (like “all of yours”). “Sua” can mean your/his/her/its, depending on context; in Brazil, for “your” it may be ambiguous, so people often use “toda a sua” with você-context or replace it with “toda a sua” + noun for clarity.
target_language_example: Eu li toda a sua mensagem.
native_language_example: I read your whole message.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens regularly in the morning. Common with routine verbs like acordar (to wake up), tomar banho (to shower), escovar os dentes (to brush teeth), and ler (to read). You can also hear "todas as manhãs" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Eu tomo café toda manhã antes do trabalho.
native_language_example: I have coffee every morning before work.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as the fixed phrase “em toda parte” = “everywhere / all over (a place)”. It can refer to something being present in many locations or spread throughout an area.
target_language_example: Procurei minhas chaves, mas havia bagunça em toda parte.
native_language_example: I looked for my keys, but there was mess everywhere.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens regularly on Mondays. "toda" + a day of the week = "every" (e.g., toda terça-feira = every Tuesday). You can also say "todas as segundas-feiras" (more explicit/plural) with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Tenho aula de português toda segunda-feira.
native_language_example: I have Portuguese class every Monday.

additional_notes: Introduces a repeated situation: each time something happens, this follows. Often interchangeable with “sempre que” (whenever).
target_language_example: Toda vez que chove, eu levo um guarda-chuva.
native_language_example: Every time it rains, I take an umbrella.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to mean the entire group: todas as pessoas (all the people), todas as coisas (all the things). It agrees with the noun’s gender/number (compare: todos os + masculine plural). Often appears after quantities like "a maioria de" (most of) or with time expressions like "todas as manhãs" (every morning).
target_language_example: Eu li todas as mensagens.
native_language_example: I read all the messages.

additional_notes: Literal phrase: todas (“all”) + as (“the”, feminine plural) + cartas. In many everyday contexts, carta means a written letter (often personal letters), as in “rasgou/queimei todas as cartas” (“he tore up/burned all the letters”). It can also mean cards (e.g., playing cards), so the exact meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Guardei todas as cartas numa caixa.
native_language_example: I kept all the letters in a box.

additional_notes: Used to refer to everything in general or every item in a set. Common in expressions like "considerando todas as coisas" (all things considered) and in more formal/religious contexts like "a causa de todas as coisas" (the cause of all things).
target_language_example: Eu já vi todas as coisas que você me mostrou.
native_language_example: I’ve already seen everything you showed me.

additional_notes: Means every child in a group. It’s feminine plural: todas (all, fem. pl.) + as (the, fem. pl.) + crianças (children). Often used with the imperfect or present to describe what the whole group was/is doing (e.g., Todas as crianças estavam..., Todas as crianças estão...).
target_language_example: Todas as crianças estão esperando o ônibus.
native_language_example: All the children are waiting for the bus.

additional_notes: Used to refer to every window in a place/area. "todas" = all (feminine plural), "as" = the (feminine plural), "janelas" = windows. Often appears with verbs like "abrir" (to open), "fechar" (to close), and "trancar" (to lock).
target_language_example: Antes de sair, verifique se todas as janelas estão fechadas.
native_language_example: Before leaving, check if all the windows are closed.

additional_notes: Used to refer to every light (bulb/lamp) in a place. Common with verbs like "apagar" (to turn off) and "acender/estar acesas" (to turn on / be on).
target_language_example: Você pode apagar todas as luzes, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you turn off all the lights, please?

additional_notes: Means something happens each morning as a routine. It can go at the beginning or end of the sentence (e.g., “Todas as manhãs, ...” or “..., todas as manhãs.”).
target_language_example: Eu caminho no parque todas as manhãs.
native_language_example: I walk in the park every morning.

additional_notes: "Todas" (feminine plural of "todo") agrees with the feminine plural noun "maçãs". Used to refer to the entire set of apples in a situation. Similar patterns: "todas as frutas" (all the fruits), "todas as casas" (all the houses).
target_language_example: Comemos todas as maçãs depois do jantar.
native_language_example: We ate all the apples after dinner.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to mean you’re referring to every one of your own things: todas as minhas malas (all my suitcases), todas as minhas perguntas (all my questions), todas as minhas ideias (all my ideas). With masculine plural nouns, use "todos os meus" (e.g., todos os meus livros).
target_language_example: Eu perdi todas as minhas chaves.
native_language_example: I lost all my keys.

additional_notes: Used when the speaker is referring to a group made up of women/girls (“amigas” is feminine plural). If your friends are men or mixed, you usually say “todos os meus amigos” (masculine plural). Often used with verbs in the plural: “todas as minhas amigas dizem/gostam/sabem/têm…”.
target_language_example: Hoje vou sair com todas as minhas amigas.
native_language_example: Today I'm going out with all my (female) friends.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens nightly (a repeated habit or routine). It can go at the beginning or end of the sentence. Contrast: "toda noite" is also common and means the same thing.
target_language_example: Eu estudo português todas as noites.
native_language_example: I study Portuguese every night.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to mean “all of our …”. It agrees with the noun: use it with feminine plural words like perguntas (questions), reuniões (meetings), tentativas (attempts), forças (forces). For masculine plural, you’d say “todos os nossos” (e.g., todos os nossos amigos).
target_language_example: Todas as nossas malas estão no carro.
native_language_example: All our suitcases are in the car.

additional_notes: Used to refer to every question in a set (e.g., on a test, in a form, in an interview). Often appears with verbs like "responder" (to answer): "responder todas as perguntas" = "answer all the questions". "Todas" agrees in gender/number with "perguntas" (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Você respondeu todas as perguntas do formulário?
native_language_example: Did you answer all the questions on the form?

meaning: 'all people' / 'everyone' (in a group or in general).
additional_notes: Literally “all the people.” Use it with a qualifier to mean a specific group: “todas as pessoas na casa” (all the people in the house), “todas as pessoas importantes” (all the important people). With “de” it often means “out of all the people”: “De todas as pessoas, eu…” (Of all people, me…).
target_language_example: Todas as pessoas aqui sabem o seu nome.
native_language_example: Everyone here knows your name.

additional_notes: Used to refer to every door in a place or situation. It’s the plural of "toda a porta" (rare) and is built from: "todas" (all, feminine plural) + "as" (the, feminine plural) + "portas" (doors). Often appears with quantity words like "quase" (almost): "Quase todas as portas...".
target_language_example: Quando chegamos, todas as portas estavam trancadas.
native_language_example: When we arrived, all the doors were locked.

additional_notes: Used literally (e.g., in a test: “all the answers are correct”) and also figuratively to mean “to know everything / have every solution,” often said when someone seems very confident or acts like they know it all. Agreement can vary: “todas as respostas estão corretas/certas” or “todas as respostas são corretas.”
target_language_example: Ele age como se tivesse todas as respostas.
native_language_example: He acts like he has all the answers.

meaning: every Monday (i.e., on Mondays; weekly on Monday).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens regularly on Mondays. It’s often short for “todas as segundas-feiras” (every Monday). You can use the same pattern with other weekdays: “todas as terças”, “todas as quartas”, etc.
target_language_example: A gente tem aula de português todas as segundas.
native_language_example: We have Portuguese class every Monday.

meaning: “all of your” (referring to feminine plural things).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to mean “all of your …”: e.g., “todas as suas joias” = “all your jewelry,” “todas as suas fotos” = “all your photos.” It agrees with what is owned (feminine plural). For masculine plural, use “todos os seus.”
target_language_example: Eu guardei todas as suas cartas numa gaveta.
native_language_example: I kept all your letters in a drawer.

additional_notes: Used to refer to every question someone has. Often appears with verbs like responder a (“to answer”): “responder a todas as suas perguntas.” Note the agreement: todas (feminine plural) matches perguntas (feminine plural). “Suas” can mean “your” (formal) or “his/her/their” depending on context.
target_language_example: Vou responder a todas as suas perguntas depois da reunião.
native_language_example: I’ll answer all your questions after the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on every occasion. Often followed by a clause with "que" ("todas as vezes que..." = "every time that..."). Can also mean "all the times" when referring back to several past occasions (e.g., "depois de todas as vezes que...").
target_language_example: Todas as vezes que eu ligo, ninguém atende.
native_language_example: Every time I call, nobody answers.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens each day (a routine or habit). Often placed at the end of the sentence, but it can also come earlier for emphasis. Common variant: "todos os dias" (also means “every day”).
target_language_example: Eu caminho todo dia depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I walk every day after work.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens regularly on weekends. It’s very common in conversation. You can also hear the plural form "todos os fins de semana" with the same meaning (often a bit more general).
target_language_example: Eu estudo português todo fim de semana.
native_language_example: I study Portuguese every weekend.

additional_notes: Used to say that all the people in a group were in a certain state or doing something. "Todo mundo" means “everyone/everybody” (literally “all the world/everyone”), and "estava" is the imperfect past of "estar" (“to be” for temporary states), often followed by an adjective (confuso, acordado) or a verb form describing an action/state (e.g., olhando, escutando, me encarando).
target_language_example: Quando eu cheguei, todo mundo estava esperando.
native_language_example: When I arrived, everyone was waiting.

additional_notes: Used to say that all people in a group (or people in general) are in a certain state or doing something. It’s made of: todo mundo = everyone/everybody + está = is (present of 'estar', for temporary states, feelings, actions, or situations). Often followed by a verb in -ndo (progressive) or an adjective (state/feeling).
target_language_example: Todo mundo está com fome agora.
native_language_example: Everyone is hungry now.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about what people in general like. "Todo mundo" = "everyone" (very common; similar to "todo o mundo"). "Gosta de" is from "gostar de" (to like) and is followed by a noun or a verb in the infinitive: "gosta de pizza", "gosta de brincar". In questions/negatives you may see "todo mundo não..." meaning "not everyone..." depending on context.
target_language_example: Todo mundo gosta de viajar nas férias.
native_language_example: Everyone likes to travel on vacation.

additional_notes: Used to say that a need or obligation applies to all people in a group (often meaning “everyone” in general). It’s followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., aprender, acreditar, checar) or by “de + infinitive” with some verbs: “precisa descer” (needs to get off), “precisa se acalmar” (needs to calm down). In speech, “todo mundo” is very common; “todos” is more formal.
target_language_example: Todo mundo precisa ter paciência.
native_language_example: Everyone needs to have patience.

additional_notes: Used to say something is common knowledge or obvious. Often appears as a complete sentence (“Todo mundo sabe.”) or followed by a clause: “todo mundo sabe que…” (“everyone knows that…”). It can also be used rhetorically/ironically, depending on tone.
target_language_example: Todo mundo sabe que isso não vai funcionar.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that this isn’t going to work.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something presented as common knowledge or obvious. Very common in speech and writing; often implies “it’s no secret that…”. You can also hear "todo o mundo sabe que" (more formal/European).
target_language_example: Todo mundo sabe que ela trabalha muito.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that she works a lot.

additional_notes: "Todo mundo" means "everyone/everybody". The "se" is a reflexive/pronominal clitic that many Portuguese verbs use: it can mean "themselves" (reflexive, e.g., "todo mundo se assustou" = everyone got scared), or just be part of the verb meaning (pronominal verb, e.g., "calar-se" = to fall silent, "juntar-se" = to join/gather). In English you usually don’t translate the "se" directly; you translate the whole verb phrase naturally.
target_language_example: Na reunião, todo mundo se apresentou rapidamente.
native_language_example: At the meeting, everyone introduced themselves quickly.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about all people. Very common in everyday speech; a more formal option is “todos têm…”. If you see “todo mundo tem de…”, it means “everyone has to / must…”.
target_language_example: Todo mundo tem dias bons e dias ruins.
native_language_example: Everyone has good days and bad days.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun with the definite article o to mean the entire thing or the full amount: todo o país (the whole country), todo o vinho (all the wine), todo o crédito (all the credit). It changes with gender/number: toda a (fem. sing.), todos os (masc. plural), todas as (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Li todo o livro em um dia.
native_language_example: I read the whole book in one day.

additional_notes: Uses the structure "todo" + "o" + noun to mean "all/whole" of something specific. Often followed by "de" to show whose money it is ("todo o dinheiro dele/dela" = "all his/her money"). You can also use it without a possessor when the context is clear ("Todo o dinheiro acabou" = "All the money ran out").
target_language_example: Eu não vou gastar todo o dinheiro de uma vez.
native_language_example: I’m not going to spend all the money at once.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with **que** (“that/which”) describing the money: **todo o dinheiro que + verb**. Common with verbs like **ter** (to have), **dever** (to owe), **ganhar/perder** (to win/lose), **roubar** (to steal), **emprestar** (to lend). Example: **todo o dinheiro que eu tinha** = “all the money that I had.”
target_language_example: Gastei todo o dinheiro que eu tinha na viagem.
native_language_example: I spent all the money I had on the trip.

additional_notes: Used to say that you have none (or almost none) left because it was stolen, spent, given away, lost, etc. It’s a noun phrase: todo (all) + o meu (my) + dinheiro (money). You can change the person/number: todo o seu dinheiro (all your money), todo o dinheiro dele (all his money).
target_language_example: Não posso sair hoje; gastei todo o meu dinheiro.
native_language_example: I can’t go out today; I spent all my money.

additional_notes: Means “all people” in general. Very common in speech and writing. Often used with singular verbs in Portuguese: “Todo o mundo sabe...” (= “Everyone knows...”). Similar to “toda a gente” (more informal in many places).
target_language_example: Todo o mundo está esperando por você.
native_language_example: Everyone is waiting for you.

meaning: all the time; the whole time.
additional_notes: Often means "constantly" (frequently/always): "Ela pensa nele todo o tempo." It can also mean "for the entire duration" of something: "Fiquei lá todo o tempo." In phrases like "todo o tempo do mundo," it means you have plenty of time (no hurry).
target_language_example: Não precisa ter pressa — eu tenho todo o tempo do mundo.
native_language_example: No need to hurry — I have all the time in the world.

additional_notes: Used to refer to every person/thing in a previously mentioned group. With people, it often means “all the men / all of them (mixed group).” For an all-female group, you usually say “todas elas.” It can be a subject (“Todos eles falam…”) or an object (“Conheço todos eles”).
target_language_example: Eu não conheço todos eles, só alguns.
native_language_example: I don’t know all of them, only some.

additional_notes: Used to include the speaker (“nós” = “we/us”). Common after prepositions: “a todos nós” (to all of us), “de todos nós” (of all of us/among us), “com todos nós” (with all of us). Often used for emphasis, similar to English “all of us.”
target_language_example: Isso afeta todos nós.
native_language_example: This affects all of us.

meaning: 'all the' (plural masculine), meaning every one of a group.
additional_notes: Used before a plural masculine noun: "todos os + noun" = “all the / every (plural)”. It agrees with gender/number: feminine "todas as" (todas as casas), singular "todo o" (todo o dia), "toda a" (toda a noite). With numbers it means “all (of them)”: "todos os três" = “all three”.
target_language_example: Eu preciso de todos os documentos antes de assinar.
native_language_example: I need all the documents before signing.

meaning: “all the students” (every student in a group).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the entire set of students you’re talking about. Often followed by a clarifier like “da classe” (in the class), “da nossa escola” (at our school). You can also say “quase todos os alunos” for “almost all the students.”
target_language_example: Todos os alunos precisam trazer um caderno amanhã.
native_language_example: All the students need to bring a notebook tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens annually or repeatedly each year. Often placed at the end of the sentence (but it can also appear earlier for emphasis).
target_language_example: A minha família viaja para a praia todos os anos.
native_language_example: My family travels to the beach every year.

additional_notes: Means every cookie/biscuit in a group. Uses masculine plural: todo (all) + os (the) + biscoitos (cookies/biscuits). In Brazil, biscoito is common for cookies; in Portugal, bolachas is more common.
target_language_example: Não coma todos os biscoitos — deixe alguns para os outros.
native_language_example: Don’t eat all the cookies—leave some for the others.

additional_notes: Used when you want complete information about something. It often follows verbs like dar (to give), anotar (to write down), saber (to know), ter (to have), lembrar (to remember), and ouvir (to hear).
target_language_example: Pode me contar todos os detalhes do que aconteceu?
native_language_example: Can you tell me all the details of what happened?

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens each day as a routine or habit. Very common with present tense (e.g., "Eu estudo todos os dias"). You can also say "todo dia" in casual speech with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Eu caminho todos os dias antes do trabalho.
native_language_example: I walk every day before work.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens daily (Monday through Sunday), often implying a regular routine. It’s common to add an exception with "exceto" (except) or "menos" (minus), e.g., "todos os dias da semana, exceto domingo".
target_language_example: O café fica aberto todos os dias da semana, mas fecha aos feriados.
native_language_example: The café is open every day of the week, but it closes on holidays.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens regularly on Sundays. Often follows the verb (e.g., "vou... todos os domingos"), but it can also appear at the beginning for emphasis: "Todos os domingos, ...". You can swap the day to make similar phrases: "todas as segundas-feiras" (every Monday), "todos os sábados" (every Saturday).
target_language_example: Eu telefono para a minha avó todos os domingos.
native_language_example: I call my grandma every Sunday.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that everything possible was tried. Common in formal or serious contexts (work, medicine, negotiations). Often appears with verbs like fazer (“to make”) or with results like em vão (“in vain”) and inúteis (“useless”).
target_language_example: Fizemos todos os esforços para chegar a tempo.
native_language_example: We made every effort to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to refer to every student in a group. Often appears with quantifiers like "nem todos" (not all) and "quase todos" (almost all). "Todos" agrees in gender/number with the noun: e.g., "todas as estudantes" (all the [female] students).
target_language_example: Todos os estudantes precisam trazer um documento amanhã.
native_language_example: All the students need to bring an ID tomorrow.

additional_notes: Means “all men” in general (often about humanity/mankind). It uses the masculine plural “homens,” which in Portuguese can refer to males specifically or to people in general depending on context. Singular is “todo homem” (“every man”).
target_language_example: Todos os homens têm direito à liberdade.
native_language_example: All people have the right to freedom.

additional_notes: Used to make a broad generalization about men, often followed by an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., iguais, mortais). Grammatically: todos (all) + os homens (the men) + são (are). Common in debates or quotes; it can sound stereotypical depending on context.
target_language_example: Nem todos os homens são assim, mas alguns são.
native_language_example: Not all men are like that, but some are.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the entire set of books in a context (“all of the books”). It often appears with an added qualifier like “todos os livros de…” (all the books by/about…), or with a relative clause: “todos os livros que…” (all the books that…).
target_language_example: Eu preciso organizar todos os livros antes de amanhã.
native_language_example: I need to organize all the books before tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Todos" means "all" and "os meninos" means "the boys" (plural of "o menino"). Used to refer to an entire group of boys. If you want to say "almost all the boys," you can say "quase todos os meninos."
target_language_example: Todos os meninos da turma chegaram cedo.
native_language_example: All the boys in the class arrived early.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean that every one of your things/people in that group is included (e.g., planos, irmãos). For feminine plural nouns, use “todas as minhas” (e.g., todas as minhas ideias).
target_language_example: Perdi todos os meus documentos.
native_language_example: I lost all my documents.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your entire group of friends. You can change it for other people or groups: "todos os meus colegas" (all my coworkers/classmates), "todos os seus amigos" (all your friends). Note the masculine plural "amigos" is also used for mixed-gender groups; for an all-female group you can say "todas as minhas amigas".
target_language_example: Todos os meus amigos moram perto daqui.
native_language_example: All of my friends live near here.

additional_notes: Used to refer to all of your children as a group. It often appears as the subject of a sentence (Todos os meus filhos...) or in comparisons/contrasts with "de": "De todos os meus filhos, ..." = "Of all my children, ...".
target_language_example: Todos os meus filhos estudam na mesma escola.
native_language_example: All my children go to the same school.

additional_notes: Used before a plural masculine noun to mean “all of our …”. It can also be used when the group is mixed or gender is unknown. For plural feminine nouns, use “todas as nossas” (e.g., “todas as nossas ideias”).
target_language_example: Todos os nossos amigos chegaram cedo.
native_language_example: All our friends arrived early.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the entire group of passengers (e.g., on a plane, bus, train, or boat). It often appears in questions like “Todos os passageiros estão a bordo?” (“Are all the passengers on board?”). With negation, “nem todos os passageiros…” means “not all the passengers…”.
target_language_example: Todos os passageiros devem apresentar o bilhete na entrada.
native_language_example: All passengers must show their ticket at the entrance.

meaning: all beings (all living things / all creatures).
additional_notes: Means “all beings” in a broad, general sense. Often appears as “todos os seres vivos” = “all living beings,” especially in science or nature contexts. In everyday speech, you’ll also hear “todo mundo” for “everyone” (people), while “todos os seres” sounds more formal/philosophical.
target_language_example: Devemos respeitar todos os seres e proteger a natureza.
native_language_example: We should respect all beings and protect nature.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean “all of someone’s …”. It’s made of: todos (all) + os (the, masculine plural) + seus (possessive, masculine plural). In Portuguese, "seus" can mean "his", "her", "your" (formal singular or plural), or "their", so context often decides who owns the thing. It must agree with the noun: feminine plural is "todas as suas"; masculine singular is "todo o seu"; feminine singular is "toda a sua".
target_language_example: Ela vendeu todos os seus livros antigos.
native_language_example: She sold all of her old books.

additional_notes: Means “all of your problems” or “all of his/her/their problems,” depending on who “seus” refers to in context. Common with verbs like falar de (to talk about) and culpar [alguém] por (to blame [someone] for). Literally: todos (all) + os (the) + seus (your/his/her/their) + problemas (problems).
target_language_example: Não me culpe por todos os seus problemas.
native_language_example: Don’t blame me for all your problems.

meaning: 'all your dreams' + 'se' (used before a verb like 'come true').
additional_notes: Used in wishes or promotional phrases, usually completed with a verb like "realizem" (come true) or "tornem realidade" (become reality). "Se" is part of the verb structure here (e.g., "realizar-se" = to come true). Often appears after "Espero que..." or on its own as a wish: "Que todos os seus sonhos se realizem!"
target_language_example: Que todos os seus sonhos se realizem neste ano!
native_language_example: May all your dreams come true this year!

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to say there are many different varieties or categories of something. Common in descriptions and general statements: "todos os tipos de + noun".
target_language_example: Eles vendem todos os tipos de comida aqui.
native_language_example: They sell all kinds of food here.

additional_notes: Used to address a group directly. It’s emphatic; often you can also just say “vocês” if the meaning is clear. It can be warm (“Eu amo todos vocês”) or hostile depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Obrigado a todos vocês pela ajuda.
native_language_example: Thank you all for the help.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a past state or condition of a whole group. "Todos" = everyone/all (people), and "estavam" is the imperfect past of "estar" (to be), often used for ongoing situations, states, or descriptions in the past. Adjectives that follow usually agree in plural (e.g., "cansados", "felizes").
target_language_example: Quando cheguei, todos estavam na sala.
native_language_example: When I arrived, everyone was in the living room.

additional_notes: Used to say that all the people in a group are doing/being something. "Todos" is plural and "estão" is the plural form of "estar" (to be for temporary states/conditions). Often followed by a gerund (-ando/-endo/-indo) like "gritando" or by an expression like "de acordo".
target_language_example: Todos estão esperando por você.
native_language_example: Everyone is waiting for you.

additional_notes: Used to include the speaker (“nós” = “we/us”). Common after prepositions: “a todos nós” (to all of us), “de todos nós” (of all of us/among us), “com todos nós” (with all of us). Often used for emphasis, similar to English “all of us.”
target_language_example: Isso afeta todos nós.
native_language_example: This affects all of us.

meaning: “we all feel” / “we all miss (someone)” (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally “all of us feel.” In the examples, it’s followed by “a tua/sua falta” (= “your absence”), which is the very common expression “sentir falta de (alguém)” meaning “to miss (someone).” Use “tua” for informal ‘your’ (tu) and “sua” for more formal ‘your’ (você/o senhor/a senhora).
target_language_example: Todos nós sentimos a tua falta aqui.
native_language_example: We all miss you here.

meaning: “we all have / all of us have.”
additional_notes: Used to make a general statement that applies to everyone, often introducing something shared (feelings, needs, faults, experiences). Word order is fixed: todos (all) + nós (we/us) + temos (we have). It’s commonly followed by a noun phrase like “nossos defeitos” (our flaws) or an abstract need like “sede de amor” (a thirst/need for love).
target_language_example: Todos nós temos dias bons e dias ruins.
native_language_example: We all have good days and bad days.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause stating something generally known or obvious. “que” links to the following idea (like “that” in English) and is usually kept in Portuguese: “Todos sabem que + [sentence].”
target_language_example: Todos sabem que amanhã vai chover.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "tomar" + "banho" to talk about washing your body (usually taking a shower, sometimes a bath depending on context). Common in questions about routine: "A que horas você toma banho?" You can add frequency or time expressions: "de manhã", "à noite", "todo dia".
target_language_example: Eu tomo banho antes de dormir.
native_language_example: I take a shower before going to sleep.

meaning: "(he/she) takes a shower (or bath) every morning."
additional_notes: "Tomar banho" means to bathe; in everyday Brazilian Portuguese it often implies "to take a shower." "Toma" is the present tense for ele/ela/você (he/she/you formal). "Todas as manhãs" means "every morning" and expresses a routine/habit.
target_language_example: Meu pai toma banho todas as manhãs antes do trabalho.
native_language_example: My dad takes a shower every morning before work.

additional_notes: From the verb "tomar" (to have/take, commonly used with meals/drinks in Brazilian Portuguese) + "café da manhã" (breakfast). Used to talk about the habit or time when someone eats breakfast. With "você", the form is also "toma" (e.g., "Você toma café da manhã?"), though in more formal speech you may hear "você toma" vs. "o senhor/a senhora toma".
target_language_example: Eu tomo café da manhã às sete antes de sair de casa.
native_language_example: I have breakfast at seven before leaving home.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **tomar** (“to take/have”) to talk about eating breakfast. You can change the subject and verb: **eu tomo**, **você toma**, **o Tom toma**, **eles tomam**. Common in Brazilian Portuguese; also heard: **tomar café da manhã** (without “o”).
target_language_example: Eu tomo o café da manhã às sete.
native_language_example: I have breakfast at seven.

additional_notes: "Tomando" is the gerund of "tomar" (to take / to have / to drink). With meals in Brazilian Portuguese, "tomar" is often used to mean “to have” (especially breakfast): "tomar café da manhã" = to have breakfast. In context it often appears with "estar" to describe what someone is doing right now: "estou/estamos/estavam tomando café da manhã".
target_language_example: Desculpe, não posso falar agora; estou tomando café da manhã.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t talk right now; I’m having breakfast.

meaning: To take a bath / to shower (to bathe).
additional_notes: Very common way to talk about bathing in general; in many contexts it can mean either a bath or a shower depending on what’s typical/clear from context. Often used with time expressions: “tomar banho à noite” (to bathe at night). Can also be used as a command: “Vá tomar banho!” (Go take a bath/shower!).
target_language_example: Vou tomar banho antes de dormir.
native_language_example: I’m going to take a shower before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Common everyday way to say you eat breakfast (literally “to take breakfast”). In Brazil, “café da manhã” is “breakfast.” You can also say “comer café da manhã” (to eat breakfast), but “tomar” is very common, especially when breakfast includes coffee or other drinks.
target_language_example: Eu gosto de tomar café da manhã cedo.
native_language_example: I like to have breakfast early.

meaning: to take care of; to look after.
additional_notes: Used when someone is responsible for a person, child, pet, or even a place/thing for a period of time (like babysitting/pet-sitting). It’s usually followed by a noun with a definite article: tomar conta do (masc. singular), da (fem. singular), dos (masc. plural), das (fem. plural). Common in requests and arrangements: “Você pode tomar conta do meu cachorro?”
target_language_example: Você pode tomar conta da minha filha por uma hora?
native_language_example: Can you look after my daughter for an hour?

additional_notes: A common way to say “have breakfast” in Brazilian Portuguese. Literally “to take the morning coffee,” but it refers to eating breakfast in general (not only coffee). Also used with a place or time: “tomar o café da manhã no hotel / às sete.”
target_language_example: Vamos tomar o café da manhã antes de sair?
native_language_example: Shall we have breakfast before leaving?

meaning: to take a bath; to take a shower (to wash yourself).
additional_notes: Often means washing yourself in general, so it can refer to either a bath or a shower depending on context. Very common with "precisar" (Preciso tomar um banho) and suggestions with "é melhor" (É melhor você tomar um banho...). Note: "banho de sol" means "sunbath" (not washing).
target_language_example: Vou tomar um banho antes de sair.
native_language_example: I'm going to take a shower before leaving.

additional_notes: Very common, neutral phrase. Often used with "ter de" / "ter que" (have to) or "precisar" (need to): "Temos de tomar uma decisão" = "We have to make a decision." You may also hear "decidir" as a shorter alternative ("Temos de decidir" = "We have to decide").
target_language_example: Precisamos tomar uma decisão hoje.
native_language_example: We need to make a decision today.

meaning: to have/drink a cup of coffee.
additional_notes: A common, polite way to invite someone for coffee or say you want coffee. In everyday speech, Brazilians often say "tomar café" or "tomar um café" (have a coffee). "Tomar" literally means "to take," but with drinks it often means "to drink/have."
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, vamos tomar uma xícara de café.
native_language_example: After lunch, let's have a cup of coffee.

additional_notes:
Polite command form (imperative) of "tomar" used to warn someone or give safety advice. Often followed by:
- "com" + noun/pronoun: "Tome cuidado com o cachorro." (Be careful with the dog.)
- "ao" + infinitive: "Tome cuidado ao atravessar a rua." (Be careful when crossing the street.)
- "para" + infinitive: "Tome cuidado para não cair." (Be careful not to fall.)
- "quando" + clause: "Tome cuidado quando estiver dirigindo." (Be careful when you’re driving.)
More informal (to one person you call "você") is "toma cuidado".
target_language_example: Tome cuidado com os carros ao atravessar a rua.
native_language_example: Be careful with the cars when crossing the street.

additional_notes: Used to warn or advise someone to avoid an unwanted result. "Tome" is the você-form command of "tomar"; in informal speech with "tu" you may hear "toma cuidado para não...". Often followed by an infinitive verb: "tome cuidado para não + verb".
target_language_example: Tome cuidado para não se machucar na escada.
native_language_example: Be careful not to hurt yourself on the stairs.

additional_notes: "Tomar café da manhã" means "to have/eat breakfast." "Tomei" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) for "I," used for a completed action. It’s very common with "ainda não" (not yet) and with time expressions like "às oito" (at eight). Literally it’s "I took morning coffee," but it’s used like "have breakfast."
target_language_example: Hoje eu tomei café da manhã cedo.
native_language_example: Today I had breakfast early.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **tomar banho** (“to take a shower/bath”). In Brazilian Portuguese, it very often means **to shower**, unless the context makes it clear it’s a bath. Common with time expressions: **de manhã** (in the morning), **à noite** (at night), **todo dia** (every day), **uma vez por dia** (once a day). You can change the verb to match the subject: **eu tomo**, **você toma**, **ele/ela toma**, **a gente toma**, **nós tomamos**, **eles/elas tomam**.
target_language_example: Depois da academia, eu tomo banho e vou trabalhar.
native_language_example: After the gym, I take a shower and go to work.

tomo um banho antes de ir

target_language_multi_word_term: tomo um banho antes de ir
meaning: “I take a shower/bath before going (to do something).”
additional_notes: tomo = “I take” (present tense of tomar). um banho can mean “a shower” or “a bath” depending on context; in everyday Portuguese it often refers to taking a shower. antes de ir means “before going (to…)” and is commonly followed by an action like me deitar (“go to bed/lie down”) or para a cama (“to bed”).
target_language_example: Tomo um banho antes de ir para o trabalho.
native_language_example: I take a shower before going to work.

additional_notes: Past tense of "tomar café da manhã" (“to have/eat breakfast”). Very common in Brazil; you can use it with different subjects: "Eu tomei..." (I had), "Você tomou..." (you had), "A gente tomou..." (we had). In Portugal, "tomar o pequeno-almoço" is more common.
target_language_example: Ela tomou café da manhã cedo antes de sair.
native_language_example: She had breakfast early before leaving.

meaning: "(he) took a bath" / "(he) had a shower".
additional_notes: Past tense (simple past) of "tomar um banho". In Portuguese, "tomar" is commonly used with "banho" to mean to bathe/shower. Which one (bath vs. shower) depends on context; you can add details like "um banho frio" (a cold shower/bath) or "um banho rápido" (a quick shower/bath). You can change the subject: "Eu tomei um banho" (I took a shower).
target_language_example: Depois do treino, ele tomou um banho e saiu.
native_language_example: After the workout, he took a shower and left.

additional_notes: Commonly used with prepositions like "no" (at/on the summit) and "ao" (to the summit). "Topo" means the top/upper part of something; "montanha" is mountain.
target_language_example: Chegamos ao topo da montanha antes do pôr do sol.
native_language_example: We reached the top of the mountain before sunset.

additional_notes: Used to say someone injured their ankle by twisting it (common in sports or accidents). It’s the past tense of "torcer" (to twist/sprain) + "o tornozelo" (the ankle). You can change the subject/person ("eu torci", "você torceu", "eles torceram") and often add a possessive: "torceu o tornozelo" or "torceu o seu tornozelo".
target_language_example: Eu torci o tornozelo jogando futebol.
native_language_example: I sprained my ankle playing soccer.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb used for a change of state or status (profession, situation, condition). Often followed by a noun/adjective: "tornar-se médico/a", "tornar-se famoso/a". In everyday speech, many speakers also use "virar" or "ficar" depending on the context.
target_language_example: Depois de muito estudo, ele se tornou engenheiro.
native_language_example: After a lot of studying, he became an engineer.

additional_notes: Past form of the reflexive verb "tornar-se" = "to become". It’s common in writing and more formal speech. Structure: "[subject] tornou-se + noun/adjective" (often with an article: "tornou-se um/uma..."). In everyday conversation, "virou" is often used instead.
target_language_example: Com o tempo, o bairro tornou-se mais seguro.
native_language_example: Over time, the neighborhood became safer.

additional_notes: Used with professions/roles/statuses to say someone became something. It’s the past (preterite) of the reflexive verb **tornar-se** (“to become”): **(ele/ela) tornou-se** = “he/she became.” Use **tornou-se uma** with a feminine noun (e.g., *tornou-se uma médica*). Common in more formal or written Portuguese; **virou** is often more casual in speech.
target_language_example: Depois de muitos anos de estudo, ele tornou-se um médico.
native_language_example: After many years of study, he became a doctor.

additional_notes: A dessert (a pie) made with apples. Very common in everyday conversation and on restaurant menus. You can use it with or without an article depending on context: "uma torta de maçã" (an apple pie) vs. "torta de maçã" (apple pie as the thing ordered/liked).
target_language_example: Vou pedir uma fatia de torta de maçã.
native_language_example: I’m going to order a slice of apple pie.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s profession or role. The verb agrees with the subject: eu trabalho como, você trabalha como, ele/ela trabalha como, nós trabalhamos como, eles/elas trabalham como.
target_language_example: Eu trabalho como enfermeira.
native_language_example: I work as a nurse.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone works with a lot of effort. It’s the verb trabalhar (“to work”) in the present tense (ele/ela/você trabalha) plus the adverb duro (“hard”). You can change the subject: Eu trabalho duro (I work hard), Nós trabalhamos duro (We work hard).
target_language_example: Eu trabalho duro todos os dias.
native_language_example: I work hard every day.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s job is at a bank. It’s the verb phrase “trabalha” (works) + “em um” (at a) + “banco” (bank). You can change the subject: “Eu trabalho…”, “Ele trabalha…”, etc. Note: “banco” can also mean “bench” depending on context, but with “trabalhar em”, it usually means a (financial) bank.
target_language_example: Meu pai trabalha em um banco no centro.
native_language_example: My dad works at a bank downtown.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone works. You follow it with a feminine noun (often places that take "uma"): "uma creche" (daycare), "uma farmácia" (pharmacy), "uma loja" (store). With a masculine place, use "trabalha em um" (e.g., "em um hospital").
target_language_example: Ela trabalha em uma escola perto de casa.
native_language_example: She works at a school near home.

additional_notes: Used to talk about having to work on Sundays (often about obligations, schedules, or rules). The preposition "aos" = "a" + "os" and is used for time expressions meaning "on" certain days ("aos domingos" = "on Sundays" / "on Sundays (in general)").
target_language_example: Eu não gosto de trabalhar aos domingos, mas às vezes é necessário.
native_language_example: I don't like working on Sundays, but sometimes it's necessary.

additional_notes: Used to talk about having a job at this place/company (“here”). You can change the time with verbs like começar a (to start): “comecei a trabalhar aqui” = “I started working here.”
target_language_example: Eu comecei a trabalhar aqui no mês passado.
native_language_example: I started working here last month.

additional_notes: Used when people collaborate toward the same goal (at work, in a team, or to solve a problem). It often contrasts with working against each other (e.g., “não uns contra os outros”). You can also say “trabalhar junto” when referring to one person with someone else (“Eu trabalho junto com ela”).
target_language_example: Se a gente trabalhar juntos, vai dar tudo certo.
native_language_example: If we work together, everything will work out.

meaning: work to do; a job to do.
additional_notes: Used to say there are tasks still pending or something that still needs to be done. Common with the verb ter: ter um trabalho a fazer (“to have work to do / a job to do”). You can also use it in plural: trabalhos a fazer (“things to do”).
target_language_example: Ainda temos muito trabalho a fazer antes de amanhã.
native_language_example: We still have a lot of work to do before tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Trabalhou" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "trabalhar" for ele/ela/você, so it describes a finished action in the past. "Duro" here means "hard" in the sense of "with a lot of effort". Often followed by "para" + infinitive to say the purpose: "trabalhou duro para..." (worked hard to...).
target_language_example: Nós trabalhamos duro para economizar dinheiro.
native_language_example: We worked hard to save money.

additional_notes: Imperative of the verb "trazer" (to bring) + the object pronoun "me" (to me). Used to ask someone to bring something to you, common in restaurants/hotels and when making requests. You can add "por favor" to be extra polite. In very formal address (to "o senhor / a senhora"), you may hear "traga-me"; in everyday speech with "você", many people say "traz" or "traz pra mim" instead.
target_language_example: Traga-me a conta, por favor.
native_language_example: Bring me the bill, please.

additional_notes: Used when talking about securing a door with a key or lock. Very common with verbs like esquecer (to forget) and lembrar-se (to remember): “esqueci de trancar a porta” / “você se lembrou de trancar a porta?”. You can specify which door with “a porta do/da …” (e.g., do banheiro = bathroom door).
target_language_example: Antes de sair, não esqueça de trancar a porta.
native_language_example: Before you leave, don’t forget to lock the door.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (por/durante treze anos = for thirteen years) or someone’s age (com treze anos / só tem treze anos = at thirteen / is only thirteen). Age can be said with ter: ele/ela tem treze anos = he/she is thirteen.
target_language_example: Ela morou no Brasil por treze anos.
native_language_example: She lived in Brazil for thirteen years.

additional_notes: Used to state an amount of money. "Trezentos" agrees in gender with the noun if needed (e.g., "trezentas pessoas"), but with "dólares" (masculine plural) it stays "trezentos". Often used with verbs like "gastar" (to spend), "emprestar" (to lend), "dever" (to owe), "ganhar" (to earn/win), and "transferir" (to transfer).
target_language_example: Eu preciso de trezentos dólares até amanhã.
native_language_example: I need three hundred dollars by tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used for age (with "ter": "Ele tem trinta anos" = “He’s thirty”) or for a duration/time span ("por/durante trinta anos" = “for thirty years”; "há trinta anos" = “thirty years ago”). You’ll often hear approximations like "uns trinta anos" (“about thirty”) and "cerca de/quase trinta anos" (“around/almost thirty”).
target_language_example: Ela tem trinta anos e mora aqui há trinta anos.
native_language_example: She is thirty years old and has lived here for thirty years.

additional_notes: Used to state an amount of money. Common with verbs like pagar (to pay), dar (to give), and emprestar (to lend). Word order is number + currency name; in Brazil you’ll often hear the currency “reais” instead of “dólares”.
target_language_example: Isso custa trinta dólares.
native_language_example: This costs thirty dollars.

additional_notes: Used to talk about durations (por trinta minutos = for thirty minutes), time difference (trinta minutos antes = thirty minutes earlier; trinta minutos atrasado = thirty minutes late), and approximate distance in travel time (cerca de trinta minutos daqui = about thirty minutes from here).
target_language_example: A reunião vai começar em trinta minutos.
native_language_example: The meeting will start in thirty minutes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration of time (for three years) or a difference in age/time (three years older/younger). With time expressions, Portuguese often uses the present tense: "Faz/Tem três anos" = "three years ago" / "it’s been three years."
target_language_example: Faz três anos que moro aqui.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here for three years.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened three years before now. It often goes at the end of the sentence (e.g., "Eu comprei... três anos atrás"), but it can also appear earlier for emphasis.
target_language_example: Nós nos mudamos para cá três anos atrás.
native_language_example: We moved here three years ago.

additional_notes: Used for age comparisons. Structure: [person] é + [number] anos mais novo/novo(a) que + [other person]. Use "novo" when referring to a male person and "nova" for a female person. You can replace "três" with any number (e.g., "dois", "cinco").
target_language_example: A minha irmã é três anos mais nova que eu.
native_language_example: My sister is three years younger than me.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (durante/pelos últimos três dias), how long something took (levamos três dias para...), or a time reference (três dias atrás = three days ago; três dias após = three days after). In speech and writing you can also say "3 dias".
target_language_example: Ficamos em Lisboa por três dias.
native_language_example: We stayed in Lisbon for three days.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has three children. In Portuguese, "filho" is literally "son" and is the masculine form; as a group term, "três filhos" can refer to three children when the group is all male or mixed. If they are all girls, you’d say "três filhas"; for a neutral word meaning “children,” you can also use "três filhos" or "três crianças" (more general, often younger kids).
target_language_example: Eles têm três filhos e moram em Lisboa.
native_language_example: They have three children and live in Lisbon.

additional_notes: A quantity phrase: number (três) + container (garrafas) + de + item (vinho). In Portuguese, you commonly use “de” after a container/measure word (e.g., uma garrafa de água, duas xícaras de café). Word order can vary in sentences (e.g., “Havia…” / “Na mesa havia…”), but the phrase itself stays the same.
target_language_example: Vamos comprar três garrafas de vinho para o jantar.
native_language_example: Let’s buy three bottles of wine for dinner.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (for) or a time interval (every). Common patterns: "por três horas" = for three hours; "em três horas" = in three hours (time it takes); "a cada três horas" = every three hours; "temos apenas três horas" = we only have three hours (available).
target_language_example: A viagem vai durar três horas.
native_language_example: The trip will last three hours.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a period of time lasting three months, often in schedules and routines (e.g., “a cada três meses” = “every three months”).
target_language_example: Vou ficar em Portugal por três meses.
native_language_example: I'm going to stay in Portugal for three months.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened three months before now. Commonly appears as just “três meses atrás” (e.g., “Fui promovido três meses atrás.”). You may also hear “há três meses” with the same meaning; many speakers combine them as “há três meses atrás,” which is very common in everyday speech but redundant (both “há” and “atrás” already mark the past).
target_language_example: Comecei este trabalho três meses atrás.
native_language_example: I started this job three months ago.

additional_notes: A specific amount of money (3,000 dollars). Used after verbs like gastar (to spend), ter (to have), ganhar (to earn/win), dever (to owe), precisar de (to need), and emprestar (to lend/loan). In Portuguese, numbers usually come before the currency word: três mil dólares.
target_language_example: Preciso de três mil dólares para pagar o conserto do carro.
native_language_example: I need three thousand dollars to pay for the car repair.

additional_notes: A specific money amount: "três" (three) + "milhões" (millions) + "de" (of) + "dólares" (dollars). Used after verbs like "ter" (to have), "precisar de" (to need), and "doar" (to donate). You can swap the number or currency: "dois milhões de euros", "três milhões de reais".
target_language_example: A empresa investiu três milhões de dólares no projeto.
native_language_example: The company invested three million dollars in the project.

additional_notes: A time expression used to say a duration (for three weeks) or that three weeks have passed. Often used with verbs like "ficar" (to stay), "passar" (to spend/time passing), or "levar" (to take): "por três semanas" = for three weeks; "três semanas se passaram" = three weeks passed.
target_language_example: Vou ficar aqui por três semanas.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay here for three weeks.

additional_notes: Used to say an action happened on three occasions. Common with past actions (e.g., "fui"), with counts like "em outubro" (in October), or after verbs like "tentar" (to try) and "prometer" (to promise). Word order is flexible, but it often comes after the verb or at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Eu já vi esse filme três vezes.
native_language_example: I've already seen that movie three times.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens in one day (a frequency). The pattern is: "[number] vezes ao dia" = "[number] times a day" (e.g., "duas vezes ao dia", "uma vez ao dia").
target_language_example: Tomo este remédio três vezes ao dia.
native_language_example: I take this medicine three times a day.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities. The pattern is: [subject] + ter + [number] vezes mais + [noun] + que + [person/thing]. In everyday Portuguese you’ll often hear just “mais … que” for comparisons, but “X vezes mais … que” makes the comparison exact. (Note: in formal math, “três vezes mais” can be ambiguous; in normal speech it’s understood as “three times as many.”)
target_language_example: A Ana tem três vezes mais livros que o irmão.
native_language_example: Ana has three times as many books as her brother.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens in one week. It commonly follows a verb: "Eu corro três vezes por semana." You can add "cerca de" (about), "pelo menos" (at least), or "no máximo" (at most): "pelo menos três vezes por semana".
target_language_example: Eu estudo português três vezes por semana.
native_language_example: I study Portuguese three times a week.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone for their opinion or to check what they believe. Often introduces a yes/no question about a situation: “Tu achas que…?” In many places (especially Brazil), people more commonly say “Você acha que…?”; “Tu achas que…?” is common in Portugal and in some regions of Brazil.
target_language_example: Tu achas que vai chover hoje?
native_language_example: Do you think it’s going to rain today?

meaning: 'you are' (with the verb estar: state, condition, location, or temporary situation).
additional_notes: "Tu" is the informal singular 'you' in European Portuguese and in some regions of Brazil. "Estás" is the 'tu' form of "estar". It’s used for conditions/states (e.g., busy, alone), location, and ongoing situations; in European Portuguese you’ll often see "estar a" + infinitive for an action happening now. The pronoun "tu" is sometimes omitted when it’s clear from context (e.g., "Estás muito ocupado").
target_language_example: Tu estás cansado hoje?
native_language_example: Are you tired today?

additional_notes: Uses the pronoun tu (“you”, singular) + podes (present tense of poder, “can/to be able to”). Common in Portugal and in parts of Brazil; in much of Brazil, people often say você pode instead. It can express permission (“you may”) or ability (“you can/are able to”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu podes me ajudar com isso?
native_language_example: Can you help me with this?

additional_notes: Used with **tu** (informal singular “you”) + **queres** (2nd-person singular of *querer*, “to want”). Common in Portugal and in parts of Brazil; in much of Brazil people often say **você quer** instead. It can be followed by an infinitive (“tu queres assistir…?” = “do you want to watch…?”) or by **que** + subjunctive to mean “you want (someone) to…” (“tu queres que ele espere?”).
target_language_example: Tu queres ir comigo ao cinema?
native_language_example: Do you want to go to the movies with me?

meaning: "Do you know how to speak...?" / "Can you speak...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask whether someone has the ability/knowledge to speak a language. Commonly followed by a language name (e.g., "Tu sabes falar português?"). "Tu" is used in Portugal and in parts of Brazil, but in much of Brazil people more often say "Você sabe falar...?". In Brazil, you may also hear "Tu sabe falar...?" in some regions.
target_language_example: Tu sabes falar inglês?
native_language_example: Can you speak English?

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular pronoun “tu” with “sabes” (present tense of saber). Common in Portugal and in some regions of Brazil; in many parts of Brazil people more often say “você sabe”. It can be a real question (“Do you know…?”) or a conversational “you know…” to emphasize a point.
target_language_example: Tu sabes onde fica a estação?
native_language_example: Do you know where the station is?

additional_notes: Used mainly in Brazil in regions where people say "tu" (instead of "você"). With "ter + de + infinitive" ("tu tens de...") it means "you have to / need to...".
target_language_example: Tu tens tempo hoje?
native_language_example: Do you have time today?

additional_notes: Used with the pronoun "tu" (informal singular "you") + the verb "ser" in the present tense ("és"). Common with adjectives or nouns: "Tu és curiosa/fabulosa/temido"; "Tu és um bom aluno." Many learners also hear "você é" for "you are" in Brazil; "tu és" is especially common in Portugal and in some regions of Brazil.
target_language_example: Tu és muito simpático.
native_language_example: You are very nice.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person you address as tu (common in Portugal and in some regions of Brazil). Often appears with de/da (“precisar de/da tua ajuda” = “to need your help”) and with agradecimentos (“obrigado/a pela tua ajuda” = “thanks for your help”). Also: “graças à tua ajuda” = “thanks to your help.”
target_language_example: Obrigado pela tua ajuda hoje.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help today.

additional_notes: Used to talk to someone (tu) about their sister. Very common in European Portuguese where "tu" and "tua" are everyday; in Brazil, "sua irmã" is often more common in many regions (and "tua" can sound more regional or more intimate). Word order is usually "a tua irmã" ("your sister"), but in casual speech you may also hear "tua irmã" without the article.
target_language_example: A tua irmã gosta de música?
native_language_example: Does your sister like music?

additional_notes: Used to ask for permission in a polite, casual way. Often followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., "Tudo bem se eu for...?", "...se eu usar...?"), similar to asking "Do you mind if I…?" or "Is it alright if I…?".
target_language_example: Tudo bem se eu abrir a janela?
native_language_example: Is it OK if I open the window?

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a set of things, actions, or a whole situation that’s already known in context. Often appears with verbs like pagar por tudo isso (“pay for all this/that”) or questions like Pra/Para que tudo isso? (“What’s all this for?” / “Why all this?”).
target_language_example: Eu não preciso de tudo isso agora.
native_language_example: I don’t need all of this right now.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the totality of things/actions in a relative clause, followed by a verb (e.g., “tudo o que você fez” = “everything (that) you did”). In English, “that” is often optional. Not to confuse with “tudo” alone (“everything”) or “o que” alone (“what/which”).
target_language_example: Anotei tudo o que você me contou.
native_language_example: I wrote down everything (that) you told me.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause referring to all things/actions connected to a male person (“ele” = “he”). Very common with verbs like pedir (to ask for), descobrir (to discover), precisar (to need), saber (to know): “tudo o que ele + verb …”.
target_language_example: Eu anotei tudo o que ele disse na reunião.
native_language_example: I wrote down everything he said in the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause describing everything you have/need/know/want, etc. It’s often followed by a verb: “tudo o que eu preciso” (everything I need), “tudo o que eu sei” (everything I know). You can also see it with a noun-like verb form (infinitive): “tudo o que eu queria fazer era…” (all I wanted to do was…).
target_language_example: Eu já disse tudo o que eu sei.
native_language_example: I already said everything I know.

tudo o que eu quero é

target_language_multi_word_term: tudo o que eu quero é
additional_notes: Use this to emphasize that there is just one main thing you want/need. It’s followed by a noun (e.g., liberdade) or an infinitive verb phrase (e.g., falar com você). Very common structure: “Tudo o que eu quero é + [noun/infinitive].”
target_language_example: Tudo o que eu quero é descansar um pouco.
native_language_example: All I want is to rest a little.

meaning: “all we can do” / “the only thing we can do.”
additional_notes: Used to say your options are limited and there isn’t much else possible. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the infinitive: “Tudo o que podemos fazer é esperar” (“All we can do is wait”). You can change the subject to match who you mean (e.g., “tudo o que eu posso fazer”, “tudo o que você pode fazer”).
target_language_example: Tudo o que podemos fazer é tentar de novo amanhã.
native_language_example: All we can do is try again tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the pattern **tudo o que + verb** (“everything that…”). **Tudo o que quero é…** is very common to mean “All I want is…”. You can change **quero** to match the subject/tense (e.g., **tudo o que eu queria** = “all I wanted”).
target_language_example: Tudo o que quero é um pouco de paz.
native_language_example: All I want is a little peace.

additional_notes: Used to refer to all the things someone possessed up to that point in time. It often appears after verbs like perder (to lose), vender (to sell), deixar (to leave/bequeath), or dizer (to say), and can be expanded with an infinitive phrase: “tudo o que tinha a dizer” = “everything (that) I had to say.”
target_language_example: Depois do incêndio, ela perdeu tudo o que tinha.
native_language_example: After the fire, she lost everything she had.

meaning: 'everything that you…' / 'all you have to do is…' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what someone will/should/needs to do: "Tudo o que você + verb". Very common in the pattern "Tudo o que você tem/tinha de fazer é/era..." meaning "All you have to do is/was...". In Brazilian Portuguese, "você" is the usual word for "you" (informal in the sense of everyday speech, but not slang).
target_language_example: Tudo o que você precisa fazer é preencher este formulário.
native_language_example: All you need to do is fill out this form.

tudo o que você precisa fazer é

target_language_multi_word_term: tudo o que você precisa fazer é
additional_notes: Used to introduce a simple instruction or the only necessary step(s). It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., fazer, perguntar, escutar, lembrar-se) or by a verb phrase. In Brazil, you can also hear the more informal/shorter version "tudo o que você precisa é".
target_language_example: Tudo o que você precisa fazer é preencher este formulário.
native_language_example: All you need to do is fill out this form.

tudo o que você tem de fazer é

target_language_multi_word_term: tudo o que você tem de fazer é
additional_notes: Used to introduce a simple instruction or the only necessary step to achieve something. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., esperar, apertar, limpar). In speech you may also hear the slightly more informal variant “tudo o que você tem que fazer é …”.
target_language_example: Tudo o que você tem de fazer é seguir estas instruções.
native_language_example: All you have to do is follow these instructions.

tudo o que você tem que fazer é

target_language_multi_word_term: tudo o que você tem que fazer é
additional_notes: Used to say the only required action is the one that follows, often to make something sound simple. Very common in spoken Portuguese. After "é" you usually use an infinitive verb (empurrar, esperar, falar, ouvir, sorrir, tomar conta). You can also swap "você" for another subject: "tudo o que eu tenho que fazer é…".
target_language_example: Tudo o que você tem que fazer é preencher este formulário.
native_language_example: All you have to do is fill out this form.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause describing the full set of things or actions being referred to. Often interchangeable with the more formal "tudo o que" in many contexts (especially in Brazil).
target_language_example: Vou fazer tudo que eu puder para ajudar.
native_language_example: I’ll do everything I can to help.

tudo que você tem que fazer é

target_language_multi_word_term: tudo que você tem que fazer é
additional_notes: Used to introduce a simple requirement or the only necessary action. Very common in spoken and written Portuguese. In casual speech, you may also hear "tudo o que você tem que fazer é" or shortened versions like "tudo que você tem a fazer é".
target_language_example: Tudo que você tem que fazer é me mandar uma mensagem.
native_language_example: All you have to do is send me a message.

additional_notes: Used to say that a situation is being managed and there’s nothing to worry about. Very common as reassurance (Tenho tudo sob controle.) or as a check-in/question (Tudo sob controle?). You can change the subject without changing the phrase: Eu tenho / Ele tem / Nós temos tudo sob controle.
target_language_example: Não se preocupe — está tudo sob controle.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — everything is under control.

additional_notes: Used to say you know, will tell, or want to know all the information/details about someone or something. Often followed by a person/pronoun (tudo sobre você/ela/ele) or a thing/idea (tudo sobre isso, tudo sobre o assunto).
target_language_example: Ela sabe tudo sobre o novo trabalho.
native_language_example: She knows everything about the new job.

additional_notes: Very common and informal in Brazilian Portuguese. It’s a shortened form of “está legal” (“it’s cool/nice”), but in conversation it often just means agreement/acceptance (“ok”). Depending on tone, it can also sound impatient or skeptical (like “yeah, right”).
target_language_example: Tá legal, eu faço isso amanhã.
native_language_example: Okay, I’ll do that tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to compare height (or something described as “high”) between two people/things. Pattern: **tão + adjective + quanto** = “as + adjective + as” (e.g., *tão alto quanto*, *tão velho quanto*). For inequality, Portuguese often uses **não tão ... quanto** (“not as ... as”) or **quase tão ... quanto** (“almost as ... as”).
target_language_example: Ela é tão alta quanto a irmã.
native_language_example: She is as tall as her sister.

additional_notes: Used after a verb to emphasize how well someone does something: “falar tão bem”, “dançar tão bem”. It often appears in questions with “Como…?” (How did you learn to… so well?). In informal speech you may also hear “tão bom”/“tão boa” depending on what is being described, but “tão bem” is for describing actions (adverbs).
target_language_example: Você canta tão bem!
native_language_example: You sing so well!

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something at the same level as someone else. It often follows a verb: “nadar tão bem quanto…”, “falar tão bem quanto…”. You can soften the comparison with words like “quase” (almost): “quase tão bem quanto…”.
target_language_example: Eu não cozinho tão bem quanto a minha irmã.
native_language_example: I don't cook as well as my sister.

additional_notes: Used to compare equal ability/quality. Pattern: "tão + (adverb/adjective) + quanto + [comparison]" = "as + ... + as". Here, "tão bem quanto inglês" usually implies speaking a language as well as one speaks English (e.g., "Falo francês tão bem quanto inglês" = "I speak French as well as English"). You can swap "inglês" for another language or thing you’re comparing to.
target_language_example: Ela fala espanhol tão bem quanto inglês.
native_language_example: She speaks Spanish as well as English.

meaning: “as well as (the)… / as good as (the)…” (when comparing how well someone does something).
additional_notes: Used for equality comparisons. Pattern: **(verb) tão bem quanto + article + person/thing** = “(do something) as well as…”. Here **o** is the masculine singular article (“the”) before a male name (e.g., **o Tom**). With a female name, you’d use **a**: **tão bem quanto a Maria**. You can also drop the article in some contexts (especially in Brazil), but **o/a + name** is common.
target_language_example: Ela fala português tão bem quanto o professor.
native_language_example: She speaks Portuguese as well as the teacher.

additional_notes: Used for comparisons of ability or performance: tão + adverb (bem) + quanto + person. You can swap “bem” for other adverbs (e.g., tão rápido quanto você = “as fast as you”). Often follows a verb like falar (to speak), ver (to see), fazer (to do).
target_language_example: Eu não cozinho tão bem quanto você, mas estou aprendendo.
native_language_example: I don’t cook as well as you, but I’m learning.

meaning: “as good as” (used to compare two people/things).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons to say someone/something has the same level of quality/skill as someone/something else. Pattern: **tão + adjective + quanto** (e.g., *tão alto quanto* = “as tall as”). Often followed by a noun or pronoun: *tão bom quanto você / o seu / qualquer jogador*.
target_language_example: Este café é tão bom quanto o do seu restaurante favorito.
native_language_example: This coffee is as good as the one from your favorite restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to comment on timing that feels unusually early. Often appears in questions like “Por que… tão cedo?” or “O que você está fazendo… tão cedo?” and can go at the end of the sentence or before a time word like “hoje”.
target_language_example: Não precisa acordar tão cedo amanhã.
native_language_example: You don’t need to wake up so early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize how stupid/silly something is or how someone feels about their own actions. Common patterns: "ser/estar tão estúpido" (to be so stupid), "me sinto/sinto-me tão estúpido" (I feel so stupid), and "tão estúpido a ponto de..." (so stupid as to...). "Estúpido" can sound insulting when aimed at someone else; it’s often used about yourself to express regret or embarrassment.
target_language_example: Eu estava tão estúpido que nem percebi o erro.
native_language_example: I was so stupid that I didn’t even notice the mistake.

additional_notes: Used to intensify the emotion “feliz” (“happy”). Often appears in patterns like “Estou tão feliz por você” (“I’m so happy for you”), “tão feliz que...” (“so happy that...”), and in comparisons with “quanto”/“como” (e.g., “não ser tão feliz quanto aparenta” = “not as happy as he seems”).
target_language_example: Estou tão feliz que eu nem consigo dormir.
native_language_example: I’m so happy that I can’t even sleep.

meaning: “as big/large as” (used for comparisons; often with “not as big as”).
additional_notes: Used to compare size, area, population, importance, etc. Structure: (não) ser + tão + adjective/adverb + quanto. With “não”, it means “not as … as”: “não é tão grande quanto…” = “isn’t as big as…”. You can also add quantities: “cinco vezes tão grande quanto” = “five times as big as.”
target_language_example: Minha casa não é tão grande quanto a sua.
native_language_example: My house isn’t as big as yours.

additional_notes: Used to compare speed (or figuratively, how quickly something happens). Pattern: “tão + adverb/adjective + quanto” = “as + adverb/adjective + as”. Often followed by a clause like “eu pude” (I could) or a person/pronoun (“quanto ele”).
target_language_example: Vou terminar tão rápido quanto eu conseguir.
native_language_example: I’ll finish as fast as I can.

meaning: “to have her/it” (ter + a = ‘have’ + feminine direct-object pronoun).
additional_notes: This is the verb **ter** in the infinitive with the attached pronoun **-la** (‘her’ or ‘it’ when the object is feminine). It’s common in the **perfect infinitive** **ter + past participle**, e.g. **tê-la feito / tê-la deixado / tê-la conhecido** = “to have done/left/met her.” The pronoun refers to a feminine noun or a woman previously mentioned.
target_language_example: Obrigado por tê-la ajudado ontem.
native_language_example: Thank you for having helped her yesterday.

meaning: 'to have him/it' (ter + o), often used in 'to have done [something] to him/it'.
additional_notes: This is the infinitive of **ter** (“to have”) with the object pronoun **-o** (“him/it”) attached after a hyphen. The circumflex **ê** appears when **ter** is combined with a clitic pronoun: **ter + o → tê-lo**. It’s very common in the **perfect infinitive** pattern **ter + past participle**: **tê-lo visto** = “to have seen him/it”, **tê-lo ajudado** = “to have helped him/it”.
