You’ll often see it after expressions like **lembrar-se de** (“to remember”) or with modals like **dever/poder** (“must/could”) to talk about a past action.
target_language_example: Eu devo tê-lo esquecido em casa.
native_language_example: I must have forgotten it/him at home.

additional_notes: This is the personal infinitive in the perfect (ter + past participle): "ter feito" = "to have done". The pronoun "-lo" is an attached (enclitic) direct object meaning "him" or "it" (often "you" in formal address, e.g., "desculpe tê-lo feito esperar" = "sorry for having made you wait"). It commonly appears after verbs like "desculpar"/"sentir muito" (apologizing) or "negar" (denying): "negar tê-lo feito" = "to deny having done it".
target_language_example: Ela pediu desculpa por tê-lo feito perder tempo.
native_language_example: She apologized for having made you waste time.

additional_notes: Present perfect of "ser" (to be), used with a plural subject (eles/elas/vocês). It describes a state or situation that started in the past and continues up to now (often with time expressions like "ultimamente", "nas últimas semanas", "desde..."). Also used in the passive voice: "têm sido enganados" = "have been deceived".
target_language_example: Ultimamente, eles têm sido muito pacientes.
native_language_example: Lately, they have been very patient.

additional_notes: Form of the verb phrase "ter medo de" (= to be afraid of). "Têm" is the 3rd person plural (they/you all) of "ter" in the present tense, used with plural subjects ("as pessoas", "as crianças", "meus pais"). It is followed by "de" + a noun ("fantasmas"), a person ("Tom"), or an infinitive to talk about an action ("sair", "viajar").
target_language_example: Eles têm medo de falar em público.
native_language_example: They’re afraid of speaking in public.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ter** in the present tense, **3rd person plural**: **eles/elas/vocês têm** = “they/you (plural) have”. **Um** is the masculine singular “a/an” (use **uma** for feminine nouns). The accent matters: **têm** (they have) vs **tem** (he/she/you singular has).
target_language_example: Vocês têm um carro?
native_language_example: Do you (plural) have a car?

meaning: a higher rank / a top-tier (higher-ranked) one.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something that belongs to a higher level in a hierarchy (for example, a stronger class of enemy, monster, soldier, etc.). In Portuguese you’ll also see it without capitals: “um rank superior”. Often implies “harder to beat / much stronger than normal.”
target_language_example: Eles chamaram reforços: um Rank Superior chegou.
native_language_example: They called reinforcements: a higher-ranked one arrived.

additional_notes: Used for traffic accidents and other mishaps (e.g., at home or work). With "acontecer", it means "an accident happened"; with "causado por", "caused by an accident"; with "se envolver em", "to be involved in an accident". In questions like "não ter sido um acidente", it suggests it may not have been accidental (maybe intentional).
target_language_example: Ainda bem que ninguém se machucou no acidente.
native_language_example: Thankfully, nobody got hurt in the accident.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a traffic accident involving a car. Very common with verbs like "sofrer" (to have/suffer) and "ver" (to see): "sofri um acidente de carro" / "vi um acidente de carro". You can also use it with "haver/ter" (there to be) or "acontecer" (to happen): "Houve um acidente de carro" / "Aconteceu um acidente de carro".
target_language_example: Houve um acidente de carro na estrada, e o trânsito parou.
native_language_example: There was a car accident on the road, and traffic stopped.

additional_notes: Used for accidents involving vehicles on the road (cars, motorcycles, etc.). Often appears with reasons for delays: "por causa de" (because of) or "devido a" (due to).
target_language_example: Houve um acidente de trânsito na avenida, e o ônibus demorou muito.
native_language_example: There was a traffic accident on the avenue, and the bus took a long time.

additional_notes: "Advogado" is a lawyer/attorney. Use "um" with a man; for a woman, say "uma advogada". In questions like "Tens um advogado?", it means having a lawyer (e.g., legal representation).
target_language_example: Preciso de um advogado para resolver isso.
native_language_example: I need a lawyer to sort this out.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine noun amigo with the indefinite article um (= “a/one”). You can use it generically (“Um amigo é difícil de encontrar...”) or to introduce someone not yet specified (“Eu considero ele um amigo”). For a female friend, use uma amiga. With de: um amigo de um amigo = “a friend of a friend.”
target_language_example: Ele é um amigo que sempre me ajuda.
native_language_example: He’s a friend who always helps me.

additional_notes: Used to talk about one of your friends (not necessarily a close friend). It’s common to say the noun + possessive after it (e.g., "um amigo meu", "uma amiga minha"). You can also negate it to mean someone is not your friend: "não é um amigo meu".
target_language_example: Vou sair com um amigo meu hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I’m going out with a friend of mine tonight.

meaning: “a friend who/that …” (introduces a description of the friend).
additional_notes: Used when you mention a friend and then add a clause with information about them. The verb after "que" is usually in the 3rd person (e.g., "que está", "que vive"). You can change the article/gender/number as needed: "uma amiga que" (a female friend who), "uns amigos que" (friends who).
target_language_example: Tenho um amigo que fala inglês muito bem.
native_language_example: I have a friend who speaks English very well.

meaning: “an animal”; also (informal) “a beast” (said about a person).
additional_notes: Literal meaning is “an animal” (any non-human creature): um animal faminto (“a hungry animal”), um animal grande (“a big animal”). When talking about a person, it can be neutral/academic (e.g., humans as animals) or informal and judgmental (“Ela é um animal.” = “She’s a beast / she’s an animal,” implying someone is cruel, rude, or out of control). In other contexts it can also be praise meaning someone is extremely strong/talented (“Ele é um animal no esporte”), depending on tone.
target_language_example: Ele é um animal no futebol.
native_language_example: He’s a beast at soccer.

meaning: a pet (an animal you keep at home).
additional_notes: Common way to refer to a household pet (dog, cat, etc.). Often used with the verb ter (“to have”) or criar (“to raise/keep”). The word estimação relates to affection/being fond of, so the idea is an animal kept as a companion, not a farm animal.
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, eu tinha um animal de estimação: um gato.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I had a pet: a cat.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a 12-month period in general (“a year”) or a duration (“for one year”). Often follows duration prepositions like por/durante: por um ano, durante um ano.
target_language_example: Morei no Brasil por um ano.
native_language_example: I lived in Brazil for a year.

additional_notes: Means a self-contained home unit in a building. Often used with verbs like morar (to live), comprar (to buy), dividir (to share), and buscar/procurar (to look for): “morar em um apartamento”, “comprar um apartamento”, “dividir um apartamento”. In Brazil, “um” is commonly used before masculine nouns; in Portugal you may also see “um” but “um apartamento” is the same meaning. Not the same as “um quarto” (a room).
target_language_example: Estamos a alugar um apartamento perto do centro.
native_language_example: We’re renting an apartment near downtown/the city center.

meaning: an artist (a creative professional, e.g., painter, musician, performer).
additional_notes: "Artista" is a common noun; use "um" for a man and "uma artista" for a woman. It can refer to many kinds of artists (visual arts, music, acting, etc.). In phrases like "nasceu um artista", it means someone was born with artistic talent ("a born artist").
target_language_example: Ela quer ser uma artista quando crescer.
native_language_example: She wants to be an artist when she grows up.

additional_notes: A common medical/emergency expression. Often used with verbs like "ter" (to have), "estar tendo" (to be having), and "sofrer" (to suffer). You can also hear "infarto" / "infarto do miocárdio" in more medical contexts.
target_language_example: Ele teve um ataque cardíaco e foi levado ao hospital.
native_language_example: He had a heart attack and was taken to the hospital.

additional_notes: Used in work contexts to talk about increasing your pay. Common with the verb pedir (“to ask for”): pedir um aumento de salário (to ask for a raise).
target_language_example: Acho que vou pedir um aumento de salário este mês.
native_language_example: I think I’m going to ask for a raise this month.

additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about a place where you keep money or do financial services (e.g., “roubar um banco” = “to rob a bank”). Note: “banco” can also mean “bench” (a seat), so context matters.
target_language_example: Preciso ir a um banco para sacar dinheiro.
native_language_example: I need to go to a bank to withdraw money.

meaning: "a bunch of" / "a group of" (often "a flock of" for animals); sometimes "a bunch of" (insulting) for people.
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to talk about a large group: um bando de pássaros (a flock of birds), um bando de coelhos (a bunch/group of rabbits). With people, it can be negative or insulting (um bando de amadores = a bunch of amateurs). It can also be used more generally like “a bunch of” with things such as questions: um bando de perguntas (a bunch of questions).
target_language_example: Tem um bando de gente esperando lá fora.
native_language_example: There are a bunch of people waiting outside.

additional_notes: Most commonly used with "tomar" or "precisar de": "tomar um banho" = to take a shower/bath; "precisar de um banho" = to need a shower. In Brazil it often implies a shower unless you specify "banho de banheira" (a bath in a tub).
target_language_example: Depois da academia, vou tomar um banho.
native_language_example: After the gym, I'm going to take a shower.

additional_notes: Uses the indefinite article “um” (“a/an”) with the noun “bebê” (“baby”). Common in contexts like adopting a baby (adotar um bebê), having a baby (ter um bebê), or talking about someone when they were a baby (quando/desde que era um bebê).
target_language_example: Eles tiveram um bebê no ano passado.
native_language_example: They had a baby last year.

additional_notes: Used to describe something positively, often meaning “nice/great” as well as “beautiful.” It agrees with the noun: masculine singular (um belo + noun). Feminine is "uma bela"; plural "uns belos/umas belas". It can also work as an intensifier meaning “quite a” (e.g., "um belo problema" = “quite a problem”), sometimes with irony depending on context.
target_language_example: Ele fez um belo trabalho na apresentação.
native_language_example: He did a great job on the presentation.

additional_notes: A compliment meaning two people look good together or make a good match. Often used with verbs like "ser" (Vocês são um belo casal) and "formar/fazer" (Vocês formam/fazem um belo casal). "Belo" can mean "beautiful" or more generally "lovely/great" in this context.
target_language_example: Vocês dois são um belo casal!
native_language_example: You two are a great couple!

additional_notes: “Bolo” is a common word for cake in Portuguese. It often appears with verbs like fazer (to make), assar (to bake), and comer (to eat). You can specify the type/flavor with “bolo de …” (e.g., bolo de chocolate = chocolate cake; bolo de Natal = Christmas cake).
target_language_example: Vou fazer um bolo de chocolate para a festa.
native_language_example: I’m going to make a chocolate cake for the party.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun to describe it positively: um bom aluno (a good student), um bom cozinheiro (a good cook). It agrees with the noun’s gender/number (e.g., uma boa…, uns bons…, umas boas…). Often combines with professions/roles and qualities (um bom pai, um bom rapaz).
target_language_example: Ele é um bom professor.
native_language_example: He is a good teacher.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone you like and trust. It can appear with different prepositions depending on the relationship: “um bom amigo meu” = “a good friend of mine”; “um bom amigo para mim” = “a good friend to me” (emphasizes that the person was supportive/helpful); “um bom amigo de Maria” = “a good friend of Mary” (Mary’s friend).
target_language_example: Ela é uma boa amiga minha desde a escola.
native_language_example: She’s been a good friend of mine since school.

meaning: “a good day” (often used to wish someone a good day).
additional_notes: Used as part of greetings and farewells: "Tenha/tenham um bom dia" = “Have a good day.” As a standalone phrase ("Um bom dia!") it can be an enthusiastic way to say good morning/good day, or a direct wish. With "estar tendo" it refers to how someone’s day is going ("Você está tendo um bom dia?" = “Are you having a good day?”).
target_language_example: Desejo a você um bom dia e boa sorte.
native_language_example: I wish you a good day and good luck.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has, offers, or is trying to get a job that is considered desirable (e.g., good pay, stability, conditions, or opportunities). Often appears with verbs like ter (to have), oferecer (to offer), conseguir/arrumar (to get/find), and encontrar (to find).
target_language_example: Ela está procurando um bom emprego na área de tecnologia.
native_language_example: She is looking for a good job in the tech field.

meaning: “a good weekend.” (used to wish someone a nice weekend)
additional_notes: Common in greetings and goodbyes, especially on Friday or before the weekend. Often used with verbs like “Desejo-te/Te desejo…” (I wish you…), “Tenha…” (Have…), or in questions like “Você passou…?” (Did you have/spend…?). You can also say “Bom fim de semana!” without “um.”
target_language_example: Bom fim de semana! A gente se vê na segunda.
native_language_example: Have a good weekend! See you on Monday.

meaning: a good man (a good person, male).
additional_notes: Used to describe a man’s character in a positive way (kind, honest, decent). Often appears after verbs like "ser" (to be) or "parecer" (to seem): "Ele é/parece um bom homem." Can also be used as a compliment when speaking to someone directly. Feminine equivalent: "uma boa mulher"; more general (any gender): "uma boa pessoa".
target_language_example: O seu pai é um bom homem e sempre ajuda os vizinhos.
native_language_example: Your father is a good man and always helps the neighbors.

additional_notes: Used to recommend or describe a location as suitable for an action. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb (fazer, montar, plantar, viver, etc.): “um bom lugar para + verbo.” You can change it for gender/number: “um/uma bom/boa lugar…”, “bons lugares…”, “boas lugares…” (usually you’ll hear “um/um bom lugar” because “lugar” is masculine).
target_language_example: Este parque é um bom lugar para caminhar e relaxar.
native_language_example: This park is a good place to walk and relax.

additional_notes: Literally “a good professor/teacher.” In Portuguese, "professor" commonly means “teacher” (not only a university professor). Use "um" because it's masculine singular; for a woman, say "uma boa professora". Often used to describe someone’s quality as a teacher or a goal (e.g., "Quero ser um bom professor").
target_language_example: Ele quer ser um bom professor e ajudar os alunos a aprender.
native_language_example: He wants to be a good teacher and help the students learn.

meaning: a long time; quite a while.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration that feels long or significant. Very common with verbs like “levar” (to take), “esperar” (to wait), and with “por”: “por um bom tempo” = “for quite a while.” Despite the literal words (“a good time”), it usually means length of time, not “having fun.”
target_language_example: Fiquei sem ver meus amigos por um bom tempo.
native_language_example: I went without seeing my friends for quite a while.

meaning: "a good job" (good work or a good job position).
additional_notes: Usually means doing something well ("good work"): Fazer um bom trabalho = to do a good job. In some contexts it can also mean a good job (position), especially with procurar/arrumar: Ele está procurando um bom trabalho = He’s looking for a good job.
target_language_example: Você fez um bom trabalho no relatório.
native_language_example: You did a good job on the report.

additional_notes: Used for a physical opening or cavity in something (a road, a shirt, the ground). With verbs like "fazer" (make), "cavar" (dig), or "aparecer" (appear). It can also be used figuratively (e.g., "um buraco no orçamento" = a hole in the budget).
target_language_example: Cuidado para não cair no buraco!
native_language_example: Be careful not to fall into the hole!

additional_notes: "Um" is the masculine singular indefinite article ("a"/"an" or "one"). Use "um cachorro" when talking about a non-specific dog or introducing one for the first time. In questions, it often means "a" dog (e.g., whether someone has a dog).
target_language_example: Eu quero um cachorro pequeno.
native_language_example: I want a small dog.

additional_notes: Means “a breakfast” (a meal in the morning). Often used with verbs like tomar (“to have/drink/eat”): tomar um café da manhã. In Brazil, café da manhã is the standard word for “breakfast” (not just coffee). In “Eu te devo um café da manhã,” it means “I owe you breakfast” (e.g., I’ll treat you to breakfast).
target_language_example: Amanhã eu pago um café da manhã pra você.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’ll buy you breakfast.

additional_notes: Used for a large road vehicle for carrying goods (cargo). "Caminhão" is masculine, so it takes "um" in the singular and "uns" in the plural ("uns caminhões").
target_language_example: O caminhão está carregado de caixas.
native_language_example: The truck is loaded with boxes.

additional_notes: Common, informal way to refer to a male person, often when you don’t know him well or you’re speaking casually (like “a guy”). It can be neutral, but depending on tone it may sound a bit dismissive. Feminine equivalent: “uma cara” is not used; say “uma garota/uma moça/uma mulher” depending on context.
target_language_example: Tem um cara na recepção perguntando por você.
native_language_example: There’s a guy at reception asking for you.

meaning: a nice/good guy (a friendly, decent man).
additional_notes: "Cara" is an informal word for "guy" (like "dude"), and "legal" means "cool/nice" (not "legal" in the law sense here). Often used to describe someone positively: "Ele é um cara legal" = "He’s a nice guy." You can also use it as a question ("Ele é um cara legal?") or with "achar" to ask someone’s opinion ("Você me acha um cara legal?"). Typically used for men; for women you might say "uma garota legal" or "uma pessoa legal".
target_language_example: Ele parece ser um cara legal, mas ainda não conheço bem.
native_language_example: He seems like a nice guy, but I don’t know him well yet.

additional_notes: "Um" means "a/an" (indefinite article) and "carro" means "car." Used to talk about a non-specific car, or to introduce a car into the conversation. For a specific car, you’ll often see "o carro" ("the car").
target_language_example: Preciso comprar um carro barato.
native_language_example: I need to buy a cheap car.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a car that is new (not used). It’s a common noun phrase: "um" (a) + "carro" (car) + "novo" (new). "Novo" agrees with "carro" (masculine singular). You can change it as needed: "o carro novo" (the new car), "um carro novo" (a new car).
target_language_example: Estou juntando dinheiro para comprar um carro novo.
native_language_example: I'm saving money to buy a new car.

additional_notes: A noun used for a small card with a picture on one side and space for a short message/address on the other, sent by mail (often while traveling). Common verbs with it: mandar/enviar (to send), passar (to hand/give). Plural: cartões-postais.
target_language_example: Vou mandar um cartão-postal para meus avós da viagem.
native_language_example: I’m going to send my grandparents a postcard from the trip.

additional_notes: Indefinite noun phrase: um (masculine “a/an”) + cavalo (“horse”). Use when talking about any horse, not a specific one; for a specific horse use “o cavalo” (“the horse”).
target_language_example: Vi um cavalo no campo.
native_language_example: I saw a horse in the field.

additional_notes: "Um" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”). "Chapéu" is a general word for “hat” (often with a brim). Common with colors and descriptions: "um chapéu preto" (a black hat), "um chapéu estranho" (a strange hat). You can also use it with "na cabeça" (“on [his/her] head”).
target_language_example: Ele está usando um chapéu azul.
native_language_example: He is wearing a blue hat.

additional_notes: "Um" = "a" (masculine singular). "Chapéu" means "hat" and is masculine (o chapéu). "Novo" means "new" and agrees with the noun: um chapéu novo. Common with verbs like usar (to wear), vender (to sell), querer (to want), precisar de (to need).
target_language_example: Comprei um chapéu novo para o verão.
native_language_example: I bought a new hat for the summer.

additional_notes: An indefinite noun phrase: "um" = "a/one" + "cigarro" = "cigarette." Used when asking for a cigarette ("Pode me dar um cigarro?") or talking about smoking one ("fumar um cigarro"). Also appears in informal bets meaning "to bet a cigarette" (a small stake).
target_language_example: Você tem um cigarro para me dar?
native_language_example: Do you have a cigarette you can give me?

additional_notes: "Um" is the masculine indefinite article meaning "a/an." "Computador" is masculine, so you say "um computador" (not *uma*). Common verbs with it: *ter* (to have), *comprar* (to buy), *usar* (to use).
target_language_example: Preciso de um computador para trabalhar.
native_language_example: I need a computer to work.

additional_notes: "Um" means "a/an" (masculine). "Computador" is masculine, so the adjective "novo" agrees with it. You can change the article depending on what you mean: "o computador novo" = "the new computer"; "meu computador novo" = "my new computer". Word order is usually noun + adjective here: "computador novo".
target_language_example: Preciso de um computador novo para o trabalho.
native_language_example: I need a new computer for work.

meaning: “a glass of” (used to order or ask for a drink).
additional_notes: Used before a beverage noun to specify the container/quantity: um copo de água, um copo de vinho, um copo de refrigerante. Very common in cafés and restaurants. (Note: for bottled or canned drinks you may also hear uma garrafa de… “a bottle of…”, uma lata de… “a can of…”.)
target_language_example: Pode me trazer um copo de suco de laranja, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you bring me a glass of orange juice, please?

additional_notes: Used when ordering or offering beer served in a glass (not a bottle/can). You can add an adjective like gelada (“cold”) to specify how you want it.
target_language_example: Para mim, um copo de cerveja, por favor.
native_language_example: For me, a glass of beer, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask for, offer, or describe drinking milk. Very common with verbs like pedir (to ask for), dar (to give), querer (to want), gostar de (to like/would like), tomar/beber (to drink), and encher (to fill). You can swap the drink: um copo de água (a glass of water), um copo de suco (a glass of juice).
target_language_example: Antes de dormir, eu sempre tomo um copo de leite.
native_language_example: Before going to sleep, I always drink a glass of milk.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or offering wine. "Um copo" means one glass (a serving in a glass), as opposed to "uma garrafa de vinho" (a bottle of wine). In polite requests, it often appears with "por favor", "eu queria...", or "eu gostaria de...".
target_language_example: Pode me trazer um copo de vinho branco, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a glass of white wine, please?

additional_notes: Used when ordering or offering water. With requests, you’ll often hear it with polite phrases like “por favor” (please) and “poderia…?” (could you…?).
target_language_example: Você pode me dar um copo de água, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a glass of water, please?

additional_notes: Used with the indefinite article "um" to refer to any crime in general, or to introduce a specific crime being discussed. Common in phrases like "cometer um crime" (to commit a crime), "ser vítima de um crime" (to be the victim of a crime), and "ser condenado por um crime" (to be convicted for a crime).
target_language_example: Ele foi preso por um crime.
native_language_example: He was arrested for a crime.

additional_notes: Refers to a supernatural evil being (common in fantasy stories), and it can also be used as an insult (“You’re a demon!”). Uses the masculine indefinite article: um demônio. Feminine: uma demônia (rare; often people still say “um demônio” regardless). Plural: demônios.
target_language_example: Ele disse que viu um demônio na floresta.
native_language_example: He said he saw a demon in the forest.

additional_notes: Used literally for something truly disastrous (an accident, a crisis) and very often as an exaggeration to say someone/something is in a terrible state: messy, ruined, falling apart, or going very badly ("Ela estava um desastre!" = she looked terrible / was a mess). With "estar/ser" it can describe appearance, condition, organization, or a situation.
target_language_example: O meu quarto está um desastre desde a mudança.
native_language_example: My room has been a mess since the move.

meaning: "a day"; also "one day / someday" (at an unspecified time).
additional_notes: With a noun like "um dia bom", it means "a (certain) day" (a single day). In stories or past events, "até que um dia..." / "um dia quando..." often means "one day" (= at some point). In the future, it commonly means "someday" (a hope or plan): "um dia vai..." / "um dia se tornará...".
target_language_example: Um dia eu quero morar perto do mar.
native_language_example: Someday I want to live near the sea.

additional_notes: Used to talk about not working/studying on a particular day. Very common with the verb "tirar": "tirar um dia de folga" = "to take a day off." You can specify when: "um dia de folga na semana" (a day off during the week / per week).
target_language_example: Vou tirar um dia de folga amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to take a day off tomorrow.

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: "um" = "a/an" (masculine singular) + "dicionário". Used to talk about any dictionary (not a specific one). You can specify the language with "de" ("um dicionário de francês" = a French dictionary) or make a bilingual pair with a hyphen ("um dicionário japonês-inglês" = a Japanese–English dictionary).
target_language_example: Você pode me emprestar um dicionário?
native_language_example: Can you lend me a dictionary?

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is among the top in a group (“one of the best + plural noun”). It agrees with gender/number: feminine plural is “uma das melhores” (e.g., uma das melhores praias). You can also change the adjective: “um dos piores” = “one of the worst.”
target_language_example: A Ana é uma das melhores jogadoras do time.
native_language_example: Ana is one of the best players on the team.

additional_notes: Common loanword in Portuguese. Often used with verbs like enviar/mandar (to send) and receber (to receive): "enviei/mnadei um e-mail" = "I sent an email"; "recebeu um e-mail" = "(he/she) received an email". You can also say "um correio eletrónico" (PT) / "um correio eletrônico" (BR), but "e-mail" is more common in everyday use.
target_language_example: Você pode me mandar um e-mail com os detalhes?
native_language_example: Can you send me an email with the details?

additional_notes: Common loanword in Portuguese. Often used with verbs like enviar/mandar (to send) and receber (to receive): "enviei/mnadei um e-mail" = "I sent an email"; "recebeu um e-mail" = "(he/she) received an email". You can also say "um correio eletrónico" (PT) / "um correio eletrônico" (BR), but "e-mail" is more common in everyday use.
target_language_example: Você pode me mandar um e-mail com os detalhes?
native_language_example: Can you send me an email with the details?

additional_notes: Used to talk about having, finding, needing, or getting a paid job: tenho/arrumei/preciso de um emprego. You can add details after it, like um emprego de meio período (a part-time job) or um emprego muito estressante (a very stressful job). Often contrasts with informal work or unemployment.
target_language_example: Estou procurando um emprego na minha área.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a job in my field.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ter" (to have) or "marcar" (to set up) to talk about an arranged date or meeting. In many everyday contexts, "um encontro" can mean a romantic date, but it can also mean a general meeting—context usually makes it clear. "Com" means "with" and introduces the person you’re meeting.
target_language_example: Tenho um encontro com o médico às três.
native_language_example: I have an appointment with the doctor at three.

additional_notes: Used with the indefinite article um (“a/an”) to talk about one specific mistake. Very common with verbs like cometer (to make/commit) and corrigir (to correct). In Portuguese, you usually say “cometer um erro” (make a mistake) rather than a direct equivalent of “do an error.”
target_language_example: Acho que cometi um erro no relatório.
native_language_example: I think I made a mistake in the report.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is a student. In Portuguese, the article changes with gender and number: um estudante (a male student), uma estudante (a female student), os/ as estudantes (students). You can add the area of study with de: um estudante de medicina (a medical student).
target_language_example: Ele é um estudante de engenharia.
native_language_example: He is an engineering student.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to praise it: um excelente jogo/filme/desjejum. For feminine nouns, use “uma excelente” (e.g., uma excelente ideia).
target_language_example: Eles fizeram um excelente trabalho.
native_language_example: They did an excellent job.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a ghost/spirit (often in scary stories or superstition): “Vi um fantasma” (“I saw a ghost”). Also appears in the common expression “parecer/estar como se tivesse visto um fantasma” = “to look as if you’ve seen a ghost” (to look shocked or very scared).
target_language_example: Ela ficou pálida, como se tivesse visto um fantasma.
native_language_example: She turned pale, as if she had seen a ghost.

meaning: a favor; a small helpful thing you ask someone to do.
additional_notes: Common in polite requests with the verb pedir: “Posso pedir-lhe/te um favor?” = “Can I ask you a favor?” You’ll often hear “Só me faça um favor” (“Just do me a favor”) to introduce a request. It can refer both to the act of helping and to the requested task itself.
target_language_example: Você pode me fazer um favor e fechar a janela?
native_language_example: Can you do me a favor and close the window?

additional_notes: Used to talk about one male child (son). In many contexts, especially when the baby's sex isn’t specified yet, it can also mean “a child/baby” (e.g., “estar esperando um filho” = expecting a baby). Plural: “dois filhos” (two sons/children) depending on context.
target_language_example: Eles têm um filho pequeno.
native_language_example: They have a young son.

additional_notes: Uses the indefinite article “um” (“a/an”) + “filme” (“movie/film”). Often used with verbs like “ver” (to see/watch), “assistir (a)” (to watch), “fazer” (to make), and “sobre” (about). You can specify genre or type with “de …” (e.g., “um filme de ficção científica” = a science-fiction movie).
target_language_example: Vamos ver um filme hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Shall we watch a movie tonight?

meaning: a bright future; a promising future.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is likely to have a successful, positive life/career ahead. Common after verbs like ter (to have) and ver (to see): “Ela tem um futuro brilhante” / “Vejo um futuro brilhante para você”. You can also say “pela frente” (“ahead of him/her”).
target_language_example: Com esse talento, você tem um futuro brilhante.
native_language_example: With that talent, you have a bright future.

additional_notes: Literally “a branch of the tree.” Used when talking about cutting, breaking off, pulling off, or removing a branch (e.g., cortar, arrancar, tirar). You may also hear just “um galho” when it’s clear you mean a tree branch.
target_language_example: O vento quebrou um galho da árvore ontem à noite.
native_language_example: The wind broke a tree branch last night.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male child or teenage boy. It can also mean “kid” in a general, informal way (but still male). In Brazil, “garoto” is common in everyday speech; in Portugal, “rapaz” is more common for “boy/young man.”
target_language_example: Quando eu era um garoto, eu brincava na rua todos os dias.
native_language_example: When I was a kid, I played in the street every day.

additional_notes: "Um" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”). "Gato" is masculine, so it takes "um" (not "uma"). Used to introduce a cat that hasn’t been specified yet; plural: "uns gatos" (“some cats”).
target_language_example: Tem um gato na rua.
native_language_example: There’s a cat in the street.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular indefinite article + adjective (um + grande) before a masculine noun: um grande sinal, um grande castelo. "Grande" can mean physical size (big) or importance/intensity (great/major): um grande perigo, um grande progresso, um grande pesadelo. With some nouns like "homem", it can mean "a great man" (admired) or simply "a big man" depending on context.
target_language_example: Precisamos de um grande esforço para terminar hoje.
native_language_example: We need a big effort to finish today.

additional_notes: Used to say that something was a very important or serious mistake. Often appears with verbs like "cometer" (to make/commit a mistake): "cometer um grande erro". You can swap in other intensifiers, e.g. "um erro enorme" (a huge mistake).
target_language_example: Se você mentir agora, vai ser um grande erro.
native_language_example: If you lie now, it will be a big mistake.

meaning: “a group of” (a number of people/animals/things together).
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to talk about several people, animals, or things as one set: “um grupo de crianças/pessoas/baleias”. With a singular verb it emphasizes the group as a unit (Um grupo de pessoas morreu...), though plural verbs are also heard in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Tem um grupo de turistas esperando na entrada.
native_language_example: There’s a group of tourists waiting at the entrance.

additional_notes: A common everyday noun. Often used with verbs like pegar (to take), trazer (to bring), levar (to carry/take along), and emprestar (to lend). In Brazil you may also hear just "guarda-chuva" without "um" when speaking generally (e.g., "Preciso de guarda-chuva").
target_language_example: Está chovendo; vou levar um guarda-chuva.
native_language_example: It’s raining; I’m going to take an umbrella.

meaning: a genius; a very smart person (often for something specific).
additional_notes: Used to praise someone’s intelligence or talent, often with "em" + a subject/skill: "um gênio em matemática" (a genius at math). It can also be said jokingly or ironically about yourself or someone else ("Eu sou um gênio!").
target_language_example: Você é um gênio em resolver problemas.
native_language_example: You’re a genius at solving problems.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone admired for bravery, great achievements, or doing something noble (real or in someone’s opinion). Often appears after verbs like “ser” (to be), “achar” / “se achar” (to think/consider oneself), and “considerar” (to consider). Feminine form: “uma heroína”.
target_language_example: Ela virou um herói para a comunidade depois do resgate.
native_language_example: She became a hero to the community after the rescue.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an indefinite/unknown man. "Um" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a”/“one”), and "homem" means “man.” In questions it often means “any man,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Vi um homem na rua ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I saw a man on the street last night.

meaning: "a man of…" (used to describe a man by a quality, role, or affiliation).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to characterize someone: *um homem de ação* (“a man of action”), *um homem de cultura* (“a cultured man / a man of culture”). It can also indicate a distinguishing feature (*um homem de seis dedos* = “a man with six fingers”) or belonging/affiliation (*um homem de Rohan* = “a man of Rohan”). Feminine: *uma mulher de…*.
target_language_example: Ele é um homem de palavra.
native_language_example: He’s a man of his word.

additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase that needs an adjective after it: “um homem muito + adjective”. Examples: um homem muito rico (a very rich man), um homem muito velho (a very old man). “Muito” intensifies the adjective (very/really).
target_language_example: Ele é um homem muito inteligente.
native_language_example: He is a very intelligent man.

meaning: “a man who …” (used to introduce a relative clause).
additional_notes: Used to describe or identify a man by adding more information with **que** (“who/that”). Very common pattern: **um/uma + noun + que + verb**. **Que** here functions like “who/that” in English, linking the noun to the description.
target_language_example: Ela procura um homem que saiba cozinhar.
native_language_example: She’s looking for a man who knows how to cook.

meaning: "a man who speaks" / "a man who can speak (something)".
additional_notes: A noun phrase made of: "um" (a) + "homem" (man) + "que" (who/that) + "fala" (speaks). It introduces a relative clause describing the man, often followed by a language or adverb: "um homem que fala latim" (a man who speaks Latin), "um homem que fala bem" (a man who speaks well). In Portuguese, "que" is used for both "who" and "that" in this kind of sentence.
target_language_example: Ela procura um homem que fala inglês.
native_language_example: She is looking for a man who speaks English.

additional_notes: Means a man who has a lot of money. Uses the masculine noun "homem" (man) and the adjective "rico" (rich). The article "um" is "a"/"an". You can change the article to "o" for "the" ("o homem rico") or make it plural: "homens ricos" (rich men).
target_language_example: Ela quer conhecer um homem rico.
native_language_example: She wants to meet a rich man.

meaning: “an idiot” (a very stupid person; an insult).
additional_notes: Used as a noun phrase, often after the verb “ser” (to be): “Ele é um idiota.” It can also appear in expressions like “fazer de alguém um idiota” (“to make someone look/feel like an idiot”). It’s rude/insulting, so avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Não seja um idiota; presta atenção!
native_language_example: Don’t be an idiot; pay attention!

meaning: a moment; a second (a very short time).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to wait briefly ("Espera/Espere um instante", "Só um instante") or to say something will take very little time ("Levará apenas um instante"). It can also mean "for a moment" when asking for brief attention ("Posso falar com você um instante?"). Often appears with emphasis words like só/mais/apenas ("só mais um instante", "apenas um instante").
target_language_example: Só um instante, já volto.
native_language_example: Just a moment, I'll be right back.

additional_notes: Means “a (male) sibling.” It’s also used figuratively for someone treated like family (e.g., “como um irmão” = “like a brother”). Often contrasts with “uma irmã” (a sister).
target_language_example: Eu tenho um irmão mais velho.
native_language_example: I have an older brother.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a method or solution: "um jeito de + infinitive" (um jeito de fazer, resolver, chegar, etc.). It can also refer to someone’s characteristic manner of doing something (e.g., "um jeito de rir" = a way of laughing). Often appears in expressions like "arrumar um jeito de" (to find a way to).
target_language_example: A gente precisa dar um jeito de terminar isso hoje.
native_language_example: We need to find a way to finish this today.

additional_notes: Used for games in general (board games, video games, children’s games) and for sports events as a single match: "um jogo de futebol" = "a soccer match." It can also be used figuratively to mean "it’s just a game" or "a mind game/manipulation" depending on context (e.g., "O amor é só um jogo").
target_language_example: Vamos assistir a um jogo hoje à noite.
native_language_example: Let's watch a game/match tonight.

meaning: a set of; a game of.
additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean either (1) a matching set/collection of items (often things that come together), e.g. um jogo de joias/panelas; or (2) a sports match or a game, e.g. um jogo de basquete/tabuleiro. Also used in expressions like "um jogo de palavras" (“a play on words/pun”).
target_language_example: Comprei um jogo de toalhas e depois assisti a um jogo de futebol.
native_language_example: I bought a set of towels and then watched a soccer match.

additional_notes: Uses the indefinite article "um" (“a/an”) with "ladrão" (male noun). Feminine form: "uma ladra". Can be used literally (someone who steals) or figuratively to mean something that “steals” time/money/opportunities (e.g., "O desperdício é um ladrão" = “Waste is a thief”).
target_language_example: Cuidado: tem um ladrão na rua.
native_language_example: Careful: there’s a thief on the street.

additional_notes: "Um" means "a/one" (masculine singular). Use it when you’re talking about an unspecified single book or emphasizing quantity (one book). Plural: "uns livros" = "some books".
target_language_example: Eu preciso de um livro para a aula amanhã.
native_language_example: I need a book for class tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say you need/want a book with the purpose of reading it. Very common with places/times: “um livro para ler no avião/no trem” (“a book to read on the plane/on the train”). You can change the noun and infinitive: “um filme para ver” (a movie to watch), “algo para comer” (something to eat).
target_language_example: Preciso de um livro para ler antes de dormir.
native_language_example: I need a book to read before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic/subject of a book. You can swap in any noun or theme after sobre: um livro sobre animais/sentimentos/história. It agrees with the noun: um livro (masc.), uma revista sobre… (fem.).
target_language_example: Você tem um livro sobre o Brasil?
native_language_example: Do you have a book about Brazil?

additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular indefinite article “um” (“a/an”) + “lobo” (“wolf”). Often appears in comparisons like “comer como um lobo” (“to eat like a wolf,” i.e., very hungrily) or in questions like “Vês um homem ou um lobo?” (“Do you see a man or a wolf?”).
target_language_example: Ele estava com tanta fome que comeu como um lobo.
native_language_example: He was so hungry that he ate like a wolf.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a long duration. Often appears with verbs like esperar (to wait): "esperar por/durante um longo tempo". You can also use it more generally to describe how long something feels: "X parece um longo tempo" (X seems like a long time).
target_language_example: Ficamos sem nos ver por um longo tempo.
native_language_example: We didn’t see each other for a long time.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a physical location or venue (a place to go, meet, stay, etc.). Often followed by more detail, e.g., “um lugar para ficar” (a place to stay) or described with adjectives like “um lugar agradável/ legal/ bom” (a nice/cool/good place).
target_language_example: Vamos encontrar um lugar tranquilo para conversar.
native_language_example: Let’s find a quiet place to talk.

additional_notes: Used to say there is an appropriate spot or space for a purpose, followed by a verb in the infinitive (um lugar para morar, um lugar para estudar) or by a pronoun/noun referring to where something should go (um lugar para eles). In speech you’ll also hear the plural: “uns lugares para…”.
target_language_example: Precisamos de um lugar para guardar as malas.
native_language_example: We need a place to store the suitcases.

meaning: a place to stay (somewhere to sleep/live temporarily).
additional_notes: Used when you need accommodation, often for a short or unspecified period (a night, a few days, or longer). Very common with verbs like “precisar de” (to need): “Preciso de um lugar para ficar.”
target_language_example: Você conhece um lugar para ficar perto daqui?
native_language_example: Do you know a place to stay near here?

additional_notes: Used when asking for or referring to a map (paper or digital). It’s the indefinite article + noun: um (a) + mapa (map).
target_language_example: Você tem um mapa da cidade?
native_language_example: Do you have a map of the city?

additional_notes: Used with the indefinite article “um” (“a/an”) to refer to any hammer (not a specific one). In everyday speech, you’ll also see it without the article when talking about the tool in general: “Preciso de martelo(s).”
target_language_example: Preciso de um martelo para consertar isso.
native_language_example: I need a hammer to fix this.

additional_notes: "Um" means "a/an" and "menino" means "boy". Used to refer to a male child (often roughly up to the teenage years). It can also be used more generally for "a kid" in some contexts, but it specifically suggests a boy (contrast: "uma menina" = a girl).
target_language_example: Há um menino brincando no parque.
native_language_example: There is a boy playing in the park.

meaning: a miracle; something amazingly unlikely or almost impossible.
additional_notes: Used both literally (a religious/divine miracle) and figuratively to mean an unexpectedly great outcome or that only something extraordinary could solve a problem. Often appears in expressions like "Esperamos um milagre" (We’re hoping for a miracle) and "Só um milagre..." (Only a miracle...).
target_language_example: Chegar a tempo com esse trânsito vai ser um milagre.
native_language_example: Getting there on time with this traffic will be a miracle.

meaning: “a million (of)”; also used informally to mean “a lot / countless.”
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to express quantity: "um milhão de" + plural ("um milhão de ienes", "um milhão de perguntas"). It’s also common as an exaggeration in set phrases like "Nunca em um milhão de anos" (“Never in a million years”) or "um milhão de vezes" (“a million times” = very often).
target_language_example: Ele tem um milhão de coisas para fazer hoje.
native_language_example: He has a million things to do today.

additional_notes: Used literally to talk about the amount 1,000,000 dollars (often USD), and also commonly as a hypothetical way to mean “a huge amount of money.” With other currencies you can swap the last part: “um milhão de reais/euros.”
target_language_example: Se eu ganhasse um milhão de dólares, eu viajaria pelo mundo.
native_language_example: If I won a million dollars, I would travel the world.

additional_notes: Used literally for time (“one minute”) and very commonly as a polite request meaning “wait a moment / give me a second.” In requests, it can mean a short moment, not exactly 60 seconds: “Espera um minuto.” You’ll also hear it with verbs like esperar (to wait), precisar (to need), dar (to give), ter (to have): “Me dá um minuto?”, “Você tem um minuto?”
target_language_example: Só um minuto, por favor — já volto.
native_language_example: Just a minute, please — I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to wait briefly, or to ask for a short amount of someone’s time (e.g., to talk). Often appears as “Só um minuto, por favor” (“Just a moment, please”) or with verbs like “espere/aguarde” (“wait”). In everyday use it usually means “a moment,” not exactly 60 seconds.
target_language_example: Um minuto, por favor — já volto.
native_language_example: One moment, please — I’ll be right back.

um modo melhor de fazer isso

target_language_multi_word_term: um modo melhor de fazer isso
meaning: a better way to do that/this.
additional_notes: Used when you want to offer (or insist on) a more efficient or correct method. Common after verbs like "deixa/deixe" (let), "permite" (allow), or "deixem-me" (let me), often introducing a demonstration: "Deixa que eu te mostre..." = "Let me show you...". "Isso" usually refers to "that" (something already being done), but in practice it can also be used like "this" in conversation.
target_language_example: Calma—há um modo melhor de fazer isso.
native_language_example: Relax—there’s a better way to do this.

meaning: “a moment”; used to ask someone to wait briefly (“one moment”).
additional_notes: Common in polite requests: "Aguarde/Espere um momento" = “Please wait a moment.” By itself ("Um momento.") it means “One moment.” It can also mean “for a moment” in the sense of a short time: "ficar um momento" = “stay for a moment.” Often used with "só" or "só mais": "só um momento" / "só mais um momento" = “just a moment” / “just one more moment.”
target_language_example: Um momento, por favor — já vou atender.
native_language_example: One moment, please — I’ll help you right away.

meaning: a lot of; lots of; a bunch of.
additional_notes: Very common way to talk about a large quantity/number in an informal, conversational tone. It can be used with countable nouns (um monte de garotos = lots of boys) and uncountable nouns (um monte de pão = lots of bread). Verb agreement is usually plural when the noun after de is plural (Um monte de turistas visitam...).
target_language_example: Tenho um monte de coisas para fazer hoje.
native_language_example: I have a lot of things to do today.

meaning: a lot of things; lots of stuff.
additional_notes: Common, informal way to say you have/did/said many things. Very frequent in speech. You can also use it with other nouns: “um monte de trabalho” (a lot of work), “um monte de gente” (lots of people). Literally it’s “a pile of things,” but it usually just means “a lot.”
target_language_example: Hoje eu tenho um monte de coisas para resolver.
native_language_example: Today I have a lot of things to sort out.

meaning: a lot of problems; tons of problems.
additional_notes: Very common, informal way to say you have many problems or difficulties. "Um monte de" literally means "a pile/mound of" and can be used with many nouns (e.g., "um monte de trabalho" = a lot of work). In some contexts it can mean "a lot of trouble" rather than just "problems."
target_language_example: Estou com um monte de problemas no trabalho esta semana.
native_language_example: I’ve got a lot of problems at work this week.

additional_notes: "Um" means "a" (masculine singular). Use "um médico" when you mean any doctor (not a specific one). If it’s a specific doctor, you’ll often use "o médico" (the doctor). The feminine form is "uma médica".
target_language_example: Você precisa chamar um médico agora.
native_language_example: You need to call a doctor now.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (“in/for one month”) or a point in the future (“in one month”). The noun “mês” is masculine, so it uses “um”.
target_language_example: Vou ficar aqui por um mês.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay here for a month.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: "um novo + noun" (e.g., "um novo método", "um novo restaurante"). It agrees with the noun’s gender and number: feminine is "uma nova"; plural is "uns novos" / "umas novas". It can also mean "a different/another" in context (something not the same as before).
target_language_example: Comprei um novo celular.
native_language_example: I bought a new phone.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a different job someone has gotten (often after leaving or losing a previous one). Common with verbs like encontrar (to find), conseguir (to get), and arrumar (to find/get—Brazil).
target_language_example: Depois de muita procura, ela finalmente conseguiu um novo emprego.
native_language_example: After a long search, she finally got a new job.

additional_notes: Used with the indefinite article "um" to mean one egg (often a chicken egg). In Portuguese, "ovo" is masculine (um ovo / o ovo). It can also refer to other kinds of eggs depending on context (e.g., "um ovo de dragão" = a dragon egg).
target_language_example: Eu vou cozinhar um ovo para o café da manhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to cook an egg for breakfast.

meaning: a pair of; a couple of.
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean “a pair of” (two of something that go together or are naturally grouped): um par de luvas (a pair of gloves), um par de tesouras (a pair of scissors), um par de peras (two pears). It can also be used more loosely to mean “a couple of” with times/occasions: um par de vezes (a couple of times).
target_language_example: Preciso de um par de sapatos novos.
native_language_example: I need a new pair of shoes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about one set of two matching shoes. Common with shopping/needs (comprar/precisar) and with descriptions like color (sapatos pretos). The plural is “pares de sapatos”.
target_language_example: Vou comprar um par de sapatos novos hoje.
native_language_example: I'm going to buy a new pair of shoes today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a single (unspecified) country. Often appears after prepositions like "em" (in) and "para" (to/for): "em um país" = "in a country", "para um país" = "to a country". The plural is "países".
target_language_example: Ela mora em um país muito pequeno.
native_language_example: She lives in a very small country.

meaning: “a piece of” / “a bit of” (a portion of something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a part or chunk of something (food, materials, objects). It’s often followed by a noun: um pedaço de madeira (a piece of wood), um pedaço de queijo (a piece of cheese). For food, English may also use “a slice” depending on the item (e.g., um pedaço de torrada = a piece of toast).
target_language_example: Você quer um pedaço de bolo?
native_language_example: Do you want a piece of cake?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a portion/slice of cake when eating, serving, or offering food. You’ll often hear it with verbs like comer (to eat), pedir (to ask for), oferecer (to offer), and servir-se (help yourself).
target_language_example: Você quer um pedaço de bolo depois do jantar?
native_language_example: Do you want a piece of cake after dinner?

additional_notes: Used when you mean a single piece/scrap/sheet of paper, often for writing or handing to someone. You can also say "um papel" for "a piece/sheet of paper" in many everyday situations, but "um pedaço de papel" emphasizes that it’s just one piece (sometimes small or random).
target_language_example: Você tem um pedaço de papel para eu anotar o endereço?
native_language_example: Do you have a piece of paper for me to write down the address?

additional_notes: Used when talking about part of a loaf (or any bread) rather than a whole loaf. Common in requests with food: "Me dê um pedaço de pão" (Give me a piece of bread). You can swap in other foods: "um pedaço de queijo" (a piece of cheese).
target_language_example: Você quer um pedaço de pão com sopa?
native_language_example: Do you want a piece of bread with soup?

additional_notes: Used when offering, requesting, or talking about a portion of pie. Often appears with "mais" (another/more): "mais um pedaço de torta" = "another piece of pie."
target_language_example: Você quer um pedaço de torta de maçã?
native_language_example: Do you want a piece of apple pie?

additional_notes: Uses the indefinite article “um” (= “a/an”) with “peixe” (= “fish”). Very common after verbs like “pegar” when talking about catching a fish (e.g., fishing). Plural: “uns peixes” (some fish) / “peixes” (fish).
target_language_example: Hoje eu peguei um peixe enorme no rio.
native_language_example: Today I caught a huge fish in the river.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to describe something as small in size or amount: um pequeno objeto, um pequeno favor, um pequeno problema, um pequeno apartamento. It agrees with the noun’s gender and number (feminine: uma pequena; plural: uns pequenos / umas pequenas).
target_language_example: Ele fez um pequeno comentário e saiu.
native_language_example: He made a small comment and left.

meaning: a plan (an idea or set of steps to do something).
additional_notes: Used with the verb ter (“to have”) and precisar de (“to need”): Tenho um plano. / Preciso de um plano. It can also mean a more concrete “plan” like an organized strategy or proposal: chegar a um plano (“to come up with/agree on a plan”). In other contexts, plano can also mean a subscription/coverage plan (e.g., plano de saúde), but here it’s the general “plan/strategy” meaning.
target_language_example: Se der errado, precisamos de um plano B.
native_language_example: If it goes wrong, we need a plan B.

additional_notes: With an article (um/uma), "policial" is usually a noun meaning a police officer. It can also be an adjective meaning "police" (e.g., "carro policial" = police car). Feminine: "uma policial"; plural: "policiais".
target_language_example: Há um policial na porta do prédio.
native_language_example: There’s a police officer at the entrance of the building.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean a small quantity/amount: "um pouco de + noun". You can use it for things you can count or not: "um pouco de pão" (some bread), "um pouco de finlandês" (a bit of Finnish). Often translates naturally as “a little,” “a bit of,” or “some,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Quero um pouco de água, por favor.
native_language_example: I want a little water, please.

additional_notes: Used when you want to go outside (or open a window) to breathe cleaner/cooler air, often to feel better, calm down, or take a break. Common with verbs like "tomar" (to get/take), "respirar" (to breathe), and "precisar" (to need): "tomar/respirar um pouco de ar fresco".
target_language_example: Vou lá fora tomar um pouco de ar fresco.
native_language_example: I'm going outside to get some fresh air.

additional_notes: Used when asking for, buying, or adding a small amount of sugar, especially in drinks or cooking. Common in polite offers and requests (e.g., “Você quer…?” / “Preciso de…” / “Adicione…”).
target_language_example: Pode colocar um pouco de açúcar no meu chá, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you put a little sugar in my tea, please?

meaning: “a little (bit) of coffee”; “some coffee” (a small amount).
additional_notes: Used to offer, request, or suggest a small quantity of coffee. Very common with verbs like beber/tomar (“to drink/have”), pegar (“to take”), and querer (“to want”): “Quer um pouco de café?” In everyday speech you can also say “um pouco de” + noun for other things (e.g., “um pouco de água”).
target_language_example: Vou só querer um pouco de café, por favor.
native_language_example: I’ll just have a little coffee, please.

meaning: a little (bit of) tea; some tea.
additional_notes:
Used to offer, serve, or talk about a small amount of tea. 
- "um pouco de" = "a little (bit of) / some" + an uncountable noun.
- Common in polite offers: "Gostaria de... ?" (Would you like...?).
- With verbs like "beber" (to drink), "oferecer" (to offer), "fazer" (to make).
target_language_example: Você quer um pouco de chá com limão?
native_language_example: Do you want a little tea with lemon?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to a small amount of food. Often appears after verbs like querer (to want), dar (to give), colocar (to put), or preservar (to save/preserve). You can replace comida with another noun: um pouco de água (a little water).
target_language_example: Você pode me dar um pouco de comida, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little food, please?

meaning: a little (bit) of money; some money.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a small amount of money. Often appears with verbs like ter (to have), emprestar (to lend), oferecer (to offer), and with the preposition de after pouco. In some contexts, it can also mean “some money” without specifying an exact amount.
target_language_example: Você tem um pouco de dinheiro para o ônibus?
native_language_example: Do you have a little money for the bus?

additional_notes: Used to say you have a basic/small amount of ability or knowledge of the French language (speaking, understanding, knowing). Often appears with verbs like falar (to speak), entender (to understand), and saber (to know), and can be swapped with other languages: um pouco de português / espanhol / inglês.
target_language_example: Eu só falo um pouco de francês, mas consigo me virar.
native_language_example: I only speak a little French, but I can get by.

additional_notes: Used to say you know or are learning a small amount of English. Very common after verbs like "falar" (to speak), "saber" (to know how), and "aprender" (to learn): "Eu falo um pouco de inglês". Often paired with "só" to emphasize limitation: "Eu só falo um pouco de inglês". You can swap in other languages: "um pouco de português / espanhol".
target_language_example: Eu entendo um pouco de inglês, mas falo devagar.
native_language_example: I understand a little English, but I speak slowly.

additional_notes: Used when you want a small amount of milk, often in cooking, coffee/tea, or shopping. You can also say "um pouco de" + noun for other things (e.g., "um pouco de água" = a little water).
target_language_example: Você pode colocar um pouco de leite no meu café, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you put a little milk in my coffee, please?

additional_notes: Used when asking someone to give you (or someone else) space or not to interfere. Very common with the verb dar (“to give”): Dê… um pouco de privacidade. Also used with precisar/poder usar (“to need/could use”): Eu preciso/poderia usar um pouco de privacidade.
target_language_example: Você pode me dar um pouco de privacidade, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little privacy, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or talk about adding a small amount of salt to food. Common with verbs like colocar/pôr (to put/add), querer (to want), trazer (to bring), and faltar (to be missing/need). Often appears as a polite request: "Você me traz um pouco de sal?"
target_language_example: Pode me passar um pouco de sal, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you pass me a little salt, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask for, offer, or indicate a small amount of water. Common with verbs like beber/tomar (to drink), colocar (to put), adicionar (to add), tirar (to take/draw). Often used as an instruction or suggestion: “Bebe/Toma um pouco de água.”
target_language_example: Você pode me dar um pouco de água, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little water, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or describe a small increase in amount, degree, or effort ("more"), or a short extension of time ("a bit longer"). Common with verbs like esperar (wait), ficar (stay), praticar (practice), se esforçar (make an effort), and with adjectives/adverbs to mean “a bit more …” (e.g., um pouco mais amigáveis = a bit friendlier).
target_language_example: Pode falar um pouco mais devagar, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you speak a little more slowly, please?

meaning: a little louder; a little taller.
additional_notes: Literally “a little more high.” With verbs like falar (to speak), it means “a little louder” (about volume). With ser/ficar (to be/to become) describing a person, it usually means “a little taller” (about height). Often used as a polite request: “Um pouco mais alto, por favor.”
target_language_example: Você pode falar um pouco mais alto? Não estou ouvindo bem.
native_language_example: Can you speak a little louder? I can’t hear very well.

additional_notes: Used to suggest or request doing something earlier than planned/than usual. Often goes after the verb (vir, partir, sair, levantar-se). You can add a time reference: "um pouco mais cedo amanhã" (a little earlier tomorrow).
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar um pouco mais cedo para evitar o trânsito.
native_language_example: Let’s meet a little earlier to avoid traffic.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or add a small additional amount of something (often with food/ingredients), or figuratively to mean being slightly closer to something ("um pouco mais de" + noun). It can also be used with abstract nouns like "atenção" (attention).
target_language_example: Você pode falar um pouco mais devagar?
native_language_example: Can you speak a little more slowly?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask for extra time to finish something or make a decision. Common with verbs like “dar”/“me dê” (give me) and “precisar de” (need). Often followed by “por favor” to sound more courteous.
target_language_example: Você pode me dar um pouco mais de tempo para responder?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little more time to answer?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to slow down (walking, driving, speaking, etc.). Often appears with verbs like ir (to go) or andar (to walk), and with por favor for extra politeness. You can also say: Pode falar um pouco mais devagar? (Can you speak a little slower?).
target_language_example: Pode falar um pouco mais devagar, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you speak a little slower, please?

additional_notes: Used to express mild worry. It often follows verbs like "estar" or "ficar" (e.g., "estou/ficou um pouco preocupado"). Agreement: "preocupado" (male) / "preocupada" (female), and it can be plural ("preocupados/preocupadas").
target_language_example: Estou um pouco preocupado com a prova de amanhã.
native_language_example: I'm a little worried about tomorrow's test.

additional_notes: Very common and friendly. It’s the diminutive of "pouco" (little), so it often sounds softer or more polite. You can use it for quantities (food, money) or time ("just a little while"). Often used in requests: "Espera um pouquinho" (Wait a sec).
target_language_example: Pode falar mais devagar, um pouquinho?
native_language_example: Can you speak a little more slowly?

additional_notes: Used with "ser" or "dar" to say something is a gift from someone ("É um presente da minha tia" = "It’s a gift from my aunt"). With "para" it shows who the gift is for ("um presente para a filha" = "a gift for his daughter"). The noun is masculine: "um/o presente".
target_language_example: Tenho um presente para você.
native_language_example: I have a gift for you.

additional_notes: Used with the verb dar (“to give”) or enviar (“to send”). Often followed by a recipient with para (“for/to”) or an indirect object pronoun: Dar um presente de aniversário para a Mary. / Ele me enviou um presente de aniversário. You can also add who it’s from with de: Um presente de aniversário do Tom (“a birthday present from Tom”).
target_language_example: Comprei um presente de aniversário para o meu irmão.
native_language_example: I bought a birthday present for my brother.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a gift given for someone’s birthday. It’s a noun phrase: "um presente" (a gift/present) + "de aniversário" (birthday) + "para" (for) + a person’s name or pronoun. You can change "um" to "o" (the), "meu" (my), "um bom" (a good), etc.
target_language_example: Preciso comprar um presente de aniversário para minha irmã.
native_language_example: I need to buy a birthday present for my sister.

additional_notes: Used when you say who the gift is intended for. Very common in shopping contexts: “Estou procurando/comprando um presente para…” You can replace the person with a pronoun: “um presente para ela/ele/você” or “um presente para o meu pai”.
target_language_example: Comprei um presente para você.
native_language_example: I bought a present for you.

additional_notes: Uses the indefinite article “um” (“a/an”) + “problema” (“problem”). Common after forms of “haver/ter” to say there is/was a problem: “Há um problema.” / “Havia um problema.”
target_language_example: Desculpe, há um problema com o meu pedido.
native_language_example: Sorry, there’s a problem with my order.

additional_notes: Used to say an issue is important, severe, or potentially dangerous. Often appears with “ser/virar/tornar-se” (to be/become) and with “temos” to point out an urgent situation (“Temos aqui um problema sério”). The adjective “sério” agrees with “problema” (masculine): “um problema sério”; plural: “problemas sérios”.
target_language_example: Se não resolvermos isso logo, vai virar um problema sério.
native_language_example: If we don’t fix this soon, it’s going to become a serious problem.

additional_notes: "Pássaro" means “bird” (often a small bird). It’s masculine: "um pássaro" (a bird) / "o pássaro" (the bird); plural "pássaros". Common in sayings like "Mais vale um pássaro na mão que dois voando" (“A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush”).
target_language_example: Vi um pássaro na janela esta manhã.
native_language_example: I saw a bird on the window this morning.

additional_notes: Used for a small rodent in general. In everyday Portuguese, "rato" often refers to a mouse, but it can also mean a rat depending on context; if you need to be specific, you may hear "rato" (rat) vs. "camundongo" (mouse).
target_language_example: Tem um rato na cozinha!
native_language_example: There’s a mouse in the kitchen!

additional_notes: “Relógio” can mean a timepiece in general. Very often it’s a watch (“um relógio” / “um relógio de pulso”), but it can also be a clock depending on context (e.g., wall or alarm clocks). Common pattern: “dar um relógio de presente” = “to give a watch/clock as a gift.”
target_language_example: Ganhei um relógio de aniversário.
native_language_example: I got a watch for my birthday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a minor illness like a cold. Common patterns: "estar com um resfriado" = to have a cold; "pegar um resfriado" = to catch/get a cold (also "devo ter pego" = I must have caught).
target_language_example: Acho que estou com um resfriado, então vou ficar em casa hoje.
native_language_example: I think I have a cold, so I’m going to stay home today.

additional_notes: "Um" is the indefinite article "a/an" (masculine singular). "Sanduíche" is a common word for a sandwich in Brazilian Portuguese. The plural is "sanduíches" (e.g., "dois sanduíches").
target_language_example: Vou fazer um sanduíche para o almoço.
native_language_example: I'm going to make a sandwich for lunch.

additional_notes: Used to refer to something kept hidden or private. Often appears with verbs like contar (to tell) and manter/guardar (to keep), and in phrases like Tenho um segredo. (“I have a secret.”) and É um segredo entre nós. (“It’s a secret between us.”).
target_language_example: Não conte a ninguém — é um segredo.
native_language_example: Don’t tell anyone — it’s a secret.

meaning: “a second”; also used as “one moment / just a sec.”
additional_notes: Literally “one second.” Used for a short amount of time (por um segundo = “for a second”) or as a quick request to wait (Um segundo! / Só um segundo! = “One moment!”). In speech it often implies “just a moment,” not an exact second.
target_language_example: Um segundo, já te ajudo.
native_language_example: One moment, I’ll help you in a second.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a person in a general, neutral way, often when contrasting humans with animals or talking about humanity as a whole. It’s more formal than just saying "uma pessoa".
target_language_example: Ele é um ser humano como todos nós.
native_language_example: He’s a human being like all of us.

meaning: a sign of; an indication of.
additional_notes: Used to say that something shows or suggests a certain quality, feeling, or situation (e.g., “um sinal de fraqueza” = “a sign of weakness”). It can also be used literally for a physical sign/symbol (e.g., “um sinal de adição” = “a plus sign/addition sign”).
target_language_example: Isso é um sinal de que precisamos conversar.
native_language_example: That’s a sign that we need to talk.

meaning: a dream (literal or figurative: a wish/ideal).
additional_notes: Used for a sleep dream ("I had a dream") or, very often, for a personal goal or ideal ("I have a dream"). It can also mean something unreal/too good to be true ("It was just a dream"). Related: "sonho" (dream), "sonhar" (to dream), "pesadelo" (nightmare).
target_language_example: Viajar pelo mundo é um sonho para mim.
native_language_example: Traveling around the world is a dream for me.

additional_notes: Used to describe an unusual or unsettling dream. Very common with the verbs "ter" (teve um sonho estranho = had a strange dream) and "sonhar" (sonhou um sonho estranho = dreamed a strange dream, but more natural is "sonhou um sonho estranho" or simply "teve um sonho estranho"). You can also add time expressions like "ontem à noite" (last night) or "esta noite" (tonight).
target_language_example: Eu tive um sonho estranho ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I had a strange dream last night.

additional_notes: Means “a smile” (noun). Common with verbs like dar (to give) in the set phrase “dar um sorriso” = “to smile / to give a smile.” Often described with adjectives: um sorriso largo (a big/broad smile), simpático (friendly), alegre (happy), forçado (forced). You can also say “um sorriso no rosto” = “a smile on (someone’s) face.”
target_language_example: Ela deu um sorriso e disse oi.
native_language_example: She smiled and said hi.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an unspecified length of time. In "Eu preciso de um tempo", it often means needing time for yourself/space (sometimes even a break in a relationship). With "durar um tempo", it means "to last a while."
target_language_example: Vou ficar fora por um tempo.
native_language_example: I’m going to be away for a while.

meaning: a gunshot; a shot (from a firearm).
additional_notes: Used when talking about a single shot fired from a gun. Common with verbs like ouvir (to hear) ("ouviu um tiro" = "heard a gunshot"), levar (to get hit) ("levei um tiro" = "I got shot"), and morrer por (to die from) ("morto por um tiro" = "killed by a shot").
target_language_example: A polícia disse que houve um tiro durante a briga.
native_language_example: The police said there was a gunshot during the fight.

meaning: a job; work; a task (a piece of work).
additional_notes: “Trabalho” is used broadly. It can mean paid employment (“I have a job”), the effort/work someone does (“They did incredible work”), or a specific task/assignment you give someone (“I gave Tom a task/job”). In school contexts, “um trabalho” can also mean a project or assignment.
target_language_example: Tenho um trabalho novo e começo na segunda-feira.
native_language_example: I have a new job and I start on Monday.

additional_notes: Used in medical contexts to talk about receiving a new organ or body part: “um transplante de + [órgão/parte do corpo]”. Often appears with verbs like “fazer” (to have/undergo) and “precisar de” (to need).
target_language_example: Ela está na fila para um transplante de coração.
native_language_example: She is on the waiting list for a heart transplant.

additional_notes: "Um" is the masculine indefinite article (“a/an”). "Táxi" is a common word for a taxi/cab. Often used with verbs like precisar de (to need), chamar (to call), and querer (to want): "Preciso de um táxi" / "Chamei um táxi".
target_language_example: Podemos chamar um táxi aqui?
native_language_example: Can we call a taxi here?

meaning: “a taxi for” (for someone), or “a taxi to (do something)” depending on context.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like chamar (to call), reservar (to book), and pegar (to take). With a person after para, it means the taxi is for that person: “Chamei um táxi para Tom.” With an infinitive verb after para (para + verb), it expresses purpose (“in order to”): “peguei um táxi para alcançar o trem” = “I took a taxi to catch the train.” Often you’ll also hear “um táxi para + place” meaning “a taxi to [a place]” (e.g., “um táxi para o aeroporto”).
target_language_example: Você pode chamar um táxi para mim, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you call a taxi for me, please?

additional_notes: Uses the masculine indefinite article: um = “a/an”. Plural is “ursos”. Often used in comparisons like “gordo como um urso” (“as fat as a bear”). Can also describe a teddy bear/toy with context (e.g., “urso de pelúcia” = “teddy bear/stuffed bear”; “urso panda” = “panda bear”).
target_language_example: No zoológico, vimos um urso bem de perto.
native_language_example: At the zoo, we saw a bear up close.

meaning: an old friend; a longtime friend.
additional_notes: Usually means a friend you’ve known for a long time (not necessarily an elderly person). Often used when you meet someone again after a while: “Encontrei um velho amigo.” You can add details with “de”: “um velho amigo de infância/da escola/de minha juventude.”
target_language_example: Ontem encontrei um velho amigo da escola no metrô.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into an old friend from school on the subway.

meaning: an old friend of mine (a longtime friend).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is your friend from a long time ago (not necessarily elderly). Word order: "um" (a) + "velho" (old/longtime) + "amigo" (friend) + "meu" (my). In Portuguese it’s common to put the possessive after the noun in this pattern: "um amigo meu/uma amiga minha" = "a friend of mine".
target_language_example: Ontem, eu vi um velho amigo meu no centro da cidade.
native_language_example: Yesterday, I saw an old friend of mine downtown.

additional_notes: Used to describe windy weather. The verb “bater” is often used with wind in Portuguese (“o vento bateu”) meaning the wind blew/was blowing.
target_language_example: Hoje está fazendo frio e tem um vento forte.
native_language_example: Today it’s cold and there’s a strong wind.

meaning: “a real / true / genuine” (used to emphasize what someone or something really is).
