additional_notes: Used before a noun to stress authenticity or intensity: um verdadeiro amigo (a true friend), um verdadeiro milagre (a real miracle), um verdadeiro gênio (a true genius). It can be positive or negative (um verdadeiro problema). Often implies “not just in name; genuinely.”
target_language_example: Ela foi uma verdadeira heroína naquela situação.
native_language_example: She was a true heroine in that situation.

additional_notes: "Vestido" is a masculine noun (o vestido), so you say "um vestido" (a dress) and "o vestido" (the dress). It’s commonly used for clothing you buy, make, or clean: "comprar um vestido" (buy a dress), "fazer um vestido" (make a dress), "limpar um vestido" (clean a dress). You can describe it with colors/materials: "um vestido azul" (a blue dress), "um vestido de lã" (a wool dress).
target_language_example: Estou procurando um vestido para a festa.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a dress for the party.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: um ótimo lugar (a great place), um ótimo livro (a great book), um ótimo professor (a great teacher). For feminine nouns, use "uma ótima" (uma ótima ideia). In greetings/wishes you often drop the article: "Tenha um ótimo dia!" = “Have a great day!”
target_language_example: Foi um ótimo jantar.
native_language_example: It was a great dinner.

meaning: “one, two, three” (counting; also a cue to start).
additional_notes: Used when counting out loud (often for kids, games, exercise, etc.). It can also be used like a countdown to begin something: “Um, dois, três, vai!” = “On three, go!” In Portuguese, commas are commonly used when listing numbers while counting.
target_language_example: No um, dois, três, todo mundo pula!
native_language_example: On one, two, three, everyone jumps!

additional_notes: Used to talk about a 12-month period in general (“a year”) or a duration (“for one year”). Often follows duration prepositions like por/durante: por um ano, durante um ano.
target_language_example: Morei no Brasil por um ano.
native_language_example: I lived in Brazil for a year.

additional_notes: Used to point out a single person/thing from a group of (at least) two. It’s masculine plural: um dos amigos, um dos leões. For feminine plural, use "uma das" (e.g., uma das pessoas). Often followed by a plural noun or by "meus/minhas/seus/suas" + plural noun.
target_language_example: Este é um dos melhores restaurantes da cidade.
native_language_example: This is one of the best restaurants in the city.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is among the top in a group (“one of the best + plural noun”). It agrees with gender/number: feminine plural is “uma das melhores” (e.g., uma das melhores praias). You can also change the adjective: “um dos piores” = “one of the worst.”
target_language_example: A Ana é uma das melhores jogadoras do time.
native_language_example: Ana is one of the best players on the team.

additional_notes: Used to refer to one person/thing within your own group (your students, employees, favorite places, etc.). It agrees in gender/number with what comes next: um dos meus alunos (one of my students, masc. plural), uma das minhas amigas (one of my friends, fem. plural).
target_language_example: Ela é uma das minhas melhores amigas.
native_language_example: She is one of my best friends.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is among the best in your personal list or experience. It agrees with the noun: for a feminine noun use “uma das minhas melhores …” (e.g., “uma das minhas melhores amigas”); for plural use “uns/umas dos/das meus/minhas melhores …”. Often followed by a noun like “amigos”, “professores”, “alunos”, “clientes”.
target_language_example: Ela é uma das minhas melhores colegas de trabalho.
native_language_example: She is one of my best coworkers.

additional_notes: Used to express a reciprocal action between two people or groups. Often appears with plural subjects (eles/elas/vocês) and with verbs like falar (to talk), conversar (to chat), flertar (to flirt), ajudar (to help), dar-se bem (to get along). Common variations: "uma com a outra" (two women), "uns com os outros" / "umas com as outras" (groups). In speech, it’s often shortened to "um com o outro" even when grammar would suggest another form.
target_language_example: Eles sempre se ajudam um com o outro quando têm um problema.
native_language_example: They always help each other when they have a problem.

additional_notes: Used to say someone belongs to the same group as the speaker (“one of us”). Also common in comparisons with qualquer (“any”): qualquer um de nós = “any one of us.”
target_language_example: Se precisar de ajuda, pode contar comigo — sou um de nós.
native_language_example: If you need help, you can count on me — I’m one of us.

additional_notes: Used to describe a mutual relationship or comparison between two people or things. Often appears with verbs like gostar de (to like), ajudar (to help), and with adjectives like diferente (different): "diferentes um do outro" = "different from each other". You may also hear variations like "uma da outra" (two women) or "uns dos outros" (a group).
target_language_example: Eles dependem um do outro para tudo.
native_language_example: They depend on each other for everything.

meaning: 'for each other' / 'at each other' (reciprocal: one to/for the other).
additional_notes: Used to express a reciprocal relationship or action between two people (or two groups): they do something to each other (e.g., look at each other) or they are a good match ("made for each other"). It changes with gender/number: um para o outro (two men or mixed group), uma para a outra (two women), um para a outra / uma para o outro (mixed pair, depending on who you’re referring to).
target_language_example: Eles sempre cuidam um para o outro.
native_language_example: They always take care of each other.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a physical location/branch where you mail letters and packages and use postal services. Often said simply as “os correios” (the post office/postal service).
target_language_example: Preciso ir a uma agência dos correios para enviar este pacote.
native_language_example: I need to go to a post office to send this package.

additional_notes: Used when talking about calling for emergency medical transport/help. Often with verbs like chamar (to call) or chegar (to arrive). In Portuguese, you can also say just “ambulância” without “uma” when speaking generally (e.g., “Chame ambulância!”).
target_language_example: Chame uma ambulância, por favor!
native_language_example: Call an ambulance, please!

additional_notes: "Arma" means a weapon; in everyday contexts it often refers to a firearm, but it can also be any weapon (e.g., a knife). It’s the feminine singular form, so it uses "uma" (a/an). Plural: "armas".
target_language_example: Ele disse que viu uma arma na mochila.
native_language_example: He said he saw a weapon in the backpack.

additional_notes: Used when you hear someone knocking (the sound of knocking) or when a knock interrupts/surprises someone. The noun phrase is built from "uma batida" (a hit/knock) + "na porta" (on the door). You can also say "uma pancada na porta" (a bang on the door) or more commonly "uma batida à porta" in European Portuguese.
target_language_example: Eu estava no banho quando ouvi uma batida na porta.
native_language_example: I was in the shower when I heard a knock at the door.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or asking for something to drink. It’s general (could be water, soda, juice, alcohol, etc.); in restaurants you might also hear “uma bebida, por favor”.
target_language_example: Eu vou pedir uma bebida.
native_language_example: I’m going to order a drink.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun: uma bela cidade (a beautiful city), uma bela voz (a beautiful voice). It can also mean “a nice/considerable” amount or quantity: uma bela quantia = a nice sum / a lot of money. For masculine, use “um belo”; for plural, “umas belas”.
target_language_example: Eles ganharam uma bela quantia com o negócio.
native_language_example: They made a nice sum from the deal.

additional_notes: "Uma" means "a" (feminine singular), and "bicicleta" is a feminine noun. Often used with adjectives after the noun (e.g., "uma bicicleta azul" = "a blue bike"). You’ll also see it with types like "bicicleta elétrica" (electric bike) and "bicicleta dobrável" (folding bike).
target_language_example: Quero comprar uma bicicleta para ir ao trabalho.
native_language_example: I want to buy a bike to go to work.

additional_notes: "Uma" means “a/an” (feminine singular). "Bicicleta" is feminine, so it takes "uma" and the adjective "nova" (new, feminine singular). You can use it after verbs like "precisar de" (to need) and "querer" (to want).
target_language_example: Ela comprou uma bicicleta nova ontem.
native_language_example: She bought a new bicycle yesterday.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to describe it: "uma boa razão" (a good reason), "uma boa escola" (a good school). It agrees with feminine nouns (compare masculine: "um bom"). Sometimes it can stand alone as "a good one" when the noun is understood from context.
target_language_example: Preciso de uma boa ideia para o projeto.
native_language_example: I need a good idea for the project.

additional_notes: Used to say something is a good plan or suggestion. Often with verbs like "ter" (to have) or "ser" (to be): "ter uma boa ideia" (to have a good idea), "isso não é uma boa ideia" (that’s not a good idea). You can also say "Uma boa ideia veio-me à cabeça" = “A good idea came to my mind.”
target_language_example: Acho que é uma boa ideia ligar antes de ir lá.
native_language_example: I think it’s a good idea to call before going there.

meaning: a good memory (ability to remember things).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "ter" (to have): "ter uma boa memória". It can refer to remembering facts, names, faces, dates, etc. You can also use it for the device meaning (computer/phone memory), but in everyday conversation it usually means mental memory.
target_language_example: Eu não tenho uma boa memória para nomes.
native_language_example: I don't have a good memory for names.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone's character in a general, moral sense (kind, decent, well-intentioned). Often said as a compliment ("Ele é uma boa pessoa!") or in questions/doubts about someone's character ("Ele é uma boa pessoa?"). Can also contrast overall goodness with flaws: "uma boa pessoa com muitos defeitos".
target_language_example: No fundo, ela é uma boa pessoa, apesar de errar às vezes.
native_language_example: Deep down, she’s a good person, even though she makes mistakes sometimes.

additional_notes: Used to justify or explain an action, feeling, or decision. It’s typically followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., "uma boa razão para ir", "...para não ir"). You can change the article to match gender/number: "um bom motivo para" is a common alternative.
target_language_example: Não tenho uma boa razão para sair agora.
native_language_example: I don’t have a good reason to leave now.

meaning: a good trip; have a good trip.
additional_notes: Used to wish someone well when they’re about to travel. It often comes with verbs like desejar (“to wish”) or esperar (“to hope”), and can be said directly as a send-off: Boa viagem! (more common than the full uma boa viagem).
target_language_example: Boa viagem e manda notícias quando chegar!
native_language_example: Have a good trip, and let me know when you arrive!

meaning: a doll; (also) a sex doll (depending on context).
additional_notes: Most commonly means a toy doll. With words like “inflável” (inflatable) or in sexual contexts, it refers to a sex doll. It can also be used figuratively about a person (often a woman) meaning “like a doll,” but that depends heavily on context and can sound objectifying.
target_language_example: Comprei uma boneca para minha sobrinha.
native_language_example: I bought a doll for my niece.

additional_notes: "Cadeira" is a common countable noun for a chair (something you sit on). Use it with the indefinite article "uma" (“a/an”, feminine singular). It can also be used in contexts like grabbing, throwing, or being strapped into a chair (e.g., a high chair: "cadeira alta").
target_language_example: Você pode trazer uma cadeira para mim?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a chair for me?

additional_notes: Used with the verb “precisar de” (“to need”): “Eu preciso de uma cadeira de rodas.” You’ll also hear it with “estar em” (“to be in”): “Ele está em uma cadeira de rodas.” Often shortened to just “cadeira de rodas” without “uma” when speaking generally.
target_language_example: Você pode me ajudar a pegar uma cadeira de rodas, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you help me get a wheelchair, please?

meaning: "a box/carton of" (a container with something inside).
additional_notes: Used to talk about quantities or a container type: uma caixa de leite (a carton/box of milk), uma caixa de sapato (a shoe box). It can also be used figuratively in expressions like "A vida é uma caixa de surpresas" (“Life is full of surprises”).
target_language_example: Preciso de uma caixa de biscoitos para a festa.
native_language_example: I need a box of cookies for the party.

meaning: a walk (a walk for exercise or leisure).
additional_notes: Used to mean going for a walk as an activity (often for pleasure or exercise). Common with verbs like "fazer" (to take/go on) or "sair para" (to go out for). You can add details with "ao longo de" (along) + a place (e.g., a river, the beach).
target_language_example: Vamos fazer uma caminhada depois do jantar?
native_language_example: Shall we go for a walk after dinner?

additional_notes: Literally “a walk in the park.” Used for a casual, pleasant walk (often for exercise or fresh air). In Portuguese it’s typically a literal phrase; unlike English, it’s not commonly used to mean “something easy” unless the context makes it clear.
target_language_example: Vamos dar uma caminhada no parque depois do almoço.
native_language_example: Let’s take a walk in the park after lunch.

additional_notes: "Camisa" is a common word for a (usually button-up) shirt. "Uma" means "a/an" (feminine singular), so you’ll often see it with colors and descriptors: "uma camisa verde" (a green shirt), "uma camisa de mangas curtas" (a short-sleeved shirt), "uma camisa de seda" (a silk shirt). With clothing you can use both "usar" and "vestir": "Ele está usando/vestindo uma camisa" = "He is wearing a shirt."
target_language_example: Preciso comprar uma camisa para o trabalho.
native_language_example: I need to buy a shirt for work.

additional_notes: "Caneta" means "pen". "Uma" is the feminine form of "a/an" and is also used for "one". Common in requests and questions: "Dê-me uma caneta" (Give me a pen), "Posso pegar emprestada uma caneta?" (Can I borrow a pen?).
target_language_example: Você tem uma caneta para me emprestar?
native_language_example: Do you have a pen you can lend me?

meaning: a ride / a lift (in someone else’s vehicle), usually free.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "dar" (to give) and "pedir" (to ask for): "dar uma carona" = give someone a ride; "me dê uma carona" = give me a ride; "pedir uma carona" = ask for a ride. Often implies a favor rather than a paid trip (unlike a taxi/Uber). You can also specify the destination with "até" (to/until): "uma carona até o aeroporto".
target_language_example: Você pode me dar uma carona até a estação?
native_language_example: Can you give me a ride to the station?

additional_notes: "Dar uma carona" means to give someone a ride (usually in a car), and "pegar/precisar de uma carona" means to get/need a ride. It’s a common, informal-friendly everyday phrase for offering or asking for transport home.
target_language_example: Se você quiser, eu posso te dar uma carona para casa depois da aula.
native_language_example: If you want, I can give you a ride home after class.

additional_notes: Used with the verb escrever (to write): escrever uma carta (to write a letter). You can say escrever uma carta para ela (“to her”) or escrever uma carta a Maria (more formal/literary, “to Maria”).
target_language_example: Vou escrever uma carta para minha avó.
native_language_example: I’m going to write a letter to my grandmother.

meaning: “a letter of …” (a letter from someone, or for a specific purpose).
additional_notes: Used before a purpose/type (“uma carta de demissão” = a resignation letter) or before the sender’s name (“uma carta de Mary” = a letter from Mary). In the second case, Portuguese commonly uses “de” where English uses “from”.
target_language_example: Recebi uma carta de um amigo ontem.
native_language_example: I received a letter from a friend yesterday.

additional_notes: "Uma" is the feminine form of the indefinite article "a/an". "Casa" can mean the physical building (house) or, depending on context, someone’s home. Common with verbs like "comprar" (to buy), "alugar" (to rent), and "morar" (to live).
target_language_example: Eles querem comprar uma casa perto da escola.
native_language_example: They want to buy a house near the school.

additional_notes: Used to describe the size of a house. The adjective grande usually comes after the noun (casa grande). With one house in mind, it commonly uses the feminine article uma because casa is feminine. It can also appear as em uma casa grande (“in a big house”).
target_language_example: Eles compraram uma casa grande perto da praia.
native_language_example: They bought a big house near the beach.

additional_notes: Used to say where a house is located. **na** is the contraction of **em + a** (“in/on + the” feminine singular), so it’s used with many countries/places treated as feminine (e.g., **na Alemanha**, **na Itália**, **na Austrália**) and also with feminine nouns (e.g., **na árvore** “in the tree”). For masculine places, you usually use **no** (em + o), e.g., **uma casa no Brasil**.
target_language_example: Eles têm uma casa na Itália.
native_language_example: They have a house in Italy.

additional_notes: A feminine noun phrase: "cerejeira" means "cherry tree" (the tree, not the fruit "cereja"). Often used with verbs like "cortar" (to cut down) and "derrubar" (to knock down/fell) when talking about removing a tree.
target_language_example: No quintal, há uma cerejeira velha.
native_language_example: In the backyard, there’s an old cherry tree.

additional_notes: Used to order or talk about one beer (one unit/serving). Very common in invitations: “tomar uma cerveja” = “have a beer.” In restaurants/bars you can say “Uma cerveja, por favor.” You can add details like “gelada” (cold) or a brand.
target_language_example: Vamos tomar uma cerveja depois do trabalho?
native_language_example: Shall we have a beer after work?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "dar" (to give) and "merecer" (to deserve): "dar uma chance (a alguém)" = to give someone a chance; "merecer uma chance" = to deserve a chance. Often followed by "para" + infinitive to say what the chance is for ("uma chance para fazer isso" = a chance to do that).
target_language_example: Você pode me dar uma chance de explicar?
native_language_example: Can you give me a chance to explain?

additional_notes: Literally “a slotted key,” used for the common flathead screwdriver. You’ll often hear it in requests (preciso de…, posso pegar…) or when describing a tool used to open/force something (para arrombar/entrar). For a Phillips screwdriver, Portuguese commonly says “chave Phillips” (also “chave estrela” in some places).
target_language_example: Você tem uma chave de fenda aqui?
native_language_example: Do you have a screwdriver here?

additional_notes: Indefinite phrase ("a" + "city"). You’ll also see it as "uma" or "uma" shortened to "uma" depending on pronunciation, and as "em uma cidade" (in a city) or "numa cidade" (= "em uma cidade"). "Cidade" often means "city" in general, but in everyday speech it can also refer to a town (especially contrasted with "o campo" / the countryside).
target_language_example: Quero morar em uma cidade maior no ano que vem.
native_language_example: I want to live in a bigger city next year.

additional_notes: In Portuguese, "cobra" can refer to a snake in general (not only the specific animal called a "cobra" in English). Used with the indefinite article: "uma cobra" = "a snake".
target_language_example: Tem uma cobra perto da porta!
native_language_example: There’s a snake near the door!

additional_notes: Used for an unspecified object (“something”) or an unspecified matter you want to check/mention (“one thing”). Very common in everyday speech; plural is “umas coisas” (“a few things/some things”), and “uma coisa legal” means “a cool/nice thing.”
target_language_example: Espera um minuto, preciso te perguntar uma coisa.
native_language_example: Wait a minute, I need to ask you something.

meaning: "something like that" / "such a thing" (often with surprise, disapproval, or disbelief).
additional_notes: Used to refer to an action, idea, or object just mentioned or understood from context. Very common in reactions: thinking, doing, buying, or saying “a thing like that.” The tone is often negative or shocked, but it can also be neutral depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu nunca faria uma coisa dessas.
native_language_example: I would never do something like that.

additional_notes: Used when you want to introduce information that matters (often before saying what it is): e.g., “I forgot to tell you something important.” In Portuguese it’s very common to use “uma coisa” (“a thing”) as a neutral placeholder, similar to English “something,” and you can switch the adjective: “uma coisa urgente” (something urgent), “uma coisa séria” (something serious).
target_language_example: Antes de você ir, preciso te dizer uma coisa importante.
native_language_example: Before you go, I need to tell you something important.

additional_notes: Uses the indefinite article “uma” (feminine) meaning “a/one”. “Criança” is feminine in grammar, so you say “uma criança” even if the child is a boy. Plural: “crianças” (e.g., “umas crianças”).
target_language_example: Há uma criança brincando no parque.
native_language_example: There’s a child playing in the park.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a camera as an object. "Uma" is the feminine singular form of "a/an" (indefinite article). You’ll often see it with a type: "uma câmera nova" (a new camera), "uma câmera japonesa" (a Japanese camera), or "uma câmera de segurança" (a security camera).
target_language_example: Preciso de uma câmera para tirar fotos da viagem.
native_language_example: I need a camera to take photos on the trip.

additional_notes: Used to pick a single item from a group: “uma das + plural feminine noun” (e.g., uma das janelas). The masculine version is “um dos” (e.g., um dos livros). Often followed by a superlative like “uma das melhores…”.
target_language_example: Lisboa é uma das cidades mais bonitas de Portugal.
native_language_example: Lisbon is one of the most beautiful cities in Portugal.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "tomar": "tomar uma decisão" = "to make a decision". Common in everyday and formal contexts (e.g., "uma decisão da corte" = "a court decision").
target_language_example: Preciso tomar uma decisão hoje.
native_language_example: I need to make a decision today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a medical condition (physical or mental): “ter uma doença” = “to have an illness/disease.” Can also be used figuratively to describe a harmful social problem (“Preconceito é uma doença.” = “Prejudice is a disease.”). Often clarified with an adjective, e.g. “uma doença grave” (“a serious illness”).
target_language_example: Ele está no hospital com uma doença grave.
native_language_example: He is in the hospital with a serious illness.

additional_notes: Common in medical/health contexts to describe a pain that is strong and usually starts suddenly (as opposed to "dor crônica" = chronic pain). It’s often followed by where the pain is: "uma dor aguda no estômago / na mão direita / aqui". You can also say it without "uma" in some contexts (e.g., "Senti dor aguda...").
target_language_example: Estou com uma dor aguda no peito desde ontem.
native_language_example: I’ve had a sharp pain in my chest since yesterday.

additional_notes: Literally “a pain of head.” Used with verbs like ter (“to have”) and estar com (“to be with / to have”): Tenho uma dor de cabeça. / Estou com dor de cabeça. It can also be figurative: Isso me deu uma dor de cabeça = “That gave me a headache” meaning it caused trouble or stress.
target_language_example: Estou com uma dor de cabeça hoje; acho que vou descansar.
native_language_example: I have a headache today; I think I’m going to rest.

additional_notes: Used when buying or listing groceries. "Uma dúzia" means 12 of something, and you can swap in other items (e.g., "uma dúzia de bananas"). Often used with verbs like "comprar" (to buy) and "precisar de" (to need).
target_language_example: Vou comprar uma dúzia de ovos para fazer um bolo.
native_language_example: I’m going to buy a dozen eggs to make a cake.

additional_notes: Used to compare something to a category or describe it approximately when you don’t have (or don’t want to use) an exact word. Often translates as “a kind of” or “sort of,” and can imply “something like” rather than a strict classification.
target_language_example: Isso é uma espécie de truque para economizar tempo.
native_language_example: That’s a kind of trick to save time.

meaning: a star (a famous person, or a star in the sky / a star-shaped decoration).
additional_notes: Often used for a celebrity: uma estrela do rock (“a rock star”), uma estrela de Hollywood (“a Hollywood star”). It can also mean a star in the sky, or a decorative star (e.g., on top of a Christmas tree).
target_language_example: Ela é uma estrela de cinema no Brasil.
native_language_example: She’s a movie star in Brazil.

meaning: “an experience” (something you lived through or tried).
additional_notes: Used for events or situations you go through (“I had an experience”), or for trying something as an experiment (“It was just an experiment/experience”). Often followed by an adjective: uma experiência ruim/má (a bad experience), uma experiência interessante (an interesting experience).
target_language_example: Visitar Lisboa pela primeira vez foi uma experiência incrível.
native_language_example: Visiting Lisbon for the first time was an incredible experience.

additional_notes: Used when asking for or giving a reason/clarification about something. Very common with verbs like "dar" (to give): "dar uma explicação" = "to give an explanation"; and with "sobre" (about): "uma explicação sobre isso" = "an explanation about that". You can also use it after stronger verbs like "exigir" (to demand) or expressions like "dever" (to owe): "Você me deve uma explicação".
target_language_example: Preciso de uma explicação antes de aceitar.
native_language_example: I need an explanation before I accept.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to a single knife. "Uma" is the feminine form of "a/one" and matches the feminine noun "faca" (knife). Plural: "facas"; "a faca" = "the knife".
target_language_example: Pode trazer uma faca, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring a knife, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a family as a unit (a household/relatives). Often appears with adjectives like "uma família grande" (a big family) or with "ter"/"querer" (to have/want): "Eu quero uma família". It can also imply “to start/have a family” depending on context.
target_language_example: Eles querem ter uma família um dia.
native_language_example: They want to have a family one day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about one thin piece cut from something (food like bread, cake, meat, watermelon, etc.). It’s a common quantity phrase when offering or ordering food. With feminine nouns you often see the contraction: “uma fatia da melancia” (= a slice of the watermelon).
target_language_example: Você quer uma fatia de pizza?
native_language_example: Do you want a slice of pizza?

additional_notes: Used with the indefinite article uma (“a”) to talk about a particular party/celebration: uma festa ótima (“a great party”). It can also be used more figuratively to mean something feels like a celebration (Cada dia é uma festa... = “Every day is a celebration...”). For “at a party,” Portuguese often uses em/numa: em uma festa / numa festa.
target_language_example: Vamos fazer uma festa no sábado.
native_language_example: We’re going to have a party on Saturday.

additional_notes: Used when talking about having or describing a daughter. "Filha" is feminine; the masculine is "filho" (son), and the plural "filhos" can mean "children" in general. Often followed by a description: "uma filha chamada..." (a daughter named...) or "uma filha que..." (a daughter who...).
target_language_example: Eles têm uma filha de cinco anos.
native_language_example: They have a five-year-old daughter.

additional_notes: “Uma” is the feminine form of “a/an” (indefinite article), used here with the feminine noun “flor” (flower). Use it when mentioning a flower for the first time or when it’s not specific; for a specific flower, you’d often use “a flor” (“the flower”).
target_language_example: Eu comprei uma flor para você.
native_language_example: I bought a flower for you.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to a single piece/sheet of paper. Also appears in the common comparison "pálido como uma folha de papel" (“as pale as a sheet of paper”). Note: "folha" can also mean “leaf” in other contexts, but with "de papel" it means “sheet (of paper)”.
target_language_example: Você tem uma folha de papel para eu anotar isso?
native_language_example: Do you have a sheet of paper so I can write that down?

additional_notes: "Foto" is short for "fotografia" and is the most common everyday word for "photo". Often used with verbs like "tirar" (to take): "tirar uma foto"; "enviar" (to send): "enviar uma foto"; "postar" (to post): "postar uma foto". You can specify who is in it with "uma foto de + person" (a photo of...) or "uma foto minha/sua/dele/dela" (a photo of me/yours/him/her).
target_language_example: Você pode tirar uma foto minha, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you take a photo of me, please?

additional_notes: Used before the person/thing in the picture: uma foto de Maria (a photo of Maria). You can also use it with a clause to mean “a photo of (when/doing…)”: uma foto de quando o Tom era bebê (a photo from when Tom was a baby), uma foto de Tom dançando (a photo of Tom dancing).
target_language_example: Você tem uma foto de mim no seu celular?
native_language_example: Do you have a photo of me on your phone?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to a photo showing someone/something. "Do" = "de" + "o" and is used before masculine singular nouns (do Tom, do meu cachorro). For feminine singular, use "uma foto da" (de + a).
target_language_example: Você tem uma foto do seu passaporte?
native_language_example: Do you have a photo of your passport?

additional_notes: Often means “a sentence” in everyday use (a complete statement). It can also mean “a phrase” (a group of words), depending on context. Feminine noun: uma frase / a frase / frases.
target_language_example: Pode repetir a frase, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you repeat the sentence, please?

meaning: a girl; a young woman (Brazilian Portuguese).
additional_notes: “Garota” is very common in Brazil for “girl” and can also mean a “young woman,” depending on context. It’s often neutral, but in some situations it can sound a bit like “girl” in English when referring to an adult; if you want a more formal/neutral option for an adult, you can use “uma mulher” (a woman). “Uma” is the feminine form of “a/an” and is used because “garota” is feminine.
target_language_example: Eu vi uma garota no ônibus que parecia perdida.
native_language_example: I saw a girl on the bus who seemed lost.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a quantity in a bottle, usually followed by a drink or liquid: uma garrafa de água/vinho/leite/cerveja. The noun after “de” is typically not preceded by an article (e.g., “uma garrafa de água”, not “uma garrafa da água”). Plural: “duas garrafas de …”.
target_language_example: Você pode me trazer uma garrafa de água, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a bottle of water, please?

additional_notes: Used to refer to one bottle (uma) of wine, especially when ordering, offering, giving, bringing, or talking about drinking wine. You can change the number: duas garrafas de vinho = two bottles of wine. In shops/restaurants you may also hear: uma garrafa de vinho tinto (red wine) / branco (white wine).
target_language_example: Você pode trazer uma garrafa de vinho para o jantar?
native_language_example: Can you bring a bottle of wine for dinner?

meaning: “a big / great (one)” (feminine), used before a noun.
additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns to mean “a large/important/major.” You normally complete it with a feminine noun: uma grande família (a big family), uma grande artista (a great artist), uma grande quantia (a large amount), uma grande diferença (a big difference), uma grande dívida (a big debt). With masculine nouns, use “um grande” (ex.: um grande problema).
target_language_example: Ela fez uma grande escolha ao mudar de emprego.
native_language_example: She made a great choice by changing jobs.

meaning: a large amount of; a great quantity of.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a lot of something (usually an uncountable noun like dinheiro, vinho, carvão, but it can also be used with countable things as “a large number of”). It’s a formal/neutral way to say “muito/muita”. The noun after “de” is often singular, and the verb may agree with either “quantidade” (singular) or with the noun that follows in more natural usage.
target_language_example: Eles produziram uma grande quantidade de energia este ano.
native_language_example: They produced a large amount of energy this year.

meaning: a story; a tale; (sometimes) a made-up story/excuse.
additional_notes: Often means a story you tell (real or fictional): "contar uma história" = "to tell a story." It can also mean an invented story/lie in context: "inventar uma história" = "to make up a story" (often as an excuse).
target_language_example: Ela contou uma história engraçada para as crianças.
native_language_example: She told a funny story to the children.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration of time (“for one hour”) or an amount of time available (“we have one hour”). Often appears with “por” (por uma hora = for an hour) or without a preposition after a verb of doing an activity (nado uma hora = I swim for an hour).
target_language_example: Eu só tenho uma hora para terminar isso.
native_language_example: I only have one hour to finish this.

additional_notes: Refers to a jacket made of leather. Often used with verbs like comprar (to buy), vestir (to put on / wear), and usar (to wear/use). You can change the article depending on the situation: uma jaqueta de couro (a leather jacket), a jaqueta de couro (the leather jacket), minha jaqueta de couro (my leather jacket).
target_language_example: Eu gosto da minha jaqueta de couro preta.
native_language_example: I like my black leather jacket.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a telephone call. Often used with verbs like fazer (to make) and receber (to receive): fazer uma ligação = to make a call; receber uma ligação (de alguém) = to get a call (from someone). In other contexts, ligação can also mean a connection/link (e.g., a train connection), but the examples here are about phone calls.
target_language_example: Vou fazer uma ligação rapidinha e já volto.
native_language_example: I'm going to make a quick call and I'll be right back.

additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns to describe something that lasted a lot of time or covered a great distance (e.g., uma longa história, uma longa vida, uma longa caminhada). The adjective “longa” agrees with the noun’s gender/number; compare: um longo dia (masculine), longas caminhadas (plural).
target_language_example: Depois de uma longa viagem, ele só queria descansar.
native_language_example: After a long trip, he just wanted to rest.

additional_notes: Used to describe a letter (carta) that is long in length or has a lot of content. You’ll often see it with verbs like escrever (“to write”) and mandar (“to send”). Word order is typical in Portuguese: indefinite article + adjective + noun (uma + longa + carta).
target_language_example: Ontem à noite, escrevi uma longa carta para minha avó.
native_language_example: Last night, I wrote a long letter to my grandmother.

additional_notes: Used with the indefinite article (uma) to refer to a language in general or one unspecified language. Often appears after verbs like aprender (to learn) and falar (to speak): aprender uma língua, falar uma língua. Note: língua can also mean “tongue” in other contexts, but in these examples it means “language.”
target_language_example: Quero aprender uma língua nova este ano.
native_language_example: I want to learn a new language this year.

additional_notes: Used to talk about any language that is not your native language (or not the main language of your country). Often used with verbs like aprender (to learn), falar (to speak), estudar (to study), and dominar (to master).
target_language_example: Estou aprendendo uma língua estrangeira para o trabalho.
native_language_example: I’m learning a foreign language for work.

meaning: "a way to" (a method of doing something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a solution or method to achieve an action that follows, typically with an infinitive verb: "uma maneira de + verb" (e.g., "uma maneira de fazer"). Often used when discussing finding solutions ("encontrar uma maneira de...").
target_language_example: Existe uma maneira de resolver esse problema.
native_language_example: There is a way to solve this problem.

uma maneira melhor de fazer isso

target_language_multi_word_term: uma maneira melhor de fazer isso
meaning: a better way to do that/this.
additional_notes: Used to suggest an improved method for completing a task. "Uma maneira" = "a way"; "melhor" agrees with "maneira"; "de fazer isso" = "to do that/this" ("isso" usually refers to what the other person is doing or something just mentioned). Often appears after polite phrases like "Deixe-me/Permita-me mostrar..." (Let me/Allow me to show you...).
target_language_example: Acho que há uma maneira melhor de fazer isso.
native_language_example: I think there’s a better way to do that.

additional_notes: "Uma" is the feminine form of the indefinite article "a/an" (also can mean "one"). "Maçã" (apple) is a feminine noun, so it uses "uma": "uma maçã". Often used to introduce an apple that hasn’t been mentioned yet (new information).
target_language_example: Eu quero uma maçã, por favor.
native_language_example: I want an apple, please.

additional_notes: "Uma" is the feminine form of the indefinite article "a/an" ("one"), used before feminine singular nouns. "Menina" usually refers to a girl/child; depending on context it can also be used more generally to mean a young woman. In sentences like "Você parece uma menina", it can be a comparison (sometimes teasing).
target_language_example: Há uma menina brincando no parque.
native_language_example: There’s a girl playing in the park.

additional_notes: Used for a message in general (spoken, written, voicemail, or text). Common with verbs like enviar (to send), mandar (to send), deixar (to leave), and with urgency: uma mensagem urgente (an urgent message). In Portuguese you often specify the type if needed: uma mensagem de texto (a text message).
target_language_example: Posso te deixar uma mensagem depois da reunião?
native_language_example: Can I leave you a message after the meeting?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like receber (to receive), mandar/enviar (to send): "mandar/enviar uma mensagem de texto" and "receber uma mensagem de texto". You can add de + person for who it’s from ("uma mensagem de texto do Tom") and para + person for who it’s to ("uma mensagem de texto para a Maria").
target_language_example: Vou te mandar uma mensagem de texto quando eu chegar.
native_language_example: I’ll send you a text message when I arrive.

additional_notes: Used to say who the message is intended for. Common with verbs like “ter” (to have) and “deixar/enviar” (to leave/send): “Tenho uma mensagem para você.” / “Deixe uma mensagem para o Tom.” In Brazilian Portuguese you’ll often hear “pra” instead of “para” in speech.
target_language_example: Tenho uma mensagem para você: vou chegar mais tarde.
native_language_example: I have a message for you: I’m going to arrive later.

additional_notes: Used to say a statement/story is not true. Often appears with the verb contar (“to tell”) in contar uma mentira (“to tell a lie”), and with ser (“to be”) in isso é/era uma mentira (“that is/was a lie”). You can also use it more broadly about an idea or situation you think is fake or not real (e.g., Tudo é uma mentira).
target_language_example: Não quero viver numa mentira.
native_language_example: I don’t want to live in a lie.

uma moeda para fazer uma ligação

target_language_multi_word_term: uma moeda para fazer uma ligação
meaning: a coin to make a phone call.
additional_notes: Used when you need a coin to use a payphone/public phone (especially before cell phones were common). It literally refers to a coin (uma moeda) needed “to make a call” (para fazer uma ligação). Word order can vary (e.g., with “no/meu bolso” inserted), but the core idea stays the same.
target_language_example: Você tem uma moeda para fazer uma ligação?
native_language_example: Do you have a coin to make a phone call?

additional_notes: "Uma" is the feminine form of "um" and works like English "a/an" or "one". Use it before a singular feminine noun: "uma mulher", "uma casa". If you mean "the woman", use "a mulher".
target_language_example: Eu vi uma mulher na rua.
native_language_example: I saw a woman on the street.

additional_notes: Used to describe a woman as physically attractive. It’s a neutral description, but in some contexts it can sound a bit direct/objectifying, so you may prefer softer options like “uma mulher muito bonita” (a very beautiful woman) depending on the situation. Word-by-word: uma (a) + mulher (woman) + muito (very) + atraente (attractive).
target_language_example: Ele falou com uma mulher muito atraente na festa.
native_language_example: He talked to a very attractive woman at the party.

additional_notes: Used to say that a plan or action is not a good choice and may lead to problems. Often appears with verbs like achar (to think), parecer (to seem), or ser (to be): “Acho que é uma má ideia”, “Isso parece uma má ideia”, “É uma má ideia”. You can also emphasize it: “mesmo” = really/actually (“Eu sou mesmo o único…?” = “Am I really the only one…?”).
target_language_example: Acho que sair agora sem guarda-chuva é uma má ideia.
native_language_example: I think going out now without an umbrella is a bad idea.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to say something is new: uma nova casa (a new house), uma nova atividade (a new activity). It’s the feminine form of "um novo" (masculine). Often followed by the noun it describes.
target_language_example: Preciso de uma nova ideia para o projeto.
native_language_example: I need a new idea for the project.

meaning: a look; a quick look (a glance).
additional_notes: Commonly used with the verb "dar" (or "dê" as a polite command): "dar uma olhada em + [something]" = "to take/have a look at". Often implies a brief or casual look, like checking something.
target_language_example: Você pode dar uma olhada no meu e-mail rapidinho?
native_language_example: Can you take a quick look at my email?

meaning: a look at that/it (“a quick look”).
additional_notes: Common in requests and offers: “dar uma olhada nisso” = “to take a look at that/it,” often implying a quick, informal check. “nisso” refers to something already mentioned (a problem, document, object, etc.). You’ll often hear it with polite commands like “dê uma olhada nisso” (please take a look at it).
target_language_example: Você pode dar uma olhada nisso pra mim, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you take a look at this for me, please?

additional_notes: Most literally means “a word.” It can refer to a single word (“Isto é uma palavra.”). In sayings or advice, it can also mean “a remark/thing said,” often with a positive tone (e.g., “uma palavra generosa” = “a kind word”).
target_language_example: Ela me disse uma palavra de incentivo.
native_language_example: She said a word of encouragement to me.

additional_notes: Used for a short stop or rest during an activity (work, studying, talking, etc.). Common with verbs like fazer (“to take”): fazer uma pausa = to take a break. Also used literally for a pause in speech: fazer uma pausa ao falar = to pause while speaking.
target_language_example: Vamos fazer uma pausa de cinco minutos.
native_language_example: Let’s take a five-minute break.

additional_notes: Literally refers to a physical stone/rock (feminine noun: a pedra). It’s also used in the common comparison “dormir como uma pedra” = “to sleep like a log/stone,” meaning to sleep very deeply.
target_language_example: No caminho, encontrei uma pedra bem grande.
native_language_example: On the way, I found a very big stone.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to describe something as small in size or amount: uma pequena história (a short/small story), uma pequena diferença (a small difference). The masculine form is "um pequeno" (e.g., um pequeno problema). Often translates as “a little” in English depending on the noun (e.g., uma pequena lesão = a minor injury).
target_language_example: Preciso de uma pequena ajuda com isto.
native_language_example: I need a little help with this.

additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t worth doing because it won’t bring a good result. Often comes with the verb "ser" ("é/foi/seria uma perda de tempo") or with "achar" ("acho que é uma perda de tempo"). You can also expand it to "uma perda de tempo e dinheiro" (“a waste of time and money”).
target_language_example: Não vou discutir isso agora — é uma perda de tempo.
native_language_example: I’m not going to argue about that now — it’s a waste of time.

additional_notes: Used when you want to ask something (“fazer uma pergunta” = “to ask a question”). Often followed by para/a + person (e.g., “fazer uma pergunta para a professora”).
target_language_example: Posso fazer uma pergunta?
native_language_example: Can I ask a question?

additional_notes: Used to refer to an individual in a general or descriptive way, often followed by an adjective or a phrase (e.g., "uma pessoa inteligente", "uma pessoa confiável", "uma pessoa com recursos limitados"). It can also contrast different “versions” of someone ("uma pessoa diferente").
target_language_example: Ela é uma pessoa muito gentil.
native_language_example: She is a very kind person.

meaning: 'a very (… ) person' / 'a person who is very (… )'.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone by adding an adjective after "muito" (very): "uma pessoa muito calma" (a very calm person), "uma pessoa muito dedicada" (a very dedicated person). "Uma" is feminine because it agrees with "pessoa" (which is grammatically feminine), even when talking about a man (e.g., "Ele é uma pessoa muito perigosa"). The adjective usually agrees with "pessoa" too (often feminine: "perigosa", "especial").
target_language_example: Meu irmão é uma pessoa muito engraçada.
native_language_example: My brother is a very funny person.

additional_notes: Used for something said or done to be funny. In questions like “É uma piada?”, it can mean “Are you joking?” or “Is this a joke?” You can also say “contar uma piada” (to tell a joke) and “fazer uma piada” (to make a joke).
target_language_example: Isso é uma piada ou você está falando sério?
native_language_example: Is this a joke, or are you serious?

meaning: to have a crush on; to have a soft spot for (a person or thing).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "ter": "ter uma queda por + someone/something". It often implies a romantic attraction when talking about a person, and a strong liking/weakness when talking about things (like chocolate). In the past, you’ll often see "tinha uma queda por..." (= "I had a crush/soft spot for...").
target_language_example: Ela tem uma queda por ele, mas nunca contou.
native_language_example: She has a crush on him, but she never told him.

meaning: "a matter of" (i.e., it's about; it depends on).
additional_notes: Used to say what something is fundamentally about (money, ethics, privacy, etc.) or what the key factor is. Very common in the pattern “É uma questão de + noun” (“It’s a matter of + noun”) and “É só uma questão de tempo” (“It’s only a matter of time”).
target_language_example: Para mim, é uma questão de respeito.
native_language_example: For me, it’s a matter of respect.

additional_notes: Used for a reply to a question/message (“uma resposta”) or for a solution to a problem (“uma resposta para…”). Common verbs: dar uma resposta (to give an answer), receber uma resposta (to receive an answer), esperar uma resposta (to wait for an answer).
target_language_example: Preciso de uma resposta até amanhã.
native_language_example: I need an answer by tomorrow.

meaning: a second chance (another opportunity, usually after a mistake).
additional_notes: Used when asking for or offering another opportunity to try again, often after doing something wrong or failing. Very common in personal relationships, school, and work. In Portuguese you often use it with verbs like "dar" (to give) and "merecer" (to deserve): "dar uma segunda chance" / "merecer uma segunda chance".
target_language_example: Você pode me dar uma segunda chance?
native_language_example: Can you give me a second chance?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a length of time ("for a week" / "it took a week") or a point in time relative to now ("a week ago" / "a week later"). It can also describe what the week was like: "uma semana terrível/difícil".
target_language_example: Demorou uma semana para o pacote chegar.
native_language_example: It took a week for the package to arrive.

meaning: a solution; a way to fix/resolve a problem.
additional_notes: Used to talk about solving a problem or resolving a situation. Very common with verbs like encontrar/achar (to find), pensar em (to think of), precisar de (to need), and ter (to have): “Tem uma solução?” = “Is there a solution?” Can also describe the type of solution: “uma solução de curto prazo” (a short-term solution), “uma solução pacífica” (a peaceful solution).
target_language_example: Ainda não temos uma solução, mas estamos trabalhando nisso.
native_language_example: We still don't have a solution, but we're working on it.

meaning: a nap; a short sleep (usually during the day).
additional_notes: Often used with the verb "tirar" ("tirar uma soneca" = to take a nap). It typically implies a quick, light rest (e.g., 20–60 minutes), and can sound affectionate because of the diminutive -eca.
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, vou tirar uma soneca rapidinha.
native_language_example: After lunch, I’m going to take a quick nap.

additional_notes: Used to say you have/prepare something unexpected for a person (often something nice): “Tenho/Temos uma surpresa para você/eles/elas.” It can also describe something unexpected to someone: “foi uma surpresa para todos nós” (“it was a surprise to all of us”).
target_language_example: Preparei uma surpresa para você.
native_language_example: I prepared a surprise for you.

additional_notes: Used to offer, invite, or talk about drinking one serving of wine. Taça is the word for a wine glass (a stemmed glass), so this is the usual way to say “a glass of wine.” You may also hear: um copo de vinho (a glass/cup of wine), but taça is more typical for wine.
target_language_example: Depois do jantar, vou tomar uma taça de vinho.
native_language_example: After dinner, I'm going to have a glass of wine.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or offering wine. "Taça" is a (wine) glass/cup used for drinks like wine or champagne, and "vinho tinto" means red wine (literally, "tinted/dark wine"). You’ll also hear "um copo de" for a regular glass, but for wine "uma taça" is more common.
target_language_example: Vou pedir uma taça de vinho tinto para acompanhar a massa.
native_language_example: I’m going to order a glass of red wine to go with the pasta.

additional_notes: "Toalha" is a feminine noun, so it usually comes with feminine articles: "uma toalha" (a towel) / "a toalha" (the towel). Common with verbs like "secar" (to dry): "secar o cabelo com uma toalha" (dry your hair with a towel). You can add adjectives after it: "uma toalha seca" (a dry towel), "uma toalha úmida" (a damp towel).
target_language_example: Você pode me emprestar uma toalha?
native_language_example: Can you lend me a towel?

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens (frequency). You can swap the time period: “uma vez por semana” (once a week), “uma vez por ano” (once a year). You can also change the number: “duas vezes por mês” (twice a month).
target_language_example: Nós fazemos uma reunião uma vez por mês.
native_language_example: We have a meeting once a month.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency. You can swap in other time periods: “uma vez por dia” (once a day), “uma vez por mês” (once a month), “uma vez por ano” (once a year). You can also change the number: “duas vezes por semana” (twice a week), “três vezes por semana” (three times a week).
target_language_example: Eu treino uma vez por semana.
native_language_example: I work out once a week.

additional_notes: Used with the verb fazer (“to take/make”) or voltar de (“to come back from”). Often followed by para/de to show destination or origin: uma viagem para Boston (a trip to Boston), voltar de uma viagem (to return from a trip). It can also be specified by type: uma viagem de compras (a shopping trip).
target_language_example: Vamos fazer uma viagem para o Rio no próximo mês.
native_language_example: We’re going to take a trip to Rio next month.

meaning: "a life" (a way of living; a person's life).
additional_notes: Used with adjectives to describe someone's lifestyle or the kind of life they live: "uma vida feliz" (a happy life), "uma vida saudável" (a healthy life), "uma vida simples" (a simple life). It can refer to a person's whole life or more generally to their lifestyle.
target_language_example: Ele quer ter uma vida tranquila no campo.
native_language_example: He wants to have a peaceful life in the countryside.

meaning: “a cup of” (a unit of measure or a drink order).
additional_notes: Used to indicate an amount/measurement (often in recipes: uma xícara de açúcar, uma xícara de farinha) or to order/ask for a cup of a drink (uma xícara de café). It’s feminine because xícara is feminine: uma xícara. In everyday conversation, people may also say um copo de (“a glass of”) depending on the container.
target_language_example: Quero uma xícara de chá, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like a cup of tea, please.

additional_notes: Used to order or talk about a single serving of coffee. "Uma" = "a/one" (feminine), "xícara" = "cup" (common in Brazil), and "de café" = "of coffee". In polite requests you’ll often hear it with "Gostaria de..." (I’d like...) or "Quer que eu lhe traga...?" (Do you want me to bring you...?).
target_language_example: Vou tomar uma xícara de café depois do almoço.
native_language_example: I'm going to have a cup of coffee after lunch.

additional_notes: Used to talk about (or offer) a single serving of hot coffee. Common in polite offers and suggestions: "Deixe-me preparar..." (Let me make...), "Preciso de..." (I need...), "Que tal...?" (How about...?). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people may also say "um café quente" when the cup is implied.
target_language_example: Posso te oferecer uma xícara de café quente?
native_language_example: Can I offer you a cup of hot coffee?

additional_notes: Used when ordering or asking for tea in a café/restaurant or at home. "Xícara" is the small cup typically used for tea or coffee. You can add details like "sem açúcar" (without sugar) or "com açúcar" (with sugar).
target_language_example: Posso tomar uma xícara de chá depois do jantar.
native_language_example: I can have a cup of tea after dinner.

additional_notes: “Uma” means “a/an” (feminine singular). “Árvore” is feminine: uma árvore, a árvore. Plural: “árvores” (uma árvore / duas árvores). Very common for describing places in nature (e.g., under a tree: “sob/debaixo de uma árvore”).
target_language_example: Há uma árvore grande no meu quintal.
native_language_example: There’s a big tree in my backyard.

additional_notes: Used to praise or agree with a suggestion or plan. Often appears with verbs like achar (“to think/find”) or ser (“to be”): “Acho que é uma ótima ideia.” / “Foi uma ótima ideia.” You can intensify with “mesmo” (“really”): “É mesmo uma ótima ideia.”
target_language_example: Vamos sair mais cedo — é uma ótima ideia!
native_language_example: Let’s leave earlier — it’s a great idea!

additional_notes: Used to pick a single item from a group: “uma das + plural feminine noun” (e.g., uma das janelas). The masculine version is “um dos” (e.g., um dos livros). Often followed by a superlative like “uma das melhores…”.
target_language_example: Lisboa é uma das cidades mais bonitas de Portugal.
native_language_example: Lisbon is one of the most beautiful cities in Portugal.

additional_notes: Used to refer to one item from your own set of things, where the noun is feminine (uma/ minhas). Often followed by a feminine noun (uma das minhas ideias/histórias/contas). For masculine nouns, use “um dos meus” (um dos meus livros).
target_language_example: Essa é uma das minhas músicas favoritas.
native_language_example: That’s one of my favorite songs.

meaning: "once" (one time); also used in frequency phrases like "once a week/month".
additional_notes: Often used to count how many times something happens (uma vez, duas vezes, etc.). In frequency expressions, it’s followed by “por” + time period: “uma vez por semana” = “once a week”, “uma vez por mês” = “once a month”.
target_language_example: Eu só fui a Lisboa uma vez.
native_language_example: I’ve only been to Lisbon once.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a reciprocal action between two or more people/animals (they do the action to each other). It agrees in gender/number with the group: masculine plural uns aos outros (mixed/all-male), feminine plural umas às outras (all-female). Often used with plural subjects.
target_language_example: Eles se ajudam uns aos outros todos os dias.
native_language_example: They help each other every day.

additional_notes: From the verb "usar" (to use/wear) + "óculos" (glasses). It’s commonly used to say someone wears glasses (in general) or wears them for a purpose: "usa óculos para ler" = "wears glasses to read." For asking a question: "Você usa óculos?" = "Do you wear glasses?"
target_language_example: Eu uso óculos desde criança.
native_language_example: I've worn glasses since I was a child.

meaning: 'using a' / 'wearing a' (with a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: "Usando" is the gerund of "usar". It can mean "wearing" when followed by clothes (e.g., "usando um jeans", "usando um terno") and "using" when followed by a tool or method (e.g., "usando um telescópio"). For feminine nouns, use "usando uma".
target_language_example: Estou usando um casaco porque está frio.
native_language_example: I'm wearing a coat because it's cold.

additional_notes: Used to describe what someone is wearing. In Portuguese, "estar + usando" is a common way to talk about something a person is wearing at that moment. "Chapéu" = hat; "preto" agrees with "chapéu" (masculine singular). You can swap the color or item: "usando um chapéu branco", "usando uma camisa preta".
target_language_example: Ele estava usando um chapéu preto na festa.
native_language_example: He was wearing a black hat at the party.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **usar** (“to use/wear”) to describe what someone has on (clothes). It often appears with **estar** to describe what someone is wearing at the moment: **Ela está usando...** (She is wearing...). In the past: **Ela estava usando...** (She was wearing...).
target_language_example: Ela está usando um vestido azul hoje.
native_language_example: She is wearing a blue dress today.

additional_notes: Used to give permission or state that someone is allowed/able to use the dictionary. It often appears with forms of "poder" (can/may): "Você pode usar este dicionário." The verb "usar" = to use; "este" = this (near the speaker); "dicionário" = dictionary. "senhoras/senhores" are polite/formal forms of address; "tu" (informal singular) and "você" (common singular); "vocês" (plural). "vós/podeis" are very formal/old-fashioned in most modern Portuguese, but still taught in some materials and used in some regions/contexts.
target_language_example: Você pode usar este dicionário na aula.
native_language_example: You can use this dictionary in class.

meaning: “to use the” (with a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular object introduced by the definite article “o” (e.g., o dicionário, o fone de ouvido, o computador). In many situations you’ll hear the contraction “usá-lo” (“to use it/him”) when “o” is a pronoun, not an article.
target_language_example: Você pode me ensinar a usar o aplicativo?
native_language_example: Can you teach me how to use the app?

additional_notes: "Usá-lo" is "usar" (to use) with the object pronoun "o" (it/him) attached using a hyphen. The verb takes an accent (usá-) when the pronoun is attached. It usually refers to an object already mentioned (e.g., a coat, a tool, a chance/strategy) and can be used with different tenses: "pretendo usá-lo" (I intend to use it), "pode usá-lo" (you can use it).
target_language_example: Se você quiser, pode usá-lo agora.
native_language_example: If you want, you can use it now.

meaning: "will end" / "is going to end"; sometimes "will turn out (in the end)".
additional_notes: From "vai" (is going) + "acabar" (to end). Used to talk about something ending in the future ("Quando vai acabar?") or how something will turn out: "não vai acabar bem" = it won’t end well. In "vai acabar por + infinitive", it means "will end up + -ing" (after some process): "vai acabar por descobrir" = will end up finding out.
target_language_example: Se você continuar assim, isso vai acabar mal.
native_language_example: If you keep going like this, this is going to end badly.

additional_notes: Formed with the verb "ir" in the present (vai) + infinitive (acontecer) to talk about a future event, often something expected or predicted. You can turn it into a question by using rising intonation: "Vai acontecer?" For other subjects: "vou acontecer" is not used (you’d say "vai acontecer" about an event); common forms are "vai acontecer" (it’s going to happen), "vai acontecer de novo" (it’s going to happen again), "isso vai acontecer" (this will happen).
target_language_example: Não se preocupe — isso não vai acontecer.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — that won’t happen.

additional_notes: Formed with ir (vai) + infinitive (chegar) to talk about a future arrival, often in the near future. Used with places (vai chegar aqui/em casa/em Lisboa) and with time expressions (logo, antes das três). In questions, it asks when someone will arrive.
target_language_example: O ônibus vai chegar em dez minutos.
native_language_example: The bus will arrive in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about rain in the near future. It’s the verb *ir* (vai) + infinitive (*chover*), a very common way in Portuguese to express the future (“going to” + verb). Often used with time words like *hoje*, *esta noite*, *amanhã*, *mais tarde*.
target_language_example: Acho que vai chover, então vou levar um guarda-chuva.
native_language_example: I think it’s going to rain, so I’m going to take an umbrella.

meaning: 'will be' / 'is going to be' (future of estar).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a future state, condition, or location (because estar is used for temporary states/locations). Common with places or situations like "vai estar fora" = "will be away/out" and "vai estar pronto" = "will be ready". Often interchangeable with the simple future "estará" in meaning, but "vai estar" is very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: A Ana vai estar em casa mais tarde.
native_language_example: Ana will be at home later.

additional_notes: Used with "ir" (vai) + infinitive (estar) to talk about the near or planned future. Often followed by a time expression (e.g., "amanhã", "em breve", "a semana toda") or a clause like "quando eu voltar".
target_language_example: Eu vou estar aqui às oito.
native_language_example: I’ll be here at eight.

meaning: “is going to do / will do” (near future with ir + infinitive).
additional_notes: "Vai" is the present of "ir" (to go) used as an auxiliary, and "fazer" is the infinitive (to do/make). Together they express a plan, intention, or prediction, similar to English “going to.” It can also appear in questions about the future: "Vai fazer sol?" = “Will it be sunny?”
target_language_example: Acho que ele vai fazer isso hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I think he’s going to do that tonight.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about the near future in Portuguese: **ir (vai)** + **infinitive (fazer)** = “going to do.” **Isso** means “that/this” (a thing/action understood from context). It changes with the subject: *eu vou fazer isso, você vai fazer isso, eles vão fazer isso*.
target_language_example: Acho que ele vai fazer isso amanhã.
native_language_example: I think he’s going to do that tomorrow.

meaning: "will stay" / "is going to stay"; also "will become" / "is going to get" (a new state).
additional_notes: Formed by ir (vai) + infinitive ficar. Used to talk about the future: (1) staying somewhere or for a period of time (vai ficar no Japão, vai ficar depois da escola, vai ficar em casa), and (2) becoming/ending up in a certain state (vai ficar feliz, vai ficar fantástico). With a verb in the gerund (e.g., vai ficar se metendo), it can mean “will keep on/continue (doing something),” often with a critical tone.
target_language_example: Se você continuar assim, vai ficar cansado amanhã.
native_language_example: If you keep going like this, you're going to be tired tomorrow.

meaning: “will stay here” / “is going to stay here.”
additional_notes: Uses the near-future construction (ir + infinitive): vai (is going to) + ficar (to stay) + aqui (here). Common for talking about someone staying (for a while) in a place. You can change the subject: eu vou ficar aqui (I’ll stay here), ela vai ficar aqui (she’ll stay here).
target_language_example: Eu vou ficar aqui até você voltar.
native_language_example: I’ll stay here until you come back.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that a situation or a person will turn out okay. Often appears as “tudo vai ficar bem” (“everything will be fine”). It can also be a question (“Vai ficar bem?” = “Will it be okay?”). Literally “will stay/become well,” but in everyday English it’s usually “will be fine.”
target_language_example: Calma, vai ficar bem.
native_language_example: Calm down, it’ll be okay.

meaning: 'will keep / will end up with' (something), or 'will get/feel' (an emotion).
additional_notes: From the verb phrase "ficar com". With things, it often means to keep, take, or end up with something (who will have it). With nouns like "saudade" or "vergonha", it means to start feeling that emotion ("to miss", "to feel embarrassed").
target_language_example: No final, eu vou ficar com a conta.
native_language_example: In the end, I'll end up with the bill.

meaning: “is going to + me” (future action affecting me).
additional_notes: Combination of **vai** (he/she/it “goes” / “is going to”) + **me** (“me”). Used to say someone/something is going to do something **to/for** you, with **me** as the object pronoun before the verb: *vai me causar* (is going to cause me), *vai me agradecer* (is going to thank me), *vai me substituir* (is going to replace me). Often corresponds to English “is going to + verb + me,” but in Portuguese the object pronoun comes before the main verb.
target_language_example: Ele vai me ligar amanhã.
native_language_example: He’s going to call me tomorrow.

meaning: “will help me” / “are you going to help me?”
additional_notes: Literally “(you/he/she) will help me.” In questions, Portuguese often drops the subject, so “Vai me ajudar?” usually means “Are you going to help me?” (you). With a name or “ele/ela,” it means “(he/she) will help me.” You can also hear “vai ajudar-me” (more formal/European Portuguese style).
target_language_example: Você vai me ajudar a carregar essas caixas?
native_language_example: Are you going to help me carry these boxes?

meaning: “are you going to let me…?” / “are you going to leave me…?”
additional_notes: From "vai" (you are going to) + "me" (me) + "deixar" (to let/allow; to leave). It’s used when asking or stating what someone will allow you to do (deixar + infinitive: "deixar entrar/sair/ir embora/saber") or where they will leave you ("deixar aqui"). Often carries impatience or insistence depending on tone.
target_language_example: Você vai me deixar falar um minuto?
native_language_example: Are you going to let me speak for a minute?

additional_notes: Uses the verb ir (vai) + infinitive (morrer) to talk about a (usually near) future outcome. Often used to predict or warn about someone’s condition (Vai morrer, se não for tratado.) or in the negative to reassure (Você não vai morrer.). Can refer to “he/she” or “you” depending on context (e.g., Você vai morrer = “You’re going to die”).
target_language_example: Se ele não for ao hospital, vai morrer.
native_language_example: If he doesn’t go to the hospital, he’s going to die.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone will need something in the future. It’s the verb phrase "vai" (is going to) + "precisar" (to need) + "de" (of). The thing that’s needed comes after "de": "vai precisar de dinheiro" (will need money). You can repeat "de" before each item in a list: "de dinheiro e de alguém" (money and someone).
target_language_example: Você vai precisar de ajuda para terminar isso.
native_language_example: You’re going to need help to finish this.

meaning: 'is going to' + 'himself/herself/itself/yourself' (introduces a reflexive verb in the future).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs (verbs with "se") in the near future: "vai se lembrar" (is going to remember), "vai se recuperar" (is going to recover), "vai se mudar" (is going to move). It can also be an imperative insult in "Vai se ferrar!" meaning "Go to hell / Screw you" (very rude).
target_language_example: Ela vai se atrasar se não sair agora.
native_language_example: She's going to be late if she doesn't leave now.

additional_notes: Used with an explicit subject (ele/ela/você/nome) to talk about a planned or expected marriage in the near or known future. It’s the verb phrase "ir" (to be going to) + "se casar" (to get married). You can add a time expression like "daqui a três meses" (in three months) or "na segunda" (on Monday).
target_language_example: A minha irmã vai se casar no ano que vem.
native_language_example: My sister is going to get married next year.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ser" to talk about what something/someone will be in the future (identity, profession, characteristics, outcomes, etc.). It’s the 3rd-person singular of "ir" + infinitive: "ele/ela/você vai ser...". For other subjects: "eu vou ser", "nós vamos ser", "eles/elas/vocês vão ser".
target_language_example: A festa vai ser amanhã à noite.
native_language_example: The party will be tomorrow night.

meaning: “is going to” + “you” (object), as in “is going to [verb] you”.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about what someone/something will do to you soon: **vai te + infinitive**. Here **vai** = “is going to” (from *ir*), and **te** = “you” as an object pronoun (informal singular). Common with verbs like *fazer* (make), *levar* (take/bring), *ensinar* (teach), *custar* (cost), *deixar* (leave/make).
target_language_example: Isso vai te ajudar muito.
native_language_example: That’s going to help you a lot.

meaning: 'will have' / 'is going to have' (also: 'there will be').
additional_notes: Combination of "vai" (from "ir", used to form the near future) + "ter" (to have). Often means someone will have something: "Ele não vai ter frio" = "He won’t be cold" (literally, won’t have cold). It can also be used impersonally to mean "there will be": "Vai ter uma boa família" = "There will be a good family" / "You’ll have a good family" depending on context. In Brazilian Portuguese, "vai ter" is very common in speech; in more formal Portuguese you may also see "haverá" for "there will be."
target_language_example: Vai ter reunião amanhã?
native_language_example: Will there be a meeting tomorrow?

meaning: 'will have to' / 'is going to have to' (must).
additional_notes: Used to say someone will be obligated/forced to do something in the future. It’s the near-future of "ter que" (to have to): "vai" (is going) + "ter que" (have to). Changes with the subject: "vou ter que" (I’ll have to), "você vai ter que", "ele/ela vai ter que", "vamos ter que", "vão ter que" (they’ll have to). Common in strong statements like "Vai ter que me matar!" meaning "You’ll have to kill me (first)!"
target_language_example: Se você quiser terminar hoje, vai ter que trabalhar mais rápido.
native_language_example: If you want to finish today, you’ll have to work faster.

meaning: "(he/she/you) is going to come back / return" (near future).
additional_notes: "Vai" is the present tense of "ir" (to go) used to form the near future: "ir + infinitive". "Voltar" means "to come back/return". So "vai voltar" can mean returning to a place, coming back at a later time, or doing something again depending on context. Person changes: eu vou voltar, você/ele/ela vai voltar, nós vamos voltar, vocês/eles/elas vão voltar.
target_language_example: Eu vou voltar amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to come back tomorrow morning.

meaning: "is going to return to" / "will go back to" (a place).
additional_notes: Used with a subject + "vai" (from *ir*, for future/plan) + "voltar" (to return) + "para" + destination. Very common for talking about someone’s plans to go back to a city/country/home. You can change "vai" for other people/tenses: "vou voltar para" (I’m going to return to), "vai voltar para" (he/she is going to return to), "vamos voltar para" (we’re going to return to).
target_language_example: Eu vou voltar para casa mais tarde.
native_language_example: I'm going to go back home later.

vai a pé para a escola

target_language_multi_word_term: vai a pé para a escola
additional_notes: "Ir a pé" means to go somewhere on foot (to walk). "Vai" is the present tense for "he/she/you (formal) goes"; with "você", the verb also stays as "vai" (e.g., "Você vai a pé..."). "Para a escola" means "to school". You can swap the destination: "vai a pé para o trabalho" (walks to work).
target_language_example: Ela vai a pé para a escola todos os dias.
native_language_example: She walks to school every day.

meaning: “goes to” / “are you going to (the) …?” (ir + a + o).
additional_notes: Used with the verb ir (“to go”) in the present tense: ele/ela/você vai (“he/she/you go”) + ao (= a + o, “to the” for masculine singular places). Common for destinations like mercado, escritório, templo. For feminine destinations, use vai à (a + a): “vai à escola”. For plural masculine, use vai aos: “vai aos Estados Unidos”.
target_language_example: Você vai ao banco hoje?
native_language_example: Are you going to the bank today?

additional_notes: From the verb "ir" (to go): "vai" is the present tense for ele/ela/você. "ao" = "a" (to) + "o" (the), used with masculine singular places like "cinema". Often used with frequency words like "sempre" (always), "frequentemente" (often), "raramente" (rarely), and time expressions (e.g., "sexta-feira à noite").
target_language_example: Você vai ao cinema hoje?
native_language_example: Are you going to the movies today?

additional_notes: Present tense of ir embora (“to leave/go away”). Used for asking when someone leaves (A que horas você vai embora?) and for stating plans or facts (Ele vai embora no próximo verão). Can also be an imperative/encouragement meaning “Go away!” (Vai embora!). Often implies departing from a place or leaving a situation.
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu já vou embora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m leaving now.

additional_notes: "Vai" is the present tense of *ir* (to go) for "he/she/it" (and also "you" in Brazil with *você*). "Para" means "to" in the sense of destination: *vai para Boston* = goes/is going to Boston. It’s very common for travel plans and schedules (buses, flights, people). It can also be used figuratively to mean heading toward a result: *vai para a morte certa* (heading to certain death).
target_language_example: Este trem vai para o centro?
native_language_example: Does this train go to downtown?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ir" in the present tense: "vai" = "(he/she/you formal) goes". "para" means "to/toward". "a" is the feminine singular definite article "the", so it’s used before feminine destinations (e.g., "a academia", "a escola"). With masculine destinations you often see "vai para o" ("o" = "the"). It can also be used for scheduled movement (e.g., a ship/train) or travel for a purpose ("a negócios").
target_language_example: Ela vai para a escola de ônibus.
native_language_example: She goes to school by bus.

additional_notes: From the verb ir (“to go”) + para a cama (“to bed”). In the examples, it’s either a question about someone’s bedtime (A que horas você vai para a cama? / Quando você vai para a cama?) or a command telling someone to go to bed (Vai para a cama!). You can change the verb form for other people: eu vou, você vai, ele/ela vai, nós vamos, vocês vão, eles/elas vão para a cama.
target_language_example: Já está tarde — vai para a cama!
native_language_example: It’s already late—go to bed!

additional_notes: "Vai" is the present tense of "ir" (to go) for ele/ela/você. Use it to ask or say how someone gets to school, often with transport: "de ônibus" (by bus), "de carro" (by car), "a pé" (on foot). You can swap the subject: "Eu vou para a escola" (I go to school), "Você vai para a escola?" (Do you go to school?).
target_language_example: Ela vai para a escola a pé todos os dias.
native_language_example: She goes to school on foot every day.

additional_notes: Present tense of the verb ir (“to go”) in the 3rd person singular (ele/ela/você vai). The preposition a (“to”) + the feminine singular article a (“the”) contract to à.
