Used before many feminine nouns: à cidade (“to the city”), à universidade (“to the university”). It can also be figurative, e.g., vai à loucura (“goes crazy”).
target_language_example: Ele vai à escola todos os dias.
native_language_example: He goes to school every day.

additional_notes: From the verb ir (to go): ele vai à escola = he goes to school; ela vai à escola = she goes to school. The "à" is a contraction of "a" (to) + "a" (the, feminine), so it literally means "to the school". Often used with frequency (cinco dias por semana) or with how someone gets there (a pé/caminhando, de ônibus, de trem).
target_language_example: Ela vai à escola a pé todos os dias.
native_language_example: She goes to school on foot every day.

additional_notes: From the verb **ir** (to go): **vai** is the present tense for **ele/ela/você** (“he/she/you”). **à** = **a + a** (“to the”), and **igreja** = “church.” Often used to talk about attending church services regularly: **vai à igreja todo domingo / toda noite / raramente**. You can turn it into a question with intonation: **Vai à igreja?**
target_language_example: Ela vai à igreja aos domingos.
native_language_example: She goes to church on Sundays.

additional_notes: Used to say something is worth the effort, time, money, or trouble. Often followed by an infinitive: “vale a pena ver/ir/fazer” (“it’s worth seeing/going/doing”). It can also be used as a question: “Vale a pena…?” (“Is it worth…?”).
target_language_example: Esse passeio vale a pena, mesmo com chuva.
native_language_example: That outing is worth it, even with rain.

additional_notes: Used to say that reading something is worthwhile (worth the time/effort). It can refer to a book, article, story, etc. Often followed by what to read: “Vale a pena ler este/esse livro.” You can also add frequency: “mais de uma vez” (more than once), “duas vezes” (twice).
target_language_example: Vale a pena ler este artigo antes da prova.
native_language_example: It’s worth reading this article before the exam.

additional_notes: Used to recommend a place (or attraction) and say the experience is worth the time/effort. It comes from the expression “valer a pena” = “to be worth it,” followed by the infinitive “visitar” (to visit). You can use it as a full sentence (“Vale a pena visitar…”) or inside another sentence (“…que vale a pena visitar”).
target_language_example: Se você estiver em Lisboa, vale a pena visitar Belém.
native_language_example: If you’re in Lisbon, it’s worth visiting Belém.

additional_notes: Used to say something is worth the effort, time, money, or trouble. Often followed by an infinitive: “vale a pena ver/ir/fazer” (“it’s worth seeing/going/doing”). It can also be used as a question: “Vale a pena…?” (“Is it worth…?”).
target_language_example: Esse passeio vale a pena, mesmo com chuva.
native_language_example: That outing is worth it, even with rain.

meaning: “It was worth it.” / “It was worth the effort.”
additional_notes: Used to say that something was worth doing despite the time, cost, or effort. It’s the past (valeu) of “valer a pena” (“to be worth it”). You can use it alone as a full sentence (Valeu a pena.) or followed by an infinitive: “Valeu a pena esperar” (“It was worth waiting”). It’s also common as a question: “Valeu a pena?” (“Was it worth it?”).
target_language_example: A viagem foi longa, mas valeu a pena.
native_language_example: The trip was long, but it was worth it.

additional_notes: From **vamos** (we go/let’s) + **fazer** (to do/to make). In conversation it often works like an invitation or decision: **Vamos fazer isso?** = “Shall we do it?” It can also state a plan/future: **Nós vamos fazer** = “We’re going to do.” You may also see it with **o que**: **O que vamos fazer?** = “What are we going to do?”
target_language_example: Vamos fazer isso hoje à noite.
native_language_example: Let’s do it tonight.

meaning: “let’s + verb” (we are going to do something ourselves).
additional_notes: Used to suggest an action to do together: vamos (let’s / we’re going to) + nos (reflexive pronoun “ourselves”), followed by a verb. Common with reflexive verbs like mudar-se (move), sentar-se (sit down), vestir-se (get dressed). In speech it can sound like “vamo(s) nos…”.
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar às oito.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at eight.

additional_notes: A repeated, urging use of "vamos" to push someone to move faster or get going. Often said when you’re impatient or encouraging someone (like "come on, come on!"). Can also be used as a general prompt to start doing something.
target_language_example: Vamos, vamos — estamos atrasados!
native_language_example: Come on, come on — we’re late!

meaning: “let’s go to the movies” / “we go to the movie theater.”
additional_notes: "Vamos" can mean either (1) an invitation/suggestion: “Let’s go…”, often with an exclamation (Vamos ao cinema!), or (2) present tense “we go” when talking about a habit (Nós/Meu amigo e eu vamos ao cinema...). "Ao" = "a" + "o" (“to the”), and "cinema" here means the movie theater.
target_language_example: Vamos ao cinema hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Shall we go to the movies tonight?

additional_notes: Used to suggest leaving or moving on. It can be an exclamation (“Vamos embora!” = “Let’s get out of here!”), a prompt (“Pronto, vamos embora.” = “Alright, let’s go.”), or a question (“Vamos embora?” = “Shall we go?”). Literally it’s “we go away,” but in everyday Portuguese it functions like an English “let’s…”.
target_language_example: Está tarde — vamos embora!
native_language_example: It’s late — let’s go!

additional_notes: “Veio” is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of *vir* (“to come”) for ele/ela/você. It often appears in questions (*Você veio aqui?*) or with time words like *hoje*, *cedo*, *de novo*, *nunca*. You can change the place word: *veio aí* (“came there/over to you”), *veio lá* (“came there/over there”).
target_language_example: Você veio aqui ontem à noite?
native_language_example: Did you come here last night?

additional_notes: From the verb **vir** (to come) in the past: **veio** = “came” (3rd person singular). **me ver** means “to see me,” and in everyday Portuguese it often implies “to visit me.” You can swap the pronoun: **veio te ver** (came to see you), **veio nos ver** (came to see us). Common with time expressions: **um dia desses** (one of these days / recently), **só no dia seguinte** (only the next day).
target_language_example: Ele veio me ver depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: He came to see me after work.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "vir" + "para". Used to say someone came to a destination: "veio para Boston" = "came to Boston". Often followed by a place, and it can also be followed by an infinitive to express purpose ("veio para se encontrar" = "came to meet").
target_language_example: Ele veio para Portugal em 2020.
native_language_example: He came to Portugal in 2020.

meaning: “look/see what …” (used to draw attention or tell someone to notice something).
additional_notes: "Veja" is the imperative of "ver" (to see) used with "você". It’s common when showing someone something you found/did, or when giving advice/instructions: "Veja o que pode ser feito" (“See what can be done”). You may also hear "Vê o que..." (more informal, in some regions).
target_language_example: Veja o que aconteceu quando eu desliguei o computador.
native_language_example: See what happened when I turned off the computer.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons of age. It almost always appears as part of the full pattern “mais velho do que eu” (“older than me/I am”), often with a number of years: “dois anos mais velho do que eu.” In everyday speech you’ll also hear “mais velho que eu” (dropping “do”).
target_language_example: Ela é cinco anos mais velha do que eu.
native_language_example: She is five years older than I am.

additional_notes: From the verb vir (“to come”) + aqui (“here”). In statements/questions, vem is the 3rd-person singular present (“ele/ela vem aqui…”). In requests/commands, vem aqui is an informal imperative meaning “come here” (often said to someone you’re on tu terms with; with você, you’ll often hear “vem aqui” as well in everyday Brazilian Portuguese, or more formally “venha aqui”).
target_language_example: Vem aqui um minutinho, preciso falar com você.
native_language_example: Come here for a sec, I need to talk to you.

vem aqui de vez em quando

target_language_multi_word_term: vem aqui de vez em quando
meaning: "comes here from time to time" / "comes here occasionally."
additional_notes: Used to say someone visits or shows up here occasionally, not regularly. "De vez em quando" means "from time to time" and can be used with other verbs too (e.g., "Eu vou lá de vez em quando" = "I go there occasionally"). In Portuguese you may also hear it without "aqui" if the place is already understood.
target_language_example: Ele vem aqui de vez em quando para tomar um café.
native_language_example: He comes here from time to time to have a coffee.

vem me ver de vez em quando

target_language_multi_word_term: vem me ver de vez em quando
meaning: "(He/she) comes to see/visit me from time to time" (occasionally).
additional_notes: "De vez em quando" means "from time to time / every now and then" (not regularly). "Vem" is the present tense of "vir" (to come) for "he/she/you (formal)", so you can change the subject: "Você vem me ver de vez em quando" (You come see me sometimes) or "Eles vêm me ver de vez em quando" (They come see me sometimes). In everyday speech, "vem me ver" can mean "come visit me".
target_language_example: Você vem me ver de vez em quando?
native_language_example: Do you come to see/visit me from time to time?

additional_notes: Used when talking about the action of selling a car owned by the person you’re speaking to ("seu" = "your"). In Brazil, "seu" can also sometimes mean "his/her" depending on context; if you want to be extra clear, you can say "vender o carro dele/dela" (his/her car).
target_language_example: Você vai vender o seu carro este mês?
native_language_example: Are you going to sell your car this month?

additional_notes: Used with a form of **estar** (e.g., *está/estão/estás*) to talk about what someone is seeing **right now**: *Você está vendo aquelas mulheres?* = “Are you seeing those women?” **aquelas** means “those” (over there / at some distance). **vendo** is the gerund of *ver* (“to see”).
target_language_example: Eu estou vendo aquelas mulheres ali perto da porta.
native_language_example: I can see those women over there near the door.

additional_notes: An imperative request/command telling someone to come to where the speaker is. It uses the polite/neutral imperative form (from "vir") typically used with "você" (and also common in written instructions). Often intensified with words like "agora" (“right now”).
target_language_example: Venha aqui, por favor, preciso falar com você.
native_language_example: Come here, please—I need to talk to you.

additional_notes: Used to call someone (or a pet) to come closer to you. It’s the formal/neutral command form (imperative) of "vir" (to come), often used with a name or a form of address (e.g., "Sofia", "garoto"). Depending on tone, it can sound friendly (calling a child/pet) or a bit firm (calling someone over to talk).
target_language_example: Venha cá um momento, por favor.
native_language_example: Come here for a moment, please.

meaning: 'to see the' (with a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: "Ver" means "to see." "A" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”), used before many feminine nouns and female people’s names/titles (e.g., "ver a sua mãe" = “to see your mother,” "ao ver a Mary" = “upon seeing Mary”). It’s simply verb + article, so it changes with gender/number: "ver o" (masc.), "ver as" (fem. plural), "ver os" (masc. plural).
target_language_example: Espero ver a professora amanhã.
native_language_example: I hope to see the teacher tomorrow.

meaning: 'to have to do with' / 'to be related to'; also literally 'to see with' (your eyes).
additional_notes: Very common in the fixed expression **ter (algo/nada) a ver com** = 'to have (something/nothing) to do with' or 'to be (un)related to'. In threats or warnings, **vai se ver com [alguém]** means 'you’ll have to deal with [someone]' / 'you’ll answer to [someone]'. In literal contexts, **ver com + [something]** can mean 'see with' (e.g., **ver com meus próprios olhos** = 'see with my own eyes').
target_language_example: Isso não tem nada a ver com você.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with you.

meaning: to see again; to see (someone/something) again.
additional_notes: Used when you expect to meet someone again or want to look at something one more time. Common in questions about meeting again ("Vamos nos ver de novo?") or requests ("Deixa eu ver de novo"). It can refer to people (meet again) or things (look again).
target_language_example: Espero te ver de novo em breve.
native_language_example: I hope to see you again soon.

meaning: “to see the …” / “to meet with the …” (masculine object).
additional_notes: "Ver" means "to see," and "o" is the masculine singular definite article (“the”). With things, it’s literal seeing (“ver o topo”, “ver o menu”). With people—especially in service/work contexts—"ver o" can mean “to see/meet with” someone (“ver o gerente”, “ver o Chef”, “ver o Tom imediatamente”). It can also be followed by a person + infinitive to mean “see someone do something” (“ver o Tom fazer aquilo”, “ver o Tom ganhar/vencer”).
target_language_example: Posso ver o quarto antes de reservar?
native_language_example: Can I see the room before booking?

meaning: “to see what …” (find out/observe what happens or what someone does).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question with o que (“what”): ver o que + verb/clause. Very common in phrases like Vamos ver o que… (“Let’s see what…”) and Esperar e ver o que… (“Wait and see what…”). Often implies waiting to find out the result.
target_language_example: Vamos ver o que acontece amanhã.
native_language_example: Let’s see what happens tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with "ver" (to see/watch) + "um filme" (a movie). Very common with "ir" to mean going to watch a movie: "ir ver um filme" = "to go watch a movie" (often at the cinema, but it can also be at home depending on context). You can also drop "ir" when you simply mean watching: "Quer ver um filme?" = "Do you want to watch a movie?"
target_language_example: Vamos ver um filme em casa hoje?
native_language_example: Shall we watch a movie at home today?

meaning: “wearing a” (used before a masculine singular item of clothing).
additional_notes: From the verb vestir (“to wear / to dress”), used with estar to describe what someone is wearing right now: estar vestindo + um + noun (e.g., um terno, um chapéu). For feminine singular clothing, use “vestindo uma” (uma camisa).
target_language_example: Ele está vestindo um casaco preto hoje.
native_language_example: He is wearing a black coat today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar + vestindo to describe what someone is wearing at the moment. You can change the last part to other clothing items (e.g., vestindo uma camisa).
target_language_example: Ele está vestindo um casaco preto hoje.
native_language_example: He is wearing a black coat today.

additional_notes: Past tense of **ver** (“to see”) + the direct-object pronoun **o** (“him/it”), attached with a hyphen (enclisis). Common in European Portuguese and in formal/written Brazilian Portuguese. In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often say **“vi ele”** for “I saw him.” Used with another verb to mean you saw someone **doing** something: **Vi-o atravessando** (“I saw him crossing”) or **Vi-o atravessar** (“I saw him cross”).
target_language_example: Vi-o na estação ontem.
native_language_example: I saw him at the station yesterday.

additional_notes: "Vi" is the simple past (preterite) of **ver** (to see) for **eu**: *eu vi* = *I saw*. It’s often followed by **o** (= *the*, masculine singular) before a noun: *vi o Tom*, *vi o carro*. You can also use it before infinitive/gerund-like structures to describe what you saw happening: *Vi o Tom chegando* (I saw Tom arriving).
target_language_example: Ontem vi o professor no mercado.
native_language_example: Yesterday I saw the teacher at the market.

meaning: “I saw a …” (past of “to see” + “a/an” for masculine nouns).
additional_notes: Used to say you saw something (completed action in the past). “Vi” is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of **ver** (“to see”) for **eu** (“I”). **um** means “a/an” before **masculine singular** nouns; for feminine nouns use **vi uma** (e.g., *vi uma pessoa*).
target_language_example: Vi um cachorro na rua.
native_language_example: I saw a dog on the street.

meaning: 'life is' (used to describe what life is like, or to define a life goal/role).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "é" ("is") with "vida" ("life"). Common patterns: "A minha vida é..." ("My life is...") to describe your situation; "O objetivo de vida é..." ("The life goal is...") to state a long-term goal; and "como a minha vida é" ("what my life is like").
target_language_example: Às vezes, a vida é difícil, mas a gente continua.
native_language_example: Sometimes life is hard, but we keep going.

meaning: "I came here to" (to express your purpose).
additional_notes: Used when you arrived somewhere with a specific goal: "+ infinitive" (falar, jogar, salvar, ver, etc.). The verb is in the past (vim = I came), so it refers to the reason for coming/arriving. Often followed by a person/object: "vim aqui para falar com...", "vim aqui para te ver".
target_language_example: Vim aqui para pedir ajuda.
native_language_example: I came here to ask for help.

additional_notes: "Vim" is the past tense of "vir" (to come): "I came". "aqui" = here. "para" introduces purpose: "to/in order to". "ver" = to see. Very common when you’re explaining why you came somewhere, often followed by a person (Tom, o senhor/a senhora, vocês, etc.). You can also say "Eu vim aqui para ver..." (more explicit) or drop "Eu" as in "Vim aqui para ver...".
target_language_example: Vim aqui para ver se está tudo bem.
native_language_example: I came here to see if everything is okay.

meaning: “twenty years” (age or a period of time).
additional_notes: Used to state someone’s age (often with “ter”: “Ela tem vinte anos (de idade)”) or to describe a duration (“por vinte anos” = “for twenty years”). In comparisons, it can mean “in twenty years” / “in the last twenty years” depending on context (e.g., “o mais frio em vinte anos”).
target_language_example: Faz vinte anos que eu moro aqui.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here for twenty years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone moving toward the speaker’s location (or the place considered “here” in the conversation). Often appears after another verb (e.g., "amar", "querer", "poder") and can be used with different tenses: "vou/vai/vão vir aqui" (will come here), "não venha aqui" (don’t come here), "está por vir aqui?" (is he about to come here?).
target_language_example: Você pode vir aqui um minuto?
native_language_example: Can you come here for a minute?

additional_notes: Used to invite or ask someone to join your group. Very common in spoken Portuguese. 'A gente' literally means 'the people' but is commonly used to mean 'we/us' (it usually takes singular verb forms: 'a gente vai').
target_language_example: Se você quiser, pode vir com a gente depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: If you want, you can come with us after work.

additional_notes: Used to invite or ask if someone will join your group and come along. "Vir" is "to come" (toward the speaker), and "conosco" means "with us". Often used as a question ("Você vai vir conosco?") or as a suggestion/invitation ("Você pode vir conosco.").
target_language_example: Se você quiser, pode vir conosco até o centro.
native_language_example: If you want, you can come with us to downtown.

meaning: "to come to my house" / "to come over to my place."
additional_notes: Used to invite someone to your home or ask when they can come. It’s built from vir (to come) + a/à (to) + minha casa (my house). Often appears in questions with different forms of address (você, tu, o senhor/a senhora, os senhores) depending on formality and number.
target_language_example: Você pode vir à minha casa amanhã à tarde?
native_language_example: Can you come to my house tomorrow afternoon?

additional_notes: Common direction instruction. "Vire" is the formal command form (used with você) of the verb virar (to turn), and it can be used by GPS, signs, or when giving someone directions. Often followed by a place like "na próxima esquina" (at the next corner).
target_language_example: Siga em frente e vire à direita no semáforo.
native_language_example: Go straight ahead and turn right at the traffic light.

meaning: to visit from time to time; occasionally.
additional_notes: "De vez em quando" means "every now and then" and is used to say something happens sometimes, but not regularly. It often appears with verbs like "vir" (to come): "vem me/nos visitar" = "comes to visit me/us." In requests/imperatives you can say "Venha" (you) or "Venham" (you all) to invite someone to visit occasionally.
target_language_example: A gente se fala sempre, mas eu só visito meus avós de vez em quando.
native_language_example: We talk all the time, but I only visit my grandparents from time to time.

meaning: to visit him (to go see him).
additional_notes: "Visitá-lo" = "visitar" (to visit) + "-lo" (him). It’s used when the verb is in the infinitive or ends in -r/-s/-z; the final consonant drops and an accent is added: visitar + o → visitá-lo. Also possible: "visitar ele" (common in speech, often considered less formal).
target_language_example: Vou visitá-lo no hospital hoje à tarde.
native_language_example: I'm going to visit him at the hospital this afternoon.

additional_notes: "Viu" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "ver" (to see) for he/she/you (formal)/it. "O" is the masculine singular definite article (“the”). With an explicit subject it’s a statement (e.g., "Tom viu o…" = “Tom saw the…”). Without a subject, it’s often used as a question in speech/writing: "Viu o…?" = “Did you see the…?” / “Have you seen the…?”.
target_language_example: Você viu o meu celular?
native_language_example: Have you seen my phone?

meaning: "(you/he/she) saw what happened" / "did you see what happened?"
additional_notes: From the verb "ver" (to see) in the simple past: "viu" = "saw". The subject is often omitted in Portuguese, so it can mean "he/she saw..." or (very commonly) a question to "you": "(Você) viu o que aconteceu?" = "Did you see what happened?" Used when reacting to an event or asking if someone witnessed something.
target_language_example: Você viu o que aconteceu ontem à noite?
native_language_example: Did you see what happened last night?

additional_notes: “Viu” is the preterite (simple past) of ver (“to see”) for ele/ela/você: “he/she/you saw.” It’s followed by the indefinite article “um” (masculine) before a singular masculine noun; use “viu uma” before a feminine noun (e.g., “viu uma casa”). Often used to report spotting something at a specific moment in the past.
target_language_example: Ele viu um cachorro na rua ontem.
native_language_example: He saw a dog on the street yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense of ver (“to see”): viu = “saw” (also the formal ‘you’/você form). Used literally for seeing a ghost, and can also be used humorously to suggest someone looks shocked, pale, or frightened (“as if they saw a ghost”). You can change the subject: Eu vi um fantasma (I saw a ghost), Você viu um fantasma? (Did you see a ghost?).
target_language_example: Ele ficou pálido, parecia que viu um fantasma.
native_language_example: He turned pale; it looked like he’d seen a ghost.

meaning: 'lives in' / 'lives at' (is based in a place).
additional_notes: From the verb **viver** (to live): **(ele/ela/você) vive** + **em** + place. Used to say where someone lives/resides. For longer-term residence, it can be similar to **mora em** (“lives in”), and **vive em** can sometimes emphasize someone’s way of life or general living situation depending on context.
target_language_example: Ela vive em Lisboa há três anos.
native_language_example: She has lived in Lisbon for three years.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "viver" (to live) in the 3rd person plural present tense: "eles/elas vivem" = "they live". "na" is the contraction of "em" (in) + "a" (the, feminine), so it’s used before feminine places ("na Alemanha", "na China") and some fixed expressions ("na mesma casa/rua"). For masculine places, you usually use "no" ("vivem no Brasil").
target_language_example: Meus avós vivem na cidade.
native_language_example: My grandparents live in the city.

meaning: “you just (did something)” / “you’ve just (done something)” (very recent past).
additional_notes: Used to say something happened moments ago. Structure: “você acabou de” + infinitive (chegar, comer, fazer, chamar, se levantar, se preparar, ser baleado). Often used in surprised or accusatory questions: “Você acabou de…?” In speech, it can shorten to “cê acabou de…”.
target_language_example: Você acabou de desligar o telefone?
native_language_example: Did you just hang up the phone?

meaning: "do you think...?" / "do you find...?" (asking for someone’s opinion).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to ask someone what they think or how they feel about something. With adjectives like "bonito" or "interessante," it often means "do you find (him/it) ...?" You can add emphasis with "mesmo" ("você acha mesmo...?" = "do you really think...?").
target_language_example: Você acha que a gente deve ir agora?
native_language_example: Do you think we should go now?

meaning: "Do you think that...?" / "Do you believe that...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion or guess about something. Very common in questions; often followed by a full clause (subject + verb). In Brazilian Portuguese, "você" is the everyday "you"; it takes 3rd-person verbs: "você acha" (not *"você achas"*).
target_language_example: Você acha que vai chover hoje?
native_language_example: Do you think it’s going to rain today?

meaning: "do you think she…?" / "do you believe she…?"
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion or guess about what a woman is doing, feels, wants, or will do. It’s built from: você (you) + achar (to think/feel/consider) + que (that) + ela (she). In questions, it often introduces another clause: “Você acha que ela vai…?”, “Você acha que ela gosta…?”
target_language_example: Você acha que ela vai ligar hoje?
native_language_example: Do you think she’s going to call today?

meaning: "Do you think he...?" / "Do you believe he...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion or guess about what a man did, wants, remembers, likes, etc. It’s the start of a question: "você" (you) + "acha" (think/feel/guess) + "que" (that) + "ele" (he). In Brazilian Portuguese, "você" is common in everyday speech; in more formal contexts you may also hear "o senhor/a senhora acha que ele...?"
target_language_example: Você acha que ele vai chegar cedo hoje?
native_language_example: Do you think he’ll arrive early today?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion or guess about you. Often followed by a verb in the past/present/future (e.g., "você acha que eu estive fazendo…", "você acha que eu preciso…"). In Brazilian Portuguese, "você" is common; in Portugal you might hear "tu achas que eu…".
target_language_example: Você acha que eu devia ligar para ela hoje?
native_language_example: Do you think I should call her today?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone for advice or their opinion about what you should do next. Often followed by an infinitive verb (aceitar, contar, esperar, etc.). In speech, it may be shortened to “Você acha que eu devo…?” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Você acha que eu deveria ligar para ele hoje ou amanhã?
native_language_example: Do you think I should call him today or tomorrow?

meaning: “do you think that this…?” / “you think that this…”
additional_notes: Used to introduce what someone thinks or believes about a situation, often followed by a verb phrase: “você acha que isso vai…?”, “você acha que isso é…?”. In questions, it usually means “Do you think this…?”. In statements (with “eu sei que…” etc.), it means “you think that this…”.
target_language_example: Você acha que isso é uma boa ideia?
native_language_example: Do you think this is a good idea?

meaning: “do you think that the …?” (about a masculine person/thing).
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion or guess. It’s made of: você (you) + acha (think/find) + que (that) + o (“the” masculine). Before a man’s name, Portuguese often uses the article (o Tom = “Tom”). For a woman: “você acha que a …?”. You can also omit the article if you’re not naming a specific masculine noun/person: “Você acha que ele…?”
target_language_example: Você acha que o seu irmão vai chegar cedo?
native_language_example: Do you think your brother will arrive early?

meaning: "Do you think you can...?" / "You think you can...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask (sometimes challenge) whether someone is able to do something. Often followed by a verb in the infinitive (dançar, consertar, fazer, ajudar). Tone depends on context: it can be a neutral question (asking if it’s possible) or a skeptical/teasing challenge.
target_language_example: Você acha que pode me ajudar com isso hoje?
native_language_example: Do you think you can help me with that today?

meaning: "do you think it is" / "what do you think it is?"
additional_notes: Used to ask someone for their opinion or guess about what something is (or which option is correct). It’s literally “you think that (it) is…”. Often appears inside questions like “O que você acha que é…?” (What do you think this is?) or “Qual você acha que é correto?” (Which do you think is correct?).
target_language_example: Você acha que é uma boa ideia?
native_language_example: Do you think it’s a good idea?

meaning: “you found” / “you thought” / “did you like…?” (past tense of achar).
additional_notes: “Você” = “you.” “Achou” is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of “achar,” which is very common and has a few meanings depending on context: (1) achar = to find: “Quanto em dinheiro você achou?” (How much money did you find?) (2) achar = to think/believe (often with “que”): “Você achou que eu era canadense?” (Did you think I was Canadian?) (3) achar = to find/consider (an opinion), often in questions like “O que você achou de…?” or “Que tal você achou…?” meaning “What did you think of…?” / “How did you like…?”
target_language_example: O que você achou do filme?
native_language_example: What did you think of the movie?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone's belief or trust in something. With ideas, religions, and supernatural things it means believing they exist (Deus, destino, milagres). With people, it often means trusting or having confidence in them: "Você acredita em nós?" = "Do you believe in us?" (Do you trust we can do it?).
target_language_example: Você acredita em vida após a morte?
native_language_example: Do you believe in life after death?

meaning: "you still" / "do you still..." (asking if something continues).
additional_notes: Used to ask whether a state, feeling, habit, or situation is still true now. Typically comes before the verb: "Você ainda + verbo...". In questions it often implies “up to now / these days” (e.g., "Você ainda trabalha lá?" = “Do you still work there?”).
target_language_example: Você ainda mora aqui?
native_language_example: Do you still live here?

meaning: “are you still …?” / “you’re still …” (asking if a state/condition continues).
additional_notes: Used with a verb/adjective or expression to check whether something is continuing. Common with emotions or states: "assustado" (scared), "brava" (mad), "tonto" (dizzy), "por perto" (around), "tendo problemas" (having trouble). "Você" is the informal/common "you" in Brazil (often used in most situations), and "ainda" means "still/yet".
target_language_example: Você ainda está cansado depois da viagem?
native_language_example: Are you still tired after the trip?

additional_notes: Used to ask or say that someone continues to live in the same place as before. Often followed by “em/na/no” (in/at) + a place (Você ainda mora nos Estados Unidos?), “com” (with) + people you live with (Você ainda mora com os seus pais?), or “por aqui” (around here/in this area).
target_language_example: Você ainda mora neste bairro ou já se mudou?
native_language_example: Do you still live in this neighborhood, or have you moved?

additional_notes: Used to talk about something the listener learned in the past. In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, you’ll often hear the pronoun dropped ("Aprendeu isso...") because the verb form already shows it’s “you” (você). Common patterns: "O que você aprendeu...?" (What did you learn...?), "você aprendeu com..." (you learned from...), "você aprendeu ... na escola?" (did you learn ... at school?).
target_language_example: Você aprendeu português sozinho ou fez um curso?
native_language_example: Did you learn Portuguese by yourself or did you take a course?

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb (e.g., aprender, estudar, trabalhar) to talk about when someone began doing something. In questions, intonation (or a question mark in writing) makes it mean “Did you start to…?”. Often followed by a time expression: quando…?, com quantos anos…?.
target_language_example: Você começou a morar aqui em que ano?
native_language_example: What year did you start living here?

additional_notes: "Você" means “you” (informal-neutral in Brazil). "Comprou" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "comprar" (“to buy”). In questions, Portuguese often uses the same word order as statements; the question is shown by intonation or a question mark: "Você comprou...?" = “Did you buy...?”
target_language_example: Você comprou esse livro ontem?
native_language_example: Did you buy this book yesterday?

meaning: “you bought this” (talking to someone, referring to a masculine item).
additional_notes: Used when asking or stating that the other person purchased a specific thing. In questions it often appears as “Onde você comprou esse …?” (“Where did you buy this …?”). “Esse” refers to something near the listener or something just mentioned, and agrees with masculine nouns (e.g., sabonete, sabão, suéter). For feminine nouns, use “essa” (e.g., “Onde você comprou essa blusa?”).
target_language_example: Onde você comprou esse livro?
native_language_example: Where did you buy this book?

meaning: "Do you know...?/Are you familiar with...?" (asking if someone knows a person/place/thing or knows how to do something).
additional_notes: "Você" = "you" (informal/neutral in much of Brazil). "Conhece" is the present tense of "conhecer". Use it to ask if someone is acquainted with a person (Você conhece aquele cara?), familiar with a place (Você conhece a cidade...?), or knows a way/method (Você conhece algum jeito de...?). For knowing facts/information, Portuguese often uses "saber" instead (e.g., "Você sabe a resposta?").
target_language_example: Você conhece algum bom restaurante por aqui?
native_language_example: Do you know any good restaurant around here?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone knows a person with a certain skill, job, or connection (often when looking for a recommendation). After "alguém que", Portuguese often uses the subjunctive when the person is unknown or hypothetical (e.g., "Conhece alguém que fale japonês?"); the indicative can also appear when the person is known/specific in context.
target_language_example: Você conhece alguém que possa me ajudar com isso?
native_language_example: Do you know anyone who can help me with this?

meaning: “do you know/are you familiar with (the) …?” (to know a person or to be familiar with something).
additional_notes: Used to ask or state whether someone knows a male person (“o Tom”, “o padre…”) or is familiar with a masculine thing/place/site (“o site…”). For feminine nouns, use “você conhece a…”. For plural, “você conhece os/as…”. Often implies personal acquaintance with people and general familiarity with things.
target_language_example: Você conhece o restaurante aqui perto?
native_language_example: Do you know the restaurant nearby?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is able to do something (physical ability, possibility, or managing to do it). It’s often followed by an infinitive verb: "Você consegue + verb" (e.g., "juntar", "sentir"). In English it’s usually "Can you…?" or "Are you able to…?".
target_language_example: Você consegue abrir a janela, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you open the window, please?

meaning: "can you do" / "are you able to do".
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s ability or capacity to do something. Often followed by an infinitive verb or a task/activity (e.g., "fazer flexões", "fazer Tom rir"). "Consegue" comes from "conseguir" (to manage to / to be able to). In some contexts it can also sound like "can you manage to..." (emphasizing difficulty).
target_language_example: Você consegue fazer isso hoje?
native_language_example: Can you do that today?

meaning: “can you see…?” / “are you able to see…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is able to see something (often because it’s small, far away, or unclear). Very common in questions: “Você consegue ver…?” In everyday speech, “Você pode ver…?” is also common and often interchangeable; “conseguir” can imply a bit of difficulty (“manage to”).
target_language_example: Você consegue ver o nome na placa?
native_language_example: Can you see the name on the sign?

additional_notes: From the verb **conseguir** (to get/obtain; to manage to do). **Você conseguiu?** can mean either “Did you get it?” (obtain something) or “Did you manage to do it?” (succeed). Used for congratulations or encouragement: **Você conseguiu!** = “You did it!”
target_language_example: Você conseguiu terminar o trabalho a tempo?
native_language_example: Did you manage to finish the work on time?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s regular habits or routines. It’s formed with the verb "costumar" + an infinitive (e.g., "você costuma fazer..." = you usually do...). In questions, it’s common for talking about typical times and activities.
target_language_example: Você costuma tomar café da manhã em casa?
native_language_example: Do you usually have breakfast at home?

additional_notes: Used to give advice, instructions, or obligations. It can sound like a strong recommendation or a rule, depending on context and tone. In the negative: "você não deve" = "you shouldn't / mustn't". You can also use it with another verb (e.g., "você deve procurar", "você deve parar") or with "ter" + past participle to express a logical conclusion: "você deve tê-lo conhecido" = "you must have met/known him".
target_language_example: Você deve descansar um pouco antes de sair.
native_language_example: You should rest a little before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to make an assumption about someone’s state or situation based on what you see/know. Often followed by an adjective (cansado, ocupado, triste) or a gerund with a feeling (sentindo dor). It can also sound like a reproach or disbelief in exclamations: "Você deve estar maluco!"
target_language_example: Você deve estar com fome depois da viagem.
native_language_example: You must be hungry after the trip.

additional_notes: Used to make an assumption about someone’s current state or feelings. In Portuguese, "deve" (from "dever") + "estar" often means a guess/probability (“must be / is probably”), not an obligation. It’s typically followed by an adjective (e.g., bêbado, cansado, orgulhoso).
target_language_example: Você deve estar muito cansado depois da viagem.
native_language_example: You must be very tired after the trip.

meaning: you should go; you must go.
additional_notes: "Você" = "you" (informal singular in Brazil, often used even in polite contexts). "Deve" (from "dever") expresses obligation/advice, so this can mean either a strong recommendation ("you should go") or a necessity ("you must go"), depending on context and tone. It’s commonly followed by a destination or purpose: "... ao trabalho" (to work), "... pra cama" (to bed), "... ver se..." (to go check if...).
target_language_example: Você deve ir embora agora.
native_language_example: You should leave now.

additional_notes: Used to give advice, instructions, or obligations. It’s followed by a reflexive verb (verb with “se”), like: proteger-se (protect yourself), cuidar-se (take care of yourself), comportar-se (behave), expressar-se (express yourself), livrar-se (get rid of), manter-se (keep yourself). In everyday speech, people also say “você deve” (without “se”) when the verb isn’t reflexive.
target_language_example: Você deve se acalmar antes de falar com ele.
native_language_example: You should calm yourself down before talking to him.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective or noun to make a strong assumption (“You must be Tom/Canadian”) or to give advice/obligation about how someone should behave (“You should be generous”). It can also appear in passive or command-like statements (“You must be punished / destroyed”). In speech, it may sound like “cê deve ser”.
target_language_example: Pelo seu sotaque, você deve ser do Brasil.
native_language_example: From your accent, you must be from Brazil.

additional_notes: Used to give advice, make a recommendation, or say what is expected. In the past form, "você deveria ter + participle" means "you should have + past participle" (something would have been better if it happened): "Você deveria ter ido" = "You should have gone."
target_language_example: Você deveria falar com ela antes de decidir.
native_language_example: You should talk to her before deciding.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or a recommendation to someone. "Deveria" (conditional of "dever") makes it sound softer and more polite than a direct command ("coma"). Often followed by an adverb or quantity, like "mais devagar" (more slowly) or "mais fruta(s)" (more fruit).
target_language_example: Você deveria comer antes de sair.
native_language_example: You should eat before you leave.

meaning: "you should be" / "you ought to be" (in a certain state).
additional_notes: Used to give advice, express what you think is appropriate, or set an expectation about someone’s emotional/physical state. "Deveria" (from "dever") is often a softer/more hypothetical way to say "should" than "deve". It’s commonly followed by an adjective (feliz, orgulhoso/a, cansado/a) or a participle (preparado/a). Adjectives may change for gender: orgulhoso (male) / orgulhosa (female).
target_language_example: Você deveria estar descansando agora.
native_language_example: You should be resting now.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or make a recommendation. It’s made of: você (you) + deveria (should/ought to; conditional of dever) + ir (to go). You can add details after it (e.g., pessoalmente = in person) or use it alone as a suggestion.
target_language_example: Você deveria ir mais cedo para evitar o trânsito.
native_language_example: You should go earlier to avoid traffic.

additional_notes: Used to say the listener is expected to know something, or that it would be useful/important for them to know it. In “Achei que você deveria saber”, it’s a gentle heads-up (“I thought you should know”). In “Você deveria saber melhor”, it’s more of a reprimand meaning “you should know better.” Uses conditional “deveria” (from dever = should/ought to).
target_language_example: Antes de assinar, você deveria saber que o contrato é por um ano.
native_language_example: Before signing, you should know that the contract is for one year.

meaning: 'you should + (a reflexive verb)' / 'you ought to + (a reflexive verb)'.
additional_notes: Used to give advice, suggestions, or mild criticism. It combines "você deveria" (you should/ought to) with "se" because many common verbs are reflexive in Portuguese (e.g., esforçar-se = to make an effort, aposentar-se = to retire, inscrever-se = to sign up/apply, envergonhar-se = to feel ashamed). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often drop the "se" in casual speech ("Você deveria esforçar mais"), but in careful/standard usage you’ll see it.
target_language_example: Você deveria se preparar melhor para a prova.
native_language_example: You should prepare yourself better for the exam.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or a recommendation to someone. "Deveria" is the conditional of "dever" (should/ought to), making it sound like a gentle suggestion rather than a strong command. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., "tentar ajudar", "tentar esquecer") or by "tentar" + "de novo/outra vez" (try again).
target_language_example: Você deveria tentar falar com ele amanhã.
native_language_example: You should try to talk to him tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone made a mistake or missed a better option in the past. It’s followed by a past participle to describe the action: "você deveria ter + (feito/ido/saído/dito...)".
target_language_example: Você deveria ter me avisado antes.
native_language_example: You should have told me earlier.

meaning: "you should have" + "me" (you should have [verb]ed to/for me).
additional_notes: Used to express criticism or regret about something the other person didn’t do in the past. Structure: você (you) + deveria (should) + ter (have) + me (me) + past participle/infinitive phrase. Common with a past participle: contado (told), dito (said), escutado (listened), visto (seen). You can also use it with an infinitive construction like "pedido para" (asked [me] to). In everyday speech, "você" is often shortened to "cê" ("cê devia ter me...") but the meaning stays the same.
target_language_example: Você deveria ter me avisado antes de sair.
native_language_example: You should have warned me before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to say someone missed something they would have enjoyed or found surprising. Common in excited/exclamatory comments (“Você deveria ter visto!”). In everyday speech, it’s often shortened to “Você devia ter visto…”. Grammar: você (you) + deveria (should) + ter visto (to have seen).
target_language_example: Você deveria ter visto a cara dele quando ouviu a notícia!
native_language_example: You should’ve seen his face when he heard the news!

meaning: “you should” / “you ought to” (advice, recommendation, mild criticism).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of dever (devia) with você to suggest what is advisable or expected: Você devia + infinitive ("Você devia parar de fumar") or Você devia ter + past participle to talk about something you should have done in the past ("Você devia ter feito isso"). It’s less direct than Você deve (present), which can sound more like an obligation.
target_language_example: Você devia falar com ela antes de tomar uma decisão.
native_language_example: You should talk to her before making a decision.

additional_notes: Uses the subject pronoun "você" (you) + the past tense of "dizer" (to say). Very common when asking what someone said or referring back to something the person told you, often followed by "que" + a clause: "Você disse que...". "Você" is used in Brazil as an informal/neutral "you" with third-person verb forms ("você disse", not *"você disseste"*).
target_language_example: Você disse que precisava de ajuda, certo?
native_language_example: You said you needed help, right?

additional_notes: Used to remind someone of what they previously said or to confirm/report their statement. Often introduces a clause with a verb in the past (e.g., estava, tinha, gostava). In conversation it can sound neutral or slightly confrontational depending on tone: “Você disse que…” = “You said that…”.
target_language_example: Você disse que ia me ajudar, lembra?
native_language_example: You said you were going to help me, remember?

meaning: “you said you wanted (to)” / “you told me you wanted (to)”
additional_notes: Used to refer back to what someone previously said they wanted. Common when reminding, confirming, questioning, or holding someone to their earlier intention. Usually followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., ajudar, nadar, ficar) or a noun phrase (e.g., mais responsabilidade).
target_language_example: Você disse que queria sair mais cedo, então vamos agora.
native_language_example: You said you wanted to leave earlier, so let’s go now.

meaning: 'would you be willing to' (to do something).
additional_notes: A polite, formal way to ask if someone is willing/ready to do something. It uses the conditional of estar (estaria) + disposto/disposta (agreeing with the person’s gender) + a + infinitive verb: "Você estaria disposto a me ajudar?" For a woman: "Você estaria disposta a..." In more informal speech you might hear "Você está disposto a..." (present) or "Você topa...?"
target_language_example: Você estaria disposto a esperar mais alguns minutos?
native_language_example: Would you be willing to wait a few more minutes?

additional_notes: Used to ask or state what someone’s temporary state/condition or situation will be in the future (busy, ready, at a place, etc.). "Você" is the common word for "you" in Brazil; in Portugal you might hear "tu estarás" or other forms depending on formality.
target_language_example: Você estará em casa mais tarde?
native_language_example: Will you be at home later?

additional_notes: “Você” = “you” (formal/neutral). “Estava” is the imperfect past of “estar” and is used for ongoing situations in the past (“you were working/thinking”), temporary states (“you were tired/aware”), and background descriptions. Often used with a gerund (-ndo): “você estava trabalhando” = “you were working.”
target_language_example: Quando eu cheguei, você estava dormindo.
native_language_example: When I arrived, you were sleeping.

meaning: “you are / you’re” (talking about your current state, location, or what you’re doing).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective (“você está confuso”), with a place (“você está conosco”), or with another verb to form the present continuous (“você está seguindo…”, “você está se sentindo…”). It’s the verb “estar” (to be) in the present for “você”; often used for temporary conditions and ongoing situations.
target_language_example: Você está ocupado agora?
native_language_example: Are you busy right now?

additional_notes: Used to check on someone’s physical or emotional state. Often said as a question ("Você está bem?"); with emphasis like "mesmo" it means "Are you really okay?". It can also be used as a reassurance/confirmation ("Você está bem, certo?" = "You’re okay, right?").
target_language_example: Ei, você está bem? Você parece cansado.
native_language_example: Hey, are you okay? You look tired.

additional_notes: Used to agree with someone or confirm that what they said is correct. Often followed by “sobre + [topic]” (“about”) or “nisso” (“about that / on that point”): “Você está certo sobre isso.” It can also be used with “em + infinitive” to mean someone is right to do something: “Você está certo em ajudar…” (Note: “certo” agrees with the person being addressed; to a woman you’ll often hear “Você está certa.”)
target_language_example: Você está certo — essa é a melhor opção.
native_language_example: You’re right — that’s the best option.

additional_notes: Used with **com** to express: (1) a temporary condition or feeling (e.g., *com calor, com frio, com sono, com fome*), often equivalent to “you’re hot/cold/sleepy/hungry”; (2) being with someone or accompanied by someone; (3) in some contexts, being romantically involved with someone (*Você está com alguém?*).
target_language_example: Você está com fome?
native_language_example: Are you hungry?

additional_notes: Literally “you are with fear.” In Brazilian Portuguese, **estar com + noun** is a common way to talk about temporary states/feelings (e.g., *estar com fome* = to be hungry). To ask what someone is afraid of, you can say **Do que você está com medo?** or **Você está com medo do quê?**
target_language_example: Você está com medo de escuro?
native_language_example: Are you afraid of the dark?

meaning: "Are you saying that…?" / "Do you mean that…?"
additional_notes: Used to check or challenge what someone just said (sometimes showing surprise, doubt, or offense). It’s the present progressive of "dizer" (to say): "você está dizendo…" + "que" + a full clause. In polite/formal contexts, you may hear "O senhor/A senhora está dizendo que…?"
target_language_example: Você está dizendo que eu não posso ir?
native_language_example: Are you saying that I can’t go?

additional_notes: Present continuous of "esperar" with "você". Often used in questions to mean “What are you waiting for?” (O que você está esperando?) or to ask who/what someone is waiting for (Você está esperando o Tom?). With "que" + verb, it can mean “Are you expecting (that)…?” / “Are you waiting for me to…?” (Você está esperando que eu faça isso primeiro?).
target_language_example: Você está esperando alguém aqui?
native_language_example: Are you waiting for someone here?

additional_notes: Uses the present continuous: você (you) + está (are) + estudando (studying). It often asks what someone is currently studying (a subject, a book, a topic) or contrasts studying with working ("estudando ou trabalhando?"). In Brazilian Portuguese, "você" is the common informal/neutral “you” in many regions, but the verb form stays third person ("você está", not "você estás").
target_language_example: Você está estudando para a prova amanhã?
native_language_example: Are you studying for the test tomorrow?

additional_notes: Present continuous of "falar" with "você". Very common in questions like "Do que você está falando?" (What are you talking about?) and with prepositions: "de" + topic/person (about), "com" + person (with/to). In Brazil, "você" is standard; in Portugal you’ll more often hear "tu estás a falar".
target_language_example: Do que você está falando agora?
native_language_example: What are you talking about now?

additional_notes: This is the present continuous (estar + gerund) used for actions in progress. With "fazer", it can mean "do" (an action) or "make" (something like food). In some contexts it also means "to take/attend" something, like a course ("Que cursos você está fazendo?" = "Which courses are you taking?"). Often used in questions: "O que você está fazendo?" = "What are you doing?"
target_language_example: O que você está fazendo agora?
native_language_example: What are you doing right now?

additional_notes: Uses the present continuous in Portuguese: **estar (você está)** + **gerund (fazendo)** + **isso** (“this”). It often refers to something happening now or around now. Very common in questions like **Por que você está fazendo isso?** (“Why are you doing this?”) and **Para que você está fazendo isso?** (“What are you doing this for?” / “For what purpose are you doing this?”). Can sound accusatory depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Por que você está fazendo isso agora?
native_language_example: Why are you doing this now?

additional_notes: Present continuous with ir (to go): "você" (you) + "está" (are) + "indo" (going). Used for movement (Aonde você está indo? = Where are you going?), leaving (indo embora = going away/leaving), direction/extent (indo longe demais = going too far), progress/performance (indo muito bem = doing/going very well), and plans/intentions (Você está indo nadar? = Are you going to go swim? / Are you going swimming?). In Brazil, "você" is common; in Portugal you may hear "você está a ir" or "tu estás a ir".
target_language_example: Você está indo para casa agora?
native_language_example: Are you going home now?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is available at a certain time/date (often to invite them to do something): "Você está livre esta noite?" It can also mean someone is free to do something: "Você está livre para ir." In context, "livre" usually means "available" rather than "not in prison."
target_language_example: Você está livre amanhã de manhã para tomar um café?
native_language_example: Are you free tomorrow morning to have a coffee?

meaning: "you are" + "(to) me" (used before a verb to mean “you are [verb]-ing to me”).
additional_notes: Used to address someone directly (você) and form the present continuous with estar (“you are …”). The unstressed object pronoun me means “me” and comes before the main verb: “Você está me dizendo…”, “Você está me ouvindo?”. Very common in questions, often expressing surprise or insistence depending on tone.
target_language_example: Você está me ajudando ou não?
native_language_example: Are you helping me or not?

meaning: "are you planning to do" (asking about someone's plans/intentions).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone intends to do, often about the near future. It’s a question form of the verb phrase "estar planejando" (to be planning) + an infinitive (here, "fazer" = to do). In real conversation it’s also common to drop "você" and just say: "O que você está planejando fazer?" or "O que você está planejando fazer depois?".
target_language_example: Você está planejando fazer alguma coisa hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Are you planning to do anything tonight?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone wants or needs, or what they’re searching for (a thing, a person, a job, etc.). It’s the present progressive of procurar (“to look for”). Very common in questions: “O que você está procurando?” (“What are you looking for?”). Often appears with “por”: “você está procurando por…”; in many contexts, both “procurar” and “procurar por” are used.
target_language_example: Você está procurando um hotel perto do aeroporto?
native_language_example: Are you looking for a hotel near the airport?

meaning: “are you ready to/for…?” (talking to one person).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is prepared for something (a noun) or ready to do something (verb in the infinitive). Examples: pronto para a verdade (“ready for the truth”), pronto para sair (“ready to leave”). In everyday speech, Brazilians often drop the subject pronoun: “Está pronto para…?”
target_language_example: Você está pronto para começar?
native_language_example: Are you ready to start?

meaning: 'you are feeling' (your current physical or emotional state).
additional_notes: Used to ask about how someone feels right now. It uses the reflexive verb "sentir-se" (to feel), so you often add an adjective after it (e.g., bem, mal, cansado/a, doente, confiante). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, you may also hear "Como você está se sentindo?" without "é que".
target_language_example: Você está se sentindo melhor hoje?
native_language_example: Are you feeling better today?

meaning: “you are trying to … me” (used before another verb).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is attempting to do something that affects you. In Portuguese, the object pronoun often comes before the infinitive: “tentar me ajudar” = “try to help me”, “tentar me assustar” = “try to scare me”. You typically complete the phrase with another verb.
target_language_example: Você está tentando me ajudar?
native_language_example: Are you trying to help me?

additional_notes: Used to describe the listener’s current state/condition: você (you) + está (are, temporary/state) + tão (so). Often followed by an adjective (cansado, linda, pálida). It can also be used with comparisons: “tão … quanto …” = “as … as …”.
target_language_example: Você está tão atrasado que vai perder o ônibus.
native_language_example: You’re so late that you’re going to miss the bus.

additional_notes: From the verb "usar". It can mean (1) using something (a chair, a phone, a tool) or (2) wearing something (clothes, earrings, makeup, perfume). It’s used to ask what someone is using/wearing at the moment: "Você está usando isso?" = "Are you using that?"; "Você está usando maquiagem?" = "Are you wearing makeup?".
target_language_example: Você está usando meu carregador?
native_language_example: Are you using my charger?

additional_notes: From "você" (you) + "está" (are) + "vendo" (seeing). Commonly used to ask what someone can see right now or to check if they can see a specific thing (often with a question: "Você está vendo...?" or "O que você está vendo?").
target_language_example: O que você está vendo na foto?
native_language_example: What are you seeing in the photo?

additional_notes: Used with the pronoun "você" (common in Brazil) + the verb "falar" in the present tense: "você fala". It can be a statement (Você fala bem. = You speak well.) or a yes/no question (Você fala coreano? = Do you speak Korean?)—in speech the intonation often shows it’s a question; in writing use a question mark.
target_language_example: Você fala inglês?
native_language_example: Do you speak English?

additional_notes: Literally “you speak French.” In Portuguese, it can be a statement (Você fala francês.) or a question just by intonation (Você fala francês?). Common variants: “Você fala francês?” (Do you speak French?), “Você fala francês bem/muito bem” (You speak French well/very well), “Você fala francês fluentemente” (…fluently), “melhor do que eu” (better than me).
target_language_example: Desculpa, você fala francês?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you speak French?

additional_notes: Used to ask or state that you spoke with someone. It’s the verb falar (to speak/talk) in the past (falou) + com (with/to). In questions, it usually means “Did you talk to …?” In statements, it means “You talked to …”. The person comes right after com: com ela (to her), com o Tom (to Tom), com a sua esposa (to your wife).
target_language_example: Você falou com o gerente sobre o problema?
native_language_example: Did you talk to the manager about the problem?

additional_notes: Form of the verb "fazer" (to do/make) with "você" (you). It’s used to ask what someone does (often meaning their job) or to talk about someone’s actions/habits. In questions, it often appears as "O que você faz?" (What do you do?).
target_language_example: O que você faz no fim de semana?
native_language_example: What do you do on the weekend?

additional_notes: "Você" is "you" (informal in some regions; in many parts of Brazil it’s the normal everyday "you"). "Fez" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "fazer" (to do/make). It’s used to talk about something the person did or made in the past. Common in questions like "Como (é que) você fez...?" (How did you do it?/How did you manage to...?). It can also mean "you had" in some expressions like "você fez muitas ligações" (you made a lot of calls).
target_language_example: O que você fez ontem à noite?
native_language_example: What did you do last night?

additional_notes: Uses **você** (“you”, informal-to-neutral in most of Brazil) + **fez** (past tense of *fazer*, “to do/make”) + **isso** (“that/this”). It’s used to say someone performed an action in the past, often followed by details: **de novo** (again), **melhor do que…** (better than…), **na segunda** (on Monday), **tudo sozinho** (all by yourself). In English you might choose “that” or “this” depending on context; Portuguese often uses **isso** broadly for “that/this thing.”
target_language_example: Não acredito que você fez isso!
native_language_example: I can’t believe you did that!

additional_notes: Used to ask or tell where someone went in the past. Often appears in questions with “onde/aonde” (where/to where): “Onde você foi?” In Brazilian Portuguese, “você” is the common word for “you” (informal in many regions, neutral in others) and it takes 3rd-person verb forms like “foi” (not “foste”).
target_language_example: Onde você foi ontem à noite?
native_language_example: Where did you go last night?

additional_notes: Uses the verb ir (to go) in the simple past: você foi = “you went.” Add para before a destination/place: foi para Boston = “went to Boston.” In questions, Portuguese often relies on intonation (no extra “did” word).
target_language_example: Você foi para o trabalho de ônibus?
native_language_example: Did you go to work by bus?

meaning: 'do you like' / 'you like' (talking to someone using você).
additional_notes: Used with "de" to say what someone likes: "Você gosta de..." (Do you like...?). With plural or specific things, "de" + article may contract: "do" (de + o), "da" (de + a), "dos" (de + os), "das" (de + as). In questions it often relies on intonation or a question mark: "Você gosta de vinho?"
target_language_example: Você gosta de música brasileira?
native_language_example: Do you like Brazilian music?

meaning: “Do you like the…?” (asking if someone likes something feminine-singular).
additional_notes: Used to ask about preferences. "Você" = you, "gosta" = like/enjoy, and "da" = "de" + "a" (“of the”) used before a feminine singular noun (e.g., a Espanha, a ideia, a sua irmã). With masculine singular nouns, use "você gosta do" (do = de + o).
target_language_example: Você gosta da comida brasileira?
native_language_example: Do you like Brazilian food?

additional_notes: Used to ask or say what someone likes. It’s followed by a noun (Você gosta de cães.) or by an infinitive verb (Você gosta de falar francês?). In questions, intonation usually marks the question; you can also add a question mark in writing.
target_language_example: Você gosta de café?
native_language_example: Do you like coffee?

meaning: “do you like playing…?” / “do you like to play…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask someone if they enjoy playing a game or sport. Often followed by what the person plays (e.g., “você gosta de jogar vôlei?”). In Brazilian Portuguese, “você” is common in everyday speech; the verb is in the 3rd-person form (“gosta”), not “gostas.”
target_language_example: Você gosta de jogar futebol nos fins de semana?
native_language_example: Do you like playing soccer on weekends?

meaning: “do you like your …?” (asking if someone likes something that belongs to them; typically with a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone whether they like something of theirs (their job, brother, computer, keyboard, etc.). It’s usually followed by a masculine noun: “Você gosta do seu emprego?” = “Do you like your job?” Here, “do seu” is a contraction: “de + o + seu” (“of the + your”). For a feminine noun, you’d use “da sua” (de + a + sua): “Você gosta da sua casa?”
target_language_example: Você gosta do seu carro?
native_language_example: Do you like your car?

meaning: 'which do you like more?' / 'you like ... more'.
additional_notes: Used to compare preferences. Often appears in questions with "de qual... você gosta mais?" (which one do you like more?) or "Você gosta mais de X ou de Y?" (do you like X or Y more?). "gostar" usually takes "de" before the thing you like: "gostar de + noun/verb". "mais" = "more".
target_language_example: Você gosta mais de café ou de chá?
native_language_example: Do you like coffee or tea more?

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of "gostar" with "você" to make polite offers, invitations, or questions about preferences. Often followed by "de" + noun ("Você gostaria de chá?") or "de" + infinitive ("Você gostaria de tomar café?"). In Brazil, it’s a common, formal-sounding way to offer something; in more casual situations, people may also say "Quer...?".
target_language_example: Você gostaria de mais água?
native_language_example: Would you like some more water?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask if someone wants to do something or to make an invitation. It’s more formal/polite than 'você quer…?'. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb: 'Você gostaria de + verb' (e.g., vir, morar, dizer).
target_language_example: Você gostaria de tomar um café comigo?
native_language_example: Would you like to have a coffee with me?

additional_notes: Polite way to invite someone or ask about their preference/interest in going somewhere or doing something. Often followed by an activity ("você gostaria de ir fazer compras?") or a place ("aonde você gostaria de ir?"). You can also use it alone ("Você gostaria de ir?") meaning “Would you like to go?”.
target_language_example: Você gostaria de ir ao cinema comigo hoje?
native_language_example: Would you like to go to the movies with me today?

você gostaria tanto de aprender Inglês

target_language_multi_word_term: você gostaria tanto de aprender Inglês
meaning: “you would like so much to learn English” / “you’d really like to learn English.”
additional_notes: Uses the conditional form “gostaria” (“would like”), which is a polite/soft way to express a desire. “tanto” intensifies the desire (“so much”, “really”). Often appears inside questions like “Por que/Por qual motivo/Por que razão você gostaria tanto de aprender Inglês?” (“Why would you like so much to learn English?”).
target_language_example: Eu queria entender: por que você gostaria tanto de aprender Inglês?
native_language_example: I wanted to understand: why would you really like to learn English?

meaning: 'have you already…?' / 'have you ever…?' (used to ask if someone has done something before, or has done it by now).
additional_notes: Used very often in questions with the adverb "já". With an action verb, it often means "ever" (life experience) or "already" (by now), depending on context: "Você já fumou?" = "Have you ever smoked?" / "Have you smoked already?". With "estar" + adjective/state, it typically means "already" (the change has happened sooner than expected or by now): "Você já está bêbado?" = "Are you already drunk?".
target_language_example: Você já visitou o Rio de Janeiro?
native_language_example: Have you ever visited Rio de Janeiro?

meaning: "Have you eaten yet/already?" or "Have you ever eaten…?"
additional_notes: Literally "you already ate." In conversation, it’s a common way to ask if someone has eaten (often meaning “yet?”). With a specific food (“Você já comeu bolo?”), it often means “Have you ever tried/eaten cake?” The time meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Você já comeu hoje?
native_language_example: Have you eaten today?

additional_notes: Uses the verb **estar** in the **pretérito perfeito** (**esteve**) with **já** to ask about past experience or whether someone has visited a place before. Very common in questions like **Você já esteve lá?** (“Have you been there?”) or **Você já esteve na TV?** (“Have you ever been on TV?”). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people also often say **Você já foi…?** with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Você já esteve em Portugal alguma vez?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Portugal?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s past experience visiting a place. It uses "já" to mean "ever/already" and the verb "estar" in the past ("esteve" = "was/has been"). Very common in travel and small talk. You can swap the place name after "em" (em Boston, no Japão, na Itália).
target_language_example: Você já esteve em Portugal?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Portugal?

meaning: "Have you ever been to…?" (asking if someone has visited a place).
additional_notes: Used to ask about life experience/travel. "já" here often means "ever" (not just "already"). "esteve" is the past of "estar" (you were/have been). "na" = "em" + "a" and is used with feminine places (e.g., na França, na China). With masculine places, use "no" (e.g., no Brasil).
target_language_example: Você já esteve na Itália?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Italy?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has visited a place at any time in their life. It uses the verb estar in the past (esteve). The preposition+article changes with the place name: no (em + o) for masculine places (no Brasil, no Canadá), na for feminine places (na França), and em (or simply drop it) for most cities/islands: Você já esteve em Paris? / Você já esteve (no) Rio?
target_language_example: Você já esteve no Brasil?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Brazil?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has already had a conversation with a person. Very common in Brazilian Portuguese in everyday situations. You can also add details after the person, e.g., “você já falou com ele sobre isso?” (“have you talked to him about that?”).
target_language_example: Você já falou com o médico sobre os resultados?
native_language_example: Have you already talked to the doctor about the results?

meaning: “have you already done (it)?” / “have you ever done (it)?”
additional_notes: Used in questions with **já** + **fez** (past of *fazer*, “to do/make”) to ask either (1) if something is finished **yet/already** (often with chores/homework), or (2) if someone has **ever** had an experience (“Have you ever taken singing lessons?”). Often followed by an object: *Você já fez a lição / a tarefa / aulas de canto?*
target_language_example: Você já fez isso antes?
native_language_example: Have you ever done that before?

meaning: 'Have you been...?' / 'Have you ever been...?' (asking about past experience).
additional_notes: Used with a destination or place: "Você já foi ao exterior?" / "Você já foi para o México?" Here, "já" often means "ever/already" and the verb is the simple past of "ir" (foi). Depending on context, it can also mean "you already left/went" (e.g., "Ele já foi" = "He already left").
target_language_example: Você já foi a São Paulo?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to São Paulo?

meaning: "Have you ever been to…?" (asking if someone has visited a place/event before).
additional_notes: Used to ask about past life experience. In questions, "já" often means "ever/already". "foi" is the past of "ir" (to go). The "à" is a contraction of "a" + "a" (to + the) and is used before feminine places/events (à China, à ópera). For masculine places you typically use "ao" (a + o): "Você já foi ao Brasil?". You can also add time: "Você já foi à Espanha este ano?"
target_language_example: Você já foi à praia aqui perto?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to the beach near here?

meaning: 'Have you been...?' / 'Have you ever been...?' (asking about past experience).
additional_notes: Used with a destination or place: "Você já foi ao exterior?" / "Você já foi para o México?" Here, "já" often means "ever/already" and the verb is the simple past of "ir" (foi). Depending on context, it can also mean "you already left/went" (e.g., "Ele já foi" = "He already left").
target_language_example: Você já foi a São Paulo?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to São Paulo?

meaning: 'have you read (it) yet?' / 'have you ever read (it)?'
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has already read something. In Brazilian Portuguese, this question is commonly formed with **você + já + verb in the pretérito perfeito**: *você já leu...?* Depending on context, it can mean either **“already/yet”** (by now) or **“ever”** (at any time in your life). You can add an object right after: *você já leu este livro?*
target_language_example: Você já leu esse livro ou ainda não?
native_language_example: Have you read that book yet, or not yet?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has heard something before. "já" often implies "already" or "ever (at some point)"; the exact meaning depends on context (e.g., "Você já ouviu esta música antes?" = "Have you heard this song before?"). Common in conversation; "você" is standard in Brazil (in Portugal, "já ouviu...?" or "você já ouviu...?" is less common).
target_language_example: Você já ouviu falar desse restaurante?
native_language_example: Have you ever heard of that restaurant?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone knows about or is familiar with a person, thing, or idea. Very common in conversation. After it, you typically use a noun or name (often with an article: de um/uma…, de o/a…, or de + name). You can also ask more formally with “O(a) senhor(a) já ouviu falar de…?”
target_language_example: Você já ouviu falar do Carnaval do Rio?
native_language_example: Have you ever heard of Rio Carnival?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has considered an idea or option. It’s often followed by a verb in the infinitive (pensou em fazer, checar, ficar) or a noun/pronoun (pensou em mim). "Já" adds the sense of "ever/already"; in suggestions it can sound like "Have you tried/considered…?"
target_language_example: Você já pensou em pedir ajuda?
native_language_example: Have you considered asking for help?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has ever tried doing something before. It’s literally “you already tried,” but in questions it often matches English “have you tried…?” You can add an infinitive after it: “você já tentou + verb” (e.g., usar, falar, fazer). “Alguma vez?” emphasizes “ever.”
target_language_example: Você já tentou reiniciar o telefone?
native_language_example: Have you tried restarting the phone?

meaning: “have you finished already?” / “are you done yet?”
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has completed something. "já" adds the idea of “already/yet.” You’ll often see it followed by a noun ("terminou sua tarefa?") or by "de" + infinitive ("terminou de falar?").
target_language_example: Você já terminou o jantar?
native_language_example: Have you finished dinner already?

meaning: “have you ever had…?” / “have you already had…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s past experience up to now. It’s made of: você (“you”) + já (“already/ever”) + teve (past of ter, “to have”). Often followed by a noun or experience (e.g., doença, problema, cliente). In questions, it commonly matches English present perfect (“Have you ever…?”).
target_language_example: Você já teve alguma alergia alimentar?
native_language_example: Have you ever had any food allergy?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has ever been to a place before (life experience up to now). "você" = "you" (informal/neutral in Brazil), "já" often means "already/ever" in questions, and "visitou" is the past of "visitar" (to visit). Typically followed by a place: "Você já visitou Roma?"
target_language_example: Você já visitou o Brasil?
native_language_example: Have you visited Brazil (yet/already)?

meaning: “have you seen…?” / “have you ever seen…?” (speaking to one person).
additional_notes: Used to ask if the listener has seen something, often at any time up to now. With “isto/antes” it commonly means “have you seen this before?”. “Já” adds the idea of “already/ever (by now)”. In Brazil, this is the usual everyday form; in Portugal you’ll more often hear “você já viu” less, and “tu já viste…?” more.
target_language_example: Você já viu esse lugar de noite?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen this place at night?

meaning: “have you (ever) seen the…?” / “have you already seen the…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has ever seen something (experience) or has already seen it (up to now). Often followed by a noun ("Você já viu o Palácio…?") or, without "o/a", by a person + an adjective/state ("Você já viu o Tom com raiva?"). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, "você" is common; more formal: "O senhor / A senhora já viu…?"
target_language_example: Você já viu o pôr do sol daqui?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen the sunset from here?

meaning: "Have you ever seen a…?" (talking about a masculine noun).
