additional_notes: Literally "have you already seen a". Used to ask whether someone has ever seen something in their life or up to now. It’s typically followed by a masculine singular noun: "um elefante", "um macaco". For feminine nouns, you usually say "você já viu uma…?"
target_language_example: Você já viu um pinguim de perto?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen a penguin up close?

meaning: “you (to me)” — used before a verb to mean “you [verb] me.”
additional_notes: Common pattern: **Você me + verb**. **você** = “you” (informal in some places; in Brazil it’s widely used), **me** = object pronoun “me” placed before the verb. Often used in requests/questions: *Você me ajuda?* (“Can you help me?”).
target_language_example: Você me empresta seu carregador por um minuto?
native_language_example: Can you lend me your charger for a minute?

meaning: "you owe me" (money or something you should do/give).
additional_notes: Used when someone owes you something—money ("Você me deve 20 reais") or more commonly an apology, explanation, favor, etc. It can sound demanding/accusatory depending on tone, especially alone: "Você me deve." In Brazil, with "você" it’s neutral; with "tu" you may hear "tu me deves".
target_language_example: Depois do que aconteceu, você me deve uma desculpa.
native_language_example: After what happened, you owe me an apology.

additional_notes: Used to remind someone of something they said or instructed you to do. Common in conversations about instructions, requests, or clarifying what was previously said. Often followed by “para/pra + infinitive” (você me disse para fazer isso = you told me to do this) or by a clause with “que” (você me disse que… = you told me that…).
target_language_example: Eu só fiz isso porque você me disse que era importante.
native_language_example: I only did that because you told me it was important.

additional_notes: Direct accusation using the polite/neutral pronoun “você” (common in Brazil). Past tense: “mentiu” is the simple past of “mentir” (to lie). Often used in questions (Por que...? Quantas vezes...?) or with emphasis/exclamation when someone is upset. Variations: “Você mentiu pra mim” (more casual, with “pra” instead of “para”).
target_language_example: Eu confiei em você, mas você mentiu para mim.
native_language_example: I trusted you, but you lied to me.

additional_notes: Used to point out that someone didn’t previously mention a fact (often with surprise or mild complaint). Follow it with a clause introduced by que. In speech, you’ll often hear it shortened to “Você nunca me disse que…” without repeating the second “você.”
target_language_example: Você nunca me disse que ia embora amanhã.
native_language_example: You never told me that you were leaving tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to negate a verb with the subject você (formal/neutral 'you' in Brazilian Portuguese). Put não before the verb: "você não veio" (you didn’t come), "você não está" (you aren’t), "você não vai" (you won’t). Often used in questions by keeping the same order: "Você não está cansado?" (Aren’t you tired?).
target_language_example: Você não tem que se preocupar agora.
native_language_example: You don't have to worry right now.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or a warning, or to say something is not allowed. It’s formed with você (you) + não (not) + dever (to should/must/owe). The strength can range from a gentle suggestion (“you shouldn’t”) to a firm prohibition (“you mustn’t”), depending on context and tone. Common patterns: você não deve + infinitive (você não deve ir, partir, rir); você não deve + reflexive verb (você não deve se perder).
target_language_example: Você não deve dirigir se estiver cansado.
native_language_example: You shouldn’t drive if you’re tired.

additional_notes: Used to give advice, warn someone, or say something is not recommended. It can sound quite direct, especially with strong verbs (e.g., "ir", "estar"). Often followed by an infinitive: "você não deveria + verbo".
target_language_example: Você não deveria falar com ele desse jeito.
native_language_example: You shouldn't talk to him like that.

meaning: “you can’t / you may not” (you are not able to, or you are not allowed to).
additional_notes: Common way to tell someone something is impossible or forbidden. Uses the verb "poder" (to be able to / can; to be allowed to / may). Often followed by another verb in the infinitive: "Você não pode + verbo" (e.g., "entrar", "fumar", "estacionar"). Depending on context, it can sound like a rule/permission (“you may not”) or a limitation (“you can’t”).
target_language_example: Desculpe, você não pode entrar sem ingresso.
native_language_example: Sorry, you can’t go in without a ticket.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say someone lacks something (physical or abstract): Você não tem coração (you have no heart). It can also express lack of options: Você não tem escolha (you have no choice). Often sounds accusatory or confrontational depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Você não tem tempo para isso agora.
native_language_example: You don’t have time for that right now.

você não tem o direito de

target_language_multi_word_term: você não tem o direito de
meaning: “you don’t have the right to” (you’re not allowed/entitled to).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is not permitted or not justified in doing something. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., fazer, estar, julgar, parar). Common in arguments, rules, and formal complaints; it can sound strong or accusatory.
target_language_example: Você não tem o direito de falar comigo desse jeito.
native_language_example: You don’t have the right to talk to me like that.

meaning: “you won’t / you’re not going to” (negative future).
additional_notes: Used to say something will not happen or to forbid/stop someone, often as a warning or threat (“You won’t escape!”). In Portuguese it’s often followed by an infinitive: “você não vai + verb” (e.g., “você não vai ver”, “você não vai escapar”). In speech, “você” is often shortened to “cê”: “cê não vai…”.
target_language_example: Você não vai entrar aqui sem convite.
native_language_example: You’re not going to come in here without an invitation.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ser" to state that someone is not something (a person/thing) or does not have a certain characteristic. It’s followed by a noun or adjective: "você não é meu parente" (noun), "você não é obrigado" (adjective).
target_language_example: Você não é a pessoa certa para isso.
native_language_example: You are not the right person for this.

meaning: “you all the time” / “you the whole time” (constantly; all the time).
additional_notes: Often used after verbs like pensar em (to think about), sentir falta de (to miss), and falar de (to talk about) to mean “constantly/all the time.” In sentence 2, “era você o tempo todo” means “it was you all along/the whole time.” Word order can vary (e.g., “o tempo todo em você”), but “em você o tempo todo” is very common.
target_language_example: Eu me preocupo com você o tempo todo.
native_language_example: I worry about you all the time.

additional_notes: Used to check if someone heard (and sometimes understood) some information, often followed by a clause like “elas disseram” (they said) or used alone as a lead-in to gossip/news. In writing, it’s usually followed by a question mark. Often shortened in speech (e.g., “Ouviu o quê?”).
target_language_example: Você ouviu o que aconteceu ontem à noite?
native_language_example: Did you hear what happened last night?

additional_notes: Used to ask about payment for something (price or method). It’s the verb pagar (to pay) in the past (pagou) with por (“for”). Often followed by an item or “tudo isso” (all that), and can appear in questions like “Como você pagou por...?” (How did you pay for...?) or “Quanto você pagou por...?” (How much did you pay for...?).
target_language_example: Você pagou por este ingresso com cartão ou dinheiro?
native_language_example: Did you pay for this ticket with a card or cash?

meaning: 'you seem' / 'you look' (it appears that you are...).
additional_notes: Used to describe an impression about someone. Common patterns: (1) "você parece + adjective" (Você parece cansado/a. = You look tired.) (2) "você parece + infinitive" (Você parece saber... = You seem to know...) (3) "você parece + noun" (Você parece um tonto. = You look like an idiot.) Adjectives usually agree with the person being described (cansado/cansada, sério/séria).
target_language_example: Você parece preocupado com isso.
native_language_example: You seem worried about that.

meaning: "You seem to be" / "you appear to be."
additional_notes: Used to comment on how someone looks or seems based on what you observe, often followed by an adjective or expression (cansado, feliz, ocupado, bem informado, encrencado). It can sound a bit personal or direct, so in sensitive situations you can soften it with "acho que" (Acho que você parece estar...) or ask a question: "Você parece estar cansado—está tudo bem?"
target_language_example: Você parece estar preocupado com alguma coisa.
native_language_example: You seem to be worried about something.

additional_notes: Used to comment on how someone appears to feel or act. It’s followed by an adjective (often a temporary state): cansado/a (tired), nervoso/a (nervous), impaciente (impatient), ocupado/a (busy). In speech, it can sound a bit direct; you can soften it with “acho que” (I think) or “um pouco” (a little).
target_language_example: Você parece estar muito preocupado hoje.
native_language_example: You seem to be very worried today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone believes, assumes, or considers. Often appears as “você pensa que…?” (“do you think that…?”) and in comparisons like “mais/menos … do que você pensa” (“more/less … than you think”). It can also describe someone’s way of thinking (“você pensa de maneira diferente”) or imply overthinking (“você pensa demais”).
target_language_example: Você pensa que vai chover hoje?
native_language_example: Do you think it’s going to rain today?

additional_notes: Used to ask or state what someone believes, often when correcting them (“not what you think it means”) or challenging them in a surprised/angry way (“Where do you think you’re going?”). In questions it can sound confrontational depending on tone and words like “que diabos” (“what the heck”). Often followed by another clause (e.g., “você pensa que ele é…” = “you think he is…”).
target_language_example: Você pensa que eu não percebi, mas eu percebi.
native_language_example: You think I didn’t notice, but I did.

meaning: "you can" / "can you…?" (ability, permission, possibility; also used to make requests).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "poder" (to be able to / can) with "você" (you). In statements it often means ability or possibility ("Você pode fazer isto." = "You can do this."). In questions it commonly functions as a polite request ("Você pode me dizer…?" = "Can you / Could you tell me…?"). Literally present tense, but in English it may be translated as "could you" for politeness.
target_language_example: Você pode me ajudar com isso?
native_language_example: Can you help me with that?

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say what someone is able/allowed to do, or to ask someone to do something politely (often as a question). In Brazil, "você" is common; in Portugal, people more often use "tu podes fazer". "Fazer" can mean either "do" or "make" depending on context.
target_language_example: Você pode fazer isso amanhã?
native_language_example: Can you do that tomorrow?

meaning: “you can do it/that” or “can you do it/that?”
additional_notes: Used to say someone is able to do something (“You can do it”) or to ask for a favor/request (“Can you do it?”). It can be made more specific with time words (amanhã = tomorrow, depois = later) or with “para mim” (for me) / “pela gente” (for us). In speech, intonation often shows whether it’s a statement or a question.
target_language_example: Você pode fazer isso agora, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you do that now, please?

meaning: “you can stay” / “you may stay”; also “you can keep (it)” (with com).
additional_notes: Ficar is flexible: it can mean “to stay” (often with por + time: por alguns dias, por um instante; or alone: Você pode ficar.) and it can also mean “to keep” when used with ficar com + noun (Você pode ficar com o lenço. = You can keep the scarf.). It can be permission (“you may…”) or ability (“you can…”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Se quiser, você pode ficar aqui mais um pouco.
native_language_example: If you want, you can stay here a little longer.

meaning: “you can stay here” / “you may stay here.”
additional_notes: Used to give permission or make an offer for someone to remain in the same place. In questions, it often means “Can you stay here…?” as a request (e.g., for a moment, for a while, tonight). “Pode” can express both ability and permission, but in these examples it’s mainly permission/request.
target_language_example: Você pode ficar aqui enquanto eu vou ao banheiro?
native_language_example: Can you stay here while I go to the bathroom?

additional_notes: Used to give permission or to say something is possible/allowed. In questions it often works like a polite request: “Can you go…?” (e.g., pick someone up, go slower/faster). Sometimes it implies a condition with "desde que" (“as long as”), or a soft “if you want” with "se quiser".
target_language_example: Você pode ir agora, mas volta antes das dez.
native_language_example: You can go now, but come back before ten.

meaning: “can you … me” / “could you … me” (asking someone to do something for you).
additional_notes: Used to make polite requests: "Você" = you, "pode" = can/could, and "me" = me (object pronoun). It’s typically followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., ajudar, ensinar, levar, ouvir, perdoar). In informal speech, many people say "cê pode me..." or use "pode me..." when "você" is already understood.
target_language_example: Você pode me dar uma mão com isso?
native_language_example: Can you give me a hand with this?

additional_notes: A polite, common way to ask someone for help. Often followed by “com + [thing]” (with something) or “a + [verb]” (to do something): “Você pode me ajudar com isso?” / “Você pode me ajudar a levar isso?” You can add “por favor” to be extra polite.
target_language_example: Você pode me ajudar a encontrar a estação, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you help me find the station, please?

meaning: “Can you help me (to)…?” / “Could you help me (to)…?”
additional_notes: Polite way to ask someone for help doing something. It’s followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., descer, descobrir, lavar, resolver). In everyday speech you can also hear “Você pode me ajudar a…?” or more informal “Pode me ajudar a…?”
target_language_example: Você pode me ajudar a carregar essas caixas?
native_language_example: Can you help me carry these boxes?

meaning: “can you give me…?” / “you can give me…”
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to hand you something or to give/provide something. Very common in polite requests, often followed by the item and “por favor”: “Você pode me dar + o/a + noun…?” In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, “você” is the usual “you” (singular) in many regions; it takes verb forms like “pode”.
target_language_example: Você pode me dar a conta, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me the bill/check, please?

você pode me dar uma carona

target_language_multi_word_term: você pode me dar uma carona
additional_notes: Used to ask someone for a lift in their car (or other vehicle). Common additions: “até a estação” (to the station), “até em casa / pra casa” (home). “Dar uma carona” = “to give someone a ride/lift”; “pra” is informal spoken Portuguese for “para.”
target_language_example: Você pode me dar uma carona amanhã de manhã?
native_language_example: Can you give me a ride tomorrow morning?

meaning: "Can you tell me…?" (polite way to ask for information).
additional_notes: Often followed by a direct object ("o preço", "seu nome") or by a question word clause: "o que" (what), "por que" (why), "quando" (when). It’s polite and common in service situations; you can add "por favor" to be even more polite.
target_language_example: Você pode me dizer onde fica o banheiro, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you tell me where the bathroom is, please?

additional_notes: A polite way to ask for instructions or an explanation. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., "chegar", "fazer", "resolver") or by a clause describing how something happened or how someone found out. You can make it a bit more formal by adding "por favor".
target_language_example: Você pode me dizer como eu faço para chegar na estação de metrô?
native_language_example: Can you tell me how to get to the subway station?

additional_notes: Polite way to ask for someone’s help with a location or place (where someone/something is, was, or can be found). Often followed by a full clause: “Você pode me dizer onde fica…?” (where … is/located) or “onde eu posso encontrar…?” (where I can find …). In Brazil, “você” is common; in Portugal, you may hear “Pode me dizer onde…?” or “Pode dizer-me onde…?” in more formal contexts.
target_language_example: Você pode me dizer onde fica a estação de metrô mais próxima?
native_language_example: Can you tell me where the nearest subway station is?

meaning: “Can you lend me…?” / “Could you lend me…?”
additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to lend you something. It’s made of: você (you) + pode (can) + me (to me) + emprestar (to lend). In Brazil, this is common with “você”; with friends you may also hear “Você/Me empresta…?” (more direct) or “Você pode me emprestar… por favor?”. Note: in standard Portuguese, money is usually lent with “emprestar dinheiro” (without “um”): “Você pode me emprestar dinheiro?”
target_language_example: Você pode me emprestar uma caneta por um minuto?
native_language_example: Can you lend me a pen for a minute?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (politely/neutral) if they are able/willing to teach you something. Often followed by "a" + infinitive: "Você pode me ensinar a + verb" (e.g., "a nadar", "a tocar piano"). You can also use it alone (“Você pode me ensinar?”) when the skill is understood from context. "Você" is the common everyday “you” in Brazil; "me" = “me”; "ensinar" = “to teach.”
target_language_example: Você pode me ensinar a cozinhar arroz?
native_language_example: Can you teach me how to cook rice?

additional_notes: Polite way to ask someone to explain something. Often followed by a direct object (isso, as regras) or by a question word + clause (como..., o que...). You can add “por favor” to be extra polite.
target_language_example: Você pode me explicar de novo, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you explain it to me again, please?

additional_notes: Polite request using você (“you”) + pode (“can”) + me (“to me”) + mostrar (“to show”). Often followed by the thing you want to see: a photo, receipt, document, directions, etc. You can soften it with “por favor” at the end.
target_language_example: Você pode me mostrar onde fica o banheiro, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you show me where the bathroom is, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (often a waiter, clerk, or friend) to bring you something. You usually follow it with the item you want, and you can add “por favor” to sound more polite.
target_language_example: Você pode me trazer a conta, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring me the bill, please?

additional_notes: Used with você (“you”) + pode (“can/may”) + ter (“to have”). It can express: (1) possibility/ability (Você pode ter sucesso. = You can succeed.), (2) permission/offer (Você pode ter este relógio. = You may have this watch.), or (3) limits/quantity (Quantos... você pode ter? = How many... can you have?). Often followed by a noun (ter bons amigos) or by an outcome/abstract idea (ter sucesso).
target_language_example: Você pode ter uma sobremesa depois do jantar.
native_language_example: You can have dessert after dinner.

additional_notes: Used to allow someone to use an object. "Você" is a common way to say “you” in Brazilian Portuguese, and "pode" can mean “can” (ability) or “may” (permission); in these examples it’s permission. Often followed by the thing being used: "Você pode usar + [item]". You can add a condition with "se quiser" (“if you want”) or "sempre que quiser" (“whenever you want”).
target_language_example: Você pode usar meu computador por uma hora.
native_language_example: You can use my computer for an hour.

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is able to see/notice something, or to state that it’s visible. Often appears in questions like “Você pode ver isso?” (“Can you see this?”). In statements, it can mean “you can see (it)” in the sense of “it’s possible/visible from here,” especially with distance or location: “Você pode ver por milhas…” (“You can see for miles…”).
target_language_example: Você pode ver a montanha daqui?
native_language_example: Can you see the mountain from here?

additional_notes: Uses the polite pronoun "você" + "pode" (can/may) + "vir" (to come). It can be a question (asking if someone is able/allowed to come) or a statement giving permission/inviting someone to come. Often followed by a time ("a que horas..."), a place ("ao meu país"), or a way/route ("por este caminho").
target_language_example: Você pode vir amanhã às 10?
native_language_example: Can you come tomorrow at 10?

meaning: 'could you…?' / 'you could…' (polite request, suggestion, or possibility).
additional_notes: "Você" = "you" and "poderia" is the conditional of "poder" (to be able to/can). It’s commonly used to make polite requests: "Você poderia + infinitive...?" (Could you + verb...?). It can also express possibility/ability in a hypothetical situation: "Você poderia ver..." (You could see...). With "ter" + past participle ("poderia ter dito/feito"), it often means "could have" (something possible in the past, often implying criticism or regret).
target_language_example: Você poderia me ajudar com isso, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you help me with this, please?

additional_notes: Used to make a polite request or ask someone to do something. It’s addressed with você (common in Brazil; in Portugal, you might hear “podia/poderia, por favor…” or “pode, por favor…”). Often followed by an infinitive verb: “você poderia, por favor, repetir… / ajudar… / parar…”.
target_language_example: Você poderia, por favor, fechar a janela?
native_language_example: Could you please close the window?

additional_notes: Used to make polite requests. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb: “Você poderia me ajudar?” = “Could you help me?” The pronoun “me” comes before the verb (me ajudar, me ensinar, me adicionar). Often used with “por favor” to sound more courteous.
target_language_example: Você poderia me ajudar com esta mala, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you help me with this suitcase, please?

additional_notes: Uses the conditional (poderia = “could”) to make the request more polite than “você pode…”. Often used as a question, with or without “por favor”. You can add details after it: “aqui” (here), “com as louças” (with the dishes), “a carregar isso” (to carry this), etc.
target_language_example: Você poderia me ajudar a encontrar a estação, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you help me find the station, please?

additional_notes: Used to make a polite request. It’s the conditional of poder (“could”) + me dar (“give me”). Very common with a noun (“você poderia me dar um copo d’água?”) or with something abstract like time/help (“você poderia me dar mais tempo?”). In Brazil, this is polite but still fairly direct; adding “por favor” makes it even more polite.
target_language_example: Você poderia me dar uma informação, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you give me some information, please?

meaning: "Could you tell me…?" (polite request for information).
additional_notes: Common polite opener before a question. Usually followed by a question word or clause: onde (where), o caminho até… (the way to…), o que (what), qual (which/what), que horas são (what time is it), quem (who). It’s formal/polite; you can add “por favor” for extra politeness.
target_language_example: Você poderia me dizer onde fica o banheiro, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you tell me where the bathroom is, please?

meaning: “Could you tell me how…?” (polite request for directions/instructions).
additional_notes: A very polite way to ask for instructions. After **como**, you can use an infinitive (**como chegar…**) or a full clause (**como eu chego…**). Often used when asking for directions: **Você poderia me dizer como chegar a/ao…?**
target_language_example: Você poderia me dizer como chegar ao aeroporto?
native_language_example: Could you tell me how to get to the airport?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to lend you something, often money or an object. It’s conditional/polite: você (you) + poderia (could) + me (to me) + emprestar (to lend). Usually followed by the item/amount: “você poderia me emprestar X?”. In Brazil, “você” is common; for extra formality you can use “o senhor / a senhora poderia me emprestar…”.
target_language_example: Você poderia me emprestar seu carregador por um minuto?
native_language_example: Could you lend me your charger for a minute?

additional_notes: Used to make a request more polite: você (you) + poderia (could) + por favor (please). Usually followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., dizer, falar, me dizer) or by the request itself. Note: depending on tone and context, it can sound either very polite (requests for help) or sarcastic/irritated (as in “você poderia por favor se mandar?”).
target_language_example: Você poderia por favor me ajudar com isso?
native_language_example: Could you please help me with this?

additional_notes: Used to say someone needs something (usually with de: "Você precisa de..." = you need ...), or must do something (with an infinitive verb: "Você precisa + verbo" = you need to / you have to ...). In questions it can sound like "Do you really need to...?" (e.g., "Você precisa ficar falando...?"), sometimes expressing annoyance or emphasis. "Você" is the common everyday "you" in Brazil.
target_language_example: Você precisa de ajuda com isso?
native_language_example: Do you need help with that?

meaning: "you need to learn to" (you have to develop the ability/habit of doing something).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone that it’s necessary or important for them to learn how to do something, or to get used to doing it. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: "aprender a" + verb (e.g., "aprender a cozinhar", "aprender a confiar"). "Você" is the common spoken/written "you" in Brazil; it can sound a bit direct depending on tone, but it’s not slang.
target_language_example: Você precisa aprender a dizer não às vezes.
native_language_example: You need to learn to say no sometimes.

meaning: "you need" (followed by a noun or infinitive with "de").
additional_notes: Used to ask or say what someone needs. After "precisa" you normally use "de" before a noun/pronoun: "Você precisa de ajuda?" (Do you need help?). If it’s followed by a verb, you use "precisar de" + infinitive: "Você precisa de esperar" (less common) / more naturally "Você precisa esperar" (You need to wait) in many contexts.
target_language_example: Você precisa de ajuda hoje?
native_language_example: Do you need help today?

additional_notes: Used to say someone needs assistance, or (with rising intonation) to offer help as a question. Often followed by an infinitive with pra/para to say what kind of help: “Você precisa de ajuda pra carregar isso?” (Do you need help carrying this?).
target_language_example: Você precisa de ajuda para encontrar a estação?
native_language_example: Do you need help finding the station?

meaning: "you need one" / "do you need one?" (referring to a masculine singular item).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun that’s understood from context or mentioned right after. It can be a statement (Você precisa de um.) or a question (Você precisa de um?). The "um" agrees with masculine nouns (um pente, um guarda-chuva). For feminine nouns, use "uma" (Você precisa de uma cadeira?). In the examples, it's often followed by the noun: "Você precisa de um assistente?"
target_language_example: Você precisa de um bilhete para entrar?
native_language_example: Do you need a ticket to get in?

additional_notes: Used to say someone needs something. "Você" = you (formal/neutral in Brazil), "precisa" = need, and "de uma" is used before a singular feminine noun (e.g., "uma licença", "uma televisão", "uma chave"). For a masculine noun, you’d say "você precisa de um".
target_language_example: Você precisa de uma caneta para preencher este formulário.
native_language_example: You need a pen to fill out this form.

meaning: “you need to do” / “you have to do.”
additional_notes: Used to tell someone what is necessary or required. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (here, fazer = “to do/make”), and then often by an object: Você precisa fazer isso agora. In Brazilian Portuguese, “você” is common in everyday speech. Depending on context, it can sound like advice (“you need to…”) or a strong instruction (“you have to…”).
target_language_example: Você precisa fazer isso hoje.
native_language_example: You need to do that today.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone that it’s necessary to stop an action or habit. After **parar de**, use a verb in the infinitive (e.g., **parar de comer / beber / mentir / perder**). Can sound direct or critical depending on tone.
target_language_example: Você precisa parar de reclamar o tempo todo.
native_language_example: You need to stop complaining all the time.

meaning: "do you prefer" / "would you rather" (asking someone’s preference).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone what option they like better. Common in questions with two choices (e.g., X ou Y?) or with an infinitive ("você prefere trabalhar/ir..."). It can also be followed by "que" + a clause to ask what someone would rather happen ("Você prefere que...?"). "Você" is a polite/common "you" in Brazil; in Portugal people more often say "prefere" or "tu preferes" depending on formality.
target_language_example: Você prefere sentar aqui ou ali?
native_language_example: Do you prefer to sit here or there?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "pretender" with "você" to ask about someone’s intention or plan, often about the future. It’s common in questions ("Você pretende + infinitive…?") and can sound a bit formal; "você vai" is a more casual alternative in many contexts. Not related to English "pretend" (fingir).
target_language_example: Você pretende estudar português este ano?
native_language_example: Do you plan to study Portuguese this year?

additional_notes: Uses the pronoun você (“you”, formal/neutral in much of Brazil) + the verb querer (“to want”). It can state what someone wants (“Você quer mais polvo?” = “Do you want more octopus?”) or sound like an offer/request, similar to “Would you like…?”. In writing, it’s usually followed by a noun (“você quer café”) or an infinitive (“você quer comer?”).
target_language_example: Você quer um café agora?
native_language_example: Would you like a coffee now?

additional_notes: Used to ask or say that someone wants to learn something. It’s most often followed by what you want to learn (a language, a skill, etc.): “Você quer aprender inglês?” You can also use it with a verb phrase: “Você quer aprender a cozinhar?” (to learn how to cook). In Brazil, “você” is common in everyday speech; in more formal contexts you may see “o(a) senhor(a) quer aprender…”.
target_language_example: Você quer aprender português comigo?
native_language_example: Do you want to learn Portuguese with me?

meaning: “do you want to buy” / “you want to buy.”
additional_notes: Uses the informal/neutral “você” (you) with the verb “quer” (want) + infinitive “comprar” (to buy). It can be a question (“Você quer comprar…?”) or a statement (“Você quer comprar…”). Often followed by what you want to buy: “uma casa”, “um carro”, “uma camisa”.
target_language_example: Você quer comprar este carro ou aquele?
native_language_example: Do you want to buy this car or that one?

additional_notes: Used when asking for clarification or specifying what someone intends (often in questions like "O que você quer dizer?" = "What do you mean?"). It can also appear inside longer sentences: "Não sei o que você quer dizer" = "I don't know what you mean."
target_language_example: O que você quer dizer com "mais tarde"?
native_language_example: What do you mean by "later"?

meaning: "you want to do" / "do you want to do".
additional_notes: Used to ask someone what they want to do, or to check/confirm someone’s intention. In questions, Portuguese often adds words like "o que é que" or "que é que" before it: "O que é que você quer fazer?" = "What do you want to do?" In Brazilian Portuguese, "você" is common in everyday speech; in more informal contexts people may say "cê".
target_language_example: Você quer fazer alguma coisa depois do trabalho?
native_language_example: Do you want to do something after work?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone where they want to go or whether they want to go (often followed by a destination like “aonde você quer ir?” or by “com” + someone, e.g., “você quer ir conosco?”). “Você” is informal-to-neutral in many places, but in some regions (like parts of Brazil) it’s the standard everyday “you.”
target_language_example: Você quer ir ao cinema hoje?
native_language_example: Do you want to go to the movies today?

meaning: "Do you want to go to the…" / "You want to go to the…"
additional_notes: "Você" = "you" (common in Brazil). "quer" is from "querer" (to want). "ir" = to go. "para" = to/for. "a" is the feminine singular article "the" and is used before many country names (e.g., a Austrália, a Alemanha). In questions, it often appears as "Você quer ir para a [lugar]?"; in statements, "Eu sei que você quer ir para a [lugar]."
target_language_example: Você quer ir para a Itália no ano que vem?
native_language_example: Do you want to go to Italy next year?

additional_notes: Used to double-check or emphasize that you’re surprised or want to confirm someone’s intention. It’s often said with a questioning tone. You can swap in other subjects too: “Você quer mesmo…?”, “Você quer mesmo fazer isso?”
target_language_example: Você quer mesmo comprar isso agora?
native_language_example: Do you really want to buy that now?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone wants another person (or people) to do. It’s followed by a verb phrase, often in the subjunctive (e.g., "Você quer que eu ajude...?"), though in everyday speech you may also hear "Você quer que a gente vai..." where many speakers would prefer "vá".
target_language_example: Você quer que eu espere aqui?
native_language_example: Do you want me to wait here?

meaning: “Do you want me to…?” (asking what the other person wants you to do).
additional_notes: Used to ask for instructions or confirm what someone wants you to do. It’s followed by a verb in the subjunctive (eu diga, eu leia, eu entre, eu vá). Often appears in questions like “O que você quer que eu…?” or “Você quer que eu…?”
target_language_example: Você quer que eu te ajude com isso?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you with that?

meaning: “do you want me to do (it)?” / “you want me to do (it).”
additional_notes: Used to ask (or state) what someone expects you to do. Literally “you want that I do,” which is why it uses the subjunctive: você quer que eu faça… It’s often followed by a specific action, or by aquilo/isso (“that/it”), and it’s common in clarifying questions like “O que (exatamente) você quer que eu faça?”
target_language_example: Eu posso ajudar, mas primeiro me diga: o que você quer que eu faça?
native_language_example: I can help, but first tell me: what do you want me to do?

additional_notes: Used to ask what the other person wants you to do. It’s the start of a longer sentence and is followed by a verb in the present subjunctive (e.g., pegue, compre, acompanhe, conte, espere). “te” = “you” (informal singular object pronoun), so this is common when speaking to one person informally.
target_language_example: Você quer que eu te ajude com isso?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you with that?

additional_notes: Used to ask if the other person wants you to go somewhere or attend something. It often implies a destination or company, e.g., “até lá” (there), “com você/o Tom” (with you/Tom). Uses the verb "querer" (to want) + "que" + subjunctive "vá" (from "ir", to go), which is the normal structure after expressing what someone wants another person to do.
target_language_example: Você quer que eu vá agora ou mais tarde?
native_language_example: Do you want me to go now or later?

meaning: “do you want to know…?” / “would you like to know…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is interested in hearing information. Often followed by a question word (o quê/por quê/por que/quem/onde/como) or a noun phrase: “Você quer saber o porquê?” (the reason/why), “Você quer saber quem…?” (who…), “Você quer saber as boas ou as más notícias?” (the good or the bad news?). In writing, it’s normally a question: “Você quer saber…?”
target_language_example: Você quer saber a verdade?
native_language_example: Do you want to know the truth?

meaning: "Do you want to be...?" / "You want to be..."
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s desire/goal to become something or take on a role/responsibility. It’s "você" (you) + "quer" (want) + "ser" (to be). In questions, Portuguese often relies on intonation (and sometimes a question mark in writing) rather than changing word order: "Você quer ser médico?" It can also be used more rhetorically/critically depending on tone (e.g., challenging someone’s choices).
target_language_example: Você quer ser professor ou prefere trabalhar em outra área?
native_language_example: Do you want to be a teacher, or would you rather work in another field?

meaning: “do you want to see (it)?” / “would you like to watch (it)?”
additional_notes: Used to ask someone if they want to see something (an object, a photo, a translation, etc.) or to watch something (a movie, a show). Often followed by a noun ("você quer ver um filme?") or by "se" + clause ("você quer ver se..." = “do you want to check/see if...”). In everyday speech, it can also introduce a suggestion: "Você quer ver uma coisa interessante?" = “Want to see something interesting?”
target_language_example: Você quer ver a foto que eu tirei ontem?
native_language_example: Do you want to see the photo I took yesterday?

additional_notes: "Você quiser" is the present subjunctive of "querer" used after phrases like "como" (as), "quando" (when), "o que" (what), "por onde" (where/which way), etc. It’s common in polite or open-ended offers: "Como você quiser" = "However you want / As you like"; "Faça o que você quiser" = "Do whatever you want". In European Portuguese, "você" is less common; you might hear "quiser" with an implied subject or "tu quiseres".
target_language_example: Você pode ligar quando você quiser.
native_language_example: You can call whenever you want.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a question or statement to add emphasis, doubt, or surprise about what the other person did/will do/needs. In Brazilian Portuguese, "você" is common in everyday speech; "realmente" means "really / truly" and often highlights that you didn’t expect it or you want confirmation.
target_language_example: Você realmente acha que isso vai funcionar?
native_language_example: Do you really think this will work?

additional_notes: Used to question or challenge someone’s belief or assumption. Often sounds skeptical or surprised, depending on tone. In everyday speech, it’s common to drop "você": "Você realmente acha que…?" / "Realmente acha que…?"
target_language_example: Você realmente acha que ele vai chegar a tempo?
native_language_example: Do you really think he’s going to arrive on time?

additional_notes: Used to question or challenge someone’s belief/opinion. It introduces a clause after acha que (“you think that”). The final o is the masculine singular definite article (“the”) and will be followed by a masculine noun/name/title (e.g., o Tom, o carro). In speech, você is often omitted: Realmente acha que o...?
target_language_example: Você realmente acha que o professor vai aceitar isso?
native_language_example: Do you really think the teacher is going to accept this?

additional_notes: Used to question or challenge someone’s belief/assumption, often showing surprise, disbelief, or mild criticism. Follow it with a clause (often in the past): “Você realmente achou que era eu…?” = “Did you really think it was me…?”
target_language_example: Você realmente achou que eu ia esquecer do seu aniversário?
native_language_example: Did you really think I was going to forget your birthday?

additional_notes: Used to question or emphasize whether someone truly wants to do something, often showing surprise, doubt, or checking if they’re sure. Followed by an infinitive (e.g., "fazer", "ir", "ficar") or by "me dizer"/"falar" + topic.
target_language_example: Você realmente quer sair agora?
native_language_example: Do you really want to leave now?

meaning: "Do you know" / "Can you" (asking if someone knows how to do something).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to ask about someone's ability or knowledge of how to do something, typically followed by a verb in the infinitive: "Você sabe + verb?". It’s the informal/neutral "you" (common in Brazil). For formal situations, you may hear "O senhor/A senhora sabe...?".
target_language_example: Você sabe nadar?
native_language_example: Can you swim? / Do you know how to swim?

meaning: "can you speak" / "do you know how to speak" (a language).
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s ability to speak a language. It’s commonly followed by the language name ("você sabe falar francês?") or by "quais idiomas" ("which languages"). In casual speech, people also say "você fala...?")
target_language_example: Você sabe falar espanhol?
native_language_example: Can you speak Spanish?

meaning: "Do you know" / "Can you" (asking if someone knows how to do something).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to ask about someone's ability or knowledge of how to do something, typically followed by a verb in the infinitive: "Você sabe + verb?". It’s the informal/neutral "you" (common in Brazil). For formal situations, you may hear "O senhor/A senhora sabe...?".
target_language_example: Você sabe nadar?
native_language_example: Can you swim? / Do you know how to swim?

additional_notes: Used with a following clause to talk about knowing the way/method (“Você sabe como chegar…?” = “Do you know how to get…?”) or to refer to something generally understood (“…e você sabe como é a Cúria.” = “...and you know what the Curia is like.”). Often followed by an infinitive (como + verb) or by a full sentence.
target_language_example: Você sabe como eu posso pagar com cartão?
native_language_example: Do you know how I can pay by card?

additional_notes: Used with a following clause to talk about knowing the way/method (“Você sabe como chegar…?” = “Do you know how to get…?”) or to refer to something generally understood (“…e você sabe como é a Cúria.” = “...and you know what the Curia is like.”). Often followed by an infinitive (como + verb) or by a full sentence.
target_language_example: Você sabe como eu posso pagar com cartão?
native_language_example: Do you know how I can pay by card?

additional_notes: Used to state or check that the other person already knows some information. Often appears with emphasis (e.g., “Eu sei que você sabe disso.” = “I know you know that.”) or as a tag question (“Você sabe disso, não sabe?” = “You know that, don’t you?”). “Disso” refers to “about that/that thing” mentioned in context.
target_language_example: Você sabe disso, então por que está perguntando de novo?
native_language_example: You know that, so why are you asking again?

additional_notes: Used with "você" (“you”) + "saber" (“to know”) + the article "o" (“the”, masculine singular). Often starts a question asking if someone knows a specific piece of information: "Você sabe o endereço?" (“Do you know the address?”). It can also introduce things like "quanto" (“how much”): "Você sabe o quanto…" (“You know how much…”). The noun after "o" may change to "a/os/as" depending on gender/number (e.g., "Você sabe a data?").
target_language_example: Você sabe o nome dele?
native_language_example: Do you know his name?

meaning: 'Do you know what…' (asking if someone knows something).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question after “what” (o que). It’s a common way to ask for information politely/neutral, often followed by a verb phrase: “Você sabe o que precisa trazer?” = “Do you know what you need to bring?” In Brazilian Portuguese it’s common; in European Portuguese you may also hear “Você sabe o que é que…?” or more informal “Sabe o que…?”
target_language_example: Você sabe o que ele quer dizer?
native_language_example: Do you know what he means?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone knows what occurred. It can also be used rhetorically to introduce the result of a story (“…and you know what happened.”). Common variations: “Você sabe o que aconteceu com…?” (to/with someone/something), “Você sabe o que aconteceu aqui…?” (in a place), “Você sabe o que aconteceu?” (general).
target_language_example: Você sabe o que aconteceu ontem à noite?
native_language_example: Do you know what happened last night?

você sabe o que eu quero

target_language_multi_word_term: você sabe o que eu quero
additional_notes: Used to say the listener already understands your preference/need, or to emphasize that what you want should be clear. Often followed by more detail (e.g., “...que você faça” = “...you to do”). As a question (“Você sabe o que eu quero?”) it can be a real question or a rhetorical/challenging one depending on tone.
target_language_example: Você sabe o que eu quero: uma resposta clara.
native_language_example: You know what I want: a clear answer.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question about a location. It can be a question (often with a question mark) or a statement. Commonly followed by a full clause: “Você sabe onde + subject + verb…?” In Brazil, “você” is common in everyday speech; in more formal contexts you may hear “o senhor/a senhora sabe onde…?”
target_language_example: Você sabe onde fica a estação de metrô?
native_language_example: Do you know where the subway station is?

meaning: “Do you know where it is?” / “You know where it is.”
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone knows the location of something (often followed by the item: “Você sabe onde está minha chave?”). It can also be said as a statement (“Você sabe onde está o problema.” = “You know where the problem is.”). Without an object, it can mean “Do you know where you are?” (talking about someone’s location or orientation).
target_language_example: Você sabe onde está o banheiro?
native_language_example: Do you know where the bathroom is?

meaning: "Do you know why the…" / "Do you know why…" (introduces a question about the reason for something).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone knows the reason for something: "Você sabe por que…?". Here, "por que" means "why" in a direct question. The "o" is the masculine definite article ("the") and can appear before masculine nouns ("o ônibus") and, especially in Brazilian Portuguese, sometimes before masculine names ("o Tom").
target_language_example: Você sabe por que o ônibus está atrasado?
native_language_example: Do you know why the bus is late?

additional_notes: Used to remind or emphasize information the speaker assumes the listener already knows. Often followed by a full clause: “Você sabe que + [sentence]”. In speech it can also introduce a reason or justification (similar to “you know, …”).
target_language_example: Você sabe que eu não posso ficar até tarde.
native_language_example: You know I can’t stay late.

additional_notes: Used to ask for the identity of a person. It’s typically followed by a verb in the past or present: "Você sabe quem disse isso?" (who said it), "Você sabe quem inventou...?" (who invented...); it can also be used in a more personal/rhetorical question like "Você sabe quem você é?" (“Do you know who you are?”). Often implies you expect the other person might know (or that you’re about to tell them).
target_language_example: Você sabe quem me ligou ontem à noite?
native_language_example: Do you know who called me last night?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone recognizes or knows a person’s identity. It’s often followed by a person or pronoun (e.g., “aquela pessoa”, “aquele cara”, “ele/ela”). It can also be said on its own (“Você sabe quem é.”) meaning “You know who it is,” usually implying the other person should recognize them from context.
target_language_example: Você sabe quem é a mulher que está falando com o João?
native_language_example: Do you know who the woman talking to João is?

meaning: “do you know about …?” / “you know about …” (to have knowledge about a topic).
additional_notes: Used to ask or state what someone knows about a subject. It’s made of "você" (you) + "sabe" (know) + "sobre" (about). In questions, Portuguese often adds emphasis with "o que (é que)" (what) or "quanto" (how much): "O que você sabe sobre…?" / "Quanto você sabe sobre…?". You can swap "você" for "tu" in some regions: "Tu sabes sobre…?".
target_language_example: Você sabe sobre algum restaurante bom aqui perto?
native_language_example: Do you know about any good restaurant near here?

additional_notes: Used to introduce information or a question about whether the listener already knew something. Very common in conversation; can sound like you’re about to share a fact or surprising detail. Can be followed by a statement in the past or present: "Você sabia que ele é/era…?"
target_language_example: Você sabia que o restaurante fecha às segundas-feiras?
native_language_example: Did you know that the restaurant is closed on Mondays?

meaning: “Did you know that…?” (introduces a fact; “o” = “the” for a masculine noun/name).
additional_notes: Used to introduce surprising or interesting information. Grammatically it’s "você sabia" (you knew) but in questions it usually means “did you know…?”. The "o" is the masculine singular article (“the”): você sabia que o Tom… / você sabia que o carro… For feminine use "a" (você sabia que a Maria…), plural "os/as".
target_language_example: Você sabia que o Paulo fala japonês?
native_language_example: Did you know that Paulo speaks Japanese?

additional_notes: Used when the subject (você = you) is also the object of the verb. It commonly appears with reflexive/pronominal verbs like deitar-se (to lie down), lembrar-se (to remember), vestir-se (to get dressed). In English, the reflexive idea is sometimes translated with “yourself,” but often it’s just understood (e.g., “Remember this”).
target_language_example: Quero que você se sente aqui.
native_language_example: I want you to sit down here.

meaning: 'do you consider yourself…?' / 'would you say you are…?'
additional_notes: Used to ask someone how they see themselves or how they would describe themselves (age, personality, identity, abilities, etc.). It’s the verb "considerar" with the reflexive pronoun "se" (yourself). Often followed by an adjective (jovem, sortudo/a) or a noun phrase (um homem perigoso).
target_language_example: Você se considera uma pessoa paciente?
native_language_example: Do you consider yourself a patient person?

additional_notes: Used to ask politely if something would bother someone: "Você se importa em + infinitive?" (Do you mind + -ing?) or "Você se importa que + subjunctive?" (Do you mind if ...?). It can also mean "to care (about)": "Você se importa com ...?" (Do you care about ...?).
target_language_example: Você se importa se eu sentar aqui?
native_language_example: Do you mind if I sit here?

você se importa com o que

target_language_multi_word_term: você se importa com o que
meaning: “Do you care about what …?” / “Do you mind what …?”
additional_notes: Used to ask (sometimes rhetorically) whether someone cares about something, usually followed by a clause with a verb: “o que acontece” (what happens), “o que (as pessoas) pensam” (what people think), etc. Note: “se importar (com)” means “to care (about)” or “to mind,” and it does not mean “to import.”
target_language_example: Você se importa com o que eles vão dizer?
native_language_example: Do you care what they’re going to say?

additional_notes: Polite way to ask permission. It’s usually followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., abrir, estacionar, fumar) or sometimes in the subjunctive (especially in more formal Brazilian Portuguese): “Você se importa se eu abra…?”. A common, slightly less formal alternative is “Você se incomoda se eu…?”.
target_language_example: Você se importa se eu sentar aqui?
native_language_example: Do you mind if I sit here?

additional_notes: Used to make a polite request, often when asking someone to do something for you. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., “falar”, “me dizer”, “recusar”, “traduzir”). You can answer politely with “Não, claro” / “Não, tudo bem” (“No, not at all”) to mean you don’t mind.
target_language_example: Você se importaria de fechar a janela, por favor?
native_language_example: Would you mind closing the window, please?

additional_notes: Used to make a very polite request. It’s usually followed by a verb in the infinitive (often with the preposition em), e.g., "você se importaria em fechar..." = "would you mind closing...". You can answer with "Não, claro" (No, of course) to mean you don’t mind.
target_language_example: Você se importaria em falar mais devagar?
native_language_example: Would you mind speaking more slowly?

meaning: “Would you mind if I…?” (polite request for permission).
additional_notes: Used to ask politely whether the other person would object to you doing something. It’s typically followed by a verb in the past subjunctive (e.g., abrisse, desse, esperasse, fizesse, saísse). Often interchangeable with “Você se importa se eu…?” (a bit more direct).
target_language_example: Você se importaria se eu usasse o seu celular por um minuto?
native_language_example: Would you mind if I used your phone for a minute?

additional_notes: Polite way to ask permission or check if something will bother the other person. Follow it with a verb in the infinitive (e.g., abrir, fazer, ligar, mudar) or a present-tense verb (e.g., eu me sento). You can also say “Você se importa se eu…?” with the same meaning. Often answered with “Não, pode.” (“No, go ahead.”) or “Sim, me incomodo.” (“Yes, I do mind.”).
target_language_example: Você se incomoda se eu fechar a porta?
native_language_example: Do you mind if I close the door?

additional_notes: From the verb lembrar-se de (“to remember”). It’s commonly followed by de/da/do/dos/das + noun/pronoun: Você se lembra de mim? (“Do you remember me?”). It can also be followed by a clause with what/which/when, etc., often without de: Você se lembra qual foi…? (“Do you remember which/what…?”).
target_language_example: Você se lembra do meu nome?
native_language_example: Do you remember my name?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone remembers something. It’s the verb phrase “(você) lembrar-se de” and it is followed by **de** + a noun, pronoun, or clause: *Você se lembra de nós?* / *Você se lembra de quando…?* In more informal speech, people often drop **se**: *Você lembra de…?*
target_language_example: Você se lembra de onde a gente se conheceu?
native_language_example: Do you remember where we met?

meaning: “do you remember …?” / “do you recall …?” (about a masculine noun or “what …”).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone remembers something. It comes from the verb "lembrar-se" (to remember) and is very common in conversation. "do" = "de" + "o" and is used before masculine nouns (do nome, do número) and also before "que" in "do que" (você se lembra do que aconteceu?). For feminine nouns, it changes to "da" (de + a): "Você se lembra da data?".
target_language_example: Você se lembra do endereço do hotel?
native_language_example: Do you remember the hotel’s address?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone if they remember a person’s (or thing’s) name. "se lembrar de" means “to remember,” and it requires "de" (often contracted: de + o = do; de + a = da). You can add what name you mean with "do/da nome de...": "Você se lembra do nome da sua professora?"
target_language_example: Você se lembra do nome daquele restaurante perto da praia?
native_language_example: Do you remember the name of that restaurant near the beach?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone remembers the content of something said or promised. It’s made of: você (you) + se lembra (remember) + de + o que (what/that which), often followed by a verb like disse (said) or prometeu (promised). In speech, "do que" can sound like "du quê".
target_language_example: Você se lembra do que aconteceu ontem à noite?
native_language_example: Do you remember what happened last night?

meaning: “did you remember to…?” / “did you remember about…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone remembered to do something (often a task or precaution). It’s the verb "lembrar-se de" (to remember), in the past: "você se lembrou de + infinitive" (e.g., fechar, ligar, trazer). You can also use it with "ter + past participle" ("você se lembrou de ter apagado…") to ask if they remember having done something. In Brazil, "você" is common; in Portugal, you might hear "tu te lembraste de".
target_language_example: Você se lembrou de comprar pão?
native_language_example: Did you remember to buy bread?

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb *sentir-se* (“to feel”). The *se* is part of the verb (not “feel someone else”): *você se sente bem?* = “do you feel well?”. Often followed by an adjective or phrase: *sortudo* (lucky), *melhor* (better), *cansado* (tired). You can change the subject: *eu me sinto…* (I feel…), *a gente se sente…* (we feel…).
target_language_example: Você se sente pronto para começar?
native_language_example: Do you feel ready to start?

additional_notes: Used to include the person you’re talking to in something (“you as well”). Often adds emphasis or comparison: "Eu consigo, e você também" (“I can, and you can too”). Word order can vary: "Você também..." (You also...), or "...você também" (…you too/as well).
target_language_example: Eu vou amanhã, e você também pode ir.
native_language_example: I’m going tomorrow, and you can go too.

additional_notes: Used with você to ask or state what someone possesses, has available, or has as a situation/condition (e.g., compromissos, namorado/a). In Brazil, você is common in everyday speech; the verb is in 3rd-person singular: você tem (not *você tens*). Often used in questions: Você tem...?, Quantos... você tem?
target_language_example: Você tem tempo agora?
native_language_example: Do you have time now?

meaning: “Do you have any …?” (asking if someone has something; singular).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has at least one of an item. It’s followed by a singular noun: “Você tem algum livro…?” (any book). For feminine nouns, use “alguma” (Você tem alguma ideia?). In the plural, use “alguns/algumas” when you mean “some.” In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, “Você tem…?” is common; in Portugal, “Tem…?” or “Você tem…?” may vary by region/context.
target_language_example: Você tem algum carregador de celular?
native_language_example: Do you have any phone charger?

meaning: “do you have any … ?” (with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has any of something. It normally needs a noun right after it (e.g., alguma dúvida, alguma notícia, alguma informação). Use **algum** (masculine) instead with masculine nouns: *você tem algum problema?*
target_language_example: Você tem alguma pergunta?
native_language_example: Do you have any questions?

meaning: “Do you have something to…?” / “Do you have anything for…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has an item, remedy, or tool for a purpose, or if they have something (news/info) to say. Typically followed by an infinitive (e.g., dizer, fazer, quebrar) or by a noun situation (e.g., para gripe = for the flu). In speech, it’s often shortened to “Tem alguma coisa pra…?”
target_language_example: Você tem alguma coisa para abrir esta garrafa?
native_language_example: Do you have something to open this bottle?

meaning: "Do you have any idea…?" (asking if someone knows or can suggest something).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone knows something, has a guess, or can propose a solution/suggestion. Very common in questions, often followed by "de" + a question word (e.g., "de quem", "de onde", "de como") or "sobre" ("about"). Can also be used to ask for a better option: "Você tem alguma ideia melhor?"
target_language_example: Você tem alguma ideia de como resolver esse problema?
native_language_example: Do you have any idea how to solve this problem?

você tem alguma ideia do que

target_language_multi_word_term: você tem alguma ideia do que
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone knows (or can guess) what something is, what will happen, or what someone wants to do. Very common in conversation; often followed by a clause with a verb (e.g., "... do que ele quer"), or by "... do que é isto". You can make it more informal by using "cê" instead of "você" in speech.
target_language_example: Você tem alguma ideia do que está acontecendo aqui?
native_language_example: Do you have any idea what's happening here?

additional_notes:
Used to confirm that someone is sure about a fact, decision, or what they said. It can be followed by:
- "de que..." + clause: "Você tem certeza de que foi ele?" (Are you sure it was him?)
- "de" + noun/pronoun: "Você tem certeza disso?" (Are you sure about that?)
In questions, it’s often said just as "Você tem certeza?" You can add emphasis with "absoluta": "Você tem certeza absoluta?"
target_language_example: Você tem certeza de que quer ir embora agora?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to leave now?

additional_notes: Used to check or challenge whether someone is certain about a fact or decision. In speech, it’s often shortened to "Tem certeza de que...?" or "Tem certeza que...?" (informal). The part "de que" introduces the clause that follows (what you’re asking about).
target_language_example: Você tem certeza de que quer sair agora?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to leave now?

você tem certeza de que o

target_language_multi_word_term: você tem certeza de que o
additional_notes: Used to ask for confirmation about something. It’s the start of a longer sentence: "Você tem certeza de que..." = "Are you sure that...". "o" is the masculine singular article (“the”) and often comes before a male name/title ("o Tom" = "Tom") or a masculine noun; with a female name/noun you’d use "a" ("Você tem certeza de que a Maria...?").
target_language_example: Você tem certeza de que o ônibus passa aqui?
native_language_example: Are you sure the bus stops here?

você tem certeza de que quer

target_language_multi_word_term: você tem certeza de que quer
additional_notes: Used to check or confirm someone’s decision before they do something. It’s a polite but direct way to ask if they really want to proceed. Often followed by an infinitive verb (fazer, esperar, sair, etc.). You can also hear a shorter version: "Tem certeza que quer...?"
target_language_example: Você tem certeza de que quer cancelar a reserva?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to cancel the reservation?

additional_notes: Used to ask for confirmation about something the other person believes or said. In writing and more formal Portuguese, you may also see "Você tem certeza de que..."; in everyday speech, "que" is very common. Can also be phrased as "Tem certeza que...?" (dropping "você") in informal conversation.
target_language_example: Você tem certeza que quer sair agora?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to leave now?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is required to do something. It’s followed by a verb in the infinitive: “você tem de + infinitive” (e.g., você tem de estudar). In everyday speech, many people also say “você tem que …”, which usually means the same thing.
target_language_example: Você tem de sair agora.
native_language_example: You have to leave now.

meaning: 'you have to do' / 'you need to do'.
additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity. It's common before another verb in the infinitive: "Você tem de + infinitive" (also often said as "você tem que + infinitive"). In questions it often appears as "O que você tem de fazer?" = "What do you have to do?"
target_language_example: Você tem de fazer isso hoje.
native_language_example: You have to do that today.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone a requirement or strong necessity. It’s formed with "ter de" (to have to) + "ser" (to be), and is followed by an adjective or noun: "Você tem de ser + [adjective/noun]". In speech, "tem de" is often pronounced like "tem que" (and many people also write "tem que").
target_language_example: Para conseguir esse trabalho, você tem de ser pontual.
native_language_example: To get this job, you have to be punctual.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone what they’re scared of. It’s followed by a noun or activity: você tem medo de cães? (dogs), de ratos? (rats), de voar? (flying). In everyday speech you’ll also hear the shorter form: Você tem medo de quê? ('What are you afraid of?').
target_language_example: Você tem medo de voar?
native_language_example: Are you afraid of flying?

meaning: "you have the right to" (you are allowed/entitled to).
additional_notes: Used to state someone’s legal or formal entitlement to do something. Very common in rules, contracts, customer service, and legal contexts (e.g., "Você tem o direito de permanecer em silêncio" = "You have the right to remain silent"). It is followed by an infinitive verb: "direito de" + verb (cancelar, negar, permanecer, etc.).
target_language_example: Você tem o direito de pedir um reembolso em até 7 dias.
native_language_example: You have the right to request a refund within 7 days.

meaning: "you have to" / "you must" (you are required to).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone is obligated or needs to do something. Very common in spoken Portuguese. It’s followed by a verb in the infinitive: "você tem que + verb" (e.g., "você tem que falar"). In speech it’s often reduced to "cê tem que". Negative: "você não tem que..." (you don’t have to...).
target_language_example: Você tem que chegar cedo amanhã.
native_language_example: You have to arrive early tomorrow.

meaning: "you have to do" (you must do it).
additional_notes: Used to express obligation/necessity. It’s built from the verb phrase "ter que" (to have to) + an infinitive: "você tem que" + "fazer". It can sound firm/strong, like giving an instruction. In questions it often means “what do you need to do?”
target_language_example: Você tem que fazer isso hoje.
native_language_example: You have to do this today.

meaning: “you have to do this” / “you need to do this.”
additional_notes: Used to say someone is required or expected to do something. It can sound like an instruction/order depending on tone (e.g., “Goste ou não, você tem que fazer isso” = “Whether you like it or not, you have to do it”). In questions (“Você tem que fazer isso?”), it asks if it’s necessary. Common variants: “você tem que” + verb (you have to…), “tem que” (more casual/impersonal), and stronger “você precisa” (you need).
target_language_example: Desculpa, mas você tem que fazer isso hoje.
native_language_example: Sorry, but you have to do this today.

meaning: "you have to go" / "you need to go".
additional_notes: Used to say someone is required or expected to leave or go somewhere. It can refer to leaving now ("Você tem que ir agora"), going to do something ("você tem que ir falar com ele" = you have to go talk to him), or going somewhere specific ("você tem que ir para fora" = you have to go outside). In speech it’s often shortened to "cê tem que ir" (informal pronunciation).
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu estou atrasado — você tem que ir comigo agora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm late — you have to go with me now.

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has something (often with a question mark/intonation): "Você tem um cartão?" = "Do you have a card?" It can also be a statement: "Você tem um coração de pedra." = "You have a heart of stone." The article changes with gender/number: um (masc. singular), uma (fem. singular), uns/umas (plural).
target_language_example: Você tem um carregador de celular?
native_language_example: Do you have a phone charger?

meaning: “do you have a…?” / “you have a…” (with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask or state possession/availability. In questions it often sounds like “Do you have a…?” and is commonly followed by a noun: “Você tem uma agulha?” = “Do you have a needle?” Use **uma** before feminine nouns; use **um** before masculine nouns (e.g., “você tem um carro?”). In Brazilian Portuguese, **você** is a common everyday “you.”
target_language_example: Você tem uma caneta que eu possa usar?
native_language_example: Do you have a pen I can use?

meaning: “you had said that…” / “you told me that…”
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something the other person said earlier. It's the past perfect of dizer (to say/tell): você tinha dito… Often used when you’re surprised, correcting a misunderstanding, or reminding someone of their earlier statement. In casual speech, Brazilians also commonly use “você tinha falado que…”.
target_language_example: Mas você tinha dito que ia chegar cedo!
native_language_example: But you had said you were going to arrive early!

additional_notes: Literally “you go,” but it’s most often used as the start of the near-future (ir + infinitive): “Você vai + verb” = “You’re going to + verb.” In questions, it can mean “Are you going to…?” / “Will you…?” Depending on tone, it can sound like a simple plan (“Você vai falar…?”) or a strong command/threat (“Você vai pagar…” = “You’ll pay…”). Often pronounced casually as “cê vai” in Brazil.
target_language_example: Você vai sair hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Are you going out tonight?

meaning: “what are you going to do?” / “you are going to do (it)”
additional_notes: Common future-with-ir structure: "você vai" (you’re going to) + infinitive "fazer" (do/make). Used in questions like "O que você vai fazer?" (What are you going to do?) and in statements like "Você vai fazer isso amanhã." (You’re going to do it tomorrow.). In the examples, "Que diabos..." adds anger/surprise like “what the hell…?”—more informal and strong.
target_language_example: O que você vai fazer depois do trabalho?
native_language_example: What are you going to do after work?

meaning: “you’re going to stay” / “you’ll be” / “you’ll end up (becoming)” (future with ficar).
additional_notes: Used with **ficar** to talk about what someone will do or what state they will be in. Common meanings: **stay/remain somewhere** (often with time: “Quantas noites…?”), **stay/keep doing something** (“ficar aí parado”, “ficar deitado”), and **become a state/condition** (“ficar com frio”, “ficar sem ar”). The tone depends on context and can sound like a real question, a warning, or mild criticism.
target_language_example: Se você não descansar, você vai ficar doente.
native_language_example: If you don’t rest, you’ll get sick.

meaning: "you are going to (do something) to/for me" / "you will (do something) to/for me".
additional_notes: Used with a verb right after it to talk about what someone is going to do involving you: "Você vai me + VERB" (e.g., "falar", "apresentar", "ajudar"). It’s the common near-future in Portuguese ("ir" + infinitive). In questions, it often implies a request or expectation ("Você vai me dar uma mão?" = "Will you give me a hand?").
target_language_example: Você vai me ajudar amanhã?
native_language_example: Are you going to help me tomorrow?

meaning: "you are going to" / "you will" (used before a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: This is the start of a future expression with the subject "você" (you) + "vai" (is going to/will) + "se", which is a reflexive pronoun. It must be followed by a verb, especially a reflexive verb like "recuperar-se" (to recover), "encontrar-se" (to meet / to meet up), or in the expression "ver-se com alguém" (to have to deal with someone / face someone). In everyday Portuguese, "você vai se + infinitive" is very common for talking about the near future.
target_language_example: Você vai se atrasar se não sair agora.
native_language_example: You're going to be late if you don't leave now.

additional_notes: Literally “you go,” but it’s most often used as the start of the near-future (ir + infinitive): “Você vai + verb” = “You’re going to + verb.” In questions, it can mean “Are you going to…?” / “Will you…?” Depending on tone, it can sound like a simple plan (“Você vai falar…?”) or a strong command/threat (“Você vai pagar…” = “You’ll pay…”). Often pronounced casually as “cê vai” in Brazil.
target_language_example: Você vai sair hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Are you going out tonight?

additional_notes: Used to ask or say that someone came/arrived, often with questions like "De onde você veio?" (Where did you come from?) or "Com quem você veio?" (Who did you come with?). In Brazilian Portuguese, "você" is common and neutral; "veio" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito).
target_language_example: Você veio de ônibus ou de carro?
native_language_example: Did you come by bus or by car?

additional_notes: From the verb "ver" (to see) in the simple past (pretérito perfeito): "você viu" = "you saw". In questions it often means "did you see...?" and can also be used like "have you seen...?" when asking if someone noticed something or saw someone/something earlier (e.g., a missing item). The subject "você" is often optional in Portuguese: you may also hear just "viu?".
target_language_example: Você viu minhas chaves em algum lugar?
native_language_example: Did you see my keys anywhere?

meaning: "did you see the...?" / "have you seen the...?" (also: "you saw the").
additional_notes: Uses the past tense of *ver* (to see): *você viu* = “you saw” / “you have seen.” With rising intonation or a question mark, it’s a common way to ask if someone saw something or someone. *o* is the masculine singular “the”; for feminine use *a* (*você viu a...*), and for plural use *os/as* (*você viu os/as...*).
target_language_example: Você viu o meu celular em algum lugar?
native_language_example: Have you seen my cellphone anywhere?

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ser** to describe identity, roles, or characteristics: *Você é especial* (“You are special”). Even though it means “you,” **você** takes the **third-person singular** form: **você é** (not *você és*). It can be used in statements or questions: *Você é estudante...?* (“Are you a student...?”).
target_language_example: Você é muito gentil.
native_language_example: You are very kind.

meaning: “You are very … / You’re too …” (before an adjective).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective to comment on someone’s qualities or behavior: Você é muito + adjective (pequeno, apertado, mentiroso, rígido, etc.). Often sounds critical depending on the adjective and tone. For “very” with nouns, Portuguese usually uses “você é muito + noun” (e.g., “Você é muito paciente.”).
target_language_example: Você é muito impaciente comigo.
native_language_example: You’re very impatient with me.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun/title to identify someone: Você é o espião. In questions, intonation (or a question mark in writing) makes it “Are you the…?”. For feminine, use “você é a…”, and for plural “vocês são os/as…”. “Você” is commonly used as “you” in Brazil and usually takes 3rd-person verb forms like “é”.
target_language_example: Você é o novo gerente?
native_language_example: Are you the new manager?

você é o único que pode

target_language_multi_word_term: você é o único que pode
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that only the person you’re talking to is capable of doing something. Usually followed by an infinitive verb (impedir, ajudar, proteger, salvar, etc.). Note agreement: for a woman, say “você é a única que pode”. You can also replace “você” with a name or “ele/ela” (e.g., “Ela é a única que pode…”).
target_language_example: Você é o único que pode resolver isso hoje.
native_language_example: You’re the only one who can solve this today.

meaning: “you are so …” (used to intensify an adjective).
additional_notes: Used before an adjective to emphasize a quality: Você é tão gentil. Often shows strong emotion and is common with exclamations (e.g., Que chato! Você é tão irritante!). In comparisons it can appear as “tão … quanto” (“as … as”): Você é tão alto quanto ele. Note: “você” is common in Brazil; in Portugal you may hear “tu és tão …”.
target_language_example: Você é tão engraçado!
native_language_example: You’re so funny!

meaning: "you are a" (used before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "ser" (é = "are/is") to identify or describe what someone/something is. "Um" is the masculine singular indefinite article; with feminine nouns, use "você é uma". Often followed by a noun (e.g., profissão, animal, tipo de pessoa).
target_language_example: Você é um estudante?
native_language_example: Are you a student?

meaning: “you are a good …” (used before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to compliment or describe someone’s ability or qualities, followed by a noun: “Você é um bom dançarino/jogador/tenista.” It must agree with the noun: bom (masc. singular), boa (fem. singular: “Você é uma boa dançarina.”), bons/boas (plural). Often also appears with “um/uma”: “Você é um/uma bom/boa …”.
target_language_example: Você é um bom cozinheiro!
native_language_example: You’re a good cook!

additional_notes: Used to ask for the opinion/guess of a group (2+ people). Literally "you (plural) think that". In Brazil, "vocês" is the normal plural "you"; in Portugal it can sound more informal (often "vocês" with 3rd-person plural verbs, as here: "acham"). You can also use it for predictions: "Vocês acham que vai chover?"
target_language_example: Vocês acham que vale a pena tentar de novo?
native_language_example: Do you all think it’s worth trying again?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people for their opinion or guess. "Vocês" = plural "you" (common in Brazil). "Acham" is from "achar" (to think/to find). "Que" = "that", and "o" is "the" (masculine singular), typically followed by a masculine noun or a man’s name (e.g., "o Tom").
target_language_example: Vocês acham que o professor vai chegar atrasado?
native_language_example: Do you all think the teacher is going to arrive late?

additional_notes: Used with the plural “you” (vocês) plus “still” (ainda) and the verb “to be” (estão).
