It’s commonly used to ask if a situation continues: “Vocês ainda estão com pressa?” (still in a hurry), “confusos?” (still confused), “em casa?” (still at home). You can follow it with an adjective (confusos), a prepositional phrase (em casa), or “com + noun” (com pressa).
target_language_example: Vocês ainda estão prontos para sair?
native_language_example: Are you still ready to go out?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to two or more people. "Vocês" = "you all" (common in Brazil); "compraram" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "comprar" for "vocês". Often used in questions about what/where/when/why someone bought something.
target_language_example: Vocês compraram tudo o que precisavam?
native_language_example: Did you all buy everything you needed?

additional_notes: Used to give advice, make a recommendation, or say what is expected for a group (“vocês” = you plural). It’s the conditional of “dever” and often sounds like a polite suggestion, but depending on context can also be a strong criticism (e.g., “Vocês deveriam ter visto” = “You should have seen (it)”). Common patterns: “vocês deveriam + infinitive” (Vocês deveriam ir) and “vocês deveriam ter + past participle” (Vocês deveriam ter visto).
target_language_example: Vocês deveriam falar com o professor antes da prova.
native_language_example: You (all) should talk to the teacher before the test.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to exactly two people. It’s the plural “you” (vocês) + “two” (dois). You can also say “vocês duas” when speaking to two women/girls.
target_language_example: Vocês dois podem me ajudar, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you two help me, please?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to two people at once (common in Brazil). "vocês" = "you" (plural), "dois" = "two" (can also be "duas" for two females), and "estão" is the verb "estar" for "you (plural) are," often followed by an adjective ("estão bem") or "com" + noun to talk about a state/feeling ("estão com fome").
target_language_example: Vocês dois estão prontos para sair?
native_language_example: Are you two ready to leave?

additional_notes: Used when addressing exactly two people together: "vocês" = you (plural), "dois" = two, and "são" = are (present of "ser"). Common for asking questions or making statements about them as a pair (e.g., a couple, friends). In European Portuguese, people often use "vocês os dois são" or "vocês os dois" for emphasis.
target_language_example: Vocês dois são muito simpáticos!
native_language_example: You two are very nice!

meaning: “you (plural) were / you (plural) were being” (imperfect past of *estar*).
additional_notes: Used with **vocês** to talk about an ongoing state, feeling, or action in the past (“you all were … / you guys were …”). Common patterns: **vocês estavam + adjective** (Vocês estavam assustadas. = You were scared.), **vocês estavam com + noun** (Vocês estavam com ciúmes? = Were you jealous?), **vocês estavam + verb (gerund)** (Vocês estavam tentando fugir? = Were you trying to escape?). In Brazil, **vocês** is the usual plural “you”; the verb stays in **3rd-person plural** (estavam).
target_language_example: Vocês estavam esperando há muito tempo?
native_language_example: Were you all waiting for a long time?

additional_notes: Used with "vocês" (you all) + "estão" (are) to talk about the current state, condition, or ongoing actions of a group of people. Common with adjectives ("Vocês estão bem?" = Are you all okay?) or with a verb in the gerund to mean "are ...-ing" ("Vocês estão tentando" = You all are trying). In Brazil, "vocês" is the usual plural "you".
target_language_example: Vocês estão prontos para sair?
native_language_example: Are you all ready to leave?

meaning: “you (plural) are with / have” (used to say you’re experiencing/feeling something).
additional_notes: In Brazilian Portuguese, estar com + noun is very common to talk about temporary states, feelings, or conditions: estar com medo (to be afraid), estar com diarreia (to have diarrhea), estar com saudade(s) de alguém (to miss someone), estar com sorte (to be lucky). It’s addressed to a group: vocês = “you all”. Often followed by a noun or noun phrase.
target_language_example: Vocês estão com fome ou querem comer mais tarde?
native_language_example: Are you all hungry, or do you want to eat later?

additional_notes: Used when addressing more than one person (vocês) and describing an action in progress (estão + -ndo). Very common in questions like “Com quem vocês estão falando?” (Who are you talking to?) and “Do que vocês estão falando?” (What are you talking about?). Often followed by de (“about”) or com (“with/to”).
target_language_example: Eu não entendi—do que vocês estão falando?
native_language_example: I didn’t understand—what are you talking about?

additional_notes: Used when talking to more than one person. In Brazil, "vocês" is the most common way to say "you" (plural) in everyday speech and it uses 3rd-person plural verb forms like "falam". Often followed by a language or topic: "Vocês falam inglês?"
target_language_example: Vocês falam português em casa?
native_language_example: Do you speak Portuguese at home?

additional_notes: "Vocês" is an informal/neutral way to say “you all” in Brazilian Portuguese (it uses 3rd‑person plural verb forms). "Fizeram" is the past (pretérito perfeito) of "fazer". It can mean “did” (actions: Vocês fizeram reserva? = Did you book/reserve?) or “made” (made peace: Vocês fizeram as pazes? = Did you make up?). Often used to talk about something completed in the past.
target_language_example: Obrigado! Vocês fizeram um ótimo trabalho.
native_language_example: Thank you! You did a great job.

additional_notes: Used to accuse or confront a group (“you all”) about something they caused or did. In Brazil, "vocês" is the common informal-plural "you" (often used even in neutral situations), and "fizeram" is past tense of "fazer". Often followed by "comigo" (to me/against me) or "para mim" (for me).
target_language_example: Por que vocês fizeram isso?
native_language_example: Why did you (all) do this?

additional_notes: Used with the verb gostar (“to like”) when talking to more than one person. It normally takes de + noun/pronoun: vocês gostam de chocolate; with articles it contracts: de + o = do (vocês gostam do meu anel?), de + a = da, de + os = dos, de + as = das. Common in questions: Do que vocês gostam? / De que vocês gostam mais?
target_language_example: Vocês gostam de música brasileira?
native_language_example: Do you all like Brazilian music?

additional_notes: Used with vocês (“you all”) + gostar (“to like”) and usually followed by de + a verb in the infinitive (gostam de trabalhar = like working) or a noun/thing (gostam de queijo = like cheese). Common in questions (Vocês gostam de…?) and statements (Vocês gostam de…). In European Portuguese, the plural “you” is often vocês too, but the verb form may vary by region/register.
target_language_example: Vocês gostam de viajar nas férias?
native_language_example: Do you all like to travel on vacation?

additional_notes: Polite way to ask a group of people what they would like to do or have. Use it before a verb in the infinitive (e.g., "vocês gostariam de entrar?") or before a noun (e.g., "vocês gostariam de café?"). In Brazil, many speakers often use "vocês gostariam de" even when addressing one person, but it’s still grammatically plural.
target_language_example: Vocês gostariam de pedir sobremesa?
native_language_example: Would you like to order dessert?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (vocês = “you” plural) whether something has happened/been done already. Often followed by a verb in the past (e.g., já ligaram? “have you called yet?”) or with estar + adjective/state (já estão com sono? “are you already sleepy?”). In questions, English often uses “already” or “yet” depending on context.
target_language_example: Vocês já terminaram o trabalho?
native_language_example: Have you all finished the work yet?

meaning: “Have you (all) already eaten?” / “Have you (all) eaten (it) yet?”
additional_notes: Used when speaking to a group (“vocês” = you all). “já” adds the idea of “already/yet,” often in questions about whether something has happened up to now. You can use it by itself to ask if people have eaten (“Vocês já comeram?”), or add what was eaten: “Vocês já comeram o bolo?” (the cake), “Vocês já comeram este prato?” (this dish). In Brazilian Portuguese, “vocês” is the normal everyday plural ‘you’; in Portugal you might also hear “vocês” but other forms are common depending on context.
target_language_example: Vocês já comeram ou ainda estão com fome?
native_language_example: Have you all eaten yet, or are you still hungry?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to more than one person. It can mean ability (“can”) or permission (“may”), depending on context. Commonly followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., ficar, usar, ver). In Brazil, many people use “vocês” in most situations (instead of “vós”).
target_language_example: Vocês podem entrar agora.
native_language_example: You can come in now.

meaning: “you (all) can do” / “you (all) are able to do” / “you (all) may do” (addressing a group).
additional_notes: Uses **vocês** (plural “you,” common in Brazil) + **podem** (present tense of *poder*: can/be able/may) + **fazer** (to do/make). Often used to give instructions (**Vocês podem fazer assim.**), suggest a possibility (**Vejam o que vocês podem fazer com isso.**), or comment on what someone is capable/allowed to do. In Portugal, **vocês** can sound more formal or less common in everyday speech, where **vós** is rare and people often use third-person forms instead.
target_language_example: Se vocês quiserem, vocês podem fazer isso amanhã.
native_language_example: If you want, you (all) can do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the plural “vocês” (“you all” / “you” in Brazil) + “podem” (can/could) + the object pronoun “me” (“me”). It sets up a request or question, and you usually add another verb right after: “vocês podem me acordar…?” (can you wake me up…?), “vocês podem me explicar…?” (can you explain to me…?). In polite requests, it’s common to add “por favor” and/or use “poderiam” (could you) for extra politeness.
target_language_example: Vocês podem me ajudar com isso, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you all help me with this, please?

additional_notes: Used to make a polite request to a group of people: vocês (“you all”) + poderiam (conditional of poder, “could”). Often followed by por favor. Can also introduce a suggestion/request in a softer way than "vocês podem".
target_language_example: Vocês poderiam falar mais devagar, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you all speak more slowly, please?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to two or more people (“vocês”) to say they need to do something or that something is necessary. Follow it with an infinitive (precisam dormir, precisam parar) or with “de” + a noun/amount (precisam de ajuda, de quantas fotografias precisam?). More formal/plural alternatives include “os senhores/as senhoras precisam”.
target_language_example: Vocês precisam de ajuda agora?
native_language_example: Do you (all) need help now?

additional_notes: Uses **vocês** (you, plural) + **querem** (they/you-plural want), common in Brazil for addressing more than one person. It can be a statement (**Vocês querem sair.** = You all want to go out.) or a question by intonation (**Vocês querem sair?** = Do you all want to go out?). Often followed by an infinitive (**vocês querem ir/sair/estudar**) or by **que** + subjunctive to express what you want someone to do (**Vocês querem que eu faça isso?**).
target_language_example: Vocês querem comer agora ou mais tarde?
native_language_example: Do you all want to eat now or later?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to two or more people. “Vocês” = you all; “querem” = (you all) want; “ir” = to go. Often followed by a destination with “para” (Para onde vocês querem ir? = Where do you all want to go?) or used as a yes/no question (Vocês querem ir comigo? = Do you all want to go with me?). In Brazil, “vocês” is the common plural “you”; in Portugal you may also hear “vocês” but other forms like “querem ir?” (implied) or “vocês querem ir?” depending on context.
target_language_example: Vocês querem ir ao cinema hoje?
native_language_example: Do you all want to go to the movies today?

meaning: “Do you (all) want me to…?” / “Do you (all) want that I…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask what a group of people wants you to do. After "querem que", Portuguese normally uses the present subjunctive (eu chame, eu fale, eu vá, eu ligue, eu conte). "Vocês" is the common way to say “you (plural)” in Brazil; in Portugal you may hear "vocês" too, but also "vós" (less common) or other forms depending on context.
target_language_example: Vocês querem que eu espere aqui ou que eu volte mais tarde?
native_language_example: Do you want me to wait here or come back later?

meaning: “Do you want me to do…?” / “What do you want me to do?”
additional_notes: Used to ask what a group of people (“vocês” = you all) expects you to do. It’s often followed by a specific action or by “o quê?” (“what?”). The verb after “que” is usually in the subjunctive: “que eu faça” (literally “that I do”), which is the normal Portuguese way to say “want someone to do something.”
target_language_example: O que vocês querem que eu faça agora?
native_language_example: What do you want me to do now?

additional_notes: Uses vocês (“you” plural, common in Brazil) + sabem (present tense of saber, “to know” facts/information). Often starts a question to ask a group for information: “Vocês sabem onde…?”, “Vocês sabem se…?”. In Portugal, people may use “vocês” in some contexts, but “vocês sabem” is especially common in Brazilian Portuguese.
target_language_example: Vocês sabem que horas começa a reunião?
native_language_example: Do you all know what time the meeting starts?

additional_notes: Used to ask (or check) who someone is, or who did something. It’s followed by a verb or clause: “Vocês sabem quem é…?”, “Vocês sabem quem ganhou…?”. In Brazil, “vocês” is the standard plural “you” in most situations.
target_language_example: Vocês sabem quem vai chegar mais tarde?
native_language_example: Do you all know who is going to arrive later?

additional_notes: Used to talk to two or more people (or to one person in many parts of Brazil, informally) using the subject pronoun vocês + the verb ser (present tense): vocês são. Often followed by an adjective or a noun (e.g., rápidos, especialistas, parentes). In questions about origin it appears as "De onde vocês são?" (“Where are you from?”).
target_language_example: Vocês são muito gentis.
native_language_example: You are very kind.

additional_notes: Used with the subject pronoun vocês (“you all”) + the verb ter (“to have”), conjugated as têm (3rd-person plural). Very common for asking a group of people (or staff at a store/restaurant) if they have something available: “Vocês têm…?” It can also mean “you all have” in statements. Often interchangeable with “Vocês possuem…?” but têm is much more natural in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Com licença, vocês têm Wi‑Fi aqui?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have Wi‑Fi here?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (vocês) for confirmation before a statement or question. It’s followed by a clause introduced by “que” (that): “Vocês têm certeza de que + [sentence]”. You can also use it as a statement: “Tenho certeza de que…” = “I’m sure that…”.
target_language_example: Vocês têm certeza de que entenderam as instruções?
native_language_example: Are you (all) sure that you understood the instructions?

additional_notes: Used to say that a group of people is required or strongly expected to do something. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., deixar, encontrar, ajudar, voltar). In speech, many speakers also say “vocês têm que” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Vocês têm de esperar aqui.
native_language_example: You all have to wait here.

additional_notes: "Vocês" is the common way to say "you" (plural) in Brazilian Portuguese. "Viram" is the past tense of "ver" (to see) for "vocês/eles/elas" and can be used in a question (often with rising intonation) or a statement. It’s used to ask if a group saw something, or to check that they noticed what happened (e.g., "Vocês viram?" = "Did you see that?").
target_language_example: Vocês viram onde eu deixei minhas chaves?
native_language_example: Did you (all) see where I left my keys?

additional_notes: Uses "vocês" (you all) + the verb "ir" (to go) in the present ("vão"). Very common to talk about near future plans: "Vocês vão + infinitive" (e.g., "vocês vão nadar?"). Depending on context, it can also mean simple future (“will”), especially in questions. Common with "votar" (to vote), "se divorciar" (to get divorced).
target_language_example: Vocês vão sair hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Are you (all) going out tonight?

meaning: to do something again; to return to doing something.
additional_notes: Used as a semi-fixed pattern: "voltar a" + infinitive (e.g., voltar a dormir = to sleep again / go back to sleep). It can express resuming an action (after a pause) or repeating it. With another infinitive like "poder", it can stack: "voltar a poder" = "be able to (do something) again."
target_language_example: Depois do intervalo, vamos voltar a trabalhar.
native_language_example: After the break, we're going to go back to work.

meaning: to go back to work; to return to working.
additional_notes: Used when resuming work after a break, time off, illness, or a pause in an activity. Common with "ter de/ter que" (have to) and "precisar" (need to): "Tenho de voltar ao trabalho". "Vamos voltar ao trabalho" can mean getting back to work right now.
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, vou voltar ao trabalho.
native_language_example: After lunch, I’m going back to work.

additional_notes: Used with a destination after "para" (a city, home, a place, etc.). It can mean returning physically (traveling back) or going back in the sense of returning somewhere you were before. Conjugate "voltar" for the subject and tense: "tenho de voltar" = "I have to go back"; "tive de voltar" = "I had to go back".
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, vou voltar para o trabalho.
native_language_example: After lunch, I'm going back to work.

meaning: to go back home; to return home.
additional_notes: Used when someone returns to their home (after being out). The verb changes with the subject (eu volto, você volta, ela volta). It often appears with time words like "hoje", "amanhã", or days of the week ("na segunda-feira").
target_language_example: Depois do trabalho, vou voltar para casa cedo.
native_language_example: After work, I’m going to go back home early.

meaning: 'go back to' (you-form command) or 'come back to'.
additional_notes: Imperative form of "voltar" addressed to "você" (also used as a polite command). It tells someone to return to a place, person, or situation: "Volte para casa" (go back home). Often followed by a location; with articles: "volte para o carro" / "volte para a sua sala".
target_language_example: Por favor, volte para casa agora.
native_language_example: Please go back home now.

meaning: Go back home; return home. (imperative: “come back home”)
additional_notes: Uses the verb voltar (“to return”) + para casa (“home”). "Volte" is the você-form imperative (also the present subjunctive used after requests/wishes: "Espero que... volte"). Often followed by a time limit: "Volte para casa antes de...".
target_language_example: Por favor, volte para casa agora.
native_language_example: Please come back home now.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "voltar para" = "to go back/return to" + a destination. Often followed by a place (city, home, prison, office). You can change the subject by changing the verb: "voltei para" (I went back), "voltamos para" (we went back), "voltaram para" (they went back).
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, ela voltou para casa.
native_language_example: After lunch, she went back home.

meaning: (he/she/you formal) went back home; returned home.
additional_notes: Past tense of "voltar" (to return/go back) + "para casa" (home). Used when someone returns to their house/home base. Often matches English "went home" or "came home" depending on context (where the speaker is). The subject can be "você" (formal you) or a third person ("ele/ela").
target_language_example: Depois do trabalho, ele voltou para casa de ônibus.
native_language_example: After work, he went back home by bus.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive: "ter vontade de + infinitive" = to feel like / want to do something (often a mild desire or mood). With "dar vontade de" it means something triggers an urge: "Dá vontade de chorar" = "It makes me want to cry." "Vontade" can also mean "will" or "power" in a more formal/literary sense (e.g., "a vontade de Sauron" = "Sauron's will").
target_language_example: Hoje estou com vontade de ficar em casa.
native_language_example: Today I feel like staying home.

meaning: feel like crying; urge to cry.
additional_notes: "Vontade de" means a desire/urge to do something. With "chorar" (to cry), it expresses an emotional impulse: "sentir/ter vontade de chorar" = to feel/have the urge to cry. It doesn’t necessarily mean you actually cried—just that you wanted to.
target_language_example: Ao ver o filme, eu tive vontade de chorar.
native_language_example: When I saw the movie, I felt like crying.

additional_notes: Commonly used to report a flight cancellation. It’s the passive past: "foi cancelado" = "was canceled" (can vary for gender/number: foi cancelada / foram cancelados / foram canceladas). Often used with possessives: "Meu/Seu/O meu/O seu voo foi cancelado." You can add a reason with "por causa de" (because of).
target_language_example: Desculpe, meu voo foi cancelado e vou chegar amanhã.
native_language_example: Sorry, my flight was canceled and I’ll arrive tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say you will stay in the current place and wait until a later event happens. Often followed by either (1) infinitive: “até ele vir/voltar” (common in everyday speech) or (2) “até que” + subjunctive: “até que ele venha” (more formal/standard). You can also drop “Eu” and just say “Vou esperar aqui até…”.
target_language_example: Vou esperar aqui até você terminar.
native_language_example: I’ll wait here until you finish.

meaning: "I’m going to do/make" (near-future plan or intention).
additional_notes: "Vou" is the present tense of "ir" (to go) used with an infinitive to talk about the near future: "vou" + "fazer". "Fazer" can mean "to do" (an action/task: "fazer isso", "fazer nada") or "to make" (create/prepare something: "fazer chá", "fazer uma construção"). You can also use it in questions like "Como vou fazer isso?" (How am I going to do that?) and "Que vou fazer?" (What am I going to do?).
target_language_example: Vou fazer isso amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to do that tomorrow.

meaning: “I’m going to stay” or “I’m going to become / get (a certain state).”
additional_notes: Literally "I go to stay" (ir + infinitive), used to talk about a decision or near-future plan. With a place/context, it often means "to stay" (not leave): "Acho que vou ficar" = "I think I’ll stay." With an adjective or feeling, it often means "to become/get": "vou ficar nervoso" = "I’m going to get nervous." It can also be used in set expressions like "ficar de dedos cruzados" (to keep one’s fingers crossed).
target_language_example: Está tarde, então vou ficar em casa.
native_language_example: It’s late, so I’m going to stay home.

meaning: “I’m going to (do something) to/for you” (vou = I’m going; te = you).
additional_notes: Used before a verb to say what you’re about to do for/to someone you address as “you” (informal singular). The “te” is an object pronoun meaning “you,” and it can mean either “to you” or “you” depending on the verb: Vou te dizer… (tell you), Vou te ajudar… (help you), Vou te pegar! (I’m going to get you!/catch you!). In more formal speech or with “você,” you’ll often hear “vou lhe…” or “vou te…” depending on region.
target_language_example: Calma, vou te ajudar a resolver isso.
native_language_example: Calm down, I’m going to help you solve this.

meaning: “I’m going to give you…” / “I’ll give you…”
additional_notes: Used to promise or announce that you will give/provide something to someone soon. It’s "vou" (I’m going to) + "te" (to you, informal singular) + "dar" (to give). Very common with objects like comida (food), informações like a hora e o lugar (the time and place), presentes (gifts), or help/services like uma carona (a ride). In more formal situations, you’ll often hear "vou lhe dar" instead of "vou te dar".
target_language_example: Calma—vou te dar os detalhes mais tarde.
native_language_example: Relax—I’ll give you the details later.

additional_notes: Used when the speaker is about to show something to the listener. It’s the near-future form with ir + infinitive: vou (I’m going) + te (to you) + mostrar (to show). In many contexts, English “I’ll show you” is a natural translation. The object can come after: “Vou te mostrar algumas fotos / onde fica / como é.”
target_language_example: Espera um segundo — vou te mostrar no mapa.
native_language_example: Wait a second—I’m going to show you on the map.

meaning: “I’m going to the movies / I go to the cinema.”
additional_notes: From **ir** (“to go”): **vou** = “I go / I’m going” (present tense). **ao** = **a + o** (“to the”), and **cinema** here means the movie theater/cinema. In the examples it’s often used with frequency expressions like **quase nunca** (almost never), **raramente** (rarely), **com frequência** (often), **de vez em quando** (from time to time), **uma vez por mês** (once a month).
target_language_example: Hoje vou ao cinema com uns amigos.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to the movies with some friends.

additional_notes: "Vou" is the present tense of "ir" (to go) for "I". Use "vou para" before a destination (a place or sometimes an activity/location): "vou para casa" (I’m going home), "vou para a cama" (I’m going to bed). Often contracts with articles: "para + a = pra" (informal), "para + o = pro" (informal). With "onde": "vou para onde quiseres" = "I’ll go wherever you want."
target_language_example: Já é tarde, vou para casa agora.
native_language_example: It’s late, I’m going home now.

additional_notes: Used to say you are going to a (usually feminine) place. It’s made of: vou (I go / I’m going) + para (to) + a (the, feminine). For masculine places, you typically use “vou para o …” (e.g., vou para o trabalho). It can refer to the near future (“I’m going now/soon”) or a habitual action depending on context.
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, vou para a praia.
native_language_example: After lunch, I’m going to the beach.

additional_notes: Used to say you are on your way to school (or that school is your destination). Often includes a time (e.g., “às sete”) or frequency (e.g., “todos os dias”). It’s the verb ir (to go) in the present tense: eu vou = I go / I’m going.
target_language_example: Agora vou para a escola, mas volto à tarde.
native_language_example: Now I’m going to school, but I’ll be back in the afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to say you are going to your home (or to the place you consider ‘home’) now or later. It’s the present tense of the verb *ir* (“to go”) with *eu* implied: *Eu vou para casa*. Often used on its own as a complete sentence (e.g., when leaving). You can add time (*às quatro*, *agora*) or purpose (*vou para casa ver...* = “I’m going home to see...”).
target_language_example: Estou cansado(a); vou para casa agora.
native_language_example: I’m tired; I’m going home now.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ir (to go) in the 1st person singular present: eu vou. The à is a contraction of a + a ("to" + the feminine singular "the"). It’s used before feminine nouns (a farmácia) and many place names treated as feminine or that take an article (a África, a Costa Rica). With masculine nouns you use vou ao (a + o).
target_language_example: Hoje vou à escola mais cedo.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to school earlier.

meaning: “I go to school” / “I’m going to school.”
additional_notes: Uses the verb **ir** (to go) in the present tense: **vou** = “I go / I’m going.” **à** is a contraction of **a + a** meaning “to the” (feminine), used because **escola** is feminine: **a escola**. Often refers to going to school as part of a routine, but it can also mean you’re on your way there right now (context makes it clear).
target_language_example: Hoje vou à escola mais cedo.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to school earlier.

additional_notes: From the verb **ir** (to go): **eu vou** = “I go / I’m going.” **à** is the contraction of **a + a** (“to the” + feminine), used because **igreja** is feminine: **a igreja**. Often used with time expressions like **domingo**, **aos domingos** (“on Sundays”), **todos os dias** (“every day”), or with frequency words like **nunca** (“never”) and **quase nunca** (“almost never”). Depending on context, it can mean a habitual action (“I go”) or a near-future plan (“I’m going”).
target_language_example: Hoje eu vou à igreja com a minha família.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to church with my family.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to continue or start doing something, often as permission (“Go ahead.”) or encouragement. It can also sound challenging/defiant depending on tone, like “Go ahead, I dare you!” (as in the third example).
target_language_example: Se você quiser perguntar, vá em frente.
native_language_example: If you want to ask, go ahead.

additional_notes: "Vá" is the formal command form of "ir" (to go), used with "você". "Embora" here means "away" (as in leaving a place). Common in requests or orders: "Por favor, vá embora" (Please go away/leave), "Vá embora daqui" (Go away from here), and in the subjunctive after verbs like "esperar/querer/preferir": "Espero que ele vá embora" (I hope he leaves). For an informal command to one person, you’ll often hear "vai embora".
target_language_example: Por favor, vá embora agora; está tarde.
native_language_example: Please leave now; it’s late.

additional_notes: Imperative (command) form of the verb ir: "vá" = "go" (formal você / also used after certain expressions with que). Used with "para" + destination/place: "Vá para Boston" (Go to Boston), "Vá para a cama" (Go to bed). With pronouns: "vá para o seu quarto" (your room, more formal) vs. "vá para o teu quarto" (your room, more informal/Portugal and some regions). Can also be used as an insult: "Vá para o inferno!" (Go to hell!).
target_language_example: Por favor, vá para casa agora.
native_language_example: Please, go home now.

additional_notes: Extremely offensive and aggressive. Literally “go (and) fuck yourself.” Uses the command form “vá” (from ir: to go) + “se” (yourself) + “foder” (to fuck). Commonly said in anger, often with insults like “cara” or swear words like “porra.” Avoid in polite/company settings; in some contexts it can also be used as a harsh “fuck off.”
target_language_example: Se você continuar me tratando assim, vá se foder.
native_language_example: If you keep treating me like this, go fuck yourself.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens repeatedly. It often comes at the end of the sentence (e.g., "Já expliquei várias vezes"). You may also hear it emphasized as "várias e várias vezes" = "over and over again / many, many times."
target_language_example: Eu já tentei ligar para você várias vezes.
native_language_example: I’ve already tried to call you several times.

additional_notes: Form of the verb "ver" (to see) + the object pronoun "-la" (her) attached to the end of the verb. The circumflex accent in "vê-" marks the stressed sound in this form. Common in more formal/written Portuguese; in everyday speech you may also hear "ver ela" depending on the region and context.
target_language_example: Quero muito vê-la de novo.
native_language_example: I really want to see her again.

additional_notes: "Vê-la" = "ver" (to see) + the direct-object pronoun "-la" (her). You often see this hyphenated pronoun attached to the verb in more formal/written Portuguese, especially with infinitives (ver, fazer, ajudar, etc.). "Novamente" means "again". In everyday speech, many people also say "ver ela novamente" (less formal).
target_language_example: Espero poder vê-la novamente em breve.
native_language_example: I hope I can see her again soon.

additional_notes: "Vê-las" = "ver" (to see) + "-las" (them, referring to a feminine plural noun like "as flores" = the flowers). The accent in "vê" marks the stressed vowel in this verb form. It’s used when the object pronoun comes after the verb (common with infinitives, e.g., "para vê-las", "preciso vê-las"). For masculine plural "them," use "vê-los".
target_language_example: Quero vê-las de perto.
native_language_example: I want to see them up close.

meaning: "to see him" (or "to see it," for a masculine thing).
additional_notes: This is the verb ver (to see) + the direct-object pronoun o (him/it), attached with a hyphen (enclisis). It often appears after infinitives or in more formal/written Portuguese. The accent in vê- marks the stressed form of ver when the pronoun is attached (compare: ver / vê-lo). Feminine and plural variants include vê-la (see her/it) and vê-los / vê-las (see them).
target_language_example: Preciso vê-lo hoje.
native_language_example: I need to see him today.

meaning: to see him again (also used as “to see you again,” formal).
additional_notes: "Vê-lo" is "ver" (to see) + "o" (him/it) attached with a hyphen (common with object pronouns). In polite/formal speech, "o" can mean "you" (male) when addressing someone as "o senhor" implicitly, so "É bom vê-lo de novo" can mean "It’s good to see you again" (formal). "Deixa-me" is informal; "Deixe-me" is more formal/polite.
target_language_example: Foi um prazer vê-lo de novo.
native_language_example: It was a pleasure to see you again.

additional_notes: "Vê-lo" is "ver" (to see) + "-lo" (him/it), used when the object pronoun comes after the verb (common after infinitives like "preciso ver"). "Novamente" means "again". In everyday speech you may also hear "ver ele novamente" (less formal/less standard) instead of "vê-lo novamente".
target_language_example: Espero vê-lo novamente em breve.
native_language_example: I hope to see him again soon.

additional_notes: This is the verb "ver" (to see) + the direct object pronoun "os" (them), attached with a hyphen. The accent (vê-) marks the stressed vowel when the pronoun is attached. Common in more formal/written Portuguese and after infinitives (e.g., "quero vê-los" = "I want to see them"). Use it mainly for groups that are masculine or mixed gender; for an all-female group, use "vê-las".
target_language_example: Quero vê-los amanhã à tarde.
native_language_example: I want to see them tomorrow afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to talk about one serving of coffee (the drink). "Xícara" is a small cup (often with a handle), so this phrase can refer to the cup itself or, more commonly, the amount of coffee in it. In Brazil, "xícara" is also used as a cooking measure (about 240 ml), but in everyday speech it usually just means a cup of coffee to drink.
target_language_example: Você quer uma xícara de café agora?
native_language_example: Do you want a cup of coffee now?

additional_notes: Used to count how many cups of coffee someone drank or usually drinks. You’ll often see it with numbers (uma/duas/três xícaras) and common verbs like tomar or beber.
target_language_example: Hoje eu só tomei uma xícara de café.
native_language_example: Today I only had one cup of coffee.

additional_notes: Used for things that happen during nighttime. With a specific day like "hoje" it often means "tonight" ("hoje à noite"). Without a specific day it usually means "at night" in general. Common pattern: "de dia" (during the day) vs. "à noite" (at night).
target_language_example: A gente se fala à noite, depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: We’ll talk tonight, after work.

additional_notes: Used for things that happen during nighttime. With a specific day like "hoje" it often means "tonight" ("hoje à noite"). Without a specific day it usually means "at night" in general. Common pattern: "de dia" (during the day) vs. "à noite" (at night).
target_language_example: A gente se fala à noite, depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: We’ll talk tonight, after work.

meaning: on TV / television (as a medium); in front of the TV.
additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like assistir (to watch) and with expressions like em frente à TV (“in front of the TV”). Here, à = a (“to”) + a (“the”), so it’s the contraction à before the feminine noun TV (a televisão). You can also hear/see na TV (“on TV”), especially when talking about something being broadcast.
target_language_example: A gente ficou em frente à TV vendo um filme.
native_language_example: We stayed in front of the TV watching a movie.

meaning: by the sea; on/along the seafront (by the shore).
additional_notes: Used to describe a place located right next to the sea (near the shore), especially houses, hotels, or neighborhoods. Often implies a seaside or beachfront area; similar to “à beira do mar.”
target_language_example: Vamos caminhar à beira-mar no fim da tarde.
native_language_example: Let’s walk along the seafront in the late afternoon.

meaning: on the verge of; about to (often something bad).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is very close to a situation happening, especially a serious negative outcome (e.g., destruction, bankruptcy, death, extinction). It’s the feminine form because it agrees with the implied word margem/beira (“edge”), and it’s followed by a noun, usually with the article: à beira da falência / à beira da morte.
target_language_example: Depois do acidente, ele ficou à beira da morte.
native_language_example: After the accident, he was on the verge of death.

additional_notes: Indicates motion/direction toward the library. It’s the contraction of "a" (to) + "a" (the, feminine singular) → "à". Used with verbs of going/returning like "ir", "voltar", "levar".
target_language_example: Eu vou à biblioteca depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I'm going to the library after work.

meaning: on the right; to the right (side).
additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or location. Common in giving directions: “É à direita” = “It’s on the right.” With “de” it specifies position relative to something: “à direita de X” = “to the right of X.”
target_language_example: Vire à direita no próximo cruzamento.
native_language_example: Turn right at the next intersection.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of going/movement (ir, voltar, levar) to say someone goes to school. "à" = "a" (to) + "a" (the), so it’s used with the feminine noun "escola". Often translated simply as "to school" (without "the") in English.
target_language_example: Eu vou à escola todos os dias.
native_language_example: I go to school every day.

additional_notes: Used to indicate position or direction. Common in directions and navigation (often contrasted with “à direita” = on/to the right). You can use it after verbs like “virar” (to turn) and “ficar” (to be/located): “Vire à esquerda” (Turn left), “Fica à esquerda” (It’s on the left).
target_language_example: O banco fica à esquerda do supermercado.
native_language_example: The bank is to the left of the supermarket.

additional_notes: "À" = "a" (to) + "a" (the), used with feminine singular places like "a estação". Often used with transport contexts: "ir à estação" (go to the station), "voltar à estação" (return to the station). If you name the station, you can say "à Estação X"; with "de trem" it’s "à estação de trem" (to the train station).
target_language_example: Vamos pegar um táxi até à estação.
native_language_example: Let’s take a taxi to the station.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (like ir, voltar, chegar) to mean going to a specific party/event. It’s the contraction of "a" + "a" (feminine singular) = "à".
target_language_example: Você vai à festa amanhã?
native_language_example: Are you going to the party tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (ir, voltar, vir) to mean going to a church building/service. It’s the contraction of "a" (to) + "a" (the) → "à" + "igreja" (church). Often appears in routines: "ir à igreja" (to go to church).
target_language_example: Eu vou à igreja no domingo.
native_language_example: I go to church on Sunday.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens at exactly 12:00 a.m. It often answers “when?” and can come after the verb (Chegamos… à meia-noite) or at the end of the sentence. Note: “meia-noite” is feminine, so it uses “à” (= a + a).
target_language_example: O filme começa à meia-noite.
native_language_example: The movie starts at midnight.

meaning: "to my" / "at my" (used before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: This is the contraction of "a" + "a minha" → "à minha". It’s used when a verb or expression requires the preposition "a" (often meaning "to"), followed by a feminine singular noun you possess: "à minha pergunta" (to my question), "à minha chefe" (to my boss). With masculine singular you usually use "ao meu"; with feminine plural, "às minhas".
target_language_example: Vou ligar à minha mãe mais tarde.
native_language_example: I’m going to call my mom later.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (especially **vir** “to come” and **ir** “to go”) to say someone is going/coming to where you live. **à** is the contraction of **a + a** (“to + the”), and it’s common to say **à minha casa** (to my house) rather than *para minha casa* in many everyday situations.
target_language_example: Você pode vir à minha casa amanhã?
native_language_example: Can you come to my house tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used after certain verbs to indicate an outcome that ends in death. Very common in set phrases like “condenado/sentenciado à morte” (“sentenced/condemned to death”) and “levar (alguém) à morte” (“to lead (someone) to death”). Also appears in “até à morte” (“until death”).
target_language_example: Ele foi condenado à morte, mas a sentença foi anulada.
native_language_example: He was sentenced to death, but the sentence was overturned.

additional_notes: Contraction of the preposition "a" + the feminine singular possessive "nossa" ("our"). Used before a feminine singular noun, often in phrases like "à nossa espera" (waiting for us) and "à nossa frente" (in front of us / ahead of us). For masculine nouns, use "ao nosso"; for plural, "aos nossos" / "às nossas".
target_language_example: Vou telefonar à nossa professora amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to call our teacher tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like responder (to answer): responder à pergunta = “to answer the question.” It’s a + a (feminine singular), contracted to à. For a masculine noun you’d use ao (a + o), e.g., responder ao professor (“answer the teacher”).
target_language_example: Você pode responder à pergunta, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you answer the question, please?

meaning: at the door; at the doorway.
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like "bater" (to knock): "bater à porta" = "to knock on the door." It can also mean someone is waiting/standing at the door: "Há alguém à porta" (There’s someone at the door). In some contexts English uses "on the door" (knocking), but Portuguese uses "à" (at/to the).
target_language_example: Tem uma encomenda à porta para você.
native_language_example: There’s a package at the door for you.

additional_notes: Used after verbs of movement like ir/voltar/chegar to indicate going to a place. It’s the contraction of "a" (to) + "a" (the, feminine) + "praia" (beach) = "à praia". Often used with "ir": "ir à praia" (to go to the beach).
target_language_example: Vamos à praia depois do almoço.
native_language_example: We’re going to the beach after lunch.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar (most common: "Estou à procura de...") to say you’re searching for someone or something. It’s slightly more formal than "procurar" or "estar procurando" and is often followed by a noun or person ("à procura de uma pasta", "à procura de uma pessoa").
target_language_example: Estamos à procura de um hotel perto do centro.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a hotel near downtown.

additional_notes: Means “to the meeting,” usually after verbs of movement/attendance like ir (to go), chegar (to arrive), and comparecer (to attend). The accent in “à” is the crase: a + a (the preposition “a” + the feminine article “a”) before the feminine noun “reunião.” Note: “reunião” looks like English “reunion,” but in Portuguese it commonly just means a (work) meeting.
target_language_example: Vou chegar cedo à reunião para falar com o gerente.
native_language_example: I’m going to arrive early to the meeting to talk to the manager.

meaning: to (someone’s) health; for health (as an effect).
additional_notes: Used with adjectives like essencial/perigoso/prejudicial and verbs like fazer bem/mal to say something is beneficial or harmful to health. Grammatically it’s “a + a saúde” → “à saúde” (to the health), often translated as “to your/their health” or “for your/their health” depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Comer mais verduras faz bem à saúde.
native_language_example: Eating more vegetables is good for your health.

additional_notes: Used when a verb or expression requires the preposition "a" and it comes before "sua" + a feminine noun (e.g., "atender a", "pertencer a"). The grave accent (à) shows the contraction of "a" + "a" (crase). "Sua" can mean "your" (formal or plural) or "his/her/its"—context tells you which.
target_language_example: Respondi à sua pergunta ontem.
native_language_example: I answered your question yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say when something happens during the afternoon (after midday). Often used with days of the week: "segunda-feira à tarde" (Monday afternoon), "sexta-feira à tarde" (Friday afternoon).
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar à tarde, depois do almoço.
native_language_example: Let’s meet in the afternoon, after lunch.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. It’s formed by **a + as** ("at" + "the" [hour]) → **às** for most clock times: **às cinco**, **às seis**, etc. With **one o’clock**, Portuguese uses **à uma** (singular). You can add parts of the day: **às cinco da tarde** (at 5 p.m.), **às cinco da manhã** (at 5 a.m.), or minutes: **às cinco e meia** (at 5:30).
target_language_example: Nos encontramos às cinco em frente ao café.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at five in front of the café.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. It’s "às" (a + as) because hours are feminine plural: às uma (at 1:00), às duas (at 2:00), etc. You can add a time-of-day phrase like "às nove da manhã" (at 9 a.m.) or "às nove da noite" (at 9 p.m.).
target_language_example: A reunião começa às nove.
native_language_example: The meeting starts at nine.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. "Às" is the contraction of "a" + "as" and is used with most clock times (às duas, às oito). With 1 o’clock you usually say "à uma" (singular). You can add parts of the day: "às oito da manhã" (at 8 a.m.), "às oito da noite" (at 8 p.m.).
target_language_example: A reunião é às oito.
native_language_example: The meeting is at eight.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something quickly because they don’t have time (often implying stress, urgency, or not doing it carefully). Common with verbs like sair (leave), voltar (return), entrar (get in), almoçar (have lunch), and ser levado (be taken) in urgent situations.
target_language_example: Saímos às pressas quando começou a chover.
native_language_example: We left in a hurry when it started to rain.

additional_notes: Used with days of the week to mean you do something on that day (often as a routine). It’s a + as (plural), so it commonly suggests “every Monday / on Mondays.” You can also say “na segunda-feira” for a specific Monday.
target_language_example: Eu trabalho em casa às segundas-feiras.
native_language_example: I work from home on Mondays.

additional_notes: Used with days of the week to mean you do something on that day (often as a routine). It’s a + as (plural), so it commonly suggests “every Monday / on Mondays.” You can also say “na segunda-feira” for a specific Monday.
target_language_example: Eu trabalho em casa às segundas-feiras.
native_language_example: I work from home on Mondays.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. It’s the contraction of “a” + “as” (at + the, for hours): a(s) + as → às. Often followed by “horas,” but you can omit it when the context is clear.
target_language_example: A reunião começa às seis.
native_language_example: The meeting starts at six.

additional_notes: Used to say the time something happens. It’s the contraction of "a" + "as" (= "at the" for clock times): "às" is used with plural hours (às duas, às sete). With 1 o’clock you usually use "à uma" (singular). You can also add "horas": "às sete horas".
target_language_example: A aula começa às sete.
native_language_example: Class starts at seven.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens occasionally (not always). In Portuguese, you can replace "ele" with other subjects: "às vezes eu" (sometimes I), "às vezes ela" (sometimes she), "às vezes a gente" (sometimes we), etc. Often appears in patterns like "Às vezes..., às vezes..." to show alternation.
target_language_example: Às vezes ele prefere ficar em casa.
native_language_example: Sometimes he prefers to stay at home.

additional_notes: A polite, common way to ask for water, especially in cafés/restaurants. You can use it alone (“Água, por favor.”) or with a quantity like “um copo de água” (a glass of water) or “uma garrafa de água” (a bottle of water). Word order is flexible: “Um copo de água, por favor.” / “Por favor, um copo de água.”
target_language_example: Para mim, uma garrafa de água, por favor.
native_language_example: For me, a bottle of water, please.

additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning water that is cold (temperature). Common in cooking instructions (e.g., cover something with cold water), for bathing (banho com água fria), and when ordering a drink (“Uma água fria, por favor” = a cold bottle/glass of water). In some contexts it can be used figuratively as “a cold shower”/“a bucket of cold water” to mean something unpleasant or discouraging.
target_language_example: Pode me trazer uma água fria, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a cold water, please?

additional_notes: Used for water at a high temperature, especially for bathing, washing, or cleaning. Common in phrases like “Não há água quente” (There’s no hot water).
target_language_example: Preciso de água quente para tomar banho.
native_language_example: I need hot water to take a shower.

meaning: "it's, so to speak" (used to soften or qualify a comparison).
additional_notes: Used when you’re speaking figuratively or making an approximate comparison—often like “in a manner of speaking.” It typically introduces a metaphor or an image rather than a literal statement, and it’s common to set it off with commas: “Ele é, por assim dizer, ...”.
target_language_example: Este bairro é, por assim dizer, o coração da cidade.
native_language_example: This neighborhood is, so to speak, the heart of the city.

meaning: “is the” / “it’s the” (when the noun is feminine singular).
additional_notes: Used to identify or define something with a feminine singular noun: “X é a Y” (“X is the Y”). It’s the verb ser (“to be”) in the present tense (é) + the feminine singular definite article (a). In phone calls, “É a + name” means “It’s + (female name)” (e.g., “É a Karin.”).
target_language_example: Lisboa é a capital de Portugal.
native_language_example: Lisbon is the capital of Portugal.

meaning: "is the capital of" (used before a feminine country/region name).
additional_notes: Used to state that a city is the capital of a place. It agrees with feminine nouns: "da" = "de" + "a" (“of the” feminine). With masculine names, use "é a capital do" (do = de + o): "Lisboa é a capital do Portugal" (rare/unnatural because people usually say "a capital de Portugal"). Most commonly you’ll also hear "é a capital de" + country name (without article): "Madri é a capital de Espanha".
target_language_example: Brasília é a capital da República Federativa do Brasil.
native_language_example: Brasília is the capital of the Federative Republic of Brazil.

additional_notes: Used to state that a city is the capital city of a country or region. Structure: [City] + é a capital de + [Country/Place]. In speech and writing, you’ll often see the country with an article (e.g., “de Portugal”, “de Cuba”, “do Brasil”, “da França”).
target_language_example: Brasília é a capital do Brasil.
native_language_example: Brasília is the capital of Brazil.

additional_notes: Used to state the capital city of a place. It agrees with the gender/number of the place that follows: use "do" (= de + o) with masculine singular places (do Brasil), and "da" (= de + a) with feminine singular places (da França). With plural names, use "dos/das". Often appears in questions like "Que cidade é a capital do... ?"
target_language_example: Lisboa é a capital do Portugal.
native_language_example: Lisbon is the capital of Portugal.

additional_notes: Used to identify a specific house (often while pointing something out or clarifying which place you mean). It’s the verb **ser** (é = “is”) + definite article **a** (“the”, feminine singular) + **casa** (“house/home”). You can also change the article for other nouns (e.g., **é o prédio** = “it’s the building”).
target_language_example: É a casa do João, não é?
native_language_example: It’s João’s house, right?

meaning: "is the key" (the most important thing for achieving something).
additional_notes: Used in the pattern “X é a chave para Y” to say that X is essential to reach/achieve Y. It can be literal (an actual key) but is very often metaphorical (“the key to success”).
target_language_example: A prática diária é a chave para melhorar o português.
native_language_example: Daily practice is the key to improving Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is essential for achieving success. Often appears in sayings and general statements (e.g., with "Diz-se frequentemente que..."). You can swap in other nouns: "A prática é a chave do sucesso."
target_language_example: Para muita gente, a disciplina é a chave do sucesso.
native_language_example: For many people, discipline is the key to success.

meaning: “is the most … (thing)” (used to say something is the most + adjective).
additional_notes: Used with superlatives: é a coisa mais + adjective (encantadora, preciosa, linda, forte) + (de/da/do) + noun, or followed by a clause: “que temos/que existe”. Very common, informal-neutral way to emphasize that something is the most important/beautiful/etc. You can also use it with masculine adjectives (e.g., “é a coisa mais importante”).
target_language_example: Este lugar é a coisa mais bonita da cidade.
native_language_example: This place is the most beautiful thing in the city.

meaning: “is the language” (used to identify what a language is).
additional_notes: Used in statements to say that a certain language is someone’s native language or is the language with a certain characteristic. Often followed by extra information (e.g., “com mais falantes…”, “mãe dela”). You can swap in another subject: “Português é a língua oficial de Angola.”
target_language_example: Português é a língua oficial do Brasil.
native_language_example: Portuguese is the official language of Brazil.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun: **a maior + (noun)** = “the biggest/the greatest (one)”. It’s a superlative idea (the #1 in size, importance, etc.). For masculine nouns, you’ll see **é o maior**. The adjective **maior** (“bigger/greater/older”) agrees with the article **a/o** (feminine/masculine).
target_language_example: Esta é a maior cidade do estado.
native_language_example: This is the biggest city in the state.

additional_notes: Used to say that a place (often a capital, region, or country) has a particular city as its largest by population or size. It’s the verb “é” (is) + “a maior” (the biggest) + “cidade” (city). Often followed by “de/da/do” to specify the area: “é a maior cidade do Japão” (…in Japan).
target_language_example: São Paulo é a maior cidade do Brasil.
native_language_example: São Paulo is the biggest city in Brazil.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the best among others. Portuguese adjectives agree with the noun: use "é o melhor" with masculine nouns (e.g., "O café é o melhor"), and "é a melhor" with feminine nouns (e.g., "A seleção é a melhor"). Often followed by a noun: "é a melhor opção" (it’s the best option).
target_language_example: Para mim, esta é a melhor solução.
native_language_example: For me, this is the best solution.

additional_notes: Used to say something is identical/equal to another thing. It agrees with a feminine noun (e.g., a ideia, a lei, a situação, a opinião). For masculine nouns, use “é o mesmo”; for plural, “são os mesmos / são as mesmas.” Often followed by “que” to compare: “é a mesma que…”.
target_language_example: Esta resposta é a mesma que a anterior.
native_language_example: This answer is the same as the previous one.

meaning: “is mine” (referring to something feminine); or “is my …” before a feminine noun.
additional_notes: Used with the verb “ser” to identify possession/relationship or to state that something is your favorite, your first time, etc. It agrees with a feminine noun: “a minha” (feminine singular). For masculine you’d say “é o meu”. Often followed by a noun: “É a minha caneca” = “It’s my mug.” It can also stand alone if the noun is understood: “Aquela caneca? É a minha.” = “That mug? It’s mine.”
target_language_example: Essa mochila é a minha.
native_language_example: That backpack is mine.

meaning: “is the most … woman” (superlative: the woman who is the most …).
additional_notes: Used to form the superlative about a woman: “(someone) é a mulher mais + adjective + (de/do/da...)” (“the most … in the world”) or “é a mulher mais + adjective + que...” (“the most … that/who…”). The adjective agrees in gender: “gentil/rica/alta/quieta”. You can swap “mulher” for another noun: “é o homem mais…”, “é a pessoa mais…”.
target_language_example: Ela é a mulher mais inteligente da turma.
native_language_example: She is the smartest woman in the class.

meaning: “is ours” / “it’s our …” (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns to identify something as belonging to “us” (our/ours), often in contrast to others: “Aquela é a nossa vizinha.” With a noun, it means “it’s our + noun” (e.g., “É a nossa família!”). Without a noun, it can mean “it’s ours,” as long as the thing being talked about is feminine.
target_language_example: Não se preocupe — é a nossa responsabilidade.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — it’s our responsibility.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is the most (superlative) in a group or compared to others. Structure: [Name] + é a pessoa mais + adjective + (de/do/da + group) or + que + verb (e.g., que conheço = “that I know”). Adjective agrees with pessoa (feminine): mais baixa, mais gorda, mais preguiçosa, etc.
target_language_example: Ela é a pessoa mais simpática da turma.
native_language_example: She is the nicest person in the class.

additional_notes: Used to strongly criticize or emphasize that something is extremely bad. It’s often followed by a clause with que (e.g., que já ouvi = “that I’ve ever heard”; que você pode fazer = “that you can do”). You can change the subject (Isso/Essa) or tense (foi/era) as needed.
target_language_example: Isso é a pior coisa que você pode dizer agora.
native_language_example: That’s the worst thing you can say right now.

additional_notes: Used to say or ask whether something is happening for the first time. Very common with the present tense in Portuguese (e.g., "É a primeira vez que estou aqui"), where English often uses the present perfect ("it’s the first time I’ve been here"). You can adapt it for formality: "a senhora / o senhor" (formal), "você" (neutral), "vocês" (plural).
target_language_example: É a primeira vez que eu venho a este restaurante.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’ve come to this restaurant.

meaning: “is the root of all …” (the main cause of something bad).
additional_notes: Usually followed by a negative noun, often "o mal" (“evil” / “bad things”): "X é a raiz de todo o mal." You can also see "de todo mal" without the article "o"; both are common. Used in serious statements about what causes problems.
target_language_example: Para ele, a mentira é a raiz de todo o problema.
native_language_example: For him, lying is the root of the whole problem.

additional_notes: Used to identify or point out something that belongs to someone: “X é a sua Y.” The possessive pronoun “sua” agrees with the thing owned (feminine singular), not with the owner. Also note that “seu/sua” can mean “your,” but it can also mean “his/her/its/their” depending on context; if you need to be clearer, you may hear “é dela” (hers) / “é dele” (his) / “é de vocês” (yours, plural).
target_language_example: Essa chave é a sua?
native_language_example: Is this key yours?

meaning: “it’s the last one/thing” (and sometimes “it’s the last time / last chance”).
additional_notes: Used to say something is the final one (the last lesson, the last window/opportunity, etc.). Depending on context, it can also mean the most recent/latest (“a última moda” = the latest fashion). In a warning, it can imply “this is the last time” (i.e., no more chances). It agrees with a feminine noun understood from context (e.g., lição, chance, vez); you may also see masculine/plural variants: “é o último”, “são as últimas”.
target_language_example: Se você se atrasar de novo, é a última!
native_language_example: If you’re late again, that’s the last time (I’ll tolerate it)!

additional_notes: Used to say something is the only option/thing/person. It’s the feminine form, agreeing with a feminine noun that follows or is implied (e.g., a única coisa, a única lei, a única maneira, a única família). For masculine nouns, use “é o único” (e.g., é o único caminho). Often followed by a noun: “É a única maneira…”.
target_language_example: Para mim, esta é a única solução.
native_language_example: For me, this is the only solution.

meaning: “is the only person who/that” (the only one who).
additional_notes: Used to say that one specific person is the only one who does something or has a certain ability/relationship. It’s often followed by a verb phrase: “é a única pessoa que me entende” (…who understands me) or “é a única pessoa que pode fazer isso” (…who can do that). You can also add details like “que eu conheço” (that I know) or “além de mim” (besides me).
target_language_example: Ela é a única pessoa que sabe a senha.
native_language_example: She’s the only person who knows the password.

additional_notes: Used with ser (é) + alérgico/alérgica + a + the allergen (food, medicine, dust, etc.). Use alérgico for males and alérgica for females: Ela é alérgica a leite. To ask a question, you can use intonation or add a question mark: Você é alérgico a…?
target_language_example: Sou alérgico a frutos do mar.
native_language_example: I'm allergic to seafood.

meaning: "that's how" / "this is how" (introduces the way something is or is done).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to explain a manner, method, or typical situation. Often followed by a verb clause: “É assim que + [subject] + [verb] …” (e.g., “É assim que fazemos…”). Can also introduce a general statement: “É assim que a vida é…” (“That’s what life is like…”).
target_language_example: É assim que se aprende português: praticando todos os dias.
native_language_example: This is how you learn Portuguese: by practicing every day.

meaning: "is quite / pretty" (used to emphasize an adjective).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective to mean “quite/rather/pretty” (a moderate-to-strong emphasis): é bastante estressante/improvável/inesperado. Note that "bastante" can also mean "enough" in other contexts (e.g., "Já é bastante!" = "That’s enough!").
target_language_example: O trabalho é bastante difícil, mas eu gosto.
native_language_example: The job is quite difficult, but I like it.

additional_notes: In Brazilian Portuguese, "bem" often intensifies an adjective after "ser": "é bem antigo" = "it’s really/very old". With comparisons, "bem" can intensify "mais/menos": "é bem mais jovem" = "is much younger". It doesn’t mean "is well" here.
target_language_example: Este restaurante é bem caro, mas a comida é ótima.
native_language_example: This restaurant is really expensive, but the food is great.

meaning: "it’s very likely that" / "there’s a good chance that".
additional_notes: Used to express a high probability. It’s often followed by the subjunctive (e.g., venha, aconteça, passe, saiba, esteja), because it introduces something uncertain or not confirmed. You can also say “é provável que” (less strong) or “é muito provável que” (similar strength).
target_language_example: É bem provável que a gente chegue atrasado por causa do trânsito.
native_language_example: It’s very likely we’ll arrive late because of traffic.

additional_notes: Most commonly, é bom simply means “it’s good/that’s good,” describing something positively: Isso é bom! It can also be used with com + noun to say someone is good with/at something (often a skill or habit): Ele é bom com números. In sentence 4, é bom com uma garrafa implies someone can handle alcohol well (a bit suggestive).
target_language_example: O café daqui é bom, mas é um pouco caro.
native_language_example: The coffee here is good, but it’s a bit expensive.

additional_notes: Used with "ser" to talk about ability/skill in a subject or activity. It’s followed by a noun or verb (often in the infinitive): "Ele é bom em matemática" / "Ela é boa em cantar". Agree "bom/boa" with the person: "Ele é bom", "Ela é boa"; plural: "Eles são bons", "Elas são boas".
target_language_example: Ela é boa em cozinhar, mas não é muito boa em dirigir.
native_language_example: She’s good at cooking, but she’s not very good at driving.

meaning: 'is beautiful/pretty' (said about a female person or feminine noun).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "ser" (é = "is") + the feminine adjective "bonita". Agree it with the noun: masculine "é bonito"; plural "são bonitas/bonitos". In questions, Portuguese often keeps the same order and uses a question mark/intonation: "Ela é bonita?"
target_language_example: A sua irmã é bonita.
native_language_example: Your sister is beautiful.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (é = “is”) to state someone’s nationality. It agrees with the subject: for women you can also say “é canadense” (same form). Common in questions: “Ele/ela é canadense?” (“Is he/she Canadian?”). You can add “mesmo?” to confirm/sound surprised: “Ele é canadense mesmo?” (“Is he really Canadian?”).
target_language_example: Ela é canadense, mas mora no Brasil.
native_language_example: She’s Canadian, but she lives in Brazil.

additional_notes: Used with the verb in the infinitive after "de": "é capaz de + infinitive". It can mean having the ability/skill to do something ("He can speak French"), or being capable of doing something (sometimes implying something extreme, depending on context: "He’s capable of anything").
target_language_example: Ela é capaz de terminar o trabalho hoje.
native_language_example: She can finish the work today.

meaning: “is able to do” / “is capable of doing”.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has the ability or capacity to do something. It’s commonly followed by an infinitive: “ser capaz de” + verb (e.g., “é capaz de fazer”, “sou capaz de resolver”). It can describe skills (“can do it”) or what someone might do in a certain situation (“might do it / is capable of doing it”).
target_language_example: Você é capaz de fazer isso sozinho?
native_language_example: Are you able to do that by yourself?

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (é) + casado to state marital status. For a female subject, use “é casada”. Often followed by “com” to say who someone is married to: “Ele é casado com uma dentista.” Questions commonly use “Você é casado?” and contrasts like “casado ou solteiro”.
target_language_example: Ele é casado, mas a irmã dele é solteira.
native_language_example: He is married, but his sister is single.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/animal cannot see with one of their eyes. You can change the subject: “Eu sou cego de um olho” (I’m blind in one eye), “Ela é cega de um olho” (She’s blind in one eye). Note agreement: cego (male) / cega (female). The more common phrasing is “cego de um olho” or “cego de um dos olhos.”
target_language_example: Ela é cega de um olho desde criança.
native_language_example: She has been blind in one eye since she was a child.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that what follows is obvious, certain, or expected. Often translates as “of course” in conversation, and as “clearly/evidently” in more formal writing. Tone depends on context: it can be neutral, reassuring, enthusiastic, or sarcastic/irritated (especially with insults or strong emotion).
target_language_example: É claro que eu vou te ajudar.
native_language_example: Of course I’m going to help you.

meaning: “is like a…” (used to make a comparison).
additional_notes: Used to compare someone or something to a noun: X é como um/uma Y (“X is like a Y”). Choose um (masculine noun) or uma (feminine noun). Often expresses similarity, not identity.
target_language_example: Este livro é como um guia para mim.
native_language_example: This book is like a guide for me.

meaning: "it’s as if" / "it’s like" (introducing an unreal or hypothetical comparison).
additional_notes: Used to compare reality to an imagined situation: “It’s as if…”. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive in Portuguese (e.g., fosse, tivesse), often expressing something that seems true but isn’t certain or is contrary to fact. Can also be used for emphasis or dramatic effect.
target_language_example: É como se eu não existisse para eles.
native_language_example: It’s as if I don’t exist to them.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (é = “is”) to describe that something is difficult in general or as a characteristic: “X é difícil.” You can add “para + person” to say who it’s difficult for: “É difícil para mim.” (Also common: “É difícil + infinitive”: “É difícil aprender…”.)
target_language_example: É difícil entender tudo tão rápido.
native_language_example: It’s hard to understand everything so quickly.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to say something is difficult to do: "é difícil de + verb" (e.g., "é difícil de resolver"). Often you’ll also see "é difícil" without "de" ("É difícil resolver este problema"), and both are common. In some cases Portuguese adds "se" before the verb ("difícil de se viver"), especially when talking about living somewhere or general actions.
target_language_example: Este texto é difícil de entender.
native_language_example: This text is hard to understand.

additional_notes: Used to state an age difference, usually followed by an adjective like **velho/velha** (“older”) or **novo/nova** (“younger”), often with **do que/que** (“than”): **Ela é dois anos mais velha do que eu.** You can change the number/unit: **é três meses mais…**, **é um ano mais…**.
target_language_example: Minha irmã é dois anos mais velha do que eu.
native_language_example: My sister is two years older than me.

é dois anos mais velho que

target_language_multi_word_term: é dois anos mais velho que
additional_notes: Used to compare ages. Structure: [person] é + [number] anos mais velho/velha que + [other person]. Use "velho" for a male subject and "velha" for a female subject (e.g., "Maria é dois anos mais velha que Ana").
target_language_example: Ela é dois anos mais velha que o marido.
native_language_example: She is two years older than her husband.

meaning: "is made of" (what something is made from).
additional_notes: Used to describe the material or components something is made from. It agrees with the subject: é feito de (masc. singular), é feita de (fem. singular), são feitos de (masc. plural), são feitas de (fem. plural). Often used with materials (pedra, papel, ouro) and with parts/components (átomos).
target_language_example: A mesa é feita de madeira.
native_language_example: The table is made of wood.

additional_notes: Used to describe what something is made from. "é" = “is”; "feita" agrees with a feminine noun (e.g., a caixa, a ponte, a casa). With a masculine noun, you say "é feito de madeira" (e.g., O móvel é feito de madeira).
target_language_example: A mesa é feita de madeira.
native_language_example: The table is made of wood.

additional_notes: Used to say what something is made from. Very common with materials (madeira, ouro, papel) and ingredients (trigo, suco de uva). You can also use it with feminine/plural subjects: “é feita de” (fem. singular), “são feitos/as de” (plural).
target_language_example: A mesa é feita de vidro.
native_language_example: The table is made of glass.

additional_notes: Used to say that an action or situation is easy. Very common with an infinitive: “É fácil + verb” (É fácil se perder. / É fácil ler.). You can add who it is easy for with “para”: “É fácil para mim/para você/para um macaco…”. The opposite is often “é difícil” (“it’s hard”).
target_language_example: Não se preocupe: é fácil aprender isso com prática.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’s easy to learn that with practice.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to say something is easy to do: “X é fácil de + infinitive” (e.g., “é fácil de usar”). You can also see “é fácil de se + infinitive” when the action refers back to the subject (more common in Brazilian Portuguese), e.g., “O esperanto é fácil de se pronunciar” = “Esperanto is easy to pronounce.” In questions, it often comes first: “É fácil de instalar?”
target_language_example: Este aplicativo é fácil de usar.
native_language_example: This app is easy to use.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ser" ("é" = "is") to describe size or height: "Aquele cachorro é grande" (That dog is big). With "o suficiente" ("enough"), it often means being old/mature enough to do something: "Você é grande o suficiente para..." = "You’re old enough/big enough to...". In questions, "É grande?" means "Is it big?".
target_language_example: Esse apartamento é grande demais para mim.
native_language_example: That apartment is too big for me.

additional_notes: Used to say that the moment to do something has arrived. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb: "É hora de comer" (to eat), "É hora de dormir" (to sleep). You can add "agora" for emphasis: "Agora é hora de...".
target_language_example: É hora de ir embora.
native_language_example: It’s time to leave.

additional_notes: Used to state equality, especially in math, measurements, and conversions. The pattern is: [X] é igual a [Y]. In speech it’s often shortened to "igual a" in equations (e.g., "cinco mais três, igual a oito").
target_language_example: Dois mais dois é igual a quatro.
native_language_example: Two plus two is equal to four.

additional_notes: Used to say that something matters or is significant. Often appears as a full sentence (“É importante.” = “It’s important.”) or with a complement: “É importante para mim” (important to me), “É importante para a economia” (important for the economy). You can also ask “Para quem é importante?” = “To whom is it important?”
target_language_example: É importante chegar cedo.
native_language_example: It’s important to arrive early.

additional_notes: Used with **é** ("is") + **impossível** ("impossible") to state that something can’t happen or can’t be done. Often followed by an infinitive: **É impossível + verbo** (e.g., *É impossível entender tudo* = "It’s impossible to understand everything"). It can also be used in questions: *É impossível…?* = "Is it impossible…?"
target_language_example: É impossível chegar a tempo sem um carro.
native_language_example: It’s impossible to arrive on time without a car.

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific thing and introduce a clause explaining it. Common in answers and clarifications: “É isso que eu quero” = “That’s what I want.” Often follows a question or contrast (e.g., “Não é isso que você queria?”).
target_language_example: É isso que eu estava tentando dizer.
native_language_example: That’s what I was trying to say.

additional_notes: Used to say someone isn’t old enough to do something, understand something, or have something. Pattern: (person) + é + jovem demais + para + infinitive (e.g., viajar, entender, ser) or + noun phrase (e.g., este trabalho). Often used with “ainda” (“still”): “ainda é jovem demais para…”.
target_language_example: Ela é jovem demais para dirigir.
native_language_example: She is too young to drive.

additional_notes: Used with "ser" + "maior" + "do que" to compare size, amount, number, age, importance, etc. It agrees with the thing being compared: "é maior" (singular), "são maiores" (plural). Common variants: "mais ... do que" (more ... than) and "menor do que" (smaller/less than).
target_language_example: Este problema é maior do que parece.
native_language_example: This problem is bigger than it seems.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective/adverb to make comparisons: **X é mais + adjective/adverb + (do) que + Y** (“X is more … than Y”). In speech, **do que** is often shortened to **que**. It can also appear in fixed-sounding phrases like **é mais calmo** (“it’s calmer/it’s more peaceful”) or **não é mais …** (“no longer …”), e.g. **Você não é mais bem-vindo** (“You’re no longer welcome”).
target_language_example: Este caminho é mais rápido do que aquele.
native_language_example: This route is faster than that one.

additional_notes: Used with **que** to compare two people or things: **X é mais alto que Y** (“X is taller/higher than Y”). With people it usually means “taller”; with objects/measurements it can mean “higher” (e.g., on the left/right, a number, a sound level). **alto/alta** agrees with what you’re describing, but in **é mais alto**, the masculine form is common when referring to a man or to something masculine.
target_language_example: Este prédio é mais alto que aquele.
native_language_example: This building is taller/higher than that one.

additional_notes: Used to compare height. Pattern: "[X] é mais alto do que [Y]" = "[X] is taller than [Y]". You can make a question by raising intonation or using a question mark in writing: "O Tom é mais alto do que a Mary?". The "do que" part means "than" in comparisons (often used with "mais/menos" + adjective).
target_language_example: Meu irmão é mais alto do que eu.
