native_language_example: My brother is taller than me.

additional_notes: Used to compare height (physical or figurative, e.g., buildings): **A é mais alto que B**. You can change the subject and keep the pattern: **sou/é/está/são mais alto(s) que...**. With women you often use **mais alta** (feminine): **Ela é mais alta que ele**. In questions: **Ele é mais alto que…?**
target_language_example: Este prédio é mais alto que o outro.
native_language_example: This building is taller than the other one.

additional_notes: Used to compare height. Structure: "ser" + "mais alto/alta" + "que" + person/pronoun. You can change the adjective for gender/number (alto/alta/altos/altas) and replace "eu" with another person (ele/ela/você/nós, etc.). In everyday speech, many people also say "do que eu" ("é mais alto do que eu").
target_language_example: Ela é mais alta que eu, mas o irmão dela é mais alto ainda.
native_language_example: She’s taller than me, but her brother is even taller.

additional_notes: Used to compare strength, ability, or overall power. Structure: [subject] + é + mais forte + do que + [comparison]. It can be literal (physical strength) or figurative (a team/opponent is stronger). In phrases like “É mais forte do que parece!”, it means something is stronger/more intense than it appears.
target_language_example: Este remédio é mais forte do que o outro.
native_language_example: This medicine is stronger than the other one.

additional_notes: Used to compare difficulty: **é mais fácil + infinitive** (“it’s easier to…”). It often appears with **do que** to compare two actions/things (“easier than…”): *É mais fácil atacar… do que…*. You may also see **mais fácil que** in informal speech, but **mais fácil do que** is generally preferred for comparisons.
target_language_example: É mais fácil aprender com prática do que só com teoria.
native_language_example: It’s easier to learn with practice than only with theory.

additional_notes: Used to say that one thing/person matters more than another. It often appears with comparisons using "que" or "do que" (“than”): "X é mais importante que Y" / "... do que Y". It’s also common in questions: "O que é mais importante?" (“What is more important?”). You can add emphasis with "para mim" (“to me/for me”): "Você é mais importante para mim."
target_language_example: Para mim, a saúde é mais importante do que o dinheiro.
native_language_example: For me, health is more important than money.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things and say one matters more than the other: X é mais importante do que Y. Common with nouns (Qualidade é mais importante do que quantidade) or with clauses introduced by o que (“what”): O que se faz é mais importante do que o que se diz (“What you do is more important than what you say”). You can change the verb for other subjects: são mais importantes do que (plural), foi/era mais importante do que (past).
target_language_example: Para mim, dormir bem é mais importante do que trabalhar até tarde.
native_language_example: For me, sleeping well is more important than working late.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things. Structure: [X] é mais inteligente do que [Y] = X is more intelligent than Y. Often followed by a person/pronoun (Maria, eles, você) or by a clause (do que Maria pensa = than Maria thinks; do que parece = than it seems). In Brazilian Portuguese, you may also hear 'do que' shortened to 'que' in casual speech, but 'do que' is standard.
target_language_example: Ela é mais inteligente do que eu pensava.
native_language_example: She is smarter than I thought.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages. Pattern: [person] é mais novo(a) do que [other person]. Use novo for a male subject and nova for a female subject. In negatives, you often hear: não é mais novo(a) do que… In Brazilian Portuguese it’s common to drop “sou” after “eu” (e.g., “do que eu” instead of “do que eu sou”).
target_language_example: Ela é mais nova do que o irmão.
native_language_example: She is younger than her brother.

additional_notes: Used with "que" to compare: "X é mais velho que Y" = "X is older than Y". "Velho" agrees with the person/thing described: "mais velha" (feminine). Can also be used for objects (car, video, etc.) to mean they’re older.
target_language_example: Ela é mais velha que o irmão dela.
native_language_example: She is older than her brother.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages. Structure: [someone/something] + é + mais velho(a) + do que + [someone/something]. Change to feminine: é mais velha do que. Common with people (age) and things like whisky (how long it has been aged).
target_language_example: Meu irmão é mais velho do que eu.
native_language_example: My brother is older than me.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ser" + "mais velho" + "que" to compare age: "X é mais velho que Y". "Velho" agrees with the subject’s gender/number (e.g., "ela é mais velha que..."; "eles são mais velhos que..."). With "qualquer um/uma", it means "older than anyone": "é mais velho que qualquer um daqui".
target_language_example: Ela é mais velha que eu, mas parece mais nova.
native_language_example: She is older than me, but she looks younger.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (é) + comparative melhor to compare things or say that one option is preferable. Common patterns: “X é melhor (do que Y)” = “X is better (than Y)”; “É melhor + infinitive” = “It’s better to…”. It can also mean “(someone) is better” in the sense of being superior at something, depending on context.
target_language_example: Acho que é melhor esperar um pouco.
native_language_example: I think it’s better to wait a bit.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things/people. Structure: [something] é melhor do que [something else]. “Melhor” agrees in number only when used as an adjective before a noun (e.g., melhores), but in this pattern it usually stays “melhor”. Often appears with possessives: “o meu é melhor do que o seu” = “mine is better than yours.”
target_language_example: A comida aqui é melhor do que a de lá.
native_language_example: The food here is better than the food there.

meaning: “is better than the …” (feminine; comparing two things).
additional_notes: Used to compare two things: X é melhor do que a Y = “X is better than Y,” where Y is a feminine noun (often omitted and implied, like “a sua” = “yours” [feminine thing]). With a masculine noun, use “é melhor do que o …” (e.g., “O meu plano é melhor do que o teu”).
target_language_example: A minha opção é melhor do que a tua.
native_language_example: My option is better than yours.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things/ideas. It agrees with the thing being described: é (he/she/it is), são (they are). You can also say “é melhor do que” (often interchangeable with “é melhor que” in everyday Portuguese).
target_language_example: Dormir cedo é melhor que ficar acordado até tarde.
native_language_example: Going to bed early is better than staying up late.

additional_notes: Used to give strong advice or a warning about what someone should do. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb: “É melhor você + verbo” (e.g., aprender, aproveitar, tomar). You can also hear “É melhor você não + verbo” for negative advice (“You’d better not…”).
target_language_example: É melhor você sair agora, porque vai chover.
native_language_example: You’d better leave now, because it’s going to rain.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is your friend. The verb “é” comes from “ser” (to be) and is used for identity/relationship (not a temporary state). You’ll often also hear the plural: “são meus amigos” (they are my friends). In speech, you might drop the subject when it’s clear: “É meu amigo.”
target_language_example: Ela é minha amiga.
native_language_example: She is my friend.

additional_notes: Used with "ser" to say something belongs to you. As a question, it often asks about ownership: "Isso é meu?" = "Is this mine?". With a noun, you usually say "é meu/minha" (agreeing with the noun’s gender): "O carro é meu" (my car), "A bolsa é minha" (my bag).
target_language_example: Este livro é meu.
native_language_example: This book is mine.

additional_notes: Used to say that something belongs to you. Portuguese possessives agree with the gender/number of the thing owned: minha (fem. singular), minhas (fem. plural). For masculine you use meu/meus (e.g., “É meu.”). You can use it with a noun (“Essa bolsa é minha.”) or without repeating the noun (“Não é minha.”).
target_language_example: Desculpe, essa cadeira é minha.
native_language_example: Sorry, that chair is mine.

meaning: “is very / is really” (used to intensify an adjective).
additional_notes: Used with adjectives to emphasize a quality: “é muito + adjective” (e.g., é muito honesto = is very honest). Although muito literally means “much/a lot,” in this pattern it usually corresponds to “very” in English.
target_language_example: Este café é muito bom.
native_language_example: This coffee is very good.

additional_notes: Used to describe something feminine (or referred to with a feminine noun like comida, ideia) as very good. With masculine nouns, use “é muito bom”. For plural, use “são muito bons/boas”. You can add “mesmo” or “realmente” for extra emphasis.
target_language_example: A sobremesa é muito boa.
native_language_example: The dessert is very good.

additional_notes: Used to evaluate something positively (“It’s very good”) or to say something is nice/pleasant, often with an infinitive: “É muito bom + verb” (e.g., é muito bom ver você = it’s really nice to see you). With people it can mean “He/She is very good (at something)” or “He/She is very good” depending on context; in that case it’s often followed by “em/para + verb/noun” (e.g., É muito bom para mudar de assunto = He’s very good at changing the subject).
target_language_example: É muito bom aprender português com você.
native_language_example: It’s really nice to learn Portuguese with you.

meaning: "is very good at" (skilled at doing something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone's ability/skill. It’s the verb "ser" (permanent/typical trait) + "muito bom" + "em" + an activity. After "em", you often use an infinitive verb (e.g., "em nadar", "em dirigir", "em fazer isso") or a noun (e.g., "em xadrez"). To negate: "não é muito bom em..."
target_language_example: Ela é muito boa em matemática.
native_language_example: She is very good at math.

meaning: "is very beautiful" (said about a feminine noun/person).
additional_notes: Used to describe something/someone feminine as very beautiful. It’s the verb ser (é = “is”) + intensifier muito (“very”) + feminine adjective bonita (“beautiful”). For masculine nouns, you say: é muito bonito. For plural feminine: são muito bonitas; plural masculine/mixed: são muito bonitos.
target_language_example: A cidade à noite é muito bonita.
native_language_example: The city at night is very beautiful.

meaning: “it is very beautiful / it’s very nice.”
additional_notes: Used to compliment something you can see or are talking about (a place, object, clothing, etc.). Often said with emphasis or an exclamation (“É muito bonito!”). You can change the subject (e.g., “O jardim é muito bonito.”) and the adjective for gender/number (bonito/bonita/bonitos/bonitas).
target_language_example: A sua casa é muito bonita.
native_language_example: Your house is very beautiful.

additional_notes: Used to complain or comment that something costs a lot. "é" = "it is"; "muito" intensifies ("very/really"); "caro" = "expensive". You can specify the thing before it (e.g., "Este vinho é muito caro") or just say it alone ("É muito caro!"). For feminine nouns, change to "é muito cara" (e.g., "A casa é muito cara").
target_language_example: Desculpe, para mim é muito caro.
native_language_example: Sorry, for me it’s very expensive.

additional_notes: Used to describe something as being very hard or challenging. You can add a subject before it (e.g., "Russo é muito difícil") or use it by itself as a full sentence ("É muito difícil...") followed by an infinitive ("de aprender", "impressionar").
target_language_example: É muito difícil encontrar um bom apartamento aqui.
native_language_example: It’s very difficult to find a good apartment here.

meaning: 'is very big/large' (or 'it's too big/large,' depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to describe the size of something. Often followed by "para + infinitive" to mean "too ... to ..." (e.g., "É muito grande para..." = "It’s too big to..."). Also commonly appears with a subject: "X é muito grande" = "X is very big."
target_language_example: Essa mala é muito grande para levar no avião.
native_language_example: That suitcase is too big to take on the plane.

additional_notes: Used to stress that something matters a lot. Common in explanations and instructions, often followed by an infinitive: “É muito importante + verb” (e.g., “É muito importante assinar…” = “It’s very important to sign…”). You can also use it with “para” to show who/what it’s important to: “X é muito importante para Y” = “X is very important to Y.”
target_language_example: É muito importante chegar cedo amanhã.
native_language_example: It’s very important to arrive early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express that someone or something matters a lot to you. It often follows the subject: "Isso/Ele/Ela é muito importante para mim." You can adjust intensity: "é importante para mim" (important), "é muito importante para mim" (very important).
target_language_example: Você é muito importante para mim.
native_language_example: You are very important to me.

additional_notes: Used to describe something you find interesting. It often follows the thing you’re talking about (subject + é muito interessante). You can change it to match the subject: é (it/he/she is), são (they are). You can also adjust intensity: é interessante (interesting), é bem interessante (quite interesting), é muito interessante (very interesting).
target_language_example: A aula de hoje é muito interessante.
native_language_example: Today’s class is very interesting.

additional_notes: Used to say someone doesn’t have the right age (or isn’t mature enough) to do something: **ser + muito jovem + para + infinitive** (é muito jovem para dirigir) or **ser + muito jovem + para + noun/pronoun** (é muito jovem para isso). You can change the person/tense: *sou/era/foi muito jovem para...*
target_language_example: Eles dizem que eu sou muito jovem para viajar sozinho.
native_language_example: They say I’m too young to travel alone.

meaning: “is much more” (used to make a strong comparison).
additional_notes: Used with adjectives or quantities to say one thing is much more/greater than another. Common patterns: “é muito mais + adjective + que/do que + …” (e.g., mais interessante, mais frio) and “é muito mais + adjective” when the comparison is understood from context. “Que” and “do que” are both common in comparisons like this.
target_language_example: Este filme é muito mais longo do que eu pensei.
native_language_example: This movie is much longer than I thought.

é muito mais velho do que

target_language_multi_word_term: é muito mais velho do que
additional_notes: Used to compare ages: “X é muito mais velho do que Y” = “X is much older than Y.” Often followed by what someone thinks/sees: “do que parece / do que aparenta (ser)” (“than he looks/seems”) or “do que você pensa que ele é” (“than you think he is”). Note: “do que” introduces the comparison (“than”).
target_language_example: Ela é muito mais velha do que parece.
native_language_example: She is much older than she looks.

additional_notes: Used to describe a feminine noun (e.g., a vila, a caixa, a possibilidade). For masculine nouns, you say “é muito pequeno” (e.g., “O apartamento é muito pequeno.”). It can refer to physical size (“The box is very small”) or to something abstract like a chance/possibility (“The possibility is very small”).
target_language_example: A chance de chover hoje é muito pequena.
native_language_example: The chance of rain today is very small.

additional_notes: Used to warn or emphasize that a situation, action, place, or person is very dangerous. Common patterns: "É muito perigoso + infinitive" (É muito perigoso nadar aqui. = It’s very dangerous to swim here.) and "X é muito perigoso" (Tom é muito perigoso. = Tom is very dangerous.). Often said on its own as a warning: "É muito perigoso!".
target_language_example: É muito perigoso atravessar a rua aqui.
native_language_example: It’s very dangerous to cross the street here.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is very useful. Often followed by “para + [person/thing]” to mean “for (someone/something)”: “É muito útil para mim” = “It’s very useful for me.” You can also use it with different subjects: “Este site é muito útil.”
target_language_example: Este aplicativo é muito útil para estudar português.
native_language_example: This app is very useful for studying Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used to say something is needed or required. Often followed by an infinitive ("É necessário reduzir os custos") or by "que" + subjunctive ("É necessário que você faça isso agora"). It can also be used alone as a short, formal-sounding question or confirmation ("É necessário?").
target_language_example: Não é necessário trazer nada; nós já temos tudo.
native_language_example: It’s not necessary to bring anything; we already have everything.

meaning: “is the” (he/it is the …, referring to a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to link a subject to a masculine singular noun phrase with the definite article “o”. It often appears in identification/classification (“Ele é o médico.”), superlatives (“é o mais…”), and definitions (“X é o…”). For feminine singular, use “é a”; for plural, “são os/as”.
target_language_example: Lisboa é o destino perfeito para um fim de semana.
native_language_example: Lisbon is the perfect destination for a weekend.

additional_notes: Used to say someone owns something (é o dono da empresa/loja/casa) or is the person in charge. Often followed by "de" or "da/do" + the thing owned. Feminine form: "é a dona".
target_language_example: Ela é a dona do restaurante.
native_language_example: She is the owner of the restaurant.

meaning: 'is the man' (used to identify or describe a male person).
additional_notes: Used with a name or pronoun to say someone is a particular man: (1) identifying someone (“Tom é o homem que…” = “Tom is the man who…”), (2) describing him (“…mais rápido do mundo” = “the fastest in the world”), or (3) saying he’s the right person (“o homem certo para este trabalho” = “the right man for this job”). In casual speech it can also be used as praise (“Ele é o homem!” = “He’s the man!”).
target_language_example: Ele é o homem que falou comigo ontem.
native_language_example: He is the man who spoke to me yesterday.

meaning: “he is the most … man” / “he is the …-est man”.
additional_notes: Used to make a superlative description about a man (homem) in a comparison set. Structure: **Ele é o homem mais + adjective + de/da/do + place** (“the richest in the city/world”) or **Ele é o homem mais + adjective + que + verb** (“the most attractive that I know”). Often paired with superlative adjectives like **rico** (rich), **atraente** (attractive), **inteligente** (smart).
target_language_example: Ele é o homem mais inteligente da turma.
native_language_example: He is the smartest man in the class.

additional_notes: Used to identify or define a specific man by adding a relative clause with que (“who/that”). Word order can change for emphasis (e.g., “Feliz é o homem que…” = “Happy is the man who…”). In everyday speech you’ll also hear “Ele é o homem que…”.
target_language_example: Ele é o homem que resolveu o problema.
native_language_example: He’s the man who solved the problem.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the largest in size/amount/importance within a group or category. It uses the superlative idea with **maior** (“bigger/greater”). It agrees with the noun: **é a maior** (feminine), **são os maiores / as maiores** (plural). Often followed by **do/da** + place/group: *do mundo* (“in the world”), *do país* (“in the country”).
target_language_example: Este shopping é o maior da cidade.
native_language_example: This mall is the biggest in the city.

additional_notes: Used to state that a country has the largest area (usually) within a region. Pattern: «[País] é o maior país da [região]». With feminine regions you use «da» (de + a): da Europa, da Ásia, da Oceania. With masculine regions you use «do» (de + o): do mundo, do continente. With plural regions: «dos/das».
target_language_example: O Canadá é o maior país da América do Norte.
native_language_example: Canada is the largest country in North America.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective to say someone/something has the highest degree of that quality: “Ele é o mais alto.” (“He is the tallest.”). It can be followed by a comparison group, often with “de” or “dos/das”: “o mais baixo dos dois” (“the shorter/shortest of the two”). Note: if you’re talking about “the least,” use “é o menos …”.
target_language_example: Este restaurante é o mais barato do bairro.
native_language_example: This restaurant is the cheapest in the neighborhood.

additional_notes: Used to say someone (a man/boy) has the greatest height in a group. It’s the superlative form of "alto" (tall): "o mais alto" = "the tallest". The group is often introduced with "de/da/do/dos" (e.g., "da família", "do time", "dos dois"). For a woman/girl: "é a mais alta".
target_language_example: O Pedro é o mais alto da classe.
native_language_example: Pedro is the tallest in the class.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is the top choice or best in a group. It can be followed by a noun (“é o melhor professor”) or a more specific description (“é o melhor … que conheço”). It also works with abstract ideas: “X é o melhor caminho” = “X is the best way/path.” Feminine form: “é a melhor” (for feminine nouns like “opção”). Plural: “são os/as melhores.”
target_language_example: Este restaurante é o melhor do bairro.
native_language_example: This restaurant is the best in the neighborhood.

additional_notes: Used to say that a place has the top reputation/quality among restaurants in a certain area. Often followed by “de + place” (é o melhor restaurante de Londres = in London) or “na/em + place” (é o melhor restaurante na cidade / em nossa área). You can swap “é” for “esse/este é” (“this/that is the best restaurant”).
target_language_example: Para mim, este é o melhor restaurante do bairro.
native_language_example: For me, this is the best restaurant in the neighborhood.

meaning: "is my" / "is mine" (used before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something belongs to you or is associated with you. Pattern: [Name/thing] + é o meu + masculine noun (e.g., apelido, mentor, chefe). For feminine nouns, use "é a minha" (e.g., "Ela é a minha amiga").
target_language_example: Este é o meu irmão.
native_language_example: This is my brother.

additional_notes: Used to say someone (or even something, like a book) is your best friend. You can swap the subject: “O João é o meu melhor amigo.” If the speaker is female, you’ll often hear “é o meu melhor amigo” (referring to the friend), but you can also say “é a minha melhor amiga” when the best friend is female. In Brazil it’s also common to drop the article: “é meu melhor amigo / é minha melhor amiga.”
target_language_example: Você é o meu melhor amigo desde a escola.
native_language_example: You’ve been my best friend since school.

meaning: 'is our' (referring to a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something belongs to or is associated with “us” (a group including the speaker). It agrees with what comes after: for feminine singular use “é a nossa”; for plural use “são os nossos / são as nossas”. Often followed by a noun phrase like “rei”, “melhor piloto”, “primeiro dever”.
target_language_example: Este carro é o nosso.
native_language_example: This car is ours.

additional_notes: Used to say that something/someone comes before all others in order, ranking, or time. Often followed by a noun ("é o primeiro dia" = "it’s the first day"), or by "de" + plural to mean “the first of …” ("é o primeiro de todos" = "it’s the first of all"). With an infinitive, you often use "a/em" ("não é o primeiro a cometer" = "you’re not the first to make").
target_language_example: Este é o primeiro dia do curso.
native_language_example: This is the first day of the course.

additional_notes: Used to identify what (or who) is causing the difficulty: “X é o problema.” It can also appear in questions like “Onde é o problema?” (“Where is the problem?”) or “O que é o problema?” (“What’s the problem?”).
target_language_example: A falta de tempo é o problema.
native_language_example: The lack of time is the problem.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or emphasize the key point in a sentence (a focus/cleft structure): “X é o que + verb/phrase” = “X is what + verb/phrase.” It can also be used on its own to confirm or point back to what was said: “É o que dizem.” (“That’s what they say.”) / “É o que estou dizendo!” (“That’s what I’m saying!”).
target_language_example: Isso é o que eu queria dizer.
native_language_example: That’s what I wanted to say.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is the thing you do/think/want/choose, usually followed by a verb (pensei, escolheria, estou fazendo) or by “mais” for emphasis (“é o que eu mais gosto/mais queria” = “it’s what I like/wanted most”). Often refers back to a previous situation or question ("That's what I thought/said/chose").
target_language_example: É o que eu mais preciso agora.
native_language_example: It’s what I need most right now.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun to say something belongs to/relates to the person you’re addressing: "É o seu carro" = "It’s your car." In questions, it often introduces the subject: "Quando é o seu próximo jogo?" = "When is your next game?" It changes with gender/number: "é a sua" (fem. sing.), "são os seus" (masc. pl.), "são as suas" (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: É o seu problema, você precisa resolver.
native_language_example: It’s your problem; you need to solve it.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun to ask or say that something belongs to the person you’re talking to: “De que cor é o teu cabelo?” (“What color is your hair?”). Often the full form is “é o teu + noun” (“is your + [masc. noun]”). On its own, “é o teu” can also mean “it’s yours” (referring back to a masculine thing already mentioned). Note: “teu” = your (informal in Brazil; common in Portugal).
target_language_example: Este casaco é o teu?
native_language_example: Is this coat yours?

additional_notes: Used to say something is the final one in an order or sequence (time, list, line, etc.). It agrees with what you’re talking about: masculine singular “o último” (dia, mês); feminine singular “a última” (aula, vez). For plural: “os últimos / as últimas”. Often followed by a noun: “é o último dia…”.
target_language_example: Este é o último trem para o centro.
native_language_example: This is the last train to downtown.

additional_notes: Used to say that a person/thing is the sole one in a group or situation. It usually agrees in gender/number: é o único (masc. singular), é a única (fem. singular), são os únicos (masc. plural/mixed), são as únicas (fem. plural). Often followed by a noun ("é o único idioma") or by "com quem/que" to mean "the only one (that/with whom)...".
target_language_example: Ela é a única pessoa que entende isso.
native_language_example: She is the only person who understands this.

additional_notes: Used to say that only one person or thing (the subject) has a certain quality or does a certain action. Often followed by a verb phrase: “é o único que sabe…”, “é o único que está…”. It can refer to a person (“the only one who”) or sometimes a thing (“the only thing that”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Ela é a única que entende o problema.
native_language_example: She is the only one who understands the problem.

additional_notes: Used to say that only one person/thing is able to do something. It’s usually followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., pode ajudar, pode esclarecer) and can change for gender/number: é a única que pode (the only [woman] who can), são os únicos que podem (the only ones who can).
target_language_example: Ela é a única que pode resolver esse problema agora.
native_language_example: She’s the only one who can solve this problem right now.

additional_notes: Used to compare something (feminine noun) with something that belongs to you. Structure: "[X] é parecida com a minha" = "[X] is similar to mine". "Parecida" agrees with a feminine thing being compared (e.g., opinião, bicicleta, cadeira). For masculine nouns, use "é parecido com o meu". You can change the owner: "com a sua", "com a dele/dela", etc.
target_language_example: A sua mochila é parecida com a minha.
native_language_example: Your backpack is similar to mine.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (é) to describe a permanent or general characteristic of something (size). Often followed by “demais” to mean “too small.” For temporary size/fit in a specific situation (like how clothes fit right now), you may also hear “está pequeno.”
target_language_example: A camiseta é pequena para mim.
native_language_example: The T-shirt is small for me.

additional_notes: Used to describe something (or someone) as ideal or without flaws. It’s the verb ser (é = “is”) + the adjective perfeito (“perfect”) in the masculine form; for feminine nouns use “é perfeita” (e.g., A casa é perfeita). Often used as a strong compliment.
target_language_example: Para mim, este plano é perfeito.
native_language_example: For me, this plan is perfect.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (é = “is”) to say that a situation, action, or person is dangerous. It can be a statement (Isto é perigoso.), a question (O Tom é perigoso?), or an exclamation (É perigoso brincar na rua!). You can add what it’s dangerous to with “a/à” (e.g., perigoso à saúde = “dangerous to your health”).
target_language_example: É perigoso andar sozinho à noite.
native_language_example: It’s dangerous to walk alone at night.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the reason or explanation for something just mentioned. Often follows a cause and then gives the consequence (or conclusion). You can also hear it as: “Por isso é que…”.
target_language_example: Está chovendo muito; é por isso que vamos ficar em casa.
native_language_example: It’s raining a lot; that’s why we’re staying home.

additional_notes: Used to explain the reason for your own action. It’s the start of a longer sentence, followed by a verb: “É por isso que eu voltei” (That’s why I came back). You can replace “eu” with another subject: “É por isso que ele/ela…” (That’s why he/she…).
target_language_example: É por isso que eu estou aqui.
native_language_example: That’s why I’m here.

additional_notes: Used to say that something can happen or can be done, or to ask if something can happen. Very common with an infinitive verb: "É possível viajar...?" (= "Is it possible to travel...?") and with "que": "É possível que..." (= "It’s possible that...").
target_language_example: É possível pagar com cartão?
native_language_example: Is it possible to pay by card?

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. It’s very commonly followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "É possível que ele chegue tarde" = "It’s possible that he arrives late"). In questions it can also sound like surprise or disbelief ("Como é possível que...?" = "How is it possible that...?").
target_language_example: É possível que eu chegue um pouco atrasado.
native_language_example: It’s possible that I’ll arrive a little late.

meaning: it is necessary; one must; it takes (e.g., money/time).
additional_notes: Used to say something is necessary or required. Common patterns: (1) "É preciso + infinitive": É preciso observar as regras. (2) "É preciso que + subjunctive": É preciso que vocês me escutem. It can also mean "it takes" when talking about what’s required to achieve something (money, effort, etc.).
target_language_example: Para aprender bem, é preciso praticar todos os dias.
native_language_example: To learn well, you need to practice every day.

additional_notes: Used on signs and in rules to say an action is not permitted. It’s the verb ser (é = “is”) + the adjective proibido (“forbidden”). Often followed by an infinitive: É proibido + entrar / fumar / fazer fotos. You may also see agreement with a noun: É proibida a entrada. (“Entry is forbidden.”)
target_language_example: Aqui é proibido fumar.
native_language_example: Smoking is not allowed here.

meaning: "it’s likely/probable that" (introduces something that is likely to happen or be true).
additional_notes: Used to express probability or a reasonable guess. Very often followed by the subjunctive: "É provável que ele chegue tarde". You can also use it in the middle of a sentence: "O Tom é provável que ainda esteja...".
target_language_example: É provável que a gente chegue depois das oito.
native_language_example: We’ll probably arrive after eight.

meaning: “it’s that you…” / “the thing is, you…”; also used for emphasis in questions (“why is it that you…?”).
additional_notes: This is basically **é que + você**. In statements it often introduces an explanation or highlights the main point: **“O importante é que você…”** = “The important thing is that you…”. In questions (often after **por que**, **como**, **onde**, etc.), **é que** adds emphasis and sounds like “is it that”: **“Por que é que você…?”** = “Why is it that you…?”. It’s common in spoken Portuguese and neutral in formality.
target_language_example: O problema é que você não me avisou antes.
native_language_example: The problem is that you didn’t let me know earlier.

meaning: 'is really' / 'it really is' (used for emphasis or to check if something is true).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize a statement (often meaning “truly/very”), or in questions to express doubt/surprise (“Is he really…?”). Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase: “é realmente triste”, “é realmente um bom rapaz”.
target_language_example: Isso é realmente importante para mim.
native_language_example: That’s really important to me.

meaning: “is rich” (has a lot of money); also “is rich in” (has a lot of something).
additional_notes: Used with the verb ser: (ele/ela/você) é rico/é rica; (eles/elas/vocês) são ricos/são ricas. It can mean financially wealthy (Meu irmão é rico.) or, with em + noun, “rich in” in a broader sense (O Japão não é rico em recursos naturais.).
target_language_example: Ela é rica, mas diz que dinheiro não traz felicidade.
native_language_example: She’s rich, but she says money doesn’t bring happiness.

additional_notes: Used to state what day of the week it is. Often appears with a time reference like “Hoje é segunda-feira” (Today is Monday) or in questions like “Hoje é segunda-feira?” (Is today Monday?). Can also be used to say an event happens on Monday: “A reunião é segunda-feira” (The meeting is on Monday).
target_language_example: Desculpa, estou cansado — é segunda-feira.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m tired — it’s Monday.

additional_notes: Used to say a place/situation is safe, or as a yes/no question: “É seguro?” = “Is it safe?” Often followed by a location with “aqui/lá/fora de…” (here/there/outside of…). Negative: “Não é seguro” = “It’s not safe.” Note: “seguro” can also mean “insurance” as a noun, but in “é seguro” it means “safe.”
target_language_example: É seguro andar aqui à noite?
native_language_example: Is it safe to walk here at night?

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ser** to ask or state who something belongs to: **Este rádio é seu?** (“Is this radio yours?”). It agrees with the thing owned: **é seu** (masc. singular), **é sua** (fem. singular), **são seus** (masc. plural), **são suas** (fem. plural). Note: **seu/sua** can also mean “his/her/their” depending on context, but in questions like these it often means “your.”
target_language_example: Esta mochila é sua ou é dele?
native_language_example: Is this backpack yours or his?

meaning: “it’s yours” (feminine form, referring to something feminine like “a bola”, “a escolha”).
additional_notes: Used to say that something belongs to “you” (informal singular: você/tu, depending on the region) and the thing owned is feminine. Often appears as “A/Esta/Essa + noun (feminine) + é sua.” Also used in set phrases like “A escolha é sua” (“The choice is yours”). For masculine nouns, use “é seu” (e.g., “O livro é seu”).
target_language_example: Esta chave é sua?
native_language_example: Is this key yours?

additional_notes: Used to downplay something or say it’s not a big deal ("It’s just..."). With an infinitive verb, it often means a simple instruction/solution: "É só + infinitive" = "You just have to..." / "All you have to do is...". In negative form, "não é só" means "it’s not just/only".
target_language_example: Não é só uma questão de tempo; é só ter paciência.
native_language_example: It’s not just a matter of time; you just have to be patient.

meaning: “it’s just a” (only a; nothing more than a).
additional_notes: Used to downplay or limit what something/someone is, often to reassure or minimize importance. It agrees with the noun: é só um + masculine singular noun (e.g., um corte), é só uma + feminine singular noun (e.g., uma fase). In speech it can sound dismissive depending on tone.
target_language_example: Calma, é só um teste.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s just a test.

additional_notes: Used to state the day of the week. Often appears with time words like hoje (today), amanhã (tomorrow), ontem (yesterday), and depois de amanhã (the day after tomorrow). In the past you switch to foi: Ontem foi domingo. You can also drop the article: É terça-feira / É uma terça-feira (a Tuesday).
target_language_example: Não posso na segunda; é terça-feira que eu tenho tempo.
native_language_example: I can’t on Monday; it’s on Tuesday that I have time.

é três anos mais velho que

target_language_multi_word_term: é três anos mais velho que
additional_notes: Used to compare ages. Structure: [person] + é + [number] + anos + mais velho/velha + que + [other person]. Use **velho** for a male person and **velha** for a female person being described. You can change the number of years (e.g., é dois anos mais velho que…).
target_language_example: Minha irmã é três anos mais velha que eu.
native_language_example: My sister is three years older than me.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons to say someone/something is 3 cm taller/shorter/longer/etc. than another: “é três centímetros mais alto/baixo/… que (ou do que) + pessoa/coisa”. Often you’ll see it as “X é três centímetros mais alto que Y” (“X is three centimeters taller than Y”). “Que” and “do que” are both common after comparatives.
target_language_example: A cadeira é três centímetros mais alta que a mesa.
native_language_example: The chair is three centimeters taller than the table.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the only thing that remains, is possible, or is available. Often followed by a verb phrase (e.g., "podemos fazer") or by "temos/tenho" to mean “that’s all we have.” In questions, it can mean “is that all that…?”
target_language_example: Desculpa, é tudo o que eu sei.
native_language_example: Sorry, that’s all I know.

meaning: “is so / is as (…as)” (used to intensify a description).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective/adverb to mean “so” (very) or “as … as” in comparisons. Common patterns: **é tão + adjective** (“is so + adjective”); **é tão … quanto/como + noun/clause** (“is as … as”); **é tão + adjective + a ponto de + infinitive** (“is so … that…”).
target_language_example: Este filme é tão bom quanto o livro.
native_language_example: This movie is as good as the book.

additional_notes: Used to compare height and say two people/things are equal in height. Structure: [subject] + é + tão + alto/alta + quanto + [person/thing]. Use “alto” for masculine subjects and “alta” for feminine subjects. You can also form a question by intonation or adding a question mark in writing.
target_language_example: Ela é tão alta quanto a irmã.
native_language_example: She is as tall as her sister.

additional_notes: Used to compare difficulty or emphasize how hard something is. Often followed by "como" to make a comparison: "não é tão difícil como..." = "it’s not as difficult as...". In questions, it can express surprise or challenge: "É tão difícil...?" = "Is it really that hard...?"
target_language_example: Aprender a pronúncia no começo é tão difícil, mas depois fica mais fácil.
native_language_example: Learning pronunciation at the beginning is so difficult, but later it gets easier.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize importance. Often followed by comparisons with quanto/como (“as … as”): é tão importante quanto/como…. With assim (“é tão importante assim?”), it often expresses doubt or surprise (“Is it really that important?”). You can also add para mim/para ele (“to me/to him”) to show who it matters to.
target_language_example: Isso é tão importante para mim quanto a minha família.
native_language_example: This is as important to me as my family.

meaning: "is a/an" (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or describe someone/something: subject + é + um + (adjective) + noun. For feminine nouns, use “é uma”. For plural, use “são” (e.g., “Eles são…”). Note: with some professions/nationalities you often drop the article (“Ele é médico”), but “é um” is common when you add description (“Ele é um bom médico”).
target_language_example: O Paulo é um professor muito paciente.
native_language_example: Paulo is a very patient teacher.

additional_notes: Used to identify something as an animal. Structure: "é" (it is) + "um" (a) + "animal" (animal). With a specific animal noun: "A raposa é um animal selvagem" (“The fox is a wild animal”). You can add adjectives after "animal" (e.g., "fiel" loyal, "perigoso" dangerous, "forte" strong).
target_language_example: Esse bicho é um animal noturno.
native_language_example: That creature is a nocturnal animal.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (é) to describe someone’s profession or identity as an artist. Often followed by more information (e.g., what kind of art they make) or an adjective like brilhante (“brilliant”) or maravilhoso (“wonderful”).
target_language_example: Ela é uma artista e faz esculturas.
native_language_example: She is an artist and makes sculptures.

additional_notes: Used to state someone’s profession/identity: "[Name] é um ator." The verb "é" is from "ser" (to be) and is used for roles/professions. For a woman, say "é uma atriz".
target_language_example: Ele é um ator famoso no Brasil.
native_language_example: He is a famous actor in Brazil.

meaning: "is a good" (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone/something positively: é ("is") + um ("a"/"an", masculine singular) + bom ("good", masculine singular). For feminine nouns, use "é uma boa"; for plural, "são bons/boas".
target_language_example: Ela é uma boa professora.
native_language_example: She is a good teacher.

meaning: 'he is a good man' (a good person, especially male).
additional_notes: Used to describe a man's character positively (kind, decent, trustworthy). Often said about someone even if you’re not close to them ("Ele não é meu amigo, mas..."). For women, you’d say "é uma boa mulher"; for a general (gender-neutral) version, "é uma boa pessoa". The literal structure is "é" (is) + "um" (a) + "bom" (good) + "homem" (man).
target_language_example: Ele comete erros, mas no fundo é um bom homem.
native_language_example: He makes mistakes, but deep down he's a good man.

additional_notes: Used to say that a city/area/specific spot is suitable for an activity (like living, visiting, studying, eating). Very common pattern: [Place] + é um bom lugar para + infinitive verb (viver, morar, visitar, estudar, comer, etc.). You can change the verb to match what you mean.
target_language_example: Lisboa é um bom lugar para estudar português.
native_language_example: Lisbon is a good place to study Portuguese.

é um bom lugar para se

target_language_multi_word_term: é um bom lugar para se
meaning: 'is a good place to (do something)' (often: to live).
additional_notes: Used to describe somewhere as suitable for an activity. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb, very often "viver" or "morar" (“to live”), as in "é um bom lugar para se viver/morar" = “it’s a good place to live.” The "se" is part of an impersonal/passive-style structure, common in Portuguese when speaking generally (not about a specific person).
target_language_example: Lisboa é um bom lugar para se visitar no verão.
native_language_example: Lisbon is a good place to visit in the summer.

meaning: "is a guy" / "is a (certain kind of) person" (about a man).
additional_notes: Used with adjectives to describe a man: "Ele/Tom é um cara + adjective". "Cara" is informal and common in everyday Brazilian Portuguese; in more formal contexts you can use "homem" or "rapaz" (depending on age). In some contexts, "cara" can be more general like "person," but it most often refers to a male.
target_language_example: Ele é um cara muito legal.
native_language_example: He’s a really nice guy.

meaning: “is a citizen” (a national of a country).
additional_notes: Used to state someone’s citizenship/nationality. Often followed by an adjective for nationality (italiano, australiano, canadense, estadunidense) or by “de + country” (cidadão do Brasil / cidadão de Portugal). In questions you’ll hear: “Você é cidadão de que país?” You can also add an adjective like “leal” to describe the kind of citizen someone is.
target_language_example: Ela é uma cidadã brasileira.
native_language_example: She is a Brazilian citizen.

additional_notes: Used to say that an action is against the law, or (more loosely/hyperbolically) that something is morally outrageous or unacceptable. Common pattern: “Em [place], é um crime + infinitive” (In [place], it’s a crime to + verb).
target_language_example: Aqui, é um crime dirigir sem carteira de motorista.
native_language_example: Here, it’s a crime to drive without a driver’s license.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something belongs to a group: “X é um dos + plural noun” (one of the + plural). It usually introduces a superlative or description: “um dos mais famosos” (one of the most famous). Feminine version: “é uma das …”.
target_language_example: Lisboa é um dos destinos mais populares de Portugal.
native_language_example: Lisbon is one of the most popular destinations in Portugal.

meaning: "is one of the best" (used to praise someone/something as top-level among a group).
additional_notes: Used to say a person or thing ranks among the top in a category. It’s followed by a plural noun (e.g., "jogadores", "países"). You can also change for gender/number: "é uma das melhores" (fem.), "são dos melhores" / "são das melhores" (plural subject). Often appears with opinion markers like "na minha opinião" or "em minha opinião".
target_language_example: Este restaurante é um dos melhores da cidade.
native_language_example: This restaurant is one of the best in the city.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (é) to identify someone as a student. It can be followed by a qualifier like universitário (“university/college”). In the negative, you typically say não é um estudante (“is not a student”).
target_language_example: Ela é uma estudante de português.
native_language_example: She is a Portuguese student.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something as outstanding in a role or category. It’s followed by a noun (usually a profession/role): “Ele/ela é um excelente professor/a.” Agree “excelente” for gender/number only in the article and noun: “é um excelente médico” / “é uma excelente médica” / “são excelentes médicos(as)”.
target_language_example: Ela é uma excelente professora.
native_language_example: She is an excellent teacher.

meaning: "is a boy" / "is a (young) kid" (for a male).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "ser" to describe someone as a boy or young male, often implying youth or immaturity depending on context. "Garoto" is a common, neutral word for "boy" in Brazil. For a girl, you’d say "é uma garota".
target_language_example: Ele é um garoto muito educado.
native_language_example: He is a very polite boy.

additional_notes: Used with a noun: "É um grande + [noun]". With "grande", position affects meaning: before the noun it often means "great/important" (e.g., "um grande homem" = a great man), while after the noun it more often means physical size (e.g., "um homem grande" = a big/tall man).
target_language_example: Ela é uma grande artista.
native_language_example: She is a great artist.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ser" to describe someone as exceptionally intelligent or gifted. It can be sincere praise, or sometimes ironic depending on tone and context. Agreement: for a woman you can say "é uma gênia" (also common to hear "é um gênio" even for women in casual speech).
target_language_example: Você é um gênio por ter resolvido isso tão rápido.
native_language_example: You're a genius for solving that so fast.

additional_notes: Used with the verb “ser” to describe someone as a man, and often followed by an adjective or description: “Ele é um homem honesto” (He’s an honest man), “um homem em quem se pode confiar” (a man you can trust). You can swap in another subject: “Meu pai é um homem…” (My father is a man…).
target_language_example: Ele é um homem de palavra.
native_language_example: He’s a man of his word.

meaning: "he is a man of..." (used to describe a characteristic or quality).
additional_notes: Used with a noun phrase after "de" to describe what someone is like (e.g., character, habits, lifestyle): "um homem de bom coração" (a kind-hearted man), "um homem de poucos prazeres" (a man of few pleasures). You can also vary the person/tense: "Ele é um homem de...", "O João era um homem de...".
target_language_example: Ele é um homem de palavra.
native_language_example: He is a man of his word.

meaning: 'he is a very (… ) man' (used before an adjective).
additional_notes: Used to describe a man's qualities: É (he) + um homem (a man) + muito (very) + adjective (inteligente, paciente, amável, etc.). In Portuguese you normally follow it with an adjective; on its own it sounds incomplete. For a woman, use: “É uma mulher muito …”.
target_language_example: Ele é um homem muito trabalhador.
native_language_example: He is a very hardworking man.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ser** to insult someone’s character/intelligence. It’s rude/offensive in most situations—use with care. **Idiota** agrees in gender/number: **é um idiota** (he/it is an idiot), **é uma idiota** (she/it is an idiot), **são idiotas** (they are idiots).
target_language_example: Não acredito que ele fez isso — é um idiota.
native_language_example: I can’t believe he did that — he’s an idiot.

additional_notes: Used with a sport or game after de: é um jogador de basquete / boliche / futebol. Jogador is masculine; for a woman you usually say é uma jogadora de. In casual speech you may also hear ele joga basquete (“he plays basketball”).
target_language_example: Ele é um jogador de futebol.
native_language_example: He is a soccer player.

additional_notes: Used to define something as a game (chess, sports, etc.). Can also be used figuratively to say something is like a game (often implying strategy, risk, or even cheating), and in questions like “Você acha que isso é um jogo?” it can mean “Are you taking this seriously?”
target_language_example: Para ele, política é um jogo.
native_language_example: For him, politics is a game.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe something as a book. Often followed by more information with "de" (e.g., "É um livro de..." = "It’s a ... book" / "It’s a book about..."). In speech, Portuguese often drops the subject pronoun: "(Isto) é um livro."
target_language_example: Isto é um livro muito interessante.
native_language_example: This is a very interesting book.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say that something is a place, often followed by an adjective or description: “X é um lugar incrível/famoso/bonito.” You can also add “de + noun” to describe the type of place: “um lugar de classe” (“a classy place”).
target_language_example: Este bairro é um lugar tranquilo para morar.
native_language_example: This neighborhood is a peaceful place to live.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ser" (é = "is") to identify someone as a boy. "Um" means "a". Often followed by adjectives or descriptions (e.g., "É um menino tímido" = "He’s a shy boy"). In Portuguese, the subject pronoun (ele = he) is often omitted when it’s clear from context.
target_language_example: Ele é um menino muito inteligente.
native_language_example: He is a very smart boy.

additional_notes: Used to say (often strongly) that a man lies or can’t be trusted. Feminine: "é uma mentirosa". Plural: "são mentirosos/mentirosas". Often used after a name or pronoun: "Ele é um mentiroso."
target_language_example: Não acredite nele — ele é um mentiroso.
native_language_example: Don’t believe him—he’s a liar.

additional_notes: Used to say that something (often a word like Tom, Brigitte, etc.) is a name, sometimes adding extra information: nationality/origin ("é um nome francês"), a description ("é um nome legal" = a cool/nice name), or details like spelling/length ("é um nome de três letras" = a three-letter name).
target_language_example: Sofia é um nome muito comum no Brasil.
native_language_example: Sofia is a very common name in Brazil.

additional_notes: Used to state that something (a place/territory) is a country. Often followed by more information with adjectives or clauses: “é um país independente/desenvolvido/grande…”. Note the structure: [Place] + é + um país. In plural: “são países”.
target_language_example: Portugal é um país pequeno, mas muito bonito.
native_language_example: Portugal is a small country, but very beautiful.

additional_notes: Used to describe a country as very beautiful. Often follows a country name: “A Itália é um país muito bonito.” You can swap the subject (the country) and keep the rest the same. In Portuguese, many country names take the article “a/o” (e.g., a Itália, a Irlanda), but some are often used without it (e.g., Colômbia).
target_language_example: Portugal é um país muito bonito, com praias incríveis.
native_language_example: Portugal is a very beautiful country, with amazing beaches.

meaning: "it’s a bit / it’s a little" (used to soften a statement).
additional_notes: Used with adjectives or adverbs to say something is true to a small degree: “É um pouco + adjective” (É um pouco assustador = It’s a bit scary). Often appears in comparisons: “é um pouco mais…” (a little more…). Can also refer to a mild sensation/feeling: “É um pouco apertada no peito” = It feels a little tight in the chest.
target_language_example: É um pouco difícil, mas eu consigo.
native_language_example: It’s a bit difficult, but I can do it.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages. It’s often followed by **que** or **do que** (“than”): *Ele é um pouco mais velho que/do que eu.* You can change **velho** to agree with the person: **velha** (female), **velhos/velhas** (plural).
target_language_example: Ela é um pouco mais velha do que o irmão dela.
native_language_example: She is a little older than her brother.

meaning: “It’s a pleasure” (nice to meet you / glad to).
additional_notes: Used as a polite, formal-friendly phrase to show pleasure or appreciation about meeting someone or doing something. Often followed by an infinitive: “É um prazer + verb” (e.g., “É um prazer estar aqui.”). With “conhecer” it means “Nice to meet you”: “É um prazer conhecê-lo(a).” You can intensify it with words like “imenso” (“É um prazer imenso...”).
target_language_example: É um prazer ajudar você hoje.
native_language_example: It’s a pleasure to help you today.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is (or might be) an issue. Often followed by an adjective (e.g., grave) or a type of problem (e.g., médico). In questions ("É um problema?"), it means "Is it a problem?"
target_language_example: Chegar um pouco atrasado é um problema?
native_language_example: Is arriving a little late a problem?

additional_notes: Used to classify or describe something by category. It’s often followed by a noun (e.g., “uma flor”, “um animal”). You can adjust for gender/number: “é uma espécie de” (similar), “são um tipo de” (they are a kind of).
target_language_example: Isso é um tipo de comida típica daqui.
native_language_example: That’s a kind of food that’s typical from here.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to emphasize that someone or something strongly fits that description (often meaning “a real,” “a true,” “a genuine”). Agree it with the noun: é um verdadeiro (masc. singular), é uma verdadeira (fem. singular), são verdadeiros / são verdadeiras (plural). Common in compliments (um verdadeiro cavalheiro) or criticism (um verdadeiro covarde).
target_language_example: Ela é uma verdadeira amiga.
native_language_example: She’s a true friend.

meaning: "is a great/excellent" (talking about a masculine singular person/thing).
additional_notes: Used to praise someone/something: subject + "é" (is) + "um" (a) + "ótimo" (great/excellent). It agrees with gender/number: "é uma ótima" (feminine), "são ótimos/ótimas" (plural). Without the article, "é ótimo" often means "it’s great" (about a situation/idea).
target_language_example: Ele é um ótimo professor.
native_language_example: He is a great teacher.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something belongs to a group: “X é um dos + plural noun” (one of the + plural). It usually introduces a superlative or description: “um dos mais famosos” (one of the most famous). Feminine version: “é uma das …”.
target_language_example: Lisboa é um dos destinos mais populares de Portugal.
native_language_example: Lisbon is one of the most popular destinations in Portugal.

meaning: "is one of my ..." (one of my favorites / one of my own).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something belongs to your group/category (often with a noun like "poetas", "pratos", "pacientes") or is among your favorites when followed by "favoritos". It agrees with gender/number: masculine plural "é um dos meus" (e.g., "autores"), feminine plural "é uma das minhas" (e.g., "músicas"). For masculine singular use "é um dos meus" + plural category (most common), or rephrase as "é um dos meus favoritos" / "é uma das minhas favoritas" if referring to a person/thing as a favorite.
target_language_example: Lisboa é uma das minhas cidades favoritas.
native_language_example: Lisbon is one of my favorite cities.

additional_notes: Used to identify/define something with a feminine singular noun: **X é uma Y**. It’s **é** (from **ser**, “to be”) + **uma** (“a/an” for feminine singular nouns). For masculine nouns, use **é um**. In Portuguese, the article usually matches the noun’s grammatical gender, not the person’s gender.
target_language_example: Aquela cidade é uma surpresa.
native_language_example: That city is a surprise.

meaning: "is an art" (something takes skill, creativity, or practice).
additional_notes: Used literally to say something is a form of art (e.g., literature, poetry), and also figuratively to mean it’s not an exact science and requires judgment, sensitivity, or practice. Common pattern: "X é uma arte".
target_language_example: Cozinhar bem é uma arte.
native_language_example: Cooking well is an art.

additional_notes: Used to identify or classify an animal as a bird. It’s the verb ser in the present (é = “is”) + uma (“a”) + ave (“bird”). You can negate it with “não é uma ave” (“is not a bird”), or add details after it (e.g., “é uma ave pequena”).
target_language_example: O tucano é uma ave colorida.
native_language_example: The toucan is a colorful bird.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns: é uma boa ideia/câmera/matéria (“it’s a good idea/camera/subject”). On its own, “É uma boa!” can mean “That’s a good idea/option!” Feminine form: uma boa (masculine would be “um bom”).
target_language_example: É uma boa ideia sair mais cedo.
native_language_example: It’s a good idea to leave earlier.

meaning: "it’s a good idea" / "that’s a good idea."
additional_notes: Used to say that a plan or suggestion is sensible or recommended. Often used in questions to ask for advice or someone’s opinion: "É uma boa ideia...?" (= Is it a good idea to...?). You can add "acho que" to soften it: "Acho que é uma boa ideia" (= I think it’s a good idea).
target_language_example: Acho que é uma boa ideia reservar com antecedência.
native_language_example: I think it’s a good idea to book in advance.

meaning: 'is a city' (used to describe a place).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "ser" ("é" = "is") to identify something as a city or to describe it: "X é uma cidade + adjective" (e.g., grande, segura, bonita). "Uma" agrees with the feminine noun "cidade". The plural is "são cidades".
target_language_example: Lisboa é uma cidade muito interessante.
native_language_example: Lisbon is a very interesting city.

meaning: "it’s something"; used to describe or emphasize a fact/quality (often with an adjective).
additional_notes: Very common with an adjective: "é uma coisa séria/maravilhosa/boa" = "it’s a serious/wonderful/good thing." Can also introduce a contrast: "X é uma coisa, Y é outra" = "X is one thing, Y is another." Sometimes used for emphasis in casual speech: "É uma coisa de louco" = "It’s crazy/insane."
target_language_example: Aprender português é uma coisa difícil, mas vale a pena.
native_language_example: Learning Portuguese is something difficult, but it’s worth it.

meaning: “is one of the” (referring to a feminine singular item).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something belongs to a group: “X é uma das + plural noun/superlative.” For masculine singular, use “é um dos” (e.g., “Ele é um dos melhores”).
target_language_example: Esta praia é uma das mais bonitas da região.
native_language_example: This beach is one of the most beautiful in the region.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as a girl. "Garota" often means “girl/young woman,” and can also be used more generally like “a girl” (similar to English). In Portuguese you can drop the subject when it’s clear from context, so "É uma garota" can mean “She’s a girl.”
target_language_example: Ela é uma garota muito inteligente.
native_language_example: She’s a very smart girl.

meaning: 'she is a very ... girl' (used before an adjective).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective after "muito": "Ela é uma garota muito amável/tímida/independente." You can replace "garota" with "menina" (girl) or "mulher" (woman). The adjective should agree with a female subject (often ending in -a, e.g., "tímida", "linda").
target_language_example: Ela é uma garota muito inteligente.
native_language_example: She is a very intelligent girl.

meaning: “is a great / big (one)” (used to emphasize size, importance, or intensity).
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns: é uma grande + noun (e.g., nação, ameaça, ilha, capital, parte, honra). Often means “great” in the sense of “important/remarkable” (uma grande honra, uma grande nação) or “big/large” in the sense of physical size (uma grande ilha). With abstract nouns it commonly means “a major” (uma grande ameaça = a major threat). For masculine nouns, use “é um grande …” (e.g., é um grande problema).
target_language_example: Esta é uma grande oportunidade para nós.
native_language_example: This is a great opportunity for us.

additional_notes: Used to say that something (often the name of a language) is a language, and it’s commonly followed by an adjective: “O francês é uma língua interessante.” You can also specify which language it is: “O francês é uma língua românica.” (Note: when naming languages in Portuguese, they’re often not capitalized: “o francês”, “o italiano”.)
target_language_example: O português é uma língua muito falada no Brasil.
native_language_example: Portuguese is a language widely spoken in Brazil.

additional_notes: "É" is the 3rd person singular of "ser" (to be), used for identity/definition. It’s often followed by an adjective or description: "É uma mulher bonita/moderna". You can also use it to emphasize someone’s status or identity: "Ela é uma mulher" (She is a woman). For men, the parallel phrase is "é um homem".
target_language_example: Ela é uma mulher forte e inteligente.
native_language_example: She is a strong and intelligent woman.

additional_notes: Used to describe a woman with an adjective that follows (e.g., rica, elegante, independente, ocupada, sortuda). You can change the subject: "Eu sou uma mulher muito..." (I am a very... woman), "Ela é uma mulher muito..." (She is a very... woman), "Você é uma mulher muito..." (You are a very... woman).
target_language_example: Ela é uma mulher muito inteligente.
native_language_example: She is a very intelligent woman.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is not a good plan or is likely to cause problems. Often appears with "Acho que..." / "Eu acho que..." (“I think...”), and it can be turned into a question to ask for someone’s opinion: "... é uma má ideia?".
target_language_example: Sair agora sem guarda-chuva é uma má ideia.
native_language_example: Leaving now without an umbrella is a bad idea.

additional_notes: Used to say you think an activity isn’t worth doing (often an opinion or criticism). It’s usually followed by an infinitive phrase (e.g., “assistir à TV”) or a noun phrase (e.g., “a escola”).
target_language_example: Para mim, esperar sem informação é uma perda de tempo.
native_language_example: For me, waiting with no information is a waste of time.

meaning: "is a person" (used to describe someone’s type/character).
additional_notes: Used with adjectives or descriptions to say what someone is like: “Ele/ela é uma pessoa + adjective/noun phrase” (e.g., legal, sincera, do povo). It’s a neutral, common way to talk about someone’s personality or who they are.
target_language_example: Ela é uma pessoa muito gentil.
native_language_example: She is a very kind person.

meaning: "is a very" (used to describe someone with an adjective).
additional_notes: Used with a following adjective to describe someone’s personality or characteristics: "[Name] é uma pessoa muito + adjective". You can also say "Ele/Ela é muito + adjective" (more direct) or "Ele/Ela é uma pessoa muito + adjective" (a bit more descriptive). The word "pessoa" is feminine, so adjectives may appear in feminine form (e.g., "uma pessoa muito simpática") even when talking about a man; in everyday speech you may also hear masculine agreement with male people.
target_language_example: O João é uma pessoa muito calma.
native_language_example: João is a very calm person.

meaning: "it's a matter of" / "it's a question of".
additional_notes: Used to say what something mainly depends on or comes down to (often followed by a noun like confiança, prioridades, gosto, tempo). Can express importance or urgency depending on context (e.g., “uma questão de segundos” = “a matter of seconds”).
target_language_example: Não é sorte; é uma questão de prática.
native_language_example: It’s not luck; it’s a matter of practice.

additional_notes: Used to praise something described by a feminine noun. Structure: "[subject] é uma ótima + noun" (e.g., cidade, pergunta, religião, piloto). It’s the feminine singular form: uma ótima. For masculine nouns, you’d use "um ótimo" (e.g., "é um ótimo livro").
target_language_example: Ela é uma ótima professora.
native_language_example: She is a great teacher.

additional_notes: Used to confirm that something is true or correct, often as a standalone reply. Can also be used within a sentence to state that a fact is true (e.g., “Isso é verdade” = “That is true”). Often appears with emphasis words like “infelizmente” (unfortunately).
target_language_example: É verdade, eu esqueci de te avisar.
native_language_example: It’s true, I forgot to let you know.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement you’re checking or confirming. Often starts a yes/no question (É verdade que…?), but can also introduce a claim (É verdade que ele mora aqui.). In questions it’s common in conversation; you can also say “É verdade?” (“Really?/Is that true?”).
target_language_example: É verdade que você mora aqui há cinco anos?
native_language_example: Is it true that you’ve lived here for five years?

additional_notes: Used to ask for confirmation about something you heard or suspect. It’s a neutral-to-slightly-challenging way to check a fact. In real speech, you’ll also hear: “É verdade que…?” (without “você”) or “É verdade?” when the rest is understood.
target_language_example: É verdade que você vai se mudar no mês que vem?
native_language_example: Is it true that you’re going to move next month?

additional_notes: Used to ask for confirmation about something you heard or suspect. "Vocês" is the plural "you" (common in Brazil), and the verb that follows is typically in the plural: "vocês fizeram", "vocês foram", etc. You can also use it as a statement: "É verdade que vocês vão embora amanhã."
target_language_example: É verdade que vocês vão viajar amanhã?
native_language_example: Is it true that you’re going to travel tomorrow?

meaning: time of year; season (period in the year).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a particular period of the calendar year, often linked to weather, holidays, tourism, or typical activities. Very common with demonstratives like “esta/nessa época do ano” (this/that time of year). Not the same as “estação do ano” (the four seasons: primavera, verão, outono, inverno), though it can overlap in meaning.
target_language_example: Nesta época do ano, as praias ficam cheias.
native_language_example: At this time of year, the beaches get crowded.

additional_notes: Used when it’s the final opportunity to do something before it becomes impossible or the moment passes. Often said with urgency or as a warning (“Essa é a sua última chance!”). You’ll commonly see it with "uma" or "a" (uma última chance / a sua última chance) and followed by "de" + infinitive ("última chance de fazer...").
target_language_example: Você tem uma última chance de me dizer a verdade.
native_language_example: You have one last chance to tell me the truth.

additional_notes: Often used with the definite article: "a última vez" = "the last time." You can add a clause with "que": "A última vez que eu vi ela..." = "The last time I saw her..." In commands, "pela última vez" means "for the last time" (a strong warning: 'I won't say it again').
target_language_example: Essa foi a última vez que eu cheguei atrasado.
native_language_example: That was the last time I arrived late.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the most recent occasion when something happened. It introduces a clause with a verb (often in the past): "A última vez em que + [event/action]...". In everyday speech, people also commonly say "a última vez que" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: A última vez em que fomos lá, estava chovendo.
native_language_example: The last time we went there, it was raining.

additional_notes: Used to single out one thing as the only one among all possibilities. It’s often followed by a clause with a verb: “a única coisa que eu podia fazer” (“the only thing I could do”) or used in questions: “Qual foi a única coisa que eu pedi?” (“What was the only thing I asked?”). You can change it for gender/number depending on the noun: “o único problema que…”, “as únicas coisas que…”.
target_language_example: A única coisa que eu quero agora é descansar.
native_language_example: The only thing I want right now is to rest.
